en: Having approached Manu as he sat with one-pointed attention, the great seers, accompanied by the commentary composed by Medhātithi,
honored him according to custom and spoke these words.
Salutation to the Supreme Brahman, whose true nature is to be known through the Vedānta, who is the cause of the three worlds, and in whom all defects have been utterly destroyed.

By means of these four verses, the distinguished authorship of this treatise and its status as a teacher of the human goal that cannot be known through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are established for the sake of its firm foundation.
For when a treatise is firmly established, its authors attain heaven and fame, which remain with them as long as *saṃsāra* endures.
And a treatise attains a firm foundation only if some people engage themselves in its study, hearing, reflection, and so forth.

Furthermore, those who act with deliberate intelligence ought not to engage in activities such as Vedic study without having ascertained their purpose. Therefore, the Teacher recited these four verses to demonstrate that this treatise is commenced for the sake of thoroughly understanding the means for accomplishing the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).

Nor should it be argued: "Without stating the purpose at the very outset, we can determine this [purpose] simply by reflecting on the sequence of the treatise as it is being expounded; what need is there for the effort of explaining it?"
Furthermore,
even though a purpose has been stated, it is not determined as long as it has not been examined further;
for not all human utterances serve as a basis for certainty regarding their meaning.

Nor is it a universal rule that every undertaking must be preceded by a full comprehension of its purpose, for we observe that engagement in the study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*) and similar acts occurs even without such a basis.
Furthermore, even among human-authored texts, the statement of a purpose is not invariably observed;
for instance:
The Blessed Pāṇini, without even stating the purpose, begins the composition of his aphorisms with the words "Now, the instruction of words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*).
To this it is said:
if the purpose were not determined at the outset, people would certainly not take up the book from the very beginning.
And since there is no such undertaking, how could they thoroughly investigate the entire treatise?

Furthermore, that very meaning which comes within the range of the intellect through a thorough investigation of the preceding and following parts becomes easy to grasp when stated briefly from the outset.
Thus it has been said:
"For it is desired by the wise in this world to maintain both the concise and the detailed exposition.
As for what was said— that even so, certainty is not attained because there is an absence of certainty regarding the meaning from human statements— [that is not the case].
In the same way, this person has the cognition "I know," but not the cognition "the object is thus.
We do not dispute here whether there is certainty or not, for that would result in excessive prolixity of the text.

Even when the engagement [with a treatise] is established despite uncertainty regarding its purpose, the arising of a doubt concerning its specific subject matter does not occur without the statement of that purpose.
For if it were not stated, there might even be a doubt as to whether this is a treatise on Dharma, a treatise on Artha, or something like an examination of a crow’s teeth.
But when the purpose has been declared, one understands: "This person is telling us, 'I shall show you the path to the highest good.'"
"And there is no harm for me in engaging [in this activity];
let it be, I shall reflect upon it"—thus is the establishment of engagement.

However, as for the engagement in the study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*), that belongs to one who is impelled by a teacher, not through the realization of one's own entitlement (*adhikāra*).
For at that time, due to being a child, he is not capable of undertaking his own office;
moreover, the accomplishment of his activity occurs solely through the instigation of others,
and it is not even made known by the formal conferral of office.
Therefore, for one who engages in that [study], there is the purpose of understanding the meaning, and from that, engagement [in practice].
But here [in this case], "the twice-born who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself elsewhere... [it is said:]
Thus ends the qualification for study for one who has mastered the Vedas;
at that time, because his intellect is fully developed, he seeks the purpose [of the study].
Furthermore, the aphorisms (sūtras) of the venerable Pāṇini are extremely concise.
There is no suspicion that it is intended to express some other meaning.
In that regard, because Pāṇini’s fame is renowned even among children, its purpose is so well-known that it is not explicitly stated.
However, this extensive treatise abounds in various explanatory doctrines and is useful for all human goals.
In that regard, nothing is lacking by stating the purpose for the sake of easy comprehension.
Furthermore, there are two types of practitioners: those who rely on reasoning (*nyāya*) and those who rely on worldly consensus (*prasiddhi*).
Regarding this, it is said: "Whatever Manu has spoken is indeed medicine."
The Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, the Sāman-chants, and those mantras belonging to the Atharvans,
as well as that which was proclaimed by the seven seers— all of that Manu has declared.

Because its power is well-known in the world through such explanatory passages (arthavāda), histories, and Purāṇas, or because it has been established by the very fame of its author—namely, that it was composed by Prajāpati, whose authority is determined by the descent of his lineage—it is for this reason alone that those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya) engage with it.
For them, even the connection with a specific author is a factor in their engagement.
It is for this very reason that the statement of the purpose is presented in the form of a question and answer.

The great sages are the questioners and Prajāpati is the speaker; furthermore, the subject matter characterized as Dharma is not something to be understood through common worldly experience, but is the exclusive domain of the scripture—a point emphasized by the statement that even the great sages have doubts regarding it. Thus, the declaration "he was questioned by them" does not mean "I was questioned."

The meaning of these four verses is that the commencement of the treatise is appropriate for the purpose of explaining such matters as the fact that the Self and Brahman possess an uncreated identity. Furthermore,
we shall demonstrate how this treatise is intent upon teaching the goals of human life by analyzing the composition of its words.
There, having approached Manu, the great seers spoke these words: "It behooves you to tell us the laws.
Being thus questioned, he replied, "Listen.
In this way, the question and the reply are both focused intently on establishing a single subject matter.

Therefore, it is stated that the *dharmas* are what are being expounded here. Furthermore, in common usage, the word *dharma* is employed for that which accomplishes the highest good (*śreyas*) and is not enjoined by means other than verbal testimony—such as perception and the other worldly instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Thus, by the connection [of the word] "let that be heard," it is stated that [this treatise] is a means of accomplishing the specific goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).
A certain distinguished person named Manu, who was perfected in the study, knowledge, and practice of numerous Vedic branches and was renowned through the tradition of the Smṛtis—
having approached him, that is, having gone directly into his presence, not by chance but by abandoning all other activities; by this effort of approaching,
the importance of the matter being asked and the authority of the speaker are made manifest.
For those who are unskilled in giving a reply do not come and question with effort one who is sitting with a one-pointed mind,
standing with a one-pointed mind, or existing with a one-pointed mind;
however, in this context, "sitting" does not mean sitting on a grass mat or similar seat, because such things are of no use.
By means of his seat, his state of well-being is indicated;
being in such a state, he becomes capable of giving a reply.
"Having approached" (*abhigamya*) refers exclusively to the act of Manu.

Regarding the act of questioning, however, there is the qualification "seated with one-pointed mind. Having ascertained that he was one-pointed—meaning his mind was undistracted—through such means as engaging in conversation appropriate to an inquiry into his welfare, [the Buddha] spoke these words, having given full attention to hearing the question.
By convention, the word *ekāgra* denotes immobility.

For one who has abandoned the contact with defects such as passion through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), stability of the mind—that is, one-pointedness—occurs during reflection on the realization of reality upon the cessation of conceptual construction.
Only in such a state is the mind capable of determining objects such as forms and sounds that are present; it is not so when joined with constructions regarding what exists or does not exist.
Alternatively, by virtue of its connection (*yoga*), the word "foremost" (*agra*) applies to the mind, because it proceeds ahead of the eyes and other senses in the apprehension of objects.
That which is joined with initial application is called "foremost" (*agra*) in the world;

the analysis of the compound is: "that which has a single point (*agra*) as its object of meditation or its object of apprehension. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound even though the members are in different grammatical cases (*vyadhikaraṇa*), because it conveys a clear meaning. Here too, one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*) is simply the cessation of distraction.
"Having honored him according to the rule":
*nyāya* is the boundary prescribed by the scriptures;

not transgressing that, having honored him in the manner prescribed by the scripture for the first approach to a guru—such as salutation, attendance, and so forth—and having demonstrated devotion and respect.
"Great sages" (*maharṣayaḥ*):

"Seer" (*ṛṣi*) means the Veda; the word "seer" is also applied to a person because of their connection with the excellence of studying that [Veda], understanding it, and practicing its meaning. And they are both great and seers.
They become "great" (mahāntaḥ) through the absolute excellence of those very same qualities,
as in the expression, "Yudhiṣṭhira is the most excellent among the Kurus.
Alternatively, they are great either due to a particularity of austerity or due to a particularity of honor and renown.
They spoke these words. "Vacana" means that by which something is spoken;
it refers to the question in the second verse that is about to be stated. Because of its proximity, that very [question] is pointed out here as "this."
Even for those who hold that the word *idam* (this) refers to a perceptible object, the question is nonetheless perceptible because it resides within the mind.
Alternatively, the term *vacanam* (speech) refers to the thing being asked about; thus, in the sense of a sentence (*vākya*), they have uttered this sentence.
But in the sense of an action (*karman*), the word *vacana* means "they asked this."
And at that time, the verb *brū* (to speak) takes two objects; by the "unspoken object" rule (*akathita-karman*), Manu is the object of the three actions.
In response to the expectation of what they said after approaching and honoring him, the second verse follows:
"O Blessed One, you ought to speak to us of the duties (*dharma*) of all the social classes (*varṇas*) in their proper order, as well as those born of intermediate castes."
The word *bhaga* refers to sovereignty, magnanimity, fame, heroism, and so forth. One who possesses these is a *bhagavat*. By that [term], there is the address "O Blessed One" (*bhagavan*).
The word *varṇa* refers to the three castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa;
the inclusion of the term "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of including the Śūdra.
Otherwise, since the great sages are the questioners, the inquiry would have been restricted to the domain of the three [higher] castes.
The "intermediate" (antara) refers to that which is between.
Due to the mixing of two castes, even a single caste may be incomplete.

Those whose origin or birth is in the intermediate [space] are called *antaraprabhava*; these include the *anuloma* and *pratiloma* offspring such as the *mūrdhāvasikta*, *ambaṣṭha*, *kṣattṛ*, *vaidehika*, and so forth.
For it is not appropriate to designate them by either of their parents' castes (*jāti*),
just as a mule produced from the union of a donkey and a horse is a different species (*jātyantara*) that is neither a donkey nor a horse.
Therefore, because they are not included within the [standard] categories of caste (*varṇa*), they are mentioned separately.
Is it not the case that those born in the natural order (*anuloma*) are accepted as being of the mother's caste?
We say: no.
For it is said, "They are called similar [to their mothers]"; thus they are similar to the mother's caste, but not of that same caste itself.
This dharma of theirs is also merely scriptural (vācanika) and not established by the very nature of things (vastusvabhāvasiddha).
Therefore, because it falls within the domain of another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), they are indeed worthy of the teacher's instruction regarding the side of dharma.
Furthermore, virtues such as non-violence (ahiṃsā) will be taught even for those who follow the inverse order.
As for the statement that they are "devoid of dharma," that is intended to mean the absence of such dharmas as vows, fasting, and so forth;
furthermore, by this, the author demonstrates that the treatise is beneficial to all persons in its true sense.
The suffix *vati* is used in the sense of "deserving" (*arhati*), meaning the manner in which a performance is worthy.

This manner—consisting of what is obligatory, what is optional, what is subsidiary, what is primary, and the restrictions regarding substance, place, time, agent, and so forth—is the domain of the root *arh*.
[This applies] in successive order.
The sequence is the order;
let that order by which the rites are to be performed also be stated, such as:
after the birth-rite (jātakarman), the tonsure (cauḍa) and the tying of the girdle (mauñjīnibandhana), and so forth.

In the term *yathāvat* ("as it is"), completeness (*kārtsnya*) regarding the meaning of the words is intended; however, since sequence (*krama*) is not itself a word-meaning, it is mentioned separately by the word *anupūrvaśaḥ* ("in succession"). The word *dharma* has its conventional usage with respect to what ought to be done and what ought not to be done—that is, injunctions and prohibitions for the sake of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*)—and also with respect to the action (*kriyā*) that has those as its object.
However, no investigation is undertaken here as to whether both [the injunction and the prohibition] constitute the primary meaning of the word, or whether one of them is secondary;
for this has been treated in detail in other texts and is of no use here.

In any case, in such statements as "The Aṣṭakā rites must be performed" and "One should not eat *kalañja*," an obligation regarding the Aṣṭakā rites is understood, and a prohibition regarding the eating of *kalañja* is understood.
Whether that action called the *aṣṭakā* is dharma, or whether it is the duty (*kartavyatā*) pertaining to its subject matter, there is no difference in the result.
Furthermore, because dharma is taught by its essential nature, it follows by implication that whatever is contrary to it is adharma.
Therefore, it is stated that both dharma and adharma are the objects of the scripture.
In this regard, the performance of the *aṣṭakā* rites is dharma, and the avoidance of killing a Brahmin and so forth is also dharma.
The non-performance of the *aṣṭakā* rites is adharma, and the commission of the killing of a Brahmin is likewise adharma.
This is the distinction between dharma and adharma.
They say that the word "arhasi" (you ought) indicates the teacher's qualification for the task of teaching by means of his capability;
for since you are capable of speaking the Dharmas, you are therefore authorized and are thus requested: "Speak!
Since it is understood through the force of the context that "whatever one is authorized to do must be performed by him," the request "Speak! is supplied as an ellipsis.
It has been stated that the word *dharma* applies to any activity whose purpose is unseen (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
In this regard, just as it is used for the *Aṣṭakā* and other such rites, so too is it used for the worship of the *caitya* and similar acts.

Since a doubt may arise as to which specific *dharmas* are intended here, the phrase "you alone" is employed both to demonstrate the particular nature of those *dharmas* and to bring forward the capacity [of the Lord] already mentioned.
For you alone, O Lord, are the knower of the true meaning and purpose of the effects of this entire self-existent ordinance, which is inconceivable and immeasurable.
You alone are solitary, without companion, and without a second;
you are the knower of the true meaning of the principles of all ritual injunctions.
"Injunction" (vidhāna) refers to the scripture, for by it rituals are prescribed.
Of that [Veda] which is self-existent, eternal, uncreated, and not of human origin— known as the Veda,
whose syllables are both perceptible and inferable;
for instance, by the text "One should offer the Agnihotra" and "With this verse, 'This thousandfold man,' one worships the Āhavanīya fire," this Veda directly prescribes the oblation.
By the use of the instrumental case in the word *etayā* ("with this"), the application (*viniyoga*) of the mantra itself is established for the worship of the Āhavanīya fire.
However, in the case of the injunction "the Aṣṭakās are to be performed," the Veda is inferred from the Smṛti.
From the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the phrase "I cut the sacrificial grass, the seat of the altar," there is an inference of the Śruti text: "With this [mantra] he cuts the sacrificial grass."
For this mantra is recited in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa), and the cutting of the sacrificial grass (barhis) is prescribed therein;
however, there is no such rule as "one should cut with this mantra.
Nevertheless, by its very form, the mantra is capable of manifesting the cutting of the sacrificial grass.
The connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices is established in a general sense through the context;
however, it is applied specifically to the cutting of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) by virtue of its own inherent capacity,
for this is the understanding here.
By virtue of the context, one should perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices with this mantra.
How so?
Because capacity, even when not explicitly stated by the phrase "as far as he may be able," is a universal auxiliary factor.
Furthermore, what can the mantra do?
It can manifest the cutting of the *barhis* grass.
Therefore, by virtue of the context and its own inherent capacity, the verbal cognition "one cuts the *barhis* with this mantra" arises in the mind.
The position of Kumārila is as follows: first, a word is cognized through conceptual cognitions (*savikalpaka-vijñāna*);
that word residing in the intellect is what is called the "Veda" as an object of inference (*anumeya*).

Its status as the Veda arises because it is brought forth by its own inherent capacity from two other scriptural passages (*śruti*), namely the sentences concerning the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices and the mantra-sentences.

Alternatively, *vidhi* means injunction (*vidhāna*), performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), or the accomplishment of a purpose (*prayojana-saṃpatti*). This [injunction] belongs to the Self-born (*svayaṃbhuva*)—that which is eternal, handed down through an beginningless succession, expounded by the Self-born or by the Veda, and which includes everything expressed by the syllables heard as well as that which is understood through the force of the meaning already apprehended. For Vedic injunction is indeed twofold.
Something may be directly expressed by the word [of the injunction].

For example, in the case of "One desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should offer a caru-oblation to Sūrya," the person desiring spiritual luster is qualified for the Saura-caru. It is understood that this procedure (itikartavyatā) for that caru, which accomplishes spiritual luster, is to be performed in the same manner as the Āgneya sacrifice.
In both cases, this cognition is nothing but verbal in nature, because it is rooted in the comprehension of words.
Both [the word and its meaning] are cognized from the word through denotation; likewise, they are cognized through the apprehension of the denoted object.
However, the distinction caused by mediation and so forth does not negate their status as verbal.

Or, for example, when water in a well is struck by the hand, it strikes another region; that [region] also becomes struck precisely through the conjunction with the [initial] strike, but not directly.
Likewise, in the case of the ejection of pebbles, their successive leaps and falls are produced solely by the initial effort.
This [case under discussion] is just like that.
In a modified ritual (*vaikṛta-karman*), there is a connection with a specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

Thus, in the case of "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," the originative injunction (*utpatti*) cannot be devoid of an entitlement (*adhikāra*); therefore, the understanding of the entitlement—"one who desires heaven"—is reached through the force of the understood meaning.

Consequently, the diversity of all injunctions consists in this very form of intentionality (*tātparya*) toward the word "all. This is intended to make known that the Smṛtis have the Veda as their source.
We shall demonstrate this in the second [chapter].
Now, it might be argued that the object conveyed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers is the injunction (*vidhi*), which consists in the form of something to be done (*kartavyatā*);
and that this is everywhere conveyed solely by the perceptible word itself.
In this regard, what is meant by the statement that "Vedic injunction is indeed twofold"? By the words "one should offer" (*nirvapet*), the *kartavyatā* (the "what-is-to-be-done") is understood;
the *itikartavyatā* (the "manner-of-doing") is understood through the force of the purpose (*artha-sāmarthya*) in the manner already described.
This is not a fault.

When it is understood that "one should offer" (*nirvapet*) or "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the sense of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*) is not fully realized merely by the fact that the meaning of the verbal root is the object;

rather, it remains incomplete as long as the other constituent parts—namely, the qualification (*adhikāra*), the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), and the manner of performance (*prayoga*)—have not been understood.
In these parts, the injunction is perceived as having an extended form;
therefore, even those aspects that are themselves of the nature of parts are not contradictory, since they are expressible by the word "injunction.
This very point he states:
"Of the inconceivable" means "of the imperceptible. For that which is perceptible is said to be experienced; it is not what is conceived, nor is it what is remembered.
Since that which is to be conceptualized is for the most part immeasurable and rooted in the words of memory,
it is not indeed cognized through direct perception;
therefore, it is said to be "immeasurable."
Alternatively, it is because that which is immeasurable (*aprameya*)— being impossible to measure by way of its extent due to its extreme vastness—
the Veda, divided into many branches and recensions, cannot be measured by all [beings];
for this very reason, it is inconceivable (*acintya*).
That which is exceedingly vast is called "inconceivable" because it is difficult to grasp.
Just as people in the world say, "What is the destination of others? It is not even fit to be thought about," so too, the mind is said to have all things as its object.
And because this [Veda] is so exceedingly vast, it is not even within the range of that [intellect].
By proclaiming through these two words that greatness consists in being the object of both external and internal organs, the Teacher encourages [the student]:
"By you alone has such a Veda been mastered; therefore, you know—that is, you understand—the true meaning (*tattvārtha*) of it, which is of the nature of what is to be accomplished."
That which is to be performed is called *kārya*.

It is that wherein a person is enjoined as the performer, such that "this must be done by you" or "this must not be done by you"; for example, the *agnihotra* and other rites are to be performed, while the eating of *kalañja* and similar acts are not to be performed.
Even a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) is indeed a form of performance.
The non-performance of the killing of a Brahmin is itself the performance of the prohibition;
for both engagement (*pravṛtti*) and abstention (*nivṛtti*) are actions (*kriyā*).
Indeed, "performance" is not said to be that which is accomplished solely by means of physical movement.
What then?
When that form has been attained, there is also its cessation;
just as one who practices what is beneficial is long-lived.
He who eats when the time has arrived and does not eat when it has not yet arrived— for him,
even abstaining from food is indeed beneficial.
Alternatively, the word "action" (*kārya*) is intended to indicate both the injunction and the prohibition.
This alone is the ultimate, ontological meaning of the Veda.

As for that which consists of the description of past events—such as "He wept; because he wept, that is the Rudra-nature of Rudra"—that is not the ontological meaning, because it forms a single syntactical unit with another injunction and, being intended for praise, lacks any finality regarding its own literal sense.
For there exists another injunction here: "Therefore, silver must not be given upon the sacrificial grass."

The passages beginning with "He wept" and ending with "therefore, before a year has passed, there is weeping in his house" form a single syntactical unit; by means of censuring the gift of silver on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), they praise its prohibition.
Thus it has been said: the Veda is an authority regarding a goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), not regarding an already established fact (*siddharūpa*);
for the subject matter of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) is of an established nature.
For the fact that the meaning of those [mantras] is something to be performed is not perceived;
rather, their purpose is perceived to be the instruction of an injunction (*vidhi*).
And if they were also intended for their own literal meaning, then their status as being subordinate to an injunction would be contradicted.
Consequently, the implied unity of the sentence would be contradicted;
and when a single sentential unity is possible, a split of the sentence is not logically justified.
Furthermore, a unity of sentence is not established by making that which is to be proven (the *sādhya*) subordinate to a statement whose purpose is an already established fact (*siddhārtha*).
For thus, nothing whatsoever is taught by the Veda as something to be done;
consequently, the Veda would be entirely devoid of authority. Furthermore, the status of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth as having injunctive meaning would have to be abandoned.
Therefore, the venerable Manu has stated that the true meaning of the Veda consists in its prescriptive form (*kāryarūpa*).
Jaimini also declared: "The Veda is authoritative regarding matters to be accomplished (*kāryārthe*); dharma is a matter characterized by injunction (*codanālakṣaṇa*).

Consequently, having established as a proven fact the capacity for proclaiming dharma due to his possession of an excellence in the complete knowledge of all things without exception, he addresses him as "O Lord" (*prabho*).
"O Lord, you who are capable of proclaiming the dharma, please expound the dharmas.
Having been thus questioned regarding the dharmas by these three verses, he promised to do so with the following verse.
Thus questioned by those high-souled ones,
Amitaujas duly honored all those great rishis and replied, "Listen."
Manu, possessed of immeasurable power, being thus questioned by those high-souled great seers, replied to them:
"Listen," in the manner previously described by him.
The object being questioned and the method of questioning are included within the word *tathā* when it expresses a manner.
Therefore, the meaning is: "having been questioned in such a manner," he replied to those questions concerning the dharmas;
or alternatively, *tathā* indicates the mere manner [of questioning].
Since the word "asked" (*pṛṣṭa*) follows from the preceding verse, the specific object being questioned is already present in the mind.
Therefore, by saying "he replied to that which was asked; listen," the fact that the question and the answer share the same object is established.
In that case, the word *tathā* serves merely to complete the meter of the verse.
In the first explanation, however, the identity of the object for both the question and the reply is conveyed by the word *tathā* itself.
The word *samyak* is an adjective qualifying the reply;
[it means] he replied correctly.
"With a serene mind" means without the involvement of anger and the like.

"Of immeasurable power" (*amitaujas*) means one whose power of speech (*vāgvibhava*) is undiminished; that is, he possesses immeasurable, infinite power, vigor, and the capacity for expression. He says "the great seers" (*maharṣīn*) because, by virtue of their greatness of soul, it is not contradictory for them to be both questioners of the Dharma and great seers.
One who constantly acts for the benefit of others is called a "Great-Souled One" (mahātman).
Therefore, although Manu himself was wise and had realized the true nature of reality—otherwise his status as a Great Sage would be untenable—he nevertheless questioned others for the sake of others.
This is because Manu possesses a preeminent and renowned authority.
Therefore, that which is said by this person is respected by the world; he is honored because of his reputation.
Thus, for the sake of introducing the treatise, we shall act as his preceptors;
and when questioned by us, he will be regarded by the people as a highly authoritative source.
Therefore, honoring all of them is not contradictory;
otherwise, what kind of honor could there be for a disciple toward his preceptor?
The form "ārcya" is the gerund (lyap) of the root *arc* preceded by the prefix *ā*.
Regarding the phrase "having honored them,

[Manu] said to them," it is here stated: if this text was composed by Manu himself, then it would be inappropriate for him to speak in the third person, saying, "Being questioned by them, he replied."
When asked, I replied: "It is logical [that Manu spoke].
Now, as for the objection: "If only one person was the author of the text, how can it be designated as 'Manu's'?"—that is not a valid challenge.
Generally, authors state their own views by way of reference to others, saying, "On this point he says," or "On this point they reply," even though they have not been asked by them in such a manner.
Whichever [author] is earlier is accepted by the world as more authoritative; thus it is said, "That is the authority of Bādarāyaṇa.
Alternatively, this is the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
However, because that tradition is recorded in the form of the *Smṛti* of Manu, it is designated as "Mānava.
He replied to those great seers.
What was that?
"Listen to that which I have been asked."
In the beginning, this was enveloped in darkness, unperceived, without distinguishing marks, beyond the reach of logic, unknowable, as if entirely asleep.
Where have they gone? Where have they fallen?

Having been asked about the doctrines taught in the treatises regarding what has "fallen," and having promised to explain those very things, [the opponent] instead describes the indeterminate state of the world—a topic irrelevant to the context and not a human goal.
This is the popular proverb: "Being asked about mangoes, he speaks of *kovidāra* trees."

Furthermore, since there is neither a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) nor a purpose regarding this subject matter, this entire chapter should not be studied at all. To this it is replied: the great purpose of the treatise is established by all of this.
In this [text], the states of transmigratory existence, from Brahmā down to the level of stationary beings, which have dharma and adharma as their cause, are set forth;
for it will be stated: "They are enveloped by manifold darkness, which has karma as its cause."
"Having observed these destinies of the living being through one's own mind—both those resulting from righteousness and those from unrighteousness—one should always fix the mind upon righteousness.

Thus, since righteousness (*dharma*) is the cause of unsurpassed sovereignty and unrighteousness (*adharma*) is its opposite, this treatise, which serves the great purpose of providing thorough knowledge of their nature, must be studied; such is the purport of the chapter.
In this context, however, the scripture consists of mantras, explanatory passages (arthavādas), and general inference (sāmānyato dṛṣṭa).
And so says the mantra:
"Darkness was hidden by darkness in the beginning; all this was an undiscernible ocean."
That which was covered by the unreal and the non-existent—He, the One, conquered it through the power of His fervor.
When the moon, the sun, fire, and other such external and internal luminaries had perished at the time of the great dissolution, there was only darkness alone;
even that darkness became enveloped by a darkness of gross form,
for at that time there was no knower whatsoever.

Therefore, because of the absence of a knower, it is said that "nothing has knowledge" and everything was enveloped in darkness. O Agni, prior to the creation of beings, all was unmanifest (*apraketam*), unknown. This world was water—possessing the nature of flowing, active; whatever was characterized by movement, all that was motionless.
By the void and subtle, even the gross was concealed; that is to say, the specific form [of the world] was dissolved within the primordial self (prakṛti).
By this much, the unmanifest state of the world has been illuminated.
By the fourth quarter [of the verse], the initial state of creation is described.
That which was one by virtue of the greatness—that is, the magnitude—of *tapas* (ascetic heat), that was born; it manifested itself through its specific nature.
The meaning is that it appeared again due to the power of *karman*.
Alternatively, in that state, by means of the greatness of the act of *tapas*, Hiraṇyagarbha was born as the Self; he came into being.
As he will state later: "Then the Self-Existent One... By means of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), even a great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) is possible;
for when destruction is observed in one part, the destruction of the whole is likewise observed.
Just as a house is sometimes seen burning and at other times an entire village is consumed by fire;
and whatever entities are preceded by an agent are all perishable, such as houses and palaces;
and this world, consisting of rivers, oceans, mountains, and so forth, is likewise preceded by an agent.
Therefore, it is inferred that [the world] will perish just like a house or similar structures.

If it is argued that its being preceded by an agent is not established, we reply: that too is proven—just as in the case of a house and so forth—by virtue of its possessing a specific configuration and other such characteristics; this is an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*).
Furthermore, we do not exert ourselves in either establishing the validity of the means of knowledge or in refuting them, because this treatise is not intended for such purposes.
For as long as this has not been examined and determined, it cannot be properly understood;
and if it were not so determined, it would be a treatise on logic (*tarka-śāstra*) rather than a treatise on Dharma (*dharma-śāstra*), and the work would result in excessive prolixity.
Furthermore, all of this will be presented with an abundance of formal analysis (*prakriyā*).
In some places the procedure is that of the Purāṇas, and in others that of the Sāṃkhyas;
whether it is known or unknown, there is no distinction whatsoever regarding merit and demerit, and thus it is not examined with precision.
If there is a need for it, it should be sought from those very sources.
However, only the explanation consisting of the coordination of the meanings of the words for this chapter is being taught; that alone we shall perform. The intended purport has already been shown:
"This world existed as darkness, like darkness."

Although the word *bhūta* has many meanings, it is used here in the sense of a simile; as in the statement, "That which is undivided among things that are divided, uncut among things that are cut, being like a universal (*sāmānyabhūta*), that is the Word"—where "being like a universal" means "like a universal. To the question, "In what respect is there a similarity between darkness and the world? he says: "unperceived" (*aprajñātam*).
Because particular natures and modifications dissolve back into their primal cause (prakṛti), they are therefore unknown through direct perception.
If it is argued that they might be known through inference,
even that lacks defining characteristics.
The characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), the mark (*liṅga*), and the sign (*cihna*)—even these are utterly dissolved in that state, because all modifications have perished in their specific forms.
It is "inconceivable" (*apratarkya*);
its nature was such that it could not even be conceived as having that form.
He refutes inference as a form of reasoning:

there is no inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*); nor is there inference based on specific observation (*viśeṣato dṛṣṭa*) that makes its nature known; therefore, it is unknowable.
In that case, it would follow that what previously did not exist at all was born; this [view] is refuted by the statement: "It was as if entirely asleep.
There is no arising of the existent from the non-existent, for it has been said: "In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed the Existent alone."
"How could being arise from non-being? and so forth, in the Upaniṣads.
Therefore, it is unknowable by means of valid cognitions whose objects are delimited;
it is understood only through such scripture.

The state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), which is the state of perfect serenity (*saṃprasāda*) attained by abandoning the conditions of waking and dreaming—as if one who was asleep were now awake—is adduced as an illustration.

Just as this Self remains in the state of deep sleep with all mental modifications (*vikalpa*) destroyed and free from the afflictions of cognition, yet it cannot be said that it does not exist, because for one who has awakened there is the recognition: "I slept happily. In the same way, this is determined by the world’s traditional scriptures (*āgama*) consisting of established facts, and by the inferences based on appearances (*ābhāsānumāna*) used by logicians (*tārkika*).
"It was" (*āsīt*);
however, that present state is not cognizable by anyone, which is why it is called "incognizable" (*avijñeya*).
The meaning is that there is no partial dissolution (*ekadeśapralaya*) in any respect.
Then the Blessed One, the Self-Existent, unmanifest yet making this world manifest, his power active within the primary elements and other things, appeared as the dispeller of darkness.
Immediately following that great night,
he is "self-existent" (svayaṃbhū), meaning he exists by himself;
he has assumed a body by his own will, and unlike the transmigrating self, his assumption of a body is not dependent upon karma.
"Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) means not appearing to those who lack the cultivation of the practice of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-yoga*).
Alternatively, it should be read as "this is unmanifest" (*idam avyaktam*);
thus, making this which is in an unmanifest state manifest, he brings it to light through gross forms and transformations.
By whose will the world manifests again—
[it] has manifested;
the word *prāduḥ* signifies manifestation.

*Tamonudaḥ* (the dispeller of darkness): *Tamaḥ* is the state of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*); he dispels it, destroys it, and then creates the world again; therefore, he is *tamonudaḥ*. The *mahābhūtāni* are earth and the other [elements].

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), their qualities—sound and so forth—are understood. He is described as such because he possesses *ojas*, *vīrya*, and the power of creation (*sṛṣṭi-sāmarthya*) that has reached those [qualities].
The great elements themselves are incapable of producing the world.
But when power (*śakti*) is infused into them by that [primordial cause], they then undergo transformation into the nature of trees and so forth.

However, it is not the great elements (*mahābhūta*) existing in the state of primordial material power (*prakṛti-śakti*), having attained the form of primordial matter (*prakṛti-rūpa*), that are intended by the term "great elements" at the beginning of the creation of the world.
There is an alternative reading: *mahābhūtānuvṛttaujāḥ* ("possessing power following after the great elements").
"Anuvṛtta" means "anugata"; this is precisely the meaning stated previously.
He who is perceivable by those beyond the senses, subtle, unmanifest, eternal,
consisting of all beings, and inconceivable— he himself has now appeared.
By means of the two pronouns "yo 'sau" (he who), he points toward the Supreme Brahman as if it were generally well-known;
that which is well-established in the Vedāntas, in other sciences concerning the self, and in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, and which is described by the qualities about to be mentioned—
that very one is said here to have "become manifest," meaning he appeared spontaneously, having taken on a body.
The root *bhā* has multiple meanings, so it is used here in the sense of "arising";
or else, it simply means "shining.
He was self-luminous, not dependent on the light of the sun or other sources.
The transcendence of the sense faculties (*indriya*) is "beyond the senses" (*atīndriya*).
This is an *avyayībhāva* compound.
That which is to be grasped by what is beyond the senses is an *sup-supā* compound.
It is apprehended by transcending the sense faculties; it is never within the range of the senses.
That by which it is apprehended is a distinct knowledge born of yoga.
Alternatively, that which has transcended the sense faculties is called the "supersensory" (*atīndriya*) mind.
Because the sense faculties are imperceptible, [the mind] is not their object.
Furthermore, just as the Vaiśeṣikas have established the inferential nature of the mind by asserting that the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is the mark (liṅga) of the mind,
it is apprehended by means of that.
And so you, Vyāsa, have said:
"He is not grasped by the eye, nor indeed by the other sense organs;
but he is perceived with a tranquil mind by those who possess subtle vision."
By those who, being serene and unpolluted by defects such as passion and the like, have attained the power of subtle vision through devotion to His worship;
"subtle" (*sūkṣma*) means atomic (*anu*), as it were— indeed, He is not the locus for conceptual constructions such as "minute," "gross," and so forth.
For he has indeed transcended all conceptual constructions;
and it is said:
"He who does not abide even in the appearance of any conceptual constructions."
It has been conceptualized in many ways through reasoning, scripture, and inference.
"Transcending difference and conjunction, existence and non-existence, succession and non-succession, and truth and falsehood—the Soul of the universe shines forth through discernment.
Thus, being subtle, it is inexpressible; it is eternal and endowed with unmanifest sovereignty that is natural, beginningless, and endless.

Even according to those for whom the station of Hiraṇyagarbha is attained through karma, there is eternality in their view because, despite having a beginning, there is no end; for the state of being the enjoyer of the fruits of creation never departs. One whose mind is thus conditioned by the thought "all beings are to be created by me," who has become the self of all beings, is called "consisting of all beings" (*sarvabhūtamaya*).

Just as a clay pot, because it is a modification of clay, has a body composed solely of clay, so too anyone who intensely contemplates anything whatsoever is said, by way of metaphorical designation, to be "composed of that," just as one says, "this man is composed of women," or "composed of the *Ṛgveda*," or "composed of the *Yajurveda*. Alternatively, according to the non-dualistic view (*advaitadarśana*), sentient and insentient beings do not exist as separate entities; rather, this entire world is a phenomenal manifestation (*vivarta*) of that [Ultimate Reality] alone.
Therefore, since transformations (*vivarta*) consist of the elements (*bhūta*), and since the [universe] is non-different from them, it is indeed logical that it consists of those elements.
But how can the manifestation of manifold forms from a single [reality] be possible, given that its oneness contradicts such diversity?
To this, the proponents of the theory of transformation (*vivartavādin*) reply as follows:
Just as waves arise from the ocean when struck by the wind, and they neither differ from it nor are defiled by it—
being in every respect indefinable in terms of either identity or difference— so too is this world the illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of Brahman.
Furthermore, the word "api" (also/even) should be understood here [to imply that the world is likewise not different from Brahman].
Abiding in its own nature, it is ungraspable; in its state of manifestation (*vivarta*), it is graspable by the senses.
Thus it is subtle.
By the word "also" (*api*), it is implied that in its gross state, it is gross.
Unmanifest and manifest;
eternal and non-eternal;
composed of the elements and yet devoid of their form.
It should be explained solely by means of the distinctions between the states of manifestation (*vivarta*);
it is inconceivable and wondrous in nature because of its union with a power that is distinct from all [other] characteristics.
Desiring to emit various kinds of creatures from his own body, he first emitted water; into that water, he cast his seed.
He, having received the name Hiraṇyagarbha through the mantras beginning with "In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose," characterized by the previously mentioned qualifications,
desiring to create— that is, wishing to bring forth— various creatures of manifold forms, first created the waters, that is, water;
[this was] from his own body, the body which had been assumed by him.
In the Advaita philosophy, primordial matter (*pradhāna*) alone is His body, because it follows His will and because it is the cause of the creation of bodies by itself.
Did He create the bodies of all the worlds through material activity, such as digging with a spade?
No, he says.
How then?
By means of a mental resolve:
"Let water arise"—thus, by mere wish.
To this, it is said as follows:
since earth and the other elements do not yet exist at that time, what is the support for the waters that have been created?
This is explained by reference to others.
It must also be stated what the support is for the Supreme Lord, the Creator, when he has assumed a body.

Or, if it is argued that because of his possession of a distinct and superior sovereignty, that power of agency is entirely different and not subject to the same constraints as the common properties of ordinary beings—this same principle should be observed in these cases as well.
Into those [waters], he emitted—that is, poured forth—his *vīrya*, his seed.
That became a golden egg, radiant as the thousand-rayed sun;
within it was born Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds.
First, the primary matter (pradhāna), which exists everywhere, becomes clay-like in form;
through conjunction with the potency (vīrya) of Hiraṇyagarbha, it attains solidity,
and that is said to have become the cosmic egg (aṇḍa).
"In gold" (*hemni*) means "golden" (*haimam*), that is to say, made of gold;
this is because of the commonality of its rays with gold.

[Objection: But this meaning is not based on scripture (*āgama*), nor is the word "like" (*iva*) heard here; so how can there be an interpretation by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) in the absence of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
It is said:
he will state that "from those two fragments, however, he fashioned heaven and earth.
And since this earth consists of clay and is not made entirely of gold, a figurative usage has been resorted to.
"Sahasrāṃśu" means the Sun; "aṃśavaḥ" means rays, and his radiance or luster is equal to those. Within that egg, Brahmā himself was born—meaning he was produced or manifested.
Brahmā is indeed Hiraṇyagarbha. The word "himself" has its meaning already explained.
By the power of yoga, having cast off the body previously assumed, he entered into the interior of the cosmic egg.
Or rather, he created the waters while still bodiless;
thereafter, he took up his own body within the egg.
Or else, he who was designated there as "another" is distinct from this Brahmā born of the egg.

And so he will say later: "emitted by him" (*tadvisṛṣṭaḥ*), meaning created by that Lord (*īśvara*). How then is it said that Brahmā was born of himself and is self-existent (*svayambhū*)? In that context, the term *brahman* refers to [the primordial cause].
This is not a fault; for a son is designated by the name of his father, as it is said:
"The self was born from the self."
This was written by the Teacher based on traditions (*āgama*) that are not limited to this [world]; nor should one be dogmatic regarding this.
It has been stated that whether he himself is born, or another is created by him, this does not serve as a basis for the designation of *dharma*.
He is designated as the "Grandfather of all the worlds" (*sarvalokapitāmaha*).
Because he is seen as unreal only by way of metaphorical designation, the grandfather is more worthy of honor than even the father.
The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of *nara*;
since they were his primordial abode (*ayana*), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.

He who is proclaimed in the scriptures as the Puruṣa, the cause of the universe, by means of the term "Nārāyaṇa" in certain places due to his possession of an excellence of power as both agent and knower—he is this very one.
There is no difference in meaning due to a difference in words.
Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and Maheśvara are one and the same entity; they do not differ merely as objects of worship.
And we shall demonstrate this in the twelfth [chapter]. It is said thus because water is designated by the word *nārāḥ*.
[Objection: But surely this is not the usage of the elders, and yet it is not well-known as such; therefore, he says: "The waters indeed are the sons of Nara.
To begin with, that Blessed One is well-known as Nara, the Puruṣa;
and the waters are his sons, his offspring.

Therefore, they are called by the word "nara. For the word "pitṛ" (father/ancestor) is seen to be applied to offspring—as in "the descendants of Vasiṣṭha are the Vasiṣṭhas" and "the descendants of Bhṛgu are the Bhṛgus"—and likewise, through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), those waters are denoted by the word "nara," as in the expression "Babhru-maṇḍu-lomaka. Because that was the former course (*ayana*), the first creation or the support while he was in the womb, for this Prajāpati, for that reason he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
Since the form *narāyaṇa* results from the analysis "he whose path (ayana) is men (nara)," the lengthening of the vowel occurs according to the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate*;
it is just like the word *puruṣa*.
Alternatively, the suffix *aṇ* is used here in the sense of a collective group (*sāmūhika*).
That cause which is unmanifest, eternal, and consisting of both being and non-being—from that was he, the Puruṣa, emitted; in this world, he is celebrated as Brahman.
It is the cause alone, not the effect; its body is not subject to the will of another; it is endowed with innate majesty.
It is said to be unmanifest and eternal, the meaning of which has already been explained.
It consists of both the existent and the non-existent.
"Real and unreal, both real and unreal"—
that which has these as its self-nature (*ātman-svabhāva*) is described in this way.
But how can there be a connection for a single thing with two contradictory properties consisting of existence and non-existence?
It is said:
because those of limited vision lack the perception of that [Self] as their object, and thus it is unfit for the conventional usage of existence, it is called "non-existent" in nature;
yet, because all of this is understood from the scriptures to have that [Self] as its cause, it is "existent" in nature.
Therefore, due to the difference in the cognizer, the conventional usage regarding Brahman is not contradictory from either perspective.
But surely, all entities are of such a nature that they are always existent by their own form and non-existent by the form of another;
why then is it said that it is "not contradictory" in the case of Brahman?
It is said:
in the Advaita philosophy, there is nothing whatsoever other than Brahman; therefore, what could that "other" be which is said to exist as its absence?
By him [Brahman] was emitted—that is, produced—the Person (Puruṣa) fashioned within the cosmic egg, who is celebrated in the world as Brahman.

He who is heard of in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts as having sat down here and there for the purpose of granting boons to the gods, asuras, and great sages of fierce austerity—he is this very one, first emitted by that Great Person, the Supreme Brahman.
Others, however, describe [the passage] beginning with "you alone" differently.
By the demonstrative pronoun "this," the world is indicated through a gesture of direct perception.

Whatever the arrangement and creation of this entire world may be, it belongs to the Self-Existent (Svayambhū); it is inconceivable, of wondrous form, manifold, exceedingly great, and immeasurable, such that it cannot be known by anyone.
Thus says the Seer (Ṛṣi):
"Who indeed knows? Who here can declare whence it was born and whence came this creation?"
Is this entire world born in dependence upon material causes (*upādāna*), or is it merely an emanation (*nairmāṇika*) as seen by a Buddha?
Is it dependent on the will of Īśvara, or is it produced solely through the power of karma, or is it an immeasurable natural occurrence?
Likewise, does it arise through the sequence of the Great One (*mahat*) and so forth, or through the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth?
You know its function, its true nature, and its purpose.
Its function is this: from the Great Principle (mahat) comes the ego (ahaṃkāra); from the ego come the non-specific subtle elements (tanmātras); from the ego come the eleven sense organs;
and from the specific gross elements (the five mahābhūtas) comes their collective effect, which extends from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
From their [the elements'] causal condition as well, the reality is the nature [of the Great One], just as the Great One consists merely of form.
The state of all modifications of the Pradhāna is called the "Great" (mahat);
thus, from Prakṛti comes the Great One.
*Prakṛti* and *pradhāna* have the same meaning.
The reality (*tattva*) of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) consists solely in the cognition "I am.
The non-specific elements (*aviśeṣas*) are characterized by being cognizable through a non-specific cognition.
"Artha" means purpose.
This subject matter is useful for a person in this manner for the sake of human goals (*puruṣārtha*), and it accomplishes this specific purpose.

Although the knowledge of the creation of the world—which belongs to the Teacher—is of no assistance whatsoever to one desiring to know Dharma, nor is it something that ought to be asked about, nevertheless, because the unequal creation of the world by the Great Sages is difficult to understand from other sources, it is worthy of inquiry at the outset.
For the mind is indeed inexpressible;
even that object which is beyond the scope of the six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), you know through the vision of the sages (*ārṣa-cakṣus*).
Furthermore, since Dharma is the domain of the Vedas, it has necessarily been understood by you. Thus, this is a praise of the speaker directed precisely toward the subject at hand.
Thus encouraged by this praise, he first speaks of the creation of the world itself, beginning with "This was" and then "From that, the Self-existent.
By these words, it is *pradhāna* (primordial matter) alone that is designated.
It exists by itself (*svayambhū*), meaning it undergoes transformation and modification into the form of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with the Great One (*mahat*).
There is no such thing as a Lord established by way of intrinsic nature (svabhāva), who would follow after the insentient *pradhāna* according to his own will.
This is simply the inherent nature of things (*vastu-svabhāva*), namely that the *pradhāna*, which is of the nature of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), undergoes transformation again and again—
just as insentient milk becomes curd through various stages such as the formation of cream.
"Bhagavān" means that the Lord (īśvara) has engaged in his own activity by way of the primary elements and so forth;
"ojas" is the vigor and capacity for his own task.
The word "ādi" (etcetera) is used here in the sense of "kind" or "classification.
By this, the unmanifest (avyakta) becomes the cause of the Great One (mahat) and the subsequent principles.
Having fallen away from its prior state during the stage of transformation, it is said that, being subtle in nature and consisting of light, it dispels darkness.
Alternatively, by supplying the word *artha* (meaning), the masculine gender is used for the primary [cause];
and the word *puruṣa* is seen to be applied to the primary cause and so forth, as in the expression: "This, however, belongs to these seven *puruṣas*."
"He who is that one" is as explained previously.
"He meditates upon" means he contemplates [the object] by way of its qualities,
because the primary cause (pradhāna) is insentient and thus incapable of meditation itself.

Just as one might bring about an effect through mere intention alone, independent of any other action, so too a thing undergoing transformation by its own inherent nature is said to "intend" without depending on the will of a Lord (*īśvara*).
[The text says: "In the beginning, he created the waters.
Their status as the "beginning" is relative to the other great elements (*mahābhūta*), but not in reference to the production of the principles beginning with *mahat*.
For he will say: "Of these seven, however... First is the arising of the principles (*tattva*), then of the elements (*bhūta*), and [finally] the potency within them.
It discharged its energy and power (*vīrya*).
Primordial matter (*pradhāna*) itself becomes the agent;
everywhere, in the production of the elements such as earth and the rest, the *pradhāna* attains solidity.
It becomes egg-shaped;
that is what is called an "egg.

Just as the principles (tattvas) arise even without the union of male and female, so too, by the power of past karma, Brahmā's body is likewise produced without a womb through his own majesty alone, like a gadfly or a mosquito.
"Emitted by that" means emitted by that primary matter (pradhāna); because his body consists of that [matter], he is said to be "emitted by that.
The rest is as before.
Whatever the true meaning here may be, we have already stated it.
These are explanatory passages (arthavādas) which are interpreted in some way through figurative speech (guṇavāda).
Having dwelt within that egg for a full year, the Blessed One,
by his own meditative power, split that egg into two parts.
That Blessed Brahmā, having dwelt for a full year within that egg, became omniscient while remaining there and reflected, "How might I emerge?
He then split that egg in two;
by that time, the embryo had reached maturity.
Since even an egg undergoes division after a certain period due to its maturation, it is said that he split that egg into two by way of the "crow-and-palm" maxim (i.e., by chance).
From those two fragments, he fashioned heaven and earth;
in between, the intermediate space, the eight directions, and the eternal abode of the waters.
The two halves are the shell of the egg;
with those two halves of the egg-shell, he fashioned— that is, he created— the heaven above,
the earth below, and the void of space in between.
The eight directions, beginning with the east, together with the intermediate directions such as southeast and so forth;
the abode of the waters in the atmosphere, the ocean, and the sky; and the earth situated in the netherworld (pātāla).
And from himself he drew forth the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent;
and from the mind, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the presiding lord who is the conceiver.
The creation of the principles (*tattva*) is now described.
That which was previously mentioned according to its constituent parts is here stated [in reverse order], as it were;
that is, he drew forth the mind (*manas*) from his own form, which is *pradhāna*.
This evolution of the principles is here described in reverse order. First from the mind [arises] the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), which is the conceiving subject;
its function is the conceit "I am."
The Lord is capable of accomplishing the task.
And [he perceives] the Great Self (mahat), all that consists of the three qualities,
and the five sense organs which gradually grasp the objects of the senses.
The principle known as "the Great" (mahat) is well-established among the Sāṃkhyas by that designation. The term "Self" (ātman) is used here in grammatical apposition with "the Great.
Furthermore, because it is woven through all created bodies by virtue of its greatness, it is conventionally referred to as the "Self."
Prior to the ego (ahaṃkāra), he created by the aforementioned method; and all things are composed of the three qualities (triguṇa).
Everything that has been enumerated and everything that will be enumerated is composed of the three qualities.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities (guṇas).
The knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas) are exclusively devoid of qualities.
Every constituent part of primordial matter (prākṛta) consists of sattva, rajas, and tamas.

The five sense-faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*) are the respective perceivers of their objects of description—form, taste, and so forth—and are the generators of consciousness. Their specific names will be stated [later] as "the ear," "the skin," and so on.
By the word "and" (*ca*), the objects—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—as well as earth and the other elements, are included.
Having arranged the subtle constituent parts of those six [gods] of immeasurable splendor within the portions of his own self, he fashioned all beings.
Having arranged subtle components within the self-measures (*ātmamātra*) of those six, he created all beings.
Therein, by means of the number six, the five *tanmātras* that are about to be described and the transcendent *ahaṃkāra* are indicated. Their "self-measures" are their own respective transformations.
From the *tanmātras* [arose] the elements (*bhūtas*), and from the *ahaṃkāra* [arose] the sense organs (*indriyas*).

Having placed the subtle components—the *tanmātras* and the *ahaṃkāra*—within the elements such as earth, which exist in the form of bodies, and having joined them according to their respective locations, he fashioned all beings, including gods, humans, animals, birds, and stationary things.
This is what is meant.

The six non-specific (aviśeṣa) constituents are the initiators of a single part of the entire universe, because the universe is originated from them. Their subtlety is established by their very designation as "tanmātras" (merely-that). Having arranged and brought those together, he fashioned from their own portions and their modifications the elements and the sense organs.
And by the word "ca" (and), he indicates that he performed the creation of the aggregate;
in the phrase "mātrāsu," the reading "mātrābhiḥ" is more appropriate.
The six subtle components of form resort to these;
therefore, the wise call that form of his "the body" (śarīra).
The *mūrti* is the body;
its constituent parts (*tadartha*) are the components that produce it.
The subtle [elements] are the six whose natures have been described, and they are called the "undifferentiated" (*aviśeṣa*).
These sense-faculties and those elements that are about to be described depend upon them;
because they arise from that [consciousness], it is said that the elements depend upon it.
Thus, their arising is dependent upon that.
And it is recited that there are five elements from [the five].
By whatever reason they serve as its substratum, for that reason the body is called the "form" (*mūrti*) of that *pradhāna*;
so say the wise.
*Manīṣā* means intelligence; those who possess it are the wise (*paṇḍitāḥ*).
Alternatively, the status of agent may be reversed:
the subtle sense organs are the agents, and [the objects] are the action.
And the parts of the sense organs, by attaining the state of being a support, are said to "support" [the sense organs].
Just as one who causes many people to eat is said to have "eaten," so too,
because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the meaning here is that they "support" [the organs] in the sense that they "produce" them.
Then the great elements, together with their functions, enter that imperishable creator of all beings, along with the mind and its subtle components.
This very Pradhāna becomes the creator of all beings;
it is imperishable and indestructible by virtue of its nature as the cause.
How does it create all beings?
From which these enter it;
what, moreover, are they?
The mind, together with its subtle components characterized as the subtle elements (tanmātras), the intellect (buddhi), the ego (ahaṃkāra), and the sense organs (indriya).
Next are the great elements known as earth, water, fire, air, and space, together with their functions.
The functions of earth and the others are, respectively: supporting, cohesion, ripening, expansion, and providing space.

In this context, *dhṛti* (stability) is maintenance; it is the staying together of that which has the nature of falling apart and scattering. It is the consolidation of what is dispersed by means of a unifying factor, just as scattered dust is consolidated and formed into a mass by water.
The digestion of food, medicinal herbs, grass, and so forth, is well known as an effect of fire (*tejas*).
"Arrangement" (*vyūha*) means a particular disposition or configuration.
"Space" (*avakāśa*) is the absence of obstruction by another corporeal form.
For in whatever place one material object is situated, there is no room for another material object;
within a lump of gold, nothing else can exist internally.
The mention of the "mind" is intended to illustrate all the sense faculties.

And by the mention of "action" (karman), either the organs of action are understood; or else, the construction is as follows: that [subtle body], endowed with subtle components, subsequently presides over the great elements. And the sense organs are included because the word "mind" (manas) is intended to be illustrative.
But from these seven immensely powerful beings,
the perishable arises from the imperishable, through subtle material constituents.
The intended meaning is simply that the gross arises from the subtle— that which is perishable emerges from the imperishable—
and not that [the gross] arises from the measures (mātrās) of six or seven principles (tattvas).
There are twenty-four principles (*tattva*).
These are the cause for the creation of all things.
Alternatively, in the creation of the body (*piṇḍa-sṛṣṭi*), only seven are the primary causes: the six non-specific principles (*aviśeṣa*) and the Great Principle (*mahat*) as the seventh.
From them the elements and the sense organs arise;
and when these have arisen, the body becomes a solid mass.
From the imperishable *pradhāna*, which has gathered all modifications and become unified, this world—multiform and scattered in many ways—is produced.
Is the primary cause (pradhāna) modified simultaneously by all its transformations in their gross forms?
No, he says:
"This [is] of them."
The sequence is exactly as previously stated:

"From primordial nature (prakṛti) comes the Great One (mahat); from that, the I-maker (ahaṃkāra); from that, the group of sixteen qualities. The word "puruṣa" is applied to this principle because it exists for the sake of the Puruṣa.
"Of those possessed of great power" means of those who are vigorous in their own tasks;
"greatness" is due to their being the cause of immeasurable transformations.
Of these, the subtle portions of form—that is, the body—are the "portions" (mātrās) for that purpose; from them this [universe] comes into being.
Therefore it is said:
"From the imperishable, the perishable [arises].
But what are their subtle constituents?

For there are no other *mātrās* belonging to those [gross] *mātrās*, by which the distinction "their subtle *mātrās*" would be logically possible. It is not that they depend on their own constituent *mātrās*;
what then?
Subtler than the subtle elements is the Great One; greater than the Great One is the Lord.
Each subsequent one among these acquires the quality of each preceding one;
whichever one is the *n*-th in this sequence, it is traditionally held to possess that many qualities.
In the preceding verse, some propose an alternative calculation of the number seven:
the five sense-faculties, beginning with the eye, when grouped together, become one;
they are designated as a single entity because they are conjoined with the single dharma that serves as the cause of awakening.
The same applies to the organs of action.
Because these two groups consist of pairs, they constitute two persons.
The five elements are taught as distinct precisely because of the difference in their effects.

Thus, in this way, those seven persons consist of their subtle constituents (tanmātra) which have the forms of objects, as well as the effects of manifestation (nirmāṇakārya), namely the tanmātras and the ego (ahaṃkāra).
The rest is the same.
And because the elements were mentioned in the preceding verse, the word "of these" (eṣām) serves as a reference back to them.

And although many statements concerning the remote [elements] are present here, nevertheless, the meaning established here—that the possession of specific numbers, agents, and qualities—is possible only for the primary elements (*bhūta*), and not for others, even though they are the subject under discussion.
Therefore, this is the meaning of the verse:
of these primary elements, whatever is the first form of each [element], that which is recited immediately after it takes on the quality through its connection with the preceding one.

By the word "quality" (guṇa), the five beginning with sound are meant. And here, "primacy" refers to the fact that space is born first, according to the order that will be stated later. Furthermore, he will explain the quality-status of sound and the others in that very same place.
Whatever object characterized by space and so forth occupies a certain ordinal position— that is, completes a certain number—
it possesses that many qualities when situated in the second or third state; [this is expressed by] the suffix *ithuk* added to the word ending in *vati*.
He possesses as many qualities as there are [stages];
situated in the second stage, he has double [the number], and so forth.
The mutual connection of the qualities of each preceding stage was stated in the first half-verse.

In that regard, they know that whatever quality is expressed by its own specific term for a given element is its "word-quality" (*śabda-guṇa*), while that which is called its "form-quality" (*rūpa-guṇa*) and so forth [is its subsequent quality].
Consequently, upon the acquisition of each preceding quality, a doubling [of qualities] would result for the elements, with the exception of space (*ākāśa*).
Therefore, it was said: "whichever one is the *n*-th [element]."
Therefore, wind has two qualities, fire has three, water has four, and earth has five.
Regarding the phrase "of each preceding one," how is it to be understood?
It must be understood here as "of each preceding one."
By means of the dual number [used] in the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ*,

as in the example *paraḥ paraḥ*; because there is no distinction between the Vedic meters (*chandas*) and the Smṛtis, and for the sake of conforming to the usage of elided forms (*lugvṛtta*), it is recited in this way.
But at the beginning, he fashioned the names and the individual actions of all beings, as well as their distinct social orders, from the words of the Vedas alone.

That Prajāpati created the names for all things, just as someone creates names for sons who have been born or for other things for the sake of practical usage— as in "vṛddhi" [is] "ā," "ai," and "au," or "dhī," "śrī," and "strī.
He established the relationship between word and meaning, such as "cow," "horse," and "man."
And he fashioned the ritual acts—those called dharma and adharma, whose purposes are unseen, such as the Agnihotra and others.
Having created these ritual acts, he established therein their specific forms and regulations: "This act must be performed by a Brāhmaṇa alone, at this time, and for this particular fruit."

Alternatively, there are rules and regulations for visible purposes, such as: "Cattle must not graze here in this region," or "This water intended for irrigating crops must not be given to that village, until we have received this service from that village.
He also performed actions for visible purposes.
Among those, the actions for invisible purposes [are known] from Vedic words or Vedic sentences.
But surely, since everything was created by Him alone and He possesses absolute sovereignty, one must say that He created this Veda for the sake of the performance and preservation of ritual action;
and the creation of the Veda will indeed be mentioned in the passage beginning with "and from Agni, Vāyu, and Ravi.
To this it is replied:
There is a difference of opinion on this point.

Some say that the Vedas were studied by him in another *kalpa*, and they were dissolved by the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*); then, in another *kalpa*, everything appears all at once, like one who has awakened from sleep, just as a verse recited in a dream might appear to someone.

Furthermore, the Veda shines forth through such statements as "The ox is to be bound for sacrifice," and "The horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal. Having seen these objects arising—recalling them instantly by means of the recollection of words—he [the Creator] thought, "This was the name of this object in another *kalpa*; let that very same one be used now," and thus he created both names and rituals from the Vedic words alone.
Alternatively, the Vedas do not dissolve even at the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*);
they remain just as they were for those persons who accept such a view.
Having fashioned within the cosmic egg a Puruṣa identical with Brahman, he taught him the Vedas;
thus that Brahmā created everything from the words of the Vedas.
Whatever the truth regarding this matter may be, it has already been stated by us.
Now, the ancient method is employed; we shall indeed demonstrate that very method.
It means, first of all, the creation of the world.

Alternatively, [he created] those names which were originally uncorrupted, and not the modern ones such as *gavi* and so forth, which arise from incapacity. "Separately" means that he did not fashion them in the same way as the body, which is merely a collection of principles (*tattva*); rather, he fashioned them separately.
The Lord created the gods whose nature is action, as well as living beings;
he also created the subtle host of Sādhyas and the eternal sacrifice itself.
Those embodied beings who are devoted to actions—human beings intent upon ritual acts—are called "karmātmānaḥ" (those whose nature is action).
For their sake, [the Lord] created sacrifice.

Those who take no delight in the meditation on Brahman, who seek fruits such as sons and cattle, and who rely on the dualistic path, are called "karmātmānaḥ" because they are devoted to the performance of ritual acts.
Since the genitive case also expresses the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*), it is understood that he created the sacrifice for their sake;
and he created the host of gods for that very same purpose.
And [he created] those whose nature is action—this word *ca* (and) is read here even though it is not in its proper place.
Immediately after the passage "His region is that of the gods," he created the sacrifice;
for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice, he created the host of gods beginning with Agni, Agni-Soma, Indra-Agni, and so forth.

Likewise, the phrase "the host of the Sādhyas, the gods" is to be supplied [to the verse]. Their separate mention is because they do not partake of the sacrificial oblation; they are merely recipients of praise, as in the passage:
"where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide."
"The Sādhyas, indeed, are the name of the gods.
There were indeed gods named Sādhyas;
or else it is like the expression "Brahmins and wandering mendicants" (where the specific term stands for the general).
In comparison with "the Maruts, the Rudras, the Aṅgirasas," the group of Sādhyas is subtle.
The mention of the Sādhyas is intended to indicate other deities as well who are not connected with oblations, such as those mentioned in the verse beginning with "venas tuṣṭūṣiṇo...
Others, however, consider these terms to be in apposition, meaning "deities who are living beings whose nature is action."
Those whose self is action—that is, whose nature is the attainment of [their own] essence—are "action-selves" (*karmātmānaḥ*).
Alternatively, they are "action-selves" because they are primarily intent upon performing actions such as sacrifices.
Certain deities are heard of in the *itihāsas* as having their very own form (*svarūpataḥ*) in sacrificial rites and the like.
Just as [the terms] Indra, Rudra, and Viṣṇu [denote deities by their own nature],
