for others, however, deityhood exists only in the act of sacrifice itself and not by their own essential form—
as in the case of the dice, the pressing-stones, and the chariot parts.
For it is not described in the case of the dice and so forth that they perform actions such as waging war against Asuras like Vṛtra, as is heard in the *Mahābhārata* regarding Indra and others;
nevertheless, they possess the status of deities (*devatātva*) in connection with the oblation (*havis*) in the hymn: "O quivering ones of the dice... and so on.
"Let these of the pressing-stones speak forth," [and] "O Lord of the Forest, firm-limbed," for the chariot parts;
and from that very [source], for the living beings.
For deities are of two kinds: those endowed with breath and those devoid of it.
Just as Indra and others are described in the Purāṇas as possessing breath and having human forms, dice and the like do not.
Furthermore, this entire elaboration of creation and so forth is based upon the perspective of the Itihāsas.
The word "ca" (and) should be understood here [to include] both sentient beings and insentient things;
for even in the view of Nirukta, there are two kinds of deities:
horses and [the deity addressed by] the mantra *mā no amitraḥ*.
"Śakuniḥ kanikradat" (The bird is crying out),
"gāva ā gāvo agman" (The cows have come, the cows have come)—
these [verses] possess the vital breath (prāṇa).
The breathless [sacrifices] have been described.
The inclusion of the term "eternal" (sanātana) is an adjective qualifying the sacrifice;
for since the sacrifice existed even in previous kalpas, it is eternal by virtue of its continuous flow.
From Agni, Vāyu, and Ravi, he milked forth the threefold eternal Brahman,
characterized as the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, for the sake of accomplishing sacrifice.
The etymologists (nairuktāḥ) maintain that there are only three deities, beginning with Agni, despite the multiplicity of their names;
therefore, it is stated according to that view:
"for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice through these three."
Because they are the recipients of the sacrifice, the fourth case is used for them.
He milked the threefold Brahman—characterized by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman and known as the Veda.
This verbal root takes two objects.
The primary action is threefold;
there ought to be a secondary second object,
yet that does not exist.
Therefore, we consider that this [action] belongs to the fifth case alone;

[the text says] he "milked" from Agni and the others, meaning he caused them to flow forth or brought them into being. But how could sounds consisting of phonemes—namely mantra-passages and Brāhmaṇa-passages—arise from Agni and the others?
What is not possible? Who is capable of asserting that potencies are unseen or non-existent?
It is not proper to conceptualize the meaning of a verb.
In that case, what is the purpose of the fifth [case-ending]?
It ought to be the second [accusative] according to the rule *duhi-yāci* (Pāṇini 1.4.51).

Furthermore, when a matter previously established by perception is stated in contradiction to that valid evidence, it does not bring satisfaction to those who rely on authoritative means of knowledge.

The contradiction has been resolved by relying on the fact that these scriptural passages refer to their own essential nature: "From Agni the Ṛgveda was born; from Vāyu the Yajurveda; from Āditya the Sāmaveda.

Since even deities such as Agni possess lordly power and Prajāpati possesses unsurpassed power, what inconsistency could there possibly be? In this view, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is also intended to be significant.

Therefore, it is established in the Bhāṣya that those which are designated as *kārakas* where the technical term *apādāna* applies are intended to be expressed as *apādāna*. How is this so according to other views? First of all, the use of the fourth case (*caturthī*) is indeed appropriate.
And these are explanatory statements (*arthavāda*).
In that regard, the second ritual act is that Prajāpati himself milked his own self;
and "milking" here refers to teaching, by virtue of the commonality of transferring [knowledge] to another.
Furthermore, there is also the fifth [case].

In that regard, the mantras dedicated to Agni appear at the beginning of the Ṛgveda; therefore, it is said, "He was born from Agni. In the Yajurveda as well, there is the mantra: "For food (iṣe) thee, for strength (ūrje) thee. *Iḍ* means food; because it resides in the intermediate region, it is produced by Vāyu through the bestowing of rain.
*Ūrj* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and that is indeed *vāyu*.
Therefore, because of the connection with the effects of *vāyu* from the very beginning, there is this comparison: "of *vāyu*.

Alternatively, since the office of the *adhvaryu*, the sacrificial duties, and all the various types of ritual movements belong to *vāyu*, by this commonality, the *Yajurveda* has its origin in *vāyu*.
Since one who lacks authority is unfit for the chanting of the Sāmans, the Sāmans are the highest forms of study, and the sun occupies the highest place.
Time and the divisions of time, as well as the lunar mansions and the planets; the rivers, the oceans, and the mountains; and that which is level and that which is uneven.
He speaks because of the commonality of the term *dharma*.
For the Vaiśeṣikas, time (*kāla*) is a substantial entity (*dravyātmā*); for others, it is of the nature of action (*kriyārūpa*).
It consists of the extension of the movements of the sun and other celestial bodies, and is characterized by recurrence.
The divisions of time are the distinctions such as months, seasons, half-years, years, and so forth;
the lunar mansions are Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, and the rest;
and the planets are the Sun and the others.
Rivers are streams;
oceans are seas;
mountains are peaks.
Level ground refers to uniform terrain free from pits and ravines; uneven ground consists of areas characterized by ascents and descents.
Desiring to create these progeny, he emitted this creation: austerity, speech, pleasure, desire, and anger.
*Rati* is the satisfaction of the mind;
*kāma* is longing or desire;
the others are well known.
He created this creation beginning with these [verses].

In this verse, the meaning is that desiring to create these progenies—the gods, asuras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, and so forth—he first created their instruments, namely the body and dharma, which possess the same nature as his own dharma. The "previous creation" mentioned here refers to that which was described in the preceding verse.
Now, what is this mode of expression, "he created creation"?
It has the same meaning as "he performed creation.
All verbal roots function to denote the general sense of "doing" as delimited by specific particulars.
"He cooks" means he performs cooking; "he sacrifices" means he performs a sacrifice.

In these cases, once the specific meaning has been understood from the verbal derivative (*kṛdanta*), the root contained within the finite verb (*ākhyāta*) becomes intent solely upon conveying the general sense of "doing. Even when that general sense has already been apprehended from some source, there must be an emphasis on factors such as tense and grammatical case (*kāraka*) so that the fault of mere restatement (*anuvāda-doṣa*) does not occur in its further expression.

Alternatively, creation—characterized by specific objects being produced and delimited by means of valid cognition—is the object of the general act of creating, just as in the expression "he nourished his own prosperity."
For the sake of distinguishing between actions, he separated dharma and adharma;
and he joined these creatures with pairs of opposites, such as pleasure and pain.
He distinguished between dharma and adharma; that is, he established them through differentiation as distinct entities: "This is indeed dharma," and "This is indeed adharma.
But is it not the case that such a distinction does not exist?
For there are actions of a dual nature, consisting of both dharma and adharma.
As they have said: "Vedic rituals are variegated because they have violence as their means;
for example, the Jyotiṣṭoma is dharma in its essential nature, but it is adharma because violence is a constituent part of it.
Therefore, he says: "But for the sake of distinguishing between actions..."
By the word "karma" here, the performance of actions—that is, their execution—is meant.
That very same thing, when performed otherwise, becomes of a contrary nature;
being dharma, it attains the form of adharma, and adharma attains the state of dharma.
For instance, violence itself:

violence performed externally is unrighteousness (*adharma*), because it falls within the scope of the prohibition, "One should not harm any living beings. Violence performed within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*) during the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice is righteousness (*dharma*), because it is characterized by a scriptural injunction (*vidhi*).
Thus, austerity (*tapas*) is *dharma*, yet that very same austerity, when performed out of hypocrisy or due to incapacity and the like, is *adharma*.

Similarly, for women, approaching a deity is *adharma*; however, for those commissioned by their elders and desiring offspring, it is *dharma* through the favor of being anointed with clarified butter and so forth.
Therefore, even though the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is identical, the distinction between *dharma* and *adharma* is established based on the difference in application (*prayoga*).
Even though they are one, there is indeed a distinction in their essential nature when viewed through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, the word "karma" is applied to the fruits of action because the effect is metaphorically designated by the cause.
By this it is meant that he distinguished the actions for the sake of discerning the division between actions and their fruits.
What, then, is the classification of the fruits of actions? To this it was said: "He joined [beings] with pairs such as pleasure and pain;
the fruit of dharma is pleasure, and the fruit of adharma is suffering."

Therefore, those who perform both [types of action] are joined with pairs of opposites (*dvandva*): through pleasure because of their performance of dharma, and through suffering because of their performance of adharma.
This term *dvandva* is used by convention (*rūḍhi*) to refer to mutually contradictory things that cause affliction, such as cold and heat, rain and sun, hunger and satiety, and so forth.
The inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*) should be understood in terms of the relationship between general categories and specific instances.

The two words "pleasure" and "pain" alone denote heaven and hell, or they signify unsurpassed bliss and extreme suffering. The word "etc. refers to specific gains such as heaven, a village, a son, or cattle, as well as their loss.
It has been stated previously that the production of karmas occurs first.
By this, it is established that Prajāpati made the distinction between their application and the distinction between their results; such is the discernment of what is to be understood.
The minute, perishable particles which are said to belong to the five elements—
along with these, this entire universe comes into being in successive order.
This is the summary:
the subtle, minute portions or constituents of the five great elements—known as *tanmātras*—are perishable;
however, because they possess the nature of transformation, they are said to be imperishable through their attainment of grossness.
Together with these, this entire world comes into being and arises,
sequentially and in stages:
from the subtle to the gross, and from the gross to the grosser.
Or rather, it is according to whatever sequence was previously stated.
Whatever task the Lord first appointed him to perform,
that very same task he himself undertook as he was created again and again.
This is its meaning:

although Prajāpati, as the Lord, is capable of creating living beings at his will during the creation of the elements, he nevertheless does not create living beings without regard for the actions performed in previous kalpas.
He causes a person to be born into that very caste which was projected by whatever kind of action was performed by him in a former kalpa, and not into another caste.

Through auspicious action, one is born into a class such as that of gods or humans for the sake of experiencing its fruit; through the opposite, one is born among animals, hungry ghosts, and so forth.

Just as the elements, the sense organs, and the qualities, existing in their primordial state (*prakṛti*) at the beginning of a kalpa, arise, so too do actions, existing in their own primordial state during the dissolution, arise again at the beginning of creation.
Therefore, this principle—that "by means of the remainder"—applies there as well.
If, then, origination depends upon karma, where is the sovereignty of Prajāpati useful, or what kind of dependent sovereignty is it?
Since the world originates when he exists, how can he be useless?
Without him, there are no stability, origination, or dissolution.
Because it is eternal, its own previously performed actions (*karma*), its will, and the transformation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) are also its causes.
From this collection of causes, this world arises, persists, and dissolves.
Even though [the Lord] is dependent [on these], his sovereignty is not impaired.
Just as here a lord, such as a king, might join his servants and others with their rewards, even so [the Lord] joins them in accordance precisely with their initial karma;
and he is not without sovereignty.
But surely this meaning is not perceived from this verse?
What, then, is understood?
It is that the Creator alone possesses sovereignty over the assignment of karma to living beings.
Whatever action—whether of a violent nature or its opposite—the Creator first assigned to a particular being at the beginning of creation, that very same action it pursues and performs.
He does not act otherwise according to his own will by depending on the instruction of his father or others;
rather, by virtue of the prior command of Prajāpati, he himself performs what is good or bad, independent of the instruction of others.
Furthermore, he is born again as one being created.
In another kalpa, or even in this very kalpa, Prajāpati himself appoints the individual souls (kṣetrajñas) as agents;
therefore, following his very injunction, they perform past actions, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
Thus it has been said:
"Though they are powerless over their own actions, they assume the role of agents;
they are impelled by the Great Lord toward what is auspicious or what is inauspicious. Thus:
"This ignorant creature is not the master of its own pleasure and pain."
Impelled by God, one may go either to heaven or even into a pit.
It is said:

if this were so, the connection between action and its fruit would be abandoned, human effort would become purposeless, and the injunctions for rituals such as the *agnihotra* and the meditations on Brahman would result in being rendered useless.
Only those who are ignorant of the true nature of the Lord would engage in actions for the sake of seen or unseen results.
But for those who believe that agency and enjoyment depend upon that [fate], there would be the consequence of non-engagement in all actions;
even when an action is performed, it would not bear fruit,
and people would remain indifferent, thinking, "We shall enjoy the results even though we are not the agents."

Furthermore, desire for agency does not arise by force among the wise, as a disease arises from unwholesome food; nor is that desire determined by the impulsion of God through the creation of the fruits of action, such that one thinks, "From this action, this agency comes about. If that were so, the statement "But in which action... would not exist.
Rather, the injunction must be understood solely from the scripture.

Therefore, that Lord first appointed that person; for in this beginningless *saṃsāra*, his status as an appointer is relative to what was first occurring, and he is the appointer because he is the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) of all things, including space and time.
Others, however, explain:
"For a self who has entered another birth, there is no dependence on the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the previous birth."
Therefore, there is a persistence of innate nature (*svabhāvānuvṛtti*).

Whatever specific species one was appointed to for a particular task, such as the killing of others, that self becomes established as belonging to that species—such as a lion—and even having abandoned the gentleness practiced during human existence, it adopts the characteristics of its species, even without being instructed by another.
It is thus demonstrated that because actions are powerful due to their being created by Prajāpati through innate nature, they cause one who has entered another species to forget previous habits.
He elaborates on this very point:
"The violent and the non-violent, the mild and the cruel, righteousness and unrighteousness, truth and falsehood—
whatever he assigned to each at the time of creation, that entered into it of its own accord."
Violent (*hiṃsra*) refers to those that cause the separation of the life-force of others, such as serpents, lions, elephants, and so forth;
the opposite of that is non-violent (*ahiṃsra*), such as the *ruru* and *pṛṣata* deer and so forth; gentle (*mṛdu*) means tender and effortless.
"Cruel" means harsh, consisting of the infliction of suffering upon others;
the rest is well known.

From this twofold karma that has arisen as established, whatever [karma] Prajāpati assigned, gave, or ordained for each being at the beginning of creation—having considered the conformity to their prior karma—that very karma the created living being enters and acquires by itself.
The state of being past time is not intended [to be expressed]; for even in the present, one observes the self-realization of a generic property (jāti-dharma) that has not been explicitly taught.
Just as the seasons themselves, at the change of seasons, assume their own respective characteristics according to the season, so too do embodied beings undergo their respective actions.
Here is an illustration:

Just as insentient things have their own natures established solely by their respective boundaries (*maryādā*), so too sentient beings do not transgress the boundaries established by Prajāpati with the assistance of the karma performed by persons. Whatever birth they are born into, they perform only that; even though they might desire otherwise, they are unable to do anything else.
This refers to the seasons, such as spring and the rest.
Its own characteristics (*svaliṅga*) are the signs such as leaves, fruits, flowers, cold, heat, rain, and so forth.
Regarding the "alternation" (*paryāya*):
whichever season has whatever alternation—that is, its own occasion for performing its function—in that [season], that very season itself undergoes that state; it does not depend upon human effort.
In spring, mango blossoms flower by themselves and do not depend on the sprinkling of water at their roots;
likewise, human actions are unseen.
There is no entity whatsoever that does not depend upon action.
For instance, the inherent nature of the rains is that which bestows rain; yet, due to the faults of the king or the faults of the realm, there may occasionally be a drought.
Therefore, the power of karma alone is irremovable.
The term *anugraha* (favor/grace) is repeated here due to the requirements of the meter.
Others, however, explain these three verses differently,
saying that by this [verse] the restriction of the inherent nature (*svabhāva-niyama*) of the potencies of karma is stated.

The meaning is that whatever fruit has been deposited by Prajāpati in a particular action, that specific action—being created again and again and being performed—partakes of that fruit itself; that is to say, it bestows it.
By this, it is established that when a sacrifice performed will bear fruit, it does not require anything else at that time;
for even service, though performed by oneself, requires the words of ministers, priests, and so forth.
The sacrifice is not like that;
rather, it requires a visible operation.
At that time, because every effect is produced by a dual cause consisting of both the seen and the unseen, the requirement for any other unseen factor is precluded.
Actions that yield desirable and undesirable fruits are the objects of injunctions and prohibitions. He illustrates actions in two ways: as harmful and non-harmful.
Violence is prohibited;

its bestowal of results such as rebirth in hell and so forth is established by the supplementary statements: "Whoever should threaten a Brāhmaṇa, whoever should threaten one belonging to me—may he be tormented with a hundred [strokes]."
She does not then deviate from her own nature;
we shall explain the specific details regarding expiations later.
Non-violence has been prescribed.
Even for that [karma], there is no deviation from its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) in bestowing its desired fruit;
rather, it is the distinction between dharma and adharma alone that accounts for this.
Prescribed action is dharma, and prohibited action is adharma; their distinctions consist of truthfulness, falsehood, and so forth.
Truth is enjoined and falsehood is prohibited;
in this manner, all the preceding and subsequent terms demonstrate specific injunctions and prohibitions.
Ritual actions possess an invariably observed relationship between cause and effect.
The example is "just as the seasonal signs";
the rest is the same.
For the sake of the prosperity of the worlds, he brought forth the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet.
For the sake of the increase of the worlds beginning with the earth;
"increase" means growth, nourishment, or abundance.
When the four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, exist, there is the increase of the three worlds.
The gods subsist upon what is given from here;
they, moreover, are entitled to perform sacrifices and other rites.
Therefore, the action performed by them causes both worlds to flourish.
The gods are impelled by human action;
from the sun rain is born—thus there is rain and prosperity for this world as well. He brought forth, that is, he produced and created, the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
"From the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet"—that is, in due order: from the mouth the Brāhmaṇa, from the two arms the Rājanya, from the two thighs the Vaiśya, and from the feet the Śūdra.
The suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*).
It occurs because the effect is, as it were, extracted from the cause.
When there is a departure, it constitutes the ablative (*apādāna*).

[The text says] he created some first Brahmin from the parts of his own mouth by means of divine power, because we observe that all people of the present day are produced from the constituent elements (*tattva*) through the medium of sexual union.
In the ultimate sense, however, this is a praise intended to demonstrate the superiority and inferiority of the social classes (*varṇa*).
Prajāpati is the most excellent among all beings; of his own body, the mouth is the most excellent;
and among all the social classes, the Brāhmaṇa is the most praiseworthy.
By this general principle, he is said to have been produced from the mouth of Brahmā;
or rather, he is said to be "from the mouth" because of the excellence of the mouth's functions, such as teaching and so forth.
For the Kṣatriya as well, the function of the arms is battle.
For the Vaiśya, there is also the work of the thighs: tending cattle while they graze with other cows, and traveling by land routes, waterways, and so forth for the purpose of trade.
For the Śūdra, there is the work of the feet: service.
Dividing his own body into two parts, he became a man with one half and a woman with the other; in her, the Lord created Virāj.
This creation is directly from the Supreme Person;
others, however, maintain that this [creation] is from that very Brahmā.
Having divided that body which emerged within the cosmic egg into two parts, with one half he became Puruṣa—that is, he became a male capable of the emission of semen.
With half [of himself], he created a woman in the manner of Gaurī and Śiva;
or rather, he fashioned her as something entirely separate.
Having created her, through the act of sexual union with her, he generated that being whose name is well-known as Virāj.
This is said:
Prajāpati approached his own daughter.
This statement regarding the act of division is based on the fact that, although husband and wife differ only in body, they are inseparable in all their functions.
O best of the twice-born, know me to be the creator of all this, whom that Virāj Puruṣa himself created after performing austerities.
"Know me—that Puruṣa whom Virāṭ created after performing austerities—to be such.
Thus, through this tradition of memory, there is nothing concerning me that remains unknown to you which needs to be described;
in the midst of that, he declares his own purity."

"The creator of all this"—by this he declares his omnipotence. The intention is that it will cause me, who possess excellence in birth and action, to be more highly trusted; and furthermore, for the sake of producing certainty, because he mentions his own human birth even though it is already known from other sources.
Just as when someone who has heard [of one's lineage] from another is asked, "Are you the son of Devadatta? and upon his saying "Yes," certainty arises;
so too, for poets, the description of one's ancestry causes shame even though it constitutes self-praise through tradition.
"O best of the twice-born" is the form of address.
The seventh [cases] are the most excellent, meaning they are the best.
Desiring to create offspring, I performed most difficult austerities and first created ten great seers as the lords of creatures.
I created—
that is, I brought forth— the ten Prajāpatis, the great seers,
after first performing extremely difficult austerities.
Austerity is practiced with great difficulty; it is extremely painful and lasts for a long time.
He names those great seers:
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada.
These [Manus], possessing great splendor, created seven other Manus,
as well as the gods, the hosts of gods, and the great seers of immeasurable power.
These seven great seers created other Manus. This term "Manu" is a word denoting office;
he who, during a Manvantara, possesses the authority over the creation or the maintenance of living beings in the manner described is called a Manu.
"Bhūritejasa" and "amitaujasas" have the same meaning.
The first, ending in the nominative case, is an adjective qualifying the Creator;
the second, ending in the accusative case, is an adjective qualifying those who are to be created, such as Manu and the others.
But are not the gods created by Brahmā alone?
True, but not all of them;
for the hosts of gods are indeed immeasurable.
For the "assemblies of gods" (devanikāya) are the abodes of the gods, such as the heavenly world (svargaloka), the Brahma-world (brahmaloka), and so forth.
And the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas; the gandharvas, apsarases, and asuras;
the nāgas, sarpas, and suparṇas; and the various hosts of the ancestors (pitṛs).

The distinction between the essential natures of the yakṣas and the others is established solely by means of authoritative sources such as history (itihāsa) and the like; it is not determined by any of the other means of valid cognition, such as direct perception.
Among them, the yakṣas are the followers of Vaiśravaṇa, while the rākṣasas include Vibhīṣaṇa and others.
More cruel than those are the Piśācas; they are inferior to the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, dwelling in impure regions such as deserts. Yet all of them are indeed harmful.

According to the traditional accounts of historians and practitioners of mantras, some of them draw out the life-force of living beings through the employment of deception and produce diseases by means of an invisible power.
The *gandharvas* are followers of the gods, preeminent in song and dance;
the *apsarases* are the courtesans of the gods, such as Urvaśī and others;
and the *asuras* are the enemies of the gods, such as Vṛtra, Virocana, Hiraṇyākṣa, and so forth.
The *nāgas* are Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and others;
the *sarpas* are well known;
the *suparṇas* are a specific class of birds, such as Garuḍa and others.
The Pitṛs, known by names such as Somapās and Ājyapās, abide in their own realm like gods;
he created their host.
Lightnings, thunderclouds, and red clouds; rainbows of Indra; meteors, atmospheric crashes, and comets; and various celestial lights, both high and low.

The middle light, visible within the belly of the clouds, is called lightning (*vidyut*); its synonyms, such as *taḍit* and *saudāminī*, are based on specific distinctions. When it becomes solidified like stone, it is called a thunderbolt (*aśani*). When it falls like raindrops or streams of rain—subtle yet visible, impelled by powerful winds, and destructive to crops and other things—it is called a hailstone (*himakaṇikā*).
Clouds are atmospheric masses consisting of water, wind, and light.
A "rohit" is a rod-like form seen in the atmosphere, appearing sometimes as blue or red;
it is occasionally attached to the solar disc, and at other times it appears in other locations.
A specific variety of that very [light] is the rainbow;
its curvature is its additional quality of having the shape of a bow.
A meteor (*ulkā*) refers to those luminous bodies seen falling in various directions during portents, emitting spreading rays at the junctions of day and night or at dusk.
*Nirghāta* refers to the sounds of portents arising from the earth or the atmosphere.
*Ketavas* are the well-known crested luminaries seen as portents;
there are also others of various kinds, such as Dhruva, Agastya, Arundhatī, and so forth.
Kinnaras, monkeys, fish, and various birds;
cattle, deer, humans, and beasts with two rows of teeth.
Beings with horse faces who dwell on mountains such as the Himavat are the *kiṃnaras*;
those with monkey faces and human bodies are the *vānaras*;
and *vihaṅgamas* are birds.
Goats, sheep, camels, donkeys, and so forth are domestic animals (*paśu*);
*mṛga* refers to the ruru deer, the spotted deer, and so forth;
*vyāla* refers to lions, tigers, and so forth.
Those who possess two rows of teeth, upper and lower, are called "those with teeth on both sides" (ubhayatodan).
And worms, insects, moths, lice, flies, and bedbugs;
all gadflies and mosquitoes, and various kinds of stationary beings.
Worms are extremely minute living beings;
insects are slightly larger than them and move upon the earth;
moths include locusts, winged insects, and the like.
"Immobile" refers to trees, mountains, and so forth;
"of various kinds" means of many different types;
and "small creatures" is treated as a singular collective compound.
Thus, by my command, all this— the stationary and the moving— was created by those great-souled ones through the power of their asceticism, each according to their own karma.
"Thus" (evam) refers back to the manner previously mentioned.
By these great-souled ones, such as Marīci and the others,
all this— the stationary and the moving— was created.
"According to their karma" means depending on whatever kind of karma a person performed in a previous life;
by the power of karma, one is born into that very birth for which it was appropriate to arise.
"By my direction" means by my command.

By performing great asceticism through the application of austerity, one attains whatever great sovereignty there may be; all of that is to be obtained through austerity—this is what he expresses by this.
I shall describe to you, according to their respective order, the nature of the karma of those beings as it is proclaimed here, as well as the sequence of their births.

Whatever kind of action—whether naturally harmful or non-harmful—belongs to which beings, that has been proclaimed exactly as it is. Now I shall explain the sequence of their births. But where was the action previously proclaimed? For in this [list] beginning with "yakṣa" and "rākṣasa," there is a designation of names, not a designation of actions.
It is said:
the understanding of their function follows from the very indication of their names, because these names are acquired on account of that function.
For instance, they are called *yakṣas* because of seizing (*yakṣaṇāt*), devouring (*bhakṣaṇāt*), or eating (*aśanāt*).
From *kṣaṇa* (moment) in secret, the *rakṣas* were born;
from *piśita* (flesh), the flesh-eating *piśācas*;
and because they flowed (*sṛta*) from the waters, they are the *apsarases*.
Because they did not obtain the liquor called *amṛta*, they are called *asuras*;
other such etymologies should also be inferred.
Regarding birth, the sequential application will be explained as "born from a womb" (*jarāyuja*), "born from an egg" (*aṇḍaja*), and so forth.
Domestic animals, wild beasts, and carnivorous animals with two rows of teeth;
as well as *rakṣas*, *piśācas*, and humans—these are born from the womb (*jarāyuja*).
These are the womb-born;
the womb (*jarāyu*) is the amnion, the bed of the embryo;
therein they first come into being.
From that, pearls are produced;
this is their order of birth.
Since there is another word *dat* which has the same meaning as the word *danta*, the form *ubhayatodataḥ* is appropriate in the nominative plural.
Birds born from eggs, serpents, crocodiles, fish, and tortoises— whatever other such creatures there are, whether terrestrial or aquatic.
Crocodiles, porpoises, and so forth;
the tortoise, which is the *kūrma*;
and those of a similar kind, such as lizards and other land-dwelling creatures.
Such are the aquatic, water-born things, such as conch shells and the like.
The gadfly, the mosquito, the louse, the fly, and the bug are born from moisture;
and whatever else is of this kind arises from heat.
Sweat is the internal moisture of earthly substances produced through contact with the heat of fire, the sun, and so forth; from that, biting insects such as gadflies and mosquitoes are born.
Furthermore, whatever else is of this nature—extremely minute creatures such as gnats and ants—that arises from warmth:
warmth is indeed sweat, or rather, heat is its cause.
Alternatively, the reading is "upajāyante" (they arise);
and one should read "ye cānye kecid īdṛśāḥ" (and whatever others are of such a kind).
All immobile beings that sprout from the earth are born from seeds or slips;
those plants which bear many flowers and fruits and perish at the ripening of their fruit are called herbs (oṣadhyaḥ).
*Udbhid* means "breaking forth";
[the suffix] *kvip* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*).
Those which are born from that are called *udbhijja*.
Having split and pierced the earth, the sown seeds give rise to trees;
all of them sprout from the seed and the stalk, and they become firm through their roots, trunks, and so forth.
The same is true for medicinal herbs.
It is appropriate [to derive] "oṣadhayaḥ" from the root *uṣ* with the suffix *ik*, as per the rule *kṛdikārād aktinaḥ*; or it is a Vedic form (*chāndasa*). This is their natural function.
"Pākāntāḥ" means those whose end is the ripening of their fruit; "anta" signifies destruction.
When the fruit has ripened, rice and other such plants perish, yet they come to be endowed with and possessed of abundant flowers and fruits.
This qualification applies to herbs and trees as far as possible.
Those which bear fruit without flowers are known as vanaspatis;
those which bear both flowers and fruit are known as vṛkṣas.
Those which bear fruit without flowers are called *vanaspati*, not *vṛkṣa*.
Those that have both flowers and fruit are *vṛkṣa*.
Due to the presence of both [characteristics], in some cases they are called both *vanaspati* and *vṛkṣa*, and *vṛkṣa* and *vanaspati* as well.
In this regard, we shall demonstrate the specific reason [for its authority];
however, we maintain that this injunction concerning the relationship between word and meaning is not like the traditional grammatical treatises (*vyākaraṇa-smṛti*).
Therefore, this is not the meaning: that those things which possess such a nature are denoted by words such as "vanaspati" (trees); rather, it is the birth of flowers and fruits that is being stated.
For that [birth] is the subject under discussion, as indicated by the phrase, "but the sequence and connection regarding birth.
The production of fruits is twofold.
Flowers arise from within [the tree] and from the flowers;
likewise, flowers [arise] from the trees.

Therefore, although the designation is such that those which bear fruit are to be known as *vanaspatis*, nevertheless, by the force of the context, a transposition of the relative pronoun (*yat*) and the demonstrative pronoun (*tat*) must be made.
Those well-known as "vanaspati" are those that bear fruit without flowers; for them, fruits are produced in the absence of flowers.
By implication, this sequence is established:
just as in the command "wrap the pillar with a cloth," when the cloth is to be wrapped, the meaning is that it must be put on [the pillar].
"Having placed a garment upon the pillar, cause him to put it on"—
this, though well known, is restated in order to establish the point expressed by the verse beginning with "by manifold darkness."
Likewise, there are various kinds of clusters and shrubs,
as well as species of grasses that grow from seeds or from stems, along with creepers and climbing vines.

Those creepers that grow from the earth in clusters, whether with a single root or multiple roots, and do not attain great growth—their collective mass is designated by the terms *guccha* (cluster) and *gulma* (bush), such as *tṛṇa* (grass) and *mūlaka* (radish) and so forth.
The distinction between these two, however, is based on whether they bear flowers or not.
Or, there are other species of grasses, such as *kuśa*, *śādvala*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, and others.
*Pratānas* are long, ground-reaching shoots of grass;
*vallīs* and *vratatīs* are creepers that, having emerged from the earth, wind around a tree or some other object and climb upward.
All of these, like trees, grow from seeds or cuttings (*bīja-kāṇḍaruham*).
Enveloped by manifold darkness caused by their past actions,
these beings possess internal consciousness and are endowed with pleasure and pain.
They are enveloped—that is, pervaded—by that darkness (tamas) for which the cause is karma known as unrighteousness (adharma);
[enveloped] by that which is multiform, serving as the occasion for the experience of various sufferings.
Although everything consists of the three qualities (triguṇa), nevertheless, for these beings, darkness is predominant, while goodness (sattva) and passion (rajas) are diminished.
Therefore, due to the predominance of *tamas*, they remain for a very long time experiencing the fruit of unrighteousness (*adharma*), constantly joined with despondency, suffering, and the like.
Because *sattva* also exists there, however, they enjoy even a slight trace of pleasure in certain states;
thus it is said: "endowed with both pleasure and pain."

Regarding "internal cognition" (*antaḥsaṃjñā*): *saṃjñā* means intellect (*buddhi*). Because of the absence of its external signs—such as outward movement, speech, and other effects in the form of physical activity—they are said to possess "internal cognition.
Otherwise, every person would be conscious only within themselves.
Alternatively, just as humans perceive the prick of a thorn and so forth beforehand, stationary beings do not;
for they require a great goad or the pain of being split by an axe and the like to have the perception of suffering,
just like living beings in states of sleep, intoxication, or fainting.
These states of existence, beginning with that of Brahmā, are declared to end here within this terrible cycle of transmigratory beings, which is constantly and perpetually moving.
This is the end, the finality; those courses of existence for which this is the limit are "ending with this.
A "course" (*gati*) is said to be the soul's connection with various bodies for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of performed actions.
There is no other course more degraded or more full of suffering than this state of being stationary.
Beyond the state of Brahman, there is no other higher goal consisting of bliss.
These states of existence are attained through auspicious and inauspicious actions known as *dharma* and *adharma*.

However, we shall explain that the attainment of the Supreme Brahman—which is characterized by liberation and consists solely of bliss—comes either from knowledge alone or from the combination of knowledge and action.
In the world of beings—the cycle of birth and death, the continuous succession of births and deaths, the transition from one species to another;
in this terrible state, which is fearsome for those possessed of negligence and indolence due to the arising of separation from the beloved and union with the unloved;
in that which is characterized by constant movement at all times, perishable, and though insubstantial, eternally terrible and never non-terrible.
"Even after remaining for a very long time in the destinies of gods and so forth, one must die"—this is eternally terrible.
Thus, by this description of how saṃsāra is caused by dharma and adharma, the great purpose of the treatise is established.
For from the treatise comes the knowledge that discriminates between dharma and adharma; therefore, it should be studied.
Having thus created all this and me as well, he of inconceivable prowess withdrew again into himself, subduing time with time.

Thus, having created this entire world—partly directly and partly by the command of Prajāpati—and having produced it and appointed me to the maintenance of the world, that Blessed One, whose power, prowess, and capacity regarding all objects were inconceivable, wondrous, and great, vanished after creating [it]; he made himself invisible, casting off the body assumed at will through his yogic power, and became unmanifest again.
Regarding the word "in himself" (ātmani):
it is not as other entities vanish into primordial nature (prakṛti) that he vanished elsewhere; rather, he [vanished] into himself.
Rather, he is dissolved into the Self itself;

for there is no other primordial nature (prakṛti) into which he might disappear, since that [Self] is the primordial nature of all beings. Alternatively, "disappearance" refers to the cessation of all worldly activities.
"Afflicting time again with time"—
the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) here should be understood as dependent on the action of "having created"; that is,
destroying the time of dissolution by means of the time of creation and maintenance.
The word "bhūyaḥ" means "again. He will state later: "The creations and dissolutions are infinite."
When that God is awake, the world thus moves;
when he, whose self is tranquil, sleeps, then everything closes its eyes.
When that God is awake—that is, when He desires, "Let this world arise; let it attain this state and endure for such a length of time"—then He acts.
He becomes endowed with mental, vocal, and physical activities, both internal and external, such as inhalation and exhalation, eating, moving about, agriculture, sacrifice, and so forth.
When He sleeps—that is, when His desire for the creation and maintenance of the world ceases—then everything closes its eyes and undergoes dissolution.
Waking and sleeping are said to be the activity and cessation of Prajāpati according to his will;
the state of being a peaceful self is the withdrawal of the state of differentiation.
When that self-existent one sleeps,
the embodied beings whose nature is action desist from their own activities, and the mind falls into exhaustion.
This verse from the previous commentary is of clear meaning:
*svasthe* means well-established;
*śāntātmavat* means having a pure nature.
Abiding in one's own self is the cessation of distinctions caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Those whose nature is action (*karmātmānaḥ*)— those for whom action is primary— are transmigrating beings (*saṃsāriṇaḥ*), knowers of the field (*kṣetrajñāḥ*), and embodied beings (*śarīriṇaḥ*).
They are described in this way because they experience a connection with a body through the connection of karma.
When that [body] sleeps or lies down, they cease from their own activities;
by this, the cessation of bodily movement is expressed.
And the mind falls into exhaustion;
by this, the cessation of internal activity is shown. Thus, dissolution is established through the cessation of both external and internal activity.
Languor is a lack of enthusiasm; it reaches, that is, attains, a state of incapacity regarding one's own activity.
But when they all dissolve simultaneously into that Great Self, then this Soul of all beings sleeps happily and in peace.
This verse should be explained by reversing the relative positions of "yat" and "tat";
otherwise, in relation to the preceding verse, a circular dependency would result.
This is what has been stated.
When one sleeps, everything closes;
one sleeps happily and at peace. The Supreme Brahman is the very nature of bliss; for it, there is no happiness during the state of sleep and no suffering at other times.
The nature of his sleep has already been described;
moreover, his state of bliss (*nirvṛti*) is constant at all times,
for that Supreme Self is not touched by the waves of the affliction of ignorance (*avidyā*), being composed solely of pure happiness.
The agency of all that [creation] is thus established.

Just as this person, having desisted from household duties, sleeps happily—feeling fulfilled because he has earned wealth useful for his home and being free from affliction, thinking "I have become one who is at peace and free from fear of injury to himself"—so too is He compared.
For Him, this world is like a family; such is the praise.
Alternatively, this verse should be explained as referring to the *pradhāna* (the primordial material cause).

In that case, the *pradhāna* "sleeps" when all beings simultaneously dissolve into it, attaining its own nature—that is, the state of the cause—and emerging from their state of modification, as many as exist within the belly of the three worlds. Furthermore, this sleep is the cessation of transformation, not the withdrawal of cognition, since the *pradhāna* is insentient.
And it is pleasant only in a figurative sense, precisely because it is devoid of volition.
But having resorted to this darkness, he remains for a long time endowed with the senses;
yet he does not perform his own action, and then he departs from the body.
Now, the death of the transmigrating person and the attainment of another body are described by these two verses:
"Darkness" (tamas) is the cessation of knowledge; having resorted to that, he remains for a long time with his senses, yet he does not perform his own functions such as inhalation and exhalation.
Then it departs, meaning it goes out from the *mūrti*, the body. Now, since the Self is all-pervading and omnipresent like space, what kind of departure can it have?
Departure is simply the relinquishing of the body acquired through karma.
Furthermore, it is not the case that a material object simply moves from one location to another.

Alternatively, some maintain that there exists another subtle body called the *antarābhava* (intermediate state), of which this departure is the exit; others, however, do not accept the existence of an intermediate state body.
As the Blessed Vyāsa has said:
"O Lord of Men, when this body has passed away, the senses indeed dwell in another body; therefore, there is no intermediate state of existence."
Even some followers of Sāṃkhya, such as Vindhyavāsin and others, do not accept the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
What is this so-called intermediate state?

When this body has perished, but before one has reached the destination—such as the mother’s womb—for the sake of taking up a second body, an intermediate, non-sensory, subtle body arises; it is that which has no contact with anything, is not burned by fire and the like, and is not obstructed by the great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Others, however, say that the *mūrti* is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). The Supreme Self, whose nature is the self of all, is like the ocean; from it the individual souls (*jīvas*) emerge due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*) and undergo differentiation, just as waves arise from the great ocean.
And as it issues forth from that [ocean], a subtle body (*liṅga*) called the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*) is admitted to accompany it.
By the power of previously accumulated merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), each individual soul (*jīva*) possesses a subtle body that serves as its place of residence.
As it is stated in the *Purāṇa*:
"It is joined with the eightfold subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), which is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) known as the vital breath (*prāṇa*)."
For one who is bound by that, there is indeed bondage; but for one who is liberated from it, there is liberation.
These five—prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna—along with the group of the five sense organs, the group of the five organs of action, and the mind as the eighth, constitute the *puryaṣṭaka*.
That body does not perish until the state of liberation (*mokṣa*).
As it has been said: "The subtle body (*liṅga*), permeated by these [elements], transmigrates in a state devoid of enjoyment."
When, having become the size of an atom, it enters— conjoined with— the seed, whether stationary or moving, then it emits a physical form.
One who possesses subtle (*aṇu*) and minute (*sūkṣma*) measures or parts is "one consisting of atomic measures" (*aṇumātrika*).
This refers either to the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city), the body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), or the selves (*ātman*) which are subtle by their very nature.
As it has been said:
"This very Self within the heart is subtler than [an atom]," and so forth.
"Seed" is the cause for the arising of a body;
"stationary" refers to that which serves as the cause for the birth of trees and the like.
"Cariṣṇu" means moving or wandering.
It enters, presides over, and becomes bound [to the body].
When it is conjoined with that [body] through the vital breaths and so forth, then it "releases its form," which means it abandons [its subtle state], binds itself, and takes on a physical body.
Thus, through waking and dreaming, that imperishable one incessantly brings this entire world of moving and non-moving beings to life and causes it to perish.
This is a summary of what was previously stated:
by means of the waking and dreaming states associated with Himself, He brings to life and causes the death of the world—both the moving and the unmoving, the stationary and the wandering.
He is imperishable and indestructible.
Having composed this treatise himself, he personally caused me to receive it according to the prescribed rule from the very beginning; I, however, [taught] the sages Marīci and the others.
Here, by the word "śāstra" (treatise), the collection of injunctions and prohibitions based on tradition (smārta) is meant, and not the physical text itself, because that was composed by Manu.
For this reason, it is designated as "Mānava" (the work of Manu);
otherwise, it would have been designated as "Hairaṇyagarbha" (the work of Hiraṇyagarbha).
Some, however, argue that even though the work was composed by Hiraṇyagarbha, its designation by the name of Manu is entirely appropriate because it was elucidated by him for many people.

Just as the Gaṅgā, although first discovered in the Himavat mountains, is designated as "Haimavatī" (born of the Himavat) despite having originated elsewhere; and just as the *Kaṭhaka* recension, due to constant study, is designated after Kaṭha—wherein, even though there are other students and teachers, the designation is made after Kaṭha because of his excellence in the exposition.
And Nārada remembers that this work consists of one hundred thousand verses composed by Prajāpati, and was subsequently abridged in succession by Manu and others;
therefore, even though it was composed by another, its designation as "Mānava" (belonging to Manu) is not contradictory.
Furthermore, the use of the word *śāstra* to denote a book is indeed observed, because it conveys the sense of being a teaching (*śāsana*).
"He caused me alone to grasp [it]," meaning "I was taught by him.
By these words—"himself," "from the beginning," and "according to rule"—the non-degeneration of the tradition (*āgama*) is expressed.
For when an author himself first teaches his own work, not even a single syllable (*mātrā*) is lost therein.
For when someone who has mastered a work from another person teaches it to yet another, there is no effort made to preserve that text;
even for the original author, having previously taught it, one might think, "I have already established this text," and thus a second-time lapse due to negligence, laziness, or the like is possible.
Therefore, it was said: "from the beginning."
The "rule" (vidhi) refers to the state of focused attention, characterized by qualities such as the teacher and disciple being single-minded;
the suffix -vati is used here in the sense of "deserving.
As for the sages Marīci and the others, I [shall speak of them].

Marīci and others are renowned for their power; by stating that even they studied this under him, he demonstrates his own status as a teacher through his connection with such distinguished disciples. Furthermore, by means of the greatness of the scripture of the great seers (maharṣis), he generates an excess of faith so that the study may not cease. Such is this great scripture that it was studied even by Marīci and the others.

If such a great soul as Manu is their teacher, it is fitting that the study of this treatise proceed from him; thus, the listeners do not cease until the completion of the scripture. In both ways, therefore, the treatise is praised.
This Bhṛgu will proclaim this scripture to you in its entirety;
for this sage has learned all of this from me in its fullness.

This scripture—this entire work—he, Bhṛgu, will cause you to hear in its entirety; he will lead it to your ears, teach it, and explain it. This is the concluding reflection upon this scripture: that the sage learned this very scripture in its fullness, without exception, from me, from my presence, having acquired and known it.

Since it is as if the knowledge issues forth from the mouth of the teacher and the disciple receives it, the suffix *tas* is appropriately used here in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*), as in the rule "from me" (*mattaḥ*).
Bhṛgu, however, possesses a more renowned power than even the great sages;
by his appointment as the expounder, it is demonstrated that this treatise has come down through a succession of arrivals from those who possess various, complete, and unsurpassed knowledges.
And for this reason, the following mode of engagement is also observed among some:
"This scripture has descended from many great souls; why should we not study it? Thus, an inclination toward engaging in study and other such activities is generated toward the scripture.
Then, having been addressed in that manner by Manu, the great seer Bhṛgu, with a joyful soul, spoke to all those sages: "Listen!"
That great seer Bhṛgu, having been thus addressed by Manu—"He shall cause you to hear [this]"—was then appointed; immediately thereafter, he said to those seers, "Listen!

With a pleased mind in the presence of his many disciples, he spoke out of great respect, thinking: "I have been appointed here"; through the honor shown to him as one fit to speak, Bhṛgu felt great self-respect, thinking, "I have been esteemed by him as an obedient servant."
Of this Svāyaṃbhuva Manu, there were six other high-souled and immensely powerful Manus belonging to his lineage, who each created their own respective progeny.
The preceptor, being questioned about the phenomena, described the origin of the world and so forth;
likewise, the disciple, having been appointed by him, began to describe the remainder of that very subject.
By the word "of this," he refers back to Manu through direct perception.
Six other Manus, known as the descendants of our preceptor who is called Svāyaṃbhuva, were born in a single lineage or family; thus they are all "vaṃśyas.

For they were all created directly by Brahmā, and because they originated from one family, they are called *vaṃśyas*. Alternatively, those appointed to a single task are *vaṃśyas*; for the designation "lineage" (*vaṃśa*) is applied to living beings through their connection to a single function.
There are two lineages of sages for grammar;
and it shows that they, having created their respective subjects, revealed that single Dharma.
In every Manvantara, whichever Manu holds authority is the creator and protector of beings destroyed in the preceding Manvantara.
Therefore, whatever offspring are created by someone, they belong to him as his own.
Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata,
the highly resplendent Cākṣuṣa, and the son of Vivasvat as well.
He points out those Manus by name; "of great splendor" (mahātejāḥ) is a qualifying epithet,
while the other names are either conventional or based on etymological derivation.
The form "vivasvatsuta" is a distinct word consisting of a compound, similar to words such as "kṛṣṇasarpa" (black snake) or "narasiṃha" (man-lion).
These seven Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva, possessed immense splendor;
each, within his own interval, produced and sustained all this world of moving and non-moving beings.
Here, seven Manus have been described by me;
elsewhere, they amount to fourteen.
This is at their respective intervals, meaning when their period of authority has arrived.
"Having produced offspring, they protected them.

"In their respective intervals" (*sve sve 'ntare*) means during the period of authority for each; that is, at whatever time the authority for creation, maintenance, and protection was attained by whichever Manu.
Others, however, consider the word *antara* to denote a specific period of time, like the words "month" and so forth.
That is incorrect;
for the period called a *manvantara* is a specific division of time associated with the word "Manu," and not [a period] in its absolute sense alone.
Eighteen nimeṣas make one kāṣṭhā, thirty of those make one kalā,
thirty kalās make one muhūrta, and a day and night consists of as many [muhūrtas].

In order to define the measurement of time for the periods of cosmic stability and dissolution, he begins to describe the divisions of time as they fall within the scope of the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*):
eighteen *nimeṣas* constitute a unit of time called a *kāṣṭhā*;
thirty *kāṣṭhās* constitute a *kalā*.
Thirty *kalās* constitute one *muhūrta*;
that is to say, thirty of those [units].
Thirty *muhūrtas* constitute a day and night (*ahorātra*).
Having extracted the verbal root *vid* (to know) as the action word, *tāvat* is the accusative plural.
Now, what is this so-called *nimeṣa*? It is the natural tremor of the eyelashes that accompanies the opening of the eyes (*unmeṣa*).
Others, however, have read it as follows: "A *nimeṣa* is the duration of time in which an unaltered syllable is pronounced."
The sun divides day and night for both humans and gods:
night is for the sleep of beings, and day is for the performance of actions.
Day and night constitute *ahorātra*.
The sun effects their division:
as long as the sun has risen and its rays are visible, there is the conventional usage of "day."
When [the sun] has set before its rising, the designation of "night" applies, whether in the world of humans or the world of the gods.
To the question, "How then is this division of day and night to be understood in places where the sun does not pervade with its rays? he says:
"Night is for sleep":
among beings who are self-luminous, there is a distinction between the commencement of activity and labor and sleep, because they are eternally illuminated.
Just as the time of manifestation for plants is fixed by their very nature, so too the activity of labor and sleep are fixed solely by the nature of time.
For the ancestors, a month constitutes a day and a night; its division is by the two fortnights.
The dark fortnight is their day for active duties, and the bright fortnight is their night for sleep.
That which is a month for humans is a day and night for the ancestors.
As for the distinction as to which is the day and which is the night, this is the division:
"this is the day" and "this is the night."
It is established within the two fortnights (pakṣa), which consist of fifteen nights each and are termed "half-months" (ardhamāsa); the meaning is that it is dependent upon the fortnights.
He states the distinction between them because one fortnight is day and the other is night, and because they possess different natures and a fixed sequence.
The dark fortnight is the day;
the bright fortnight is the night.
The reading "from activities and movements" (karmaceṣṭābhyaḥ) is appropriate, just as [in the case of] "for sleep" (svapnāya).
It is precisely the state of being for that purpose which is intended as the state of being the object; therefore, the locative case is used here due to the requirements of the meter.
For the gods, a year consists of day and night; their division is as follows:
the northern course (udagayana) is their day, and the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is their night.
Twelve months of human beings constitute one day and night for the gods.
Furthermore, there is a division of the year by means of the northern course (*udagayana*) and the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*).
Among these, for the sun as it proceeds toward the northern direction, there are six months of the northern course.
*Ayana* means going or abiding.
In that direction, the sun rises for six months;
when it has turned back from there, it is the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*).
For indeed, having moved toward the southern direction and abandoned the northern, it makes its rising.
Now learn, in brief and in their proper order, the measure of each individual Yuga within the day and night of Brahmā.

Brahmā is the creator of progeny; learn from me in brief, that is, concisely, the measure of his world—the duration of its nights and days (ahorātra) and of the Yugas. This verse is intended to state the summarized meaning of each individual Yuga which is about to be described, and serves to focus the attention of the listeners.
And thus they awaken;
listen! This renewed promise regarding the division of time already under discussion is for the purpose of indicating that this is a separate section.
Therefore, the matter about to be explained is not merely a supplement to the commencement of the treatise, but pertains to *dharma* as well.
And so he will say: "They know the day of Brahmā to be meritorious";
the meaning is that merit arises from the knowledge of that [day].
They say that four thousand years constitute the Kṛta Yuga;
its dawn (saṃdhyā) lasts for as many hundreds of years, and its twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is of the same duration.
Because they are the subject under discussion, the divine years are understood here;
and thus the author of the Purāṇa says:
"O twice-born ones, this has been sung by the sages according to the divine reckoning."
The number of yugas is proclaimed according to the divine measure alone.
Those four thousand [years] constitute the period known as the Kṛtayuga.
The twilight (saṃdhyā) of that Kṛtayuga is likewise four hundred years; the portion of the twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is of the same kind and the same measure, meaning it consists of four hundred years.
That which possesses the continuity of the nature of both past and future time is the *saṃdhyā*.

The *saṃdhyāṃśa* is the conformity to the characteristics of both times, wherein there is a slight persistence of the qualities of the preceding age and a greater prevalence of those of the age yet to come.
In the other three [ages], along with their junctions (saṃdhyā) and sub-junctions (saṃdhyāṃśa),
the thousands and hundreds decrease by one.

In the three ages other than the Kṛtayuga— namely the Tretā and the others— along with their respective junctions (saṃdhyā) and sub-junctions (saṃdhyāṃśa), there occurs a decline or diminution. In the Tretā age, there is a loss of one thousand [years] compared to the Kṛtayuga.

In this way, from the Tretā age comes the Dvāpara, and from the Dvāpara, the Kali; thus there are three thousand years for the Tretā, two for the Dvāpara, and one for the Kali. In each case, hundreds of years are diminished in both the *saṃdhyā* and its *saṃdhyāṃśa*.
A distinguished collection of days is called a *yuga*; its specific divisions are the *kṛta* age and so forth.
In the phrase "so many hundreds," the long vowel *ī* should be understood as a mnemonic device (*smṛti*).
Here, it serves as a memory aid.
The compound *samārāraḥ* consists of so many hundreds (*tāvatāṃ śatānām*).

Since the word *tāvat* ends in the suffix *-vat*, it receives the designation of "number" (*saṃkhyā*) by the rule *bahugaṇavatuḍati*. Once it has the designation of "number," the designation of *dvigu* applies by the rule *saṃkhyāpūrvo dviguḥ*. Consequently, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *dvigoḥ*, which is an exception to the suffix *ṭāp*.
[The meaning is: that of which a hundred is the measure (*parimāṇa*).
The suffix *vatup* is applied according to the rule *yattadetebhyaḥ*.
By the rule *ā sarvanāmnaḥ*, the final vowel is replaced by *ā*.
Otherwise, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as *tāvanti śatāni yasyāḥ*, since the word *śata* ends in *a*, the suffix *ṭāp* would have to be applied according to the rule *ajādyataṣṭāp*.
The intention is that when that [action] has been performed, there would then be "a hundred" [of such actions].
This cycle of four ages (caturyuga) which has been enumerated at the very beginning,
consisting of twelve thousand [years], is called an age of the gods (devayuga).

The phrase "this which" is a common worldly idiom used to refer back to a subject introduced by way of a collective whole— namely, this cycle of four ages (*caturyuga*) whose number has been determined as four thousand years and so forth prior to this verse. Twelve thousand of these four-age cycles are called a *yuga* of the gods.
The meaning is that twelve thousand cycles of four yugas is what is called a "divine yuga" (devayuga);
the suffix *aṇ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*) following the word *sahasra*.
The analysis of the compound is: "that in which the measure is twelve thousand cycles of four yugas."
A thousand divine yugas, by calculation, should be known as one day of Brahmā; his night is of the same duration.

One thousand divine yugas constitute one day of Brahmā; his night is of the same duration, namely one thousand divine yugas. The connection is that "one thousand" refers to the total number calculated by enumeration.
This restatement is for the purpose of completing the verse;
for there is no conventional usage of "thousand" and so forth without a number.
The instrumental case is used here in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).
Those people who know day and night understand that the holy day of Brahmā lasts for a thousand yugas, and his night is of exactly the same duration.
That whose end is a thousand yugas is "yugasahasrānta" (lasting for a thousand yugas).
Those humans who know this are "knowers of day and night.
In response to the question "What [happens] to them?", the connection is that "merit accrues to them."
The knowledge of the measure of a Brahma-day is meritorious; therefore, it should be known—through this praise, there is the comprehension of an injunction.
At the end of that night, he who has been asleep awakens;
having awakened, he creates the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent.
That Brahmā, having experienced sleep during that long night, awakens;
thereafter, he creates the world once again.
The sleep of Brahmā is of the nature previously described.
For he does not sleep like an ordinary person, owing to his constant state of awakening.
In this regard, he describes the sequence of creation with the words, "the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent.
But was it not previously stated that "he created water alone at the beginning"?
Some say that dissolution is of two kinds: the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) and the intermediate dissolution (*avāntarapralaya*).
This sequence applies to the intermediate dissolution;
furthermore, in this context, the mind (*manas*) is not included among the [twenty-four] principles (*tattva*), because it has already arisen previously.
What then? The meaning is that Prajāpati, having awakened, creates—that is, he directs—the mind for the purpose of creation.

In the second case, however, regarding the doctrine of the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), since the mind has the Great Principle (mahat-tattva) as its cause, the mind is indeed the Great Principle; consequently, there would be a loss of the previously stated sequence.
For it is said in the Purāṇa:
"Manas, mahat, mati, buddhi, and mahattva are proclaimed; these words are declared to be synonyms for the Great One (mahat). Thus it is said.
Impelled by the desire to create, the mind undergoes transformation and brings forth creation;
from that, space is born, and they know sound to be its quality.
Although this creation of reality has already been described,
it is stated once more in order to explain the specific details that were not mentioned:
"It undergoes transformation" means it acts with particularity, being impelled by Brahman.
From that which was impelled, space is born;
of that space, there is a quality called sound.
A quality is said to be dependent, and space is its substratum.
For sound cannot exist without space.
From ether, undergoing transformation, there arises the pure and powerful wind, the bearer of all fragrances; it is indeed considered to have the quality of touch.

The arising of one primary element from another primary element is not accepted, because it is admitted that all primary elements arise from the *mahat* (the Great One); therefore, it is explained as follows: immediately after space, from the *mahat* undergoing transformation and having attained the state of the mere quality of touch (*sparśamātra*), wind is born.
It carries all perfumes, both pure and impure;
yet it itself is pure, holy, and powerful.

Whatever modification exists in the form of activity—characterized by trembling, throwing, moving upward, downward, or sideways, and so forth—all that which is moved or vibrated is dependent upon the wind; it is in order to demonstrate this that [the wind] is described as "powerful.
Furthermore, the ablative case-endings used later on are not intended to express the sense of being produced from something.
Rather, they should be construed as follows: "immediately after the wind."
From fire also, as it undergoes transformation, there arises a radiant light that dispels darkness; this is said to possess the quality of form.
By the two words "virociṣṇu" (shining) and "bhāsvat" (luminous), which have the same meaning, its self-illumination and illumination of others are established:
it is itself radiant and it illuminates other things.
And from light, undergoing transformation, water is said to arise with the quality of taste;
from water, earth arises with the quality of smell—such is the creation from the beginning.
Taste, beginning with the sweet, is a quality of water; smell, both fragrant and foul, is a quality of earth.
Thus say the Vaiśeṣikas: "Smell exists only in earth."
These are the innate qualities of each [element], yet they become intermingled through association;
thus it has been said: "Whichever one is the *n*-th.
And this enumeration of the qualities is useful for the contemplation of the inner self (*adhyātmacintā*).
For it has been said by the author of the Purāṇa:
"In this world, those who contemplate the senses remain for ten manvantaras;
those who contemplate the elements remain for a full hundred, and those who contemplate the ego remain for a thousand."
Ten thousand great-souled ones who contemplate the ego remain free from fever; however,
one hundred thousand remain as those who contemplate the unmanifest.
Having attained the Person who is devoid of qualities, no further enumeration exists.
That divine yuga which was previously stated to consist of twelve thousand [years],
multiplied by seventy-one, is here called a manvantara.
Seventy-one divine yugas constitute the period of time known as a manvantara.
The Supreme Lord, as if in play, repeatedly brings about innumerable Manvantaras, as well as creation and dissolution.
"This number does not exist" means they are "innumerable.
But is it not the case that a specific number is heard in the *Jyotiḥśāstra* and other texts, namely that there are fourteen *manvantaras*?
It is said in reply: [the term refers to] the impossibility of counting them individually.
For they are indeed innumerable due to their recurrence,
just as there are twelve months; likewise,
the recurrence of both creation and dissolution is truly uninterrupted.
"He creates this as if playing.
Play arises from a desire for pleasure;
however, because He has all His desires fulfilled and because His nature consists solely of bliss, creation and withdrawal are not prompted by play.
For this very reason, the word "even" (api) is employed here.
The resolution to this has already been stated previously:
that even out of mere playfulness or curiosity, the activity of kings and others is observed in the world; such is the view of the knowers of Brahman.
In the Kṛta age, Dharma was complete with all four quarters, as was Truth;
no acquisition whatsoever occurred for humans through unrighteousness.

That which has four feet is "four-footed" (*catuṣpād*). Since sacrifice and the like constitute *dharma*, and since *dharma* has the nature of something to be performed, it lacks a physical body; therefore, the word "foot" (*pāda*) here does not denote a limb of a body. What then? It denotes merely a portion.
For *dharma* has no body, whether in human form or in the form of animals, birds, and so forth.
Thus, being endowed with its own four parts, it is called "four-footed.
Therefore, this Dharma was complete and four-footed during the Kṛtayuga.
Regarding the sacrifice, while it is in the state of practical application, there are four officiating priests: the Hotṛ, the Brahmā, the Udgātṛ, and the Adhvaryu.
The four castes or the four stages of life are the performers;
in every respect, whatever dharma is declared in the Veda was at that time practiced in its entirety, without even a partial deficiency and without any loss of quality.
The number four is mentioned for the sake of abundance.
In this same way, it should be applied to generosity and the other perfections as well: the giver, the object, the recipient, and the purity of intention.
Alternatively, they are sacrifice, generosity, austerity, and knowledge;
as he will state later: "Austerity is supreme."
Alternatively, *dharma* is the sentence that establishes the teaching; and its four feet are the four classes of words:
nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and particles (*nipāta*).
And so it is said:
"Four are the measured steps of speech; those Brahmins who are wise know them—those who are masters of their minds, capable, learned, and righteous."
But nowadays,
the three [fires] are hidden in the cave; they do not stir,
for they do not shine forth.
Humans speak the fourth speech.
Vedic people say that one-fourth [of the Veda] has been lost.
This means that originally no Vedic statement was interrupted, nor was there any division of Vedic branches (*śākhā*); but nowadays, much has been interrupted.
And "all this is indeed truth" is the syntactical connection (*anuṣaṅga*).
Even though truth, being ordained, constitutes *dharma*, it is taught separately for the sake of emphasizing its primacy, or else for the sake of indicating its causal nature.
Truth is the cause of the performance of all *dharma*.

But those who are untruthful perform certain actions for the sake of winning over the world while abandoning others; yet, due to the inherent nature of the age, no sacred scripture, knowledge, or wealth accrues to or comes to the practitioner by means of unrighteousness—that is, by a prohibited path. Men do not acquire knowledge through unrighteousness, nor do they earn wealth thereby.
Since knowledge and wealth are the causes for the practice of Dharma, their purification is stated here as the cause for the true existence of all dharmas.
In other [ages], dharma exists by means of tradition (āgama), but it is diminished quarter by quarter;
and through theft, falsehood, and deceit, dharma departs quarter by quarter.
In the ages other than the Kṛtayuga, Dharma declined quarter by quarter from that which was known as the Veda; in each successive age, it was diminished and removed by one quarter.
The branches of the Vedas disappeared because of the deficiency in men's power of comprehension and retention.
Even that Dharma currently practiced, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites, is likewise falling away quarter by quarter due to theft and other such corruptions.
Because the officiating priests, the sacrificers, the donors, and the recipients are possessed of these defects, dharma is not accomplished according to the rules;
consequently, the fruit as previously described is not obtained.
Therefore, the connection between theft and the other causes of the destruction of dharma with the respective ages is not intended to be numerical, since all of them are observed even today.
In the Kṛta age, people are free from disease, have all their goals accomplished, and possess a lifespan of four hundred years;
however, in the Tretā and subsequent ages, their lifespan decreases by one quarter in each.
Because of the absence of unrighteousness, which is the cause of disease, they are free from disease;
"disease" means illness.
Indeed, all four castes have achieved their intended goals.
*Artha* means purpose. Alternatively, it refers to those optional rites (*kāmya-karman*) for which all purposes are accomplished;
that is, because there is no obstruction, the complete attainment of the fruit occurs without impediment.
Regarding the phrase "with a lifespan of four hundred years":
one might object that it is heard in the *Āyurveda* that he lived for sixteen hundred years;

therefore, they say that the word "hundred years" here indicates a stage of life, meaning that they live through four stages of life, and do not die before their full span of life, nor do they die without having reached the fourth stage of life.
For this very reason, he says in the second half-verse that "age diminishes. Since the increase of age was stated previously, it is logical that its diminution is mentioned subsequently.
[The term] "by quarters" means:
And here there is no fourth part (*pāda*) [of the lifespan], but rather merely a portion (*bhāga*);
the meaning is that the lifespan is diminished by way of its parts.
