Thus, some children die, some youths, and some those who have reached old age.
A full lifespan is difficult to obtain.
The lifespan of mortals declared in the Vedas, as well as the blessings resulting from ritual actions, bear fruit in the world according to the age, as do the powers of embodied beings.

Some say that the lifespan prescribed in the Vedas, required for Vedic rites such as those lasting a thousand years and so forth, bears fruit according to the age (yuga); it is accomplished in accordance with the specific age, not in all ages.
Today, no one lives for a thousand years.
Whoever lives for the full duration lives for a hundred years;
others do not respect this [interpretation],

because in long-term sacrificial sessions (*dīrghasattra*), the word "year" is established as referring to days, and because otherwise there would be a contradiction with other injunctions, resulting in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
For this is the textual passage there: "Fifty-five threefold years," and so forth.
In that context, three days are already established because the Gavāmayana is the archetype;
however, since the specific number "fifty-five" is not otherwise established, it must be enjoined as a new prescription.
If another "year-ness" were understood [in addition to the previously mentioned], there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
In that case, one must necessarily resort to the interpretation of one [term] as a restatement (*anuvāda*).

The word "year" (*saṃvatsara*), whether referring to solar, civil, or other measures, is indeed seen to be used elsewhere as well for a collection of days consisting of three hundred and sixty [days] without distinction.
Therefore, it is appropriate that this very [period] is restated by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as "days.

Others, however, argue that in the *mantras* and *arthavādas*—such as "O gods, there are indeed a hundred autumns before us" and "Man has a lifespan of a hundred years"—the word "hundred" (*śata*) is listed among the names for "many," and "multiplicity" (*bahutva*) is not fixed;
for according to the [particular] age, people may be long-lived or short-lived.
However, according to the explanation based on what has been heard, in the Kali age all people have a lifespan of only one hundred years.
Alternatively, regarding those rites for one desiring long life, no specific measure is mentioned there; in such cases, the measure should be understood as varying according to the age (yuga).
[This applies to] blessings.
There are also other Vedic injunctions concerning results,
pertaining to optional rites (*kāmya-karma*).
Although longevity is itself a desired result, it is taught separately because of its preeminence.
For it has been said: "Life is indeed the supreme desire;
power is extraordinary capacity, the possession of qualities such as *aṇimā* and so forth, the power of cursing, and the granting of boons.
The phrase "they bear fruit according to the age" is to be applied in every instance.
The duties of men in the Kṛta age are of one kind, those in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages are different,
and those in the Kali age are yet another, in accordance with the decline of the ages.
This is the conclusion regarding the difference in the intrinsic nature of things due to the difference in time as previously stated.
The word *dharma* does not refer exclusively to sacrifices and the like; rather, it applies to the mere qualities of things.
Other qualities of things arise according to each age, as was shown earlier.
Just as the nature of things is one in spring, another in summer, and yet another in the rainy season, so it is also with respect to the ages (*yuga*).

And this "otherness" here does not mean that causes produce a different effect by abandoning the effect they were previously seen to produce; rather, it is due to the diminution of their power because the effect arises in an incomplete form.
Thus he says: "in accordance with the decrease of the ages."
Diminution means deficiency.
Austerity is said to be supreme in the Kṛta age, knowledge in the Tretā;
they say sacrifice alone is the path in the Dvāpara, and charity alone in the Kali age.
This other distinction regarding the nature of the ages (yuga) is now stated.
Since there is no injunction in the Veda for austerity and the other duties according to the specific divisions of the ages, all of them must be performed at all times.
This [present] restatement, however, must be explained in some way or another as a mere descriptive reference (anuvāda).
For it is described thus in the Itihāsas:
austerity is paramount, and it yields great fruit;
those who are long-lived and free from disease are capable of practicing austerity.
With this intention it is said:
knowledge has the internal as its object;
therefore, self-restraint within due to bodily affliction is not excessively difficult.
In the Dvāpara age, however, sacrifice is predominant because it does not involve great hardship;
as for charity, it does not require physical exertion, nor internal restraint, nor is it excessively dependent upon great learning, and thus it is easily accomplished.
But for the sake of protecting this entire creation, that one of great splendor assigned distinct duties to those born from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet.
The division of time has been explained;
now the qualities of the Brāhmaṇas and others are being described. This is the introduction to that section.

For the sake of the protection and preservation of the entire creation and all the worlds, the immensely radiant Prajāpati ordained and established the duties—concerned with both visible and invisible goals—for the four social orders (varṇas), beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, who were born from his mouth and other parts.
Now those actions are being described.
He ordained for the Brāhmaṇas teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, and receiving gifts.
The protection of subjects, giving, sacrifice, study,
and non-attachment to sense objects— this, in brief, is the duty of a Kṣatriya.
Objects are said to be things such as the sounds of songs that give rise to longing; non-attachment therein means not indulging in them again and again.
The protection of cattle, giving gifts, performing sacrifices,
studying, trade, money-lending, and agriculture are the duties of the Vaiśya.
Trade (*vanikpatha*) is the acquisition of wealth through commercial activity via land routes, water routes, and so forth;
it consists of procuring goods from other regions for use [by the king], in whose kingdom one resides.
Lending at interest (*kusīda*) is the investment of wealth for the sake of profit.
But the Lord ordained only one duty for the Śūdra:
to serve these very castes without malice.
The Lord Prajāpati ordained a single duty for the Śūdra:
"You must perform service toward these— Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas—
with freedom from envy and without reproach."
One should not harbor even the slightest dejection toward him in one's mind.
Service consists of attending upon him, performing tasks conducive to his needs, massaging his body, and so forth; this involves following his will.
For a Śūdra, this is for the sake of visible worldly benefit.
And because it is not prescriptive, the phrase "only one" does not prohibit giving and the other [virtues].
The injunction for these actions will occur later;
therefore, we shall demonstrate there itself the specific nature of the sacrifices and so forth through their distinctions.
The human being is proclaimed to be more pure above the navel;
therefore, his mouth has been declared by the Self-Existent One to be the most pure of all.
A person is pure down to the ends of the feet;
from the navel upward he is exceedingly pure;
and even more so is the mouth.
And this was spoken by the Puruṣa himself, the cause of the world.
What follows from that?
To this he says:
"Because of being born from the head, because of seniority, and because of upholding the Veda."
According to dharma, the Brahmin is the lord of this entire creation.
The "highest limb" is the head;
from that comes the origin or birth of the Brāhmaṇa. He is also the eldest, having been created by Brahmā before the other castes.
Because of his upholding of the *brahman*, that is, the Veda—
for it is specifically ordained for him—
therefore, due to these three reasons, the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of the entire world, as it were.
A master is to be approached with humility, and one must abide by his command within the bounds of dharma.
"Dharmataḥ prabhuḥ" means that the master is authoritative regarding dharma; the suffix *tasi* is used here because [the word *dharma*] belongs to the group beginning with *ādi*.

For the Self-Existent One, having performed austerities, first created him from his own mouth for the purpose of conveying the offerings to the gods and ancestors, and for the protection of this entire world.
This is for the sake of specifying the three aforementioned reasons;
for even in the case of another person, the head is the principal part.
Furthermore, the Self-Existent One created that Brāhmaṇa from his own mouth.
And having performed austerity, this [being] arose from his head.
He states the primacy [of the eldest] first:
that which is performed with reference to the gods is *havya*; that which is performed with reference to the ancestors is *kavya*.

For the purpose of "carrying them," that is, for the purpose of conveying them toward the gods and the ancestors— the gerundive suffix (*kṛtya*) in *abhivāhyāya* must somehow be understood as expressing the abstract action (*bhāve*), because the root *vah-* is transitive. And by means of that action, the protection— that is, the preservation— of the entire three worlds is accomplished.
The gods subsist on what is given from here [the earth];
they, in turn, ripen and cause the plants to ripen by means of cold, heat, and rain.
Thus, there is protection through mutual assistance.
What being is greater than he, whose mouth the dwellers of heaven always consume the sacrificial offerings to the gods (havya), and the ancestors consume the offerings to the manes (kavya)?
This demonstrates the previously mentioned carrying of the oblations and so forth.
Those whose abode or home is the third heaven (tridiva) are thus called; they are the gods dwelling in heaven.
The gods attend upon the food eaten by a Brahmin.
In the *śrāddha*, the feeding of Brahmins intended for the Viśvedevas is prescribed as a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the ancestral rite (*pitrya*);
it is with reference to that [standard] that this is stated.
What is "other," "additional," or "superior" (*śreṣṭha*) than that? This [question] is forgotten by the author himself.
The gods and the ancestors occupy the highest and middle stations and are not perceptible; they have no other means of sustenance except for the feeding of Brahmins. Therefore, the Brahmin is great.
Among beings, those endowed with breath are the best; among those endowed with breath, those who live by intelligence are the best;
among the intelligent, men are the best; and among men, the Brāhmaṇas are traditionally held to be the best.
Those entities on earth—whether stationary, such as trees and the like, or moving, such as worms, insects, and so forth—are designated by the term "beings" (*bhūta*).
Among them, those living creatures capable of activities such as eating and moving about are superior;
for they experience pleasure more acutely.

Among them, those who live by their intelligence—such as dogs, jackals, and others—are able to distinguish between what is beneficial and what is harmful; for when tormented by heat they seek shade, when afflicted by cold they seek sunlight, and they abandon a place that lacks food.
Among these, humans are superior, and among humans, the Brahmins are superior;
for they are the most worthy of honor in the world and are not treated with contempt by anyone.
For upon the killing of such a person, there is a great penance based solely on his caste.

Among Brahmins, those who are learned; among the learned, those whose intellects are refined; among those of refined intellect, those who perform their duties; and among those who perform their duties, those who know Brahman.
The preeminence of the learned arises from their eligibility for sacrifices and other rites that yield great fruits; among them,
those who have perfected their understanding—
having fully mastered the true meaning of the Vedas— are not defiled by the Buddhists and others.
They too are the performers and practitioners of those actions;
for they are not harmed by performing what is enjoined and by avoiding what is prohibited.
Even they [are surpassed] by those who know Brahman, because of their identity with the nature of Brahman.
For in that regard, Ānanda is indeed inexhaustible.
When the specific qualities of a Brāhmaṇa—such as learning and the like—have been shown, someone might despise a Brāhmaṇa who possesses only his caste;
to prevent this, it is said:
"The very birth of a Vipra is the eternal embodiment of Dharma."
For he, having arisen for the sake of the Dharma, is fit for becoming Brahman.
Birth itself—indeed, the very origin—is the caste of the Brāhmaṇa, the eternal embodiment and form of Dharma.
He is born for the sake of Dharma and is consecrated by the second birth, the initiation (*upanayana*).
For that birth for the sake of Dharma leads him toward, and results in, the state of Brahmanhood.
Having cast off the body of *dharma*, one becomes a partaker of supreme bliss; such is the praise.
For when a Brāhmaṇa is born upon this earth,
he is born as a lord over all beings for the protection of the treasury of Dharma.
"He exists above the entire world" expresses his preeminence by way of being superior;
"he is the lord of all beings" expresses his sovereignty.
For the protection of that which is called the "Dharma-treasury," there arises the accumulation of material goods, which is the [material] treasury;
by way of analogy, the accumulation of Dharma is called a "treasury."
Everything that exists within this world belongs to the Brāhmaṇa;
by virtue of his preeminence and noble birth, the Brāhmaṇa indeed deserves all this.
Fearing that one who is not content might commit a transgression by engaging again in receiving gifts and the like, he provides this resolution:
"All this wealth existing within the three worlds belongs to the Brāhmaṇa as his own;
herein no 'receiving' exists."
He takes it by virtue of his lordship, not by virtue of being a recipient;
this is a statement of praise, not an injunction. For this very reason, the word *arhati* (he is worthy) is used.
Noble lineage is the excellence of being well-born.
A Brahmin eats only his own, wears his own, and gives away his own;
it is through the Brahmin’s compassion that other people enjoy their sustenance.
That which he eats in another’s house in the form of hospitality and so forth is indeed his own; one should not think, "This is another's cooking.
He clothes himself.
Whether he obtains a garment by asking or without asking, it is not for the sake of acquisition, but rather for the purpose of clothing himself.
Let alone what he takes for his own use—therein he has ample authority—even that which he gives to others, though belonging to another, is not improper for him.
*Ānṛśaṃsya* means compassion.
By virtue of his great being, kings upon the earth utilize their own wealth;
otherwise, if he were to think, "I shall take this and employ it for my own purposes," then everyone would become destitute and useless.
For the sake of discerning his [the king's] duties, as well as those of the remaining [classes], the wise Svāyambhuva Manu composed this treatise in due order.

This verse is intended to demonstrate the fruit of the entire praise of the Brāhmaṇa. This treatise, which possesses such great purpose, was composed for the sake of the discernment of duties—that is, for the purpose of discerning which actions are to be performed and which are to be avoided—by that Brāhmaṇa who is most exalted by his own ultimate majesty. Furthermore, it was fashioned—that is, created—for the remaining classes, beginning with the Kṣatriyas, in due order; primarily for the Brāhmaṇa, but by extension also for the Kṣatriyas and others.
This should be studied with diligence by a learned Brahmin and correctly expounded to his disciples; it must not be taught by anyone else.
"It should be studied" and "it should be expounded"—these *kṛtya* suffixes denote fitness (*arha*) and not an injunction (*vidhi*).
From the second chapter onwards, the treatise will proceed;
for this first chapter is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
There is no prohibition here whatsoever.

Therefore, just as in the expression "rice for the king's meal," this is a praise of the rice and not a prohibition against others eating it, so too here, the phrase "not by anyone else" is not a prohibition; rather, it is solely a praise of the scripture.

The Brāhmaṇa is the most excellent in the entire world, and this is the scripture among all scriptures; therefore, it is fit to be studied and expounded by such a learned Brāhmaṇa, and it cannot be studied or expounded by anyone in general.
For this very reason, he says "with effort" (*prayatnataḥ*).

As long as great effort has not been exerted, and as long as the self has not been refined by other treatises such as logic (*tarka*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), and hermeneutics (*mīmāṃsā*), it is impossible to expound this [work].
Therefore, by the term "study" (*adhyayana*), "listening" (*śravaṇa*) is indicated.
For in that context, learning is useful for the sake of proficiency, not for mere recitation.

Indeed, if there were an injunction regarding study, proficiency would result only through the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) [of the act]; nor is it reasonable to say that in an injunction, hearing is indicated by means of study.
It is not proper to maintain that an element of an injunction has the purpose of being merely indicative (*lakṣaṇārthatā*).
In the case of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), however, it is not a fault if it is a figurative statement (*guṇavāda*) that conforms to other means of valid cognition.
Therefore, this scripture has the three social classes (*traivarṇika*) as its qualified audience;
and this will be explained specifically later on.
A Brahmin who studies this treatise and whose vows are well-praised is never tainted by the defects of action born of mind, speech, or body.
Having thus praised the scripture by way of its connection to the purpose of the Brahmin, he now praises it directly:
one who knows this scripture becomes "one whose vows are praised," meaning he becomes a performer of the complete observance of restraints (*yama*) and disciplines (*niyama*).

Having learned from the scripture that there is transgression (*pratyavāya*) in failing to perform them, and out of fear of that, he performs all the restraints and disciplines according to the scripture; he performs everything exactly as prescribed.
By practicing [this], one is not smeared by, nor bound to, the defects produced by the transgression of prescribed duties and the performance of prohibited actions.
He purifies his lineage and seven ancestors and seven descendants;
indeed, even he alone is worthy of this entire earth.
He becomes a purifier of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*). A "row" (*paṅkti*) is said to be a gathering arranged in a distinguished sequence; he purifies that, making it stainless.
All the wicked become non-wicked through his presence.

They are worthy of receiving the earth as far as the ocean's edge, including seven ancestors— those born of their own lineage such as fathers and so forth— and seven descendants yet to be born in the future.
For the knowledge of phenomena is the cause for the authority to receive [gifts];
moreover, by this means all phenomena are known.
This is the most excellent means of securing well-being; this increases the intellect;
this constantly brings renown; and this is the supreme state of ultimate bliss.
*Svasti* is the non-perishing of a desired object;
*ayana* is the act of reaching or attaining.
That by which *svasti* is attained is *svastyayana*.

It is superior to other [acts] such as recitation (japa) and burnt offerings (homa), for their performance is not possible without a scripture; therefore, because it is the cause for the performance of those [other acts], this [scripture] is superior.
Alternatively, it is the very sentences that convey the knowledge of dharma which are more excellent, whereas actual performance is laborious; hence it is called "superior."
This increases the intellect;
for when a treatise is studied, the growth of the intellect is well-established through the illumination of its meaning and the unraveling of its knots.
This brings renown; one who knows the Dharma gains fame when questioned by those in doubt.
That which is for the sake of fame is "famous" (*yaśasya*).
Fame (*yaśas*) is renown due to possessing qualities such as learning and magnanimity.

The "highest good" (*niḥśreyasa*) is so called because it is the cause of the attainment of that joy characterized by heaven and liberation—which is not intermingled with suffering—and because it is the cause of the knowledge and action that lead to its attainment; thus it is the supreme excellence.
In this Dharma, the merits and faults of actions have been declared in their entirety,
as well as the eternal conduct for all four social classes.
Now, he states the independence of his own treatise regarding its subject matter through its complete treatment thereof:

"Whatever dharma there may be, all of it has been stated in this treatise in its entirety. This is a hyperbolic praise (atiśayokti) meaning that one need not rely on other treatises for the knowledge of dharma.
In this treatise, Dharma has been stated in its entirety— that is, without remainder—
and also the merits and defects of actions.
The "merits and defects" of actions refer to the desirable and undesirable fruits of rites such as sacrifices and [prohibited acts] such as the killing of a Brahmin.

For completeness is thus achieved when there is the essential nature of the action (*karmasvarūpa*), the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), the specific result (*phalaviśeṣa*), the connection with a specific agent (*kartṛviśeṣasaṃbandha*), and the distinction between obligatory and optional rites (*nityakāmyatāviveka*).
All of this was promised by the term "virtue and defect" (*guṇadoṣa*).
When "dharma" is stated, the inclusion of the word "action" (*karman*) is for the purpose of completing the meter.
"For all four castes" is also for the sake of completeness;
it means that whoever is authorized in the Dharma, everyone such as these attains the Dharma from this [source].
And conduct is indeed eternal.
Dharma, which has conduct as its authority, is called "conduct. We shall examine this further in the second [chapter].
It is eternal, handed down through an ancient lineage, and was not initiated by those of the present day.
Conduct is the supreme dharma, as declared in the Śruti and in the Smṛti;
therefore, a self-possessed twice-born man should always be constantly engaged in this.

The supreme and most excellent dharma is that conduct which has been declared in the Śruti, the Veda, as well as that which is declared in the Smṛtis. Therefore, one who possesses self-control and desires his own welfare should be constantly devoted to this dharma of conduct; he should perform it perpetually.
Since the Self exists in everything, it is stated that the suffix -matup is used because it follows a secondary derivative (taddhita).
A Brahmin who has fallen away from right conduct does not enjoy the fruit of the Vedas;
however, one who is endowed with right conduct shall partake of the full fruit.
This is another way of praising right conduct (*ācāra*). One who has fallen away from right conduct, being devoid of right conduct, does not obtain the fruit of the Vedas.
It has been stated that the "fruit of the Vedas" refers to the fruit resulting from the performance of rites prescribed by the Vedas.

This is a censure stating that if one performs Vedic rites in their entirety and without deficiency, yet falls away from proper conduct (*ācāra*), one does not obtain the fruit—such as the desire for a son—from them.
This same point is stated by way of its opposite: "But one who is endowed with proper conduct obtains the full fruit of optional rites.

Regarding this, some say that because of the word "complete," even one devoid of proper conduct has a connection to the fruit of optional rites, though not the attainment of the entire fruit; but that is of no consequence, because this is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
Thus, having seen through conduct the course of Dharma, the sages took up conduct as the supreme root of all austerity.

Whatever austerity there may be—whether breath control, silence, restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), the *kṛcchra* penance, the *cāndrāyaṇa*, fasting, and so forth—the root for the production of the fruit of all that is right conduct (*ācāra*). Therefore, sages seeking the fruit of austerity accepted that very conduct as the root, that is, as the cause. For the sages have seen, through conduct, the course—that is, the attainment—of Dharma;
for even austerity, though it causes great hardship, does not bear fruit for one devoid of conduct, according to the Vedic revelation.
And [he taught] the origin of the world, the very procedure for the formative rites (saṃskāra),
the practice and observance of vows, and the supreme rule for ritual bathing.
The dharmas have been stated here;
furthermore, for the sake of engaging the listener, the infinite fruitfulness of the dharma has been declared by the words "ending with this" and so forth.

In that regard, thinking "this [ocean] is beyond the senses, infinite, and difficult to cross," they might become despondent; therefore, to generate enthusiasm, he recites the table of contents (*anukramaṇī*), which consists of a summary of the meaning of the treatise.
"There are only this many subjects here, not too many, which can be understood by persons endowed with faith.
Thus, when the path taught in brief is undertaken, it does not become difficult to endure.

Furthermore, "the origin of the world" includes everything such as the measurement of time, the distinctions between the nature of reality, and the praise of the Brāhmaṇas, all of which are contained within the origin of the world.
And this has been stated as a commendatory exposition (arthavāda), not as an object of valid cognition;
it refers to the ritual procedures (saṃskāra-vidhi) and the practice of observances (vrata-caryopacāra).
The *saṃskāras* are those beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*).
Their *vidhi* is the duty to be performed;
for the student (*brahmacārin*), it is the practice (*upacāra*), the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), or the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) regarding the observance of vows.
This is the subject matter to be known in the second chapter.
The ritual bath is a specific sacrament for one returning from the teacher's house.
The acquisition of a wife, the characteristics of marriages, the procedure for the great sacrifices, and the eternal ritual for ancestral offerings (śrāddha).

The "attainment of wives" refers to the taking of a spouse; the "characteristics" of the various forms of marriage, such as the *brāhma* and others, as well as the means for obtaining them, serve as the cause for understanding their essential nature. The "great sacrifices" (*mahāyajña*) are the five, beginning with the *vaiśvadeva*.
The *kalpa*—the rule, the procedure, and the manner of performance—of the *śrāddha*, which is the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*), is [herein set forth].
The inclusion of the word "other" (*para*) and the inclusion of the word "eternal" (*śāśvata*) are for the purpose of completing the meter.
This is the subject matter of the third chapter.
The characteristics of the modes of livelihood, the vows of a Snātaka,
what may and may not be eaten, purity, and the purification of objects.
The application of the duties of women, asceticism, liberation, and renunciation itself;
the entire duty of kings, and the adjudication of legal cases.
The rules for questioning witnesses, the law concerning men and women,
the law of partition, gambling, and the removal of thorns [criminals].
The conduct of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, the origin of the mixed castes, the duties of the social orders in times of distress, and likewise the rules for expiation;
The definition of the modes of livelihood (*vṛtti*)—the means of subsistence consisting of the acquisition of wealth, such as service and so forth;
the observances (*vrata*) of a *snātaka* who has completed his Vedic studies and returned from the teacher’s house, such as "one should not look at the rising sun" and so forth;
this is the meaning of the fourth [section].
Regarding what may and may not be eaten: five types of five-nailed animals are edible; inedible items include onions and the like.
Purity consists of that produced by time, such as at birth and so forth, as well as the purification of objects with water and other means.
The application of women's duties refers to their connection [to stages of life], such as being a girl, a young woman, and so on.
This is the section on the fifth case.
*Tāpasya* means "beneficial for an ascetic" (*tāpasa*).
An ascetic (*tāpasa*) is one whose primary practice is austerity (*tapas*), namely a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*); his duty is *tāpasya*.
Liberation is the dharma of the wandering mendicant,
and renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is indeed a specific form of it;
and that will be demonstrated in that very [section].
The sixth chapter, however, concerns this:
the entirety of the dharma—both that which has visible results and that which has invisible results—of a king who is authorized to protect the earth and has attained sovereignty;
this is the subject matter of the seventh chapter.

The "decision regarding legal matters" such as debts and the like refers to the determination reached after deliberation by cutting through doubt; it is the ascertainment of what is to be performed. As for the "rule regarding the examination of witnesses," it is mentioned separately because of its preeminence.
This is the eighth topic:
the law concerning husband and wife, namely their mutual conduct when staying together in one place or when separated by travel;
and the law concerning the division of inheritance.

Gambling: the rule concerning that subject is expressed by the word "gambling. The clearing away of thorns and the like—namely, thieves, forest-dwellers, and so forth—is the means for expelling them from the kingdom.
Although partition and so forth need not be mentioned separately— since they are included among the eighteen titles and are thus already subsumed under the phrase "and [other] effects"—
they are nevertheless mentioned separately due to the division of the chapters.
The "conduct" (*upacāra*) of Vaiśyas and Śūdras refers to the performance of their own respective duties (*svadharma*).
In this ninth [chapter],
he will describe the origin— that is, the birth— of those of mixed castes such as the Kṣattṛ, Vaidehaka, and others,
as well as the law for times of distress (āpad-dharma), which is the duty pertaining to those who, while unable to subsist by their own occupations, face the loss of life.
This [is explained] in the tenth [chapter];
the rules for expiation are in the eleventh.
The journey through saṃsāra itself, which arises from the threefold karma;
the supreme good resulting from actions; and the examination of the merits and defects of those actions.
Transmigration through cyclic existence:
the possessor of attributes (dharmin) is characterized by its attributes (dharma).
The transmigrating person is the self (ātman); its "going" is the attainment of another body after leaving the present one.
Alternatively, the worlds such as the earth and so forth, which are the objects of saṃsāra, are what is meant here;
going there is as described previously.
It is threefold—superior, inferior, and middling—and arises from karma, having virtuous and non-virtuous actions as its cause.

Not only have the destinies caused by action been described as leading to the supreme good (niḥśreyasa), but also that inner knowledge which is the means to it— since there is no other excellence beyond it—
and an examination of the merits and defects of actions, both those prescribed and those prohibited.
In this treatise, Manu has declared the eternal laws of regions, the laws of castes, the laws of families, and the laws of heretical sects and groups.
This very point confirms the statement regarding completeness:
those ten duties (*daśadharma*) are to be practiced in a specific region, not throughout the entire earth;
the duties of caste (*jātidharma*) are based on castes such as the Brāhmaṇa and so forth.
"Family traditions" refers to those practices initiated by renowned lineages.
"Heretics" refers to those who follow prohibited vows and conduct based on external traditions; the "dharmas" therein belong to these heretics who abide in improper actions.
A *gaṇa* is a corporation consisting of merchants, artisans, actors, and so forth;
the Blessed One, Manu, has declared all those categories of persons in this treatise.
Just as Manu formerly spoke this scripture when questioned by me,
so too do you now learn it from me.
Awakening is for the purpose of focused attention.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Mānava Dharmaśāstra*, in the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu;
thus [ends] the commentary on Manu composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi.
The First Chapter.
Now begins the Second Chapter:
That which is practiced by the wise, by the virtuous, and constantly by those free from aversion and attachment.
Learn that Dharma which has been approved by my heart.
The first chapter, which was intended to reveal the true nature of the subject matter to be expounded in this treatise, has been concluded;
and the description of the creation of the world and so forth has been explained as merely supplementary to that. Now, the treatise itself begins.

In this regard, because the subject matter promised [at the outset] has been interrupted by the description of the creation of the world and so forth, it has been forgotten; therefore, for the sake of reconnecting with it, he informs the disciples once again:
"That dharma which you have desired to hear, listen now as it is being spoken by me; having become attentive, hear it.
In the first chapter, five or six verses were intended to establish the purpose and other preliminary matters.
The supplementary portion consists of explanatory praise (*arthavāda*);
if that is not correctly understood, there is no great harm in the thorough knowledge of *dharma*.
But here, *dharma* itself is directly taught.
Therefore, the purpose of restating it is that this meaning must be ascertained by those who possess attentiveness.
The word *dharma* has the sense already explained, referring to the performance of the *aṣṭakā* and other such rites;
however, proponents of external systems consider even the wearing of ashes, skull-bones, and so forth to be *dharma*.

To exclude that [misunderstanding], the qualifying words beginning with "by the learned" (*vidvadbhiḥ*) are used. The "learned" are those whose intellects have been refined by the scriptures and who are skilled in the knowledge of the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of cognition (*prameya*).
Furthermore, these "learned" are those who know the meaning of the Vedas, and no others.

Those who have accepted the authority regarding *dharma* from sources other than the Veda are indeed ignorant, because they grasp the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its objects (*prameya*) in a distorted manner.
This is determined in its true nature through Mīmāṃsā.

"The virtuous" (*santaḥ*) are the righteous; they are those who, having ascertained the meaning through the means of valid cognition, exert themselves for the sake of attaining what is beneficial and avoiding what is harmful.
The beneficial and the harmful are established through direct perception;
the unseen is characterized by injunctions and prohibitions. Those who stand outside the practice of these are called non-existent.
Therefore, both knowledge and practice are included here.
The word *sat* cannot be used in the sense of "existence," because that would be purposeless;
for whatever is practiced by someone must necessarily be something already existing.
"Service" refers to the habit of performing religious observances.
By using the word "bhūta" (past), he indicates that this has been practiced since beginningless time;
this dharma of the Aṣṭakā and so forth was not instituted by anyone in the present age, unlike other dharmas.
He demonstrates this very point by means of the word "eternal" (*nitya*):
this Dharma exists as long as saṃsāra lasts;
whereas all external dharmas, being promulgated by foolish and immoral persons, disappear again even after having found an opportunity for some time.
For delusion does not persist for a thousand eons;
even though right knowledge is obscured by ignorance, it attains purity upon the destruction of that [ignorance].
Indeed, its purity cannot be destroyed.
By those who are free from hatred and passion.
This is the second cause for the practice of external dharmas.
Delusion has been explained previously.
By this, greed and the other [afflictions] are meant, since the mention of passion (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*) is intended as an illustration.
Through greed, they engage in mantras, tantras, and so forth;
or else, greed is included within passion and hatred.
Those who are attached to the means of enjoyment for themselves, being incapable of living by any other means, subsist by wearing sectarian marks (*liṅga*) and so forth.
As it has been said: "The wearing of ashes, carrying a skull-bowl, nakedness, and two saffron-colored garments are the livelihood of those devoid of intelligence and manliness.
Hatred is the cause of performing contrary practices.
For those dominated by hatred are not at all capable of ascertaining reality; therefore, they determine what is indeed non-dharma to be dharma.
Alternatively, both attachment and hatred are obstacles to the ascertainment of reality.

Even when there is some mere knowledge of the scriptures and one has attained the designation of "learned," the performance of contrary actions is possible due to the presence of attachment and hatred.
Even though they know the scriptures correctly, some people practice unrighteousness such as giving false testimony for the purpose of harming someone they dislike or benefiting someone they love.
It is impossible to determine with certainty that their performance is rooted in the Veda, because other causes—namely passion and hatred—are possible. Therefore, such conduct must be prohibited.
Here an objection is raised:

the word "by the good" (*sadbhiḥ*) has been described as signifying goodness (*sādhutā*). But what kind of goodness does he possess, if it is possible that he might engage in unrighteousness (*adharma*) due to passion and hatred?
Therefore, it should not be said that they are "free from hatred and passion. Rather, it is stated as a reason:
because they are devoid of passion and the like, they are therefore "saintly" (sat).
And here it is demonstrated that there is an absence of the predominance of passion and hatred.
It is not the case that the cause is utterly and completely annihilated without remainder for one who has reached the state capable of its absence;
for thus says the Śruti: "Indeed, for one who possesses a body, there is no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant."
Attachment (*rāga*) is greed for the enjoyment of sense objects.
Aversion (*dveṣa*) is the activity directed toward the prevention of that [enjoyment].
Greed (*lobha*) is stinginess (*mātsarya*), a desire characterized by non-sharing, such that one thinks, "May this person not possess wealth, fame, and so forth."
These are mental phenomena (*cittadharma*).
Alternatively, attachment (*rāga*) is affection for sentient things such as wife, son, friends, and kinsmen; greed (*lobha*) is longing even for insentient things such as wealth.
[This is] by way of the heart (*hṛdayena*).
By the word "heart" (hṛdaya), he refers to the mind (citta);
and the "acquiescence" of the heart is its clarity.
For this is the established state.
The principles such as the intellect (buddhi) and so forth reside within the heart.
Even though the deluded engage in external acts of violence, the eating of forbidden food, and the like under the impression that these are dharma, nevertheless, their hearts experience anguish;
whereas in the performance of Vedic rites, the mind finds complete satisfaction.
Therefore, this is the meaning of all this:
I do not teach such a doctrine in which these faults exist;
rather, it is that which is practiced by such great beings, or wherein their own minds proceed.
Therefore, great reverence is appropriate toward the teachings that are being proclaimed.
Alternatively, "heart" (*hṛdaya*) refers to the Veda; for when it has been studied, it abides in the heart by way of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and thus it is the "heart."
And thus, a triad is included here.
Even if some activity were to occur for someone simply out of their own grasping without prior investigation, it would still be appropriate only in this case;
this is what is expressed by the phrase "this is permitted by the heart."
Furthermore, as for the principle that "the path is that which the great multitude has taken," that too applies here;
for in this matter, the learned are free from desire, have acted in the past, and are beyond reproach in the world.
And if it were argued that such activity lacks authoritative basis, even that is established by the authority of the Veda itself.
By this, an inclination toward engagement in every respect is produced.
Others, however, explain this verse as referring generally to the definition of dharma:
"That which is practiced by such persons is to be understood as dharma."
This definition applies to everything—whether ordained by the Vedas, prescribed by the Smṛtis, or obtained through traditional conduct.
However, in this context, the reading "understand that Dharma which is practiced by these [persons]" is appropriate.
To have desire as one's sole motive is not praised, yet here there is no such thing as being entirely free from desire;
for the study of the Vedas and the performance of Vedic ritual action are themselves objects of desire.
One whose motive for engaging in action is the desire for results is "kātmā"; the state of being such is *kāmātmatā*.
By the word *ātman*, it is expressed that this [desire] is predominant;
it is not praiseworthy, but rather censurable.
And thus, from this censure, when an inference of prohibition is made, it is understood that [these acts] should not be performed.
By implication, this is a prohibition of all optional rites such as the Saurya and others.
Or rather, why should we specify "of the Saurya and others"? [The prohibition applies to all.]
Every performance of action is for the sake of achieving a result, not for the sake of the mere completion of its own form;
nor is there any action whatsoever that is fruitless.

As for the injunction "one should not engage in vain exertion," this refers to [offerings] poured into ashes or the pursuit of news regarding other regions and kings; even in those cases, there exists a result of the action.
However, because the primary fruit for a person—such as heaven or a village—which serves both seen and unseen purposes, is absent, it is called a "vain effort. Now, it might be argued:
"Let the action itself possess a fruit."
One should not form a desire for that object; the result will come about through the very nature of things.
In this regard as well, rites such as the Saura sacrifice are fruitless;
it is understood that the result is that which is desired.
"It will not come to be for one who does not desire it. Furthermore, no worldly activity is observed to be independent of an intention toward a result;
nor is there any such distinction stated in the Vedic revelation that, in the case of Vedic rituals, a result should not be intended.
In that regard, since desire for those Vedic studies that yield specific fruits is prohibited, there would be a contradiction with the Veda if one were not to engage in them;

however, as for the obligatory rites (*nitya*), there is no such engagement [forbidden] in the first place. Furthermore, because no specific distinction is made, if one were to cease from worldly activities, there would be a contradiction with perceived reality (*dṛṣṭavirodha*).
Thus, this consequence arises: nothing at all should be performed by anyone; rather, everyone should remain silent.
To this it is replied:
as for what was said regarding the undesirable consequence of a prohibition applying to optional rites such as the Saurya sacrifice and others, that will be addressed later.
"He enjoys here all desires exactly as they were intended.
For if there were a prohibition [of action], how could there be intention, and how could there be the attainment of desires?

As for the objection that [the injunction] would apply even to worldly matters because no specific [subject] is mentioned, the specific [subject] is indeed already implied there, since "dharma" is the topic under discussion in the phrase, "Learn that dharma."

As for what was said—that since no fruit is heard of in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), there is no possibility at all of an intention for a fruit, so what is the use of a prohibition?—to that also it is replied: because of the absence of a fruit, someone who does not correctly understand the meaning of the scripture might not engage [in such rites]; and having observed that engagement preceded by an intention for a fruit in the case of rites like the *saurya* sacrifice where a fruit is explicitly heard, one might, through general inference (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), assume that whatever is to be done is done for the sake of a fruit, and thus intend a fruit even where none is heard. It is for the purpose of precluding this that the present [text] is commenced.

Although this is the logical principle—that whatever is heard in scripture as having a fruit must be performed exactly so, and even that which is taught by the scripture as a duty despite being fruitless (such as rites indicated by terms like "as long as one lives") must be understood as having a fruit through the *viśvajit*-principle in the absence of an explicit statement—nevertheless, there is no possibility of performing such acts otherwise; yet, for those who are unable to grasp this principle, it is established by means of a direct scriptural injunction.

For while understanding through formal reasoning involves effort, understanding from a direct statement is lighter and easier; thus, acting as a friend, [the author] teaches a matter established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Although this word *kāma* is seen to denote "passion" (*hṛcchaya*), since that is impossible here, *kāma* means "desire" (*icchā*) or "longing" (*abhilāṣa*), as these are synonymous.
In this context, considering what is to be said later, the meaning will be established as follows: one should not engage in every instance out of a longing for results.

But the opponent, considering the meaning of the word "kāma" to be merely the state of having desire—that is, the mere connection with desire—objects: "And here there is no such thing as being without desire.
The meaning is that in this world, no activity whatsoever exists for one who is free from desire.

Let alone agriculture, trade, and the like performed by those of developed intellect; even the acquisition of the Veda—the study of the Vedas—which a child is made to do by his father and others while being beaten, that too does not occur without desire.
For study consists in the utterance of sounds;
and utterance does not arise without a desire [to speak], like the sound of a thunderclap.
If one desires it, why then is one being beaten?
That very [desire] is produced by such a wish;
however, the distinction is simply this: in the case of an intended object, it arises spontaneously.

Furthermore, even that "discipline of action" (karmayoga) prescribed by the Veda and enjoined by the Veda—such as the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices—which is understood to be obligatory, would not be attained [by one who lacks such desire].
For it is not possible for one who lacks desire to perform the renunciation of one's own property for the sake of a deity;
therefore, if the state of being motivated by desire is prohibited, it follows that all rites prescribed by the Vedas (śrauta) and the Smṛtis (smārta) would be prohibited.
Desire indeed has its root in volition; sacrifices are born of volition;
vows, restraints, and duties—all are traditionally held to be born of volition.
And therefore, having clarified what was stated—that the essential nature of a sacrifice cannot be accomplished without desire—he says this:
"The mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is the root of sacrifices and the like, as well as of desire.
One who intends to perform sacrifices and the like necessarily forms a mental resolve.
And when a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is being formed, its cause—desire (*kāma*)—must necessarily be present, even if it is undesirable;

just as for one who seeks to cook and produces fire, smoke, which shares the same cause, arises as an unintended byproduct. In that case, it is impossible to claim that "sacrifices and the like will be performed, yet desire will not arise."
Now, what is this so-called *saṃkalpa* (volition), which is the root of all action? It is said:
it is that which is called the mental visualization (*cetaḥ-saṃdarśana*), immediately after which aspiration (*prārthanā*) and determination (*adhyavasāya*) arise in succession.
For these mental activities constitute the root of all engagement in action;
indeed, no physical activities are possible without them.

To explain: first, the determination of the nature of an object—namely, the cognition that "this object accomplishes this purposeful action"—is what is intended here by the term *saṃkalpa* (volition).
Immediately following that, there arises a prayer, which is desire;
that itself is *kāma*.
When the desire "How may I accomplish this by means of this" exists, one resolves, "I shall do it," and determines it; that is resolve (*adhyavasāya*).

Thereupon, one engages in the external activity involved in acquiring the means of accomplishment. For instance, a hungry person first perceives the act of eating; then he desires it, thinking, "May I eat"; then he resolves, "Having desisted from other activities, I shall eat"; then he says to those who are the agents, the instruments, the locus, and the authorities: "Prepare the kitchen," or "Bring [the food].
But if this is so, sacrifices and the like do not arise from mere intention (*saṃkalpa*) alone, but rather from intention, prayer (*prārthanā*), and resolution (*adhyavasāya*).
In this regard, what is meant by the statement that "sacrifices arise from volition" (*saṃkalpa*)?
There is no fault here, because volition is the primary cause.
For this very reason, it will be stated later: "No action whatsoever is seen to belong to one who is devoid of desire."
Vows (*vratāni*): A mental resolve is a vow, such as that which is prescribed: "This must be performed by me for as long as I live," as in the case of the *snātaka* vows.
The duties of Yama consist of prohibitions such as non-violence and the like;
engagement in what ought to be done and desisting from what is forbidden do not exist without volition (saṃkalpa).
No action whatsoever is ever seen here in this world that is performed by one who is free from desire;
for whatever one does, all that is the movement of desire.
In the preceding [verse], scriptural engagement and withdrawal were explained as being dependent upon volition (*saṃkalpa*).
The distinction here is that it is stated that even in worldly activities, they are dependent on that [volition].
In this world, at any time whatsoever—even while awake—no action can ever occur as something to be performed for one who lacks the desire [to do so].
Whatever action one performs—whether worldly or Vedic, prescribed or prohibited—all that is the movement of desire (*kāma*).
Because it is the cause, it is said to be the movement of desire alone.
This situation is extremely precarious: being driven by desire is not praiseworthy, yet there is no performance of any rite whatsoever without it.
To this, he replies:
"One who conducts oneself rightly toward these [virtues] goes to the world of the immortals;
and here, one enjoys all desires exactly as they were intended."
One should conduct oneself correctly regarding those sensual pleasures. What, then, is correct conduct?
It is that whatever has been heard exactly as it was taught should be practiced in that very same way.

In the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), no fruit should be intended, because none is mentioned [in the scriptures]. In the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), however, there is no prohibition, because they are heard [in scripture] as such; indeed, those rites are understood through injunction precisely as means for attaining a fruit.
The performance of those [obligatory rites] by one who does not desire a fruit would be a doing of what is not prescribed [as having such a fruit].
In the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), the intention for a fruit is nothing but delusion;
for a fruit does not arise merely from an intention when its status as a means to that fruit has not been established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Acting in this way, one goes and attains the state of the immortals (*amaralokatā*).

"Immortals" (*amara*) refers to the gods; their "world" (*loka*) is heaven. Because they dwell there, the word "world" is applied to the gods through the non-distinction between the location and that which occupies it, as in the expression, "the beds cry out."
Therefore, this compound is as follows: "amaraloka" means those who are both immortals (*amara*) and worlds (*loka*); "amaralokatā" is the state of being that.
The meaning is that one attains the status of the divine host, which is to say, one attains divinity.
It is stated in this way for the sake of metrical conformity (*vṛtta*).

Alternatively, *amaraloka* means that which beholds or sees the immortals (*amarān*); the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), and from that form, the suffix *bhava* (denoting "belonging to" or "being in") is added.
He becomes one who is seen by the gods;
by this manner as well, the attainment of heaven alone is expressed.
Or else, he is beheld in the world like an immortal.
And this is a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda).
Here, heaven is not enjoined as a result, because there is an absence of results for obligatory rites (nitya), and because various distinct results are heard in the case of optional rites (kāmya).
Therefore, by the term "attainment of heaven," the successful completion of the performance of the scriptures is actually expressed through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).

The meaning is that the purpose for which the performance of actions is undertaken is thereby accomplished. In that regard, the purpose of obligatory (nitya) rites is either the non-occurrence of transgression (pratyavāya) or the fulfillment of the injunction's requirement. In the case of optional (kāmya) rites, however, [the result is obtained] exactly as intended and exactly as prescribed in the scriptural injunctions.

At the time of performance, having resolved upon the specific fruit of whichever action has been heard of in scripture, and having intended it with the mind, thinking "May I obtain this fruit from this," one then enjoys—that is, attains—all desires, that is, all objects of longing.
Thus, the occurrence of a dilemma is avoided, because desire for all objects is not prohibited;
rather, what is prohibited is the desire characterized by the longing for a fruit in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*).
The perfection of the means (sādhana-saṃpatti), however, is indeed for the sake of specific desires.
But the exponents of Brahman (brahmavādinaḥ) consider that the phrase "being of the nature of desire" (kāmātmatā) is intended to exclude rites such as those dedicated to Sūrya.
Actions performed with a longing for results become of the nature of bondage; however, one who acts without desire, following the principle of offering everything to Brahman, is liberated.
This was said by the Blessed One Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana: "Do not become one whose motive is the fruit of action;
likewise, due to the incompleteness of the means and through folly, you have become a performer of ritual acts."
"And because of the aiming for a fruit, the ritual is considered impure.
There are many alternative interpretations here, but they have not been shown because they lack substance.
The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as are the Smṛtis and the conduct of those who know it;
likewise, the practice of the virtuous and the self-satisfaction of one's own conscience.
What is the connection here?
For it has been promised that "dharma" is what is to be explained,
and that [dharma] is characterized by affirmation and negation.

In this regard, it is not necessary to enjoin that "the Veda is the root of Dharma," or "the Veda should be known as the root of Dharma," or "it should be relied upon for the authority of Dharma," because this is established even without such an instruction.

For the fact that the Veda is the root of Dharma is not something to be understood through the instructions of Manu and others; rather, it is established by its own nature: because it produces cognitions of objects that are uncontradicted, because it is authorless (*apauruṣeya*), and because there is no suspicion of false statement due to defects arising from human contact; and since the word is inherently free from defect, its self-evident authority (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) is established just like perception.

Now, it might be argued that, having restated the validity of the Veda as established through reasoning (*nyāya*), the fact that the *smṛtis* of Manu and others are rooted in that [Veda] is made known by means of a specific statement.
That too is not correct;

for even in that case, there remains a dependence on prior cognition. Furthermore, since memory is subject to error, deception, and so forth, these are eliminated by the acceptance [of the tradition] by great men (*mahājana*) and other factors. Moreover, because the perception of supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārtha*) is impossible for a human being, and since such a person's own experience is established, it is concluded that the memory of the meaning of the Vedas must indeed be rooted in the Veda itself.
For a recollection concerning the meaning of an action performed by those who know the Veda is not possible;
moreover, since the Veda itself serves as the source, there is no occasion to postulate another source.

Nor is it appropriate to say that the phrase "the tradition and conduct of those who know it" is merely a restatement intended to show the lack of authority of external Smṛtis, because their lack of authority is already established by logic alone.

For it is impossible for the Śākyas, Bhojakas, Kṣapaṇakas, and others to have a connection with the Veda, by virtue of which their [teachings] could be authoritative regarding their own subject matter on the basis of being rooted in it; because they do not themselves accept this, because they declare the Veda to be non-authoritative, and because they teach matters that contradict the directly perceived Veda.
Among these, the impossibility [of such a connection] exists in those Smṛtis because of the prohibition against the study of the Veda.
For if Buddhists and others were indeed students of the Veda, then the consideration would arise as to whether or not [their teachings] are rooted in it.
But where that connection is utterly remote, what suspicion can there be of its being rooted in that?
Furthermore, they themselves accept other sources transmitted through tradition, such as: "I see with my divine eye the good and bad destinies of the mendicants.

Thus, all outsiders—the Bhojakas, Pāñcarātrikas, Nirgranthas, Ānarthavādins, Pāśupatas, and so forth—accept the authors of their own systems to be extraordinary persons or specific deities who have directly perceived those objects; yet they do not consider even their *dharma* to be rooted in the Veda.
Furthermore, matters that contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the Veda are taught therein.
For instance, while those such as the Saṃsāramocakas assert that violence (*hiṃsā*) is dharma, it is here explicitly prohibited by direct perception.
Likewise, elsewhere bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*) is accepted as non-dharma, whereas here there is the injunction: "One should bathe day after day; one should resort to sacred fords."
Likewise, the slaughter of the animal dedicated to Agniṣṭoma is accepted in some cases as a cause of sin, yet it is contradicted by the injunction for the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
Similarly, others maintain that all sacrifices and oblations are for one's own benefit; however, they are understood through various injunctions regarding deities to have diverse divinities.
Therefore, there is a contradiction.

As for those who say: "Just as in the case of acceptance and non-acceptance, or the times for the *udita* and *anudita* oblations, since we observe contradictions with direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), it is possible that there exists another Vedic branch—whether extinct or not extinct—that contains injunctions for matters contrary to that [direct revelation].
For the branches of the Veda are infinite;
how could they all be directly perceived by a single person?"
"And its destruction is possible.
In that regard, there might exist such a Vedic branch (*veda-śākhā*) in which this practice of eating from a vessel made of human bone, wandering naked, and so forth, would have been taught.
To this it is replied:
We do not say that it is impossible for the Veda to teach contradictory meanings;
rather, because those two [options] are of equal status, there is no conflict between the two alternative applications.
In this case, however, the Veda is merely to be inferred.
Furthermore, there is no occasion for a conceptual construction that contradicts direct perception;
nor can certainty be established by mere possibility alone.
Indeed, the positive operation of direct perception, which contradicts it, is certain; and what is uncertain does not sublate what is certain.
Furthermore, we shall elaborate upon the position regarding the destruction of the Vedic branches (*śākhotsāda*) later in this very verse.

In every case, there is an interconnection between the directly revealed scriptures (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) and the *smṛtis* of Manu and others—sometimes through a mantra, sometimes through a deity, and sometimes through injunctions regarding ritual materials (*dravya*).
Since such an interconnection is not possible in the case of external [scriptures], they lack authoritative validity (*aprāmāṇya*).

In this way, conduct (*ācāra*) as well—when practiced by those learned in the Vedas for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*)—possesses authority just like the *Smṛtis*, because its source is possible.
Conversely, improper conduct lacks authority because visible causes and the like are possible, and because error and the like are possible for the ignorant.
The same applies to self-satisfaction (*ātmatuṣṭi*).

And if the authority of the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and established customs is derived from the teachings of Manu and others, then how is the authority of Manu and others established? For in that case too, their authority must derive from other teachings, such as the Smṛti statement, "And Manu declared the traditional law," and so forth. How, then, is the authority for that established?
Therefore, that "this is a valid means of knowledge" and "this is not a valid means of knowledge" is to be determined through reasoning, not by mere instruction;
thus, this verse is useless,
and the subsequent ones are of the same nature.
To this it is replied:

Here, those authors of *Dharmasūtras* who compose literary works with the intent of establishing the meaning of categories for the sake of instructing unlearned persons—just as they record the performance of the *Aṣṭakā* and other rites after having themselves understood their obligatoriness from the Veda for the purpose of making others understand them—likewise [record] the authority of the Veda and so forth, which are established by other means of knowledge.

This is because there are certain practitioners who are incapable of discerning reality through reasoning, due to the absence of an intellect capable of such processes as induction (*ūha*) and exclusion (*apoha*).
For their sake, even a matter established by logic is taught like the instruction of a friend.
In this regard, that very fact which is established by logic—that the Veda is the root of Dharma—is restated here: "The Veda is the root of Dharma.
Since the Veda has been established through reasoning as the source of Dharma after being examined, no suspicion of its lack of authority should be raised here.

Furthermore, there are in the world instructors who teach matters established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as: "One should not eat while suffering from indigestion, for diseases arise from indigestion.
Nor should it be said that those who are unable to understand through reasoning that the Veda is the root of Dharma will likewise not believe it on the strength of its verbal testimony alone;
for it is observed that some people, regarding certain persons as authoritative (*āpta*), accept their word as valid without even investigating it.
Thus, this entire treatise is rooted in logic (*nyāya*), not in the Veda.
We shall demonstrate on appropriate occasions elsewhere—in works such as the *Vyavahāra-smṛti*—wherever they are based on logic.
As for how the *Aṣṭakā* and other rites are rooted in the Veda, that will be pointed out right here.
By the word "Veda," the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* [Vedas], together with the *Brāhmaṇas*, are denoted.
And these are well-known to have distinct divisions among students by virtue of other statements;
students, refined by an unbroken tradition of instruction, recognize them as "this is the Veda" upon merely hearing it, just as one recognizes "this is a Brāhmaṇa."

In that regard, even within the collection of sentences beginning with "I praise Agni" (*agnim īḷe*) and "Agni is indeed the lowest of the gods" (*agnir vai devānām avamaḥ*), and ending with "Thou gatherest together" (*saṃ sam id yuvase*) and "Then the Mahāvrata" (*atha mahāvratam*), the word *veda* is employed; and this applies even to the individual sentences that constitute its parts.
Furthermore, there is no distinction between primary and secondary usage as there is in the case of words such as "village" (*grāma*).
For the principle is this: words that function for a whole also function for its constituent parts.

For the word *grāma* (village) is most commonly established in usage as referring to a collection [of houses]; however, through its connection with words such as "the village is burned," it applies to a part of that collection. Even when only a few huts are burned, people in common parlance say, "the village is burned.
Alternatively, even in that case, it refers to the collection itself.
Burning, though occurring in only one part, is designated as belonging to the whole;
for the connection of the whole with an action occurs precisely through its parts.
This very connection of the whole with an action is that which belongs to the parts.
For it is not possible to perceive or touch a whole apart from its parts;
yet the word *veda* is etymologically explained:
it is called *veda* because from it they know (*vidanti*) the object characterized as *dharma*, which cannot be known by any other means of valid cognition.
And that knowledge arises from each individual sentence, not from the entire collection of chapters and sections denoted by the words "Ṛgveda" and so forth.
Thus, the penalty of tongue-cutting prescribed for the recitation of an example refers even to a single sentence;
the inclusion of the word "entirety" (*kṛtsna*) in the injunction "the whole [Veda] is to be mastered" is for the purpose of ensuring the study of every sentence of the entire Veda.
Otherwise, one might become proficient by studying only a few sentences, rather than the entire Veda.
We shall examine this point hereafter.
And that Veda is divided in many ways.

The Sāmaveda has a thousand paths through its divisions such as the Sātyamugri and Āṇāyanīya; the Adhvaryus (Yajurveda) have one hundred and one branches through divisions such as the Kāṭhaka and Vājasaneyaka; the Bāhvṛcyas (Ṛgveda) have twenty-one branches through divisions such as the Āśvalāyana and Aitareya; and the Atharvaṇa is ninefold through divisions such as the Maudaka and Paippalādaka. Now, it may be objected that some do not even consider the Atharvaṇa to be a Veda, since [the scriptures] state: "The triple knowledge consists of the Ṛks, Sāmans, and Yajus"; "The sun moves with the three Vedas, never lacking them"; and "One should observe the vow pertaining to the three Vedas. In such passages, the name of the Atharvaṇa does not appear anywhere.
Furthermore, a prohibition is heard: "Therefore, one should not recite [the Veda] with the Atharvaṇa.

For this reason, they declare the followers of the Atharvaṇa—who are outside the Trayī—to be heretics (pāṣaṇḍins). That is incorrect, because the learned (śiṣṭas) engage with the Veda without making such a distinction.

The term "Śruti" is also used for the *Atharvāṅgirasa* texts; thus, "Śruti" and "Veda" have the same meaning. Furthermore, being denoted by the word "Veda" is not the sole reason for the sentences concerning the *Agnihotra* and other rites to serve as authoritative means of knowing *dharma*, since we observe the usage of the term "Veda" even for the *Itihāsa* and *Āyurveda*, as in the statement: "The *Itihāsa-Purāṇa* is the fifth Veda among the Vedas."
What then? [It is authoritative] because, while being of non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*), it makes known the matters to be practiced and is free from error.
All of that exists in the Atharvaveda as well, since rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma are taught there just as they are in the Yajurveda and other Vedas.
The misconception of some that it is not a Veda arises because of the abundance of teachings therein concerning rites rooted in malevolent magic (*abhicāra*).
For malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) are prohibited because they result in the separation of the life-force of others;
yet these very rites are primarily practiced by the royal priests (*rājapurohita*) who belong to the Atharvaṇikas, and for that reason they are censured.
As for the argument that the Atharvaveda is not mentioned in passages such as "not empty of Vedas," these are merely explanatory statements (*arthavāda*).
What is the point of explaining or not explaining that?
This statement—"the three Vedas," "the triple knowledge," and so forth—is intended with the distinction of mantras in mind.
For there is no fourth class of mantra apart from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, since the *praiṣas*, *nivids*, *niṃgadās*, *indragāthās*, and so on, are all included within these very categories.
In the Atharvaveda, the *carcas* themselves are recited as mantras;

therefore, this [Atharvaveda] is indeed the Ṛgveda from the perspective of the mantras. As for the prohibition [of it being a separate Veda], that serves to prove the opposite, since a prohibition is only logical when there is a prior possibility of occurrence.
Or this is its meaning: one should not mix the ritual acts prescribed by the three Vedas with the mantras studied in the Atharvaveda.
In the Vācaḥstoma sacrifice, all Ṛg-verses, all Yajus-formulas, and all Sāman-chants are employed; therein, there is a prohibition of those studied in the Atharvaveda.

That Veda is a distinguished collection of words, of non-human origin, known as Mantra and Brāhmaṇa, divided into many distinct recensions (śākhās); it is the root of Dharma, the authoritative source, and the cause for its full comprehension.
The "cause" (kāraṇa) is the root.

And that [Veda] is the cause for Dharma with respect to the Veda and the Smṛtis solely by way of being an indicator (jñāpaka), not by way of being a producer (nirvartaka), nor by way of being a cause of subsistence (sthitihetu), as in the case of a tree.
Furthermore, the word "Dharma" has been explained previously.

That which is to be performed by a person as a means to the highest good (*śreyas*), by a nature distinct from what is cognized through perception and other means of knowledge, is such that agriculture, service, and so forth constitute what is to be performed by a person; and its nature as a means to that [good] is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Furthermore, the manner in which the production of rice and other crops results from agricultural activity and the like is also indeed cognizable through perception and other means of knowledge.

However, the status of sacrifice and other such acts as means—by virtue of their form involving the mediation of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) and so forth—is not cognizable through perception or other ordinary means of knowledge.

Furthermore, "welfare" (*śreyas*) consists in the attainment of desired results such as heaven or a village, which is generally denoted by the word "pleasure" (*sukha*); the attainment of results such as disease, poverty, unhappiness, or hell, which is generally denoted by the word "pain" (*duḥkha*), as well as the avoidance thereof.
Others, however, maintain that welfare consists in the nature of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) and the like.

This dharma is understood from the words of the Brāhmaṇas containing injunctive suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like, and in some cases also from mantras such as, "One should sacrifice *kapiñjala* birds for the sake of spring," and so forth. Among these, sentences joined with words of desire (*kāmapada*) convey that the performance is for the sake of a specific fruit, such as: "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya," and "One desiring a village should offer the *sāṃgrahiṇī* oblation to the Viśvedevas."
Those [rites] are not performed by one who does not desire a fruit;
as for others which are presented as obligatory by terms such as "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*), they are not undertaken for the sake of a fruit, because no fruit is mentioned.

Nor can a fruit be postulated even when none is mentioned—as in the case of "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit"—because these [obligatory rites] are understood as duties to be performed even without a fruit, due to terms such as "as long as one lives."
In that regard, by failing to perform them, there is the fault of transgressing the meaning of the scriptures;
therefore, those [prescribed acts] are performed for the sake of avoiding that fault.
Regarding the prohibitions as well—such as "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed" and "Liquor must not be drunk"—the principle is exactly the same.
For the avoidance of prohibited acts is not for the sake of attaining a fruit, but rather for the sake of avoiding transgression (pratyavāya).
"Entire" means complete;
there is not a single word, syllable, or even a fraction of a syllable that does not lead to dharma.
Here they raise an objection:

"But surely, the Veda consists of injunctions (vidhi), explanatory passages (arthavāda), mantras, and names (nāmadheya); and it has been stated that Dharma has the nature of something to be performed (kartavyatā).
In that case, it is logical that only injunctive sentences should be the authority for Dharma."
For from them, the obligation to perform actions such as sacrifices is understood:
"One performs the *agnihotra*," "One performs [the sacrifice] with curd," "That which one offers in the evening to Agni and Prajāpati," and "One desiring heaven performs [the sacrifice].
For here, the action called *agnihotra* is understood as something to be performed.
In that very context, "with curd" (dadhnā) is the substance;
"and for Agni" (yad agnaye ca) is the deity;
and "one who desires heaven" (svargakāmaḥ) is the qualification.

As for such passages as "Agni indeed is all the deities; Agni alone is the divine Hotṛ priest; he invites the gods and offers the oblation," and likewise, "Prajāpati cut out his own omentum" and so forth—by these, no duty to be performed is taught.
They merely restate a past event or something else that is not applicable to the present time:
"In the past, the omentum was cut out by Prajāpati from himself."
"Let it be torn out; what is the use of this to us?

Likewise, even though fire possesses the nature of all deities, that [universal nature] is not employed in a rite dedicated to Agni, because the purpose of the designation is fulfilled by the word 'Agni' alone.
If there were another deity, then because of that otherness, there would be no designation of Agni at all."

Since even the invocation (*āvāhana*) has been prescribed by another scriptural statement, such as "O Agni, bring hither the gods" (*agnim agna āvahe*), the passage beginning with "He invokes the gods and offers oblations" (*sa devān āhvayati ca juhoti ca*) is redundant. Furthermore, as for the mantras—such as "Death was not, nor was immortality then; where did the well-faring one fall today without return? (*na mṛtyur āsīd amṛtaṃ na tarhi sudevo adya pated anāvṛt*)—which express meanings such as lamentations over the course of existence (*bhāvavṛtta*), what dharma do they establish?
At that time, death had not come into being, nor had immortality, which is life.
Before the creation of beings, because they had not yet come into existence, there was no life for anyone, nor was there death; for at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), everyone is dead.
Whether death exists or not, nothing is taught here that needs to be done by this [statement].

Thus, he is a "good god" (*sudeva*), a man of great merit equal to a deity, who today might fall into a pit—that is, one who would cast himself into a pit from which there is no recovery (*anāvṛt*), meaning no returning or reviving.
Purūravas, deceived by Urvaśī, lamented;
such is the origin of that name.

[Expressions] such as "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," or "one should sacrifice with the *balabhid*," do not enjoin any purpose, action, or substance, because the action is enjoined by the verb (*ākhyāta*) and because terms like *balabhid* do not denote a substance.

Furthermore, since the *soma* sacrifice is already established by its very nature through the injunction of the unmanifest (*avyakta-codanā*), it is not necessary to laboriously assume that the term denotes a substance.
Therefore, dharma is not taught by means of names.
Consequently, how can it be said that "the entire Veda is the root of dharma"?
It is said:
