And that [marriage] is prohibited by the rule: "beyond the seventh degree from paternal relatives and beyond the fifth degree from maternal relatives."
In this country as well, practices such as eating together with one who has not been initiated are by no means accepted as being in accordance with *dharma*.
Nor is it possible for a practice that contradicts the *smṛti* to possess authority, because it is remote from the *śruti*.
From practice (*ācāra*), the *smṛti* must be inferred; from the *smṛti*, the *śruti*.
Smṛti, however, leads one to infer a direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*) that is not separated from it.
Furthermore, this is because such customs as these involve the apprehension of a cause:
[for example], those desiring a beautiful maternal cousin married her out of fear of the king, thinking, "Let there be no punishment for approaching a maiden."
Others, however, being ignorant, have grasped the literal meaning of the verse, "By that path his fathers have gone," and have accepted it as a mandatory rule (*dharma*).

Furthermore, although the expiation has been heard in the text, "One should not take these three as wives," they maintain that this is merely a cause for error, implying that women other than these three are not prohibited.
We shall explain how this is not the actual meaning of the passage.
Furthermore, there is no authority for those traditions of memory and practice whose causes are perceptible;
as the venerable Bhaṭṭa has stated:
"That which is contradictory, that which is censured, that which has a perceptible purpose, and that which has a perceptible cause [is not authoritative]."
This Smṛti, which is based on the possibility [of its origin], would not have the Śruti as its root.
Therefore, these are explanatory passages (arthavādas) intended to praise the regions, serving as supplements to the injunction that "the twice-born should resort to these countries.
*Pāraṃparya* means succession (*paraṃparā*).
A succession is a continuous flow in which one person approaches another, that one approaches yet another, and from him yet another—in this manner it proceeds.
*Krama* is the non-interruption [of the sequence]; that which has come from, or reached, that [is *kramaja*]. *Saṃkīrṇayoni* refers to the intermediate [classes].
[It refers to] the *varṇas* together with those.
Kurukṣetra, Matsya, Pañcāla, and Śūrasena—
this is indeed the land of the Brahmarṣis, which follows immediately after Brahmāvarta.
These are merely designations;
Kurukṣetra and Samantapañcaka are well known. It was there that the Kurus met their destruction.
"Perform good deeds quickly; they will be your protection here"—this is the etymological derivation.
Words such as *matsya* and others, ending in the plural number, denote regions.
"The region of the Brahman-sages" (*brahmarṣideśa*) is a collective designation.
The land created by the gods is Brahmāvarta.
Since the Brahman-sages are slightly inferior to the gods, this land is inferior to Brahmāvarta due to its connection with the Brahman-sages;
thus it is said to be "immediately following Brahmāvarta," meaning slightly different from it.
The negative particle *nañ* has the sense of "slight," as for example when they instruct, "A patient should drink barley-gruel that is *anuṣṇā*" (not-hot), meaning it is slightly warm.
The word *antara* expresses difference, as in the expression, "There is no small interval (*anantaram*) between women, men, and water; there is a great interval (*mahad antaram*)."
From the presence of a twice-born man born in this region,
all men on earth should learn their respective duties.
In these regions, such as Kurukṣetra and others, they should learn—that is, seek to understand—their respective conduct and customs from the presence of the twice-born Brāhmaṇas born therein.
By the phrase "in that region," this is explained.
The region situated between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, extending eastward from Vinaśana and westward from Prayāga, is proclaimed as Madhyadeśa.
In the northern direction is the Himalaya mountain; in the southern direction is the Vindhya.
Vinaśana is the place where the Sarasvatī disappears;
Prayāga is the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Taking these regions as boundaries, one should know the central region named Madhyadeśa;
it is called Madhyadeśa because it is neither too superior nor too inferior, and not because it is situated in the middle of the earth.
From the eastern ocean to the western ocean,
the wise know that the land between those two mountains is Āryāvarta.

The region situated between the eastern ocean and the western ocean, as well as that which lies between the two mountains—the Himavat and the Vindhya—as taught in the preceding verse, is called Āryāvarta by the wise and the learned.
Noble people (āryas) dwell there, arising again and again;
even though Mlecchas may repeatedly invade it, they do not remain there for long.
The prefix *āṅ* here denotes a limit (*maryādā*), not an inclusive extension (*abhividhi*). Therefore, the islands of the ocean are not included in Āryāvarta.
These are taken as the boundaries of the region in the four directions.
In the east lies the eastern ocean, in the west the western [ocean], and in the north and south the Himavat and Vindhya mountains.
Since these two are taken as the boundaries, they themselves do not possess the status of Āryāvarta.
Therefore, since it might follow that there is no residence [of Āryas] there, he says this:
That land where the black antelope roams by its own nature should be known as the land fit for sacrifice; beyond that is the land of the Mlecchas.
Where a black-and-white, black-and-yellow, or black-spotted antelope roams or dwells— that is,
where its birth or origin occurs naturally in that region, and not merely where it has been brought from another land for reasons such as excellence or as a gift and has resided there for some time—
that region should be understood as *yajñiya*, fit for sacrifice.
Therefore, beyond the region where the black antelope roams lies another land, the Mleccha country.
The Mlecchas are well known;
they are those excluded from the four castes, born of inverse unions (pratiloma), and unauthorized [for Vedic rites], such as the Medas, Andhras, Śabaras, Pulindas, and others.

Nor is the status of this place as the locus of the sacrifice enjoined by this [text], as in the case of "one should sacrifice on level ground," because of the use of the present tense in the word *carati*.
For it is not possible to perform the sacrifice at the very moment one has begun to move;
rather, the place is the locus of the sacrifice by way of supporting the liquids and other substances that depend upon the factors of action (kārakas), such as the agent who performs its means.
Furthermore, it is impossible for two corporeal entities to occupy the same place at the same time.
Nor is it logical to resort to indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding a different time, because indirect indication is improper when a direct injunction (*vidhi*) is possible.
As it was stated in the *Śūrpādhikaraṇa*: "For this is what is being enjoined."

But is it not the case that the contained (*ādheya*) need not necessarily pervade its entire locus (*ādhāra*), such that the fulfillment of the meaning of "locus" would occur only through the pervasion of the whole locus—as in the expression "oil in sesame seeds"?

Rather, even by a contained object connected to only one part, the status of being a whole locus is established—as in "he sits in the palace" (*prāsāde āste*) or "he stands upon the chariot" (*ratham adhitiṣṭhati*).

For in this way, since the region consisting of a collection of villages and cities, delimited by boundaries such as rivers and mountains, is the subject under discussion, one who moves even in a single part, such as a mountain or a forest, makes the whole [region] his locus.
Therefore, this is not a fault, for it is impossible for two corporeal things to occupy the same location.
It is replied:
there is no injunction here stating that "one must sacrifice."
The injunctive suffix is heard after the root *jñā* (to know), not after *yaj* (to sacrifice).
In that context, what is heard is the fitness for sacrifice; that is, "this place is fit for sacrifice.
And that fitness for sacrifice is possible even in the absence of an injunction.

In these regions, the materials required for sacrifice—such as *darbha* grass, *palāśa* leaves, and *khadira* wood—are generally found; furthermore, those qualified to perform sacrifices—the members of the three higher castes who possess the threefold knowledge (*traividyā*)—are seen only in those very regions.
Therefore, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of their fitness for sacrifice based on these facts.

The statement "the *kṛtya* suffix should also be understood [as such]" has the sense of a superimposed injunction; like the passage "one should offer with wild sesame gruel," it is merely an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) in the form of an injunction.

Furthermore, as for what was said—"but beyond this is the land of the barbarians" (*mleccha-deśa*)—this too is generally a restatement (*anuvāda*), for in these lands, people are generally barbarians.

However, the Mlecchas are not defined by this connection with a specific region, because they are well-known by themselves, just like the Brāhmaṇa and other castes. Now, if it is argued that this term "Mleccha country" is applied by way of its meaning— that is, as the country of the Mlecchas— then if the Mlecchas were somehow to invade even the region of Brahmāvarta and establish their residence there, that very place would indeed become a Mleccha country.

Likewise, if some king of the Kṣatriya or other caste, being of virtuous conduct, should defeat the Mlecchas, establish the four castes [in his realm], and settle the Mlecchas as outcastes (cāṇḍālas) just as in Āryāvarta, he too would be fit for sacrifice. For the land is not inherently defiled; rather, it becomes defiled through association, like ground contaminated by impure substances. Therefore, even outside the aforementioned regions, provided the necessary conditions are met, one belonging to the three higher castes must certainly perform sacrifice, even in a land where the black antelope does not roam.

Therefore, this is a restatement (anuvāda) to be understood as follows: "That is the land fit for sacrifice; beyond that is the land of the Mlecchas"—this is a supplement to the subsequent injunction.
The twice-born should diligently seek refuge in these countries;
however, a Śūdra, distressed for a livelihood, may dwell in any place whatsoever.
He now states the rule for which purpose the description of the distinctions between countries was given:

members of the twice-born classes, even if born in another country, should resort to these regions such as Brahmāvarta and the like. Having abandoned their birthplace, they should make an effort to take refuge in regions such as Brahmāvarta.
On this point, some say that this injunction regarding residence in these specific regions has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
Even though eligibility (*adhikāra*) might exist elsewhere, one must dwell in these particular regions.

In that case, since the eligibility would have to be inferred, either this injunction for residing in these regions is to be understood as being for the sake of purification, like bathing at sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā.

Just as some waters are more pure, so too some portions of land are pure, as stated in the Purāṇa. Alternatively, heaven might result from the mere act of resorting [to such a place] independently, like the Viśvajit sacrifice. In that case, both of these positions remain unestablished.
If a resort that has not yet been attained is enjoined, then even a qualification might be postulated;
regarding this, it is considered which of the two positions is logical.
However, because the performance of obligatory and optional rites is possible in this very region according to the method already stated, they are indeed obtained for those who are qualified.
For it is not possible to perform the entirety of the dharma outside of this region.

To illustrate: first, in places such as Kashmir on the Himalayas, those afflicted by cold are not qualified for the external twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), nor is the study of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) possible according to the rules, which require one to go out from the village either to the east or to the north.
For indeed, bathing in rivers and the like day after day is not possible during the winter and the cool seasons;
and this very fact is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the expression "the twice-born.
No region whatsoever becomes a "barbarian land" (*mlecchadeśa*) by its own nature merely because of the absence of contact with barbarians.
Otherwise, if one were a Mleccha merely by connection with that region, how could there be the status of being twice-born?
Now, it might be argued: "One does not become a Mleccha by mere travel, but rather by residing [there]."
And that [position] is refuted by this;
yet that is not [correct], for here "resorting" (saṃśraya) is what is heard.
And for one who exists in another region, that [act] consists of abandoning that [former place] and establishing a connection with another region;
it is not the taking up of a residence by one who is already residing there.
Otherwise, he would have stated it simply as: "Having abandoned these regions, one should not dwell elsewhere."

Now, if it is argued that once the taking of refuge is established, that statement is intended for the purpose of excluding others, then it would constitute a *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification). And such a specification entails three defects.
Furthermore, there is the abandonment of the directly stated meaning (*śrutārthahāni*), as [the literal sense] would be "one should not abandon these places."
When the literal meaning is possible, figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is not appropriate;
for this very reason, there is no recourse to the sense of "having been so in the past.

Therefore, this is an indicative mark (liṅga): it is not that men become barbarians (mleccha) by virtue of their connection to a place, but rather that a place becomes a barbarian land (mlecchadeśa) by virtue of its connection to men.

Since service to the twice-born is prescribed for the Śūdra, he is always entitled to reside in the same region as them; however, if he cannot subsist there, residence in another country is permitted.

When, due to having a large family or an inability to perform service, the twice-born person he has depended upon might not be able to support him, then he may live in another country where the acquisition of wealth is possible.

Even there, he should not dwell in a land abounding in Mlecchas, but rather in a land fit for sacrifice (*yājñiya*); for if he were surrounded by Mlecchas, it would be impossible to avoid contact through such activities as traveling, sitting, and eating, which would lead to the risk of his becoming like them.
"Emaciated by livelihood" means afflicted by the absence of livelihood.
"Livelihood" (vṛtti) refers to wealth sufficient for the maintenance of oneself and one's family.

The emaciation resulting from its absence is designated as being "connected" to it; just as a famine caused by the absence of rain is designated as being "caused by the rains," even though it is actually caused by the lack of rain.
By saying "in whichever [one]," he expresses the lack of restriction.
This origin of Dharma has been proclaimed to you in brief;
now learn of its manifestation and the duties of the social classes.
The statement of the summarized meaning of the entire text and its subject matter is for the purpose of non-forgetfulness.
"Yoni" means the cause. "Samāsena" means by way of summary or condensation.

"And origination" is a reflection upon the subject matter of the first chapter. The phrase "of all this" refers to the creation of the world, which he points out after having made it perceptible through his intellect.
The duties to be performed by the social classes are the "class-duties" (varṇadharma).
Learn them;
the distinction is that they are to be explained in detail.

In this regard, the authors of the *Smṛtivivaraṇa* elaborate that dharma is of five kinds: the dharma of caste (*varṇadharma*), the dharma of life-stage (*āśramadharma*), the dharma of both caste and life-stage (*varṇāśramadharma*), occasional dharma (*naimittika*), and the dharma of quality (*guṇadharma*).
Among these, that which proceeds by depending solely on birth and does not rely on distinctions of age, life-stage, and so forth, is the dharma of caste;
for example: "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed," and "Liquor must not be drunk by a Brāhmaṇa."
This is the duty (dharma) for one who possesses only caste, up until the final exhalation [of life].
As for the duty of the stages of life (āśramadharma), where caste alone is not taken into account, rather the undertaking of that specific stage of life is relied upon;
as, for example, in the case of a student (brahmacārin) regarding the tending of the sacred fire, the kindling of fuel, and the practice of begging for alms.
The dharma of caste and stage of life depends on both;
for example, "the bowstring made of murvā grass is for the Kṣatriya," and so forth.
This is an illustration of its not being worn in another stage of life nor by another caste.

However, the first undertaking is the duty of initiation (*upanayana-dharma*), not the duty of a stage of life (*āśrama-dharma*). And initiation is for the purpose of [entering] a stage of life; it is not itself a duty of that stage.
Purification by liquidation and so forth are occasional (*naimittika*) duties.
"Based on virtue is the duty of virtue," "and he must be protected from six [things]," and so forth; these are the duties of a consecrated Kṣatriya by virtue of his great learning.

Thus, it has been shown that everything is included by the mention of "letter" (varṇa); however, internal subdivisions are established from that very [mention]. Furthermore, there are properties of non-letters (avarṇadharma) that depend solely upon the nature of being a person (puruṣatva).
Those too would have to be stated with their distinctions;
in this way, other distinctions as well should be inferred.
Furthermore, the mention of "phonemes" (*varṇa*) here is for the sake of illustration, not for the purpose of excluding those produced from within [the mouth].
For this proposition is merely a restatement of that which was previously asserted.

For the twice-born, the purifying refinement of the body, beginning with the rite of impregnation (*niṣeka*), should be performed through meritorious Vedic rituals; it leads to purification both in this world and after death.
The application of mantras refers to Vedic rituals; here, "Vedas" is intended to mean the mantras. Those utterances which belong to them are what is meant by that term.

Therefore, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied because [the word *veda*] begins with the vowel *a*; or else, the term "Vedic" (*vaidika*) is used figuratively because [the Smṛti] is rooted in the Veda. Furthermore, by the word "action" (*karman*), action in the form of a procedural method (*itikartavyatā*) is intended.

And thus, since the sacramental rites beginning with *niṣeka* (conception) must be performed by means of ritual actions (*karma*), the distinction between the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is established.
Here, *niṣeka* is the primary act (*pradhāna*), while the recitation of mantras constitutes the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
*Niṣeka* is the depositing of semen into the womb.
He is the beginning of that collection of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra-kalāpa*) which will be described and extends up to the initiation (*upanayana*).
The singular number in the term "bodily purification" (*śarīra-saṃskāra*) is used with reference to the entire group.
Furthermore, by the word "purification" (*saṃskāra*), that which brings about the body endowed with its qualities is expressed.
In this context, *niṣeka* is that which brings about [the birth], while the others are producers of specific qualities.
This very point is expressed by the word "purifying" (*pāvana*).
It is called purifying because it purifies—that is, it removes impurity.
"Both after death and in this world":

because one is qualified for all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) actions here—whether their fruits are seen or unseen, such as the *Kārīrī* sacrifice or the *Jyotiṣṭoma*—it is said that [the teaching] benefits both worlds.
"By means of merits" means by means of what is auspicious and propitious.
The distinction between the meanings of the words *puṇya* and *pāvana* is that they bring about good fortune and dispel misfortune, respectively.
The term *dvijamanām* is intended to exclude the Śūdra; furthermore, this is a specification of those who are to undergo the sacraments (*saṃskāra*).
And by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the members of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) are understood;
for at that time, they are not yet twice-born (*dvijanman*).
By means of the fire-oblations performed for the fetus, and by the rites of birth, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle,
the taint derived from the seed and that derived from the womb are wiped away from the twice-born.

The purpose of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) has been stated: the purification of the body is both sanctifying and meritorious. Regarding that, its sanctifying nature is defined as the removal of defects from what is defiled. To the question, "But how can the body be defiled? he replies:
"Namely, that which pertains to the seed and that which pertains to the womb.
That which exists in the seed, or that which has the seed as its cause, is "pertaining to the seed" (*baijika*);
likewise for "pertaining to the womb" (*gārbhika*).
Sin (*enaḥ*) is invisible evil that causes suffering.
Because it serves as the instrumental cause for the seed and the womb, only their purity is mentioned here.
Semen and blood constitute the seed of the person.
Furthermore, they are impure by their very nature;
even the womb is indeed defiled due to the transmission of defects.
Therefore, the impurity caused by that [womb] is wiped away and removed from the person by means of purificatory rites (saṃskāras).
He now points them out, naming some of them and characterizing others by the specific sacraments they perform:
"by the oblations pertaining to the womb," which are performed when a child has been conceived in a woman's womb.
Or, they are called "gārbha" because they are intended for the sake of conception; in that regard,
the woman is merely the instrument,
while the fetus itself is the actual agent.
Furthermore, because they are performed for that purpose, the *homas*—namely the *puṃsavana*, *sīmantonnayana*, and *garbhādhāna*—are for its sake.
The word "*homa*" is used as an illustration for ritual action (*karman*) in general;
for indeed, the *garbhādhāna* is not itself a *homa*.
And the specific forms of the ladle, deity, and so forth for these rites are to be understood from the Gṛhya-smṛtis;
just as it is with the oblations pertaining to the womb (gārbha-homa), so it is with the sacrament called the birth-rite (jātakarma),
and likewise with the tonsure ceremony (caula).
The term *cauḍa* refers to the purpose of the tonsure (*cūḍā*). The *mauñjīnibandhana* is the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*),
for it is at that time that the girdle made of *muñja* grass is bound.
Therefore, by this, the rite of initiation (upanayana) is indicated.
*Nibandhana* is simply *bandhana* (binding);
the prefix *ni-* serves to complete the meter.

The purificatory rites (saṃskāras) designated by names such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*) and others, joined in a copulative compound, are indicated by the instrumental case as being for the purpose of cleansing. Furthermore, every purificatory rite imparts some specific quality—whether visible or invisible—to that which is to be purified, whether that object has already fulfilled its purpose or is intended to fulfill another task. For instance, in the injunction "one threshes the rice" (*vrīhīn avahanti*) or "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*), the removal of the husks and chaff imparts a visible quality to those who are about to accomplish the sacrifice.

"Having removed the garland from his head, he places it in a clean place"—from this rule regarding the disposal (*pratipatti*) of a used and disarrayed garland, it follows that there is an unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) quality specific to the garland.
Therefore, the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) mentioned here are for the purpose of removing impurity from the *śrī* (the body).
Furthermore, no removal of odor is observed in the body through such means as contact with earth and water.
Therefore, this purification— characterized by a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*)— should be understood as being like the purification of time such as [the period] from birth onwards.
Purified by this purification, one becomes entitled to perform the rites prescribed in the Śruti and Smṛti,
just as clarified butter purified by mantras is used in a burnt offering (*homa*).
In worldly affairs, however, purification occurs through the purification of the substance itself, as in the case of clarified butter used for eating and the like.
For instance, the touchability of a young boy is established merely by the fact that "his limbs are purified with water";
likewise, it is said: "There is no impurity resulting from touching him."
But how, then, can these have the status of being for the sake of ritual action (*karmārthatva*)?
It is logical that the act of purifying (*utpavana*) serves the purpose of the clarified butter (*ājya*), because it is enjoined within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of that specific rite;
however, these external [acts] are not heard of as being within the context of any particular ritual action.
Therefore, it is difficult to maintain that the purpose of the action resides in the person by way of him being the agent.
Furthermore, when there is no utility for the result, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) itself cannot be what is brought about by its own nature;
for if that were the case, the status of being a preparatory act (*saṃskārakarma*) would be lost, and it would instead become a primary act (*pradhānakarma*).

Furthermore, [if one were to argue that] "therefore the refinement of the body (*śarīrasaṃskāra*) must be performed," then the second [type of] scriptural hearing (*śruti*), namely "when a boy is born, before he is touched by others," would be sublated; there would be a disruption of the application (*viniyogabhaṅga*), as in the case of "he offers the *śatru* oblations.
In that case, many inconsistencies would arise, such as the necessity of postulating a new qualification (*adhikāra*).
To this, it is replied:

We do not state that the definition of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) consists in having that [principal] as its purpose (*tādarthya*) based on the authority of scripture and so forth; rather, it is the quality of being helpful (*upakārakatva*).

And that is possible even in the absence of being an auxiliary, as in the case of the injunction for the fire-laying (*ādhāna*) and the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*).

For here there are no direct scriptural statements (śruti) and so forth; since [the texts] such as "one offers in the Āhavanīya" have already assigned the Āhavanīya and other fires to their functions, and because their essential nature is non-worldly, their establishment is achieved solely through the injunction for laying the fires: "In spring, a Brāhmaṇa should lay the fires."
Therefore, the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) is employed in the sacrifices by way of bringing about the *āhavanīya* and other sacrificial fires;
yet it is not a subordinate element (*aṅga*).
Likewise, the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) also assists the sacrifices by way of producing the comprehension of the meaning [of the texts].

Thus are these *saṃskāras*. This is the procedure for the initiatory rites (*adhyayanavidhi*) of one so consecrated; for one who has completed the purpose of the initiatory rites, there is marriage; for one who has performed marriage, there is the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*); and for one who has established the fires, there is eligibility [for Vedic study]. Thus, there is a utility for external personal *saṃskāras* in the performance of ritual duties. Furthermore, because of the mention of the *niṣeka*, the father’s authority extends to all of them as well.
And likewise, there is a mantra at the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*): "Truly, you are the self named 'son'.
For it is prescribed that one must produce offspring and instruct one's offspring:
"Having discharged the three debts... and so forth.
Therefore, they say that a son who has been instructed is "worldly" (*lokyam*).
Instruction consists in the imparting of one's own office, and we shall explain that this occurs through the teaching of the Veda, culminating in the comprehension of its meaning.

For this very reason, the sacraments (*saṃskāra*) are beneficial to both: in the injunction for the procreation of offspring, they benefit the father; and in the rites to be accomplished by means of the refined youth, they benefit the boy.
Therefore, the right belongs to the father; in his absence, to one who occupies his position.
Thus it has been said: "But those who have not been consecrated should be consecrated by their brothers who have already been consecrated."
He now shows, by way of illustration, those actions in which the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) of the student are beneficial:

"By private Vedic study, by vows, by burnt offerings, by the threefold knowledge, by sacrifice, by sons, by the great sacrifices, and by ritual sacrifices, this body is made fit for union with Brahman."
The act of recitation is intended here by the word *svādhyāya*. This [term] "by one learned in the three Vedas" (*traividyena*) is the specification of its object;
for even when there is an intervention, a connection characterized by meaning exists, according to the principle that "whatever has a semantic connection with something [is connected to it]."

Therefore, even though there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the relationship between object and subject is established by changing the case-ending; the meaning is "by the study of the three Vedas.
The word *traividyam* refers to the three Vedas themselves;
its formation is established according to the rule for words such as *cāturvarṇya*.

Alternatively, "by self-study" refers to the study of the Vedas; "by the threefold knowledge" refers to the comprehension of their meaning; "by vows" refers to those such as the *sāvitra* and others performed by the religious student (*brahmacārin*);
and "by oblations" refers to those which are performed at the time of the instruction for the vows.

Alternatively, the kindling of the fire with fuel-sticks in the evening and morning by a religious student (*brahmacārin*) is referred to by the term "oblation" (*homa*) because of the commonality of its connection with the fire as a substratum.
Now, one might ask: is the placing of fuel-sticks not an oblation, such that it is said [to be called so] due to a commonality of connection?
They reply that it is not, because sacrifice (*yāga*) and oblation (*homa*) must be accomplished by means of substances fit for consumption.
How then? It has been stated: "One should, unwearied, offer oblations with those [verses] to the fire in the evening and in the morning."
By figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the placing of fuel sticks (*samid-ādhāna*) is expressed by the word "oblation" (*homa*).
Just as the substance being offered is cast into the fire, so too are the fuel sticks intended for the purpose of kindling.
Therefore, on the basis of this commonality, the act of kindling itself is called an oblation.
For in the originative injunction, it is heard: "One should place the *samidh* fuel-sticks";
[the phrase] "one should offer with them into the fire" (*juhuyāt tābhir agnim*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for another purpose, as we shall explain later.
And there is no fault of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in a restatement.
But this is logical: that sacrifice (*yāga*) and oblation (*homa*) are accomplished by means of substances that are merely pure.
And this being so, many injunctions become meaningful as they are intended, such as: "He casts the grass-bundle (*prastara*) with the *sūktavāka*."

For in that case, they say the sacrificial grass-bundle (prastara) is the substance and that one performs the sacrifice by carrying it; moreover, by virtue of the scriptural statement, that very act is indeed a sacrifice.
Furthermore, for some, even the darbha grass is edible.
How [is it] in the case of the *śākalahoma*?
If it is argued that even there the originative injunction is "for he places wood-shavings (*śakala*) on the fire," then what is the status of the *grahayajña*?
One should offer fuel-sticks (*samidh*) for each of the *graha*s, such as the *arka* and others.

Therefore, wherever it is heard in the originative injunction that "one should offer oblations," even in the case of wood and other materials, there too it is indeed a *homa*, because of the connection with a deity.
[This is] by means of sacrifice (*ijyā*) and the satiation of gods and sages.
This, then, is the collection of ritual duties for one who has been initiated during the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*).
Now follow the duties of the householder:
by means of sons through the rite for procreating offspring,
and by means of the five great sacrifices beginning with the sacrifice to Brahman.
"By sacrifices," such as the *jyotiṣṭoma* and others prescribed by the revealed scriptures (*śruti*).
Now, if these ritual acts had some other purpose, then external purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) intended for producing fitness for those specific entitlements would be meaningful;
therefore, he says: "This body is made fit for Brahman."

Brahman is the Supreme Self, the causal Person; this body belonging to Him is His physical form, which is fashioned by all these rites prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti. And its connection with Brahman consists in attaining His very nature; for that indeed is the supreme human goal.
Other types of relations need not be sought after, since everything whatsoever is already established as a cause [of liberation].
Thus, the attainment of liberation is stated.
By the word *brāhmī* and by the word *tanu*, the Puruṣa who presides over that [body] is indicated.
For these purificatory rites (saṃskāras) pertain to his body;
and it is he alone who attains liberation upon the dissolution of the body into the five elements.
Others, however, say that [the rite] renders one fit for the attainment of the state of Brahman.

For the attainment of the state of Brahman does not occur through ritual actions alone; indeed, liberation results from the combination of wisdom and action. One who has been purified by these [actions] becomes qualified for the meditations on the Self. Thus says the Śruti: "O Gārgī, he who performs sacrifices, offers oblations, practices austerity, studies, or gives gifts, without knowing this Imperishable—one's [efforts] become merely finite."

But is it not the case that the attainment of Brahman is not heard in scripture as the fruit of these actions? For instance, the obligatory rites (*nitya*) have no fruit mentioned at all; and if one were to postulate such a fruit, there would be the consequence of human authorship (*pauruṣeyatva*).

Furthermore, since permanence (*nityatā*) is understood through words such as "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*), the *viśvajit*-maxim (*nyāya*) does not apply here either. If it were argued that this [action] has fruit solely on account of this very scriptural statement, then it would follow that only those seeking liberation (*mokṣa*) would have the qualification (*adhikāra*) for it; in that case, its status as a permanent duty (*nityatva*) would be lost, and there would consequently be a contradiction with the Śruti. If it is argued that no one performs what is fruitless, and thus [the injunction] would be purposeless (*anarthakya*), then let it simply not be performed.
The purpose of a means of valid cognition is the comprehension of the object of cognition;
if that has been accomplished, its purposiveness is established.
And here, there is indeed the comprehension of what is to be done.
And when that [obligation] exists, its non-performance constitutes a transgression of the meaning of the scripture, and from that follows demerit (*pratyavāya*).
It is precisely regarding such a matter that the understanding of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others arises from the linguistic usage of the elders:
for a servant or similar person who does not perform what is to be done by someone who has issued a command—whether seeking wages or not—does not receive his wages, or else he is joined with demerit.

In that regard, since no fruit is explicitly mentioned, the non-occurrence of a fruit is not what constitutes the transgression (*pratyavāya*) in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*); rather, it is the connection with suffering.
In this way, the universal qualification of all persons for the obligatory rites is established.
Therefore, there is no fruit whatsoever for the obligatory rites.
But the fruit of optional rites (*kāmya-karman*) is indeed something else; it is not liberation (*mokṣa*), because that is what is heard [in scripture].
In that case, how can this supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*) be accomplished through the performance of all ritual actions?
For this very reason, some explain this as a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

The ritual procedure is for the purpose of praise. And here, the term "belonging to Brahmā" (brāhmīyam) is interpreted figuratively by relying on some basis whatsoever. [It means] that which is for the purpose of reciting the Veda (brahman), and that which qualifies one for its rituals.
If that is so, how is it that Gautama stated there are forty *saṃskāras*?
For in that context, even the *somasaṃsthā* sacrifices are mentioned as *saṃskāras*;
yet it is not possible for primary rituals (*pradhānakarman*) to be considered *saṃskāras*.
Nor can this be explained as a mere explanatory eulogy (arthavāda), because there is no distinction [between the cases].
In that instance [of the former], there was praise by superimposing the status of being a residual refinement of the self's qualities;
likewise here too, having equated the refinements with the [other] refinements by superimposing an equality of results, [the text] declares the necessity of performing the refinements.
And thus, it is not extracted from the section on formative forces (saṃskāra);
furthermore, the statement "praise is being performed" is a description in the present tense,
not an injunctive suffix.
In that case, how is it understood that the attainment of Brahman is the fruit?

Nor are ritual actions enjoined here, such that—given the requirement for a qualification (*adhikāra*)—there could be an indication of a fruit despite the use of the present tense, as in the case of "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) in the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice.
Therefore, all of this is stated solely for the purpose of praising the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*).

Even those who describe a distinction—namely, that the fruit of obligatory rites (*nitya*) is the attainment of Brahman, while that of optional rites (*kāmya*) is exactly as stated in the scriptures—that too is without authority, because all of this is merely explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Furthermore, it has been established that the performance of obligatory rites is accomplished even without a [desirable] fruit;
thus it is said: "To be motivated by desire is not praiseworthy."
Before the cutting of the umbilical cord, the birth-rite (jātakarma) is prescribed for the male child;
it includes the ceremonial feeding of him with gold, honey, and clarified butter, accompanied by sacred mantras.
Vardhana means cutting.
"Jātakarman" is the name of this rite;
its specific form is to be understood from the Gṛhya-smṛtis.
Of what rite, then, is "jātakarman" (the birth-rite) the name? To that end it is said: "The consumption of gold, honey, and clarified butter.
They designate the child by the word "asya" (of this), or rather, they indicate that among the constituent acts of this jātakarman, the primary one is this consumption performed with mantras.
The meaning is that it must be performed with a mantra along with its accompaniment (*samantraka*).
Since no specific mantra is mentioned here, and because the *Smṛtis* share a common purpose, what is stated elsewhere is understood to apply here as well.
Therefore, it should be understood that the rite is to be performed "with mantras" by means of those mantras which are included in the *Gṛhya-smṛtis*.
If the Gṛhya-smṛtis are to be relied upon, then even the specification of the substances should not be made;
for it is recited there: "Clarified butter and honey, with a rubbing of gold; one should cause [the child] to eat with gold, saying: 'I give to you of honey and clarified butter.
Furthermore, there are many Gṛhya-smṛtis, and the mantras for each Gṛhya rite differ, as do the various procedures (itikartavyatā); we do not know which of these should be adopted.

Now, if it is argued that the designation by school (caraṇa) will serve as the restrictive factor—such that the instruction regarding birth-rites (*jātakarman*) and so forth would be useless because they are already established through that very designation; and that whatever is designated as "the Gṛhya of the Kaṭhas," "the Gṛhya of the Bahvṛcas," or "the Gṛhya of the Āśvalāyanas," the person associated with that designation will perform what was taught therein—it is replied: [The objection continues: "In that case, the instruction regarding the birth-rite and so forth would be purposeless, since it is already established by that [designation] alone. For whatever is designated as 'the Gṛhya of the Kaṭhas,' 'the Gṛhya of the Bahvṛcas,' or 'the Gṛhya of the Āśvalāyanas,' the person associated with that [designation] will perform what was taught therein. To this, it is said: [The following refutation follows].

Through the specification of the substance and other factors, the oneness of the ritual action (*karman*) is clearly understood; for thus is the establishment of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*): "This very substance is this [same] one, and this ritual action bears that same name; therefore, this is indeed that. It is recognized through repeated observation by virtue of its association with those qualities.
And since there is unity [of the dharma], that part which is not mentioned in any one [text] may be brought from another without contradiction;
just as a single ritual act is recognized through all Vedic branches (*śākhā*), so too is it recognized through all the *smṛtis*.
As for the uncertainty regarding which [text] should be adopted due to the multiplicity of the *Gṛhya-smṛtis*, [it is resolved as follows]:

Since all [scriptural sources] are equal in their authority, those that have the same object are to be treated as alternatives (*vikalpa*), while those with different objects are to be combined (*samuccaya*).

However, the designation of a *caraṇa* (Vedic school) is not at all a restrictive factor; for the connection of a person with a *caraṇa* is not fixed by that designation, just as in the case of *gotra* and *pravara*.
Whichever branch has been studied by someone, that person is designated accordingly as a "Kaṭha" or a "Bahvṛca.

Furthermore, there is no restrictive rule regarding study stating that "this specific person must study this specific branch," for there is indeed the study of multiple branches, as evidenced by the injunction: "Having studied the Vedas... (vedān adhītya).

In that regard, all designations proceed for those who study three Vedas; some say they are Kauthumas, Kaṭhas, or Bahvṛcas, and in such cases, one must necessarily accept an option. However, for one who studies a single branch, it is proper for him to perform exactly what is prescribed by the Gṛhya-sūtra with which his own branch is designated.
For he alone is capable of performing exactly what has been prescribed; it is precisely his own ritual formulas (*śākhā-mantra*) that have been studied by him, and he is able to employ them.
Or rather, he knows that very [branch] which has been chosen.
And the study of the Veda is for the purpose of performing rituals, so that one may study as many mantras as are useful for those rituals.
It is said:
the study of the Veda is by virtue of the injunction for private recitation (*svādhyāya-vidhi*);
one who has not studied the Veda has no entitlement [to perform rites].
Nor is the study [of the Veda] prompted by ritual action;
therefore, this designation—such as "the Gṛhya of the Kaṭhas" or "the Gṛhya of the Vājasaneyins"—is based solely on the application of specific mantras.
In whichever branch (śākhā) certain mantras have been studied, that Gṛhya-sūtra in which those mantras are predominantly employed is designated accordingly.
The *Gṛhyasmṛti* is an authoritative means of knowledge;
although it is designated as "this [work] of the Kaṭhas," it certainly brings about the comprehension of its own meaning for the *Bahvṛcas* as well.
The Veda and the *smṛtis* alike have the obligation to convey their own meaning.

Furthermore, once the duty to act has been understood, if no specific agent is heard mentioned, one's own entitlement [to perform it] would not exist—just as, for example, the *tanūnapāt* fore-offering belongs to the Vasiṣṭhas; or else, [entitlement] would be lost due to a prohibition.
But neither of these two cases applies here.

Nor can it be assumed that the *Bāhvṛcya* (the Ṛgveda) is not authoritative for the Kaṭhas, or that the *Kāṭhaka* is not authoritative for the Bahvṛcas; for he who is a Kaṭha is the very same person as an Akatha, provided there is no study of that particular recension.
But the lineage is fixed; thus [the opponent's position] is inconsistent.
This very point is expressed by the saying: "He who abandons his own sutra and proceeds according to another sutra—whatever he studies therein, its meaning can be practiced."

Therefore, if one should bypass the branch (*śākhā*) one has studied oneself and perform rituals according to a branch studied by one's father or others, and should likewise adopt their *Gṛhya* manual, he incurs the fault of abandoning his own branch.
Alternatively, there is the abandonment of the branch on the part of the father and others, by whom the youth was not taught the branch studied in the traditional sequence.
In this case, the youth is not at fault.

When this boy, having lost his father, should personally take refuge with a teacher—just as Jābāla did—then, by the scriptural injunction "one should study that [branch] by which one's fathers have gone," it would be proper for him to study that very branch.
If, however, the study of his own ancestral branch (*ātmaśākhā*) is not possible, then he may abandon his own branch.
Therefore, this conclusion stands.
In all Smṛtis, the entire set of rites beginning with the birth-ceremony (jātakarman) is taught.

Among these, those parts which serve different purposes are to be combined; those that are contradictory are to be treated as options; and those that serve the same purpose are likewise [to be combined].
The word "of a male" (puṃsaḥ) is used for the purpose of excluding females and neuter persons.

Others, however, consider the human purpose (pumartha) not to be intended [as a specific gender], because the term "of the twice-born" (*dvijanmanām*) generally introduces the three castes as the subjects to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*). And since the subject to be consecrated is the primary referent (*uddeśya*), a qualifying attribute such as gender or number is not intended to be significant in relation to that primary referent.
Just as in the injunction "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), even though the singular number is used, all cups are indeed cleansed.
"One should feed the man who has been afflicted by fever at the end of the day";
thus, this same time for eating applies even to a woman afflicted by fever. And so, there is a prohibition against what would otherwise have been obtained [at other times].
"This rite for women is to be performed without mantras; this is the procedure for women.
And regarding eunuchs, it is observed that there is the taking of the hand [in marriage] if there is a desire for wives on the part of those such as the impotent.
To this, it is replied:

This word *pumān* is not a term denoting the human species like the word *nara*, such that the gender expressed by the case-ending would not be intended to be significant. For this [word] everywhere denotes the specific characteristic (*liṅga*) in the form of procreation, pertaining to both stationary and mobile beings, as well as to those with form and those without form. Indeed, in this context, the gender is the meaning of the nominal stem itself.

For it is appropriate to speak of the intention or non-intention [to express] a meaning that is denoted by a case-ending (*vibhakti*), because the mere utterance of a case-ending does not have a single purpose; rather, it possesses utility even by expressing other meanings such as the object (*karman*) and so forth.
In this case, however, if there were no intention to express it, the masculine word-form would result in being utterly meaningless.
Just as in that very case, the meaning of the nominal stem *graha* is intended to be expressed in order to avoid the redundancy of the sentence;
yet, if it were argued that there is no intention to express the mere meaning of the suffix,
then the entire word-meaning— even when serving as a qualifier of that which is being indicated— would not be intended to be expressed.
Just as in the case of the rule "for whom both oblations [are spoiled]," even though the word "both" (ubhaya) is heard, that same expiation applies even if only one of the two—curd or milk—is lost;
the word "both" is not intended to be restrictive.
Regarding this, some offer the following resolution:
This is not the same as that;
for the five-platter offering does not have the oblation as its purpose.
Rather, the entitlement to perform it is contingent upon the destruction of the oblation.

In this case, however, the grammatical refinements (*saṃskāra*) pertain solely to the meaning of the word *māṇavaka*. This distinction, moreover, is not a governing factor; for fear of splitting the sentence (*vākyabheda*), the intention to express the qualifier is not admitted.
Even if it were for the sake of that [purpose], the syntactical split (vākyabheda) would not be avoided;
therefore, this is the solution:
this very sentence is the originative injunction (utpattivākya) of the birth-rite (jātakarman).
This begins with the phrase "by means of Vedic rites.

In that context, the male alone is specified as the one to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*). If his [gender] were not intended to be significant, the sentence would be purposeless, just as in that very same context the word *havis* (oblation) is intended to be significant.
If this were so, then the Śūdra would also attain [the right to study], since no specific caste has been mentioned;
yet he will not attain it, because [Vedic study] is accomplished through mantras.
Alternatively, the phrase "of the twice-born" (dvijanmanām) will serve as a supplementary statement to complete the sentence.

And at that time, [the person] was not specified as being the object of the injunction, such that—once the person to be refined (*saṃskārya*) were understood from that very [specification]—one might suspect that the word "man" (*pumsaḥ*), like the word with two genders, was intended as non-significant (*avivakṣita*).
However, for women, the injunction is appropriate even though [the rite] was not previously established;
the same applies to the observation of the wife even for a eunuch (*klība*).
One whose semen is wind-like, one who is impotent, one who possesses both sets of sexual characteristics, or one whose organs have not functioned;
because these conditions are difficult to determine at the time of purificatory rites such as the birth ceremony (*jātakarman*) and because they can be remedied, they do not exclude eligibility.
Furthermore, a characteristic that is not fixed does not preclude eligibility, just as the lack of property (*adravyatva*) does not; for the lack of property is not fixed like one's caste (*jāti*).
Even he who is without wealth becomes possessed of wealth; having been poor for a long time, one becomes very wealthy in a single day.
For the killing of such a eunuch, purification is achieved by [carrying] a load of straw.
For that [Self] is unconditioned and unapproachable; it does not abide for the sake of peace for anyone.
Therefore, these sacraments (saṃskāras) are established as belonging only to men, and they are prescribed by these [rules];
by another rule, those for women are performed without mantras.
For a neuter person, they do not exist at all.
One should perform the naming ceremony for him on the tenth or the twelfth day,
or on an auspicious lunar date, at a favorable moment, or under a constellation endowed with excellent qualities.
On the tenth or the twelfth lunar day, one should perform the naming ceremony for that child;
the causative sense (*ṇij-artha*) is not intended here.
Thus, the *Gṛhya-sūtra* states: "Having raised [the child] on the tenth day, the father gives him a name."
"Name" (*nāma*) is indeed "name-giving" (*nāmadheya*).
That word by which one is called upon for specific tasks is a "name.

Because the rite of birth (*jātakarman*) is the subject under discussion in the phrase "prior to the cutting of the umbilical cord," the tenth and twelfth days from birth are intended here, and not lunar dates.

In this regard, some explain that the mention of the tenth day is intended as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the cessation of impurity, and they supply the word "having passed" (*atītāyām*), so that [the meaning becomes]: "when the tenth day has passed for a Brāhmaṇa, on the twelfth for a Kṣatriya, and on the fifteenth for a Vaiśya.
That is incorrect.

Since there is no authoritative evidence for [the application of] secondary figurative indication (lakṣaṇā), this rite shall be performed during the period of impurity (āśauca) as well, just like the birth-rite (jātakarman).
However, if the feeding of Brahmins is prescribed in some instance, then figurative indication would be appropriate;
if the tenth and twelfth days possess the qualities to be described hereafter, then it should be performed on those two days.
If not, then on another auspicious day;
"auspicious days" refers to the second, fifth, and so forth.
"Auspicious" means praiseworthy; the ninth, fourteenth, and other such empty lunar days (*riktās*) are inauspicious.
A *muhūrta* is the ascendant (*lagna*), such as Aquarius and so forth;
it is "auspicious" when it is not occupied by malefic planets and is aspected by the two [benefic] teachers (*guru*).
The purity of the ascendant is understood from astrology (*jyotiṣa*).
And "when the lunar mansion is endowed with auspicious qualities":
the lunar mansion refers to Śraviṣṭhā and so forth; that day on which it becomes endowed with such qualities.
And the qualities of the lunar mansion consist in being free from cruel planets, malefic planets, planetary conjunctions (viṣṭi), and the vyatīpāta yoga.
The word *vā* signifies conjunction;
by it, it is taught that [the rite should be performed] on an auspicious lunar day (*tithi*), under a pure asterism (*nakṣatra*), and at an auspicious moment (*lagna*).
And this conjunction is to be understood through astrology (*jyotiṣa*).
And this is the ultimate truth:
it should not be performed before the tenth or twelfth lunar day;
and at a later time, it should be performed on that very day when the lunar mansion and the ascendant are completely pure.
Now he prescribes what kind of name should be given, both in terms of its form and its meaning:
"The name of a Brāhmaṇa should be auspicious; that of a Kṣatriya should be endowed with power;
that of a Vaiśya should be connected with wealth; but that of a Śūdra should be contemptible."

In this regard, intending to determine its essential nature (*svarūpa*), he says: the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) is that "māṅgalya" means that which is beneficial for auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) or that which is good therein.
"Auspiciousness" (*maṅgala*) is the accomplishment of a desired object, such as long life, abundant wealth, and so forth, which results in the fruit of happiness both seen and unseen.
The very denotation of that [object] constitutes the word's "beneficiality" (hitatva) and its "correctness" (sādhutva); thus, the formation of the secondary derivative (taddhita) is established.
Correctness is not intended here to mean merely the communication of the accomplishment of a desired object;
rather, it is the accomplishment of that which is wished for by the very utterance of the word.
From a compound (samāsa), the attainment of longevity, the attainment of wealth, the acquisition of a son, and so forth, are understood;
or from a secondary derivative (taddhita) expressing benefit, cause, or purpose.

In that regard, within the Gṛhya texts, the use of words ending in a taddhita suffix is prohibited by the rule: "One should perform what has been prescribed [by the sūtra], not what is formed by a taddhita."
Even in a compound, there is the unification of the two words into a single meaning; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of employing too many syllables.
For he will state the rule regarding the secondary word (*upapada*) as "possessing the word *śarman* for a Brāhmaṇa.
In that case, when the name consists of four or three syllables and the word *śarman* is used as the secondary word, the name becomes five or six syllables long.
And that [name] has been prohibited; therefore, one should make it consist of two or four syllables.

Consequently, whatever is generally desirable to everyone and not blameworthy—such as a son, cattle, a village, a daughter, wealth, and so forth—the words denoting these things are to be employed as names, ending with the suffix *śarman*.
By this, the inclusion of such terms as Gośarman, Dhanaśarman, Hiraṇyaśarman, Kalyāṇaśarman, and Maṅgalyaśarman is established.
Alternatively, "mangala" is dharma, and that which accomplishes it is called "maṅgalya. What, then, is that which accomplishes dharma?
It refers to these words for deities: Indra, Agni, Vāyu, and so forth.
Likewise, there are the words "ṛṣis," such as Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and Medhātithi;
for them, too, there exists the means for accomplishing dharma.
"One should satisfy the sages and meditate upon those who have performed meritorious deeds.
"A man desiring prosperity, having awakened at dawn, should recite the names of the deities, the sages, and the twice-born who have performed meritorious acts."
And by the inclusion of the auspicious, that which is inauspicious—such as Yama, Death, and so forth—is excluded; as is that which is meaningless, such as "Ḍittha" and other names based on mere whim.
For a Kṣatriya, [the name] should be endowed with power;
that is, it should be joined with strength and expressive of power.

*Anvaya* is connection; the connection between a word and its meaning is precisely the relationship of signifier and signified. *Sāmarthya* is power; by whatever [name] one is designated, such a name should be given to a Kṣatriya.
"Subduer of enemies," "Duryodhana," "Protector of Subjects," and so forth;
by such distinctions, the designation of names serves as a mark of caste.
Likewise, for a Vaiśya, [the name] is connected with wealth.

And here, it is not merely synonyms that are understood—such as *dhana*, *vitta*, and *svāpateya*—but rather the manner in which the cognition [of wealth] occurs. This may be either through the employment of words such as "wealth" (*dhana*) and so forth, or through the connection with the object itself; for example, one who performs the act of giving wealth is called "one of great wealth" (*mahādhana*), or "one possessing cows" (*gomān*), or "one who acquires grain" (*dhānyagraha*).
This should be understood in all cases.
Thus, there is the use of words such as "possessed of strength" (*balānvita*) and "endowed with wealth" (*dhanasaṃyukta*).
Otherwise, he would have simply said, "one should give the names of strength."

Because words denoting strength and the like are very few, whereas individual persons are infinite and their distinctions difficult to ascertain, the cessation of linguistic usage would surely result.
[Examples include] "śūdra" as a term of contempt, and "kṛpaṇaka," "dīna," or "śabaraka" as terms for the wretched and the lowly.

The name of a Brāhmaṇa should end with a word meaning "shelter" (śarman); that of a Kṣatriya should be endowed with a word meaning "protection" (rakṣā); that of a Vaiśya should be joined with a word meaning "prosperity" (puṣṭi); and that of a Śūdra should be joined with a word meaning "servant" (preṣya).
In this context, the mention of the essential form (*svarūpa*) and the sequence of recitation [are established by the rule], with an auspicious word at the beginning and the word *śarman* at the end;
this has been illustrated accordingly.

However, this does not apply to the names of Kṣatriyas and others, because the feminine form of the word *rakṣā* is heard [in their case], making grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with masculine [names] impossible.
Therefore, because they share a single commencement and because of established usage, the term "artha" (meaning/purpose) is to be understood everywhere;
and because there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*).
That which is auspicious (*maṅgalya*) is also meaningful for the sake of merit (*śarmārthavat*).

*Śarma*, *śaraṇa*, and *āśraya* mean happiness; by the inclusion of the term "meaning" (*artha*), words such as *svāmidatta* and *bhaṭṭabhūti* are also included. For example: Indrasvāmī, Indrāśraya, and Indradatta.
Its being the basis is thus understood;
in this manner, it should be inferred in all cases.
Now, what is this "cause" (hetu)? Is it a conjunction (samuccaya) due to the difference in the sentences?
One might ask: "Why is there not a combination [of both], as in 'one should sacrifice with rice' and 'one should sacrifice with barley'?
It is replied:
this is merely an observation of indicative marks (liṅga), because the text is of human origin.
If an alternative were intended, he would have said "maṅgalyam" or "śarmavat" for the sake of brevity;
for in the case of a split sentence, there is a double utterance of the verb,
which makes it cumbersome.
Protection (*rakṣā*) means guarding, nourishing, increasing, and preserving; for example, "Govṛddha" and "Dhanagupta. A servant (*preṣya*) is a slave (*dāsa*).
A slave of a Brahmin is one who belongs to a Brahmin; a slave of a deity is one who belongs to a deity.
For women, [the speech] should be easy to pronounce, gentle, clear in meaning, captivating, auspicious, ending in long vowels, and characterized by benedictory expressions.
Since the term "of a man" (*puṃsaḥ*) is the subject under discussion, this is prescribed because [the name] would otherwise not apply to women.
"Easy to pronounce" (*sukhodyam*) means that which is easily uttered;
a woman's name should be one that can be pronounced with ease even by women and children.

For the most part, the transactions of women are conducted with other women and children; and because they lack proficiency in their own grammatical formulation, they do not have the capacity to utter every refined (saṃskṛta) word.
Therefore, it is taught specifically for them;
however, it is not permitted for men that what is difficult to pronounce be uttered.
The examples are Maṅgaladevī, Cārudatī, Suvadanā, and so forth. The counter-examples are Śarmiṣṭhā and Suśliṣṭāṅgī.
Akrūra is used when it does not express the meaning "not cruel."
"Harsh in meaning" refers to that which has a cruel sense, such as "ḍākinī" or "paruṣā.

"Clear in meaning" is that whose meaning is not to be understood through further explanation, but produces comprehension of the meaning for both the learned and the unlearned upon being heard alone. "Unclear in meaning" is, for example, "kāmanidhā" or "kārīṣagandhyā."
Just as with the expression "the treasure of desire," [it is understood that] "by means of her, desire remains right there";
so too, as long as it has not been explained, it is not understood.
In this way, the explanation that Kārīṣagandhyā is the daughter of Kārīṣagandhi is required.
*Manoharā* is that which is pleasing to the mind and brings about well-being;
*Kālākṣī*, however, is the opposite.
*Śarmavatī* and *Rudravatī* are auspicious names.
"Viparīta" means "not my portion"; that which has the long vowel at its end is [the word] "viparīta," meaning "autumn."
"Āśīrvāda" means that which utters a blessing (āśis);
it is a designation (abhidhāna), that is, a word (śabda).
Between these two [terms], there is a descriptive compound (viśeṣaṇasamāsa).
Therefore, that in which something exists is found to be designated by a blessing, such as "having a son," "having many sons," or "one who upholds the lineage.
For these meanings are the objects of blessings;
conversely, their opposites are "inauspicious" and "without auspicious marks."
Now, what is the difference between an auspicious word (*maṅgalya*) and a benediction (*āśīrvāda*)?
None at all.
However, they are mentioned separately for the sake of completing the meter and the sense.
In the fourth month, the child's first exit from the house should be performed;
in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana), or whatever auspicious rite is desired in the family.
In the fourth month from birth, the infant child must be taken out of the house for the purpose of seeing the sun;
he should be kept within the inner chamber for three months.
The mention of the "infant" (śiśu) is intended to include even a Śūdra.
Thus, in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) takes place;
for five months, the child’s diet consists solely of milk.
Alternatively, one may follow whatever auspicious and propitiatory rites are well-known in the family, such as offerings to Pūtanā, Śakunika, or the Ekavṛkṣa, for the welfare of the child.
Or rather, that [rite] should be performed at a specific time;
and this is a remainder of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, the name is obtained according to family custom, even apart from the previously stated characteristics.
Indrasvāmī, Indraśarmā, Indrabhūmi, Indraghoṣa, Indrarāta, Indraviṣṇu, Indradeva, Indrajyoti, Indrayaśas, and so forth—these arise according to the distinctions of family lineages.
The tonsure ceremony for all twice-born classes must be performed according to dharma in either the first or the third year, as enjoined by the Vedas.
*Cūḍā* means a crest or tuft of hair;
the ritual performed for that purpose is *cūḍākarma*.
This *cūḍākarma* refers to the specific arrangement and fixing of the hair on certain parts of the head.
In the first or the third year; there is an option based on the favorable position of the planets.
The statement "because of the injunction of the Veda" is a restatement, since its authority has already been established by the fact that it is rooted in that very [Veda].

Alternatively, by the word "śruti," not only prescriptive sentences are meant, but rather the *mantras*. And these, like [the mantra] "The people who perform the tonsure ceremony... (*cūḍākarma yāñ janāḥ*), manifest an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*); for instance, [the mantra] "What one should cleanse with the razor" (*yat kṣureṇa mārjayeta*) and so forth. By this, it is stated that this ritual act is accompanied by *mantras*.
When there is a requirement for a specific rule, the domestic (gārhya) injunction is accepted.
Therefore, this sacrament does not apply to a Śūdra, because of the mention of the "twice-born" (dvijāti).
However, the shaving of the hair at an indefinite time, which is naturally required for a Śūdra, is not prohibited.
One should perform the initiation (*upanayana*) of a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception;
that of a Kṣatriya in the eleventh year from conception; and that of a Vaiśya in the twelfth year from conception.
The year spent in the womb is that from which the eighth year is reckoned;
by association with the word "womb," the year is indicated,
for in its primary sense, the womb cannot be designated as having an "eighth year."
In that [year], one should perform the *aupanāyana* for a Brāhmaṇa.
*Aupanāyana* is simply *upanayana*; the suffix *aṇ* is used in its own sense (*svārthika*).
The lengthening of the final vowel of the second member of the compound is according to the rule "it is seen in other cases as well" (*anyeṣām api dṛśyate*).
Alternatively, due to its Vedic character (*chāndasatva*), there is vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) for both members of the compound.
For "initiation" (*upanayana*) is a sacramental rite well-known among those who know the Vedas in their *Gṛhya-smṛtis*, synonymous with "tying the sacred girdle" (*mauñjībandhana*).

It is called *upanayana* because by means of it one is led near (*upanīyate*) or brought into the presence of the teacher for the purpose of studying one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*), as if to build a wall or a mat [for that purpose].
This is the name for a distinguished sacramental rite (*saṃskārakarman*).
For a king, it is on the eleventh year from conception;
that is, for a Kṣatriya, it should be performed in the eleventh year from birth or from conception.

This word *rājan* denotes the Kṣatriya caste and does not depend upon the possession of qualities such as consecration (*abhiṣeka*), because we observe its usage in that sense in the scriptures, and because it occurs in association with words denoting the Brāhmaṇa and other castes.
Furthermore, since the word "Kṣatriya" is seen in injunctions regarding specific qualities— such as in the rule "the girdle of a Kṣatriya is made of bowstring"—
we shall explain that any usage of the word *rājan* for anyone other than a Kṣatriya, such as a Vaiśya who is a lord of a territory, is figurative.
When the primary sense is absent, the secondary sense is accepted;
and thus the author of the Gṛhyasūtras states: "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year, a Kṣatriya in the eleventh, and a Vaiśya in the twelfth.

And the venerable Pāṇini likewise accepts this very principle, for by stating that "the function of a king is kingship" (*rājñaḥ karma rājyam*), he asserts the status of the word *rājya* as the derivative base (*prakṛti*) in relation to the word *rājan*, thereby declaring that the meaning of the word *rājan* is established through sovereignty over a territory.
In this manner, for a Vaiśya, [initiation] should take place in the twelfth year from conception.
The initiation of a Brahmin who desires spiritual luster should be performed in the fifth year;
that of a King seeking power in the sixth; and that of a Vaiśya desiring prosperity in the eighth.

One designates offspring according to the father’s dharma, thinking, "May my son be endowed with Vedic luster (brahmavarcasī)"; thus, by the father's desire, the son is designated as belonging to that [desire].
Since the son is a child, such a desire is not possible for him.
But surely, if it is accepted that the fruit of an action performed by one person accrues to another, does this not result in the fault of "attaining what was not done" (akṛtābhyāgama)?
And even though this result occurs without being desired, it is stated thus by transcending the boundaries of verbal testimony, authoritative means of knowledge, and logical reasoning;
this is not a fault,
for this will be like the Śyena sacrifice.
One performing the Śyena sacrifice does it for the purpose of malevolent magic, and the one against whom the magic is directed dies.
Now, it might be argued that this result belongs only to the one who desires it;
for the sacrificer indeed desires the death of his enemy.
Since that very [result] is obtained [by the one who performs the initiation], the fruit does not go to the non-agent.
Here too, the result characterized by the possession of a distinguished son belongs to the initiator alone.

Just as a father experiences joy through the health of his son, so too [does he experience it] through the son's Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*); therefore, that fruit belongs to the agent who is the one authorized [for the rite]. For the determination of the meaning of a scripture follows the logical connection (*anvaya*).
And here, the syntactical connection (anvaya) is understood as "this must be done by the son precisely because he desires the fruit";
furthermore, there is no authority for abandoning the syntactical connection exactly as it is heard.
By this, the benefit performed for the father after death by the son is also explained.
For even in that case, the son is the agent and the satisfaction of the father is the fruit;
likewise, there is the indicative mark: "The self, indeed, has the name 'son'.
Indeed, by the father himself, the *śrāddha* has in reality already been performed with the self as the recipient, since the procreation of offspring was undertaken for this very purpose.

Just as in the *Sarvasvāra* sacrifice, when the sacrificer has died, the agency for even those subsequent ritual acts belongs to the sacrificer himself— by means of the injunction, "O Brāhmaṇas, complete the sacrifice," and because at the conclusion of the performance he is the employer of the officiating priests through the giving of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) or their selection— so too here, since the son is produced for that purpose, whatever is performed for the sake of the father, such as the *śrāddha* and other rites, is considered performed by the father himself.
Spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) consists in being endowed with Vedic study and realized knowledge.
Strength (*bala*) is internal capacity, both spiritual (*brāhma*) and physical.

The power of enthusiasm (*utsāha-śakti*) and great vital energy (*mahā-prāṇatā*) constitute the internal [strength], while the external consists of the excellence of elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, and the treasury. As it has been said: "The excellence of one's own limbs and the acquisition of external resources."
*Īhā* means exertion;
it refers to business activities such as agriculture and trade conducted with abundant wealth.
In all cases, the counting of years begins from conception (*garbha*), for the term "from conception" (*garbhāt*) is understood to carry over [from the preceding rule].
The Sāvitrī does not expire for a Brāhmaṇa until the sixteenth year,
for a Kṣatriya until the twenty-second, and for a Vaiśya until the twenty-fourth.
Thus, the two primary optional times for initiation have been stated.

Now, if the boy has not been initiated due to the absence of the father or some other cause such as illness, and the prescribed time has thus elapsed, it might follow that he is no longer eligible for initiation; for even though the time is a subordinate factor (*aṅga*), the qualification ceases in its absence, just as the *agnihotra* sacrifice is not performed when the morning and evening times have passed.
Therefore, this [next section] is commenced as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to provide for cases outside the prescribed times.
Up until the sixteenth year from conception, the eligibility of a Brāhmaṇa for initiation (*upanayana*) does not cease.
By the word *sāvitrī*, the rite called initiation—which has the recitation of that [verse] as its means—is indicated.
"It does not pass beyond" means that it does not become a time that has elapsed.
Thus, up to the twenty-second [generation] of the *kṣatrabandhu*— meaning one belonging to the *kṣatriya* caste—
the word *bandhu* is sometimes used in a derogatory sense, as in the expression: "How do you know your own [lineage], O wretched Brahmin (*brahmabandhu*)?"
Regarding the word *jñāti* (kinsman), as it is said:
"The state of being a village-dweller, a community-member, a kinsman, and an associate—even for Mahendra, this is inaccessible; how much more so for those who rule over portions of the earth?"

Regarding the rule "the suffix *cha* is applied after a word ending in *jāti* when it denotes a substance and signifies a *bandhu*," since the first two meanings are impossible here, the third meaning is adopted.
Thus, "the twenty-second year" (*dvāviṃśa abdaḥ*) is the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*).

The suffix denoting completion (*pūraṇapratyaya*) applies up to twenty-four; although it would have been applicable here as well, it was not employed out of consideration for the meter, yet its meaning is nonetheless understood.
For it is impossible for the number twenty-four, which refers to a collective whole, to function as a limit (*avadhi*).
The twenty-fourth part of that, however, is the year as the limit;
they explain the prefix *ā-* as inclusive (*abhividhi*),
and they cite a scriptural indication (*liṅga*) as evidence.
"One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa with the Gāyatrī, a Rājanya with the Triṣṭubh, and a Vaiśya with the Jagatī.
And for these meters, two quarters are completed within such a period of time;
during that much time, they remain powerful and do not abandon the social classes (varṇas) that serve as their own substrata.
But when the third stage has passed, they become devoid of vigor, their capacities diminished, and they reach their end,
just as it is said that a man of five hundred years is an elder. And for this reason, thinking "we have not been honored by him," they abandon that caste.
Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa does not have a *gāyatrī* *sāvitrī*, nor a Rājanya a *triṣṭubh*, nor a Vaiśya a *jagatī*.

That *ṛc* whose deity is Savitṛ is "Sāvitrī"; and that [Sāvitrī] should be understood as the *gāyatrī* which has been shown and prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. Likewise, for a Kṣatriya, the *triṣṭubh* Sāvitrī is "Ā kṛṣṇena."
For a Vaiśya, [the verse] "jagatī viśvā rūpāṇi" [is used].
Beyond this time, all three of these, having become unrefined through the lapse of the Sāvitrī initiation, become Vratyas, despised by the Aryas.

From this time forward, beyond [the limit], all these three castes—the Brāhmaṇas and the others—when their respective time for initiation has passed, even if it is a secondary period, become unrefined (*asaṃskṛta*), that is, they have not undergone initiation; they are fallen from the *Sāvitrī* and have missed the initiation. They are designated by the name *vrātyas*, and are censured—that is, reviled—by the noble and learned.
This verse is intended for the purpose of establishing the conventional usage of the designation "Vrātya";
however, their unfitness for initiation has already been established by the preceding [verse].
The Noble Ones have stated that he is "condemned.
What, then, is this condemnation? He says:
