"For never, even in times of distress, should these impure [practices] be performed according to rule."
He should not enter into matrimonial or blood relations with Brāhmaṇas.

Having made these Vrātyas—who are unpurified and have not performed the penance—perform three *kṛcchra* penances according to the rule, whatever rule for penance has been taught by the scripture, one should never, even in some emergency or under any circumstance whatsoever, enter into social relations with them; that is, one should not perform such acts together with them.
Does this mean a prohibition of all relations?
No, he says: "those of the *brāhma* [spiritual] and *yauṇa* (marital) kinds."
*Brahman* is the Veda;
the relationships based upon it are officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts.
One should not act as one for whom these are performed, nor should one act as an officiant for them.
Thus, they are not to be taught, nor should one study from them;
however, because those who know the meaning of the Veda have the right to accept gifts, this also constitutes a "brahmic" relationship.
A "matrimonial" relationship consists in the giving and taking of a maiden.
The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is for the sake of illustration.

From this observation of the fault [of neglecting initiation], it is understood that for the purpose of avoiding the state of being a *vrātya*, even in the absence of a father, the boy—provided he is of mature intellect—should himself cause himself to be initiated.
For this rule regarding the teacher is optional (*kāmya*).

In that regard, if someone does not proceed [to become a teacher] because he does not desire the status of an *ācārya*, then the student must request him by means of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth.

Thus, the Śruti records: "Satyakāma Jābāla went to Hāridrumata Gautama, saying, 'Sir, I shall live as a religious student; please instruct me,'" whereby he himself requested the teacher for the purpose of initiation (*upanayana*).
Students of the Veda should wear,
in their respective order, the skins of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, and the goat, as well as garments made of hemp, flax, and wool.

Although the word *kṛṣṇa* applies to any object endowed with the quality of blackness—as in "a black cow" (*kṛṣṇā gauḥ*) or "a black blanket" (*kṛṣṇaḥ kambalaḥ*)—nevertheless, in this context, it is understood to refer specifically to the deer because of another Smṛti text and due to its association with the *ruru*.
The *ruru* is a particular species of deer; the *basta* is a goat.
In all cases, whether referring to a modification or a part, the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix is applied.

A Brāhmaṇa [should wear] a black antelope skin, a Kṣatriya a *ruru* deer skin, and a Vaiśya a goat skin; they should wear these, that is, cover themselves with them. Furthermore, there are garments made from hemp, flax, and wool.

The word "ca" (and) indicates a conjunction. In that context, "upper garments" (*uttarīya*) refers to materials such as hemp; "leather" (*carma*) refers to upper garments by virtue of propriety; and "cloths" (*vastra*) refers to those used for covering the private parts.
The connection is not with every [item] for each one individually in sequential order, nor is it by way of inversion; rather,
the first student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) is connected with the first hide and garment, and the second with that situated in the second position,
as has been demonstrated.

But surely, even without an explicit statement, this is established from common worldly usage alone; for instance, in the case of "pulverized by the thunderbolt, cast down by the wind, and burned by fire," there is a sequential understanding of the connection: pulverized by the thunderbolt (*vajra*), cast down by the wind (*anila*), and burned by the fire (*agni*).
It is replied:
This would indeed be so if there were a distinct specification and an equality in number.
But here, because of the employment of the singular term "brahmacārins," no sequence is understood; for there are three types of *brahmacārins*, and six [items] are assigned:
three skins and three garments.
However, when the term "in sequence" (ānupūrvya) is included, the order conveyed by another sentence is adopted.
Thus, after being connected with the hides, the word *brahmacārī* is repeated and then connected with the garments;
consequently, the equality of number is established.
It was precisely regarding such a subject that the venerable Pāṇini made this effort: "The subsequent mention of an equal number [of elements] follows the order of enumeration."
The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of muñja grass, triple-stranded, even, and smooth;
that of a Kṣatriya should be a bowstring made of mūrvā fibers; and that of a Vaiśya should be made of hempen threads.

Muñja is a species of grass; a girdle made from it is *mauñjī*. That should be made as the girdle or waist-band for a Brāhmaṇa, serving as a middle-binding. It should be triple, meaning consisting of three strands.
It is even, being neither thin in some places nor thinner in others;
rather, it is even throughout.
It is smooth, endowed with the quality of thinness, and polished.
Furthermore, for a Kṣatriya, the *jyā* is the bowstring;
that may sometimes be made of leather, sometimes of grass, or a rope of *bhaṅga*, *umā*, and so forth.
For this reason, he says "maurvī" (made of *mūrvā*).
When that [bowstring] has been removed from the bow, it should be used as a waistband (*śroṇībandha*).

Even though the triple-stranded and other qualities of the girdle pertain only to the *mekhalā* made of muñja grass, nevertheless, because it would result in the destruction of the bowstring's own nature, it is not used [as a waistband].
A product of hemp fibers is a *śāṇatāntavī*.
The vowel lengthening of the second member occurs because it follows the rules of Vedic grammar (*chāndasa*).

Alternatively, when the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is applied to the word *tantu* alone, it is then connected with *śaṇa*; thus, "made of hemp" (*śaṇatāntavī*) means that which is related to hemp. A product of the material (*prakṛti-vikāra*) is designated by its connection to that material.
"Devadatta’s grandson [offers] cow-ghee";
"the cord, the thread, should be made of hemp or muñja grass like the girdle"—
thus the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras have very clearly stated the properties of the threefold nature and so forth for the girdle of a Vaiśya.
If muñja grass is unavailable, however, they should be made from kuśa, aśmantaka, or balvaja;
they should be triple-stranded with one, three, or five knots.
In this context, they maintain that the word "ādi" (and so forth) has been elided;
thus, [the phrase] "in the absence of muñja grass and so forth" is understood.
Furthermore, the use of the plural number in the word "kartavyāḥ" (they are to be performed) is more appropriate.
The distinction of the girdles is clearly evident due to their connection with different castes;

however, if they were connected to a single caste, the plural number would have to be based solely on the difference between individual instances. Furthermore, the term "of the Brahmin" (*viprasya*), which is the subject under discussion, would have to be modified to the plural form.
And there would be an option only if there were a single object;
yet an option is not appropriate when a possible course exists.
Therefore, in the absence of *muñja* grass, [one uses] *kauśa* grass.
In the absence of jute, one may use *aśmantaka*; for hempen fibers, one may use *balvaja*. By the mention of "grass" and "medicinal herbs," *kuśa* grass and others are included.
This is a restrictive rule concerning substitutes.
Even in the absence of *kuśa* grass and the like, something else similar to *muñja* grass and so forth should be used. It is triple-stranded with a single knot;
this distinction in the number of knots is not according to the distinction of social classes (*varṇa*).
Rather, each case is subject to individual deliberation.

Even regarding this breaking of knots on girdles made of *kuśa* grass and the like, which is enjoined as a distinction of dharma, it should be understood that this applies even when the practice according to other *smṛtis* is variable.
The sacred thread of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of cotton, twisted upward and triple-stranded;
that of a Kṣatriya should be made of hempen threads, and that of a Vaiśya should be made of woolen threads.
By the word *upavīta*, a specific manner of arranging the garment is expressed;
as he will state: "when the right hand is raised.
And that is merely a religious duty (*dharma*).

Cotton-ness (*kārpāsatā*) does not exist in that [thread]; therefore, the substrate (*dharmin*) is characterized by its property (*dharma*). That which possesses this particular arrangement is called "cotton" (*kārpāsa*).

Alternatively, the suffix *-a* in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) should be applied because it belongs to the *arśa-ādi* group, as in the case of "sacred thread" (*upavīta*), meaning "that which has an upward turn" (*upavītavat upavītam*).
It is turned upward; that is, it is wound around toward the upper direction.
"Trivṛt" means threefold.
This upward winding is prescribed for that which has attained the state of thread from the spinning-wheels and has been made threefold.
Having joined the three strands together and formed them into the shape of a rope by winding them upwards, one should make the sacred thread (*upavīta*) with it.
And that rope should be worn as a single strand, or three, five, or seven;
for it receives the name *yajñopavīta* (sacrificial thread) due to its connection with the sacrifice.
It is figuratively designated as such because it is raised up for the purpose of the sacrifice.
In this regard, because the *iṣṭi*, *paśu*, and *soma* sacrifices are one in their nature as sacrifice (*yajña*), they are made to have a single thread (*ekatantuka*).

Alternatively, because they are accomplished by means of the three fires, or due to the distinction between the *ahīna*, *ekāha*, and *satra* types, they are made to have three threads (*tritantuka*).
Or, because there are seven forms of the *soma* sacrifice (*somasaṃsthā*), there are seven threads.
There are three libations [to be performed] at the three junctions of the day; thus there are five.
In the absence of a thread, it may also be done with a cloth or similar material. This has been stated in another Smṛti.
*Avi* means a sheep; its thread is *sūtra*. That which is made from that is *āvikasūtrika*. The suffix *ṭhañ* should be applied because it belongs to the *adhyātmādi* group.
Alternatively, one should read the word as *avikasūtrika*.
And in that case, the formation of the word is accomplished by the suffix *ṭhan* used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).
According to the Dharma, a Brāhmaṇa deserves staffs made of bilva or palāśa wood; a Kṣatriya, of vāṭa or khadira; and a Vaiśya, of pīlu or udumbara.

Even though there is a mention of a pair [of staffs] in the rules for the qualities [of the staff], because singularity is heard in the injunctions— such as "having taken the desired staff, with its hair-end" (*keśāntakaḥ*) and "the staff of a Brahmin is made of Bilva or Palāśa wood"— it is understood that one carries a single staff (*ekadaṇḍa*).
In the *Gṛhya-sūtra* it says, "The staff of a Brahmin is made of Bilva or Palāśa," and in the *Gautama-dharma-sūtra* only the taking of a single staff is mentioned.
In this context, the mere existence of the staff is heard [in the expression] "they deserve staffs" (*daṇḍān arhanti*).
These staffs are to be applied to the religious students (*brahmacārin*);
as for the question "in what action?", that will be stated here and later in the phrase "having received what is desired" (*pratigṛhyepsitam*).
And since punishment is the means for that apprehension, the singular number was intended; therefore, the dual number is used here.
It is a restatement of what is already established, as in the expression: "If it rains, many people will practice agriculture.
*Bilva*, *palāśa*, *vaṭa*, *khadira*, *pīlu*, and *udumbara* are the specific names for particular species of trees.
"Bailva" means a modification or a part of the *bilva* tree;
this applies everywhere in the same way.
Furthermore, these [examples] are intended merely for illustration.
Because of the statement, "All [these] are worthy of sacrifice," they deserve these punishments in the matter to be described hereafter,
according to dharma and according to the scriptures.
The staff of a Brahmin should be made according to the measurement reaching to the hairline;
that of a king should reach the forehead, and that of a Vaiśya should reach the nose.
The word *daṇḍa* denotes a specific form;
a long piece of wood measured by its length is called a *daṇḍa*.
In response to the inquiry as to what its length is, he says:
"Keśāntagah" means he goes to or reaches the hair-limit; it refers to one whose measure extends to the crown of the head.
Starting from the tips of the feet up to the crown, reaching the hair-limit, is "keśāntagah. Alternatively, "keśāntaka" means one for whom the hair is the limit (the end).
The letter *ka* is an affix added at the end of a compound (*samāsānta*).
A punishment consistent with this measure should be inflicted or caused to be inflicted by the teacher upon the Brāhmaṇa.
"Reaching the forehead" means extending as far as the forehead; that is, its measure is up to the limit of the forehead.

Since that which is measured by only four finger-breadths up to the forehead alone cannot be designated by the term "staff" (daṇḍa), it is explained thus: [the staff] reaches from the tips of the feet up to the end of the forehead;
likewise, for a Vaiśya, it reaches as far as the nose.
All those [reeds] should be straight, without blemishes, pleasant to behold,
not causing alarm to men, possessed of their sheaths, and undamaged by fire.
"Upright" means straight, not crooked;
"all" is a restatement, because there is no distinction from what has been previously mentioned;
"unblemished" means without holes.

Their appearance is gentle and pleasing; they possess a serene countenance, their complexion is pure, and they are free from bristling agitation. They cause no distress, and neither themselves nor others—whether human beings or animals—should be made to feel distressed by them.
The phrase "of men" is for the purpose of illustration. "With bark" means unplaned. "Unspoiled by fire" means not touched by lightning or by a forest fire.
Having accepted his desired staff and having paid homage to the sun,
he should circumambulate the fire from left to right and go about for alms according to the prescribed rule.
Once the skins have been donned, the binding of the girdle must be performed;
having bound the girdle, the initiation ceremony (upanayana) must be performed; and once the sacred thread (upavīta) has been placed, the taking up of the staff (daṇḍa) follows.
Having taken up a staff, one should worship the Sun, Āditya.
Standing facing him, the worship of Āditya should be performed with mantras dedicated to the deity Āditya;
the understanding of these mantras is derived from the Gṛhya texts.
If there is any other procedure, it follows from that very source.
That which is common to all is stated here:
having circumambulated the fire, having gone around it on all sides.
He should practice; he should perform alms-gathering (*bhaikṣa*).
Alms-gathering (*bhaikṣa*) is the collection of alms (*bhikṣā*).
"He should beg" means he should request;
"according to the rule" is a restatement of the rule that will be explained below.
By the word *bhikṣā*, food such as cooked rice in a very small quantity is meant.
An initiated member of the highest twice-born class should go about for alms using the word "bhavat" at the beginning;
a Kṣatriya, however, should place it in the middle; and a Vaiśya, at the end.
In this context, the word *bhaikṣa* refers to the statement used in requesting alms. For it is that [statement] which can be preceded by the word *bhavat*, not the object such as food and so forth.

Furthermore, since women are instructed as the first ones from whom alms are to be sought, and because the person being requested in a request must be addressed, the feminine form of the word *bhavat* ending in the vocative case should be employed.
In this case, it is the sequence itself that is restricted as having an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*),
whereas the employment of words occurs according to their actual meaning, as in "give alms" (*bhikṣāṃ dehi*).
But how is the meaning of a refined (*saṃskṛta*) word obtained when women are being addressed?
And they do not understand that the *saṃskṛta* [language] is the constant means of instruction (*upanayana*), and that the utterance of words is stated to be its constituent part (*aṅga*).
Furthermore, corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) are impermanent;
therefore, their conjunction with that which is eternal is not possible.

In the same way, when the learned hear incorrect words, they recall the correct words through a partial similarity and thereby comprehend the meaning. This is because, according to the view that an incorrect word indicates its meaning through inference, the word *gā* leads one to infer the word *go* by virtue of their similarity.

Therefore, because meaning is understood from this, women will likewise understand the meaning from these [words] by recollecting the connection that has arisen between them and the learned, due to their similarity to the learned.
Moreover, these three words consist of very few syllables, are well-known everywhere, and are easily understood even by women.
For example: "O Kṣatriya, you who are among the people (bhavan-madhya), give alms (bhikṣām) to me (bhavati)."
Likewise, the compound *bhavaduttaram*—meaning "that which has the word *bhavat* as its subsequent member"—is the sense of the compound; that is, the sentence [beginning with] *bhavat*.
By the use of the past-participle suffix (*-ta*) in the word *upanītaḥ*, he shows that this very same rule applies even to the daily practice of wandering for alms (*bhaikṣyacaraṇa*).

By concluding the section on initiation (*upanayana*) with the words, "This indeed has been declared as the rite of initiation for the twice-born," he states that this same rule applies even to the alms-gathering (*bhaikṣya*), which is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the initiation.

Because it would otherwise be a modification, this [rule] would either be merely an ancillary part of the initiation (*upanayana*), or—by the force of the past-participle suffix—it would override the context and apply to begging for the sake of livelihood alone.
Thus, this duty applies to all begging: both that which is an ancillary to the one being initiated, and that which is for the purpose of daily livelihood.
He should first beg for alms from his mother, or his sister, or his own maternal aunt— whichever among these would not treat him with contempt.
Words such as "mother" and so forth have well-known meanings. "Nija" means a uterine sister;
and she who would not treat him with contempt.
"Vimānanā" means contempt; "it is not given" refers to a refusal.
And thus it is said in the Gṛhya-sūtra: "One should first beg from one who does not refuse, or from a woman who does not refuse.
For that alone is the primary priority which belongs to one who is being initiated.
Day after day, however, one should not resort to [conduct] out of fear of being dishonored.
Having collected that food without guile, as much as is required,
and having offered it to the teacher, he should eat while facing east, pure and having sipped water.
The word "having gathered" (samāhṛtya) indicates gathering from many [sources];
it should not be understood that many [verses] are to be taken from a single source.
As for the word "that" (tat), it refers to that which has immediate proximity to the word in the context of the function's meaning, and not to the introductory element belonging to the general topic.
For the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras have prescribed that "one should cook the *anupravacanīya* [oblation]," not the eating of alms;
and they state that "one should remain for the remainder of the day," and that the initiation (*upanayana*) occurs after one has already eaten breakfast.
Therefore, the eating of alms is not an integral part (*aṅga*) of the initiation ceremony.
One should beg only as much as is necessary for the fulfillment of the purpose known as satisfaction;
one should not beg excessively.
One should report to the teacher without deceit; one should not conceal prepared food with coarse food and present coarse food to the teacher.
Thinking, "He will surely not accept this poor food," [the disciple] makes it known that "this offering has arrived. If the teacher does not accept it, the disciple may eat it with permission.
Furthermore, how is it that the offering (*nivedana*) does not serve solely for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa-saṃskāra*), given the authority of historical tradition (*itihāsa*)?
Thus, the Blessed Vyāsa demonstrated in the narrative of Tritakūpa that [the food] was taken by the teacher;
and as for what is heard in some places, namely, "one should eat when permitted."
Having sipped water, he faces the east.
Some say that this facing east during the sipping of water follows immediately from the preceding rule;
however, that is incorrect.
The restriction regarding direction, "facing east or north," will apply to the ritual sipping of water (ācamana);
therefore, it is connected specifically with eating. [He should be] pure.

The sight of outcasts and the like, visiting impure places, stepping over them, spitting, and so forth—these are prohibited by this [rule] for one who has already performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) at the time of eating.
One who eats facing the east gains long life; facing the south, one gains fame;
facing the west, one gains prosperity; and facing the north, one indeed eats the truth.
Eating while facing the east has been prescribed as a constant rule for one who is free from desire.
Now, the rules pertaining to specific desires are stated:
"One should eat facing the east for the sake of longevity (*āyuṣya*)."
If longevity is obtained from that food, then it is "conducive to longevity" (*āyuṣya*); by this, the following meaning is established: one who desires longevity should eat facing the east.
There are two applications regarding the east: the obligatory (*nitya*) and the optional (*kāmya*).
One who desires longevity should intend for that as the fruit.
But the other is not like that.

Just as the obligatory *agnihotra* is performed repeatedly by one desiring heaven, so too for one desiring a result, the obligation—though it is obligatory—is fulfilled through a single performance (*tantra*).
In the same way, one desiring fame [should perform it] facing south.
These are indeed injunctions for those who desire [the results].
"Desiring prosperity" (*śriyam icchan*):
this is formed with the suffix *śatṛ* from the root *śrī* followed by the denominative suffix *kyac*.
Alternatively, there is a reading ending in "m," namely *śriyam*, meaning "conducive to prosperity" (*śriyai hitam*), similar to words such as *āyuṣyam*.
Because it is a part of a living being, the root *bhuj* is used here in its own primary sense;
thus, one speaks of "enjoying" (*bhuṅkte*) the *ṛta*.
"One obtains prosperity from eating"; thus, the reading "śriyam" ends in the accusative case. Alternatively, the dative case is used in the sense of "for the sake of that," as in "pratyak śriyai."
*Ṛta*, truth, and sacrifice, or their fruit, heaven (*svarga*).
One desiring heaven should eat facing north.

Even in the absence of an injunctive suffix (*vidhi-pratyaya*), since [the act] is not otherwise established, the understanding of its injunctive purpose arises through the postulation of the fifth mood (*pañcama-lakāra*) and so forth.

Thus, this eating according to the division of the directions is for the sake of specific results. However, eating in the intermediate directions—which follows by implication—is set aside by the constant rule of facing the east.
Furthermore, this optional injunction does not concern the eating of alms-food for the student alone; rather, it pertains to the mere act of eating for householders and others as well.

Likewise, the statement "he eats" (*bhuṅkte*)—as opposed to "he should eat" (*aśnīyāt*), which is the subject under discussion—is an indicative mark (*liṅga*). Otherwise, [the author] would have pointed to "he should eat," since that alone is understood without doubt as referring to the subject at hand. But when the term "he eats" is used, a doubt arises: does this refer to the very same subject at hand expressed by another word, or does it denote merely the act of eating as a general verbal meaning? In such a case, because the verb is repeated, there is the comprehension of a different meaning rather than the recognition of the subject at hand.

As for the argument that, due to the absence of an injunctive suffix, this is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) and is thus a supplement to what precedes— a solution already stated in the rule *vacanāni tv apūrvatvāt*—

and that there is no reason for it to form a single syntactical unit with what precedes, such as the criterion of being incomplete when separated; even if, by the extension (*atideśa*) in the rule *uttareṣāṃ caitad avarodhi*, the duty of the religious student (*brahmacārin*) were to apply to all persons, there would nonetheless be no [specific] fruit [for such a person].

For when there is a desire for a specific quality, they do not admit an application based on extended application (*atideśa*). Some maintain that [the rule] "one desiring cattle should fetch water with a *godohana* vessel" and "one desiring vigor should use *khādira* wood" is not intended to apply to modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).
Having sipped water, a twice-born man should always eat his food with a concentrated mind;
and having eaten, he should sip water properly and touch the cavities of his head with water.

The two words *ācamana* and *upaspṛśati* are understood from the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) to have the same meaning, denoting a specific purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the purpose of purification.

Even if *upaspṛśati* is listed in a different sense [in grammatical lexicons] and *camu* refers merely to eating, nevertheless, because they are seen used with prefixes in this specific sense, it is precisely that meaning which is perceived.
Although the root *spṛś* has a general scope of application, its actual usage is the determining factor.
The root *gaḍi* is taught [in grammatical treatises] as denoting a specific part of the face;
and it is used for the cheek alone, not for any other part.
The terms *puṣya* and *siddhi* are taught as denoting the asterisms in general, yet they function to denote specific ones.
The word *dhāyyā* is recited as referring to any *sāmidhenī* verse in general, yet it also applies specifically to those inserted (*āvāpikī*) verses;
therefore, the meaning is "having sipped water," which is likewise the sense of the expression "having touched [water]."
And that [detail] will be prescribed later on.

Furthermore, a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between these two is observed: having stated "one should perform the ritual ablution (*upaspṛśet*) at all times," he says "one should sip water three times" (*trir ācāmet*).
Therefore, the meaning is that they refer to the same act.

Although it was already stated, "Having sipped water," the repetition regarding the sipping of water for the purpose of eating is for the sake of indicating immediate sequence: one should eat immediately thereafter and not allow it to be interrupted by another activity.
And so the Blessed Vyāsa said:
"O Hari, I shall dwell among those who always eat while five parts [of their bodies] are still wet."
Śrī indeed spoke thus:
"The two hands, the two feet, and the mouth—this is the fivefold state of being moistened.
And that belongs to one who eats immediately after sipping water, not to one who delays."
In this context as well, he will state in the section on the observances of a *snātaka* that "one should eat with wet feet";
we shall explain how there is no redundancy between these two rules.

The inclusion of the word "always" (*nitya*) is so that the rule regarding eating might not be understood as pertaining specifically to the religious student (*brahmacārī*) by virtue of the immediate context, but rather as a rule for eating in general, established by direct instruction.

Regarding this, some say that the mention of the "twice-born" (dvija) is for the purpose of establishing a duty for every eater, and that the mention of "constantly" (nityam) is a mere restatement (anuvāda).
They do not think correctly;
for if the word "twice-born" did not apply to the student (brahmacārin) under discussion, then it might indeed be so.
But when this designation applies to that [action] as well, then the sublation of the context cannot be perceived without the inclusion of the word "eternal" (nitya).
[The agent] is composed,
observing both the substance being consumed and its own inherent power.

For one whose mind is distracted, there would be neither the avoidance of food that is contrary to the teacher's instructions or that causes burning sensations, nor the eating of what is wholesome to one's constitution.
After eating, one should perform the ritual rinsing (upaspṛśet).
The removal of ointments of oil and other substances has been explained in the section on the purification of materials.
When that has been performed, this sipping of water (ācamana) is prescribed for one who has eaten.

On this point, some hold the view that one sipping is for the purpose of purification, while a second must be performed for the sake of an unseen spiritual merit (adṛṣṭārtha), according to the rule: "Having slept, having sneezed, and having eaten.
And thus it is recited: "One who has already sipped water should sip again."
We shall establish this in the fifth [chapter].
The word "properly" (samyak) reiterates the specific nature of the act of sipping water;
one should perform everything exactly according to the rule that has been stated.
And one should touch the apertures with water;
the apertures are the openings in the head.
But has this not already been stated: "And one should touch the apertures with water"?
Some say that this is for the purpose of excluding the self and the head.

When one, being already pure, sips water solely for the purpose of purification before eating, or when there are those for whom there is one sip of water after eating for the sake of purity and another for an unseen (transcendental) purpose—in those cases, the self and the head are not touched during the rite for the unseen purpose; however, such a rite for the sake of purity does indeed arise.
The application of that [act] which has its constituent parts complete will be stated [later] in the rule: "One desiring purity should always sip water.
Alternatively, it is for the purpose of recognizing the ritual procedure: this sipping of water is scriptural, not worldly.
For one who knows the connection with specific constituent parts, when the possessor of those parts (the principal act) is indicated, the recognition "this is that very same thing" is established.

And therefore, where it is heard in scripture that "one should sip water" (ācāmet), it is not understood as the mere consumption of any substance whatsoever; rather, what was stated—that it refers to a scriptural purificatory rite (saṃskāra) together with its accessories—is thereby demonstrated.
One should always honor one's food and eat it without disparaging it;
upon seeing it, one should rejoice, feel serene, and welcome it in every way.
That which is eaten is called "food" (*aśana*), referring to cooked rice, flour-cakes, cakes, and so forth.
One should perceive that food, when brought for the purpose of eating, as being the form of the deity; for this food is indeed the supreme deity.
Since it is the cause of the sustenance of all beings by virtue of being their creator, perceiving it in such a way constitutes its worship.
Alternatively, "meditating" means cultivating the realization that whatever is for the sake of one's life belongs to Me; thus, by always honoring it, one worships Me.
Or, worship consists of receiving [the food] after bowing with prostrations and the like. And one should eat this without disparaging it.
Even when causes for contempt arise—whether due to the food being poor quality or because of its unwholesome preparation—one should not despise the food.
One should not reject it by saying such things as, "What is this that is being eaten? It is disgusting and causes an imbalance of the bodily elements.
However, if it is of such a nature [that it must be rejected], then one should not eat it; but if it is not so, one should eat it without disparaging it.
Upon merely seeing it, one should rejoice;
one should be satisfied and pleased, as if returning from a long journey upon seeing a son, wife, or others,
and one should become serene.

Having abandoned even the turbidity born of other causes by beholding food, one should take recourse in mental clarity and rejoice. Rejoicing (*pratinandana*) is the expression of praise for prosperity.
"May we be ever-yoked with this"—this is the expression of joy (*abhinandana*) which demonstrates zeal.
"In every way" (*sarvaśas*) means at all times.
Because of the understanding that the option (*anyatarasyām*) applies as a fixed alternative (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the suffix *śam* should be applied in the sense of the locative case.
Or rather, it should be read as "sarvadā" (at all times).
For food that is always honored bestows strength and vigor;
however, when eaten without honor, it destroys both of these.
This is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) supplementary to the preceding injunction, not an injunction regarding a result.
For if it were an injunction regarding a result, this injunction would be optional (kāmya), intended for one desiring vigor and one desiring strength;
consequently, the word "constant" (nitya) would be untenable, as it is said that "eating is indeed constant when honored."
Therefore, this rule of facing east is to be observed for as long as one lives;
for food eaten without being honored destroys both strength and vigor.
Strength (*bala*) is capacity—the power to lift heavy loads and so forth without fatigue.
Even for one who is emaciated, there is vigor and great vitality;
there is development of the limbs, and he becomes large-bodied and possessed of great strength.
One should not give the leavings of food to anyone, nor should one eat between [meals];
one should not overeat, nor should one go anywhere while still impure from food.

Food contained in a vessel that has been defiled by contact with the mouth is called *ucchiṣṭa* (leavings); one should not give that to anyone. Since this [rule] alone establishes the prohibition regarding *snātaka* vows, the specific prohibition concerning Śūdras will be explained in that very context.
Although the fourth case-ending (*caturthī*) was expected, the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for the purpose of prohibiting the mere relationship [of giving].
Even for those who do not understand that "this has been given to us," food should not be prepared for them, such as dogs, cats, and the like.
For in this case, the full meaning of "giving" is not fulfilled; there is merely the cessation of the giver's ownership, but no acquisition of ownership by another.
The word *antara* signifies the intermediate state.
There are two times for eating: evening and morning;
one should not eat at any other time.
Alternatively, the word *antarā* refers to an interval.
Having abandoned the activity of eating, one should not eat again that same food previously taken in the vessel after it has been interrupted by another action;
however, a specific rule is recited in another Smṛti: "interrupted by rising and sipping water.
Some, however, explain "interruption" as referring to an interval [of time].
It is heard in the scripture: "Having touched the vessel with the left hand and having taken a portion with the right, he offers it into his mouth for the vital breaths.
In that context, immediately after that favoring of the vessel with the left hand, one should not engage in overeating—that is, eating in excessive measure.

And this cause of ill health is intended to illustrate [the dangers of] heavy, incompatible foods, and so forth. From the instruction on causes, one should understand from the *Āyurveda* that eating in moderation means one should eat only as much food as does not fill the stomach and is properly digested.
The belly has three parts: one and a half parts for food, half a part for drink, and one part for the movement of the bodily humors (*doṣa*);
otherwise, there is ill health. Furthermore, one should never go anywhere while still having remnants of food.
Therefore, having removed the remnants and restored that very spot to a state of purity, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) in that same place.
Excessive eating is detrimental to health, detrimental to longevity, and detrimental to rebirth in heaven;
it is non-meritorious and despised by the world; therefore, one should avoid it.
He explains that the prohibition against overeating is based on observable grounds:
ill health is the onset of disease; suffering from fever, abdominal ailments, and the like;
and the loss of life through cholera and similar conditions constitute a lack of longevity.
"One should protect oneself from all sides"—because this involves transgressing the protection of the body and so forth, it leads to the loss of heaven.
The attainment of hell follows from the absence of heaven. It is non-meritorious and brings about misfortune.
One who is hated by the world is censured for eating excessively;
therefore, for that reason, one should avoid overeating and should not do it.
A Brahmin should always perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma-tīrtha;
he may use either the Kāya or the Traidaśika, but never the Pitrya.
By the word *tīrtha*, a sacred place for water is denoted;
it is called a *tīrtha* because it stands (*tiṣṭhati*) for the purpose of crossing over (*tāraṇa*) and for liberation from sin (*pāpapramocana*).
In some instances, however, a *tīrtha* is a path for descending into water (*udakāvataraṇamārga*), in the sense that "by means of this, people cross over" (*taranti anena*).
But here, however, it is said that the term *tīrtha* refers to a specific portion of the palm that holds water;
or rather, the word *tīrtha* is used figuratively by way of praise,
for water does not abide there permanently.
With that [water] he should touch [his lips], that is, sip water;
the phrase "with the Brāhma [mantra]" is also solely for the purpose of praise,
meaning "that of which Brahmā is the deity."
For a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) does not possess the status of a deity, because it lacks the nature of a sacrifice and is devoid of mantras.
The patronymic suffix denoting a deity is applied by superimposing upon it the nature of a sacrifice through certain attributes, such as its being a cause of purification;
[this applies] both for the purpose of constant ritual purity and as an auxiliary to a rite.
Who is Prajāpati? That which has him as its deity is *kāya*. Likewise, that which has the thirty-three (*tridaśa*) as its deity is *traidaśika*.
When the suffix *devatā-ṇi* is applied to the word *tridaśa*, the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of the same meaning (*svārthe*).
And the status of being a deity is as before.
One should perform the ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) at these sacred fords (tīrtha).
The mention of the "vipra" is not intended to be restrictive.

For he will state the specific rule for Kṣatriyas and others; and a specific injunction—such as "but the king [should drink] water reaching his throat," and so forth—is not tenable unless there is a general application [of the rule] already established.
Nor [should one eat] at a *pitrya* rite, that is, one dedicated to the ancestors, at any time whatsoever.
Even when [the ancestors] have become unfit for the Brāhma and other sacred sites due to boils, pustules, and so forth—
surely the ancestral rite (*pitrya*) would not apply simply because it was not prescribed?
There is indeed a doubt on this point.
In order to indicate that this is the *pitṛtīrtha* (the sacred part for the ancestors), it must necessarily be stated that "of those two, [the thumb-base] is the paternal";
yet no specific function for it is mentioned here.
Since there is an expectancy for a function, one might suspect a connection with the function under discussion due to its being the subject at hand.

Now, however, since there is a prohibition [of other options], the understanding of what is to be done arises from the designation "pertaining to the ancestors" (pitrya) itself: the ancestral rites, such as the libation of water and so forth, must be performed with this *tīrtha*.
In this way, the praise becomes relevant.

Furthermore, because the *brāhma* and other *tīrthas* are enjoined by direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*), it is appropriate to mention this [pitrya *tīrtha*] in order to remove the doubt that might arise in its absence.
They declare that the *brāhma* sacred site is at the base of the thumb;
the *kāya* site is at the roots of the fingers; the *daiva* site is at their tips; and the *pitrya* site is below those two.
The base of the thumb is its lower part;
the region of its palm is the *brāhma* tīrtha.
He says that the interior of the hand is the palm.
The Brahma-line is at the end of the great line (mahārekhā), facing oneself, in the middle of the hand;
the body is above the staff-line (daṇḍarekhā) at the base of the fingers;
and the divine (daiva) is at the tips of the fingers.
Although the word "finger" (*aṅguli*) is subordinate at the root [of the compound], it is connected with the word "tip" (*agra*) because of its mutual expectancy.
In the phrase "the paternal [portion] is below those two," there too is a connection between the subordinate word "finger" and the thumb (*aṅguṣṭha*).
And here, the ring finger (pradeśinī) is intended;
the space below those two is the ancestral (pitrya).
This is explained thus on the strength of other Smṛtis and the established usage of the learned, because a literal connection [of the words] is impossible.

And as for the conch: the *brāhma* *tīrtha* is below the thumb and before the tip-line; that between the forefinger and the thumb is the *pitrya*; that on the front of the joint of the little finger and the palm is the *kāya*; and the tips of the fingers are the *daivika*.
One should first sip water three times, then wipe the mouth twice;
one should also touch the sense- openings with water, as well as the self and the head.
One should sip water three times from one of the prescribed apertures (*tīrtha*), causing it to enter the stomach through the mouth.
Then, following that consumption of water, one should wipe the mouth—that is, both lips—twice by repeated application.
Here, "wiping" (*pramārjana*) refers to the removal of the particles of water adhering to the lips using the hand moistened with water.
How much less so with the hand?
This is because of established custom or because of the context concerning the *tīrtha*.
Furthermore, the phrase "only with water through the *tīrtha*" heard later in the text is also drawn back [to apply here].
And because the act of wiping has a visible purpose, the word "mouth" (*mukha*) refers here to the specific part already mentioned.

One should touch the apertures (*khāni*), which are the cavities, with water held in the hand; "touching" (*sparśana*) is itself what is meant by "sprinkling" (*upasparśana*). And since the mouth is the subject under discussion, this rule for touching applies specifically to the primary apertures.
And Gautama says that one should touch the apertures of the head;
by "the self," he indicates either the heart or the navel,
for in the Upaniṣads it is stated that "one should behold the self within the heart."
Therefore, this touch belongs to the heart, which is the pervasive self, the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*);
for it is impossible for that which is formless to possess touch.
It is recorded in some Smṛti texts that "one should not touch the navel," and by this we understand [the heart] to be the navel.
The head is well known.
And because the Smṛtis have a single purpose, it is understood that one should wash the hands up to the wrists and so forth;
likewise, silence of speech is the restraint of speech, and there is the sprinkling of the feet.
In the Mahābhārata, even the washing of the feet is shown.
One who knows the Dharma and desires purity should always sip water that is neither hot nor frothy through the proper part of the hand, in a secluded place, facing either the east or the north.
The word "hot" (*uṣṇa*) is intended as an indication of boiling water;
for it is thus recited: "with unboiled waters.
And in this way, waters heated by summer heat or naturally hot are not prohibited.
The mention of "foam" (phenagrahaṇa) is intended to indicate bubbles as well;
for it is recited [in other texts] as "with inferior foam and bubbles.
The phrase "at the proper place (tīrthena), he who knows the Dharma" is merely for the purpose of completing the meter.
"One who desires to attain purity" (*śaucepsuḥ*) means one who wishes for purification;
otherwise, one does not become pure.
"Always" means not only in the context of eating,
but rather, it applies even to the purification of semen, feces, urine, and so forth.

In the act of consuming water, the instrumental case is used because it functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*); this rule does not apply only to those waters being consumed, but also to those serving as the cause in acts such as sprinkling the feet.
We, however, maintain that even in the act of consumption, water is indeed the instrument, for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*) is not a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) performed upon the water itself.
[This should be done] in a secluded and pure place.
For a secluded place, generally being unpopulated by people, is pure; [the practitioner should sit] facing east or north. The word "face" (mukha) is connected with each [direction].

"Facing either east or north"—for thus it was recited by Gautama. And the compound should be analyzed as follows: "one whose face is toward the northeast" (*prāgudaṅmukha*). This is not a *bahuvrīhi* containing a *dvandva*, but rather a *bahuvrīhi* itself.

If it were a *dvandva* compound with internal composition (*garbha*), there would have to be the suffix *-a* (the *samāhāra* ending) due to the rule for compound-final elements; nor could it be a *itaretarayoga* [copulative] compound either,
for it is impossible for both directions to face forward simultaneously.
In that case, it would follow that one part of the ritual rinsing (ācamana) must be performed facing east and another part facing north; yet the ritual rinsing is not a single localized act.
Furthermore, the purpose of the directions is not something to be adopted [as a subordinate factor] such that the two [directions] could be connected by depending upon each other.

Nor are the words "east" (prāk) and "north" (udak) well-known as denoting the "invincible direction" (aparājitā)—as in the case of "southeast" (dakṣiṇapūrva) and so on—such that they would be understood as a directional compound (dik-samāsa) or a possessive compound (bahuvrīhi).
Therefore, this is not a bahuvrīhi compound containing another mode of operation;
hence, there is an option.
And it has been cited in another Smṛti: "One should begin the purification facing either the east or the north."

Just as in the case of "the Bṛhat and Rathantara Sāmans in the six-day [sacrifice]," where the Bṛhat is used on some days and the Rathantara on others, rather than both Sāmans being combined on a single day; so too,
although the sipping of water (ācamana) by means of the *tīrtha* has been mentioned,
its specific measure has not been stated.
Therefore, for the sake of defining that [distinction], he says:
"The Brahmin is purified by water reaching the heart; the Kṣatriya, by water reaching the throat; the Vaiśya, by water that has been sipped; and the Śūdra, by water merely touched at the extremity."
They go to or reach the heart; thus they are "heart-reaching" (*hṛdgāḥ*).
The suffix *ḍa* is applied according to the rule "it is seen in other cases as well.
By means of a division of the yoga-rule, the substitution of *hṛd* for *hṛdaya* is established.

He is purified; that is, he attains purity and his impurity is removed. "Water" refers to a quantity measuring slightly less than a handful (*culuka*), reaching the throat—that is, pervading as far as the throat. By means of such water, a *bhūmipa*—a Kṣatriya—is purified. Sovereignty over the earth is ordained for the Kṣatriya.
By that well-known activity, the kṣatriya caste is characterized;
had the intention been to speak of sovereignty, he would have mentioned it specifically among the duties of a king.
A vaiśya [is characterized] by those [drops of water] which have been tasted, that is, those which have entered the interior of the mouth.
Even those [waters] that have not reached the throat are causes of purification for a Vaiśya;
for a Śūdra, they are so by being touched at the end (anta).
The suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārthe*), according to the rule beginning with "ādyādi."
This word *anta* has the sense of "nearness," as in "he went to the edge of the water," which is understood to mean "near the water.
It also has the sense of "part" or "portion."
The term *vastrānta* (end of a garment) and *vasanānta* (end of a cloth), occurring in both cases, require another related entity to be specified: "the vicinity of what? or "the part of what?

In this context, since the sipping of water (*ācamana*) for other parts has been prescribed by means of specific locations (*tīrtha*), it is understood here that [the sipping] is performed by the edge of the tongue and the lips.
However, the sense of "vicinity" is not possible, because the prescribed act of sipping cannot be accomplished by mere proximity.
There is also sipping (prāśana) during contact;
for when something is touched by the tongue and lips, the tasting of its flavor is inevitable.
In this context, a slight reduction from the quantity prescribed for a Vaiśya is intended.
For a Vaiśya, [the area of purification] extends as far as the root of the tongue; for a Śūdra, it is the tip of the tongue.
Because water is liquid, the transgression of the limit cannot be avoided; however, impurity occurs only when one inevitably reaches beyond it.

Furthermore, this entire division of the *tīrtha*s applies to the sipping of water with the right hand, because the fitness of the hand [for such acts], as well as the practice of using the right hand (*dakṣiṇācāratā*), are prescribed as duties pertaining to the person.
And for this very purpose, this is stated regarding this specific limit.
When the right hand is raised, the twice-born is called *upavītī*;
when the left is raised, he is *prācīnāvītī*; and when it hangs from the neck, he is *nivītī*.
But surely, categories of things established in common worldly usage are also relied upon in the treatises on Dharma.

The statements of Manu and others are not intended for the purpose of defining the technical meanings of words, like the *abhidhāna-kāṇḍa* (lexicographical sections) of grammar or traditional law codes (*smṛti*).
We have already stated that if they provide definitions for meanings that are not widely known, how can they be subject to censure?
Moreover, there is another purpose here as well:

so that when the sequence for sipping water (*ācamana*) is being taught, it may be understood that wearing the upper garment (*upasaṃvyāna*) and so forth are constituent parts (*aṅga*) of that sipping.

Even though the wearing of the sacred thread (*upavīta*) is always established—whether for the sake of a religious observance (*vrata*) or for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*)—nevertheless, if it is done without that [thread], the sipping, even if performed, would remain incomplete.
If this statement or rule did not exist, there would be a deficiency in the ritual and a fault on the part of the person.

Furthermore, even if one performs the sipping of water (*ācamana*) without the sacred thread (*upavīta*), it is as if it were not done at all; moreover, there would be a fault, for drinking water while impure is forbidden.

But how is it that the sacred thread alone is a constituent part of the sipping of water, when other things are also prescribed here, such as wearing the thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīti*)?
It is said:

the *prācīnāvīta* is prescribed by its own specific term for the ancestral rite (*pitrya-karman*); since it has thereby attained its purposeful application, it cannot be treated as an optional alternative to the *upavīta*, which has not yet fulfilled its function.
Likewise, the *nivīta* is purposeful in the context of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*).

Although there is no specific application for the *nivīta* here, nevertheless, because the various *smṛtis* share a single purpose, its application elsewhere indeed renders it meaningful here as well.
The mention of "taking the hand" is intended to indicate the arm; for in common worldly usage, one whose arm is raised is called *upavītī*.
Furthermore, we shall explain that the *upavīta* is to be worn at all times.
One is not called *upavītī* merely because the left hand is raised;
one is called *prācīnāvītī* when the right hand is raised.
This is a name derived from a compound word.
The absence of compound, however, is for the sake of conforming to the meter.
In the phrase *kaṇṭhasajjane*:
"clinging to the throat" means attachment or placing [the hand] upon the throat.
When either an arm of the garment or of the thread is raised, then one becomes *nivītī*.
Having cast the girdle, the antelope skin, the staff, the sacrificial thread,
and the water-pot into the water when they are worn out, he should take others with the appropriate mantras.
The discarding of those that have been damaged in water and the taking up of others is prescribed here;

the sequence of discarding and taking up is exactly as heard in the text. And because of this repeated mention, these [acts] do not constitute a mere subsidiary part of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).
For if it were an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of that [sacrifice], its disposal would necessarily occur only at the conclusion of its performance.
What then? It is worn as long as one's period of Vedic studentship (*brahmacarya*) lasts.

Now, is it not possible that there might be no means of disposal for those [sacred fires] which, by chance or through human force, are extinguished before the completion of the ritual acts, even at the very time of initiation (*upanayana*)?

Furthermore, there is a subsequent taking up for the sake of completing the application, as in the case of a potsherd; because of this subsequent taking up, it is inferred that there is a holding [of the staff].
It is said:
first, the grasping of the staff has been enjoined, and likewise the binding of the girdle.
In that regard, the arrangement of the thread must certainly be performed as an integral part of the initiation ceremony;
once it has been performed, the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled.
What does it matter afterwards whether those [threads] are lost or not lost?
And when the limbs are destroyed, a specific performance (*pratipatti*) becomes an auxiliary to the ritual act (*karmopakāraka*).
Yet, no purpose is prescribed for those [limbs] such that, for the sake of accomplishing it, there would be a formal scriptural injunction (*vācanika-upādāna*) regarding a specific time.
Furthermore, because the purpose has not been performed, the repeated taking up [of the limbs] prompted by that purpose is said to be established by the sense of the matter itself.

Therefore, because of the injunction for practice and because of the mention of "taking up" (upādāna), wearing [the water-pot] is an ancillary part (*aṅga*), and it does not terminate with the performance [of the rite].
For, since it is mentioned as being on the same footing as the *kamaṇḍalu*, which persists after the time of initiation (*upanayana*), their persistence in subsequent stages is also understood;
and that [persistence] is an ancillary part of the vow (*vrata*).

Therefore, because of the context, the girdle and other items serve both purposes: they are for the sake of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), and once the initiation has concluded, they are seen to persist as long as the state of studentship (*brahmacarya*) lasts.
Furthermore, the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) must be made for the purpose of holding water, precisely because of this injunction regarding its disposal.
Otherwise, the disposal would be conditional, occurring only when the water-pot exists.

In that regard, since it is said, "Having taken up the staff, one should wander for alms," the carrying of the staff is established as being an ancillary part of the practice of begging by virtue of the sequence; thus, it occurs even when wandering for purposes other than begging due to established custom.
However, one does not always carry the staff in the palm of the hand while standing, sitting, lying down, eating, and so forth.
Accordingly, he will later prescribe the *brahmāñjali* (the hollowed hands joined at the heart) for the study of the Veda (*svādhyāya*).
The phrase "as with the mantra" reiterates the taking [of the staff] according to the procedure for initiation (*upanayana*);
and in that context, there is a mantra for the girdle (*mekhalā*), not for the staff (*daṇḍa*).
The tonsure ceremony (keśānta) is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year,
for a member of the royal caste (rājanyabandhu) in the twenty-second, and for a Vaiśya two years after that.
The sacrament known as *keśānta* (the tonsure) should be performed for a Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year from conception; regarding the precise nature of this rite,
the *Gṛhya-sūtra* alone is the authority.
"In the twenty-second [year] plus two" means for one who has twenty-two years with two additional years;
or alternatively, "time" alone is the referent of the compound,
meaning at a time two years beyond the twenty-second year.
Regarding the phrase "of a Vaiśya":
it is the years that are the things to be numbered by the word "two," for they are indeed the subject under discussion.
This entire rite for women, however, should be performed without the recitation of mantras,
for the purpose of purifying the body at the proper time and in the proper sequence.
This sequence for women is to be performed entirely without mantras.
Starting from the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), this is the sequential order of the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*);
that is to say, it is the entire collection of rites along with their prescribed procedures.
He states the purpose for women as well, just as for men, namely for the sake of refinement (*saṃskāra*) and for the sake of the body's purity:
"at the proper time," meaning without transgressing that time at which a particular sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) has been prescribed.
The *avyayībhāva* compound occurs in the sense of "not exceeding the meaning of the word" (*padārthānativṛtti*) and "similarity" (*yathāsādṛśya*);
it should be understood in the same way regarding "sequence" (*krama*).

Since the repetition (*āvṛti*) has been prescribed as being devoid of even a single mantra, there is no possibility of obtaining [the recitation] in a manner that deviates from the proper time and sequence; therefore, the prohibition is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*) intended merely to complete the meter.
This much was intended to be said: that these [rites] for women are performed without mantras.

Since the preceding statement regarding the prohibition of mantras would imply that the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) for women—just like the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) and others—is also to be performed without mantras, this [verse] is commenced to preclude that.
"The marriage rite is declared to be the Vedic sacrament for women;
service to the husband is their residence with the teacher, and household duties are their tending of the sacred fires."

The Vedic sacrament known as *upanayana*, which is intended for the purpose of receiving the Vedas, is for women the rite of marriage (*vaivāhika-vidhi*). That which occurs at marriage, pertains to marriage, and is accomplished by marriage is [the sacrament].
Therefore, since marriage is ordained in the place of *upanayana*, the statement regarding its attainment refers to marriage.

And if its cessation were marriage, which performs that function, then alas! the study of the Vedas would be attained, as would the practice of vows; let it be that initiation (*upanayana*) does not take place. Both of these [study and vows] are likewise precluded by service to the husband or residence with the teacher.

Since she serves, attends upon, and honors her husband, that very service constitutes her residence with a teacher (*guru*). One must undertake study while residing with a teacher, but since she has no residence with a teacher, how could there be study for her?
"The purpose of the household" refers to domestic duties, such as cooking, managing the household goods, and supervision—those which will be described in the ninth chapter.
Regarding the passage beginning with "and for the accumulation of wealth," etc.:
the very act of placing fuel on the fire that a religious student performs every morning and evening constitutes her household duty.
Furthermore, by means of this fire-ritual, the entire collection of restraints and observances belonging to the religious student is implied.
And this has been stated thus, because marriage constitutes the attainment of initiation (*upanayana*):

just as for a man, from the time of initiation onwards, there exist Vedic, Smṛti-based, and customary injunctions, whereas prior to that there is freedom of action, speech, and diet; so too for women, there is freedom of action prior to marriage, and thereafter they have the entitlement to perform Vedic and Smṛti-based rites. Or rather, the construction of the words is as follows.
For women, marriage alone is the Vedic sacrament that constitutes their *upanayana*.
Although marriage is not technically an *upanayana*, it is figuratively designated as such even in the absence of the formal initiation.
What is the similarity between marriage and the *upanayana* that justifies this designation? To this, he says: "service to the husband," and so forth.
The conclusion of the section:
This rite of initiation for the twice-born has been declared; it is meritorious and manifests their true birth. Now, learn the application of ritual duties.
This concludes the section on initiation (*upanayana*).
Everything stated here is for the purpose of initiation.
But does it not follow that the tonsure (*keśānta*) should likewise be included?
No, because its performance is prescribed at its own time even before the initiation has been completed;
for even that which is recited within a specific context may serve a different purpose through the force of the sentence.
And thus, the *keśānta* ceremony is accepted by some as being applicable even to one who has returned home (*samāvṛtta*).
That which pertains to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) is *aupanāyanika*;
the lengthening of the final vowel of the second member is as previously explained.
Birth (*utpatti*) is the production from one's mother and father.
It is called "productive-revelatory" (utpatti-vyañjaka) because it manifests, illuminates, and renders manifest that [quality] which possesses attributes.
Although [the person] is born, he is equal to one unborn so long as he is not initiated, due to the absence of entitlement;
therefore, this injunction is productive-revelatory.

The meaning of "meritorious" has already been explained. Listen now to that which is about to be declared: the duty—that which must be performed by one who has been initiated—which constitutes his connection, relationship, or qualification with respect to those rites.
Having initiated the pupil, the teacher should first instruct him in purification,
as well as in proper conduct, the fire-ritual, and the twilight devotions.
One should train and instruct [the student] in ritual purity (śauca) from the very beginning.
By the expression "from the beginning," it is not intended that the instruction in purity must precede [the rules on] conduct and so forth;
rather, these [topics] are mutually unordered in their sequence.

He will explain that the instruction for the vows (*vratādeśana*) occurs immediately after the initiation (*upanayana*), and the study of the Veda follows once the Vedic vows have been instructed. Therefore,

because the kindling of the fire and the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) involve the recitation of mantras, the recitation of mantras— which would otherwise not be applicable before the instruction for the vows— is here prescribed.
Purity (śauca) is not restricted to a specific time; therefore, it must necessarily be taught on that very day. The same applies to conduct (ācāra).
Consequently, the statement "this [is taught] at the beginning" is for the purpose of showing respect, and does not enjoin that purity must be the first thing taught.
Purity consists of the single [cleansing] on the penis and so forth, ending with the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).

Proper conduct (ācāra) includes rising to meet teachers and others, offering them a seat, saluting them, and so forth. The fire-rite (agnikārya) is the performance of the fire-installation rite and the kindling of fuel-sticks (samit).
The worship of the twilight consists in the meditation upon the Sun and the contemplation of His true nature; this is the worship of the twilight.
Or rather, [it refers to] "the morning twilight" and so forth.
This is the rule for the vow.

Now he states the rules for study: "But one who is about to study, having sipped water according to the scriptures, facing north, with hands joined in the *brahmāñjali*, wearing light clothing, and with senses subdued, should be taught."
The *lṛṭ* (future tense) suffix should be understood here as referring to what is about to happen:
one who is about to engage in study, about to begin study, or, in other words, desiring to study. He should be taught while facing north.
In the Gautamiya [tradition], however, it is said that the disciple faces east and the teacher faces west.
"Having sipped water according to the scripture" recalls the previously mentioned rule for the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).

Regarding the phrase "by whom the *brahmāñjali* was made": because [the class] beginning with *āhitāgni* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, there is the posterior placement of the past participle (*niṣṭhānta*). Alternatively, the reading is *brahmāñjalikṛt*.
"Laghuvāsā" means one whose garments are washed;
by washing, the two garments become light.
Therefore, through this lightness of the garment, its purity is indicated.
Alternatively, if this student wears coarse clothing such as wool, he might not feel a blow when struck during a distraction of mind, and thus he would not properly recite [the text].
Furthermore, if the garment were removed, it would cause distress to the teacher;
and if the body were uncovered, the fool would experience great pain when struck with a rope or similar object.
Therefore, wearing light clothing serves a visible purpose.
One who has conquered—that is, restrained—both sets of sense organs is called "one who has mastered his senses" (*jitendriya*).
This means he should not look here and there, he should not hear whatever may come to his ears, and he should remain attentive to his study. Thus it is said.
At the beginning and at the conclusion of the recitation of the Veda, one should always clasp the feet of the teacher;
having joined the hands together, one should study, for that is known as the *brahmāñjali*.

Although this word *brahman* has many meanings, it is understood here as referring to the Veda because of the context of study (*adhyayana*). This locative case [in *brahmaṇi*] is one denoting the occasion (*nimitta-saptamī*) for its commencement.
And because the context is specifically that of study, this undertaking refers to the act of studying that subject; it is the first recitation by a person.
In this regard, the term "foot" (pāda) is used; however, the initial syllables of the Veda—namely *agnim īḷe*, *iṣe tvā*, and *agna āyāhi*—are not what is here called the "beginning."
For its status as a cause is not possible, because it is eternal;
indeed, a cause is something that occurs only occasionally.

By this, the following is meant: one who is about to begin the study of the Veda should perform the clasping of the teacher's feet, and having done so, he should then pronounce the syllables of his own recitation; however, once the act of study has already commenced, he should not clasp the feet again.
But surely, the commencement is the first moment of the action, and that is the cause;
and it is logical for that which exists to be a cause, just as life is [the cause of the Agnihotra].
In this regard, even a past event such as the burning of a house is a cause, for it is heard of as such in those very contexts.
Therefore, it is logical that the study and the clasping of the feet should indeed be performed together.
It is replied:
the term "commencement" refers to the resolve to teach, not to the first moment of the action.
As soon as the teacher says, "Study," the student resolves to do so;
therefore, immediately following that, there is the clasping of the feet. This is for the purpose of pleasing the mind of the teacher who has set out to provide assistance.

Just as in the world someone praises one who has acted to help them, saying, "Surely we have been liberated from this evil by you," so too is this request wordless: "I have approached for the sake of study. For a teacher is not to be importuned with the words, "Teach me!"
Only the formal approach (*upasadana*) to him must be performed for the sake of full awakening, as this is the occasion for study;
therefore, once the approach has been made, there is the utterance of the syllables of the Veda. Moreover, it is said that one should study with the hands joined together.
In that context, one who is studying would transgress the rule for clasping the feet [of the teacher].

"End" (*avasāna*) means completion, the cessation of study. Although the word *brahma* is subordinate in relation to the commencement [of the recitation], nevertheless, because the end requires something to refer back to and because it is proximate, its connection is understood to be with the word *brahma* itself, as no other term has been heard.

The inclusion of the word "always" (*sadā*) is intended so that this rule may apply at the beginning and end of future performances [of the recitation] every day; otherwise, it would apply only to that primary commencement which immediately follows the instruction for the vow (*vratādeśa*).

Now, the *Anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice is enjoined at the commencement of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*; it occurs only at that commencement of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* performance which takes place immediately after the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), and not at the commencement of the monthly performance.
As long as the daily recitation—measuring approximately two chapters—has not been completed, starting from the morning until its conclusion, the act of study remains a single unit.

Even if there should be some interruption in the middle, once it resumes, it does not deserve to be called a "new beginning"; therefore, the act of approaching the teacher by touching his feet is not performed again.
Furthermore, it is recited in another Smṛti: "The clasping of the teacher's feet [should be done] every morning, day after day.
Having joined and brought them together so that they are closely attached to one another, one should study.
That well-known configuration of the two hands known as "the tortoise" (kacchapa) should be performed in that manner;
for that is indeed the *brahmāñjali*.
This is an explanation of the meaning of the term.
The clasping of the teacher's feet should be performed with crossed hands:
the left foot is to be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand.
The act of clasping the feet of the teacher mentioned in the preceding verse should be performed with crossed hands.
To explain what kind of crossing of the hands must be done, he says:
the left foot is to be touched—that is, contact is to be made—with the left hand; however, one should not remain pressing down for a long time.
And this exchange occurs between the two hands by their simultaneous movement toward each other's directions.
Standing in front and facing the teacher, one must perform the salutation by clasping his feet;

in that act, the left hand is led to the right path and the right hand to the left, so that the left foot is touched by the left hand and the right foot by the right hand—this is the exchange of the hands.
Others, however, read "vinyastapāṇinā" (with hands placed).

Since the placing [of the hands] is already established by the mere act of touching, one should not touch with only the tip of a finger out of fear of being burned—just as one would avoid touching a red-hot iron ball—but rather the two hands should be placed or laid down.
They explain that squeezing, which causes pain, is forbidden.
But when the pupil is about to begin his studies, the teacher, always alert, should say, "Recite, sir! and he should stop when the pupil says, "May there be a pause."
The words beginning with "adhyeṣyamāṇam" have been explained previously.
This is the injunction regarding the teacher:
when the teacher desires to have the student recite, he should then address him, saying, "Recite, sir! (adhīṣva bho).
The teacher must not be troubled by one who has not been invited, [thinking], "Teach me this recitation.
And it is said:
"One should study only when summoned."
Having uttered this word "virāmo 'stu" (let there be cessation), he should begin—that is, he should desist. Who?
The teacher alone, because of the indication by the nominative case.
Alternatively, he may return when dismissed by his teacher, not of his own accord.
This is explained as follows: when the teacher says, "Let there be a cessation," then the student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should cease.
Others, however, maintain that this rule applies to the time of cessation for any student who has completed his studies, as well as for the sub-teacher (upādhyāya).

And likewise, another Smṛti states: "Having recited the Vedic study, at the time of cessation, one should touch the earth with the forefinger and say 'Svasti' among the Yajus; 'Vispaṣṭam' among the Sāmans; 'Virāmaḥ' among the supreme Ṛks; and 'Āramaḥ' among the Atharvans. 'Atandrita' means not lazy;
'tandrā' and 'ālasya' mean drowsiness and indolence."
Through connection with that [laziness], a person is called "indolent" (*tandrita*);
by abandoning laziness, one is "not indolent" (*atandrita*).
And this is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
There is no lethargy or fatigue here. However, one should not entertain this doubt: that this rule is for one who is free from lethargy, while there is another for one who is lazy.
One should always place the Praṇava at the beginning and at the end of the Veda;
that which is not preceded by Oṃ flows away, and that which is not followed by it falls apart.

In this case as well, according to the previously stated principle, one should place the *praṇava* at the beginning and at the end of the *brahman*; it should be understood that this refers to the act of recitation concerning the *brahman*. The word *praṇava* is a synonym for the syllable *oṃ*.
And so he will say later: "That which is not preceded by *oṃ* flows away.

The inclusion of the word "always" (*sarvadā*) is intended so that this may be a rule pertaining solely to the injunction for Vedic study; otherwise, due to the context, it would apply only to the student (*brahmacārin*) for the purpose of formal acquisition.

This being the case, it becomes established for all instances: both for the purpose of non-forgetting, and for householders and others who are told, "One should study one's own portion of the Veda day after day."
However, he will prescribe [its use] by its own name for the twilight recitation (*saṃdhyājapa*) and other such acts, saying: "This syllable and this [verse].
Nor is this a Vedic rule such that it would apply whenever one begins the utterance of any Vedic sentence whatsoever.

Therefore, the *praṇava* is not used at the beginning of oblation-mantras, recitations, scriptural expositions, *yājyā*-verses, and so forth, nor in any other instance of uttering a Vedic sentence for the purpose of illustration.

Therefore, it is established that the constant recitation of the Veda, as prescribed by the injunction for the study of one's own branch of scripture (*svādhyāya-adhyayana-vidhi*), is for the sake of dharma.

As for the application of the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), its purpose of marking the commencement of daily recitation is already established simply by the continued application of the rule regarding the constant time of recitation.
The explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for this is: "That which is not preceded by Om flows away."
In the beginning, at the start, Brahman that is not preceded by *oṃ* flows away;
[it becomes] "made with *oṃ*" (*omākṛtam*), meaning refined by the word *oṃ*.
This is a compound formed as "the means (*sādhana*) has been performed" (*kṛta*).
Alternatively, "oṃkṛta" refers to that Brahman in which the syllable *oṃ* has been uttered; the inversion [of the word order] occurs because it begins with a vowel (*sukhādi*).
And the word "afterwards" (*parastāt*) refers to the conclusion.
By means of the particle *ca*, it is connected with the phrase "not preceded by *oṃ*" (*anoṃkṛta*).

By both terms, "it flows away" (*sravati*) and "it falls apart" (*viśīryati*), the fruitlessness of study is established. This is also a deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) meaning that the Veda (*brahman*) which has been studied becomes fruitless when employed in ritual action (*karman*). Just as milk or the like poured for the purpose of cooking is said to "flow away" when it leaks and spills here and there from a cracked vessel before reaching the state of being cooked, so too is this described.
The destruction of that which has reached its fruition, become condensed, and attained the state of being experienced—that is disintegration (viśaraṇa).
Sitting upon grass-blades pointing eastward, purified by means of purifiers,
and cleansed by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), he then becomes worthy of the syllable Om.
The word *kūla* signifies the tips of *darbha* grass.
"Sitting near them" (*paryupāsīnaḥ*) means seated upon those *darbha* blades with their tips pointing eastward.
