The status of these as the object of the action arises from the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the prefix *ā* in the rule *adhi-śīṅ-sthāsām ātmanepadam*, which prescribes the *ātmanepada* endings for the roots *śī*, *sthā*, and *ās*.
In the phrase *pari upa ā āsīnaḥ*, the prefix *ā* should be understood here as being joined [to the preceding word];
the words *pari* and *upa* are meaningless [in this context].
He has been purified—that is, brought to a state of purity—by means of *pavitra* blades of *darbha* grass.

The *aghamarṣaṇa* and other such mantras are not denoted here by the word "purifier" (*pavitra*), because at that time those [mantras] have not yet been studied by the religious student (*brahmacārin*).
Nor do blades of *darbha* grass become instruments of purification merely by their existence, since they perform no action.
With regard to their intermediate operation, another Smṛti text indicates the touching of the vital breaths (*prāṇopasparśana*).
And Gautama said: "The touching of the vital breath with *darbha* grass,
sitting on seats with the tips pointing eastward,
and being purified by three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*)."

The breath (*prāṇa*) is the air that moves through the mouth and nose; its *āyāma* is its restraint, its retention within the body, and the prevention of its exit to the outside. Regarding this, the measurement of the duration of retention is recorded in another Smṛti, as is the recollection of the mantra:
"The Gāyatrī, together with the Śiras, joined with each *praṇava*..."
One should recite [the mantra] three times while restraining the breath; that is called prāṇāyāma.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha has also taught the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*).

The limit for cessation is precisely at the end of the mantra, because no other [limit] is prescribed; and since all the Smṛtis have a single purpose when there is no contradiction, the performance here should likewise be exactly thus.

But would this not result in a circular dependency: the *oṃ* syllable should not be performed until the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) has been completed, yet breath-control does not conclude without the *oṃ* syllable?
This is not a fault;
for the instruction "one should recite it three times" refers to the mental recollection of the syllable *oṃ* during breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*),
since the utterance of sound is impossible for one whose breath has been restrained.
Although recitation (*japa*) is accomplished through some form of vocal activity, in the case of the study of one's own Vedic texts (*svādhyāyādhyayana*), however, utterance is intended.
This is because the act of study is of such a nature; for this verbal root [√adhi-i] refers to an action involving sound, and sound, which is perceivable by the ear, is not grasped by the mind alone.
Moreover, this is not a property of the syllable *oṃ* such that it would follow [as a requirement] even when it is uttered in other contexts;
for it has been stated that it should be performed at the commencement of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*).
If it were indeed a property of the syllable *oṃ*, it would follow [unnecessarily] in worldly sentences such as "we say *om*," and so forth.

Gautama, however, has stated: "The three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) consist of fifteen measures (mātrās). By the word *mātrā*, the duration of an unmodified vowel such as *ā* is meant. In this context, because of the contradiction, the time mentioned in other Smṛtis does not apply; nor is there the recitation of mantras, for even those breath-restraints that do not include the syllable *oṃ* exist there. Thus, there is no occurrence of the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
Therefore, the ellipsis is that one ought to perform the *oṃkāra*;
this is when the entire compound is used as a conventional term (*rūḍhi*) denoting the *praṇava*.
But when [the suffix] *kāra* has the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), [it refers to the individual sound].
The utterance of this very word "om" is the *oṃkāra*; at that time, there is no dependence on another word.
Having stated that [the act] must be performed by means of the word *praṇava*, he here restates it as "*oṃkāram*"; therefore, these two have the same meaning.
And thus it has been shown.
Prajāpati milked forth from the three Vedas the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*, as well as the words *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*.

This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) for the preceding injunction. Regarding the syllable *oṃ*, which consists of a collection of three phonemes, he states the etymological derivation of each one:
from the three Vedas—that is, from the three collections of knowledge—he "milked out" (*niraduhat*), meaning he extracted it, just as clarified butter is extracted from curd.
Not only the three syllables, but also this other [set]: bhūr, bhuvaḥ, svar.
From the three Vedas alone, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out foot by foot that which is the "Tat" of this Sāvitrī verse.

This explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the origin of the *gāyatrī* verse beginning with "tat savitur vareṇyam" is intended for its injunction; and in the preceding verse, the injunction of the *vyāhṛtis* also follows from that very explanatory passage. The sequence, however, is understood from the order of recitation.
And he will say:
"Reciting this syllable and this [gāyatrī] preceded by the vyāhṛtis..."
"He milked" means he extracted [the essence].
Although that [word] "tat" could be taken as a representative reference (*pratīka*) for "that of Savitṛ we choose," it cannot be considered as consisting of three feet;
rather, it must be understood as consisting of exactly three feet.
And as for the statement "the Sāvitrī has three feet," there are other Prajāpatis such as Kaśyapa and others;
therefore, he specifies [the source] as "Parameṣṭhin," which refers to Hiraṇyagarbha.
For he is established in the supreme state, characterized by non-return;
and this [recitation] of the Sāvitrī is for the sake of showing the highest degree of reverence,
since it is said that she was directly extracted from the Vedas by Prajāpati himself, the foremost of all.
A Brahmin who knows the Vedas, by muttering this syllable and this [Gāyatrī] preceded by the Vyāhṛtis during the two twilights, becomes endowed with the merit of the Vedas.

Even though this occurs within the context of the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*), this is an injunction for the twilight recitation (*saṃdhyā-japa*) because it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*).
In that regard, there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *gāyatrī*, while there is an injunction for what was previously unestablished (*aprāpta-vidhi*) concerning the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis*.
On this point, someone says:
This is not an injunction regarding the twilight ritual (*saṃdhyā-vidhi*), because it is not the subject under discussion (*aprakaraṇāt*).
For if it were an injunction, it would pertain to the religious student (*brahmacārin*), since he is the one under discussion;
yet such a ritual is not possible for him.

For here one is called "a knower of the Veda," yet that person who has just been initiated does not possess the status of a knower of the Veda. Moreover, the fruit mentioned here is that he becomes endowed with the merit of the Veda.
The rule for the daily twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) is not for the sake of a fruit.
Nor do we know what this so-called "Vedic merit" (*vedapuṇya*) is, by means of which this yoga is called "recitation" (*japa*).

If, first of all, the intended merit is that which results from the study of the Veda, and the intended "union with Vedic merit" is the attainment thereof—then, regarding this very injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyavidhi*) under discussion, there is no fruit whatsoever other than the comprehension of the meaning, because no such [fruit] is heard in scripture and because the comprehension of the meaning is already perceived. Thus, even a mere assumption [of another fruit] is not possible.
Furthermore, the rule for householders and others, namely that "one should study one's own Veda daily," is also indeed obligatory.
As for the mention of rewards therein—such as milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey—that is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
Therefore, this is not [an optional] injunction.

For all of this is intended to be enjoined when it is a prescriptive rule (*vidhi*); however, when this is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), then "reciting" refers to the study that is the subject under discussion, and the phrase "by the merit of the Veda" is also interpreted in some way or another. To this, it is replied:
It has already been stated that the context is set aside by the direct statement.
Precisely because the terms "knower of the Veda" (*vedavid*) and "twilight" (*saṃdhyā*) do not connect with the subject matter under discussion, this injunction applies elsewhere.
The injunction is simply this: "One should mutter these three at the two twilights."
The term "knower of the Veda" (vedavit) will be restated [as a qualification for all].
If it is argued that while being a knower of the Veda is possible for householders and others, it is not possible for a student (brahmacārin), what is the use of its possibility in his case?
For, since this is a restatement of what is already established, all those belonging to the various stages of life (āśrama) possess the entitlement.
For if the term "knower of the Veda" were a qualification of the agent, the religious student (brahmacārin) would have no entitlement [to the rite].
But how can this be a restatement? Because it would result in the fault of splitting the sentence (vākyabheda).
When the rite of twilight devotions (saṃdhyā-vidhi) has arrived, the Praṇavas and Vyāhṛtis are not yet established there and must therefore be enjoined.
In that context, if it were further enjoined that [the person] "should be a knower of the Veda," there would be a syntactical split (vākya-bheda).
For when a ritual action is already established, it is not possible to enjoin multiple matters simultaneously.
However, a mere restatement of the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis* is not possible here;
therefore, this is the meaning of the sentence:
regarding what was stated—that one should mutter the *Sāvitrī* during the two twilights—there is this further qualification: one should mutter it preceded by the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis*.
Furthermore, the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is intended merely as an illustration.
As for what was said— that a fruit is heard in this context while this rite of the twilight (saṃdhyā) is obligatory— what contradiction could there possibly be?

The desire will pertain to that very quality as being eternal; from that [act] which has the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis* as its qualities, this fruit arises—just as cattle are the fruit of the *agnihotra* when it involves the fetching of the *godohana* vessel, by virtue of the force of the sentence: "For one desiring cattle, he should fetch [the water] with the *godohana*."
This was stated with reference to the student; however, this is not an optional injunction (kāmya-vidhi).
For in another Smṛti, this injunction is clearly stated as being indeed obligatory (nitya):
"One should recite the Gāyatrī together with its head (śiras), preceded by the Vyāhṛtis."
Thus,
you yourself have stated that there is an understanding of the fruits;
for this is the meaning of the phrase "by the merit of the Veda."

One should apply oneself to reciting this triad because of the merit that is declared in the Veda for the performance of the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), and not merely to the *gāyatrī* alone. Merit (*puṇya*) is indeed *dharma*, since the *smṛtis* are rooted in the Veda; thus, even that which is declared in the *smṛtis* is designated as the "merit of the Veda" (*vedapuṇya*). What, then, is the merit of the Veda? It is that which is taught therein. Therefore, by reciting these three, one partakes in the merit of the Veda. Furthermore, the merit of the Veda is that which is proclaimed in it. Consequently, one who recites this triad obtains the merit of the Veda. Thus, it is established that one should recite the triad. And so it has been said: "The *gāyatrī* is the mother, the *sāvitrī* is the father, and the *triṣṭubh* is the grandfather. By reciting these three, one attains immortality. Therefore, one should recite the triad. And so it has been said: "The *gāyatrī* is the mother, the *sāvitrī* is the father, and the *triṣṭubh* is the grandfather. By reciting these three, one attains immortality. Therefore, one should recite the triad. And so it has been said: "The *gāyatrī* is the mother, the *sāvitrī* is the father, and the *triṣṭubh* is the grandfather. By reciting these three, one attains immortality. Therefore, one should recite the triad. And so it has been said: "The *gāyatrī* is the mother, the *sāvitrī* is the father, and the *triṣṭubh* is the grandfather. That which is produced from the Veda while it is being recited can also be said to belong to it; however, because of its unique nature, it is more appropriate to designate it as "that which is made known" rather than "that which is produced. Sacrifices and the like produce dharma, whereas the Veda alone is its communicator.

As for those who claim that the final quarter [of the verse] has the following force— that what was stated as "for the sake of eternal self-satisfaction" means that one achieves one's purpose through the mere recitation of the *trika* during the twilight (*saṃdhyā*)—
that too is incorrect; for if that were the case, it would be optional (*vikalpeta*) with respect to that prescribed rule.

In that case, there would be an occasional sublation of the rule of constant recitation; and when sublation is not possible, one should not accept sublation. The term "this syllable" is a reference to the syllable *oṃ*.
But is it not the case that this is not a single syllable, but rather two or three? It is replied: [it is].
By the word "syllable" (akṣara), both a vowel alone and a combination of consonants are expressed;
here, however, it refers to that which is under discussion [in this context].
And this is the Sāvitrī verse: "tat savitur vareṇyam."
"Preceded by the *vyāhṛtis*" means that which has the *vyāhṛtis* at its beginning.
Only the three *vyāhṛtis* under discussion here are to be understood, because this [term] refers to what is under discussion; it does not refer to the seven ending with "Satyam."
But by practicing this triad externally a thousand times, a twice-born man is freed from even great sin within a month, just as a snake is freed from its skin.
"Outside" refers to an unenclosed place;
by this it is meant:
outside of villages and towns, in the forest, on a riverbank, and so forth.
"Having practiced and repeated a thousand times.
Now, is it not the case that repetition is already conveyed by both the suffix *kṛtvasuc* and by the word "having practiced" (*abhyasya*)? In that case, there would be redundancy.
There is no fault, because of the relationship between the general and the particular.
By the word "repeatedly" (abhyasya), practice in a general sense is expressed; when there is a requirement for a specific detail, [the term] "a thousand times" (sahasrakṛtvaḥ) is used.
Nor is both [the general and the particular] understood from the suffix -kṛtvasu alone, because that suffix requires a specific action to which it refers.
For when it is said, "Devadatta five times during the day," the meaning of the sentence is not completed until it is stated, "as much as he eats.
Now, one might object that even by the word "repeatedly" (abhyasya), no specific action is expressed.
True.
It is understood that one should practice that which has been introduced as *japa*;
"repetition" (*āvṛtti*) means service performed again and again;
[this applies] even to great sin.
And "great sin" refers to such things as the killing of a Brahmin;
he is liberated even from that, how much more so from minor offenses (*upapātaka*)?
The particle *api* is used here in the sense of possibility, not in the sense of conjunction.
The understanding of a conjunction through the mention of distinct entities is as in the case: "Devadatta has authority here, and Yajñadatta also.
Such is not the indication here.
From which secondary sins (*upapātaka*), then, is this liberation said to be?
The killing of cows and similar acts are minor offenses (*upapātaka*).
For each of these, penances have been prescribed in the tradition along with their secret rites.
Or, he may know those which were not performed—though no means of avoidance was stated—and yet, because they were inevitable, he knows that they were indeed committed.
Even for them, the daily obligatory rites such as the *saṃdhyopāsana* serve as expiations.

If this were indeed an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), then he would have stated it right there [in that context], just as [he says]: "Restraining his food, one should indeed recite the *saṃhitā* of the Veda three times.
Furthermore, if this were an expiation, the entire section on expiations (*prāyaścitta-prakaraṇa*) would be rendered useless.
For who, being cursed by fate, would abandon an expiation that is accomplished through mere recitation and instead resolve upon hardships that rob the body and life?
And it has been said:
"If one should find honey on an arka tree, why would he go to the mountain?"
When a desired object has already been attained, what wise person would exert effort toward it?
Likewise:
"For a wise man does not buy what can be obtained for one *paṇa* with ten *paṇas*.

And there is no basis for syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the subject matter (*prakṛta*), such as the requirement of being dependent when divided, by which this could be stated as a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) supplementary to it.
To this it is replied:
this is indeed a positive injunction;
this ritual application is solely for the purpose of liberation from evil.

As for what was stated—that an option (*vikalpa*) is not established when the injunctions are unequal—in this case, the purpose of the option will apply specifically to the expiation consisting of recitation (*japa*).
Since the removal of all sins has been declared to be accomplished by means of the *aghamarṣaṇa* and other such rites, there is an option between these and the present one;
for in the case of the *aghamarṣaṇa*, a three-day fast (*upavāsa*) has been prescribed.
In this case, one becomes pure by eating while performing the monthly rite;
therefore, one does not perish through an excessively arduous penance, which would result in an unequal injunction.
Alternatively, this is the purification for a sin committed previously, when a divine affliction has been indicated by such signs as the ill-omened state of the planets.
Therefore, there is liberation; it is said that he is liberated from what is undesirable; therefore, he is released.
The meaning is that he is not connected with the fruit of those actions. "Like the skin" means as a snake becomes freed from its worn-out skin.
By this, the destruction of sins without remainder is established.

As for that inauspicious karma performed in the past which is indicated by skin diseases and the like, many expiations (prāyaścitta) have been prescribed for it in other Smṛtis; we shall demonstrate those very expiations in the section on Prāyaścittas.
With this very intention it has been said:
"For those who mutter prayers and offer oblations, no downfall is seen."
One who is deprived of this Ṛc, as well as of his own timely ritual action,
whether born of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya lineage, incurs censure among the virtuous.
One who is separated from this Sāvitrī, having neglected the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) and abandoned the private recitation of the Vedas (svādhyāya),
incurs reproach— that is, censure— among the virtuous and the distinguished.
What kind of reproach does he incur? To this he says: "By his own action at the [proper] time.
When the time—defined by the rule "until the sixteenth year"—has passed while he remains uninvested, he is censured.
Thus, even though initiated, one who is fit for the commencement of Vedic study but is devoid of the Sāvitrī becomes a *vrātya* (an outcast).
That which is the common ritual action (*svakriyā*) of the three [castes] is what is indicated here;
and that is indeed the initiation (*upanayana*).
In this way, the word "time" (*kāla*) is meaningful.

If the intention were to express one's own duty, such as study and so forth, it would have been sufficient simply to say "by one's own action. The word *yoni* is a synonym for birth (*janman*) and conveys the sense of caste (*jāti*);
the meaning is "belonging to the caste of Brahmins and so forth."
This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) intended for the purpose of expiation (prāyaścitta) for a Vrātya.
The three imperishable great utterances preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*,
together with the three-footed *Sāvitrī*, should be known as the mouth of Brahman.
Those which have the syllable *oṃ* at their beginning are called "preceded by *oṃ*.
The "Great Utterances" (*mahāvyāhṛti*)—which are the very subject under discussion—are these words: *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*.
They are "indestructible," meaning imperishable.
This is stated because the result takes a long time to manifest;
otherwise, the qualification "all words are eternal" would be meaningless.
This three-footed Sāvitrī verse, beginning with "tat savituḥ," is the mouth of Brahman.

Because it is the first, it is designated as the "mouth"; therefore, the statement "this should be studied at the beginning" is its explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Alternatively, it says this very thing: that the "mouth" is the door or the means by which the attainment of Brahman occurs through this [study].
He who studies this day after day for three years without weariness reaches the supreme Brahman, becoming like the wind and possessing the form of space.
He becomes all-pervading and omnipresent like space; he becomes one whose form is space and whose nature is space.
However, "form" here does not mean a physical body, because space lacks a body.
Now, what is this Brahman that is said to undergo the attainment of form?

He is of the nature of the bliss of the Supreme Self, from whom these individual souls (kṣetrajñas) emerge like waves from a mass of water tossed by the force of the wind; just as those waves become identical in form with that [water] when it is in a state of perfect stillness,
so too do these selves become of that same nature.
Furthermore, all of this will be explained in detail in the twelfth chapter.
This study of the Gāyatrī is enjoined as recitation (*adhyayana*), not as silent chanting (*japa*); nor is there a counting of repetitions.
From the expression "without sloth" (*atandrita*), it is understood that it should be performed many times.
For when performed only once, there is no fear of negligence;
this is the rule for one who seeks liberation.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the supreme austerity;
there is nothing superior to the Sāvitrī; and truth excels silence.

The syllable *oṃ* is the single syllable; it is the supreme Brahman because it is the means for attaining Brahman. Its recitation (*japa*) and the contemplation of its meaning lead to the attainment of Brahman; thus it is so described.
"Om" is the designation for Brahman;
for thus they say, "The Praṇava is its designator. Why is that supreme, that most excellent?

The meditation on the syllable *Oṃ* excels over other meditations on Brahman—such as "One should meditate on food as Brahman" and the instruction "The sun is Brahman"—because it is stated that its attainment comes from mere study, and because the Word itself is heard to be Brahman;
for it is said: "He who is proficient in the Brahman of Sound attains the Supreme Brahman."
For every object of meaning is not beyond verbal usage, and the syllable *oṃ* is the root of all speech.
Thus says the Śruti: "Just as all leaves are pierced by a pin, so too is all speech pierced by the syllable *oṃ*;
indeed, this whole world is the syllable *oṃ*."
"Being pierced through" means following after, or attaining the state of being its substratum.
But how is it that all speech is pierced through by the syllable *oṃ*?
First, it has been stated that Vedic speech is preceded by the syllable *oṃ*.
According to the statement of Āpastamba, "Even worldly [utterances] may begin with those [sacred words]," this has been explained otherwise in the *Upaniṣadbhāṣya*; however,
it is not presented here as it is of no use in this context.
The term *prāṇāyāma* refers to the restraint of the breath accompanied by a specific procedure, just like the ritual of sipping water (*ācamana*).
It is the supreme austerity (*paraṃ tapaḥ*) compared to the *cāndrāyaṇa* and other penances. What, then, is its excellence?
This is devotion;
there is no mantra-knowledge superior to that of Sāvitrī.
"Of these" is a term of praise.
Truth is superior to silence;
silence is said to be the restraint of speech,
and the fruit obtained from truthful speech is greater than that of such restraint.

In the case of speaking the truth, the injunction is also fulfilled; however, in the case of silence, there is merely the performance of the prohibition against falsehood. This verse is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
All Vedic rites of oblation and sacrifice flow away;
however, the Imperishable should be known as the Imperishable, which is indeed Brahman and Prajāpati.
Whatever Vedic oblations there may be, such as the Agnihotra and others, and whatever sacrifices there may be, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others—all of these perish and do not become complete;
or rather, their fruit leaks away and quickly vanishes.
But this imperishable syllable known as Oṃ is to be known as the imperishable, having inexhaustible fruit.
For one who has become Brahman, there is no further falling back into saṃsāra;
therefore, because its fruit is inexhaustible, it is called "akṣara" (the imperishable).
One word "akṣara" is the term to be defined (*uddeśya*), while the second is a technical name (*saṃjñāśabda*) and an etymological verb-based term (*kriyāśabda*).
That very thing is Brahman;
Prajāpati is indeed the syllable Om;
this is a hymn of praise.
The mention of the verbal roots *juhoti* and *yajati* refers to the two [roots]; the meanings conveyed by these actions are sacrifice (*yāga*) and oblation (*homa*).
The plural number is used with respect to the individual instances.
Alternatively, this is a reference to the meanings of the verbal roots themselves, namely *juhoti* and *yajati*.
Actions distinct from those are giving and so forth.
This is a *dvandva* compound consisting of "the offerings and sacrifices" (*juhoti-yajati*) and "actions" (*kriyā*);
the oblation (*homa*) and the sacrifice (*yāga*) are mentioned separately because of their predominance.
Regarding this, some maintain that the praise of the syllable *oṃ* mentioned here is for the purpose of prescribing its recitation even by itself;
for it is not merely a supplementary detail (*śeṣa*) to the context under discussion, as there is no subsequent reference back to it.

In the case of the Vaiśvānara sacrifice, however, the qualities such as "eightfold" are indeed supplementary, as seen in the passages: "In that it is an offering on eight potsherds, he purifies him with the *gāyatrī* and with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*)," and "In that it is on nine potsherds, he bestows brilliance upon him by means of the *trivṛt*."

In all cases, when it is possible for a passage to form a single syntactical unit (ekavākya) by depending on the term *vaiśvānara*, there can be no assumption of a separate injunction (*vidhyantara*) through the postulation of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). However, here [in the case of "the syllable is to be known"], there is no dependence on what precedes, nor is there a further reference back to the *sāvitrī* and so forth.
Therefore, since the meaning of the sentence is fully completed by its own constituent words alone, it is not a subordinate element of anything else.
In the phrase "it is to be known," the suffix -kṛtya functions as an injunctive;
and because of its connection with the word *brahman*, that which is to be known is to be meditated upon and cultivated as having the nature of Brahman.
And when that is being cultivated, what is called "mental recitation" (*mānasajapa*) is thereby accomplished.
The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is ten times superior to the ritual sacrifice (vidhiyajña);
the whispered recitation (upāṃśu) is a hundredfold more effective, and the mental recitation (mānasa) is declared to be a thousandfold.
Sacrifice that is the object of an injunction is "injunction-sacrifice" (vidhiyajña), such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others.

That ritual action which is enjoined by the command "one should sacrifice" and is performed through external activity with the completion of all its constituent parts, including the officiating priests and so forth, is what is called "injunction-sacrifice" here;
however, recitation (japa) is not a sacrifice.
It is spoken of as a sacrifice by way of praise and figurative usage;
therefore, it is not a ritual sacrifice (*vidhiyajña*).
It is distinguished, excellent, and the most eminent sacrifice, surpassing the *jyotiṣṭoma* and others by ten qualities.
By this, the great fruitfulness of recitation (japa) is stated:
whatever fruit is obtained from sacrifice, that very same fruit is obtained in even greater measure through recitation.
And it is not logical that recitation should have a greater fruit than the sacrifices prescribed in the Śruti.
For if that were the case, who would undertake sacrifices consisting in the destruction of one's body and wealth?
Therefore, this is merely a commendation, similar to the statement: "By the final oblation, one obtains all desires."
This is its meaning: that very fruit, such as heaven and so forth, is obtained; however, unlike in the world, it is due to a specific excellence of effort.

Because there is no distinction in the sacrifice itself, there is a distinction in the magnitude of the fruit: whatever fruit belongs to whichever sacrifice—whether heaven, a village, a son, cattle, or the like—that is obtained through the recitation (*japa*) of that [mantra].
When whispered (*upāṃśu*), it is a hundredfold, such that another person does not hear it even if standing nearby.

A *sāhasra* [recitation] is one that possesses a thousandfold [merit]. That which is contemplated merely through the activity of the mind (*manovyāpāramātreṇa*) is a mental recitation; it has the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśu*) and so forth, having as its object mere muttering (*japamātra*). This is because it is distinguished from the subject under discussion by the phrase "which has been studied" (*yo 'dhītaḥ*). Therefore, these qualities apply everywhere—whether it be the recitation performed for expiation (*prāyaścitta*), for pacification (*śāntika*), or for prosperity (*ābhyudayika*). It is called *sāhasra* because it has a thousand [units].
Since the qualities (*guṇa*) are the subject under discussion, the existence of a thousandfold qualities is understood;
furthermore, the word *guṇa* here denotes a constituent part.
And the abundance of the fruit is understood through the connection [between the parts and the whole].
The four types of cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), together with the ritual sacrifices (vidhiyajña),
are all not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of silent recitation (japayajña).
The great sacrifices (*mahāyajñāḥ*) are called the cooked sacrifices (*pākayajñāḥ*); excluding the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), there are four such sacrifices.

When these are performed according to the prescribed rules (*vidhiyajñāḥ*), being thus endowed and accompanied by them, [the other sacrifices] do not equal even a sixteenth part (*kalām aṃśam*) of it.
They do not equal even a sixteenth part.
Alternatively, *arhati* is used in the sense of "worthiness" regarding the valuation of a limb;
by adding the suffix *tip* to the word *arha*, the form *arhanti* is produced.
A Brahmin shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whether he performs other rites or not, one who is friendly toward all is called a Brahmin.
One may attain perfection—whether it be the attainment of desired fruits or the realization of Brahman—through recitation alone (*japya*).
One should not harbor doubt in this regard, such as:
"How can that which is to be obtained through great exertions like the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and through meditative contemplations (*bhāvanā*) be accomplished by recitation?"
It is indeed established. One might perform other impermanent rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma;
or rather, one should not perform even those, since the Brāhmaṇa is said to be "friendly" (maitra).
"Friend" (*mitra*) is indeed "friendliness" (*maitra*).
A brahmin should be one who delights in friendliness toward all living beings;
and how can there be friendliness in the injury of an animal during the *agniṣomīya* sacrifice?
This is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda), and not a prohibition of the ritual acts involving animal parts, because it is understood as a supplement to what precedes it;
furthermore, those [acts] are prescribed by direct Vedic revelation (pratyakṣa-śruti).
The rule regarding the muttering of prayers (japa) has already been passed.
A wise person should exert effort in restraining the senses as they roam among alluring objects, just as a charioteer restrains his horses.
"One should apply effort toward the restraint of the senses"—this much is the meaning of the scripture;
the remainder is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) up until the injunction for the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*).
Restraint (*saṃyama*) consists in avoiding engagement with prohibited objects, as well as the avoidance of excessive attachment even to those that are not prohibited.
In this regard, the avoidance of what has been prohibited is established by those very prohibitions themselves.
This collection of verses is intended to prohibit excessive attachment even toward things that have not been specifically prohibited.
This is precisely what he says:

"Moving among objects" means acting with independence through the inherent power of things. "Covetous" refers to those objects which are called "alluring"—objects that carry away, attract, appropriate for themselves, and bring a person under their control; they are thus "covetous" objects. "Moving among them" means wandering about in various and specific ways.
If the senses did not act with particularity, then what could even unavoidable objects do?

Or, let the senses be unrestrained; if the objects themselves are rejectable, then the self is still easily restrained by a person. Since both are at fault, effort must be applied, for these [senses] are indeed difficult to control.

Just as a charioteer, the driver of horses yoked to a chariot, exerts effort in restraining and controlling them—though they are by nature prone to wavering—so that they do not, against his will, carry him along a wrong path but instead submit to his authority; in this same way, the senses must be brought under control.
I shall correctly explain, in due order and as they truly are, those eleven sense-faculties which the wise of old have spoken of.

This enumeration of numbers is to be understood through other means of knowledge and is not the primary subject matter of this treatise; however, it is explained here out of goodwill. The ancient sages have already spoken of them;
I shall describe them further on by name and by function.
"Succession" means being free from confusion.
Because of the mention of "preceding," this systematic arrangement was not devised by logicians alone; rather, it has been established by previous teachers as well.
Those who do not know this are ridiculed by the world as "not belonging to the tradition" (nāgamika); therefore, this [succession] should be understood.
The well-known categories of things have already been explained previously.
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth; the anus, the generative organ, the hands and feet, and speech is recorded as the tenth.
The ear and the other [senses] are well known.
Because of the distinction between their physical bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there is the dual number "the two eyes" (*cakṣuṣī*);
elsewhere, however, there is the singular number because the capacity (*śakti*) supported by them is one.
The *upastha* is that which emits semen in the male and is the receptacle for the *rajas* (menstrual fluid) in the female;
because these two are mentioned as a copulative compound (*dvandva*) and are parts of a living being, they are treated as a singular unit.
*Vāk* refers to the palate and other organs that manifest sound, denoting a specific part of the body.
This is a designation by name.
Of these, the five sense organs are the ear and so forth in their respective order;
the five organs of action are said to be the anus and so forth.
He now states their function for the purpose of determining their essential nature;
for they are not themselves perceptible.
The sense-faculties (*buddhīndriyāṇi*) are the instruments that produce cognition, being the causal factors of the intellect.
The genitive case is used here in the sense of the relationship between an action and its instrument.
The word "beginning with" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the ears and so forth" (*śrotrādīni*) is intended to mean "in succession," so that it should not be understood as signifying a category or type.
"Successively" (anupūrvaśaḥ) means in order.
Since order depends upon spatial arrangement, the systematic arrangement mentioned in the preceding verse is relied upon here:
[first] the organs of action.
In this context, action is intended to be that which consists of vibration.
The eleventh is to be known as the mind (manas), which by its own quality partakes of the nature of both;
when it is conquered, these two groups of five become conquered.
The mind is the eleventh among the sense-faculties. Volition is the specific quality of the mind; by means of it, both the auspicious and the inauspicious are willed.

Alternatively, because it is rooted in volition (saṃkalpa) regarding the engagement with their respective objects among both the cognitive organs (buddhīndriya) and the active organs (karmendriya), it is said to be of a dual nature.
When that [volition] is conquered, these two groups—the group of cognitive organs and the group of active organs—each consisting of five as previously described, are thereby conquered.
This is the exposition of the principles (tattva).
Through attachment to the senses, one undoubtedly incurs fault;
but by fully restraining them, one attains perfection.
"Consequence" (prasaṅga) means being intent upon that.
By means of that which has become the cause, one encounters—that is, reaches—both seen and unseen faults.
There is no doubt here; this is certain.

Having fully restrained those senses, he then attains—reaches without remainder—the perfection consisting in the acquisition of his intended goals, which is the fruit of performing the rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti.
Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects;
rather, it increases all the more, like a fire fed with sacrificial butter.
Let alone the longing for sense objects, which is not pursued due to the instructions of the Teacher;
rather, even the visible pleasure arising from cessation [of desire] occurs.

For instance, even when sense objects are being enjoyed, they produce an even greater greed; yet for one who has eaten his fill, who is satiated, and who has reached a state of extreme satiety, there arises a longing in the heart: "How can I eat more? It is only because of incapacity that one does not proceed to do so.

Therefore, this cessation is not possible through enjoyment; desire—that is, longing—is never appeased or turned back by the consumption and service of objects of desire, those things that are longed for and yearned after.
On the contrary, it increases even more, like fire with its black trail when fed with sacrificial butter.
And desire is of the nature of suffering;
for one who has not experienced its flavor, desire does not arise.
This is the enumeration of reality.
And it has been said:
"Whatever rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women there are on earth—all that is not enough for even one person; realizing this, one should attain tranquility."
Whether one should attain all these or whether one should renounce them entirely,
the renunciation of all desires is superior to their attainment.
Relying upon the previously stated reason as its basis, this concluding verse is recited:

"When desire increases through indulgence, therefore, he who is a seeker of desires might obtain all these objects and enjoy them like a youthful lord of many realms; whereas he who renounces these—touching them not even slightly—is like a celibate youth. Of these two, the one who renounces is superior to the one who obtains and enjoys them; he becomes exceedingly excellent. Thus it is said: "he who would renounce."
And this is directly perceived by oneself.
These senses, corrupted by sense-objects, cannot be so effectively restrained by abstinence as they can by constant application of knowledge.
If this is so, then it follows that one should simply dwell in the forest, for there the sense-objects are not present;
and since they are not present, they will not be indulged in.
To address this, he says: "The senses are to be restrained not by non-indulgence."
He would be devoid of happiness;

yet they remember that one should not let the forenoon, midday, or afternoon pass fruitlessly, but should devote them to dharma, artha, and kāma according to one's ability. Furthermore, the maintenance of the body does not occur without indulgence.
However, this is stated as a prohibition against craving (*gardha*).

And that craving [is abandoned] through knowledge—namely, the knowledge of the defects inherent in sense objects as taught in the scriptures such as "it is a pillar of bone bound together with sinews"—and through one's own direct experience of their unpleasantness as a result of ripening (*vipāka*).
What is the fruit of ripening? Through the cultivation of the contemplation of initial defects and the practice of dispassion (*vairāgya*), longing gradually ceases.
But it cannot be abandoned all at once;
rather, it must be done constantly—that is, at all times.
This is an adjective qualifying "knowledge."
They have become corrupted;

because they are defects, they are called "corrupted" precisely because they have proceeded as such. This suffix *śas* is employed here and there by great sages such as Vyāsa and others, in expressions such as *nityaśaḥ*, *anupūrvaśaḥ*, *sarvaśaḥ*, and *pūrvaśaḥ*.
Effort must be made to establish its correctness.
In that regard, under the rule for the suffix *śas*, it is recited: "after a word in the singular number and in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*).
Therein, the meaning of repetition must somehow be indicated.
Others, however, describe *śasat* as the form of the root *sthā* (to stand) with the suffix *kvip*;
this is a neuter adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*),
meaning "by means of knowledge that is eternally established."
The Vedas, renunciation, sacrifices, observances,
and ascetic penances never attain perfection for one whose inner disposition is corrupted.
In this context, "dharma" refers specifically to ritual injunctions;
the Vedas are those [injunctions] concerning their subject matter, such as study and recitation;
and "tyāga" (renunciation) refers to giving, by way of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Alternatively, even though the consumption of honey, meat, and so forth is not explicitly forbidden, their avoidance is prescribed here because such abstention yields a fruit;
for one whose disposition— that is, whose mind— is utterly corrupted,
these means of accomplishing results do not lead to success (*siddhi*) at any time whatsoever.
Therefore, at the time of performance, one must not have the mind directed toward desired objects and the like.
It is indeed possible to fix the mind upon the ritual action by setting aside all other conceptual constructions;
for by this statement, the abandonment of thinking about sense-objects has been prescribed as an auxiliary factor (*aṅga*) in rituals.
In the absence of that [mindfulness], action would be fruitless.
For this is a defect of the state of being: that one who has engaged in the performance of an action abandons devotion to it and fixes the mind upon vices.
That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled,
neither rejoices nor becomes dejected, should be known as one who has conquered his senses.
Having heard the sound of flutes, songs, and the like, or having heard words such as "you are Bṛhaspati," he does not rejoice.
Having heard harsh, rough, and abusive speech, he does not despond; he does not experience mental suffering.
Despondency (*glāni*) means weariness (*kheda*).

Having touched garments such as those made of *rāṅkava* wool or *kauśeya* silk, as well as blankets made of goat hair (*kutapa*), he experiences them with equanimity. Likewise, he remains the same whether beholding beautifully dressed young women and actors or seeing an enemy;
and he eats with equal indifference both milk-rice mixed with much ghee and coarse *kodrava* grain.
For one who smells both devadāru oil and camphor and the like in equal measure,
it should be practiced in such a way that one is not touched by pleasures or pains that are purely mental;
in this manner, his senses become conquered.
But it is not by mere non-activity alone;
this much extent of restraint is to be resorted to.
But surely, a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) must avoid association with women with great effort; why then is the acceptance of prepared alms-food prohibited?
To this he says: "If even one among all the senses leaks..."
Therefore, his wisdom leaks away like water from the foot of a leather water-skin.
The genitive case is used here in the sense of specification (*nirdhāraṇe*).

If even a single sense-organ leaks—that is, if it functions independently in its own object and is not restrained—then his wisdom (*prajñā*) leaks away, as does his fortitude (*dhairya*), even with respect to the objects of the other senses.
A *dṛti* is a vessel made of the hide of a goat or similar animal for carrying water and the like.

Even though his other [senses] are restrained, if water flows from even a single foot, it all leaks away. For one whose mind is intent upon sense objects due to greed for them, neither the fortitude accumulated through the practice of knowledge nor right knowledge itself truly manifests the meanings accessible through logic and scripture.
Having brought the collection of senses under control and likewise restrained the mind,
one should accomplish all goals through yoga without wasting the body.
He explains:
although the mind is indeed a faculty, it is mentioned separately because of its preeminence.
"Village" means a collection.
Having brought the senses as well as the mind under control,
he should accomplish— that is, bring to completion— all goals achievable through rites prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti,
without emaciating or afflicting his body.
"By way of yoga" means by means of proper method.
For one of a delicate constitution, sudden exposure to hard seats, black antelope skins, and so forth, causes suffering;
it is for this reason that this is stated.

Those for whom food is well-prepared and refined, and whose bedding and such are soft, should not abandon those things abruptly; rather, their opposites should be brought to a state of habituation through a gradual process.
This gradual engagement is called "yoga.
And in this context, the connection is with the phrase "having brought [them] under control through yoga."
Or rather, it should be construed as "according to the place through application. One should not remove the body from its proper position;
whatever is appropriate for the body, one should not abruptly withdraw that.
Or "yoga" means intent;
the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the third case.
One should protect the body with intent.
One should stand reciting the Sāvitrī during the morning twilight until the sun appears;
but during the evening twilight, one should always remain seated until the stars are clearly visible.
The morning twilight is that which occurs in front [of the sun] at dawn; the evening twilight is that which occurs at sunset. One should stand during those times, reciting the Sāvitrī.
Rising from his seat, he should remain in one place with his movement ceased;
the Sāvitrī has already been stated as "tat savitur vareṇyam," for there are indeed recitations of it.
The rule regarding the syllable *oṃ* and so forth is for the purpose of the twilight recitation (*saṃdhyājapa*) in this verse: "this syllable and this [mantra]";
"until the sight of the sun" means until the Blessed Lord Āditya is seen.
This is the specific instruction regarding the time for recitation and the location. Now, what is the need for a formal rule? For the twilight (*saṃdhyā*) ceases precisely at sunrise.
To explain: that is called twilight when darkness has not entirely vanished, nor has the light become fully manifest.
And it is said:
"That which is light in heaven and darkness on earth is designated as Time, the offspring of Savitṛ.
It is also stated in the *Nirukta*: "The lower portion belongs to Savitṛ," as is known from the *Paśusamāmnāya*.
On what basis is it said that "Rāma is below" and "Kṛṣṇa is below"?
Furthermore, at the rising of the sun, darkness recedes from all sides;
and when the characteristics of both have not yet ceased, it is the twilight, possessing the characteristics of both night and day.
And this accusative case in "saṃdhyām" is used to express continuous connection;
by that, it is meant that one should remain until the time of twilight.
Beyond that, independence [of duration] is established as a matter of course.
Some say that this is not a case of the accusative used for absolute connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*).

Rather, according to the Vārttikakāra’s rule that "time [and distance] becomes designated as the object (*karman*) of intransitive verbs," the accusative occurs there simply because it is an object (*karman*).
As for the rule "of time and distance in absolute connection," that applies where a word expressing an action is not employed.
The river is crooked for a *krośa*, yet it is auspicious throughout the entire night; furthermore,
the domain of a verbal root that possesses an object is as in "one studies for a month," whereas here, in the case of "one should stand during the twilight," the root *sthā* is intransitive.
Therefore, the instruction regarding the ritual procedure is intended to establish the performance of both standing and sitting for the sake of attaining the entirety of the *saṃdhyā*.
However, the time of commencement is not explicitly stated here, as it is already implied by the word *saṃdhyā* itself;
for that which is the very beginning of the *saṃdhyā* period is precisely the beginning of its ritual injunction.

For the twilight period is not long like the time of the full moon and other such occasions; if there were a delay, it would indeed be difficult to perceive because of its extreme subtlety, like the rising and falling of the ends of a balance scale. The conclusion of night and the commencement of day have their sequence unperceived. The venerable Sun moves with extreme speed; thus, astronomers maintain that his transition from one zodiacal sign to another, once he has finished traversing one, takes only a moment (*truṭi*).
In this way, the rising and setting [of the sun] also mark the beginning and end of the day.
Before sunrise it is night; once the sun has risen, it is day.
And by this [definition], there is no twilight (*saṃdhyā*), because the night ceases precisely with the rising of the sun.
For this very reason, there is engagement in the performance [of rites] when one is near sunrise and sunset;

and there is cessation when the sun and the stars are clearly visible, because he who performs the worship for such a duration necessarily fulfills the injunction at the primary time. And for this same reason, that which is intended here by "twilight" (saṃdhyā) is the entire period pertaining to the sun (sāvitra), not that which is calculated according to the science of astronomy (jyotiḥśāstra).

And that has already been stated previously. If this is so, then for those for whom this alone is the time for the Agnihotra, it would follow as a consequence that there is no twilight ritual (saṃdhyā-vidhi); what kind of objection is this?
It is indeed logical that the Smārta [rite] is set aside by the Śrauta;
moreover, there is no contradiction here,
for it is possible to offer the oblation both while standing and while sitting.
But surely, it is not only standing and sitting that are prescribed for the two twilights; rather, the recitation of the *trika* is also enjoined.
And how could one, while reciting the *sāvitrī*, utter the mantra for the fire-oblation? Let there be a sublation of the recitation.
First, standing and sitting are not contradicted in the case of the primary act;
moreover, according to the maxim "when a subordinate element is omitted, the principal remains," suppression of the recitation is appropriate because it is merely a subsidiary (aṅga).
Furthermore, the status of those two [standing and sitting] as the primary acts is established by their direct connection with the injunction through the words "he should stand" and "he should sit."
However, *japa* (recitation) is subordinate because, by virtue of its present participle suffix (*śatṛ*), it is understood as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, the connection with the qualification applies only to standing and sitting, as seen in the passages: "He who [stands] during the morning [prayer]" and likewise, "Standing thus, he removes the sin of the night.
As for what was stated by someone else—that here "standing" is the subordinate factor and the act of recitation is the primary one—that is incorrect.
"For from that, indeed, we have heard of the fruit"— to this it is replied:
this is not an injunction for one who possesses desire.
Whence is the mention of a fruit?

As for the misconception that there is a restatement of a fruit in the passage beginning with "Oṃ" (praṇava), stating that one is joined with the merit of the Veda, that has been resolved in that very same place.
Therefore, standing and sitting are the primary [requirements].
Alternatively, the Agnihotrin may recite the Sāvitrī once or repeat it three times;
by that much, there is no lapse of the time for the Agnihotra.
According to the rule "having eaten, he is released in the evening," the rite is not thereby obstructed.
The word *aśna* denotes a long period of time;
by that much, the purpose of the twilight (*saṃdhyā*) rite is fulfilled.
For the limit defined by the sight of the sun is merely an ancillary detail (*aṅga*).

The Agnihotra sacrifice is to be performed by those who have risen for the *uditahoma* and have completed their twilight (*saṃdhyā*) rites. However, according to Gautama, the meaning of the sūtra "as long as the light [of the sun] is visible" is that this duration of time is what is called *saṃdhyā*.
It is not a subsidiary element of the ritual (*vidhyaṅga*).
In this regard, there is no repetition of the rite during that specific time.

Just as in the injunction "one should sacrifice on the full moon," the rite is not repeated merely because of the time, so too with the statements "the morning twilight while the stars are still visible" and "the evening twilight while the sun is still present"; even that is a definition of the time, and it is this duration of time that is expressed here by the word "twilight" (*saṃdhyā*).
In that regard, the ritual pertaining to the *saṃdhyā* (twilight) is to be performed.

In this context, if one performs standing, sitting, and recitation (*japa*) for even three or four units of time (*kālakalā*) within that period denoted by the word *saṃdhyā*, which lasts for only a *muhūrta*, the purpose of the injunction is indeed fulfilled.
For here, unlike in the case of Manu, a pervasion of the entire duration of the time is not prescribed.
In every respect, the rites of the *agnihotra* and the *saṃdhyā* can be performed even if they occur at the same time.
The word "always" (*sadā*) expresses their obligatory nature;
it refers to both twilights.
He should sit; "sitting" means remaining in a non-upright posture, being seated. "Ṛkṣa" means a lunar mansion (nakṣatra).
[He should remain] until its disappearance.

The phrase "until the sight of the sun" (ārkadarśanāt) must be supplied here with the word *ākāra*. The term *samyak* is an adjective qualifying both "seeing" (*darśana*) and "cultivation" (*vibhāvanā*).
When the sun has its orb fully complete, and the stars are radiant, endowed with their own light, and not overwhelmed by the splendor of the sun; [at that time, one sees the moon].
Standing while reciting prayers during the morning twilight, one removes the sin committed at night; sitting during the evening twilight, however, one destroys the impurity created by day.
The subject matter here is stated as follows:
it removes—that is, dispels—that fault (doṣa) born from the practice of what is prohibited;
"naiśam" means occurring at night, that which was committed during the night.
Thus, the word *enas* has the same meaning as *mala*.
Furthermore, this expiation does not apply to every sin committed during the day or at night;
for if it did, the specific instructions for particular expiations such as the *kṛcchra* would be rendered useless.
According to the common worldly saying, "If one should find honey on an arka tree, why would one go to the mountain?"— what then [is the point]? Rather,
that minor sin which was committed unintentionally, which cannot be avoided, and for which no specific expiation has been prescribed, departs [by this means].

When one is asleep, subtle injury to living beings occurs through the movement of hands or turning over in bed; scratching the itch of the private parts is prohibited on the grounds that one should not touch them "without cause"; and impurity arises from the flow of saliva and so forth. Furthermore, there is the persistence of impurity not caused at that specific time due to the practice of what is prohibited.
It is with this very intention that it is said: "He should be known as perpetually impure, being devoid of the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana)."
Thus, there is no occurrence of impermanence, because such a fault never exists.

Furthermore, while walking on a path during the day, if one encounters the sight of another man's wife and, upon the manifestation of a mental transformation born thereof, engages in angry and vulgar speech; [this is also a case].
They dispel those two twilight rituals.
But he who neither remains during the morning nor performs worship in the evening is to be excluded from all the duties of the twice-born, like a Śūdra.
By stating that there is a transgression for its non-performance, he establishes its obligatory nature (*nityatā*).
He who does not remain standing during the morning twilight (*saṃdhyā*) nor sits down during the evening twilight should be known as equal to a Śūdra.
He is to be excluded from all duties of the twice-born (*dvijāti*), such as the offering of hospitality and other forms of respectful treatment, and is to be cast out.
Therefore, the *saṃdhyā* must be performed daily in order to exclude equality with the *śūdra*.
This is the statement regarding the qualification [for the rite].
And here, both standing and sitting are prescribed for the recitation (*japa*).
That which is connected with the qualification (adhikāra) is primary; anything else connected to it is auxiliary (aṅga).
Restrained and established in the daily rite near water,
he should go to the forest with a concentrated mind and recite the Sāvitrī.

This is another rule for Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). Because it is not mentioned in the same context as the previous rule for the purpose of memorizing the text, it is distinct from that. "Outside the village" refers to a desolate place in the forest.
Having gone there and reached the vicinity of water— in places such as rivers or ponds—
in its absence even in vessels such as water-pots (kamaṇḍalu) and the like;
being restrained, pure, and diligent.
Being composed and having abandoned all mental distraction,
one should recite even the Sāvitrī;
provided that it is not possible to do so due to some pressing business involving the study of many hymns, sections, chapters, and the like.
"Abiding by the rule for daily rites (*naityaka*). *Naityaka* means that which is constant (*nitya*).
One whose wisdom is established understands that "this rule is indeed constant."

Furthermore, the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*)—the purpose of which is apprehension—is the archetype (*prakṛti*); this [meditation], being its modification (*vikāra*), adopts its properties.
Consequently, the syllable *praṇava* (Om) and other such properties as "with the tips of the grass blades pointing eastward" (*prākkūlān*) belong to the Brahman.
Others, however, explain that "injunction" (*vidhi*) means "mode," "method," "procedure" (*itikartavyatā*), and so forth.
One who relies upon that procedure (*itikartavyatā*) which must necessarily be performed by a perpetual celibate student (*nitya-brahmacārin*) in the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*);

for the obligatory nature (*nityatva*) of this injunction is to be understood from such scriptural passages as, "For that is remembered as the perpetual sacrifice of Brahman" (*brahmasatra*). Of these two, the first explanation appears to be the more reasonable.
For the word *vidhi* is not commonly known to denote "manner" (*prakāra*).

Furthermore, if by the word *naityaka* the rule (*vidhi*) for the religious student (*brahmacārin*) were intended, then in the passage "there is no suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) in the *naityaka* [rite]," that very same thing would be denoted by the word *naityaka*; consequently, the prohibition of suspension of study would apply to that very case.

Furthermore, there is no restriction regarding days unfit for study (anadhyāya) in relation to the auxiliary sciences of the Veda, in the daily private recitation (svādhyāya), and indeed in the mantras used for fire offerings (homa).
The "auxiliaries" (*upakaraṇa*) are the helpful sciences (*upakāraka*), namely the *vedāṅgas* such as the *kalpasūtras*, *nirukta*, and so forth;
when these are being recited, there is no requirement for strict adherence even during periods of suspension from study (*anadhyāya*).
For regarding the *anadhyāyas* and the mantras used for fire-oblations (*homa*), the rules of suspension are not to be strictly observed.
One should study during non-suspension periods;
or rather, there is the reading "na nirodhaḥ. There is no cessation of study during the non-suspension periods.

Even though the rule of non-study during forbidden days (*anadhyāya*) is a property of the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), and that injunction has the *svādhyāya* as its object, and the *svādhyāya* is the Veda, whereas the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) are not denoted by the word "Veda"—nevertheless, because they are interspersed with Vedic sentences, the notion [of them being the Veda] might arise; therefore, it is stated for the sake of clarity.
Or rather, this is an illustration:
just as there is no period of non-study regarding the Vedic auxiliaries, so too there is none regarding the Veda.

Regarding the mantras in the *agnihotra* oblation, or those in other *sāvitra* and propitiatory (*śānti*) oblations— this is mentioned for the sake of illustration— one might think that the rule of non-study during forbidden periods (*anadhyāya*) applies only to the mere utterance of Vedic sentences that are auxiliary to rituals, such as the mantras for constant recitation (*japa*) and the ritual directions (*praiṣa*). Thus, one who would conclude that there should be no recitation of the mantras for the oblation and so forth on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight and other such times is corrected by this matter established through reasoning, which is here being restated.

The enumeration of days unfit for study (*anadhyāya*) is prompted by the injunction for the recitation of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana*); it is not a duty pertaining to the Veda itself. Therefore, there is no prohibition of study regarding mantras that are ancillary to ritual acts (*karmāṅga*).
This refers to the obligatory rule for daily recitation (*naityaka-svādhyāya*), which is enjoined for members of all stages of life (*āśrama*) by the preceding statement.
In the daily recitation there is no suspension of study, for that is remembered as the "Brahma-sacrifice";
it is meritorious, offered with the oblation of the Veda, and consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ*-call even during times when study is otherwise suspended.
This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) supplementary to the preceding rule.
For this reason, there is no suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) for the daily recitation (*nāityaka*), because that is remembered as the "Brahma-weapon" (*brahmāstra*).
Just as a sacrificial session (*satra*)—such as the sacrificial session of a thousand years and so forth—is constantly ongoing and never interrupted, so too is this [daily recitation].

The Brahma-sattra is that which is accomplished through the study of the Veda; and because it is a *sattra*, it must never be interrupted, for if it were interrupted, its status as a *sattra* would not exist.
He now applies this nature of being a *sattra* by means of a metaphorical construction.
The study of the Veda is one oblation offered; another sacrifice is offered by means of the Soma-oblation.
The root *hu* (to offer) is used here in the sense of non-cessation, because verbal roots have multiple meanings.
By the word "Brahman," the act of studying that [Veda] is indicated.
The study of the Veda is compared to an oblation; this is a compound formed according to the rule "vyāghrādibhiḥ" (Pāṇini 2.1.56).
Whatever study is performed on a day when study is forbidden is like a *vaṣaṭ* offering.

Just as at the end of a sacrificial verse (*yājyā*), the continuity of the rite is maintained by the *vaṣaṭ* call, so too the study of the Veda on the fourteenth day and other forbidden days occupies the place of that *vaṣaṭ* call.
By the word "vaṣaṭ," the word "vauṣaṭ" is indicated. That which is performed by it is "yukta" (joined) or "saṃskṛta" (refined).
[The compound] "sādhanakṛt" is a tatpuruṣa compound.
For one who, being self-restrained and pure, studies the Veda according to the prescribed rule for a year,
this [sacrifice] constantly yields milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey.
This is a supplementary injunction to the primary rule,
and that [primary rule] has been established as obligatory;
and regarding what is obligatory, the mention of a fruit is merely an explanatory praise (arthavāda).
Furthermore, there is no injunctive suffix (vidhivibhakti) by which,

according to the principle that "when one thing has two purposes, there is a conjunction [of acts] and a separation [of results]," milk and the like could serve as the cause for a distinct entitlement (*adhikārāntara*).

And since a permanent entitlement (*nitya-adhikāra*) is already established, the principle of the *rātrisatra* does not apply, whereby milk and the like would otherwise be postulated as having no other fruit.

Therefore, this is merely an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise). Its basis is the statement regarding the "flowing forth" (*prakṣaraṇa*) of milk and other substances through the acquisition of cattle by means of receiving gifts and so on, which results from the world's respect for one who studies.

He who studies the Veda as his own sacred recitation (*svādhyāya*) for a year—that is, for a full year—according to the rule, sitting on grass-blades pointing eastward, self-restrained with controlled senses, and pure through bathing and other rites; for that person, it flows, streams, and gives constantly throughout his life, as long as he lives.
This is the *svādhyāya*.
"Payodadhi" (milk and curd).
Others, however, consider that dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are expressed by the words "milk" and so forth:

milk is dharma because of its commonality with purity; curd is artha because it is a cause of nourishment; ghee is kāma because of its commonality with affection; and honey is mokṣa because of the unification of all flavors.

Whatever human goal there may be, all of it is attained through the study of the Veda in just one year, let alone over a longer period of time. Since these are merely explanatory statements (*arthavāda*), one should not insist on determining the precise literal meaning of words such as "milk" and so forth.

Having undergone the initiation ceremony, a twice-born man shall perform the tending of the sacred fire, the practice of begging for alms, sleeping on the ground, and doing what is beneficial for his teacher, until his formal return home (samāvartana).
Kindling the fire with fuel-sticks every morning and evening is "kindling the fire-god.
Not ascending a bedstead means sleeping on the ground;
however, it does not mean specifically sleeping on the bare earth.

Service to the teacher, characterized by fetching water-jars and so forth, consists of attending to his needs; that which performs such assistance must be carried out for as long as one lives. This is to be performed until the completion of the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*), ending with the ritual bath (*snāna*) that marks the departure from the teacher’s household, because this service is for the purpose of fulfilling the injunction to study the Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana-vidhi*).

Since the persistence [of duties] lasts as long as one's undertaking of the student life (*brahmacarya*) and its constituent practices, and their cessation follows from the abandonment of those, this is already established.

The repetition of the examples of fire and fuel, however, is for the purpose of enjoining the performance of that entire collection of duties—distinct from those previously mentioned—by subsequent stages of life (*āśrama*) as well.
Thus says Gautama: "And this is not in conflict with the subsequent stages."
Now, why is it not thus: that these [beings] persist as long as they practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*), while others, however, turn back even before that?
Another *smṛti* has been shown on this point:
"And restrictive rules (*niyama*) follow the principal; such is the principle when there is a possibility [of its application]."
Since it means "beneficial for the teacher," the dative case is appropriate by virtue of its connection with the word *hita*.

The son of the teacher, one who is obedient, a giver of knowledge, righteous, pure, trustworthy, capable, a provider of wealth, virtuous, and one's own kinsman— these ten are to be taught according to the Dharma.
He will state that "of all gifts, the gift of the Veda (brahmadāna) is preeminent.
In this regard, the following verse is intended to define the characteristics of a worthy recipient (*pātra*) for whom knowledge should be given;
furthermore, this rule concerning teaching is stated here in connection with the duties of a religious student (*brahmacārin*).
The son of the teacher:
service, attendance, performing whatever household tasks are necessary according to one's ability, and massaging the body.
The giver of knowledge: whatever text is not known to the teacher, which has been somehow learned by the student—whether concerning wealth, pleasure, the arts, or dharma.
This teaching is [given] through the discipline of knowledge (*vidyā-viniyama*).
A righteous person (*dhārmika*) is one for whom the primary focus is the performance of rituals such as the *agnihotra*.
A pure person (*śuci*) is one who is purified by earth and water, as well as by purity of purpose (*artha-śuddhi*).
The three terms "righteous" (*dhārmika*), "pure" (*śuci*), and "virtuous" (*sādhu*) are a tautology, like the expression "ox and bull.
"A trustworthy person" (*āpta*) refers to one who is close, such as a friend or a kinsman.
"Capable" (*śakta*) means one who possesses the ability to comprehend and retain [the teachings].
He is a giver of wealth;
his own son who has been initiated [is to be taught],
and even those previously initiated by others may be taught.
Now, it is said that this is the "nature of things" (dharmatā), for through these [virtues] being cultivated, the Dharma comes into being;
and the purpose is served by what is seen.
In that case, whence is the assumption of the unseen (adṛṣṭa)?
Who said it is a conceptual construction?
What is the conceptual construction regarding what was heard?
For it was heard directly that "the tenfold nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is to be studied."
But the Teacher says: "The established rule of the Dharmaśāstras is being stated here:
by teaching these [students], there is no transgression of dharma; however, when one teaches for the sake of wealth, the dharma characterized as the 'gift of knowledge' does not occur."
One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks improperly;
for even though he knows, a wise man should behave like one who is dull-witted in the world.

If a student who has not formally approached the teacher destroys [the text] while reciting—whether by omitting a syllable or reciting it with a wrong accent—the teacher must not say anything unless asked, such as: "You have destroyed this; it should be read like this.
However, even if the student does not ask, the teacher must speak [if the error is obvious].
Even if he asks, the teacher must still not speak if he asks in an improper manner.
"Since I have a doubt regarding this matter, it is right for you to instruct me"—this is the proper method of inquiry according to the duty of a disciple.

Otherwise, even though he knows the answer, he would behave in the world like one who is dull-witted or mute, remaining silent like an ignorant person. This prohibition against removing doubts without being asked pertains specifically to the subject matter of the scriptures.
In judicial procedure, however, he will state: "Whether appointed or unappointed, one who knows the Dharma ought to speak.
Others, however, maintain that this applies without distinction.
He who speaks unrighteously and he who asks unrighteously—
one of these two perishes or incurs enmity.

He states the fault incurred by transgressing this prohibition: "He who, when questioned regarding what is not dharma or questioned in an unjust manner, declares, 'This is what was taught to be studied,' and he who asks [the question]— [both incur sin]."
Both of them die before their time;
or, if one is the transgressor, he alone dies. If, when questioned unjustly, he does not speak, then the questioner alone dies; or if he speaks in reply, then both die.
By this demonstration of the fault in an improper question, the questioner’s method of questioning is shown to be unjust;
or else, he incurs hatred or becomes an object of dislike in the world.
Where neither virtue nor wealth is found, nor even a corresponding desire to listen,
there knowledge should not be sown, just as one would not sow good seed in saline soil.

What was stated as "ten [persons] should be taught according to the law" is a brief restatement of that very point by way of another method, not an expression of a new meaning, because it is a restatement of what is already under discussion.

The word *artha* should be understood as referring to mere benefit (*upakāra-mātra*), since teaching has previously been said to occur even through the exchange of knowledge (*vidyā-vinimaya*). Such persons are suitable for being taught.
"Great for great things and small for small things.
In this context, *vidyā* (knowledge) is that by which every object is found—that is, known; thus, *vidyā* consists of both the recitation of the text and the comprehension of its meaning.
One who provides no assistance should not be taught, nor should an explanation of the meaning be given to him.
"Barren soil" (ūṣara) is said to be that portion of ground where, due to defects in the earth, a seed does not sprout even when it is entirely present;
whereas auspicious and excellent grains such as rice are sown with plows and other implements.

In this way, knowledge sown in a [suitable] field indeed bears great fruit. And it should not be thought that teaching for the sake of taking wealth constitutes "wages," for in that case, the engagement does not precede a prior agreement on the measure of payment, such as: "If you give this much, then I shall teach this much."
This refers to the form of service;
it does not mean by the mere scent of assistance to the teacher's purpose.

As for the statement that one should not previously render any service to the teacher, this is not a prohibition against prior service; rather, it means that when one is about to bathe and has been formally commanded, the teacher’s purpose must be accomplished to the best of one's ability.
That negation is merely a supplement to that [preceding statement] and is not a separate sentence.
A teacher of Brahman should die only together with his knowledge;
even in the midst of terrible calamity, he must never sow it in barren soil.
The word *sama* means "together with.

It is fitting for a proponent of Brahman—that is, a student of the Vedas—to meet death while his own body is worn out by [the study] that has not been imparted; it is not, however, [fitting] to impart it to an unworthy recipient.
By this it is understood that teaching must necessarily be performed by one who has studied the Veda, and not merely for the sake of livelihood.
Nor is the qualification restricted solely to one who desires a fruit, as is the case with the giving of water and the like.
Thus says the Śruti: "He who, having studied the Vidyā, does not teach it to one who asks, would be a destroyer of his duty;
he would shut the door to the highest good."
One should teach this; it is a great source of glory. The seers declare it to be the sovereign authority of speech. All this is established upon this yoga.
Those who know thus become immortal.
By the statement "he would be a destroyer of his duty," the Śruti itself, reiterating the fault in not teaching, makes known its necessity.
"In barren soil" (iriṇe) means where the three previously mentioned purposes are absent.
"Even in terrible calamity" (āpadi) means even in a most distressing emergency.
The absence of instructed disciples is said to be a painful calamity;
and this occurs when [the duty] is mandatory.
For if [teaching] were obligatory, then in the absence of a primary [disciple], the cessation of teaching would follow through the employment of a substitute disciple.
Just as [one proceeds] with wild rice (*nīvāra*) in the absence of *vrīhi* rice,
so too in this state there is simply a cessation of the entitlement to teach;
