it is like the cessation of honoring guests when there is an absence of hospitality characterized by the aforementioned qualities.
By the term "he should sow," teaching is expressed through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by means of the properties of a seed;
for just as a seed sown in a field indeed yields abundant fruit, so too does knowledge.
Others, however, explain it as referring to the calamity caused by the lack of wealth.
"Even by one who is extremely destitute, it is better that he die rather than sow in barren soil;
thus, 'one should protect oneself from all [harm]'—this injunction is not transgressed even when such a means of livelihood as teaching exists.
This is incorrect.
One who gives wealth does not [give] to a barren field (iriṇa), because the word *iriṇa* is a restatement of what was previously mentioned.
Furthermore, if one does not even give wealth, how could an engagement with that [recipient] in times of distress be possible, such that it would need to be prohibited?
Knowledge approached a Brahmin and said: "I am your treasure; protect me.
Do not give me to a scorner, so that I may remain most powerful."
This too is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda).
Knowledge, having assumed a physical form, approached a certain teacher and said:
"I am your treasure; protect me."
What, then, is your protection?
Do not give me to one who is envious, contemptuous, or abusive;
do not cause me to commit abuse against one who reviles you.

And thus, in this way, I shall become most heroic and pre-eminently the accomplisher of your task; "heroism" (vīrya) refers to an excellence of capacity in the fulfillment of a purpose. As for the reading "śevadhiṣṭe 'smi," with the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*, that is an imitation of a Vedic usage.
But speak to that brahmin alone whom you know to be pure, self-restrained, a celibate student, a guardian of the treasure, and vigilant.
To whatever disciple you may know to be pure, disciplined, with senses restrained, devoted to effort, and practicing celibacy— to him speak of me.
For he who guards and protects a treasure is one who, being vigilant, does not become negligent nor stumble, because of his total devotion to that task.

From this explanatory passage (arthavāda), it is understood that [the initiation] should be given to all disciples who possess these qualities, such as being capable, having obtained [the necessary materials], and being givers of wealth.
He who acquires the Veda from one who is reciting it without permission is guilty of the theft of Brahman and falls into hell.

When someone, while studying for the sake of practice or explaining [the text] to another, has another person approach him and grasp that Veda which was previously unknown to him, or dispel his doubt, this fault is said to belong to the former.

Until permission is granted—[the latter should say], "Just as these are studying under you, so may I also study; please deign to grant me permission"—he should learn only after having obtained such permission.
Otherwise, the study of that Veda is like theft.
Thus, that student, joined with this thief of the Veda (*brahmacaura*), reaches hell, a place of great torment.
The ablative case in *adhīyānāt* is used according to the rule "the ablative is used for the source in connection with a verb of acquisition" (*ākhyātopayoge*).
Alternatively, because the act of departing is implied, it is as if the Veda itself were departing from the student.
Or, with *lyap* [the suffix -ya] when there is an object;
having heard one who is studying, he acquires it—that is, he learns.
Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual knowledge, one should first pay homage to the person from whom that knowledge was received.
The incidental discussion is concluded; now the procedure for salutation is commenced. "Laukika" means that which exists in the world, namely, the training in worldly conduct.

Alternatively, it is the knowledge of the arts of singing and instrumental music; or the knowledge of the treatises concerning the arts by Vātsyāyana and Viśākhila; or the Vedic [knowledge], which is prescribed by rule and concerns the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the Smṛtis;
or the spiritual science (ādhyātmikavidyā), which is the science of the Upaniṣads concerning the Self.

Or, because the body is metaphorically designated as the "self," this Vedic knowledge should first be used to greet that person who was the teacher from whom one learned it. At the first meeting, the act of bringing [the teacher] face-to-face by means of a word— used in the manner to be described for the purpose of uttering a blessing— is the meaning of the verb *abhivādayati*.
"Previously" means first. By that [rule], he is to be addressed; however, his own speech need not be awaited, for at that time he would be the one returning the greeting.
If it is argued that the word "pūrva" (first) is redundant because the meaning is already established by the word "abhivādayet" (should salute), that is not so;

for when this word is present, this specific meaning is obtained. Indeed, by examining the meanings of the verbal root and the prefix, one understands merely the act of speaking while facing [the other].
It certainly occurs even for one who has been awakened by another;
however, those who explain [the verse] as "those who were previously [teachers] to one's own parents" should be disregarded, as that is irrelevant to the context.
A Brahmin who is well-restrained is better, even if his essence consists only of the Sāvitrī mantra,
than one who is unrestrained, even if he knows the three Vedas, eats all things, and sells all things.

This is a praise of the rules of conduct such as salutation and so forth. He whose essence and primary focus is the *sāvitrī* alone is described in this way; that is, one whose study consists of the *sāvitrī* alone.
A Brahmin is better and superior if he is well-restrained, meaning his self is governed by the scriptures.

One who is unrestrained—even if he knows the three Vedas and is learned in the scriptures—eats everything; that is, he consumes whatever is censured by worldly custom, even if it is not explicitly forbidden.
Likewise, he is a seller of all things.
The mention of eating and selling is for the purpose of illustration; it implies other prohibited acts as well.
This is what is meant:
just as one is censured for abandoning other observances, so too is one censured for abandoning rising to greet [a guest] and so forth.

Now, as for the question "How is it that *varaṃ vipraḥ*?"—since it ought to be *varo vipraḥ*—some say that because a specific [term] is expressed following a general introduction, this is "better" (*varam*); what is that? It is that he is a Brahmin who is well-restrained (*suyantritaḥ*). Others, however, say that the word *vara*, having entered into various genders, also exists in the neuter gender.
One should not sit together with a superior on a bed or seat already occupied by him;
while remaining on one's own bed or seat, one should rise to meet him and offer salutation.
The term "śayyā cāsanaṃ" (bed and seat) is a dvandva compound in the singular form according to the rule that the genus of inanimate objects is singular;
one should not occupy or sit together with a superior—such as a teacher or one more advanced in knowledge and so forth—on such a thing.
Is this the case for every instance? No.
"No," he says; "there is no fault regarding that which is used as a bed or a seat, even if it is artificial,
provided it is a stone slab or the like."
And he will say, "One should sit together with the teacher"; this [present rule] is a restatement of that very point.
Others explain it as "in what is frequented" or "occupied.
One should not enter there even at a later time; it is not merely a prohibition against sitting together.
For that [distinction] is indeed established by what is about to be stated;
and when a positive injunction is possible, a mere restatement (anuvāda) is not appropriate.
Regarding this, some explain the distinction based on traditional practice (ācāra).
That which is known as the teacher’s exclusive bed or seat—where the teacher lies down or sits—there the disciple shall not sit, whether in his presence or out of his sight.
However, where these two actions have been performed by the teacher in some way or another, the prohibition applies only when he is not present.
It is precisely such conduct that is called *adhyācarita* (habitual practice), and not merely any place occupied through the relationship of owner and property.
Furthermore, if someone superior arrives while one is seated on a bed or a seat, one must rise from there and perform a salutation.
As for the phrase "seated on a vehicle or a seat," that refers to descending from what has been designated as a seat for a teacher;
its meaning is that one must abandon the bed or seat by standing upon the ground.
However, this rising to greet a superior who is not an *aguru* is possible only for one who remains seated on his seat.
For the vital breaths of a young man indeed rise upward when an elder approaches;
he recovers them again by rising to meet him and by saluting him.
This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding the former [case].

When an elder—meaning one of advanced age—is approaching or coming, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), which are the causes of life and consist of the internal winds, exit upwards from the mouth of the youth—the young man. Abandoning the function of the downward breath (*apāna*), they seek to effect the severance of life.
When one rises and performs a salutation, by that act they become capable of maintaining their life as before;
they proceed and are restored to life.
For one who is habitually respectful and constantly attends upon the elders, four things increase: longevity, virtue, fame, and strength.
He is one who addresses everyone first and is habituated to saluting others as is appropriate; this refers not merely to the utterance of the word of salutation itself.
By the word "habit" (*śīla*), the absence of regard for personal gain is expressed.
He constantly attends upon his elders with kind words and the like.
For by serving him with assistance according to one's ability,
four things increase for that person:
longevity, the Dharma, and the tree of fruits such as heaven in the next world.
And the two [powers], glory and strength, have been mentioned previously;
this explanatory passage (arthavāda) is also a cause for understanding the fruit [of the action].
After the initial salutation, a Brahmin greeting an elder should announce his own name,
saying, "I am so-and-so by name."
When another person is addressed by name, directed toward a benediction, or asked a question regarding their welfare, that is an *abhivāda* (salutation).
Following this salutation—that is, immediately after the word expressing the salutation—one should utter this word: "I am named so-and-so.
Here, the pronoun *asau* (that one) denotes every particular [person].
This particular use of words is for the purpose of bringing [the other person] face-to-face: "I am saluting you" means you are being brought face-to-face for the sake of a blessing.

Then, having understood the request, he begins to offer a return salutation, a blessing, and so forth. For this cannot be expressed by using a general pronoun; [otherwise], not understanding the request, whom would he address with a blessing? Moreover, it is heard in the tradition that "one should announce one's own name."
In that case, when it is said, "I am this one named Devadatta," one would perform the salutation;
however, because of the lack of purpose for the word "this one" (*asau*), there is no determination of its meaning.
Furthermore, the authors of the Sūtras also conduct their discourse according to other systems of tradition (*smṛti*).

Just as Pāṇini uses terms such as "the second case" (*dvitīyā*) in the rule *karmaṇi dvitīyā*, so too here [in the Yajñasūtra] it is stated, "this [is] also [the case]," thereby extending its own name by analogy; this is also formulated as a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) in the Yajñasūtra.

If this is so, since it is already established by the phrase "one's own name" (*svaṃ nāma*) alone, the word "this" (*asau*) in the expression "this name" (*nāma*) is redundant. [Reply: It is for the purpose of employing the word "name" (*nāma*).
How so?
One should proclaim one's own name, saying, "I am this name," meaning,
"I am such-and-such by nature. Because they share the same referent, they consider these two to be interchangeable.

In these two verses, this much is established as the form of the salutation formula: "I, named Devadatta, salute you, sir" (*abhivādaye devadattanāmāhaṃ bhoḥ*). By the subsequent verse, the word "sir" (*bhoḥ*) will be prescribed [for the elder].

Because of the mention of "one who is superior" (*jyāyāṃsam*), there is also a salutation for those who are equal or inferior; however, this specific manner [of address] does not apply to them, because it pertains specifically to one who is superior.
To those who do not understand the meaning of one's name,
a wise man should say "I am [so-and-so]," and he should do the same for all women.

Since even an unlearned person might be entitled to a formal salutation (*abhivādana*) according to rule due to their superior wealth and other such factors, this [verse] is intended to preclude that.
Any unlearned persons who do not understand the refined name when it is uttered for the purpose of a salutation—
thinking "we have been saluted by him"— and who, being ignorant of grammar, do not comprehend the refined language (*saṃskṛta*), those men and women should be saluted by the wise.

These [fools] do not comprehend the Sanskrit being spoken; therefore, omitting even a portion of the formal injunction—namely, the mention of one's own name—they should say only this much: "I salute you" (*abhivādaye 'ham*). If they still do not understand even that, they are to be saluted even with common vernacular (*apabhraṃśa*). It is for this purpose that the term "wise" (*prājña*) is included. Having recognized their incapacity for understanding, one should adapt the practice of salutation accordingly; one must not adhere strictly to the literal instruction alone.
The same applies to women as well.
The inclusion of the term "all" refers even to the wives of gurus who are knowledgeable in the application of refined language (*saṃskṛta*).

Others, however, maintain that one who is known by a nickname, such as Vanamālīvarṇa, should not use the name given by his father because it is not well-known; since what is well-known is not [merely] a name, he should instead proclaim his own [nicknamed] name.
Others, however, explain that [certain people] do not know how to return a greeting.
Since the rule "in returning a greeting, except for a Śūdra" prescribes a protracted vowel (*pluta*) at the end of the name,
one should simply say "I am he" (*aham ity eva*) to those who do not know that [rule].
In the context of presenting the purposes of grammar, the author of the Mahābhāṣya has demonstrated this:
"Those ignorant ones who do not know the protracted vowel (*pluti*) at the end of their name during a return greeting—
against them, if one has lived abroad, one may speak as one wishes, just as one would toward women."
They say that by the force of another Smṛti text, this word "abhivāda" (greeting) actually functions in the sense of "pratyabhivāda" (the return greeting).

If this were not explained in such a way, then the rule "he is not to be greeted by a learned man" would imply a total prohibition of greeting in every respect; in that case, there would be a contradiction with another Smṛti text which says, "he should say, 'This am I'. However, when it is explained in this manner, that prohibition is based on praise and is not an injunction; it is interpreted accordingly to follow this specific purpose.
In a salutation, one should utter the word "bhoḥ" at the end of one's own name;
for the seers have declared that the state of being "bhoḥ" is the very essence of names.
One should utter the word "bhoḥ" at the end of one's own name.
The inclusion of the word "one's own" is for the purpose of excluding the person being saluted. The remainder is a commendatory statement (arthavāda).
And it is not only at the end of the syllables of the name, but also after those [syllables] [one says], "I am.
For here, the particle *iti* is used for the purpose of delimiting the application;
it must be employed in exactly this way.

Moreover, in the case of an ill-taught usage such as "O Devadatta, I am [here]," when comprehension is delayed, the manifestation [of the word's meaning] would occur only after a long time; thus, there would be a contradiction regarding the function [of the word]. In a case where the connection is obstructed, someone might not even be attentive.
The "existence of its own form" (*svarūpabhāva*) is the being (*sattā*) of its own form.
Alternatively, when there is the actual form (*svarūpa*) of those names that are to be saluted, it occurs in place of them; therefore, there is the cessation of those names.
The word *bhāva* may be derived in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāvasādhana*) or in the sense of an agent (*kartṛsādhana*).
Or, the locative ending in *svarūpabhāve* should be read [as *svarūpe bhāve*].
The state of being "bho" (*bhobhāva*).
That which is the becoming, that which is the essential nature of the word *bho*, is the essential nature of nouns.

Just as someone is addressed by grasping their name, saying, "Devadatta, listen!", so too the word *bhoḥ*, ending in the vocative case, is remembered by the sages as being used precisely for the purpose of addressing.

When greeting a Brahmin, one should say, "May you be long-lived, O gentle one. Furthermore, at the end of his name, the letter *a* should be pronounced with the preceding vowel lengthened to a protracted (*pluta*) sound.
When a salutation has been performed, the one who returns the salutation—the father who is being saluted—should be addressed thus: "May you be long-lived, O gentle one" (*āyuṣmān bhava saumya*).

The word *iti* indicates a manner; it serves to include other such expressions as "May you be long-lived," "May you be of great longevity," "May you live for a long time," and so forth, which are well-established in the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).
The letter *a* at the end of the name of that person who is being greeted in return must be pronounced as a protracted vowel (*pluta*).
"Protracted" (*pluta*) is a technical term for a vowel consisting of three morae (*mātrā*).
The mention of the letter *a* is intended to illustrate the same rule for the letters *i* and the others as well.
And the state of being final (antatva) should be understood as independent [of other conditions].
It applies even to that which is the final vowel of a word ending in a consonant.
This is a qualification of the vowel *a* which is about to undergo prolation (*pluta*), referring specifically to the preceding syllable.
In this context, "syllable" (akṣara) refers to a consonant.
That which is joined with a preceding [vowel] is thus described.
This is what is meant:
The vowel *a* that is not adventitious (*āgantu*) should not be protracted (*pluta*). Rather, only that which already exists within the name itself should be protracted.
And all this explanation is by virtue of the authoritative tradition (*smṛti-sāmarthya*) of the Blessed One Pāṇini.
Furthermore, regarding the application of words and their meanings, the venerable Pāṇini is more authoritative than Manu and others.
And he records that in the case of a return greeting (*pratyabhivāda*) addressed to one who is not a *śūdra*, there is a protracted vowel (*pluti*) for the final syllable (*ṭi*).
By the term *ṭi*, that which begins with the final vowel is denoted.
The mention of "Brahmins" is not intended to be restrictive;
this same rule applies to Kṣatriyas and others as well,
for the practice established by other Smṛtis is exactly thus.
And there is no other rule for these.
An example here is: "O venerable Devadatta! [The vocative ending is elided].
For one whose name ends in a consonant: "O venerable Somasharman, prosper! [The final vowel is lengthened].
That brahmin who does not know how to return a greeting is not to be greeted by a learned man; he is exactly like a śūdra.
The statement "one who does not know the return-greeting" implies that such a person should be addressed in this way; thus, [the word] *abhivādasya* is redundant and does not cohere [with the rest].
This is not so;
rather, the construction is made as follows: "the return-greeting corresponding to the greeting."

For one who performs a salutation by uttering their own name, a prolation (*pluti*) should be made at the end of that name. However, for one who salutes saying, "I, sir," there is neither the utterance of a name nor a prolation.
The phrase "not to be saluted" is a prohibition against the utterance of the word "salutation."
The salutation should be performed exactly as prescribed, and not with such forms as "I, sir" (*ahaṃ bho*), because that has already been shown previously.
This very point is understood from the example of the *śūdra*:
even for a *śūdra*, being of advanced age, the state of being worthy of salutation and being the first to speak is desired.
The word "viduṣā" is for the purpose of completing the meter.
Upon meeting a Brāhmaṇa, one should ask about his welfare; a Kṣatriya, regarding his freedom from illness; a Vaiśya, regarding his security; and a Śūdra, regarding his health alone.

When a greeting has been offered and returned, and a friendly rapport has been established, this restriction of words based on differences in caste is intended for an inquiry made out of a desire to know.
This restriction of caste applies to those who are to be questioned, not to the questioners.
Furthermore, because these [questions] do not have entirely different meanings, this restriction of their specific form is prescribed.
The words *ārogya* (health) and *anāmaya* (freedom from disease) have the same meaning.

Likewise, the words *kṣema* (security) and *kuśala* (well-being) are not absolutely different either. Although the word *kuśala* denotes proficiency, here it refers to the non-departure of the body and its constituent elements (*saṃyogin*).
These must necessarily be employed;
there is no prohibition against others as well, according to one's inspiration, for the sake of desiring specific distinctions.
This is likewise shown in a certain chapter of the Mahābhārata.
Some argue that because of the expression "having come together here" (*samāgamya*), this question does not concern a teacher or similar superior, but rather concerns only those of equal age;
for approaching (*abhigamana*) a teacher is prescribed by rule, whereas coming together (*samāgama*) occurs by chance.
However, since there is indeed a "coming together" even within the context of formal "approaching," this argument is trivial.
One who knows the Dharma should address an initiated person by name only if he is younger; otherwise, he should address him using the honorifics "bho" or "bhavat" placed at the beginning.

At the time of returning a greeting and on other occasions, one who is initiated for the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices—from the initiation ceremony (*dīkṣaṇīyā*) until the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*)—should not be addressed by name; that is, his personal name must not be uttered. By the word "even" (*api*), it is inferred that there is a prohibition against uttering the name of an elder brother even if he has not been initiated, provided he is younger—that is, junior or born at a more recent time.
And likewise Gautama says: "One should mention the name and lineage of the guru with respect.
Respect (*māna*) means worship; the name should be taken preceded by that [respect]. For example: "The Lord Janārdana Miśra.
How, then, should one who has been initiated conduct conversation for the sake of business?
"Preceded by 'bhoḥ' or 'bhavat':

having first employed the word 'bhoḥ', one should address this initiated person using derivative terms such as 'dīkṣita' or 'yajamāna'. However, the mention of his name preceded by the word 'bhoḥ' is not permitted."
When it is stated that "that address which has the word *bhobhavat* preceding it" is [the form], they explain the rule because these two words cannot be used together in a single sentence.
When one is engaged in conversation with him, he should be addressed using the vocative case ending with the word *bhoḥ*.
However, when one describes his qualities in his absence, one should employ [the forms] such as "this was done by His Honour the Dīkṣita" or "His Honour does this."
And since only the nominal stem (prātipadika) "bhavat" has been employed, it must be used together with its ending when it enters into a relationship with a case-suffix.
But toward a woman who is the wife of another and not related by birth,
one should address her as "Madam," "O auspicious lady," or "Sister."
When conversation with a woman occurs for a specific purpose, it should be conducted in this manner:
"Whether you are another's wife (*patnī*), or whether you are a sister (*bhaginī*).
This word *bhavat* ends in a feminine suffix; in the vocative case, its vowel has been shortened.

In the phrase "it becomes" (*bhavatīti*), the particle *iti* indicates that the very form of the word itself—altered by the reversal of its original meaning—is intended to communicate the sense to another; as in the case of *subhage* for *bhaginī*, where it denotes a specific manner of address.
Since the governing rule is "he should speak," it is established that the actual phonetic form of the word is what is being grasped.
Furthermore, when addressing her as a teacher, she should be addressed with such words as "O Mother," "O Illustrious One," "O Younger Sister," "O Daughter," "O Long-lived One," and so forth.
Because of the mention of the "wife" (*patnī*), this rule does not apply to a maiden (*kanyā*).
Furthermore, she is unrelated by birth (*yonitaḥ*);

for those who have not attained kinship through either the maternal or paternal line—such as the daughters of one's maternal uncle and so forth—he will state a different rule for them in the verse beginning with "the women who are female relatives and connections" (*jñātisaṃbandhiyoṣitaḥ*).
But surely that [point] is established by that very [rule], since this general rule finds its application elsewhere; what then is the use of the phrase "and also unconnected"?
One need not strive to point out such redundancy here, for this is a work composed in verse.
Upon rising, one should address maternal uncles, paternal uncles, fathers-in-law, officiating priests, and teachers who are younger than oneself, saying, "I am so-and-so."
Because of the plural designation "gurūn," it is not only the specific person mentioned here as a guru who is understood;

rather, like the term in Gautama’s [Dharma-sūtra], it is a general word denoting those who are senior by virtue of wealth and so forth. "To them" refers to those younger than one's own age, such as a sister's son and others, who are inferior in years relative to oneself.

One's own name is indicated by saying "I am so-and-so," and the use of the word "I" following that is permitted. This is what should be done for those who have arrived after one has risen from one's seat.
The use of the word "bhoḥ" in a salutation is prohibited; and it is stated in the Gautama-sūtra that those who are to be saluted should rise up.
A maternal aunt, the wife of a maternal uncle, a mother-in-law, and a paternal aunt are to be honored like the wife of one's guru; they are equal to the wife of a guru.
And these [wives] are to be honored like the wife of one's guru by rising to meet them, saluting them, offering them a seat, and so forth.

Although this is already established by the phrase "like the wife of the guru," the specific statement "they are equal" (samāḥ) permits that other duties toward the guru’s wife—such as obeying her commands and the like—may also occasionally be performed.
Otherwise, because of the context, the term "to be honored" (saṃpūjyāḥ) would refer exclusively to the matter of salutation.
Women with grey hair are also mentioned [in this context];
for those who are younger as well, this very same rule of salutation applies.
The wife of one's brother of the same caste should be saluted every day;
however, upon returning from a journey, the wives of one's paternal kinsmen and maternal relatives should be saluted.
It should be understood that this refers to one's elder brother. "To be clasped" means to be saluted by touching his feet.
"Savarṇā" means belonging to the same caste.
However, for women of the Kṣatriya and other castes, the duty toward their paternal and maternal relatives applies even to the wives of their brothers; likewise,
the duty toward the women of one's paternal and maternal kin applies when one has returned from a journey—
that is, upon returning from travel abroad.
For it is not possible for one who is away from home to perform the formal salutation (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*).

"Kinsmen" refers to those on the father’s side, such as paternal uncles and so forth; "relatives" refers to those on the mother’s side, such as fathers-in-law and so forth. Since this salutation is of the nature of an act of reverence, it is performed toward their elders; younger members do not deserve such honor.
One should maintain a conduct toward one's father's sister, one's mother's elder sister, and even one's own elder sister as toward a mother; yet the mother is more venerable than they.

Regarding the sister of one's father and the sister of one's mother—in such a case, as well as toward one's own elder sister, the same conduct prescribed for a mother is extended by analogy. Now, it might be argued that this very rule has already been stated for the mother’s sister and the father’s sister in the passage beginning, "The mother’s sister, the maternal uncle’s wife," and so forth. To this it is replied: [the present rule serves to clarify the application].
In that context, it was stated, "like the wife of a guru";
here, however, it is said, "the conduct is like that toward one's mother.
This is not a difference.
For the conduct toward the wife of one's guru is equal to that toward one's mother.
Some say this is restated in order to state that the mother is more venerable than those [others], namely the two sisters and the father;
for when the mother gives an order and the sisters and others do as well, the mother’s order is to be carried out, not theirs.
Nor should it be said that this [rule] is already established by the principle that "the mother excels in terms of reverence," because that statement is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
Others, however, maintain that there is a difference in the conduct required toward the teacher’s wife and the mother:
for the teacher’s wife, the prior command and so forth are mandatory.
However, due to affection since childhood, there may be a change [in status] for the mother;
in that regard, the distinction between the maternal aunt and the paternal aunt is based on both designations.
In childhood, the fondling is indeed equal toward one's own sister.
"But for one whose childhood has passed, there is a state of being worthy of worship like the wife of a guru.
Nor is this established by this [text] alone;

for if there were not two distinct statements, then by the mere phrase "conduct toward her is like that toward a mother," only the cessation of salutation (abhivādana) pertaining to the context would be understood.
Furthermore, the extension of affectionate conduct is prescribed as follows:
friendship among citizens is said to be based on a ten-year seniority; among artists, it is based on a five-year seniority;
among Vedic scholars, it is based on a three-year seniority; and among blood relations, it is established even by a very small difference in age.
It was stated previously that "the vital breaths indeed depart when old age approaches the young. In that regard, after how many years does one become old?
For in the world, the conventional designation of "old" occurs upon the graying of the head; this [verse] is for the purpose of defining that.
Friendship with fellow citizens is said to exist even when there is a difference of ten years from birth;
therefore, one who is more than ten years older becomes an elder, yet he should be treated like a friend, as it is said: "O sir! or "Friend!"
"Jyeṣṭha" means more than ten years old.
"Ākhyā" means a designation;
it refers to a youth whose designation is "ten years."
This is a three-membered *bahuvrīhi* compound.

There is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) because the years are the cause for the designation [of the friend], since the distinction between the cause and the thing caused is not intended to be expressed.
And this much is the meaning contained within the compound: that one who is born before ten years [of age] is indeed a friend.
The "pure ones" are the citizens;
the mention of "city-dwellers" is for the sake of illustration, as this same rule applies to village-dwellers as well.
Whosoever reside in a single village, provided that there exists a cause for mutual proximity between them, they are friends.

However, among those who possess some skill in arts such as sculpture, singing, or instrumental music, he who is older by five years is a *sakha* (friend/peer), and beyond that, he is *jyeṣṭha* (elder). Among those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyas*), friendship exists for three years.
Even among those of the same caste or lineage, he who is older by even a short time—by just a few days—is *jyeṣṭha*.
But how long is this "very short time"? It is certainly not a year;
for since it is specified as "prior to three years," when it is further described as "short," it is understood to be less than that.
Furthermore, because of the use of the singular number, it is not two years, nor even one year;

for the qualification "for a short time" would otherwise be untenable. For the object denoted by the word "year" has a definite measure, and that which is deficient by even a single day and night does not possess the status of being a year.

Therefore, by the word "short," he refers to time in general; and its specific qualification is that it is less than a year. Furthermore, the word "api" (also/even) should be understood as having the sense of "eva" (indeed/exactly).
Friendship occurs in a short time, whereas seniority requires a long duration;
this should be understood to apply to those of equal qualities and of the same caste.
By this, the worldly definition of "elderly" is set aside in favor of a relative one.
Others, however, explain:

"By this [phrase], seniority (*sthaviratva*) is not indicated; rather, it is simply friendship (*sakhitva*). If the definition of a 'senior' were based on literal [chronological] sequence, then one would be a friend for such a duration of time, but thereafter [the other] would be the elder."
And this is the meaning of the verse:
those friends lived together in one city for ten years;
through association with experts in the sixty-four arts, they mastered them in five years.

Among those who dwell together even for a short time with their own kind, there is indeed friendship; therefore, not everyone of equal age is a *vayasya* (companion), but rather this alone is the defining characteristic: namely, being of equal age.
This is logical;
however, it contradicts the following verse,
for in that [verse], the priority belongs to the caste (jāti), not to the age (vayas).
And if seniority were declared by this much time alone, then it would be logical that even the suspicion regarding those of a different caste would not be averted;
furthermore, previous commentators consider the first explanation alone to be correct.
One should recognize a ten-year-old Brahmin and a hundred-year-old king as father and son; yet, of the two, the Brahmin is the father.

The "ten-year-old" is the time consisting of ten years from birth, which serves as the delimiting factor; the Brahmin is the delimited object of that time. Neither his high or low status nor his emaciation and so forth can be measured by time; rather, it is some activity of his [that is measured]. And that activity, beginning from birth, is constantly inherent [in him] and is characterized solely by the maintenance of life.
"In this way, for a hundred years"—
these two should be understood as father and son;
when these two are compared, the Brāhmaṇa is the father.
The meaning of this section is that even a Kṣatriya who is very old must rise to greet and salute a Brāhmaṇa, even if the latter is of only a few years' standing.
Wealth, kinship, age, ritual action, and learning as the fifth—these are the grounds for respect; each subsequent one is weightier than the preceding.
The way in which birth is a cause of superiority has been explained:
one of superior birth is to be honored by one of inferior birth.
Now, the relative strength and weakness of those factors—such as salutation and other forms of honor—that serve as causes for honoring among those of equal birth are being stated.
In this context, age is mentioned again for the purpose of determining strength and weakness.
Here, connection with wealth and so forth is everywhere a cause for honor;
namely, the possession of wealth and the possession of kinsmen are grounds for respect.
This is the meaning here:
it is not merely the distinction of kinship—such as being an uncle or a maternal uncle—that is the cause for honor; rather, one who honors his relatives and has many relatives is to be revered.
It should be understood that "age" is what is preeminent.
And it is generally employed in this very sense,
as in: "Even though he has reached maturity, that son must always be instructed by his father."
And as long as youth is a cause for honor, that has already been stated as being called "the ten years.
Ritual action (*karman*) refers to devotion to the performance of rites prescribed by the *Śruti* and the *Smṛti*.
Knowledge (*vidyā*) is the understanding of the meaning of the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) and their ancillaries (*upakaraṇa*).

[Objection: But surely it is said, "The learned man sacrifices; the learned man officiates at a sacrifice. Since one who lacks knowledge has no entitlement to perform ritual acts, how can rituals be a cause for attaining knowledge without that very knowledge?
[Response: This is not a fault.
What is intended here is excellence (prakarṣa).
Excellence in knowledge is the cause for [receiving] honor;
however, even one with very little knowledge may be fit for the performance [of rites].
Whoever knows as much as he does is authorized to that extent.
The qualification for knowledge is not based on scriptural injunction alone, but rather on its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*).
For how could one who is ignorant of the nature of ritual action—such as an animal, which performs actions instinctively—be qualified?
Indeed, such a being might be able to perform recitation and austerity after hearing a few sentences from the Smṛti.
However, the understanding of Vedic statements assists in rites such as the Agnihotra.
Even in that case, one is qualified only to the extent that one knows;
he who understands the meaning of the Agnihotra passages is qualified for them.
Knowledge of other ritual acts is not helpful in that regard. Now, it might be argued:
"The entire Veda is to be mastered"—thus, this injunction concerning the whole Veda extends until its full comprehension is attained.

In that regard, when the comprehension of the entire Veda is to be accomplished, how is this possibility of partial comprehension feasible, such that it is said: "He who knows the meaning of the Agnihotra passage is qualified [for the rite] even if he does not know the meaning of other passages"?
To this it is replied: First of all, the study of at least one recensional branch (*śākhā*) must necessarily be performed.

In that regard, one who has studied a single recensional branch (*śākhā*) and has ascertained its meaning is qualified [for the ritual], even though he has not ascertained the meaning of other recensions. But is it not the case that the subject matter of the scripture (*śāstrārtha*) is everywhere one and the same?
Even if there is indeed a difference in the sequence of words and phonemes, the form of the scripture itself is undivided.
Or rather, comprehension arises through proficiency in the categories (padārtha) and logic (nyāya);
and neither the categories nor the logic differ from one Vedic branch (śākhā) to another.

In this regard, by whatever reason the meaning of one recensional branch (śākhā) is determined, that same [reason] exists for another branch as well; it does not require a different etymological derivation. Therefore, if one branch is understood, all [branches] are indeed understood.
This is true.
Let there be no difference regarding those rites, such as the Agnihotra and others, which are taught in one [branch] and are likewise taught in other branches;
however, certain rites are not taught at all in some branches—

for example, in the Āśvalāyana school of the Ṛgveda, the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the Śyena and other malevolent rites, as well as other [rites] such as the Soma sacrifice, the Vājapeya, and the Bṛhaspatisava.
In this regard, one is qualified for those rites such as the Agnihotra and Jyotiṣṭoma that are dependent upon the Vedic recension (śākhā) one has studied.
However, how could a student of that particular recension know the rituals prescribed in another recension that he has neither studied nor heard?
Furthermore, these Soma sacrifices are not obligatory (nitya), such that one would have to seek out another recension to fully understand them out of fear of the sin incurred by non-performance.

Although the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires) is not recited there [in that specific branch], there is nevertheless an injunction for the *āhavanīya* fire in the passage, "He takes out the *āhavanīya*. Not understanding its purpose from common worldly usage, one asks, "What is this *āhavanīya* for which there is an *ādhāna*? and thus searches for another branch [of the Veda].
Thereupon, one thoroughly examines the entire section on *ādhāna* as it is recited in that other branch.

Having heard the scriptural injunction, "Thus, having sacrificed with either the New Moon oblation or the Full Moon oblation," one searches for another recension (śākhāntara) to determine the specific form of these two rites. In the same way, regarding any other optional (kāmya) or obligatory (nitya) performance, if any collection of subsidiaries—whether pertaining to the Adhvaryu or the Udgātṛ—is not mentioned therein, one must understand that by investigating another recension. However, there is no possibility of knowing through one's own study those subsidiaries that are to be performed and are taught only in another recension.
However, for one who studies many branches [of the Veda] and is devoted to its meaning, all of this is directly perceived.
Furthermore, the performance of ritual action is possible even without such [extensive] knowledge;
or rather, the performance is possible even with only slight proficiency.
But for one whose knowledge is stainless and whose fields of knowledge are to be explained, that knowledge is a ground for honor.
The suffix *īyasun* is used here in the sense of comparing two things to determine which is "more" (*garīyaḥ*).
One who knows the fourteen fields of knowledge is honored by virtue of that knowledge alone, even if they are disqualified due to being lame, blind, destitute, or otherwise.
Regarding their conflict, he states the relative strength and weakness: "Whichever is subsequent is weightier.
If one person possesses wealth while another has many kinsmen, the one with kinsmen is to be honored over the one with wealth;
for that which is subsequent to another is more important than it.
Likewise, the age of a relative is more important than that [wealth], and that [age] is established as more important even than the aforementioned wealth.
Therefore, the statement of Gautama is appropriate: "But sacred learning (*śruta*) is weightier than all [others], because dharma has its root therein.
How can there be a suffix denoting excellence (*prakarṣa-pratyaya*) in the word *garīyaḥ*, given that the preceding [factors] do not possess weightiness at all?

If it is argued that although both are heavy, the upper garment possesses a greater heaviness, and therefore wealth does not [possess such a degree] relative to the former, we reply: when a general heaviness is intended for the collection as a whole, the suffix *īyasun* is appropriate when one wishes to express the excellence of the other.
*Māna* means honor; its *sthāna* is the cause or basis for it.
Alternatively, if the reading is *mānyasthānāni*, it should be understood as containing an implied sense of the abstract noun;
that is, "grounds for being honored" or "causes of being honored."
It has been stated that when each quality is present individually, the subsequent one is superior.
Now, however, in a case where two preceding qualities belong to one person and a single subsequent quality belongs to another, how is it determined? To this he says:
"Among the five [qualities] in the three castes, those that are more numerous and possess greater virtues [prevail]."
Wherever such persons may be found, even a Śūdra who has reached the tenth stage is worthy of honor there.

Among these five grounds for respect, he in whom there are more, many, and not all [of them] is the one to be respected; in that case, the status of being "another" (paratva) should not be given much weight.
One may have wealth and kinsmen, another two [of these], and another is advanced in age.
In that regard, concerning the former sublater:
even if there is multiplicity, if they are not superior, and one [instance] of a single [type] is extremely preeminent, then there is equality;
it does not, however, constitute the status of being a sublater of the other.
This is because [the later rule] achieves its purpose in relation to a single [instance].

However, if there are many qualities that are exceedingly superior, then even when there is equality in number—where the preceding rules have the same number as the subsequent ones—the relationship of sublation (bādhyabādhakabhāva) does not arise on the basis of priority alone.
What then? It is simply a matter of generality.

But surely, since it is stated that "he who possesses qualities is worthy of honor" in this context, it would be logical for the preceding rule—even if it has the same number of syllables—to be set aside by this one.
This is not so;
for when the qualities are equal, this [present] rule has already fulfilled its purpose.
Just as between two learned men, one being [learned] and the other also [learned], the one whose learning is excellent and endowed with virtue is praised;
so it is in all cases.
Among the three castes—the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas—[the same applies].

If these qualities are more numerous and more excellent even in a Kṣatriya, then the Kṣatriya is to be honored by a Brāhmaṇa of inferior qualities, even though the latter is superior by birth. Likewise, the Vaiśya is to be honored by the Kṣatriya;
and likewise, even the Śūdra is to be honored by all three twice-born classes, up to the tenth generation.
The tenth stage is said to be the final state;
this is an indication of extreme old age.
And thus, for a Śūdra, wealth and kinsmen are not grounds for respect toward those of the three higher castes, because of the mention of the "tenth stage."
However, ritual action (*karman*) and knowledge (*vidyā*) are not possible for him at all, because he lacks the qualification for them.
By the word "many" (*bhūyāṃsi*), mere abundance is intended, not the specific number of "plurality.
Consequently, it is established that [the term] also has two objects.
For there is no evidence that this word *bahu* expresses only a numerical value;
moreover, this is not the word *bahu*, but rather the word *bhūyas*, which is seen used in various places in the sense of "excess.

Furthermore, in the phrase "the answer here is more [convincing]" (*bhūyān*) and "I shall be joined with greater success" (*bhūyasābhyudayena*), even the plurality of the suffixal meaning is not intended to be expressed.
For this plural number is used when expressing a genus;
indeed, if it were intended to refer to a single individual possessing qualities, that individual would not be the cause for measurement.
Consequently, the previously established understanding would be sublated.

And by stating that even a Śūdra [attains the goal] at the tenth decade, he shows the lack of intention [to restrict the rule to higher castes], since he declares that the excellence of age alone is the cause for measurement;
and such is the established practice as well.
The way must be yielded to one who holds a wheel, to one in his tenth decade of life, to the sick, to one carrying a heavy load, to a woman, to a *snātaka*, to a king, and to a bridegroom.
This other mode of worship is mentioned as incidental:
one who possesses a chariot, a rider of a carriage, or one mounted on a vehicle such as a cart—
his path should be yielded.
That portion of ground by which one travels from a village or other location to another place is called a *paddhati* or a path.
If, on that path, a chariot should come from behind or from the front, then a pedestrian should move aside from that section of the road to avoid obstructing its passage.
One who stands in the tenth stage (*daśamīstha*) is one whose age is fully advanced.
A sick person is one who is excessively afflicted by disease;
a burdened person is one who has taken up heavy goods such as rice and the like; he too, being unable to approach [the teacher] in the prescribed manner, is to be favored.
A woman [is to be approached] solely by virtue of her being female, regardless of her caste, qualities, or relationship to her husband.
And here, "king" (rājā) is intended to mean the lord of the realm, not merely a member of the Kṣatriya caste;
for it will be concluded later with the term "pārthiva," where a pārthiva is defined as one who is the lord (īśvara) of the earth (pṛthivī).
But surely, since the word *rājan* is heard at the beginning, it is more appropriate that the word *pārthiva*, occurring in a subsequent sentence, refers to that very same person;
for the word *rājan* is known to denote the Kṣatriya caste. Since it appears in the opening statement and its primary meaning has not yet been contradicted, it must be accepted in its literal sense.

In the passage concerning Bala and others, however, since the use of the word *pārthiva* is possible through the duty known as the protection of the earth—which is prescribed for the Kṣatriya caste and depends upon that [caste status]—it is improper to take it as referring to another caste.
To this, it is replied:
no other [meaning] is heard here in the scripture.

Regarding the statement, "A *snātaka* is entitled to honor from a king": therein, the fact that a *snātaka* is to be honored by anyone merely belonging to the *kṣatriya* caste is already established by the rule, "A ten-year-old Brahmin [is equal to a king].
For it has been stated that in that context, the word "ruler of the earth" (*bhūmipa*) is intended as an indicator for the *kṣatriya* caste in general.
And because the term "king" is used as an illustration, this duty is understood to apply also to a Kṣatriya who is a lord of subjects;
[the rule is that] when one has set out for a wedding,
the path must be yielded to these [persons].
The meaning [of the word] is merely "giving," and giving consists in moving away from the path;
for this very reason, the dative case was not employed.
Among those gathered together, the *snātaka* and the king are to be honored;
and between the royal *snātaka* and the king, the *snātaka* receives the honor due to a monarch.

Among those who have come together and assembled in one place, the two—the *snātaka* and the king—are to be honored by means of the gift of the customary path. "Receiving honor from the king" (*nṛpamānabhāk*) means he receives or obtains honor from the presence of the king;
the genitive case is used here in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*).
However, there is a mutual optionality regarding the wheel and the other [requisites],
and that depends upon capacity.
But that twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the Kalpa and the Rahasyas, him they call an Ācārya.
This [work] is undertaken for the purpose of defining the meanings of words such as "ācārya" and so forth; for their usage in the world is figurative,
and this [definition] has not been established by the traditional authors of word-meaning relations, such as the teacher Pāṇini and others.
Furthermore, this recollection (*smṛti*) concerning the meaning of the term "teacher" is rooted in worldly usage, not in the Veda, like the *smṛtis* of Pāṇini and others.
For here no duty to be performed is enjoined;
rather, the meaning is established in the form of a fact—namely, "this is the meaning of this word"—and is not something to be accomplished.
Having initiated—that is, having performed the *upanayana*—he who teaches the Veda, that is, causes it to be grasped, is an *ācārya*.
Here, "grasping" refers to the memorization of the sequential order of the sentences, independent of any other student.
The word "kalpa" is intended to indicate all the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*).

The *rahasya* (secret) refers to the *Upaniṣads*. Although they too are included by the very term "Veda," they nevertheless have a second designation, namely *vedāntas*. Considering the word *anta* (end) to mean "proximity," one might think that these are not [part of] the Vedas; therefore, the term *rahasya* is employed to dispel such a doubt.
Others, however, describe *rahasya* as the meaning (*artha*) of the Veda.
Therefore, the status of being a teacher (*ācārya*) is not accomplished by the mere grasping of the essential form [of the texts], but rather from that accompanied by their exposition.
Thus it is stated in the *Abhidhānakośa*: "He who explains the meanings of the mantras is called an *ācārya*. The mention of "mantras" is intended as an illustration for Vedic sentences in general.
And on this interpretation, the comprehension of the meaning would also be prompted by the injunction to become a teacher, not merely the mere recitation.
Consequently, everyone would be compelled to perform the study of their own Veda (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) by everyone else.
Even if the performance is prompted by another, the student’s own purpose would still be accomplished through the *svādhyāya-vidhi*.

In that case, when the teacher does not engage [in teaching] because the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*) is optional (*kāmya*), then the performance of the purpose of the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*) would not be attained;
consequently, the injunction for Vedic study would have to be considered obligatory (*nitya*).
Furthermore, the word *rahasya* is not well-known as denoting the meaning of the Vedas.
Therefore, the purpose of grasping the secret [teachings] has already been stated previously;
or rather, it is mentioned separately because of its preeminence.

As for the statement "and he explains the meanings of the mantras," this is simply a lack of recollection, since there is no evidence that the word *mantra* is intended as an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, the purpose of this injunction is the impelling of the intention to recite;
thus, once the student has grasped the nature of the Veda, the injunction for the office of the teacher is fulfilled.
But he who teaches a portion of the Veda, or even the Vedāṅgas,
for the sake of his livelihood, is called an Upādhyāya.
One who teaches even a single portion of the Veda— whether it be a *mantra* or a *brāhmaṇa*—

or who teaches merely the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) devoid of the Veda, or indeed the entire Veda, for the sake of livelihood— that is, for the sake of a profession and not by virtue of the injunction for becoming an *ācārya*— is an *upādhyāya*, not an *ācārya*.
He who teaches the entire Veda to one who has been initiated by another is not an *ācārya*.
Likewise, he who, even after initiating a student, does not teach him the entire Veda is also not an *ācārya*.

If this is so, and since the definition of an *upādhyāya* consists in teaching a portion [of the Veda] while the definition of an *ācārya* consists in performing the initiation (*upanayana*), then what is the definition of one who neither initiates nor teaches the entire Veda?
He was neither a teacher nor a preceptor,
nor was any other name of his heard;
it is said thus.
By the phrase "whether little or much of what has been heard," it is shown that this teacher is inferior to an *ācārya* but superior even to an *upādhyāya*;
furthermore, the two words "api" and "punaḥ" are for the purpose of filling out the meter.
That Brahmin who performs the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony according to the rules, and supports him with food, is called his guru.
By the mention of "conception" (*niṣeka*), this instruction regarding the father's status as a teacher is intended.
"Conception" (*niṣeka*) refers to the emission of semen; it is the first among those rites.
By the inclusion of the word "first," all the purificatory sacraments (*saṃskāras*) are understood.
He who performs these [rites] with food, and he who honors him— alternatively, there is the reading "and increases him"—
the meaning is the same, because honoring is logically possible only by means of food.
This is a statement of another meaning regarding this boy;
it is certainly not a subsequent reference (anvādeśa),
for there has been no prior mention of the boy here.
It is not so;
for whom else would the acts of impregnation and so forth be performed?
Furthermore, the designation is made by implication, not merely by way of direct designation.
He who performs those [rites] is,
being thus deficient in these two qualities, merely a progenitor and not a teacher (*guru*).
Nor should it be thought that, in the absence of being a teacher, he is not to be honored.
He alone is to be honored above all else;
and so the Lord Vyāsa said:
"The father is the master, the source of the body, the doer of what is dear, the giver of life, and the guru."
"And the father is the visible deity who instructs in what is beneficial.
The mention of the "Brahmin" is for the sake of illustration.

He who, being chosen by someone, performs for that person the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), the cooked sacrifices (pākayajñas), and the soma-sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and others, is called his officiating priest (ṛtvij) in this world.
The ritual act that produces the fires, such as the Āhavanīya and others, is called *agnyādheya*;
it is prescribed by the injunction: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the fires in spring.
The *pākayajñas* include the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other such sacrifices.
The *makhās*, such as the *agniṣṭoma* and others, are soma-sacrifices;
the word *makha* is a synonym for *kratu*.
He who performs these rites for someone is called that person's *ṛtvij* (priest).
The words "of whom" (*yasya*) and "his" (*tasya*) demonstrate a relationship of connection.
He alone who performs these rites is called his officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), and not anyone else.
All these terms, beginning with "teacher" (*ācārya*), are words denoting a relationship.

"Chosen" means requested and having performed the formal selection according to the scriptural injunction. Because of the context of respectability, the designation "officiant" (*ṛtvij*) is taught here; for indeed, there is no occasion for officiants among the duties of a religious student (*brahmacārin*).
This definition is stated within the scope of [showing] that he is to be honored like a teacher (*ācārya*) and others.
He who truly fills both ears with the Veda should be known as both mother and father; one should never act treacherously toward him.
He who covers both ears with the Veda—that is, by teaching the Vedas—should be known as mother and father.
This is not an injunction that the teacher is to be designated by the words "mother" and "father";
for the words "father" and "mother" have well-established meanings, just like the word "teacher" (ācārya) and others.
Janaka means father;
jananī means mother. These terms are used figuratively for the purpose of praising the teacher.
As in the expression, "The Vāhīka is an ox.

For in the world, mother and father are renowned as being of ultimate benefit; they produce one's welfare, nourish one with food and the like, and exert themselves for the sake of their son even without regard for their own bodies. Therefore, because of his great helpfulness, the teacher is praised by means of them.
He who assists in the acquisition of knowledge is superior to all other benefactors.
This is an adverbial phrase meaning "unfalsely.
By that which is unfailing, true, and by the Brahman described through its syllables, accents, and phonemes, one should not act with malice toward him.
"Apakāra" means malice, as well as contempt toward that [teacher].
Once the grasping of the completed text has occurred, one should not harbor malice even at a later time.
And so says the author of the *Nirukta*:
Those Brahmins who, having been instructed by their teachers, do not respect them in word, thought, or deed—
meaning they do not show respect but rather treat them with contempt— are exactly like those [already mentioned].
Disciples are not to be fed by the teacher;
they do not serve for his enjoyment.
In the same way, that learning does not benefit them;
there is an alternative reading, *ātṛṇatti*, which means "it pierces" or "perforates the ears. By this metaphor, it is precisely the act of teaching [without comprehension] that is being described.
"Indeed, that man is said to have unpierced ears through whom what has been heard has not entered the range of his hearing.
This is a prohibition against malice toward all teachers— whether *ācāryas*, *upādhyāyas*, or *gurus*— even by one who has completed his studies.
Ten preceptors equal one teacher; a hundred teachers equal one father;
but a mother exceeds a thousand fathers in respect.
The prescription of the precedence [of one relative over another] is according to the order of their praise:

the teacher is superior to the sub-teacher (upādhyāya), the father is superior to him, and the mother is superior even to him. The mention of the number ten and so forth is merely for the sake of praise.
The intention is to express that each subsequent one is superior to each preceding one;
for this very reason, there is the statement: "A thousand [cows] for the father;
he exceeds ten teachers."
He is superior to ten preceptors. But how, then, is the accusative case used here? The word *ati* is a karmapravacanīya (governing particle).
Passing beyond the preceptors one after another, he excels them; he is endowed with an extraordinary degree of reverence.
Alternatively, *atireka* means "excess"; the verbal root [in this context] refers to overcoming that which is caused by such excess.
Thus, by the intensity of his reverence, he surpasses the preceptors.

The expression "atiricyate" (is exceeded) is used with the reflexive subject (*karmakartṛ*), and the use of the accusative case is not contradictory because of the inclusion of the term "bahulam" (frequently) in the rule *duhipacyoḥ bahulaṃ sakarmakayoḥ*.

Now, one might object: "It will be stated immediately below that 'the father who bestows the Veda is more venerable,' yet here the superiority of the teacher over the father is being asserted; these two are mutually contradictory.
This is not a fault.

Here, the teacher (*ācārya*) is intended as an instructor according to the etymological view (*nairuktadarśana*), meaning one who causes [the student] to grasp proper conduct (*ācāra*) through mere refinement and the instruction of conduct; for it is said that "an *ācārya* is so called because he makes one grasp conduct. Furthermore, there is no such restriction that linguistic usage must proceed solely by means of technical terms established within one's own system;
for the word "guru" is conventionally defined here as referring to a father, yet it is employed in various places to refer to a teacher as well.

Therefore, this superiority of the father [is established] over one who provides only slight assistance, such as merely performing the initiation (*upanayana*), who imparts proper conduct (*ācāra*) but does not provide instruction;

and when this sequence is intended, in the case of their simultaneous presence, the mother is to be saluted first, then the father, then the teacher (*ācārya*), and then the sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*).
When the principal teacher and the father who performs the sacraments are both present, what is the order of precedence? To this he says:
"Between the biological progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is the more venerable."
For the birth of a Brahmin from the Veda is eternal, both in this world and after death.
The progenitor who gives birth and the giver of the Veda who teaches—both of these are fathers.
Of these two fathers, the father who gives the Veda is the more venerable.
Therefore, when the father and the teacher are together, the teacher is to be saluted first.
Here he states an explanatory passage (arthavāda) that serves as a reason: "For it is a birth from Brahman. Birth for the purpose of grasping Brahman is "birth from Brahman" (brahmajanma).
This is a compound formed according to the *śākapārthiva* class [of compounds].
In this context, the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) is the "birth from Brahman.
Alternatively, the very acquisition of the Veda (*brahmagrahaṇa*) is the birth. That [birth] of the Brahmin is eternal and constant; it is beneficial both after death and in this world.
One should understand that the birth which occurs when his mother and father produce him together through desire is merely his physical conception within the womb.
These two verses are an explanatory praise (arthavāda).
One should understand that "origination" refers to when his mother and father produce and give birth to this child in secret, driven by mutual desire and under the sway of passion.
The birth and arising of that child consists in being born from the womb in the mother’s belly and acquiring the major and minor limbs;
and those entities for which there is such an arising perish in that very same way.
Therefore, what is the use of that arising for which destruction follows immediately?
But that birth which the preceptor, having mastered the Vedas, produces for him according to the rule with the Sāvitrī mantra— that is real, and it is free from old age and death.
But that birth of his which comes from the teacher is indestructible.

Since the attainment of heaven and liberation results from the performance of rituals once the Veda has been received and its meaning understood—and since all of this is rooted in the teacher—he is the most excellent.

That caste (jāti) which he produces, and that second birth known as the initiation (*upanayana*) which brings about the praise of birth as a "second birth," is made true by the *Sāvitrī* and its recitation; that caste is ageless and immortal.
Although these words have identical meanings, they are nevertheless employed here with the intention of expressing a superior quality of the birth known as "upanayana" over the birth from a mother;
for old age and death do not occur for a *jāti* (caste/class) in the same way they do for living beings.
Furthermore, its indestructibility can be established by means of only a single word.
And that is not what is being established here.

The construction of the words is as follows: "The birth which a teacher who has mastered the Vedas produces according to rule through the *sāvitrī*—that is, by means of the entire set of rites constituting the initiation (*upanayana*), since the word *sāvitrī* is used as a designation for those rites—that birth is superior.
Here, *jāti* means birth (*janma*).
One should know that person to be a teacher in this world by virtue of that service rendered through sacred learning, whoever assists one with their learning, whether it be little or much.
The meaning is that whichever teacher benefits a student with sacred learning (*śruta*)—
whether little or much, as this qualifies the action—
one should know even such a teacher to be a guru who has benefited him with a small amount of learning.
However, this interpretation is superior:

"Of whatever learning"—whether it concerns the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, other sciences, or the arts of logic—whatever little or much of it there is, by that one assists; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

That which is "learning" (śruta) and that which is "assistance" (upakriyā)—this is "learning-assistance" (śrutopakriyā). Through that act of assistance, because it is the cause of it, the word "learning" is used in grammatical apposition with "assistance," as in the expression "learning-assistance."
In that case, the conduct due toward a guru must be observed, or else one is designated by that [same] term, as is recorded in tradition regarding words such as "teacher" (ācārya) and so forth.
One who brings about a Brahmanic birth and is a teacher of his own duty becomes,
according to dharma, the father of an elder even if he is a mere child.
The birth for the purpose of grasping Brahman is the "Brahmic" birth; the one who performs that [birth] is the initiator (upanayana).
He is the instructor and teacher of one's own duty through the exposition of the meaning of the Vedas.
Such a person, though a child, becomes the father of an elder or senior Brāhmaṇa.
In that case, even the elder brother must behave toward him as he would toward a father.
But how can a younger brother initiate an elder?
For initiation is prescribed for the eighth year.
As long as one has not studied and mastered the Vedas, one is not qualified for the injunction regarding the appointment of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*).
If that is so, then in this context, the "birth of a Brāhmaṇa" does not consist of the initiation (*upanayana*), but rather the acquisition of the Vedic study itself;
its agent is the one who causes it to be taught.

He who instructs and explains one's own duty, which is the meaning of the Veda, becomes a father; according to dharma, the duties of a father must be performed toward him. "According to dharma" means that his status as a father is established on the basis of dharma.
Furthermore, those duties are not established as being related to the father of the teacher or the expounder;
therefore, it is prescribed that "one should behave toward a Kṣatriya as one does toward a Brāhmaṇa."
The youthful sage Kavi, son of Aṅgiras, taught his fathers;
having encompassed them with his knowledge, he said to them, "O little sons!"
This is an *arthavāda* known as a *parakṛti*, serving as a commendatory statement for the rule regarding conduct toward one's elder set forth previously.

A young child named Kavi, the son of Aṅgiras, taught those who were his elders—his paternal uncles, maternal uncles, their sons, and others—who were equal to his father; that is, he caused them to study.
And on occasions requiring a summons, he called out to them, "O little sons, come here!"
Having embraced them through knowledge, having accepted them, and having made them disciples.
Filled with indignation, they questioned the gods regarding that matter;
and the gods, having assembled, said to them, "The child has spoken what is right for you."

Addressed with the invocation "O little sons," which placed them in the position of fathers and the like, they were moved to indignation and filled with anger; they questioned the gods regarding that matter—the address using the word "sons"—asking, "By this boy we are thus addressed;
is this appropriate?"

Being thus questioned, all those gods held a consultation; having assembled and reached a unanimous decision, they spoke to these ancestors of Kavi, saying: "The child has spoken what is just and appropriate for you."
The ignorant one is indeed a child, while the giver of mantras is a father;
for they call the ignorant one a "child," but the giver of mantras a "father."
For one does not become a child merely by being young; rather, even an old man is a fool if he is ignorant.
The term "giver of mantras" is illustrative:
he who gives, teaches, and explains the mantras—that is, the Vedas—is the father.
The word "vai" indicates another scriptural tradition;
this scripture of the gods is indeed ancient. Likewise, the phrase "they say" (āhuḥ) indicates a traditional report (aitihya), which is instruction from others.
Those who came before us also said that an ignorant person is a fool and a child;
however, one who imparts the mantras is called "Father. The use of the particle *iti* indicates that the preceding words refer to the literal form itself.
Since it is heard from another source that the word "bāla" denotes merely one who lacks knowledge,
and for this reason there is an absence of the accusative case ending after the word "bāla."
In reality, this Śaiśava Brāhmaṇa from the Chāndogya has been described by the author of the Smṛti.
The seers did not establish dharma by means of years, nor by gray hair, nor by wealth, nor by kinsmen; he among us who is learned in the Vedas is great.
This is a praise of the teacher.
The word *hāyana* is a synonym for *saṃvatsara* (year).

One does not become great and worthy of honor through many years—that is, by being advanced in age—nor by gray hair, nor by white hair on the head, beard, and body, nor by much wealth, nor by kinsmen.
The previously mentioned grounds for respect are applicable here.
One does not become great by means of all [sciences] combined; rather, it is through a single science alone.
For this reason, the sages established [this rule].
The sages,

having perceived the meaning of the Vedas in their entirety, have determined and established this Dharma. He who is an *anūcāna*— one who has performed the recitation (*anuvacana*), that is, the teaching of the entire Veda along with its auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*)— he is our great and most excellent one.
The root *kṛ* functions in the sense of establishing, not in the sense of producing what has not existed.
The seniority of Brahmins is by knowledge, that of Kshatriyas by valor,
that of Vaishyas by grain and wealth, and that of Shudras alone by birth.
This too is merely an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).
That which was stated—that knowledge alone is superior to wealth and the other [means] when combined—is precisely what is indicated here in detail:

the superiority of Brahmins is by virtue of knowledge, not by wealth and so forth; that of Kṣatriyas is by virtue of valor (*vīrya*). Valor consists of skill with material resources and firmness of vital breath.
Among Vaiśyas, seniority is determined by grain and wealth.
Since grain is mentioned separately, the word "wealth" (dhana) refers to gold and the like, following the analogy of the expression "Brahmins and wandering mendicants" (*brāhmaṇaparivrājaka*).
A Vaiśya who possesses great wealth is the eldest.
The suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the third case (instrumental) because it belongs to the group beginning with *ādi*;
[here] the third case is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).
One does not become old merely because one's head is gray;
even a youth who has studied the Vedas—the gods recognize him as an elder.
One is not called "old" merely because his head has turned white and the hair upon it is grey.
How then? Even one who is young and in the prime of life, if he has studied [the Vedas], the gods know him as an elder; they call him so.
For it is said that the gods are the knowers of all things; this is a praise.
Just as an elephant made of wood, as a deer made of leather, so too is a Brahmin who has not studied; these three merely bear the name.

This is a praise of study and the student. Just as a wooden elephant made from timber with an axe or other tools is fruitless and does not perform the work of an elephant, such as slaying enemies for kings; likewise, a Brāhmaṇa who does not study is equal to wood and is not qualified for anything.
A leather deer—whether it be a hide product or another animal made of leather—is fruitless and does not perform tasks such as hunting.
These three bear only their names, but not their actual purpose.
Just as a eunuch is fruitless with women, just as a cow is fruitless with another cow,
and just as a gift given to one who lacks knowledge is fruitless, so too is a Brahmin who knows not the Rigveda fruitless.
A eunuch, a hermaphrodite, or one incapable of sexual intercourse with women is fruitless among women;
just as a bull is fruitless among cows, so too is a Brahmin who is ignorant of the Rigveda and unlearned in the Vedas fruitless.
Seven or eight verses have already passed, intended for the praise of the student and the teacher. Now, however, the mind of a disciple who lacks faith yet continues to study may become distracted.
One who desires righteousness (*dharma*) should instruct living beings toward their welfare through non-violence alone, and should employ speech that is sweet and gentle.
When anger arises in a teacher, he is prohibited from excessively resorting to such acts as beating or harsh speech.
For the sake of their welfare, he should provide instruction to living beings— namely wives, sons, slaves, pupils, and uterine brothers— through non-violence, that is, without striking them.
By the inclusion of the word "bhūta" (real), it should not be understood as referring only to the disciple.
Well-being (*śreyaḥ*) is the attainment of visible and invisible fruits; instruction (*anuśāsana*) is for that purpose.
Alternatively, *upadeśa* refers to teaching without a formal text, or to the teaching and exposition of a treatise (*śāstra*).
In this context, excessive beating and shouting are prohibited as far as possible;
however, slight beating with a rope or a split bamboo cane is indeed permitted.
How, then, should they be established on the path?
And his speech should indeed be sweet and preceded by conciliation;

with pleasant, gentle words, and not with a loud, arrogant, crow-like, or harsh tone. Even when saying something pleasing, one should say: "Study, my son; do not let your mind be bound elsewhere. Having quickly completed this lesson with faith, you shall immediately sport with your bright playmates.
As for one who does not approach [the study] with such faith, the rule stated by Veṇudeva applies to him.
One who desires the Dharma should employ and instruct [others] in this manner;
thus, the duty of teaching becomes preeminent.
He whose speech and mind are pure and always perfectly guarded indeed attains the entire fruit that is taught in the Vedānta.
When there is a cause for agitation, whether from the teacher or from another, if his speech and mind do not become turbid, and even when turbidity has arisen,
they remain properly guarded such that there is no intent to harm others nor any undertaking of action for their affliction— this is the proper guarding of speech and mind.
