The inclusion of the word "always" (sarvadā) is for the purpose of establishing this as a duty for every person, and not merely for the teacher at the time of teaching.
He indeed attains everything.
"Vedāntas" refers to the established conclusions (*siddhānta*) of the Vedas.

Regarding the word *siddha*, there is an elision of the word *atyanta* (extremely), just as in the expression *siddhe śabdārthasaṃbandhe* (when the relationship between word and meaning is extremely established).
Whatever established conclusion regarding the meaning of Vedic statements has been accepted by those learned in the Vedas—namely, that "this is the fruit of this ritual"—he obtains all of that fruit.
By speaking thus, it is stated in this verse that restraint of speech and mind constitutes both a duty of the ritual (*kratudharma*) and a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*).

For if it were not a duty of the person alone, then in the absence of any deficiency in the ritual, why would one who is unrestrained in speech and mind not obtain the full fruit, such that it is said: "the self-restrained one obtains everything"?

Others, however, explain the Vedāntas as the *Rahasyabrāhmaṇas*. According to them, whatever fruit is accepted for the obligatory (*nitya*) rites and for the fruitless restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), one attains all that fruit, which is characterized by the attainment of Brahman. If it is asked how the obligatory rites can have the attainment of Brahman as their purpose, there exists the view of certain [authorities] that this is indeed so.
Alternatively, the "end of the Veda" refers to the completion of its study; consequently, one obtains that fruit which results from the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*).
However, if explained in this way, it would follow that [the injunction to study] has as its sole purpose the injunction to teach.
One should not be a wounder of others even when afflicted, nor should one have a mind intent on deeds that harm others;
one should not utter that speech by which another is agitated, for such speech does not lead to the higher worlds.
This is another quality pertaining solely to the purpose of a human being (*puruṣārtha*):

one who does not speak such unpleasant words as are "wound-tearing" (*aruṃtuda*)—that is, words that pierce the vital points (*marman*), cause pain, touch the very core, and produce extreme agitation through insults—even when one is afflicted and tormented by another. One should not speak such disagreeable things.

Likewise, one should not commit acts of malice toward others, harm others, or engage in the thought or action intended for that purpose. Alternatively, one should not even direct the mind or intellect toward such malice or action. Furthermore, one should not utter that speech by which another person is agitated, even if it is spoken in jest.
One should not utter even a single portion of such a statement, because from that portion, through the context of the meaning and other factors, the indication of another meaning is perceived;
for such speech is *alokyā*, which obstructs the attainment of the heavenly worlds and the like.
A Brahmin should always tremble at honor as if at poison;
he should always long for dishonor as if it were nectar.

When begging for alms, whether at the house of a celibate student or from a teacher who teaches for a livelihood, one should not allow the mind to be disturbed if there is no honor; rather, one should recoil from honor itself and should not value even that which is given out of reverence. One should always desire and long for contempt and disdain as if they were nectar.

The genitive case is employed by superimposing upon the verb *ākāṅkṣet* ("should desire") the sense of the root *adhi-i* ("to expect"), on account of its similarity to the word *utkaṇṭhā* ("longing").

But is it not the case that what is unhonored is unfit to be eaten? True; this [rule] is for the purpose of preventing agitation of the mind, but it does not mean that such food is declared fit to be eaten.
One should remain equanimous toward both honor and dishonor; furthermore, one should not seek out dishonor.
For a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*), even alms-food given with contempt is acceptable.
Moreover, this is not "acceptance" (*pratigraha*) in the sense that would apply to the rule: "he who accepts what is honored [is purified]."
For he who is held in low esteem sleeps in happiness and wakes in happiness;
he moves through this world in happiness, while the scorner perishes.
This is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) for the preceding injunction, intended to demonstrate its fruit:
he is not disturbed by insults; he sleeps in peace.
Otherwise, being consumed by hatred, he would not obtain sleep in any way whatsoever.
Once awakened, he who is intent on that [insult] finds no peace;
yet when he rises from his bed, he moves about his duties with ease.
But he who is the perpetrator of the insult perishes by that very evil.
By this gradual method, the twice-born man, having refined his self, should while dwelling with his teacher slowly accumulate the austerity conducive to the attainment of Brahman.
The twice-born person, whose self has been refined and brought to maturity by this sequential application, should accumulate austerity (*tapas*).
The phrase "by this" refers back to everything that was stated as the duty of the religious student (*brahmacārin*), beginning from the point where it says "being about to study.

By this collection of injunctions, when practiced sequentially through this sequential application, one accumulates austerity—that is, the refinement of the self characterized by freedom from blemish.

Just as freedom from blemish (*niṣkalmaṣatva*) comes about through austerities such as the *cāndrāyaṇa* and others, so too does it come about through this collection of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) intended for the acquisition of the Veda.
Therefore, one should accumulate it—gradually, without haste—and acquire and increase it.
"Order" (*krama*) refers to the sequence: having done this, that must be done; beginning with the syllable *oṃ*, and so forth.
"Connected with that" means that the performance [of the rite] has a connection with that;
"for the sake of attaining Brahman" means for the purpose of attainment.
Attainment consists of both study and understanding.
The entire Veda, along with its secret portions, must be mastered by the twice-born through various specific austerities and vows enjoined by the rules.

By means of various and manifold specific austerities, such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, and by gradually emaciating the body through practices such as eating once a day or eating only at the fourth meal-time, and by performing the vows prescribed in the *Gṛhya-smṛtis*— such as the *Upaniṣad-vrata* and the *Mahānāmnikā-vrata*— the entire Veda must be mastered.

As for those who say that the word *tapas* used in the previous verse refers to the duties of a student (*brahmacārin*), and that here too those same specific forms of austerity are intended, they do not think correctly; for these are already included by the word *vrata* itself.
Indeed, according to the scriptures, *vrata* denotes a restrictive observance (*niyama*).
Furthermore, because the word *vrata* is a general term, its application to the *mahānāmnikā* and other such observances is established.
Therefore, ascetic practices such as fasting and the like are intended here.
Regarding the word "Veda" used in the singular in this context, some consider the singular number to be intended.

Although, due to the use of the suffix -tavya, the Veda appears to be the primary object to be refined by virtue of its application, nevertheless, both according to the injunction and in terms of the actual fact, it is subordinate to the comprehension of meaning.

And when the quality [of the Veda] is intended to be expressed, this activity of the student regarding the subject matter of the Veda—which culminates in the comprehension of its meaning—is determined by an examination of the function of the injunction.

For here, the meaning of the injunction is this: "One should effect the comprehension of the meaning by means of the Veda that has been studied. Otherwise, its status as something to be refined (*saṃskāryatva*) cannot be established; for everything that is refined is so done as a subordinate element (*śeṣabhūta*) toward some other purpose to be accomplished.

Furthermore, the observed purpose of the Veda once it has been studied is the generation of an understanding of its own meaning; otherwise, even though its primacy is heard [in scripture], it would have to be abandoned, as in the case of the injunction "he offers groats.
The verbal root [of study] also has the sense of understanding alone, for "acquisition" (adhigamana) is said to be knowledge (jñāna).
It is traditionally taught that all roots meaning "to go" (gam) mean "to know" (jñā).
Furthermore, the grasping of the Veda's own form has already been enjoined by such rules as "one should study [the Veda] with hands joined," and so forth;
by this [present rule], its extension up to the grasping of its meaning is established.

Considering that the intention [to express singularity] alone has not been established for the study of multiple Vedas, the phrase "having studied the Vedas" (*vedān adhītya*) will be restated as a counter-exception.
Even if the study of multiple Vedas exists, where would the intention to express singularity be useful? It is certainly useful.
When even a single branch (*śākhā*) has been studied, the requirement of the injunction "one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied" is fulfilled.
However, the study of multiple Vedas occurs by virtue of personal desire; for if it were not impelled by an injunction, what madman would afflict himself with the chewing of ivory cups?
There certainly exists another injunction here, namely "having studied the Vedas," and that applies to one who desires its specific fruit.
And the fruit [of study] is heaven.
Now, if something—such as streams of clarified butter or something else—is recorded in the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) of this injunction, then that alone must be the fruit.

For the injunction regarding the religious student (*brahmacārin*) has as its object the comprehension of meaning and possesses a visible purpose; since comprehension is seen to be useful for the performance of rituals, it is the learned person who is entitled to perform the ritual.
The study of each individual Veda is for the sake of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit) alone.

Otherwise, since the injunction for *svādhyāya* (Vedic study) would be fulfilled by the study of a single Veda, the statement "having studied the Vedas" and so forth—which occurs in the absence of an injunction for [specific] *dharma*—would be entirely purposeless. To this, it is replied:

How could this position be consistent, given that there is this single injunction—"the Veda is to be mastered"? If it is argued that this injunction is not for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*), because it is an injunction of purification (*saṃskāra-vidhi*) and because its utility lies in the performance of visible rites, then the same applies to the study of multiple Vedas as well;
for even in that case, this very same principle holds true.
Furthermore, there would be a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*).

In some cases, there is a connection with obligatory and optional rites by way of understanding, according to the rule for the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*); in other cases, it is directly for the sake of a result.

Now, if it is thought that "having studied the Vedas" is a separate injunction (*vidhi*) and not something prompted by the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa-vidhi*), and that only one who desires its specific fruit is entitled (*adhikṛta*) here—then [the following applies].
That is incorrect;
nor is this a different injunction.

Rather, when there is no intention to specify a number regarding the very injunction under discussion, it restricts the study of five, six, seven, or more branches—which would otherwise be undertaken according to one's capacity—to the triad [of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas].
Furthermore, no injunction such as "one should study" is heard here;
rather, the injunction here is "one should dwell in the householder stage of life.
Moreover, that which was stated regarding the intended significance of the number is utterly irrelevant.
For the intention to express a number arises from the application (*viniyoga*), not from the derivation (*upapādana*).
And that application prescribes the study for the purpose of Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*).
The predominance understood from the two accusative endings does not depart because of [the word] *artha* being subordinate.
For if it were understood in this way, even the cup (*graha*) would be intended to be singular in "one cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*),
because even though it is the primary element, it indeed possesses the status of an instrument (*sādhana*) with respect to the cleansing;
yet it is not denoted as such by the word.

Just as in the injunction "one offers with the *graha* vessels," the *graha* serves as a subordinate factor even in the act of offering (*homa*), so too, by virtue of both its denotation and its application, the Veda (*svādhyāya*) possesses primacy. And since it possesses primacy, its singular number is not intended to be significant.
Well then, if the purpose of the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*) were fulfilled by the mastery of even a single Veda, one would have to state the purpose of studying multiple Vedas;
we shall discuss this in the third [chapter].

Now, if this injunction extends as far as comprehension, then even when the Veda has been mastered in its formal aspect, as long as the comprehension of the meaning has not arisen, the performance of restraints and observances (*yama-niyama*) such as abstaining from honey and meat would not cease in the interim.

What fault is there in that? It contradicts the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). For the learned, even when listening to the meaning of the Veda while it is being recited, do not avoid honey, meat, and so forth.
This is not a fault;
for there is another Smṛti text stating, "Having studied the Veda, one should bathe. In that context, the word "having studied" refers merely to the recitation of the text.
And by the phrase "one should bathe," the cessation of the restraints and observances that are auxiliary to the rule for Vedic study at its proper time is indicated.
Just as honey and meat are prohibited, so too is bathing.
In that context, when bathing is permitted, by virtue of association and because they belong to the same category, honey, meat, and the like are also permitted.
However, sexual intercourse with women is prohibited by another scriptural statement, namely, that one's celibacy (*brahmacarya*) must remain unbroken.
And even in the event of its transgression, nothing is lost regarding the injunction for Vedic study at the time of comprehending the meaning;
for at that stage, it is not a constituent part [of the study], since all restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) terminate with the initial formal undertaking (*grahaṇa*).
However, this prohibition pertains to the human purpose [of procreation].
For this very reason, if there is some accidental emission, the penance for an *avakīrṇin* does not apply.

Indeed, the emission of semen by one established in a vow (*vratastha*) is a transgression; and one established in a vow is not eligible for this penance for a minor offense (*upapātaka*), such as the *Cāndrāyaṇa*.
What, then, is the reason for taking "one should bathe" as a defining characteristic?
It is said:
this bathing is not, first of all, of the nature of washing the body with water, because that would entail the consequence [of the act] having an invisible (adṛṣṭa) purpose.
Furthermore, because the observances of the student (*brahmacārin*) lack a defined limit, and because this [Vedic study] is logically established as their required rule by providing that very limit;
however, those observances do not require another limit in this way.
For they exist for the sake of the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*); therefore, their cessation alone constitutes their limit.
And its cessation occurs through the cessation of its object;
and study is its object;
the cessation of that [study] is indeed perceptible.
True, provided that for someone the [Veda] should consist solely of what is heard (*śruta*).

However, even though it is not explicitly heard, its object—the comprehension of meaning which constitutes the result—also becomes an object [of the injunction] because otherwise the injunction would be impossible as a rule for mental cultivation (*saṃskāra-vidhi*).
For if it were restricted solely to the hearing and recitation of the text, its status as an injunction would be contradicted.

For the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*) consists in its capacity to prompt the performance of its own object; and this object consists of the end to be accomplished (*kārya*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). And that [object] is nothing other than the meaning of the injunction itself.
The effect, the instrument, and the object are not [the primary factors here], because they are included within a single word.
The meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is delimited by the sense of the roots such as *adhi* (to study) in the form "one should study" (*adhīyīta*).
The performance of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) constitutes the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
In that case, it is not possible for this injunction to bring about the performance of its own object;
for the fulfillment of all injunctions regarding their own objects occurs only through the mediation of the performance of their respective objects,
and the performance of the object of this [injunction] is already established by the force of another injunction.
For there is indeed an injunction for the teacher: "Having initiated the pupil, he shall teach him the Veda.
And the accomplishment of study is not possible without teaching.

Therefore, the teacher, in order to fulfill his own duty, impels the boy toward study; and since one who has not been impelled by the teacher cannot possibly perform it, [the teacher acts] having understood this himself.
Therefore, it must necessarily be accepted that [the study] is impelled by an injunction of the teacher.
Since its performance is established when it is so impelled, there is no purpose whatsoever for the student in the injunction to study one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*).
Consequently, because it is impossible for it to be an impeller, what kind of injunctive nature could this injunction possess?
When the destruction of its own nature would otherwise result, that specific method is sought by which its status as an agent [of action] may be obtained.
In this regard, it is certain that this is an injunction for refinement (*saṃskāra-vidhi*); and a refinement is never without fruit.
Since, when there is study, one perceives a composition of meaning— whether it be of such or such a kind— and since that [perception] is useful for the performance of all those respective rites,
the injunction is understood from the duty to produce an understanding connected with the subject matter of the Vedic study.
And although, by the very nature of things, understanding arises immediately after the grasping of the sentence, it does not yet possess a definitive form.
Therefore, in whatever manner certainty arises, it is in that respect that the injunction functions as the impeller.
Certainty arises through investigation by way of the exclusion of doubt and other such states;
and such investigation is not obtained from any other source.

It is not for the sake of the injunction regarding the teacher, because that is fulfilled by the mere act of study. Nor is it prompted by a visible purpose; for what would not be accomplished by a person without inquiry, such that he would exert himself for its sake?
If it is argued that inquiry is undertaken at will, just as one desiring a village or the like acts spontaneously, then, since human desire is unrestricted, some might simply not engage in inquiry.
If one were to reflect [on this] immediately after the study [of the Veda],
then, because this portion has not yet been attained, and since the scope of an injunction consists of that which is not yet attained, there exists the operation of the injunction.

Therefore, since study is already established by other means, and since the comprehension associated with it arises from the very nature of things in an indeterminate form—which has no purposeful efficacy in itself—then even when that [study] exists as a mere purificatory act (*saṃskāraka*), it is only determinate knowledge that is useful for the performance of fruitful rites. Since such determination is achieved through inquiry (*vicāra*), and since that inquiry must necessarily be performed at a fixed time, this injunction stands as one whose culmination lies in inquiry, in order to ensure its completion.
Thus, there arises a requirement for restrictive rules (*niyama*).

Does [the study] terminate with the hearing and recitation [of the Veda], or does it terminate with the investigation of the meaning for the purpose of generating a certain understanding that is implied [by the text]?
Therefore, in view of this requirement, the phrase "having studied the Veda, one should bathe" provides the limit [for the study].
In that case, since there is no distinction between the subject matter at hand and the requirement, the figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is appropriate.
Now, why is it said that there is "understanding without having heard," when it is indeed heard that [the Veda] is to be mastered?
In the Veda and in other Smṛtis, it is recited: "One studies the Veda" and "The private recitation (svādhyāya) is to be studied.
Furthermore, since this [work] is rooted in the Smṛti of Manu, its meaning is indeed not different from that Smṛti.
This realization (adhigama) has the intention of awakening [the object] already projected;
or rather, realization is simply the grasping of its own nature,
while its culmination in awakening is obtained by that very same principle.

Nor is there any inconsistency or irregularity in this single rule, wherein one portion of its subject matter is applied by means of the teacher’s injunction, while that same [teacher] is the motivator for another portion; thus, there is no disparity.

What is untenable here? Nothing, because it is understood as being for the sake of the purpose itself. As for what was said—that the study of multiple Vedas is appropriate for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*)—we shall provide the refutation of that under the rule "thirty-six years" (*ṣaṭtriṃśadābdikam*).
The word *veda* denotes a branch (*śākhā*) consisting of a collection of sentences from both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas.
Since the word *veda* is observed to be used even for a single sentence that is a part of it, the word *kṛtsna* (entire) is employed to eliminate that doubt.

Even if the study were not yet complete when one sentence has been studied—because other sentences would also be denotable by the word *veda* and because [the study] is a purificatory act (*saṃskārakarma*), like the [sacrificial] cup (*graha*)—nevertheless, the inclusion of the word *kṛtsna* is for the sake of clarity.
Others, however, explain the word "entire" (*kṛtsna*) as referring to the constituent parts (*aṅga*).
For the word "Veda" denotes a collection of sentences of a specified extent;
in that regard, if even a single *ṛc* verse is missing, the Veda has not been studied.
Therefore, the word "entire" (kṛtsna) is intended to include the study of the auxiliary sciences (aṅga).
Accordingly, another Smṛti states: "The Veda with its six auxiliaries is to be studied by a Brāhmaṇa as a duty without [any specific] motive.
Now, one might object that what is understood here is simply that "whatever is the Veda, that is the entire [Veda]."

Furthermore, the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) are not denoted by the word "Veda"; therefore, how could there be a connection with them? As for the traditional injunction (*smṛti*) that "the Veda with its six auxiliaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*) should be studied," in that case, the auxiliaries are included by their own specific term.
But here, since the word "entirety" (kṛtsna) is a qualifier of the Veda, how could the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) possibly be included? It is replied:
this Smṛti is rooted in the injunction, "One's own Veda (svādhyāya) is to be studied."
And that [study] is established as culminating in realization;
since realization is not possible without the [auxiliary] limbs, the inclusion of those limbs is established by implication.
Therefore, the knowledge of grammar, etymology, prosody, and hermeneutics is also necessitated by the injunction.
Thus, having accepted that the limbs are for the sake of the whole, it is appropriate to employ the word "entire" (*kṛtsna*) as an indicator.

In this regard, just as the hands, feet, and so forth are called the "limbs" of a person because they are its constituent parts, the *Nirukta* and other sciences are not in that way the constituent parts of the Veda;
nevertheless, they are called "limbs" of the Veda figuratively.
It is said that without them, the Veda is not capable of conveying its own meaning; therefore, the term *adhyāsa* (superimposition) is used here like [the term] "limbs" (*aṅga*).
Thus, by virtue of being superimposed as the Veda, the word "entirety" (*kṛtsna*) becomes appropriate. This is what is meant by "together with the secret" (*sarahasya*).
The Upaniṣads are the secret [teachings]. Although they possess the status of being Veda, they are mentioned separately because of their preeminence.
A twice-born man of the highest order, desiring to perform austerity, should always practice the Veda;
for the study of the Veda is said to be the supreme austerity for a Brahmin in this world.

The repetition, which is already established as being for the purpose of grasping [the meaning] by virtue of being supplementary to the subject matter (*prakṛtaśeṣatayā*), is restated for the sake of praise (*stutyartha*), and is not a further injunction (*vidhyantara*).
The word *sadā* (always) refers precisely to the time of recitation.
The word *tapaḥ* (austerity) refers to scriptural practices such as the restriction of food and so forth, which produce physical hardship.
In this context, however, the term *saṃskāra* (refinement) produced by that [penance] is used figuratively to denote the capacity for granting boons, pronouncing curses, and so forth.
One who is "about to perform penance" (*tapsyan*) is one who desires to acquire it through penance; here the verbal root refers to the heat (*saṃtāpa*) which is a constituent part of the acquisition.
Because the status of the object as the agent (*karmakartṛtva*) is not intended to be expressed, the *parasmaipada* (active voice) ending is employed.
The second half-verse, which states the reason, is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
For Vedic study is indeed a certain form of eminent austerity; therefore, Vedic study is praised by attributing to it a fruit equal to that which is superior to it.
Truly, that twice-born man performs the highest austerity even unto his fingertips,
who, though wearing a garland, studies his own Veda daily to the best of his ability.
This is another explanatory restatement (*arthavādānuvāda*) regarding the rule for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*) found in the *Vājasaneyaka-Brāhmaṇa*.
The connection is with the phrase "even unto the tips of the nails. The particle *ha* indicates traditional report (*aitihya*).
Since the excellence of austerity is already understood from the word *parama*, the mention of "the tips of the nails" indicates an excellence even beyond that which is already excellent.
Even the tips of the nails, though devoid of life, are pervaded by this austerity.
For austerity such as the *kṛcchra* and others, because it does not pervade the tips of the nails, does not bestow its fruit in its entirety.
But this [term] also encompasses those [other meanings], which is why it is praised.
Regarding "tapyate tapaḥ":
since *tapas* takes *tapas* as its object, the suffix *yaṅ* and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) are applied.
"He who, though garlanded": one who possesses a garland (*sragvī*) is called a person wearing a wreath of artificial flowers;
by this, he demonstrates the abandonment of the vows of a religious student (*brahmacārin*).

Even if one has abandoned the duties of a student (*brahmacārin*), if he studies the Veda daily—according to his capacity, even if only a very small amount—he too is endowed with the highest human goal.
This is a praise; it does not mean that study is prescribed after the abandonment of the restrictive rules (*niyama*).
That twice-born man who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in other matters,
quickly falls to the status of a Śūdra while still alive, along with his lineage.
For those for whom the word "entire" (*kṛtsna*) is intended to include the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), since the study might otherwise occur in an indefinite order, the sequence is now fixed:
first the Veda is to be studied, and thereafter the auxiliary sciences.

However, for those for whom the word is used to remove the suspicion that even the Veda itself might be incomplete, the study of the Veda alone is already established as occurring after the *traividya* vow.
The study of the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) is not permitted unless the Veda has first been mastered.

That twice-born man who, without having studied the Veda, exerts excessive effort and application in another treatise, in the auxiliary sciences, or in the texts of the schools of logic (tarka-śāstra), attains the status of a Śūdra even while still alive—
“āśu” meaning quickly or immediately.

"Together with one's lineage" means together with the continuity of sons, grandsons, and so forth. Since it is impossible to prohibit effort—that is, excessive exertion—it follows that upon its completion, other branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) are studied as occasion demands.
The statement regarding the attainment of the status of a *śūdra* is an expression of extreme censure.
Because of the word "twice-born" (*dvija*), this rule regarding the sequence applies to one who has been initiated (*upanīta*).

Prior to initiation, however, the study of the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*)—such as phonetics (*śikṣā*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), and so forth—is not prohibited, provided they are not mixed with Vedic sentences.
But surely, the auxiliary sciences are implied by the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya-vidhi*)?
And the student, directed by the teacher, performs that procedure.
Before the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), since the teacher does not exist, how could there be the possibility of studying the auxiliary sciences?
This is not a fault.
Therefore, they say that a son who has been instructed is "worldly"; thus, he who is to be consecrated by his father will teach him grammar and other subjects prior to the initiation ceremony.
The eligibility of the twice-born for various [sacrificial rites] has been heard [in the scriptures].
In this regard, because [the term *dvija*] is like the word *ācārya* and others [which have multiple meanings], he speaks in order to determine its specific meaning:
"The first birth is from the mother; the second is at the tying of the girdle (*mauñjībandhana*)."
The third [offering] is for a twice-born man during the initiation for a sacrifice, as enjoined by the Śruti.
The first birth of a man is from his mother;
the second is at the binding of the girdle of muñja grass, that is, at the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). The short vowel [in *mauñjibandhane*] is due to the rule *ṅyāpoḥ bahulam*.
The third [birth] occurs during the initiation (*dīkṣā*) for sacrifices such as the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
Initiation itself is heard of in scripture as being a birth; thus it is said: "The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) again and again make him an embryo when they initiate him.
Three births are declared by the Veda for the twice-born (*dvija*).
But if this is so, does it not follow that one becomes a twice-born (*dvija*) at birth?
Let it be so;
nevertheless, for the designation "twice-born," the initiation (*upanayana*) is the cause.

And based on that designation [of being a "twice-born"], there is eligibility for the performance of rites prescribed by the Vedas (*śrauta*), the Smṛtis (*smārta*), and customary practice (*sāmayikācārika*).
The mention of the first and third births is for the purpose of praising the second birth;
that [second birth] is the best among all births.
For one who has not been initiated is not entitled to perform a sacrifice at all, whereas one who has not been invested with the sacred thread is not entitled to anything whatsoever.
Others, however, considering the commonality of being "first," regard the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) as the initiation for sacrifice.
For even that [establishment of the fires] has its origin in birth; he who does not establish the fires is indeed as if unborn.
In that regard, his birth as a Brahmin is marked by the tying of the girdle;
at that time, Sāvitrī is said to be his mother and the teacher his father.

Among these three births, that which is the birth of Brahman is the initiation (*upanayana*), characterized by the tying of the girdle of muñja grass and marked by the binding of the sacrificial cord.
In this regard, the Sāvitrī is his mother; for it is through her being recited that he is brought to completion.
And by this, he shows that the recitation of the Sāvitrī is the principal element in the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), for it is for that purpose that the boy is brought near;
the father is the teacher (*ācārya*);
birth is brought about by the mother and father.
Therefore, by way of metaphorical description, even in that context, the Ācārya and Sāvitrī are spoken of as the mother and father.
It has been stated that [the student] is marked by the binding of the girdle of muñja grass.
In that regard, because of the fastening of the cord, the teacher might be honored like a father; for that purpose, it is said:
"Because of the imparting of the Veda, they declare the teacher to be a father."
For no ritual action whatsoever is prescribed for him prior to the binding of the girdle of munja grass.
They call the teacher "father" because of his imparting of the Veda;
this is due to teaching the entire Veda, not merely from the recitation of the Sāvitrī verse which is a constituent part of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).
"Imparting" means causing the student to undertake the utterance of the syllables of the Veda.

If this is so, then as long as the teacher has not attained the status of a father, the boy does not undergo his second birth. And as long as he has not attained the state of being twice-born, he would be free to act as he pleases, just as before the initiation ceremony. Therefore, it is said: "For prior to the tying of the girdle of muñja grass, no rite—whether based on the Śrutis, the Smṛtis, or established custom—that serves an invisible purpose (adṛṣṭārtha) is applied to this boy; nor is he entitled to perform them therein."
Immediately upon the *upanayana*, one becomes entitled to all the duties of a twice-born man.
But surely, because of his lack of learning at that stage, how could he be so entitled?
It is for this very reason it was said: "The pupil and the sacrificer [are both under the teacher]."
He must be instructed by the teacher;
thus it has been said: "And he should teach him the rules of purity and conduct," and as Gautama stated regarding the regulations beginning with the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).
The duty of the teacher, however, extends until the completion of the Veda.
One should not utter the Veda, except for the offering of the *svadhā* libation;
for he is equal to a Śūdra as long as he is not born [into the knowledge] of the Veda.
The phrase "until the tying of the girdle of muñja grass" is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].
Alternatively, the determination of the limit is established by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating "or as long as he is not born into the Veda.
*Brahman* here means the Veda; one should not cause him to recite that.
This is the father’s instruction:
that one should protect [the child] from drinking intoxicants and the like, just as one protects him from the utterance of Vedic syllables.

Some, however, describe this very prohibition against the articulation of Brahman as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the study of the auxiliary sciences such as grammar prior to initiation (*upanayana*).
They explain that one should not be told [the meaning] by his father for the sake of instruction; however, there is no fault in a child reciting some indistinct Vedic sentences on his own.
But this is not correct, for it is stated in another Smṛti: "One should not utter the Brahman."
And in an explanatory passage (arthavāda), it is heard: "For he is indeed equal to a Śūdra.
This means that just as a Śūdra incurs fault, so too does this person.
By the word *svadhā*, food prepared for the ancestors is meant here.

Alternatively, the ancestral rite (*pitrya-karman*) is expressed by the word *svadhā*. That mantra by which this [oblation] is poured out—that is, offered and conveyed—is called *svadhā-ninayana*, such as "May the ancestors be purified" (*śundhantāṃ pitaraḥ*), and so forth. Excluding that [mantra], no other mantra should be recited.
From this very [text], it is understood that the offering of water, the *navaśrāddha*, and so forth for the father must be performed by one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*).
However, regarding the *pārvaṇaśrāddha* and other such rites, there is no entitlement because of the absence of sacred fire (*agnimattva*).
For that will be explained in the section concerning the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka*.
And we shall establish this point in detail in the third [chapter].
For one who has undergone the initiation ceremony (upanayana), the instruction in the observances (vratādeśana) is prescribed,
as well as the formal reception of the Veda (brahmagrahaṇa), in due order according to the rules.
By the statement "the teacher, having initiated the pupil," the sequence of purification, conduct, and study has been stated.
Therefore, one should recite [the texts] in that very same order.
Since study would follow immediately after initiation, this [next section] is commenced for the sake of establishing a different sequence.
For one who has been initiated, the vow of the three Vedas and so forth must be performed;
thereafter, the Veda is to be studied.
For the student who has undergone initiation, the instruction of the vows is both prescribed and carried out by the teachers.
This is accepted solely on the authority of the treatise (*śāstra*).
Therefore, the very desire for what ought to be done (*kartavyatā*) is established as the pursuit (*eṣaṇā*).
Consequently, the mention of "the Veda, which is Brahman," according to this sequence and preceded by the injunction, is a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to complete the verse.
Whatever skin, thread, girdle, staff, and garment have been prescribed for him, those same items he must employ even during his religious observances.
The authors of the Gṛhyasūtras have taught certain rites designated as "vratas" for one who desires to take up a portion of the Veda or a year's study;
this practice of the vow (*vratacaryā*) is the collection of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*).

In that regard, regarding the commencement of another vow upon the completion of a previous one, the same rules that apply to the initiation (*upanayana*) apply to the instructions for the vows (*vratādeśa*).
Now, what is the disposal of those [vows] previously undertaken? They are cast into water.
But was it not already stated regarding those previously acquired [elements]:
"What is the status of those that have perished?
Their function, as enjoined by the scriptures, ceases upon destruction, and their cessation occurs through the acquisition of others"?
Whatever hide is prescribed for a particular religious student— such as that of the black antelope for a Brāhmaṇa and that of the Ruru deer for a Kṣatriya—
the same should be understood to apply to his staff and other such items,
as well as to his specific observances (vratas).
Because it is the subject under discussion, the word "vow" (vrata) refers here to the instruction of the vow (vratādeśa).
A student living with his teacher must observe these rules,
fully restraining the collection of his senses for the sake of increasing his own ascetic merit.
This verse is intended to proclaim the importance of the collection of restraints (yama) and observances (niyama) that are about to be described by treating them as a separate section.
Thus, what was previously stated must certainly be performed;
however, this [present teaching] is even more significant than that, and when practiced, leads to a great fruit.

The mention of the "student of sacred knowledge" (*brahmacārin*) is for the purpose of connecting [this section] as a distinct context (*prakaraṇāntara*), lest one suspect that these are not its specific duties. If these were indeed the duties of the student alone, why then is this called a "distinct context"?

Because these [duties] possess a superior excellence compared to the previous ones, and because they share common characteristics, it is designated as a "distinct context" despite this degree of difference.
The remaining words are restated merely for the sake of completing the verse.
One should serve, that is, one should practice these which are about to be described;
they are indicated by the word "these" (imān) because they are present in the mind.

"Living with the guru" means living in the presence of the guru for the purpose of studying knowledge; by this, he expresses constant proximity. "Having restrained the collection of the senses" refers to the path previously mentioned.
"For the sake of increasing austerity" means for the sake of the self-purification (*ātmasaṃskāra*) produced by the performance of the injunctions for study.
He now states those rules previously promised:
Having bathed daily and being pure, he should perform the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors,
as well as the worship of the deities and the placing of fuel on the sacred fire.
Having bathed daily and being pure—that is, having removed all impurity through bathing—one should perform the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors.
However, if one is already pure, one need not necessarily bathe.
Since bathing is prescribed here as a cause for purification by the mention of "purity," it is not to be performed as a mandatory observance (vrata) like those of a Snātaka.
For this very reason, bathing is prohibited in another Smṛti;
that prohibition refers to bathing with clay for the purpose of beautification.
However, Gautama has prescribed bathing in this manner: "He floats like a staff in the waters."
The removal of impurity should not be performed by scrubbing with the hands and so forth.
In the absence of contact with feces and the like, that impurity which arises from sweat or is innate due to contact with cloth-dust and such does not render one impure;
for that is of a fixed nature.

And likewise, the Brāhmaṇa text—“What indeed is the impurity? What is the deerskin? What are the beard-hairs? What is austerity?”—shows that such wearing of dirt is itself a means for achieving dharma.
But how, again, is it understood that bathing has the purpose of purification?
For it is not the case that one who is both bathed and pure, being characterized by both qualities, is then employed in rites for the gods.

Because one who has bathed lacks impurity, and because bathing is prescribed for one who has already performed purification, sipping water (*ācamana*), and so forth—according to the rule "having bathed and sipped water, he should sip water again"—the purity of one who has bathed is understood to be such that even when the occasion [for bathing] exists, the act of bathing is mentioned again [here]. Furthermore, this other *smṛti* text serves to prohibit [bathing] in the absence of the occasion of impurity;
thus, it will provide a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to the rule "one should bathe after having studied the Veda" once the injunction for Vedic study is completed.
One should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the gods, sages, and ancestors.
This is understood to be exactly like the offering of water (*udakadāna*) to the gods and others as prescribed among the duties of a householder, because of its association with the word *tarpaṇa*.
As it is said, "That which one satiates with water," and likewise, "He satiates the deities," the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras have declared this rite to be accomplished by means of water.
And this is known as "water-satiating" (udakatarpaṇa).
Those gods are enumerated by the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras, beginning with Agni, Prajāpati, Brahmā, and so forth.
Their satiation does not consist in producing physical satiety; rather, it is the casting of handfuls of water directed toward them.
Therefore, this [offering] is stated to be a sacrifice consisting of water as its substance;
for otherwise, it would not possess the status of a deity. For it is recorded in tradition that a deity is the recipient of a sacrifice, not the agent of satisfaction.
For this indeed is the defining characteristic of a deity: deities are recipients of hymns (*sūkta*) and recipients of oblations (*havis*).
In that regard, they partake of the hymn by virtue of being the object of praise, and they partake of the oblation by virtue of being the recipient of the offering.
Furthermore, by way of figurative usage (*guṇavṛtti*), the term expresses their status as the recipient of the water-offering intended for their gratification.
The act of giving to a teacher and others is understood through the ownership [of the recipient] directed toward them by means of [the gift of] cows and so forth.
The deity, too, is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*);
because of this commonality of being a recipient, it is said that [the deity] "is satisfied."

If this were for the purpose of satisfying the deities, then it would be a purificatory rite (*saṃskārakarma*) consisting of the libation of water; however, it is not possible for deities to be the objects of such purification,
for they have never been used [for a purpose], nor will they ever be used.
Furthermore, it is not possible for one who has neither performed nor will perform a ritual act to possess the status of a *saṃskāra*.
As for the sages (*ṛṣi*), they are those whose lineage (*ārṣeya*) belongs to a particular sage;
for example, among the Parāśaras, [the lineage] includes Vasiṣṭha, Śakti, and Pāraśarya.

The authors of the Gṛhyasūtras, however, have specified the seers who perceived the mantras as those to be offered libations to, namely Madhucchandas, Gṛtsamada, and Viśvāmitra. Since the word "seer" (ṛṣi) is used without qualification, both [the general category of seers and the specific ones] would be applicable; yet, because the Gṛhyasūtra is a specific Smṛti, it is proper to accept only those [specific seers] mentioned therein.
The ancestors (pitaras) are those who have passed away before; they consist of the fathers and grandfathers, as well as the sapindas and the samānodakas.
The libation for the ancestors (pitṛ-tarpaṇa) is indeed the act of satiating them.
This will be explained explicitly in the section on the rules for the śrāddha ceremony.
Regarding the worship of deities (*devatābhyarcanam*), some ancient authorities have reflected on this: "What indeed are these so-called 'deities' for whom this worship is prescribed?
If they are those depicted in paintings or manuscripts—such as the four-armed one holding a vajra in his hand and so forth—then worldly people refer to them as 'images' (*pratikṛti*)."
Therefore, the designation "deity" in that context is figurative. Now,

those [deities] which are understood from Vedic injunctions related to hymns and oblations, as well as from mantra-texts— and which those who know the relationship between words and their meanings remember as Agni, Agni-Soma, Mitra-Varuṇa, Indra, Viṣṇu, and so forth— if this is the case,
then their status as deities is due solely to their connection with those ritual actions, not due to a connection with an external object.
In that case as well, whatever deity is enjoined for a particular oblation belongs to that oblation alone;
for instance, in the rule "the eight-potherd [cake] is for Agni," the deity belongs to the *puroḍāśa* cake dedicated to Agni, not to the *caru* offering dedicated to Sūrya.
And this is their conclusion: since the primary sense is impossible, it is logical to accept the secondary sense, and this is also supported by established practice.
Therefore, this procedure for worship pertains specifically to images.

As for the reality (tattva) involved here, we shall explain it under the section on "the deity of the gods" (*devadaivatya*) in the context of the vows (*vrata*). The offering of fuel (*samid-ādhāna*) consists of the throwing of wood chips into the fire in the evening and in the morning.
One should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, savory flavors, women,
all fermented acids, and indeed the harming of living beings.
Honey is that produced by bees;
however, because *mādhvīka* is an intoxicant, it is prohibited even before initiation, according to the rule: "A Brahmin should always avoid intoxicants.
This also applies to meat, even that which has been consecrated (*prokṣita*) and so forth.

By the word "fragrance" (gandha), substances such as camphor and agallochum—which possess an excellence of sweet scent—are excluded through a figurative indication based on their relationship [to the quality]. The prohibition concerns the enjoyment of these [substances] for anointing the body and so forth;
however, as for the fragrance itself, which issues from its own locus and comes [to the senses], it is impossible to prohibit.

In that case as well, there is no prohibition even against what occurs spontaneously; however, if it is done out of a desire for enjoyment, such as with heavy incense and the like, there is indeed a fault.
Therefore, when a preceptor is engaged in cutting down a sandalwood tree or similar wood, there is no fault in smelling its fragrance as it arises from the very nature of the object itself.
Such a fragrance is perceived because of its association with flower garlands.
However, that odor of medicinal ghee for leprosy, putrid wood, and so forth, which is not of such a nature as to cause madness of the heart, is not prohibited.
*Mālya* is a flower strung together;
*rasas* are the sweet, sour, and other tastes.
But surely, since that which is devoid of rasa cannot be eaten, the very function of the life-force (prāṇavṛtti) would not exist?
True;
what is prohibited are substances such as molasses and the like when they consist of rasa alone in an excessive degree.
In the act of preparing the food, there is a prohibition even of those things included within the substance itself;
or rather, this is a prohibition against attachment to prepared food that has been thoroughly refined,
as it has been said:
"He who fears wealth as if it were a snake, sweet food as if it were poison,
and women as if they were ogresses— he attains knowledge.
Others, however, consider [the arts] to be the erotic (śṛṅgāra) and so forth.

One should not cultivate the nourishment of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) by watching plays and the like, or by listening to poetry. As for the view of others— that *rasa* is that which exists as an internal liquid within sugarcane, myrobalan, and so forth, like water— and that what is prohibited is the juice when it has been squeezed out and separated,
but not that which remains within them— this is incorrect.
For the word *rasa* is not commonly known as a synonym for liquid. Furthermore, that which is appropriate to end with consumption for a particular thing is precisely what is prohibited in its case;
therefore, the prohibition applies to the eating of honey and meat, not to their seeing or touching.

Even in the case of perfumes and garlands, the taking up [of these items] is prohibited because of the conceit of adorning the body, but not their grasping by the hand or other means in any way whatsoever.

Likewise, women are prohibited [from being taken] through the connection of sexual intercourse; and it is precisely out of apprehension of that [prohibition] that he will later prohibit looking at them and touching them.
And thus Gautama says: "Beholding or touching women when there is suspicion of sexual intercourse.
Sour substances (*śuktāni*) are those that have acquired a sour taste either through mere fermentation or through contact with another substance;
their prohibition is established precisely because they pertain to the duties of the twice-born.
The repetition [of the word "sour"] is for the purpose of including that which is figuratively sour;
by this, harsh and rough words are prohibited.
As for what was stated by Gautama—that "words may be sour"—this inclusion of "all" is for the purpose of making this very point explicit.
Having referred to "sour liquids" (*rasa-śuktāni*), the word "all" (*sarvāṇi*) is prescribed;
thus, the inclusion of [speech] in a secondary sense (*gauṇa-parigraha*) becomes established.
However, those who explain it thus—that by the word "sour" (*śukta*) there is a prohibition of liquids, and by the word "all" there is a prohibition of mental words—should be asked this:
Why is the inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) not intended for the purpose of prohibiting those things whose prohibition is already established by their meaning?
For if that were the case, it would follow that curd and other such substances that have turned sour would also be prohibited.
However, if the prohibition is explained as having its purpose already stated by relying on what is already established, then there is no fault whatsoever.
Since the killing of living beings such as mosquitoes and flies might occur through negligence, this prohibition is reiterated for the purpose of careful avoidance;
or else, it is for the purpose of making it an ancillary part of the rule for Vedic study (*svādhyāya*).
For not only is there a transgression of the prohibition intended for human welfare in the case of killing, but there is also a transgression of the purpose of the rule for Vedic study.

If it is asked, "Why is this not postulated in the case of mother-of-pearl and similar objects as well?"—the answer is that in those cases there is scope for another object [to account for the error]; and when an alternative explanation exists, the uselessness of a single uniform object is a more serious fault.
Anointing the body, applying collyrium to the eyes, wearing shoes, carrying an umbrella,
as well as desire, anger, greed, dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments;
Anointing (abhyaṅga) is the rubbing of the head and body with unctuous substances such as clarified butter and oil;
collyrium (añjana) is for the eyes.
The mention of the eyes is for the purpose of completing the meter.

Furthermore, the prohibition regarding these two applies to their use for the purpose of adorning the body, not for medicinal purposes, as they are mentioned in association with perfumes, garlands, and so forth.
"Sandals" refers to leather footwear, not merely [wooden] shoes.
And the carrying of an umbrella—whether by one's own hand or by the hand of another—is prohibited in both cases.
Lust (*kāma*) is passion (*rāga*); the [desire] for procreation (*manmatha*) is established by the very prohibition of women. Anger (*krodha*) is wrath (*roṣa*).
Greed and delusion;
these two, egoism and possessiveness, are mental factors (*cittadharma*).
Dancing is the movement of limbs for the delight of common people, as well as the application of dramatic performance (*abhinaya*) according to the systems seen in the works of Bharata and others.
Singing (*gīta*) is the demonstration of the musical notes beginning with *ṣaḍja*.

Instrumental music (*vādana*) is the production of pitched sounds using instruments such as the lute (*vīṇā*) and the flute (*vaṃśa*), as well as the striking of drums such as the *paṇava* and *mṛdaṅga* in accordance with rhythmic timing (*tāla*).
Gambling, idle gossip, slander, as well as falsehood; gazing at and touching women, and injury to others.
Gambling is the playing with dice;
betting on cocks and other animals is prohibited because the word "gambling" (dyūta) is a general term.
Idle talk with people refers to verbal quarrels over worldly matters without cause, or the seeking out of news regarding regions, or engaging in questioning.
Slander (*parivāda*) is the speaking of another's faults out of envy (*asūyā*).

Falsehood (*anṛta*) is when that which was seen or heard in one way is spoken of in another way. In all cases, one should avoid these; thus, by the force of the context, the accusative case is understood.
Regarding women, there are gazing and touching.
Gazing (*prekṣaṇa*) is the examination of the configuration of their limbs, [thinking] "this limb of hers is beautiful" or "this is not.
Touching (*ālambha*) is embracing.
And these two [lying and causing harm] are forbidden for a child when there is a suspicion of sexual intercourse, according to the literal sense.

"Harm" (upaghāta) means injury or doing wrong; it refers to the obstruction of someone in the accomplishment of some purpose, such as obtaining a maiden in marriage and so forth. When questioned, even if one is unfit [to speak], one must not state that one is unfit; rather, one should remain silent, because lying is prohibited.
One should always sleep alone and never let semen spill;
for by spilling semen out of desire, one destroys one's own vow.
One should always sleep alone and never spill one's semen, even in a non-vaginal place; for [spilling it] in a vaginal place is already precluded by the prohibition against women.
Regarding this, there is an explanatory statement (arthavāda): "For by spilling [semen] out of desire (*kāma*). Here, "desire" (*kāma*) means intention (*icchā*).
By emitting—that is, discharging—the semen through manual manipulation or sexual intercourse with a woman, one violates and destroys one's own vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
A twice-born student of sacred knowledge who, while dreaming, unintentionally emits semen,
shall bathe, worship the sun, and recite three times the verse beginning with "punar mām."
The expiation for an *avakīrṇin* is prescribed for the intentional violation of a vow; however, this [following rule] is stated for an unintentional act.
The mention of "sleep" is not intended to be significant; rather, "unintentionally" (*akāmataḥ*) alone is the cause [for this expiation]. For indeed, desire cannot arise in a dream.
Therefore, even if semen should somehow flow involuntarily while one is awake—like a drop of one's own impure blood—one must perform this very same penance.
Having unintentionally emitted semen, one should perform this penance and mutter the verse beginning with "punar mām."
He should fetch a water-pot, flowers, cow dung, earth, and kusha grass—
as much as required— and he should go out for alms every day.
He should fetch water-jars and other such items as many as are necessary for the teacher’s purpose;
this is mentioned by way of illustration,
and he should also perform whatever other blameless work is useful for the household.
This verse has the purpose of establishing that one should not cause [the disciple] to perform despicable acts, such as the wiping away of leftovers, except for his teacher;
for service toward the teacher has been prescribed in general terms.
The analysis of the compound is: "whatever the extent of these [duties]."
And he should go for alms day after day.

Here, "alms" refers to prepared food that is extremely small in quantity, sufficient only for sustenance. Because the word "food" (*anna*) is employed in the prohibition against eating from a single person's meal, it is understood here as referring specifically to food.
Because of the grammatical coordination in the statement, "Having collected alms and having offered them, one should eat," it is established that the alms consist of prepared food.
For if dry grain were begged, how could there be eating of it?

Furthermore, if [the food] were collected at the teacher's house while still being cooked, it would have the nature of raw material for alms (*bhaikṣaprakṛti*), not the status of alms (*bhaikṣatā*) itself.
By common usage, such alms alone are so called;
[it means] "day after day.
But surely, from the very statement "one should subsist constantly on alms," the practice of going out for alms day after day is already established.
The inclusion of the word "daily" (nitya) is for the purpose of prescribing the means of subsistence.
Even with stale food, provided it is mixed with fats such as ghee, one may subsist; for that reason, it is said that one should eat after begging day by day.
One must not, however, consume on a subsequent day whatever was begged on a previous day, even if it is mixed with some fat, by way of an exception [to the rule against eating stale food].
He specifies those from whom alms are to be obtained: "A student,
being self-restrained, should daily collect alms from the houses of those who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifices, who are praiseworthy in their own duties."

And those who are not deficient in their knowledge of the Vedas, being endowed with the study of the Vedas; and who, having the qualification for sacrifices, are performers of them—meaning they are not deficient, not excluded, but rather possessed of that [qualification];
and who are praiseworthy in their own duties;
and for whom there is no qualification for sacrifice, they are devoted to other auspicious works.
Alternatively, those who are praised for their own occupations are said to be those who are content with their own livelihood alone and do not subsist on such occupations as usury and the like.
From their houses, one should collect alms—meaning one should take them after having requested them—being self-restrained and pure. The phrase "daily" is a restatement (anuvāda).
One should not beg for alms from the family of the teacher, nor from the families of one's paternal or maternal kinsmen;
however, if houses belonging to others are unavailable, one should avoid each preceding house in favor of the next.
Even though he possesses these qualities, he should not beg in the house of his teacher.
First, he should not seek it from his own family or lineage; nor should he receive it even from the paternal uncles and others belonging to the teacher's family.
"Relatives" refers to those on the father's side who are fellow students (*brahmacārin*); [he should not beg] in their family either.

Nor should one form such a connection with relatives on the mother’s side, such as maternal uncles and so forth, thinking, "among my teachers and kinsmen"; for they are already included by the word *kula* itself in the phrase "the family of the teacher. From whom, then, should he beg?
Apart from these, [one may seek alms] from other houses.

If there is no gain— that is, if it is impossible to obtain [alms] from other houses— then if the entire village is occupied by teachers, kinsmen, and relatives, and there are no others at all, or if those who exist do not give food, one should beg even from these houses.
In the absence of others, he should first beg from a kinsman; in his absence, from a relative; and in his absence, from the teacher’s household.
Or, if those previously mentioned are unavailable, he may wander through the entire village,
restraining his speech and remaining self-controlled, while avoiding those who have been accused of crimes.

In the absence of those previously mentioned who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifice, he may wander for the sake of subsistence throughout the entire village, disregarding distinctions of caste, while avoiding only those who are accused—that is, those notorious for having committed sins—even if their sin has not been witnessed. And so says Gautama: "The practice of wandering for alms among all castes is prescribed, with the exception of those who are accused or outcasted."
Having restrained his speech, he should not utter any other word than that pertaining to alms, from the time he sets out until he has obtained the alms.
Having brought fuel from afar, he should place it in the open air;
and evening and morning, he should unwearyingly offer oblations into the fire with that fuel.
The mention of "distance" (*dūra*) is intended as an illustration for a location that is not possessed by anyone.
It is said that the forest is far from the village, and therein there is no ownership by anyone.
For if the meaning of "distance" were not illustrated, the meaning of the treatise would be unsettled, as one could not determine how far "far" actually is.
Having fetched it— that is, having brought it—
one should place it, that is, set it down,
in the open space above the house.
For indeed, it is not possible to place a treasure-trove in the sky, which is without support.
One should offer oblations with them in the evening and in the morning;
as for the bringing [of the materials], it may be done at that time or at another time according to one's wish.
They say that placing [the wood] in the air is for a purpose not immediately visible;

however, others say that the wood being brought down from the tree becomes wet, and this should be understood as occurring right there, either on top of the house or on another structure such as a wall.
If one who is not ill fails to go on his alms-round and fails to kindle the sacred fire for seven nights, he shall perform the penance of an *avakīrṇin*.

Without having performed for seven nights—that is, for seven days—the continuous service of the sacred fires, gathering fuel, and begging for alms, one who is not ill—that is, being free from disease—should perform the penance called *avakīrṇi-vrata*, the nature of which will be described in the eleventh [chapter]. This is intended to demonstrate the gravity of the offense; however, this is not the only penance applicable here.
For in another Smṛti, a different expiation is prescribed here: "An oblation of clarified butter with the *savitṛ* [verse] or the *retasyā* [verse].

Furthermore, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) here: if this were an expiation, then, like sexual intercourse with a woman, it would have been recited as a causal factor in the section on the expiation for a student who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*).
As for those who explain that both of these must necessarily be performed for seven nights:
In that case, there is a fault due to non-performance;
however, for one who has completed the seven nights, there is no fault in not performing it thereafter.
And those seven days are taken from the beginning, starting from the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).
This is incorrect, because it contradicts the rule "one should perform [this] until the return ceremony," and because it also contradicts the immediately following verse.

One who observes the vow should always subsist on alms; he should not eat the food of a single person. It is traditionally taught that for one observing the vow, subsistence on alms is equal to fasting.
But is it not already heard in scripture that "one should go for alms day after day"?
For in this way, the practice of begging for alms serves a visible purpose;
and it has also been stated that "one should eat after having offered [the food] to the teacher."

Furthermore, that eating is not a refinement of alms-food (bhaikṣa) such that it would serve as a means of livelihood. Some say that this is restated in order to state that "one who observes the vow must not eat from a single person's food.
This too is incorrect, because the eating of food from a single person is already prohibited by the word *bhaikṣa* itself.

The collection of alms is called *bhaikṣa*; therefore, how could there be the possibility of eating food from a single source? All of this is restated for the purpose of permitting that [eating] for ancestral rites (*pitrya*).

He should maintain himself by means of alms; he should sustain his life through food obtained as alms. He should not eat food belonging to a single person, nor should he consume the food of a single mendicant.
Furthermore, one should not entertain the suspicion that he must not eat what belongs to a single owner, but rather [avoid] what belongs to many owners who are undivided brothers.

"Eating the food of one" (*ekānnāda*) means he eats or consumes the food of a single person; this refers to a religious student (*vratī*, *brahmacārī*). The word "vratī" is understood from the context itself and is included merely to complete the meter of the verse.
In this regard, there is an explanatory passage (arthavāda):
that mode of life consisting solely of subsistence on alms for one observing the vow, which is the maintenance of the body, is recorded in tradition as having a fruit equal to fasting.
In a rite dedicated to the gods, he should eat like one observing a vow; in a rite for the ancestors, he may eat at will when invited, like a seer (ṛṣi); his vow is not thereby violated.
This is an exception to the instruction regarding subsistence by begging in specific circumstances:

when a meal for the gods (*devadaivatyam*) is being prepared—meaning when Brahmins are being fed with the gods as the intended object—and when a meal for the ancestors (*pitryam*) is being prepared—meaning when one is invited or requested on behalf of the ancestors—one may eat food from a single source at will;
however, one should not beg for it oneself.
And that [food] is like that of a *vratin*, meaning it is not inconsistent with the vows and is devoid of honey and meat.

By the two words "like a *vratin*" (*vratavat*) and "like a seer" (*ṛṣivat*), one and the same meaning is expressed; there is no distinction established by a difference in ritual action between the village and the forest.
However, the double mention is for the sake of the meter.
If the Vaikhānasa sage were permitted to eat that [food], then even meat would be permitted for a religious student (*brahmacārin*).
For it is said, "He may consume even what comes from a village," and thus there is the eating of meat.
That which has the gods as its deity is *devadaivatyam*.

And that feeding of Brāhmaṇas is prescribed in divine rites such as the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; it is also prescribed in rites such as the Āgrahāyaṇī, where it is stated: "Having fed the Brāhmaṇas, one should cause them to recite benedictions. In this context, this is the authorization. Others, however, consider that feeding of Brāhmaṇas which is performed on the seventh lunar day and so forth, dedicated to deities such as Āditya, to be "devadaivatyam" (having the gods as its deity).
That is incorrect;
for there is no connection with a deity in the act of eating, since that is not a means of sacrifice (*yāga*).

Nor is a deity merely that which is intended (*uddeśyamātra*), because if that were so, it would follow [absurdly] that the teacher (*upādhyāya*) and the house are also deities in such cases as "he gives a cow to the teacher" and "he sweeps the house."
For the eater has a perceptible connection with the food;
however, the sun is not an instrument (kāraka), nor is it the intended object (uddeśya) like the house, nor is the meal for its sake.
Indeed, the accusative case-ending indicates that the food is for the sake of the eater, not for the sake of the sun.
Nor has it been stated anywhere that "one should feed Brāhmaṇas with the Sun and so forth as the intended recipient.
If it is argued that the injunction is inferred from established practice (*samācāra*), we say no; for its source is already perceived, namely, the external Smṛtis.
Indeed, there exists such a source in the form of those Smṛti texts.
In that case, the meaning of the scripture would be that one should gratify the deities by feeding Brahmins;
however, this meaning cannot be so construed.
For the purpose of the scripture does not consist primarily in the gratification of the deities, but rather in the primary purpose of the injunction itself.
Furthermore, in this injunction, there is no connection with the deities intended—such as Āditya and others—either by way of the object [of the rite] or by way of the qualification [of the agent].

For they are not a causal condition (*nimitta*) like the breaking [of a vessel], nor are they desired as being related to oneself like cattle and so forth, because they do not possess a nature that can be enjoyed.
If it is argued that rather the satisfaction residing in them is what is desired;
That [satisfaction] also requires another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its own establishment, and such a means does not exist;

for the satisfaction resulting from the sun and so forth is not established by perception or other means in the same way as cattle and the like, whereby it could be connected with a Vedic injunction for an optional sacrifice (*kāmyeṣṭi*).
But as for the notion that "my lord will cause [me] to sacrifice for his own desired fruit," this too is to be disregarded due to a lack of authoritative evidence;
nor is there any injunction regarding this matter that serves as proof.
For that [injunction] enjoins a person by means of its own connection with the known qualification of the performer; it does not, however, make known the existence of that which is desired.

For the injunction measures itself as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in the sense that the object of desire—already known through another means of knowledge—is a qualification of the performer, being related to the performer as something to be accomplished through performance.
Now, this sacrifice is for him, and the eating is its disposal (*pratipatti*).
Let it be so, if that is the practice of the learned.
First of all, it cannot be proven that the food is not directly related to the deity;
however, its connection mediated by the sacrifice is not denied.
Furthermore, one does not engage in this [act] with the thought that it is a sacrifice; rather, [one thinks], "When the Brahmins have been fed, the deity will be pleased.
Therefore, the deity is neither the agent of the act of feeding nor a qualifier of the agent.
Consequently, there is no connection [with the deity] by way of being its object.
Nor is there the status of being the intended recipient (*uddeśyatva*) for the sun and so forth;
for it is he to whom food is given who is the intended recipient of that meal,
and that [food] is given to the Brahmins.
Nor is it merely that which is being addressed [as a deity] that one gives a cow to or sweeps the house for; for if that were so, it would follow that the house and the teacher would also be deities.
But then, how can there be the feeding of Brahmins at a rite for the ancestors?
For even in that case, the ancestors could not be the deities.
Nor does the oblation (homa) possess the nature of being for the ancestors (pitrya), because another deity is heard [in the scripture];

since the satisfaction of the ancestors is not established by any other means of knowledge in the same way as the satisfaction of Āditya and others, it cannot be the object to be accomplished (sādhya) in relation to the injunction.
Regarding this, they say:
For here the satisfaction of the ancestors is indeed established.
Because the self is imperishable, the ancestors are established; and for them, a connection with a body is brought about through their past actions (*karma*).
For the offering of food (*bhojana*) is the primary element here.
For its fruit is declared to be that one obtains abundant merit by feeding [the ancestors];

and that fruit consists in the satisfaction of the ancestors. This satisfaction is merely a state of pleasure; it does not arise as the result of the act of eating characterized by satiety, as is the case for human beings.
There is a certain satisfaction of the ancestors resulting from their own past actions for those who have been born into that particular birth;
this verbal root expresses mere satisfaction, whereas satiety is a specific quality,
which is to be understood through other means of valid cognition.
And it should not be objected here: "The son is the agent; how can the fruit go to the agent when it accrues to the fathers?
For those who know the principles of logic do not say that these Vedic rites grant their fruit to another.
This is because, in this case, the fathers themselves are both the authorized performers and the agents.
By the very procreation of offspring, all this has been accomplished by the ancestors;
for it was with this very purpose that he was produced, thinking, "He will perform benefit, both seen and unseen.

Consequently, just as in the *Sarvasvāra* sacrifice, due to the absence [of the sacrificer], the deceased possesses agency through the direction, "O Brāhmaṇas, complete my sacrifice," regarding the subsidiary elements belonging to the subsequent period.
The same should be understood here as well;
however, this is the distinction:
in that case, the performers are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who are engaged for another purpose and hired for wages for the sake of their livelihood.
In this case, however, the son is indeed impelled by that injunction.

Just as a father who is impelled by the injunction of procreation has the authority to perform the sacramental rites for his son’s sake—since that injunction extends up to the point of instruction—so too does the son have the authority to perform the *śrāddha* and other rites for the sake of his father.

Likewise, while the father is still living, the rite for the elders must certainly be performed [by the son], according to the rule: "But when [the parents] are aged, both mother and father [must be honored]."
In this way, his [the father's] destiny has also gone [to that state].
Furthermore, this entitlement is not optional like the Vaiśvānara sacrifice; for it is said:
"One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when a son is born."
"He who, upon the birth [of a son], performs this sacrifice becomes indeed purified, radiant, an eater of food, and endowed with sensory power.
Thus, for one desiring such fruits as a son, the father has the entitlement to perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice; however, it is not mandatory, unlike the *cūḍā* ceremony and others.
But here, since it is said that "the rite for the ancestors (pitrya) must be performed until death," it is lifelong.
The view that "there is no Vedic fruit for the performer" is otherwise refined as follows:

just as in the case of the Vaiśvānara sacrifice, the fruit—characterized by the father's possession of a distinguished son—belongs to the father alone, and the fruit does not go to the non-performer; likewise here too, that fruit, which is the father's joy, belongs to the son alone.
