In both cases, it is not contradictory that the fruit accrues to the father who performed the act;
for by the very production of offspring, such a fruit is desired, and thus there is no occurrence of a fruit unintended by the ancestors.

If the ancestors are not the deities (*devatā*) in the *śrāddha*, how then can this rite be called "pertaining to the ancestors" (*pitrya*), given that [the suffix -ya] is a *taddhita* derivative denoting a deity?
We say it is because of the commonality of being the intended recipient (*uddeśyatva*).
In the case [of the *śrāddha*], the ancestors are designated [as recipients] with the thought, "This feeding of Brahmins is for the sake of your benefit.
However, in the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the ancestors are indeed the deities (*devatā*) themselves.
They do not consider the ancestors to be the deities in the *śrāddha* rite;
rather, that the Brahmins are fed is analogous to the offering (*avadāna*) of clarified butter, sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), and so forth, into the fire.
Such is this [act].
And thus, the Brahmins attain the status of fathers;
therefore, at the time of serving the food, the fathers alone are to be intended, [with the thought], "This is for you, not mine.
The Brahmins, however, occupy the position of the Āhavanīya fire.
The only distinction is this: whereas the oblation is thrown into the *āhavanīya* fire, it is instead placed before the Brāhmaṇas, who take it up for themselves.
Nor is the *śrāddha* not a sacrifice; for there, the utterance of *svāhā* is intended for the deities, as is seen in the case of the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other offerings.
Therefore, even though it is a sacrifice, the *śrāddha* rite will have the ancestors (*pitṛs*) as its purpose.
The fact that the ancestors possess the status of deities and are recipients of the fruit [of the rite] will not be contradicted.
Regarding the third [section], we shall explain something related to that which has not yet been stated.
Therefore, it is established that the Ādityas and others are not the deities in the feeding of Brāhmaṇas.

But is this definition not also too narrow? For we observe the usage of the term "deity" even in the absence of a connection to a sacrifice, as in the case of that which is intended as the goal (*uddeśya*) in a sacrifice;

and furthermore, there is the worship of deities, as in the injunction, "one should approach the deities" (*daivatāny abhigacchet*). Neither worship nor approaching by means of walking with one's feet toward the deities is possible [in those cases].
This is not a fault.
Where there is an injunction regarding a deity, this procedure of worship shall apply—whether in the case of the Vaiśvadeva deities or those connected with the Agnihotra and other rites.
But even so, it is not tenable;
for the status of a deity as an object of worship is impossible, because that would entail the loss of its essential nature.
For if it were the object of the act of worship (*pūjākarma*), it would be the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) of the sacrifice.
It has been stated that nothing happens to [the deity] apart from another action;
for a factor of action (*kāraka*) is a capacity (*śakti*), and that capacity differs with each action.
Furthermore, since that [kāraka] is understood through its function (*kārya*), it is logical that its distinction [from other kārakas] extends as far as its function persists.
Therefore, that which is a recipient (*saṃpradāna*) remains precisely a recipient; it does not incur the status of being an object (*karman*).
How then is it that in the expression *pācakāya dehi* ("Give to the cook"), the agent of the root *pac-* (to cook) becomes the recipient of the root *dā-* (to give)?
With his limbs wounded by arrows, he went along helpless while being gazed upon with side-long glances by his beloved;
the resolution to this has been stated:
because the distinction between power and the possessor of power is merely figurative, the expression "he goes having eaten" is established.
Therefore, if this concerns the object of worship, there is no attainment of a deity; if, on the other hand, the deities are Āditya and the rest, there is no injunction for worship.
For when a deity is already established, worship is not enjoined with reference to it.
Nor are Āditya and the others general terms for "deity," in the way that the word "cow" applies to the Śāgaleya and other breeds.
To this it is replied: It is true that the sun and so forth are not deities by virtue of their own nature;
this term is a relative one.

The meaning of "deity" is to be understood solely from the injunction: that for which a specific oblation is prescribed is its deity. It has been stated that Agni himself is not the deity in a rite other than the Āgneya sacrifice.
However, a ritual of worship cannot exist without one who is being worshipped.
Furthermore, deities are traditionally heard of as objects of worship.

In that regard, if worship in the primary sense is possible for the sake of a deity, then sacrifice itself must be understood as worship. Since that [sacrifice] is beautiful, when there is no hearing of a specific substance or deity, this [textual passage] should be understood as a restatement (anuvāda) intended to prescribe the time of the forenoon.
Therefore, it is effectively stated that the rites for the deities (daivata) should be performed in the forenoon.
Why is it said that "the deity is not heard"?
For there is no explicit word "deity" [in the text].
This word "deity" (devatā) is not used in a general sense;
it refers to those whose status as deities is observed elsewhere, for whom this rule of worship is prescribed.
Therefore, Agni, Āditya, Rudra, Indra, Viṣṇu, Sarasvatī, and others such as these are to be worshipped.
And for the purpose of worship, there is the presentation of incense, lamps, garlands, offerings, and so forth.
Among these, fire has a direct connection [to the deity].
And as for that [offering] to the sun, because it resides at a great distance, one casts fragrances and other substances in a pure place while intending it for him.
Since the true nature (*svarūpa*) of Indra and the other deities is not perceptible, they are enjoined in that manner by means of the very words "Indra" and so forth.

Although worship has as its primary object that which is being worshipped, nevertheless, when those being worshipped are subordinate to some other purpose, it is the act of worship itself that is understood as the duty to be performed.
For if the material substance (*dravya*) were primary, it would be impossible for it to be the subject of an injunction.
These [actions] are twofold, being either subordinate (*guṇa*) or principal (*pradhāna*), according to the principle that "those by which a substance is intended to be prepared" are subordinate.
However, it is logical [to consider them principal], as in the case of hymns of praise (*stuti*) and ritual injunctions (*śāstra*).
Just as a hymn of praise does not exist for the sake of the object of praise, so too this act of worship does not exist for the sake of the object of worship.

If it is argued that there is no mention of the roots *stu* (to praise) and *saṃstu* (to recite), it has been stated here [in the commentary] that the accusative case is used because it is observed in the case of groats (*saktavaḥ*).

Likewise, in the injunction "one should perform circumambulations to the right of the clay, the cow, and the deity," the practice of moving to the right (*dakṣiṇācāratā*) is prescribed. Ritual acts for the gods (*daivāni karmāṇi*) are to be performed with the right hand.
For it is not possible for a deity to have a location by way of the southern path, as in the case of clay and other such things, because the deity is formless.
Thus, [the statement] "one should approach the deities" is untenable;

since it is impossible to reach the vicinity of a deity through the activity of moving one's feet, and since the root *gam* has the meaning of "knowledge," how does "approaching" (*abhigamana*) differ from "remembering"? (smaraṇa).
One should approach the deity; at the time of the ritual action, one should meditate upon her with the mind, meaning that one should avoid mental distraction known as agitation.
Thus, this traditional rule (smṛti) has its source clearly perceived:
"One should meditate with the mind upon whichever deity the oblation has been taken for."
But surely this too is already established because the intended designation would otherwise be impossible.
There is no fault here, as it is possible for there to be both an objection and confusion.

In this way, common usages such as "the property of the gods," "the cattle of the gods," and "the wealth of the gods" are to be understood as referring to cattle and other items that have been set aside for the sake of those [gods].
In matters concerning punishment (*daṇḍādhikāra*), however, they maintain that the legal dealings regarding deities apply only to their images (*pratikṛti*);
otherwise, there would be a breakdown of established order.

Since images—which are the assumed forms of deities—are related to them through an assumed relationship of owned and owner, that which belongs to them is what is referred to as "deity-property" (*devadravya*) in such passages as: "But the property of deities, Brāhmaṇas, and kings should be known as the highest [sanction]. Etc.
For there is no relationship of master and servant among the deities; since the primary meaning is impossible, only a secondary (gauna) meaning should be accepted.
What, then, is the secondary meaning here?
For everywhere, the comprehension of a secondary meaning arises from the connection with a common quality.
In cases such as "The boy is fire," [the metaphor arises] because one perceives those qualities in the white boy;
and those qualities are ascertainable through perception and other means of knowledge.

But here, since the meaning of the deity is to be understood only through its ritual function (*kārya*), and since no specific nature (*svarūpa*) is understood from that function, how could there be an ascertainment of common qualities in the images?
To this it is replied:

because such forms are heard in the mantras and explanatory passages (arthavādas), and these are explained as being figurative descriptions (guṇavāda), those who—failing to perceive their basis—grasp the literal meaning and thus establish that Indra and others possess such forms, perceive a similarity in the images; therefore, the figurative nature [of the usage] is entirely appropriate.

As for those who claim that the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas for the Vaiśvadeva rite at the Śrāddha itself constitutes the offering to the deities (daivadevatya), their statement is redundant; since that rite is an auxiliary part of the ancestral rite (pitrya), it is already included by the mention of the "ancestral" (pitrya).
Furthermore, because the term is a general one, how can a specific meaning be understood?
If it is argued that this is due to association (sāhacarya), then that would only hold if the ancestral rite were not already encompassed by the word "pitrya."
The maxim of the cow and the bull also applies only when there is no difference in the object.
This duty has been taught by the wise as belonging solely to the Brāhmaṇa;
however, for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, this duty is not prescribed in this manner.

This practice of eating food from a single source and so forth, which has been prescribed, was taught by wise and learned men after they had obtained it from the Veda; however, they do not approve of this for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya.
For them, there is never any eating that is not obtained through begging.
But surely, is it not the case that only Brāhmaṇas have the entitlement to eat at a Śrāddha feast?
Since it is stated, "Those who are worthy of being fed there, and those who are to be avoided,
[should be known] regarding the most excellent Brahmin," the entitlement to receive gifts belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone;
so how can there be this prohibition for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya?

And this is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*), not an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*); furthermore, prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*) depend upon something that has already been established. It is said:
For Brahmins who have finished eating, the disposal of the remaining food is prescribed by the rule: "One should provide for one's kinsmen.
In this context, there is no regard for caste; whoever is one's kinsman, he is the one to be fed by him.
Furthermore, in that case, Kṣatriyas and others are not connected as recipients, but rather it is the kinsmen [who are intended].
Therefore, there is a prohibition of this attainment.
Whether constantly urged by his teacher or even without being urged,
he should apply himself to his studies and to the welfare of his preceptor.
Even if not urged by the teacher and even if not formally appointed, one should apply oneself with effort to the study of the Veda.
But has it not been stated that "one should study when summoned"? How, then, can application be prescribed for one who has not been urged?
This is stated for the sake of the remaining qualities by one who has mastered a portion of the Veda;
in that regard, the command of the teacher need not be awaited.
Likewise, whatever is beneficial to the teacher—such as fetching water-jars and so forth, or massaging him when he is fatigued—that too must be performed even without being commanded.
Restraining his body, speech, organs of perception, and mind, he should stand with palms joined in reverence, gazing at the face of the teacher.
Having arrived from somewhere, he should remain gazing at the face of the guru and not sit down;
restraining his body,
he should not move his feet or hands, nor laugh, nor say anything that is useless.
One should restrain the faculties of cognition.
Whatever possesses a marvelous form, one should not contemplate that again and again in the presence of the Guru;
this applies to the ears and the other senses as well.
The restraint of the eyes is accomplished simply by looking toward the face of the teacher.
One should restrain the mind and, with the mind, abandon worldly conceptualizations such as the undertaking of household chores or the filling of store-rooms.
Since it has already been stated that "one should exert effort in self-restraint," that prohibition is intended for the purpose of forbidding attachment.
In the presence of the guru, not even the slightest movement of the senses should be permitted toward an object that is not expressly forbidden;
one should remain with palms joined in the *añjali* gesture, hands folded like a *kapota* bird.
He should always have his right hand raised, be sweet in conduct, and well-restrained;
and when told, "Be seated," he should sit facing the teacher.
The hand must be withdrawn not only from the sacred thread (*sūtraka*), but also from the garment (*vāsas*).
The inclusion of the word "constantly" (*nitya*) indicates that this withdrawal of the hand is required not only while standing, nor only at the time of study, but rather at other times as well.
One should maintain good conduct (*sādhvācāra*); that is, one's behavior, including speech and interaction, should be excellent and irreproachable.
Because of the requirement that [the precepts] be observed constantly, one must not engage in vulgar speech and the like even when the teacher is not present.
Being well-restrained in speech, mind, and sight, with self controlled,
one should avoid even the slightest fault.
One who acts according to his own will is said to be "uncovered" (anāvṛta) in the world; the opposite of that is "well-covered" (susaṃvṛta).
Others, however, believe that one should remain with the body covered by a garment in the presence of the teacher and should not remove the upper robe;
thus one should stand.

But when the teacher says "Be seated," either by this word or by a movement of the eyebrows and so forth— for the purpose is to communicate an injunction, and communication does not consist solely in the operation of words— then he should sit, that is, he should take his seat facing him, directly opposite.
In the presence of the teacher, he should always have inferior food, clothing, and dress;
he should rise before him and go to bed after him.
In the presence of one's teacher, one should eat inferior and meager food.
This "meagerness" may be in terms of quantity or, in some cases, in terms of preparation.

If one has obtained from alms such prepared side dishes as clarified butter, curds, milk, and so forth, then—if that same kind of food has not been eaten by the teacher at the same time while eating together with him—[one should eat it].
If such food as that [of the teacher] is not prepared in the house, then it must be discarded by him.

However, if the teacher also has such food, then a reduction [in the student's portion] must be made. As for clothing, if the teacher’s garment is made of wool, then the student must not wear one made of cotton or similar materials.
Dress refers to ornaments, decorations, and the like;
that too is inferior,
because it is always contrary to celibacy.
For this very reason, the assumption of [specific] dress is prescribed;
moreover, ornamentation is not desired for a religious student (*brahmacārin*).
At the end of the night, he should rise first from his bed, or having perceived the occasion for rising from his seat, he should rise first—that is, before—his teacher.
Finally, at the time of sleep, he should lie down on his bed after the teacher has slept, and he should sit upon his seat [only] after the teacher has sat down.
One should not engage in responding or conversing while lying down,
nor while sitting, nor while eating, nor while standing, nor with one's face turned away.
*Pratiśravaṇa* is the act of responding when being called upon or being assigned a task;
*saṃbhāṣā* is the exchange of words in dialogue with the teacher. These two are *pratiśravaṇa-saṃbhāṣe*.
Lying down on his own bed with his limbs cast upon it, he should not practice— that is, he should not perform [the rite]; nor should he do so while sitting, having sat down upon a seat.
Not while eating;
not standing in one place without moving, remaining upright;
nor, moreover, with his back turned.
One should not perform [the rite] while standing with one's back turned toward the direction in which the Guru is seen.

Standing, one should attend to one who is seated; approaching, one should attend to one who is standing; going out to meet, one should attend to one who is coming toward oneself; and running, one should attend to one who is running.
How then?
When he gives an order while seated, then [the other], standing up from his seat, should respond and converse;
but if [the teacher] is standing, [the student] should go toward him.
When the teacher stands and gives an instruction, one should approach him facing him, having walked several steps toward him;
"āvrajata" means coming, having gone out to meet him, that is, having gone directly toward him.
The prefix *prati* denotes direction toward (*ābhimukhya*).
Running after one who is running with speed, or likewise following after one who is staying behind.
Facing one who has turned away, approaching the presence of one who is far off,
bowing down before one who is reclining, and standing at the command of one who is present.

Likewise, when the teacher has his back turned, the disciple should sit facing him. If the teacher happens to turn around and sends him away, the disciple should go in that direction, face him, and perform what was previously prescribed. "Having approached" means having come near to one who is at a distance.
Even when [the teacher] is seated or lying down, one should approach him having first bowed, becoming humble and bending the limbs;
for it was stated previously that one should "approach" even while standing nearby in attendance, provided one has indeed bowed.
In the presence of his teacher, his bed and seat should always be low;
within the teacher's range of vision, he should not sit as he pleases.
"Low" means not elevated; it is "low" in comparison to the teacher's bed and other such items.
Because of the inclusion of the word "constantly," this applies even after the period of student life (*brahmacarya*).
And "in the sight of the teacher": wherever the teacher sees him, he must not sit as he pleases—such as by stretching out his legs or leaning his body against things.
The mention of "taking a seat" is intended to indicate all physical movements in general;
that is, one should not engage in any action at will.
One should not utter his name alone, even in his absence;
nor should one imitate his gait, speech, or gestures.

One should not utter or pronounce the name of this guru alone, even in his absence, unless it is accompanied by such titles as *upādhyāya*, *ācārya*, or *bhaṭṭa*. Nor should one imitate him— that is, one should not act like an actor— by mimicking his gait, saying, for example,
"In this manner our guru walks away."
"Speech" refers to [speaking] quickly, slowly, at a medium pace, and so forth;
"action" refers to eating in such a manner, tying a turban in such a manner, turning around in such a manner, and so on.
This prohibition against imitation applies when done with the intention of derision.
Wherever censure or even slander of the guru arises,
one should cover one's ears or depart from that place to another.

In whatever place, amidst a gathering of wicked people, there occurs the disparagement of one's teacher—the recounting of faults already committed, censure, or the attribution of non-existent defects—one should cover one’s ears with the fingers or other means and block them;
or else, one should depart from that region for another place.
From slandering others one becomes a donkey; indeed, a reviler becomes a dog; one who consumes another's property becomes a worm, and one who is envious becomes an insect.
This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) supplementary to the preceding prohibition;
therefore, it should be explained as follows:
having heard slanders, one becomes a donkey.
In the case of a dropped *lyap* suffix, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used for the object of the cause; that is, having heard the censure.
A "reviler" (*nindaka*) is one who hears the reviling; he is called a "reviler" by way of figurative usage (*upacāra*).
Likewise, a "preparer" (*saṃskartṛ*) is a slaughterer (*avaghātaka*).

From the very prohibition of hearing [the teachings], the prohibition of direct realization is established as well. One who consumes [the teacher's wealth] while living off the guru, who follows crooked paths, who is envious, and who cannot endure the prosperity and advancement of the guru, burns within.
Since these two [meanings] have not been previously established, this is an original injunction (*apūrvo vidhiḥ*).
In the case of *parivāda* and *parīvāda*, the lengthening of the vowel occurs because of the rule "after the suffix *ghañ*, [the vowel is long] diversely when not referring to a human being."
One should not pay homage to him while standing at a distance, nor when angry, nor in the presence of a woman;
and if one is seated in a vehicle or on a seat, one should descend before saluting him.
In this context, the offering of perfumes, garlands, and so forth by means of sending another is prohibited.

Since agency is equal whether an act is performed by oneself or caused to be performed by another—because the status of being an agent is traditionally attributed even to the instigator—it might follow that one could worship through another; it is with this understanding that the prohibition against worshipping through the mouth of another is established.

There is no fault if one is unable [to perform the salutation] while staying in another village, for we observe such usage as: "While the teacher is going to another village, you should salute him," or "Having gone there, he saluted him.
One should not be angry;
since anger toward the guru is impossible, even if anger arises from some other cause, the clarity of mind resulting from abandoning it at the time of worship is what is intended.
Others read "kruddham" (angry).
He was not standing near or in the presence of a woman, that is, a lover;
rather, because he was intent on honoring his guru and performing the full range of service, anyone who might fear mental distress [on the part of the guru] is thereby prohibited.
Therefore, it is explained as "of a woman.
A vehicle (*yāna*) refers to a cart (*gantrī*) and so forth;
a seat (*āsana*) refers to a stool (*pīṭhikā*), a couch (*mañca*), and so forth.
Then, having descended and stepped down, one should offer salutation.
While in the previous rule "standing on a bed or seat" rising from the seat was prescribed, by this [rule] descending is enjoined.
For rising from a couch or a seat is possible even for one who has not yet descended.
In that case, descending is not possible for one who has not risen;
therefore, since this [rule] alone establishes it, the inclusion of the word "seat" (*āsana*) in the phrase "bed and seat" (*śayyāsana*) would be purposeless.
It is not purposeless.

If the disciple perceives that the teacher has arrived from the western direction while he himself is facing away, then, remaining on his seat, he should turn around in haste and rise up facing him; however, he should not rise and then turn back toward him. For in that case, the act of turning to face him would be interrupted by the act of rising, and consequently, the teacher might become angry.
Even when one who was previously turned away rises, the teacher should think: "He has not risen for my sake; his rising was caused by some other circumstance.
Therefore, the mention of the seat is meaningful in both cases.
One should not sit with one's teacher either upwind or downwind;
nor should one say anything at all in a place where the teacher cannot hear.

When the wind comes from the direction where the teacher is situated toward the place of the pupil, or from the pupil's place toward the teacher's place, those are respectively "against the wind" (*prativāta*) and "with the wind" (*anuvāta*). One should not sit with the teacher in either of these positions— one against the wind and the other with the wind— but rather, one should position oneself so as to be served by a crosswind relative to the teacher.
In that place where there is no hearing—that is, in a place where one cannot be overheard—one should not mention anything concerning the teacher, whether it pertains to himself or to others.
Where the teacher does not hear clearly, yet perceives through the movement of the lips and so forth that this person is conversing with someone related to him, one should not mention that either.
One may sit together with one's teacher on vehicles drawn by oxen, horses, or camels, on palanquins, on stone slabs, on mats, and on rocks, wooden planks, or boats.
The word *yāna* (vehicle) is connected with each [term] individually. That which is stated as a vehicle by means of cows, horses, and camels is "cow-horse-camel-vehicle" (*go'śvoṣṭrayāna*).
Just as in the case of *dadhighaṭa* ("curd-pot") and similar compounds, there is an elision of the word *yukta* ("yoked to" or "connected with").
However, there is no mounting upon items such as the back of a horse when they are used alone.
If the word "vehicle" (*yāna*) were understood as being independent [of its specific context], then perhaps permission would be granted;
yet, from established practice (*samācāra*), occasional permission is observed.
On the ground level of a palace, an upper story, or similar structures, sitting together is established as being just like on the ground floor of an ordinary house.
A *prastara* is a spread made by scattering grasses such as *darbha*;
a *kaṭa*, however, is well known as being made from reeds, *vīraṇa* grass, and so forth.
A stone is one found on a mountain peak or elsewhere;
a plank is a wooden seat such as a boat-cloth and so forth;
a boat is a vessel for crossing over water.
By this, it is also established in the case of a jar and so forth.
When the teacher’s teacher is present, one should behave toward him as toward one's own teacher;
and without being permitted by one's teacher, one should not pay homage to one's own teachers.
The conduct toward a guru has been described; now it is extended by analogy to other cases.
Since this entire [section] pertains to the duties of Vedic study, "guru" here should be understood as the *ācārya*.
When that person's own guru is present, one must behave toward him as one would toward a guru.

Since he is "nearby," he need not go to his [own] home for the purpose of salutation and so forth. While residing in the teacher's house, if he has not been dismissed—that is, not permitted—by the teacher, he should not go to salute his own elders, such as his mother and father. However, when his own elders come to him while he is staying in the teacher's house, he need not wait for the teacher's permission to salute them. Why is this? Because the mother and father are objects of absolute reverence.
Even for one engaged in saluting paternal uncles, maternal uncles, and others, there is no obstacle whatsoever to the practice of venerating elders;
indeed, all this effort is solely for the purpose of propitiation.
Regarding the question of what the order of salutation should be when mother, father, and teacher are present together, it has been stated that the mother is the greatest of all.
However, there is an option between the father and the teacher;
for since the teacher's dignity is ordained through the superimposition of the status of "father," therefore the father is superior.
And since it has been stated that "the father who imparts the Veda is more venerable," therefore [the father] is the teacher;
hence, this is an option.
This same constant conduct is required toward teachers of knowledge, toward one's own parents,
and toward those who forbid unrighteousness as well as those who give beneficial instruction.
This is also an extended application (*atideśa*).
Teachers other than the *ācārya*, such as the *upādhyāya* and others, are "teachers of knowledge" (*vidyāguru*).
One should behave toward them in exactly the same manner, performing duties such as those beginning with "the body itself," and so forth.
"Among those of one's own birth," such as elder brothers, paternal uncles, and so forth,
"constant conduct" means the conduct due to a guru. However, for teachers of knowledge, with the exception of the *ācārya*, it lasts only as long as the acquisition of that knowledge.
Even when friends forbid one from unrighteous acts— such as improper conduct or adultery— if,
due to an internal inclination toward such acts, one desires to perform them, a friend or similar person should restrain that friend from such misdeeds even by seizing him by the hair.
Therefore, one should behave toward such a person, even if they are of equal or inferior age, as one would toward a teacher.
Or rather, those who teach what is beneficial in the form of a method, free from books,
are called "noble ones" (abhijana) because they are teachers of what is beneficial.
One should always behave toward those who are superior as one does toward a guru—
toward the son of a guru, toward a teacher, and toward the guru’s own kinsmen.

"Superiors" (*śreyāṃsaḥ*) are those who possess excellence in wealth, age, learning, and so forth, relative to oneself. Toward them, one should always maintain the conduct due to a teacher (*guru*) as far as possible, such as salutation, rising from one's seat, and so on.
In this context, many words have already been explained.
In their case, the application [of the rule] does not incur fault due to the force of the context;
for one need only say "in matters of welfare," and the phrase "like a guru" is implied.
The phrase "the mode of life" (*vṛtti*) and so forth is already established.
All of this is to be inferred by oneself throughout this entire treatise;
likewise regarding the teacher’s son and the preceptor.
By the mention of the "teacher" (ācārya), the status of being an instructor is indicated.
If the teacher is absent and his son teaches for a few days, then one's conduct toward him should be as toward the teacher.
There is an alternative reading: "toward the teacher’s sons and likewise toward noble men."
The word "ārya" denotes one who possesses virtuous qualities or belongs to the Brāhmaṇa caste,
as seen in the usage, "An Ārya is superior to a Śūdra.
Furthermore, this rule of conduct is not prescribed for every son of a teacher.
"And likewise toward one's own kinsmen of the teacher.
The inclusion of the word "own" (sva-) is for the purpose of referring to those belonging to the teacher's lineage;
here, the mere fact of being related to the teacher's lineage is the cause [for such conduct], and neither age nor learning is taken into account.
Whether he be a child, of equal age, or a pupil, the son of a teacher who teaches during a sacrificial rite deserves honor just like the teacher himself.

For those who do not read [the word *ācārya*] in the previous rule as a qualification of the teacher’s son (*guruputra*), it would follow that the conduct due to a teacher should apply toward any person of the same caste who is virtuous and teaches; this specific rule establishes an exception to that.
A teacher’s son deserves honor and worship like a teacher only while he is teaching, not when he is not teaching.
But surely, since the conduct due to a teacher is occasioned by the acquisition of knowledge, it would already apply to the teacher’s son while he is teaching, just as it does to the teacher?

Since this [subsistence] is established even for one who is younger than a Brahmin by virtue of the illustration of the "child-Brahmin" (śaiśava-brāhmaṇa), the phrase "a child or one of equal age" need not have been stated for that purpose either.
True;
however, this mode of life is prescribed even for one who is not an Ācārya, namely, one who teaches the Veda or a portion of the Veda.

But this person is not a *grāhaka* (one who causes one to grasp); he merely teaches for a few days or for a portion of a day. Therefore, since he is neither an *ācārya* nor an *upādhyāya*, this rule is prescribed for one who has not [otherwise] attained that status. From this very statement, it is understood that for another teacher—such as one whose mantras are incomplete—one should not perform the full range of duties toward a guru.
Furthermore, for those who read the word *ācārya* in the preceding [text], this is restated for the sake of what follows.
And he will state "and the removal [of hair]" (utsādanaṃ ca). Or [it refers to] a disciple at a sacrificial rite (yajñakarmaṇi). The mention of "sacrificial rite" is for the sake of illustration.

Even if [the teacher] has taught only a certain limb—whether a portion of the Veda consisting of the Mantra section or some part of the Brāhmaṇa section—he is nevertheless to be honored like a guru, provided he is the son of a guru.
Therefore, it has been stated that if one learns some branch of knowledge from him in this manner, one must behave toward him as toward a guru; for such is the purpose of this introductory statement.

As for those who explain that by the word "teaching" (*adhyāpayan*) the capacity to teach is indicated—thinking that if one is capable of teaching, he may teach or he may not; provided he has mastered the Veda, he is to be regarded like a guru—their explanation is indeed literal. However, the suffix *śatṛ* has the sense of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), according to the rule: "The suffix *śatṛ* [is used] in the sense of a characteristic or a cause of an action.
And here, the action mentioned is that he deserves respect as a guru.
One should not perform the massaging of the limbs, the bathing,
or the eating of the leftovers for the teacher’s son, nor should one wash his feet.
One should not perform the rubbing or massaging of one who has been anointed with oil; nor should one perform the washing or rinsing of the feet for the teacher’s son.
Precisely because of this prohibition, even though it is not explicitly stated, it is understood that this [behavior] should be performed toward a teacher.

However, when the teacher’s son himself becomes the teacher—by virtue of being suitable for teaching the entire Veda—then there exists, on account of his own status, the practice of eating his leftovers and so forth;
that is not prohibited by this [rule].
By this, there is a prohibition of that which is extended by analogy (ātideśika), but not of that which is directly taught (aupadeśika).
The wives of one's gurus who are of the same caste (varṇa) should be honored like the gurus themselves;
however, those who are of a different caste should be honored by rising from one's seat and by salutation.
The wives of the guru are the guru’s consorts;
they are of the same caste (*savarṇāḥ*), meaning they belong to the same social class.
They are to be honored like the guru himself through such acts as carrying out his commands.
"But for those of a different caste, [one should show respect] solely through rising to meet them and saluting them.
Because of the plural number [in "rising and saluting"], the sense of "and so forth" (*ādi*) is included here;
by that, [qualities such as] being pleasant and beneficial, as well as [the rules regarding] movement and non-imitation, are also extended [to this case].
Anointing, bathing, massaging the limbs,
and the dressing of the hair— these should not be performed by the wife of one's teacher.
Anointing (*abhyañjana*) is the smearing of the hair and body with clarified butter, oil, and so forth.
Rubbing (*udvartana*) is the massaging of the limbs;
because it serves a similar purpose, washing the feet is also included.
In every respect, any kind of attendance that is to be accomplished through physical contact is entirely prohibited;

and he will state the reason later, saying, "This is the nature of women. Furthermore, the grooming of the hair refers to the arranging and styling of it, as well as the parting of the hair with saffron, vermilion, and other substances.
This has been stated for the sake of illustration;
by this, even the adorning of the body, such as the anointing with sandalwood paste, is prohibited.
A young wife of the guru, however, should not be saluted by touching her feet here by one who has completed twenty years of age and understands virtues and faults.
"By one who has completed twenty years" means by a youth.
For a child up to sixteen years of age, there is no offense.
One who has completed twenty years is described in this manner.
This time is intended to mark the emergence of youth; for this very reason, it says "by one who discerns virtues and faults.
Here, "virtues and faults" refer to the pleasure and pain born of desire, or—when directed toward women—to the qualities of beautiful form and ugly form, or to steadfastness and fickleness.
In every respect, the number of tantras is twenty.
This is the very nature of women: the corruption of men in this world. Therefore, the wise do not become negligent regarding women for the sake of their own welfare.
This is the nature of women: that they cause men to fall from their fortitude;
for through association, women lead men away from their vows.
Therefore, for this very reason, they do not become negligent.
They avoid women from afar;
negligence consists in making physical contact and so forth.
This is the inherent nature of things: that when a young woman is touched, she produces a mental agitation caused by desire.
In that regard, even mental agitation is forbidden; let alone other forms of passionate involvement in vulgar conduct—such as with women, who are *pramadā*.
For in this world, women are indeed capable of leading astray both the ignorant man and even the wise man who has fallen under the sway of desire and anger.

Nor should it be thought that because one’s senses have long been restrained, there is no fault for one who knows that even looking upon the wife of a guru with a wicked mind is an extremely grave sin, while touching her feet and so forth is not.
For both he who recognizes such faults and he who recognizes none at all are equal regarding women;
since in this matter, learning is of no avail.

Women are capable of leading—meaning, bringing to—a person who is under the sway of desire and anger onto every wrong path, an improper course, and an object of sense that is contrary to worldly conduct and sacred scriptures;
for the meaning is that he is one who becomes bound by desire and anger.
Furthermore, this is intended as an illustration of various types of calamities.

Excepting one who is extremely childish, one who is extremely aged, or one who has attained the excellence of yoga—by whom the human qualities of cyclic existence have been utterly severed without remainder—there is no man whatsoever who is not drawn by women, just as iron is attracted by a magnet.

Nor does this power belong to the women themselves; rather, it is due to the very nature of things that the minds of men are agitated upon seeing young women, especially those who are celibate students.
One should not sit in seclusion with one's mother, sister, or daughter;
for the powerful collection of the senses drags away even a wise man.
Therefore, one should not sit in a secluded place, such as a deserted or empty house; nor should one, free from apprehension, engage in touching the limbs or similar acts.
For the aggregate of the sense-faculties is exceedingly fickle; it drags away, carries off, and renders even a wise person—one whose self is restrained by the scriptures—subject to its control.
However, on this earth, a young man should, according to the prescribed rule, perform a salutation to the wives of his elders who are themselves young, saying, "I am so-and-so."
The word "kāmam" indicates a lack of approval;
this is connected with what follows, namely, "clasping the feet after one has been away from home.
However, the prostration at the feet on the ground is indeed permitted.
This rule applies when a young man [meets] young women, or when two youths [meet each other].
However, if he is a child or a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), and she is an elderly woman or the wife of a teacher, then the clasping of her feet (*pādopasaṃgrahaṇa*) is not prohibited.
The phrase "I am so-and-so" is a restatement of the rule previously mentioned.
"According to the rule" means with the hands separated.
Having returned from a journey, one should clasp the feet of the teacher’s wives every day and offer salutations,
keeping in mind the dharma of the virtuous.
Upon returning from a journey, he should grasp [the teacher's] feet, touching the left with his left hand and so forth; this should be done every day, day after day,
and the salutation should be performed by prostrating on the ground.
Reflecting that "this is the duty and the conduct of the virtuous and the learned," he [should act].
Just as a man obtains water by digging with a spade,
so too does one who is intent on service obtain knowledge residing in the teacher.
This is the fruit of the entire procedure of service (*śuśrūṣā*);
it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for the injunction regarding Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*), by means of propitiating the teacher.

Just as a certain man, digging the earth with a spade or a hoe, obtains water without difficulty, so too does this person, intent on serving the teacher and devoted to attending upon him, acquire the knowledge residing in the teacher.
He may be shaven-headed, or he may have matted hair, or he may have a single lock of hair tied in a topknot;
the sun should never set or rise while he is still in a village.
He should have his hair shaved entirely, becoming *muṇḍa*;
or he may be *jaṭila*.
*Jaṭā* refers to locks of hair that are extremely matted together; one who possesses such is *jaṭila*.
"Having a topknot-tuft" means one whose tuft (*śikhā*) is itself a matted lock (*jaṭā*);

he should maintain his tuft in the form of a matted lock. Alternatively, he may be shaven (*muṇḍa*), as prescribed for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice. Furthermore, he should act in such a way that while staying in a village, the sun does not set behind him—that is, it does not go down [while he is there].
The mention of "village" is intended to indicate the "town" as well.
He should contemplate the time of sunset while in the forest;
likewise, he should act so that the sun does not rise upon him in the village, just as it happens for a *brahmacārin* staying in the forest. Even at sunrise, he should conduct himself in this manner.
[The text refers to] "this" student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) under discussion.
Others, however, explain that the word *grāma* refers to "village-like" behaviors such as sleeping and so forth, and that [the sun] should not set while he is engaged in them;
for this reason, the author will later say "while he is lying down."
Therefore, this prohibition of sleeping during the two twilights does not apply to staying in the forest at that time;
for a young student might be afraid.
However, Gautama has stated that the practice of performing the twilight prayers outside [the village] begins after the *godāna* ceremony.
And the Godāna vow is performed in the sixteenth year; having reached that age, he is able to perform the twilight devotions in the forest.
If the sun should rise while he is sleeping out of his own volition,
or if it should set while he is unaware of it, he shall fast for the day while reciting [the sacred texts].
In this case, one should perform the following expiation:
if the sun should rise while a religious student (brahmacārin) is lying down under the sway of sleep, it would cause him to incur the fault of being pervaded by its own rising.
The term *abhi* is used here as a *karmapravacanīya* according to the rule *abhir abhāge*.

Then, regarding the second [case], "toward one who is lying down" means toward one who has fallen asleep in such a manner; or if [the sun] should rise during the time of sleep, as characterized by being thus asleep,
one should fast for the day while reciting [the mantra].

Some say that if the morning [Sāvitrī] is missed, the day is for recitation and fasting, while the meal is taken at night; but if the evening [Sāvitrī] is missed, the night is for recitation and fasting, while the meal is taken in the morning.
The word "day" is used for the sake of illustration.
They also cite the statement of Gautama: "One should stand during the day without eating, and after sunset, one should spend the night reciting the Sāvitrī."
That is incorrect;
in both cases, it is proper that the expiation (prāyaścitta) occurs during the day alone, because there is no evidence that the word "day" (dina) is intended merely for illustration.
For this [word], being dependent on that [context], does not convey its own primary meaning.
And this is independent [of time];
therefore, an option is appropriate.
In that regard, he for whom no illness arises while staying awake the entire night shall recite at night; another, however, shall do so only by day.
And the recitation (japa) is of the Sāvitrī alone, according to the statement of Gautama.
Now, one might ask: how is Gautama to be accepted as an authority in this matter?
It is said in reply:
This sentence is dependent [on further specification] because that which is to be recited has not been indicated;
when such dependence exists, the understanding of a specific detail is appropriate based on another scriptural passage (*śruti*).
However, in this case, there is an indication of time.
Gautama does not require a waiting period for another time, as there is no interval to be expected.
Alternatively, since an expiation is prescribed for the passing of the twilight [prayer], the recitation of the Sāvitrī is already established.
And it is logical that there is nothing superior to the Sāvitrī.
[It is] by way of acting according to one's desire;
that is, he who sleeps at the time of twilight knowing [it to be so],
or through lack of awareness.
Lack of awareness (*avijñāna*) means not realizing that "this is the time for the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) for one who has been asleep for a long time.
This is what is meant:
this very same expiation applies to both transgressions committed intentionally and those caused by negligence.
Furthermore, for one who transgresses the twilight prayers that neither rise nor set [i.e., the morning and evening *saṃdhyā*], the penance is fasting and the omission of obligatory rites.
Alternatively, for one who transgresses the scriptures through acting according to his own will, that itself constitutes ignorance.
For he who goes to sleep while the sun is setting, or wakes up while the sun is rising,
and fails to perform the penance, shall be joined with great sin.
This is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) concerning the previously mentioned rule for penance:
"corrupted by the setting" means one who has set while the sun is still visible; likewise, "corrupted by the rising" [means one who has risen while the sun is still visible].
If one does not perform the previously mentioned expiation,
then one becomes bound by great sin, not by a small one;
that which is called "unseen sin" (adṛṣṭapāpa) is the cause for experiencing sufferings such as those in hell.
Having sipped water and being purified, he should always, with a concentrated mind, attend to both twilights in a clean place, reciting the prayers to be recited according to the rule.
Thus, there is a great fault in the rising and setting [of the sun].
Therefore, having sipped water (ācamya), being pure, intent, and composed— having removed mental distraction and the distraction caused by those actions—
one should mutter the prayer to be muttered (*japya*) known as the *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī* in a clean place.
One should worship during both twilights;
for it is precisely these two twilights that are to be worshipped here.
And "worship" (upāsana) in this context refers to a particular state of mind.
Alternatively, one should worship the blessed Savitṛ at both twilights;
for the mantra has him as its deity, and therefore one should worship him alone. With all mental constructs withdrawn, one should become single-mindedly focused upon him.
This is a restatement (anuvāda) of the injunction previously mentioned;
only meditation (upāsana) is what is to be enjoined.
Others, however, say that this verse is for the purpose of enjoining [the conditions] such as "in a clean place" (śucau deśe).
This is a redundancy on their part;
for it has already been enjoined that "every action that is to be performed must be done by one who is pure," and when there is contact with an impure place, how can there be purity?
If a woman or a person of lower status should perform any virtuous act, one should practice all of that with diligence; furthermore, one should do whatever brings the mind joy.
If a woman is the wife of a teacher, or if one is a junior or younger relative,
having received instruction from the teacher, one should practice the three aims of life beginning with dharma that are superior; all of that one should practice.
For it is possible that both of them have acquired knowledge of this through contact with their teacher.
A *śūdra* who serves as a teacher’s attendant is a junior;

if he should instruct [the student] thus: "The anus and the penis are washed with clay and water; wash your hands thoroughly; you have forgotten the sequence of clay and water; your own teacher was previously seen by me many times while I was giving him water for the washing of the anus; he first performs purification with water and then with clays"—if he should instruct in such a manner, being endowed with such conduct, he may do so.
Likewise, the teacher’s wife should instruct him in the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
He should perform all of that with diligence and faith;
he must not despise it by thinking, "This is practiced by women and Śūdras."
The phrase "one should practice" (samācaret) here intends instruction preceded by actual practice;
for it will be said later: "Dharma, purity, and things to be accepted from all sources.
It may even happen that the teacher himself commands: "O Brāhmaṇī, cause this one who stands in the place of a son to sip water according to the prescribed rule."
And one should tell him: "For the sake of purifying urine and feces, earth and water must be applied.
In that regard, his word is to be followed: "Take the earth in this manner," or "Wash with water in this manner.
Alternatively, the practice of purifying iron, stones, water, and so forth, as observed by women and Śūdras in the house of a teacher (guru), is to be accepted as authoritative.

This verse is appropriate for the purpose of establishing the authority of those customs (ācāra) related to women and Śūdras that have been thus far described. But is it not the case that the authority of all customs related to those who do not know the Veda is already established?
This has not been stated.
For not even the slightest practice of those who do not know the Veda can be authoritative.
If, however, there is a basis for its authority in a connection with those who know the Veda, then that alone is the authority; what is the use of mentioning women?
Moreover, in such matters, the authority of the practices of women and Śūdras is not intended.
For if that were the case, he would have stated it precisely in the section concerning the definition of validity (*prāmāṇya*).
Therefore, the ultimate point is that this introductory discussion (*upodghāta*) is for the purpose of defining the term *śreyaḥ* (the highest good).
Alternatively, this is a restatement of the validity of the Teacher’s words.
Even that which a woman or a Śūdra might say is fit to be performed, how much more so that which is taught by a teacher?
And as for the matter where his mind would find delight and satisfaction—
that too has been explained under the rule "one's own satisfaction" (Ātmatuṣṭi).
In every respect, this verse does not have much purpose.

It is said that the good consists of dharma and artha, or of kāma and artha, or even of dharma alone; or it may be that artha alone is the highest good in this world—such is the established doctrine regarding the three aims of life.

"That which is praiseworthy, that which, when practiced, does not harm one in this world or the next, and that which is called the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) in the world—what indeed is that? Thus he explains, acting as a friend.
This matter is not rooted in the Veda, nor is it a definition of word-meanings like the terms "teacher" (*ācārya*) and so forth.
Rather, every person who desires the highest good engages in action [for its sake].
In this regard, it is said: "This is the highest good; for its sake, effort must be exerted.
Therein, he first sets forth the opinions of others: according to some, dharma and artha constitute the highest good.
Dharma consists of the injunctions and prohibitions prescribed by the scriptures;
artha consists of cattle, land, gold, and so forth.
This alone is the highest good (śreyas), because human happiness is dependent upon it.
Another view holds that there are two aims: desire (*kāma*) and wealth (*artha*).
Desire is indeed the primary aim of human life, for pleasure is the highest good; wealth, too, is an aim because it is a means to that [pleasure].

For thus the Cārvākas say: sensual pleasure alone is the sole human aim; wealth is its means; and as for dharma, even if it exists, dharma itself is superior to all, because everything has its root in it.
And it is said: "From dharma come both wealth and pleasure."
"Only wealth," say the merchants who live by trade;
but the established conclusion is that it is the three aims of life (*trivarga*).
Therefore, even wealth and pleasure should be pursued provided they do not conflict with dharma, but never when they do so conflict.
And so Gautama says: "One should not let the forenoon, midday, or afternoon pass fruitlessly; one should devote them to dharma, artha, and kāma according to one's ability.
The group consisting of these three is the *trivarga*;
this term is conventionally established for the three when they are combined.
The teacher, the father, the mother, and an elder brother must not be treated with contempt even by one who is distressed, especially by a Brāhmaṇa.

No one else whatsoever should be disregarded, but these [brahmins] especially so; the meaning is that there is a greater penance required in this case. Even by one who is *ārta*, i.e., afflicted by them.

"Insult" (avamāna) means contempt; it consists of the failure to offer the honor that is due, as well as humiliation, which is termed disrespect. The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is for the sake of completing the meter.
The teacher is the embodiment of Brahmā; the father is the embodiment of Prajāpati;
the mother is indeed the embodiment of the Earth; and one's own brother is the embodiment of oneself.
This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) concerning the preceding [verse]:
that which is the Supreme Brahman, well-known from the Vedānta Upaniṣads—of that, the teacher is the form, the body;
"form" (mūrti) is used here in the sense of being like a physical form.
Prajāpati Hiraṇyagarbha is his father;
this very earth is his mother, by virtue of the common quality of being able to bear a burden. And heaven is his own uterine brother—this is praise for the self, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
All these, being forms of deities endowed with greatness, destroy when they are insulted, and when propitiated, they unite one with desired objects;
thus, teachers and others are praised as being equal to them.
The suffering that parents endure for the birth of human beings cannot be repaid, even in a hundred years.
This is another praise by way of restating the actual facts:
both the mother and the father undergo suffering for their children from conception until the tenth year;
the mother's suffering consists in bearing the fetus.
Childbirth is the taking of life for women;
and the effort of concealing what has been born is suffering.
This is personally experienced by everyone.
[This applies] even for the father, beginning from the initiation ceremony (upanayana) until the explanation of the meaning of the Vedas.
Here, by the word "origin" (saṃbhava), the period from conception until death is meant.
For that [conception] does not bring affliction; rather, it is these rites occurring at subsequent times that do so, for they are accomplished through hardship.
No repayment, no discharge of debt, and no equal return for that kindness can be made for even many hundreds of lifetimes, let alone in a single birth;
yet, it is said that the repayment toward one's mother and father is achieved through the giving of incalculable wealth or by rescuing them from great calamity.
One should always do what is pleasing to those two and to the teacher at all times;
for when these three are satisfied, all ascetic merit is fully accomplished.

Therefore, one should always, for as long as life lasts, do whatever is pleasing to those two—mother and father—and to the teacher; one should not consider oneself finished by doing it once, twice, or thrice.

When those three—the teacher and the others—are satisfied and propitiated through devotion, the fruit that is obtained by performing all forms of austerity, such as the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances, for many groups of years, is obtained simply from their satisfaction.
Service to these three is said to be the highest austerity;
one should not practice any other duty without being authorized by them.
How, then, can the fruit of austerity be obtained through service to one's mother and others without [actual] austerity?
Because this is the supreme austerity of all: the serving of their feet.

Without being permitted by them, a young student might practice another form of dharma that contradicts such service—such as bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and so forth, or vows and fasts that wither the body and cause mental distress to them.
Permission must also be obtained even for the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice,
because a prohibition against contempt has been established;
for in the case of great undertakings that are to be accomplished through the expenditure of much wealth and effort, those who are faltering might become objects of contempt.
However, in the performance of obligatory rites (nityakarman), permission is not beneficial.
For those three worlds are indeed these three stages of life;
those three Vedas are indeed these, and those three sacrificial fires are said to be these.
This is stated because of the non-difference between cause and effect.
Because they are the cause for attaining the three worlds, they themselves are called the "three worlds.
And these same three are the other three stages of life (*āśrama*) beyond the first stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*).
The fruit that is obtained through the three stages of life beginning with the householder's stage is obtained by those three when they are satisfied;
for they are themselves the three Vedas, since their fruit is equal to the recitation of the three Vedas,
and they are themselves the three sacred fires.
Because the fruit of performing rites accomplished by fire is obtained through service to him,
this too is merely a form of praise.
The father is indeed the Gārhapatya fire, the mother is remembered as the Dakṣiṇa fire, and the teacher is the Āhavanīya fire;
this triad of fires is most venerable.

This designation of the father and others as the *gārhapatya* fire and so forth is based on a certain commonality. The *tretā* consisting of fires—that is, the *tretā* of the consecrated fires—is the weightier one, which yields great fruit.
The etymological derivation of the word *tretā* is: "that which has gone (*itā*) for the purpose of protection (*trāṇa*), having been attained (*prāptā*) for the sake of protection."
By being heedful in these three, a householder shall conquer the three worlds;
shining with his own body, he rejoices in heaven like a god.
By being heedful toward these and not failing in their propitiation,
and likewise through such propitiation, a householder would conquer the three worlds, take possession of them, and attain sovereignty over them.
For the service rendered by a son who is in the stage of a householder is of benefit to his father and others;
for at that time, they have become old.
[The son shines] blazing, beautiful, or manifesting by his own splendor alone.
Like a god, like the sun, he rejoices in the heavenly world.
By devotion to one's mother one attains this world; by devotion to one's father, the middle world;
and by service to one's teacher, one likewise attains the world of Brahmā.
This world is the earth;
because it bears weight, the mother is equal to the earth. Through devotion to the father, the intermediate world, the atmosphere, [is equal to the father].
Prajāpati is said to be the father;
and according to the etymologists (nairukta), Prajāpati occupies the middle station.
For he is either the protector (pātā) or the guardian (pālayitā) of living beings through the act of raining.
The world of Brahmā, the world of Āditya; the instruction is that "Āditya is Brahman. "World" (loka) means a specific place; he partakes of it, that is, he attains it.
These are merely explanatory passages (arthavāda);
one should not be dogmatically attached to them.
Furthermore, one who desires worldly sovereignty has no authority over its propitiation.
This is not an optional injunction;
rather, the status of being a father is the sole occasion here, and failure to perform it constitutes a transgression of the sacred law.
All duties are honored by him by whom these three are honored;
but for him by whom these are not honored, all ritual actions are fruitless.
"Respected" means honored.
By the term "respected," one's intent to reciprocate is indicated;
for whoever is respected strives to repay that kindness with satisfaction.
Alternatively, "respectful" (ādṛta) means "completely satisfied.
Since it is impossible to be completely satisfied with the infinity of Dharma, this indicates an eagerness to bestow the fruit [of the ritual].
All his actions quickly become granters of results.

For one by whom these three are honored and fully satisfied through service, all actions—meaning all rites prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti—are fruitful; however, whatever auspicious deed is performed with a desire for results when they have not been propitiated, all of that is fruitless.
All actions refers to all ritual acts based on the revealed and traditional scriptures.
This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). For the rule of propitiation is for the sake of human welfare;
by transgressing it, a person incurs demerit and is obstructed from enjoying the desired fruits, even when those fruits have been acquired through karma.
Therefore it is said: "All his actions are fruitless."
As long as those three live, he should not serve anyone else;
he should constantly perform service toward them alone, devoted to their pleasure and welfare.
The meaning of this verse has been explained:
it was stated that one should not perform any other action, whether visible or invisible, without their permission;
one should always practice service toward them alone.
He is devoted to what is pleasant and beneficial.
That which is both pleasant and beneficial is as follows:
that which causes delight is pleasant, and that which provides protection is beneficial.
Whatever one performs for the sake of the next world without causing them distress,
that one should announce to them through thought, word, and deed.
That whose fruit is enjoyed in another world, in a future birth, is called *pāratrya*;
this is a Vedic (Chāndasa) form.
Without contradicting the service [to his elders], whatever other duty he may perform, he should report each of those to them; that is, he should make them aware of them.
The inclusion of the term "without causing obstruction" was made for this purpose:
one should not cause those who are opposed to grant permission in such cases.
This is intended to prevent a person of upright nature from granting permission when requested, even while disregarding the harm it would cause to himself or others.
By means of thought, speech, and action;
the offering is not for the sake of some unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha), but rather one should demonstrate through action exactly what kind of permission has been granted.
Alternatively, the connection should be made in this way:
Whatever one may perform for the sake of the next world through thought, word, or deed, all that one should offer to them.
For a person’s duty is indeed completed within these three;
this is the supreme dharma directly perceived, while any other is called a secondary dharma (upadharma).
The word *iti* signifies completion and conveys totality.
Whatever duty must be performed by a person, and whatever human goal (*puruṣārtha*) there may be—when these [deities] are propitiated, that [duty] is completed and becomes fully accomplished.
This is the supreme and most excellent *dharma*, by virtue of its directness.
Furthermore, other subsidiary duties (*upadharma*) such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice function as attendants (*pratihāra*), not like the king himself; this is the praise [of the king].

[The following] is the prohibition against showing contempt, the doing of what is pleasing and beneficial, the non-performance of that which is contrary to his interests even if it ought to be done, and likewise the non-performance of that which is not contrary but has not been authorized.
The remaining collection of verses is *arthavāda* (explanatory praise).
One who possesses faith should acquire auspicious knowledge even from a lowly person; one should accept the supreme Dharma even from an outcaste, and a jewel of a woman even from a base family.

A disciple who is faithful—whose inner self is embraced by a sense of conviction—and who is diligent, may learn from even a person of inferior birth (*avarāt*) that auspicious knowledge, which is the science of logic such as the *Nyāya-śāstra* and so forth; or else, that which is merely beautiful, adorned with the pure sciences of poetry, dramaturgy (*Bharata*), and the like, or the science of mantras (*mantra-vidyā*) which is not conducive to *dharma*. He should learn it from such a person.

However, "auspicious knowledge" here should not be understood as Vedic knowledge; for while there will be a rule permitting it in times of distress (*āpad*), it is certainly not desired in the absence of distress.
But as for that which is impure—whether it be the illusion of Śambhu, sorcery, trickery, and so forth—that is never [to be practiced].
Furthermore, the "last" refers even to a Cāṇḍāla; and "dharma" beyond even that is that which is other than the Veda and the Smṛtis, namely, worldly (laukika) dharma.
The word *dharma* is also used in the sense of "established order" (*vyavasthā*).

Even if a *caṇḍāla* were to say, "This is the law here," meaning, "Do not stay long in this place, nor bathe in this water; this is the custom of the villagers here, or a boundary established by the king," one should not think, "I must follow the teacher's word; fie on this wretched *caṇḍāla* who commands me!
Nor should one entertain the thought that the highest dharma is the knowledge of the reality of Brahman.
For it is not possible for those such as Caṇḍālas to possess that thorough knowledge, because they lack the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas;
nor can it be obtained from any other source,
for there is no instruction regarding Brahman comparable to the syllables of a mantra for scorpions.
Like a "jewel among women" (*strīratna*);
or, it may be analyzed as "she who is both a woman and a jewel.
This follows either the rule "that which is compared [is placed first] with *vyāghra* and so forth," or the rule "the qualifier [is placed first] with the qualified."
When any superior object whatsoever is called a "jewel" (*ratna*), then [the comparison] is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
But if only emeralds, rubies, and so forth are denoted by the word "jewel," while its application elsewhere occurs due to a commonality of excellence, then it is a simile (*upamita*).

A woman who possesses an excellence of luster, form, and grace, or who possesses auspicious marks such as grain, much wealth, and sons, may be brought from even a low family or one deficient in ritual acts.
This is the introductory context for the rule "from one who is not a Brahmin," though it is demonstrated by way of an impossibility.
Nectar should be taken even from poison, a well-spoken word even from a child,
virtuous conduct even from an enemy, and gold even from filth.
The preceding passage is a supplement to the injunction that "in times of distress, one may study even from a non-Brahmin.
By this, a common worldly saying is used as an illustration;
for thus do people in the world say: "That which is good should be accepted even from what is bad."
Even in poison, that which is nectar must certainly be accepted, just as a swan takes milk from water.
This was said with reference to certain elixirs (*rasāyana*) which contain poison.
Even if a child should suddenly utter some well-spoken word or an auspicious blessing at the start of a journey or similar occasion, that too is to be accepted.

The conduct of even enemies and others that is practiced by the virtuous constitutes the behavior of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*). It should not be rejected on the grounds that it was performed by someone who is hateful;
this is a very well-known illustration: gold is [pure] even from impurity.
Just as these [qualities] are perceived even when based on what is non-existent, so too is the study [of the Veda] from one who is not a Brahmin.
Women, jewels, as well as knowledge, dharma, purity, eloquent speech, and various arts— these are to be accepted from everyone.
Just as gems and jewels, even when acquired from Śambaras, Pulindas, and others, are pure, so too are sciences and the like. Furthermore,
crafts such as the cutting of variegated leaves— which are non-defective and not censurable— such as the cleaning of clothes, the dyeing of cloth, and weaving,
are to be accepted and adopted by those possessed of resolute and extreme fortitude, regardless of the specific caste of the person from whom they are taken.
Because there are many such statements as "even from poison, nectar [is obtained]," all these are *arthavādas* (explanatory passages) due to their being of a uniform character.
In times of distress, study from one who is not a Brahmin is prescribed;
likewise, following and serving the teacher must continue for as long as the study lasts.
But this is the rule here:
"distress" refers to the state of being a teacher of Brahmins;
the time of distress is "the time of distress."
Since the meaning "in times of distress" (*āpad*) is already established, the inclusion of the word "time" (*kāla*) is for the purpose of completing the meter.
There is an alternative reading: *āpatkalpa*.
*Kalpa* means "arrangement" (*kalpana*); thus, these [rules] are prescribed and taught as the arrangement to be followed in times of distress.

If the teacher, having commenced instruction, should leave for another country—either due to a penance or some other cause—and abandon the pupil, and if no other Brāhmaṇa teacher can be found in that region; and if, because of the pupil's childhood, traveling to a distant land is impossible, then he may study from a non-Brāhmaṇa, namely a Kṣatriya, or in his absence, from a Vaiśya. Since the context concerns the Veda as a whole, the term "Veda" is specifically enjoined here.

Although here the word *abrāhmaṇa* denotes the human nature residing in the three castes other than the Brāhmaṇa caste, nevertheless, the Śūdra is not included here, because he lacks the qualification for teaching.
Teaching presupposes study;
yet, if one were to transgress the scriptures, it is possible even for a Śūdra to have studied the Veda, just as it is possible for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas to be teachers.
That too is not the case;
for it is traditionally taught that the dissolution of the body occurs upon its retention.
Therefore, because of the severity of the punishment, this act is inferred to be a great misdeed.

Through the habitual practice of censurable acts and through association with such persons, a student (*brahmacārin*) would incur extreme corruption. If it is argued that because teaching is prohibited for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, they must incur an equal degree of fault [as a Brāhmaṇa], there is a distinction here:
where both the punishment and the penance are heavy, there the fault is great; but where they are light, the fault is small.
Furthermore, there are no great punishments or penances for teaching Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, as there are for serving Śūdras.
Moreover, two acts are censured—studying and teaching—whereas for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, there is only one [such censure].
Contact with those who have been forbidden from teaching is permitted by this very rule; it does not cause any fault.
However, there is no authority whatsoever for association with a Śūdra who has studied what is forbidden;
furthermore, "following" (anuvrajyā) constitutes service.
Since service such as salutation and washing of the feet is prohibited, it follows that "service" here refers exclusively to following and nothing else.
As long as there is study, as long as there is grasping.
A disciple desiring the unsurpassed goal should not dwell for life with a non-Brahmin teacher, nor even with a Brahmin who has not mastered the Vedas.

Residing with a non-Brahmin teacher for the purpose of study was previously mentioned as applicable even to the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*); this is now specifically prohibited. "Permanent residence" means residing for the duration of one's life; "he shall not reside" means he shall not do so.
"Let him dwell" means:
because of the relationship between the general and the particular, the connection "let him dwell" is to be understood as follows:
dwelling directed toward the teacher; let him dwell in that.
Having completed his studies, he should go elsewhere.
But surely, since only study was permitted, how could there be the possibility of permanent residence?
This is not a fault.
Since it has been stated that his residence is with a guru, and a guru is defined as one who teaches,
a doubt therefore arises:
[is this the case] even when the Brāhmaṇa is not a learned scholar?
The word *vā* has the sense of "also.

Even if a Brāhmaṇa is today not one who has studied the Vedas (*anūcāna*), nor is he endowed with good conduct and noble birth, nor is he habituated to explaining and studying [the scriptures]—by the term "one who recites after" (*anuvacana*), these qualities are also indicated; for since non-residence is established precisely because of the lack of worthiness in one who does not recite after [the teacher], these qualities are implied.
In this context, "goal" (gati) is intended to mean the attainment of supreme bliss;
it is unsurpassed, meaning there is nothing superior to it. Desiring that—namely, liberation in the form of the bliss of the Supreme Self—one seeks it.
But if he should desire to dwell permanently in the family of his teacher,
he should attend upon him with diligence until the liberation of the body.

If he should desire lifelong residence in the teacher's family—that is, perpetual celibacy (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya*)—then, being disciplined and devoted to that end, he should attend upon this teacher until the release from his prosperity, meaning as long as the body is sustained.
That Brahmin who serves his teacher until the completion of his body goes directly to the eternal abode of Brahmā.
This is the injunction regarding the fruit of lifelong celibacy (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya*).
"The completion of the body" means the renunciation of life;
he who serves and attends upon his teacher until that time [of death].
That Brahmin goes to the abode of Brahman—the eternal seat—meaning that he does not return to the cycle of transmigration.
He goes by a direct, untroubled path;
he is not obstructed by any other state of existence, such as birth as an animal or as a human being.
In the view of the Itihāsas, by the word *brahman* is meant a specific deity with four faces; his *sadma* (abode) is a specific place located in heaven.
For the proponents of Vedānta, however, *brahman* is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); its *sadma* is its very own nature, which is the attainment of that state of being.
One who knows the Dharma should not provide anything to the teacher beforehand;
however, when he is about to perform the final bath and is commanded by the teacher, he should procure an offering for the teacher according to his ability.

This prohibition regarding the giving of wealth to the teacher applies to the *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong student), because the rule for providing wealth to the teacher is prescribed for one who is about to perform the ritual bath (*snāsyan*),
and there is no such bath for the *naiṣṭhika*.
Furthermore, it is the *naiṣṭhika* who is the subject under discussion.

For the *upakurvāṇa* (the student who is still under training), however, there certainly exists the obligation to assist from the time of initiation (*upanayana*) until the final bath (*snāna*). When possible, he should give according to his ability.
