Before the final bath, he should "assist" the teacher by giving something; since the verbal root here has a prefix and means "to give," the fourth case (*caturthī*) is used for the recipient of that action.
Alternatively, one should also apply the rule that "the mention of the action itself [is required]," whereby the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) is established.
The phrase "one who knows the Dharma" is a restatement.
When the time for the ritual bath has arrived, the preceptor commands him, "Bring such-and-such an object";
then [the student], according to his ability, brings as much as he is able.
"For the sake of the guru" means this belongs to the guru;
he should fetch— that is, bring near— whatever the guru has need of.
But is this not a prohibition against the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) performing services for his teacher?
For these are not two separate statements—one being a prohibition and the other an injunction to perform services for the teacher.
Rather, the injunction is that at the time of the ceremonial bath (snāna), the service to the teacher must necessarily be performed.
The prohibition is supplementary to that [injunction].
Furthermore, if the assistance [to the teacher] were prohibited, the injunction for all forms of service would become meaningless.
Moreover, giving alone is not what constitutes assistance; if it were, only the assistance consisting of wealth would be prohibited, and not other forms such as doing what is pleasant or beneficial.
But if it is an explanatory passage (arthavāda), then its non-literal nature is not a defect;
moreover, syntactic unity (ekavākyatā) is understood here.
Bringing pleasure to his guru, he may offer a field, gold, a cow, a horse, or at least a parasol and sandals; or grain, garments, or even vegetables.
It has been stated that one should perform what is indicated for the sake of the teacher; however, not everything must be done—this is the purpose of this verse.
If the teacher should command something contrary [to dharma], such as "Bring the wife of so-and-so" or "Give away your entire property," that must not be performed.
What then? A field; by "field" (kṣetra) is meant the ground where grain grows.
"Hiraṇya" means gold.
The word "vā" (or) signifies an option;
they are not to be given together.
Finally, in the absence of other items, even an umbrella and sandals [are to be given];
because of the use of a copulative compound (dvandva), they are to be given together.
In the case of "clothes" (*vāsāṃsi*), the number is not intended to be significant in all instances.
"Bringing pleasure" (*prītim āharan*)—this is connected to the preceding [phrase] as "he should bring this.
Or, in the reading *prītam āharet*, the completion of the action occurs right here. Or, it may be read as *prītim āvahet*.
One should bring grain and so forth in order to produce pleasure;
or rather, pleasure itself is said to be brought about as something to be acquired.
Consequently, it is established that the mention of material substances serves merely as an illustration.

It is understood that whatever else is of this kind—producing joy, such as jewels, pearls, coral, elephants, horses, carriages, chariots, and so forth—that too should be given. And thus says Gautama: "At the conclusion of his studies, the teacher is to be invited with wealth;
he should bring it if it be his own property acquired through his own effort, and if not, he should acquire it by begging and other means."
But when the teacher has indeed passed away, one should behave toward the teacher’s son who is endowed with good qualities,
or toward the teacher’s wife, or toward a sapinda relative, just as toward the teacher.
This is the instruction for the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*).

In the absence of the teacher, he should live with the teacher’s son who is endowed with qualities such as Vedic learning (*śrotriya*), or with the teacher’s wife—that is, the wife of the teacher—or with one who is a *sapiṇḍa* of the teacher himself.
And there, he should behave toward him as toward the teacher, performing everything such as the offering of alms-food and so forth.
The word *dāra*, ending in the plural number, is recorded by grammarians as denoting "wife";
however, the authors of the legal codes (*smṛtikāra*) employ it even in the singular, as in the passage: "When one's wife is endowed with virtue and offspring, one should not take another."
When these [objects] are unavailable, one who is disciplined in standing, sitting, and moving about,
and who practices service to the sacred fire, shall perfect his own body.

The non-existence of all these [qualities] is their absence, or alternatively, their deficiency. When these are absent, one should apply oneself to the service of the fire: smearing the fire-sanctuary, fueling the fire, and—due to the rule of constant proximity like that toward a teacher—sitting day and night like a servant; this is the service of the fire. Performing it, one should "perfect" the body, meaning one should exhaust the physical frame. Just as a blind man is called "one who has eyes," so too does the text say "he should perfect."
"Staying and sitting" (sthānāsana) is the mode of life (vihāra); one who possesses that should never merely sit, but should live in this manner.

Others, however, think that "staying and sitting" refers to the posture such as the Svastika used at the time of meditation, while "wandering" (vihāra) refers to something else, such as wandering for alms.
The Brahmin who conducts himself in this manner, remaining unbroken in his celibacy,
goes to the highest abode and is not born here again.
The word "thus" refers back to the lifelong practice of celibacy (*naiṣṭhika-vṛtti*).
He who thus practices celibacy—unfallen and unswerving—attains the highest station, characterized by the realization of the Supreme Self.
He is not born again in this world; he does not enter into the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*).
It attains the form of Brahman.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Mānava Dharmaśāstra*, in the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu;
thus [ends] the *Manubhāṣya* composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi.
The second chapter;
now the third chapter: The vow pertaining to the three Vedas consists of practicing [the student's life] under a teacher for thirty-six years.
It may be half of that, or a quarter, or even until the time of its acquisition.

The two types of religious student (*brahmacārī*) previously explained were the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) and the temporary student (*upakurvāṇa*). By the statement, "He who serves his teacher until the completion of the body," the lifelong studentship has been described;
by the phrase "until the return [from the teacher]," another alternative [the temporary studentship] is also indicated.
In this regard, by the very acquisition of the name "naiṣṭhika" (one who has reached the final goal), the remainder of the time limit is easily understood as being characterized by that [name].
One who goes to the end—that is, to completion—is a *naiṣṭhika*.
By the sacred text itself, the duration is prescribed as "until completion."
By this sequential application for one who is still a student,
through various specific austerities and vows enjoined by the rules.
The entire Veda is to be mastered.

Thus, when the specific number is not intended to be expressed, the study of one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or more recensions (*śākhā*)—which is otherwise obtained according to one's capacity—is here regulated. Furthermore, "the vow pertaining to the three Vedas" (*traivedika-vrata*) must be observed.
The collection of the three Vedas is called *trivedī*; that which has the purpose of grasping those [three] is "pertaining to the three Vedas" (*traivedika*).

The act of grasping is included within the term *vṛtti*, because the acquisition of the Vedas has been prescribed previously. *Vrata* refers to the collection of duties pertaining to the religious student (*brahmacārin*). *Caryam* means that which is to be practiced.
The suffix *kṛtya* denotes an injunction (*vidhi*).
Thus, when it might be concluded that the sequence for the acts beginning with "fetching" (*āharaṇa*) ends with "grasping" (*grahaṇa*), he says: "lasting thirty-six years.
Even after the Veda has been grasped, the [prescribed] period must be completed.

If *dharma* is the purpose of the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana-vidhi*), and that injunction for Vedic study ceases once the [text] has been mastered, then for what purpose is the twelve-year observance of vows (*vrata-caryā*) continued after the mastery?
This is to say too little;
for this same question would have to be raised even regarding those subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) subsequent to the primary sacrifices (*yāga*) such as the Āgneya in the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites.

When it is understood that the fulfillment of the injunction's purpose occurs only through the performance of all the constituent parts—including those subsidiaries that provide remote assistance and those joined by a specific sequence—then the injunction itself is established solely through the word of the exhortation (*paricodanā*). Now, if one objects: "There exist alternative views (*pakṣas*) ranging from the great [penance] down to the lighter ones, such as taking half or even a quarter of that; since these exist, who indeed would care for such a great effort and very long duration, namely the twelve-year observance? [Response: This is not so. For the following reasons: (1) because the penances prescribed by Manu and others are intended for those who have committed a minor offense (*upapātaka*); (2) because they are prescribed for those who have lost their caste (*patita*) due to the non-performance of expiation; (3) because they are prescribed for those who have committed a sin through negligence (*pramāda*) while being capable of performing penance; (4) because they are prescribed for those who have committed a sin unintentionally (*abuddhipūrva*); (5) because they are prescribed for those who have committed a sin once; (6) because they are prescribed for those who have committed a sin while being of sound mind; and (7) because they are prescribed for those who have committed a sin while being capable of performing penance. Furthermore, the twelve-year penance is prescribed for those who have committed a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) intentionally and repeatedly. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Moreover, the twelve-year penance is prescribed for those who have committed a mortal sin intentionally and repeatedly, whereas the other penances are prescribed for those who have committed a mortal sin unintentionally, or for those who have committed a minor offense intentionally or unintentionally. Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the twelve-year penance is prescribed for those who have committed a mortal sin intentionally and repeatedly, whereas the other penances are prescribed for those who have committed a mortal sin unintentionally, or for those who have committed a minor offense intentionally or unintentionally. Thus, there is no contradiction. Moreover, the twelve-year penance is prescribed for those who have committed a mortal sin intentionally and repeatedly, whereas the other penances are prescribed for those who have committed a mortal sin unintentionally, or for those who have committed a minor offense intentionally or unintentionally. Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the twelve-year penance is prescribed for those who have committed a mortal sin intentionally and repeatedly, whereas the other penances are prescribed for those who have committed a mortal sin unintentionally, or for those who have committed a minor offense intentionally or unintentionally. Thus, there is no contradiction. Moreover, the twelve-year penance is prescribed for those who have committed a mortal sin intentionally and repeatedly, whereas the other penances are prescribed for those who have committed a mortal sin unintentionally, or for those who have committed a minor offense intentionally or unintentionally. Thus, there is no contradiction. This injunction regarding purificatory rites (saṃskāra-vidhi) is primarily concerned with Vedic study (svādhyāya), because it arises in connection with that act of study.

Furthermore, injunctions regarding purificatory rites do not by themselves entail a qualification for performance; rather, they enter into another injunction that possesses such a qualification by means of the object to be purified.

Just as the act of threshing rice—expressed in the injunction "one threshes the rice"—attains a connection with the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) by means of purificatory rites such as the removal of the husks and chaff from the rice that serves as the material for the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) used in the Āgneya and other sacrifices, and not independently of them—it is precisely that [connection] which is understood as the thing to be accomplished;
for in this way, the status of the Veda as something to be refined (*saṃskārya*) is established, and it cannot be maintained otherwise unless it is subordinate to something else.
It is observed that the comprehension of meaning follows immediately after the study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*).
Therefore, this study extends until the comprehension of the meaning, just as the threshing of grain extends until the production of rice.
However, there is this distinction:
because it is studied within a specific context, the threshing immediately establishes a connection with another injunction that has already obtained its authority.

This [injunction], however, because it is studied as a non-contextual (anārabhyādhīta) rule, culminates in comprehension; and since it is understood to be useful for the performance of all rites that yield fruits, it constitutes an entitlement (adhikāra).
Likewise, the very cessation of the meaning of the injunction is intended as the specific fruit.

For the fact that an injunction serves the purpose of man (puruṣārthatva) is understood through established linguistic usage; whether that [purpose] occurs directly or through a mediated sequence makes no difference.

Furthermore, because it falls under the heading of "that which is being traversed" (*gamyamāna*), this injunction (*vidhi*) itself independently enforces its own performance, even though the comprehension of meaning is useful within the context of the scriptural injunctions regarding obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites.

As for those who maintain that [the study of grammar] shares the same functional purpose as the injunctions for the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices by way of the comprehension of meaning, and who claim that the excellence of that very result arises from a specific effort—what wrong has been done to them by the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa-vidhi*)? Why is it so strenuously denied that they share the same functional purpose?
If you say, "It would result in the Veda being non-authoritative," let it be so.
An object established by the force of reasoning cannot be abandoned merely on account of some practical purpose;
rather, one reasoning is sublated by another that is more powerful.

However, if this [injunction] were to have the same function as the injunction for making someone a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), its very nature as an injunction would be lost, because its own meaning would not be intended to be expressed.

This is the same even when [the rite] enters into the *jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices. However, when this injunction is independent and enforces its own performance as a constituent of equal rank [with the main sacrifice], then it is performed joined with its own *itikartavyatā* (procedure). In that case, among the various optional alternatives—both lighter and heavier—once the result is accomplished by the lighter one, the performance of the heavier ones brings about a specific distinction in the very purpose of the injunction.

Just as in the case of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), where it is stated that "one [cow] should be given," "three should be given," "twelve should be given," and so forth—once this injunction (*vidhi*) has been performed, whether the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is explicitly heard, implied, or inferred by its own capacity—this is a distinction of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇabheda*), not a distinction in the relationship [of the act]. In every respect, we cannot escape being touched by both [factors], provided that this injunction both compels the performance of its own purpose and serves as an auxiliary to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other rites.
Now, what is this nonsensical babble, contradicting itself from beginning to end?

It was stated previously that the injunctions for ritual refinement (*saṃskāra-vidhi*) do not directly relate to the qualification (*adhikāra*); however, this [present] injunction is independent and compels the performance of its own specific purpose.
Just as this [injunction] is not connected with a qualifying factor mentioned in a particular [text], the implied qualification is not incompatible even with the injunctions for ritual refinement.
This is not a distinction if the performance prompted by this injunction is intended to pertain to the portion consisting of the comprehension of the meaning.

Since the mere recitation [of the Veda] is enjoined by the rules for the teacher (*ācāryavidhi*), it would follow that the preparatory injunctions (*saṃskāravidhi*) are accepted as being connected to that [recitation] as their governing authority (*adhikāra*).

Alternatively, if the performance [of those rites] is prompted by them because they assist other injunctions, then study would belong to one who is already qualified [for ritual action], and there would be no qualification for one who has merely completed his Vedic studies. In that case, the qualification of a *śūdra* would be difficult to prevent.
Furthermore, it would not follow that one hears the meaning of the Veda immediately after its study.
For as soon as one happens by chance to learn from some source that a Vedic ritual named Jyotiṣṭoma has heaven as its fruit, at that very moment one would have to learn its procedure;
and at that same time, one would have to study the mantras used by the sacrificer that are useful for it.
On this point, some offer a rebuttal by means of the principle of the "dependent" (*āśrayin*).

For just as the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other such offerings possess a dual nature—being both purificatory acts (*saṃskārakarma*) and purposeful acts (*arthakarma*)—so too the study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāyādhyayana*), by virtue of following the application of its designation and because it is observed to result in the comprehension of the fruit of the action, is both a purificatory act and a purposeful act that bears fruit.
Therefore, its status as having a prescriptive injunction (*sādhikāra*) is established.
Who, then, is the qualified person? We say it is the initiated youth of the three higher castes;
for this is prescribed among the duties of the religious student (brahmacārin).
For the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth convey the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*), which consists in a mandate (*niyojya*) that is invariably connected [to a result].

In that regard, when there is a requirement for a specific qualification (*viśeṣa*), in some cases the qualification is provided by the words themselves, as in "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāmaḥ*) or "one should perform the Agnihotra as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam agnihotraṃ juhoti*).

In other cases, such as the Viśvajit sacrifice and others, although not explicitly heard in the text, it must be inferred by the force of the capacity for denoting a related meaning (*anvitābhidhāna-sāmarthya*).
In some cases, it is understood through the context, the inherent power of the subject matter, and also by considering other injunctions;
all of this is present here.
The student under training (*brahmacārī*) is the subject under discussion.
Furthermore, the comprehension of the meaning arises through the inherent capacity of the entity (*vastu*),
and that [comprehension] is applicable to all injunctions, because it is the learned who are entitled [to perform them].
Others, however, do not accept this.
Its status as a subordinate element (*adhikāra*) is understood precisely by virtue of its being a purificatory injunction (*saṃskāravidhi*),
because purificatory acts are performed for the sake of that which is to be purified.
Furthermore, if no specific change were observed in the object to be purified, then, like the case of parched grain (*saktu*), its nature as a purificatory act would be lost.
Moreover, there is a distinction here characterized by the comprehension of an action that bears fruit.

As for the argument that it is "like the *sviṣṭakṛt* [offering] and so forth," that is incorrect because it results in the loss of its nature as being inaccessible through the knowledge of verbal roots and suffixes; thus, it possesses both forms [of injunction and instruction].
Therefore, it is established that this injunction is independent and pertains to the student (*māṇavaka*).

And for this reason, [the study of the Veda] must be performed by its own inherent force alone, and not through the implication of an injunction regarding qualification for rituals such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa, as is the case with acts like threshing.
In the same way, the study of multiple Vedas is to be understood.
For even there, since the purpose of the injunction is accomplished by means of a single Veda, why study multiple Vedas?
However, it is logical [to understand the injunction] as referring to the abundance of fruit;
and the fruit is as previously described, not the milk, curd, and so forth mentioned in the supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*).

This being the case, for one who studies a single Veda, the study of those mantras useful for ritual actions that are not recited in his own branch (*sva-śākhā*) is permitted by implication at the time of performing the ritual, due to the efficacy [of the injunction].

Although [the word] "having studied" (*adhīta*) [is used] in the context of eligibility for one who has studied the Veda, others, however, consider that in the injunction "The Veda with its six limbs is to be studied by a Brāhmaṇa as a duty without motive" (*niṣkāraṇo dharmaḥ*), the term "without motive" (*niṣkāraṇa*) functions as a word establishing eligibility (*adhikārapada*). "Without motive" means without aiming at any purpose (*prayojana*); it must be performed like an obligatory rite (*nityakarman*). For, without its status as a provider of eligibility, no syntactic connection is possible through the medium of the subject matter, such as being an action, an agent, or a qualifier thereof.

Therefore, even though it is an injunction for a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra-vidhi*), there is no contradiction in its having either an implied qualification (*gamyamānādhikāratva*) or an explicitly stated qualification (*śrūyamāṇādhikāratva*).
Others, however, consider the absence of a qualification to be superior precisely because it is an injunction for a purificatory rite;
for a qualification is sought only for the purpose of obtaining a specific mode of performance (*anuṣṭhāna-viśeṣa*).
And this [fact] is established here precisely by the observation of a specific object to be refined (*saṃskārya*). Prescriptions for refinement depend upon a purpose;
in this case, it is the fruit of the action itself that is to be accomplished by the injunction.
And that [period] established by ritual action, characterized by the formal reception [of the Veda], is indeed seen to be non-contradictory.
Since no specific division is mentioned here, the understanding of the division is derived from another Smṛti: "Brahmacarya for twelve years for each Veda.
But which three Vedas are intended here?
"The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda. "Then why is the Atharvaveda not a Veda? "Who says such a thing?"

However, in this case, as it has been heard, since the removal of the need for refinement (saṃskāryatva-nirbarhaṇā) results in the attainment of the performance of that injunction through its culmination in the comprehension of meaning—
given that such comprehension is useful for the performance of all ritual acts—
the Atharvaveda is rich in instructions on malevolent magic (abhicāra) and the like.
Therefore, rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma are not enjoined [by this text],
nor is there any subsidiary (aṅga) belonging to them;
for the completion of all their subsidiaries, including the duties of the Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, and Udgātṛ priests, is accomplished by the three Vedas alone.
Furthermore, the primary injunctions for the production [of rituals] such as the Jyotiṣṭoma exist only within the three Vedas;
the office of the Brahman priest also exists only within the three Vedas;
and the word "tri" (three) denotes a number.
Furthermore, numerical words do not function without depending upon some single entity.
Therefore, only those [Vedas] whose purpose here consists in the instruction of that specific task can be designated by the word "three.
And the Atharvaṇa does not enter into that task.
In that regard, there are no primary injunctions for the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such sacrifices, nor are there injunctions for their constituent parts.
In the Śyena and other malevolent (abhicāra) sacrifices, the same officiating priests (ṛtvij) are employed and the same procedure (itikartavyatā) applies;
even the specific details that differ are taught within the three Vedas themselves.

Therefore, since there is no co-inclusion of the *Ṛgveda* and *Yajurveda* with the *Sāmaveda* in a single ritual act, the designation "three Vedas" would otherwise be untenable; thus, the *Atharvaveda* is not included here. However, because it is denoted by the word "svādhyāya," its inclusion within the scope of the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) is not contradictory. "Half of that" refers back to the number thirty-six.
Half of that is eighteen years;
here too, the calculation of divisions is six years;
here too, it is a quarter.
A "quarter" (pāda) is that same number divided into four parts;
[in this case] nine years constitute the fourth part.
There are three for each Veda.
But how can the Veda be mastered in three years?
There may be someone who is most exceptionally intelligent.
Another says:
Dharmas are not prompted by the very nature of the act of grasping; rather, they are prompted by the injunction (*vidhi*) regarding that object.
In that case as well, once the grasping has ceased, if the observance of the rules is maintained for certain days during the period of study, the purpose of the scripture is thereby accomplished.

The performance of the subsidiary rites (*aṅgakalpa*) would be for the sake of the injunction regarding private recitation (*svādhyāya-vidhi*); by that alone, there would be the designation of one as a "graduate by vows" (*vrata-snātaka*) upon the completion of the vow, even if the formal study has not been finished. Therefore, the prescription of a specific time [for the conclusion] is appropriate.
Without three years [of study], one does not become a *vratasnātaka*.

Although some traditional authorities (*smaranti*) maintain that "the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) occurs upon the completion of the Veda," nevertheless, its application is indeed stated by way of metaphorical usage (*upacārāt*) for the completion of the vows as well.
That [position] is incorrect.
Even though they are enjoined by a scriptural injunction, it is proper that the observances (*vrata*) last only as long as the study;
for they are prescribed in connection with the study,
and thus they ought to endure only for the duration of the study.
For indeed, by the word "only" (*eva*), if this is a separate sentence, then the three-year period of vows begins even before the Veda is mastered;
however, if it is a single sentence meaning that the period lasts until the mastery of the Veda, then there is no cessation of the vows as long as the Veda has not been mastered.
By the use of the particle "only," they favor precisely this latter position.

If there is no cessation [of study] when the Veda has not been grasped, how then is there a distinction in designation as a *vratasnātaka* (one who has bathed after the vows) and a *vedasnātaka* (one who has bathed after the Veda)?
We shall explain this in the fourth [chapter].
"Thirty-six years" (*ṣaṭtriṃśadabda*) means thirty-six years taken together; that which pertains to that is "thirty-six-yearly" (*ṣāṭtriṃśadābdika*).
In this way, there is that which pertains to the three Vedas (*traivedika*);
that which has half of that measure (*tadardhaparimāṇa*), namely *tadardhika*;
likewise, there is that which consists of a quarter (*pādika*) and that which ends with the learning [of the texts] (*grahaṇāntika*).

In all these cases, the suffixes *ini* and *iṭhan* are used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). However, it cannot be maintained that "whatever has a certain measure, that [measure] belongs to it."
Having studied the Vedas— either all four, two, or even one— in the proper sequence,
and having remained inviolate in his student discipline (*brahmacarya*), he should enter the stage of the householder (*gṛhasthāśrama*).
The study of three Vedas has been prescribed;
the study of one or two Vedas, not being otherwise established, is now provided as an alternative.
It has been explained that the word "veda" refers to a specific recensional branch (śākhā).
One should study three branches—one from each of the Vedas, or two, or even one—but not from only a single Veda.
The triple Veda is recited as "trividyā. Having studied and mastered the Veda according to the aforementioned observance of vows, [one should proceed].
One should dwell in the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*).
He will describe the essential nature of the householder stage in the passage beginning with "A twice-born man should marry a wife," etc. "He should dwell" means he should practice [it].
Verbal roots have multiple meanings; the prefix *āṅ* is used here in the sense of a limit. By conventional usage, one who has taken a wife is called a "householder" (*gṛhastha*).
The word *gṛha* (house) denotes a wooden structure;

that collection of items consisting of injunctions and prohibitions prescribed for it is expressed by the word *āśrama* (stage of life). For example, for one who has been initiated, there is the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*) until the return home (*samāvartana*), and for one who has performed the marriage ceremony, there is the householder stage (*gārhasthya*).
He whose celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is unviolated and unbroken—that is, who has desisted from sexual union with women—is described in this way.
Furthermore, a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) should be observed here:
by means of the conventional usage of verbal forms, one should be of unviolated celibacy and then enter the stage of the householder (*gṛhasthāśrama*).
If there were a single unified statement [regarding the sequence], then in the event of a transgression, the very qualification for the householder stage (*gārhasthya*) would be lost.

However, since it is prescribed here as being for the sake of the person’s own welfare (*puruṣārtha*), one is subject to expiation (*prāyaścitta*) upon its violation; yet, one does not thereby cease to possess the qualification.

Furthermore, in the injunction "having studied, one should dwell [in the family]," only the sequence (*paurvāparya*) is intended to be expressed, not that marriage must occur immediately after study. This is because the sequence is established by the suffix *-lyap* (denoting what precedes), and immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is not the literal meaning of the word.

Consequently, it follows that between the study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*) and marriage, there is occasion for hearing the treatises on grammar and other sciences for the purpose of understanding the meaning of the Veda.
For only a learned person is qualified for the householder’s life, not an ignorant one as might be the case under the rule governing Vedic study alone.

Even though during childhood one possesses characteristics similar to those of animals and is incapable of realizing one's own qualification, nevertheless, one is made to perform [the duties] by the father or the teacher.
In reality, the authority belongs to those two alone.
The father has authority over the instruction of his offspring because the injunction for procreating offspring is fulfilled by that much;
and "instruction" consists in the imparting of the two authorities regarding what is prescribed and what is prohibited.
In that regard, when someone does not understand even while being instructed, they are guided by the hand like a blind person;

just as one is held back from touching fire or falling into a well by means of a firm grasp of the hand, so too [is one restrained] from drinking intoxicants and the like, even though their results are unseen.
Or, just as one is made to take medicine and the like against one's will, so it is with respect to the categories taught in the treatises.
But when he has attained some degree of proficiency, then he should be enjoined thus: "You ought to do this and that.

This being the case, once the boy has studied the Veda, he must be awakened by his father or teacher in this manner: "You have mastered the Veda; you are now qualified for the desire to know its meaning, and therefore you ought to hear its auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*).
By this much, the father's obligation to procreate offspring is fulfilled.
Thus it has been said: "To what extent, then, is one considered to have been produced [as a student]? To the extent that he has himself accomplished his duty.

Therefore, this remains established: marriage does not take place merely by having studied, as long as the meaning of the Veda has not been mastered. And thus, the construction of the words should be made as follows.
Having completed his studies, even when the formal act of study has ceased, he should remain one whose *brahmacarya* (celibacy) is unviolated.
Since the cessation [of the vow] has already occurred, this repetition is intended to signify the end of other restrictive rules, such as the avoidance of honey, meat, and so forth.
Therefore, all these rules must be observed for as long as the period of study lasts.
But when the study is completed and at the time of understanding the meaning, one must indeed desist from women; service to women is not to be performed.

Although the word *brahmacarya* is etymologically derived as the undertaking of a vow for the sake of grasping the *brahman*, we shall demonstrate that its usage in that context is intended solely for the desisting from women.
This is according to the sequence.

By the very same well-known order of recitation among students, first comes the *catuḥṣaṣṭi*, and then follows the *brāhmaṇa* which begins with the continuous account of one's lineage, starting from the father and grandfather.
For in such a matter, speakers do not say, "not by family, nor by conduct, nor by order. By this, it is established that the very branch (*śākhā*) studied by one's ancestors must not be abandoned.
One should first honor with a cow that son who is well-known for his own duty, who inherits the father’s Vedic legacy, and who is seated upon the marriage bed wearing a garland.
One should first honor with a cow that person who inherits the legacy of the Veda (*brahmadāyahara*).
He is called *brahmadāyahara* because he takes—that is, appropriates—both the Veda (*brahma*) and the legacy (*dāya*).
"Legacy" (*dāya*) means wealth, as it is given; the "Veda" (*brahma*) is the scripture; and "taking" (*haraṇa*) means acquisition.
Having mastered the Vedas and having received his share of the inheritance from his father, he enters the state of a householder, for one who is destitute lacks the qualification [to do so].
However, if the father is destitute, then, for the sake of ensuring the continuity of the lineage, he should acquire wealth and marry him.
Others, however, consider the phrase "the gift of the Veda" (*brahmadāya*)—referring to the father—to be a restatement of the previously mentioned rule.
But surely it has been stated that the teacher has the authority to instruct the student; why then is it said here that [the son] is the heir to his father's Vedic knowledge?
It is replied:
for one whose father exists, that very father is his teacher.
In the absence of the father, or if he is incapable, another person has the authority [to perform the initiation].
By the adoption of another teacher, the father’s authority indeed ceases;
there is no distinction whether the father teaches himself or by means of employing another.

As for what they say— that because the fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is prescribed as a constant rule in the injunction "the fee is a boon" (*varo dakṣiṇā*) during the initiation (*upanayana*), it must necessarily involve another person as the agent— that is incorrect;
for this injunction, "the fee is a boon," occurs specifically within the context of the initiation.
The one who initiates [the student]— whether he be the father or the teacher— neither of these two requires a separate act of bowing when they are engaged in their own respective offices;
for the giving of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is for the purpose of causing bowing,
and bowing is not required from one who is already engaged in another office.

Therefore, since the word *dakṣiṇā* lacks the sense of bowing down (*ānamana*), it should be understood by implication as a designation for a gift intended for transcendental merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*), like the giving of gold.

Furthermore, the father himself must make [the son] a master with such wealth that the granting of the boon becomes possible for him. Now, if this insistence is maintained—that the term *dakṣiṇā* cannot occur except in the sense of a gift given for the purpose of bowing down—[then the following applies].
"Or rather, when the primary meaning is possible, a metaphorical sense (lakṣaṇā) is not logical.

If that is so, then in the case of one whose father is neither in that position nor an *ācārya*, when he initiates himself like Satyakāma, the injunction regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) will apply to him.
And it has been established that even such a person, having slightly departed from childhood, indeed possesses the qualification for the purification of the self.

Therefore, the father’s authority is twofold: either when he initiates [the son] himself, or when he appoints another teacher. This applies to one who has become "established" (pratīta)—that is, turned toward entering the householder stage of life—but not to a lifelong student (naiṣṭhika), even when he has completed the purpose of the injunction for study and is about to enter the village.
"Wearing a garland":

this is for the purpose of illustrating all those rules whatsoever that have been prescribed by the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras regarding the rite of the honey-mixture (madhuparka). "Seated on a couch" means seated upon a costly bed or sofa.
He was lying down, worthy of the honor of worship;
[he was honored] with a cow and the *madhuparka* offering.
This procedure regarding the *madhuparka* is prescribed as an optional alternative in the tradition.
Therefore, by the word "cow" (go), a specific ritual action for accomplishing that [result] is indicated. One should "honor" (arhayet), that is, worship;
according to the context, this refers to either the father or the teacher.
"First" means prior to marriage. "Well-known" (*pratīta*) refers to [the fact that he is known] by his own duty (*svadharma*); this is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
There is no difference in the connection whether one says "one who takes the inheritance of Brahman by his own duty" or "one should honor him by his own duty."
Having been permitted by his teacher, having bathed and returned home according to the prescribed rule,
the twice-born man should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks.
Even when the completion of the Vedic study and vows has occurred, he should bathe—having been permitted and authorized by his teacher.
By the word "bathing" (snāna), a specific sacramental rite (saṃskāra) prescribed in the Gṛhyasūtras is indicated, marking the end of the duties of a religious student (brahmacārin).
How this term functions as an indication (lakṣaṇā) has been explained previously.

On that very day, having undergone some rite prescribed by the authors of the *Gṛhyasūtras* consisting of the worship with *madhuparka*, he has returned from the teacher’s house to his father’s house; this is a restatement (*anuvāda*). All of this is already established as a supplement to the injunction "he should marry" (*udvaheta*), and not as a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the marriage itself.
Therefore, even for one who has studied the Vedas while remaining in his father’s house, marriage certainly takes place even though a formal return (*samāvartana*) is impossible.
Some consider the *samāvartana* (the returning home) to be the ritual bath (*snāna*) that is an integral part of marriage.

If it is argued that a distinction [between them] is understood from the use of the gerund suffix (*ktvā*), then in that case, he will describe the *samāvartana* as a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) consisting of a bath that is an integral part of marriage;
for there, the bath is indeed prescribed with specific details, such as "by the *snātaka*," and so forth.
Alternatively, the statement regarding "returning" (samāvṛtti) intends the abandonment of restraints and observances (yama-niyama).
The meaning is that one who has returned has entered back into his former state, which is devoid of such restraints.
And the statement regarding the abandonment of restraints intends a specific [limited] scope.

For the restraints and observances (*yama-niyama*) of a *brahmacārin* are indeed superior, whereas those of the subsequent stages are not; the phrase "according to rule" (*yathāvidhi*) is used here just as it was in the expression "by his own duty" (*svadharma*).
A twice-born man should marry a wife.
"One should marry" constitutes the rule for marriage (*vivāha*).
Marriage is a sacramental rite (*saṃskārakarma*), as indicated by the use of the accusative case in the word "wife" (*bhāryām*).
Furthermore, prior to marriage, there exists no wife for whom the sacrament of marriage could be performed, just as there is no application of collyrium for an eye that does not yet exist.
What, then, is accomplished by marriage?

Just as in the case of "he cuts the sacrificial post" (yūpa), that to which acts such as cutting are performed is called a sacrificial post; likewise, it is through marriage alone that one becomes a wife.
By the word "marriage," the taking of the hand (pāṇigrahaṇa) is meant.
And that is what is primary here;
for thus they record: "marriage is the act of taking a wife, the grasping of the hand.
Here too [the author] will say: "the sacrament of grasping the hand," indicating that it has the offering of parched grain and so forth as its constituent parts.
And all of that must be understood from the Gṛhya-sūtras.
Because of the mention of "a maiden" (*kanyā*) in the rule, "One should not marry a tawny (*kapilā*) maiden," this sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) pertains to a maiden and not to women in general.
Furthermore, we shall explain that in this context, the word "maiden" refers to a female who has not yet engaged in sexual intercourse with a male.
"Of the same caste" means belonging to the same class as oneself.

"Endowed with auspicious marks" (lakṣaṇānvitām): "marks" (lakṣaṇāni) are signs such as color, lines, and moles that indicate non-widowhood, progeny, and wealth, as understood from the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra); "endowed with" (anvitām) means possessed of these; the meaning is "endowed with auspicious marks."

Although a characteristic may also be indicative of what is undesirable, one should marry such a woman by means of those very scriptures that indicate [auspicious traits]; therefore, she who possesses auspicious characteristics is to be regarded as "characterized" (*lakṣaṇavatī*).
In common usage, the word *lakṣaṇa* is employed specifically to indicate what is intended as desirable;
thus, it is said of a woman who possesses auspicious marks that "this man is well-characterized" (*salakṣaṇa*) and "this woman is well-characterized."
In this regard, an investigation into the qualification (*adhikāra*) must be undertaken.

Because it is a rite of consecration (*saṃskāra-vidhi*), its performance is established just like the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*). For just as the establishment of the fires is performed for the sake of accomplishing the *āhavanīya* and other fires—which are auxiliary to the obligatory and optional rites by serving as their medium—so too is marriage. This is because marriage, by means of producing a wife, serves both visible and invisible human goals.

Thus, when a man’s inclination toward sexual gratification would otherwise result in a mere pursuit of women in general, the prohibition against approaching maidens or the wives of others ensures that the lustful man finds the cessation of his distress within his own wife.
"One must practice the Dharma together"—because she has authority over all dharmas, the accomplishment of the unseen human goal (adṛṣṭa-puruṣārtha) depends upon her.
Regarding this, some reflect as follows:
those possessed of passion perform marriage on their own initiative for the sake of accomplishing the visible goal, in the manner previously described.
And for those who have performed their marriages, that marriage may occur for the purpose of accomplishing the performance of rites according to the rules prescribed for the twice-born.
For one whose attachment to women has somehow ceased, there is no marriage.

Since there is no entitlement to perform rites in the absence of marriage, and since there is no fault in the non-performance of rites by one who lacks such entitlement, it is not contradictory for even a person without an āśrama to remain in that state while not performing the duties pertaining to the goals of human life.
This is incorrect;
for just as desire is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), so too is dharma a motivator in its status as a human goal.
Indeed, everyone acts for the sake of accomplishing some human goal.
If this were the case, then statements such as "having remained without an āśrama for a year" and so forth would be untenable;
we shall examine this matter thoroughly on the occasion of the discussion regarding the options for the āśramas in the sixth [chapter].
He now shows what kind of girl should be married:
"She who is not a sapinda of the mother and not of the same gotra as the father is recommended for the twice-born in the rite of marriage for sexual union."
A woman who is not a *sapiṇḍa* of the mother and who belongs to the same *gotra* as the father is recommended for the rite of marriage.
The mention of *sapiṇḍa* is intended to indicate maternal relatives;
for according to another *smṛti*, the *sapiṇḍa* relationship for women extends to the third generation on the mother’s side.
However, marriage beyond three generations on the mother's side is not intended; rather, it is intended beyond the fifth.
For Gautama recites thus: "Beyond the seventh on the father's side and beyond the fifth on the mother's side.
Therefore, since there is no consistency with the literal hearing [of the text], the absence of *sāpiṇḍya* must be explained as being due to maternal connection, in accordance with other Smṛtis.
By this it would have been stated that a wife born in the lineage of one's mother does not exist [for him].
And the limit is precisely that of Gautama.

Therefore, she who is born in the lineage of the maternal grandfather or the great-grandmother should not be married until the fifth degree, due to the proximity of kinship within the line of the sons.

Therefore, there is a prohibition against all maternal aunts and their daughters, as well as all those born from the lineage of the maternal great-grandfather, because there is no distinction in their status as kinsmen (*bandhu*).
Furthermore, she who is not of the same *gotra* as the father [is also prohibited];
*gotra* is traditionally recorded in the Smṛtis as the lineage of Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, Garga, and so forth.

Those of the same lineage (*gotra*) do not intermarry; the Vasiṣṭhas do not marry among the Vasiṣṭhas, nor the Gargas among the Gargas. However, in the case of the Vasiṣṭhas, there is a prohibition even against one who shares the same maternal *gotra*. Indeed, having married a woman of the same *gotra* as well as one with the same *pravara*, [one incurs a fault].
Having abandoned her, the twice-born man should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
likewise for [marrying] the daughter of a maternal uncle or one belonging to the mother's lineage.
Gautama, however, recites: "Marriage is with those who do not share the same *pravara*.
In that case, even if the *gotra* is the same, if there is a difference in the *pravara*, marriage would be permissible;
but that is incorrect, because in another *smṛti* both are prohibited by the rule: "She who is not born of the same *ṛṣi* and *gotra*."
"Ārṣeya" and "pravara" have the same meaning.
But how can there be identity of lineage (*samānārṣeyatva*) when there is a difference in *gotra*? Why should this not be the case if [the connection] is recorded in tradition?
This matter has the Śruti and Smṛti as its authority; it is not within the scope of direct perception, such that there could be a contradiction.
But who, indeed, are these so-called "pravaras"?
This which is said is far too little.
This also must be explained: what indeed is this so-called "brahminhood" (*brāhmaṇatva*), and likewise, what is this so-called "clan" (*gotra*)?

Just as there is a distinction such as brahminhood despite the commonality of being human, so too, despite the commonality of brahminhood, there is a division of clans such as Vasiṣṭha and others; and within each clan, there are those who share the same ancestral seers (*samānārṣeya*).
For one whose clan is such-and-such, the invocation of the lineage (*pravara*) must be performed by means of those [names].
The same applies to the prohibition against marriage as well.
Furthermore, the authors of the Sūtras record the *pravara* lineages in connection with the distinction between *gotras*, stating: "For whomsoever this *gotra* belongs, these are his *pravaras*.
And the distinction between *gotras* is made by those born of that very *gotra*.
It is recorded that they remember, "We are Parāśaras," or "We are Upamanyus.

Even though they remember their *pravara*s (ancestral sages) just as they do their *gotra*s (lineages), nevertheless, because of the great number [of *pravara*s], they might perhaps forget them; therefore, having made the *gotra* a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), the memory of the *pravara*s was composed.
However, they do indeed remember the *gotra*.
And there is no characteristic mark whatsoever by which one could say, "He who is of such-and-such a form belongs to this lineage";
in that regard, memory extends only as far as the lineage,
which is the state of having a similar nature within the continuum.
Furthermore, this distinction between *gotra* and *pravara* applies to Brāhmaṇas, not to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas;
for thus says the author of the Kalpasūtra: "Because of [the rule] regarding the priesthood for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.

Although this statement would be appropriate in the context of *pravara* even as a prohibition of what was otherwise applicable when there is a designation of a specific *gotra*, nevertheless, they have no traditional recollection (*smaraṇa*) of their *gotras*.
What then is the rule regarding the limit for kinsmen even in the marriage of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas?
It is said:
this [rule] concerning "beyond the seventh from the paternal kinsmen" applies to all social classes (varṇas).
Here too, she must be of a different *gotra*; by the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that she must also not be a *sapiṇḍa*.
Thus, the term *sapiṇḍa*, being carried over from the previous context, serves—as before—to indicate all those related by kinship.
By this, the prohibition is established for women descended from the father’s sister, as well as for other women in the lineage of the great-grandfather, up to the seventh person.
The *sapiṇḍas* are recorded in tradition as extending up to the seventh generation;
others, however, say that *gotra* refers to the lineage (*vaṃśa*),
in which case there is no requirement for a specific limit.
As long as it is known that we belong to a single lineage (*ekavaṃśa*), there is no marriage;
even in this view, the phrase "and not a *sapiṇḍa*" (*asapiṇḍā ca*) continues to apply.
Consequently, as before, there is a prohibition against marrying the daughters of one's father’s sister and others.
But under this view, the prohibition regarding those of the same ṛṣi and gotra would be difficult to establish;
for in that case, the thought "we belong to the same lineage" does not exist there. It is said in reply:
They support this with historical evidence;

for therein they describe how the seers, such as Vasiṣṭha and others, were the original founders of the lineages, and those born from them are the *gotras*. Their sons and grandsons, through their association with qualities such as excellence in asceticism and learning, became most renowned as the *pravaras*.
This very restriction is established from another Smṛti.

However, this point must be examined here: regarding the phrase "those with the same *pravara*," does the identity consist in the name or in the number? And if it consists in the identity of name, does the prohibition apply where all [the *pravaras*] are identical, or even when only one is identical?

In that regard, if *pravara* status were determined by the collective group, then when some member of a group has died and another person is born into the group, a different collective would have arisen; thus, because the *pravara* would no longer be identical, marriage would be prohibited.
In this way, there would be marriage between the Upamanyus and the Parāśaras, for their *gotras* are distinct.
Some are Upamanyus and others are Parāśaras; according to the aforementioned principle, there is a distinction in their *pravara* lineages.
The *pravara* for the Upamanyus is Vasiṣṭha, Bhāradvāja, and Ekapāt;
for the Parāśaras, it is Vasiṣṭha, Gārgya, and Pārāśarya.
Now, if the status of being a *pravara* belongs to each individual, there is a prohibition even when only one is common;
for example, "beans should not be eaten," and they are not eaten even when mixed [with other things]. What, then, is the correct view here?
Each one possesses the status of being the *pravara*.
For thus is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) observed:
"He chooses one, he chooses two, he chooses three"—in this way, each one is understood as a single unit.
Even when there is equality in that respect, he states that "there is no marriage among these.
The mention of the "twice-born" (dvijāti) is for the sake of illustration;
for even in the case of a Śūdra, [the rule] exists: "up to the seventh from the father's side and the fifth from the mother's side."
The taking of a wife is the act of taking a wife, the deed of taking a wife;
in this context, it means that which is prescribed as praiseworthy through praise. It is sexual union.
"Maithunī" means born of sexual union; "amaithunī" means not born of sexual union.
This is connected with the word "of the father," meaning she is produced solely from the father's seed as soon as she is born.
Since *niyoga* (the rite of appointment) is prescribed for her, there is no prohibition by the aforementioned qualifications for one born through it.
Therefore, she is separately prohibited by the term "amaithunī" (one who has not had sexual intercourse).
Consequently, a woman born of a *niyoga* marriage should not be married out of desire, because she is *maithunī* (having had sexual intercourse).
Others, however, read the word as *amaithune*.
She is praised for the purpose of dharma in the act of taking a wife, but not for sexual intercourse;
this is a commendation, not a prohibition.
Such a wife, even though there is sexual intercourse, exists solely for the sake of dharma.
Even if they are great and prosperous in terms of cattle, goats, sheep, wealth, and grain,
one should avoid these ten families in forming a marriage alliance with women.
This is a deprecatory explanatory passage (arthavāda) for the prohibition that is about to be stated.
"Prosperity" (samṛddhi) means success;
"wealth" (dhana) means power (vibhava).
"Even great" means even excellent. To qualify the types of wealth, he says: "cows, goats, sheep, wealth, and grain. The suffix *tasi* is used here in the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārthe*).
And with cattle, goats, sheep, and grain.
The mention of "wealth" (dhana) is for the purpose of qualifying the cattle, goats, and so forth;
that is, those cattle, goats, and others which take the form of wealth.
For "kūṭasaṃpannatā" refers to grain;
"strīsaṃbandha" refers to marriage. A "strīsaṃbandha" is a connection for the purpose of obtaining a wife.
Families that neglect their religious duties, those lacking male progeny, those devoid of Vedic study, those with hairy anal folds,
and families afflicted by consumption, chronic disease, epilepsy, leucoderma, or leprosy.

A family in which the rites such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*) and other sacraments (*saṃskāra*) have been abandoned and are no longer performed, and in which the daily five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) and so forth are not observed; and a family that is "without men" (*niṣpuruṣa*), meaning one where only women give birth.
Where generally only girls are born and not males;
where there is no desire for the study of the Vedas; and where [the people] are hairy and afflicted with hemorrhoids.
The two families are indicated by a copulative compound treated as a singular.
It is endowed with many long hairs on the arms and other parts.
Hemorrhoids (*arśāṃsi*) are fleshy growths attached to the anal organ; for they cause pain because they are of the nature of a disease.
*Kṣaya* is the disease of pulmonary consumption (*rājayakṣmā*).
*Āmayāvin* refers to one with weak digestion whose consumed food does not properly digest.
*Apasmāra* is that which causes impairment such as the loss of memory.
*Śvitra* is a white discoloration on the body characterized by fissures;
*kuṣṭha* is well known.
All these words, which denote specific diseases, are indicated as being formed with possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*) beginning from *romaśa*.
Earlier commentators have described the basis for this prohibition as being observed [in common experience]:
"The offspring of two-footed beings follow the lineage of their mother;
therefore, the progeny of those whose actions and so forth are inferior would also possess that same character."
And diseases are contagious;
for it is thus stated in medical treatises: "All diseases are transmissible, with the exception of dysentery."
One should not marry a girl who is tawny, nor one with an extra limb, nor one who is diseased;
nor one who is hairless, nor one with excessive body hair, nor one who is talkative, nor one who is reddish-brown.
The previous prohibition was based on family lineage;
this one, however, is based on essential nature.
She whose hair is tawny or golden in color is a *kapilā*.
"Excessive-limbed" means having six fingers;
"sickly" means afflicted by many diseases and seized by an illness difficult to treat.
The suffix *ini* occurs here in the sense of abundance (*bhūman*) or in the sense of constant connection (*nityayoga*).
"Without hair" means hairless;
"hair" refers here to both body hair and head hair.
It means the absence of all hair on the upper arms and the two shanks.
Talkative even when there is very little to say, she speaks excessively and harshly;
she has tawny eyes due to an eye disease, or her eyes are round, brownish, or tawny.

One should not marry a woman whose name is that of a lunar mansion, a tree, or a river; nor one named after a low-caste person or a mountain; nor one named after a bird, a snake, or a servant; nor one with a terrifying name.
A lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) is, for example, *Ārdrā* or *Jyeṣṭhā*, which take their names from those [mansion names].
A tree is, for example, *Śiṃśapā* or *Āmalakī*, which takes its name from that [tree name].
A river is the *Gaṅgā* or the *Yamunā*, which takes its name from that [river name].

"Ṛkṣāṇi ca vṛkṣāś ca nadyaś ca" is a *dvandva* compound; "tāsāṃ nāmāni" is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the names of those"; then, with the second word "nāma," there is a compound with elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*). Examples include *antyanāmikā*, *barbarī*, *śabarī*, and so forth.
Mountains such as the Vindhya and Malaya; the suffix [denoting "belonging to"] is applied as in the previous case, forming a compound. Birds named Śukī and Sārikā.
*Ahi* means a snake; *vyālī* and *bhujaṅgī* are names for a female serpent.
*Preṣyā*, *dāsī*, and *ceṭī* mean a servant girl or slave. *Darani* means a woman who causes fear. *Bibhiṣaṇa* is a name meaning "fear-inducing. *Ḍākinī* refers to a female demon (*rākṣasī*).

One should marry a woman whose limbs are unimpaired, who has a pleasing name, whose gait is like that of a swan or an elephant, and whose body hair, hair, and teeth are fine, and whose limbs are soft.
"Avyaṅgāṅgīm":

she whose limbs (*aṅgāni*) are not deficient (*avyaṅgāni*) is so called. Although the word *avyaṅga*—like words such as *pravīṇa* (skilled) or *udāra* (noble)—is etymologically derived as "one whose limbs are not deficient," nevertheless, because it is more appropriate for the second word *aṅga* to denote the whole (*avayavin*), the word *avyaṅga* expresses the perfection of the physical form (*saṃsthāna*).
"Gentle" means sweet;
herein, the ease with which women speak is demonstrated.
She walks like a swan or like an elephant.
Her gait was graceful and slow, like that of swans or elephants;
the word *tanu* does not mean "small," but rather refers to proportion. One is called *tanvaṅgī* ("slender-limbed") when she is neither too stout nor too thin.

She whose limbs are soft, pleasant to the touch, not hard, and not rough—such a woman he should marry; since the context concerns a maiden, he should marry a maiden. If this is so, then the prohibition beginning with "not hairless" is redundant, because by this very injunction, it is established that she who does not possess these qualities is unfit for marriage.
This is true;
however, when a single meaning is presented through both the mode of affirmation and the mode of negation, it is understood clearly.
Furthermore, in this context, the word "maiden" (kanyā) refers, by virtue of the subject matter, to women who have not experienced sexual intercourse.

And so Vasiṣṭha says: "One should marry a suitable wife who has not experienced sexual intercourse. Furthermore, a woman consecrated by one man cannot be consecrated again by another, because that which has already been performed cannot be performed again.

Therefore, even if a married woman whose union with her husband has not yet occurred becomes unchaste due to some circumstance such as her husband's absence abroad, there can be no marriage for her to another man, despite her still being technically a maiden.
Thus, this statement by Vasiṣṭha is recited in the middle [of the section];
it is also stated elsewhere: "One should marry a woman who has had no prior husband, who is younger than oneself, and who has brothers."
A prudent man should not marry a girl who has no brother or whose father is unknown, for fear that she may be a *putrikā* (an appointed daughter).
One should not marry her who has no brother,
due to the suspicion of her being an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), that is, due to the suspicion that she might be an appointed daughter; that is,
by this doubt or uncertainty that "perhaps the status of an appointed daughter was once established for her by her father."
And how does this doubt arise?
If it were not known whether the father had departed for another country or had died,
and she were given away by her mother or by the father’s sapindas.
It is recorded in the Smṛti that when the father is absent and the time has arrived, these [sons] must also give [the portion];
we shall demonstrate this Smṛti passage later.
However, while the father is still living, there is no suspicion regarding her status as an appointed daughter (*putrikā*).
For he himself said, "Whether it has been done or not," and the word *vā* (or) should be understood in the sense of *cet* (if). If the father is not known, then the maiden must not be married.
Others, however, declare that these two negations are independent:
"If the father were not known, she would be considered as one born of an unknown man"—this is a negation regarding a girl secretly born;
and such is the connection [of the text].
One should not marry a girl who has no brother, out of fear that she might be a *putrikā* (an appointed daughter).
The phrase "out of fear that she might be a *putrikā*" is not to be connected with the clause "it would not be known" (*na vijñāyeta*).

In this section, wherever there is no prohibition based on visible grounds—as in the verse beginning "and one who is not a *sapiṇḍa*"—if such a rule is transgressed, the very essence of the marriage is not accomplished.

Therefore, a marriage contracted with a woman of the same *gotra* and so forth, even if performed, is as good as not performed. This is because marriage, like the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires), consists in the comprehension of its injunctions; thus, it ceases to exist due to the transgression of its injunctions.

Just as in the injunction for the *ādhāna*, if any subsidiary element is not known, there is no production of the *āhavanīya* fire and the rest in its absence, so too, a woman of the same *gotra* does not attain the status of a wife.
Therefore, even that which merely resembles a sacrament performed for such [a woman] must be abandoned.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha and others prescribe expiation (*prāyaścitta*) even for such a marriage;

although the deficiency belongs to the rite itself due to the transgression of the prohibition regarding its constituent parts, rather than being a direct fault of the person, nevertheless, there is an expiation based on scriptural injunction.
Alternatively, approaching a woman of the same lineage (*sagotrā*) is prohibited;
if one engages in activity for that purpose, the penance (*prāyaścitta*) prescribed for it shall apply.

However, regarding the prohibition against those of deficient ritual status (*hīnakriyā*) and so forth, since its basis is the observation of visible worldly consequences, the marriage is nullified; she does not become his wife, and there is no abandonment of her.
Thus, for this very purpose, the phrase "even though they are great" is recited as a distinction from the preceding prohibition, for the sake of praise;
and such indeed is the practice of the learned:
one may sometimes marry a woman who is like Kapilā and so forth, but never one of the same lineage (sagotrā).
For the twice-born, a wife of the same caste is recommended for the rite of marriage;
however, for those who proceed out of desire, these following [wives] may be taken in descending order.

In the injunction "A twice-born man shall take a wife" (*udvaheta dvijo bhāryām*), although there is the use of the accusative case—which indicates that the wife is the primary object and that marriage is a subordinate act—the singular number is intended to be significant. This is because it is an *uddeśya* (the subject of a restatement) within an *anuvāda* (a restatement). Just as in the case of "He cuts the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ chinatti*), when something whose essential nature is already known from another source is restated elsewhere for the purpose of prescribing a different function, the restatement is made of that very thing exactly as its nature was previously understood; as in "He cleanses the house" (*gṛhaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*). This is because a restatement is dependent upon prior knowledge.

For the number of *grahas* (cups) is already known from such statements as, "The Adhvaryu takes these ten cups at the morning pressing," and their function is understood from the injunction, "He offers with the *grahas*. Therefore, because the word *graha* depends on this prior knowledge, its number is not intended to be significant. In the present case, however, the meaning defined as "wife" is not established by anything else and must be understood from this very sentence; therefore, it is perceived exactly as it is heard in the text. Just like the meaning of the nominal stem itself, the number is also intended to be significant.

This will be explained in detail through reasoning in the fifth [chapter]. When the intention to designate a number is established, even though the second marriage has been performed, there is no status of "wife," just as when the *āhavanīya* fire is already present, there is no second *āhavanīya*.
And since the taking of another wife is permitted under certain circumstances, this [section] is commenced for that purpose.
With this very intention, it is stated in the Gautama-sūtra: "If one's wife is endowed with both virtue and offspring, one should not take another; but in the absence of either one, one may do so.
"Savarṇā" means belonging to the same caste.
First of all, she is recommended as the primary choice for one who has not yet taken a wife of a different caste.

However, if after marrying a woman of the same caste, he by some chance finds no pleasure in her, or if his efforts toward procreation do not succeed, then—regarding activity motivated by desire—these women of the same caste who will be mentioned below are to be known from the scripture as superior alternatives.
Therefore, this constitutes an exception to the rule of having only one wife and the restriction to a wife of the same caste.
But surely, in the case of marriage with a woman of the same caste (*savarṇā*), dependence is understood;
it is not the plurality of women of the same caste that is intended.
At any rate, what is understood here is the transgression of the number one.
If [marriage] with a woman of a different class is permitted, who would prohibit [marriage] with a woman of the same class?
Likewise, Gautama has stated without qualification: "But when one of the two is lacking, he should perform [the rite].
Furthermore, in the subsequent verse, the phrase "she and his own" indicates that marriage with a woman of the same class exists.

A Śūdra woman alone is prescribed as a wife for a Śūdra; she and one of his own caste (svā) are prescribed for a Vaiśya; those two and one of his own caste for a Kṣatriya; and those three and one of his own caste for a Brāhmaṇa.

When there is a distinction of caste, there is a restriction regarding those of the same caste (*savarṇa*). Just as for a Brāhmaṇa, three [wives] beginning with the Kṣatriyā are permitted, so too for a Śūdra, women of lower birth such as washerwomen and carpenters would be obtained;
therefore, this rule concerning a wife of the same caste (*savarṇā*) is stated.
However, the woman of superior caste was not previously obtained because of the mention of the sequence;
she [the Śūdra] and his own [caste woman] belong to the Vaiśya,
and those two [the Vaiśya and the Śūdra] and his own [caste woman] belong to the Rājanya.
Thus, regarding the Brahmin as the first-born:

when an exposition ought to be made according to the sequence of the castes starting with the Brahmin, the exposition made by proceeding from the Śūdra serves to reinforce the very point previously stated—
that there is an option according to the order [of preference], and not necessarily a conjunction.
For it is taught that, even in times of distress, a Śūdra woman is never prescribed as a wife for either a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya, regardless of the circumstances.

Even if a Śūdra woman were exceedingly beautiful, and a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya were of heroic nature such that they might fall into even the tenth stage of life, nevertheless, they should not marry a Śūdra woman.
This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda).
In no account whatsoever—not even in any historical narrative or legend—is this ever taught or described.
"In a grave emergency" means in an excessive emergency.
Since it was permitted in the preceding case but prohibited by this [rule], there is an option (*vikalpa*).

Now, one might object: "An option is appropriate when two scriptural characteristics (*śāstralakṣaṇa*) coincide regarding a single subject, such as the taking or not taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup; however, it is not appropriate here, because [this rule] prohibits an activity characterized by passion (*rāga*)."
Furthermore, a Śūdra woman does not possess the characteristics prescribed by the scriptures;

rather, the meaning of the previous scripture is that engaging with her out of mere passion is not prohibited. However, since the prohibition concerns those characterized by the scriptures, a Śūdra woman is certainly not to be married.
Intending exactly this, Yājñavalkya stated: "That which is said regarding the acceptance of a Śūdra woman as a wife by the twice-born—that is not my opinion.
To this, it is replied:
In every case, an alternative is resorted to precisely because the instruction would otherwise be purposeless.

If there were an absolute prohibition against Śūdras, then only the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas would be subject to the counter-exception (pratiprasava) regarding permission in times of distress. Both the scriptural counter-exception and this prohibition would be rendered useless, since [the marriage with] a woman of the same caste (savarṇā) is already established by rule.
Thus, this permission and its prohibition are each mutually contradictory and must be considered as alternatives.
But surely, in the case of an alternative, there is freedom of choice;
and since that is established by the very fact of the counter-exception (*pratiprasava*), a prohibition need not even be stated.

The marriage of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya is not subject to such freedom of choice as that of a Śūdra woman; however, this is more serious except in times of distress (*āpad*). But it is proper to understand this: since the exclusion of non-similar-class women (*asavarṇā*) is effectively accomplished by the rule restricting [marriage] to one's own class (*savarṇā*), the subsequent exclusion of the Śūdra woman indicates that the exclusion of other non-similar-class women is not absolute. And because it is not absolute, this understanding arises—that in times of distress, or when a wife of the same class is unavailable, a Śūdra woman must not be married, while the others may be married.
Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry women of low birth,
quickly reduce their own families, along with their progeny, to the status of Śūdras.
This is a deprecatory explanatory statement (arthavāda) serving as a supplement to the preceding prohibition.
[The term] "low-born" refers specifically to the Śūdra, because she alone was the subject under discussion and because of the concluding statement, "they lead their lineages to the state of Śūdras.
These twice-born men, through delusion—that is, through lack of discernment born of greed for wealth or due to the influence of desire—cause their families to descend to the state of Śūdras.

The sons born of her are indeed Śūdras, as are their sons and grandsons; thus it is said that they are "with progeny. Progeny (saṃtāna) refers to the continuous succession of offspring, such as sons, grandsons, and so forth.
According to Atri and the son of Utathya, one who marries a Śūdra woman falls [from his caste];
according to Śaunaka, by the birth of a son; and according to Bhṛgu, by having offspring from her.

"He who finds a Śūdra woman"—that is, he who marries a Śūdra woman—"he falls," meaning he becomes as one fallen. "Atri, the son of Utathya"—the commentary (*upaskāra*) states that this is the opinion of those two. This half-verse, for its part, is a supplement to the preceding prohibition.
This is another treatise [intended] because of Śaunaka’s statement regarding the birth of a son;
having permitted approaching a Śūdra woman during her season, it prohibits such an act by stating that "the birth of a son occurs during the season on even nights."
The meaning is that one should not approach a Śūdra woman even during her fertile period;
this is because Bhṛgu was her offspring.
This, moreover, is another Smṛti text.
He whose offspring are those very children born of a Śūdra woman is called "one who has such offspring"; the state of being that is "having such offspring.
This is the opinion of Bhṛgu:
even during the fertile period (*ṛtu*), one may approach women who are more suitable for procreation, provided they have already borne children.

Furthermore, the mention of "fallenness" (*patitatva*) here is merely a form of censure and does not imply that he possesses the legal status of an outcaste (*patita*), such as [the rule] that water should be poured for one who has fallen;
this we shall explain later.
By taking a Śūdra woman onto his bed, a Brāhmaṇa goes to a low state;
by procreating a son upon her, he is indeed fallen from his Brāhmaṇahood.
This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).
If one procreates a son through her, he then falls from that very Brahminhood;
it is merely a censure, meaning that the offspring lacks the status of a Brahmin.

And because of the masculine designation in the word *sutaḥ*, even though there is phonetic coalescence (*samānasaṃhitā*) in the phrase *sutotpatter*, it is specifically the birth of a son (*putrotpatti*) that is intended;
this has been shown accordingly in the statement, "The even nights are to be avoided."
But for him whose rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests have that [greed] as their primary motive, neither the ancestors nor the gods will eat; he does not go to heaven.
This prohibition applies at all times.
Even if, for some reason, a Śūdra woman is married, these rites—of which she is the primary object—must not be performed.
Furthermore, the meaning is that there is no entitlement to perform religious duties (dharma) with her as there is with the women of the three higher castes.
Since she has obtained authority by virtue of being his wife, this is a prohibition;

therefore, for one who employs wealth for his own religious duty (*svadharma*), her permission is not required, as is the case with the wives of the twice-born. However, in matters other than those pertaining to religious duty—namely, in regard to wealth and pleasure—that permission must certainly not be disregarded.
The employment of her in those tasks is not prohibited as if she were a servant; thus, there would be no fault in having her perform duties such as threshing at a *śrāddha* ceremony and the like.
However, she must not be made to perform tasks such as serving food.
