In this context, "divine" (*daiva*) action refers to rites such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, as well as the feeding of Brahmins for the sake of the deities, as was explained under the rule regarding those observing a vow (*vratavat*).
"Pitrya" refers to ancestral rites such as the *śrāddha* and the libation of water (*udaka-tarpaṇa*).
"Ātitheya" refers to the honoring of a guest (*atithi*), including providing food, water for the feet, and so forth.
But is there not already a prohibition [against this] in the rule: "with another woman of the same caste who is present"?
Not at all;

for it is heard there [in the source text]: "By one who is established. This implies that when a woman of the same caste (*savarṇā*) is in her season (*ṛtumatī*) but somehow not present, the duty would otherwise apply as it does in the case of a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya wife.
Moreover, this is not a prohibition regarding eligibility; rather, it concerns the inspection of the clarified butter (*ājya*) and similar acts.
It is prescribed as a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) that "the clarified butter is to be inspected by the wife.
In the case of the word "wife," since it is established that for ritual purposes any woman who has been taken [as a wife] may be employed, there was previously an unrestricted application.
Just as [a rite] may be performed by any one of several wives of the same caste, this prohibition is for the purpose of ensuring that it is not performed even by one of a different caste.
Her preeminence is due to her being the authorized [wife].
The statement, "The ancestors and gods do not eat from him," expresses the fruitlessness of his ritual actions.
And he does not go to heaven;
even if a guest eats, the fruit thereof—such as heaven and so forth—does not accrue to him.

The mention of "heaven" is intended to indicate the fruit of honoring a guest, and it is a restatement of what has been said [in other texts] regarding [the act being] "conducive to wealth and fame," and so on.
For one who has drunk the saliva of a low-caste woman, for one who has been defiled by her breath,
and for one who has begotten a child upon her, no atonement is prescribed.
This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).

"Vṛṣalīphena" means the mouth-liquor of a low-caste woman (*vṛṣalī*); it refers to one by whom that has been drunk. The compound is analyzed with the final member placed first (*paranipāta*), as in the case of *palāṇḍubhikṣitā* ("one who begs for onions") and similar expressions.
Regarding the alternative reading *vṛṣalīpītaphenasya*: the analysis of the compound is "that whose foam has been drunk" (*pītaḥ pheno yasya*). Thus, it is *vṛṣalyā pītaphenaḥ*.
The compound is formed by the rule of *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) beginning with "the third case" (*tṛtīyā*).
In the analysis of the compound *pītaḥ pheno vānena* ("the foam was drunk by him"), there is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) with *vṛṣalyāḥ* ("of the low-caste woman").
However, the meaning remains the same across all types of compounds.

When two people are engaged in union, kissing the lower lip and so forth necessarily occurs; by means of that concomitant attribute (*sahacāridharma*), the connection to sexual intercourse (*maithuna*) is indicated.
Moreover, due to the context, this is a supplementary rule to the prohibition of marriage and not an independent statement;
for if it were an independent statement, the practice of *niyoga* (levirate) would be highly esteemed as being permissible except for kissing and the like.
Therefore, one who approaches a Śūdra woman while avoiding kissing and such acts does not transgress any point of the scriptural injunction.
And "of one born of her" means of one who approaches her during her fertile season;
"there is no expiation" means there is no purification—this is an expression of extreme censure.
Learn now, in brief, these eight forms of marriage for women among all four castes, which are beneficial or harmful both in this world and after death.
This is a brief introduction to what is about to be explained:
[factors] beneficial and non-beneficial; some are beneficial, while others are not.
"Eight" is the specification of the number;
"samāsaḥ" means a compendium;
"strīvivāhāḥ" refers to marriages for the purpose of consecrating a woman.
What, moreover, is this so-called marriage?

It is the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) performed for the purpose of making a girl—who has been obtained through the proper means—one's wife; it consists of the necessary procedures and constituent parts, culminating in the sight of the Seven Sages, and is characterized by the taking of the hand.
The Brāhma, the Daiva, as well as the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya, and the Āsura; the Gāndharva, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca is the eighth and lowest.
These are the names of those indicated as eight by number;
the mention of the "lowest" is for the purpose of censuring the Paiśāca form.
I shall declare to you all that which is the duty for each caste, as well as the virtues and faults belonging to each, and the merits and demerits regarding procreation.

"Dharmya" means not departing from dharma; that is to say, it is prescribed by the scriptures. And as for the "qualities and defects" of a particular marriage, they are so called because they are the causes of desirable and undesirable results. "In procreation" means in the birth of offspring.
Virtues are virtues, and faults are faults;
the burden-bearer alone possesses the virtues and faults characterized by heaven, hell, and so forth, while their purpose—the attainment of heaven and so on—follows as a matter of course.
Such indeed they are.
Even though the meaning has already been understood, they speak again for the sake of further comprehension.

One should know that for a Brahmin there are six [marriages] in the regular order, for a Kshatriya four [starting] from the lower ones, and for a Vaishya and a Shudra only those [same ones], which are lawful and not demonic.
There are six forms of marriage for a Brāhmaṇa in their proper sequence;
"sequence" means order, that is, the enumeration of names in successive order.
[The same applies] for a Kṣatriya.
The word *kṣatra* denotes the Kṣatriyas.
One should know that its four lower [forms of marriage]—the Āsura, Gāndharva, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca—are for them.
For the Vaiśyas and Śūdras, those same [forms] are prescribed, excluding the Rākṣasa.
The wise know that four of the first [forms of marriage] are recommended for a Brāhmaṇa;
the Rākṣasa alone for a Kṣatriya; and the Āsura for Vaiśyas and Śūdras.

This prohibition of the Āsura and Gāndharva forms applies to the Brāhmaṇa because of the prescription of the Brāhma and other forms for him. Likewise, for the Kṣatriya, only the Rākṣasa form is permitted, not the Gāndharva or Āsura;
for the Vaiśya and Śūdra, only the Āsura form is allowed.
There is an option (*vikalpa*) between those [forms of marriage] that are prescribed and those that are prohibited.

Consequently, when that which is prescribed as obligatory (*nityavat*) is absent, one may proceed with the optional ones. Furthermore, if a man were to engage in those acts both prescribed and prohibited immediately—without regard for the absence of the specifically prescribed form—the author of the treatise has shown that the man would incur fault and undesirable offspring would be produced, as indicated by the passage beginning "and the merits and demerits in the procreation. However, this does not mean the cessation of the essential nature of marriage itself, as is the case with marrying a *sapiṇḍa* relative.
Of these five, three are considered lawful and two unlawful in this world;
the Paiśāca and the Āsura forms should never be performed.
This Smṛti rule concerns Kṣatriyas and others, not Brāhmaṇas, because it would contradict [the rules] regarding the Rākṣasa form of marriage;
for a Brāhmaṇa ought not to perform killing or wounding, since this practice is logically applicable only to the domain of Kṣatriyas and others.
Among the five types of marriages, however, the three beginning with the Prājāpatya are lawful (dharmya).
Two [forms of marriage] must not be performed: the Paiśāca and the Āsura.
Although the Prājāpatya is not applicable to Kṣatriyas and others, it is prescribed for them; likewise, the Rākṣasa is prescribed for Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
This constitutes the prohibition of the Āsura and Paiśāca forms.
This is the established rule in this matter:

for a Brāhmaṇa there are six forms of marriage. Among them, the Brāhma form is the most excellent of all; inferior to that are the Daiva and Prājāpatya forms; even inferior to those is the Ārṣa; then the Gāndharva; and even inferior to that is the Āsura.

For those for whom this verse concerns only the Brāhmaṇa, they hold the view that even for a Rākṣasa marriage, it applies to a Brāhmaṇa who has settled into the conduct of a Kṣatriya; and even for one engaged in improper acts (vikarman), while he is subject to penance for killing or wounding, there is neither a Rākṣasa marriage nor a [prohibited] Vivāha. In that regard, the superiority of the Brāhma form is demonstrated by its very fruit.

The deficiency of the other three [castes] due to the absence of prohibition is established precisely by the statement regarding the reduction of the fruit. Furthermore, since the Āsura form is prescribed for Vaiśyas and Śūdras, it is understood as an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) for Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas;
moreover, the injunction "six" is a positive prescription (*vidhāna*).
Therefore, it is conceptual construction;
and that [construction] occurs by way of conventional determination.
Its reliance [on such determination] is equal, since no other possibility exists.

For an option (*vikalpa*) is established here just as in the case of rice and barley, precisely because a combination (*samuccaya*) is impossible due to the prescription of multiple forms of marriage.

Even if a combination were possible and it were performed accordingly, such [a marriage] would yield inferior results in terms of both merit (*dharma*) and offspring. Furthermore, for a Kṣatriya, the Rākṣasa form is primary, since it is prescribed as an option through four verses.
By the phrase "four [forms]," the Asura, Gāndharva, and Paiśāca forms are also included; however, by the rule "the Rākṣasa is the one for a Kṣatriya," these are prohibited.

Therefore, they are optional alternatives, not primary forms. Furthermore, because the context is dependent on the subject at hand, the injunction regarding the single Rākṣasa form applies specifically to that case.
Regarding the Prājāpatya form, there is no specific enumeration [of its prohibition];
therefore, even for a Kṣatriya, the Prājāpatya is equal to the Rākṣasa.
Likewise, for Vaiśyas and Śūdras as well, the Prājāpatya is traditionally prescribed as a constant rule and is not prohibited.
The Āsura and Paiśāca forms, however, are both prescribed and prohibited for them.
The Rākṣasa form is prohibited by the rule "not for those who are not Rākṣasas," while it is prescribed by the rule "three are lawful.
For a Brāhmaṇa, the Paiśāca form does not exist at all; for Kṣatriyas and others, the Brāhma, Daiva, and Ārṣa forms are established as permissible.
Whether performed separately or combined, the two forms of marriage previously mentioned—
the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa— are recorded as lawful for the Kṣatriya.
The phrase "separately" is a restatement (*anuvāda*), since this has already been established by the preceding [text].
The term "mixed" (*miśrau*) is what is being enjoined (*vidhīyate*), because the other two forms, the Gāndharva and Rākṣasa, have been prescribed as independent [of one another].
This statement regarding mixing is made because it was not otherwise obtained, just like the case of rice and barley (*vrīhi-yava*).

In the injunction "one should sacrifice with rice" or "with barley," there is an option (*vikalpa*) because two substances are prescribed independently of one another as being applicable to the performance of a single sacrifice; it is not a case of mixing.
For if there were mixing, neither the purpose of the scriptural rule regarding rice nor the purpose of the scriptural rule regarding barley would have been fulfilled.
Likewise, in this case, when a single girl is to be accepted, two means that were previously unestablished are simultaneously prescribed.

Its scope is as follows: when a maiden is in her father’s house and, having somehow come within the range of his vision while he is there, she is described by a female messenger and likewise falls in love with him, yet being dependent on others, she does not obtain union; then, having made an agreement with the suitor, she causes herself to be led away, saying, "Lead me from here by whatever means possible. If he, through his superior skill, carries her off by killing and cutting [her relatives], then this constitutes the *gāndharva* form insofar as there is a mutual union by desire, and it constitutes the *rākṣasa* form insofar as there is "killing and cutting."
These two marriages belong only to the Kṣatriya;
this is a restatement that those two are lawful for the Kṣatriya as previously enjoined.
Others, however, say: when a Kṣatriya enters into many marriages, he may marry one by the Gāndharva rite and another by the Rākṣasa rite; this is the view concerning mixed forms.
Alternatively, the phrase "all [women] by either one" refers to each [class] individually;

by this it is understood that for a Kṣatriya, there is no restriction regarding these two [classes], whereas among the Prājāpatya and other forms of marriage, she must marry with the same class as the one he first married.
Now he states their essential nature:
"Having covered [the girl] and having honored her, and having invited a man of learning and good character himself, the giving away of a daughter is proclaimed as the Brāhma rite."
"Having clothed him":
what is intended is a specific kind of clothing, since other [clothing] is already obtained by its very nature;
that is, having caused him to be dressed in an excellent garment, according to the place, according to possibility, and with a cloth appropriate [to the occasion].
"Having honored" means having performed worship with special affection and special hospitality by means of these ornaments, such as bracelets, earrings, and so forth.
By this act of clothing and honoring, since there is no authoritative evidence for the connection of either the bride or the groom [alone], the benefit must be applied to both.
To one who possesses learning and virtuous conduct;
furthermore, other excellent qualities mentioned in another Smṛti should be observed: "He should be young, wise, beloved by the people, and carefully examined regarding his virility."
When one has not previously requested [the bride's hand],
but having invited her by sending one's own men, brings her to one's presence and gives a bride-price,
that gift is the Brāhma dharma marriage.
Although the word *dharma* is non-specific in its denotation, it must be understood here as referring specifically to that [marriage] because of the preceding context.

The definition is that the *brāhma* marriage consists of obtaining a wife without asking for her, preceded by honoring [the bridegroom]. Now, one might object: "Is it not improper to say that marriage has the purpose of taking a woman [as a wife]?"
This gift extends up to the point of marriage;
the purpose of the gift does not cease before the marriage is performed,
for that indeed is the time for her formal acceptance.
Furthermore, giving is not completed in the absence of acceptance;
giving is not merely the cessation of one's own ownership,
for it extends until the attainment of ownership by another.
And so he will say: "The completion of those [rites] should be known by the wise at the seventh step.
Thus, the maiden must be given away at the very time of the marriage ceremony.

Accordingly, the author of the Gṛhyasūtra demonstrates the ritual procedure (*kāṇḍikadharma*) for the Brāhma marriage at that very time. As for the giving [of the girl] prior to the marriage, that is merely a statement of formal agreement (*upasaṃvādana*).
For if that [agreement] is not made, the completion of the marriage at the intended time is not certain;
someone might not give what was previously stipulated, or the other might perhaps not accept it.
Therefore, before the marriage, a formal agreement must be made: "This girl shall be given by you, and she shall be taken by me."

Just as an internal sacrifice (*antaḥkratu*), which possesses its own auxiliary elements and whose purpose is established even without being explicitly enjoined, is excluded from the category of external rites by implication; so too, those who maintain that— just as the gift of a substance such as a cow, when given for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), is accomplished through a reception preceded by a mantra, and it is for this reason that it was stated "and likewise in the case of duties consisting of giving"—
hold that here marriage stands in the place of the mantra of reception.
And thus, "taking in hand" (upayamana) and "marriage" (vivāha) have the same meaning; and "taking in hand" is the act of making one's own.
For the venerable Pāṇini indeed records this traditional rule: "The root *yam* with the prefix *upa* is used in the sense of making one's own."
Therefore, marriage is for the purpose of taking a maiden [as a wife].
That is incorrect;
for marriage is for the purpose of making one who has already been taken a wife.
There is no injunction stating that one should accept [the bride] by means of this ritual act;

nor are the marriage mantras of the nature of formulas for acceptance, such as the mantras "I accept you with the impulse of the god" (*devasya tvā pragṛhṇāmi*). As for the statement "by his own hand," that is not contradictory.
Marriage, too, has the nature of being its own cause;
for while ownership in general is established through the act of giving, it is through marriage that a specific form of ownership is created.
This is not "property" (*sva*) in the same sense as cattle or other goods, which can be employed according to one's will; rather, it is [ownership] by virtue of her being a wife (*jāyātvena*).

For the relationship characterized by husband and wife is indeed a specific form of the master-servant relation; and so [the author] will demonstrate later: "In marriages, the giving away for the sake of auspiciousness and well-being is the cause of ownership."
When a sacrifice has been properly extended and the officiating priest performs his duty,
the giving away of a daughter after she has been adorned is declared to be the divine (daiva) rite.

In an extensive sacrifice such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, once the ritual procedure has been commenced, the giving of a daughter to the officiating priest (ṛtvij), specifically the Adhvaryu, who has performed the rites for her sake;
the phrase "having adorned" is a restatement (anuvāda), because every form of giving a maiden is of this nature.
This is a general injunction: "Having clothed and adorned [the girl], one should cause her to be wed."
But surely, it is heard in scripture that a cow, a horse, a mule, and so forth, are given as sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests;
nowhere, however, is the giving of a maiden enjoined as being for the sake of the sacrifice. What, then, is the relevance here of "being for the sake of the sacrifice"?

When a sacrifice has commenced, that which one gives to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is the *daiva* form of marriage. Furthermore, there is the scent of a reciprocal service in its performance; for even when given without reference to a specific task, it certainly produces a particular inference regarding the inclination to perform that task for one who is engaged in it.
On account of this degree of connection through assistance, the divine [marriage] is inferior to the Brahma [marriage].
Having taken one or two pairs of cattle from the bridegroom according to the law,
the giving of the daughter according to the prescribed rule is called the Ārṣa rite.
A cow and a bull constitute a pair;
having accepted one or two from the bridegroom, the giving away of the girl is the Ārṣa rite. This is the law (dharma).
This is simply a matter of dharma; one should not entertain the notion of a sale here, because there is no repayment of high or low interest—this is the intended meaning.
Having addressed the couple with the words, "May you both perform dharma together," and having honored them, the bestowal of the maiden is recorded as the Prājāpatya rite.
The *prājāpatya* [form of marriage] is that gift which is made after establishing a formal agreement (*paribhāṣā*) and binding [the couple] with the words, "Dharma must be practiced by both of you.
The mention of "dharma" is intended as an illustration;
the meaning of this statement of agreement is that there shall be a commonality of purpose and security regarding dharma, artha, and kāma.
Only the word *dharma* is uttered as "let [you] perform dharma together," but not "let [you] perform dharma, wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*) together.
However, that word *dharma* is explained as being intended to indicate (*upalakṣaṇa*) both wealth and pleasure by virtue of other legal codes (*smṛti*).

If one does not transgress her in matters of dharma, wealth, and pleasure, then she is given to you; thus, at the time of marriage, for one who has made a compact and accepted its terms, the formula "let [you] perform dharma together" should be recited precisely during that giving.
Although the joint performance of wealth (*artha*) and pleasure (*kāma*) is intended, it is not mentioned because it is not the subject under discussion.
Thus says Gautama: "In the *prājāpatya* rite, let them perform their duty together.
By the inclusion of the word "mantra," he shows that the form [of the ritual] as prescribed for the qualified person must be employed, just like a mantra.

Indeed, it is not appropriate to criticize the concordance of Great Beings regarding their desire for the welfare [of others], for this is understood from other Smṛtis. By this very agreement, there is no deficiency in him due to fault;
for here, there exists on the part of the donor a desire for benefit through his own excellence.

This statement is expressed by its own word (*svaśabda*); however, this is not a restriction of the speech solely to the giver. Since the requirement is already established by the word "having repeated" (*anubhāṣya*), the word "speech" (*vāk*) would be redundant, because the organ of speech is the instrument for repetition. Thus, the author of the *Gṛhya-sūtra* says: "Having said, 'This is the truth for you,' he should cause the bridegroom to say, 'This is the truth for us.'"
And the word "anu" expresses the ascertainment of that very object which has already been reached by speech.
Having given wealth to the kinsmen and to the bride herself according to one's ability,
the giving away of the daughter at one's own will is called the Āsura dharma.

The Āsura marriage consists of giving the woman’s property to the girl’s kinsmen—such as her father and others—and to the girl herself, and then taking the girl away; it is called "taking" (*ānayana*) because she is given away.
By the phrase "out of one's own will" (*svācchandyāt*), meaning out of one's own desire and not according to the scriptures, he indicates its distinction from the Ārṣa form;
for in that case, there is a scriptural restriction, namely, "one pair of cattle."
In this case, however, the choice depends on qualities such as the maiden's beauty and good fortune.
The mutual union of the maiden and the groom through their own desire is to be known as the Gāndharva marriage; it is based on sexual union and arises from passion.
And by "will" is meant the union through mutual desire and the coming together in one place of the man and the maiden;
this is its censure: "arising from sexual intercourse. That which has sexual intercourse as its purpose is *maithuna*; that which is conducive to it is *maithunya*.
This very point has been made clear by the term *kāmasaṃbhava*.
"Source" (*saṃbhava*) means that from which something arises;
thus, it is called *kāmasaṃbhava* because desire is its source.
The forcible abduction of a maiden from her home while she is crying out and weeping, after having killed, wounded, or broken down [her defenses], is called the Rākṣasa rite.
What is intended here is simply that the abduction of a maiden from her family by force, having overcome them by violence, constitutes the Rākṣasa form of marriage;
the words "having killed" and so forth are merely descriptive restatements (*anuvāda*).
If someone who intends to carry her away by force encounters resistance, then the acts of killing and so on necessarily follow.

If, having recognized the extraordinary power of the slayer, they were to remain indifferent out of fear for their own lives, then he would indeed become a *rākṣasa*; in that case, killing and so forth must necessarily be performed—
having killed him with a wooden staff or the like, or having struck him,
or having cut his limbs into pieces with blows from a sword or similar weapon.
Having broken through walls, fortresses, and the like,
[he takes] a maiden who is crying out and weeping and is unwilling;
this is the distinction from the Gāndharva [form of marriage].
Crying out loudly with words such as "I am being carried off by one who has no protector! Save me! constitutes *krośana*.
Weeping is the shedding of tears.
This is the duty for a woman who is terrified.
When one approaches a woman in secret while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged,
that most sinful form of marriage is known as the Paiśāca, the lowest of all.
The lack of consent is equal for both the Rākṣasa and the Paiśāca forms;
in the Rākṣasa, there is killing, while in the Paiśāca, there is deception.
"Asleep" means overcome by sleep.
One who approaches a woman who is intoxicated, drunk, under the sway of liquor,
or distracted and deprived of her senses by a fit of wind,
in secret and out of view, engaging in sexual intercourse— this is the *paiśāca* marriage; it is the most wicked of all marriages and a cause of sin.
From that, a legitimate offspring (dharmāpatya) is not produced.

Here, because the Gāndharva, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca [forms] share grammatical coreferentiality with the term "marriage" (*vivāha*) as their primary sense, it is held that these are merely unions through abduction or voluntary approach, independent of the sacramental rite of taking the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa-saṃskāra*).
For them, even in the case of the Brāhma and other [forms], because of the coreferentiality between "giving" (*dāna*) and "marriage," the sacramental rite is excluded.
And how it does not cease has been shown accordingly.

By way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the word "marriage" (*vivāha*) is used for the giving away [of a girl] for the purpose of marriage. However, regarding the *gāndharva* form, it was described by the Blessed One Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana in the union of Duṣyanta and Śakuntalā as being "without fire and without mantras. From that observation, it follows that while the sacramental rite of taking the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa-saṃskāra*) exists, it is devoid of mantras and so forth.
Regarding the Paiśāca form, however, there is disagreement as to whether it is primarily an act of approaching [the woman];
yet her status as a maiden (*kanyātva*) does not depart, because that is removed by the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*).

Consequently, since the prohibition—"the mantras of taking the hand are established only for maidens"—does not apply here, there certainly exists a connection with the sacramental rites accompanied by mantras.
And that prohibition was made for the purpose of prohibiting [the marriage of] a consecrated girl (*saṃskāra*);
for she, having been consecrated by mantras, has lost her status as a maiden (*akanyā*).
Therefore, let there first be sexual intercourse; after that, there is no fault of marrying a non-maiden.

And thus we have the view that Karṇa was born of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*). For if maidenhood were lost through sexual intercourse with a man, how could this linguistic expression—"the son of an unmarried girl is *kānīna*"—be possible? However, if "unmarried girl" (*kanyā*) refers to one who has not undergone the sacramental rites (*asaṃskṛtā*), then it is logical that Karṇa and others are the sons of an unmarried woman.

If it is argued that, according to the primary interpretation, the possibility of procreation from a maiden exists—since marriage with such a woman is described in the Itihāsas and other texts—then one might ask: what is the purpose of the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) once the connection of sexual pleasure has already been accomplished through intoxication by liquor and the like?
To this, it is replied:

Even though the status of being a woman or a man has ceased and the prohibition against approaching a maiden has been transgressed, nevertheless, the performance of the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) is for the sake of establishing a joint entitlement with her; furthermore, it is performed so that approaching her would not constitute "approaching a maiden" [in a technical sense].
This marriage is censured as being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) due to its connection with the transgression of the prohibition against approaching a maiden.
That is incorrect.

For in the world, this word "kanyā" (maiden) denotes a woman who has not had sexual intercourse with a man, regardless of whether she depends on the state of having undergone sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*). Even those whose virginity has been violated by men are not designated as "maidens," even if they have not yet received the sacraments.
Furthermore, there is no offense of violating a maiden (*kanyāgamana*) in approaching those women who have taken up residence in brothels.

Although the words *kumārī* and *kanyā* are intended to denote the first stage of life, nevertheless, in the context of marriage rites, they refer specifically to a woman who has not yet been enjoyed by another.

Thus, when one requests as a wife a girl wearing the dress of a maiden (*kumāra*) whose sexual intercourse with a man has not become publicly known, others understand her to be "not a *kumārī*" because her maidenhood (*kaumāra-bhāva*) has perished;
furthermore, there would be a loss of the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*).

For the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite) must indeed be performed with the recitation of mantras, such as "May Viṣṇu prepare the womb. But it is impossible to perform the preparation of what has already been prepared; in that case, the application of the mantra would be non-factual (*ayathārtha*). Furthermore, there is no application of mantras for an unmarried woman in the *paiśāca* form of marriage, because the hearing of those [mantras] is prescribed for one who is married.
Furthermore, it is not logical to assume that [sexual intercourse] is prescribed for marriages other than the Paiśāca form, because no such distinction is heard in the texts.
Therefore, many such defects follow if one adopts the view that "approaching" (upagama) refers to actual sexual intercourse.

Consequently, the root *gam* preceded by the prefix *upa* should be understood as referring to activities aimed at sexual union—such as embracing, hugging, and kissing—due to their association with and purposefulness toward that end.

As for the statement "the son born of an unmarried girl" (*kānīna*), since the primary meaning is impossible there, it is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as referring to the absence of sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*).
As for the observation of sacramental rites, that occurs only in certain cases;

even though it is said, "she who is consecrated while pregnant, whether her condition be known or unknown," in that case, he who was the one who approached [the woman] is not the one who performs the consecration.
But this is not the Paiśāca form of marriage;

for in the Paiśāca rite, she is given to the very man by whom she was enjoyed, and he alone performs her consecration. However, the consecration of a pregnant bride is based solely on scriptural injunction.
And all of this will be explained more precisely again in the ninth [chapter].
Others think that "approaching" (*upagamana*) is primary; for if it were not primary, the prohibition against "going" (*gamana*) would be untenable.
For if approaching were primary, then that alone would constitute marriage, since there is no other [form of marriage] due to the reasoning just stated.
Consequently, there is no scope for that prohibition, because [the following occurs]: through mutual desire the Gāndharva form arises, by force the Rākṣasa, and otherwise the Paiśāca.
There is no other mode by which that prohibition could have its scope.
However, it does have a scope: where there is a forcible approach in secret, or where a girl is given away by her parents but not consecrated with the sacred rites.
Nor is this [act] Gāndharva, because there is an absence of the maiden's consent;
for that very reason, even the husband does not have the status of one who approaches a maiden, since another object [of desire] is possible.

Therefore, because the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) is prohibited for one whose virginity is destroyed, because it serves as a means just like the Brāhma and other forms [of marriage], and because the term "marriage" (*vivāha*) is applicable therein just as in those cases, the meaning of "approaching" (*upagama*)—by virtue of the force of the context—is indeed figurative.
And the distinction among these is as follows: that which is obtained unasked, like land, gold, and so forth, is *brāhma*;
that which is distinguished by the status of being a priest (*ṛtvij*) is *daiva*; and that which is [obtained] with a pair of cattle is *ārṣa*.
The *prājāpatya* form [of marriage] is established by the rule of the scriptural statement: "Let both of them practice dharma together, whether with or without solicitation.
The remaining types are easily understood through their distinctions.
The secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix in words such as *brāhma* is used in the sense of "for this purpose" (*arthe*).
And the connection with Brahmā and others is superimposed for the sake of praise;
this applies to all [the other classes] as well.
"This Paiśāca [language] is fit for Piśācas"—this is a censure.
For the foremost of the twice-born, the giving away of a daughter with water alone is distinguished as the best;
for the other castes, however, it is by mutual desire.
Regarding the gift of a daughter to the foremost of the twice-born—the Brāhmaṇas—it is praised that the gift is made with water alone when one gives a daughter.
When one gives a daughter to a Brāhmaṇa, then one should give her with water alone.
But how, then, is water the instrument of the gift?
For there is no giving without those [waters]; indeed, one gives the gift of alms preceded by the word "namaḥ" with water.
This is because of the rule regarding such matters.
Alternatively, by the restrictive phrase "only with water," he excludes the Ārṣa, Āsura, and Prājāpatya forms of marriage.
For in that case, water alone is not the cause; rather, there is also the taking of property such as a pair of cattle, as well as the formal agreement (*saṃvit*).
By this, the following is meant:

just as when property such as a cow or gold is given, nothing is stipulated—such as "this cow must be tended by you alone" or "such grasses must also be provided"—so too a daughter may be given; one should not require the son-in-law to enter into a stipulation out of affection for his daughter.
"And wealth should not be accepted from him.

However, in the case of Kṣatriyas and others, if there is a mutual desire—that is, a reciprocal longing—between the bride and the groom, then the giving should be performed; otherwise, it is not so, as in the case of the Brāhma marriage.
Others, however, explain [it differently].
"Or having taken wealth, or even with water alone"—this is for the purpose of mutual desire.
In this view, it is made known that the Brāhmaṇa's [authority] extends to all subjects.
O Brahmins, listen as I correctly proclaim all the specific qualities of these marriages that have been declared by Manu for each of them.
He recalls what was stated [previously]: "And those which are the merits and defects of each.

Since many [topics] were promised to be discussed, this restatement is appropriate for the sake of specific knowledge, indicating that "this matter is being stated by means of the verses to be recited therein.
In the phrase "of these marriages," the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).
"Thus, O Brahmins, listen to all those qualities of each marriage that have been proclaimed by the teacher Manu.
Bhṛgu addresses the great sages:
'Proclaim them correctly, without error, and without confusion.'"
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman who has performed meritorious deeds liberates ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first from sin.
The ancestors of the lineage are the father, grandfather, and so forth;
the descendants are the son, grandson, and so forth.
He liberates them from sin—that is, he delivers them from the torments of hell and other such states.
A son born of a wife wedded according to the *brāhma* rite— if he is a doer of good deeds and a performer of meritorious acts—
[delivers] the ancestors who have gone to the other world;
for this word "father" (*pitṛ*) is a synonym for the deceased (*preta*), since the designation "father" cannot otherwise apply to the lineage of sons and so forth.
The word "ten" is connected with each of the words "prior" and "subsequent," because of the designation "twenty-first.
Furthermore, this is an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda);
therefore, one should not ask how it liberates those who have not yet come or those who have not yet arisen.
However, for ancestors, liberation from sin certainly occurs through auspicious acts such as *śrāddha* performed by their descendants; this will be explained in the section on *śrāddha*.
Therefore, what is meant by the statement "he liberates ten generations from sin" is that ten persons in a family are born free from sin—this is the intended basis.
A son born of a woman married according to the Daiva rite delivers seven generations of ancestors and seven of descendants;
a son born of a woman married according to the Ārṣa rite delivers three of each; and a son born of a woman married according to the Kāya (Gāndharva) rite delivers six of each.
One who is married according to the divine rite is "divinely wedded" (daivoḍhā); born of her is "born of a divinely wedded woman" (daivoḍhāja);
a son (suta) is a male child (putra).
Who is Prajāpati?
He is the deity of that marriage which is called *kāya*.
Although there is no actual connection with a deity in the sacramental rite characterized by the taking [of the hand], the status of being a deity is figuratively attributed to Prajāpati.
Furthermore, although there is a sacrifice to Prajāpati in that context, it is common to all forms of marriage and is not the cause for the designation "Kāya.
Moreover, there would be no application [of this term] to the Āsura and other [inferior marriages],
for there is no sacrifice associated with Āsura marriages.
In the term *kāyoḍha*, the shortening [of the vowel] occurs according to the rule: "The forms *ṅī* and *āp* are frequently shortened in technical names (*saṃjñā*) and in Vedic meters (*chandas*).
Now, it might be objected: whatever yields a lesser fruit is mentioned later;
therefore, it would be more appropriate for the *ārṣa* [offspring] to be mentioned after the *prājāpatya*.
There is a reason why the Prājāpatya rite, which yields a superior result, is mentioned later;
for in the rule "of the five, three are lawful," the inclusion of the Prājāpatya is intended, otherwise it would refer to the Ārṣa.
In the four forms of marriage beginning with the Brāhma, sons endowed with Vedic luster and esteemed by the learned are born in due order.
It was stated that "at the time of procreation, [one considers] merits and demerits";
this very point is expressed by the authors of the Smṛtis using the term *anupūrvaśaḥ*, meaning "in successive order.
Furthermore, *brahmavarcasa* refers to honor and renown resulting from the excellence of sacred learning, study, and realization.
Those who possess these qualities are endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*).
This word ends in the suffix *-in*. They are approved and authorized by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), beyond reproach, and not hated—that is to say, beloved.

And therefore, because [the word *mati*] does not have "understanding" (*mati*) as its meaning, it does not fall within the scope of the rule *matibuddhi-*, nor is there a prohibition of compounding by the rule *ktena ca pūjāyām*.
Furthermore, when a general relationship is intended to be expressed, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is employed.
Endowed with beauty, virtue, and excellence, wealthy and renowned,
possessing abundant enjoyments and most righteous, they live for a hundred years.
Form (*rūpa*) is a captivating appearance;
essence (*sattva*), which is a quality (*guṇa*), will be explained in the twelfth [chapter]. "Endowed with these" means possessed of both of them.
The wealthy are those possessing riches; the famous are those renowned for their endowment with qualities such as learning and heroism;
those with sufficient enjoyments are those constantly provided with an abundance of the means of pleasure, such as garlands, ointments, song, and instrumental music.

"Bhoga" (enjoyment) is non-separation from the previously mentioned means of happiness; those who possess such enjoyment in its entirety—complete, unimpaired, and full—are "paryāptabhogāḥ" (those with sufficient enjoyments).
Those intent on the practice of dharma are "dharmiṣṭhāḥ" (the most virtuous).
For some, the word "dharma" is a term denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*).
Therefore, from this word expressing a quality, the suffix of excellence (*ātiśāyika*) is applied:
"they live for a hundred years."
But among the remaining [prohibited] types of marriages, sons who are cruel, speakers of untruth,
and haters of the Veda and Dharma are born.
Regarding marriages other than the *brāhma* and others—namely the *gāndharva* and so forth—those who speak cruelly and untruthfully are called "speakers of cruelty and untruth.
"Cruelty" (*nṛśaṃsa*) refers to vulgar and abusive speech directed toward one's mother, sister, and others;
"untruth" (*anṛta*) is well known.

*Nṛśaṃsānṛte* means cruelty and falsehood; the etymology of the word refers to those whose habit it is to speak such things. *Brahmadharma* means the duty of the Veda, that is, the meaning of the Veda; they hate, revile, or do not have faith in that.
For this very reason, there is the censure: "in ill-considered marriages."
Through blameless marriages with women, one's offspring become blameless; through blameworthy ones, they become blameworthy among men. Therefore, one should avoid those who are blameworthy.
This is a brief demonstration of the results of the various forms of marriage.

Those marriages which are prescribed for a particular person are "blameless" (anindita); the offspring—characterized as sons and so forth—of those who have married according to these [forms] becomes blameless, meaning it is praiseworthy.
By means of "blameworthy" (nindita) ones—that is, those that are prohibited—the offspring becomes blameworthy, meaning censurable.
Therefore, one should avoid censurable actions so that one's offspring may not be partakers of suffering.
The sacramental rite of taking the hand (pāṇigrahaṇa) is prescribed for women of the same caste;
this following rule is to be known for the marriage ceremony when the castes are different.

What is called "taking the hand" (pāṇigrahaṇa) is a sacramental rite (saṃskāra) prescribed by the authors of the Gṛhya-sūtras; it is taught, ordained, and established as something to be performed in the case of women of the same caste (savarṇā) being married. Regarding the act of marriage with women of a different caste (asavarṇā), the following rule shall be understood to apply.
An arrow should be grasped by a Kṣatriya woman, a goad by a Vaiśya maiden,
and the hem of a garment by a Śūdra woman when marrying a man of higher caste.

A Kṣatriya woman being led by a Brāhmaṇa should take hold of an arrow held in the Brāhmaṇa’s hand, because the taking of an arrow is prescribed in place of the taking of the hand. A goad is the instrument used to cause exertion in oxen, by which they are pained while being driven, just as the elephant-goad is for elephants. A Śūdra woman should take hold of the fringe of the garment.
By those of superior caste, such as the Brahmin and other castes, in the matter of learning [the Vedas] and marriage.
He should approach his wife during her fertile period, always remaining devoted to his own wife; observing that vow, he may go to her out of a desire for pleasure, except on the forbidden lunar days.
Marriage has been described.

Once it is completed and the status of wifehood has been attained, since the possibility arises that one might approach her by one's own desire on that very day, this [rule] is commenced to prevent that:
one should not go to her immediately after the marriage on that very day; rather, one should wait for the time of her season (*ṛtukāla*).
The authors of the Gṛhyasūtras, however, have stated that from this point forward, the two shall eat food free from pungent salt, remain celibate, and sleep on the ground— either for three nights,
twelve nights, or a year. In that regard,
even if the period of a year has elapsed, there is no sexual intercourse during the intervening fertile season.
Thus, from this time forward, there is no approaching [the wife] except during her season;
in this way, these two Smṛtis are not in conflict.

However, regarding the three-night period and so forth, there is an option: those who are intensely tormented by passion may engage in sexual union, whereas those who possess self-control must observe celibacy.

*Ṛtu* is defined as a specific state of the female body characterized by the appearance of menstrual blood, a period capable of conceiving a fetus; and because "appearance" is used figuratively, even when this [blood] has ceased, it remains subject to the time-periods to be described hereafter. The time of that [period] is called *ṛtukāla*.
Alternatively, by association, the season (*ṛtu*) is simply time (*kāla*).
Thus, there is a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇasamāsa*):
one whose vow is to approach [his wife] during the season is "one who approaches during the season" (*ṛtukālābhigāmī*).
The suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of "vowed to" (*vrata*), as in "one who sleeps on the bare ground" (*sthaṇḍilaśāyī*) or "one who does not eat at a funeral feast" (*aśrāddhabhojī*).

The meaning of *syāt* is "should be" (*bhavet*). Although the injunctive suffix (*vidhivibhakti*) is directed toward the verb "to be" (*asti*), it nevertheless establishes the operation of approaching; thus, "he should be one who approaches" (*abhigāmī syāt*) means "he should approach" (*abhigacchet*).
For one who does not approach [his wife] cannot be considered an "approacher. But what kind of vow is this?
Is it that one must necessarily approach her during the fertile period (*ṛtu*), or rather that one must approach her only during the fertile period?
This is what is being said: Is this a restrictive rule (*niyama*) or an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*)?
But surely, according to the treatises, a "vow" (*vrata*) is called a restrictive rule.
And since this suffix *ṇini* occurs in that very context, how can a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*) be suspected? It is said in reply:
We shall demonstrate that even in the case of *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification), there exists both scriptural authority and the nature of a restriction (*niyama*).
What, then, is the distinction between these two? A restriction (*niyama*) is a specific type of injunction (*vidhi*).
Now, what is an injunction (*vidhi*)? It is a word that makes known something to be performed (*kartavyatā*), such as: "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra.
For, without this statement, there is no way to understand that the Agnihotra is to be performed from any other source whatsoever.
Restriction (*niyama*), moreover, is that where there is an optional possibility [of performance] without a statement for the sake of establishing the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
For example, in the injunction "one should sacrifice on level ground," only a location in general is implied by the prescription of sacrifices such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices;
for the performance of a sacrifice is not possible without resorting to some location.
And place is of two kinds: level and uneven.
When one should sacrifice on a level place, then this statement is merely a restatement (anuvāda).

But when, due to the unrestrained nature of desire, one wishes to sacrifice on an uneven place, then this statement is purposeful as it enjoins a level place; for once a level place has been enjoined, an uneven place is not resorted to, because it was not enjoined.
By implication, there is the cessation of that [unauthorized act].
For when performance is based on an injunction, why would one perform what is not enjoined? Indeed, if one were to do so, the accomplishment of the performance as prescribed would not be achieved.
And here is an example from the Smṛti:
"One should eat food facing the east.
This implies that for one who is eating, eating occurs by chance while resorting to whichever direction may happen to be present.
In that regard, sometimes the east is reached and sometimes another direction;
for when the east is reached, the other is not, and when the other is reached, the east is not.
Thus, regarding the position of not being reached [by the sun], the statement "one should eat food facing the east" is spoken for the purpose of an injunction.
In that regard, by transgressing [the rule], one abandons the purpose of the scripture (*śāstrārtha*).

Thus, in this case, approaching [one's wife] according to one's own whim rather than during the fertile period (*ṛtu*), or failing to perform the approach which is prescribed as an option, would result in the violation of the scripture.
Just as other matters ordained by the scripture become causes for penance when they are transgressed, so too is the failure to follow the prescribed approach.

Now, when approaching [one's wife] during the fertile season (*ṛtu*) or outside the fertile season (*anṛtu*) occurs through the impulse of passion (*rāga*), there is the injunction: "One should approach her during the fertile season. In that case, the following restriction is sought: "One should approach her only during the fertile season and should not go to her outside the fertile season.

Just as in the rule "five five-nailed animals are edible," although the state of being edible applies by implication to five-nailed animals such as the hare for the purpose of satisfying hunger, it would also apply by extension to others such as monkeys;
yet in that case, the application does not occur indiscriminately.

When there is a simultaneous possibility of application both there and elsewhere, the statement "five five-nailed animals are edible" results in a restriction (parisaṃkhyā) for the purpose of excluding others; such is the case here. Now, is it not said that restriction possesses three defects?
For three defects would arise there: the abandonment of one's own purpose, the assumption of a purpose for another, and the sublation of what has been established.

When, by positive implication (*anvaya*), the eating of five-clawed animals is understood from the statement "five five-clawed animals are to be eaten," that [eating] is abandoned because the sentence is intended to prohibit anything other than those.
Furthermore, the prohibition is not explicitly heard; therefore, there is the assumption of a purpose for another.
And because of the state of being desirous, the consumption of all objects that would otherwise result is precluded;
thus, by this [argument], there are three defects in the restrictive injunction (parisaṃkhyā).
This is not sound.

When there is a purpose and the literal meaning of the Vedic text is impossible, it is not contradictory for the sentence to have as its aim the avoidance of meaninglessness. An injunction (*vidhi*) applies when [an action] is absolutely unestablished; a restrictive rule (*niyama*) applies when it is optionally established;
and an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) applies when it is established both there and elsewhere, as in the case of the nails.
What, then, is appropriate here?
Since the definition of *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) exists in that it excludes what is already established both there and elsewhere, this is a *parisaṃkhyā*.
For approaching [one's wife] is established as occurring both during the fertile period (*ṛtu*) and outside of it.
But it is not that "that which is during the season is [therefore] outside the season.
Just as when there is a desire to eat, the restriction regarding that meal is "not at a *śrāddha*," yet one does not remain eating only non-*śrāddha* food by abandoning all food;
so too here, since there is distress, the restriction regarding that act of approaching is understood to be "one should not approach outside the season."
Furthermore, since the desire to go arises from a specific purpose, it is logical that the statement is dependent upon the knowledge of the proper time;
otherwise, an uninitiated matter would be taught.

Moreover, because the injunction for procreating offspring must be performed by one who has already married, and because such procreation is possible during the fertile period (*ṛtu*), going [to one's wife] is already established as a duty.
Furthermore, for one who has already fathered a son, the procreation of a second son is not prescribed;

for when the injunction "one should procreate offspring" intends singularity, the purpose of the injunction is fulfilled. Nor can the act of sexual intercourse itself be enjoined as having an invisible (transcendental) purpose.

Because it falls under the category of rules concerning purification (saṃskāra), because the assumption [of an independent injunction] is impossible, and because approaching during the fertile period is implied by the injunction for procreating offspring; furthermore,
if the phrase "one should approach her during the fertile period" were intended to prohibit non-periodic intercourse,
then in that case, the rest would be a mere reiteration (anuvāda) or a restrictive exclusion (parisaṃkhyā).
For in that case, there is meaningfulness even through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of another sense.
And by doing so, there is no contradiction with Gautama’s [rule].
Thus it is stated there: "One should approach [one's wife] during her season, or at all times except for those occasions that are prohibited."

The alternative "or at all times" (*sarvatra vā*) is intended to permit acting according to one's own will; it does not, however, establish a restrictive rule (*niyama*) for both the fertile period (*ṛtu*) and the non-fertile period (*anṛtu*).

Furthermore, if in the preceding [injunction] there were a restriction that "one should approach [the wife] during the fertile period," then in the case of "or at all times," the word "he should approach" (*upeyāt*), being employed here as well, would necessarily have to be understood as a restrictive rule because of the uniformity of the context. For it is not logical that the same word, when not uttered again, should have a different meaning.

It has been stated that the purpose of restriction is not applicable elsewhere than during the fertile period (*ṛtu*). Therefore, the injunction regarding approaching one's wife during the fertile period is for the purpose of prohibiting it outside that time.
In that regard, for one who has not yet fathered a son, there is indeed a restrictive rule (*niyama*) due to other scriptural injunctions.

But one who has already fathered a son may act according to his desire; however, regarding intercourse outside the fertile period or when it is forbidden, he is again permitted by the wife's wish, as it is said: "He should approach her according to that vow, except on the forbidden days.
Here, the word "that" (tad) refers back to the wife.
The meaning is this: "one who has that vow" (*tadvrataḥ*) refers to one for whom the taking of her hand is the vow.

Even without the desire for pleasure, if a son has been born for the sake of offspring, he may approach her during the fertile period (*ṛtu*); or, if no son has been born, he may approach her even outside the fertile period out of a desire for sexual union, but he must do so with her as the object of his vow and not according to his own whim.
Alternatively, the word *tat* (that) is to be understood as referring back to "the desire for pleasure" (*ratikāmyayā*) as well, because this is a work of the Smṛti tradition.

Out of a desire for pleasure, he may go elsewhere as well, except on the forbidden days (*parvan*). In this very context, a grammatical elision (*akāra-śleṣa*) is to be understood; the remainder of the sense is "out of a lack of desire for pleasure on his own part.

However, according to the explanation already given, there is nothing here that requires such an elision, nor is there any connection [of the word] even without it, since the pronoun *tat* is subordinate within a compound.
He will describe the auspicious days: the new moon, the eighth day, the full moon, and the fourteenth day. He is devoted to his own wife.
One should be devoted to one's own wife, intent on cultivating affection for her;
or rather, one should take pleasure only with one's own wife and not take pleasure with the wives of others—this is the prohibition against the wives of others.
This vow must be observed constantly throughout one's entire life.
Therefore, this is established: there are three statements here. "One should approach [one's wife] during the fertile period" is the first.

The second is in the form of a restatement of the rule for one who has not yet produced a son. The third concerns one who is impelled by his wife: [he may approach her] during the fertile period and even outside it, except on the forbidden days, but not out of a desire for sexual pleasure.

"Devoted to his own wife" is the third [rule]. And the construction of these words is as follows: he should approach her during the fertile period for the sake of offspring; however, out of a desire for pleasure, he may approach her even outside that vow, provided he remains devoted to his own wife.
The natural menstrual period of women is traditionally said to consist of sixteen nights,
together with four other days that are censured by the virtuous.
This verse is for the purpose of defining the seasons;
this matter is to be understood from medical and other such treatises, and is not based solely on scriptural injunction.
The same applies to these two verses beginning with "In even [conception days] sons [are born]."
Those sixteen nights constitute the natural menstrual period (*ṛtu*) for women month after month.
Because it is based on another source of authority, the phrase "month after month" is understood even though it is not explicitly stated [in the verse].
That which occurs by nature is "natural" (*svābhāvika*); it refers to that which happens for those whose constitution is healthy.

For some women, even when the time has arrived, [menstruation] may be prevented by illness and the like; conversely, through the use of medicines such as ghee and sesame, or by the power of sexual union, it may occur even out of season.
Therefore, those nights are called the natural *ṛtu*. By the other four [verses], [the author] states:

The four days which are censured by the virtuous—during which touching, conversing with women, and so forth, are forbidden—begin from the first appearance of menstrual blood. The mention of "days" (*ahar*) is intended to indicate full twenty-four-hour periods (*ahorātra*). Together with these [four days].
Of these, the first four, as well as the eleventh and the thirteenth, are censured; the remaining ten nights, however, are praised.

Among those nights, the first four following the initial appearance of blood are censured; there is no approaching [sexual intercourse] during them. During those three, even physical contact is forbidden due to impurity. But regarding the fourth night, although purity is attained through bathing according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha, sexual enjoyment is not permitted, because all four nights are declared to be contemptible.

The eleventh and the thirteenth [days] are also censured; thus, approaching them is prohibited. Here, "eleventh" and "thirteenth" refer to the days starting from the onset of the menses, not to lunar dates (*tithi*).

Because of the connection with "nights" as the subject of selection in the phrase "of those," it is understood that what is being selected must belong to the same class, just as in the expression, "the black one among cows is rich in milk."
This prohibition against traveling for six nights is for the sake of an unseen spiritual result (adṛṣṭārtha).
The remaining ten nights are commended;
since the prohibition applies to the six, the excellence of the ten is already established and is merely restated here.
Sons are born on even nights, and daughters on uneven nights; therefore, one desiring a son should approach his wife during her season on the even nights.
Among those ten nights, the ones that are even—namely the sixth, eighth, tenth, twelfth, fourteenth, and sixteenth—if he approaches his wife on these, sons are born;
on the odd nights, daughters are born.
Therefore, for the sake of achieving the birth of a son, he should approach and have sexual intercourse with his wife during her menses on the even nights.
This is a restatement;
this too is indeed a restrictive rule: that one who has not yet fathered a son should not approach [his wife] on the odd-numbered nights.
When the male seed is in excess, a male is born; when the female seed is in excess, a female is born.
When they are equal, a neuter is born, or sometimes both a male and a female; when they are diminished or scanty, the opposite occurs.
The semen is the virile seed of the man, and the blood is that of the woman.
It was stated by the venerable Vasiṣṭha that "a person is produced from the combination of semen and blood.
When the male seed is more abundant than the female seed, a son is born even on non-even days; likewise, when the female seed is more abundant, a daughter is born even on even days.
This is for the purpose of performing the act of approaching even on odd nights for one desiring a son.

It is taught that when a man considers himself well-nourished through the use of aphrodisiacs and food, possessing superior virility, and perceives some degree of decline in the woman, then he who desires a son should approach her.
Furthermore, "superiority" here does not refer to quantity, but rather to quality.
Some say that when a male and a female are mixed, it is "puṃs" (masculine), while others read it as "apumān" (neuter) meaning "napuṃsaka. Still others read it as "sāmya" (equality).
When there is equality between the two, it results in either a male alone,
or a male and a female. When, during the process of conception, the wind divides the mixed semen and blood equally— one portion in one place and an equal amount in another— then twins are born.
In that case, even when the division [of the humors] is equal, if the female seed (strībīja) is in excess, a female is born; if the male seed (puṃbīja) is in excess, a male is born.
If the seed is diminished in its essence (sāra), there is a reversal: either the non-conception of a fetus or the birth of a neuter being.
Avoiding women on the eight censurable nights and the other [four],
he remains a celibate student (brahmacārī) regardless of which stage of life (āśrama) he inhabits.

If, while avoiding women during the six censurable nights and the other eight non-censurable nights, he approaches them only when two nights remain— provided it is not on a sacred festival day (*parvan*)— then he remains a true celibate (*brahmacārī*) and attains the fruit of celibacy,
regardless of which stage of life (*āśrama*) he dwells in.
This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).

However, there is no permission for [sexual] intercourse during the night in the stages of life such as the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), because the subduing of the senses is prescribed for all stages of life other than the householder's. Furthermore, the repetition [of the term "night"] can be understood as a mere explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). These nights are to be avoided, not necessarily in sequential order; rather, two nights are permitted so that one may engage in intercourse at will, provided it does not occur on a festival day (*parvan*). What, then, is the fruit of celibacy (*brahmacarya*)?
Since no specific distinction is heard [in the texts], heaven [is the result].
However, in some places it is heard that "the student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) does not fall," meaning he is not defiled by minor transgressions.
A wise father shall not accept even the slightest bride-price for his daughter;
for by accepting a bride-price out of greed, a man becomes a seller of his offspring.

This is a prohibition against taking a bride-price (śulka) from an Asura marriage, because later on there is the mention of "accepting wealth for the sake of the girl. A wise man— one who knows the faults of such a seizure— should not accept even a small amount of wealth or property [from the groom].
One who accepts [the bride] is joined with the fault of selling one's offspring.
But what is this so-called *śulka*? It is that which is taken from the groom preceded by conversation.
Where, however, there is bargaining with high and low prices and the determination of a price based on the qualities of the girl, that is indeed a purchase (*kraya*).
But here, even for a girl of great qualities, the wealth given is very small,
or she is taken without prior verbal agreement.
This is not the proper rule for selling; therefore, he is censured by attributing the nature of selling to it.
Those kinsmen who, out of delusion, live off the property of women—
whether it be their vehicles or their clothing— are sinners who go to a downward state.
This is a supplement to the preceding [verse]: "Wealth derived from women" refers to those things received from the groom at the giving away of a daughter;
and "relatives," such as the father and others, who live off it out of delusion.
As it has been said: "Having given wealth to his kinsmen," this refers to wealth such as gold, silver, and so forth,
as well as women and vehicles.
A vehicle such as a horse, or clothing— even this much, such as clothing, vehicles, and so forth, is never to be used for one's livelihood, let alone more than that.
He declares the fruit for those who subsist [on such wealth]:
those wicked men, by practicing what is forbidden by the scriptures, go to a low state, that is, to hell;
or alternatively, he will demonstrate in the ninth chapter that these are the "women's wealth."
Those kinsmen who, out of delusion, subsist upon these [prohibitions]— namely, the father and his kin, the husband and his kin,
as well as vehicles and the like,
and likewise clothing.
Because of the presence [of the word] in the cognition of women, a verbal proximity (śābda-saṃnidhi) is postulated, just as in the case of "the king's man"— [the question being] "whose?"—
[the answer is] "the king's."
Regarding the rite of the seers (*ārṣa*), some say that a pair of cattle is the bride-price (*śulka*); but that is surely false.
Whether it be small or large, such a thing is indeed nothing other than a sale.
A cow and a bull constitute a pair of cattle;
some say that this may be accepted, but Manu’s opinion is that this is indeed false and incorrect.
The meaning is "not to be given.
Even a small [gift] is thus;
one who possesses few means is "small."
In this way it becomes great; the sale is exactly of that same extent.
When the kinsmen do not take a fee for them, that is not a sale;
it is merely a token of honor for the maidens and an act of pure compassion.
Is the acquisition of wealth from a bride-price (*śulka*) considered a sale?
We say: no.
When the kinsmen, being authorized over the maiden, take or seize it for their own benefit, then that constitutes a sale.
The "arhaṇa" (offering) regarding the bride refers to the acceptance of wealth for the sake of the girls; that constitutes their honor and worship.
The girls themselves feel great esteem toward themselves, thinking, "We are such that we are to be married after being given wealth.
Furthermore, they become objects of veneration elsewhere as well, [thinking], "These women are fortunate."
Or rather, ornaments and the like should be made with that wealth; therefore, they become highly esteemed and beautiful.
Compassion (*ānṛśaṃsya*) means freedom from evil; there is not even the slightest scent of unrighteousness (*adharma*).
Thus, by this explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), the acceptance of wealth for the sake of the maiden is enjoined.
These women should be honored and adorned by their fathers, brothers, husbands, and brothers-in-law, who desire abundant prosperity for them.
The bride’s relatives must give [the girl] not only after receiving a boon, but they must also give her;
because of the association with the term "father" (pitṛ), the word "father" refers here to the grandfather, paternal uncles, and so forth,
and thus the plural number is used.
Alternatively, the plural number is used with reference to individual instances;
likewise, [the plural] "by husbands" refers to fathers-in-law and so forth with reference to individual instances.
*Devaras* are the brothers of the husband.
They are to be honored.
On occasions such as the birth of a son, they are to be honored with invitations, providing shelter, great respect, and diligent offerings of food and the like.
They are to be adorned.

They should be adorned with garments, ornaments, ointments for the limbs, and so forth. In this regard, those who desire much auspiciousness— meaning those who wish to obtain, or who desire to attain, everything denoted by the word "much," such as desirable and lovely things like the prosperity of sons and wealth, health, and freedom from humiliation— [should act accordingly].
This injunction is for the sake of the fruit.
Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice;
where they are not honored, all rituals there become fruitless.
The deities rejoice, are satisfied, and become gracious;
being gracious, they endow their masters with the very fruits they desire.

However, where they are not worshipped, all actions—such as sacrifices, oblations, and gifts—and whatever offerings are made with the intention of propitiating the deities, are fruitless; such is the meaning of this explanatory passage (arthavāda).
A householder should perform the domestic rites according to the rules in the nuptial fire,
as well as the performance of the five great sacrifices and the daily cooking.
The section on marriage has been concluded.

One should perform the domestic (gṛhya) rites in that fire in which the marriage was performed; this includes the rites to be accomplished by means of the fire, such as the Aṣṭakā, the Pārvaṇa-śrāddha, the Homa, and so forth, as taught by the authors of the Gṛhya-smṛtis.
As for the five great sacrifices (pañcayajña) which will be described hereafter, their performance (vidhāna)—that is, their execution—should likewise take place in that very same fire.

Although it has been stated that the performance of the five sacrifices (pañcayajña) is prescribed without distinction, nevertheless, the Vaiśvadeva oblation is accomplished by means of fire, whereas in the case of water-libations and the like, nothing is to be done with fire.
How then is there the instruction that "the performance of the five sacrifices is to be done in the fire"?
Some say that even a single locative case-ending (saptamī) is differentiated according to the difference in its objects.

Therefore, the term "five sacrifices" (pañcayajña) is employed here as a designation for a single portion of those five sacrifices. Alternatively, in the phrase "the rule for the five sacrifices," the word "in the fire" (agnau) is not to be construed [with this], because the Vaiśvadeva oblation has already been established as having the fire as its locus by the preceding [text].
Thus, the connection should be made as follows: "The householder, moreover, should perform the rule for the five sacrifices."

In the phrase "in the fire," the word "fire" is required [as the locus] for both the domestic rites (*gṛhyakarman*) and the daily cooking. The word "house" (*gṛha*) denotes a wife; thus, one who has taken a wife—that is, a householder accompanied by his spouse—should perform this and that [rite].

Regarding marriage, some authors of the Gṛhyasūtras have stated that the fire is to be established by churning the two kindling woods (*araṇi*); others have stated that one should bring fire from wherever it is burning and offer oblations into it.
By this statement that [the rite] is "domestic" (*gṛhya*) in that context, the maintenance of the fire is effectively implied.
On this point, some say:
even for a Śūdra there is the maintenance of the nuptial fire (*vaivāhikāgni*), because he too has the entitlement to perform *pākayajña* sacrifices;
nor is any specific caste mentioned here, for only the term "householder" (*gṛhī*) is heard.
Even a Śūdra may be a householder, for the taking of a wife has been prescribed for him as well. This very point is stated elsewhere:
"A householder should perform the Smārta rites every day in the marriage fire."
Thus it is said.
To this, it is replied:
"The domestic rite [is to be performed] in the nuptial fire"—so it is heard in the scripture.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as a ritual action called "gṛhya" (domestic) in itself.
In this context, that which is spoken of by the authors of the Gṛhyasmṛtis should be understood as "gṛhya" through metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā).

And the rituals prescribed by the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras are enjoined only for those of the three higher castes, not for the Śūdra; for it is said: "Having explained the Vaitānika (Śrauta) rites, we shall now explain the Gṛhya rites."

The purpose of this restatement of what has already been said is precisely this: that those who alone have the entitlement to perform the *vaitānika* (sacrificial) rites are the same ones who have the entitlement to the *gṛhya* (domestic) rites; it is not, as explained by others, for the sake of the acquisition of those specific duties (*dharma*).

For if that were intended, he would not have stated, "Its times for kindling and offering have been explained by [the rules for] the *agnihotra*. Nor is it logical to define *gṛhya* simply as "that which occurs in the house" (*gṛhe bhavam*).
The word *gṛha* (house) denotes either a hall (*śālā*) or a wooden structure (*dāra*).

First of all, no specific ritual action is traditionally prescribed for which the house serves as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), such that one could refer back to "the house" and then enjoin the duties of a householder (*gṛhin*) with respect to it.
Furthermore, even those rites that consecrate the house, such as the examination of the building site (*vāstuparīkṣā*) and so forth, pertain only to the three higher castes, not to the Śūdra.
Now, as for the statement regarding wood, it is of no consequence because it is already covered by the phrase "the householder [should perform] even there.
Furthermore, as for another Smṛti text stating,
"The householder should perform the rites prescribed by the Smṛti every day in the marriage fire," [it refers to that].
Or even when taken at the time of giving by the donor, it is [to be offered] into the Śrauta fires used for the Vaitānika rites.
Thus, here too, because no specific distinction is made— such as "something [is] Smārta"— there is indeed a dependence on something else;
for not every Smārta rite is possible in the fire,
nor is there any evidence that it has the fire-oblation (homa) as its object.

For it is not necessarily the case that an oblation (homa) must have fire as its locus. Therefore, it should be stated that what is taught by the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras is "Gṛhya" (domestic ritual).
For these two Smṛtis merely restate the rites prescribed by the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras.
And likewise, from where could a Śūdra’s formal acquisition of the sacred fire (agniparigraha) come?

Furthermore, another [text] is recorded there: "The Śrauta [rites] are performed in the Vaitānika fires. In that case, this must necessarily be understood as referring to the three higher castes (traivarṇika).

Otherwise, one would have to accept a difference in the intended meaning of a single word—namely, that the same term refers to all four castes in the former instance and to the three castes alone in the latter.
Furthermore, when non-difference is possible, difference is not logical.
"Daily" (*vāhikī*) means occurring every day;
that cooking for the purpose of eating which takes place every day must be performed in that very same fire.
A householder has five slaughterhouses: the hearth, the grinding stone, the broom, the mortar and pestle, and the water jar; by using these, he causes slaughter.
This is an instruction regarding the qualification for the performance of the five sacrifices.
"Sūnās" are like slaughterhouses;
they refer either to places where animals are killed for the purpose of selling meat, such as marketplaces and the like, or to those activities performed that produce meat and are thus causes of sin.
In this way, even the kitchen hearth and so forth are equal to slaughterhouses by way of metaphorical attribution, because they are causes of evil;
for there is no direct prohibition of them in the treatise,
nor is there any general prohibition.
For indeed, there would be no one who lacks a desire to destroy suffering;
nor is any action seen to be accomplished by that [suffering] which is prohibited by another statement.
Furthermore, an inference of a prohibition cannot be drawn from this very statement alone, because it is understood as forming a single syntactical unit with the subsequent [statement].
Alternatively, if it were intended as a prohibition, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Furthermore, how could one accomplish with another entity the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by the meaning of this word—the attainment of those five sacrifices?
Moreover, the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) have not been stated.
By this, the prohibition of any other thing that serves the same purpose as those [fire-hearths] is stated.
Or rather, these sacrifices would belong to one who, out of greed for another's food, would go to a river or similar place for the sake of water;
for if the prohibition of the fire-hearths and so forth were intended, then he would have recited this very word for the purpose of prohibition—what need is there for inference?
