A direct statement is more powerful than its own [implied] word.
If, however, it were for the purpose of expiation, its mention in the eleventh book would be appropriate;
for by means of prohibitions alone, there would simply be non-performance.
Furthermore, because items such as the hearth are unavoidable, their prohibition is impossible;
and if there is no prohibition, how can there be an expiation?
Therefore, the five great sacrifices are not for the purpose of destroying faults.

What then? He states the eternality of sacrifices by way of their being eternal, for the purpose of expiating the false defects superimposed upon the eternally connected [elements] such as the hearth (cullyādi).
It is recited that the initial phoneme [of *yajña*], namely *ya*, is labio-dental (*dantoṣṭhya*).
"He is struck" means he is destroyed by his evil deed through the loss of body, wealth, and so forth;
or "he is bound" means he is made subject to another by sin—this is the meaning of the root *bandh* (to bind); or "he is driven."
"Carrying" (*vāhana*) means engaging in one's own function.
When a hearth or similar object performs its own task—which has been appropriately attained according to its fitness—it is said to be "carrying" by performing that task through those [means].
A hearth (*cullī*) is a place for cooking, such as a frying pan and so forth.
A *peṣaṇī* is a grinding stone or a millstone;
*upaskara* refers to household utensils such as bowls, cauldrons, and the like;
and a *kaṇḍanī* is that by which rice and other grains are pounded.
A water-jar is a receptacle for water.
For the purpose of expiating all of those [sins] in due order, the great seers have prescribed five great sacrifices for householders to be performed every day.

For the sake of expiating those slaughter-places, such as the hearth and so forth— in order to purge the defects arising from them— the sequence of purification consists of smearing the hearth, planing the grinding stone, and so on;
these five great sacrifices (pañca-mahāyajña) have been ordained by the great seers (maharṣi) as duties to be performed daily by householders who maintain a domestic fire.

The word *gṛhamedhin* refers to the stage of the householder (*gṛhasthāśrama*). Regarding the phrase "every day," since no specific time limit is mentioned, it is understood to mean "as long as one lives."
And from this, its permanence is established;
"great sacrifices" (mahāyajña) is the name for these rites.

Teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman; the libation to the ancestors is the sacrifice to the Pitṛs; the burnt offering is the sacrifice to the gods; the bali-offering is the sacrifice to the spirits; and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men.
This is the rule regarding their essential nature (*svarūpa*).
By the word "teaching" (*adhyāpana*), "studying" (*adhyayana*) is also included, since the author will state later that "recitation is an *ahuta* sacrifice.
Furthermore, even recitation does not require pupils.
And it is heard generally from the Ṛṣis through Vedic study in the *Ṛṇāvedana-śruti*: "From the Ṛṣis [one is freed] by Vedic study.
Therefore, both teaching and studying, as far as possible, constitute the *brahmayajña*.
He will state later that the libation (*tarpaṇa*) consists of food and the like, or water.
The offering made by a person into the fire for the deities to be mentioned hereafter,
as well as the remnant offered into the mortar and other such vessels, is that which pertains to the spirits (bhūta).
"Bhauta" means "having the Bhūtas as its deities";
this is the name of a specific ritual act,
for in that context, the offering of the *bali* is prescribed with the word "Bhūta" in the phrase "to the Bhūtas who roam by day."
By virtue of association, this entire group of rites is designated by the term *bhūtayajña*.

Just as among the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, although only one oblation is the *vaiśvadeva-āmikṣā*, the entire festival is referred to as "one should sacrifice with the *vaiśvadeva*" [as a whole]. The word *bali* refers to an offering made without fire (*anagnihoma*).
The wise remember that the *devejyā* is the offering to the gods;
the honoring and propitiating of guests is the *nṛyajña*.
But how, one might ask, is the private recitation of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*) a sacrifice?
For in that [recitation], no deities are worshipped, nor even mentioned;
rather, only the syllables of the Veda are uttered with their meanings unintended.
And it has been said regarding the repetition of the words of the sacred tradition (āmnāya): "Some say they are meaningless."
True;

in the case of praise, the word "sacrifice" (yajña) is used figuratively, as is the word "great" (mahat). Furthermore, in the context of honoring guests, the word "sacrifice" is also used figuratively.

Although it is possible for the guest (*atithi*) to function as a deity (*devatā*), nevertheless, in the original injunction, it is heard that "one should feed" and "one should honor" [the guest], but not that "one should sacrifice to guests.
This is just as in the case of the phrase, "whatever rite [is performed] for the king of men.

These five sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) are not to be performed simultaneously, because they lack a connection to a single common qualification (*adhikāra*), as separate qualifications are heard for each.

If there is a connection to a single qualification (*adhikāra*), then even if three or four [rites] have been performed, nothing would truly be accomplished as long as what was required remains unaccomplished. Just as in the case of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices—the *āgneya*, *agnīṣomīya*, and *upāṃśuyāja*—the qualification is not established by performing only one or two of them.
Or, as in this very context, regarding the *vaiśvadeva* oblation, if there is an interruption of any of the deities ending with *sviṣṭakṛt*, the qualification for the oblation is not fulfilled.
Furthermore, it is heard that there is an entitlement for each [of these] individually:
"One should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Veda (svādhyāya)," and "One should be constantly devoted to the rites for the gods (daiva).
Through the connection with the words of entitlement, there is a separate application [of the injunctions].
Furthermore, regarding the *ātithya* (hospitality), another qualification is heard in the scripture: "it is conducive to wealth and fame.
In that regard, four [of these duties] are under one's own control, whereas hospitality (*ātithya*) depends upon the presence of a guest.
Moreover, a guest is not to be invited, because there is no such thing as "hospitality" in the absence of a guest.
For we shall state that a guest indeed becomes present of his own accord.
Therefore, if one should incur sin by performing one of the five [daily duties] while neglecting the others, the performed does not become unperformed.

Consequently, even for one who is not authorized to perform the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice due to being without a sacred fire (*anagnika*), there certainly remains the authority to perform the private Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*), the water libation (*udakatarpaṇa*), and so forth.

Furthermore, since other Smṛtis mention that the taking up of the sacred fires (*agniparigraha*) may occur at a different time [than marriage], it is not necessarily the case that "taking up" refers only to marriage. For the Smṛti says: "The fire is preceded by the wife, or preceded by the inheritance. Now, one might object: for one who has not performed a marriage, the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) will take place at the time of inheriting the estate.
For this would indeed be so if the injunction for establishing the fires were for its own sake;
however, the establishment of the fires is for the sake of the fires,
and the fires are for the sake of ritual action.
Furthermore, ritual acts are prescribed for one who has a wife as his companion, not for one alone.
Even when certain authors of Gṛhya-sūtras state that one should perform the Śrāddha after having established the Parameṣṭhi-prāṇa fire, that too applies only to one who has a wife;
for that alone is the time for its establishment.

Nor is it the case that there is no *śrāddha* for one who does not maintain the sacred fires; for this [rite] is prescribed even for one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*), with the exception of the pouring of the *svadhā* offering. Furthermore, he cannot perform the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*), because eligibility for that requires learning, whereas at present he lacks such knowledge.
However, on the basis of scriptural injunctions, the *śrāddha* must be performed according to one's capacity, just as in the case of the *niṣādasthapati*.
But when the fire is maintained by an uncle or others, since learned persons (*vidvats*) are available, there is no entitlement for one who is unlearned (*avaidya*).

If, however, the laying of the fires (*agnyādhāna*) is prescribed specifically within the section on *śrāddha*, then, having laid them as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of that rite, they shall be abandoned once the *śrāddha* has been completed.
Some, however, cite another Smṛti: "The Vaiśvadeva oblation should be performed even in a worldly fire; others say it should be done with dry food."
He who does not neglect these five great sacrifices according to his ability,
even while living constantly in the household, is not tainted by the defects of the slaughterhouse.
In this context, permanence is being enjoined,
while other factors are restated; even if these [rites] are deficient in their qualities, they must be performed according to one's capacity.

This too is already established because of its permanence. Therefore, [the phrase] "according to possibility and according to capacity" uses the suffix *tasi* due to its inclusion in the group beginning with *ādi*.
The meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*) alone is "he causes to neglect" (*hāpayati*), because the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇij*) is not intended to be expressed.

Alternatively, "neglect" (*hā*) is derived from *han* with the suffix *kvip* according to the rule for the *saṃpadādi* group; then, from that [root] ending in *hā*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of "causing to reach" (*āpayati*), where *āp* takes *kvip* in the agentive sense. From that resulting nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the causative suffix *ṇic* is added in the sense of the verbal action itself.
Thus, "he does not cause to neglect" (*na hāpayati*) means "he should not abandon."
This is a praise [of the householder], meaning that while living in his own home, he is not bound by the sin of the slaughterhouses (sūnās), which are inevitably present there.
He who does not offer sustenance to these five— the gods, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself— does not truly live, even though he breathes.
The praise of the prescribed rule is achieved by censuring its non-performance.
Some read it with the dative case:
"To the deities, guests, and dependents, to the ancestors, and likewise to oneself."
"One does not offer [the oblation] to five.
For here, "offering" (nirvāpa) means giving, not merely the preparation of something for that purpose;
because it is the primary action in connection with that [giving], the dative case is appropriate.

He who does not give to these every day—even while breathing, even while living, even while possessing inhalation and exhalation—does not truly live; he is as good as dead, because there is no fruit in his life.

Furthermore, the "dependents" (*bhṛtyāḥ*) referred to here should be understood as those mentioned in the verse beginning with "but [one's] mother and father in their old age," and not slaves, because the giving to them is contingent upon their labor.
Alternatively, they may refer to those such as *garbhadāsas* (slaves from birth) who, though incapable of labor in their old age, are nonetheless seen to be subject to obligatory support.
The maintenance of old oxen and other such animals is mandatory; we shall explain this in the section on partition.

And it has been stated by Gautama: "He must support those whose means of subsistence have failed. Furthermore, there is the offering to the deities and the oblation into the fire, as well as the presentation of the *bali* on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) to the Vaiśvadeva deities—that is, to the deities of the New and Full Moon sacrifices—or, according to the connection with the formula "I offer you, acceptable to Agni," what other kind of offering could there be?
Therefore, because they are already included by the mention of the deities (*devatā*), there is a separate mention of the spirits (*bhūta*).
The mention of the self (*ātman*) serves as an illustration:

just as for the self there is no life without food, and thus the consumption of food is inevitable for its sake—since life is a desired object and because of the injunction that "one should protect oneself from everything"—so it is also with respect to the deities and the others.
The unoffered (ahuta), the offered (huta), the likewise well-offered (prahuta),
the offering to Brahman (brāhmya-huta), and the consumed (prāśita)— these they declare to be the five sacrifices.
By these words, the prescription of these [five sacrifices] is found in a certain Vedic branch (veda-śākhā).

Therefore, in order to demonstrate that the prescription of the five great sacrifices (pañca-yajña) is rooted in the Śruti, he refers to them again by means of their well-known names. The second purpose of employing different designations is to indicate that whatever dharma has been prescribed in that context under the names of "oblation" (āhuti) and so forth, even if it was not explicitly mentioned here, must also be included.
As in the case of the Brahma-yajña, śrāddha, marriage, and other such rites.

Recitation is the *ahuta* sacrifice; the fire-oblation is the *huta*; the offering to the spirits is the *prahuta*; the oblation to the elemental beings is the *bhautika bali*; the worship of the foremost of the twice-born is the *brāhmya huta*; and the libation to the ancestors is the *prāśita*.
That sacrifice which is called the "unoffered" (ahuta) should be understood as silent recitation (japa).
This is because of the scriptural injunction, "One should honor the seers through self-study," whereby the study of the Veda constitutes the purpose of japa;
or alternatively, it refers to the act of mental recollection within the sphere of internal activity.
In both cases, the root *jap* (to mutter) is taught for both audible speech and mental recitation.
*Huta* is an oblation poured into the fire; *prahuta* is an offering made to the spirits (*bhūta*).

Although this is indeed an oblation (*homa*), because oblations are generally well-known as being performed in the fire, there might be the doubt that the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*) is not an oblation;
therefore, it is called "the offered" (*prahuta*) by way of praise, meaning it is an oblation in an eminent sense.
The worship of the foremost of the twice-born, the Brāhmaṇas, is the "oblation to Brahman" (*brāhmyaṃ huta*).
The rite of hospitality consists of honoring the foremost of the twice-born.
One should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas and to the rites dedicated to the gods here in this world;
for it is by being engaged in the rites dedicated to the gods that one sustains this entire universe, both moving and unmoving.
He clarifies by this what was stated regarding the five great sacrifices— that there is a distinct entitlement for each one individually, rather than a single collective entitlement: when,

due to defects such as poverty or some other cause, the performance of hospitality and the like cannot somehow be accomplished, then one must remain constantly engaged in self-study (*svādhyāya*) during the rites dedicated to the gods (*daiva*).
The offering into the fire for the deities of the Vaiśvadeva is the rite pertaining to the gods (*daiva*).
Although the *bhūtayajña* and *pitṛyajña* also possess a divine character, it is specifically the offering into the fire that is called "divine" here due to the context.
Regarding this, he states an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*):
Engaged in divine action and devoted to it, he sustains—that is, supports—the moving and the unmoving, the stationary and the wandering;
the meaning is that he becomes the cause of the maintenance of the entire world.
But how does the sustenance of the entire world come about through the oblation poured into the fire? To this he says:
"The oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born; from rain comes food; and from that, living beings."
The oblation (*āhuti*)— that is, the sacrificial offering such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa*— which is being offered and cast into the fire by the sacrificer,
reaches the sun in an invisible form.
Since the sun is the bringer of all essences (*rasa*), it is said that the essence of the oblation reaches the sun.
Therefore, that essence, ripened by time within the rays of the sun, is born in the form of rain;
from that comes food, such as rice and other grains;
and from that come all creatures, that is, all living beings.
Thus, by offering into the fire, the sacrificer acts for the benefit of the entire world;
this is a supplement to the preceding injunction, and not one whose purpose is restricted to the literal meaning of the words as heard.
For if it were so [restricted], only one who desires rain would have the qualification [to perform it].
And that has not been heard [in the scripture];
since a connection is possible as a supplement to the subject matter under discussion, there is no occasion for such an assumption.
Just as all living beings depend upon the wind for their life,
so do those in the other stages of life depend upon the householder.
By another method, he shows the necessity of performing the great sacrifices:
Vāyu is the vital breath (prāṇa); depending upon it, all beings live.
For there is no life for one who is without breath; indeed, the maintenance of breath is itself life.
The word *jantu* denotes living beings in general.
The inclusion of the term "all" implies that even the life of gods and sages, despite their extraordinary powers, is dependent upon the wind (*vāyu*).
Thus, the householder is equal to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) for those in all stages of life (*āśrama*).
Therefore, the meaning of the injunction is that one must be the means of subsistence for all.
Although, by the mention of "others," those in other stages of life (āśramins) than the householder are understood, nevertheless, this is not intended to exclude the householder;
for the giving of hospitality and so forth is specifically enjoined for the *snātaka*.
Therefore, the mention of "the others" is for the purpose of establishing their equality with the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*).
Furthermore, it is not heard [in scripture] that they exist by themselves or for themselves, nor do they attain the maintenance of a body and family;
thus, the compound *itarāśramāḥ* means "those other stages of life."
Since members of all three other stages of life are daily supported by the householder alone with both knowledge and food,
therefore the householder’s stage is the most excellent.

Since all three other orders of life are supported and benefited by the householder through knowledge arising from the exposition of the meaning of the Vedas and through food, therefore the household order is the eldest and best.
In the reading *gṛhī*, it is a bahuvrīhi compound; in the reading *gṛham*, it is a descriptive determinative (viśeṣaṇasamāsa) compound, namely "the eldest order" (*jyeṣṭhāśrama*).
Here too, the phrase "by the householders alone" is a restatement based on propriety; it is not a prohibition against forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*) and others from teaching and so forth.
For the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), this is indeed prescribed: "He should perform these very same great sacrifices.

As for the wandering mendicant (*pravrajita*), although he is equal toward all beings and thus the infliction of harm is forbidden by the rule "he should not undertake [actions]," nevertheless, the exposition of the meaning of the Vedas is prescribed in the *Bhikṣu-śāstra*.

Furthermore, because of the injunction regarding the excellence of the practice of cultivating knowledge and dispassion, there is no excessive effort required from those two [the forest-dweller and the mendicant] in the exposition of the meaning of the Vedas.
Since celibates (brahmacārins) lack the means for their own livelihood, they cannot act as teachers; and since they are instructed to subsist on alms, how could there be the giving of food?
Therefore, because this is generally possible only for householders, it is stated that [the rites] are performed by householders alone.
This must be maintained with effort by one who desires imperishable heaven and absolute happiness in this world— this which is difficult for those of weak faculties to maintain.
That is the householder’s stage of life (gṛhāśrama).
It should be maintained with effort and practiced by one who desires imperishable heaven and seeks happiness in this world—
that happiness which has no end whatsoever.
The word "atyanta" (extreme) indicates permanence. An "āśrama" that is "adhārya" means it is impossible to maintain for those with weak faculties.
This is what is meant.

Since sexual union with women, well-prepared food, and so forth are inevitable for a householder, there is a fault in the attachment of the senses to their objects; therefore, it is said that he must maintain himself with effort [in restraint] compared to other stages of life (*āśrama*). Even here, there is great control over the senses: one must not approach [one's wife] outside her season, one must not approach the wives of others, and one should eat only the remnants of the food [offered to the gods and ancestors].
The restraint that must be observed when sense objects are present is difficult to practice.

Regarding the phrase "imperishable heaven," this does not mean that all the duties of a householder have heaven as their fruit, because some are obligatory (nitya) and others are heard to have different fruits.
Even those acts whose fruits are not heard of [in scripture] but are imagined to have heaven as their fruit—there is no reason for specifying them alone in this restatement (anuvāda).
Therefore, this is a restatement of the intended fruits of prescribed acts;
nor is this a separate qualification (adhikāra).
It could indeed be said that these [rites] last for as long as one lives, and that they are for one desiring heaven;
for by the phrase "by one desiring happiness here," they are understood to be equivalent to what is not subject to injunction.
Indeed, it is not possible here to understand the phrase "by one desiring happiness" as being the fruit of the ritual action, because no specific distinction is indicated.
For all pleasure is perceived as delimited by specific gains such as village boys and the like;
if it were merely pleasure without such delimitation, it would be nothing other than heaven (*svarga*),
and that is not something belonging to this world.
Therefore, this is a restatement for those who desire to attain happiness in this visible world.
For other ascetics—those belonging to the other stages of life—dwell in misery, whether they have tree roots as their shelter or live in the houses of others.
Thus, this is indeed a restatement.
By virtue of its similarity to that [preceding statement], this too is merely a restatement:
"Sages, ancestors, gods, living beings, and likewise guests—these expect [support] from householders; therefore, one who understands his duty must act toward them."
These [gods and others] solicit from householders—that is, from those living as family men—and desire to take [offerings].
"Desire" refers to the longing for the instruction on how to obtain benefit for themselves.
Therefore, one who understands what is established by the scriptures must perform the duty toward these gods and others, such as the prescribed fire-oblations (homa) and so forth.
"Family" refers to one's wife.
Even by an ordinary person, that which is bound together with great effort should not be rendered fruitless; how much more so, then, the praise of a deity?
One should honor the sages through the private recitation of the Vedas, the gods with burnt offerings according to the rule,
the ancestors with śrāddha rites, men with food, and the elemental spirits with the bali offering.
The very same meaning as "one should study one's own Veda" (svādhyāyam adhīyīta) is expressed by "one should honor the sages with one's own Veda" (svādhyāyenārcayed ṛṣīn).
That which is performed with devotion at a śrāddha—namely, the offering of water for the feet, the arghya, garlands, and ointments—is what is called "honor" (arcā);
furthermore, this is a statement of praise.
Nor is there the performance of both recitation and the worship of sages;
for those mantras addressed to deities such as Agni praise the sages.
Therefore, the statement "one should honor the sages with recitation" is merely a commendation.
Alternatively, the sages Marīci and others are not intended here; rather, it is the Vedas themselves.
Furthermore, the word *svādhyāya* is a term for an action and does not denote the Vedas here, as in the injunction "one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied.
By this, the following is meant: one should honor the Vedas through study, practicing them according to the prescribed rules, because otherwise such honoring would be impossible.
In this case as well, worship is merely figurative;
for in the *homa* sacrifice, the deity is not the primary factor, since the deity is a mere instrumental factor (*kāraka*).
[One worships] the ancestors with the *śrāddha*.
In this matter, the injunction is exactly as it has been heard;
that will be determined in the section on the rules for ancestral rites (śrāddha).
One should honor men, such as guests, mendicants, and so forth.
The meaning is that one should give food to them preceded by worship.
Day after day, he should offer the śrāddha with food and drink,
or even with milk, roots, and fruits, bringing satisfaction to the ancestors.
One should give; one should perform the *śrāddha* ceremony day after day, every single day.
The extension of the ritual procedure occurs by means of the name.
The rite for the ancestors known as *śrāddha* is prescribed for the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).
Its specific performance details are extended [to the present case] by this very name, "śrāddha."
"With food and drink" (annādyena):
this is a restatement of [the rule] beginning with "with sesame, rice, barley," etc.;
its intended meaning will be explained further below.
"Udakena" means with water; "payaḥ" means milk.
At the fivefold sacrifice performed for the sake of the ancestors, one should feed even a single Brahmin;
however, in that regard, one should not feed any twice-born man for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva offering.

Since the term *śrāddha* implies a specific injunction, when that entire injunction is applicable, certain portions of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) are set aside; thus, one should not feed anyone here [in this context].
Furthermore, in this *anvāhika-śrāddha*, there is no feeding of twice-born men intended for the Viśvedevas as part of the *vaiśvadeva* rite.
Regarding this, some say:
The repetition of the phrase "one should feed [him] when food is ready" indicates that this is an original injunction (*apūrvatva*).

Therefore, this *śrāddha* consists solely of feeding a single Brāhmaṇa with the ancestors in mind; there is no other procedure (*itikartavyatā*) such as the water-offering vessel (*arghapātra*), the fire-oblation (*homa*), and so forth.
Celibacy (*brahmacarya*), the prohibition of Vedic study (*svādhyāyaniṣedha*), and the like do not apply here.
"One should feed even a single Brahmin"—
because the rule "one for each of the three [ancestors] in both cases" is not an injunction, it does not establish what was previously unestablished; thus,
this [rule] enjoins that one should feed at least one, though many may be fed if possible.

"For the sake of the ancestors" means for the purpose of satisfying the ancestors. "Pertaining to the five sacrifices" (pāñcayajñika) means that which arises from or is included within the five great sacrifices.
The term *pāñcayajñika* is applied to the *śrāddha* rite;
however, this libation (*tarpaṇa*) is not itself the *pāñcayajñika*.
Therefore, there is a conjunction of both the libation and the feeding [of Brahmins].
But there will be this distinction: that he satisfies [the ancestors] with water alone.
A Brāhmaṇa should daily perform an oblation in the domestic fire with the Vaiśvadeva food that has been prepared, according to the prescribed rule, for these deities.
The cooked offering (pāka) intended for the Viśvedevas is called Vaiśvadeva.
Furthermore, the word *viśvadeva* signifies "all" (*sarva*), and here it serves as an indication for the recipients (*saṃpradāna*).
By this, its purpose for guests and others is also stated.
Once [the food] is prepared, one should perform the *homa* for these deities who are about to be mentioned.

By the word "prepared" (*siddha*), it is shown that the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) accompanied by the mantra "For the god thee" (*devasya tvā*) should not be performed; the meaning of the injunction is simply that once the cooking is complete for all purposes, the *homa* and other rites should be performed. [This is stated] in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*.
This is an instruction regarding the performance of the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other rites according to the prescribed rule.
It states the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) consisting of sweeping, sprinkling water around the fire, and so forth, which is obtained through established custom and preceded by the formal injunction.
The word "Brāhmaṇa" is intended to indicate that the entitlement for this applies to members of the three twice-born castes.
"Every day" means constantly.
The mention of the deity is for the purpose of obtaining the utterance of "svāhā.
Because of the use of the genitive case, the formulation would otherwise be "this is for Agni."

However, the oblation is offered to the gods either by means of the word "devatā" or with the utterance of "svāhā," because the *vaṣaṭkāra* is prescribed again at the end of the *yājyā* verse; whereas in the case of domestic (*smārta*) oblations, the *vaṣaṭkāra* is absent,
but the utterance of "svāhā" occurs everywhere.
And when that exists, the ritual application is "Svāhā to Agni."
First to Agni and to Soma, then to both of them together,
to the Viśvedevas, and also to Dhanvantari.
"At the beginning" is a restatement, since it is already established that Agni comes first according to the order of recitation; those two [offerings] are separate oblations.
And for those two taken together, the application is "to Agni and Soma" and "to the Viśvedevas."
A single oblation indeed for Dhanvantari, svāhā!
To Kuhū, to Anumati, and to Prajāpati;
together with Dyāvāpṛthivī, and likewise finally to Sviṣṭakṛt.
"Together with Heaven and Earth," "to Heaven and Earth, svāhā!
Likewise, at the end, for the Sviṣṭakṛt:
"Sviṣṭakṛt" is a term denoting a specific quality.
And Agni is subordinate by his very nature, because of the statement in another Smṛti, "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," and because he is prescribed in the Śruti for all burnt offerings (sarvahomas).

Although the result is established by the reading "at the end" (antataḥ), the explicit statement is made to show that since additional oblations are prescribed in another Smṛti, if they are to be combined, the insertion (āvāpa) must be performed before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.
But surely, because the oblation (*homa*) is one, an option regarding the deity is appropriate. Why, then, is the oblation one?
Because this very [text] is the originative injunction (*utpatti*) of the oblations: "To Agni," "To Soma," and so forth.
And in that case, because they are already occupied by specific deities at the very moment of their origination, the oblations are understood to be distinct.

Having thus correctly offered the oblation, he should present the bali-offering to Indra, Antaka, Appati, and Indu, along with their followers, while circumambulating in a clockwise direction toward all the quarters.

Being devoted to the meditation on the deity with right and undistracted mind, having thus offered oblations into the fire for these deities, one then proceeds clockwise through all the directions in their respective order:
first to the east, then to the south; this is the clockwise rotation.
Indra is the nearby lord, and Indu is in every direction;
another says that Indu has no share of the oblation.
If the offering of the bali were not made with this word, how could Indu have a share of the oblation?
It has been explained that the *baliharaṇa* offering is indeed the same as the *homa* oblation.
Furthermore, for fear of breaking the meter, the specific form of the word is not intended here; thus, the enumeration must be performed using the very terms employed in other Smṛtis:
"to those with their followers and elephants" (*sanugebhyaḥ*).
*Anuga* means followers or attendants; thus, *tatpuruṣa* [is used]. Accordingly, there is the usage "to the attendants of Indra" (*indrapuruṣebhyaḥ*) and so forth.
One should cast [the food] at the door with "To the Maruts," and also into the water with "To the Waters";
likewise, one should offer it upon the pestle and mortar with "To the Vanaspatis."
Here, the instrumental suffix (*itikaraṇa*) is intended to express the form [of the word];
"in the waters" (*apsu*) indicates the locus;
and "from the waters" (*adbhyaḥ*) is the designation of the deity.
The phrase "to the lords of the forest" refers to the pestle and mortar;
since they form a dual compound with a singular sense (*dvandvaikavadbhāva*), the two substrates are not treated as optional alternatives.
By virtue of the function of the subordinate element in the designation, it is logical that the repetition applies to the principal element, namely the oblation.
Furthermore, it is not possible to establish a connection with the oblation for the pestle and mortar as a single unit, because their distinctness is perceived even there;
for, unlike milk and water, their blending together is impossible.

In that case, if the offering were made upon the mortar, the oblation would not have been performed upon the other [the pestle], and if it were made upon the pestle, it would not have been made upon the mortar.
Furthermore, an oblation cannot be divided into parts because its measure is fixed;
therefore, in this case of a dual designation, it is logical that the offering be made into one of the two conjoined [fires].
One should place [the offering] for Śrī at the head and for Bhadrakālī at the feet.
One should offer an oblation to Brahmā and Vāstoṣpati in the center of the dwelling site.
The *ucchīrṣaka* is the head-position, which is the refuge of the well-known deities; there one should offer an oblation (*bali*) to Śrī.
From the feet—that is, in the lower part of the house—one offers to Bhadrakālī.
Her place is also in the eastern part of the door.
Others say that the *ucchīrṣaka* is the head-end of the house-bed and the feet are its lower end;
therefore, this oblation is performed either on a bed or the like, or on a spot of ground at the place where the householder sleeps,
for Brahmā and Vāstoṣpati.
Even though there is a dual designation, these two oblations are distinct: "to Brahmā" and "to Vāstoṣpati.

However, where there is duality of deities as in the case of Agni-Soma, one employs either a joint mention or a collective mention, as in "of those two together" and "together with Heaven and Earth," because their association is not otherwise well-known. *Vāstu* means a house; [the offering is made] in its midst.
And one should cast an offering into the air for all the gods,
as well as for the spirits that roam by day and those that roam by night.
Because of the word "ca" (and), this is indeed a single oblation:
to the Viśvedevas, either in the open space of the house or having gone outside the house;
to those who roam by day, and to those who roam by night.
The phrase "to the beings" (bhūtebhyaḥ) is to be supplied [to the following].
Some say that these two oblations are offered separately in the evening and in the morning as "to those who roam by day" (divācārebhyaḥ);
that is incorrect.
He will later describe the *amantrahoma* (oblation without a mantra) for the evening.
By this prohibition of the mantra, let there be no intentionality directed toward the verbal expression; however, by what means is mental intentionality (*mānasa uddeśa*) to be excluded?
For without that [mental intention], the accomplishment of the oblation is not possible.
But this must be stated: how is this understanding of the distinction arrived at? If it is argued that it is by the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras themselves, let it be so.
One should offer a bali on the back part of the house for the prosperity of all food;
however, one should carry all that remains of the bali to the south for the ancestors.
This is the remainder of the two previous oblations.
The first half-verse is for the purpose of prescribing the *ādhāra* [foundation].
That which is the dwelling situated above the dwelling is the "upper site" (*pṛṣṭhavāstu*).
One should also offer an oblation upon the upper part of even a single-roomed house to those who roam by day and those who roam by night,
for the prosperity of all food.
The dative case here is used in the sense of "being for the sake of that" (tādarthye), not in the sense of a recipient (saṃpradāne).

This is because no oblation (*homa*) or similar act is explicitly mentioned; because the word *bali* is a subordinate element (*pūrvaśeṣatvāt*) to what precedes it; and because the two preceding oblations require a substratum (*ādhāra*).
Furthermore, nowhere in another Smṛti is the entirety of all food (*sarvānnabhūtiḥ*) heard of as being a deity (*devatā*) in the Vaiśvadeva rite.
Therefore, this is its meaning:
this [rite] must be performed for the sake of the preparation of all food; when this offering (baliharaṇa) has been made, all foods become [fully prepared].
For while it is appropriate to understand the meaning through the well-known sense of the individual parts, the postulation of a collective meaning has already been addressed.
Alternatively, some unseen purpose must be postulated with respect to the deities.

Because of the inclusion of the word "remnant" (*śeṣa*), the offering should be performed after having set aside the remainder of the *bali* in a vessel; the *bali* offerings are not to be taken directly from what remains in the cooking pot.
"To the south" means in the southern direction; that is to say, facing toward it.
"All" refers to whatever quantity has been taken.
One should slowly scatter [the remains] on the ground for dogs, outcasts, dog-cookers, those afflicted with foul diseases, crows, and worms.
Having set aside food from the vessel, one should place it on the ground for the benefit of dogs and others;
"those with diseases" refers to those suffering from leprosy, consumption, and so forth;
"birds" refers to winged creatures.
It should be done slowly so that it does not become mixed with the dust raised from the ground.

The mention of "ground" is not for the purpose of prohibiting [giving] from a bowl; rather, it means that one should not give directly into the hand of an outcaste, a fallen person, or one afflicted with leprosy.
This is a rule concerning the manner of providing assistance.
For this very reason, this verse is recited with the genitive case, not with the dative ending.
For birds, [the offering] should be placed in such a place where they eat without fear of dogs and other predators.
"Of worms" means in such a place where their presence occurs.
Thus, the Brahmin who constantly honors all beings goes by a straight path to the supreme abode, his very form consisting of radiance.
This is the conclusion of the preceding section.
Because of the use of the word "all," one must also assist with food other animals that may be found in the village, such as deer, chickens, cats, and so forth.
The root *arc* here signifies "favoring" or "benefiting," not "worship," because it is impossible for dogs and similar creatures to be worshipped.
And this is stated for the purpose of precluding contempt; it is recited as "he does not favor [them].
He attains the supreme station, the abode, Brahman, by the straight path.
He does not wander through the many wombs of saṃsāra.
What, then, is this prescription of results?
We say: it is not so.
It has been stated that this rule is obligatory (*nitya*); and regarding an obligatory act, the mention of a fruit is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*),
for no injunction (*vidhi*) is actually heard here.
"He goes" is a statement in the present tense.
"Having a body of light" means having a body consisting solely of light; it is not connected to a body composed of the five elements, but rather he exists as one whose very nature is consciousness.
Alternatively, freedom from stain is indicated by this.
The meaning is that one becomes pure in nature.
Furthermore, this is compassion for living beings;
since there is no connection with sin when there is no transgression of the scriptures, purity is indeed appropriate.
Otherwise, since evil is of the nature of impurity, he would not be of the form of light;
and it is likewise logical that when evil is absent, one attains the supreme abode, which is most excellent and of the nature of non-suffering.
Having performed this rite of offerings in this manner, one should first feed the guest;
and one should give alms to the mendicant and to the religious student according to the prescribed rule.

He will describe the characteristics of a guest (*atithi*). When such a person has arrived, one should first feed him—that is, provide him with food—before all other eaters present in the house. And one should give alms (*bhikṣā*) to a mendicant (*bhikṣu*) who asks for it.
By the word "bhikṣā" (alms), a gift of food of very small quantity is meant;
for it is said that a "prasṛti" is a bhikṣā,
and this is well known in the inner apartments.
It should be given according to the rule to a *brahmacārin*;
however, it should not be given according to the rule even to another mendicant (*bhikṣu*) who is of a heretical (*pākhaṇḍa*) or similar nature.
But for a *brahmacārin*, the rule is that the giving of alms must be preceded by the recitation of benedictions (*svastivācana*). This is the procedure.
Alternatively, [the term] "bhikṣu" refers to a wandering mendicant, and "brahmacārī" to one in the first stage of life;
the word "ca" (and) is placed out of its logical position for the sake of the meter.
It should have been read as "brahmacāriṇe ca" (and to the student of sacred knowledge).
In that case, however, there would be no giving to a forest-dweller (vānaprastha).

Therefore, [the term] *bhikṣu* means "one who begs," and the inclusion of the word *brahmacārin* serves as a qualification for him alone. By this, the giving of alms from all three stages of life (āśrama) is necessarily authorized.
But in the case of heretics and the like, as with outcasts and others,
assistance to mendicants is indeed prescribed according to one's ability by the inclusion of the term "all."
Whatever merit a householder twice-born man obtains by giving a cow to his teacher according to the prescribed rite,
that same merit he obtains by giving alms.
The gift of food to one who asks should always be given according to one's ability;
this, however, is a different matter.
That fruit which one obtains by giving cows to a teacher is obtained by giving alms, for it is not distinct from the vow regarding cows.
In another *Smṛti*, it is heard that the gift of a cow (*godāna*) yields all fruits and even serves the purpose of liberation from sin.
Regarding those minor benefits for which an equality of fruit with great benefits is stated, one should understand that, as in the world, there is a distinction in the magnitude of the fruit;
that very fruit is obtained, but not for a long duration.
For this principle is inexpressible; for what wise man would buy with ten *paṇas* that which can be obtained for one?
If the results were equal, the great effort [required by the former] would result in pointlessness.
Some read the text as "the teacher according to rule" (*ācāryaḥ yathāvidhi*).
In this context, the negative particle (nañ) should be understood as having a limited scope, as in the word "alpagu" (one who has little merit). Merit is the dharma; its fruit is [the result].
One should respectfully offer even alms or a vessel of water, according to the prescribed rule,
to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the true meaning of the Vedas.
Now, since it was stated "according to the rule," that very rule is being explained.
The mention of the water-pot (*udapātra*)—and not merely the giving of alms—is intended to show that this applies to all people at all times.
"Having honored" means having worshipped.
That gift for which there is a prior injunction is "prescribed by rule" (*vidhipūrvaka*). The word *pūrva* signifies a cause; the meaning is that this [gift] has the scripture as its cause.
Or, the injunction (*vidhi*) is the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*), and that must be performed first.
It has been stated previously regarding the giving of alms: "He gives with respect, having honored [the recipient].
One should offer—that is, give—to that Brāhmaṇa who knows the true meaning of the Veda, its ultimate, certain significance.
"To a Brāhmaṇa" is the restriction regarding caste (*jāti*);
"to one who is learned" is the restriction regarding quality (*guṇa*).

Therefore, whatever is to be given should be given to a Brāhmaṇa, and that [gift] should be preceded by honor to one who knows the meaning of the Veda; thus, there is an injunction of three matters. Since the entire passage is directed toward the object of giving, and because it is of human origin (*pauruṣeya*), there is no injunction of various distinct forms of meaning.
There is a fault in giving when [the recipient] has attained [such status].
The offerings to the gods and ancestors of ignorant men perish,
for they have been given by donors to Brahmins who have become like ashes through delusion.
The nature of the document that should be given was described previously;
by this [verse], there is a prohibition against giving it on an invalid document. "They perish" means they become fruitless.
*Havya* refers to those offerings, such as the feeding of Brahmins, which are performed for the sake of the deities;
*kavya* refers to other offerings, such as *śrāddha* rites, which constitute parts of ancestral ceremonies (*pitryakarman*).
[These are offered] when [the body] has become ashes.
"Attained the state of ash" means having become ash;
or, the word *bhūta* is used in the sense of a comparison, meaning "like ash," just as one says "become wood. But what is the similarity with ash?
Just as that which is useless, being of the nature of refuse, is to be discarded, so too such a Brahmin is to be excluded from ritual acts; this is the intended meaning.
The connection is that [these gifts] perish for men who do not understand.
They were given by donors out of delusion.
The statement "by those who do not know, out of delusion" is a restatement;
for that which is rejected by the scripture is done only out of delusion.
But what are those who have not become ashes?
He says:
[they are those] in whom offerings have been cast into the fires of the mouths of Brahmins, which are perfected by knowledge and austerity.
And it delivers one from misfortune and indeed from great sin.
Those who are enriched by knowledge and austerity are distinct from others; they have become like ash [in comparison].
"Enrichment" (samṛddhi) means preeminent excellence.
Those who are endowed with extensive learning and great austerity are described in this way.

Even though knowledge (*vidyā*) and austerity (*tapas*) belong to the whole [the Brahmins], they attain grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the mouths, which are their constituent parts, through a connection with that which is connected to them [the whole].
In the expression "the mouths of the Brahmins are fires," a compound is formed because *vyāghra* and others belong to the class of words known as *ākṛtigaṇa*.

Just as an oblation poured into fire is fruitful, while an oblation poured into ashes is fruitless, so too this kind of food placed into the mouth of a Brahmin is called an "oblation"; thus, it is the food itself that is being praised.
Sacrifices, fire-offerings, and the like are well known for their great fruit;
therefore, that which is less renowned is compared by means of its most celebrated quality:
it delivers one from misfortune.
When life is beset by hardships such as illness, enemies, or oppression by kings, it rescues and protects one from them; one is not touched by such [calamities].
Furthermore, it saves one even from great evil in the next world, such as rebirth in the hells and other lower realms.
Not only is such a recipient required for rites pertaining to worldly prosperity (*ābhyudayika-karman*),
but even that which is given for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) should be bestowed solely upon one who possesses those qualities.
To a guest who has arrived, one should offer a seat and water,
and having prepared food according to one's ability, one should give it in accordance with the prescribed rule.
[This refers to one who has] arrived on his own initiative, not one who has been invited;
for an invited person does not become a guest.
Furthermore, he will state the place of arrival: "where [the host's] wife or even the sacred fires are."
One should provide water for the seat;
first the water intended for washing the feet, then the seat, and then the food.
The phrase "having prepared according to one's ability" is an adjective qualifying the food.
Having prepared the food with special care, one should give it and feed [the recipient] according to the prescribed rule.
That gift in which the rule comes first is described in this way.
The meaning is that "vidhi" refers to the scripture (śāstra), which is the prior cause and the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Even for one who constantly gathers grains by gleaning and offers oblations into the five fires,
a Brahmin staying unhonored takes away all his merit.
Even for one who is extremely poor, it is not proper to neglect the honoring of guests; [this applies even to one] who gathers [grain], that is,
who picks up the ears of corn remaining after the field has been harvested.
And this is intended as an illustration of the restriction of one's livelihood.
Even for one who offers oblations into the five fires, if he—

who is perfected in the performance of the scriptures yet extremely poor— does not honor a guest who has arrived with gifts of food and so forth, then that performance of his, that restraint of livelihood, becomes fruitless.
Consequently, the guest takes away, seizes, and renders fruitless all well-performed merit;
for he dwells unhonored. Therefore, "one should honor him" is the meaning of the injunction.
From the indicative mark "dwelling," this rule applies when [the guest] has arrived in the evening.
There are five fires: the three sacrificial fires (tretā), the domestic fire (gṛhya), and the social fire (sabhya).
Now, what is this fire called the social fire?
Thus they have said:

For one who has gone abroad to another village, where a common (laukika) cooking is performed; or in the case of a great sacrifice (mahāsādhana), that fire which is carried from the domestic hearth (gṛhyāgāra) into many houses for the purpose of removing the cold—that is the *sabhyāgni*. In that case, what [fire] is used there for the *homa*?

To whatever extent there is a rule that these [offerings] are for householders, from this very statement they believe that the Vaiśvadeva-homa exists even for one who is away from home, even in a common fire (*laukika*).
They cite the Smṛti text: "One should offer oblations wherever one sees a well-kindled fire licking at grains of rice or barley, or dried grain."
In this regard, however, you say:
"The knowledge of the five fires is taught in the Upaniṣads;
therein, the forms of those fires are conceptualized."
The meditation performed in that form and the knowledge [attained] therein are conceived as the *homa* (oblation).
For that [meditation] is held to yield a fruit superior to all Vedic ritual acts (*śrauta-karman*).
Thus it is traditionally taught there: "The thief of gold, the drinker of liquor, the violator of the teacher's bed, and the slayer of a Brahmin—these four fall, as does he who associates with them."
He demonstrates the necessity of this duty through an exceptional praise: that even the fruit obtained from the five [great sacrifices] perishes if the guest is not honored and not turned away.
Although there is a rule for feeding the guest even at the morning meal, the expiation for its omission is greater in the evening.

Regarding the phrase "according to one's ability" (*yathāśakti*) in the previous verse, those who consider it to refer to food say: "Guests should be honored according to one's ability—whether they be one, two, or many."
Grass, ground, water, and fourthly, kind speech—
these are never lacking in the homes of the virtuous.

If, due to poverty, the giving of food in the evening is not possible, one should not think: "The primary thing is the feeding of the guest, and since I do not have that, what is the use of this person who has entered my house? For even for one who is incapable [of providing food], the rule for honoring a guest may be fulfilled by the gift of grass and so forth. Alternatively, this rule does not terminate with the meal alone; rather, bedding and other such things must be given to one who will stay overnight.
The mention of "taking grass" is intended as an illustration for [making] a bedding. "Ground" refers to a place for sitting, lying down, or walking about.
"Kind speech" refers to words that are pleasant and beneficial, or the introduction of a discourse, and so forth.
Even in the absence of food, these [offerings] are not withheld from a virtuous guest who has arrived; rather, they are given at all times.
A Brāhmaṇa staying for even a single night is traditionally called a guest (atithi);
because he stays only temporarily, he is therefore called a guest.
Since the meaning of the word "guest" (atithi) is not well-known in common worldly usage, he states its definition:
the status of being a guest belongs to one who stays for a single night in another's house;
and that applies to a Brāhmaṇa, not to any other caste.

On the second day, regarding the ritual of worship, there is freedom of choice (*kāmacāra*). One who desires a specific excellence of prosperity (*abhyudaya*) has authority for that [second day], but it is not mandatory (*naiyamika*). Accordingly, Āpastamba shows that one who desires a fruit has authority for the second and subsequent nights: "By staying for one night, one conquers the earthly worlds; for a second, the intermediate [worlds]; for a third, the divine worlds. Thus he demonstrates the eligibility for the second and following nights for one seeking a result.
Right here, for the sake of strengthening [the argument], he states the etymological derivation: "For 'sthiti' (staying) is impermanent;
this word is derived from the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *ati*;
its formation is somehow accomplished through the *auṇādika* suffixes."
One should recognize as a guest a Brahmin who comes from another village, as well as a traveling companion,
when he has arrived at the house, or even where the sacred fires are maintained, including one's wife.
One who dwells in the same village is not a guest, even if he arrives at the time of the Vaiśvadeva offering;
this excludes a fellow traveler, a fellow student, and a friend.
For regarding him, there will be a rule later on: "A Vaiśya, a Śūdra, and a friend."

Even one who associates with him in every way through various jests, conversations, and the like—though he may not have been seen before—is designated by the term "companion" (*sāṃgatika*) and thus prohibited [from being treated as a guest].
Furthermore, for this householder who has gone abroad, even a guest endowed with all auspicious marks is not [the one intended];
rather, one should recognize as such a guest whoever has arrived at his home.

Wherever his permanent residence is—that which is called his dwelling place—even if he is away on a journey, his wife and his sacred fires constitute his home; thus, even when the householder is absent, they remain his guests.
Therefore, just as he makes arrangements for the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, and other rites while traveling, so too must he make arrangements for the guest.
From the word "or" (vā), however, it is understood as follows:
when one is traveling abroad together with one's wife and sacred fires, then even for one staying in another village, there is indeed a guest—
even though he is not present in the house— provided his wife and sacred fires are there.
And therefore, if one should dwell abroad with his wife while the sacred fires remain at home, there is no obligation to honor guests;
the word "or" (*vā*) refers to the rule "one should know [the guest] when he has arrived at the house," and not to a mutual relationship between the wife and the fires.
Those foolish householders who subsist on the food provided by others go,
after death, to the state of cattle belonging to those who gave them that food.
"Worship" (*upāsana*) means its practice.
This is a censure directed at that Brahmin who, with such an attitude, attends upon this or that person— just as a guest inevitably receives food—
yet he whose character is such only "worships" the cooked food belonging to another, and never [gives it himself].
By that karma, after passing away, one goes to or attains the state of a beast, such as the species of an ox and so forth.
To the giver of food and other things, [the recipient] attains the state of an elephant, a donkey, or a horse in that person's house.
This is the fault of the householder who has prepared the *sthālīpāka* offering.
A guest brought by the setting sun in the evening must not be turned away by the householder;
whether he arrives at the proper time or an improper time, he must not remain in the house without eating.
Evening time begins with sunset and ends with the onset of night (*pradoṣa*).
At that hour, a guest who has arrived must not be turned away nor refused; he is to be honored with food, a bed, a seat, and so forth. By whom? By the host.
By "gṛhamedhin" [is meant]:
*medha* is sacrifice;
*gṛhamedha* is a designation for the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*).
In this context, the qualified person is a householder—
that is, a *gṛhastha*.
The term "married by the sun" (*sūryoḍha*) is a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*), meaning he was "led" or "brought" [to the marriage] by the sun.
Because he has been brought by fate, he must necessarily be honored.
Whether he arrives at the second time— that is, when the time for the Vaiśvadeva offering has arrived— or at an improper time, such as after the evening meal has already concluded,
no householder should allow him to dwell in his home without eating.
If there is a remainder, it should be offered;
if not, the cooking must be performed twice.
One should certainly not eat that food oneself which one does not offer to a guest;
for the honoring of guests brings wealth, fame, long life, and leads to heaven.
When a guest is present, one should not personally consume superior food—such as soup, ghee, curd, sugar, and so forth—until it has been given to him.
However, that which is for the sick, such as gruel, meat broth, or bitter decoctions, should not be given to one who does not desire it;
there is no fault in consuming such things if they have not been given.

In every respect, this is intended to mean that one should not eat prepared food oneself, nor should a guest be fed inferior food; such is the purport of this. "Dhanya" means that which is beneficial for wealth or the cause of wealth;
the words *yaśasya* and so forth are to be understood in the same manner.
This is an explanatory praise (arthavāda) because feeding guests is an obligatory duty; for when a guest is present, [the act of feeding] is already established as a prior requirement.
Since it is possible to construe it as a commendatory statement, it is not proper to assume a separate injunction.
One should provide a superior seat, lodging, bed, escorting, and attendance for those who are superior; inferior treatment for those who are inferior; and equal treatment for those who are equal.

When many guests arrive simultaneously—whether they are equal, inferior, or superior—the assignment of seats and other provisions must take their qualities into account, and not be done without distinction.
"Seat" refers to a grass mat (*bṛsī*) and the like;
"lodging" refers to a place of rest.
"Bed" refers to a couch and the like;
"following" means walking behind one who is departing;
"attending" means remaining in his presence by engaging in conversation near him.
This is the highest among the highest:
one should follow a superior person for a long distance; a middling person, not too far; and an inferior person, only a few steps.
But when the Vaiśvadeva offering has been completed, if another guest should arrive, one should give him food according to one's ability; however, one need not perform the Bali offering for him.
The food intended for all purposes is indeed designated by the term *vaiśvadeva*.
When that has been completed—that is, when it has been finished, all have eaten, and the food is entirely consumed—if another guest should arrive, one should give him freshly cooked food;
however, one must not take a portion from that [original] cooking for the offering.
An oblation into the fire is not intended here, nor merely the offering of bali;
for the oblation into the fire and the bali-offering pertain to the morning and evening cooked meals, and not to those in between.
Thus he will say later: "But in the evening, of the food... and so forth.
And thus, even if one were to cook several times during the day, nevertheless the Vaiśvadeva offering would not be repeated for each cooking;
rather, it should be performed according to one's capacity, either by means of a specific consecration or otherwise.
A Brahmin should not proclaim his own family and lineage for the sake of food;
for by praising them for the sake of food, he is called a "vomit-eater" by the wise.
This instruction regarding the guest is incidental.
One who seeks food should not announce or declare, "I am of such-and-such a family, the son of so-and-so.

"One's own family and lineage" refers to one's own family—namely, one's paternal ancestry beginning with father and grandfather—and one's *gotra*, such as Garga or Bhārgava, or even one's personal name.

A "slip of the lineage" (*gotraskhalita*) refers to when another name is uttered with the intention of referring to a different name; this is what is being described. Furthermore, even the study of other *smṛtis* is prohibited; that too must not be reported.
This is its explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

Thinking, "I shall seek food for the sake of eating because I am born of a renowned family and caste"—for this purpose and by this reason, praising and proclaiming one's own lineage and clan, one is called by the wise "an eater of vomit," meaning one who eats or swallows what has been vomited or disgorged.
A Kṣatriya is not called a guest in the house of a Brāhmaṇa;
rather, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, a friend, a kinsman, and even a teacher [are so designated].
Even if a Kṣatriya is traveling on a journey, he is not a guest when the time for the first meal has arrived;
therefore, one need not necessarily give to him.
The same applies to Vaiśyas and Śūdras as well.
Friends and kinsmen who are equal to oneself are not guests;
however, a teacher is to be treated like a lord, as it is said that the act of cooking must be announced to him.
But if a Kṣatriya should come to the house in the manner of a guest, one may,
at will, feed him as well once the Brahmins have finished eating.
In this regard, the characteristics of a guest are having one's provisions for the journey exhausted, residing in another village, and arriving at the time of the meal.
If a Kṣatriya comes to the house in such a form, then he too should be fed.
By the mention of "feeding," other forms of service are excluded.
However, speaking words that are both pleasing and beneficial is prescribed for anyone who has arrived at one's house without distinction;
and this is the proper time for such a meal.
After the Brahmins and Vedic scholars have eaten—whether they are guests or non-guests residing in the house, or those who were fed first—he should then be fed.
The word "kāmam" expresses the absence of a restrictive rule;
the meaning is that this injunction is optional (kāmya) and not obligatory (nitya). And since no specific desire is mentioned, heaven is [the result] among the particular fruits.
Alternatively, "blessed," "glorious," and so forth, should be connected here.
If a Vaiśya or a Śūdra also arrive at his household as guests,
he should feed them along with his servants, practicing kindness toward them.
The duty of a guest is *atithidharma*;
those two in whom that exists are "possessors of the duty of hospitality" (*atithidharmin*).
And the duty of a guest has been explained previously.
The "family" refers to the household; one should feed even a Vaiśya and a Śūdra who have arrived there, just as one would a Kṣatriya.
However, the time for feeding those two is after the time for the Kṣatriya, since it is said:
"One should feed those two along with the servants."
In this context, "servants" refers to slaves.
Their time for eating is before all others—guests, kinsmen, and relatives—who have already eaten, and prior to the husband and wife.
The word "together" (saha) indicates merely simultaneity of time.

"Practicing benevolence, compassion, and pity" means making them one's standard, or relying upon them—so much is the sense. By this, he precludes their being objects of worship; for one who is to be favored and pitied is not an object of worship.

If it is possible to bestow favor upon those who deserve compassion, then it should be done by one seeking spiritual prosperity; however, the transgression of a guest does not arise from the mere non-performance [of such favor].
This is what is meant:
the merit derived from favoring those deserving of compassion is superior to that of feeding a guest, whereas no merit inferior to that [of feeding a guest] arises from the former.
Furthermore, he should, together with his wife, feed friends and others who have come to his house out of affection, providing them with ordinary food according to his ability.
"Friends" refers to those for whom he is a companion or a friend;
the word "etcetera" (ādi) includes various types such as kinsmen, relatives, associates, and fellow students— excluding the teacher—
and those who have approached him with affection.
Since the guest and dharma are the subjects under discussion, the term "with affection" (saṃprīti) is used for the purpose of prohibition [of eating without it].
One should feed them;
that is, having prepared the food with excellence—that is, having refined it.

The word "according to one's capacity" (*yathāśakti*) is used as an elliptical expression for "capacity. Whatever capacity one possesses and whatever kind of refinement a person deserves, that very same refinement should be performed with respect to him,
together with his wife.
The time for the husband's meal is the very same as that for the wife, because there is no separate time for her meal;
for it has been stated thus: "But the remainder [of the food] belongs to the couple.
In the Mahābhārata, the wife's eating after the husband is demonstrated.

In the dialogue between Draupadī and Satyabhāmā, Draupadī, while explaining the duties of women, said: "I eat the remaining food after all my husbands have eaten. Eating the remnants of the husband's meal is the duty of women.
Therefore, it is not prescribed that friends and others should eat at the same time as the wife."
Nor does "eating from a single vessel" mean eating together; rather,
it means that they should not be fed alone,
but that his wife should also eat there.
And therefore, the rule that "the husband and wife [should eat] what remains" is here set aside.
If the husband has someone more worthy who must be waited for, or if he should not eat due to a lack of appetite, then the wife should eat in his place;
in this way, their mutual affection will be manifested.
One should feed these— married women, young girls, the sick, and pregnant women—
immediately after the guests, without making any distinctions among them.
"Suvāsinyah" refers to newly-wed brides, women whose husbands are living, daughters-in-law, and daughters.
Others, however, say that even those who have given birth are called "suvāsinyah" provided their fathers-in-law and fathers are still living.
One should feed these very persons immediately after the guests, following them directly.
One should feed the guests at the same time as those who have already begun their meal;
others, however, read "agra" (before),
without reflecting on this.
One should not entertain such doubt as to how children can eat while guests have not yet been fed.
But that unwise person who eats before giving to these [beings] does not realize, while eating, that he is being devoured by dogs and vultures.

If an unwise person, ignorant of the meaning of the scriptures, eats first—before giving food to these [beginning with] guests and ending with servants—he is eaten by dogs and vultures as a ghost (*preta*).

He does not realize that such a meal is his own being devoured by them. For the deluded mind thinks, "I alone am eating here," but he does not perceive that such food is actually the devouring of his own body by dogs and vultures.
It is stated thus because it is the fruit of that.
Then, after the Brahmins and his own servants have indeed finished eating,
the husband and wife should afterwards eat what remains.
The *vipras* are the guests, and the "own" (*sva*) refers to kinsmen and others.
When they have finished their meal, the husband and wife—the couple—should eat what remains.

The word "afterwards" (*paścāt*) is stated so that it may not be thought that eating should occur first, even though the designation "remnant" (*śiṣṭa*) applies once something has been set aside for them.
This first half-verse is a restatement intended for the purpose of prescribing the time for the meal of the husband and wife.
Having honored the gods, the sages, human beings, the ancestors, and the household deities, the householder should thereafter eat the remains.
This is merely a restatement of the previously mentioned rule for the performance of the five sacrifices and the time for the householder's meal;
however, others describe it as an injunction for a different purpose.
In the preceding [verse], it was prescribed that the husband and wife should eat their remaining food at the same time.
By this [verse], the wife is excluded and only the husband is enjoined;
consequently, before the servants and even before the husband, the wife should eat,
or having prepared [the food] in this manner, he should feed her.
This too will be appropriate;
otherwise, if one were to assume the meaning to be "she should not eat with them [the brothers] as her husband," there would be a disruption of the syntactical connection of the word as it is heard.
As for the observation found in the Mahābhārata, that is merely an observation and not an injunction; if it were an injunction, it would be subject to optionality.
That is incorrect, because this is a restatement (anuvāda).
Nor is there a contradiction with the singular number in the word "householder" (gṛhastha), since husband and wife have a joint entitlement;
and in that case, because the sense of "together" is predominant, there is no occasion for the dual number.
Just as in the injunction "a Brahmin should establish the sacred fires," although there is joint entitlement with his wife, the singular number is not contradicted;
for what reason?
Because in that case, one is the primary agent while the other is subordinate.
Furthermore, a quality (guṇa) is not capable of producing its own number;
therefore, because the primary referent possesses the number one, even though there is an entry into the meaning of "husband" (paty-artha), the singular alone is appropriate.
The single word *gṛhastha* applies to the wife as well, and that occurs when there is a desire to express them together (*sahavivakṣā*).
And that [act] occurs because the two primary elements or the two qualities are objects of a single cognition.
Therefore, the wife's meal does not precede that of the man.
Thus, it is established that this is a restatement (anuvāda) for the sake of strengthening the comprehension [of the rule].

Those who, considering the word "deities" (*devatā*) in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—"one should worship the deities of the household"—to be connected with the injunction "one should worship," maintain that the injunction for worship is indeed figurative (*gauṇa*).

For it is not possible for the primary meaning of "deity" to be the object of worship; since the status of being a deity is primary only insofar as it is connected with sacrifice (*yajis*) and praise (*stuti*). And thus he says, "the deities of the household."
The term *gṛhyāḥ* means "those belonging to the house";
and these are merely representations,
for it is not established that those who have become the recipients (*saṃpradāna*) of a sacrifice possess a connection with the house.
For them as well, the term "deity" is used figuratively and does not refer to an object of worship. Why is this so?
Because it is logical that those [deities] who are to be sacrificed to by a householder are called *gṛhyāḥ* (belonging to the household).
He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin;
for it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists of what remains from a sacrifice.
He who cooks or causes food to be cooked for his own sake—thinking, "I am hungry," or "This pleases me"—reaps only evil; he stores it up, takes it in, and does not consume even a morsel of the food.

Therefore, one who is not ill should not cook food for himself. However, for one who is ill, it is proper to resort to whatever means necessary to sustain the body, even by transgressing other rules, because of the scriptural injunction: "One should protect oneself by all possible means."
Thus some have explained its meaning;
this is incorrect because it contradicts another Smṛti, for they say as follows:
Whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is dear to one in one's home,
that very thing should be given to a virtuous person by one who desires that it become inexhaustible.
"Beloved" means desired and longed for.
And if it were not cooked, how could there be the possibility of giving such a thing? Therefore, this is its meaning: [it refers to the state of being ready].
First of all, there is no such thing as a "regular" (nitya) cooking intended for a specific purpose;
its purpose lies in [cooking] when friends, kinsmen, and others have arrived.
Otherwise, if the cooking were not intended for a specific recipient, the giving of food to guests and others would be enjoined.
Therefore, this is what is meant:
this fault applies to one who eats without having given [food] to them;
or else, when everyone, beginning with the guests, has eaten, one should not cook again for one's own sake.
And likewise Vasiṣṭha says: "The husband and wife should eat what remains;
when everything has been consumed, there is no further cooking;
it is the eating of the remnants of a sacrifice."
This is indeed a praise of the aforementioned practice of eating the remnants.
A "sacrifice" refers to the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites; "remnants" refers to what remains after [the deities] have been served, and this is the consumption of that.

It yields a fruit equal to those [sacrifices], namely, that which is prescribed for virtuous householders devoted to the performance of the scriptures, consisting of the remnants left over after guests and others have eaten.
One should honor with the honey-mixture (madhuparka) a king, a sacrificial priest, a snātaka, a teacher, a dear father-in-law, and a maternal uncle, again after a full year has passed.
In connection with the topic of honoring guests, a specific form of worship for certain other venerable persons who have come to one's house is now prescribed.
"A king" refers to one who has been consecrated, not merely any member of the Kṣatriya caste;
for this is an exceedingly great honor, and every Kṣatriya does not deserve it.
For it is not appropriate that he be mentioned together with the *snātaka* and the teacher;

nor is equality of honor with the teacher appropriate for him, as is shown by an indicative mark (*liṅga*). For instance, the *Brāhmaṇa* on the *Ātithyeṣṭi* sacrifice says, "Just as when a king of men has arrived," and in the procedure for the *madhuparka*, it states, "A guest is like a cow-slayer," which indicates that this refers to a king of men.
Therefore, this worship should be performed by a Kṣatriya or a non-Kṣatriya who is a lord of the realm;
however, for a Śūdra, there is no possession of mantras.
But is it not the case that the recitation of mantras is forbidden for a Śūdra?
But this does not apply to Brāhmaṇas and others when the ritual gift is intended for a Śūdra.
This is not a fault,
because even for those [lower castes], there is the recitation of mantras such as "bhūtebhyas tvā."
But is it not the case that in the Mahābhārata, the ritual of the madhuparka is also heard of as being performed by a Śūdra?
"He himself duly offered him a worthy seat,
and the madhuparka and a cow to that Blessed One."
"To the Blessed One Vāsudeva, Vidura [offers]..."—
the term *madhuparka* is applied here to the curd used as its constituent ingredient out of devotion.
A word may be used for that which serves a particular purpose, just as in the expression "clarified butter is indeed life."
The word *rājan* refers to a lord of the countryside and does not apply to every mere Kṣatriya.
They say that a son-in-law is "dear" (*priya*),
and a *snātaka* is so by virtue of both learning and vows.

Otherwise, all officiating priests and teachers are indeed *snātakas*. For those established in the various stages of life (*āśrama*), the practice of begging for alms is prescribed, but not eating according to the duty toward a guest.
Alternatively, the term *snātaka* refers to one who has recently completed the study of the Vedas.
One should honor and worship these [guests].
The term *madhuparka* is the name of a ritual act;
its specific nature is to be understood from the *Gṛhya-sūtra*.
"Those for whom a year has passed" (*parisaṃvatsarān*) is an epithet qualifying those worthy of honor, such as kings; it refers to those by whom a full year has been completed or exceeded.
