If they arrive after a year has elapsed, then they are worthy of the *madhuparka* offering; prior to that, they are not.
Some explain it thus:
if they arrive before the end of the year, then even though the year has not yet elapsed, he receives another offering for the first offering.
Others, however, say:
Their worship is annual, not to be performed until their arrival;
according to this view, arriving before that time does not constitute an obstacle to the worship.
There is an alternative reading: *parisaṃvatsarāt* (after a full year).
The meaning is that for as long as one year has passed, they remain [impure]; after that, however, they are to be honored again.

When a sacrificial rite is at hand, both a king and a learned Brahmin (śrotriya) are to be honored with the honey-mixture (madhuparka); but this rule does not apply when there is no sacrifice—such is the established tradition.
Some maintain that this [rule] is intended for the purpose of obtaining [the guest] even before a year has passed, provided that a sacrifice is the occasion;
others, however, say that it is a restatement (upasaṃhāra) of the previous rule concerning the king and the learned Brahmin (śrotriya).
For if it were not a restatement, the phrase "but not when there is no sacrifice" would be untenable.
In this context, the "learned one" (*śrotriya*) is either the *snātaka* previously mentioned, or indeed the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) himself;

for it is prescribed that the offering of the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) is to be made to him when a sacrificial rite is about to commence. Even if he should sacrifice with Soma more than once within a year, they should perform the sacrifice for him only after he has been offered the guest-offering (*arghya*).
In this way, this Smṛti will have its basis established;
otherwise, a basis would have to be inferred.
Others, however, believe that the word "learned in the Vedas" (śrotriya) refers to all the officiating priests and others.

And likewise, Gautama has stated this without distinction: having said, "The *madhuparka* [is offered] upon the arrival of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), the teacher (*ācārya*), the father-in-law (*śvaśura*), the paternal uncle (*pitṛvya*), and the maternal uncle (*mātula*)," he further stated, "[This applies] prior to [the completion of] a sacrifice or a marriage.
Therefore, for all those worthy of the *arghya* offering, there should be eligibility for the *arghya* even before a year [has passed] when a sacrifice is the occasion;
however, the prohibition "but not at one who is not sacrificing" should be understood as applying prior to a year, and not after.
In this second quarter-verse, there is a manifold understanding of the reading;
some recite it as:
*tate yajña upasthitau*.
This is their meaning:

if the two [guests] arrive—that is, have been invited and brought—once the sacrifice has already commenced (*tate*), then this performance of the *madhuparka* rite is for them; it is not, however, performed when the sacrifice is merely about to begin (*prārabhyamāṇe*).
This position is refuted by some:
since the injunction "the initiated one does not give" prohibits all giving on the part of the initiated, the permission to give the *madhuparka* would be contradictory to that.
Nor can it be said that this is not an act of giving, because the injunction "he should honor him" (*arhayet*) prescribes this as an act of worship.
Since there is the offering of curd and the offering of meat and other foods in the *madhuparka* ceremony,
it might be argued that one is simply consuming what belongs to another.
If this were the case, there would be the fault of theft.
If it is argued that this is not so because of the scriptural statement, then the sense of "giving" (dadāti) certainly exists;
for the root *dā* has been enjoined, as in the injunction: "one should give the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*)."
Therefore, it is contradictory.
There would be a contradiction with the statement "the initiated one does not give" only if the word *yajña* referred exclusively to Soma sacrifices.
Since the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) and others are also sacrifices, this injunction will apply to them as well.
This is not correct; for if that were so, it would contradict established custom.
Indeed, the learned do not bring the *madhuparka* for an *arghya* guest anywhere other than at Soma sacrifices.
Conduct consists of reverence for the Vedas;

therefore, this reading alone is appropriate: "when a sacrificial rite has arrived. It is those who are about to begin a sacrifice who honor a guest with the *madhuparka*, not those whose sacrifice is already in progress.
Therefore, we do not even consider this:
let there be a cessation of giving that is obtained in a general sense, but not of that which is specifically enjoined as its object.
And "sacrificial act" (yajñakarma) refers to that which is both a sacrifice and an action; when that has arrived—that is, when it has been reached—[the rule applies].
In the evening, when food has been prepared, the wife should offer a Bali oblation without reciting mantras;
for this is called the Vaiśvadeva, which is prescribed for both morning and evening.
The first [daily offering] has been described;
now the second cooking is being explained.

At evening, which is the end of the day and the onset of night (*pradoṣa*), the entire procedure for a *pākayajña* must be repeated for the food prepared there, with the exception of the *brahmayajña* and the *pitṛyajña*.
But is it not the case that only this much is heard:

"one should offer the bali"? And since the offering of the bali is well known as being the sacrifice to beings (bhūtayajña) alone, how can there be an oblation in the fire or the giving of gifts to guests and others in that context?
Now, the word *vaiśvadeva*—in the sense that "this is indeed called the *vaiśvadeva*"—establishes its applicability to all [offerings].

This is prescribed for all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*). Whether it is performed in the evening or in the morning, it is exactly the same in the evening as it is in the morning; it is for this very purpose that the word "morning" is used.
Otherwise, since it is already prescribed for the morning, why is this [same act] prescribed for both evening and morning?
If that is the case, then the *brahmayajña* and the *pitṛyajña* must also be performed. It is replied: [they need not be].
Because of the statement "of the prepared food," only that which can be accomplished with food should be performed;
however, the *brahmayajña* accomplished through Vedic study is not to be done, nor is the libation (*tarpaṇa*) accomplished with water.
And thus the connection is made.
One should offer an oblation (*bali*) of the prepared food.
This rite, known as *vaiśvadeva*, is prescribed for both times of day once the food has been prepared.
It is explained in this way because of the words "food" (*anna*) and "for all gods" (*vaiśvadeva*).
"Without a mantra":
by the word "mantra," there is prohibited a vocal utterance addressed to a deity that ends with *svāhā*, such as "To Agni, svāhā! and so forth;
for no other mantras are prescribed for use in the *vaiśvadeva* offerings.
And among those [Vedic texts], the status of being a *mantra* is expressed by way of praise;
however, there is no status of being a *mantra* for those not recited in one's own Vedic study (*svādhyāya*).
A certain portion of the *svādhyāya*, consisting of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, *Sāman*, and so forth, is designated as "mantra" by those who study the Vedas.
Furthermore, the understanding of the meaning of words arises from conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).

Nor are those words by which the offering of oblations (*baliharaṇa*) and other rites are performed recited anywhere [in the Vedic texts]. Rather, based on the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) that "one should perform the *homa* for the gods beginning with Agni," and by another statement that "the sacrificial food (*havis*) is delivered to the gods either with the utterance of *svāhā* or with the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*," the utterance of *svāhā* is prescribed for all *homas*, while the utterance of *vaṣaṭ* is regulated for the end of the *yājyā* verse, as it is stated: "He utters *vaṣaṭ* at the *yājyā*."
The dative case is prescribed when used in conjunction with the word *svāhākāra*.

Therefore, because the sacrifice has the deity as its intended object (*uddeśya*), and because the status of being an intended object for the deity arises from the form understood through words—and since this is appropriate only through words—this construction is performed, such as "Svāhā to Agni" and so forth.
If that is the case, and those [words] are prohibited, how then is the accomplishment of the sacrifice possible?
For as long as the dedication has not been performed—such that [the thought] "this is not for you, nor is it mine"—the completion of the essential nature of the sacrifice does not occur;
indeed, a sacrifice is not merely an act of relinquishment devoid of dedication.
This is true.

When the [use of] the word is prohibited, the wife will perform the assignment of the deity mentally, just as a Śūdra utters a salutation (*namaskāra*). For him, the salutation is permitted as a non-mantric substitute; since it is said that "for the Śūdra, the mantra is replaced by a salutation," the salutation is permitted for him, but not the word for the deity.
And in that case, it has been stated that success [in the rite] comes from the employment of a deity.
However, here the honorable ones say: "For a Śūdra, the utterance of *svāhā* is replaced by a salutation (*namaskāra*), but the mention of a deity is not prohibited.
Now, who is the performer in the evening Vaiśvadeva oblation?
It has been stated that the wife herself, because of her proximity, will perform [the rite] without mantras, just as in the case of the *bali* offering.
Having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires should, at the waning of the moon,
perform the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha every month.
This other obligatory *śrāddha* is prescribed as distinct from the optional *śrāddha* dedicated to the Viśvedevas.

It is to be performed at the waning of the moon, on the new-moon day (*amāvāsyā*). Even then, it is not to be done at just any time; rather, it is to be performed after having completed the *pitṛyajña*.
Having performed that Piṇḍapitṛyajña which is prescribed by the Śruti,
and since its time is thus obtained for this [rite] as well—
it has been stated that "the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is on the new moon day in the afternoon"— [one should proceed].
Even for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (anāhitāgni), the application of the *aupāsana* fire certainly exists;
and thus it is said:
"In this manner, one who has not maintained the sacred fires, having cooked [the oblation] in the perpetual [fire]," and so forth.
"One possessing fire" means one who possesses either the nuptial fire or the fire brought at the time of inheritance. The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is not intended to be restrictive;
it is desired [to apply] to the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya as well.
Thus, it is stated without qualification in other Smṛtis:
"the piṇḍānvāhāryaka";
this is the name of this Śrāddha.
It is brought forth or performed subsequent to the rice-balls (piṇḍas);
therefore, it is called *piṇḍānvāhāryaka*. It occurs every month and every following month; thus, it is *māsānumāsika* (monthly).
The compound expression *māsānumāsam* denotes a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) pertaining to months;
that is to say, it means "it should be performed month after month.
And from this, its obligatory nature (*nityatā*) is established.

Although the understanding of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) arises from the word *anumāsam*, the word *māsa* is redundant; nevertheless, in poetic composition, such prolixity is not taken into account.
*Śrāddham* is also merely a name [of the rite], while *kuryāt* constitutes the injunction (*vidhi*).
The wise know that the monthly śrāddha for the ancestors is the anvāhārya;
and that should be performed with effort using commendable meat.
The *anvāhārya* is the sacrificial fee for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) at the two Śrauta rites of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
This monthly *śrāddha* performed on the day of the new moon is the *anvāhārya* for the ancestors (*pitṛs*).
Just as the priests are gratified by the *anvāhārya*, so too are the ancestors gratified by the *śrāddha*.
By this, he states that the *śrāddha* is for the sake of the ancestors (*pitṛ*).

Just as the *darśa* and other sacrifices are for the sake of deities such as Agni, the ancestors are not [the direct recipients] in the *śrāddha* in that way; rather, the *śrāddha* is solely for the purpose of benefiting them.
And thus, the genitive case in "of the ancestors" (*pitṝṇām*) is used.
For if it were merely a deity, its absence from the dative case would be improper.
In one view, there is a different reading and a different meaning:
"The wise know the *anvāhārya* [to be] the monthly [offering] for the *piṇḍas*."
By this [statement] as well, its necessity is asserted, just like the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*);
however, it is not an ancillary part (*aṅga*) [of another rite]. That very [rite] is to be performed with *āmiṣa*, that is, with meat.
By means of what is praised, not prohibited, or specifically prescribed—
as he will state, "for two months with fish-meat"—
this is the primary ritual procedure (*mukhya-kalpa*).
In its absence, curd, ghee, milk, cakes, and so forth will be prescribed;
and meat as a condiment for the food consisting of boiled rice and the like.
However, this alone is not the sole food, since [the author] will later state: "and the accessories such as soups and vegetables," as well as "as many as there are and with whatever foods."

Furthermore, are all the rites—such as the fire-oblation (homa), the feeding of Brahmins, and the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa)—equally primary and denoted by the word "śrāddha," or is some part here subordinate and some primary?
It is said in reply:

because of the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in expressions such as "one should feed at a śrāddha" and "the śrāddha was eaten by him," it is understood that the feeding of the Brahmins is the principal element.
And so it is said:
"In that regard, I shall declare in their entirety those who are to be fed and those who are to be avoided among the best of the twice-born, as many as there are, and with which foods."

In that regard, concerning this śrāddha, I shall now explain all of the following: which of the best of the twice-born Brāhmaṇas are to be fed and which are to be avoided; how many and of what number they are—such as "two for the gods" and so forth; and with which foods they are to be served—such as sesame seeds, rice, barley, and so forth.
Listen to this, for this is what must be primarily accomplished here.
Without these, the *śrāddha* is not considered performed.

Furthermore, regarding any other constituent part—whether it be an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) or a direct auxiliary (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*)—if that is incomplete, the *śrāddha* is not considered performed; it would not be endowed with its full quality.
Therefore, they are mentioned again for the purpose of declaring their preeminence.
One should feed two at a rite for the gods and three at a rite for the ancestors, or one at each; even if very wealthy, one should not engage in excessive elaboration.

Although it would have been more appropriate to explain the specific details of the matter already promised in that same sequence, nevertheless, because what remains to be said here is very brief, he sets aside the point that "one should feed those who are to be fed" and instead provides this specification of numbers:
one should feed two Brahmins with reference to the gods,
and three for the sake of the ancestors.
Or, one [guest] may be invited for both occasions—one for the divine rite and one for the ancestral rite.

Although in the term *pitrye* (for the ancestors), the deity is enjoined by the word *pitṛ* (father) in the sense of "this is for the father," nevertheless, the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are the intended recipients.
In that case, one should feed one person for each ancestor, and not just one person for all of them, because they are distinct deities.
And it has been stated by the author of the *Gṛhyasūtra*: "But certainly not one for all; this is explained by the [rule regarding] rice-balls (*piṇḍa*).
The meaning is that just as a single rice-ball is not offered for all [ancestors], likewise a single Brāhmaṇa is not fed.
Here too, he will say: "He should invite at least three."
That invitation is solely for the purpose of providing food, not for the sake of some unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Therefore, it should be understood that in the rite for the ancestors (*pitṛkṛtya*), one should invite three [Brahmins] each;
thus he says: "And one should not feed those who are inferior."
And having established this, the statement "even each single learned person" should likewise be understood as "one for each one.

Furthermore, it is not the case that "each one in both places" is being prescribed here; rather, this is a restatement intended to prohibit an extensive [application]. It is just like saying, "Eat poison, but do not eat in his house."

If that is so, then this rule as well—"two for the gods"—would not exist, since it too can be accounted for by another purpose. If, however, this rule exists because [the number] was not otherwise established, then why would the rule "one for each" not also exist?
To this, he says:
Let it not be that even one of the two is prescribed; from what, then, is the understanding of the number derived? From the rule: "One should invite at least three."
But surely, there is no mention of "deities" (daiva) in that [verse].
Rather, the number is understood from another Smṛti: "Or odd numbers according to one's enthusiasm," and "Even numbers for the deities.
Furthermore, if this were a rule prescribing a specific number, then since there would be no possibility of exceeding it, the prohibition [of exceeding] would be meaningless.
Therefore, as many Brahmins as can be fed without those faults occurring that arise from a large-scale performance should be fed;
in rites for the ancestors (pitrya), an odd number, but in rites for the gods (daiva), exactly two—
even one who is exceedingly prosperous and extremely wealthy.
It would not proceed in detail;
nor is this prohibition of detail intended for an unseen purpose.
What then?
Hospitality, the proper time and place, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins—these five things elaborate rituals destroy; therefore, one should not seek elaboration.
These faults arise;
a detailed account is not pursued here.
However, if it is possible to provide hospitable treatment and so forth, then one should act according to one's enthusiasm.
*Satkriyā* (proper hospitality) refers to the specific preparation of the food.
*Deśa* (place) refers to ground sloping toward the south and so forth, as will be stated in the phrase "in clean open spaces.
*Kāla* (time) refers to the afternoon, when the sun has moved past midday.
Purity pertains to oneself, to Brāhmaṇas, and to servants. The "attainment" of Brāhmaṇas is the acquisition of virtuous Brāhmaṇas;
these qualities must necessarily be accomplished.
And they perish in detail;
"detail" means deficiency.
Furthermore, this [deficiency] would entail an overabundance of Brahmins.
Therefore, one should not desire it, nor should one perform it.
This well-known performance for the deceased, called the ancestral rite (pitrya), occurs at the waning of the moon;
for one engaged in that, it is always merely a worldly performance for the dead.
This rite called *pitrya* is not like those rites for the gods (*daiva*), which have no purpose for the deities; rather,
it is the well-known and celebrated performance of funeral rites (*pretakṛtyā*) or service for the deceased,
performed at the waning of the moon.
*Vidhu* is the moon; its waning is the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). There is an alternative reading, *tithikṣaye*;
however, the reading *vidhikṣaye* is faultless.
This is how it should be applied there:
"pitrya" refers to the rite enjoined by the ritual rules, performed in the ancestral home;
[the word "tasmin" refers] to that ancestral rite.
For one who is disciplined, devoted to that,
and constant in its performance,
it stands by him just as a funeral rite does for the deceased.
Even for that preta, a service such as the *śrāddha* and other rites is performed by his sons;
in this manner, it is established that the fruit of the *śrāddha* is the non-interruption of the lineage of sons, grandsons, and so forth.
Furthermore, one who desires that fruit does not have the entitlement [to perform this rite], because its obligatory nature (*nityatva*) has already been established.
Others, however, maintain that this is a different qualification intended for one who desires the non-interruption of the lineage;
it is a worldly duty, meaning it is based on traditional law (smārta).
Sacrificial offerings to the gods and the ancestors must be given by donors only to one learned in the Vedas;
what is given to such a most worthy Brahmin yields great fruit.

To a *śrotriya*—one who has studied an entire branch (*śākhā*) consisting of both mantra and brāhmaṇa, including the *chāndasa* (Vedic phonology)—to him should be given the *havyas*, those offerings prescribed for the Viśvedevas as part of the meal at a *śrāddha*;
and the *kavyas*, those meals intended for the ancestors. To the most worthy one.
The Arhat possesses both worthiness and fitness for veneration. One born of a great family is honored—one who is born into a noble lineage and is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct.
What is given to such a person, whether out of faith or otherwise, yields great fruit.

Or rather: a gift given to one who is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*) is fruitless; to one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) but lacks qualities such as noble lineage and knowledge, it yields little fruit; but to one who is most worthy (*arhattama*), it yields great fruit.
By feeding even a single learned man at a rite for the gods or the ancestors, one obtains abundant fruit; but not by feeding many who are ignorant of the mantras.
He demonstrates what was stated regarding "for the sake of attaining arhatship":
by feeding even a single learned person, one obtains abundant fruit;
and "learnedness" has been explained as the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas.
As it has been said: "Even many who do not know the mantras.
The mention of "mantras" is intended to indicate the Vedas.
The meaning of the injunction is that, in the absence of five who are learned in the Vedas, one may feed even a single learned person.
Puṣkala means abundant, nourished, and vast.
One should examine from afar a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas;
he is the proper recipient for offerings to the gods and ancestors, and he is remembered as a guest.
One should not be fed simply because he has mastered the Vedas.
Rather, one should examine him from afar with skill, seeking to know the complete purity of both his maternal and paternal lineages.

As it has been said: "Those who are [traced] ten generations back on both the mother’s and father’s side, who have practiced learning and austerity, and who are distinguished by meritorious deeds—those whose Brahminhood is established on both sides"—this is the examination from afar.
Likewise, there is the understanding of the Veda through its study, comprehension, performance of rites, and realization according to reality.
One who has reached the "pāra" of the Veda—that is, its completion—is a *vedaparaga*. One does not become worthy [of this status] merely by reciting the Vedic *saṃhitā* or the *brāhmaṇa* alone.
From this very perspective, it is understood that by the word *śrotriya*, even one who studies but a single portion of the Veda is denoted.
That [person] is a *tīrtha* for offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*).
A *tīrtha* is like a bathing-place; it is called a *tīrtha* because they descend there to take up water.

Therefore, just as those seeking water obtain it by traveling along the correct path, so too do the *havya* and *kavya* offerings reach the ancestors through such a Brāhmaṇa; this is the praise [of him].

Furthermore, regarding other acts of sacrifice, public works, and charity, just as a gift is given without hesitation to a guest who has arrived of his own accord, and that which is given yields great fruit, even so, *havya* and *kavya* should be given without hesitation to such a Brāhmaṇa, for they result in great fruit.
For where a thousand times a thousand who are ignorant of the Ṛgveda may eat,
a single person who knows the mantras, being pleased, is worth all of them according to dharma.
"Of those who do not know the Ṛgveda" means those who do not know the meaning of the Ṛgveda;

this is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa), because for those who do not know the Ṛgveda, there is no possibility [of being a recipient] at all, due to the restrictive rule that [the gift] must be given "only to one learned in the Vedas" (*śrotriya*).
The compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) has not been applied because of its archaic character (*chāndasatva*) and for the sake of metrical convenience (*vṛttānurodha*).
For they recite thus:
"One might even turn a bean into a bean-paste, but one should not disturb the meter."
Alternatively, "anṛcā" is the nominative plural;
the connection is "as a thousand non-Vedic singers (anṛcāḥ) eat," just as in the expression "a thousand cows."

A single person who knows the mantras and understands the meaning of the Vedas—being pleased, satiated, and fed—is equal to all those who do not know the Ṛgveda; he takes them into himself, makes them his own, and attains non-difference from them.
And when there is this non-difference, the understanding arises that the fruit which is obtained by feeding thousands of such [ignorant] people is obtained in a single [learned] person.
This censure of the ignorant is for the purpose of enjoining the learned.
Furthermore, it is not being said that those numbered in the thousands and the one [learned person] have equal results;
for since the injunction applies to the learned, there is no possibility at all of its application to the unlearned.

Even if, in the absence of a learned person, the phrase "to a Śrotriya indeed" might suggest a partial application to the unlearned, nevertheless, so that there be no prohibition of the extensive [gift], the literal meaning of the text remains possible.
Offerings for the ancestors and oblations to the gods should be given to one preeminent in knowledge;
for hands smeared with blood are not purified by blood alone.
To one who is superior or more distinguished by knowledge and learning, the *kavyas* (offerings to the ancestors) should be given.
This refers to the simile of hands smeared with blood:

hands smeared with blood become stained even more excessively when wiped with blood; they do not become clean. In the same way, an unlearned Brahmin, being fed at a funeral rite, leads the ancestors even further downward.
For as many mouthfuls as one who is ignorant of the mantras consumes at offerings to the gods or ancestors,
for that many mouthfuls does that deceased person consume glowing spikes, spears, and iron balls.
Even though this occurs within the section on ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), this is a restatement of the fault pertaining to the eater based on the direct statement of the text;
as it has been said:
"Therefore, an ignorant man should fear from whatever source that gift may come."
Thus:
the *śūla* and *ṛṣṭi* are specific types of weapons; an *ayoguḍa* is an iron ball.
For the sake of which the *śrāddha* was commenced, that person is made by the messengers of Yama to eat blazing, heated iron balls.
However, upon seeing Vyāsa, it was concluded that this fault belongs to the host and not to the eater;

nor does it belong to the ancestors. For it is not logical that those who have died should incur a connection with guilt for another’s transgression of a prohibition, as that would result in the fallacy of "the acquisition of what was not done" (*kṛtābhyāgama*) and other such faults. If indeed such a Brahmin was fed by the son, what offense has been committed by the deceased?
But surely, by this same logic, even the benefit conferred upon the ancestors by a son would not be established?
It would not be established if the *śrāddha* and other rites were not enjoined for that purpose;
however, in this case there is no such injunction stating that one desiring to benefit the father must act in this way, as in the case of the *śyena* sacrifice.
As for the statement, "The hungry ghost consumes that much," this is applicable even in connection with the one who feeds [the Brahmins];
for it is a logical connection that "he whose Brahmin of such a kind eats at the *śrāddha* obtains this fruit.
Furthermore, this prohibition against feeding the ignorant is topical to the present context.

In the transgression of that [rule], there is a deficiency in the ritual action; and when there is such a deficiency, the very cessation of the entitlement to perform the *śrāddha* constitutes a fault.
The ancestors obtain benefit from the assistance provided by the *śrāddha*;
therefore, it is logical that the son incurs sin (*pratyavāya*) upon the violation of the injunction.
Rather, what does that statement of the Blessed Vyāsa mean?
"Whatever number of morsels of sacrificial oblation one who is ignorant eats,
he shall go to the abode of Vaivasvata and swallow that many iron spikes."
There is an alternative reading, "pretya" (having died). This refers to the state of death belonging to the enjoyer alone;
one who is ignorant [of the mantras] should not consume [the offerings] at rites for the gods or the ancestors.
Some twice-born are devoted to knowledge, others likewise to austerity; some are devoted to austerity and Vedic study, and others are devoted to ritual action.
The classification of qualities is stated in order to praise knowledge (*vidyā*) above all other qualities, and this praise is for the purpose of making gifts to the learned.
Those who possess excellence—that is, a state of culmination—in knowledge, which is *vidyā*, are called "those established in knowledge" (*jñānaniṣṭhāḥ*), meaning those qualified for knowledge.
Because it conveys the intended meaning, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed even when the members have different case-relationships (*vyadhikaraṇa*).

Those who have intensely studied the meaning of the Vedas and are devoted to them are described in this way; this should be understood to apply everywhere to compounds ending in *niṣṭhā*. Furthermore, *tapaśca svādhyāyaśca* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing a *dvandva* within it.
Austerities include the Cāndrāyaṇa and other such practices; self-study refers to the study of the Vedas; and rites refer to the Agnihotra and other such rituals.
It should be understood that all these qualities are to be combined together in all cases.

For the presence of a single quality does not confer the status of being a worthy recipient upon one who is devoid of other qualities; rather, some excellence in someone is what is expressed. Just as the word *niṣṭhā*, meaning "completion," indicates "excellence," so too one who has reached that [excellence] is said to be *tatpara* (intent upon that).

Even when all qualities are present, if there is excellence in one and the other qualities are mediocre, one indeed becomes a worthy recipient (*pātra*). However, if even one quality is not excellent, they do not attain the status of a worthy recipient despite the presence of all other qualities.

Furthermore, a collective [interpretation] is explained, by which it was stated in the second [chapter] that for one devoid of knowledge, there may still be the actual performance of ritual action (*karmānuṣṭhāna*).
Others, however, explain that the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) is one who is established in knowledge;

for his practice of self-knowledge is specifically prescribed through the renunciation of action (*karmanyāsa*). Or, the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) is one who is established in austerity (*tapas*).
For he is called an ascetic (tāpasa); indeed, in the summer he should practice the "five-heat" penance (pañcatapas).
Those established in austerity and sacred study (svādhyāya) are celibate students (brahmacārins);
those established in ritual action (karman) are householders (gṛhasthas).

For this reason, those who do not belong to any stage of life (anāśramin) are excluded; likewise, the authors of the Purāṇas state: "One should never perform a Śrāddha for those who stand outside the four stages of life."
Offerings to the ancestors (kavya) should be diligently established among those devoted to knowledge;
however, offerings to the gods (havya) should be offered according to the rule to all four [classes] alike.
He states the purpose for the classification of the qualities:
*kavya* refers to that which is given with the ancestors in view;
the meaning is that these [offerings] are to be established in, that is, bestowed upon, those who are devoted to knowledge (*jñāna*).

Because of the mention of "effort," in the absence of that [effort], even among those belonging to the four [castes], those established in knowledge are the most worthy recipients for the ancestral rite (pitrya), just like [those who are so for] the sacrificial offering (havya).
For it has been said: "Among all worthy recipients, they are the most worthy recipient."
The meaning of the verse is that the gift of food is to be given without distinction to all four [classes].
*Nyāya* refers to the scriptural injunction.

If one's father is unlearned in the Vedas but his son has mastered the Vedas, or if the son is unlearned in the Vedas but the father has mastered the Vedas; [in either case, the merit belongs to the learned one].
This verse is intended to present a doubt.
One should know the elder of these two to be the one whose father is a Vedic scholar;
however, the other deserves honor for the sake of honoring the sacred mantras.

Having raised the doubt—"Of these two, which is superior: one whose father is unlearned but who himself has mastered the Vedas and studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches (sāṅga), or another whose father has mastered the Vedas but who himself is a fool?"—the author states the established conclusion:

between these two—the one who is himself learned in the Vedas (*svayaṃ-śrotriya*) but has a foolish father, and the one who is himself a fool but has a father learned in the Vedas—one should know that the latter, who has a father learned in the Vedas, is superior, praiseworthy, and fit for the *śrāddha* ceremony.

The other [type of person] is not invited with the thought that he is a Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of honoring him, but rather because the mantras he has studied are honored therein. No worship of mantras is prescribed in the *śrāddha*; therefore, such a person should not be fed.

By means of two verses, through the presentation of a doubt and its resolution in the form of an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*), it is stated that both the father’s status as a *śrotriya* and one’s own status as a *śrotriya* are causes for being fed at a *śrāddha*, and not merely one’s own status as a *śrotriya*.
However, it is not prescribed that one who does not study himself becomes a fit recipient of food simply by virtue of his father being a *śrotriya*.
As it has been said: "One should examine [the guest] from afar.
By this, the examination regarding Vedic study is restricted to the two types of persons mentioned here.
However, the examination of caste and qualities pertains even to persons superior to him;
therefore, because it is intended to state specific distinctions regarding that very person, there is no tautology.
One should not feed a friend at a śrāddha; rather, one should win him over with wealth.
One should feed at a śrāddha that twice-born man whom one knows to be neither an enemy nor a friend.
This prohibition applies even when there is an existing excellence of prior qualities such as being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), on account of [pre-existing] friendship and so forth.
One should not feed a friend at a *śrāddha* ceremony—one who shares the same joys and sorrows and is indistinguishable from oneself.
The "winning over" of this friend consists in making him one's own through other means, namely, through the cultivation of friendship.
Alternatively, benevolence (*maitrya*) consists in non-interruption, which is to say, providing assistance.
One should not only feed a friend, but even an enemy or adversary; indeed, one should feed whoever one knows to be neither an enemy nor a friend.

Where there is neither passion nor hatred, nor any other connection such that one might suspect a motive for affection or a purpose for action—since the mention of "enemy" and "friend" is merely illustrative;
likewise, it is precisely because of the suspicion of such a connection that the maternal grandfather and others are mentioned as secondary options (*anukalpa*).

If there is even the possibility of giving a gift to an enemy for the sake of establishing friendship, and this "establishing of friendship" constitutes *saṃgraha* (conciliation), then the inclusion of the "enemy" need not be made.
It will be for the sake of clarity of meaning.
For one whose ancestral rites and sacrificial offerings are dominated by friends,
there is no fruit after death from those ancestral rites or sacrifices.
This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) for the preceding prohibition.
This word "friend" (*mitra*) has the abstract state as its primary meaning; thus, it refers to those things characterized by friendship or characterized by benevolence (*maitrī*).
Therefore, it applies as a remainder to both types of friends.
A gift made with a deity as the intended recipient, or a mere feeding of Brahmins for the sake of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), is characterized as an oblation (havis);
there is no fruit after death.
But surely, because the agents are not the same, the effect cannot arise?
The agent of the action is the man who performs the *śrāddha* rite; the result belongs to his existence as qualified by the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*).
Some say that the word *pretya* is a distinct term denoting the other world, classified as a particle (*nipāta*).

Now, if the fruit were also the agent of the action, then that fruit would not come into being even after death—that is, even upon approaching [the agent] closely; it would not attain the state of being experienced.

That lowest of the twice-born who, out of delusion, forms friendships through a śrāddha offering, falls from heaven and from the world of those who perform śrāddhas, for he is a friend to the śrāddha.
He who, out of delusion and ignorant of the meaning of the scriptures, forms friendships with those unworthy through a spirit of faith, falls from heaven;
the meaning is that he does not attain heaven.
He is said to "fall" because of his lack of connection to the commonality [of the virtuous].
Just as one who has attained heaven and then fallen from it is no longer connected with heaven, so too is this person.
By this, it is precisely the non-attainment of the fruit of the *śrāddha* that is being stated;
for in that way, it remains applicable as a general rule for all cases.
*Śrāddhamitraḥ* means one for whom faith (*śrāddha*) is a friend;
because it is the cause for gaining friends, faith itself is the friend, hence it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
He is the lowest among the twice-born.
The mention of the "twice-born" (dvija) is for the sake of illustration;
even a Śūdra should not entertain friends as guests at a meal.
But surely, because he is not a Brāhmaṇa, a Śūdra cannot even attain the status of a friend?
If it is argued that this conventional rule was established by the Śūdras— that Brāhmaṇas should not be friends with [Śūdras],
and that the practice of friendship exists only among those of equal caste and not between those of higher and lower castes—
this too is not correct.
For thus Śvetaketu Āruṇeya said: "I have a Kṣatriya friend among the Pañcālas.
Furthermore, the prohibition regarding a "friend" is explained for the purpose of indicating a general relationship;
for Brāhmaṇas can be financial associates of a Śūdra, and even the relatives of a Pāraśava [Śūdra].
That sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) which is given for a communal feast is declared by the twice-born to be of the Piśācas;
it remains right here in this world like a blind cow in a single house.
The word *sam* functions in the sense of "together. That by which one eats together is *saṃbhojanī*.
For it is through loving-kindness (*maitrī*) that eating together proceeds.
Or, communal dining is intended here as eating together;
this practice of gathering friends at a *śrāddha* is the custom of *piśācas*.
Street-people are *piśācas*.
That sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā) remains only in this world; it is not capable of yielding fruit in the hereafter.

Just as a cow remains in one particular house when blind, so too does this sacrificial gift remain only here; it serves only the purpose of one's friends and is not able to provide benefit for the ancestors.
Giving is the sacrificial fee.
Just as one who sows seed in barren soil does not obtain fruit,
so too the giver who offers an oblation to one ignorant of the Ṛgveda does not obtain the fruit.
*Iriṇa* means saline soil. That field where, due to a defect in the ground, the seed sown does not sprout is *iriṇa*;
it is where the sower, the farmer, does not obtain the fruit.
In this way, having offered oblations to the gods and the ancestors to one who is "anṛca"—meaning devoid of Vedic study—one does not obtain the fruit.
The term *anṛce* ends in the locative case;
the word *ṛc* is used here as an indicator for the Vedas in general.
By giving a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a learned man according to the prescribed rule, one makes both the giver and the recipient partakers of the fruit, both in this world and after death.
It is logical that the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) given to a learned man makes the givers partakers of its fruit;
however, what kind of fruit do the recipients enjoy?
If it were an unseen (adṛṣṭa) result, that would be improper, because the act of receiving has not been enjoined [as a duty], and people engage in it only for the sake of obtaining a visible reward.
If it is seen, then it is seen even by one who is ignorant.
True;
this is a mere eulogy.
Such is this gift for the learned man that even the recipient becomes a partaker of unseen merit;
how much more so the giver, even regarding visible results?
After death there is heaven, and in this world there is fame; as one practices according to the scriptures, people offer words of praise, saying, "He acts in accordance with the treatises."
The phrase "according to rule" is a restatement [of what has been previously established], as is the statement "and he gives thus in matters of dharma."
One may, if one wishes, honor a friend at a śrāddha ceremony even if he is not worthy, but not one who is hostile; for an oblation consumed by an enemy becomes fruitless after death.
One should diligently feed at the śrāddha a Bahvṛca who has mastered the Veda,
or an Adhvaryu who has reached the end of his recensional branch, or a Chandoga who has completed his study.

The terms *vedapāraga*, *śākhāntaga*, and *samāptika* denote those who have studied an entire Vedic branch (*śākhā*) together with its mantras and Brāhmaṇas; they do not refer to those who have studied only the mantra-saṃhitā, nor the Brāhmaṇa, nor even a portion thereof. Furthermore, those who study only a single branch of the Veda are also called *śrotriya*.
Therefore, to exclude that [unqualified recipient], it is stated: "It should be given to a *śrotriya*. A *śrotriya* is one who has studied the Veda;
and the word "Veda" denotes a branch (*śākhā*) consisting of both mantra and brāhmaṇa.

This [statement] is for the purpose of ensuring that even one who has studied only a portion [of the Veda] might be included, lest he be excluded on the grounds that he must study the entire branch (*śākhā*).

Now, it was stated that those belonging to the stages of life (*āśrama*) are to be fed; however, for those who have not studied their entire *svādhyāya*, the possibility of entering the householder stage (*gārhasthya*) and the other stages does not exist at all.
For it has been stated thus: "The entire Veda is to be mastered.
This would apply even to a *brahmacārin* who has commenced the study of the Veda but has not yet completed it;

for completeness (*kārtsnya*) is expressed by all these synonymous terms—"one who has gone to the further shore of the Veda," "one who has reached the end of the various recensions (*śākhā*)," and "one who has completed [it]."
Since the purpose is accomplished by a single word alone, the utterance of multiple words with various forms but a single meaning is for the sake of conforming to the meter.
"He goes to the further shore of the Vedas" (*vedānāṃ pāraṃ gacchati*). One who has the completion of a branch (*śākhā*) is "one who has reached the end" (*samāptikaḥ*).

The *adhvaryu* is one who studies a branch of the *Yajurveda*; this word *adhvaryu* is not a term denoting a specific type of officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). Rather, it refers to the *pravacana* (the oral tradition) of the *Adhvaryus*.
Due to his connection with the study of that [tradition], a person is called an *adhvaryu*.

A *chandoga* is one who studies the Sāmaveda. In another *smṛti*, he is called a *trisāhasravidya* (one possessing three thousand-fold knowledge) and a *samāptika* (one who has completed [the study]). In that context, the word "thousand" (*sahasra*) refers to the Sāmaveda because of its connection with a thousand songs; thus, one for whom these three thousand-fold branches of knowledge exist is a *trisāhasravidya*.
The *Tāṇḍava-mauktika* and the *Sāmagāna*—these are the three branches of knowledge (*vidyās*) of that *Sāmaveda* which has a thousand paths.
The *Daśatayī*, the *Catuḥṣaṣṭi*, and the *Brāhmaṇa* belong to the *Bahvṛca*.
Others, however, consider this verse to be intended for the purpose of excluding the followers of the *Atharvaveda*.
If he intended to speak of completeness, he would have said this:
"One should feed that twice-born man who has studied an entire branch of the Veda."
But is this not equally applicable to the prohibition of those who study the Atharvaveda?

In that case as well, it would have been possible to say: "Upon its prohibition, one should generally not eat from the house of an Atharvaṇika"; for thus he would have expressed the understanding of the prohibition by its own specific term, which is more concise.
This is not so;
for is the negation of one thing understood through the prescription of another, or is the negation expressed by its own word?
Manu’s composition of the instruction on dharma is varied.
If any one of these, being duly honored, should eat at a person's śrāddha,
the satisfaction of that person’s ancestors shall be eternal for seven generations.
Someone might think that since it was stated [in verse 128] "three for the ancestral rite" (*pitṛkṛtye*),

and since those who study various Vedic branches (*nānāśākhādhyāyin*) were mentioned in the preceding verse, there would be no application of this rule to fellow students (*sabrahmacārin*). This [verse] is intended to remove that doubt.
Any one of these three types of those learned in the three Vedas (traividya) is worthy of being fed.
This is what is meant:
those who study the same Vedic branch (śākhā) or those who study different branches are worthy of being fed.
"Honored" means worshipped, requested with water for the feet (*argha*) and other offerings;
"satisfaction extending to seven generations" means it pervades seven persons.
Because the *anuśatika* group is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*), there is vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) in both members of the compound.
This is intended to indicate the greatness of time;
the satisfaction of the ancestors lasts for a long duration.
As long as seven generations of descendants—sons, grandsons, and so forth—are born or will be born, the ancestors remain satisfied by such gifts to Brahmins.
This [lineage] is eternal; it does not cease in the interim and arise again.
How much more so, then, that it remains established for all time?
This indeed is the primary rule for the offering of sacrificial oblations (havya) and ancestral offerings (kavya);
however, this secondary practice should be understood as that which is always performed by the virtuous.
Beginning with the section on the *pitṛyajña*, twenty-five verses have been passed; therein this much meaning has been stated:
a *śrāddha* must be performed on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).
A learned man who has studied the Vedas, whose conduct is virtuous, who is of renowned lineage, and who is the son of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*)—provided he is not a relative—should be fed.
The remainder is all for the purpose of explanatory praise (arthavāda).
This first method (kalpa) or rule just mentioned is the primary one, namely that which is given at a śrāddha to one who is not a relative;
however, this which is about to be described should be understood as the secondary method (anukalpa).
That which is performed by way of substitution in the absence of the primary [element] is called an *anukalpa* (secondary alternative).
The passage beginning with "always" (*sadā*) and so forth is for the purpose of praise.

One should feed the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the sister’s son, the father-in-law, the teacher, the daughter’s son, the husband of a sister, a relative, the officiating priest, and the person for whom one performs sacrifices.
A sister’s son is a *svasrīya*.
A *viṭpati* is a son-in-law (*jāmātṛ*), because the word *viṭ* signifies offspring.
Others are *atithis*.
For even in the world, he who is the lord of all subjects, having come to one's house, is called by the word *viṭ*;
while *bandhu* refers to a kinsman, such as a *śāla* or one of the same lineage (*sagotra*), and so forth.
One who knows the Dharma should not examine a Brahmin for a rite dedicated to the gods;
however, when a rite dedicated to the ancestors has arrived, he should examine him with great care.

This is not a prohibition against examining Brāhmaṇas for rites dedicated to the gods; rather, its purpose is to permit those who are one-eyed, afflicted with elephantiasis, and so forth, to participate occasionally in rites for the gods.
When the time for the ancestral rite (śrāddha) has arrived, one should diligently perform an examination [of the guests], but not for rites dedicated to the gods.
Occasionally, one may even feed those who are about to be mentioned [in the following verses].
Nevertheless, we shall demonstrate those [cases] where they are permitted.

Others, however, maintain that this verse is merely an introduction intended for the diligent avoidance of what will be prohibited in the upcoming section on prohibitions; it does not, however, intend to permit those who are one-eyed and so forth at rites for the gods.
Manu has declared those Brahmins who are thieves, outcasts, eunuchs, or those who follow the lifestyle of atheists to be unworthy of offerings made to the gods and the ancestors.
A thief is a robber;
an outcaste is one who has committed any one of the five great sins (mahāpātakas);
a eunuch is a neuter, one with both sexual organs, one whose semen is wind, or a sterile man.

Nāstikas are the Lokāyatikas and others who maintain the view that "there is no gift, there is no oblation, and there is no other world. Their conduct (*vṛtti*) or behavior is their practice; lack of faith is the "nāstika-conduct" (*nāstika-vṛtti*). Those who possess this are "those of nāstika-conduct.
This is a compound in which the latter member [of the first term] has been elided (*uttarapadalopī-samāsa*).
Since the term "atheists" (*nāstika*) alone would have sufficed, the recourse to the compound *vṛtti-pada* is for the purpose of completing the verse.
Alternatively, they are so called because their livelihood (*vṛtti*), that is, their means of subsistence, depends upon atheists.
Manu has declared them to be unworthy of *havya* and *kavya*, [the offerings] to the gods and the ancestors.
The mention of Manu is for the purpose of showing respect for the prohibition, since all dharmas have been declared by Manu.
One should not feed at a śrāddha those who have matted hair but do not study the Vedas, nor those with shaggy hair, gamblers, nor those who officiate as priests for groups of people.
The "matted-haired one" (jaṭila) is a religious student (brahmacārī), for this specific type of hair is prescribed for him as an option: he may be either shaven-headed or matted-haired.
Furthermore, the matted hair is merely an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa) of the religious student; therefore, even being shaven-headed is prohibited for him.
And there is a prohibition against such a person if he is not studying his lessons.
But surely, since it is said that "gifts are to be given only to one learned in the Vedas" (*śrotriya*), there can be no possibility at all for one who has not studied;
for if one who has begun his studies but has neither yet mastered nor grasped the Veda were to receive [a gift], how could such a person be included?
Indeed, because of the statement "one who has reached the further shore of the Veda" (*vedapāraga*), how could there be any possibility for one who has merely begun his studies?
In that case, even one who has studied the Veda but has not mastered it is intended here by the term "one who does not study.

Alternatively, someone might think that by the phrase "even a daughter's son who is observing a vow," it is the status of being a daughter's son (*dauhitrata*) alone that is required here, and not the act of studying; for that reason, this [rule] is stated.
Since there is a prohibition against one who does not study, it is understood that one who is learned (*vidvas*) has the entitlement [to perform the rite].
He has coarse hair, with blood-stained locks, and his sense faculties are impaired;
for they provide this etymological explanation of him:
"Even the *dūrvā* grass, or even a mere patch of green turf, serves as his clothing."
For he is covered by *dūrvā* grass and by shame; even in the absence of garments, he conceals his private parts with that much alone.
A gambler is one who plays at dice. And those who officiate for groups or assemblies [of sacrificers].
For a sacrifice is prescribed for Vrātyas who have been readmitted through the Vrātyastoma and other rites;
yet, officiating at such a sacrifice is prohibited by the rule: "Having performed the sacrifice for Vrātyas [one is excluded].
To this we reply:
He who performs sacrifices for many people even one by one, or who acts as a priest for many on multiple occasions, is also not one whose food should be eaten.
Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "And he who has many patrons for sacrifice, and he who initiates many [pupils].
Some say that because of the mention of the *śrāddha*, this prohibition applies only to ancestral rites (*pitrya*) and not to divine rites (*daiva*).
That is incorrect; for that [offering] is also a constituent part of the *śrāddha*, and it is therefore proper to refer to it by the word *śrāddha*.
Physicians, temple-priests, meat-sellers,
and those who live by trade— these should be avoided at offerings to the gods and the ancestors.
Physicians are those who practice medicine;
*devalakas* are those who attend to idols.
Both of these are prohibited on account of their means of livelihood.
However, if they are for the sake of dharma, there is no fault in being a physician or a temple-priest;
those who sell meat are butchers.
In the reading with the accusative case-ending, the verb from the preceding verse is to be supplied.
Those who live by trade through forbidden articles of commerce are prohibited;
such forbidden articles will be described in the tenth chapter.
Therefore, those who subsist by such means are to be avoided in both cases.

But those who sell meat are forbidden from doing so even for the sake of dharma. Suppose someone has offered meat to another person who needs it—for instance, one who requires the offered meat for use in a *homa* sacrifice with clarified butter (*ghṛta*)—and he exchanges that meat for the butter; this exchange serves the purpose of dharma. Since the term "selling" (*vikraya*) applies to such an exchange as well, those who sell meat even for the sake of dharma are likewise prohibited.
A servant of a village or of a king, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth,
one who opposes his teacher, one who has abandoned the sacred fires, and likewise a usurer;
A *preṣya* is one who carries out orders; he is someone who is sent by a village for some task wherever it may be. Likewise, there is a royal messenger (*rājapreṣya*).
One with deformed nails, one with black teeth;
one who opposes his teacher in verbal discourse and otherwise acts in a manner that obstructs or is antagonistic toward him;
and one who has abandoned the sacred fires, whether the threefold set or either of the two domestic fires (tretā or āvasathya).
A usurer (*vārdhuṣi*) is one who lives by interest when there exists another means of livelihood;
for it is said that "the lending of grain at interest is called usury (*vārdhuṣitva*).
Such a traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) applies only to its own specific context.
For grammarians, who live by their knowledge, remember the word *vārdhuṣika* even in reference to things other than grain;
and they are more authoritative in the recollection of word-meanings due to their specialized application.

One afflicted by consumption, a cattle-herder, one who marries before his elder brother, one who has been expelled from his caste, a hater of Brahmins, the elder brother whose younger brother married first, and one who belongs to a communal group (gaṇa).
A *yakṣmī* is one afflicted by disease; others say it refers to one seized by pulmonary consumption (*rājayakṣman*). A *paśupāla* is one with a staff in hand, who lives by that occupation.
A *nirākṛti* is one who, despite possessing the requisite qualification (*adhikāra*), is devoid of the performance of the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*).
Even in the present day, one who is not supported by others is called a *nirākṛti*.
For thus it is said in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*: "He who does not worship the gods, nor the ancestors, nor men."

As for those who recite, "One who has not studied the Vedas, one who lacks learning, one who possesses no wealth, and one who is an outcaste (nirākṛti) are declared [unfit]," they do not understand the relationship between words and their meanings.
For such a person, there is simply no eligibility here [for Vedic study], due to the restrictive rules for those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*).
Furthermore, the etymological derivation of *nirākṛti* exists in the sense of "one who rejects" (*nirākartā*) the gods and so forth.
Furthermore, when there is an intention to express the non-difference between the property (dharma) and the possessor of the property (dharmī), the usage with the suffix *ktin* is also justified.
This verbal root preceded by the prefix *ni-* functions in the sense of "excluding" (*apavarjana*).

Those who are excluded (*nirākṛta*) are said to be those who have been set aside (*apavarjita*), as in the expressions "excluded from a meal" (*bhojanāt nirākṛtāḥ*) or "excluded from an office" (*adhikārāt nirākṛtāḥ*).

*Ākṛti* means turning away (*avarjana*); that which has turned away from this [proper form] is *nirākṛti*. Furthermore, *ākṛti* means configuration (*saṃsthāna*); likewise, it should be understood as expressing contempt, as in the case of "one of ugly appearance" (*durākṛti*), who is thus prohibited.
And it is said: "One who is endowed with speech, physical form, age, and conduct."
One endowed with speech is eloquent and possesses a sharp faculty of speech;
one who is garrulous is not to be honored.
One endowed with beauty has a pleasing arrangement of limbs.
"One endowed with youth";
"the gift to the young is first, then to those of similar age," so say some.
Or rather, this word *vayaḥ* is a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*) ending in the suffix *ktic*.
A "hater of Brahman" (*brahmadviṭ*) is one who hates Brāhmaṇas or the Veda, because the word *brahman* denotes both meanings, as it is recorded that "one who knows Brahman is called a Brāhmaṇa.
A "group" (*gaṇa*) is a community;
those who live together through a single activity are denoted by the word *gaṇa*, and the Brāhmaṇas learned in the four Vedas (*cāturvidya*) are included therein.
The *parivettṛ* (the younger brother who marries before the elder) and the *parivitti* (the elder brother so superseded) are of the nature that will be described hereafter.
One who is of bad character, one who has broken his vows, the husband of a low-caste woman, the son of a remarried woman, one who is one-eyed, and he in whose house lives a paramour;

Cāraṇas, naṭas, nartakas, gāyanas, and the like are performers (kuśīlavas). An *avakīrṇin* is one who has violated his vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). A *vṛṣalī* is a Śūdra woman; her husband is [the subject].
And they consider that this applies when no other [wife] exists;
specifically, for one who is the husband of a *vṛṣalī* alone and has no wife of the twice-born classes.
Why is this so?

In another section, a summary of censurable practices is heard in the words, "these censurable practices. Furthermore, marriage with a Śūdra woman is not censurable for anyone, as it is permitted; and that [marriage] is permitted for one who has already performed a marriage with a woman of his own caste.
Therefore, since there is no wife of the same caste, the husband of a *vṛṣalī* is prohibited here; [the term] *paunarbhava* refers to one born of a *punarbhū*, that is,
a woman who has been married again.
He will state in the ninth chapter: "or abandoned by her husband.
*Kāṇa* means one who is defective in one eye.
And he for whom there is a *upapati*—that is, a paramour of his wife—who exists while the wife remains [in his household].
He is censured for his indifference;
as it has been said: "The killer of the embryo transfers his guilt to the one who eats the food, and the unfaithful wife transfers hers to her husband."
One who teaches for a fee, one who has been taught by a teacher for a fee,
one whose pupil is a Śūdra, a Śūdra who is a teacher, one who is corrupt in speech, and the Kuṇḍa and Golaka sons.
A "teacher for hire" (*bhṛtakādhyāpaka*) is one who stands as a teacher while being paid wages.
Regarding the term "wages" (*bhṛtaka*): he is one who proceeds on the basis of a contract, saying, "I will teach the Veda [to you] if you give me so much.
For this is the well-known form of wage among porters and the like.

However, he who, without first determining "I shall teach this much for this much wealth," teaches according to a verbal agreement and receives payment for the purpose of teaching, is not a teacher for hire (*bhṛtakādhyāpaka*). Teaching performed when the amount of wealth to be given has not been previously fixed is what is prescribed; thus is one "taught by a teacher for hire."
One who, possessing developed intelligence, studies after personally providing the fee (*bhṛti*)—like Satyakāma—is described in this manner.
However, for one who is taught by his father or others after they have provided the fee in the absence of another teacher, there is no state of reprehensible conduct.
For a child must be turned away from prohibited things by his father.
This has been stated: "The student and the one for whom one sacrifices [are both included] under the teacher.
For a Śūdra, the student is the teacher in the sciences such as grammar, and the teacher is indeed a Śūdra himself.

Even though he is a subordinate member [of the compound], there is a connection [to the prohibition], because this is a Smṛti scripture and because the status of having reprehensible conduct applies to all [classes].
And having a Śūdra as one's teacher is censured, but not any other [transgression].
One who is corrupt in speech is a speaker of harshness and falsehood;
others say he is "accused" (abhiśasta).
The *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* will be explained below.
Having abandoned one's mother, father, or teacher without cause,
and having entered into association with outcasts through Brahmanical or matrimonial connections;

He who abandons his mother, father, and teacher when there is no [just] cause—since the word *guru* is a general term, it also applies to the *upādhyāya*; however, some explain that if this were the case, the mention of "mother and father" would be unnecessary, as they are already established as *gurus* by virtue of their nature; therefore, they maintain that here the *ācārya* alone is intended by the term *guru*.
That is incorrect.
If the mention of "mother and father" were absent, the word *guru* would apply to the father alone, according to the maxim of the artificial and the non-artificial (*kṛtrimākṛtrimanyāya*).
However, when they are mentioned separately, its status as a general term is established, as in other treatises where it is said, "The teacher is the best among gurus."
And one should abandon a father who is a regicide and so forth, which are causes for abandonment.
Abandonment of mother and father consists in the failure to perform service such as attending to their feet, and a lack of devotion toward their propitiation;
the same applies to a teacher.
When there is a teacher capable of instructing, yet he does not teach, and the student studies elsewhere by abandoning him;
or when one has entered into association— that is, established a connection— with those who have fallen from their status (patita),
whether through Vedic connections such as officiating at sacrifices or teaching, or through matrimonial connections such as giving a daughter in marriage and so forth.
But surely, he is to be avoided precisely because he is fallen (*patita*).
Some say that one falls after a year of associating with a fallen person; this prohibition does not apply before that time.
Now, what is the meaning of the expression "having entered into a connection through association"?

In this context, the word "relation" (*saṃbandha*) does not denote conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth as it is understood by the Vaiśeṣikas and others; rather, it is action itself that is called "relation" because it is the cause of relation.
Furthermore, the word "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), as found in the definition of officiating at sacrifices and the like, indicates relation in its most general sense.
One who sets fire to a house, a poisoner, one who eats from a vessel belonging to another, a seller of Soma,
one who travels by sea, a bard, an oil-presser, and a forger;
One who burns a house or a dwelling; "gara" refers to that which gives poison, and the mention of *gara* is for the purpose of illustration, including poisons (*viṣa*) and the like as well.
He eats the food of a *kuṇḍa*;
likewise that of a *golaka*, because the mention of the *kuṇḍa* is intended as an illustration.
He sells *soma*.
The "plant" is *soma*; he who sells it, whether for the purpose of sacrifice or for medicinal purposes.
Others, however, say that the "plants" refer to sacrifices such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* which have *soma* as their means.
Although the sale of these [sacrifices] is impossible—since an action is incorporeal—nevertheless, this prohibition exists because such a practice is observed among the ignorant.

For we see that even the ignorant speak thus: "Whatever good deed has been performed by me, let that be yours. Here, "good deed" (*sukṛta*) refers to the merit (*dharma*) accomplished through virtuous acts.
And likewise: "Between the night you were born and the night you shall die—in this interval, may I seize your world, your merit, your life, and your offspring, if you should betray me."

Just as with oaths, so too one who makes a gift or a sale by word of mouth is excluded; and for this very reason, the impropriety of such acts as giving oaths, making gifts, or selling when performed by mere speech is inferred. He who goes upon the ocean—that is, the great sea—is [excluded].
A *bandī* is a reciter of praises;
a *tailika* is one who grinds sesame seeds and other such grains;
a *kūṭakāraka* is one who speaks falsely in witness-depositions.
One who quarrels with his father, a gambler, a drunkard,
one afflicted by a foul disease, one accused of a crime, a hypocrite, and a seller of liquids.
"He who disputes with his father and speaks harshly" refers to one who litigates in a royal court by means of the sequence of plaintiff and defendant for the sake of a share of property and so forth.
And thus Gautama says: "those who have become estranged against their father's will.

As for the statement "one who opposes his guru," how is this not a redundancy? It is explained as follows: [the former refers to the specific act of litigation, while the latter refers to general opposition].
Obstruction (*pratirodha*) is one thing, and dispute (*vivāda*) is another.

Whatever object is intended by the teacher, the explanation of the means by which that might be accomplished is "obstruction. Even regarding a matter that is logically sound, the act of thwarting the teacher's desire for it constitutes the state of being an obstructor.
"Pratirāddha" is an alternative reading for that term.
One who has "assaulted" (pratirāddha) means one who has struck the teacher directly with his hands or other limbs, or one who has resisted him by dealing blows such as slaps.
In this interpretation, the subject matter of the dispute is established as being different [from the previous case].
A *kitava* is one who causes gambling to take place, namely the master of the gaming house (*sabhika*).
As for one who gambles himself, he has already been prohibited previously.
Others read "kekara" [instead of *kitava*], explaining that a *kekara* is a drunkard.
And he has a sidelong glance, with a gaze extending one and a half [the length of his body]; others have timid eyes,
but he has pupils like the wings of a parrot.
A liquor-drinker is one who drinks *surā* or other intoxicants such as *ariṣṭa*; being a drinker of *surā*, he is excluded precisely because of his fallen status.
A person afflicted by a foul disease is one suffering from leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).
For he is utterly censurable in the world; it is appropriate to designate him as one afflicted by a "sinful disease" (*pāparogin*).
And precisely because of this prohibition, in the term *yakṣmin*, not every person seized by illness is understood; who then? One who suffers from consumption (*kṣayin*).
For if everyone were included, since [the meaning] would already be established by that alone, the term *pāparogin* would not have been used.
One who is "accused" is one who is well-known in the world as a perpetrator of either a major (pātaka) or minor (upapātaka) sin, even in the absence of certainty regarding his having committed it.

A "hypocrite" (dāmbhika) practices dharma through deception for the sake of gaining the favor of the world; he does not act out of the conviction that it is his duty. A "seller of liquids" is a seller of poison.
For this is its designation:

"one who betrays through whispering" (upāṃśubhedī), "one who administers poison" (rasadaḥ), "one who administers poison" (rasadaḥ), "an agent" (sattrī), and so forth; one who administers poison is called a *rasada*.

One who makes bows and arrows, one who is the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is still unmarried, one who betrays a friend, one who lives by gambling, and likewise one who is a teacher of his own son.
He who, like an artisan, fashions bows and arrows,
and he who is the husband of an *agredidhiṣū*—
the word *didhiṣū* is connected with both [terms], like the eye of a crow.

If it is argued that such a connection is obtained because this is a treatise on traditional law (smṛti)— for even marks on the body, clods of earth, and so forth, are conventionally established for the sake of traditional law and serve to convey meaning—
then it should not be asked how a single word, situated within a compound, can be connected to two things of different categories.
For Gautama has prohibited two things;
here too, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the distinction of the relationship:
the compound consists of two words.
For there is no such person as one called an *agredidhiṣūpati*; these two [categories] will have their definitions stated later. [Also excluded is] a betrayer of friends (*mitradhruk*).
One who betrays a friend;
one who acts to obstruct the affairs of a friend;
and one whose livelihood is gambling—that is, one for whom gambling is the means of subsistence.
But has this not already been stated in the verse, "The gambler, the drinker of intoxicants"?

It is not necessarily only one whose livelihood is gambling who is the instigator of gambling; rather, it is also one who does not know how to play himself, or who does not play out of fear of his elders.
However, the addict, being cursed by the gods, causes another to play.
The second word, *kitava*, has that same meaning. Alternatively, it refers to those who live by gambling, who are pillars in the gambling hall, and who speak falsehoods;
he whose son is such a teacher or instructor.
The primary status of being a teacher is not possible in the case of one's own son.
One suffering from epilepsy, one with scrofulous swellings, one afflicted with leucoderma, as well as a slanderer, a madman, a blind man, and likewise a reviler of the Vedas— these should be avoided.
These are specific types of diseases:
*bhrāmarī* (a state of wandering delusion) and *apasmārī* (epilepsy).
In *gaṇḍamālī*, rows of pustules (*piṭakā*) arise in the shape of a garland on the cheeks and the throat.
A *śvitrin* is one afflicted with white leprosy. A *piśuna* is a backbiter who reveals the secret vulnerabilities of others; a *karṇejapa*.
An *unmatta* is one whose mind is unsettled due to a disturbance of the bodily humors (*dhātu*), or who is possessed by a *piśāca*; such a person speaks or acts at random.
"Blind" means one who is deficient in sight. "One who reviles the Vedas"—
but is it not the case that by the very term *brahmadviṣ* ("hater of Brahman"), since the word *brahman* has multiple meanings, the reviler of the Vedas is already included?
It is not so;
blame and hatred are distinct.
Hatred is a mental factor (*cittadharma*), whereas blame is the disparagement of that [hatred] by means of the word "displeasure" (*aprīti*).
One who trains elephants, horses, or camels; one who lives by means of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras);
one who raises birds; and likewise a teacher of warfare.

A trainer of elephants and the like is one who disciplines them and teaches them their movements. One who lives by means of the stars is an astrologer; by the word "stars," the science of astronomy (jyotiḥśāstra) is indicated, and one who subsists by that is a jyotiṣika.
One who raises birds such as hawks for the purpose of hunting;
and a master of combat, that is, an instructor in the science of archery (dhanurveda).
He who diverts watercourses and delights in obstructing them,
he who constructs houses, acts as a messenger, and likewise plants trees;
"Srotāṃsi" refers to the sources of water; he is one who breaks them.
Having broken the embankment, he leads [the water] to another place for the purpose of irrigating rice and other crops.
And he delights in the obstruction of those very same currents.
An *āvaraṇa* is a covering;
it conceals that area from which water emerges.
A builder is one who instructs on the arrangement of houses, one who lives by the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*), such as a master mason (*sthapati*) or a carpenter (*sūtradhāra*).
But he is not the one who designs his own dwellings;
he is a messenger, a servant of the king, to be employed like a slave.
For a messenger is dispatched specifically for matters such as peace and war.
One may plant trees for a price;
however, there is no fault in doing so for the sake of Dharma, because it is an irreproachable practice.
The planting of trees is ordained: one who plants ten mango trees does not go to hell.
One who dabbles with dogs, one who lives by falcons, a defiler of virgins, a violent person, one who subsists on the service of Śūdras, and a priest for a multitude.
One who plays with dogs is a *śvakrīḍī*;
one who keeps dogs for the purpose of play;
or one who lives by means of hawks through buying, selling, and so forth.
The previously mentioned "bird-keeper" is one who maintains birds confined in cages and the like;
the "defiler of virgins" is he who makes a maiden non-virgin;
the "cruel" one is naturally fierce and devoted to killing.
"One who lives by the livelihood of a *vṛṣala* through service and so forth for *śūdras*;
'one whose sons are exclusively *vṛṣalas*'— this is an alternative reading for *vṛṣalaputraḥ*."
"By those who have only Śūdra offspring" refers to one of reprehensible conduct;
"the priest of the deities of *gaṇas*" refers to those well-known sacrifices for groups (*gaṇayāgas*).
One devoid of proper conduct, one who is impotent, a constant beggar, one who lives by agriculture, one with elephantiasis, and one who is censured by the virtuous— these are likewise [excluded].
"Worldly custom" refers to the conventional practice of employing honors and the like for those who have come to one's home; he is devoid of that.
A "weakling" (klība) is one of little strength, whose enthusiasm is broken regarding what ought to be done.
A "beggar" is one who always begs, and one who causes distress to others through begging.
This is the inherent nature of things: that one who is being solicited feels agitation at the request.
[The suffix] *yu* is applied after roots such as *nand* in the sense of the base itself, and *ka* is added in the same sense.
A "farmer" (*kṛṣijīvī*) lives by farming performed by himself; however, when other means exist, he may live even by farming not performed by himself.
One with elephantiasis is one whose single foot is large;
he is ill-fated and censured by the virtuous, being loathed by the good even in the absence of any fault.
A sheep-butchers, a buffalo-herder, the husband of a woman previously married to another, and a carrier of corpses— these indeed must be avoided with great effort.
One who moves about with sheep and rams—that is, one who engages in trade such as buying and selling them, or one for whom their wealth is primary—is a *aurabhrika*.
Likewise is a *māhiṣika*.
One whose wife has another man before her is her husband, that is, her maintainer.

He who performs the marriage rites again for a woman who has been given to another or wedded by another becomes her husband once more; such a man is called a *paunarbhava* (the husband of a remarried woman) according to the scripture. He who carries out or escorts the deceased—these must be avoided with great effort.
A learned man who is the best among the twice-born should avoid, in both circumstances, these lowest of the twice-born, whose conduct is censurable and who are unworthy of the company at a meal.
