Their conduct— that is, their performance of actions— is censured and condemned; thus,
those such as the one-eyed are identified by the signs of past faults,
while those such as thieves are identified by faults currently being experienced through perception and other means.
In both cases— whether for the rite of the gods (daiva) or the rite of the ancestors (pitrya)—
one should avoid them, meaning one should exclude them;
for those who are "unfit for the row" (apāṅkteya) do not deserve a place in the row.
The suffix *ḍhak* should be applied in the sense of "becoming. Their very unworthiness is understood through their exclusion from the row [of diners];
they do not deserve to eat together with other Brāhmaṇas.
For this very reason, they are called "corrupters of the row";
those who sit together with them also become corrupted.
For a Brahmin who has not studied the Vedas is extinguished like a fire of straw;
one should not offer sacrificial oblations to him, for an offering is not poured into ashes.
Just as these thieves and others are defilers of the assembly, so too is one who has not studied; this repetition is for the purpose of establishing that he possesses an equal fault.

Others, however, explain it as being intended to allow for the occasional inclusion of those who study—such as the one-eyed and others—in rites for the gods, provided they do not currently engage in reprehensible conduct.

A Brahmin who does not study is to be avoided; however, even to one who does study, neither *havya* nor *kavya* is given—this is precisely the purpose of mentioning *havya* here. One who does not study is to be avoided solely with respect to *havya*, as well as those whose conduct is seen to be censurable.

Therefore, those who are prohibited in both cases by scriptural statement should be excluded from rites for the gods (*daiva*) as well as for the ancestors (*pitrya*); others, however, are to be excluded from rites for the ancestors alone.
And so says Vasiṣṭha:
"Now, if one is learned in the mantras but afflicted with bodily defects that defile the company..."
"Yama declared him irreproachable; he alone is a sanctifier of the assembly.
Regarding the phrase "he is extinguished like a grass-fire":
just as a grass-fire is unable to cook sacrificial offerings, yet is extinguished and even blown out by the mere offering of the oblation.
In whichever fire that which is offered does not become ashes, there is no fruit from that oblation; for thus it is heard in scripture: "One should not offer into a fire that is not kindled."
"Agni, indeed, is all the deities.
Thus, a Brahmin who has not studied [the Veda] is equal to a fire made of straw.
This very point he expresses by saying, "for an oblation is not poured into ashes."
Just as a grass fire first turns to ashes and nothing is offered into it, even so such a Brahmin is not to be fed.
I shall explain in its entirety the fruit that arises for a giver after death from giving to those unworthy of the company at a rite for the gods or for the ancestors.
He states the result of this prohibitive rule:
those who are worthy of the row (*paṅkti*) are *paṅktyas*;
those who are not *paṅktyas* are *apaṅktyas*.
The establishment of the form [of the word] is due to the observation of forms such as *daṇḍin*.
Whatever arising of fruit—that is, whatever production of fruit—occurs for the donor from giving to those [recipients], all of that I shall now declare; therefore, be attentive.

Whatever is eaten by twice-born men who have not observed their vows, as well as by those such as a younger brother who marries before his elder, and by others excluded from the company at meals— that indeed the Rākṣasas consume.

Those who are without vows, unrestrained, and devoid of scriptural conduct— such as those who marry before their elder brothers (*parivettṛ*) and others— though they are outside the pale of the scriptures, are nevertheless mentioned separately either for the sake of specific recollection or to indicate the gravity of their fault.
Others who are excluded from the company at meals (*apaṅkteya*) include the one-eyed (*kāṇa*), the club-footed (*ślīpadin*), and so forth.
Whatever food is eaten by them at the śrāddha, that is consumed by the Rākṣasas, the enemies of the gods, and not by the ancestors.
Therefore, it is meant to be said that such a śrāddha becomes fruitless.
The mention of the Rākṣasas is a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda).

He who, while his elder brother remains, enters into the union of marriage and the sacred fire-sacrifice, is to be known as a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder); the elder brother, however, is a *parivitti*.
One born first, at the beginning, is called an *agraja*, a uterine brother;
for it is thus recited:
"The sons of paternal uncles, those born of other wives, and likewise the sons of other women..."

"There is no fault in superseding [an elder brother] when there is a union with a wife and the *agnihotra* fire. In this context, "elder" refers to a uterine brother; provided that he remains unmarried and has not yet established the *agnihotra* fire.

The word *agnihotra*, though denoting the ritual act, is employed here in the sense of its purpose, namely the installation of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*), because it refers to the cessation of its primary function. A specific distinction is recited in another Smṛti:
One who is insane, a sinner, a leper, an outcast, a eunuch,
or afflicted with pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman) is not fit to wait upon [the preceptor].

This [statement] is also intended as an indication of those who lack eligibility; therefore, even one who is excluded from the company at meals (apāṅkteya) is included. A specific time is further required.
And thus says the Smṛti: "He should wait for eight years; some say for six.
This number of years is to be understood as starting from the time when the younger brother has reached the age for marriage;
and the time for marriage is the completion of the rules for Vedic study.
But is it not the case that this was recited in the section concerning those who have gone abroad?
Indeed, having introduced the period of exile for women when their husband has gone abroad, the text beginning with "brothers" and so forth was recited.
True.
In another sentence, the direct connection of the word *proṣita* is understood;

however, in the case of a connection in yet another sentence, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be stated, and such does not exist— as in the rule "an extended application [is indicated] by a circumflex accent" (*svaritenādhikāraḥ*).
Furthermore, the word "that" does not occur here;
nor is that sentence incomplete without reference to it.
Moreover, Vasiṣṭha has used the word "fire" without qualification to include even the fire prescribed by the Smṛtis.
Some maintain that this rule applies even to a father who has not performed the *ādheya* (consecration) of the sacred fires,
on the grounds that the term "eldest" (*agraja*) is etymological and thus the father is also an eldest.
Even if this were so, the same [rule] would apply to any other person who is an eldest.
Furthermore, this conventional usage of "elder" and "younger" does not apply to father and son;
for it is also recited in another Smṛti: "and among brothers, the elder [is the one]. Thus, the *parivitti* is the elder, the first-born brother.
The elder brother who remains unmarried, the younger brother who marries before him,
and she by whom he is superseded— all these go to hell, with the giver and the officiating priest as the fifth.

In this context, he provides a prohibition—by way of demonstrating the faults—of others related to supersession as well. One who is superseded by marriage is called a *parivitti*; one who performs the supersession by marrying before his elder brother is called a *parivettṛ*. Thus, the act of superseding the elder brother is termed *parivedana*.
And by whichever girl she is surrounded,
they all go to hell;
the giver and the officiating priest are the fifth among those who go to hell.
The "giver" (dātā) is the father or other relative, as they are the ones under discussion in this context regarding the girl.
The "sacrificer" (yājaka) is one who performs the *homa* at the wedding, or one who acts as the instructor therein.

Alternatively, he may be the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) for the *jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices of those very individuals—the superseded elder brother (*parivettṛ*), the superseded younger brother (*parivitti*), and the giver of the girl.

Therefore, the elder brother must act in such a way that he does not become an obstacle to the marriage of his younger brother. The younger brother, too, must wait for the appropriate time— whether it be twelve, eight, or six years—
and the girl should not be given in marriage to such a person.
The term is a bahuvrīhi compound containing a dvandva within it, meaning "those for whom the giver and the sacrificer are the fifth."
He who, out of lust, becomes attached to the wife of his deceased brother—
even if she has been authorized by religious law— is to be known as a *didhiṣūpati*.

One who, having engaged according to the law of *niyoga*, should feel passion—that is, cultivate affection—upon approaching the wife of his deceased brother, [doing so] out of desire; that is, by transgressing the rules of *niyoga* and abandoning the injunction that it be "once at each menstrual period," he should perform acts such as firm embraces and kissing out of longing for desire, or engage repeatedly, or his mind should undergo a transformation; one who is thus manifested as being impassioned through signs such as the lover's loving gaze, embraces, and endearing words is to be known as a *didhiṣūpati*.

The definition of the husband of an *agredidhiṣū* (a woman whose younger sister has married before her) is to be known from another Smṛti text: "While [the elder sister] is still living, he is the husband of an *agredidhiṣū*.
However, some say that this verse does not exist at all in the traditional recension (*samāmnāya*), and they claim that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) [cited] is incomplete.
When the definition of two [types of men] is to be established, it does not apply to those who perform what ought not to be done.
Furthermore, in another Smṛti, both of these are defined: "The wise call him *didhiṣūpati* who marries a woman previously married to another."
But that Brahmin for whom the Agredidhiṣū herself is the wife of his household is called an Agredidhiṣū.
But that is not possible here, because the husband of a woman previously married to another has already been prohibited separately.
Therefore, the *didhiṣūpati* must be someone else.
Two types of sons, the Kuṇḍa and the Golaka, are born from another's wife:
the Kuṇḍa is he who is born while the husband is alive, and the Golaka is he who is born when the husband is dead.
When the husband is alive and his wife resides in his house, a son who is born secretly, either as a paramour's child or through the husband's indulgence, is called *anyajāta* or *kuṇḍa*.
But when [the husband] is dead, he is a *golaka*.
Some maintain that these two are sons born of an unauthorized union (*aniyuktāsuta*).
That is incorrect;
because those two are not Brahmins, they do not qualify [for the rites].
Therefore, the Kuṇḍa and Golaka are born from an unauthorized union (niyoga).

But how is it that for those born of women not formally appointed (*aniyuktā*) or of women who are not one's own (*asutayoḥ*), there is non-Brahminhood, whereas for the other two [categories], there is Brahminhood?
Because in the definition of caste (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), the term "wife" (*patnī*) is employed, as in the phrase "among wives of equal status from all castes.
Furthermore, the word *patnī* is a relative term, just like the word *bhartṛ* (husband).
Furthermore, the term *patnī* (wife) is derived in connection with the sacrifice (*yajña*), and one person has no entitlement to perform a sacrifice together with the wife of another.
If this is so, then by the same logic, those born through *niyoga* likewise do not possess Brahminhood;
we shall resolve this in the tenth [chapter].

Or, let there be no Brahminhood for either the son of an appointed woman (*niyuktā*) or the son of an unappointed woman (*aniyuktā*). But has it not been argued that, in the absence of Brahminhood, since there is no possibility of its attainment, a prohibition is untenable?
This will be established simply by the prohibition against those who have fallen from their status (*patita*).

Falling away (*patana*) means the loss of the duties of the twice-born (*dvijāti*). Since [eating at] a *śrāddha* is a duty of the twice-born, how could it be possible for one who has fallen away? Furthermore, the prohibition is recorded in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) regarding those who are thieves or outcasts (*patita*).
But those beings born in the field of another cause the destruction, both here and after death,
of the sacrificial offerings (havya) and ancestral gifts (kavya) given by the donors.

Regarding the plural form "jātyākhyāyām" (in the case of a generic designation), the word "prāṇinaḥ" (living beings) refers to those who disregard the designations such as "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth; they are worthy of being designated simply as "living beings" and do not deserve any other designation. Therefore, they destroy the *havya* and *kavya* offerings, rendering them fruitless for the donors, that is, the givers.
Because terms such as *parivettṛ* and others are not well-known in the world and are not recalled by common usage, this definition is formulated for the sake of establishing their precise meaning.
As many worthy guests as an unworthy person looks upon while they are eating,
for that many the foolish donor receives no fruit from that act.
Those who are worthy of the row are called *paṅktyas*.
Being worthy of sitting and eating together with the virtuous in one place constitutes being a *paṅktya*; due to the absence of that quality, they are *apaṅktyas*.
As many learned, ascetic, and Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) as he sees eating in the row, for that many there is no fruit known as the satisfaction of the ancestors (*pitṛtṛpti*).
Therefore, thieves and the like should be removed from that place by one performing a śrāddha;
"bāliśa" means a fool.

A blind man, upon seeing [the gift], destroys the fruit of ninety [gifts]; one with a squint, that of sixty; one with leucoderma, that of a hundred; and one afflicted by a foul disease, that of a thousand given by the donor.
But surely, how can there be sight for one who is blind, such that it is said, "the blind man having seen [it] at ninety"?
True;
by this, proximity to that place is indicated.

To whatever extent is the range of vision for one with sight, from that extent of unobstructed space, the blind man is to be excluded; the one-eyed man, from sixty. This does not mean that he is to be fed beyond that point.
The reduction in the number [of days] merely indicates a lightening of the fault for the purpose of specifying a particular penance.
One afflicted with *śvitrī* (vitiligo) is called a leper (*kuṣṭhī*);
one suffering from a "sinful disease" (*pāparogī*) is well known.
As many Brahmins as one who performs sacrifices for Śūdras may touch with his limbs,
for that many [offerings], the donor shall not obtain the fruit of the meritorious gift.

Regarding the phrase "as many Brahmins as he touches with his limbs while seated in the row," here too, the touching of the limbs is not intended; rather, as before, it refers to proximity to that location.
The fruit is that which arises from the ritual offering.
"Paurtika" refers to that which pertains to *pūrta* (meritorious works).
That fruit which arises from giving outside the sacrificial altar is *paurtika*.
Even a Brahmin who knows the Vedas, having accepted a gift from him out of greed,
quickly goes to destruction like an unbaked clay vessel in water.
By way of incidental discussion, this [verse] declares that one who officiates for a Śūdra is not to be accepted as a recipient of gifts.

Even if a man who knows the Veda accepts wealth belonging to such a Śūdra-officiant—this being a restatement of the fact that he does so out of greed—he too goes to destruction; he is deprived of the desired object, whether it be wealth, sons, cattle, his own body, or other possessions.
How much more so, then, one who does not know the Veda?

It will indeed be stated that for one who knows the Vedas, there is no great fault in accepting gifts. An "unbaked vessel" (āmapātra) refers to a container such as a shallow bowl made of unbaked clay;
it is cast into the water.
What is given to a seller of Soma becomes excrement; to a physician, pus and blood;
what is given to a temple-attendant is lost; and what is given to a usurer finds no firm foundation.
He is born into that birth where excrement becomes his food;
likewise for a physician,
[the treatment] is lost, fruitless, or causes distress.
For lost wealth produces agitation;
"unstable" (apratiṣṭham) refers to that which has no existing foundation or standing.
Through various kinds of words, the fruitlessness of such a gift and the connection with fault for the donor are demonstrated.

Regarding the terms "vanished" (naṣṭa) and "unsupported" (apratiṣṭha), one should not suspect that there is no difference in their meaning, because there is a distinction in their functional effects (kārya).
That which is given to a trader brings no fruit either in this world or the next;
it is like an offering poured into ashes, even so when given to a twice-born man born of a remarried woman.
This also is to be explained as before:
the eating of a merchant is forbidden,
but not his presence in that place.

For there is no such basis here as there was previously, where proximity [was established] through the secondary sense (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "having seen" (*vīkṣya*) in reference to a place within the range of vision;
moreover, rebirth will be discussed in the ninth [chapter].
But regarding other unworthy persons, those listed as unfit for the company,
the wise declare that their food is fat, blood, flesh, marrow, and bone.

Those such as the blind and others who are recited in this section on demonstrating the fruit of giving to those unworthy of the company (*apaṅkti*), and others such as thieves who are specified in their respective sections—when these are fed, these things accrue to the giver: fat, blood, flesh, and so forth.
He is born into such a species where these constitute his food, namely among the species of worms, carnivorous beasts, vultures, and the like;
thus say the wise who know the Vedas.
This is the meaning of all [the texts]:

when those unworthy of the company are fed, the obligation of the *śrāddha* is not fulfilled; and since this rule is mandatory (*nitya*), the fault of transgressing the injunction necessarily follows if it is not performed.
Learn in their entirety those foremost of the twice-born who purify the row when it has been defiled by one unworthy of the company— those best of the twice-born who are the sanctifiers of the row.
Listen to those Brāhmaṇas by whom a row— a gathering defiled or corrupted by the aforementioned unworthy persons— is purified and rendered faultless;
I shall describe them in their entirety, without omission, in the verses to follow.
The other words are of the nature of explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

Just as one who eats in a row, if he is corrupt, defiles those who are not corrupt, so too does one who purifies the row (*paṅktipāvana*), by virtue of his own excellence of qualities, remove the defects of others; such is the meaning.
And by this, the eating of those unworthy of the row is not permitted; rather, it means that one who purifies the row must necessarily be sought out.

And once such a person has been found—if others have not been examined with extreme care even back through three generations—and if they are not found to possess any defects, then they must be fed even if [the other criteria] are lacking; this is the purpose of the instruction regarding those who purify the row (*paṅktipāvana*).
Those who are foremost in all the Vedas and in all the expositions,
and who are born of a lineage of Vedic scholars, should be known as the purifiers of the assembly.

"Foremost" means the most excellent; those who have thoroughly mastered the Vedas by dispelling all doubts are so called. And "foremost in all the *pravacanāni*" refers to those by whom the meaning of the Vedas is proclaimed and explained; these are the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) of the Vedas.
Those by whom the Veda with its six limbs has been studied and is being studied,

and who are born into a lineage of Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) such that their fathers, grandfathers, and so forth are likewise— surely it is precisely such persons as these who are prescribed as those to be fed; in that case, what excellence is there [in them] such that they are now called "purifiers of the assembly" (*paṅktipāvana*)?
The giving of something to those who are learned is prescribed only when they possess Vedic scholarship (*śrotriya*); however,
learning is not mentioned here,
nor is the status of being a sanctifier of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*) established by it.
For the status of being a "purifier of the assembly" (paṅktipāvana) depends upon specific qualities; it is not appropriate when there is a deficiency of those qualities.
Therefore, this [rule] is intended for the purpose of giving to a mere Śrotriya in the absence of a learned man (vidvat).
What is stated here is that, in the absence of a learned man, giving to a Śrotriya is indeed primary (mukhya), not secondary (gauṇa).
The plural number is used with reference to individual instances;
the particle *ca* serves as a conjunction for accumulation.

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who maintains the five sacred fires, one who knows the Trisuparṇa hymns, one who is learned in the six Vedāṅgas, one born in the lineage of those who gave their daughters in marriage according to the Brahma rite, and one who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāman; these are the ones [to be honored].
The portion of the Veda known as the *triṇāciketa* belongs to the Adhvaryus and begins with the words "pītodakā jagdhatṛṇāḥ" and so forth.
Because of his connection to the study of that [text], a person here is called *triṇāciketa*.
Furthermore, a specific vow is prescribed for those who study the *triṇāciketa*.
He by whom that has been performed is "one who has thrice kindled the Nāciketa fire.
Here too, it is the person who is spoken of only figuratively.

One should not think that mere [performance of this rite] constitutes the quality of being a sanctifier of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*); rather, this additional quality should be seen as a cause for sanctifying the assembly when it is conjoined with qualities such as being a master of the Vedas (*śrotriya*).
The knowledge called *pañcāgnividyā* is recorded in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*; its fruit is described in the passage beginning with "the thief of gold," and so forth.
By virtue of his connection to the study of that [knowledge], a person is also called *pañcāgni*, as before.
Others, however, maintain that one who possesses five fires—namely, the three *tretā* fires and the two consisting of the *sabhyā* and *āvasathya* fires—is *pañcāgni*.
In this context, the term *sabhya* refers to that which is employed in many regions specifically for the purpose of dispelling cold during the great ritual performance (*mahāsādhana*).

The mantra called *trisuparṇa* is found in the *Taittirīyaka* and the *Bāhvṛcya*, as in the passage beginning, "Those Brahmins who recite the *trisuparṇa*," and so forth. One who knows the Veda with its six ancillaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is a *ṣaḍaṅgavid*.
One who is born from the lineage of a woman given in marriage according to the *brāhma* rite of giving is called a *jyeṣṭhasāmaga*.
He is so named because he sings the *jyeṣṭha-dohā* sāmans found in the *Āraṇyaka*.
In this case as well, he is called "Puruṣa" because of his chanting of the Sāman or his observance of that vow.

One who knows the meaning of the Vedas, an expounder, a celibate student, one who bestows a thousand [cows], and one who has reached a hundred years of age— these Brāhmaṇas should be known as purifiers of the assembly.
He knows the meaning of the Veda. But has it not already been stated that he is one who knows the six auxiliary sciences?
True.
He who, even without [the help of] the ancillary sciences (*aṅga*), understands [the Veda] by his own wisdom, is intended here as one who knows the meaning of the Veda.
Alternatively, this is a restatement made again and again of that very same point:
those who lack knowledge of the meaning of the Veda are not worthy of the *śrāddha*, even if they possess other qualities.
One who expounds and explains the meaning of the Veda itself,
one who is a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*),
and one who gives a thousand [cows].
"He who has given a thousand cows by employing a term without qualification"—
this is logical,
because the word *sahasra* is a synonym for "many"; thus the meaning is "he who gives much" or "he who is generous."
For there is no means of valid cognition for the enumerability of cows;
even in the Veda it is stated, "Cows are indeed the mothers of sacrifice.
When there is an injunction without qualification, cows are understood [to be intended].
"One whose life-span is a hundred years" means one who is advanced in age;
for he, by virtue of having fully ripened his impurities (*kaṣāya*), attains purification.
He is called "one whose life-span is a hundred years" because his lifespan consists of a hundred [years].
The years are to be understood as innumerable, according to established usage;
or else, the word "hundred" has the sense of "many," meaning a long life,
and what is intended here is the state of advanced age.
But it is stated in the Gautama-smṛti: "Some say that the gift [of a maiden] should first be given to young men, as in the case of the ancestors.
It is for this very purpose that they explain the inclusion of the term "celibate student" (brahmacārin) here;
for he is indeed of early age.
On the day before or on the very day when the Śrāddha rite is about to take place,
one should properly invite at least three Brahmins who possess the qualities already described.

The types of Brāhmaṇas who are to be fed have been described; now, the subsequent procedure is stated. On the day before the Śrāddha is to be performed—whether on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) or the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī)—that is, on the fourteenth or twelfth day prior to it, one should invite the Brāhmaṇas when the Śrāddha is to take place on the following day.
"On the following day" means on that very same day;
here, the option depends on one's observance of the rules.
He who is able to maintain the rules does it on the preceding day, while he who is unable does it on that very day.
And because of the observance of additional precepts, there is great fruit.
When an invitation is to be made, it should be preceded by a formal request, followed by the engagement [of the monks] and their acceptance.
Those of whom three are the minimum are called "at least three" (*tryavara*).
If they are extremely few, then there are three;
however, if one has the capacity, it is said that there should be an odd number according to one's enthusiasm.
The remaining collection of words is for the purpose of completing the verse.
"Upasthite" means when [the time] has arrived;
"yathoditān" means as previously described.
A twice-born man invited to a rite for the ancestors should always remain self-restrained;
he should not recite the Vedas while that śrāddha lasts.
One invited to a *śrāddha* for the ancestors should remain self-restrained;
with a controlled mind, he should observe celibacy (*brahmacarya*), practice other restraints and observances (*yama-niyama*) such as the vows of a *snātaka*,
and adhere to the "vows of man" (*puruṣavrata*) which include prohibitions against dancing, singing, and so forth, as these are prescribed as integral parts of the ritual.
The performer of the *śrāddha* must act in such a way that the invited Brahmin remains restrained in his senses from the moment of invitation onwards; otherwise, the *śrāddha* would be defiled.
Furthermore, he should not recite the *chandāṃsi*, that is, the Vedas.
What is prohibited here is that study which consists of the vocal utterance of Vedic syllables.
However, the recitation of mantras (*japa*) is not prohibited at the time of the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and other such rites;
it should be performed by one for whom that *śrāddha* is to be done.
At a *śrāddha* dedicated to the ancestors, he should remain self-controlled, as if he were one who has been invited to a *śrāddha*.
The syntactical construction of the words is: "and he too shall be self-restrained and of restrained mind.
Therefore, from the time of the invitation of both the eater and the performer [of the rite] onwards, the restriction and the suspension of study are equal for both.
For the ancestors attend upon those twice-born who have been invited;
they follow them like the wind and wait upon them as they sit.
"One must be self-restrained when invited"—this is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for this injunction.
For the ancestors attend upon the invited Brahmins in an invisible form, entering their bodies just as one possessed by a spirit or a demon;
they follow them like the wind.
Just as the vital breath (prāṇa), which is like the wind, follows a person who is walking and does not abandon one who is walking, so too do the ancestors become like the wind;
they attend upon the seated Brahmins,
following them when they walk and sitting down when they sit.
The meaning is that the invited twice-born ones become embodiments of the ancestors;
therefore, they must not be invited as independent individuals.
But if that best of the twice-born, having been invited according to the rule for offerings to the gods or the ancestors,
somehow transgresses, that sinner shall go to the state of a pig.
"Ketita" means invited to offerings for the gods (*havya*) or the ancestors (*kavya*).

Having accepted the invitation— that is, having agreed to partake in the *śrāddha* meal— if he somehow transgresses it by failing to present himself at the time of the meal, or fails to maintain celibacy (*brahmacarya*), then that Brāhmaṇa goes to the state of a pig.
"Perhaps through desire or by forgetting"—
the phrase "in accordance with the rule" (*yathānyāyam*) is for the purpose of completing the meter.
Others, however, say:
Non-acceptance of that which is being requested is itself a transgression;
thus it is stated in the *Śrāddhakalpa*: "One who is invited by one who is blameless should not neglect [the invitation].
And this [position of yours] is incorrect.
One's engagement in a *śrāddha* is prompted by desire, not by scriptural injunction;
therefore, if one does not accept it when that desire is absent, what fault is there?
But he who, having been invited to a śrāddha feast, rejoices with a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī),
incurs all whatever evil deed has been committed by the giver.
The term *vṛṣalī* is intended to indicate women in general, because celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is prescribed universally.
Therefore, even a Brāhmaṇī woman is indeed a *vṛṣalī*.
He demonstrates the etymological derivation [of the word] as "she who lusts after" (*vṛṣasyati*) and "she who agitates" (*cālayati*) her husband.
Therefore, this is the meaning:

with respect to the meal, for one who on that day rejoices and delights with a woman—producing even conversation, embracing, and so forth, out of a desire for sexual union with her—this fault applies to him. Whatever evil or sin belongs to the donor who performs the *śrāddha*, all of that is transferred to him.
By this, only the connection with an undesirable result is indicated;
otherwise, where the giver is a performer of merit, there would be no fault whatsoever.
"Modana" means the arising of joy.
Therefore, one should not even engage in conversation, embracing, or similar acts with them.
Free from anger, devoted to purity, always practicing celibacy,
having laid down their weapons, these highly fortunate ones are the Pitṛs, the deities of old.
They are free from anger, devoid of wrath, and devoted to purity.
Purity (*śauca*) means cleanliness, whether through earth and water, through expiation, or through internal purification.
"Constantly" is a qualification of purity;
therefore, in cases such as spitting, one must perform ritual sipping (*ācamana*) and so forth at that very moment.
A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) avoids sexual intercourse with women.
"Those who have laid down their weapons":
by whom weapons (*śastra*) have been laid down (*nyasta*), that is, abandoned.
The mention of "weapons" is intended to indicate violence involving physical force (*daṇḍapāruṣya*).
"Highly fortunate" (*mahābhāgāḥ*): being endowed with qualities such as nobility and wealth constitutes "high fortune.
Since the ancestors possess such a form and they enter into the Brāhmaṇas, this meaning is enjoined by way of an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) that those [Brāhmaṇas] must assume that very form.
The "ancient deities" are those known as the ancestors (pitṛs); the praise here is that even in another kalpa these were indeed deities.
The term "ancient" (pūrva) is used because the ancestors were worthy of worship in former times.
Since the origin of all these [castes] has been explained in its entirety,
learn now those regulations by which they are to be served.
The origin of these ancestors, as well as which ancestors are to be honored by whom— such as the Somapas by a Brāhmaṇa and the Haviṣmants by a Kṣatriya, and so forth—
all of that shall now be stated in its entirety; listen and understand it.
The phrase "by means of observances" is a restatement (anuvāda), since they have already been enjoined previously by the words "one should be self-restrained";
the plural number is used because of the multiplicity of the observances.
The sons of all those sages— Marīci and the others, who were the sons of Manu Hiraṇyagarbha— are recorded as the classes of Pitṛs.
Hiraṇyagarbha is Prajāpati;
his son is Manu Hairaṇyagarbha.
And so it was stated in the very first chapter: "Having thus created all this, including me... and so forth.
The sons of that Manu—Marīci and the others, as well as Atri, Aṅgiras, and so forth—and the sons of those sages, these are the groups of ancestors (pitṛgaṇa).
But surely, fathers and the rest are the ancestors of everyone;
for thus it is enjoined: "One should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) to the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather."
Likewise, it is stated: "From this point forward, sons should give to three [ancestors].

In that regard, why is it said: "The sons of the ṛṣis are the ancestors named Somapas, belonging to the Brahmins"? Furthermore, one cannot understand this as an option—namely, that one should give either to the Somapas or to the father and grandfather.
Therefore, it is heard in the scripture that "at birth, [the rite] must be performed by the son";
furthermore, the word "son" (putra) is a relative term. Likewise, [it is said]: "but he whose father has passed away... and so forth.
Therefore, the meaning of this section must be stated.
It is said:
this is a praise that serves as a supplement to the preceding injunction.
In this context, their status as recipients (saṃpradāna) is not heard [in the scripture].
But is there not the rule that they are "to be treated metaphorically" (upacaryāḥ)?
This root *car* cannot be the subject of a grammatical rule in its general sense of "acting."
That which is called "observance" (upacāra) is not recognized in the Veda as being anything like a gift or a sacrifice;
for this term is generally used, like the verb *karoti*, with reference to an action that is proximate,
and the *śrāddha* is that which is proximate.
In that case, since [the act] has already been enjoined with respect to a specific recipient, it cannot be enjoined again; furthermore, there is no proximity of something to be enjoined.
And for that which is proximate, the *carati* suffix is sublated.
Even as for the usage in common parlance, "those who are to be treated as gurus," there too what is understood is service characterized by washing the feet and so forth.
That [interpretation] is also not possible for the ancestors mentioned above;
furthermore, since the meaningfulness of the passage is established through its natural syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*), there is no possibility of postulating a different meaning.
And if the Somapas and others were intended as deities in the *śrāddha* according to their respective castes, then the description of their lineage would be appropriate.
But if it is intended as a praise, everything becomes logical.
This [text] is commenced for the sake of engaging someone whose intellect might be impaired and who would be disrespectful toward ancestral rites due to hatred for their father.
Do not think thus: "The ancestors are merely the forms of deceased men; if they are not gratified, what harm will they do at the *śrāddha*, or what benefit will they provide if they are gratified?"
Since these possess great power,
and since Hiraṇyagarbha is the lord of the entire world, his son is Manu, and they are his grandsons; for this very reason, they are called "the sons of the sages" (ṛṣiputra).
The sons of Manu are not anyone else; rather, they are the sages of renowned power, such as Marīci and others.
Their sons are the *pitṛs*.
And there are various types of practitioners who are especially inclined toward such explanatory statements (*arthavāda*).
And those who maintain that the visualization (*dṛṣṭi*) of Soma-pās and others should be applied to the ancestors are to be disregarded due to a lack of authoritative evidence;
for there is no such statement here as there is when the visualization of Brahman is taught in relation to the sun.

Furthermore, as for those who say that one should offer to the ancestors after having grasped their lineage-names (*gotra-nāman*), that [lineage] is "Soma-pās" and so forth according to the distinction of castes (*varṇa*).
That too is incorrect;
this is a designation of names, not a designation of a lineage (*gotra*), because we hear the expression "of the Somapas.

If it is argued that even if it were a name for a lineage, the word *nāma* (name) would still be appropriate, then in that case, there would be a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) in the designation of the lineage, such as "the lineage of the ancestors is the Somapas," rather than "the ancestors are the Somapas."

Now, if it is argued that the designation of a "continuum" (*saṃtāna*) is seen by way of a metaphorical application of non-difference based on the lineage (*gotra*), as in the case of saying "Babhru is Mandu," to this it is replied:
Here, this must be examined— what indeed is this so-called "lineage"?

The "primordial man" (*ādipuruṣa*) is the founder of the designation, most renowned through his possession of qualities such as knowledge, wealth, heroism, and magnanimity, by whom the family is designated.
If this is so, then there exist internal subdivisions of lineages (*gotra*) for all [classes], such as the Brāhmaṇas and others.

Furthermore, people born in that lineage remember what kind of person their ancestor was, thinking, "We are born in the family of such-and-such a person"; therefore, designation by that very [ancestor] is appropriate.
For no one remembers the Somapās as a lineage (gotra), as one does the Bhṛgus, Gargas, and Gālavas;
moreover, it is appropriate for Brāhmaṇas to designate their lineages by those very names,
for those are indeed the primary lineages.
In its conventional sense, the word "lineage" (*gotra*) does not apply there;

for this definition—that lineage is the primordial person who establishes the designation—does not exist for those [lineages], because these lineages are beginningless, like the castes of Brāhmaṇas and so forth.
Indeed, it is not the case that only after the birth of Parāśara do certain Brāhmaṇas receive the designation "Pārāśara."
This being the case, it would follow that the Veda has a beginning;
therefore, because of its eternity, one must rely on that very same lineage (gotra) in rites such as the libation of water (udakatarpaṇa).
Those who create new designations, however, are not eternal; they are merely contemporary.
Furthermore, it is not appropriate in Vedic ritual to employ an impermanent designation when a permanent one is available.

Therefore, for Brāhmaṇas, after making the dedication with words such as "May this *svadhā* and water be for Gārgya" or "for one of the Garga lineage" according to their specific *gotra*, they should then utter the personal name and perform the offering of water and other rites.
For Kṣatriyas and others, however, no such usage of *gotra* exists.
For it is not the case that Kṣatriyas and others remember their lineage as fixedly as a Brāhmaṇa does;
therefore, their lineage is merely worldly, consisting of a most famous founder who established the name.
Consequently, they are designated by that lineage in rites such as the *śrāddha*, even though it is a name that has a beginning in time.
However, those Kṣatriyas do not deserve to be designated by such lineage names as "Havirbhuj" and so forth in the context of Śrāddha and other rites.

As for those who say that for those whose fathers' names and so forth are unknown, the Śrāddha and other rites are enjoined using these terms—such as "I invoke the Somapas; Svadhā to the Somapas"—this too is not correct.
For it is indeed said that those who are ignorant of names [call them] "grandfather" and "great-grandfather.

And if the meaningfulness [of these terms] were not obtained as a supplement to the subject matter by way of being an explanatory passage (arthavāda), then alternative interpretations might be resorted to;
however, when a connection as a single syntactical unit is possible, it is not right to adopt a meaning based on the assumption of a split in the sentence.
The sons of Virāṭ, known as the Somasads, are remembered as the ancestors of the Sādhyas;
and the Agniṣvāttas, renowned throughout the world, are those of the Marīcis.
These verses are explanatory statements (*arthavāda*) regarding the *śrāddha* rite, because they form a single syntactical unit with it as a whole.
For the Sādhyas are not taught to be the recipients (*saṃpradāna*) of the *śrāddha*, since the Sādhyas are deities (*devatā*).
And deities have no entitlement (*adhikāra*) to ritual acts, because they lack the status of being those who are to be enjoined (*niyojya*).

For a deity cannot be commanded, because that would entail the loss of its status as a deity. Since there is a qualification [to perform an act], agency must be admitted; and if there is agency, how can there be the state of being a recipient (*saṃpradāna*)?
Nor is there any other form of deity. The sons of Virāj are called the Somasads; they are the ancestors of the Sādhyas.
Such obligatory ritual must necessarily be performed, since even the Sādhyas, who were former gods and have already accomplished their duties, worship the ancestors.
The Agniṣvāttas are the ancestors of the gods, such as Indra and Agni; they relish the sacrificial offerings, such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa*, cooked in the fire.
The Mārīcas are those born from Marīci;
they are world-renowned and famous.
The Barhiṣads, born of Atri, are remembered as the progenitors of the Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Uragas, Rākṣasas, Suparṇas, and Kinnaras.
All these beings, beginning with the Daityas, are not entitled to the study of the scriptures; they are mentioned merely for the sake of explanatory praise (arthavāda).
Their true nature is well-known from the Itihāsas.
The Suparṇas are a particular species of birds.
The Kinnaras, horse-faced beings, and animals—
such is this ancestral karma that even the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rakṣasas, who cause the destruction of sacrifices, do not transcend it, as do the animals who lack consciousness and memory;
those born of Atri are named Barhiṣads.
Among the Brahmins they are called Somapas; among the Kshatriyas, Havirbhujas; among the Vaishyas, Ajyapas; and among the Shudras, Sukalinas.
The meaning of this verse has already been explained previously.

They drink the *soma*, namely Indra and the other deities of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices; they are the "eaters of oblations" (*havirbhujas*), namely the deities who consume the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and the cake (*puroḍāśa*).
The *ājyapās* are the deities of the two libations (*āghāra*), the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*), and so forth.
They are called *sukālins* because they "make the time good" (*sukālayanti*), that is, they bring the ritual action to its proper conclusion.
The deities for the *karmāpavarga* oblation are those prescribed in such [mantras] as "ayāścāgne 'nabhiśastīś ca" and so forth.
The Somapas were the sons of Kavi; the Haviṣmats were the sons of Aṅgiras;
the Ājyapas were the sons of Pulastya; and the Sukālins were the sons of Vasiṣṭha.
The *havirbhujas* alone are the possessors of the oblation (*haviṣmantas*). Bhṛgu is the sage (*kavi*);
they remember Uśanas as the one who speaks the wisdom of the seers (*kāvyam*), and [they likewise remember him] as a descendant of Bhṛgu (*bhārgavam*).
Just as these deities are the sons of the seers, so too are your ancestors of the very nature of deities; do not hold them in contempt.
One should designate the *anagnidagdhas*, the *agnidagdhas*, the *kāvyas*, the *barhiṣads*,
as well as the *agniṣvāttas* and the *saumyas*, as belonging exclusively to the Brahmins.
Soma is "unburnt by fire," for it has no cooking by means of fire; therefore,
those deities who are worshipped with it are also called "unburnt" and "prosperous" because they possess that same quality.
In this way, sacrificial offerings such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa*, which are burnt by fire, are cooked by the fire;
those deities who are worshipped with them are "burnt by fire" (*agnidagdha*).
The connection is to be understood in the same manner as previously explained.

Those who are called "cremated by fire" (agnidagdha), one should designate them as such; those who are "not cremated by fire" (anagnidagdha), one should designate them as "drinkers of Soma" (somapa). The same applies to the "Kavyas" and the "Barhiṣads."
The sons of Kavi are the Kāvyas, and they are said to be the Soma-drinkers among the sons of Kavi;
the Barhiṣads are said to be born of Atri.
This restrictive particle "eva" (only) is not to be understood as applying strictly to each respective case.
For in that case, the meaning would be as follows:
[the offering] is for the ancestors of Brahmins alone, and not for those of Kṣatriyas and so forth;
and that contradicts what was stated previously.

Nor are these mentioned as fathers by way of a distinction of caste, such that their connection with [the status of] Brāhmaṇas and so forth would have to be asserted by separating them from that [general category].
Therefore, the particle *eva* (only) must be extracted and connected in this manner: "one should point out only the Agniṣvāttas and only the Saumyas.
The mention of the *vipra* (Brāhmaṇa) is for the purpose of indicating the Kṣatriyas and others, since it is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
These ancestors of such names are heard of in the Veda: "the Agniṣvātta ancestors, those who were cremated by fire, and those who were not cremated. Having cited these mantras, he explains them.
Or rather, the connection is made thus:
one should designate as "ancestors" only those of the learned brahmins (vipras) who are referred to by these specific terms, namely one's own paternal ancestors.

Nor should one entertain the suspicion that there is a difference in meaning due to a difference in words; the mention of the "Brahmin" (vipra) is for the purpose of indicating the qualified person (adhikārin) by virtue of his preeminence, for an indication is made by means of the principal, as in the expression, "The king is going."
Furthermore, regarding these principal groups of ancestors that have been proclaimed,
it should be understood that their sons and grandsons here are infinite.
These, however, are the principal classes of ancestors, beginning with the Somapas;
their sons and grandsons are also infinite in number,
and they too are indeed ancestors.
From this statement regarding the restriction of the names, it is understood that the Soma-drinkers and the others are not the intended recipients (*uddeśya*).
For if their sons and grandsons— the fathers— were indeed the intended recipients, then no name for them would have been recorded in the tradition.
Therefore, it is determined that this is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda).
The singular form "putrapautram" is used because it belongs to the class beginning with "gavāśva" and so forth.
"Anantakam" means immeasurable.
The suffix *ka* is used in the sense of the word's own meaning (*svārtha*).
From the sages were born the ancestors; from the ancestors, gods and humans;
and from the gods, the entire world—both moving and stationary—in due order.
The ancestral rite (pitrya-karma) should not be regarded as inferior to the divine rite (daiva-karma);
rather, it is the most preeminent,
because the ancestors are the eldest-born of the gods.
For indeed, the sequence of creation is as follows: from the sages (ṛṣis) the ancestors (pitṛs) were born, and from the ancestors the gods (devas).

From the gods, everything else in the world—whether moving (cara), i.e., mobile, or stationary (sthāṇu), i.e., immobile—arose in due order; this sequence was stated in the first chapter. The discussion of explanatory passages (arthavādas) has now concluded.
Even water given with faith in silver vessels, or in those adorned with silver, conduces to inexhaustible results for them.
The vessels should be made of silver, the bowls of silver;
in the absence of those, they should be made of wood, copper, or gold, provided that one part is joined with silver.

And this vessel to be given is the vessel intended for a full meal consisting of ghee, honey, and other condiments; it is in regard to such a vessel that this requirement of being made of silver is prescribed.
Whatever involves the offering of rice balls (piṇḍa) and so forth must be performed with both hands;

likewise, the pouring of water upon the rice balls, the washing (avanejana), and other such acts must also be done with both hands, because of the scriptural injunction that these are to be performed "with the hand [held] in the *apasavya* position.
However, as for the daily libation of water (*udakatarpaṇa*), that may be performed either with the hand in the *apasavya* position or with the left hand.
For this has been recited in the section on ancestral rites (śrāddha).
That is not so; for even a subsidiary part of a rite that is not part of the current context may be taught as an independent injunction (anārabhyādhīta).
In that very context, there is a statement:
"Let it be; it would be a restatement (anuvāda).
It is also [the case] with water."

The word "api" (even) indicates praise for the vessel. Let alone the giving of refined food; even if merely water is given in a silver vessel, through its connection with the quality of silver, it becomes inexhaustible and serves as a means for the inexhaustible.
The meaning is that it becomes the cause of inexhaustible satisfaction.
The phrase "with faith" is a restatement, as it is prescribed for all types of giving.
For the twice-born, the rite for the ancestors (pitṛkārya) is superior to the rite for the gods (devakārya);
for it is traditionally taught that the rite for the gods is the preliminary nourishment for the rite for the ancestors.
That which is performed with reference to the gods is the rite for the gods (daiva).
After that, the rite for the ancestors (pitṛkārya) is distinguished; it is specifically designated as that which must be performed. By this, he declares the preeminence of the ancestral rite.
In this context, it is stated that the "divine" (daiva) is a constituent part of the ritual action.
He clarifies its status as a constituent action:
for the feeding of Brahmins, which constitutes the divine portion, is the nourishment and cause of increase for the rite dedicated to the ancestors (pitṛkārya).
The primary [offering] is not for oneself; it nourishes only the ancestors.
One should first employ a deity as their protector;
for the *rakṣas* plunder a *śrāddha* that is devoid of protection.

"Protection" (ārakṣa) means that which has become a protection; thus it is said to be for the purpose of protection. Alternatively, the word *bhūta* is used in the sense of a comparison, meaning "as if for the sake of protection.
When it is for the sake of protection, one should first appoint—that is, invite—a divine Brāhmaṇa and seat him upon a seat.
There is another explanatory passage (arthavāda): in the Itihāsas, it is said that certain invisible beings, the Rākṣasas, plunder— that is,
they snatch away— the Śrāddha offering from the ancestors.
Which gods, then, are to be designated?
First, in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*, from the application (*viniyoga*) of the mantra "We invoke the Viśvedevas," the Viśvedevas are understood.
It is also stated in the Purāṇa: "The Śruti says, 'the Viśvedevas'."

That which begins and ends with the divine succeeds; that which begins and ends with the ancestors does not. But one who strives for what begins and ends with the ancestors perishes quickly, along with his lineage.
The beginning and the end are "ādyantau.
That which has the divine (daiva) for its beginning and end is "daivādyanta.
The commencement (upakrama) of the śrāddha must be performed with the rite dedicated to the gods (daiva).
Therefore, the invitation of the gods must be performed first.
The conclusion occurs at the end;
once the Brahmins associated with the ancestors have been dismissed, the dismissal of the gods must be performed afterwards.
Even in the case of giving perfumes and other such items, they consider them to begin with the divine (daiva);
however, for those objects, it is not possible for both the beginning and the conclusion to be by means of the divine, because that would entail the consequence of repetition.
Furthermore, this rule of beginning and ending with the divine pertains to the ritual procedure (*prayoga-dharma*), not to the nature of each individual object.
Regarding items such as perfumes and garlands, the procedure is specified according to the distinction of whether they are directed toward the gods;
this is accomplished precisely through the sequence of engagement [already established].
First of all, the invitation must be performed beginning with the deities.

It is logical that the commencement of other categories occurs from the very same point where the first category was commenced, because one category necessitates the commencement of another category. As it has been said: "Because the qualities whose time for manifestation is determined by their inherent nature commence from that [very point]."

One should strive to perform that śrāddha rite; this is the injunction, while the remainder is an explanatory praise (arthavāda). It should not end with the rites for the ancestors (pitrya) and so forth.

Since the beginning and end with [the word] *daiva* has been prescribed, the prohibition against beginning and ending with *pitrya* should be understood as a mere explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), like a common worldly sentence;
for in the world, having enjoined something, one prohibits its opposite even if that opposite is not otherwise established, according to the principle:
"Action disciplines the substance, not the non-substance."
He perishes quickly along with his lineage;
this is a deprecatory explanatory statement (arthavāda) intended to show that [such an act] yields no fruit for one's progeny.
Therefore, all activities such as serving food and so forth must be performed beginning with the gods.
As for the serving of food and so forth in between, or the giving of drinks and so forth to those who are thirsty, that should be offered to whichever person first develops the desire;
for if it were offered to one who does not desire it merely out of compliance with him, there would be a subversion of the primary injunction: "one should gladden the Brahmins."

Likewise, suppose one person is fond of sweet flavors while another is accustomed to sour flavors; in that situation, where there are various kinds of foods to chew and eat, as well as fragrant drinks, if—despite the availability of many beverages—one were not to provide a flavor suited to the other's constitution out of consideration for someone else, then disease would be produced in him.
Therefore, the completion of the treatment itself depends on fate and other such factors.
One should smear a pure and secluded place with cow dung and,
with great effort, ensure that it slopes toward the south.
Pure means not defiled by ashes, bones, skulls, and so forth;
secluded means spacious and not crowded with many people;
sloping toward the south means inclining toward the southern direction.
One should strive to prepare such a place;
if such a place is not available by nature, one should act in such a way that it is prepared through one's own effort.
And one should smear that place with cow dung.
The clay and other materials are removed, because there is a rule for smearing with cow dung.
The ancestors are always satisfied by what is offered in open spaces, on clean riverbanks, and in secluded places.
"Opportunity" refers to a location.
"Pure" means naturally clean places such as forests that produce clarity of mind.
"Riverbanks" refers to sandy shores and the like near rivers.
This is another rule regarding secluded and solitary sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
Consequently, there is no requirement for smearing with cow-dung, because of the statement "he should prepare [the site]."
Where purity must be achieved, there this rule applies;

however, in things that are pure by nature, fitness is attained simply by the fact that they have been washed with water. In these regions, the ancestors become exceedingly satisfied by a *śrāddha* performed through what has been given or done.
When separate seats covered with sacrificial grass have been prepared,
he should cause those Brahmins, who have duly sipped water, to sit down upon them.

One should not give a single seat— such as a long-washed plank or similar object— to all [the guests] when they have been prepared, arranged, and assigned separately according to their respective divisions. The mention of "separately" (pṛthak) implies that they should be seated in such a way that they do not touch one another.

He should cause those previously invited to sit upon sacrificial grass (barhis) where mats of darbha grass have been spread, after they have touched water, bathed, and performed the ritual of sipping water (ācamana).
Having seated those blameless brahmins upon their seats,
he should worship them with fragrant perfumes and garlands, beginning with the gods.
After seating [the deity], one should worship with perfumes and garlands.
One should offer perfumes such as saffron, camphor, and so forth;
garlands are strings of flowers.
The term "fragrant" (*surabhi*) is an adjective qualifying the garland (*mālya*).
One should not offer flowers that are scentless.
This adjective is equally applicable to perfumes (*gandha*); since there exist perfumes that are unpleasant, it is used for the purpose of excluding them.
Alternatively, [it may be done] with fragrant incenses;
the mention of "fragrant" is independent [of other qualifiers].
Having first given to the Brahmins representing the gods, one should then give to those representing the ancestors.

However, they say that this mention of "beginning with the deity" (daiva-pūrva) is for the purpose of establishing a rule that the items [of the meal] must start with that [deity] prior to the commencement of eating;
but for those who have already commenced eating, there is no such rule regarding drinks, side dishes, and so forth. Otherwise, what would be the purpose of stating it again?
"Untainted and blameless Brahmins"—
this is a restatement;
it is a prescription specifically for such individuals.

Alternatively, even though there is an indication of the suffix meaning (*bhūtapratyaya*), this is merely a prohibition against the performance of the action denoted by the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*).
What is intended is that one should not feel aversion toward it and should not revile it, as will be stated later.
Scholars consider it better to abandon only the meaning of the suffix than to abandon the meaning of the entire word.
For in the case of a restatement, the entire word would indeed be meaningless.
Having brought water for them, along with sesame seeds and purifiers (pavitra),
the Brāhmaṇa, being authorized by the Brāhmaṇas, should perform the rite in the fire together with the Brāhmaṇas.
When they have been anointed, adorned with garlands, and are smelling fragrant incense, water for the *argha* offering should be presented;
by that same [water], sesame seeds along with *pavitra* blades should also be offered.
The word *pavitra* refers to *darbha* grass.
Having brought water for those Brahmins and given it to them, being permitted by them, he should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*).
The grammatical connection is: "being permitted by the Brahmins, he should perform [it].
They should all give permission simultaneously.
The statement of seeking permission is also obtained by implication;
for they would not grant permission if not requested.
Consequently, interrogative statements such as "I shall perform [the rite] in the fire" or "I will perform [it]" are understood.
The formula for seeking permission is also obtained by implication.
All of this must be performed using correct (sādhu) words.

This has been demonstrated by the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras: "One should seek permission, saying, 'I shall perform [the rite] in the fire' or 'I will perform [it],' and they should say, 'Om, do so.'"
Having first performed the satiation of Agni, Soma,
and Yama according to the rule, he should afterwards satisfy the ancestors with the offering of the sacrificial oblation.
That which is to be performed in the fire is now stated.
The genitive case for "of the fire" (agneḥ) is used in the sense of the dative;
Agni is the single deity.
The phrase "to Soma and Yama" indicates that these two possess the status of deities, just like Agni and Soma.
Having first performed the satiation of these two deities by means of the offering of the oblation (*havis*), one should afterwards satisfy the ancestors.
The meaning is that one should perform the offering of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa-nirvapaṇa*) and the feeding of the Brahmins.
In the Gṛhyasūtras, however, other deities are prescribed;
for those who have no Gṛhyasūtra, this statement regarding the deities serves as their guide.
*Āpyāyana* means nourishment.
"The deities thrive through the oblation" is an explanatory passage (arthavāda).
In the absence of fire, however, one should place [the offering] directly into the hand of the Brahmin;
for that twice-born one is called "fire" by the Brahmins who perceive the sacred mantras.

This rule is stated for the absence of the Smārta fire—whether it be the nuptial fire or the ancestral fire (dāyādi). However, regarding the ordinary (laukika) fire, its presence or absence need not be considered, because of the prohibition against performing the Pitṛyajña in it; as he will state later: "The oblation belonging to the Pitṛyajña is not performed in the ordinary fire."
But how, then, can there be an absence of that fire?

For it has been stated that the time for a *śrāddha* occurs when one who is away from home is without fire, yet possesses the requisite materials, a worthy Brahmin, and the proper place; it is not said to be restricted solely to the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).
In that context, this rule is prescribed for when one who is away from home encounters a person who purifies the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*) or obtains materials such as the *kālaśāka* vegetable.
But how can one who is away on a journey have the entitlement to perform a *śrāddha*?
If his wife is traveling abroad, the sacred fire must likewise remain present right there;
for it is not desired that the fire be separated from either the wife or the sacrificer.
For it is thus heard in the tradition that the sacred fire must not be left behind by one who is traveling abroad.
Now, if a householder were to travel alone, then there would be an absence of the fire.

However, because he [the husband] acts as the intermediary and because the ritual authority is joint, when the wife is not present, how can there be an application of the common fire to the *śrāddha* in the absence of her consent?
For when a substance is common property, if one party does not consent, the act of relinquishment simply does not take place.
Now, it might be argued that by this same logic, the performance of *śrāddha* at sacred sites (*tīrtha*) would also not be possible.
In this regard, the following statements are contradicted:
"A śrāddha at Puṣkara is inexhaustible, and asceticism there yields great fruit;
one should know that it is exactly the same at the Mahodadhi and at Prabhāsa."

This is not a fault; for one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) and goes on a pilgrimage to holy sites (*tīrthayātrā*) together with his wife, it would be appropriate [to maintain the fires]. But here, there is travel abroad with the wife; in that case, there is no absence of the sacred fire.
If [the husband departs] alone, then because he does not know his wife's consent, he lacks authority.
It is said in reply:
when departing on a journey, he asks permission of his wife, saying, "I shall employ the wealth for a religious purpose."
Having obtained permission for that, he will be qualified [for the rites].
Furthermore, prior to initiation (*upanayana*), when the maintenance of the sacred fires (*agniparigraha*) does not exist, this rule shall apply;
and there is indeed the qualification for *śrāddha* even for one who has not been initiated.
It has been shown that [the term] is used because of the bringing of the *svadhā* offerings.

Furthermore, for one who has performed the ritual bath (*snāta*) but has not yet married, there is an absence of the sacred fire (*agnyabhāva*) in the event of the death of a parent or similar circumstances.
Now, it may be objected that the *Kāṭhaka* recites that the formal adoption of the fire (*agniparigraha*) occurs upon the death of the *Parameṣṭhin*.
This [fire] is to be seen as belonging to one who has taken a wife, not merely to a *snātaka*.
For two times are prescribed for the *smārta* fire: that beginning with marriage (*bhāryādi*) or that beginning with inheritance (*dāyādi*).

In this regard, for one by whom the fire was not maintained at the time of marriage—either because he remained undivided from his father or because, while living together with his elder brother, the rule applies that "for brothers who are undivided, there is a single religious duty"—this [second time] is his second occasion, namely, "except at the time of inheritance."
This very time for giving is when the father dies;
it is with reference to this that it is said:
"Having become pure, one should give to the ancestors, and having brought the fire from the frying pan, one should attend to it."
If the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) were not an integral part (*aṅga*) of the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*),
then it would follow that its performance does not occur prior to that rite, nor does the *śrāddha* itself exist [prior to it];
furthermore, there would be no abandonment [of the fires].
This is recited: "This is the Aupasada fire; in it, the Pākayajña [is performed].
And even in the Pākayajña, one who is without a wife has no entitlement;
for the clarified butter (ājya) must be inspected by the wife.
Regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "And the wife shall undertake the vow.

It cannot be maintained that this undertaking of the vow and the gazing at the clarified butter (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*) will belong to the wife only when she is present, because they are enjoined as being obligatory (*nityavat*).
Consequently, it follows that the injunction must be performed [by her].
But is it not the case that the father's death alone is not the time for inheritance?
For it is recited thus: "Having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the sons should then divide [the estate]";
this is the time for partition (*vibhāga*), not for the inheritance itself (*dāya*).
Even in the case of partition, this restriction does not apply, because it is stated that "the separation of the property-holders is lawful.
And its legality arises from the fact that those who have been divided perform *śrāddha* rites separately and offer hospitality and other honors individually.
Furthermore, statements such as "they should not offer the *navāśrāddha* together" refer to subjects who have completed their education.

One who has acquired only a slight knowledge [of the Vedas], having married with the thought, "Lest through an excess of passion I should transgress the restriction regarding my own wife," and being intent upon the study of the meaning of the Vedas, is told this—namely, "Having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, they should divide [the inheritance]"—once his studies are completed in just one year.
At that time, for one whose wife has died and who desires to take another wife, there is an absence of the sacred fire (*agni*) until he has obtained a wife;
for since it is stated as a rule of existence that "one must sacrifice only together with a wife," there is no taking up of the fire for one who has not yet married.
This being the case, in the absence of fire, one should cast the oblations into the hand of a Brāhmaṇa.
Of which Brāhmaṇa?
Into the hand of any one of those who have been invited—either of that one seated for the rite dedicated to the gods (daiva), or of another invited guest.
For that which is [the statement] "Agni... is indeed an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda); this is agreed upon by those who perceive mantras and by those who know their meaning.

The ancients speak of these best of the twice-born as gods who are free from anger, easily propitiated, and intent upon the nourishment of the world; they are to be honored at the ancestral rite (śrāddha).
This is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda);
it establishes the nature of the Brahmins as being divine.
Fire is the deity.
In that regard, the deities consume what is offered through his mouth;
a brahmin is also of such a nature,
for the deities indeed consume even what is placed into his hand.
What, then, is the form of the deities by which even a brahmin is said to possess the form of a deity? To this he says: "those who are free from anger. How do they speak?
To demonstrate that purpose, he says:
"The oblations of clarified butter (ājyāhuti) should be cast into the hands of those Brahmins who possess such a nature.
However, others say:
Previously, by the words "free from anger" and so forth, the qualities such as freedom from anger were prescribed for those invited on behalf of the ancestors who are to be praised;
by this [verse], the distinction is made that these apply to those invited on behalf of the gods. Thus he says: "the gods at the śrāddha."
The ancient sages speak thus;
or rather, it should be read with the accusative ending:
"these ancient gods, the Sādhyas, who have arisen in this kalpa."
They are engaged in nourishing the world;
thus they partake of the offerings of the faithful.
In this regard, one should not think: "These people act out of greed for their own sake, seeking happiness in this life; therefore, why is worship offered to them?"
Since they nourish the world—the earth, the intermediate space, and the heavens—therefore no contempt should be shown toward them.
Having performed the entire circumambulation with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (aprasavya) around the fire,
he should pour water upon the ground with his left hand.
Regarding the rite to be performed in the fire for Agni, characterized by the casting of oblations with the formula "To Agni, svadhā, obeisance," that must be done *apasavya*.
It should be performed with the right hand, not with the left, nor with both; for there is a prohibition against using both hands together, stating they must be released from both hands.
Some maintain that the term *apasavyena* was used specifically to preclude the possibility of performing the rite with the use of both hands joined together.
But this is improper:
regarding those oblations which are offered into the fire, it is prescribed that their procedure (*āvṛt*)—that is, their circumambulation—should be performed counter-clockwise (*apasavya*).
One should perform the oblations ending toward the south, not toward the north, as is done in rites for the gods.

One should cause the oblations to be performed with a ladle, but not facing north; rather, one should face south, just as water is offered through the *pitrya* (southern) *tīrtha*. Because of the inclusion of the word "all," other acts such as serving food and so forth must also be performed *apasavya* (with the sacred thread over the right shoulder).
One should pour out the water with the hand in the *apasavya* position.
Alternatively, there is the reading "śanaiḥ" (slowly).
The meaning here is as follows:
otherwise, by the phrase "with silver vessels," the rule regarding the left hand would be intended for the purpose of obtaining silver vessels.
The turning around, the turning back again.
Then, having formed three balls from that remainder of the sacrificial food with a concentrated mind,
he should offer them facing south according to the very same rite prescribed for the water libation.
Having formed three *piṇḍas* from that food which was taken in the vessel for the purpose of the *homa*—the remnant of what was offered—one should offer them by facing the southern direction.
One should cast them upon *darbha* grass, intending them for the ancestors (*pitṛs*).
A solid mass of substance is denoted by the word *piṇḍa*.
Therefore, one should not give food that is clearly visible;
nor [food] with water,
according to the "water-rite" (audaka-vidhi) which was just described as beginning with "with the sacred thread over the right shoulder" (apasavyena), and so forth.
In this regard, a doubt arises:

should the consecration of the oblation (havis) be performed by taking a portion from that very food which was prepared for feeding the Brahmins, or should a separate sacrificial porridge (caru) be prepared?
And what should be the quantity of that oblation?

For in this case, there is no possibility of a specific measurement such as "four handfuls" and so forth; this has already been examined. Since no specific rule is heard, one may act according to one's desire.
The measure is that by which the accomplishment of the purpose is achieved.
And because of the extension of the rules for water-offerings, the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍas) is performed with one's own hand, using the apasavya method, and not with silver vessels.
The inclusion of the term "concentrated" (samāhita) is for the purpose of completing the meter.
Having then offered those rice-balls with self-restraint according to the prescribed rule, he should wipe that hand upon those Darbha grasses for the sake of the "partakers of the smearings."

Having offered those rice-balls upon the *darbha* grass, he should wipe that hand on those very *darbha* blades upon which the offering of the balls was made; for according to another *Smṛti*, the wiping takes place at the roots of the *darbha*. Others, however, maintain that it is not merely the food or water adhering to the hand that is to be wiped onto the *darbha* grass.
Even if nothing at all should adhere to the hand, one must nevertheless wipe the hand on the *darbha* grass;
for this is not merely a ritual act of disposal (*pratipattikarma*),
such that it would not be performed in the absence of a specific purpose stated in the injunction.

It is not heard here that one should wipe what has stuck to the hand; rather, it says "the hand itself. But surely it is heard [in another text] that this applies to those who partake of the smearings (*lepabhāgin*);
therefore, in the absence of a smearing, the rule would not apply.
Therefore, why is it said that even if nothing at all should touch one's hand, one must still perform [the act]?
It is replied:
physical food itself never actually touches [the hand].
While the morsels are being passed around, the essence of the food transfers to the hand due to contact with the heat;
that very thing is called the "lepa" (smeared residue).
The genitive case in the phrase "of those entitled to the lepa" (lepabhāginām) expresses the relationship between the wiping away and those [residues].
Furthermore, there are no visible recipients of the *lepa* (food smeared on the ground) whose relationship as owner and so forth could be established with that *lepa*.
Therefore, one should either meditate in the mind, "May this portion be for the recipients of the *lepa*," or designate them by means of speech.
Others, however, declare that those ancestors who preceded the great-grandfather are the "partakers of the smearings" (lepabhāgin).

According to this view, if their names are not known, the dedication should be performed using such expressions as "to the father of the great-grandfather" and "to the grandfather of the great-grandfather.
Because of the use of the singular number in the word "hand," it indicates that the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) is to be made with one hand, specifically the left (apasavya).
The term "prayataḥ" (purified) is a restatement, because [the state of purification] has already been prescribed.
The phrase "according to the rules" (vidhipūrvakam) incorporates the ritual procedure seen in other scriptures.
Śaṅkha states: "One should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) with perfumes, garlands, incense, clothing, and prepared offerings."
If the rule heard here were stated merely according to one's own opinion, then the phrase "according to the prescribed rule" would be redundant;
therefore, the expression "according to the prescribed rule" is intended to include the rules from other scriptures.
Having sipped water, turned away from it, and slowly restrained his breath three times,
he should pay homage to the six seasons and to the ancestors with the appropriate mantras.
Having offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) upon the darbha grass, he should turn toward the northern direction by way of the left;
for in another Smṛti it is stated: "turning to the left, having turned toward the north."
Standing facing north, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).
Having sipped water, he should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*);
that is to say, having restrained and completely suppressed the vital breaths (*asūn prāṇān*).
And in this context, there is no injunction such as "the Gāyatrī with the Śiras," and so forth. It should be done slowly, so that there is no excessive strain; thus he said:
