Having restrained the vital breaths according to the recitation,
one should perform a single prostration facing that very [direction],
saying "Homage to Spring," and so forth.
And one should pay homage to the ancestors with the appropriate mantra,
using the mantra beginning with "Homage to you, O ancestors" (namo vaḥ pitaraḥ).
The salutation to the ancestors should be performed facing the funeral cakes (piṇḍas);
for another Smṛti states that this is done by way of circumambulation.
He should slowly pour the remaining water near the rice balls;
then, with a concentrated mind, he should smell those rice balls in the order they were placed.

From the very same vessel from which the pouring of water upon the *darbha* grass was previously performed before the offering of the rice balls (*piṇḍa*), one must again pour water near the rice balls, that is, in their vicinity.
The mention of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) is for the purpose of disposing of that water;
for in this way, the word "remainder" becomes appropriate.
And therefore, if that [fire] should somehow cease to exist, there is no further pouring back [of the ashes];
however, in the Gṛhya texts, it is stated that the pouring back must always be performed.
And he should smell those rice-balls.
Smelling is the perception of the fragrance.
Regarding the domestic ritual, however, it is stated that one should consume the sacrificial porridge by "inhaling" it (*prāṇabhakṣa*).
This is done according to the order in which they were offered: to the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather.
"Concentrated" completes the verse.
Having taken very small portions from each of the balls of food in successive order,
he should first cause those very Brahmins who are seated to eat according to the prescribed rule.
"An extremely small measure" means a minute portion or fragment;
that very [portion] which belongs to the Brahmin who has been seated for the sake of the father—some small amount from his *piṇḍa* must be caused to be eaten by him.
"In due order" has already been explained.

In this context, because the word "that" (tat) refers back to what has been previously mentioned, there is no mention of the subject at hand in the phrase "the absence of fire"; rather, it refers to something else that was previously [stated] as edible.
While his father is still living, he should perform the offering for his ancestors alone;
or else, as in the case of a Brahmin, he should cause his own father to partake in that Śrāddha.
It has been stated that "one should offer rice-balls (piṇḍas) to the ancestors.
Who, then, are these so-called ancestors?
For the word *pitṛ* has multiple meanings; it refers, for instance, to one's progenitor.
The term "father" (*pitṛ*) is seen as a relative noun, as in "Janaka is my father.
Those who have previously passed away, such as one's father and others, as well as other deceased relatives, are called "fathers" (*pitaraḥ*).
Accordingly, mantras such as "Homage to you, O fathers" (*namo vaḥ pitaraḥ*), which end in the plural number, are suitable as recited formulas (*nigada*).
For this very reason, [the names] are not substituted in a *śrāddha* for women;
phrases such as "Obeisance to you, Mother! Obeisance to you, Grandmother! are not performed. Therefore, in the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, substitution is made for the number, but not for the nominal stem.

And thus the author of the Sūtras states, "One should modify the mantras as if they were singular," and so forth. In this manner, the modification (*ūha*) is performed in the formula "Obeisance to you, O Father. He who performs the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for a brother, a paternal grandfather, or others, modifies it accordingly: "Obeisance to you, O Brother," "Obeisance to you, O Paternal Grandfather," "Obeisance to you, O Uncle," and so on.
The Śrāddha for paternal uncles and others who are childless is ordained by the rule:
"Whoever receives from whom, he should give to him.
Furthermore, although the word *pitṛ* (father/ancestor) denotes specific deities, it also applies to the eternally immutable reality.
For the authors of the *Nirukta* enumerate the Pitṛs as being situated among the deities, stating: "The Maruts, wearing Rudrākṣa beads, are the Pitṛs.
Thus, since the word *pitṛ* has multiple meanings, he speaks in order to determine the specific sense:

while the father is being maintained—that is, while the father is living—one should offer [the oblation] to the three ancestors—the grandfather, the great-grandfather, and their father—as is indicated by the use of the plural number.
And likewise, it is stated in the Gṛhyasūtra: "To those whom the father gives [the offering], to them the son should give; this applies if both father and son have maintained the sacred fires.
Now, it is objected: "But they say that the fourth ball does not go [to anyone].
True.
In this case, no fourth rice-ball is offered.

He states another alternative: "or like the Brahmins. Just as Brahmins are honored after being invited and while observing vows such as celibacy, in the same way, the father should be fed by one whose father is still living.
The term *śrāddha* refers to the ancestral rite, and by extension, the food intended for that rite is also called *śrāddha*.
In this context, the sole criterion for being fed is the status of being a *pitṛ* (ancestor); neither caste (*jāti*) nor personal qualities (*guṇa*) need be considered.

For thus they say: "The *śrāddha* is for the sake of pleasing the ancestors. Since the purpose there is to bring satisfaction to the deceased, what disrespect could there be toward one who is still living, such that one would not feed him?
The word "one's own" (*svakam*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*), since its meaning is already established by the fact that it is a relative term.

Here, the beneficial meal for the father is enjoined; however, there is a contradiction [if one were to interpret it otherwise] because of the rule: "This offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa-nirvapaṇa*) on *darbha* grass must be performed for the ancestors.

For if the *darbha* grass were in the place of the vessel, then—given that the living father possesses ownership over the gift and thus only a small portion would be eaten—it would not be logical [to speak of the father eating the entire offering].
For while one's own property may be applied according to one's will during one's lifetime,
the offering of collyrium and such things into that funeral ball (piṇḍa) is not appropriate, as it would entail the fallacy of the "half-old woman" principle;
for there is no purpose served for the father by anything consecrated with collyrium and the like at this point.
Therefore, the offering of collyrium and other items is for the sake of an invisible (transcendental) purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

However, that which is devoid of collyrium and the like might sometimes be fit for the consumption of oneself, one’s father, or another; thus, this would be like the "half-old woman" fallacy (*ardhajaratīya*).
Therefore, according to this view, the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍanirvapaṇa*) is directed toward two ancestors: the grandfather and the great-grandfather.

The authors of the Gṛhyasūtras, however, record that for one whose father is living, there is neither the Piṇḍapitṛyajña nor the Śrāddha; rather, there is simply the non-commencement of that rite, or its conclusion at the point of the oblation (homānta).
But he whose father is deceased while his grandfather is still living should,
having pronounced his father’s name, pronounce the name of his great-grandfather.
By the mention of the father's name, his invocation, the offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍa), and the feeding of the Brahmins are indicated. One should recite the name of the great-grandfather;
one should not offer [the piṇḍa] to a grandfather who is still living.
Rather, they record in the traditional law (smṛti) that one should offer [the oblation] from that [portion] to the father's ancestors, beginning with the grandfather.
"Or the grandfather may eat that śrāddha," so Manu declared;
"or, being duly permitted, one may perform it oneself at will."
Just as one whose father is living is fed, so too is the grandfather;
having obtained permission from the grandfather, he should perform the rite himself. Beyond that, he should give to two ancestors, or to the great-grandfather alone.
This is the meaning of the two [phrases]: "this" and "at will, himself."
Having placed the water with sesame seeds and the *pavitra* grass into their hands,
he should offer them the first portion of that *piṇḍa*, saying, "May there be *svadhā* for them."

Regarding what was stated—that one should cause [the recipient] to eat a very small portion from the funeral cakes (piṇḍas)—this is the rule for the time and the place thereof. A portion of the cake must be taken from the front part; having offered darbha grass and water with sesame seeds, one should then present that share of the cake.

Saying, "May there be *svadhā* for these," the word "these" (*eṣām*)—a pronoun—is used to include specific names. Thus the connection is made: having uttered whatever names belong to those [ancestors], one should say, "May there be *svadhā*."
Therefore, when used in conjunction with the word *svadhā*, the dative case must be employed in the instruction, as in "May *svadhā* be for Devadatta" or "May *svadhā* be for Yajñadatta.
In this interpretation, there is no contradiction with other treatises.
Holding the vessel containing the increased portion of food with both hands,
he himself should gently place it near the Brahmins while meditating upon the ancestors.

Having personally taken with both hands a vessel filled with food from the kitchen or similar places— a "vardhita," meaning a vessel full of food— one should place it near the Brahmins, that is, set it down in their presence in the place where the Brahmins are being fed.
Others, however,
explain that the word *vardhita* refers to a rounded mass of food.

If one were to think, "I am offering this to you," while meditating on the ancestors in the presence of the Brahmins and then place it there—just as one does with the scattered offerings (vikiro)—that would be improper.
For [the author] will later state: "Having initiated him, one should serve him everything."
Therefore, this is the placing of it after it has been brought from another location for the purpose of serving.
The food that is brought forth and placed between both hands,
the evil-minded Asuras suddenly snatch away.
Food should be brought forward and served with both hands, and not with one alone;
"serving" (pariveṣaṇa) is indeed the same as "bringing forward" (upanayana).
Therefore, in that case as well, this very rule previously stated applies.
This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda):
when food that has been released— that is, set aside and not yet grasped— by both hands is brought forward for the purpose of serving, the Asuras seize it— that is, destroy it— by force,
by means of their power.
Those of evil mind are the wicked-souled ones;
the asuras are the enemies of the gods. The word "of both" (ubhayoḥ) is in the locative case, denoting location.
"Released," "not ploughed," and "not remaining" [are examples].

Furthermore, case endings denoting agents (kāraka-vibhakti) occur even when a negation is present, as in: "He does not come from the village," "He does not sit on the seat," and "He does not fast for three nights."
With self-restraint and concentration, he should first place upon the ground the various side dishes such as soups and vegetables, as well as milk, curd, ghee, and honey.
The *guṇas* (condiments) are the *vyañjanas* (side dishes).
The subsequent detailed explanation is for the purpose of illustrating these very points.
One should arrange the soups, vegetables, and so forth on the ground itself; one should serve them using the bare earth, not on wooden vessels, platters, or the like.
Various kinds of food and edibles, roots and fruits,
as well as heart-pleasing meats and fragrant drinks.
Edibles (*bhakṣya*) include parched grains, fried cakes, and the like;
for that which is solid and distinct is called edible because it is swallowed.
Food to be eaten (*bhojya*) includes items such as *ghṛtapūra* (butter-filled cakes) and so forth.
Having brought all that, he should serve it slowly and with great concentration,
remaining pure and extolling all its qualities.
Having brought [the food] near the Brahmins and having presented all of this,
one should then serve it;
"serving" (pariveṣayet) consists in taking up the vessel for eating and offering it.

Although serving while [the guests] are eating requires being in close proximity, nevertheless, the food should be placed near them in such a way that it does not come into contact with the leftovers of those who are eating.

"Proclaiming the qualities" means that while announcing the qualities of the substances to be eaten or consumed—such as their sourness and so forth, saying "this is sour," "this is sweet," or "this is sugary"—one should give whatever they prefer; this is the connection with what will be said later. The phrase beginning with "gently" (*śanakais*) is a restatement for the purpose of completing the verse.
One should never shed tears, nor become angry, nor speak untruth;
one should not touch food with the foot, nor should one shake it.
*Asram* means weeping or crying;
one should not shed it, nor should one do so.
Generally, in occasions such as funeral *śrāddha* rites, the shedding of tears arises from recollecting the suffering born of separation from what is beloved.
That is prohibited.
However, there is no fault in tears of joy falling spontaneously;
one should never, at any time, shed tears [of grief].
One should not become angry, nor should one harbor anger.
This prohibition regarding false speech is for the sake of ritual action, as it is already forbidden for the sake of human purpose.
One should not touch food with the foot, whether it be the leavings of another or not.
And one should not shake or cause this food to tremble;
having picked it up with the hand or another limb, one should not throw it away again.
Others, however, explain that the shaking performed for the purpose of removing dust and the like from a garment must not be done over the food.
Tears send the hungry ghosts (pretas) away; anger, enemies; falsehood, dogs;
touching with the foot, the rākṣasas; and shaking off [the dust], evildoers.
The explanatory statement (arthavāda) for this is as follows:
the shedding of tears causes the Śrāddha to go to, that is, reach, the departed spirits (pretas);
it does not become a benefit for the ancestors (pitṛs).

In this context, *pretas* are intended to be a specific class of spirits similar to *piśācas*, and not those who have recently died before the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has been performed. *Rākṣasas* are to be understood as being like *bhūtas* and *pretas*.
*Aris* (enemies) are well known.
Likewise, those who have committed evil deeds, who practice wickedness, and who are sinners.
Whatever may please the learned Brahmins, that he should give without envy;
and he should engage in discussions concerning the Veda, for this is what is desired by the ancestors.
Whatever food, condiment, or drink they might desire, he, being free from stinginess and greed, should give it;
"matsara" is a name for greed.
It should be pleasing and generate joy.
*Brahmodyāḥ*:
those which are raised or told regarding the *brahman*, that is, the Veda; such as the battle between the gods and the asuras, the slaying of Vṛtra, the deeds of Saramā, and so forth.
Alternatively, [those such as] "Who indeed wanders alone? and so on.

The reading is "brahmādyāś ca kathāḥ" (and discourses on Brahmā and others). This means discourses and conversations concerning the meaning of the principal mantras and so forth, expressed in worldly language.
The statement that "this is desired by the ancestors" is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
At a rite for the ancestors, one should indeed cause [the guests] to hear the Vedic recitation, the treatises on Dharma,
as well as narratives, histories, Purāṇas, and supplementary texts.
Svādhyāya is the Veda; the works of Manu and others are the Dharmaśāstras;
and the Ākhyānas are those such as the Sauparṇa and Maitrāvaruṇa which are recited in the Bāhvṛca (the Ṛgveda).
The *itihāsas* are the *Mahābhārata* and others;
the *purāṇas* are those composed by Vyāsa and others, consisting of descriptions of creation and so forth;
and the *khilas* are the *Śrīsūkta*, *Mahānāmnikā*, and others.
Being satisfied himself, he should gladden the Brahmins and feed them gradually;
he should repeatedly encourage them with food and by praising their virtues.
Even when there is a cause for it, one should not manifest one's own suffering in any way, such as by long sighs and the like; rather, one should act as if joyful.
One should gladden the brahmins with songs and so forth performed by others, or with jokes that are unobjectionable and arise spontaneously in the course of conversation.
If someone should become weary while the private recitation is being performed for a long time,
then one should desist from that and delight them with narratives, songs, and the like;
one should feed them gradually.
One should feed [the patient] with agreeable words such as, "Take a few morsels; this is excellent food," and so forth.
One should speak gently and not with agitation, using food such as milk-rice and the like.

One should encourage [the recipient] toward eating by presenting food endowed with flavor through its qualities (*guṇa*) and its constituent parts (*vyañjana*), prepared for the purpose of giving. Standing before them, one should repeatedly say things such as, "These cakes are delicious," or "This milk-rice is flavorful," while holding the vessel in hand; this is what is meant by "incitement" (*paricodanā*).
One should diligently feed even a daughter's son who is observing a vow at a śrāddha;
one should provide a kutapa blanket as a seat and scatter sesame seeds upon the ground.
In the case of a secondary alternative, it is stated with effort that the daughter's son (dauhitra) is to be fed.
A *kutapa* is a cloth made in the shape of a blanket from goat-hair threads;
it is well known as a *kambala* among the people of the North.
One should offer that seat;
not only on the occasion of a daughter's son, but at other times as well,
because it will be stated that "three things are purifying at a śrāddha," and thus it pertains to the śrāddha in general.
And one should scatter sesame seeds over the earth; one should cast sesame seeds upon the ground.
At a Śrāddha feast, three things are purifying: a daughter’s son, a woolen blanket, and sesame seeds.
And in this regard, they praise three qualities: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste.
"Purifying" means sanctifying or that which brings about goodness. The first half-verse is a restatement (anuvāda), while the latter half contains the injunction (vidheya).
Purity (*śauca*) consists in avoiding contact with impure things,
or the cleansing, according to the scriptures, of impurity produced through negligence by means of earth, water, and so forth;
it also includes the unhurried and confident performance of activities such as eating.
All the food should be very hot, and they should eat while remaining silent;
nor should the twice-born, when asked by the donor, speak of the qualities of the sacrificial offering.
Just as "hot" refers to that which is excessively hot or has passed beyond the state of being hot,
and just as "praparṇa" (leaf-fallen) means one from whom the leaves have fallen,
so too [the term applies] to all food and its qualities.
This injunction regarding heat applies only to that food for which hot food is appropriate, and not to curd-rice and the like, which would be unpleasant and disease-inducing if served hot.
In such cases, it would contradict the rule that "one should gladden the Brahmins. Furthermore, because of this injunction for hot food, the entire quantity of food should not be served at once.
For indeed, food becomes cold for those who eat much;
therefore, one should give again after they have eaten.
Nor should it be said that giving to those already eating is improper because it would be leftover food.
The rule for eating is precisely of this nature: it is the activity of the eater until satiety. For in this case, the rice and other foods are not connected [to the rite] as things to be accepted.
For this very reason, the mantra for receiving gifts is not employed there in the case of boiled rice and other such items.
"Vāgyataḥ" means those by whom speech (*vāk*) is restrained (*yata*) or controlled;
the inversion of the word order is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

Or, [the compound] *vāgyataḥ* is a *kṛt* compound meaning "one for whom speech is restrained" (*sādhanaṃ kṛtā*). In that case, the word *yataḥ* expresses the agent; "restraint" (*niyamana*) is the prohibition of activity, and the activity of speech is the utterance of sounds, which is here prohibited.

One should not utter words that reveal [the recipient's] identity or describe the qualities of the sacrificial oblation. The virtuous who eat with pleasure remember that nothing is intended for the giver by such speech.
But is this not already established by the very restriction of speech?
True;
yet it must not be performed even by means of gestures and the like.
The root *brū* functions in the sense of "establishing" [a meaning];
thus, "they would say" (*brūyuḥ*) does not refer merely to the utterance of sounds.
As long as there is heat in the food, as long as they eat with speech restrained,
so long do the ancestors eat— until the qualities of the sacrificial offering have been described.
This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) for the preceding injunction;
"uṣman" means heat.
Whatever one eats with one's head wrapped, whatever one eats facing south, and whatever one eats while wearing shoes— that indeed the Rākṣasas consume.
"Enveloped" means by a turban (*uṣṇīṣa*) and so forth;
for in the North, they wrap the head with cloth strips (*śāṭaka*).
As for those who explain that one's head is also enveloped by hair in the form of a topknot (*cūḍā*), they are not proponents of a logical argument.
Your hair is being braided, not your head;
yet the hair itself is not the head,
for it resides upon the head.
However, there is no prohibition regarding the Sūtra;
for in that context, the worldly convention of "wrapping" does not apply.
Since a fault is mentioned for one facing south, it permits eating even while facing a direction other than the south when the space is small.
Otherwise, since the rule prescribes facing north (*udaṅmukha*), how could there be any possibility of facing south?
*Upānahau* refers to leather footwear for protecting the feet.
Others, however, explain that *upānahau* means leather sandals.
"The Rākṣasas eat, not the ancestors"—this is a censure.
A Caṇḍāla, a boar, a cock, and likewise a dog,
a menstruating woman, and a eunuch— these must not look at the twice-born while they are eating.
The *varāha* is a boar,
and that is the domestic variety.
Although it is heard in the scripture that "they should not look [at food] because of the proximity of a dog," nevertheless, the learned do not approve even of the mere proximity of its location.
And likewise, another action such as "the boar [smells] with the nose" and so forth is heard in the form of an explanatory passage (arthavāda).
For smelling is not possible for one who is not looking;
rather, this is a restatement of the nature of those things already present.
The pig sniffs about;
the cock flaps its wings. Therefore, one should give [the offering] in an enclosed space—this is the injunction.
This is the purpose [of the rule]: even in an unenclosed place, one should give [the gift] provided there is an absence of defects.
A *ṣaṇḍha* is a eunuch.
Whatever is looked upon by these [outcastes] during the giving of a house, at a meal,
or at an offering to the gods or the ancestors, that goes astray from its proper course.
At home, in the *agnihotra* and other rites, or in propitiatory homas (*śānti-homa*) and the like; in giving, regarding objects such as cows, gold, and so forth;
for the sake of prosperity (*abhyudaya*).
Where Brāhmaṇas are fed for the sake of dharma—
whether at a divine oblation such as the New- and Full-Moon sacrifices,
or at a ancestral rite (śrāddha).
Whatever action is being performed that is observed, it goes astray from its true nature;
for whatever purpose it is undertaken, one instead cultivates its opposite.

Although this occurs in the section on ancestral rites (śrāddha), nevertheless, by virtue of the syntactical connection (vākya), this prohibition applies elsewhere as well, such as in the case of fire-oblations (homa) and so forth.
The pig destroys [the merit] by its smell, the cock by the wind of its wings,
the dog by the casting of its gaze, and one born of the lowest caste by touch.
A cock kills by means of the wind produced from its wings;
this has already been explained.
Their presence should be warded off at such a distance that they remain unable to see [the victim].
A *caṇḍāla* is one born of the lowest caste by nature;
furthermore, it has been explained that [actions such as] touching and so forth refer to the actions under discussion and do not intend to denote the essential nature [of the agent].
Therefore, this objection—that because there is a general prohibition against touching a *caṇḍāla*, the prohibition would be redundant since no [touching] could possibly occur—is not tenable.
Therefore, the Śūdra is one born of the lowest caste; and for him, the prohibition against touching the Śrāddha of the twice-born does not apply to his own [ritual].

Even if that were intended, this fault regarding the touch of food, drink, and so forth is not what is being stated here; rather, it refers to the touching of a place that has been appropriated, such as a riverbank and the like, which is unenclosed.
For the purification of such a place by means of wind, sunlight, and so forth has been declared.
Therefore, since there is such an attainment, the prohibition is appropriate.
Whether he be lame, or one-eyed, or even a servant of the donor,
or one with deficient or redundant limbs— one should remove him as well.
A servant is a hired laborer;
by the use of the word "also," others such as kinsmen who happen to be present by chance are likewise to be removed.
One should have them moved away from that place.
A lame person is one whose gait is impaired, such as one who cannot walk;
one with deficient or redundant limbs is a eunuch, a person with contracted hands or feet, one suffering from elephantiasis, and so forth.
When a Brahmin or even a mendicant has approached for the sake of food, he should,
with the permission of the Brahmins, honor them according to his ability.
A Brahmin who has arrived as a guest, or a mendicant Brahmin seeking alms, he should honor according to his ability, being permitted by the Brahmins engaged in the meal;
he should worship him with food or by giving alms,
for that day’s cooking is intended solely for that purpose.
Having gathered food of all kinds and sprinkled it with water,
he should cast it upon the ground in front of those who have finished eating, scattering it about.
The word *varṇa* should be understood here in the sense of "kind" or "manner.

Having brought together all kinds of side dishes (*vyañjana*) and food, having mixed them into one, and having sprinkled them with water, one should, after those who have eaten and are satiated have declared "We are satisfied," cast or scatter [the remainder] before them— not in just one place, but scattered upon the ground.
Not in bowls;
nor even on clean ground—what then? He will say, "The scattering [of food] is upon *darbha* grass.
Śaṅkha states that one should perform the scattering once or thrice.

The remnants of the meal and whatever scattering of food has been offered upon the *darbha* grass shall be the portion for those who have died an unnatural death and for women who were devoted to their families.
"For them who have died before three years [of age], there is to be no consecration with fire (agnisaṃskāra) as long as they remain uncremated.
The leavings in the vessels and the scattering of food upon the Darbha grass constitute their share.
Indeed, the word *bhāgadheya* denotes a share (*bhāga*) itself; for there is no benefit from a Śrāddha rite for them."
"Of those who abandon" refers to teachers and others;
or alternatively, it refers to those who abandon their wives—women of good family (*kulayoṣit*)—who have not been seen to commit a fault.
However, in the independent version where the word is *kulayoṣitām*, they explain that "women of good family" refers to unmarried maidens.
Therefore, the remnants should be assigned to them.
Nor should it be said, "The remnant is impure; how can it be fit as a portion? For by virtue of this scriptural statement, there is no impurity, just as in the case of the remnants of Soma.
The remnants that have fallen upon the ground are declared to be the share for the class of servants who are upright and free from deceit at the ancestral rite.
The manner of disposal for what remains in the bowl has been stated previously;
by this [verse], it is declared that what falls on the ground as leavings is for the sake of the class of servants.
*Ajihma* means not crooked.
He is honest and not indolent;
such is the portion for that class of servants.
Therefore, a large amount should be given, so that it falls upon the ground while he eats.
Until the rite of sapindikarana is performed for a deceased member of the twice-born caste,
one should offer a śrāddha meal without a deity and present a single pinda.

For a twice-born person who has passed away, until the rite of *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*—that is, until the rite known as the "offering together with the rice-balls" (*sahapiṇḍadāna*)—must be performed for the one who died first.
This offering together with the rice-balls must not be performed with the two preceding ancestors.
How, then, should it be performed?

"And he should offer one piṇḍa"—the word "and" (ca) has the sense of "only" (eva); therefore, he should offer that single piṇḍa to that deceased person alone. For a Brāhmaṇa should be fed for that very purpose.
In another Smṛti, a further specific procedure is recorded: that [the rite] is devoid of the invocation (āvāhana) and the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa).

By the term *agnaukaraṇa* here, the request for permission with the words "I shall offer into the fire" is prohibited, but not the oblation (*homa*) itself. For indeed, in the Gṛhya-sūtras, the oblation is prescribed specifically with reference to the Śrāddha for the deceased (*preta-śrāddha*).
Regarding the time at which the rite is to be performed and for how long, these should be sought from other Smṛti texts:
"The first [śrāddha] is on the eleventh day;
it should also be performed on the anniversary of death (mṛtāha), and every month for a year."
"And the annual *śrāddha* is indeed like the monthly one.
Likewise, in the *Kāṭhaka*, it says "thus the annual [rite].
And the mention of the eleventh day is for the purpose of indicating the cessation of ritual impurity (*āśauca*).
For it is heard in the sacred tradition (*śruti*) that "having become pure, one should offer [the oblation] to the ancestors.
Indeed, the authors of the *Gṛhya-sūtras* record that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite takes place at the end of a year.
And this *śrāddha* is the *ekoddiṣṭa* type, while the act of offering (*nirvapaṇa*) is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of that.

As for the argument that, because of the Vedic injunction "one should give to the ancestors," and because the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has not yet been performed, it is not proper to give here to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—
since a Smṛti cannot override a Śruti— [that is incorrect].
But when the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed for him according to the Dharma, the sons must perform the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) by means of this very same procedure.

But when the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, then one should offer [the oblations] to three [ancestors] by this very procedure (*āvṛt*), according to the rules for the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha; "procedure" (*āvṛt*) here means the ritual method.
One should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha preceded by the deities (*daiva*).
One should feed the ancestors (pitṛs) alone;
in this case, however, one should not designate the deceased (preta).
Here, the "ancestors" refers to the grandfather and others who have already been incorporated through the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite and have entered the class of the ancestors (*pitṛvarga*).
One should feed them.
Furthermore, in that context, the deceased (preta) is to be invoked among those very Brahmins; for his rite is for the sake of uniting him with all of them, so that he may be joined with them.

As for what was stated by Viṣṇu—"One should feed Brahmins for the deceased, for the father of the deceased, for the grandfather of the deceased, and for the great-grandfather of the deceased"—even there, it is not heard [in the source] that one should feed them separately.

In this regard, just as an oblation intended for many deities is offered once as a single act directed toward those many deities, so too it is not at all unreasonable that a Brāhmaṇa might be fed while directed toward many [ancestors].
For in this way, the scriptural mention of "together" (*saha*) is upheld, and in the rite for the ancestors (*pitrya*), an even number of guests is not fed.
According to the view of those for whom the rule is "one for each" or "one for both," a single person is fed on behalf of all.
This is how it should be understood.
But if this were so, would it not follow that for the rite for the ancestors, the injunction "three" would apply to all the deities collectively?
In that case, all [the deities] would be designated for each individual Brahmin, and even there, no separate mention is made.
How is it that it does not exist?
For it is recited in the Gṛhya-sūtras: "But certainly not one [offering] for all;
this has been explained by the rules regarding the rice-balls (piṇḍas)."
Furthermore, he says that one should pour the water from the vessel of the deceased (preta) into the vessels of the ancestors for the sake of the *argha* offering.
In that case, since there is no vessel prepared for the deceased, from which vessel would the *argha* water be given?
If it were from the combined vessel, that is incorrect; for that [water] was prepared for the grandfather and others, not for the father.
Furthermore, it is not logical for there to be a different purpose [for the pouring] from that which was intended for another purpose.
If one were to perform the pouring after having already offered the *argha*,
then— having already offered the *argha*— the statement that "one should pour for that purpose" would contradict the rule that the pouring is for the sake of an independent *argha*.
In the manner described here, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Now, who is this one called a *preta*? It is because after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) is no longer offered to the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*), since he has entered into those very [ancestors].
And thus says the Smṛti:
"He who joins a deceased ancestor for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed with a separate *piṇḍa* becomes a destroyer of the ritual injunction and is born as a slayer of his father."
For indeed, [the offering] is prescribed for him as distinct [from others],
and not as one common to all;
and the mantras, such as "those who are equal" (*ye samānāḥ*) and so forth, express this very same meaning.
To this it is replied:

this word *preta* does not function through its connection with the action of the root *i* (to go). This is a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*); one who has died is called *preta*, and now [this being] is called *preta*.
For one who has gone a long distance on a journey is not called a *preta*.
Yet, there is an application of the term *preta* through its connection with the action [of dying], without distinction, to both those who died previously and those who die now.

Thus, the Śruti says, "Those who depart from this world together," which shows the use of the term *preta* for one whose death has not been long. Furthermore, the rule "food for the *preta* for three days" refers specifically to one who has just passed away.
As for the phrase "with a separate *piṇḍa*," this is its meaning:
after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the *ekoddiṣṭa* should not be performed;
whenever a *śrāddha* is to be performed, it must always be offered to the three ancestors, specifically to the three paternal ancestors on the anniversary of their death.
It is not for the father alone;
thus, by the phrase "in this very manner," the procedure for the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha is extended [to the *ekoddiṣṭa*].

Now, one might object: the word "by this very" (*anayaiva*) is understood as referring back to the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), because pronouns denote what is proximate, and it is the rule for the *ekoddiṣṭa* that is proximate.
It is not so.
For if, even when the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, [the rite] were to be performed for only one person, then the very mention of a distinction would be untenable.

Furthermore, the word "but" (*tu*) indicates a difference in the procedure under discussion: this rule applies to the *asapiṇḍa* rite; however, once the *sapiṇḍa* rite has been performed, this [rule] should not be considered applicable.
Therefore, although it is separated [in time], the *pārvaṇa* rite is extended [to the annual śrāddha] because it remains present in the mind.

Furthermore, if after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, the *ekoddiṣṭa* were to be performed, then if one were to say "giving to three [ancestors]" on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), what would be the distinction?
Is there not the same purpose there as well, namely, "performing the rite together with the *piṇḍas*"?

Furthermore, in the *Mānava-śāstra*, there is no well-known rule regarding "another time" such as "on the anniversary of death every year" and so forth, by virtue of which this [present rule] could be explained as referring specifically to that.

Consequently, due to this lack of distinction, *ekoddiṣṭa* rites would apply everywhere. In that case, it would contradict the statement in the *Mahābhārata*, which, after introducing the sacred fords (*tīrtha*), says: "He indeed first gratified his ancestors with a *śrāddha*."

As for another Smṛti text stating, "And indeed, the annual Śrāddha is like the monthly one," even there, by the word "monthly" (māsika), the Śrāddha on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) alone is intended, because that serves as the archetype (prakṛti) for all Śrāddhas;
for it is in that [new moon Śrāddha] that the ritual rules (dharmas) are traditionally taught.
It is not appropriate to designate the Śrāddha performed every month throughout the year by the term "monthly."
For no specific characteristics of that [ekoddiṣṭa] are recorded by which it might be distinguished [from the pārvaṇa].
However, even here there exists the rule: "The first ekoddiṣṭa is on the eleventh day; for a Kṣatriya, on the thirteenth," and so forth.
Therefore, it is not appropriate to designate the ekoddiṣṭa by the term *māsika*.
For it is called "monthly" (*māsika*) because of its connection with the time of a month;
yet its connection is not with the month alone, since a connection with other times has also been shown.

Because it is stated that "having become pure, one should offer to the ancestors," and because the rite may be performed after the month as well as omitted during the month, it is not designated by the term "monthly" in this context.

Because the term "Paurṇamāsika" (pertaining to the full moon) is heard in connection with the origin [of the rite] on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), because the monthly *śrāddha* for the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) is fixed, because there is no connection with any other time, and because it possesses the same ritual characteristics (*dharma*), the extension of those characteristics to it is appropriate. The *āma-śrāddha* (raw-food *śrāddha*) also has the *pārvaṇa* as its archetype (*prakṛti*). Since giving to three [ancestors] would follow from that archetype, the status of being an *ekoddiṣṭa* (offering for a single ancestor) is specifically prescribed.
As for the statement of Yājñavalkya:
"The [śrāddha] should be performed on the anniversary of death every month for a year, and likewise annually; the first [śrāddha], however, is on the eleventh day."
In that case as well, such a procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is prescribed;
for there too, it is understood that the new-moon sacrifice (*amāvāsya*) alone is the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Therefore, even when the Ekoddiṣṭa is connected with the time of a month, it is not logical to extend its specific properties (*dharmātideśa*) to other [rites].
For one mendicant does not beg from another mendicant;
moreover, that [mendicant] is a modification of whatever [source] he comes from.
Furthermore, faith is indeed one and the same.
Therefore, there is no evidence for the general term *māsika* (monthly rite) to have as its specific scope the *ekoddiṣṭa* (single-offering rite). The same applies to the text of Yājñavalkya.
If there were a reference to what immediately precedes it, then an extension (*atideśa*) of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* would result.
For immediately after that, this is heard:
having recited "this is the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*" and "prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*," what follows immediately thereafter is stated as "on the day of death," and so forth.
Therefore, disregarding proximity, the new moon (*amāvāsya*) alone is thus designated because of its inherent ritual quality (*dharmavattva*).
Furthermore, the mantras illuminate our position even more clearly:
"Be united with your former ancestors. Here, those who exist together with their former ancestors are referred to as "be united" (*saṃsṛjyadhvam*); the plural number is used for the sake of honor.
And thus the author of the *Nirukta* says: "These very dawns (*etā u tyā uṣasaḥ*).
[He explains: "The plural number is used for the sake of honoring this single dawn alone.
Now, as for the phrase "you must mingle together" (*saṃsṛjyadhvam*), those balls (*piṇḍas*) into which [the water] is poured are being referred to.
And that which is deposited [with the formula] "by the ancestors" (*pūrvebhiḥ pitṛbhiḥ*) is, as before, expressed in the plural;
thus, the plural form in "by the ancestors" (*pūrvebhiḥ*) will be used according to its conventional application.
Otherwise, if the phrase "be united" (*saṃsṛjyadhvam*) were intended to designate the ball being deposited, the plural form in both instances would have to be assumed to be non-literal.
This too is of no consequence, because each individual ball is joined with a portion of the [other] balls; for it is said:
"Having set aside the fourth ball, one should divide it into three parts and place them upon the balls."
Therefore, there is no simultaneous expression of multiple substrata here by which a plural number could be justified.

Since each [element] is denoted individually, how could the plural form "saṃsṛjyadhvam" (you should mix together) be construed as a logical consequence? Furthermore, because it denotes that which is being deposited as a mass by means of the word "pūrvebhiḥ" (by the former ones), the designation "ebhiḥ" (by these) would not be appropriate. It is spoken of as if it were something remote.
Moreover, this mantra is not injunctive (vidhāyaka), such that we would strive to determine its meaning [as a prescription];
rather, it is expressive (abhidhāyaka). And its quality as an expression is established through its application (viniyoga).
And *viniyoga* (application) is *saṃsarga* (association), and it is that which makes [the application] manifest.
Number (*saṃkhyā*) here is not applied (*viniyukta*), nor is its manifestation attained; it is connected merely by way of possibility. And its comprehension occurs prior to the mantra.
As for those who say that the word "fourth" is logically applicable as being prior [to the grandfather],
on the grounds that the father is first and thus, in relation to him, the great-grandfather is the fourth—
this too is not correct.
Having set aside four balls for the ancestors, the fourth ball becomes that of the deceased (preta) alone;
this Śrāddha ceremony begins with the ancestors, not with the deceased.
For it is said: "One should feed the ancestors alone; one should not designate the deceased again."

Even for one who follows the sequence beginning with "this first ball is for the deceased (preta), then that for his father," and so forth, this restriction is established: it is prescribed that the division into three parts and the placing [of the portions] upon the balls apply specifically to that which is the fourth.
For such is the extent of that statement: "having divided the fourth ball into three, he should offer it.
In that context, because of their immediate proximity, the connection between the word "fourth" and the verb "should offer" is understood.

Regarding the phrase "having divided into three parts," when there arises the expectation as to what it is that is to be divided into three, the *piṇḍa* (ball of food) mentioned in proximity is connected [to that action].
Since the sentence is rendered complete by that much alone, there is no authority for connecting it with the word "fourth.
In that case, since any [of the four] might logically be subject to division, the determination is made on the basis of another Smṛti.
"Having offered four balls of rice according to each name,
the giver of the balls should divide the first one into three parts with the two verses beginning 'Those who are equal'.
The status of being "first" is intended with respect to the act of giving, and not because of a connection to a primordial person.

For instance, the great-grandfather would have to be prior to the grandfather, and the grandfather would likewise be prior to the father; thus, due to this lack of terminus, there would be no comprehension [of the lineage]. However, "giving" (*dāna*) is established by a fixed sequence as being the first. And so, since the rite is qualified by the term "the fourth," even across the three acts, it is logical that the division of the first portion should follow the order of giving, in accordance with other Smṛti texts.
Therefore, as for what was stated in the *Kāṭhaka*—that "the division [of property] for one who has died previously is seen to be desired"—what is this "desirability"?

And as for what was said—that for this very reason there is no giving to him, because he is already included [within the others]—that is of no consequence; for it is stated in the scripture: "It is not given, and the fourth funeral ball (*piṇḍa*) does not go to him."

Likewise, regarding the statement "the *piṇḍa* proceeds to three," there is his own reading: "one should again designate the deceased (*preta*)," which has been explained as prohibiting a further offering when the deceased is already included among the ancestors (*pūrvapreta*). This reading does not exist for the purpose of prohibition; rather, the particle *ca* is read in the sense of conjunction.
Or, even if that reading were present, the same principle should be understood here as was stated regarding the prohibition of a separate *piṇḍa* in the case of one who has undergone *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.
As for those statements:
"After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, every year the son should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* for his parents; otherwise, it is the *pārvaṇa*."
Regarding such passages as these: if these sentences actually exist, then what is the use of proclaiming the name of this new-moon day?
Furthermore, these sentences are not found in any of the well-known Smṛtis accepted by the learned.
Therefore, there is no specific indicative mark by which we may conclude that the funeral cakes for the ancestors who have passed away previously are deposited [on this day].
Therefore, proper conduct must not be abandoned;
this very position has been shown to be consistent with reason.
Consequently, due to differences in opinion, some have proposed the view that the offerings made by ancestors [should be treated] according to the principle of "cutting off" (apaccheda).

When a twice-born person has passed away, one should perform the Śrāddha rite without the *daiva* (divine) portion and offer a single *piṇḍa*, until the *asapiṇḍa-kriyā-karma* (the rite of non-ancestral connection) is completed.
In this matter, when the father has died but the grandfather is still living, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite should be understood as optional (*pākṣika*).
When one does not accept the rule that "one does not offer [the oblation] by bypassing a living person," then,
according to the alternative view that "this [grandfather] should be placed at the head," the deceased father must be united with the ancestors by bypassing the grandfather.

In this same way, even for a deceased son, the father must perform [the rites] by means of an option (vikalpa). Likewise, upon the death of a childless wife, this very rule applies to one whose mother is still living. "Others should perform [the rites] for those who are negligent, and they [the sons] for her"—by "sons" (sutaiḥ) is meant "offspring" (apatyaiḥ).
Even though the mention of "son" includes others who occupy his place, there is no prohibition if it is not by means of his own specific term.
That fool who, having eaten at a *śrāddha*, gives the leftovers to a *vṛṣala* goes headfirst to the Kālasūtra hell.
Although the taking of the fault lies with those who eat at the *śrāddha*, nevertheless, this is an instruction for the performer [of the rite].
Therefore, he should act in such a way that [the guests] do not give [the food],
just as in the case of the restriction regarding the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
A *vṛṣala* is a *śūdra*.
"With head downwards" means with feet upwards.
The mention of *śrāddha* is used so that it may not be understood as referring to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite already under discussion.
If one who has eaten at a śrāddha ceremony approaches the bed of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī) on that same day,
his ancestors lie for that entire month in her excrement.
They say that this term "vṛṣalī" is intended as an indicative mark for any woman in general;
they provide an etymological derivation:
she is called a *vṛṣalī* because she "desires a male" (*vṛṣasyati*), that is, she causes her husband to waver.
And that [intercourse]—whether with a Brahmin woman or any other—is entirely prohibited;
likewise, another Smṛti states: "On that day, he should remain celibate and self-restrained.
By the word *talpa*, sexual union is meant.
It is not merely a prohibition against ascending a bed;
the mention of "day" (ahar) is intended to indicate a full day-and-night (ahorātra),
so that the prohibition would apply even at night.
The statement "it is excrement" is a deprecatory explanatory passage (arthavāda) intended to cause desistance.
Regarding his ancestors who eat at the śrāddha,
this too is to be explained as before.
But this is logical: that there is a restriction for both.
This duty of the eater is occasional (naimittika), being enjoined when the occasion is the eating at a śrāddha;
and from the context, it also serves the purpose of the ritual act.
Having asked, "Was it well-tasted? he should then cause those who are satisfied to rinse their mouths;
once they have rinsed, he should dismiss them with the words, "May you all be happy."

Having given water for sipping (*ācamanika*) and food and drink, they should be asked with the word "Was it well-tasted? (*svaditam*). Furthermore, according to another Smṛti, this question should be made after taking up some of the food;
for there is a certain disposition in some people such that, even when food is present, they do not seek it out due to restraint despite a desire for it, yet they take what is already within reach.
One should offer water for sipping to those who are satiated;
however, others maintain that they should be asked with the words, "Are you satisfied?
and once their satisfaction is known, they should be gratified with the word, "It was well-prepared."
He will state later that one should say to the father, "It was well-eaten" (*svaditam*).
One should also dismiss those who have sipped water (*ācānta*) with the words, "May you rest at your ease" (*abhito ramyatām*).
*Abhitaḥ* means on both sides; the meaning is: "May you remain as you wish, either right here or in your own home."
Immediately after that, the Brahmins should say to him, "Svadhā astu";
for in all rites for the ancestors, the utterance of "svadhā" is indeed the supreme benediction.
After those who have eaten have been granted permission to go home, the word *svadhā* should be uttered;
*svadhākāraḥ* means the utterance of the word *svadhā*,
which is a supreme benediction.
In all rites for the ancestors, whether the śrāddha offerings consist of cooked food or uncooked food.
Then, once they have finished eating, he should present the remains of the food;
he should act according to what they say, being authorized by the twice-born.
The food that has been eaten should be offered to them; they should be asked, "Is this sufficient? and one should act according to their response once permission has been granted.
Therefore, it should not be employed for any other purpose without having been authorized.
At a rite for the ancestors, one should say "it is well-savored" (svaditam); at a rite for cattle, "it is well-cooked" (suśṛtam);
at a rite for prosperity, "it is excellent" (saṃpannam); and at a rite for the gods, "it is pleasing" (rucitam).
Even another person who has arrived at that time should likewise delight [the recipient] with these words.
However, another says: "With these words, one should seek permission for the undertaking of eating and so forth;
therefore, the performer of the *śrāddha* should speak thus out of a desire for his own satisfaction."
"May you relish [the food]" (*svadadhvam*); for it has not yet been relished. Or rather, the reading may be "may he relish" (*svadatu*).

This explanation, which conveys this meaning, depends upon other *smṛtis* and established custom; therefore, those who have begun eating should be gratified by the performer of the *śrāddha* or by another in this manner.
In a cow-pen, while the cows are standing in certain places, one should say, "It is well-cooked";
the response "So be it" is understood everywhere.
In rites for the gods, one says "It is pleasing" (rucitam) or "It is approved" (rocitam).
The afternoon, as well as darbha grass, the preparation of the site, sesame seeds, abundance, refinement, and eminent brahmins— these are the perfections for śrāddha rites.
The śrāddha should be performed before midday.
These items are the requisites for śrāddha rites;
they must be prepared.
Even though it is stated without qualification, [the afternoon rule] does not apply to all *śrāddhas*.
For another *smṛti* states:
"The rite for the gods (*daivika*) should be performed in the forenoon, but that for the ancestors (*paitṛka*) in the afternoon."

"The *ekoddiṣṭa* [rite] is at midday, while that performed on account of prosperity (*vṛddhinimittaka*) is in the morning. "Vāstu" means a dwelling; its "preparation" (*saṃpādana*) consists of sweeping, whitewashing the walls with lime and the like, smearing the floor with cow dung, and ensuring it slopes toward the south. "Sṛṣṭi" means liberal distribution; it refers to the giving of food and condiments without stinginess.
*Mṛṣṭiḥ* means cleansing;
it is a particular preparation of food.
Others, however, explain it as follows:
This perfection is the power of manifestation; however, it is not non-creation in the absence of these [factors].
Darbha grass, the strainer, the forenoon, and all kinds of sacrificial foods (haviṣya),
as well as whatever purifying means were mentioned previously, should be understood as the perfections of the oblation.
Darbha grasses are well known.
"Purifiers" refers to the mantras.
"Haviṣya" means things suitable and fit for the sacrificial oblation; these will be described in the preceding verse.
Purity is that which purifies and consists of pure conduct;
and that which was mentioned previously:
the preparation of the site, the creation, the cleansing, and the Brahmins who are preeminent and endowed with learning and good character.
The perfection of the *havya* (oblation).
*Havya* refers to sacrifices and the like performed for the sake of the deities, as well as the feeding of Brahmins;
the word *havya* indicates divine ritual action (*daivika-karman*) in general.
The food of sages, milk, Soma, meat that is not seasoned,
and salt that is not processed— these are said by their very nature to be sacrificial oblations (havis).
The "sage" (muni) is one who dwells in the forest (vānaprastha); his foods are wild products such as *nīvāra* rice and the like.
This is merely illustrative, for it includes cultivated grains such as *vrīhi* rice as well;
thus, the term "all" (*sarva*) is used in the subsequent verse.

And later on, having introduced the passage beginning with "the sacrificial oblation which lasts for a long time," there is an enumeration of cultivated grains as well, namely "sesame, rice, barley, and beans.
*Payaḥ* means milk;
by virtue of both traditional law (*smṛti*) and established custom, its derivatives such as curd and so forth are also included.
*Soma* is a specific type of plant.
*Anupaskṛta* means authorized and unrestricted;
for example, meat from a slaughterhouse (*sūnāmāṃsa*) and the like are *anupaskṛta*.
Regarding the term *akṣāralavaṇam*, a doubt arises here: is it a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) containing a copulative compound (*dvandva*), or is it simply a negative compound?
Is it "not salt and alkaline," or is it that a specific kind of salt called *kṣāralavaṇa* is prohibited, while other [salts] are permitted?
*Lavaṇa* must be understood in this way;
for when a compound contains a *dvandva*, two distinct functions must be resorted to,
and there is a difference in the connection of the negative particle (*nañ*) with each individual member.
That becomes heavy by its very nature; when no specific substance is mentioned, this [grain] is to be understood as the oblation (*havis*).

In general injunctions such as "one proceeds with what is fit for oblation" (*haviṣyeṇa vartate*) or "one eats from the morning meal onwards what is fit for oblation" (*haviṣyāt prātarāśād bhuṅkte*), that which is fit for oblation is to be known.
Having dismissed those brahmins, being self-restrained, silent, and pure,
and looking toward the southern direction, he should request these boons from the ancestors:
The preceding verse was incidental;
now he states the remainder of the subject at hand:
"having dismissed [them] and granted permission for them to dwell as they please."
After those Brahmins have finished eating, he should look toward the southern direction and request these boons—the desired objects—from the ancestors; that is, he should pray to his own ancestors.
While meditating on his own ancestors, he should make this request: "If you are pleased with us, may this be accomplished for us. Thus should he petition.
What, then, are those boons that should be requested? To this he says:
"May our givers increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give."
This verse is to be recited as a mantra.
Having thus performed the offering of the oblations, immediately thereafter one should cause those rice-balls to be consumed by a cow, a Brahmin, a goat, or fire, or else cast them into water.
Immediately after that, following the request for the bride, one should cause the balls of food (piṇḍas) offered to the ancestors, consisting of cows and other items, to be consumed.
"Consumption" here means simply casting them into the fire.
There is an alternative reading: *prāpayet* (should cause [them] to reach [the fire]).
Some perform the offering of the rice-balls only after [the meal];
others feed them to birds, or cast them into fire or water.
After the feeding of the Brahmins has been performed, some prepare the sacrificial oblation (havis);
others cause it to be eaten by birds;
this is a more extensive procedure than the former.
The fire is the digestive heat;
this has merely been restated as previously mentioned.
And this offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) is intended to take place subsequently in the vicinity of the food remnants.
Then, the devoted and lawful wife, intent on the worship of her ancestors and desiring a son, should properly eat the middle *piṇḍa*.
This is the procedure for the first and last balls; as for the middle one:
of those balls, the wife who desires a son should eat the one that is in the middle.
She who is not deluded by desire for sensual pleasure, whose rule is:
"The husband alone is to be served by me, and no transgression must be committed even in thought"—she is a devoted wife (*pativratā*) and one devoted to her husband.
She is intent upon the worship of the ancestors and rites such as the *śrāddha*, and is full of faith.
One should exert effort in propitiating that [deity] and so forth;
one should eat properly according to the rules for sipping water (ācamana) and other such observances.
She gives birth to a long-lived son, endowed with fame and intelligence,
wealthy, possessed of offspring, virtuous, and likewise righteous.
Having consumed that bolus, she gives birth to a son;
he is endowed with *medhā*, which is the power of comprehension,
and with *sattva*, a quality well-known among the Sāṃkhyas, which is manifested as courage, energy, and so forth.
Having washed his hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should provide food primarily for his kinsmen;
having given respectfully to his kinsmen, he should also feed his relatives.
When the rice-balls have been offered, he should wash those two hands;
then he should perform the ritual of sipping water (ācamana).
He should act so as to reach or attain the ancestors, for they go toward or arrive at their kin (jñāti-prāya).
One should give to the kinsmen;
having given respectfully to them, one should also give to the relatives.
Kinsmen (jñātayaḥ) are those of the same lineage (sagotra), while relatives (bāndhavāḥ) are those on the mother’s and father-in-law’s side.

To this it is replied: regarding what was said, that one should act according to what they say—if they have said, "Let this food reach our houses," then what becomes of the Vaiśvadeva oblation and the other rites? Another cooking must be performed.
Alternatively, the offering of the remnants of the food is prescribed as a constant duty for its own sake, with the instruction:
"When it is said, 'The food remains,' they should say, 'To those who are dear. However, this would be merely optional if they were to accept it.
That remnant of food should remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed;
thereafter, one should perform the domestic bali offering—thus the law is established.
While they are eating, whatever remains clinging to the vessels used for eating or has fallen on the ground must not be wiped away from that place until the Brahmins have departed.

Then, once the *śrāddha* rite is completed, the domestic offering (*gṛhabali*) should be performed, followed immediately by the Vaiśvadeva oblation, the daily rites, the feeding of guests, and so forth; this is because the word "bali" is intended to be illustrative.
Others, however, hold that the word "bali" is more commonly known to refer specifically to the sacrifice to the spirits (*bhūtayajña*).

Therefore, they say that the oblation into the fire is not contradicted by what precedes it. Nor should it be argued: "When a rite for the ancestors has already commenced, how can another rite be performed within its midst?

For just as performing the morning and evening oblations (*homa*) on the previous day is not contradictory to a *śrāddha* performed according to the two-day ritual procedure (*dvyahakalpa*), so too is the *vaiśvadeva* oblation belonging to the *aupāsana* fire.
By that [rule], the ritual items subsequent to the *bhūtayajña* are displaced forward, but not those prior to it.
To this it is replied:

if the *vaiśvadeva* oblation were performed before the fire, then the *baliharaṇa* would follow immediately after the *śrāddha*; in that case, the *devayajña* and the *bhūtayajña* would become separated by an interval.
Consequently, there would be a disruption of the sequence;
furthermore, this would not constitute a subversion of the time for the Vaiśvadeva, because it would result in the omission of the time for the ancestral Śrāddha.
Therefore, the performance of all the Mahāyajñas must follow after the Śrāddha.
I shall explain in its entirety that oblation which, when offered to the ancestors according to the prescribed rules, serves for a long time and even for eternity.
The word *cirarātra* signifies a long period of time.

That which conduces to infinity—that is, which arises for the sake of long-term satisfaction—I declare both of these; this is stated for the purpose of making a formal vow (*praṇidhāna*). To the word *kalpate*, the term *preta* (becomes) is to be supplied.
When sesamum, rice, barley, beans, water, or roots and fruits are offered according to the prescribed rule,
the ancestors of men remain satisfied for one month.
The mention of sesame seeds and the other items is not for the purpose of excluding other grains, but rather to demonstrate the specific fruits resulting from those already mentioned;
even when these are given according to the rules, the ancestors remain gratified for a month.
The subsequent phrases, such as "the ancestors of men [are pleased] according to the rules," are merely for the purpose of completing the meter.
For two months with the flesh of fish, for three months with the flesh of the deer,
for four months with the flesh of sheep, and for five months indeed with the flesh of birds.
*Urabhra*s are sheep;
*śakuni*s are wild birds such as chickens and the like;
and *matsya*s are fish such as the *pāṭhīna* and others.
For six months with the meat of a goat, and indeed for seven with that of the spotted deer;
for eight months with the meat of the black antelope, and for nine with that of the ruru deer.

*Ruru*, *pṛṣata*, and *eṇa* are words denoting specific species of deer; [the forms] *raurava*, *pārṣata*, and *aiṇeya* are secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) formed in the sense of "made from" or "belonging to."
They are satisfied for ten months by the flesh of boars and buffaloes,
but for exactly eleven months by the flesh of hares and tortoises.
And the *varāha* is the wild boar.
But with cow's milk, milk-rice,
and the meat of a vārdhrīṇasa for one year, the satisfaction lasts for twelve years.

Because the connection of what is explicitly stated (*śruta*) is stronger than that of what is inferred (*anumita*), the connection is with "cow's milk" (*gavyena payasā*), and not with the "meat" (*māṃsa*) mentioned in the context.
Others, however, reading the word *ca* as having the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), explain it as: "with meat, with cow's milk, or with *pāyasa*";
*pāyasa* is a derivative of milk, such as curds and so forth.
Rice cooked with milk is well known;
*vārdhrīṇasa* is an old goat,
for it is recited thus in the *Nigamas*.
But those who perform the sacrificial rites call that "vārdhrīṇasa" which drinks from three vessels, whose senses are decayed, which is white, aged, and uncastrated, used in the ancestral ceremonies.
He who drinks such that three things touch the water—the two ears and the tongue—is one who drinks with three, and is thus called a *tripiba*.

As for the expiation prescribed by Śaṅkha for eating beef, that should be understood to apply to occasions other than the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), the eighth-day offerings (*aṣṭakā*), and ancestral rites (*śrāddha*).
Black potherbs, large-scaled fish, the flesh of the rhinoceros and red deer, honey,
and all kinds of food fit for sages are prescribed for the sake of infinite results.
*Kālaśāka* is a well-known distinguished vegetable; it refers either to the black variety of *vāstūka* or to the *śalyaka* plant. *Mahāśalkāḥ* are said to be porcupines.
Others, however, say that "fish" refers to those with scales; "khaḍga" is the rhinoceros; and "loha" is a black goat as well as one that is entirely red.
Likewise, a black goat, a red goat, and so forth lead specifically to infinity.
The word "loha" (iron) refers, by way of indicating its color, to a goat endowed with that particular color.
Iron is black and copper is red; the word "loha" (metal) is applied to both.
Although this color may also occur in sheep and other animals, commentators explain that based on the authority of other Smṛtis, only the goat is intended.
Others, however, say that by the mention of a part of its name—just as Devadatta is called simply "Datta"—the bird named Lohitapṛṣṭha (Red-back) is indicated.
And proper conduct should be sought in both cases.
"Honey" refers to that produced by bees.
In all instances here, what is intended is the arising of an excess of joy, and not the literal time as it is heard.
For in that case, there would be non-performance for twelve years;
therein it would contradict the rule that "the ancestral rite must be performed until death."
Whatever one may offer mixed with honey on the thirteenth lunar day,
that too shall indeed be inexhaustible during the rainy season under the Maghā constellation.
Whatever food is combined with honey on the thirteenth lunar day, during the rainy season, and under the Maghā constellation— on those occasions,
it becomes truly inexhaustible.
There is a combination of the season, the lunar mansion, and the lunar day; however,

according to the statement of Āpastamba, even on the thirteenth, eighth, and tenth days during the rainy season, and under the Maghā asterism, there is no such requirement for their specific conjunction.
Thus indeed he said: "And [the merit] is even greater under the Maghās."

May there be one born in our family who would give us milk-rice mixed with honey and clarified butter on the thirteenth day [of the lunar fortnight], when the shadow of an elephant falls toward the east.
This is said with reference to the present thirteenth day, which is endowed with the qualities of the year and so forth:
"In this manner the ancestors pray:
'May there be such a person born in our family—one of superior qualities—who might offer us milk-rice mixed with honey and clarified butter on the aforementioned thirteenth day.'"

Likewise, when the shadow of the elephant—that is, the *kuñjara*—has moved toward the eastern direction (*prākchāye*), meaning at a time other than the afternoon; during the remainder of the day, the elephant’s shadow becomes long and directed eastward. Alternatively, the reading is *prākchāyam*.
For Brahmins are fed in the shade;
however, if the primary rite cannot take place in the shade due to its smallness, it should be performed in another location nearby.
Since it is a subordinate element, when possible, the principal rite must be performed with all its constituent parts in the elephant's shadow itself.

As for what they explain— that an eclipse of a planet is called "the shadow of an elephant" (hasticchāyā) because Svarbhānu, the son of Asura, having become an elephant, pierced the sun with darkness— that is incorrect.
For in that case, the application of the word "elephant" is figurative;
moreover, in another Smṛti, the shadow of an elephant is mentioned separately from eclipses of the planets, as in the passage: "the shadow of an elephant, and the eclipses of the moon and sun."
Whatever one gives according to the rule, properly, and endowed with faith,
that becomes infinite and inexhaustible for the ancestors in the hereafter.
The repetition "whatever... whatever" indicates that all food which is not prohibited is permitted;
the phrase "according to rule" (*vidhivat*) is a restatement for the sake of clarity.
It is this [quality], namely "endowed with faith" (*śraddhāsamanvita*), that is enjoined here.
It should be given with faith;
thus given, it becomes infinite and inexhaustible for the ancestors in the world beyond.
"Infinite" means there is no restriction regarding the duration of time.
"Indestructible" means that there is no depletion by measure;
it exists at all times and is abundant.
In the dark fortnight, from the tenth day onwards— excluding the fourteenth—
the lunar days are commended for the śrāddha rite, just as these are not so other days.
From the mention of the tenth day and so forth, it follows that there is the production of an excellence of fruit.
However, [the rite] should also be performed on other days provided that faith exists;
but on the fourteenth day, there is indeed a prohibition.
By performing [the rites] on even lunar days and under even asterisms, one attains all desires;
but by performing them on odd lunar days, one obtains abundant progeny for the ancestors.
The "odd" days are the second, fourth, and so forth.
The "odd" lunar mansions (*ṛkṣa* or *nakṣatra*) are those such as Bharaṇī and the rest. The lunar days (*tithi*)—the first, third, fifth, seventh, and ninth—are called "odd."
The second, fourth, sixth, eighth, and tenth are even; likewise, the eleventh and so forth are to be seen as odd. This should also be understood regarding the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).
[This fulfills] all desires.
And those objects of desire are presented as distinct in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
"Abundant offspring" means offspring nourished by wealth, knowledge, power, and men; thus it is "abundant."
Just as the latter fortnight excels the former fortnight,
so too does the afternoon excel the forenoon for one performing a śrāddha.
The first fortnight is the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), and the latter is the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa).
The months begin with the bright fortnight of Caitra.

Just as for a śrāddha rite the dark fortnight is superior to the bright fortnight and yields more excellent fruit, so too, by virtue of specific scriptural statements, the afternoon is superior to the forenoon.
It is understood that [the śrāddha] must indeed be performed even in the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) at times.
But surely there ought to be a well-known illustrative example;
yet no distinction regarding the śrāddha has been stated for the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) as compared to the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Some say that this is understood from the phrase "on the tenth day and so forth of the dark fortnight. However,
we say this:
According to the principle expressed in the sūtra "But because of the statement, since it is not previously established," that which is not prohibited can serve as an example;
thus, even a positive injunction (vidhi) can be understood from the very statement of the example.
Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, with the rite performed correctly from left to right, unwearied,
and holding darbha grass in his hand, he should perform the ancestral rite according to the rule until its conclusion.
Whatever rite pertains to the ancestors, this is the rule for that ritual.
The constituent elements have been explained previously.
It should be performed by one who is untiring—that is, by one who is not lazy—and who possesses faith.
"Until the end," meaning until death; the sense is that this rule is to be observed for as long as one lives.
"With darbha grass in hand":
regarding this, it has been said, "Darbha grass is the purifier."
That darbha-grass [ring] with its ends tied together is called a *pavitra*.
One should not perform a Śrāddha at night, for that is declared to belong to the Rākṣasas;
nor during either of the two twilights, nor when the sun has only just risen.
But surely, since the afternoon is specifically prescribed, how could there be application [of the rite] during the night and so forth?
If it is argued that this is indicated by the statement of a particular opinion— that it exists elsewhere as well—
then that is true.
Regarding the statement "the afternoon is superior to the forenoon," since that specific designation exists only in relation to something else, a general cognition arises.
Therefore, some say that the forenoon itself is at times its other subsequent time.

As for the phrase "the eclipse of the moon and sun," it would apply even during the night and so forth in the case of lunar eclipses and the like; [the specification of time] is for the purpose of excluding that.

And therefore, because of the prohibition [of bathing] during twilight when there is an eclipse of the moon or sun, and because of the injunction [for it at other times], there is an option (*vikalpa*). Others, however, say that the time of midday is distinct from both the forenoon and the afternoon; by this very prohibition, it is indicated that one should perform [the bath] even then. And regarding the sun, since it belongs to the forenoon, the prohibition applies to the sun when it has first risen.
"Rākṣasī" is a figurative expression (arthavāda).
By this procedure, one should perform the Śrāddha here three times a year—
during the winter, summer, and rainy seasons— and the Pāñcayajñika rite daily.
One should perform the *śrāddha* three times a year according to the previously mentioned procedure and sequence of rites, beginning with the invitation on the day before;
as to which months these are, he says: "in the winter, summer, and rainy seasons.
This rule of performing it thrice a year is an alternative to the practice of performing it every month.

That which is recited among the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña) is to be performed daily. Its procedure consists solely of this: wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), with the sacrificial cord over the right arm (apasavya), facing north, and feeding Brāhmaṇas. It is for this very purpose that it is mentioned again.
"In this way, the rule for three years applies to one who has not maintained the sacred fires"—thus the ancients explain; however, they alone know what constitutes the authoritative proof.
The oblation pertaining to the ancestral sacrifice is not prescribed for the common fire;
nor is there a *śrāddha* without the *darśa* for a twice-born who has maintained the sacred fires.
The oblation that constitutes a part of the ancestral sacrifice (paitṛyajñika) is not prescribed for the common domestic fire (laukika-smārta);
it is not enjoined by the scripture as something to be performed therein.
Therefore, it should be performed three times a year by one who has not maintained the sacred fires (anāhitāgni).

Although that which has been performed even three times is indeed considered "performed" in the case of a worldly fire, nevertheless, with respect to the year-long period, it remains as if unperformed.
For one who eats a *prastha* is considered "not having eaten" if he has eaten less than that.
The earlier commentators explain this as a supplementary explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) belonging to what precedes.
But this is logical:
if it is said that when a worldly fire has not been formally consecrated for marriage and the like, no oblation (homa) forming part of a śrāddha should be performed in it;
