and by the prohibition of the oblation, it is implied that other rites distinct from that [oblation] may be performed.

Otherwise, since the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* is prescribed as a constituent part of the rite even for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*sāgnika*), there would be no entitlement to perform the *śrāddha* at all for one without such fires (*anagnika*).
Just as a blind person lacks entitlement to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) due to the inability to perform the inspection of the clarified butter (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*),
this being the case, it is made known that for one with fires the *śrāddha* is performed with the fire-oblation (*homa*), whereas for one without fires it is performed even without that.
And thus, this alone is the scope of the phrase "in the absence of fire.
Even those who explain that the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is intended here, and that the oblation performed therein does not exist in the worldly or Smārta fire—they too do not speak correctly.
Let it be so for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) regarding its obligatory nature; however, [the rule] such as "having cooked, he should offer" would apply.
They say that for one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), there is a prohibition against performing a *śrāddha* without the new moon day (*darśa*), even during eclipses and the like;
however, this contradicts established custom.

Others, however, read the text as "not without the new moon," meaning that the monthly *śrāddha* must be performed by the fire-maintainer, and for him there is no rule requiring it only three times a year.
Others maintain that this reading does not exist at all;
what then is its meaning?

It means that for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), rites such as the *maghā-śrāddha* do not necessarily occur apart from the new-moon *śrāddha* (*dārśa*); thus, for him, only the new-moon *śrāddha* is obligatory.
But for one who has not maintained the sacred fires, even those rites prescribed for the winter season and other times are obligatory.
When that best of the twice-born, having bathed, gratifies the ancestors with water,
he thereby obtains the entire fruit of the performance of the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña).
By this [verse], the optional nature of that *śrāddha* called *pāñcayajñika*, which is prescribed as being performed "day after day," is stated.
By performing the libation of water (*udakatarpaṇa*) after bathing, one obtains the very fruit of the performance of the *pitṛyajña*.
As for what was said—that "one should feed even a single person"—there is no rule that it must necessarily be performed.
The heating and satiation [of the body] must certainly be performed.
They call the Vasus the fathers, the Rudras the grandfathers, and likewise the Ādityas the great-grandfathers; such is this ancient Vedic revelation.
This [verse] is intended for one who, out of hatred for his father, does not engage [in the rite], so as to induce him to do so.
The deities—the Vasus and others—residing in the three worlds, and the ancestors who partake of the rice-balls (piṇḍa), are identical;
therefore, these [ancestors] should be regarded as deities.
This Vedic revelation is heard in the Veda;
therefore, it is ancient because the Veda is eternal.
One should always be an eater of vighasa, and always an eater of amṛta;
vighasa is the remnant of what has been eaten, while amṛta is likewise the remnant of a sacrifice.

By the first quarter of the verse, that which was prescribed as the eating of food remaining after the meal of guests and others is here restated. Scriptures are renowned for concluding with auspiciousness because they are characterized by auspiciousness. A rite dedicated to the gods is more highly esteemed than one dedicated to the ancestors.
"Remnant of the sacrifice" (yajñaśeṣa).
By this, the consumption of the remnants of oblations from the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices is stated to be equal to *vighasa*.
With the subsequent half-verse, his very affection is expressed through his exposition of the meaning of the Vedas.
Since the injunction [of these two] is seen in a certain branch [of the Veda], this [text] removes any confusion:
"one who eats vighasa" (vighasāśī) means one who eats the remains of an offering;
"one whose food is nectar" (amṛtabhojanaḥ) means one whose meal consists of nectar.
"Bhṛtyaśeṣa" (the remainder of the servants) should be understood as that which remains after the servants have eaten.
If the reading is "bhuktaśeṣam" (the remainder of what was eaten), it should be understood by implication as that which remains after guests and others have eaten.
Others, however, maintain that because of the context, it should be understood as the remainder of what was eaten at a śrāddha ceremony.
And likewise, another Smṛti states: "One should eat while served by one's ancestors.
Regarding this meal, some say it is an ancillary part (aṅga) of the Śrāddha rite;
others, however, say that this is a restriction on eating for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha).

Since the section concerning the *śrāddha* has not yet commenced by the very statement "they call them Vasus," it should be understood that "the remnant of the sacrifice" refers to the remnant of the substances employed for the sacrifice.
All these rules for the five sacrifices have been declared to you;
now hear the rules for the livelihoods of the foremost among the twice-born.

For previously, the concluding summary of the rule for the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) as "pertaining to the five sacrifices" (*pāñcayajñika*) was intended solely for the sake of auspiciousness. With the second half of the verse, there is an introduction to a portion of the subject matter of the chapter to be explained hereafter;
these two [halves] serve the purposes already stated.
The "foremost of the twice-born" are the Brāhmaṇas; their "livelihoods" (vṛttayaḥ) are their means of subsistence, that is, their occupations.
Alternatively, they are the "principal livelihoods" of the twice-born.
We shall demonstrate this very point later on; thus it is well known.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
There is a certain venerable *Manusmṛti*, for which Medhātithi’s commentary is indeed appropriate;
yet that [commentary] has vanished by the power of fate, such that no manuscript of it can be found anywhere.
King Madana, together with the son of Araṇa, had this restoration carried out by having manuscripts copied here and there from various regions that had been brought from afar.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Commentary on Manu, composed by Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi Svāmin, son of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Virasvāmin.
Now begins the fourth chapter: Having lived the first quarter of his life with his teacher, a twice-born man,
having taken a wife, shall dwell in his house during the second quarter of his life.
He states the meaning of the two preceding chapters in brief for the sake of recollection.
The purpose of the second verse is to indicate that this is the rule for the means of livelihood (*vṛtti*) pertaining to the duty of the householder (*gārhasthya-dharma*).

Since the duration of life is not fixed, it would be inappropriate to establish a division into four parts for those in the stages of life (*āśrama*); therefore, this verse serves to restate the prescribed time-periods for the stages of life.

And although this might somehow be justified with reference to the statement, "A man indeed has a lifespan of a hundred years," nevertheless, because another limit is prescribed for studentship in its own context by the rule "until the taking of the [final] bath" (*grahaṇāntikam*), and because in the householder stage as well another time is understood from the rule "when the householder sees [his hair turning grey]," it is inferred that [the former] is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). The phrase "the first quarter of life" refers to the first part of the lifespan relative to birth.
Having lived with the teacher and practiced celibacy, he should then dwell in the householder stage after marrying during the second or fourth quarter of his life;
he should fulfill the duties of the householder's stage and reside therein.
A Brahmin should live in times of non-distress by adopting a livelihood that involves no injury to living beings, or at least very little injury.

The "malice" intended here is the state of mental distress characterized by weariness that arises in another person who is being entreated with "Give! Give!", and not physical injury itself, since the latter is prohibited universally for all.
Regarding "with little malice":
if one cannot manage without begging, then one should ask for only a small amount; this is what is meant by "little malice."
That mode of conduct which serves as a means of livelihood, such as agriculture, service, and so forth—in whatever mode of conduct no harm comes to another—that should be resorted to.
This is a general instruction:
having fully established oneself [in that], one should live.
The rule for the tenth [stage] will occur in times of distress (*āpad*).
From this instruction, it is understood that there is also another mode of livelihood (*vṛtti*) besides those that are about to be mentioned;
otherwise, if the general instruction were restricted solely to the specific cases to be mentioned, it would be entirely purposeless.

And by that [rule], officiating at sacrifices and teaching are included; even though lending money (*kusīda*) is not mentioned among the "immortal" (*amṛta*) occupations and the rest, it is nevertheless permitted.

As for the very slight livelihood of gleaning (*uñchavṛtti*) which has been adopted, that indeed involves little harm. And so says Gautama: "Agriculture and trade are permissible, provided they are not performed by oneself."
And [this applies to] the indolent as well.
This rule concerns mere subsistence; the accumulation of wealth, however, must be achieved only through the specific duties that will be prescribed hereafter.
For the sake of accomplishing the mere necessities of life,
one should accumulate wealth by means of one's own irreproachable occupations, without causing distress to the body.
In the preceding section, the means for daily livelihood were stated; by this [verse], the rule regarding the accumulation of wealth is taught.
One should effect the accumulation of wealth through one's own occupations, and those occupations will be described later.

He states the purpose of accumulation: "for the sake of accomplishing mere sustenance. One should not undergo the hardship of accumulating wealth for the sake of enjoyment; rather, it is for the sake of accomplishing mere sustenance.

Sustenance (*yātrā*) is the maintenance of oneself and one's family; the measure of that is "mere sustenance" (*yātrāmātra*); its accomplishment (*prasiddhi*) is its fulfillment; that which has this as its goal is "for the sake of that" (*tadartha*).
The performance of obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) is indeed included within the maintenance of the self (*ātmasthiti*); for one who does not perform them, there is no maintenance of the self.

As it is said: "He who does not offer the five [fires] does not truly live, even though he breathes. Alternatively, even if an act is prescribed by scripture, that which the world censures must certainly be avoided.

Just as for a man of noble birth who has enjoyed great wealth, his livelihood might be obtained through some means such as receiving gifts from one of inferior lineage who has acquired fortune, even if that person is of the same caste;
thus his body remains free from hardship,
whereas service and trade involve great suffering due to long journeys and other such trials.
Such things should not be done;
"accumulation" (saṃcaya) means the guarding of what has been gathered into a heap.
Now he states those occupations by name:
"One may live by means of *ṛta* and *amṛta*, or by *mṛta* or *pramṛta*, or even by *satya* and *anṛta*; but never by the livelihood of a dog."
In some cases, praise is understood from the name alone;
and the purpose [of such praise] is the engagement with those who are censured when those who are praiseworthy are absent.
In that regard, "the dead" and "the deceased" are utterly censured.
Even more than that, there is truth and falsehood, since it was said by that very same [author]: "Or even by that one lives.
The word *api* (even) is intended to indicate a lack of approval.
Having indicated them by name, he explains their essential nature:
"Ṛta" should be known as gleaning ears of grain; "amṛta" is that which is obtained unasked;
"mṛta" is alms obtained by begging; and "pramṛta" is traditionally held to be agriculture.
*Uñcha* and *śila* together constitute *uñchaśila*;
that is to be known as *ṛta*, equal to the vow of truthfulness (*satyavrata*).

*Uñcha* is the gathering of the *pulāka* (grains) that have fallen from the field—such as rice and other crops—as they are being carried to the house or the threshing floor, which were overlooked by the owner; that is *ṛta*.
In this regard, one should not entertain the thought, "This belongs to another; I will not take it.
Indeed, for one who has fallen from a threshing floor, taking ears of grain—whether already harvested or unharvested—that possess many stalks, is *śila*.
It is *amṛta* (nectar), because it brings about extreme joy when obtained without being asked.
"Alms begged are like a dead thing.

Since the meaning is already established by the word "begged" (*yācita*) alone, the use of the word *bhaikṣa*—which ends in a collective secondary suffix (*taddhita*)—indicates that many people should be asked for alms, and one person should not be harassed.
Thus it is said: "with little injury."

Since the word *bhikṣā* is generally established in usage regarding prepared food (such as in the phrase "for the sake of purifying oneself, one should eat alms-food" and so forth), the term *yācita* (solicited) is employed here to indicate a general sense. Therefore, this is not merely the begging for prepared food; for if one possessed a sacred fire (*agnimān*), there would be a contradiction with the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites due to the use of food cooked on another's fire. Nor is this begging solely for the purpose of eating; rather, it is for the purpose of maintaining life.
Furthermore, the maintenance of a householder is not accomplished by food alone; rather, it requires whatever is necessary for the household.
Therefore, one must beg even for firewood, water, clothing, and so forth, as well as household utensils such as cooking pots and their lids.

For a religious student (*brahmacārin*), however, since cooking is impossible according to the rules at the time of eating, his begging for alms is understood to concern only food that has already been prepared.

Furthermore, this word *bhikṣā* (alms) also expresses the quantity pertaining to the substance being begged for; as in the expressions "he does not give even a mere *bhikṣā* when asked," or "a *prasṛti*-measure is [the standard] *bhikṣā*. Therefore, begging for cattle, gold, and so forth is not authorized by the term *prasṛta*, since such requests are for the purpose of formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) and the like.
But is not the acceptance of alms also indeed a form of receiving (pratigraha)?
It is not so; "receiving" is merely the act of taking.
It is only in the specific sense of formal acceptance that the root *grah* preceded by *prati* is employed.

Therefore, it is not by mere acceptance alone; for even one capable of receiving may find that the act of receiving is inferior. Acceptance occurs when one receives what is being given with the thought of spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and preceded by a mantra.
However, in the case of alms (*bhaikṣa*), there is no recitation of the mantra "devasya tvā," nor is there such recitation in the giving and receiving of gifts out of affection and the like.
Furthermore, there is no conventional practice of "receiving" (*pratigraha*) in that case;
therefore, this which is denoted by the terms "dead" (*mṛta*) and "not dead" (*amṛta*) is indeed a different thing from receiving.

Consequently, in this context, neither for one who is being asked nor for one who is not being asked does there arise an expectation of some other benefit due to the [recipient's] greatness of being (*mahāsattvatā*), such that it would be logical for the giver to have regard for the caste and other qualities of the recipient.
Thus, for one who receives what is being given out of compassion, there is no "receiving" [in the ordinary sense].
But is it not the case that giving out of compassion is solely for the sake of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*)?
We say: no.
And in that case, there is no requirement for the ritual of giving; rather, it arises from the practice of compassion or from the desire to benefit others.
Just as in the case of providing beneficial instruction and the like, the recipient does not require consideration of their caste or other such factors, so it is with giving out of compassion.
Furthermore, the learned do not insist upon such a gift being made specifically "to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the true meaning of the Vedas."
For this very reason, even non-Brāhmaṇas who have fallen into a state of wretchedness and accept what is given by another do not rely upon the Brāhmaṇical mode of life known as *pratigraha*.
This is established:

although there exists a distinction between receiving what was requested and what was unrequested, the meaning of the terms "dead" (*mṛta*) and "not dead" (*amṛta*) is not determined by that alone, because a different scope has been demonstrated.
This same form [of activity] also exists in the cases of officiating at sacrifices and teaching:
some person, having performed the sacrifice, obtains the status of a priest, while another is requested [to do so];
the same should be applied to teaching.
Therefore, any livelihood obtained through begging is designated by the word "death," because it brings about wretchedness and is thus like death;
however, agriculture is even more sinful than death,
for the pulling of the plough is the bearing of a heavy burden.
And that, indeed, is the work of the people.
Trade involves both truth and falsehood, and one may indeed subsist by it;
however, service is declared to be the "dog's livelihood," therefore one should avoid it.
It should not be thought that the scripture permits both truth and falsehood in trade;
rather, this is a statement regarding the inherent nature of things:
greed itself is falsehood.
From the statement "one should live," trade is for the sake of livelihood alone, not for the accumulation of wealth.
Service is the "dog's way of life" (*śvavṛtti*);
for just as a dog is driven about and obtains its food with difficulty, so too is the servant.
Service means being sent on errands;
wherever one is sent for work, whether appropriate or inappropriate, one is a servant.
Therefore, those who approach the king with superior activities such as the use of weapons and so forth are not "dog-livers" (those following the dog's way of life).
He may possess grain sufficient for a granary, or grain sufficient for a jar;
he may have enough for three days, or he may not even have enough for tomorrow.
It has been stated that the accumulation of wealth should be undertaken for the maintenance of oneself and one's family, and that one should not resort to hardship merely for the sake of enjoyment.
However, it was not specified whether this should be acquired daily or all at once in an amount sufficient for a long period;
regarding this, the following is commenced to address the matter of the delay of time.
Because it conveys the sense that "he has grain in the granary," this is a *vyadhikaraṇa* (non-co-referential) *bahuvrīhi* compound.
There is an alternative reading, *kuśūladhānyakaḥ*;
in this case, *kusūladhānyam* means "grain measured by a granary," and the suffix *-ika* is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) to indicate that he possesses such grain.
A granary made of bricks and other materials is called a *kusūla* or a *koṣṭha*;
by this term, the measure [of grain] is indicated here. In that regard, one should collect only as much as fits [into it].
Furthermore, there is no fixed restriction regarding the storage vessel;
even for one who possesses a large estate, including many servants, kinsmen, wives, slaves, children, cattle, horses, and so forth, as much as is required for their annual subsistence is permitted.
For it will be said: "He who has food for three years..."
The mention of "grain" (*dhānya*) is also not intended to be restrictive;
there is no fault for one who acquires even gold, silver, and so forth, provided it is sufficient for that duration of life.
The meaning of the statement is that, in any case, one must not acquire more than that.
A *kumbhī* is a small water-jar (*uṣṭrikā*).
The traditional authorities remember that by this term, a store sufficient for six months is indicated.
That which lasts for three days in this world is called *tryahaihika*.
He who accumulates food for the sake of the daily requirements of his family is one who provides for three days (*tryahaihika*).

Regarding the term *śvastana*—meaning food belonging to tomorrow (*śvas*)—one should form a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) by adding a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) in the same manner as before. One who provides for the immediate moment is one who provides for the present (*sadyas-tātkālika*).
What has been earned on that day should be spent on that very day.
He states the established rule regarding this distinction:
"Among these four types of twice-born householders,
each subsequent one should be known as superior in terms of dharma and as the greatest conqueror of the world."
Whichever accumulation is made over a very short period of time, that becomes superior and more abundant through its dharmas; and from the abundance of dharmas, there arises an abundance of fruit,
becoming the supreme conqueror of the world.
One conquers the worlds, abides in them through sovereignty, and takes possession of them as objects of enjoyment.
When excellence is intended to be expressed, the word *tamas* [is used]. Since no specific distinction is mentioned, "the world" (*loka*) is understood to mean heaven (*svarga*).
Therefore, the established rule here is as follows:

One who has a large family—meaning one with many children, whose sons have not yet been divided, and whose daughters have not yet been married—is a "kusūladhānyaka" (one who possesses a granary of grain). However, one who is advanced in age, who has obtained sons, and for whom the legal formalities have been completed, should resort to the other methods of livelihood to the extent that he attains tranquility.
Among these, one performs six duties; another proceeds with three;
one with two; but the fourth lives by means of the Brahmasattra.
Among these householders, such as those who possess granaries full of grain and so forth, one is a performer of the six duties (*ṣaṭkarmā*).
For him who possesses great property, as previously described, there are six occupations for his livelihood.
What, then, are they?
The occupations under discussion are gleaning, living by a handful of grain, receiving gifts, begging, and agriculture and trade.
Teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts are included here because of the inclusion of both "begged" and "unbegged" [gifts].
One who has a large family should combine all modes of livelihood for the sake of accomplishing his constant duties, including even agriculture and trade.

As for those who explain the six duties—teaching, studying, and so forth—as being recited in the first chapter, there is a contradiction with the context [of this passage], and the mention of studying and the rest is purposeless, since they have already been prescribed elsewhere.
Another [teacher], Kumbhīdānya, says that one proceeds by means of three;
he considers the prefix *pra-* to be meaningless, as in the expression "as far as one proceeds (*yāvad vartate*), so far one proceeds (*tāvat pravartate*)."
And subsistence is the attainment of stability;
among those things mentioned, excluding agriculture and trade in whatever place they may occur,
the one who stores grain in a jar (kumbhīdhānyaka) is indeed more praiseworthy than the former.
For he will state that such a livelihood is censured by the virtuous, referring to "cowherds or traders.

As for what was said by Gautama—"agriculture and trade, provided they are not performed by oneself, and usury"—this applies even when there is no distress; yet even in that case, where one does not perform the work oneself, a fault certainly exists, though it will be a minor one.
One [type of robe] is obtained from two [sources].
Here too, excluding what is obtained through solicitation, two of the three [remaining types] are taken according to their possibility;
even that which is not solicited is accepted as long as it is sufficient for three days.

The fourth, however, lives by means of the *brahmasattra*. The *brahmasattra* is a mode of livelihood consisting of either *śila* (gleaning) or *uñcha* (gathering single grains). Because it occurs continuously, it is like a *sattra* (sacrificial session); it is not a mode of livelihood to be completed on a single day, and thus it is called a *sattra*, owing to its daily and constant performance.
The word *brahman* is a synonym for *brāhmaṇa*. This sacrificial session (*satra*) belongs to them.
Therefore, this preceding detailed exposition of the *vṛtti* should be understood as referring exclusively to the *brāhmaṇas*.
Regarding the Kṣatriyas and others, however, [the author] will explain it in various places.

But how is it possible to subsist by the practice of gleaning ears of grain (*śiloñcha*), given that the falling of ears and grains occurs only in the fields or threshing floors during the autumn and summer seasons?
To this, it is said:

Thinking, "I shall acquire [grain] for the summer months from those grown in summer, and for the autumn months from those grown in autumn," he would be one who subsists on a six-month supply, not one who provides only for the morrow.
However, it is possible otherwise as well: that he may somehow take up as much rice and other grains as are available.
True;
it is not sufficient for that meal. While he is gathering [food], when he obtains enough, he will eat it, because the five types of food and so forth are not available.
And likewise, in the *Mahābhārata*, one who subsists by gleaning ears of grain (*śiloñcha*) and eats only at the end of the fortnight (*pakṣāntāśana*) is described.
If it is argued that this very person, being a householder in this state, has become an ascetic (*tāpasa*), [we reply: even so, living from day to day (*aśvastanikatva*) would be contradicted;
for he would then be one who remains as long as provisions are available, not one who lives from day to day.

For one is called "one who does not store for the morrow" (*aśvastanika*) who earns what is necessary for subsistence day by day and spends it on that very day, not setting aside anything for a second day.

And if food does not cease even daily for one who lives by gleaning ears of grain (*śiloñcha*), how could he be one who does not store for the morrow? Furthermore, how could such a person maintain his own life and support his wife and children?
For this very reason, some explain the passage differently, beginning from the point where it says, "another proceeds with three."

By the three [means]— sacrificing for others, teaching, and receiving gifts— and by the two [remaining], with the exclusion of receiving gifts because it is inferior, sacrificing for others and teaching are understood.
Teaching is the "Brahma-sacrifice" (brahmasattra),
for that is sufficient for one's livelihood.
As for the statement, "subsisting by means of *śila* and *uñcha*," that refers to someone entirely different from the four previously mentioned types.
To this it is replied:
he who takes ten or twelve grains of barley or rice, measured by the *śila*, from many people, sufficient only for the journey of a single day, is one who subsists by *śila*.
But he who gathers [grain] one by one for the sake of sustenance is one who lives by gleaning (uñchavṛtti).
In another Smṛti, this is called the livelihood of the Yāyāvara;
and for this reason, it is appropriate even as a lifelong practice.

There is no contradiction with the performance of rites such as the Vaiśvadeva, nor is there the fault of failing to support one's wife and children, because he accepts only an extremely small amount from the alms he has requested.
Subsisting by means of gleaning ears of grain and picking up single grains, and being devoted to the Agnihotra,
he should always perform only the Iṣṭi sacrifices prescribed for the new moon, the full moon, and the solstices.
*Parva* means the end of an *ayana*; those [sacrifices] occurring at those two times are called *pārvāyaṇāntīya*.
Having applied the suffix *aṇ* in its own sense (*svārthika*), the suffix *cha* must be added because the word ends in a *vṛddhi* vowel.
The *parveṣṭi* refers to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), and the sacrifice at the end of the *ayana* is the one named *āgrayaṇa*.
By the use of the term "exclusive" (*kevala*), optional sacrifices (*kāmyā iṣṭayaḥ*) are prohibited.
Even the Vaiśvadeva oblation and the Bali offering do not occur daily for him;
for he does not always possess sufficient wealth.
Therefore, because of the mention of "only" (kevala), there is a cessation of the great sacrifices (mahāyajña).
But would not the Agnihotra also cease for him?
For that too is accomplished solely by means of material substances (dravya).
He will perform the fortnightly oblations.
If it is asked how his wife's maintenance shall be provided,
she too will resort to that same means of livelihood.
And when the wife is unable to observe this vow, then the husband also has no entitlement [to it].
If it is asked, "How can the wife's livelihood be maintained for one who is engaged in the Cāndrāyaṇa and other such observances?"—
this is not a valid objection, because she shall eat what remains after guests and others have been served.

But surely, because of the absence of the Vaiśvadeva oblation, it would not be proper for the wife to eat even when her own property exists, since both husband and wife are enjoined to eat only the remains of the sacrifice (vighasa).
Therefore, she will perform the Vaiśvadeva with her own property, as there is permission to take from the wife's property for religious duties.
This is not so.
In that state, the duty consists solely of the *agnihotra*; the *vaiśvadeva* oblation does not apply.
Or, let it be granted; but how then shall she live who possesses no wealth?
Therefore, he whose wife is incapable [of assisting] is not authorized for the livelihood of gleaning ears and picking grains; "subsisting" means maintaining himself, i.e., keeping himself alive.
One should never follow worldly conduct for the sake of a livelihood; rather, one should live the pure, straightforward, and honest life of a Brahmin.

What is called "worldly conduct" (*lokavṛtta*) is that by which a person of ordinary nature and little strength conducts themselves—through hypocrisy and speaking pleasant but untrue things, such as saying, "You are Viṣṇu," "You are Brahmā," "Victory to you! or "Live long!"—as well as through various jesting conversations. This must not be done for the sake of livelihood or for the purpose of a means of subsistence.
But there is no fault for one whose nature is playful. "Upright" (*ajihmām*):
he who has one thing in his heart and another outwardly is called "crooked" (*jihma*).

One whose nature is characterized by hatred and envy shows what is unpleasant to those who speak [the truth]. One who performs the *agnihotra* ritual for the sake of gaining worldly status through gifts and the like, rather than out of faith in the meaning of the scriptures, is a hypocrite (*śaṭha*).

Even though crookedness (*jaihmya*) and deceit (*śāṭhya*) are qualities of the self (*ātman*), livelihood is designated as "straight" (*ajihmā*) and "honest" (*aśaṭhā*) through the metaphorical treatment of them as non-different from it.
It is called "pure" (*śuddhā*); purity consists in not being mixed with other modes of livelihood and in being free from the two aforementioned faults.
Although this meaning can be conveyed by a single word, it is expressed through many words out of deference to the meter, as in the expression "cattle and bulls" (*gobalīvarda*).

Now, how is there an accusative case in the phrase *brāhmaṇajīvikāṃ jīvet* ("he should live the life of a Brahmin"), since the root *jīv* is intransitive? Furthermore, how can the same verbal root be used twice in a single sentence?
For there is no relationship of the probandum and the probans in the case of "going" [being] "one who goes.
It is said in reply:
because of the relationship between the general and the particular, the relationship of the probandum and the probans is not contradictory.

Just as in the expression "he has nourished the horse-nourisher" (*aśvapoṣaṃ puṣṭaḥ*), the root *jīv* occurs in the sense of "subsisting" (*vartana*) when it functions as a subordinate member of an action; therefore, its transitivity is established, and thus there is no fault.
He should live and pursue the means of livelihood.
In order to strengthen the practice of subsisting on what is obtained every three days or on the morrow, he has stated this enumeration:
"Seeking happiness, one who desires ease should remain self-restrained by relying upon supreme contentment;
for happiness has contentment as its root, while the opposite is the root of suffering."
One should resort to contentment; one should not endure the hardship of begging with the thought, "May I become a source of livelihood for many.
One who seeks happiness should be self-restrained. Self-restraint is the absence of desire for wealth beyond what is necessary for one's sustenance.
Contentment is the root of happiness for the wise;
its opposite, discontent, is the root of suffering.
It is a great wretchedness for the learned when their desired object is not attained.
Therefore, one should resort to contentment.
A twice-born Snātaka, living by any one of these modes of livelihood,
should observe these vows which lead to heaven, long life, and fame.
The "storehouse" (nidhi) is the object of subsistence (vṛtti), and it is expressed by the word "subsistence" (vṛtti).
Therefore, [the phrase] "by any one [of these]" does not depend on that [storehouse], because the rule for cessation [of the vow] is prescribed by means of any one [of the other sources].
Consequently, for one who lives by a combination of subsistences and who has obtained paternal wealth, eligibility for the vow is not appropriate.
Otherwise, there would be only a single mode of living.
These are the vows (*vrata*).
A mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is called a vow; it is of the form: "This, prescribed by the scriptures, must be performed by me," or "This must not be performed."
Some say that the fruits of observing vows consist of heaven, long life, and fame;
therefore, they claim that those who desire such fruits have the qualification for these vows.
That is incorrect.

If this were the case, it would follow that [the self] is impermanent; consequently, the mention of "eternal" (*nitya*) in the subsequent verse would be contradicted. Furthermore, their eternity is made known in the Veda by the passage: "For as long as he is joined with sin... and so forth.
If heaven and the like were construed as objects of desire (*kāmyatvena*), they would not attain the status of qualifiers for the qualified person (*adhikṛta*).
One should perform one's own duty as declared in the Vedas constantly and without laziness;
for by performing that according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal.
Because the Smṛtis are rooted in the Veda, it is heard [in scripture] that "it is declared in the Veda.
One's own duty (*svakarma*) refers to the collection of observances (*vrata*) to be described hereafter;
it is called "one's own" because it has been prescribed for oneself.
One should perform this constantly throughout one's life,
being untiring and free from laziness,
observing this vow according to one's ability.

By this, he states that when there is the capacity, one should perform the practice as far as possible. Thus it has been said: "Or, by mentally observing that entire conduct in its entirety, [one attains] the supreme goal, which consists in the attainment of the state of Brahman."
One should not seek wealth through excessive attachment, nor by contrary actions,
nor even in times of distress from here and there among speculative matters.
That in which a person becomes attached is what is intended by the term "attachment" (prasaṅga), such as singing, instrumental music, and so forth;
for it is in these that those possessed by passion seem to become stuck.
Therefore, one should not seek nor acquire wealth through singing, instrumental music, and the like.

One should not desire other [means of livelihood] that are contrary [to dharma], prohibited by the scriptures, or unsuitable for one's family, provided that the wealth inherited from one's father and ancestors is being utilized and is sufficient to maintain one's station.

One should not, even when fallen into distress, proceed by accepting gifts from just anyone; rather, one should act with force through the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous, for he will permit even this in times of distress.
One should not become attached out of desire to any objects of the senses,
and one should mentally restrain excessive attachment toward them.
The objects of the senses are their respective domains, such as forms, tastes, and so forth; one should not be attached to them, nor should one cultivate an excessive addiction to them.
Enchanting young women, the music of the flute, delicious flavors, the fragrance of camphor and other scents, and passionate touch—these are the sense-objects;
one should not indulge in them to excess.
"Out of desire" means by reason of the predominance of desire.
One should be a constant practitioner even toward all those [objects] that are like things unasked for;
however, there is indeed the danger of excessive attachment to them.
By this, the means of cessation is explained.
For attachment to objects cannot be turned away by the object itself; rather, it must be turned away by the mind through the cultivation of its opposite.
First, there is the difficulty of its occurrence.

One should reflect on how even those things previously enjoyed become inherently tasteless in an instant, how they are subject to destruction, and how attachment to them leads to falling into hell due to scriptural prohibitions;
as it has been said: "These [pleasures] cannot be [enjoyed] in such a way [as one desires]."
One should abandon all worldly pursuits that obstruct one's Vedic study;
maintaining oneself by any means whatsoever, for that indeed constitutes the fulfillment of one's purpose.
All those matters that are contrary to the study of the Vedas must be abandoned, such as attending upon kings or ministers' households.

Furthermore, for one who is attached to this worldly course of life, there may be excessive gain from agriculture, usury, and so forth, by which he will support himself; then, being possessed of family wealth, his female and male slaves will become numerous.

Indeed, the sense of having accomplished one's duty and achieved one's purpose for this *snātaka* is this: that he, being constantly devoted to Vedic study, somehow or other maintains his small family.
One should conduct oneself here by practicing conformity in dress, speech, and intellect with respect to one's age, occupation, wealth, learning, and lineage.
In the word *vayasaḥ*, the genitive case is used in relation to similarity (*sārūpya*).
In *veṣavāgbuddhi*, there is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*).
In the word *sārūpyam*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).
Therefore, this is the meaning: dress and other such attributes appropriate to one's age and so forth should be adopted.
"Correspondence" (sārūpya) means appropriateness (aucitya), because it is impossible for anything else—such as physical form—to possess similarity [to that specific state].
"Dress" (veṣa) refers to the arrangement of the hair, garments, and so forth.

In that regard, in the first stage of life there is the wearing of a topknot; in youth, the wearing of locks of hair such as the *kauntala* and so forth; and in old age, the wearing of matted hair or shaving the head. Speech should be appropriate to one's age. Likewise, the intellect: first it involves the pursuit and maintenance of the three aims of life (*trivarga*); later, for one who is aging, it consists solely of the preeminence of dharma.
Dress should be in accordance with one’s occupation and in accordance with one’s wealth;
indeed, it ought to be in conformity with one’s family. For even if such things as bright teeth, red lips, and elaborate hair-styles are ostentatious, they do not bring about arrogance.
Thus it has been said: "The sphere of his activity is worldly convention."
This is what is meant: this is not for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*), because its meaning has already been determined by others;
rather, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) based on worldly convention. By acting in this way, one conforms to worldly behavior and does not incur the world's hatred.
One should constantly study the scriptures that increase the intellect, which are auspicious and beneficial, as well as the Vedic Nigamas.

The Itihāsas and Purāṇas increase the intellect; the treatises on logic (tarka-śāstra), such as those of Bṛhaspati and Uśanas, are beneficial; the sciences of medicine, astronomy, and so forth—which have perceptible purposes—are "beneficial" (hita) because they provide assistance, since the science of polity (artha-śāstra) is taught separately;
and the Vedic Nigamas—the Nirukta, Grammar, and Mīmāṃsā—are the means for understanding the meaning of the Vedas.
If, however, "ṛc" were taken in its conventional sense, it would result in a purposeless (adṛṣṭa) effect.
For in whatever manner a person masters a treatise,
in that same manner he understands it, and his discernment finds delight in it.
"Attainment" (*samadhigama*) means "adherence" (*abhiniveśa*), which is to say "repeated practice" (*abhyāsa*).
One "knows" (*vijānāti*) means one knows specifically (*viśeṣeṇa*).
This is evident even in the case of a text being practiced repeatedly, insofar as it exists [in the mind].
Then his consciousness becomes pleasing;
the meaning is that it becomes radiant.
This is a statement regarding the root of the preceding mindfulness.
Because "liking" (ruci) has the sense of "desiring," there is no status as a recipient (saṃpradāna) according to the rule *rucy-arthānām*.
One should never, according to one's ability, neglect the sacrifice to the sages, the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the spirits, the sacrifice to humans, and the sacrifice to the ancestors.

The restatement of the great sacrifices (mahāyajña) prescribed in the third chapter is for the purpose of specifying particular details; and those details will be explained later with the words "without exertion" (anīhamānaḥ). Others, however, hold a different view.
The repetition in the section on vows (*vratādhikāra*) is for the purpose of establishing a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
Therefore, one should make such a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "As long as I remain in the householder stage, I shall not neglect the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*).
However, one should not entertain the doubt that the repetition is intended to enjoin [the practice] twice over.
For no injunction is heard here;
it is merely stated that "one should not let [it] lapse.
And because it is obligatory, the lapse is already established as a possibility.
There is no reason for a difference in ritual action based on the recognition of what has been prescribed,
whether one offers cooked food according to one's ability, or raw food, or roots and fruits.
Some people, who are learned in the scriptures on sacrifice, constantly offer these great sacrifices into the senses themselves, remaining free from worldly desire.
Some householders who know the science of sacrifice offer these great sacrifices into the very senses; they accomplish them.
But who are they?
Those who are free from worldly striving.

Those who do not desire wealth— such as those who have renounced household affairs and those who practice the vow of bodily abandonment— and even those who subsist by gleaning ears of grain or single grains, as well as the lame and others, accept this very rule;
for the author will later state regarding them that "if there should be a desire for a wife," implying they may take a wife if they so wish.
Furthermore, these [servants] have no entitlement to the five sacrifices;
because they lack property, they receive only their maintenance, and not even more for the purpose of performing ritual acts.
The root *hu* (to sacrifice) indicates the state of being accomplished through the sense of "doing" (*karoti*).
For a specific action, namely sacrifice (*yāga*), cannot become the object (*karman*) of another specific action, namely oblation (*homa*);

for it is not the case that one says "he cooks the cooking" (*pacati pākam*). However, it is indeed the case that one says "he performs the cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*) or "he performs the sacrifice" (*yāgaṃ karoti*).

However, actions that have a general object as their domain—such as *icchati* (desires), *śaknoti* (is able), and *jānāti* (knows)—render the substance and the object of action as their means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Furthermore, it is observed that a particular instance serves the purpose of indicating a general characteristic, as in: "This cow is to be avoided with the foot."
And thus, some explain this *homa* as the very restraint (*saṃyama*) of the senses.
Others [cite] from the *Prāṇasaṃvādopaniṣad*: "Whatever food comes first, that is to be offered as *homa*; the first oblation he should offer with 'To Prāṇa, Svāhā! and so forth.
Still others, however, maintain that this *homa* is precisely the method of meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*) taught in the subsequent verse.
And thus, their syntactical unity is perceived.
Now, one might object that in the subsequent passage, the vital breath (prāṇa) in speech is not a sense organ;
this is not a fault.
The mention of the "faculties" (indriya) is for the purpose of indicating their internal nature;
what is intended here is that [the result] is not to be accomplished by external means.
Some offer the breath into speech and speech into breath at all times,
perceiving in speech and breath the inexhaustible completion of the sacrifice.
When this person exhales, he should then meditate thus: "I offer speech into breath.
And while speaking, he should meditate: "I offer breath into speech.
By this much alone, the five sacrifices are accomplished.
If they were eternal, they would not need to be taught for the sake of a result;
moreover, those who know the Self are authorized here.
For this matter has been prescribed in detail in the Upaniṣads, in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, regarding the meditation on the five fires.
It is inexhaustible in terms of its fruit, because its fruit is non-return.
Other brahmins always perform those sacrifices with knowledge alone,
perceiving with the eye of knowledge that their ritual action has its root in knowledge.
By means of those sacrifices—the great rites naturally performed—they worship; that is, they fulfill their qualification regarding them.

Therefore, because there is a difference in meaning, the relationship between the goal and the means (sādhya-sādhaka-bhāva) is established in the expression "they worship with sacrifices," just as in the case of the term "one who has sacrificed with the Agniṣṭoma."
But how can the accomplishment of sacrifice be through knowledge?
Sacrifice consists essentially in the relinquishment of a substance for the sake of a deity;
and knowledge is not of such a nature.
It is said:
by the phrase "they sacrifice," the accomplishment of the purpose of sacrifice is intended here.
If the accomplishment of that purpose arises from knowledge, for what reason, then, is there the performance of ritual actions?
For it is impossible for the performance of ritual action to occur without an object [of knowledge].

Now, if this thought arises—that since the text "and he who knows this thus" declares that even knowledge is a means to the fruit, there is no need for the performance of ritual action—that is incorrect; because, being subordinate to something else, that statement is merely an explanatory praise (arthavāda).
To this it is replied:

We have already stated that those who know the Self and are free from desire are the ones qualified; it is they alone who are intended by the term "knowers," not those who merely understand how to perform ritual actions.
For those who remain in the household state as renunciants of Vedic ritual (*vedasaṃnyāsika*), this cultivation of the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) is prescribed;
and for the great sacrifices that are accomplished through material substances, the attainment of self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*) is thus prescribed.

However, regarding the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) and the libation of water (*udakatarpaṇa*), he will explain in the sixth chapter that they are indeed to be accomplished through ritual action (*karma*).
In this context, he states an explanatory passage (arthavāda) regarding the nature of the cause: "having knowledge as its root.
Knowledge is the root of this activity;
knowledge is the root of every performance of ritual action.
For one who is ignorant is not able to perform anything;
thus it is said, "The wise man should sacrifice.
They see with the eye of knowledge.
Knowledge is like the eye;
just as form is perceived by means of the eye, so too is it known through knowledge.
That "knowledge" is not intended to mean the Veda alone.
One should always offer the Agnihotra at the beginning and end of day and night;
likewise, one should perform the Darśa sacrifice at the end of the half-month and the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice as well.
Terms such as *agnihotra* and others are well known in the Śruti and the Gṛhya-smṛtis as denoting specific ritual acts;
they are prescribed therein along with their respective procedures (*itikartavyatā*).
This [text] is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of them, and not an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*), because it merely describes their form (*rūpa*).

Only the obligation regarding the subject of the oblation (*homa*) is heard in the scripture, but neither the substance nor the deity [is mentioned]; furthermore, names such as *agnihotra* require a specific referent. Therefore, it is understood that the specific details must be supplied by other scriptural texts.
If this is so, then since the duty is understood from that very source, this [present text] would be purposeless;
however, it is for the sake of corroborating the meditation under discussion regarding the renunciation of Vedic study (*vedasaṃnyāsika*).
Just as some offer the breath with speech, and by means of knowledge alone, the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) are accomplished.
"This case is just like that.

And what is this objection—"Why is there a repetition?"—since it would follow as a logical flaw that whatever is stated in one part of all the *Śrutis* and *Smṛtis* is merely repeated elsewhere? Furthermore, a general solution has already been stated: "There is no tautology because the recipients of the teaching differ."

Just as there is a difference in sense faculties due to the difference among perceivers— since not everyone is able to see with a single eye, and many sense faculties are thus purposeful— so too is there a difference in Vedic branches (*śākhā*) and a difference in Smṛtis.
Now, if it is asked, "Why is the form [of the Veda] not mentioned?"—
this too is not a fault.
Since there is a difference in the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for each branch, which one should be designated? To designate all of them would be cumbersome;
to designate only one would entail the abandonment of the others.
That too is indeed an objection;
and it has been stated that this is a restatement (anuvāda), not an injunction (vidhi).
For such an objection would apply only if it were an injunction.
"Why is there a further injunction when it has already been prescribed elsewhere?
[The answer is: "At the beginning and end of day and night.

Here there is no correspondence in order (yathāsaṃkhya); rather, it means at the beginning of the day and at the beginning of the night, and likewise at the end of the day and at the end of the night.
By this [term], the two times of evening and morning are encompassed;
therein, for those who offer at sunrise, it is at the beginning of the day, and for those who offer before sunrise, it is at the end of the night.
The word *dyu* is a synonym for "day."
"Always":
the fire-oblation (homa) must be performed every day, morning and evening, for as long as one lives.
The phrase "one should sacrifice with the New Moon [offering]" is to be supplied here.
For in that context of origination, there is no such injunction as "one should offer an oblation"; rather, it says "one should sacrifice with the Darśa.
And this [statement] is a restatement of that; for this very reason, an ellipsis is supplied.

For this very reason, even though no specific distinction is heard [in the texts], the New Moon sacrifice (darśa) occurs at the end of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), that is, at the end of the half-month, and the Full Moon sacrifice (paurṇamāsa) occurs at the end of the bright fortnight (śukla).
Thus says the Śruti: "One should sacrifice with the Darśa on the day of the Darśa, and one should sacrifice with the Pūrṇamāsa on the day of the Pūrṇamāsī."
At the end of the grain harvest, a twice-born man should perform the sacrifice of new grain; likewise, at the end of each season, he should perform the seasonal sacrifices (adhvara);
at the end of the sun's course, he should perform the animal sacrifice; and at the end of the year, he should perform the Soma sacrifices.

The word *sasya* refers to grain such as rice and the like; its *anta* means its exhaustion. When the previous crops have been exhausted, one should perform the sacrifice with new grain; that is to say, one should perform the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice.

In this context, neither the exhaustion of the previous grain nor the arrival of the new grain is the occasion for the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice; rather, it is the eating of new grain by one who has not yet performed the *āgrayaṇa* that is prohibited.
This is why it is said: "One should not eat new grain without having sacrificed.
Therefore, the meaning is that the consumption of new grain [must be preceded] by the *āgrayaṇa*.
They explain [the rule] as "one should sacrifice with that.

However, under this view, because the previous crop is absent and the new crop exists—whether from another source or not—and in the absence of a desire to eat [it], the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice would not be obligatory. Alternatively, if "the end of the crop" (*sasyānta*) is understood as an indicator for the emergence of the new harvest, then one would incur the fault of eating without having sacrificed.
Therefore, these are two distinct sentences:
"One should not eat without having sacrificed" is the first, and "at the end of the grain" is the second.
By the mention of "the end of the grain," the production of the grain itself is intended; since that [production] is a fixed event, its occurrence serves as the occasion for the rule.
However, the exhaustion [of provisions] is not fixed, for even those who possess wealth deal here in grains sufficient for three years.

For this very reason, the author of the Sūtra states: "One should not eat the new crop without having offered the Agnihotra," and likewise, "When one is satisfied by the rain, then one should sacrifice with the Āgrayaṇa.
Similarly, there is this other rule prescribing a specific time: "In autumn, the new grain [is to be eaten]."
In that regard, he for whom there is no exhaustion of the previous grain harvest attends to the autumn season, but the other does not;
thus, both [injunctions] possess purposefulness. Otherwise, it would have been stated simply as: "Upon the production of new grain, one should sacrifice with the New Grain Sacrifice."
But for one who says, "One should not eat food without having performed the sacrifice of the new grain," for him there is a waiting for autumn even when the new grain has already arisen;
and because the arising of the new grain is the occasion [for the rite], the *Āgrayaṇa* must necessarily be performed at the end of the season, even in the absence of a desire to eat the new food.
By the observation that "the season is the year," this performance of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices is prescribed;
by the word *adhvara*, those very sacrifices are intended.
[They are performed] at the beginning of the two solstices (*ayana*) and at the end of the two solstices.
And those two solstices are the southern and the northern;
therein, the animal sacrifice is to be performed twice a year.
However, the author of the Sūtra says: "It may be every six months or yearly."

"At the end of the year": the word *samā* is a synonym for "year," and its "end" (*anta*) is its completion in the winter season. However, this injunction for the *saumika* sacrifice does not apply there; rather, it applies when that [winter] has passed and spring has arrived.
And thus says the Śruti: "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma every spring.
These are the obligatory rites;
the overall purport is that they must be performed somehow or other, even by one who has renounced the Vedas.

A twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires and desires to live a long life shall not eat new grain or meat without first having performed the sacrifice for the new harvest and the animal sacrifice.
The term "possessor of fire" (agnimān) here refers to one who has established the sacred fires (āhitāgni), because of the context concerning religious observances (vrata).
For that sacrifice, there is a Vedic injunction regarding the observance:
"One should not eat meat without having sacrificed with an animal victim, nor should one eat new grain without having performed the Āgrayaṇa offering."
He states the fruit resulting from the observance of the rules:
"One who desires to live a long life.
By the word *āyuḥ* (life), the continuous functions of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths are meant.

And as for the second [view], even though *jīvati* is intransitive, it is [considered transitive] with respect to the action of desiring (*iṣ*). A verbal root ending in the desiderative suffix (*san*) also functions in the sense of desire. In this view as well, the object of *iṣ* is not something external, but is the meaning of the base itself; furthermore, the desire is subordinate to that which is about to be desired. This is because "the base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together," a principle that applies not only to forms ending in *san* but elsewhere as well.

Even in this view, by the word *āyus* (life), time will be indicated, since [the sacrificer] desires living for a long time. In that case, it must be understood as having the nature of time; for although it is not an action (*karman*), it receives the designation of "action" according to the rule: "For non-actions, there is the status of being an action. And this is the rule for one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) regarding the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), as well as for the *āgrayaṇa* offering.
Even for one who maintains the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*), the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice is prescribed as a mandatory rule in the *Gṛhya-smṛtis*.
As for the statement "in autumn, the new grain," that refers to rice (*vrīhi*) and millet (*śyāmāka*), not to barley (*yava*).
Nor is there a harvest-sacrifice (*sasyeṣṭi-yāga*) for every kind of crop, nor for beans (*māṣa*), pulses (*udgādi*), and the like.
Since it has been stated that this [text] is dependent upon other treatises and is not itself prescriptive,
and since the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice is prescribed in other treatises with rice, *śyāmāka* millet, and barley,
yet no other grain is to be consumed if the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice has not been performed; [the present text serves as a restrictive injunction].

As for what was stated without qualification—"one should not eat grain"—if that were intended as a general prohibition, he would have said simply: "One should not eat the *āgrayaṇa* offering of rice, millet, and barley until one has offered the *agnihotra*.
Thus it was recited by the author of the Sūtra: "The *āgrayaṇa* [is performed] of rice, millet, and barley; one should not eat grain until the *agnihotra* has been offered."
Therefore, this word "sasya" does not have a strictly restricted scope.
For his fires, greedy for new grain and meat, if not honored with the offering of new grain and animal sacrifice, desire to consume his very life-breaths.
He establishes permanence itself by pointing out the fault of non-performance:
the fires of this *āhitāgni*, not honored with new grain and for which no oblations have been offered, desire—that is, wish—to devour his very life-breaths.
"Gardhin" means one who has *gardha*; *gardha* is an excess of longing, and the suffix *-in* is used here in the sense of possession.
No guest should dwell in his house without being honored to the best of one's ability, whether with seats, food, beds, water, or roots and fruits.
This which was stated for the sake of what follows is now restated:
no guest whatsoever should dwell in a house unhonored;
every guest must be made to dwell in the house with honor.
"According to one's capacity":
whether it be one, two, or many—however many can be honored—all are to be honored with seats and other such items.
This is intended to provide for those staying there preceded by such honor; however, it is not said that the ownership of all seats, food, and beds is entirely relinquished.
Since roots and fruits are mentioned separately from the list of rice-gruel, meat, cooked grain, and ghee, they should be given when these other items are unavailable.
One should not honor, even with a mere word, heretics, those who persist in improper actions, those who act like cats, rogues, sophists, and those who behave like herons.
Based on the indicative force of the word "should dwell" (*vaset*), some say that this is a prohibition against offering hospitality in the evening to heretics and the like;
however, that is incorrect, for what is being excluded here is their status as objects of worship.
However, it is not said that the giving of food and so forth must occur in every single case;
for even for those eating during the day, a stay of a few moments is certainly possible.
Therefore, "one should dwell" is not a defining characteristic of the evening time alone.

In this context, "heretics" (*pāṣaṇḍinaḥ*) refers to those who bear external sectarian marks, such as the red-robed ones, the naked ones, the Carakas, and so forth. "Those engaged in improper occupations" (*vikarmasthāḥ*) refers to those who, when not in times of distress, subsist by the livelihood of another caste;
for example, a Brāhmaṇa living by the occupation of a Kṣatriya, or a Kṣatriya by the occupation of a Vaiśya, and so on.
Those who follow the "vow of the cat" are hypocrites;

they perform the *agnihotra* and other rites for the sake of winning over the world, thinking, "Let us desire houses and such," and not because these are their own duties as enjoined by the scriptures.
They are deceitful, having one thing in their heart and another in their speech.

Having promised to provide assistance to someone, they disregard their duty and do not perform it; these are the rationalists and nihilists who maintain a fixed conviction that there is no other world, no gift given, and no oblation offered.
Those whose conduct is like that of a crane are indeed hypocrites; they are distinguished from [the others] by a slight difference.
This distinction will be shown between them mutually, even by mere words.
Let alone the giving of seats and such; even welcoming words preceded by worship, such as "Welcome, please sit here," should not be spoken.
However, the giving of food is permitted even from outcasts (śvapaca) and others.
Thus, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, concerning the gift of food alone, has recorded in tradition: "One should not inquire about [the donor's] birth nor his learning."
The meaning is that one should not engage in the search for a worthy recipient here.
One should honor with offerings to the gods and the ancestors those householders who are śrotriyas, having completed their Vedic studies and vows; one should avoid those who are the opposite.

The Vedas, the sciences, and the vows—those by whom these have been mastered, having reached completion therein; various types of *snātakas* are included here. Among them, the *veda-snātakas* are those who have studied the Vedas.
The *vidyāsnātakas* are those who have completed their inquiry into the meaning of knowledge.
Because of its proximity to the term "knowledge" (*vidyā*), it is understood here as referring specifically to the Veda;
for that alone is, in reality, true knowledge.

The vows consist of those lasting thirty-six years and so forth. Even when the desire to know the Veda and its meaning has been fulfilled, the ceremonial bath (snāna) does not take place immediately; rather, there is also the view that the period of thirty-six years and so on must be completed. Others, however, who bathe after three years even without having studied the Veda, are called *vratasnātaka*s.
The objection that "how can there be a ceremonial bath for one who has not studied the Vedas? is invalid.
[Objection: But for what purpose is the mention of the *śrotriya* (one learned in the Vedas), since the status of a *snātaka* is already established by that alone?
[Response: It is for the sake of excellence (*atiśaya*).
By this, those śrotriyas who are devoted to the study of the Vedas and householders who are married gṛhamedhins are intended.

This does not mean that mendicants, ascetics, and celibate students (brahmacārins) are unworthy of honor; rather, because they subsist on alms, the status of a guest (atithi) is not possible for them.
For the religious student (*brahmacārin*), there is no dwelling other than at the teacher's house; for the ascetic (*tāpasa*), none other than in the forest;

and even for the wandering mendicant (*pravrajita*), who may enter a village only for the sake of alms, there is no dwelling in a village. Therefore, although it might somehow be possible for those in other stages of life (*āśrama*) to dwell elsewhere than in a house, this [rule] regarding the householder (*gṛhamedhin*) is the general rule.

With offerings to the gods (havya) or the ancestors (kavya)— whether in rites for the deities such as those for peace and so forth, or in ancestral rites (śrāddha) for the fathers— only those [who possess the aforementioned qualities] are to be honored.
Those who are the opposite, namely those who have not taken the vow of studentship (asnātaka), are to be avoided even if they lack the previously mentioned defects.
A householder should give according to his ability to those who do not cook for themselves,
and he should share with all beings without causing hardship to his own dependents.
Some say that those who do not cook for themselves—namely, celibate students (*brahmacārin*) and wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*)—are the ones [to whom gifts should be given].
That is incorrect, for giving to them is indeed prescribed as a constant duty, as in the rule: "One should give alms to a mendicant.
Therefore, one should give according to one's capacity to those who are poor and live by begging, such as heretics (*pākhaṇḍin*) and others.
It lasts as long as it can be sustained and as long as it can be cooked;
and because it is characterized by the absence of the act of cooking, this is indeed the gift of prepared food and its sharing.

One should also share whatever other wealth one possesses— such as fuel, clothing, medicine, and so forth— and give away some portion of it to all beings. This word "beings" (bhūta) denotes the world consisting of conscious entities.
Just as it is said, "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this that has come to be," [the distribution of wealth] applies only to sentient beings,
because it is impossible for insentient things to receive a share for the sake of benefiting them as if they were sentient.
Therefore, according to the view that those possessing the nature of growth are sentient, a distribution of wealth for the purpose of watering and so forth must also be made for trees and the like.
This word *bhūta* has many meanings. In some cases it occurs in the sense of "preeminence," as in: "This Brāhmaṇī is a *bhūta* (an eminent person) in this house.
In other cases it denotes a *piśāca*, as in: "He is possessed by a *bhūta*."
In some cases, it is used in the sense of "contrary" (viparīta), as in "he says what has happened" (*bhūtam āha*).

In some cases, the word *bhūta* refers to a past time, as in "the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is past. And in some cases, it refers to a specific deity, as in "an offering (*bali*) to the *bhūtas*."
In some cases, it denotes merely that which possesses consciousness, as in "one should not harm living beings" (*bhūtāni*);
in some cases, it denotes attainment, as in "the moon is a great being" (*mahad bhūtam*);
and in some cases, it functions as a metaphor, as in "he is like a poem" (*kāvyabhūtaḥ*).
In some cases, it expresses arising, as in "Devadatta’s son has been born. But here, that which is the meaning of the word has already been explained.
In the phrase "from the elements" (*bhūtebhyaḥ*), the dative case is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*).
Without causing obstruction;
having set aside what is sufficient so that there is no suffering for oneself or one's family, one should share the surplus.
Thus it is said: "without causing hardship to one's dependents."
A Snātaka who is perishing from hunger may seek wealth from a king, or from his patron for whom he performs sacrifices, or from a resident pupil; but not from anyone else—this is the settled rule.

The mention of "the king" is intended as an illustration for those of wealthy status; and so he will say later: "The lord of the earth should be entreated by those who are suffering and desiring base metals or wealth."
Therefore, although the word "rājan" primarily denotes the Kṣatriya caste, nevertheless, upon consideration of other treatises, it is understood to signify the lord of a territory (*janapadeśvara*).
For lords of territories possess abundant wealth;
thus, what is meant is that one should accept gifts from those who are exceedingly prosperous in cattle, goats, sheep, wealth, and grain.
That being the case, the principle of "without causing harm" is upheld;
for the wealthy, when giving, are not excessively afflicted. However, there would be fault in one who takes from their own possessions.
Furthermore, if the word "king" were used in its primary sense, the acceptance of gifts from Brahmins and others would be prohibited;
in that case, there would be a contradiction with all the Smṛtis.
For it is stated in another Smṛti: "One may accept uncooked food from praiseworthy members of the twice-born classes and from a Śūdra who performs service."
Even regarding the prohibition, "one should not accept gifts from a king," the word *rājan* refers exclusively to the lord of a realm (*janapadeśvara*).
Furthermore, the prohibition there does not apply to a Kṣatriya, because of the statement, "from one not born of the *rājanya* [caste].

For this very reason, the prohibition therein does not apply to one belonging to the Kṣatriya caste; if that were the case, the phrase "from one not born of the *rājanya*" would not need to be stated.
For those who are not born of the Kṣatriya caste do not become Kṣatriyas.
Therefore, this is the established rule here: acceptance [of gifts] should be made from a Kṣatriya king who acts according to the scriptures, but not from any other;
likewise for the sacrificer and the pupil.
The genitive case here expresses dependence on wealth; alternatively, the form *tasantau* (nominative dual) should be read.
Because these two words denote the cause of an action, it is implied that one should live by means of officiating at sacrifices and teaching.

Others, however, say: because other means such as theft and so forth result in minor offenses (upapātaka) and are prohibited, one may live by propitiating the Lord through a gift of favor or by means of reciting benedictions;
yet this person is not a servant, for that mode of livelihood is forbidden.
Thus, because he has rendered assistance, one may accept gifts even from a patron for whom one does not perform sacrifices;
for the obligation persists even when the relationship has ceased.
"Falling into distress" means...
When the wealth of the father and others is available, [the rite] should not be performed; this has been stated as "when resources are sufficient.
This present [verse] is a restatement of that very point.
And this is not a matter of emergency (āpaddharma). For exhaustion is not an emergency; rather, it is the absence of acquired wealth.
An emergency, however, consists in the absence of prescribed means and the depletion of one's resources.

Even when there is an abundance of grain and wealth, if food is exhausted during a famine or similar crisis, the state of having no food available for hospitality while one is afflicted by hunger is "calamity" (*āpad*); whereas the dejection of one who, though not hungry, lacks wealth due to poverty is "distress" (*avasāda*). This is the distinction between these two. However, one should not accept [gifts] from anyone else who possesses only a small amount of wealth and food and is thus incapable of providing assistance.
A learned Snātaka shall never suffer from hunger if he is capable;
nor, while possessing wealth, shall he wear worn-out or dirty clothes.

And if one should be thwarted in some business for the sake of wealth, one should not at that very moment resort to the duties of distress; rather, one should strive again until it succeeds. As it has been said: "One should seek prosperity until death."

Therefore, even if by some chance the destruction of a crop should occur for one who is farming due to a lack of rain or other causes, he should not, on account of this loss alone, suddenly become dependent on the food of others through begging.
When there is a valid means of livelihood, worn-out and dirty clothes are not permitted, nor are they permitted when wealth and resources exist.
Having trimmed his hair, nails, and beard, self-controlled, wearing white garments, and pure,
he should be constantly engaged in the private recitation of the Veda and in what is beneficial for the self.
This "cutting" refers specifically to the cutting of the dental floss; this cutting is mandatory. For this very reason, he says "pure."

For one with long hair, bathing and other such acts would be accomplished only with great difficulty, leading to laziness as well as the consequence of impurity. However, if one were devoted to bathing even while hair and so forth grow long, then the wearing [of them] would not be faulty. "Self-controlled" (dānta) means free from arrogance.
He is pure regarding his affairs through the causes prescribed by the Vedas, such as sipping water with soft and excellent materials,
and he is constantly devoted to the study of the Veda;
although this matter has already been stated, it is repeated again and again for the sake of emphasis.
Beneficial practices for oneself consist of remedies for disease and so forth, as well as the avoidance of indigestion, excessively heavy food, and burning food, and so on.
He should carry a bamboo staff, a water-pot containing water,
a sacred thread, a Vedic text, and two auspicious golden earrings.
The wearing of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and the ear-ring (*kuṇḍala*) constitutes contact with the body.
Furthermore, whichever limb is the appropriate place for the placement of an object, it should be applied to that very spot;
for example, the ear-ring on the ears and the sacred thread on the body, because the ornament for the ear is designated by the name *kuṇḍala*.
Furthermore, because a thread fastened around the neck becomes an *upavīta* by being raised over the right arm,

and because it serves a visible purpose, there is always contact with the limbs via a staff and so forth. For instance, the carrying of a staff is for the sake of support when one is weary, and for the sake of warding off cattle or other attackers that may come face-to-face.
Since purification is prescribed with water that has been drawn out, the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) is enjoined by virtue of its being the required receptacle.
And because it serves the same function, it excludes vessels such as jars (*kalaśa*), but not items such as earrings or bracelets.
Therefore, the water-pot must contain water for the purpose of removing the impurity caused by excrement, which is to be cleansed by water.
And it has been said: "One should not remain impure for even a moment when one has the capacity [to purify oneself].

Regarding the phrase "when one has the capacity": if the water previously taken was used, or otherwise unavailable, and the cause of impurity—such as the discharge of phlegm or spittle—has arisen, then in the absence of water, being impure is not a fault.
Nevertheless, he will state that bathing is required upon the discharge of urine or feces: "But one who is distressed, having discharged bodily waste either without water or even in water..."
"Having bathed outside with his clothes on"—
and purity is prescribed at every step in another Smṛti;
thus indeed said the blessed Vasiṣṭha.
Fire is said to be pure in water, in the hand, and in wood;
therefore, having wiped the water-pot with both hands and water, [one should carry it].
Manu Prajāpati has prescribed the fire-circumambulation and the oblation;
having performed these and his necessary duties, one who is most skilled in purification should sip water for rinsing.
Baudhāyana also stated, beginning with "Now, the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) should be carried," [continuing]: "Therefore, having performed purification and having wiped the water-pot,
this wiping of the object is indeed the rite of circumambulation by fire (paryagnikaraṇa)."
Likewise,
even while remaining in his previous state of impurity, he should carry a water-pot;
a wise man should not despise it, nor fear it, nor find fault with it.
Furthermore, this term [for "purity"] is based on specific formal characteristics and does not depend upon the genus (*jāti*);
therefore, this very same purification applies to an object made of clay, gold, or silver, and is not connected to the inherent genus of the material itself.
However, in the case of contact with urine and the like, the purification pertaining to the inherent genus of the material must be observed.
