Washing the hands, however, is required because of impurity resulting from contact with a person who has not yet finished eating. Thus Gautama says in some places, "having placed [the water] nearby for the sake of purification.
Therefore, here too, what is intended is merely placing [the water] nearby, not taking it up by oneself.
The *veda* is a handful of *darbha* grass; its purpose is for touching the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) with those *darbhas*, and so forth.

Therefore, those [materials] whose purpose is transcendental (*adṛṣṭārtha*) have a constant connection with the body, whereas for those whose purpose is visible (*dṛṣṭārtha*), their presence is constant, but their actual employment depends on the specific requirement.
"Auspicious" means beautiful in appearance; by its form, and through heating, cutting, and rubbing, it is pure gold.
One should never look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting;
nor when it is eclipsed, nor when it is reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky.
"Afflicted" means eclipsed by a planet;
"situated in water" means reflected in water;
one should see it situated in the middle of the sky—that is, in the atmosphere—but not at the time of midday.
One should not step over a calf’s tethering rope, nor run while it is raining, nor look at one's own reflection in water; such is the rule.
The "calf-line" (*vatsatantrī*) refers to a rope for tethering calves, or a row of calves; one should not leap over it nor step across it. Thus says Gautama: "One should not walk over a calf-line.
Its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is its physical configuration.
Because of the mention of "one's own," the beholding of another's form is not excluded;
such is the retention, this is the certainty established in the treatises.
One should circumambulate clockwise clay, a cow, a deity, a Brahmin, clarified butter, honey, a crossroads, and well-known trees.
For one who has set out, the rule regarding conditions encountered on the way— such as clay and so forth—
is as follows: the clay and other materials should be taken with the right hand,
and the clay should be lifted up in this manner.
For thus another treatise recites in the section on ritual procedure (*prasthānādhikāra*): "having circumambulated clockwise";
"deity" refers to one depicted on a cloth or similar medium for the purpose of worship.
Gautama, however, recites: "one should follow the temples of the deities while keeping them to the right."
According to worldly convention, one should understand that "devatāyatana" refers to temples such as those of the four-armed Mārtaṇḍa;
furthermore, he will speak of sacrificial halls (*yajñagṛha*) later on.
*Madhu* is honey because of its great excellence (*mahācaryāt*), and also because it is recited among the auspicious items.

The "well-known trees" (*vanaspati*) are large in size; they are well-known great trees by virtue of their dimensions or the excellence of their flowers and fruits, such as the *udumbara* and others. There is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "The *udumbara* is indeed nourishment (*ūrj*).
However, those who claim that these [trees] possess superior qualities must be disregarded, as they rely solely on rootless tradition as their authority.
One should not approach a woman even if one is intoxicated when her menses appear;
nor should one sleep with her on the same bed.
Even if one is heedless and afflicted by the arrows of desire,
one should not approach a woman upon seeing her *ārtava*— the monthly menstrual blood well-known to occur every month.
And one should not lie down on the same bed with her.
If it is argued that this is already established by the prohibition against physical contact itself, we say no;
for this is a specific vow (*vrata*), and it constitutes a distinct form of penance (*prāyaścitta*).
For when a man approaches a woman who is overwhelmed by her menses,
his wisdom, vigor, strength, sight, and even his lifespan diminish.
"Rajas" refers to the menstrual flow mentioned previously; "overwhelmed by it" means connected with that.
This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) regarding what precedes.
For one who avoids her when she is overwhelmed by the menstrual flow,
wisdom, splendor, strength, vision, and even lifespan increase.
The mention of "increase" is indeed a form of praise.
He should not eat together with his wife, nor should he look at her while she is eating,
sneezing, yawning, or sitting at her ease.
The statement that "the mouth of women is always pure" is an assertion of purity, while the prohibition regarding "the leavings of women and Śūdras" is a restriction;
both are established through a distinction of scope.

Among these, the assertion of purity is understood to concern women in the context of sexual intercourse, based on the observation of another Smṛti text stating, "And women [are pure] during the connection of sexual pleasure."
Therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the prohibition should also be understood as applying to women who are not objects of passion, such as one's mother, sister, and so forth.

For "passion" (*rati*) here does not mean mere affection; rather, it is a specific state of being caused by the god of love (*manmatha*), consisting of desire and the like preceded by the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).
Consequently, there is purity regarding those women endowed with such [passion], while there is a prohibition regarding those who are the opposite.
Since eating with one's wife would otherwise be occasioned by the purpose of sexual pleasure (*ratinimitta*), this statement—"one should not eat together with one's wife"—is commenced.

Alternatively, if by the mention of "association" (*saṃsarga*) a specific kind of sexual union for one who lusts is intended, then purity is achieved merely through kissing; in that case, there would be no occasion for eating together with one's wife.
In this regard, this further statement is for the purpose of making known the vow (*vrata*).
Consequently, a lifelong resolve (*saṃkalpa*) must be made such that eating together with one's wife does not occur.

And since this "eating together" (*sahabhojana*)—which shares the same basis, the same time, and the same place—is enjoined as the object of the negative particle (*nañ*), it is suspected that its meaning is already established by the prohibition against consuming the remnants of another's meal (*ucchiṣṭa*).
Furthermore, this specific meaning of "together" (*saha*) is derived from other means of valid cognition, such as another scriptural injunction or established usage;
for the meaning of the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is simply that which depends on something else.
Thus, one may also feed others, such as friends and so forth, with the words, "He should feed [them] together with his wife."
In this context, a common substratum for the act of eating is not understood; rather, it refers to the eater’s sharing of the same location or the same time with his wife.
Others, however, explain "leftover" (*ucchiṣṭa*) as that which has been abandoned after eating. But when there is only one wife, they share the meal together for the sake of a single purpose.
If it were explained in this way, however, eating together with a Śūdra would be prohibited, and established usage would be abandoned;
for the designation "impure" (ucchiṣṭa) arises from contact with him, and that [designation] exists even through eating together.
Some, however, maintain that only eating in the same place and at the same time is prohibited, because the instruction has a visible purpose.

Due to differences in individual nature, one man might not be satisfied with a woman who eats much, while another places his trust even in one who eats very little; thus he behaves deceitfully, thinking, "She eats but little before me.
Other such restrictive rules are likewise inconsistent.
Furthermore, one should not look at her while she is eating.
For if she were eating while being watched, her husband would not find it pleasing due to the distortion of her form caused by her having her mouth wide open.
As for sneezing, it is the sound produced when the nose is filled with wind residing in the head; because this too involves a deformity of the face, there would be no pleasure in that either.
Yawning consists of the prolonged exhalation of breath through a gaping mouth or the stretching out of the limbs and minor members of the body.
That too is exactly so;
she may sit as she pleases, with her hair unbound or her limbs cast upon the ground.
A twice-born man who desires spiritual luster should not look at a woman applying collyrium to her own eyes, nor one who is anointed with oil, nor one who is uncovered, nor one who is giving birth.
Anointing another woman indeed brings her beauty;
for though she is uncovered and her garment removed,
people especially desire her when she is veiled.

A woman whose limbs are uncovered, who is about to speak very skillfully, and whose entire form is not well-proportioned in every respect— being thus naked, she is not to be looked upon by one desiring splendor (*tejas*). Splendor consists of the brilliance of complexion as well as the application of energy and enthusiasm.
One should not eat food while wearing only a single garment, nor should one perform a bath naked;
one should not void urine on a path, nor in ashes, nor in a cow-pen.

Even though the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is always present, because it does not cover [the body] and because it is taught as distinct from the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), he is "clad in one garment. A second garment, such as one for covering the limbs, may be used at the time of eating;
however, this is not the case for urination.
In this context, the mention of "urine" is intended to include "excrement" by implication.
"On the road" means on a carriage-way; "in a cow-pen."
Wherever or in whatever direction the cows go to graze.
Neither on ploughed land, nor in water, nor on a funeral pyre, nor on a mountain;
neither in a ruined temple nor ever on an anthill.
In a city, it refers to a stack of bricks for the sake of fire;
the mention of "mountain" is intended as an illustration for forests and gardens,
for there will likewise be a specific prohibition regarding "the summit of a mountain."
Furthermore, if there were a general prohibition [against urinating], it would entail the undesirable consequence that those living on mountains would be unable to urinate;
a *valmīka* is a mound of earth formed by insects.
Neither in pits inhabited by living beings, nor while walking, nor while standing;
neither having reached a riverbank, nor on the summit of a mountain.
Neither walking nor standing;
since walking and standing are prohibited, sitting is permitted.
And not on the bank of a river, nor in the water of the river.
That which gives rise to the suspicion of contact is "nearby" (āsanna);
the summit or peak of a mountain is its *śṛṅga*.
While looking at the wind, fire, a Brahmin, the sun, water, or likewise cows,
one should never discharge feces or urine.
Because wind and the other elements are present [in the body], one should not look even while glancing at a limb while urinating.
Furthermore, since wind is formless (*arūpa*), its perception is to be understood as an illusion caused by the movement of colored clods of earth and so forth propelled by it.
However, this prohibition does not apply to the wheel of wind (*vāyucakra*) when it is dissociated [from the body].
For the wind blows from every direction.
This is its explanatory praise (arthavāda):
"The wisdom of one who urinates facing fire, facing the sun, facing the moon, water, or a twice-born man, or facing a cow or against the wind, perishes."
Some do not recite this verse in this chapter.

[Objection: Since the rule for urination prescribes facing the north, and since the sun rises in the east, how could there be a situation where one would be facing it, such that facing the sun would need to be prohibited?
[Response: This is a mere explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), like the passage "not in the atmosphere, nor in the sky."
Alternatively, one might step toward the northern direction during the northern solstice; such a possibility exists.
Or, the prohibition may refer to the subject under discussion [the daily ritual].
They read the word as "pratisaṃdhyam" (at every twilight).
That is incorrect;
for there is the permission that "at the twilights, as during the day," and because the suppression of natural urges is prohibited.
Therefore, one should read "prativātam" (against the wind).
This is a supplement to what precedes: [the suffix] *śatṛ* or *tasant* [is applied] after the root *mih*.
Of a person who urinates, or from urination.
Having set aside wood, clods of earth, leaves, grass, and the like, he should pass by,
restraining his speech, being pure, with his body covered and his head veiled.
"Having set aside" means having concealed [the ground] with wood and so forth; one should urinate upon that.
Alternatively, "setting aside" (tiraskāra) means an obstruction; having covered the ground with wood and so forth, one should discharge [urine].
In that case, the reading with the third case ending would be clearer.
One should void urine and excrement by using wood, a leaf, or grass;
restraining one's speech, being pure, using clods of earth, and remaining free from food remnants; with limbs covered and the private parts concealed.
"Veiled" means having covered the head; it is stated elsewhere that "the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) is worn over the ear."
One should void urine and excrement facing north during the day;
at night one should face south; and during the two twilights, one should face as one does during the day.
The voiding and casting away of urine and excrement.
In shade or in darkness, by night or by day, a twice-born man may perform [the purification] facing whichever direction is comfortable, as well as when there is fear of danger to life.
Shadow (*chāyā*) is the obstruction of sunbeams by walls, doors, and so forth.
Darkness (*andhakāra*) is the hindrance to light caused by clouds, mist, Rāhu, or night.
"One whose face is according to pleasure" means one who has a pleasant countenance.
One should recite in whichever direction one feels comfortable;
this rule applies when the direction is not known due to darkness.
"Endangering life" means causing pain to life.
And fear is that produced by thieves and the like.
One should not blow on a fire with one's mouth, nor look at a naked woman;
one should not throw impure things into the fire, nor warm one's feet over it.
The fire should be fanned with a bellows or similar means.
One should not look at a naked woman, except during sexual intercourse; so says another Smṛti.
"Not impure" (*amedhya*): sacrifice (*yajña*) is pure (*medhya*), and that which is for its sake is pure;
"impure" (*amedhya*) refers to what is unfit for sacrifice (*ayajñiya*), such as onions, urine, feces, and so forth.
One should not throw it into the fire.
Having lifted one's feet, one should not warm them directly over the fire.
However, there is no fault in warming them over the fire for the purpose of inducing perspiration and so forth, provided they have been shielded [from direct contact].
One should not place it beneath oneself, nor should one step over it;
one should not treat it as if it were underfoot, nor should one cause any injury to living beings.
One who is on a bed should not place a fire-vessel beneath it;
"upadhāna" means a support or a place;
"avalaṅghana" means going by leaping.

One should not do that by which the feet of one who has not jumped down from a height would be placed upon it; nor should one perform anything that causes harm to living beings—that is, anything that inflicts pain on life, such as traveling with excessive speed or force.
One should not eat at the time of twilight, nor should one travel or lie down;
nor indeed should one scratch the ground, nor should one remove a garland from oneself.
The time of twilight is the period of junction;
lying down is sleep;
he will prohibit the private recitation of the Vedas.
In another Smṛti, however,
it is said that one should avoid exactly four activities during the twilight hours:
eating, sexual intercourse, sleep, and likewise the recitation of sacred texts.
"And one should not scratch at all. This prohibits scraping or tearing up the ground;
however, it does not prohibit the arrangement of letters using a stylus or similar tools.
One should not remove from oneself a garland (*sraj*).
A *sraj* consists of strung flowers;
one should not, by oneself, take it off from one's neck or head because it has withered or become heavy.
By implication, it is stated that one should remove [the impurity] by means other than these;
some maintain that this entire procedure applies specifically to the twilight (saṃdhyā).
One should not discharge urine, feces, or spittle into water,
nor anything else smeared with impurity, nor blood, nor poisons.
*Lohitam* means blood.

The plural form *viṣāṇi* (poisons) is used to indicate the distinctions between artificial and natural poisons, the distinctions between stationary (*sthāvara*) and mobile (*jaṅgama*) poisons, or the various types such as *gara* and so forth.
One should not sleep alone in an empty house, nor should one wake a superior person; one should not converse with a woman in her courses, nor go to a sacrifice unless invited.

An empty house is one where no one dwells. One who is inferior should not awaken a superior person— whether by means of conduct or other qualities— by saying, "This is proper for you," or "This is improper," nor by providing logical arguments, instructions, or the like.
A *udakyā* is a woman in her menses;
one should not engage in conversation with her.
Nor should one go to a sacrifice unless he is formally initiated (*avṛta*).
One should not go to a sacrificial ground uninvited;
however, Gautama says one may go at will for the purpose of seeing it.
Therefore, this prohibition regarding eating and so forth at a sacrifice applies to one who is not invited.
In the fire-sanctuary, in a cow-pen, in the presence of Brahmins,
during Vedic study, and while eating, one should keep the right hand raised.
This word *goṣṭha* signifies a dwelling place; it is a distinct word derived from a form resembling a compound.
The plural number in *brāhmaṇānām* is intended to be significant. The mention of the "hand" (*pāṇi*) is for the purpose of indicating the arm (*bāhu*).
In the case of eating where one is the agent oneself.
One should not prevent a cow from suckling, nor should one tell anyone about it;
likewise, a wise person, having seen a rainbow in the sky, should not point it out to anyone.
One should not prevent a cow—whether one's own or another's—from drinking water or milk;
nor should one tell anyone [to do so].
This rule applies prior to the time for milking.
However, at the time of milking, the pouring out [of milk] is prescribed. Because of the use of the feminine gender, there is no prohibition regarding the prevention of male calves.
*Indrāyudha* is the rainbow of Śakra, which is called *vijñānacchāyā* (the shadow of cognition) among the Kashmiris.
"In the sky" is a restatement (anuvāda).
Some, however, say that there is no fault in seeing [the sun] when it is situated on a mountain or the like; for that purpose, it says "in the sky."
One should not dwell in an unrighteous village, nor in one where diseases are exceedingly prevalent;
one should not set out on a journey alone, nor should one reside for long on a mountain.
A village where unrighteous people—those who commit major sins (pātaka) and minor sins (upapātaka)—dwell in great numbers is called "unrighteous" by association with them;
one should not dwell there.
The mention of a "village" is intended to indicate any place of residence.
Therefore, there is also a prohibition against [staying] in that city.
A marshy region (*anūpa*) is full of diseases;
one should not dwell in a dry region (*jāṅgala*) that is likewise full of diseases.
One should abandon that region where diseases have arisen due to the influence of fate;
one should not set out on a journey alone, without a companion.
One should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra, nor in one filled with unrighteous people,
nor in one overrun by hosts of heretics, nor in one infested by men of the lowest castes.
Sovereignty over a territory is kingship.

One should not dwell in a territory where the Śūdras hold power. Kingship consists of the seven constituent elements (prakṛtis), beginning with the minister, the commander-in-chief, and the judicial officer.
This prohibition of residence applies where all the inhabitants belong to the Śūdra caste.
But is this not already established by the rule "one should not dwell among the unrighteous," since a place "surrounded by unrighteous people" would necessarily include such a case?
This is not a fault.
The previous prohibition applied where they reside;
this one, however, applies even if they are residing elsewhere but happen to be present in another location—nevertheless, one must not dwell in that place.
Thus, the inclusion of the term "enclosed" (*āvṛta*) is used here.
One should not stay in a region that is occupied by these [heretics].
Likewise, regarding a country overrun by heretics (*pāṣaṇḍijanaiḥ*):
although they are unrighteous because they stand outside the Veda, they nevertheless possess a sense of dharma; for this reason, they are mentioned separately.
"Afflicted by the last ones" means being connected with them;
or alternatively, "afflicted" means tormented,
as for example the Vāhlīkas are [tormented] by the Mlecchas.
One should not eat food from which the oil has been extracted, nor should one practice excessive satiety;
one should not eat too early, nor too late, nor having already eaten in the evening, should one eat again in the morning.
He for whom oil has been brought [as a substitute] must avoid oil-cakes, vegetable broth, and meat;

for him, there will be a re-allowance of sacrificial remnants and preparations of milk that have stood overnight. The plural number is used with reference to buttermilk, inspissated milk, and so forth.

For curd itself is indeed a direct modification; had it been intended that only that [curd] be produced, he would have simply mentioned "curd. Therefore, its purpose is not for the sake of prescribing [it].
For curd does not possess the quality of being stale;
therefore, this prohibition does not apply to products derived from milk such as buttermilk, *takra*, *kilāṭa*, and so forth.
One should not eat to excess, nor should one seek satiety.
In that regard, there are three portions of the stomach:

one for solid food, another for liquids such as water, and another for the movement of the vital airs (*vāyu*); thus one should eat. One should not eat too early in the morning, while the sun has only just risen.

For those who are emaciated, [the meal] should be taken after one watch has passed in the forenoon; for others, at midday. One should not eat too late in the evening at the time of sunset, nor should one eat in the evening if one has already eaten and is satisfied in the morning.
Therefore, one should eat with desire [for more] at both times.
Thus it has been said: "Eating in the evening and in the morning is the meal ordained by the gods for human beings.
However, if one should be satiated in the morning, one need not eat in the evening.
Alternatively, it is explained as follows:
"He should not eat in the evening or in the morning" means that he should not satisfy himself at both meal times;
and thus Yājñavalkya speaks of a slight meal in the evening.
One should not engage in useless exertion, nor drink water with cupped hands;
one should not eat food in one's lap, nor ever be a seeker of idle curiosity.
Futile activity (*vṛthāceṣṭā*) is an operation that provides no benefit in either the seen or the unseen worlds;
for example, being intent upon news of other lands and such. When the two hands are joined together, it is the *añjali*.
Therefore, one should not drink water;
by the mention of "water," there is no prohibition against milk and the like.
Nor [should one drink] from the hollow of the hands.
"Eatables" refers to roasted grains, cakes, and the like;
one should not eat these while holding them on one's lap, that is, upon the thighs. By the use of the term "eatables," fruits are also prohibited [from being eaten in this manner].

However, since food such as flour-gruel (*saktu*) and boiled rice (*odana*), when offered without any liquid seasoning, is unfit for consumption, there is no possibility of it being placed in one's lap.
"Curiosity" (*kutūhala*) refers to an excessive longing arising from the thought, "What could this be? in the absence of a definitive conclusion. "Never" (*jātu*) means at no time whatsoever.
One should not dance, nor indeed sing, nor play musical instruments;
one should not clap hands, nor shout, nor, being impassioned, engage in conflict.
Dancing is a specific kind of bodily movement, well-known in the world. Singing is the production of sound through the notes of the scale, such as Ṣaḍja and the rest.
And this prohibition applies to worldly [dancing and singing], not to Vedic ones, because those are prescribed by rule.
Musical instruments refer to the lute, flute, drum, and so forth. Playing these oneself is prohibited; however, there is no prohibition against them being played by musicians.
For there is no authority for the claim that this [term] is derived from a causative (*ṇic*) stem rather than a simple root.

"Clapping" (*āsphoṭanam*) refers to the repeated striking of the hands against the ground, such as when clapping *karamarda* fruits; it is a sound produced by the hand. "Screaming" (*kṣveḍā*) is the production of an indistinct sound with the teeth, commonly known as *kṣveḍanikā*.
The other is *valgana*.
One who possesses passion (*rāgī*), when satisfied, should not cause opposition; he should not create conflict.
When [the practitioner] is afflicted, there is no prohibition.
The suffix ṇic must be applied after a word ending in the kṛt-suffix ghañ.
One should never wash one's feet in a vessel made of bell-metal,
nor should one eat from a broken dish or one that is defiled by its nature.

One should not wash one's feet in a bronze vessel; this applies even to a broken vessel, meaning one that is cracked in some part. In the case of vessels that are completely shattered, the prohibition follows as a matter of course.
However, in the case of leaf-cups and the like, because they are not conventionally designated as "broken vessels," there is no fault even if they have holes.
"State" (bhāva) refers to the intention within the heart;
that in which the mind finds no satisfaction.
Or, in the case of a sound-defiled object such as a spittoon and the like,
even there, such clarity of mind does not arise.
One should not wear shoes, clothing,
a sacred thread, ornaments, a garland, or a water-pot that have been worn by others.
One should not carry a water-pot held by others such as one's father;
Gautama states that it may be washed if one is unable [to obtain another].
A *karaka* is a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*); even if it was held by one's father or others, carrying it is contrary to established custom.
This is intended to be of the nature of a relative connection;
it is pure only for that person to whom it belongs, and not for anyone else.
Ornaments include such things as ivory bracelets and the like.
Some maintain that because of their association with items of little value such as water-pots and the like, there is no prohibition regarding gems, pearls, and so forth.
One should not travel with draft animals that are untrained, nor with those afflicted by hunger or disease;
nor with those whose horns, eyes, or hooves are broken, nor with those whose tails are deformed.
Untamed and untrained oxen, horses, mules, and so forth—
those capable of bearing the yoke— are yoked to carry the burden;
this is an illustration that includes carts and other such vehicles.
The inclusion of the word "cow" (go) implies that travel by those who are not yoked to the burden, or by those who are merely untamed, is not permitted.

A bull whose horn is broken possesses horns only as long as it remains a bull; this does not apply to horses and the like. "Tail" (vāladhi) refers to the tail; those "disfigured by it" are those whose tails have been cut off and so forth.
One should not travel with such a person;
indeed, the act of mounting [the same vehicle] is prohibited by another Smṛti.
One should always travel with horses that are well-trained, swift, endowed with auspicious marks,
and perfected in color and form, without excessively prodding them with the goad.
Some, even though they are arrogant, do not adopt discipline;
for that reason, it says "by the disciplined," meaning those who are well-trained.
"By the swift" means by those who go quickly.
"Endowed with the marks" means possessed of auspicious curls and so forth, not having a bare head or similar defects;
"endowed with color and form" means with a beautiful color such as gold or crimson, and with form, which is a particular excellence of configuration.
And its excellence is to be known from the science of characteristics (*lakṣaṇavidyā*). Even while striking excessively— that is, causing pain—
they break apart when being driven excessively again and again with the goad, the hook, and so forth.
The morning sun, the smoke from a funeral pyre, and a broken seat should be avoided;
one should not clip one's nails or hair, nor should one tear at the nails with the teeth.
When the sun has first risen, the period of three *muhūrtas* is designated as "morning sunlight" (*bālātapa*).
The "smoke of the deceased" (*pretadhūma*) is that which arises from a corpse being cremated.
A "seat" (*āsana*) is one that is broken, perforated, or shattered.
This is what should be avoided:

one should not cut one's nails or hair oneself out of addiction; however, when they have grown excessively long, one should have them trimmed by a barber. Furthermore, one should not tear off even long nails with one's teeth.
Others, however, connect the text as follows:
"One should not cut one's nails or hair with the teeth";
thus, one should not even cause the nails to fall by means of the teeth.
For in the art of scratching with the nails, amorous women tear open various parts of the body with their claws.
One should not crush a clod of earth, nor should one tear grass with the fingernails;
one should not perform fruitless action, nor anything that results in future unhappiness.
*Vimardana* is the breaking into pieces of a clod of earth associated with clay;
some, however, say it refers even to a clod of earth associated with lime and the like.
And *mardana* of clay is the repeated throwing up and dropping [of it], or its kneading with the hand.
And this crushing [of grain] that is prohibited is that which occurs through acting at random, and not for a purpose such as purification and the like;
for the mention of "fruitless" [grain] was drawn forward [to this point] from earlier.
Since this is already established by that very [rule], the present undertaking is for the sake of specifying a particular expiation.
*Karaja* means nails;
it does not mean action. But is it not the case that fruitless action is already excluded by the rule, "One should not perform useless exertion"? Indeed, it is so.
On this point, they say:
"Movement is an activity consisting of the primary elements;
however, in this context, there is an exclusion of the general category."
Therefore, one should avoid conceptualizations such as those of a kingdom of the mind.
"The future" refers to a time yet to come;

for from a certain action, unhappiness or suffering arises in a future time, just as from indigestible food, or like the expenditure of great wealth without considering the maintenance of one's family.
One should not do that.
In this regard, there is an explanatory passage (arthavāda):
"The man who crushes clods of earth, cuts grass, or bites his nails, as well as the informer and the impure person, quickly goes to destruction."

From this very mention of "clod" (*loṣṭha*) alone, it is understood that the previously mentioned term *mṛlloṣṭham* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). For if both [elements] were intended as primary, the mention of "clay" (*mṛd*) would have been made here just as in the case of the clod, since it too is easily crushed by the hand; thus, the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) was necessary.
Since mortar is hard, its kneading is accomplished only with effort; therefore, it does not occur at all when there is no purpose [for it].
However, the kneading of a lump of clay by hand occurs naturally for some men.
It is this [latter] that is excluded.
He is habitually a cutter of grass;
he gnaws his nails with his teeth;
he is a slanderer, a backbiter, and a whisperer into the ear.
He who explains the faults of another, whether real or unreal, in their absence—
being "impure" in the sense already explained—
he quickly goes to destruction.
This is not like other Vedic fruits, which have no fixed time [for their realization]; rather, in this very life, there is soon a separation from wealth and so forth, that is, destruction.
One should not engage in contentious debate, nor should one wear a garland outside [the house].
Riding on the backs of oxen is in every way censured.

That mutual disputing regarding worldly treatises or matters which is carried out with obstinacy, such as by making a wager and so forth—that which is self-aggrandizement—is *vigṛhyakathā* (disputatious discourse).
It is "external garland":
one should cover with a cloth a garland worn around the neck that is outside the garment.
And such is the traditional practice:
others say that "outside" refers to an uncovered place;
they state that one should not wander about with garlands openly displayed in such places as city streets and the like.
Alternatively, "external fragrance" and "external garland" refer to that whose scent is not clearly perceived;
thus another Smṛti text states: "One should not wear a scentless garland, except for one made of gold.
Furthermore, regarding "riding on the back of cows," this prohibits mounting cows directly, except when using a saddle.

"In every respect" means that even when there is an obstacle such as a pack animal, since it is not a vehicle for riding on the back, there is no prohibition against yoking it to a cart or similar conveyance.
One should not enter an enclosed village or house except through the gate,
and at night, one should avoid the roots of trees from afar.

In the case of an enclosed village—such as one surrounded by a fence or wall—entry is prohibited except through the gates; however, in the case of an unenclosed village, entry may be made at will even through the gates.
One should never play with dice; one should not carry one's sandals oneself;
one should not eat while reclining on a bed, nor with food held in the hand, nor while seated on a seat.
"Even without a wager, one should not play with dice even in jest.
The mention of "even" (*api*) is for the purpose of indicating that this applies to sticks (*śalākā*) and other such implements as well;
thus, there is a prohibition against all forms of gambling.
One should not, having personally taken leather footwear—meaning sandals—in one's own hand or with a staff or other implement, carry them to another place.
This prohibition applies specifically to one's own footwear, because the word "himself" (*svayam*) is the subject under discussion;
therefore, there is no prohibition regarding footwear belonging to a teacher or others.

One should not eat while sitting on a bed, a couch, or similar furniture; nor should one eat by placing a morsel in the hand, or by placing food on a seat that is not separated from the vessel or other such items.
This specification regarding the lack of separation refers to the food, not to the eater.
One should not eat anything mixed with sesame after the sun has set;
nor should one sleep here naked, nor go anywhere while still impure from food.
When the sun has set;
the accusative case is used because *prati* functions as a *karmapravacanīya*.
And he is not impure from food remnants.
But is this not already prohibited among the duties of the religious student (*brahmacarya*),
and has its status as a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*) been made known?
It is not merely for that purpose [of the sacrifice].
True;
this instruction is for the purpose of making known its nature as a vow (vrata).
Therefore, a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) should be made for the duration of one's life.
One should eat with wet feet, but one should not go to bed with wet feet;
eating with wet feet, one attains a long life.
One should perform this rite at the beginning of the action.
One should eat with wet feet; and one should not sit down while massaging one's feet until one is fully satiated.
One should lie down; while on the bed, one should not toss the limbs about.
"Lying down" (saṃveśana) means the joining of the limbs upon the bed.
He states its fruit: "long life."
This is not a rule for one who desires long life; rather, as before, it is obligatory.
The mention of "long life," however, is merely an explanatory praise (arthavāda).
One should never enter a difficult place that is beyond the range of sight;
one should not look at feces or urine, nor should one cross a river by means of one's arms.
One should not approach, nor step upon, nor go toward a difficult place such as a mountain that is hard to climb, or a forest dense with trees, shrubs, and creepers;
one should not even bring it within the range of sight, for there is the apprehension of the presence of hidden dangers such as snakes or thieves.
The mention of "the eye" is intended as a definition for valid means of knowledge such as scripture and so forth,
not for excrement or urine.
"Beholding" (*udīkṣaṇa*) refers to the examination [of an object] by means of its color and other qualities.
And since examination occurs through prolonged observation, for that very reason it should not be performed;
however, there is no fault if it is seen by chance somewhere.
Furthermore, crossing a river by swimming with one's arms is forbidden for one who is healthy, but not when there is fear of wolves and the like.
One who desires to live a long life should not step upon hair, nor ashes, bones, or potsherds, nor cotton seeds, nor husks.
*Kapālikāḥ* means broken fragments;
*dīrgham āyuḥ* means long life.
The second [case ending] has been explained.
One should not dwell with those who have fallen from their caste, nor with Caṇḍālas, nor with Pulkasas;
nor with fools, nor with the arrogant, nor with outcastes, nor with those who live on the outskirts of society.
But has this not already been stated [in the rule]: "not in a place crowded with unrighteous people, nor one infested by outcasts"?
We say: no;
in that case, residence was what was prohibited.
In this context, however, "co-residence" (saṃvāsa) is explained as follows: one should not live as a householder in the village where they reside.
Co-residence with them consists of social interaction through acts such as giving and receiving, cultivating friendship, living near their houses, sharing the same shade, and so forth.
And because of the inclusion of the word "obstructed" (*āvṛta*), abundance [of such persons] is understood there;
its meaning is that one should not dwell even near a village where they are numerous.
But here, even in the absence of abundance, dwelling nearby and so forth is prohibited; this is the distinction.
The *pulkasas* and *niṣādas* are born from a *śūdra* woman.
The "outcastes" (*antyāḥ*) are the barbarians (*mlecchas*), such as the *medas* and others.

The term "lowest-of-the-low" (*antyāvasāyin*) refers to one born from a *caṇḍāla* father and a *niṣāda* mother; this will be explained in the passage beginning with "a *niṣāda* woman [from a *caṇḍāla*]" and so forth.
They are self-conceited, arrogant with pride, and haughty on account of wealth and other such things.
One should not give counsel to a Śūdra, nor his leavings, nor food prepared for sacrifice;
one should not teach him the Dharma, nor prescribe a religious vow for him.
One must not provide instruction regarding what is beneficial or harmful to a Śūdra concerning matters seen or unseen;
that is to say, one must not act as a counselor to a Śūdra. Furthermore, this prohibition concerns [counseling] for the sake of livelihood.
However, there is no fault [in teaching] out of friendship and the like;
for Śūdras can indeed be family friends,
and out of friendship, one must certainly provide beneficial instruction.
And since a Brāhmaṇa’s friendliness is authorized toward all social classes (*varṇa*), he is called a "friendly Brāhmaṇa.

As for those who, having introduced the point that "one should not speak to one who does not ask," argue that this is appropriate because it is established in other treatises (stating), "one should not speak to anyone unless asked," that is incorrect.

For in that context, regarding the subject of Vedic study, one should not speak unasked—such as "this has been ruined by you"—when someone else is making an error concerning the accents or phonemes, or some other lapse. And thus, in this connection where it is said that "these [students] are not to be taught," it was stated: "one should not speak without being asked.
The meaning of this is that one should say nothing at all to a non-pupil who, when not asked, recites with wrong accents or wrong syllables.

Regarding the term "nocchiṣṭam" (not impure from food): this word *ucchiṣṭa* refers to a state of impurity (*aprāśastya*) caused by eating. Even one who has voided urine or feces is called *ucchiṣṭa* if he has not sipped water for purification (*anācānta*), as we shall explain later: "One who is *ucchiṣṭa* should not touch [anything] with his hand."
The term *ucchiṣṭa* (remnant) is used predominantly in connection with eating (*bhujisaṃbandha*).
For when one is eating, that which remains inside or outside [the mouth] becomes a remnant through contact with the interior of the mouth.
Thus, the phrase "hair of the beard has not entered the mouth" indicates that only what has entered the mouth—excluding the beard itself—renders something a remnant.
Consequently, the term *ucchiṣṭa* (remnant) is applied to the eater, to the food being eaten, and to the vessel or other receptacle.
In some instances, however, it also signifies "that which remains after use," as in the expression, "the sacrificial oblation (*havir-ucchiṣṭa*) is the priestly fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
In that context, according to established usage, what is held in a vessel, connected to a person who has eaten, and only slightly consumed, is called *ucchiṣṭa*.
Even that which is pure, such as rice placed in a vessel, though not touched by the eater, is nevertheless avoided due to its association [with him] according to established custom.

In this regard, the injunction "the leavings (ucchiṣṭa) should be given" and the prohibition "not the leavings" refer to the same subject and may be treated as alternatives based on the distinction between a truthful Śūdra and an untruthful one, or by the differentiation of the types of sacrificial remnants (haviḥ-śeṣa).
Alternatively, "leavings" refers to what remains in the cooking pot after guests and others have eaten—essentially stale food—and that must not be given to a Śūdra.
To this it is replied: because of its association with the term *jīrṇa* (worn-out), it is proper to understand this very [meaning];

and since the prefix of the root *śiṣ* denotes that which remains after being used, its application is not contradictory, as it functions in accordance with that sense—just as in the expression *havirucchiṣṭa* (the remnant of the sacrificial oblation) and *dakṣiṇā* (the sacrificial fee).
In this way, there will be no contradiction between these two [scriptural] traditions, even though in common usage those worthy of sipping water (*ācamana*) are generally seen here in the text.
As for the statement, "and the rules of purification are like those of a Vaiśya," that refers to the case of *dāsa*s and *śūdra*s;
we shall demonstrate that it is understood as referring specifically to what has been left over after eating.
"Not *haviṣkṛtam*":
that which has been made for the oblation (*haviṣe kṛtam*), i.e., prepared for the purpose of the oblation.
This is a compound with a plural [final member] because of the prohibition against what is prepared for the sake of another.
By the principle of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikā*), everything that possesses even the slightest scent of sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is thereby prohibited.

Consequently, this establishes a prohibition for the oblation intended for the purpose of sacrifice, as well as for the remnant of the oblation already offered, and for the oblation that has been left over after being partially consumed.
Thus, the verb *karoti* ("he does") is employed here in its general sense of action, as in the expression "it has been done" (*tathā ca kṛtam*).

The statement "that which has been prepared and intended for the sake of the oblation" implies that even in the case of what remains as leavings, as long as there is the original intention (*saṃkalpa*), it is designated as *haviṣkṛta* (prepared for the oblation); thus, the prohibition is understood to apply to it in every state, except when it is no longer properly so designated. Others, however, have explained it as "mixed with the oblation" (*havirmiśra*).
And because of the prohibition of the mixed [case], there is also a prohibition of the solitary [case].
It has been stated that when there is a prohibition of one who is mixed with another, it is like the case of a Brahmin.
But how, when there is a prohibition of the mixed, is there a prohibition of the solitary?

A subordinate negation of a conjunction can sometimes be stated by means of a simple negation, in cases where even though two things are conjoined, they appear as distinct from one another; or where, while a form is perceived by the eye, there is an application of it through taste and so forth—in such cases, linguistic usage based on that [conjunction] certainly occurs. For example, when balls of parched grain are mixed with wine and the like, even though the form of the wine is not concealed, because there is the cognition of it, the expiation for drinking wine must indeed be applied.
But even so, since liquor that has attained the state of a solid mass lacks the nature of a liquid, its drinking would not be possible.
This is not a fault; for "drinking" is mentioned here as a conventional expression based on the general rule.
However, it is indeed the act of ingestion that is prohibited;
for this is a section concerning what may and may not be eaten,
and "eating" (bhakṣaṇa) here refers simply to the act of ingesting (abhyavahāra).
Its specific qualities include drinking, eating, chewing, and so forth.
Furthermore, since odor is perceived even when it lacks a [perceptible] substrate, the existence of a substance cannot be inferred from it;
for even when camphor and the like are at a distance, their odor is still perceived.
In the conceptualization of the perception of the parts of a subtle substance, there would be a dimension of the substance [in those parts].
However, where there is a state of unification of two conjoined things and no cognition of them as distinct, injunctions and prohibitions cannot operate upon the substrates alone;
just as in the case of the instruction "milk is to be drunk," when milk and water are mixed and both are drunk, it is neither milk nor water, because they have become a different substance.
For in that case, the color is one thing and the taste, shape, and so forth—which serve as the cause for the cognition of it—are another; thus, it is a distinct substance.
If this were so, then when wine and water are drunk together, if they were [distinct], the penance for drinking wine would not apply, because it would be a different substance.
This is not a fault, for wine overpowers other tastes, just like a bitter taste.
Therefore, due to the recognition of the taste, that very penance indeed applies.

However, in cases where there is a large quantity of water and only a small amount of liquor or the like, we shall carefully determine the penance for contact (*saṃsarga*) in a specific section [of this work].
Consequently, a prohibition based solely on the substance may also extend to its contact.

Just as when it is said that "māṣa beans should not be eaten," even those mixed with other things are not permitted; for what reason would a substratum of contact exist in that which is not in contact? When it is said, "Bring water from the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā," one does not bring water from the Gaṅgā alone, nor from the Yamunā alone.
If it is argued that this refers only to customary conduct (*samācāra*), then only such conduct should have been cited as the example. Furthermore, one must not instruct him in the Dharma.

But surely, by the prohibition against giving excessive gifts concerning both seen and unseen matters—expressed without distinction in the rule "not to a Śūdra"—the prohibition against instructing him in the Dharma is already established.
True;
however, the repetition is for the sake of indicating what remains.
Consequently, the instruction regarding the expiation becomes authorized.
We shall demonstrate this point in the section concerning "abandoning one who has come for refuge.

Others, however, say that one should not instruct others in the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for rites such as the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* or the *pākayajña* by acting as their officiating priest (*yājaka*) and so forth.
On this matter, they raise an objection: if instruction in the Dharma is forbidden for a *śūdra*, how then can he possess knowledge of the Dharma?
And since performance is not possible for one who lacks knowledge, it follows that the *Dharmaśāstra* would be useless if its performers were Śūdras.
This objection is not valid;
for it is possible for a Brāhmaṇa—who has transgressed prohibitions out of desire for gain—to act as an instructor.
For the injunction regarding the gift of one's entire property does not employ the killing of a Brahmin as its means;
rather, it is the desire for gain that functions as the motivator.
But is there not a scriptural statement: "And he should proclaim it to the others"?
Regarding the attainment of the means of livelihood,
for this very reason the following is the subject at hand: "A Brāhmaṇa should know the means of livelihood for all according to the rule,
and he should proclaim them to others."
However, for one who has taken refuge with a Śūdra, instruction must certainly be given;
for it is forbidden to live together with those who are ignorant, as they would transgress injunctions and prohibitions, according to the rule: "Not with fools, nor with the arrogant.

As for what some commentators explain—that by these two rules, "one should not instruct him" and "nor should one teach him," the instruction of the Dharmaśāstra or the exposition of its meaning is prohibited—[that is incorrect].
One [aspect] is the study of the treatise (*śāstra*), and the other is the explanation of its meaning;
however, instruction that is not based on a formal text (*agranthaka*) has not been prohibited by anyone.
For those who speak thus, since it is established that "it is an investigation of that very treatise," [the objection] is redundant.
Here they say:
the word "dharma" refers to treatises for the purpose of understanding phenomena, such as grammar and so forth;
for that is not a treatise on dharma (dharmaśāstra) because it does not teach regarding objects beyond the senses, due to the absence of prohibitions [therein].
However, it exists for the purpose of understanding the *Dharmaśāstra*.
For a grammarian is indeed able to extract the profound meaning of a sentence by following the meanings of individual words.
Furthermore, because it is a *Dharmaśāstra*, it is mentioned separately since it would otherwise have been included under the term "treatise" (*śāstra*).

This is logical, provided that no one should say: "How can there be application to the subsidiary parts for one who is not authorized regarding the primary part? For the Veda and the Smṛti-śāstra constitute the primary part, and in those, the Śūdra has no authorization.
And one should not prescribe a vow for him;
by the word "vow" (vrata), the *kṛcchra* penances are meant, as seen from the usage "by these vows.
One should not instruct those [penances] to one who desires prosperity.
However, instruction is indeed intended for the purpose of expiation.
As for the observances of a *snātaka*, there is no possibility of their application because he is not a *snātaka*.

Likewise, the *Sāvitrī* and other rites do not apply due to the absence of Vedic study, and study is impossible due to the absence of initiation (*upanayana*), since the three castes are mentioned in the injunctions for that initiation.
For he who teaches him the Dharma and he who prescribes the vow sink together with that very person into the darkness called "the unrestrained."

This is a deprecatory explanatory passage (arthavāda) for the preceding prohibition. By the phrase "together with him," he states the fault of both: the one who listens and the one who causes [the listener] to hear.
It sinks, it plunges; that is to say, it reaches that.
One should not scratch one's own head with both hands joined together;
nor should one touch it while impure from food, nor bathe without using it.
The prohibition concerns both hands simultaneously—joined together, closely pressed, and mutually joined. By the word "with the hands," he prohibits the arms from being joined;
by the word "of oneself," he excludes another person.
Therefore, there is no fault in having someone else scratch [the head] when it is covered;
because of the mention of the "head," there is no fault regarding the back and so forth.
And one should not touch the head oneself.
Some say that one should touch oneself with another limb; that is not correct, because "with the two hands" is the subject under discussion.
Nor should one bathe without the head.
This is the rule for the daily (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) baths.
[Objection: But why should this apply to the worldly bath of one who is perspiring?
[Response: Because it forms a single syntactical unit with the injunction for bathing.
The requirement for a prescribed bath is logical due to its proximity [to the context]. However, in common worldly usage, there is no such rule, and thus it is not established [as a mandatory rite].
Furthermore, this verb *snāti* refers to the cleansing of all parts of the body with water, cow’s urine, and so forth, as well as to cleansing excluding the head.
In that context, when touching a Caṇḍāla or similar person, even that which is incidental is prohibited, yet one should not bathe without it;
for there exists a worldly bath that is headless, as evidenced by the rule: "But one who has bathed his head [should apply] oil [to the rest]."
One should avoid seizing the hair and striking the head;
moreover, having bathed one's head, one should not touch any part of the body with oil.
Some maintain that this applies without distinction, whether to oneself or to another;
others, however, connect it with the subject at hand, "oneself.
Furthermore, this prohibition is occasioned by anger.
However, the grasping of the hair of a passionate woman during sexual union is not prohibited.

Regarding the term *śiraḥsnānam*, it is a case of inverted word order (*paranipāta*) because it belongs to the class of irregular compounds beginning with *rājadanta* (meaning "that by which the head has been washed").
The compound *śiraḥsnāta* is formed by the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*).
The limb is not one's own.
One should not accept gifts from a king who is not born of the Kṣatriya lineage, nor from those who possess a slaughterhouse, a water-wheel, or a tavern flag, nor from those who live by prostitution.

It has been stated that "one should seek wealth from a king. This word "king" (*rājan*) is observed to be used for a ruler of a realm even when he is not of the Kṣatriya caste, as in the expression "the kingdom of Brāhmaṇas.
In this context, regarding both the injunction for receiving gifts and its prohibition, the term is understood to refer to the ruler of a realm.

Regarding the phrase "one not born from a *rājanya*": since sovereignty over a realm can arise from any of the social classes (*varṇas*) through desire for it, this is specified as an exception; one should not accept [the office] from a king who lacks birth or origin (*prasūti*) from a *rājanya*, that is, from a *kṣatriya*. Thus, one should not take [it] from such a ruler of a realm.
Even from a *kṣatriya* who is greedy and acts contrary to the scriptures—according to the prohibition that will be stated later—one should not accept gifts.
A "butcher" (*sūnāvan*) is one who lives by the sale of meat preceded by the slaughter and immolation of animals;
he is well known in the world as a "scavenger" (*khaṭika*).
A *dvaja* is one whose merchandise is liquor, living by its purchase and sale;
a *veśa* is the profession of prostitution, and whoever lives by that—whether woman or man—is so designated.
A cart is equal to ten slaughterhouses; a banner is equal to ten carts;
a brothel is equal to ten banners; and a king is equal to ten brothels.
This is for the purpose of making known that each subsequent [offense] carries a greater gravity of fault;
the remedy for such cases will be explained later.
A king is considered equal to a butcher who maintains ten thousand slaughterhouses; therefore, accepting gifts from him is a terrible thing.
A butcher acts with a knife;
he drives [the animals], meaning he employs them for the sake of accomplishing his own ends.
This is terrible and fearsome, because it is a cause for rebirth in hell and other such states.
By way of a partial statement, there is a censure regarding the acceptance of gifts from a king:
"He who accepts gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures shall,
in succession, go to these twenty-one hells."
Greedy and habitually seizing from neighboring lords and others,

he acts contrary to the scriptures; having understood [the requirements of] learning and virtue, he nevertheless transgresses the treatises and conducts himself by means of unjust punishments, the abduction of others' wives, and so forth.
Having experienced the fruit in one place by way of succession, one goes elsewhere.
The word "hell" (naraka) denotes unsurpassed suffering;
alternatively, it denotes a specific location by implication from hearing that it consists solely of suffering.
The number twenty-one is a figurative explanation (arthavāda).
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava and Raurava,
the hell Kālasūtra, and likewise Mahānaraka.
Saṃjīvana, Mahāvīci, Tapana, Saṃpratāpana,
Saṃhāta, Kākola, Kuḍmala, and Pūtimṛttika.
The Iron Spike, the Residue, the Path, the Śālmalī River,
the Forest of Sword-leaves, and the Iron Saw.
The three verses have a clear meaning.
Knowing this, learned Brahmins who discourse on the Veda and desire the highest good after death do not accept gifts from a king.
This is the concluding summary of the preceding injunction prohibiting acceptance [of gifts] from a king:
knowing that accepting gifts from a king is the cause of various sufferings, such as rebirth in hell, learned Brahmins should not accept gifts from a king.
"In the hereafter," meaning in another existence, "those who desire" means those who long for "welfare," that is, spiritual well-being.
The word *pretya*, however, is another term that resembles a gerund (*lyabanta*). "Brahman" refers to the Veda; they speak it, that is, they recite it.
The mention of "the learned" (*vidvat*) and "those who proclaim the Brahman" (*brahmavādin*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the intensity of their suffering.
Moreover, there is a fault in accepting gifts from them;
for it will be said later: "Therefore, even a wise man should fear [them]."
One should awaken during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and reflect upon dharma and artha,
as well as the physical disciplines rooted therein and the true meaning of the Vedas.
The night consists of three watches; its final portion is the *brāhma-muhūrta*.
One should abandon sleep during that time, and having awakened at that hour, one should reflect upon the Dharma and its purpose.
Furthermore, one should consider what kind of physical hardship arises when practicing a particular teaching.

If a teaching is of little benefit yet produces great bodily suffering and contradicts other teachings, one should abandon it. Even if wealth is acquired through service and the like, if it causes excessive hardship, that too should be avoided.
"One should protect oneself from all sides.
Without reaching certainty, one should do nothing;
nor should one engage in conceptual constructions such as those of a kingdom of the mind.
For this is the nature of men: even in the absence of external activity, conceptual constructions of the mind arise in the form of longing for the property of others and so forth.
It is for the purpose of ceasing these that this [Vedic injunction] exists for the sake of man.
At that time, the true meaning of the Veda is to be considered in terms of the relationship between the goal to be accomplished (sādhya) and the means of accomplishment (sādhana).
One should contemplate the secret knowledge of the Self and practice it according to the method of Vedānta;
or else, one should investigate the meaning of that Veda which pertains to the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*).

One should determine through one's own intellect: "This is the injunction, this is the meaning, this is the nature of the rite, this is the deity here, this is the substance, this is the qualified person (*adhikārī*) here, and this is the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)," and so forth.
Due to the differences in opinion among commentators, one should examine the reasons [adduced] to determine whether this is correct knowledge or this is an error.
Having risen and performed his necessary duties, purified and composed,
he should stand for a long time reciting prayers during the morning twilight, and likewise at its proper time during the evening twilight.
Immediately thereafter, when the night has turned to dawn, one should leave the bed. The necessary evacuation of urine and feces is generally performed by men at that time.

In that regard, the necessary renunciations are described as the cleansing of the mouth and teeth and so forth; having performed these and completed his purification, he should sip water according to the rule beginning with "one [application] on the penis.
Being composed by setting aside other discursive thoughts, he should remain at the twilight devotions. Reciting the Sāvitrī, he should fix his mind for a long time upon the Blessed Sun.
The time for the twilight ritual (*saṃdhyā*) is said to extend until the sun is visible;
however, for one desiring long life, one should recite [the mantra] for even longer than that. For this purpose, the previously mentioned twilight rite has been set aside.
And as for the subsequent twilight, it should be performed at its proper time, beginning from the moment of sunset and continuing even after the appearance of the stars.
By virtue of their long observance of the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*), the seers (*ṛṣis*) obtained long life,
as well as wisdom, fame, renown, and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
He now demonstrates the purpose for which this injunction exists:
one who desires the fruits such as longevity should perform the twilight recitation (*saṃdhyājapa*) for a long duration.
Even though [the rite] is obligatory (*nitya*), this specific fruit results from the quality of its length.
This applies to one who has gone abroad without his sacred fires;
for any other, however, there would be an obstruction of the time for the *agnihotra* due to the performance of the elaborate twilight (*saṃdhyā*) rites.
The "elaborate twilight" is so called by virtue of its specific qualities.
The word *saṃdhyā* occurs here in the sense of the ritual procedure for recitation and so forth that accompanies the *saṃdhyā*.
The term *dīrghasaṃdhya* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those whose *saṃdhyā* is long. The mention of the *ṛṣis* is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).
Having performed the ritual commencement (upākarma) according to the rules on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada,
a Brahmin, being disciplined, should study the Vedas for four and a half months.
The full moon day conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇā is called Śrāvaṇī;
likewise for Prauṣṭhapadī. Having performed the rite known as the Upākarma on that day, one should study according to the prescribed rule.
The previously mentioned rule beginning with "prākkūlān" is recalled; he is intent upon that [rule]. "Chandāṃsi" means the Vedas.
This word *chandas* refers to the Veda and does not refer to the *gāyatrī* meters and so forth.
Therefore, this is the supreme injunction even for one who studies the Brāhmaṇas and other such texts.
And it is indeed appropriate in both cases, as there is no difference in the suffix (*pratyaya*).
This distinction is established:
the Chandogas perform the *upākaraṇa* on the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada, while the Bahvṛcas and Adhvaryus do so on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa.
On the Puṣya day, a twice-born man should perform the external dismissal of the Vedas (chandasām utsarjana),
or when the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha has arrived, during the forenoon.
When four and a half months have passed, the *utsarjana* (concluding rite) should be performed under the Puṣya asterism.
The ritual for the *utsarga* has been handed down by the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras.
"Outside" means in an unenclosed place.
The specific nature of these two rites, the *upākarma* and the *utsarga*, is to be understood from the *Gṛhya-sūtras*.
Having thus performed the formal dismissal of the Vedic meters outside according to the scriptures,
one should cease [the study] for a "bird-night" (two nights and one day), or for that very single day and night.
Having performed the *utsarga*, one should not study for two days and one night—
that is, for that day and night;
and for the second day only, not the night— during this much time one should desist and not study.
The night with its two sides [of days] is "pakṣiṇī.
Alternatively, the day on which the suspension of study is performed and that very night constitute a period of non-study;
on the second day, one should study.
But according to the first view, the second day is declared to be a non-study day, while study is permitted during the night.
From this point forward, one who is self-restrained should recite the Vedic hymns during the bright fortnights,
and one should recite all the auxiliary sciences of the Vedas during the dark fortnights.

Therefore, after this rite of renunciation has been performed, one should study the *chandāṃsi*— the Vedas consisting of the collection of *mantra*s and *brāhmaṇa*s— during the bright fortnights (*śuklapakṣa*s), and one should study the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*s),
such as phonetics (*śikṣā*), sacrificial manuals (*yajñasūtra*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), and so forth, during the dark fortnights (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*s).
One should not study indistinctly, nor in the presence of Śūdras; having studied the Veda at the end of the night while fatigued, one should not go back to sleep.
That in which the manifestation of phonemes and vowels is not clear is "indistinct" (*avispaṣṭa*); and that generally occurs in the rapid (*drutā*) mode of recitation.
"At the end of the night" (*niśānte*) means during the final portion of the night.
When one who has risen from sleep studies, he should not then lie down again until he becomes weary;
nor, being exhausted at the end of the night, should he lie down after studying the Veda—such is the disciplined manner of recitation.
A twice-born man, being disciplined, should always recite the Vedic meters according to the prescribed rule, as well as those composed in the *brahma-chandas*, except in times of distress.
The *chandāṃsi* intended here are the *gāyatrī* and other meters; by them, the *brahman* consisting of the *ṛc* and *sāman* is "made" (*kṛtam*), meaning it is "joined" (*yuktam*).
Since the root *kṛ* has multiple meanings, its sense here is explained as follows:

just as one says "make cow-dung" (*gomayān kuru*) in the sense of gathering it, or "make a back" (*pṛṣṭham kuru*) in the sense of massaging it, so too here it functions in the sense of the root *yuj* (to join).
"Brahman" and "meter" (chandas) are "brahmacchandasi"; that which is made or joined by these two is "brahmacchandaskṛta.

"Brahman" refers to the Brāhmaṇa; in the Yajurveda, "brahman" refers to the sacrificial formulas (yajūṃṣi) and the mantras associated with the Gāyatrī and other meters. They recite [these] in one and the same location.
Just as in the Bāhvṛcya and Chāndogya [recensions], the mantras are divided such that they appear in one text while the Brāhmaṇa appears elsewhere,
so too, because of this difference in form, it is appropriate that the Vedas are distinct; thus have the predecessors explained it according to what has been stated.
The previous rule is set aside in times of distress.

In times of distress, for a teacher who is absent, or for one who is occupied with the distribution among many deities and thus lacks proficiency, there may be a lapse of memory; therefore, in such times of distress, this [strict] division need not be observed.
One who is studying should always avoid these occasions of non-recitation,
as should one who is teaching disciples according to the prescribed rule.
One who is studying should avoid these following occasions of non-study (anadhyāya),
as should one who is teaching.
The mention of "teaching" is intended to include those who do not study, for the purpose of grasping and for the sake of practice.
"Always" does not mean from the very beginning [of the term];
rather, it refers even to the fifth month and a half, starting from the *upākarma* ceremony.
This is a restatement for the sake of the students.
When the wind is audible to the ear at night, and when it stirs up clouds of dust by day—
those who know the rules of study declare these two occasions during the rainy season to be times unfit for study.
*Anila* is wind (*vāyu*).
It blows with speed; where a sound is heard due to the friction of one wind against another within the air, that is the wind called *karṇaśrava*.
That which is heard by the two ears is *karṇaśravaḥ*.
The compound is *sādhanam kṛtā* (accomplished by means).
The mention of "ear" (*karṇa*) is for the purpose of indicating a specific state;
it is heard precisely by the two ears.
Therefore, whenever the sound of wind is heard in this manner, one must not study. "Pāṃsusamūhana" means that which sweeps up dust or gathers dust;
"pāṃsu" means dust.
And this is an illustration; it applies equally to such wind as well.
Whenever and wherever it rains, if such a wind blows, for that duration there is no study (*anadhyāya*).
Those who know the rules of study are those who know the procedure for teaching.
Manu has declared that when there is lightning, thunder, and rain, or when there is a falling of great meteors, study is prohibited for the remainder of the day.
*Vidyut* means lightning;
*stanitam* means thundering.
Because these are presented as a copulative compound (*dvandva*), there is a suspension of study when these occur together simultaneously.
The radiance of luminous bodies falling from the sky is called a *maholkā* (great meteor); their "convergence" (*saṃplava*) refers to their falling both here and there.
The term *ākālika* denotes that same period of time starting from the moment of the omen until the following day.
The mention of *manu* is for the purpose of completing the verse.
Others [hold it] for the sake of conceptual differentiation.
One should know that when these [phenomena] appear while the sacred fires have been kindled, then one should know it to be a time unfit for study; likewise, so too when clouds are seen out of season.
This is not a time of non-study at any hour when these [phenomena] have arisen; rather, it refers to when the fires have been made manifest—meaning, at the time of the twilights (saṃdhyā).
For at that time, the fires are invariably made manifest with the desire to offer oblations.
The word *prāduḥ* signifies manifestation.
Regarding "out of season": the rainy season is the *ṛtu*; other than those [two seasons], autumn and so forth constitute the out-of-season period.
In that regard, regarding the "sight of clouds," the phrase "when the fires have been made manifest" is to be understood as a necessary condition.

One should know that these— thunderclaps, earthquakes, and the eclipses of the luminaries— are occasions for the suspension of study (anadhyāya) lasting until the same time the next day, even during the proper season.
A thunderclap is a sound of atmospheric portent;
among the luminaries such as the moon, sun, Jupiter, and so forth, it refers to their eclipsing, the appearance of halos, and their mutual oppression—
even during the proper season.
The inclusion of the word "also" (api) is intended to convey that, it is said, portents are not counted during the rainy season.

But when the fires have been kindled, if there is the sound of lightning and thunder, the suspension of study shall last as long as the light remains; for the remainder of the night, it is as [regulated] as during the day.
Regarding the conjunction of three [factors], it was previously stated that [the time for recitation] is not restricted by the night;
by this [present rule], it is stated that even when two [factors] conjoin, it lasts as long as the light remains.
"Stanita" means thunder, and "niḥsvana" means sound; thus, "stanitaniḥsvana" refers to the sound of thunder.

"Lightning and the sound of thunder" (*vidyutstanitaniḥsvanam*) is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). When both of these have arisen during twilight, there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) as long as the light remains.
The sun is the light by day;
Agni is the light by night.
When [the sun] has risen during the morning twilight, there is no study as if it were still day; however, at night, there is none.
Thus, there is a suspension of study during the evening twilight and at night, but there is no fault in studying in the morning.
Regarding the three topics under discussion—lightning, thunder, and rain—there is a specific instruction for lightning and thunder by dividing them;
rain remains as the remainder. When that third [rain] is observed, the previously mentioned suspension of study lasting until the same time [the next day] applies.
With reference to that, it is said: "as by day, so also by night";
[this refers to] light such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, which is more well-known.
The reading is "śeṣam" (the remainder).
The remaining [period] while the oblation is being offered is a cause for the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*).
Now, why was it not stated thus: "But the remainder is remembered as lasting until the same time [the next day]"? The composition of Manu’s verses is diverse.
For those who desire perfection in dharma, there shall be a perpetual suspension of study in villages and cities, as well as wherever a foul odor is present in every respect.
Those who desire proficiency in the Dharma should not study it in villages or towns.
Furthermore, the word "Dharma" refers here to the fruit of Dharma, such as heaven and the like;
or alternatively, proficiency in Dharma consists in its being unadulterated by non-Dharma (*adharma*), whereby the purpose of the injunction is performed in its most complete form.
And for this reason, an exemption is granted to one who is incapable [of studying].
"Foul odor" means a loathsome smell; when that reaches the path of the nose, there is no study. "In every respect" means even when it is the smell of a corpse, in all cases.
There is a suspension of study when a corpse is inside a village, in the presence of a low-caste person (vṛṣala),
while weeping is occurring, or when there is a great crowd of people.
"In which a corpse is contained" means one in which a corpse remains within the village until it has been removed;
"of a vṛṣala" does not here refer to a Śūdra, because that [impurity] has already been prohibited previously by the rule "not in the presence of a Śūdra person."
Rather, unrighteousness is characterized by that which is predominantly unrighteous.
Therefore, there is a prohibition against one who is of evil conduct and against being in his proximity. "While weeping" means when the sound of weeping is present.
The word *rudya* refers to a place where there is merely the sound of weeping;
*samavāya* refers to a gathering of people.
One should not study in such a place where many people have assembled together for some purpose.
Alternatively, the meaning is "when people are weeping in a crowd";
it is a prohibition when many are weeping. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used in the sense of the agent, which is a Vedic usage.
While in water, at midnight, when voiding excrement or urine,
while impure from food, or after eating at a *śrāddha* ceremony, one should not even mentally contemplate [forbidden things].
Midnight consists of four muhūrtas;
that indeed is the "great night.
It comprises two muhūrtas from the first half of the night and two from the latter half.
"In water" means situated in a river, a pond, or the like.
Recitation [of mantras] while submerged in water is not prohibited—such as the *aghamarṣaṇa* and others—because it does not constitute a state of being unfit for study (*anadhyāya*).
Others read the word as "at sunrise" (*udaye*).

At the time of the sun's first rising, there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*). One is considered "impure" (*ucchiṣṭa*) by virtue of being connected with eating as long as one has not performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*);
even one who has voided urine or feces is indeed called impure prior to performing *ācamana*.
Others say that [the term] refers merely to the occasion for sipping water (*ācamana*); by this, even one who has spat or performed similar acts is included,
as well as [one who does so] even mentally.
It is not that mental reflection on these [topics] is permitted except during the non-periods of study;
rather, this is for the purpose of emphasizing the gravity of the faults associated with these specific occasions.

Having accepted an invitation to an Ekoddiṣṭa rite, a learned twice-born man shall not recite the Veda for three days during the period of impurity following the death of a king or during an eclipse of Rāhu.
That which is intended for one person alone is called *ekoddiṣṭa*, namely the *navaśrāddha*.
Having accepted the invitation—that is, having agreed—to that [ceremony], there is a suspension of Vedic study (*anadhyāya*) for three days starting from the time of the invitation.
Likewise, the moon is the king; its *sūtaka* (impurity) is the flow of nectar toward Rāhu.
By the word "and" (ca), that of the Sun is also included.
Alternatively, the *sūtaka* of a king who is the lord of a country refers to the festival of the birth of a son;
