the *sūtaka* of Rāhu refers to the eclipse of the Moon and the Sun, which is commonly known as a *grahaṇa*.
As long as the fragrance and the smear of a single funeral feast (ekānudiṣṭa) remain on the body of a learned Brahmin, so long should one not recite the Veda.

Regarding the *āmaśrāddha* performed for a single person: as long as the scent and the smear of that [food] remain on the body during the performance of the śrāddha, there is a suspension of Vedic study (*anadhyāya*).
This is a different rule from the preceding one.
On the second day, having bathed and removed that scent, one is fit for study.
And this is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) that one should not study even when there is no odor or stain, as long as the food eaten has not been digested;
by the word "of the learned" (viduṣaḥ), he reiterates that only such a person is entitled to eat at a śrāddha feast.
One should not study while lying down, nor with feet raised, nor having crossed one's legs; nor after eating meat, nor food from a birth-impurity (sūtaka).
"With legs extended" means with one foot placed upon the other; "with legs joined" refers to sitting on a bed, chair, or similar seat with the feet together.
"Avasakthikā" is the binding of the knees and the middle [of the thighs] with cloth or other materials.
"Āmiṣa" means meat.
The mention of *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) is intended to illustrate [the category of] impurity due to death (*śāvāśauca*) and so forth as well.
In mist, at the sound of an arrow, during both twilights,
on the new moon and fourteenth days, and on the full moon and the Aṣṭakā days;
*Nīhāra*, *diṅmoha*, and *dhūmikā* are synonyms;
it is that by which the quarters are made as if covered with mist and dust.
*Bāṇaśabda* is the sound of arrows, the whizzing noise of shafts.
Others recite and explain it as being dental-labial, citing "vīṇā" and "bāṇa" as examples;
for its usage is seen in the Mahāvrata [rite],
in the phrases "it has a hundred strings" and "the lute has no strings."
On the fourteenth day of both fortnights,
and on all the *aṣṭakās*— that is, all the eighth days— according to both the other Smṛti texts and established custom;
others, however, read the text simply as "on the eighth days."
The new moon day destroys the teacher, and the fourteenth day destroys the disciple; the Brahma-eighth and the full moon likewise destroy them; therefore, one should avoid those days.

The explanatory passage (arthavāda) for the preceding [rule] serves to establish its obligatory nature. Therefore, in cases where there is nothing to indicate its obligatory status, that non-study is optional.
And the author will state later: "One should always avoid only these two."
One should avoid those [times] from the practice of Vedic study.

A twice-born man should not recite [the Veda] during a rain of dust, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze, when jackals howl, or when dogs, donkeys, and camels are barking, nor while in a row [of people].
A jackal is a *gomāyu*;
its crying is the making of sound.
There is no study when dogs, donkeys, or camels are standing in a row and making noise.
In each individual row of the same kind.

One should not study at the edge of a cremation ground, at the edge of a village, or even in a cow-pen; nor after wearing a garment used for sexual intercourse, or after accepting food offered at a funeral rite (śrāddha).
The word *antaḥ* expresses proximity;
it means "near the cremation ground" and "near the village.
*Govraje* refers to a place where cows go (*vrajanti*) to graze.
A cow-pen is a cattle-fold.
One should not study while wearing that very garment which was worn at the time of sexual intercourse;
for the word "maithuna" (sexual intercourse), by association, refers here to the garment used at that time.
One should not study even after having taken food consisting of dry grains and the like that was prepared for a *śrāddha* ceremony.
Whether it be animate or inanimate, whatever may be related to a funeral rite (śrāddha), upon touching that there is no study; for the twice-born is traditionally said to have his hand as his mouth.
That which is given for the purpose of a *śrāddha*, such as cooked rice and other foods, is commonly known as "śrāddhika"; it is for the sake of excluding this that the following is stated.

It is not only the acceptance of rice, grain, and so forth during a *śrāddha* that causes the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*), but also anything else, whether animate—such as a cow—or inanimate—such as a pair of garments.
Having accepted that [gift] at the time of its reception and having touched it with the hand, one should not recite;
for that very thing is his food.
One whose mouth is the hand is called *pāṇyāsya*.
This shows that eating at a *śrāddha* and the acceptance of goods for its sake are equal [in their prohibitive status].
One should know that when a village is plundered by thieves, during a panic caused by fire, and during all extraordinary portents, the suspension of study lasts until the same time the following day.
"Upapluta" means afflicted or beset.
Where many thieves fall upon a village for the purpose of slaughter, one should not study there.
"Sambhrama" refers to a state of agitation where fear is produced by fire that has broken out, such as from a house fire, even if the house and so forth have not yet been consumed.
There is no period of non-study (*anadhyāya*) that is limited by time;
rather, starting from the time the event occurs until the same time on the following day, it remains so.

Furthermore, in the case of other miraculous portents (*adbhuta*), whether celestial, terrestrial, or atmospheric—such as stones floating in the air or the appearance of celestial bodies during the daytime—the same rule applies.
On the occasion of the *upākarma* and the *utsarga*, a suspension of study for three nights is prescribed;
on the *aṣṭakā* days and on the nights at the end of the seasons, it is for one day and night.
Regarding the *utsarga*, a period of one day and night was previously mentioned; this [present rule] provides an alternative of three nights.
Regarding the *upākarma*, it is a new injunction.
The *aṣṭakās* are the three or four eighth days following the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī during the dark fortnight.
Although a fast for a full day and night has been prescribed for all eighth days (aṣṭamīs), nevertheless, this undertaking is indeed appropriate for the sake of the obligatory (nitya) rite.
Furthermore, in this entire section, the option (vikalpa) depends upon whether the purpose has already been fulfilled.
The phrase "for a day and night" is to be supplied [from the previous rule] to the [specific] eighth days at the end of the seasons (ṛtvantāsu).
There are six seasons.
When among them the preceding one ceases and the succeeding one begins, there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*).
The mention of "night" is intended as an illustration.
One should not study while mounted on a horse, nor on a tree, nor on an elephant; nor on a boat, nor on a donkey, nor on a camel; nor while standing on a mound, nor while traveling in a vehicle.
A barren tract (*īriṇa*) is a region outside the village, devoid of water and grass, also known by the synonym *ūṣara*.
A vehicle (*yāna*) refers to a cart, chariot, palanquin, and so forth; there is a prohibition against traveling by such means.
Not during a dispute, nor in a quarrel, nor in an army, nor in battle;
not immediately after eating, nor while indigestion persists, nor after vomiting, nor when there is acidity.
A dispute is preceded by verbal abuse;
an outburst is mutual striking with sticks and the like;
an army consists of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
*Saṅgara* means battle.
Even when not in battle, there is a prohibition for one who is stationed with an army.
According to another *smṛti*: "Immediately after eating, as long as the hands are still moist."
"Indigestion" (*ajīrṇa*) refers to food eaten on the previous day that has not yet been digested on the following day.

"Vomiting" (*vamana*) is well known. Regarding "sour eructation" (*śuktaka*), even if there is no indigestion, it refers to the day [of the offense] or the following day when such an eructation occurs.
Nor should one study without having first taken leave of a guest, while a strong wind is blowing,
when blood is flowing from the body, or when one has been wounded by a weapon.

The mention of the "guest" (atithi) is intended to indicate the learned person (śiṣṭa). A guest is a learned person who arrives unexpectedly; when such a person has come to the house, he should be requested [to study], saying, "We shall apply ourselves," and having been permitted by him, one may study.
Accordingly, another Smṛti states: "And when a learned person has arrived at the house."
When the wind, Māruta, blows with great force—
it was indeed already stated that [the sound] is heard by the ear and so forth;
this is true.
Therefore, there is a prohibition against [storing] for longer than that, or even for more than a year;
or else, it "blows" (vāti), meaning it becomes completely dried up, since the root *vā* has the sense of drying.
Furthermore, the mention of "wind" (*māruta*) is intended to indicate wind in general.
Even when the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) are wasting away due to the fatigue of Vedic study, it is a time unfit for study (*anadhyāya*).

When the wind (*māruta*) increases, there is a distinction in the relationship [of the terms], as the locative cases "in the one who ordains" (*vidhāyini*) and "the student" (*adhyetari*) belong to different grammatical substrata (*vyadhikaraṇa-saptamī*).
When blood has flowed out by means of leeches and the like, or when the body has been wounded by a weapon and blood has flowed out.
There is syntactic unity with the passage beginning with "the limbs" (*gātra*).
One should never recite the Ṛgveda or the Yajurveda while the sound of the Sāmaveda is being heard;
likewise, after having completed the study of the Veda, or after having studied the Āraṇyaka.
When the sound of the *sāman* is being heard, one should not recite the *ṛc*s or *yajus*s.
There is no prohibition regarding the *ṛgveda* and *yajurveda* brāhmaṇas.
Furthermore, when the *pañcaviṃśa* [stotra] is being heard, this prohibition applies to both the *ṛc*s and *yajus*s as well.
"The end of the Veda" is where the Veda reaches its conclusion, namely the end of the Mantras and the end of the Brāhmaṇas. The Āraṇyaka is a specific portion of the Veda;
having studied that, no other text should be studied.
The Ṛgveda has the gods as its deities; the Yajurveda belongs to humans;
the Sāmaveda is remembered as belonging to the ancestors; therefore, its sound is impure.
Regarding the sound of chanted *sāman* verses, it is stated that there is a suspension of Vedic study (*anadhyāya*) for the *ṛc* and *yajus*.
In this regard, the following is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): "The gods (*deva*) are its deities; thus it is 'deva-daivatyam,' meaning it is intent upon the praise of the deities."
The *ṛcas* are for the most part primarily concerned with praise;
therefore, it is said that they have the gods as their deity (*devadaivatyā*).

Since human beings are primarily characterized by action (*karman*), and since the *Yajurveda* teaches a great abundance of rituals, the *Yajurveda* is called "human" (*mānuṣa*) on account of this correspondence.
The word *mānuṣa* denotes the human species;
because of the superimposition of non-difference [between the Veda and its users], it is said that "the Yajurveda is human.
*Pitrya* means beneficial for the ancestors (*pitṛ*).
The ancestors (pitaras) are indeed its deities; thus it is heard through some connection with the word "ancestor" in whatever manner.
There are three worlds, and there are exactly three presiding authorities over them:
the gods are the deity of heaven, humans of the earth, and the ancestors of the intermediate space (antarikṣa).
Thus there are three Vedas.
Since two [of them] are stated to be connected with gods and humans, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the Sāmaveda belongs to the ancestors (*pitrya*).
Its sound is impure.
In this context, the impurity of that sound (dhvani) should not be understood as being ultimate (paramārthataḥ).
Rather, just as one must not study in the presence of impure things, so too in the presence of that [sound]; thus, the basis for impurity is the general principle.
And this prohibition of the Ṛgveda and Yajurveda applies when the Sāman is being sung, according to the context of the injunction for Vedic study, not during the performance of a sacrifice.
Knowing this, the wise daily practice the essence of the three Vedas in sequence first, and afterwards they study the Veda.

Knowing this connection with the presiding deities of the three worlds—as in the statement "The Ṛgveda has the gods as its deity," and so forth—the wise and learned first practice the essence extracted from the three Vedas, namely the Praṇava, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Sāvitrī, and subsequently study and recite the Veda according to the stated sequence. By that study of this triad, the three worlds and the three deities become encompassed.
Although this matter was already stated in the second chapter, it is repeated here again.
Just as one does not study during periods forbidden for study, so too one does not study that which has not been previously learned from the essence of the three Vedas.
If a domestic animal, a frog, a cat, a dog, a snake, a mongoose,
or a rat passes between [the teacher and the student], one should know that the study of the Veda is suspended for a day and a night.

"In the case of intervening [sex], it refers to between the teacher and the student, or among those who are studying together. "Day and night" means a full day and night. In the Gautama-smṛti, however, a three-day fast and separation from one's home are prescribed.
And regarding the study [of the Veda] in a cemetery, this very same rule applies;
however, in this case, an option is to be understood.
A twice-born man should always diligently avoid two occasions for the suspension of study:
an impure place for Vedic recitation and his own impurity.
Because of the inclusion of the term "constant" (*nitya*), there is an option regarding the occasions for non-study (*anadhyāya*) mentioned previously.

Even among those, it has already been shown that for some there is merely constancy; this applies where the term "constant" occurs or where there is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), such as "the new moon day kills the teacher.
Furthermore, the impurity of the ground consists in its contact with unclean things such as bones, female genitals, male genitals, and so forth.
But regarding the self, it will be explained in the fifth [chapter].

Even though these two [periods] are non-study periods within the context of the injunction for formal study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), they nevertheless apply to the daily obligatory recitation (*naityaka*);
for one who is impure is not entitled [to perform such rites].
And so says the Brāhmaṇa: "Of this very sacrifice there are two occasions when study is suspended: when one is personally impure, and when the place is [impure].
Furthermore, the Brahma-sacrifice is a constant recitation.
On the new moon day, the eighth, the full moon, and the fourteenth,
a twice-born Snātaka should always remain celibate, even during the fertile period.
"He should be a celibate student (*brahmacārī*).
The duty of a celibate student—namely, the abstention from sexual intercourse—is extended [to him] here, and not [other duties] such as wandering for alms;
for, due to the connection with the phrase "even during the fertile period," that very [abstention] first comes to mind.
Others, however, desire the abstention from honey and meat on these days as well;
in that regard, another Smṛti text should be cited:
"On the sixth, the eighth, the new moon, and the fourteenth of both fortnights..."
One should avoid [these acts] on the full moon day, and likewise with regard to oil, meat, sexual intercourse, and shaving.

Others, however, say that "brahmacārī" is the specific name for one belonging to a particular stage of life (āśrama). Therefore, when it is applied to a householder or others who abide in a different stage of life, it serves as an extended application (atideśa) by way of indicating the dharma intended for the acquisition of the Veda.
[The meaning is: "He should be a brahmacārī."
For a word used in reference to one thing conveys the sense of "like that" (vatyartha) when applied to another.

Since all the duties of a religious student (*brahmacārin*) would otherwise apply [to the snātaka], the explicit statements—"he should perform [the duties] such as tending the sacred fire, kindling the wood, and begging for alms until his formal return (*samāvartana*)"—and "the householder is one who eats the remnants," exclude those [student duties].
Thus, only the prohibition of honey, meat, and sexual intercourse is extended [by analogy] to him.
But since the word *brahmacārī* is well-known as referring exclusively to the cessation of sexual intercourse, this [objection] is trivial.
One should not perform a bath after eating, nor when ill, nor at midnight; nor should one bathe constantly with clothes on, nor in a body of water that is unknown.
This is not a prohibition [of bathing] because there is no possibility of performing the obligatory daily bath after having eaten;
for in another Smṛti, the sequence of activities is heard as "bathing, the great sacrifices, and eating the remnants.
Nor does it apply to bathing necessitated by touching a Caṇḍāla and so forth, because that would contradict the rule: "One should not remain impure even for a moment."
Therefore, this prohibition applies to that which is characterized by desire and serves as the cause for removing heat and the like.
An "afflicted person" (ātura) is one seized by disease;
even though he is impure, there is a total prohibition against bathing for him, because one must protect oneself from all sides [even through impurity].
What, then, is its purification?
Cleansing with mantras, sprinkling, discarding the garment, and so forth must be performed.
The "great night" (*mahāniśā*) consists of four *muhūrtas* on both sides of midnight.

As for those who explain that "great night" refers to the time such as the beginning of winter (*hemanta*), their interpretation is a misinterpretation because it contradicts the injunction for the morning bath during the months of Māgha and Phālguna.
Nor is there any authoritative basis for the claim that this is a prohibition regarding winter nights, since a second occurrence of the word "night" (*niśā*) is absent [in the text].
The phrase "with garments" (*vāsobhiḥ*) indicates by implication that the prohibition applies when there is a multiplicity of garments due to cold and similar conditions.
By one [rule], it is indeed prescribed that "one should not bathe naked";
by two [rules], there is no restriction;
and by many [rules], there is a prohibition.
A reservoir is a receptacle for water; it is "unknown" because its depth is uncertain and due to the danger of crocodiles and other such creatures; "constantly" means at all times.
One should not intentionally step upon the shadow of deities, a teacher, a king, a *snātaka*, an *ācārya*, as well as one who has brown hair or is consecrated for a sacrifice.
In this context, the "representations" (pratikṛti) are the deities, because their shadow-forms arise therein.
The "guru" is the father;
the "ācārya" is the one who performs the initiation (upanetā).
The specific mention of "distinction" (bheda) is for the purpose of removing the extension of respect [due to a maternal uncle] by analogy;
therefore, this rule does not apply to maternal uncles and the like.
Some say that because it contradicts established custom, this is not correct, and that the distinction should be understood as being like the expression "ox and bull" (govalīvarda).
*Babhru* means the tawny color;
it refers to a substance endowed with that quality.
Here, *babhru* refers either to a cow or to the Soma plant, as the word *babhru* is seen used for both in the Veda.
"Out of desire" means there is no fault if it was not preceded by conscious intent.
At midday, at midnight, after eating a śrāddha meal containing meat,
and during both twilights, one should not frequent a crossroads.

At midday, at midnight, or during the "great night" (mahāniśā), having eaten a *śrāddha* meal containing meat, one should not indulge [in sexual intercourse], nor should one remain there for a long time.
If, by some chance, while traveling to a village or elsewhere, there is no other path except through a crossroads (*catuṣpatha*), then mere contact with it is not prohibited.
Some, however, construe the particle *ca* in this manner.
Having eaten at a *śrāddha* or any other meal containing meat,
one must investigate the established custom regarding this particular relationship;
otherwise, a mediated connection cannot be established.
One should not intentionally step upon fragrant unguents, the water used for bathing, feces, urine, blood, phlegm, spittle, or vomit.
Udvartana refers to substances such as ground flour used for rubbing the body to remove oil and impurities;
apasnāna refers to water that has already been used;
and niṣṭhyūta refers to things like betel rolls which, although not in the form of phlegm, have been spat out after being consumed.
The "foundation" (adhiṣṭhāna) is that which stands upon it.
[There is] no fault if it was done intentionally or preceded by ignorance.
One should not serve an enemy, nor the companion of an enemy, nor one who is unrighteous, nor a thief, nor the wife of another.
One should never engage in sending gifts, sitting or standing together, or conversing about matters such as housing and honors with an enemy,
a foe, one who is unrighteous, a sinner, or one who lives by dishonest means, nor with a thief or a robber.
Precisely because of this specific mention of "difference," it is not every non-virtuous person who is meant; rather, it is as has been explained.
"Another's wife" means a woman.

By the use of the term *yoṣit* (woman), it is not only a legal wife (*patnī*) that is intended, but also one who is kept (*avaruddhā*), because both cause enmity and because the prohibition is based on visible faults for both parties due to their association.
Furthermore, the mention of "wife" (*dāra*) later on is for the purpose of showing an excess of invisible defects;
it is not, however, to be understood that because of a general designation as "woman" (*yoṣit*), the specific meaning of the word "wife" is understood through an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
This is not an explanatory passage for this [context].
This sentence is indeed distinct.
Indeed, there is nothing in this world so detrimental to longevity as a man's pursuit of another's wife in this life.
Eating food that causes indigestion, stealing gold, and the like—none of these are so detrimental to longevity or so destructive to one's life-span as is sexual intercourse with another's wife;
for such an act entails fault both in its visible and its invisible consequences.
One who desires prosperity should never, under any circumstances, despise a Kṣatriya, a serpent, or a learned Brāhmaṇa, even if they are weak.
Disrespect, lack of regard, absence of reverence, and contempt;
even those who are emaciated and currently unable to show affection.
For these three, when treated with contempt, may utterly consume a man;
therefore, a wise person should never hold these three in contempt.
He shall consume the man who treats them with contempt; for three things, when insulted, are capable of burning:
a Kṣatriya by his gaze and his power, a serpent by its venom, and a Brāhmaṇa by his silent prayers, burnt offerings, and invisible spiritual power.

Therefore, "these three are eternal" is the conclusion. Having first set forth the defects [of violating them], the conclusion is stated again for the sake of ensuring diligent avoidance. And from this excessive diligence, the gravity of the expiation is also inferred.
One should not despise oneself because of former failures;
until death one should seek prosperity, nor should one consider it unattainable.
Failure is the lack of success regarding wealth and so forth at the time of acquiring wealth through agriculture and other means.

In that situation, one should not despise oneself by thinking, "I am unfortunate and devoid of merit; I have not obtained wealth on this occasion, so how shall I obtain it at another time? One should not harbor such despondency.
Until death, one should seek prosperity.
Until the final breath, one who desires to acquire wealth must not abandon it;
nor should one consider this prosperity difficult to attain.
Thinking, "My resolve will certainly succeed," one should proceed toward its acquisition without taking into account unfavorable planetary positions or other such obstacles.
There is a well-spoken verse by someone:
"The base count upon the positions of the planets [as fate], neglecting human effort; for those incapable of exertion, nothing is impossible for the persevering."
By this, he shows the following:

one who thinks, "I am not in a miserable state; since wealth is obtainable through the afflictions [of ritual labor], I am not authorized for the establishment of the sacred fires and so forth; therefore, I have escaped the affliction of performing the *agnihotra* sacrifice"—such a person does not think correctly.
Therefore, one should strive for that purpose.
One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak a truth that is unpleasant;
nor should one speak a pleasant falsehood—this is the eternal dharma.
Speech employed for a purpose is restricted to truth;
one should speak what is true according to what has been seen and heard, and that which is pleasant.
This is the second rule:
the recounting of another's qualities, such as nobility and so forth, even on some occasion when one has not seen them oneself;
likewise, [the announcement] regarding the birth of a son and so on—such as "O Brahmin, a son has been born to you"—should be spoken truthfully, even if it serves no purpose of one's own.
If that [truth] were not known to him,
there would be something true, whether pleasant or unpleasant;
thus, the son of a Brahmin showed what was pleasant, and so forth.

O Brāhmaṇa, just as one should not speak an unpleasant truth— such as "your daughter is pregnant"— even though that pregnancy of the daughter is a fact, it must not be disclosed because it is unpleasant;
rather, when there is another way, one should remain silent.
"Surely, out of affection, one should say 'she is not pregnant' when she is pregnant; therefore, he says: 'And one should not speak an untruth that is disagreeable.
Thus, he who has had the first direct realization is not permitted to remain silent regarding it;
this is the eternal law."
The Veda is eternal and constant; because it is ordained by that [Veda], Dharma is also eternal.
One should say "bhadraṃ bhadram" (well-being, well-being) or simply say "bhadram" (well-being);
one should not engage in dry enmity or dispute with anyone.

In this context, they explain the elision of the negative particle (*nañ*) in the first instance of the word "bhadra" as follows: one should say that what is "not auspicious" (*abhadra*) is "auspicious" (*bhadra*).
The use of the particle *iti* is for the purpose of illustration.
Established words such as *kalyāṇam*, *maṅgalam*, *siddham*, and *śreyaḥ* should be employed.
Even if the preceding word is intended merely for illustration, expressions such as "one with sight" for a blind person or "one who is wise" for a fool are thereby obtained.
Alternatively, the word *bhadram* itself should be used in such instances.
One should not engage in "dry hostility"— that is, boastful speech devoid of any purpose such as wealth or other interests.
In this way, a dispute in a royal court becomes merely "dry" and so forth,
even if it is initiated by someone who is incompetent.
One should not travel too early in the morning, nor too late in the evening, nor when it is high noon;
one should not travel with an unknown person, nor alone, nor with outcastes.
The word *atikalya* refers to the break of dawn; one should not go out at that time.
At *atisāya*, the time of the evening twilight, one should not travel with an unknown man, nor should one go without a companion, especially with *vṛṣalas* or *śūdras*.
One should not despise those who have missing limbs or extra limbs, those deficient in learning, those advanced in age, those lacking beauty or wealth, or those of low birth.
Those with deficient limbs are those such as the one-eyed, the leprous, the humpbacked, and so forth.
Those with redundant limbs are those who have an excess of body parts, such as those suffering from elephantiasis and the like.
Those devoid of learning are fools.
Those who have passed beyond their youth are extremely aged;
those devoid of beauty have deformed features, such as being flat-nosed or one-eyed;
and those devoid of wealth are poor.
"Deprived of wealth" means lacking or excluded from riches; "deprived by birth" refers to those of low birth, such as the *kuṇḍas*, *golakas*, and others;
one should not revile them.
"Reproach" (ākṣepa) means contempt.
For these [persons], the very act of addressing them with these words constitutes contempt.
A Brahmin who is impure from eating should not touch a cow, a Brahmin, or fire with his hand;
nor, while in good health, should he look at the hosts of luminaries in the sky while remaining impure.

"Ucchiṣṭa" refers here to one who has eaten without having sipped water (anācānta), or one who has voided urine or feces; indeed, the word "ucchiṣṭa" denotes merely that which is impure. Thus, the touching of cows and other such beings by one who is *ucchiṣṭa* is prohibited.
By the word "impure" (aśuci), he will later describe the expiation (prāyaścitta). The mention of "limbs" (prāṇi) is not restrictive;
contact with another part of the body is also not permitted.
There is no prohibition against [seeing] when it is screened by clothing or other such things. One should not look at the host of luminaries in the sky;
one must be healthy and not afflicted by illness.
Because of the statement "in the sky," there is no prohibition of the light on earth, namely fire.
Having touched these while impure, one should always touch the vital breaths with water,
as well as all the limbs and the navel with the palm of the hand.
Even though the term is used without qualification, the "vital breaths" (prāṇas) are said to be specifically those located in the head, such as the eyes and so forth;
for the word *prāṇa* is seen in the Veda, in the *Prāṇasaṃbhava Upaniṣad*, as denoting the eyes and other sense organs.
The "limbs" (*gātrāṇi*) refer to the shoulders, knees, feet, and so on.
Having taken water with the palm of the hand, one should touch [the body].
Unless he is ill, he should not touch his own orifices without a specific reason,
and he should avoid touching all the hairs of his private parts.
Without a specific cause, such as the need for scratching,
one should not touch one's own cavities— the apertures of the eyes and so forth—
nor should one avoid those secret parts located in the armpits and the genitals by means of the ordinary act of touching.
The employment of another verb is for the sake of completing the verse;
others, however, say that by the mention of another verb, the act of seeing is prohibited.
He should be devoted to auspicious conduct, self-restrained, and have his senses conquered;
he should constantly recite prayers and offer oblations into the fire without weariness.
Auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is the attainment of desired longevity, wealth, and so forth.

For that purpose, one should always be devoted to practicing auspicious conduct (*maṅgalācāra*), which consists of touching yellow pigment (*gorocanā*), forehead marks (*tilaka*), auspicious fruits, and the like; being endowed with such [conduct], one should be constantly intent upon its practice.
Now, it has already been stated that conduct is indeed an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
True;
by this, an unseen purpose is stated.
For if [the practice] were performed with the notion that it is seen [in its results], someone might become indifferent due to observing its failure.
To that end, it is stated again:

for instance, at the time of departure, when one is close to setting out, there is the mention of saluting curds and the like, seeing white garments, the cry of a *kapiñjala* bird to the right, or a crow on a fruit-bearing tree to the right—such things as these should be observed for the sake of auspiciousness, while the opposite should be avoided.
One who has conquered the senses is free from longing for sense objects.
Although this has been stated more than once for the sake of human purpose, it is stated again here to prevent a lapse in practice.
Since an oblation can be performed in a place other than the fire, he says "he should sacrifice into the fire";
the term "unwearied" is a restatement of what was already mentioned.
For those who are endowed with auspicious conduct, who are always self-restrained,
and who constantly engage in recitation and burnt offerings, no misfortune exists.
Misfortune— consisting of natural inauspicious omens, calamities sent by fate, disease, loss of wealth, separation from loved ones, and so forth—
is thus averted for those who follow these auspicious practices.
By this, too, their permanence is affirmed, even though they serve the purpose of producing specific results.
For no one seeks the cessation of calamities caused by fate;
therefore, the mention of "constantly" (*nitya*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Even if someone were to seek it, this injunction would still apply constantly.
And thus, its purpose is twofold: the performance of one's eternal duties and the cessation of falling into ruin.
One should constantly recite the Veda at the proper times without weariness;
for they declare that to be his supreme duty, while any other is called a secondary duty.
It has been stated that "one should both recite and offer oblations.
In that regard, he first states the means for the recitation: "One should recite the Veda itself";
the remainder is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
"At the proper time" means at whichever time [is appropriate]; this is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in a distributive sense (*vīpsā*).
For one should recite the mantra at the very moment that worldly activity does not interfere.
Other rites, such as the Agnihotra and others, have fixed times;
however, for the recitation of prayers (japa), purity alone is the time.
This is the primary duty.
*Upadharma*:
"near to dharma" (*dharmasya samīpe upadharmaḥ*).
This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound in which the proximity is the predominant factor, not an *avyayībhāva*.
According to the rule "comparisons [are formed] with words expressing common properties" (*upamānāni sāmānyavacanaiḥ*), just as in the case of the example:
the censure of other religious duties is for the purpose of praising the recitation of the Veda, not for the purpose of prohibiting it.
Through constant study of the Vedas, through purity, through austerity,
and through non-injury toward living beings, one remembers one's former birth.
Non-malice is non-violence.
"Beings" refers to those that are stationary and those that move.
These four practices, which result in the recollection of past lives, are to be performed throughout one's entire life.
Birth (jāti) is another existence;
it is the former state of being (pūrvabhava).
Remembering his former birth, the twice-born practices the Brahman;
and through the constant practice of the Brahman, he enjoys infinite bliss.
Now, one who desires a desired fruit strives for everything;
yet, the recollection of past lives is not invariably pleasant such that it could be described as the fruit of the fourfold practice beginning with the study of the Vedas.
To this he says: remembering his former birth, he knows Brahman, studies it, and becomes full of faith therein.
Such is the practice of Brahman by which one remembers a previous birth;
remembering it, one again engages in that practice.
And from that practice cultivated over many births, there follows the bliss characterized by the attainment of Brahman.
He attains—that is, reaches—an eternal state from which there is no return.
By the word "infinite" (ananta), a specific kind of bliss is indicated: the soul's complete satisfaction that requires no further means. This eternity is established by the term "eternal" (ajasra).
Such happiness is attained, and it does not diminish.
Although the meanings are the same, they are not redundant,
just as in the expression "carrying vṛttaka and purīṣa," where *vṛttaka* refers to water and *purīṣa* to excrement.
In this context, one is a conventional term (rūḍha) and the other is an etymological term (kriyā-śabda):
*purīṣa* means that which is capable of filling (*pūraṇa-samartha*), while *vṛttaka* means water.
One should constantly perform the Sāvitra and Śānti oblations on the Parvan days;
and one should always worship the ancestors on the Aṣṭakā and Anvaṣṭakā days.
The nature of the previously mentioned oblations is now stated:
they are dedicated to Savitṛ (sāvitrāḥ), having Savitṛ as their deity,
and they are to be performed on the festival days of the full moon and the new moon.
The *homa* offerings are for the purpose of pacification, having the objective of averting what is undesirable.

Furthermore, regarding the substance, it is heard in all *homa* rites where no specific substance is prescribed that "the clarified butter (*ājya*) which is taken in the *dhruvā* vessel is indeed for the sake of this entire sacrifice.
Moreover, the locative case in the word "on the joints" (*parvasu*) should be understood as having the sense of the accusative.
Fire is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the oblation (*homa*), but it is never the object (*karman*).
The items to be offered are recited as fried grain, clarified butter, meat, parched barley flour, curd, milk, parched grain, ground flour, and so forth;
and these oblations are *apūrva* (unprecedented).
Whatever procedure (*itikartavyatā*) follows from the customary practice has been shown previously.

Regarding the *aṣṭakā* rites: after the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī, there are the three eighth days of the dark fortnights; according to some, these are the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the winter and cool seasons (*hemanta-śiśira*), as stated in the traditional texts.
Therein, one should honor the ancestors with a *śrāddha*.
The word *pitṛ* refers to one's deceased father and ancestors;
the *anvaṣṭakās* are those same [days], namely the ninth lunar days.
One should perform the voiding of urine at a distance from the dwelling, as well as the washing of the feet and the disposal of the remains of food, keeping them far away indeed.
That by which the feet are sprinkled, such as water and so forth, is "foot-sprinkling" (pādāvasecana);
one should throw that away from a distance.
Alternatively, one should perform the washing of the feet itself at a distance.
*Niṣeka* means sprinkling (*pariṣeka*).
Even water used for bathing with oil and other substances can be designated by the term *niṣeka*.
This refers to the casting away at a distance of that which remains after use and is to be discarded.
For that is more commonly known by the term "niṣeka" (conception).
One should perform the preparation of unguents, bathing, cleaning the teeth, applying collyrium,
and the worship of the deities during the very morning.
In the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) praising the limbs of the sacrificial animal, it is heard [in the Veda]: "The anus is Mitra.
Therefore, here too, by means of figurative identification (*abhedopacāra*), Mitra is the anus; purity pertaining to that is *maitra*.
Adornment (*prasādhana*) refers to the dressing of the hair, anointing with unguents, and so forth.
Alternatively, the method for purifying the qualifier and the qualified terms is as follows:
even if one has not defecated, one must perform the washing of the anus in the morning.

Just as rinsing the mouth is prescribed because the flow of saliva and such is inevitable for one who has slept, so too this washing of the mouth and the lower parts of the body must necessarily be performed, even without a specific cause.
Others, however, say that *maitra* (the duty toward friends) consists of performing what is beneficial for friends; this should be performed even before all other internal duties.
Furthermore, since there is not even a moment’s delay for one who is impure, its priority should be understood in relation to one's own personal tasks.
In that case, the term "forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇa*) is intended merely to indicate priority over other duties, and not to exclude the afternoon.
Alternatively, Mitra is Āditya;
thus, the worship of him is "maitra" (pertaining to Mitra).
On the sacred festival days (parvan), he should visit the deities, righteous and most excellent brahmins, the Lord for the sake of protection, and his teachers.
One should salute the elders, offer them one's own seat,
wait upon them with palms joined in reverence, and follow behind them as they depart.
One should, with vigilance, always practice the conduct of the virtuous, which is the root of dharma, properly established in one's own duties as proclaimed by the Śruti and Smṛti.
For through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct, desired offspring;
through right conduct, inexhaustible wealth; and right conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
Nor is this person, endowed with qualities such as learning, being established [as the object of the rite];
for these qualities are sought after by the subjects.
Thus it has been said:
What is done with that cow which is neither a milch-cow nor pregnant?
What is the purpose of a son being born who is neither learned nor righteous?
Even that which is inexhaustible and abundant— meaning that which cannot be exhausted even by improper calamities—
and even that which is "markless," such as moles or spots upon the aggregates (the body) that indicate misfortune such as poverty,
conduct destroys even that.
For by being devoted to such conduct, unrighteousness is destroyed.
For a man of evil conduct is censured in the world;
he constantly partakes in suffering, being diseased and short-lived as well.
Even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks, the man who possesses good conduct,
is full of faith, and is free from envy, lives for a hundred years.
Whatever action depends on another, that one should avoid with effort;
whatever depends on oneself, however, that one should practice with diligence.

That which is performed for the benefit of oneself and others through the solicitation of another is avoided as being dependent on others; however, this does not apply to activities such as officiating as a priest (*ārtvijya*), which are accomplished through one's own livelihood (*vṛtti*).
For that is indeed under one's own control.
It is precisely with regard to such matters that the hiring of servants and the like is undertaken.

Nor does this [text] prohibit even that which is dependent on others for one who has been initiated, because it is improper for a Smṛti to subvert a Śruti, and because the Smṛti has its scope in the matter already mentioned.
However, that which is under one's own control—even if it be a very small amount of wealth—one should personally perform the act of helping others, however slight that help may be.
When obligatory duties cannot be fulfilled and there is no wealth available for the maintenance of one's family, begging must indeed be performed, provided there is no other means available.
"Rather, I shall sacrifice specifically, I shall give specifically"—this is his intended meaning:
that even when some measure of wealth exists, one should remain devoted to contentment.
Everything dependent on another is suffering; everything dependent on oneself is happiness.
One should know this, in brief, to be the defining characteristic of happiness and suffering.
He censures begging:
"Whatever is dependent on others is entirely suffering.
Let alone standing at the door of another's house; even following after them is a wandering both in this world and the next."
As for that which you said—
that even at the mere thought of begging, my heart does not endure—
it is surely no doubt a creation of Māyā, and not the work of the Self-born Creator himself.
In brief, this is the definition of suffering: whatever there is of begging;
and this is happiness: the absence of longing.
Whatever action one performs that brings satisfaction to one's inner self, that one should perform with effort; but one should avoid the opposite.
The repetition of "satisfaction of the self," which was mentioned previously, is for the purpose of recollection;
its object is indeed perception.
That action which, when being performed, does not give rise to hesitation or doubt—that is what should be done.
But that in which the heart finds no satisfaction should be avoided.
One should not harm one's teacher, a lecturer, a father, a mother, a preceptor, Brahmins, cows, or any ascetics whatsoever.
The *ācārya* is the one who initiates [the student];
the *pravaktṛ*, *adhyāpaka*, and *vyākhyātṛ* are the instructors;
and the *guru* is someone other than those two, such as a paternal uncle, a maternal uncle, or the like.
The term "all" (*sarva*) is used to include all ascetics engaged in penance as well as even those who have committed sins;
for there, the harming of all living beings without distinction has been prohibited in various contexts.
Some maintain that the repetition [of the prohibition] is for the purpose of excluding even *ātatāyin* assailants from the rule regarding teachers and others;

however, the passage beginning with "But one who [kills] a teacher, or a child, or an elderly person" is an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) serving as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to this very point.
But the Teacher (*Upādhyāya*) says:
This is not a prohibition;
rather, this is a restrictive exclusion (paryudāsa) intended to enjoin a specific intention, similar to the rule: "One should not look at the rising sun."
Therefore, when effort has been exerted, this constitutes a prohibition of the intention (*saṃkalpa*).
Alternatively, speaking ill is indeed violence (*hiṃsā*), as seen from the usage: "He struck her with various words.
Or else, the root *han* is employed in the sense of performing an adverse action.
One should avoid atheism, reviling the Vedas, and disparaging the deities;
one should also avoid hatred, arrogance, pride, anger, and harshness.
Nihilism (*nāstikya*) consists in the determination that the objects established by the authority of the Vedas are false.
Censure (*nindā*) is the presentation [of those objects] through words [with the intent of disparagement].

This occurs when, due to a defect in one's disposition—not as a formal dialectical objection (*pūrvapakṣa*)—one says: "The Veda is self-contradictory; there is no truth here. Regarding tautology (*punarukta*), it is likewise [a defect arising from such a disposition].

The deities are Agni and the others; their "insult" (*kutsanam*) is indeed censure (*nindā*). Just as people say of fate, "We have been struck down by a cursed fate," so it is with regard to the gods. "Hatred" (*dveṣaḥ*) is a lack of affection caused by envy and other such motives.
Stambha is inflexibility due to egoism;
māna is egoism as self-conceit, such as thinking "I am learned" or "I am wealthy";
amarṣa is anger, which is harshness and severity.
Anger is that which is preceded by hatred.
One should not raise a stick against another, nor, when angry, should one strike them down;
except for a son or a pupil, whom one may strike for the sake of correction.
That by which one is subdued is "punishment" (*daṇḍa*), such as the hand, a stick, a whip, a rope, or a split bamboo cane.
Being angry, one should not exert it against another, nor should one brandish it;
for the purpose of striking, one should not even cast it obliquely.
"Throwing down" means bringing them into contact with one's body with force.

One may strike the son and the pupil with the heel, a bamboo splinter, or an open hand-palm, as will be explained in the eighth chapter, but not with a staff. And these should not be done out of anger; rather, they are for the sake of correction and instruction, in case they act restlessly out of childishness.
Just as [the ears] behind the body, they should be struck slightly.
The mention of "pupils" is intended to include female and male slaves as well, because their function is the same.
A twice-born man who merely threatens a Brahmin with the intent to kill him wanders for a hundred years in the Tāmisra hell.

Since beating is prohibited without distinction regarding all objects, these five verses are intended to show the excessive gravity of the fault in performing that act against a Brāhmaṇa. Having "threatened"—that is, having merely raised a staff or similar object with the intent to kill or the desire to strike, even without actually letting it fall—one is cooked in hell for a hundred years; one revolves there, experiencing the fruit of that action.
Having intentionally struck [another] out of anger even with a blade of grass,
one is born for twenty-one lifetimes in states of woe.
"Aggression" means an outburst of anger, not in jest;
it is done intentionally.
"Twenty-one births."
*Jāti* means birth;
the suffix *-āka* is meaningless, as in the word *pralambaka*.
"Birthplaces of the wicked" refers to animals in the animal realm who experience abundant suffering.
Let alone objects such as a staff that cause immediate pain;
even from being struck with a blade of grass, there is the experience of hell for a long duration.
A man who, through lack of wisdom, causes blood to flow from the body of a Brahmin who is not fighting, incurs very great suffering after death.
"Blood" means red blood;
that which one causes to flow from limb after limb of a Brāhmaṇa by striking him with a sword or similar weapon while he is not fighting—
provided he is not desiring to fight according to the duty of a Kṣatriya, like the teacher Droṇa.
"Very great suffering in another birth after death, such as in hell," is a restatement [of the fact] that this results from a lack of wisdom;
for a wise person, through knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures, would never act in such a manner.
For as many particles of dust as the blood takes up from the surface of the earth,
for that many years shall the shedder of that blood be devoured by others in the next world.
In the case of a slight blow, the aforementioned fruit [of merit] is attained.

But if the blow is more severe, then for as many years—as many as the number of particles of dust, ash, or fragments of soil that the blood falling from the body of the Brahmin onto the ground collects—the perpetrator who sheds that blood shall be devoured by dogs and jackals in the next world, the hereafter.
Therefore, a learned man should never even threaten a twice-born person;
he should not strike him even with a blade of grass, nor should he cause blood to flow from his body.
This is a summary of the preceding rule prohibiting the three actions, which concerns the lifting and lowering [of weapons];
the meaning is that one must never do so, even in times of distress.
For that man who is unrighteous, whose wealth is based on falsehood,
and who always delights in violence— this one does not prosper in happiness here.
This is a general supplement to the prohibition against all violence:
unrighteousness (*adharma*) consists of acts forbidden by the scriptures, such as approaching women who should not be approached; one who practices that is an unrighteous person (*adhārmika*).
Furthermore, for whom falsehood itself is wealth.
He who, having spoken untruthly in witness-giving, legal adjudication, and the like, acquires wealth through bribery;
and he who, delighting in violence, being intent on harming others either due to a persistent enmity or for the sake of material gain—
neither of these prospers in happiness, nor does he attain happiness in this world.
Even if he suffers for his righteousness, he should not turn his mind toward unrighteousness,
seeing quickly the reversal that befalls those who act unrighteously and commit evil.
Dharma is the standard of the scriptures;
conducting oneself according to it, even if one suffers or meets with distress, one should not set the mind upon unrighteousness.

For although unrighteous people may be seen to possess great wealth through theft, bribery, deceit, and the like, nevertheless their downfall is soon observed, such as the loss of their wealth and other misfortunes.
Therefore, one should not deviate from the Dharma.
Having become a friend, he has shown the matter as it was perceived. Now he states the meaning of the scripture:
"An unrighteous act committed in this world does not bear fruit immediately, like a cow."
But turning back slowly, it cuts away the very roots of the doer.
This is said because the times for the results of Vedic actions—whether auspicious or inauspicious—are indefinite.

Unrighteousness (adharma), when practiced or performed, does not bear fruit immediately; it does not yield its result at once. For in the Veda, it is heard that the results of prescribed and prohibited actions consist solely of pleasure and pain.
However, no specific time is understood [from the injunction].

For the function of the sentence, even when intent upon making known what is to be done (*kartavyatā*), culminates merely in the cognition of the connection between the ritual action and its fruit; it does not imply a specific time for those actions that possess fruits.
As for obligatory (*nitya*) rites, however, their duty to be performed does not arise from a fruit.

Even in the case of avoiding what is prohibited, one who desires the cessation of the sufferings of hell and so forth has no entitlement [to perform such acts] other than by virtue of the prohibitions in the scripture.
That prohibition, however, makes known that the performance of what is prohibited results in suffering.
To explain this more precisely would entail excessive prolixity; therefore, we shall desist.
"Like a cow.
This is an illustration by way of similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
Just as the earth, when sown with seeds, does not immediately become possessed of various crops, but rather depends upon ripening—such is the similarity (*sādharmya*) of Vedic action.

Also by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*): just as a cow or a beast yields fruit immediately through carrying or milking, so it is not with merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). The mention of "demerit" is for the purpose of demonstrating that there is no fixed rule regarding the time when merit also bestows its fruit. "Being turned around" means being accumulated over time.
It "cuts off," that is, severs, the roots of the agent who performs what is forbidden. By the severing of the roots, the total destruction of everything is indicated;
just as trees and other stationary beings do not grow again once their roots are cut, so it is for those who commit unrighteous acts.
If it does not bear fruit for oneself, then for one's sons; if not for the sons, then for one's grandsons; but an unrighteous act committed never fails to produce its result for the doer.

This is improper: that it is said the fruit of an action performed by one person goes to another. Vedic actions yield their fruit to the agent; the principle of Vaiśvānara does not apply here, because there is no scriptural statement [to that effect].
Indeed, the state of being for the sake of sons and so forth is not heard [in the scripture] here.
True;
yet when a son is being tormented, the father who is afflicted experiences even greater suffering.
Therefore, suffering belongs to the doer alone.
It is not contradictory that even for a son, that fruit [of suffering] arises from his own previously committed karma in a former body;
the same should be understood regarding grandsons as well.
"Grandsons" refers to the sons of one's sons.
Since the *saṃhitā* (the phonetic combination) is the same for "adharma" as it is for "dharma," both dharma and adharma are included [in the compound].
One prospers through unrighteousness for a time, then sees auspicious things;
thereafter one conquers one's rivals, but finally perishes along with one's very roots.
He prospers— that is, he attains growth— through unrighteous means such as treachery against his master;
at that very time,
having acquired wealth or a village, he then beholds and experiences auspicious things characterized by the abundance of many servants, cattle, horses, and so forth.

Consequently, one conquers and overcomes rivals and enemies who are impoverished; however, those established in the Dharma, being free from any crookedness, do not suffer from such [defeat]. Therefore, for them, the very word "poverty" is a defeat in terms of sovereignty.
And having existed thus for some time, they are uprooted along with their roots—along with their sons, kinsmen, wealth, and relatives—and utterly destroyed.
Therefore, the Dharma must not be abandoned.
One should always take delight in truth, righteousness, noble conduct, and purity;
and one should instruct disciples in accordance with dharma, restraining speech, arms, and belly.
Truth (*satya*) is the state of speaking of things exactly as they have been perceived.
Dharma consists of injunctions and prohibitions within the domain of the revealed scripture (*śruti*).
Although truth possesses that same nature, its separate mention by the Veda is for the sake of emphasizing its excellence.
Untruth is inherent in the nature of men;
therefore, it is repeatedly prohibited with great effort.
Noble conduct (*āryavṛtta*) is right behavior (*sadācāra*).
The noble ones are the refined; their conduct is their practice. One should take delight therein; "delight" means complete satisfaction.
In these matters, contentment is enjoined by this [rule].
Having observed other such practices as well, one should cultivate serenity of mind.
Furthermore, disciples—namely wives, sons, slaves, and students—are to be instructed according to the Dharma.
The qualities beginning with "behind the body" and so forth [are the following]:
being restrained in speech, arms, and stomach;
and being moderate in speech, whether there is a purpose or not, which constitutes restraint of speech (*vāk-saṃyama*).

Restraint of the arms is the non-inflicting of harm upon anyone by relying on the strength of one's arms. Restraint of the belly is the absence of gluttony (*anaudarikatā*), which is the state of not eating excessively.
Gluttony (*audarikatā*) is excessive eating; it is characterized by a craving for specific delicacies and eating frequently at the houses of others.
"Even though a point has already been stated, it is stated again; for that which is beneficial should be spoken of many times"—this is the resolution of the charge of tautology in all cases.
One should abandon wealth and pleasure if they are devoid of righteousness, and one should also abandon righteousness if it results in future suffering and is censured by the world.
The threefold aggregate of human goals (*puruṣārtha*) has been described.

Someone, considering them to be equal, might object: "Just as Dharma is practiced by setting aside wealth (*artha*) and pleasure (*kāma*), so too is there Dharma that is opposed to them, such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and others.

For that [Dharma] is opposed to wealth because of the giving of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and the like, and it is opposed to pleasure because of the injunction of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for one who is consecrated."
In this way, one should not pursue even wealth and pleasure if they involve the abandonment of Dharma.

Regarding the rule "one should not harm living beings," where desire for something involves violence resulting in a continuous chain of enmity, that [rule] serves to prohibit such an object. However, where both wealth and pleasure are sought through the harming of someone, some might argue that there is no fault of violence; it is to dispel such a misconception that this is stated:
one should abandon or avoid such wealth and pleasure where there is a conflict with Dharma.
Having thus stated that dharma is more powerful than everything else, he says that even it must be avoided in certain circumstances: "And [one should avoid] dharma that results in unhappiness.

*Udarka* means the subsequent time; that for which this [subsequent result] is unhappy—such as when one gives away all one's possessions out of the thought, "This man is righteous and possesses great merit," or when one performs a ritual bath at riverbanks or secluded spots because many common people see it there.
Such bathing occurs for the sake of material gain, whereas the expectation of being seen while acquiring merit is for the sake of gaining a reputation for being virtuous.
And as for giving to those who are like crows at a sacred ford (*tīrthaka*):

such a gift is indeed a *dharma*, because it serves to establish one's reputation as a donor; yet it differs from [giving to] them [in its merit]. Alternatively, that which the world censures as blameworthy—such as the killing of a cow, which is not to be slain, and the eating of its meat—is even more reprehensible in the world than [the killing of] other animals.
Furthermore, this prohibition is based on a visible foundation, like the prohibition against touching a snake.

Thinking "this matter has been enjoined," common people—lacking in learning and unaware of the truth—would proclaim the unrighteousness of the sacrificer; and because of their great number, even the learned, failing to understand that the basis for this [prohibition] is well-established, would likewise avoid him.
Thus it is said: "When the king is righteous... and so forth.

This has been stated and explained by the predecessors; thus it is understood that it is not logical for a Smṛti to annul what is enjoined by a directly perceived Śruti. However, this following example is more appropriate.
The practice of *niyoga* (levirate), though ordained by the *Smṛti*, is not performed because it is censured by the world.

Likewise, when someone supports a young woman who has no protector out of compassion, if there is apprehension regarding public censure—thinking, "He finds her desirable precisely because she is a woman"—that is a practice censured by the world.
One should not be fickle with hands or feet, nor fickle with the eyes, nor crooked; one should likewise not be fickle with speech, nor have a mind intent on deeds that harm others.
"Fickle with hands and feet":

the compound is formed by means of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) following the rule for the third case (*tṛtīyā*). And "fickleness" consists in the grasping and moving away of objects, even those not currently being used by the hand.
One should not engage in visual fickleness, such as gazing at the wives of others or looking at paintings,
nor should one form the intention to perform actions intended to harm others.
By that path by which his fathers have gone, and by which his grandfathers have gone—by that path of the virtuous he should go; going by that, he does not come to harm.

Whatever practice has been performed by one's father and others, with whom affection was cultivated, with whom the marriage of daughters and so forth was contracted, and whichever Vedic branch was studied—that very path is to be followed.
Acting in this way, one does not come to harm, is not oppressed, and is not censured in the world.
Others, however, say that for the ignorant, this is merely a means among human duties such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and the like, like the royal drum for the Mlecchas and others.
The Agnihotra and other such rites, however, depend solely upon their own specific cognitions.
Here, they raise an objection:
if a practice performed by one's ancestors and so forth is without a foundation, how can it possess the nature of Dharma?
If there is a source [for the practice], then that will apply to the son as well; what is the use of mentioning the father and others?
This objection has already been answered by the statement that "this is an instruction for the ignorant who do not know the source.

Others, however, say that where doubt does not cease even when investigating with great care, and where the meaning of the sentence can be understood in two ways, one should follow the path practiced by the fathers and others.
This too must be considered:
for there is no such thing as a means of valid cognition that is eternally doubtful;
indeed, a sentence must necessarily be fixed upon a single meaning.
Or, among those things conceptualized as objects, one should follow the conduct practiced by one's father and others, because others have practiced it;
thus he says "the path of the virtuous.
This means that if some unrighteousness was previously practiced by one's father, grandfather, or others in any way, it is not to be resorted to; hence he says "the path of the virtuous."
With officiating priests, family chaplains, and teachers; with maternal uncles, guests, and dependents; with children, the elderly, and the sick; and with physicians, kinsmen, relatives, and friends.
One should not engage in dispute with one's mother or father, sisters, brothers, sons, wife, daughters, or the group of servants.
"One should not associate" is to be connected with each [term].
"Dependents" refers to those who have come for refuge and live off one's support.
"Physicians" refers to the learned or medical practitioners.
Relatives (*jñātayaḥ*) are those on the father’s side;
kinsmen (*saṃbandhinaḥ*) are those related by marriage; and blood relations (*bāndhavāḥ*) are those on the mother’s side, such as the daughter of one’s mother’s sister and so forth.
"Jāmayah" refers to sisters and those living in one's own household.
"Vivādaḥ" means conflict, opposition, or hostile behavior, as well as verbal quarreling.
One should not engage in these with them.
By abandoning disputes concerning these, one is liberated from all sins;
and by conquering these, a householder conquers all these worlds.
Whatever sinful connection arises from these disputes being engaged in, the non-doer has no connection with it;
thus it is said that "he is liberated from all sins.
Furthermore, the statement that "by conquering and disregarding these, he conquers and appropriates all worlds" is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
The teacher is the lord of the world of Brahmā; the father is the master of the world of Prajāpati;
the guest is the lord of the world of Indra; and the officiating priests are the lords of the world of the gods.
The teacher is the lord and master of the world of Brahmā; when he is satisfied, the world of Brahmā is attained. Therefore, by virtue of his qualities, he is called the Lord of the World of Brahmā.
In the world of Prajāpati, the father is the master.

Sisters-in-law are in the world of the Apsarases; kinsmen are in the world of the Viśvedevas; relatives are indeed in the world of the Waters; and one's mother and maternal uncle are in the world of the Earth.
The young, the old, the emaciated, and the afflicted should be known as lords of space;
an elder brother is equal to a father, and one's wife and son are one's own body.
The wife and son are one's own body, one's very own physical frame; the shadow, the group of servants, and the daughter are likewise. The son-in-law is the ultimate object of pity.
Therefore, one should always endure being insulted by these without any feverish agitation.
The circle of servants is one's own shadow;
just as a shadow is constantly following and is not an object of anger, so too is the circle of servants.
A daughter is pitiable, to be commiserated with, and worthy of compassion.
Being reviled by these aforementioned harsh words, being dragged down, and being provoked to anger, he should endure—that is, he should be patient.
"Free from fever" means one in whom fever does not exist; and by the absence of fever, the lack of agitation in the mind is indicated.
For just as there is agitation of the mind in one who is feverish, so it is for one who is angry.
Alternatively, there is another reading: *asaṃjvaraḥ*.
*Saṃjvara* means feverish distress;
that is negated by the negative particle *nañ*.
Even if one is capable of receiving gifts, one should avoid attachment to them;
for by accepting gifts, one's spiritual luster (brāhmaṃ tejaḥ) is quickly extinguished.
What is obtained from another person prompted by an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is "acceptance" (*pratigraha*).
In that regard, even if one is capable—that is, competent—one should avoid "prolixity," meaning further engagement.
Competence consists of the perfection of learning, study, and virtuous conduct, as well as knowledge of the substances and the ritual procedures.
Therefore, although it has already been stated that "the ignorant man should be afraid," this is repeated here for the sake of what follows.
He shows this:
"Without knowing the lawful rule regarding the acceptance of material gifts,
a wise man should not accept them, even if he is perishing from hunger."
One should not accept gifts for the sake of enjoying sensual pleasures and the like without discernment.
What is meant by this is that one may accept gifts for the maintenance of one's own family and for the fulfillment of obligatory duties, but not otherwise;
even if one is perishing from hunger, one should not accept gifts, even if by so doing one undergoes distress.
"Emaciation" (avasāda) is the lack of growth of the body;
alternatively, the connection is made as "the righteous rule regarding the acceptance of substances.
What, then, is that righteous rule?
Having understood the righteous purpose, the mantras for receiving gifts, and the deities of the various substances—such as "gold for Agni," "a cow for Rudra," and so forth.
He states the excessive fault incurred by an ignorant person in accepting specific types of gifts:
"But an ignorant man who accepts gold, land, a horse, a cow, food, clothing, sesame seeds, or clarified butter is reduced to ashes like wood."
"He becomes reduced to ashes like wood.
Just as wood burnt by fire is reduced to ashes, so too a Brahmin who is not endowed with knowledge becomes reduced to ashes when accepting these substances, such as gold and the like.

Gold, life-span, and food; land, a cow, and likewise fuel that nourishes the body; a horse, sight, and skin; clothing, ghee, splendor, sesame seeds, and offspring—[these are the rewards for giving these things].

The earth and the cow burn—that is, consume—the body, which is the physical frame; gold [burns] life, where there is a transformation of the grammatical case, and "it burns" must be supplied as the verb. In the same way, the verb must be supplied in the phrases "the horse [burns] the eye," and so forth.
But a twice-born man who is without self-restraint, who does not study the Vedas, and who delights in accepting gifts,
sinks along with that very recipient, just like one in water using a stone as a raft.
He who possesses no austerity,
who does not study nor cause others to study—
by the mention of "study," learning as such is indicated.
When both this knowledge and austerity are combined, they serve as the cause for the qualification to receive gifts.
One who has fallen away from both qualities yet still desires to receive gifts sinks down and goes to the lower realms along with that gift.
Along with whom?
Since no other [recipient] is specified and the donor is present, it is understood that [the gift is given] "together with him.
The recipient relies upon him as one would rely on a raft for the sake of crossing over oneself.
However, one who is such an unworthy recipient leads both the donor and himself downward, just as a stone-raft does in water.
An "ashmaplava" is a raft made of stone. A raft is that by which one crosses to the further shore, such as a boat or the like.
In this regard, just as one who has mounted a stone for the purpose of crossing a river sinks in the water along with the stone-raft, so too does he go.
For both the one who gives to a brahmin and the brahmin who receives from such a person go to hell.
Therefore, an ignorant person should fear whatever gift he might receive;
for even by a very small amount, the ignorant man sinks like a cow in the mud.

Therefore, out of fear of hell, the ignorant fool should be afraid of receiving gifts; he should tremble and, in short, should not accept them. Let alone gold and other such substances—even by accepting a small amount of worthless material such as tin or lead, the ignorant man sinks like a cow in a muddy quagmire.
A knower of dharma should not give even water to a twice-born man who acts like a cat,
nor to one who acts like a heron, nor to a sinner, nor to one who is ignorant of the Vedas.
The duty of the recipient has been explained;
now the duty of the giver is being stated.
By the word "also" (api), all that is fit to be given is excluded [from the previous rule].
Even water, where it is not withheld from anyone, should not be given to them; how much less any other substance?
This is a prohibition against giving other substances expressed through hyperbole (atiśayokti);
however, there is no prohibition regarding water, because water serves all purposes.
But has it not already been stated that one should not honor those who follow the "vow of the cat" even with mere words?
True;
in that case, honoring was forbidden, but here, giving is permitted.
And that [prohibition] applies to wealth, not to anything else;
thus, the double negation becomes meaningful.
Furthermore, as he will state later: "wealth acquired even according to the prescribed rule."
Therefore, the giving of food with contempt to heretics and the like is not prohibited.
On this point, someone says: although "one who does not know the Veda" (*avedavid*) is heard [in the text], one must also consider "one who has not studied [the Veda]" (*anadhīyāna*).
For it is stated that giving is prescribed for those who have merely studied the Veda.
Nor is it proper to give a gift for the sake of desire to those who are hypocritical.
He should be asked this:
"Where, moreover, has giving been prescribed for one who merely studies the Vedas but is devoid of knowledge?"
If it is argued that [gifts] should be given only to one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), [we reply:
no, because there is no established rule for giving to one who is most worthy (*arhattama*) in the absence of learning;
furthermore, other scriptural passages such as "the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is for the learned" exist within the same context.
Therefore, by reflecting upon that and considering the function of both qualifiers, it is understood that [the gift] must be given.
Consequently, we see no reason for abandoning the literal meaning of the text.
As for the claim that parity is illogical—
What indeed is improper regarding a matter that is to be understood through verbal testimony?
One who acts according to the "vow of a cat" is a *baiḍālavratika*;
one who possesses the "vow of herons" is a *bakavratika*.
When the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is not intended to be expressed, the locative case (*saptamī*) is used;
when the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is intended to be expressed, the dative case (*caturthī*) is appropriate.
For wealth, even if acquired through lawful means, when given to these three types of persons,
results in misfortune for both the giver and the recipient in the next world.
It is thus stated that the giving of food is not prohibited by the taking of wealth;
even if acquired according to rule— by means such as receiving gifts from the virtuous or through purchase in a manner permitted by the scriptures—
such a gift leads to the detriment of both the giver and the receiver in the next world.
Just as one who attempts to cross water with a boat made of stone sinks,
so too do the ignorant donor and recipient sink to the bottom.
Just as one who crosses by means of a boat or other float made of stone or rock sinks and disappears beneath the water when attempting to cross,
so too do the ignorant donor and recipient [sink].
One should derive *pratīcchakaḥ* by adding the causative suffix *ṇic*—on the basis of the sense "he causes acceptance"—and then the suffix *ṇvul*.
An alternative reading is *pratīpsakaḥ*;
in that case, it is derived from the desiderative form of the root *āp-* with the suffix *ṇvul*.
But the meaning for both is indeed one and the same.
One who carries the banner of Dharma while being always greedy, deceitful, and a deceiver of the world;
one who follows the "cat-vow," violent, and a subverter of all—such a person should be known as a hypocrite.
These two words are used figuratively (*upacāreṇa*).

And among the various grounds for figurative usage, only that which serves as the reason for the employment [of the word] is applicable here; this is for the purpose of establishing the object of the negation of the restriction [that the word refers only to its primary sense].
Dharma is like a banner (*dhvaja*).
Because [the class] beginning with *vyāghra* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, it forms a compound;
sometimes it is a *karmadhāraya* for the sake of meanings such as "all wealth" (*sarvadhanādi*).
From that, the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is applied in the sense of "this belongs to him."
He who practices Dharma solely for the sake of reputation, and not out of devotion to the scriptures, is described thus:
he practices Dharma only where people can see him and has it proclaimed by his own men, thinking, "Through the renown of being righteous, I shall obtain gifts and other benefits.
He is greedy, envious, and miserly.
One who deceives or cheats the world is a *lokadambhaka*. One who acts with guile is a *chādmika*;
*chadma* means a pretext or fraud.

A righteous person takes what was entrusted to him in secret and does not reveal it publicly; yet this "righteous" person reveals what was told to him in private, saying, "What was said in his presence does not go elsewhere. It is observed that someone tells another thing out of trust, only for it to be spoken back to the very person from whom it was meant to be hidden; such is malice toward others. Furthermore, he is a detractor who seeks to deceive everyone and cannot endure the virtues of others.
Such a person is to be known as one who follows the "vow of a cat.
He is a deceiver; he deceives. The suffix *ka* is applied here according to the rule *ātaś copasarge*.
Then, the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*). "The deceiver of all" (*sarveṣām abhisaṃdhaka*) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
Some recite a verse regarding this point:
"He whose banner of Dharma is always raised high like the banner of the gods,
yet whose sins remain concealed— that is called the 'cat-vow' (baiḍāla-vrata).
This very meaning is stated here in brief.
One who possesses even a single one of these qualities should be known as a "cat-vowed" hypocrite (*baiḍālavratika*).
From this very verse, it is inferred thus:
