since no specific distinction is heard regarding the phrase "and concealed sins," and because all of these constitute sin, the Teacher has instructed his disciples in both ways.
Some have been taught this verse, while others have been taught it previously;
both are authoritative.

Therefore, although in the case of "Devadatta has armlets, earrings, broad shoulders, and a large chest," the status of being a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatva*) is understood of these qualities taken together, nevertheless, in this context, each of these is a defining characteristic individually.
A twice-born man who looks downward, who is deceitful, intent on accomplishing his own ends, crafty, and falsely humble, is one who practices the "heron-vow."
The characteristic of the *bakavrata* (heron-vow) is looking downward;
or rather, it is having a low gaze.
"Low" (*nīca*) means dejected (*dīna*).
He is always active in some way or another, obtains [wealth] from somewhere, and even takes it from the lowliest.

*Niṣkṛti* means cruelty; one who acts with that as his primary motive is a *naiṣkṛtika*, a speaker of improper words. He is falsely humble, resorting to courtesy and modesty, yet he is an obstacle to what needs to be done.
A cat feigns sleep when it desires to seize its prey;
likewise, one who practices the Dharma with hypocrisy is called a "cat-vowed" person (*baiḍālavratika*). The same applies to one who follows the "heron-vow" (*bakavrata*).
For cranes, while catching fish, display contempt for other aquatic creatures;
nevertheless, their very intention is directed toward seizing fish.
By "vow" (vrata) is meant an action that has been habitually practiced.
The non-redundancy of the words has been demonstrated.
Nevertheless, it might be argued that there is no fault because it is a definition;
for a definition is indeed something not yet known.
By stating [the point] repeatedly, the meaning becomes easy to grasp.
What, then, is the difference between one who observes the "vow of a cat" (baiḍālavratika) and one who observes the "vow of a heron" (bakavrata)?
It is said:
This one, being intent on accomplishing his own purpose, does not obstruct the work of another;
the former, however, out of envy, destroys the work of another even when his own purpose has not been achieved.
Those Brahmins who observe the vow of the heron and those who bear the marks of a cat fall into the Andhatāmisra hell because of that sinful action.
This verse has been explained by its own words.
One should not perform a vow after committing a sin merely under the pretext of dharma;
by concealing one's sin with a vow, one practices deception upon women and Śūdras.

Having committed a sin, one should not perform a vow as an expiation merely by invoking the name of Dharma; that is, while declaring "I am performing this vow for the sake of Dharma," he proclaims it in the world, saying, "I have no need for expiation. Yet, in reality, he performs it solely for the purpose of expiation.
This must not be done.
One should not deceive women or Śūdras with such a vow after having concealed and denied the sin.
An expiation should generally be performed publicly, except in the case of secret [offenses].
Such Brahmins, both in this world and after death, are censured by those who discourse on the Veda; and whatever vow is practiced through hypocrisy goes to the Rākṣasas.
In this world, by the very nature of things (*padārtha-svābhāvya*), whatever fruit arises from an action performed even with another purpose as its objective, that fruit certainly comes to pass.

For instance, one engaged in the service of a teacher under the command of a superior does so thinking, "I am carrying out the teacher's word for the sake of merit (*dharma*)," and not for the sake of sensual pleasure;
yet, due to the inherent nature of the matter (*artha-svābhāvya*), it nevertheless produces sensual pleasure.
Thus, some think: "Vows are for the purpose of removing evil;
even when they are performed with another objective, they do not abandon their essential nature.
In this way, my act of atonement will serve both purposes."
"I shall become renowned in the world as an ascetic, and I shall cast off my sin"—
it is for the sake of turning back such a person who possesses this kind of thought that this [teaching] is commenced.
In that case, this vow, though performed and observed under a pretext, goes to the *rakṣasas* and becomes fruitless; the meaning is that it does not remove sin.

Not only does it fail to achieve its purpose, but such Brahmins who practice vows in this manner are censured and condemned by those who discourse on the Veda (*brahmavādins*), namely the learned ones who know the authority of the Vedas.
He who, being without the marks, subsists by the livelihood of one wearing the marks,
takes upon himself the sin of those who wear the marks and is born in the womb of an animal.
The wearing of emblems (liṅga) pertains to each stage of life (āśrama):

for instance, the student (brahmacārin) wears a girdle and so forth; the householder (gṛhastha) carries a bamboo staff, a water-pot, a sling, and so on; the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) wears skins, rags, matted hair, and so forth; and the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka) wears ochre-colored garments, a staff, and so on.

He who, though belonging to no [specific] stage of life, wanders through the world for the sake of alms and subsists upon this attire, takes away the sin (enas) of those who bear such emblems and satisfies their debt.
He is born in the animal realm, in the womb of animals such as dogs, jackals, and the like.
Furthermore, one should not entertain the suspicion here that the sin of those wearing sectarian marks transfers from them to him and moves about within him; for such a thing is impossible.
What is understood is the prohibition against wearing the outward signs of another [sect].
Even though there is no explicit prohibition, that [prohibition] is understood from the deprecatory explanatory passage (arthavāda) itself.
One should never bathe in water reservoirs belonging to others;
for by bathing there, one becomes tainted by a portion of the misdeeds of the person who constructed the reservoir.
A *nipāna* is a reservoir of water so called because people drink from it or go to it;
it includes ponds, wells, tanks, and the like.
One should never bathe in such a reservoir belonging to another that was constructed by that other person for their own sake and has not been relinquished for universal use.
All bathing—whether daily, occasional upon touching a Caṇḍāla or others, or for the purpose of removing sweat from heat—is prohibited here.
Regarding a transgression of this rule, he states the fault:
whoever is the maker of a water-reservoir becomes tainted, that is, connected with, some portion or part of whatever evil deed has been committed.
This is a deprecatory explanatory statement (arthavāda) which serves as a supplement to a prohibition.
One who enjoys his vehicles, beds, seats, wells, gardens, and houses when they have not been given to him shall incur a fourth part of the sin.
One who makes use of vehicles and other items belonging to another that have not been given shall incur a fourth part—that is, one-fourth—of the sin pertaining to that [theft].
Regarding this, someone says: "Because of the expression 'not given,' even things prepared for general use must not be utilized.
That is incorrect, because the context concerns what belongs to another.
Nor are those [offerings] belonging to another;
for that has been properly relinquished.
It has already been explained previously that the mention of the "fourth" part was not intended to be definitive.
One should always perform one's bath in rivers, in natural pools dug by the gods, in tanks, in lakes, and also in pits and springs.
All rivers are "dug by the gods" (*devakhāta*).
Therefore, since it is impossible for them to be both [human-dug and god-dug], that characteristic must be recited as being expressed by the term "dug by the gods.
For ponds and the like may be dug by the gods, but they can also be dug by humans.
Nor are they dug by the gods;
rather, its greatness is characterized solely by the fact that its author is not remembered.

A wise person should constantly practice the restraints (yamas), but not exclusively the observances (niyamas); for by failing to practice the restraints while devoting oneself solely to the observances, one falls.
The *yamas* are of the nature of prohibitions, such as "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed," "Liquor must not be drunk," and so forth.
The *niyamas* are of the nature of observances, such as "One should always recite the Veda alone," and so forth.
One should not [neglect] the *niyamas* constantly.

By this, it is not said that the observance of the *niyamas* is unnecessary; rather, it is stated that the *yamās* are more obligatory than the *niyamas*. Thus he says: "One who fails to perform the *yamās* falls [from his status];
for when there is a lapse in the *yamās*, [the sin] such as the killing of a Brahmin [occurs]."
Because he has fallen [from his status], he is no longer entitled to perform the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and other rites;
however, this is not the case when there is a mere lapse of a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
Thus, too, is the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).
"One who possesses the observances (*niyama*) but is not devoted to the restraints (*yama*) falls; however, one who possesses the restraints but is lazy regarding the observances does not perish.

Without first examining the observances with his intellect, he should not apply his mind excessively to those consisting mostly of restraints. Thus it is for those for whom *yama* and *niyama* are technical designations.
Non-violence, truthful speech, celibacy, freedom from guile, and non-stealing— these five are both the restraints (yamas) and the observances (vratas).
Absence of anger, service to the teacher, purity, moderation in diet,
and vigilance— these are the five observances (niyamas) and the minor vows (upavratas).
The relative gravity or lightness of these [transgressions] is also established by this verse;
therefore, it is not by this that the practice of the *yamas* is enjoined, nor the non-practice of the *niyamas*, since both are prescribed by those scriptures.
The section on religious observances (*vrata*) was concluded by the preceding verse;
now the section on prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*) begins:
"One should not eat at a sacrifice performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*), nor likewise at one performed by a priest for an entire village (*grāmayājika*)."
A Brahmin should never eat at a sacrifice offered by a woman or a eunuch.
In this regard, first of all, even food obtained from any source whatsoever is prohibited for one who has a desire for it.

A Brahmin should not eat at a sacrifice that has been commenced by one who is not a Śrotriya—that is, one who has not studied the Vedas—or at a sacrifice performed by officiating priests (ṛtvij) who are not Śrotriyas; nor should he eat where a village-priest (grāmayājī)—one who performs sacrifices for an entire village—is offering oblations, or where a woman performs the Homa.
For in the Chāndogya, the performance of the Agnihotra sacrifice by women has been mentioned by the authors of the Gṛhya-smṛtis; therefore, observing this [practice], he prohibits it.

Alternatively, this prohibition applies to a sacrifice where the woman is the principal figure, the husband is afflicted by defects such as poverty, and the woman is arrogant due to her dowry and the power of her kinsmen.
A *klība* is a eunuch.
This is offensive to the virtuous wherein these people offer oblations;
this is contrary to the will of the gods, therefore one should avoid it.

This is an explanatory supplement (arthavāda) to the preceding prohibitory rule. "Unseemly" (aślīla) means something not praiseworthy for the virtuous (sādhu), that is, for the cultured (śiṣṭa). For it is there that these people offer oblations and perform sacrifices.
It is contrary to and opposed to the gods;
therefore, one should avoid going to such a place.
One should never eat food belonging to those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted; nor food into which hair or insects have fallen, nor that which has been intentionally touched by a foot.
As long as there is an association with intoxication and the like, these [foods] are unfit to be eaten.
Others consider it to be a matter of frequency;
one should not eat the food of that person who is frequently intoxicated or addicted to liquor.

Likewise, for one who is dominated by anger, extremely irritable, and generally sickly, afflicted by various diseases and ailments; [food] that is infested with hair and insects, or corrupted through contact—
wherein some insects cause corruption when dead but not when alive, such as flies and house-lizards.
Others, however, [are those] while still alive.
The mention of "insects" (kīṭa) is for the purpose of indicating small creatures such as worms and moths;
the mention of "hair" (keśa) is, according to established custom, for the sake of showing nails, body hair, and impurities such as eye-secretions.
If it is touched intentionally with the foot out of desire, there is an offense; however, if it is done through negligence, there is no fault.
That which has been looked upon by a killer of an embryo, touched by a woman in her courses,
pecked by a bird, or even touched by a dog;

A "bhrūṇahan" is a slayer of a Brahmin; by him it must be looked at, that is, examined with precision. This is merely an illustration [of the rule]; it applies to other outcast sinners as well. However, there is a prohibition regarding anything touched by such sinners.
The prohibition regarding one touched by them is established simply by the injunction for bathing.
A *udakyā* is a woman in her menses; the prohibition applies to one touched by her, not to one merely looked upon by her.

Now, it may be objected: since the author will later state that even one who touches such a person must bathe, and thus impurity is already established by that very rule, how could there be any possibility of eating for one touched by such a person?
It is said:
that food should be eaten after being washed;
or rather, as has been stated, the mention of the "slayer of an embryo" (bhrūṇahan) is for the purpose of illustration.
In this regard, someone might think that [the prohibition] is for the purpose of illustrating those things recited in the verses of the Divākīrti;
likewise, there would also be a prohibition even for that which has been looked upon by a woman in her courses.
By this, that which has been touched by a dog is explained.
Therefore, it is said that [the mention of] "outcastes" (patita) is for the purpose of illustrating others as well.
Thus, in this context, [the term] applies appropriately to those such as the outcaste and the woman who has recently given birth (sūtikā).
The inclusion of the term "udakyā" (a menstruating woman) is for the purpose of indicating the woman who has recently given birth.
"By a winged creature":
a winged creature is a bird, and according to common usage, this refers to carnivorous ones such as vultures, crows, and the like, but not to swans and similar species.
Food smelled by a cow, and especially food announced [beforehand], as well as the food of a multitude, the food of a courtesan, and that which is despised by the learned; [these one should avoid].

*Ghuṣṭānna* is that which is given after being publicly announced to some petitioner who has not been invited, without specifying particular recipients such as those in a monastery or those attending a sacrificial session;
or it is that which, having been promised to one person, is given to another.
For this verbal root is taught in the sense of "accepting" (*pratipatti*) or "understanding" (*jñāna*).
In the absence of that [guest], they remember that eating at sacrifices, weddings, and so forth, without being invited, is prohibited.
Furthermore, this term *gaṇa* refers to a collective; therefore, there is no designation of a *gaṇa* for brothers who are undivided.

This is because of the statement, "For undivided brothers, a single religious duty (*dharma*) prevails," and it has been shown in the ninth [book] that their single duty consists precisely of acts such as hospitality, according to the rule: "The eldest alone shall take the paternal wealth in its entirety."
And its inclusion demonstrates that one has the authority [only] over those duties which must necessarily be performed.
Even though it is common property, there is a prohibition against others who are not included therein.
A *gaṇikā* is a courtesan.
"Despised" means censured;
even by a learned man who knows the meaning of the Vedas,
such things as lotus stalks and grain-husks, though they are edible.
The food of a thief, a singer, a carpenter, a usurer, one who has undergone initiation, a miser, and one who is bound or shackled;
A singer is one who lives by singing; however, for others, singing such as that of the *aparāntaka* style and so forth is indeed prescribed.
A miser is one who is stingy.
The distinction between the two who are bound with fetters is this: one is restrained by mere words, while the other is constrained by ropes and iron shackles.
Others read the word as *viśada* instead;
they explain that *viśada* means "suffering" (*kaṣṭa*).
The food of one who is accused of a crime, of a eunuch, of an unchaste woman, and of a hypocrite;
as well as food that is sour, stale, or the leavings of a Śūdra—[these must not be eaten].
A *puṃścalī* (unchaste woman) is anyone who engages in sexual relations with any man whatsoever.
Now, it might be argued that the food of a courtesan (*gaṇikā*) is already prohibited;
however, this is not so.
A courtesan is one thing, and an unchaste woman is another.
A courtesan lives by the profession of a prostitute;
an unchaste woman, however, is one whose senses are restless.
A hypocrite is one who observes religious duties with deceit, such as those who follow the "cat-vow" (*baiḍālavratika*) and others.
The food of a Śūdra is forbidden specifically for the purpose of [prescribing] particular penances, because the eating of the leavings of anyone is generally prohibited.

Others, however, say that "the leavings of a Śūdra" refers to food remaining in the cooking vessel that is fit to be eaten, which is called "leavings" (*ucchiṣṭa*) when it remains after a Śūdra has eaten.
However, there is an alternative reading: "as well as the leavings of one who is not a guru.
"Leavings" (ucchiṣṭa) refers to that which becomes impure through contact with another person, as well as what has been abandoned after eating.
For if it were one's own [leavings], there would be no abandonment before eating, since one would be consuming only a single mouthful.
Nor is it the practice of the learned that, having eaten food given once, one should rinse the mouth again and eat what has been taken up in another vessel;
likewise, one should not eat food in such a manner,
nor should there be an interruption by other actions such as rising from the seat during the meal.
Therefore, there is no fault in touching [the food] before it is finished, prior to the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), or after it;
however, as for eating together, even though there is contact with another person, it does not constitute "eating leavings" because it is a distinct matter.
In this context, the father eats together with his son and others from what has been left over.
Accordingly, Āpastamba and others, by mentioning the location, censure eating together with one who is uninitiated (*anupanīta*) as a general rule, but not with one who is initiated (*upanīta*).
However, under this view, there would be a prohibition against eating together with those of a different caste;
thus, another form of intervention (*vyavadhāna*) must be assumed.
However, that which has been abandoned after being eaten is called *ucchiṣṭa* (leavings) because of its connection with the meaning of the verbal root, even if it belongs to another person.
The food of a physician, a hunter, a cruel person, or one who eats the remnants of another's meal;
the food of a fierce person, the food of a woman who has recently given birth, and food from which others have already sipped water before leaving it for ten days.
In another *Smṛti*, a specific distinction is heard: "The *śalya* is one who lives by dancing;
the *mṛgayu* is a deer-hunter, one who kills deer for the sake of hunting or for the purpose of selling meat."
One of cruel and crooked nature is difficult to propitiate.
An "eater of leavings" is one who eats forbidden leavings.
An "ugra" is a specific caste.
The use of the word *rājā* (king) is seen in the Veda:
"He is fierce like one who sits in the middle.

And there is no other prohibition for that [eating of a king's food]; nor is it heard as being prohibited by way of demonstrating a fault, since the prohibition is derived from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "The food of a king takes away one's splendor."
*Sūtikānna* is that food prepared for the sake of a woman who has recently given birth; even if it is prepared by members of her own family, it is unfit to be eaten.
It is *anādya* (not to be consumed) for ten days, until the tenth day has passed.
Therefore, although for Kṣatriyas and others the period of impurity (*āśauca*) ends after ten days, nevertheless, [the food] must not be eaten during those ten days.

There is an alternative reading, "sūtakānnam" (the food of those in a birth-impurity). By the word "sūtaka," those persons who possess that impurity are indicated; those in whose family there is a birth-impurity are such that their food is not to be eaten for ten days.

This prohibition applies to that view according to which the impurity (*sūtaka*) for all [relatives] lasts ten days; however, when the view is that the impurity belongs only to the parents or only to the mother, then one must not eat as long as the impurity persists. The mention of "not yet ten days" is intended to indicate the cessation of the period of impurity.
Therefore, for Kṣatriyas and the other castes, whoever has a period of impurity (*āśauca*) for a certain duration, he is one whose food is not to be eaten for that long.
Although "the food of one in *sūtaka* before ten days have passed" (*sūtakānnam anirdaśam*) ought to have been read [there], it is placed after the word *paryācānta* due to metrical requirements.
Others, however, have explained the mention of *anirdaśa* as being independent.

By the word *sūtaka*, the period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*) is indicated. The milk of cows and other animals [is forbidden] during the ten-day period. "Paryācānta" means that which is separated from the purification rite of sipping water; if one sips water for some reason while in the middle of a meal, then what has been left over after eating must not be consumed again.

One should not eat meat that has not been honored, meat obtained for no purpose, the food of a woman who has no male relatives, the food of an enemy, the food of a city official, the food of an outcast, or food upon which someone has sneezed.
That which is given with contempt to one worthy of honor is "unhonored" (anarcita);

however, this does not apply to a friend or similar persons. "Meat prepared in vain" (vṛthāmāṃsa) is that which has not been offered as a remnant in the worship of the gods and so forth, but was prepared solely for one's own sake.
A *avirā* is a woman who has neither a husband nor a son.
A *dviṣan* is an enemy.
A *nagarī* is the mistress of a city, even if she is not a queen.
That upon which one has sneezed, where a sneeze has been made.
The food of the slanderer and the liar, of one who sells the results of sacrifices,
of an actor and a tailor, and likewise the food of an ungrateful person— [these should be avoided].

A slanderer (*piśuna*) is one who betrays a matter told in confidence, or one who speaks of another's faults in their absence. A liar (*anṛtī*) is one who gives false testimony. A seller of sacrifices (*kratuvikrayaka*) is one who, having performed a sacrifice (*kratu*), sells it by saying, "Let the fruit of my sacrifice be yours," and gives it away for a price.

Although from the perspective of ultimate reality there is no selling of a sacrifice, nevertheless, this prohibition applies to one whose livelihood is of such a kind, or who engages in it through the deception of others.
A *śailūṣa* is an actor;
others say it refers to one for whom his wife is a commodity for sale.
A tailor is a *sauccika*.
An ungrateful person (*kṛtaghna*) is one who destroys a benefit received;
moreover, he engages in harming his benefactor rather than repaying him, even though he is capable of doing so.
Of the blacksmith, the Niṣāda, the stage-player,
the goldsmith, the basket-maker, and likewise the seller of weapons.
The *karmāra* is an iron-smith.
The *niṣāda* will be mentioned in the tenth [chapter]. The *raṅgāvataraka* is one who enters the arena, such as a wrestler (*malla*) and others, distinct from actors (*naṭa*) and singers (*gāyana*).
Alternatively, one who is curious attends every performance;
a *veṇa* is one who lives by playing musical instruments;
a seller of weapons is a vendor of swords and the like, whether already finished or unfinished; and a *vāyasa* is a seller of [such items].
[One should avoid the food] of dog-keepers, of liquor-sellers, of a laundryman,
of a dyer, of a cruel man, and of one in whose house a paramour resides.
Those who keep dogs for the purpose of hunting and the like are "dog-keepers" (śvavantaḥ).
Liquor-sellers (śauṇḍikāḥ) are those addicted to intoxicants or those who live by trading in them.
Cloth (cailam) means a garment; he cleanses (nirṇenakti) it, that is, washes it.
This is a synonym for a dyer;
a *rajaka* is one who applies colors such as indigo to garments.
A *nṛśaṃsa* is one who praises or lauds men (*nṛn*) in the world, who is well known as a bard (*bandī*).
Alternatively, "nirdaya" means cruel;
"upapati" means a paramour, specifically one who dwells as a lover in the house of his wife.
They also tolerate those who have a paramour, those who are entirely dominated by women, food from a deceased person within ten days of death, and anything that causes dissatisfaction.
The former is one who is unaware of his wife's paramour;
this one, however, having become aware, remains patient and does not exercise restraint over his wife.
Nor is the food of that ignorant man—who has a paramour elsewhere than at home—to be eaten.

Those who are conquered by women—those for whom the wife alone in the house is both the manager and the appropriator, while the husband himself is not the master of his own dependents—are under her control in every respect.
Their food is like that of the deceased during the period of impurity following a death; those born of such families are persons whose food should not be eaten.
The mention of "within ten days" is intended to indicate the specific time-period.

When the mention of "within ten days" (*anirdaśa*) in the preceding [verse] independently prohibits food from those connected by impurity (*āśauca*) without distinction, this [present rule] refers to food prepared for the deceased (*pretānna*), even for a friend, kinsman, or the like who themselves are not subject to impurity.
The food of one who, out of compassion, proceeds to perform the fourth-day *śrāddha* and so forth, is not to be eaten.
The "tenth-day," "ninth-day," "fourth-day *śrāddha*," "eighth-day," and so on, are described in the *Rāmāyaṇa* as well as by other authors of the *Gṛhyasūtras*.
That which causes dissatisfaction is that which, when being enjoyed, does not produce satisfaction of the mind.
The food of a king takes away one's splendor; the food of a Śūdra, one's Vedic luster;
the food of a goldsmith, one's lifespan; and the food of a leather-cutter, one's fame.
Now he shows the result of transgression:
for one who eats the food of a king, there is the destruction of vital energy (*tejas*).
In this same way, it should be understood in all cases.
Terms such as "goldsmith" (*suvarṇakāra*) and so forth denote those who subsist by means of specific crafts.
Those who fashion gold for the sake of their livelihood are called "goldsmiths.
The same should be understood for washermen (*rajaka*) and others as well.

"He cuts the skin" means he slices the skin; "leather-cutters" refers to those who live by that occupation—this is their conventional designation. In this context, for those cases where there is no prior prohibition but only a fault is heard, a prohibition must be inferred from that very fact.
The food of artisans destroys one's progeny, and that of a washerman destroys one's strength; the food of a multitude and the food of a courtesan cut one off from the higher worlds.
Artisans, such as cooks and the like, are those whose occupations are not excessively censured;
this is their distinction from mere craftsmen (*śilpin*).
"Destruction of the people" means their non-production.
The food of a physician is pus; the food of an unchaste woman is semen;
the food of a usurer is excrement; and the food of a seller of weapons is filth.
The food and meal of a physician is equal to pus;
his semen is his vital faculty;
and his excrement is his impurity—all of which are one and the same.
Regarding those others who have been successively proclaimed as persons whose food should not be eaten,
the wise declare that their food consists of skin, bone, and hair.

Regarding those others who have been declared unfit to be fed in this section, even beyond those specifically mentioned in the rules of practice—the food of such persons consists of skin, bone, hair, and so forth;
whatever fault there is in consuming their skin, that same fault applies to their food as well.
Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one must fast for three days;
having eaten it intentionally, or having consumed semen, feces, or urine, one must perform the Kṛcchra penance.
Fasting for three days means not eating at all; if this is done unintentionally— that is, without prior awareness— one should perform a *kṛcchra* penance if it was done intentionally.
And since that *kṛcchra* must be consistent with other Smṛti texts, it refers to the *taptakṛcchra*.

In that regard, for the consumption of semen, feces, or urine, the *taptakṛcchra* is prescribed; for drinking [these] unintentionally, one should consume hot milk, ghee, water, or air for three days each—this is the *taptātikṛcchra*. After that, his purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) is performed.
Furthermore, the statement regarding penance (*prāyaścitta*) outside of its specific context is intended to demonstrate the gravity of the fault.

Because of the use of the genitive case in the phrase "of any one of these" (*anyatamasya*), they consider this penance to apply only to food defiled by its source of possession (*parigraha-dūṣita*), and not to that which is defiled by time, its inherent nature, or contact.
For there are four kinds of food unfit for consumption, such as that which has turned sour or has been kept overnight.
That which is corrupted by time includes things such as fermented liquids and stale food; that which is corrupted by association includes things such as those mixed with intoxicants;
and that which is corrupted by its own nature includes things such as garlic.
Regarding that which is defiled by appropriation among those foods whose nature is unfit to be eaten,
it is said here:
"True."
There are four kinds of food that should not be eaten;
there is also the instruction regarding the sixth.
However, if this expiation did not apply to sour gruel and the like, then their inclusion in this context would be entirely purposeless.
For in the fifth [chapter], there is no prohibition of those two;
therefore, their mention here is solely for the purpose of penance.
In that case, then, what is the purpose [of mentioning them] there?
We shall explain that very point there.

Although the consumption of what is censured and what is unfit to be eaten has been mentioned, as well as the rule regarding having eaten the food of those whose food should not be eaten—all of that will be determined in detail according to its divisions in the eleventh book.
A learned twice-born man should not eat cooked food from a Śūdra who does not perform ancestral rites (śrāddha);
however, in the absence of other means of subsistence, he may accept from him raw grain sufficient for a single night.
The consumption of food from a Śūdra has been prohibited without qualification;
now, its specific scope is stated as "from one who does not perform Śrāddha. But where, then, was the Śūdra's food prohibited?
Regarding the passage "and the leavings of a Śūdra," one might object:
"In that case, does this mean there is no food other than the leavings of a Śūdra?
We reply: "No."
Thus, the connection there is as follows: one should not eat the food of a Śūdra, nor the leavings (ucchiṣṭa) of anyone else.
As for what was explained previously—that it represents the view of earlier authorities—we have also described it accordingly.
By the word "śrāddha," the performance of *pākayajña* and other rites prescribed for a Śūdra is indicated by means of metonymy (*lakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, one should not eat cooked food belonging to anyone other than a virtuous Śūdra who does not perform those [prescribed] rites;
or, according to another reading, "one who lacks faith" (aśraddhin).
The meaning is "one who lacks faith.
And likewise, in the following verse, he states the very primacy of faith with the words "of the generous one.
*Āma* refers to unhusked, dry grain, such as rice and the like.
Likewise, "one-night" means sufficient for a single day, not much.
Having deliberated upon both— the miserly Vedic scholar and the liberal usurer— the gods ordained that their food be equal.
A Brahmin who is endowed with all virtues— since the term *śrotriya* is intended to indicate [the possession of] learning— he is a learned man devoted to the performance of prescribed duties;
yet, if he is miserly and wretched, he does not welcome a friend, a kinsman, a guest, or a petitioner, nor does he strive to give anything to anyone.
The other is a usurer, one of evil deeds who lives by lending at interest.
Then there is the generous and noble man, full of faith, who rejoices when guests arrive at his home and honors them with food and other offerings out of faith.
Regarding these two, the gods weighed their food on a scale and established that it was equal.
Even if one person is virtuous and of righteous conduct, he may nevertheless be marred by stinginess;
for it is said that greed destroys all virtues.
And even if the other is full of faith, he may still be unworthy due to the defects of his past actions.
Having thus reflected and deliberated, the gods established that these two were equal.
Prajāpati, having approached them, said: "Do not make the unequal equal;
that which is purified by faith from the liberal giver is to be accepted, while the other is to be rejected."
Prajāpati came to the gods and said, "Do not act thus; such an unequal settlement is unjust.
The gods asked, "Which of these two is superior?
Prajāpati spoke again.
The food of one who is generous and faithful is pure and sanctified by that faith; or [the food] of a usurer is likewise sanctified by faith.
Other food—that of a learned Vedic scholar—is defiled by his ritual actions and is therefore not praiseworthy.
This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) in the form of a dialogue between the gods and Prajāpati.
One should not eat with respect even from a virtuous person who lacks faith; however, one may eat even from a Śūdra if he possesses faith.
With faith, one should constantly perform sacrifices and works of public utility without sloth;
for when performed with faith using wealth acquired through righteous means, those two become inexhaustible.

*Iṣṭa* refers to sacrificial rites such as the *yajña* performed within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*); *pūrta* refers to other acts performed outside of that for the sake of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*), such as honoring guests.
These two must be performed with faith (*śraddhā*).
Likewise, they come with "welcome" wealth—those riches which arrive by means of learning, heroism, austerity, a daughter, and so forth.
Thus, both become inexhaustible and yield inexhaustible fruit.
However, those [gifts] which are not "welcome" do not have inexhaustible fruit, yet they are not without fruit either.
For in that way, ownership is produced by them as well, and by means of that [ownership], sacrifices and so forth must be performed. Furthermore,
no prohibition against usury and the like is heard in the context of sacrifice, giving, and so forth, such that it would be a subsidiary part (aṅga) of those acts.
Therefore, as many causes for the attainment of heaven as there may be, by means of the wealth acquired through them, sacrifices and other rites should be performed;
however, there will be variations in the excellence or deficiency of the result.
What, then, are those praiseworthy means of acquiring wealth? To this it is said:
[wealth] obtained through learning, heroism, austerity, a daughter, a client, a pupil, or inheritance.
Wealth is of seven kinds and pure; both of these [the giver and the receiver] are likewise of that same kind.
In that context, learning and austerity are the causes for receiving gifts.
Even though there is only one act of receiving a gift, it is described as distinct due to the difference in its causes.
Furthermore, the qualities of the recipient should also be understood therein by implication.
If the donor is not extremely wicked, then what has come from him is pure.
By the words "sacrificer" (yājya) and "pupil" (śiṣya), officiating at sacrifices and teaching are respectively understood.
"Inherited" (anvayāgata) refers to that which has come down from one's father, grandfather, and so forth.
That which was obtained from the father-in-law's house at the time of giving the daughter in marriage;
that which was obtained by valor for a Kṣatriya;
and the lineage of the daughter—all these are common property to all.
That which is obtained through idleness, agriculture, trade, crafts, service, or following others,
as well as that received from one who has rendered a favor, is declared to be "spotted" (śabala).

Service consists of acting as a messenger, being employable according to one's master's will, following orders, and being agreeably affectionate. Among these, money-lending, agriculture, and trade are not for the non-Vaiśya; they are indeed prescribed specifically for the Vaiśya.
Service, namely the attendance upon the twice-born, is indeed commended for the Śūdra;
any other [occupation], however, is censured for him.
By the use of the term "variegated" (śabala), it is indicated that the fruit [of such service] is not long-lasting.
That fruit lasts for as long as one lives. That which is acquired through gambling, theft, distress, hypocrisy, violence, or by means of deceit is declared to be "black" (kṛṣṇa).
A *pārśvika* is one who stands by the side; he acquires wealth through bribery and the like.
Having learned of someone’s acquisition of wealth, he says, "I will cause it to be given to you, provided that you give me something"; he who accepts [this offer] is a *pārśvika*.
He is neither the doer nor the instigator, but remains on the sidelines; he does not accept [the wealth] out of ignorance.
And just as one stands as a guarantor for a debtor after having taken [a pledge],
so too is there hypocrisy (*pratūpaka*) and deceit (*dāmbhika*).
Deceit (*vyāja*) consists of the sale of saffron and other substances adulterated with safflower and the like.
Affliction is the causing of pain to others; taking by stealth is theft;
and by force is violence.

But surely, through theft and forceful seizure, ownership itself does not arise, because they are not enumerated among the causes of ownership in the text: "One becomes an owner through inheritance, purchase, partition, acceptance of a gift, or finding [lost property]," as well as "learning, craft, wages, service," and so forth; likewise, "there are seven righteous ways of acquiring wealth. If it is argued that from this very statement the two [theft and force] are indeed causes of ownership, then how is it that "what is enjoyed by force is not digested [i.e., does not become one's own]"?
Some, however, say that this reading "dyūtacauryārti" does not exist at all; rather, it is "vairyārti.
That which is taken from an enemy at the time of making peace—when one gives because of being deprived of power, saying, "If you give this much, then I shall make peace with you"—is what is meant.

"Seizing by force" (*sāhasam*) does not mean taking by means of physical violence; rather, it refers to that which is acquired at the risk of one's life, such as by means of a sea voyage or through the secret purchase of goods prohibited by the king.

Others, however, maintain that ownership is not contradicted by seizure by force or by possession over time, because force is primary only at the initial moment of seizure; even in the absence of force, ownership arises there through possession characterized by non-negligence.
But where there is enjoyment of power from the very beginning throughout all time, it is said that "it is digested" (i.e., the matter is settled).
Therefore, both [views] are not contradictory.

It is logical that ownership does not arise through theft or force, because such acts are categorized as distinct types of acquisition, and because other authors of the Smṛtis do not include them among the causes of ownership.

One should constantly practice the duty of giving, both that which pertains to sacrifices and that which pertains to public works, with a state of complete contentment whenever a worthy recipient is encountered, according to one's capacity.
The compound *dānadharmas* refers to acts such as the construction of ponds and the like;
it is a *smāhāra-dvandva*.
Alternatively, it is a *karmadhāraya*, meaning "that which is both a gift (*dāna*) and a religious duty (*dharma*)."
By the mention of "dharma," he indicates the state of being bound by joy and so forth;
by "bhāva," he means with a contented and serene mind, having encountered a worthy recipient, [giving] gifts such as vows and the like.
Thus it is meritorious and external to the altar.
Whatever may be asked for should be given by one free from malice;
for a worthy recipient will surely arise who delivers one from all [suffering].
Whatever may be asked for, even if it is very little, it must be given when one has been requested.
When there is doubt as to whether a person is a worthy recipient (pātra) or not, and no certainty exists, something small should be given, but not too much.
Furthermore, if there is doubt due to [ambiguous] speech, one should not give.
A worthy recipient (pātra) will eventually arise;
what kind of recipient? One who saves and protects [the giver] from every cause for falling into hell, that is, from every sin.
Regarding the statement "to a Brahmin who knows the true meaning of the Vedas," this is the basis for doubt: it is an exception (apavāda) concerning a small amount of wealth.
The giver of water obtains satisfaction; the giver of food, imperishable happiness;
the giver of sesame seeds, desired offspring; and the giver of a lamp, supreme vision.
Satisfaction is the absence of affliction by hunger and thirst;
and that belongs to one who is wealthy and free from disease.
By this, it is stated that the fruit [of the action] is the possession of great wealth and freedom from illness.
It is inexhaustible happiness.
Since it is not specified otherwise, it is understood that this is not happiness derived from material requisites; "inexhaustible" means lasting for as long as one lives.
The giver of food provides prepared food such as barley-meal and boiled rice, as well as raw materials such as unhusked rice;
the gift of a lamp should be made at a crossroads or in an assembly of Brahmins.
The giver of land obtains land; the giver of gold, long life;
the giver of a house, the finest dwellings; and the giver of silver, supreme beauty.
One attains sovereignty over the earth; one obtains gold and fine gold;
from silver, one obtains the most excellent form.
The giver of clothing attains the same world as the Moon; the giver of horses attains the same world as the Aśvins;
the giver of a draft-ox attains abundant prosperity; and the giver of a cow attains the realm of the Sun.
He is looked upon like the moon and becomes pleasing to behold for everyone;
according to the Itihāsas, he attains that particular celestial abode called Candraloka.
He attains the same world as the Aśvins—that is, the companionship of those possessing horses—and acquires a great many horses.
Furthermore, by beholding the two Aśvins, one attains their world.
By giving a bull—an ox capable of drawing a cart—great and abundant prosperity arises for the giver, consisting of an abundance of cattle, goats, sheep, wealth, grain, and so forth.
One also attains the station, the realm, of Bradhna, the Sun.
One of great majesty comes to be above all,
whether it be heaven or the realm of the sun.
In another Smṛti, a specific excellence of fruit is heard of as depending on a specific [quality] of the vehicle.
A milch cow with golden horns and silver hooves, well-behaved, covered with cloth, accompanied by a bronze vessel, and given along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), should be donated.

In the reading *sudakṣiṇā*, other items such as gold and so forth should also be given there; or, the word *su-* should be understood in the sense of "excellent," meaning that cow is an excellent sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
*Kāṃsyopadohāḥ* is an alternative reading.
*Kāṃsya* is a specific measure;
the meaning is that she yields much milk when milked with that [measure].
One who desires specific results should adopt the procedure seen in other Smṛtis, such as: "Having made the ground covered with forms and adorned with pearl-ploughs," and so forth;
likewise, "If she is a Kapilā cow, she delivers [the ancestors] even up to the seventh generation of the family."
A cow with her calf, facing both ways, [is equal to] as many eons as there are hairs on her body.
This is the fruit of the gift of a tawny cow that has a calf;
when a "cow with two faces" (ubhayatomukhī) is given, she causes one to reach heaven for as many thousands of years as there are hairs on her body, she delivers one, and she liberates one from sins.
In the *Bhārata*, it is stated that the gift of a cow yields all fruits.
Even water and other such gifts are heard in scripture to have heaven as their fruit:
"By giving land, cattle, food, clothing, water, sesame seeds, clarified butter, shelter, a house, or gold, one is glorified in heaven."
The house is the place of residence.
One who gives a vehicle and a bed obtains a wife; one who grants fearlessness obtains sovereignty;
one who gives grain obtains eternal happiness; and one who gives the Veda attains equality with Brahman.
Sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is lordship (*īśvaratva*), that is, mastery (*prabhutva*).
Happiness (*sukhitva*) is well-being (*saukhya*).
Grains (*dhānya*) are rice, black gram, green gram, and so forth.
The specific fruit of sesame seeds has been stated.
Brahman is the Veda; he who teaches and explains it bestows that [fruit].
[The result is] equality with Brahman (brahmasārṣṭitā).
*Arṣaṇa* means "flowing. *Ṛṣṭiḥ* means "an arrow" or "a spear. He whose *ṛṣṭi* is equal (*samā*) is *sārṣṭiḥ*.
Due to Vedic usage (*chāndasatvāt*), there is the substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-*.
The root *ṛṣ* means "to go.
Alternatively, *sārṣṭi* is "flowing forth" (*arṣaṇa*).
The state of being that is *sārṣṭitā*.
In both cases, it is stated that this "samānagatitva" of Brahman means its state of equality.
Of all gifts, the gift of the Veda is preeminent:
that of water, food, cattle, land, clothing, sesame seeds, gold, and clarified butter.
This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) for the preceding injunction.
"Gifts" (*dānāni*) refers to the objects to be given (*deyadravya*),
or it refers to the act of giving itself.
The gift of Brahman consists in the study and exposition of the Vedas;
water and other such gifts are mentioned because they are the most excellent among all gifts.
With whatever disposition one bestows whatever gift, one receives that very same thing, honored in return with that same disposition.
This word "bhāva" refers to a mental state (*cittadharma*).
With whatever kind of disposition—whether with a serene mind, faith, and respect—one gives, one receives exactly that;
or if one gives without faith, with contempt, with a defiled mind, or with disdain, one likewise obtains the same.
Furthermore, this does not refer to the intentionality of a substantial category;
rather, it refers to the fruit.
This is what is being stated.

One obtains that specific pleasure which is to be accomplished by that specific substance. For if the intention were directed toward the genus [of the substance], then in the case of giving medicine to a sick person, one would receive medicine;
yet since that is useless for one who is not ill, that person too would be excluded.
Therefore, one obtains exactly that same joy, such as exhilaration and so forth, which belongs to the giver;
thus, it is stated that by the gift of medicine at all times, health is attained.
Alternatively, "bhāva" refers to the desire for a result, thinking, "May this be mine."
Whatever substance one gives with a specific fruit in mind, one obtains that very thing;
by that same disposition and with that same intention, one receives exactly what one desires—this is what is meant.
Thus, it is demonstrated that all substances can yield every kind of fruit.
He who accepts what has been honored, or he who gives what has been honored—both of them go to heaven; but in the reverse case, they go to hell.
It should be given preceded by worship,
and it should be received in exactly that same manner;
one must not give with contempt— this is the intended meaning of the verse.
"Adored" is an adverbial modifier of the action.
One should not be proud of one's asceticism; one should not speak untruth even after performing sacrifices;
one should not revile Brahmins even when distressed; and one should not boast after giving a gift.
One should not feel pride because of the austerity one has performed.
One should not think in one's mind, "I have practiced extremely intense austerity that was very difficult to perform.
Having sacrificed—that is, having performed a ritual—one should not speak untruth.

Although [the prohibition] was already established without distinction, its restatement as a human goal (puruṣārtha) is for the purpose of making known that it is an auxiliary (aṅga) of the sacrifice;
for if one transgresses the prohibition, the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites become deficient in their constituent parts.
Even when afflicted or distressed, one must not revile or disparage Brāhmaṇas.
Having given away goods such as cattle and the like, one should not proclaim before anyone, "This was given by me."
Sacrifice perishes through falsehood; austerity perishes through pride; longevity perishes through reviling Brahmins; and the merit of a gift perishes through boastful proclamation.
This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) for the preceding prohibition:
by means of falsehood as its cause, the sacrifice perishes—that is, it leaks away and becomes fruitless;
that purpose for which it was performed is not accomplished.
Thus it is in all cases.
One should gradually accumulate merit, like termites building an anthill,
for the sake of a companion in the next world, without causing pain to any living beings.

If one is unable to perform great acts of charity, great austerity, or great sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others, then one must not remain indifferent. Rather, one should gradually accumulate merit through small gifts, slight austerity, assistance to others according to one's capacity, and the recitation of prayers (*japa*) and burnt offerings (*homa*) prescribed by the *Smṛtis*,
just as ants and termites build up a mound of earth little by little.

"For the sake of a companion in the next world" is a restatement of the fruit of dharma. "Without afflicting any living beings": even when begging for the sake of dharma, one must not cause affliction to living beings.
For in the next world, neither father nor mother remain for the sake of companionship;
neither son, nor wife, nor kinsman remains—only the Dharma remains.
This is a restatement of what has occurred:
in another birth, no friend, relative, or anyone else has the power to rescue one from the sufferings of hell and so forth for the sake of companionship;
rather, it is only the Dharma practiced while living that rescues one.
A living being is born alone, and alone indeed it perishes;
alone one experiences the fruit of good deeds, and alone likewise that of evil deeds.
Just as a living being, a creature, is born alone and not together with friends, kinsmen, and so forth, and likewise perishes alone— friends and kinsmen do not undergo death along with him—
even if a wife or another devoted person should kill themselves at the time of his death, nevertheless that act of dying is entirely separate.
By this, they do not experience oneness of womb, as was the case with Atri.
In this way, good and evil deeds are experienced separately as well.
But has it not been stated that "neither son nor wife"?
To what extent is it true that a son indeed benefits his deceased father through rites such as the *śrāddha*, and likewise the wife?
True;
this statement is intended to mean that only a righteous son becomes such [a helper].
Just as someone becomes a companion to another who is living by taking him by the hand, so too does a son benefit one who has died solely through the medium of dharma.
Having cast off the dead body upon the earth like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, the relatives depart with averted faces; dharma alone follows him.
It goes along with [the body].
This is established by direct perception and is stated for the sake of thorough reflection:
having cast the corpse of the deceased upon the earth like a useless log, the relatives turn away and depart.
But dharma alone follows the person.
Therefore, one should always gradually accumulate merit for the sake of a companion;
for with merit as a companion, one crosses over the darkness that is difficult to traverse.
This is a summary:
"Darkness difficult to cross" refers to that which is crossed with difficulty;
"darkness" means suffering.
Even that becomes easier to cross with dharma as a companion;
for one does not sink into such darkness—this is the meaning.
A person who is preeminent in dharma and whose sins have been destroyed by austerity is swiftly led to the next world, radiant and possessing a body of ether.

One for whom dharma is primary is *dharmapradhānaḥ*, meaning one who is devoted to dharma and a performer of actions as they have been prescribed. "With sin destroyed by austerity" (*tapasā hatakilbiṣam*): even if some transgression has somehow been committed through negligence, his impurity is destroyed by austerity—that is, by expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*). When the fault born from that transgression of the sacred word (*śāstra*) has been eliminated by such expiation, he leads [the deceased] to the radiant other world; he leads or causes him to attain the other world, the celestial realm of the gods, such as heaven and so forth.
Who? By virtue of the context, it is Dharma itself.
"The embodied person" (śarīrin):
one who possesses a body (kha-śarīra) by means of his own body (kha).
His body is not composed of the five elements as it is for other men;
rather, his body is space itself, which is Brahman.
By this, his omnipresence is expressed.
One who desires to lead his family to excellence should always form alliances with the most eminent;
he should avoid those who are inferior.
Because the "excellent" (uttama) is of many kinds, there is a distributive repetition (vīpsā) with reference to it:
some are excellent by birth, some by learning, and some by conduct;
or else, due to the diversity of relations, any relation whatsoever that is fit for any particular excellent person.

One who desires to lead his lineage to excellence, eminence, and preeminence should enter into alliances—characterized by the giving away of a daughter and so forth—with those who are superior and most excellent in terms of birth and other such qualities;
he should avoid those who are inferior and low.

Since the avoidance of the inferior is already established by the injunction to associate only with the superior, this statement of avoidance is intended to permit the use of middling persons when superior ones are unavailable.
The lowest means those who are base.
By approaching only the most excellent and avoiding the inferior, a Brahmin attains preeminence; by the opposite conduct, he falls to the state of a Śūdra.
By associating with and forming connections with the superior, a Brāhmaṇa attains excellence.
The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is intended to illustrate the case of the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya as well.
By transgression—that is, by acting in the opposite manner and forming connections with the inferior through pratiloma unions—he descends to the state of a Śūdra.
It is stated that because the genus does not depart, it attains identity with that [object].
Firm in action, gentle, self-controlled, and not associating with those of cruel conduct,
one who is non-violent and possesses such vows shall conquer heaven through self-restraint and charity.
One who possesses firm resolve regarding duties is one who acts with steadfastness;
whatever he undertakes, he necessarily brings to completion, and having begun a task, he does not desist before finishing it.
The meaning is that he is not fickle.
Thus it has been said: there is the reaching of the end of what has been commenced;
one is gentle and not harsh;
and there is no association with those of cruel conduct, such as thieves and the like.
He should not form any association with them;
likewise, through self-restraint and charity, he may conquer— that is, attain— heaven,
provided he remains observant of his vows.
Maintaining this vow and discipline,
one should be understood as "self-controlled" (*dānta*)— meaning patient toward the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*)— since self-control (*dama*) is mentioned separately.
One should accept from everyone fuel-wood, water, roots, fruits, food that is offered, honey, and the gift of safety.
*Edhas* is fuel, such as wood and the like;
*anna* is food, whether cooked or raw;
*abhyudyata* means brought forward and presented before one.

All this may be accepted from anyone, except from outcasts (patita), those accused of crimes (abhiśasta), Caṇḍālas, and others of the inverse castes (pratiloma); it may be accepted from a Śūdra or from another person who has committed only slight sins.
Honey refers to that produced by bees (mākṣika).
"Abhaya" (fearlessness) is like a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*);
this is for the sake of providing an illustration.
For "acceptance" (*pratigraha*) is the taking possession of another's property by one's own will, and it does not consist of the form of food.
For in this case, no one’s ownership is withdrawn, nor does anyone’s ownership arise anew;
therefore, the term *dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial fee) is used here by way of praise.

Just as providing protection from thieves and the like to even outcasts (*caṇḍāla*) and others in a forest or wilderness is not considered a fault, so too there is no fault in accepting these pieces of wood and other such items.
This rule applies when there is no emergency;
however, in an emergency, he will state that [food] may be accepted even from Caṇḍālas and others.
Furthermore, the word "offered" (abhyudyata) is connected only with "food" due to proximity, not with "firewood" and the other items.

Therefore, among the *edhas* and other such items, a request that is not contrary to dharma is permitted; for it is said, "Acceptance [of gifts] should be made from righteous twice-born men," which implies that it is not obtained from unrighteous twice-born men or from a Śūdra.
Furthermore, the solicitation of specific types of objects is desired.
For that purpose, this [is stated].
Prajāpati considered alms that have been brought forward and offered, even if they were not previously solicited, as acceptable— even from one who has performed evil deeds.
By this specific qualification, it is stated that other substances in excess of the alms-food are also to be accepted.

Furthermore, the word *bhikṣā* (alms) is used here in a commendatory sense; it is not intended to mean alms-food alone, even though this term denotes a small quantity of prepared food. Indeed, because alms-food is so small in quantity, it does not entail excessive fault, and for a religious student (*brahmacārin*), it is prescribed as being acceptable from all social classes (*sarvavarṇika*).
In this way, other things similar to it have also been seen by him with this specific distinction.
The word *bhikṣā* is employed with the intention of expressing such a meaning;
for instance, in the Mahābhārata:
Having gone together to the workshop of Bhārgava, those two high-souled sons of Pṛthā approached Pṛthā,
and being exceedingly delighted, they [presented] Yājñasenī to her.
"O Bhiksus," thus did those two foremost of men announce.
"Brought forth" (*āhṛta*) means carried to that place where the recipient is stationed;
"offered" (*upahṛta*) means placed before him, announced by word or gesture that it may be accepted.

That alms which is "unasked for beforehand"—meaning it was not previously requested by the recipient, either directly or through another, nor had the donor previously stated, "I have this wealth; please accept it out of favor"—but is instead provided unexpectedly and offered at that very moment with a revealed intention—such alms Prajāpati Hiraṇyagarbha considered (or deemed) acceptable even from one who has committed evil deeds. Why? Because they are to be accepted even from such a person.
One who possesses evil, sinful karma is called "one of evil-doing."
The ancestors do not eat for fifteen years,
nor does the fire carry his oblation, for him who treats her with contempt.
Now follows the explanatory passage (arthavāda) censuring non-observance:
"Furthermore, if anyone disregards this [rite], his ancestors do not eat nor accept the śrāddha offering;
and Agni does not carry the oblation to the gods."
The meaning is that no fruit is obtained from rites performed for the ancestors or for the gods.
Regarding this, someone says:
even if it is not utilized, such a thing must necessarily be accepted for the sake of favoring the donor.
But that is incorrect;
for it is said that this acceptance of what is unasked is free from fault,
as this is indeed a counter-exception.
And there is a counter-exception to what has been prohibited;
for while the attainment [of a woman] through worldly desire was prohibited, that very same [attainment] is now permitted as a counter-exception.
One should not refuse a bed, a house, kusha grass, perfumes, water, flowers, jewels, curd, parched grain, fish, milk, meat, or vegetables.
One should not reject nor refuse beds and other such items, even if they have not been brought forward;
if these goods are already present in the house and someone says, "I shall bring this and that," one should not decline them when they are offered.
Desiring to support his teachers and dependents, and wishing to honor the deities and guests, he may accept gifts from all sources; however, he himself should not find satisfaction therein.
There are many types of gurus through direct instruction and extension of instruction; dependents (bhṛtya) who have sought refuge are enumerated in another Smṛti:
"The aged mother and father, a virtuous wife, and an infant son."
Desiring to uplift those who are sinking from hunger,
and wishing to honor deities and guests for the sake of fulfilling his daily obligatory duties (*nityakarman*),
he should accept gifts from all— both from the virtuous and from the unvirtuous.
But one should not satisfy oneself with it;
for satisfaction consists of the cessation of hunger and enjoyment, which one should not perform.
That [food] should be accepted solely for the sake of the teacher and others, and not for one's own sake.
How, then, should one maintain oneself? To this he says: "But when the teachers have passed away, or living at home without them,"
Seeking his own livelihood, he should always accept it from a virtuous person.
If, after [the elders] have passed away or departed, or even while they are still living, one dwells separately from them;
and the mention of "gurus" is intended to include all dependents as well;
then, seeking—meaning requesting—one's own livelihood or means of subsistence, one should accept it from "sādhus," that is, from righteous persons.
Since caste is not specified here, there is acceptance [of gifts] even from a righteous Śūdra;
thus it has been said: "One should not eat the food of a Śūdra," and so forth.
A partner in business, a family friend, a cowherd, a slave, and a barber—
these among Śūdras are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant].
One who is called an *ardhasīrī*, an *ardhika*, a *kuṭumbī*, or a *bhūmikarṣaka* [is a sharecropper].
The terms *gopa* and *dāsa* are relative words (*saṃbandhiśabda*):
whoever herds someone else's cattle is entitled to eat from that person's food.
And he who offers himself, saying, "I am your refuge; I shall dwell with confidence in you"—he who thus surrenders himself is also one whose food may be eaten.
Whatever his nature may be, whatever he intends to do,
and how he might treat him, in that manner one should present oneself.
He clarifies the very act of self-surrender:
what kind of soul this Śūdra may have— what his lineage is, what his country, what his craft,
and what he desires to do.

"I have resorted to you for various tasks, whether for the sake of dharma or for some other purpose, such as the protection of the royal palace. Or, 'just as one might serve,' means that I shall attend upon you with this craft, serving you by performing all household duties such as saluting your feet. In this way, when everything is offered, the self is said to be offered. Others, however, considering the word *ātman* in the verse "The self, indeed, is named son" (*ātmā vai putranāmāsi*) to refer to offspring, say that this [verse] declares that the food of that Śūdra whose daughter is married according to his desire is fit to be eaten.
That is incorrect;
for first of all, this word "ātman" is not clearly applied to a daughter,
since the word "putra" is far more commonly established as referring specifically to a male.
Furthermore, there is no purpose in teaching by means of an indirect expression;
it would have been proper simply to say, "and he who gives his daughter.
Others, however, explain that the mention of "one who offers half" and so forth is intended as an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa) for the Śūdra.
By this, it is established that the food of a Pāraśava and of a father-in-law is fit to be eaten.
He who represents himself as something other than what he truly is when among virtuous people is a doer of evil; he is a thief in the world of darkness, a stealer of his own self.
One who, while being unrighteous and contrary to reality, speaks otherwise among the virtuous and disciplined, saying "I am righteous";
or one who, having relied on one purpose, displays another—such a person is the greatest evildoer among all evildoers;
he is a thief, a robber.
While another thief is one who steals property, this one, however, steals his very self; thus there is an extreme degree of censure.
All expressible objects are fixed, rooted in speech, and issued forth from speech;
he who steals that speech is a man who commits every form of theft.
Because of the eternal relationship between word and meaning, meanings are said to be fixed within speech, that is, in the word.
They are said to be rooted in speech because the speaker’s manifestation of his own intention is dependent upon it; they are said to be rooted in that [speech].
They are said to have issued forth from speech because they arise from it, and because the listener’s comprehension is likewise dependent on it, they are said to have issued forth from speech.
And one need not strive here to resolve any suspicion of tautology, because this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) that serves as a rebuttal of the matter in whatever way possible.
Whoever steals—that is, robs—that speech, saying one thing but performing another, acting with one intention while displaying something else, he is a perpetrator of all thefts.
There is no substance, such as gold or the like, which has not been stolen by him; this is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended for the purpose of censuring the speaking of untruth.
Having discharged his debts to the great seers, the ancestors, and the gods according to the prescribed rule,
and having entrusted everything to his son, he should live maintaining an attitude of equanimity.
This is stated as another alternative for the householder:

having fulfilled his debt to the great sages through Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), to the ancestors through the procreation of offspring, and to the gods through sacrifices— as it is said, "one is burdened by three debts"— and having performed these three, once his son has attained legal capacity, he should entrust the entire management of the household and family affairs to him,
renounce them, and continue to live in the home itself, remaining impartial and having abandoned egoism (*ahaṃkāra*).
One should remain having completely abandoned the notion of "this is my wealth," "this is my wife and children," and "these are my male and female slaves.
The state of equanimity (*mādhyasthya*) consists in the abandonment of craving for one's own possessions through the realization: "I belong to no one, and no one belongs to me.
Furthermore, this renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) applies to desires and to actions performed for visible results, but not to all actions whatsoever.
We shall demonstrate this later.
One should always reflect alone in solitude upon what is beneficial for oneself;
for by reflecting alone, one attains the supreme good.
Once the renunciation of all actions has been performed, this must specifically be done by him:

being alone and without companion, without conversation, in a place that is undisturbed, secluded, and solitary, he should reflect—that is, meditate—upon what is beneficial; he should practice those meditations on Brahman prescribed in the Upaniṣads.
Through such reflection and through that practice, he attains and reaches the supreme good known as liberation.
Thus has been declared the eternal mode of life for the Brahmin householder,
as well as the auspicious ritual of the Snātaka vows, which increases one's inner strength.
The summary of the chapter's subject matter:
This eternal and perpetual mode of life for a householder Brahmin has been declared.
However, that which will be mentioned for times of distress is non-permanent.
Because of the mention of the *vipra*, this rule (*kalpa*)—the procedure (*vidhi*)—pertains only to the vows of a Brāhmaṇa *snātaka*.
"Goodness" (*sattva*) is a personal quality; it is that which causes his increase.
"Śubhaḥ" means "praśastaḥ" (praiseworthy);
this is a term of praise.
A Brahmin who lives according to this conduct, being learned in the Vedas and the Shastras,
is eternally freed from impurity and is glorified in the world of Brahma.
This is the statement of the fruit for all of this.

A Brahmin living by this, being learned in the Vedas and the Shastras, becomes free from stain; "stain" refers to the sin born of the transgression of prohibitions, which has been removed or eliminated through expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*).
By this, the following is meant:

By performing what is enjoined, by not practicing what is prohibited, and because whatever was somehow done has been expiated through penances, he is glorified in the world of Brahman; that is, he attains greatness in a particular location within the world of Brahman.
According to another philosophical view, it is established that he becomes one with the nature of Brahman.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Commentary on Manu, composed by Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi, son of Bhaṭṭa Vīrasvāmin.
Now begins the fifth chapter:
Having heard these duties of the *snātaka* as they have been declared,
the sages spoke thus to the high-souled Bhṛgu, who was born from fire.

Having heard those duties prescribed for the student (*brahmacārin*) and the householder (*gṛhastha*) in the three preceding chapters, the sages Marīci and others questioned their teacher Bhṛgu regarding this matter about to be stated. Now, one might object: since the term "the graduate" (*snātaka*) is heard here [in the next chapter], what is the purpose of mentioning the "student" (*brahmacārin*)?
It is said:
this is a recitation of what has already been stated;
the duties of the religious student (*brahmacārin*) have indeed already been declared.
The phrase "the high-souled one, whose origin is from Fire" (*analaprabhavam*) is an epithet of Bhṛgu; it refers to him whose birth or origin (*prabhava*) is from *anala*, that is, from Agni.
But was not Bhṛgu already stated in the first chapter to be the offspring of Manu, in the passage beginning "I, desiring to create progeny..."?
True;
it is a figurative statement (arthavāda).
It was said thus because his birth from Agni into the presence of Bhṛgu was heard [in scripture], and it was spoken based on that very observation.
And thus is the etymological explanation:
"From the heated semen, that which first blazed forth became yonder sun; that which was second became Bhṛgu.
Or rather, this is stated figuratively.
"Because of the commonality of brilliance, it is an emanation like that of fire.
One should not, however, insist here on which of these two positions is more logical,
for this treatise does not have that as its primary purpose.

This entire sequence of questions and answers is intended to demonstrate the gravity of the defect regarding food that is about to be described. Food defiled by its inherent nature is more serious than food defiled by its acceptance;
for a defect in the essential form is stronger than a defect arising from a relationship, because it is internal.

But surely, previously a more extensive penance was heard for unintentional [consumption], namely, "fasting for three days"; whereas this [present rule] states, "one should fast for a day in the case of the remaining [substances]. How then can this be considered more severe?
It is said:
this refers to the category of garlic and similar substances;
for by eating those intentionally, one falls [from his status], and thus the penance for a fallen person applies.
O Lord, how does death prevail over those brahmins who, as previously described, perform their own duties and are learned in the Vedas and the scriptures?
He now demonstrates that which was asked by the great seers (maharṣis). "Thus" (evam) refers to the operation of the treatise;
"as has been stated" (yathoktam) refers to the meaning of the treatise.

By this composition of the treatise, such Dharma as has been declared—[the author] will later state that "this which has been declared is for the twice-born," because the mention of the *vipra* (Brahmin) is intended to be illustrative. How does death prevail? [Does it do so] in the stage of a *snātaka* or in the stage of a student (*brahmacarya*)?
For it is fitting that they should live out their full lifespan, living for the duration of a human life;
since the lifespan of humans is one hundred years, it is not proper for them to die before that through premature death.
For it has been said: "Indeed, one obtains long life through right conduct, by those who recite prayers and offer oblations."
The righteous Bhṛgu, son of Manu, did not say anything to those great seers;
instead he said, "Listen to the fault by which Death seeks to slay the Brahmins."
Through the lack of study of the Vedas, the abandonment of proper conduct,
laziness, and defects in food, death seeks to strike down the Brahmins.
But surely, since the question "Is it not proper for those who perform their own duty? was asked, the subsequent text beginning with "by which fault" would not be appropriate as an answer?
It is said in reply: the passage beginning with "through non-practice" is stated by way of illustration.

Just as the practices you have previously adopted—such as the non-study of the Vedas and so forth—are causes of death before one’s full lifespan, so too is the defect of food which is about to be described.

Even when the study of the Vedas and other such duties exist, that which was previously mentioned as one's own duty (*svadharma*) does not [prevent death]; rather, this defect of food is more serious.
And because it constitutes a separate section, it is stated here.
Garlic, leeks, onions, and mushrooms,
as well as anything produced from impure substances, are unfit to be eaten by the twice-born.
Substances such as garlic and the like are well known in the world.
The word *kavaka* is a generic term;
it is understood to refer to what is commonly known in some places as *kṛyāku*.
The *chatrākas* are indeed mushrooms (*kavakas*).
For it is with the word *kavaka* that they are prohibited, and with the word *chatrāka* that the penance will be stated [in the verse]: "The *chatrāka* and the village pig.
Furthermore, no distinct entity named *chatrāka* is well-known [in common usage].
Nor is it proper to understand that whatever has the shape of a mushroom (*chatrāka*) is therefore a mushroom simply on the basis of a commonality of syllables and phonemes;
for if that were the case, it would follow that there is a prohibition contradicting established practice regarding *suvarcalā* and other such items.
Therefore, only those things which are indeed mushrooms (*kavaka*) are mushrooms (*chatrāka*).
And likewise the author of the *Nirukta* states: "The *kṣuṇṇa* is the *ahicchatraka*, because it is crushed (*kṣudyate*).
Therefore, those white-colored things that grow on unplowed ground and on ground that has grown gradually are *kavakas*.
And he will say: "The *kavakas* are terrestrial."
And it has been shown [in the commentary] that they are "as if trampled by a foot.
This refers to those things which are crushed by a kick of the foot;
therefore, there is a prohibition against those things that grow from trees or shrubs and bear that same shape.
Mushrooms (*kavaka*) and *kukuṇḍa* fungi are explained in medical treatises (*vaidyaka*).
However, this explanation is not like that of words such as "cow" (*go*) and so forth;
the word *kavaka* is used for mushrooms both in the medical science and in common worldly usage.
Therefore, certainty regarding the meaning of medical and other treatises is derived from this [text],
and that has been demonstrated.
However, even those substances such as garlic which possess similar color and smell have been prohibited by Viṣṇu.
