In the case of the worldly [action], the engagement occurs either out of desire for meat or out of hatred; in the case of the Vedic, however, it is prompted by the scripture, which states, "This is for the sake of the sacrifice."
It shone forth completely; that is to say, it attained full manifestation.
He who harms harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure finds no happiness anywhere, whether he is alive or even dead.
The letter *a* here should be understood as being elided for the purpose of negation.
And because non-harmful beings are excluded by this negation, there is no prohibition regarding [the killing of] snakes, tigers, and the like.
He who does not desire to inflict upon living beings the afflictions of bondage and slaughter,
seeking the welfare of all, attains ultimate happiness.
The afflictions (*kleśa*) are indeed bondage and slaughter,
or alternatively, acts such as mutilation.
He who does not wish to perform these— by whom even mutilation itself has not been committed— is one whose very desire for such objects has ceased.
Not only does he cause no harm, but because he desires to seek the welfare of all, he enjoys ultimate happiness.
Whatever one meditates upon, whatever one does, and wherever one fixes one's delight—
that one attains without effort, provided that one harms nothing whatsoever.
Whatever he thinks of, such as a bride-price or an offering,
and whatever object he fixes his delight and desire upon with intention,
that he obtains without effort and in a very short time.
Whatever action one performs, one attains its completion immediately after its accomplishment, without any obstacle.
For meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings, and the slaughter of living beings does not lead to heaven; therefore, one should abstain from meat.
He demonstrates that the entire collection of verses prohibiting violence is supplementary to the prohibition of eating meat:
as long as living beings have not been killed, meat does not come into existence;
and violence brings about excessive suffering.
Therefore, one should avoid meat.
But surely there is indeed meat from those who have died naturally; why then is it said "without having killed"?
This is a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*).
Furthermore, the flesh of those who have died naturally is simply not obtained because it is a cause of disease;
for meat is not eaten without being given,
and there is no giving of that which causes disease.

Regarding the phrase "it arises": because meat is caused by violence (*hiṃsā*), the designation of an agent is entirely consistent with the identity of the agent [in both actions]. Alternatively, regarding the phrase "it arises" and "not conducive to heaven" (*na ca svargya*):
it is not intended merely that it is not a cause for the non-arising of heaven, but rather that it is a cause for the suffering of hell and so forth.
Having thoroughly considered the origin of meat and the slaughter and imprisonment of embodied beings, one should desist from eating all kinds of meat.
The growth of the embryo occurs within the womb, a place of impurity, originating from the impurities of semen and blood;
likewise, there is killing and binding of embodied beings caused by that [womb].
Having thoroughly observed all this with a discerning intellect and having investigated it according to reality.
One should desist from the eating of all meat, even that which is not prohibited, let alone that which is forbidden;
this is an explanatory praise (arthavāda).
It does not mean, however, that meat should be understood as inherently impure in its true nature.
For that sentence is not intended to enjoin impurity.
He who does not eat meat, avoiding the manner of a Piśāca,
becomes beloved in the world and is not afflicted by diseases.
He who, having abandoned that rule of worshipping the gods, does not eat [the meat], but rather eats it according to the rule,
attains the affection of the world;
he becomes beloved by all.
And [regarding] diseases:
for one who is emaciated, weak, or otherwise afflicted, if he eats meat, a disease arises;
therefore, it too must be eaten according to that very same rule.
Thus, by eating in this manner, one is not afflicted by diseases;
otherwise, even while eating meat, one is indeed afflicted by diseases,
as in the case of a *piśāca*.
Piśācas are a specific class of animals; they eat meat without regard for ritual injunctions.
Therefore, anyone else who eats in that same manner is censured as being like a piśāca.

The one who consents, the one who dismembers, the one who kills, the buyer and the seller, the one who prepares the meat, the one who serves it, and the one who eats it— all these are considered slayers.
If another person, for their own purpose, approves of someone being killed by yet another, thinking, "Well done, this killer is doing it," that person is the approver (*anumantṛ*).
The butcher (*viśasitṛ*) is one who performs the dismemberment of the slain body.
The server (*upahartṛ*) is the one who brings the food.
All these, such as the "eater," are killers.

When the status of being a killer is superimposed upon those who do not actually kill—such as those who perform the preparation, sale, and so forth of the meat—it is intended as a censure; however, in reality, they are not killers at all.
For in common worldly usage, the act of killing has the result of the loss of life.
Its agent is understood from the Smṛti to be the slayer.
According to the specific rule that "the independent one is the agent," he who effects the separation of life from living beings is called the killer;
and acts such as buying and selling are indeed distinct from that.
But is this not also merely a traditional teaching (*smṛti*), stating that "these people, beginning with the consenter, are killers"?
This is not an authority regarding the relationship between words and their meanings; rather, it concerns *dharma* and *adharma*.
For in that regard, the venerable Pāṇini is more highly qualified.
Furthermore, Manu and others employ worldly objects as established in common usage; they do not remember a rule for the relationship between words and their meanings.
For these individuals are users [of language], not its original creators. But is it not the case that they do remember such things as "he asks that teacher"? Indeed, they do remember them.
True;
there is no contradiction with the scriptures or the traditional law (smṛti) in that regard,
nor do those statements have any other purpose.

In this case, however, since it is possible to justify [the statement] as an explanatory passage (arthavāda) even by means of a secondary purpose, one cannot determine that there is actual agency in killing. As for those who say, "If there is no eater, there is no killer," implying that killing is motivated solely by eating, and that the prompter is traditionally recorded as the agent—
therefore, the status of being a killer is indeed primary.
Therefore, it is argued that the expiation prescribed for the killer alone is appropriate for the eater.
To this we reply: that is incorrect;
for there is a separate expiation for those who have been killed and for the one who relishes the flavor, stated as: "having eaten meat that is unfit to be consumed..."
Furthermore, that which was stated regarding agency by way of being an instigator does not exist at all;
for this is its definition:
"He who, through commanding or entreating, impels one who is independent."
"He is both the agent and the primary cause, not another [who acts] figuratively.
For the killer indeed proceeds by being motivated by the desire for life, thinking, "I shall live by selling meat," but he is not commissioned by the eater.
Now, if it is argued that the status of an instigator consists in performing an action conducive to that [result], [the response follows].
"One who, having resolved to perform an action, intends to provide assistance therein is an instigator (*prayojaka*).
This too does not exist here at all.
For what is appropriately denoted by the term "provision" (*saṃvidhāna*) is the placing of instruments, the rendering of the trembling animal powerless, and the bringing forward of the sword.
Without that [purpose], the action is not accomplished.

Now, if it is argued that that for whose sake the undertaking of an action occurs is the instigator (*prayojaka*), then in the case of "he causes the boy to study" (*māṇavakam adhyāpayati*), the boy would obtain the designation of agent (*kartṛ*) based on the cause of teaching; for studying is not the object of the act of causing to study.
Furthermore, he does not engage in killing with reference to anyone [other than himself].
By means of this, there would be for him an inclination toward eating that which is harmful for the sake of determining its nature. All these beings strive for their own welfare;
no one remains still for even a moment thinking, "I must benefit another. Thus, he is one whose desires are fulfilled.
Now, for one who has set out for their own sake, the undertaking would be purposeless without someone to consume [the result];
but when such a person exists, it becomes fruitful. And the fruit is the motivator.
And since that [act] depends upon the eater, the eater is the instigator by way of a causal chain.
If that were so, then one who is killed out of hatred would be the instigator of the killer;
consequently, the very person being killed would become the killer.
For indeed, without hatred, the status of being a killer is not possible.
Likewise, in the case of killing a Brahmin as well, the giving away of all one's possessions is a factor that brings about the sin.
For without a recipient, the act of receiving is not possible; therefore, not only would the recipient incur guilt, but the giver as well.

And a beautiful woman, while guarding her virtue, might incur blame if she were gazed upon by a lustful man whose heart was being consumed by the arrows of Love and who displayed an excess of longing.
Therefore, this is not the definition of an instigator.

For those two—the killer and the eater—are engaged in their own respective interests; like the proverbial "lost horse and burnt chariot," they experience mutual assistance, but neither is the instigator of the other.
This has been determined with precision in the verse beginning with "Of Śūdras, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Brāhmaṇas."
He who desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another,
without having first worshipped the ancestors and the gods— there is no doer of more demerit than he.
This censure applies to one who eats meat for the sake of excessive nourishment,
and not out of apprehension regarding the danger of disease arising;
for it says:

Regarding the phrase "those who wish to increase [their merit]," even for such a person, there is no fault if they fail to worship the ancestors and gods due to some illness; however, it is not the case that there is no fault when worship is simply not performed because it is somehow impossible to do so.
He who might perform the horse sacrifice every year for a hundred years,
and he who does not eat meat— the merit and fruit of these two are equal.
The consumption of the meat of hares and other animals remaining from the worship of the gods and others is permitted.
One who desists from that [eating] enjoys the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
The fruit of the horse sacrifice consists of the attainment of all desires, the conquest of all [worlds], and so forth.
Nor should it be objected here: "How can there be equality of fruit for the abstention from meat when it involves great effort and the expenditure of much wealth?
For this restraint itself is exceedingly difficult to perform.
Furthermore, the principle that "as in the world, the distinction of fruit arises from the measure [of the effort]" indeed prevails here.
Therefore, there is no fault in [interpreting this as] an injunction regarding the fruit;
however, we say that this is merely an explanatory passage (arthavāda).
For this reason, the statement "a hundred years" is easily reconciled under the view that it is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise);
for it is not possible for the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) to be enjoined every year,
nor is it possible for one to perform it for a hundred years, because it is impossible for an eligible person to live for such a length of time.
"Merit and fruit" (puṇyaphalam) is merit and its fruit;
this is a collective dvandva compound.
For in a genitive tatpuruṣa compound, there would be a lack of semantic connection (asāmarthya).
One does not obtain that fruit by subsisting on pure fruits and roots or by eating the food of sages, which one obtains from the total avoidance of meat.
"Pure" means fit for the gods.
"Foods of sages" refers to grains such as *nīvāra* that ripen without being ploughed.
This is indeed an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).
"He shall eat me in the next world, whose flesh I eat here"—
the wise declare this to be the true nature of "meat" (māṃsa).
The etymological explanation of the name is an explanatory praise (arthavāda):
"He shall eat me. The pronoun "he" (sa), which refers generally, is made complete in its sense by the appropriate object: "him whose meat he eats."
There is no fault in eating meat, nor in liquor, nor in sexual intercourse; this is the natural inclination of living beings, but abstention from them yields great fruit.
From the passage beginning with "Food for the vital breath" up to this verse, there is merely a collection of explanatory statements (arthavāda).
Only two or three verses contain prescriptive matter.
Just as in the rule, "There is no fault in eating meat when one has purchased it or produced it oneself," so too is this verse.
But it is heard here that abstention bears great fruit;
through many expressions of censure, such a refinement has arisen [in people] that no meat whatsoever should be eaten.
[The author] says, "There is no fault in eating meat," for the sake of the livelihood of living beings.
There is no fault in consuming what remains after the worship of the gods, or when the aforementioned occasions such as the desire of a Brahmin arise;
however, if they wish to eat,
the renunciation preceded by the resolve, "I shall not eat," yields great fruit.
Since no specific fruit [of the action] is mentioned, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that heaven is the fruit.

Likewise, [the prohibition applies] to drinking liquor for Kṣatriyas and others, but to sexual intercourse for all castes, except with a menstruating woman or at forbidden times. This limited engagement regarding small amounts is what is sanctioned by the scriptures.
The activity of living beings has as its purpose the maintenance of the body;
thus says the author of Āyurveda:
"Food, celibacy, and sleep—these three are considered [the pillars of life]."
"For intoxicants and women indeed cause the support of life.
This [statement] refers to one who is able to live even without them; for such a person, abstention yields great fruit.
And this is mentioned merely as an illustration.
The same applies to other abstentions whose objects are neither prescribed by the learned nor prohibited by them.

Where there is an injunction for a person who is inclined toward action, and the purpose is the production of an excellence of pleasure that is not censurable— or where abstention from something leads to a result, such as eating honey, eating choice food, wearing a woolen garment (*rāṅkava*), and so forth— and likewise, such is the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).
And the venerable Vyāsa has said this:
"But as for those actions which, though neither enjoined nor prohibited, are performed out of attachment—such as laughing, scratching, and so forth—abstaining from them leads to dharma."
I shall now proclaim the purification for the deceased, as well as the purification of objects,
for all four castes, duly and in their proper order.

The mention of "even for the four" is for the purpose of making it known that the duties prescribed in general do not accrue to a Śūdra without such effort. "Purity among the deceased for the living" is a compound formed according to the rule *sup-supā*.
And this purification, like that of the *apreta*, is caused by a specific occasion (*nimitta*).

Therefore, although the statement regarding purification is formally asserted, nevertheless, because purification is dependent upon impurity and because both are established through the authority of the scriptures, impurity is mentioned first, even though it was not explicitly asserted at the outset.

Upon the death of one whose teeth have not yet emerged, or who has just emerged, or whose tonsure ceremony has been performed, all relatives remain impure; the same is declared regarding birth-impurity (sūtaka).
They remember that one who has just been born is even more tender than one whose teeth have appeared;
thus, this is merely a general statement made without such distinction, since the differentiation regarding the periods of impurity will depend upon that [specific detail].
For example, in another Smṛti, immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is heard of in such passages as "until the eruption of teeth" and "likewise when a child is in a foreign land."
An infant who has not yet cut its teeth is to be understood as such;
and thus, for men whose tonsure has not been performed, this one-night period of impurity is established even in the case of one whose teeth have appeared.
In this way, these two Smṛti texts are non-contradictory regarding the subject of infants, through a distinction of their respective scopes.
And purification for one night applies until the performance of the *cūḍākaraṇa* (tonsure ceremony);
for he will state that for those whose tonsure has been performed, there is a three-night period,
and that "the Brahmin shall be purified after three nights prior to the initiation (*upanayana*), and thereafter [immediately]," and so forth.

However, those who describe these alternatives—namely, that impurity (*āśauca*) due to death lasts ten days according to the divisions of age—and who connect them out of order based on other *smṛtis* and established practice, [asserting]: "Ten days for one who has been initiated (*upanīta*); four days for one not initiated; three days for one whose tonsure (*muṇḍa*) has been performed; one day for one whose teeth have appeared; and immediate purity (*sadyaḥśauca*) for one younger than a younger brother," and so forth;

and likewise, three or four days for one whose *cūḍā* ceremony has been performed—in their view, the alternative based on conduct (*vṛtta*) and Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), which is well-known from other *smṛtis*, would not be established as an option.
We shall demonstrate that further on.
One is said to be "dead" (mṛta) because of the cessation of all activity, since the verb *sthā* preceded by the prefix *sam-* is seen to signify the stopping of activity.
"Relatives" (*bāndhavāḥ*) refers to those who are *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas*.
And regarding *sūtaka*, this refers to the birth of a son and similar occasions;

thus it is said, "all relatives are impure," and by this [statement] its connection is established. But how, in this case, is there an understanding of a distinction based on age, since the phrase "one whose tonsure has been performed" indicates a connection with a specific sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*)?
In the case of "and when the initiation has been performed," this is indeed heard [in the scripture].
For this very reason, it is not at all heard how long a period of time is prescribed for one who has performed the tonsure ceremony (*caula*).
It is said: [as follows].
Because of the association with the phrase "born after the appearance of teeth" (*dantajātānujāta*), the term *kṛtamuṇḍa* (one who has been shaven) is understood to signify the time [of tonsure].
And that time here refers to the first or third year.
Although the shaving of the head in the first year is optional, if that were adopted, the rule "immediately upon the appearance of teeth" would be contradicted.
That too is incorrect.
What is the limit [of the period] for one who has had his head shaved?

Because of the word "and" (*ca*), it is understood that [the rule applies] to one who has had his head shaved and also to one who has received the initiation (*upanayana*), since a different designation comes into use upon the attainment of another sacrament (*saṃskāra*).
In this way, there will be consistency with this Smṛti rule even in the passage "until the eruption of teeth, [impurity lasts] immediately.

Furthermore, in the rule "for three nights until the initiation of the vow (*vratādeśa*)," the mention of "initiation of the vow" is intended solely as an indicator of time. Otherwise, since the time for a Brāhmaṇa is not fixed but occurs specifically in the eighth year, and the same applies to the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya, no specific time would be stated for the Śūdra at all.
In that case as well, because of the statement "for all [castes], [the impurity lasts] for a full [period] once childhood has passed," therefore,
from the eighth year onwards, there is full impurity for all four castes, since that period exists even for the Śūdra. However,

according to the view in which the initiation (*upanayana*) of the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya is observed to take place in the eleventh year, then no specific period would have been prescribed for the Śūdra.
In that case as well, for one whose childhood has passed, the period is complete; for one still in childhood, it is three nights.
Regarding the cessation of childhood, another Smṛti states: "A child is said to be [so] prior to the eighth year," while others say, "One remains a boy until the sixteenth.
Even for those who maintain that childhood ceases at sixteen, purification lasts for exactly one month from the age of eight onwards.
Thus it is recited: "But after six years, the purification for a Śūdra is monthly.
Elsewhere it is recited: "For one of eight years, a month.
Now, is it not the case that this arrangement according to the divisions of age is obtained from the very statements that are about to be mentioned?
What is the purpose of this heading, "one whose teeth have appeared"?
True;
it is for the sake of easy understanding.
Impurity on account of a death is prescribed for ten days among sapinda relatives;
it may last for three days or even one day until the collection of the bones has taken place.
The definition of *sāpiṇḍya* will be stated.
The phrase "prior to the collection [of the bones]" (*arvāk saṃcayanāt*) will be explained as an elliptical expression for four days;
for there is a scriptural statement that for one who has maintained the sacred fires, the collection takes place on the fourth day.
And this alternative depends upon [the completion of] the life-stages (*vṛtta*) or the study of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*).
Thus, another Smṛti states:
"A Brāhmaṇa who is united with the Veda and the sacred fires becomes pure after one day."
One who possesses only the Vedas becomes free from qualities after three days, and one who is devoid of qualities after ten days.
In that regard, for one who maintains the three Vedas and possesses the sacred fires, the period is one day; for one who maintains two Vedas, it is three days;
but for one devoid of qualities, it is ten days.
Immediate purification was taught by Gautama;
and that applies specifically to a Brāhmaṇa for the sake of not interrupting his Vedic study.
In that regard, there are other ritual acts.
In both cases, for ten days the food of the family is not eaten;
giving, receiving, burnt offerings, and Vedic study are suspended.
Thus, these and other such ritual acts are suspended;
however, because the Veda of one who has studied much perishes if not recited, the private recitation (*svādhyāya*) is not suspended.
Likewise, an option (*vikalpa*) is appropriate when there is a dependence on a livelihood.

For one who lives by the six occupations, there is a ten-day period; for others [who live] by three [occupations], there is a four-day period according to this rule; and for one [who lives] by two [occupations], there is a three-day period.
Since one is not authorized to accept gifts and so forth during a ten-day impurity, even the mere maintenance of life would be difficult to achieve.

However, for those who hold that there are four stages of life and four periods of impurity, and thus establish a connection between them respectively according to the stage of life—for them, a ten-day period would apply when [the child] has teethed, whereas when one dies after being initiated (*upanīta*), there would be only a single day.
In that case, there would be a contradiction with other Smṛti texts and established practice. Now, if a connection is made in reverse order (prātilomyena) in order to avoid this contradiction—

namely, that the impurity lasts ten days for one who has been brought home, four days for one whose tonsure has been performed, three days for one whose teeth have appeared, and one day for one whose teeth have not yet appeared— [then the following applies].

In this case as well, an option is appropriate due to the contradiction with the rule "for those whose tonsure ceremony has been performed, [impurity lasts] for three nights," since a three-night period is prescribed by its own specific term; for the four-day period is established as having a different scope based on a difference in livelihood (*vṛtti*) and a difference in the accumulation of wealth.
In this way, there is syntactic unity with another Smṛti text through the phrase "from one day.

Otherwise, if the option were explained as being based on a difference in age, by what means would an option be obtained in the Mānava Śāstra that depends upon the distinction between one's livelihood and Vedic study?

Therefore, according to this statement of Gautama, for one who possesses a livelihood even without daily acceptance of gifts—such as one who has a granary full of grain (*kusūladhānya*)—and who is devoted to sacred study (*svādhyāya*), purification occurs immediately upon the mere recitation of the Veda.

Even regarding those ritual rules (*kalpa*) that prescribe a period of three days and so forth, for those who accept gifts for the sake of their livelihood, purification occurs after that same duration, based on this very view of Gautama.
Otherwise, he would have simply said, "of a Brāhmaṇa who is engaged in sacred study," rather than saying, "for the purpose of not interrupting sacred study."

Therefore, although it is heard in scripture that "purification occurs after one day" and so forth without qualification, it must nevertheless be understood as referring to specific ritual acts; for this reason, [the author] states that for a Brahmin, the period is ten days as if it were a constant rule, saying, "A Brahmin is purified in ten days.
For there would be no purpose in repeating what has already been stated otherwise.
Therefore, this alternative must be explained by means of a logical method.

Furthermore, where there is immediate purification for those such as children, and a three-night period for those such as those who have shaved their heads, since there is no such alternative in those cases, there is purity for all ritual acts.
The sapinda relationship ceases with the seventh person;
however, the status of being a samānodaka persists as long as the birth and the name are not forgotten.

Based on the recognition of lineage (*anvaya*), the consciousness of kinship, and the continued application of the term "relative" (*bāndhava*), those born of the same lineage are called *sapiṇḍas*, extending up to the seventh generation.

According to the rule that "the son should give to those to whom his father gives," even when the father and other ancestors are living, six generations are considered *sapiṇḍas* by virtue of their fitness.

Although the offering is made to the ancestors and one is the seventh from oneself, therefore the grandfather, great-grandfather, and others born of the preceding lineage are designated as *sapiṇḍas*.
The six ancestors are the *sapiṇḍas* on the paternal side; the six descendants, beginning with the son, are likewise [the *sapiṇḍas*] on the maternal side.

Since the designation of *sapiṇḍas* is obtained through their co-occurrence in a single act of offering the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*), this same co-occurrence applies to the son and others when performed by the grandson and so forth. Therefore, all those to whom one gives and with whom one becomes a recipient of the gift are designated as *sapiṇḍas*.

Since the offering of the *piṇḍa* in that context serves as a defining characteristic (*avadhy-upalakṣaṇa*), it is like saying "one should come at the time of the conch-blowing," which refers to the specific moment marked by the sound of the conch.

Therefore, what is meant is this: those who belong to the lineage of one's great-grandfather—starting from that great-grandfather himself down to the seventh generation—are his *sapiṇḍas*. This should be understood in the same way for one's own lineage and for the lineages of the father and so forth.
The counting must be performed starting from the point where the distinction begins, up to the limit of the seventh degree.
Just as those who share one common ancestor, starting from that ancestor and extending down to the seventh generation, are considered *sapiṇḍas* everywhere;

and since being born into that lineage is the defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) rather than relying on caste (*jāti*), even those of different castes, such as Kṣatriyas and others, are *sapiṇḍas* of Brāhmaṇas and the like.

For this very reason, in cases of impurity (*āśauca*) arising from their birth and so forth, the period for a Brāhmaṇa is ten days alone, whereas for them [the Kṣatriyas, etc.], it remains their own respective time, such as twelve days and so on.
Therefore, for everyone, purification occurs at its own prescribed time even upon birth or other events that have a non-sapinda as their cause, or a non-sapinda as their cause.
For Kshatriyas and others, the sapinda relationship extends to three generations with respect to a Brahmana.
And so says Shankha:

If many persons born of the same lineage have separate fields and are distinct individuals, they share a single funeral offering (piṇḍa) but have separate rites of purification; however, the offering itself extends through three generations.

"Pṛthakkṣetra" means [sons] born of women of different castes. "Pṛthagjana" refers to those who, even if they are of the same caste as those with separate fields (*pṛthakkṣetra*), have multiple mothers; for that reason, both terms are employed. "Ekapiṇḍa" means those who are *sapiṇḍas*.
However, their periods of purification are distinct, being determined solely by the cause of their own caste:
for a Kṣatriya and others when a Brāhmaṇa is in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka) and so forth, it lasts ten days; and when a Brāhmaṇa is in a state of birth-impurity, it lasts twelve days for them.
Likewise, there is another distinction: the offering of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) recurs through three [generations].
It occurs in exactly three persons.

With respect to those of the same caste, for Kṣatriyas and others, the *sāpiṇḍya* of a person is like that of a Brāhmaṇa; however, with respect to those of different castes, this statement can establish that the *sāpiṇḍya* extends to three persons, because of the inclusion of specific qualifications such as "born of one [father] but from separate wombs."
This very point is clarified by this Smṛti:
"The Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, heirs, and those who are well-disposed kinsmen of a Brāhmaṇa—
if there is impurity (āśauca) among them, the purification of the Brāhmaṇa is held to occur after ten days."
And [the texts state], "by six, by three, or by one," and so forth.
As for women of different castes, however, purification occurs at the time of their husband's death, provided he is still living.
And it is said:

In the case of birth or death among slaves and wives born of anuloma unions, the period of impurity shall be equal to that of their master; however, if the master has died, it shall be according to the paternal lineage.
Others read the first quarter-verse as "asavarṇāsutānām" (of those born of wives of a different caste).

If this reading exists, then even for Śūdra sons who reside in the father's house and remain dependent on him, the period of impurity is ten days and so forth, calculated with respect to the father's caste.
And here, "servants" refers to those who work for wages.
However, regarding those who are born slaves (*garbhadāsa*), another rule is heard:
"Artisans, craftsmen, physicians, as well as male and female slaves, kings, and royal servants are proclaimed to be pure immediately (*sadyaḥśauca*). Thus it is said.
In this manner, their purity should be understood as pertaining only to physical contact, and not, however, to activities such as giving gifts or eating.
Since these terms are based on specific actions, one might ask: does purity apply in the absence of those actions, or are all activities prohibited, or are only certain ones permitted?
Because of the phrase "for the sake of not obstructing the king's business," when a need arises, those very actions that come to mind are what are intended.
And such is the established practice.
But is it not the case that no prohibition against touching is heard here? For it is recited in another Smṛti:
After the collection of the bones, the touching of the limbs is prescribed;
likewise, another [impurity] lasts for three or four days, after which a Brāhmaṇa may attain purity through touch.
Purification shall occur on the eleventh day in the case of both birth and death impurity.
Hārīta states: For a Kṣatriya, there is contact [with the corpse] on the sixth or seventh day, and purification regarding food after twelve days;
for a Vaiśya, there is contact on the eighth or ninth day, and purification regarding food after a fortnight;
for a Śūdra, there is contact on the eleventh or twelfth day, and purification regarding food after a month.
Likewise, there is another statement regarding contact:
"A Brahmin becomes pure in ten days for food, while the others [Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras] are purified in twelve, fifteen, and thirty days respectively."
And these alternatives are to be established according to the requirements of the purpose, depending on whether [the master] possesses good qualities or lacks them.
In all cases, for a Brāhmaṇa, food-servants (bhaktadāsa) defile him by contact after three or four days;
however, slaves from birth (garbhadāsa) do so immediately.
The same applies to the other castes as well.

Wherever this immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is prescribed, in all such cases there must be a bath and the changing of clothes. It will be made known later that "whatever purification is ordained for each specific object [applies here too]."
"Even for unmarried girls, the sapinda relationship extends through three generations;
however, for women who have sons, it is understood to extend through three male ancestors," says Vasiṣṭha. This refers specifically to the period of impurity (āśauca).
The rule regarding marriage has been shown.
It is established that the limit is the seventh person; six persons are *sapiṇḍas*.
Upon reaching the seventh, the relationship ceases.
The state of being *samānodaka* (distant kinsmen) is the designation of *samānodaka*.
Regarding the non-knowledge of birth and name:
"birth" means that this person was born into our family; "name" refers to [the lineage] from such-and-such a father, grandfather, and so forth.
If neither is perceived, there is cessation; therefore, even if only one of the two is known, it should be understood that the water is undesirable.

Having entered a river or another body of water, bending down so that the water reaches the navel, facing south, and having taken up water with the right hand over the left, they should return without looking back.
In the case of birth as well, it should be exactly the same; however, the *sūtaka* (impurity) belongs to both the mother and the father.
The *sūtaka* belongs to the mother alone, while the father becomes pure by performing ritual ablution (*upaspṛśya*).
Thus it is regarding birth among sapindas.

Just as the rules of ten days and so forth were established for death with respect to one's livelihood through the six duties and the like, and with respect to the smallness or greatness of one's Vedic study, so too in the case of birth, the mere impurity is extended [by analogy] without limitation of time.
And by implication, since no specific distinction is grasped, there is the acquisition of all those [consequences] connected with it.

But if there were an extension [of the rule] limited by time (*kālāvacchinna-atideśa*), then, because of its primacy, the connection with the ten-day period alone would apply to Vedic study and the like;

or else, due to proximity in the text, it would be satisfied by the single day in preference to the ten days and so forth, and thus there would be no connection with the other periods such as the three days.

In that case, this Smṛti—which prescribes [the rules] for death and birth-impurity (*mṛta-sūtaka*) in a general manner when there is a need regarding conduct and Vedic study, and which establishes [the period] based on mere birth without regard for qualities and the like in the case of birth—would be contradicted.
Furthermore, established custom (*samācāra*) would be contradicted.
[Objection: In that case, would not the rules of three days, one day, and so forth also apply to women who have given birth, thereby contradicting established custom?
To this it is replied:
If this were a mere alternative (vikalpa),
then the eon (kalpa) would have remained exactly as it was;
for in that case, the word "but" (tu) would be more appropriate.
Furthermore, the word *sūtaka* does not denote impurity (*aśauca*) itself;
rather, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it would indicate the impurity associated with *sūtaka*.
And since secondary indication functions through association, it is more appropriate for it to indicate precisely the state of untouchability (*aspṛśyatā*).
And if all types of impurity were intended, he would have simply stated "impurity" [in the rule], namely, "impurity belongs to the mother alone.
Therefore, since another Smṛti text speaks of three nights of untouchability, its absence here implies an option between those two: the birth-impurity (sūtaka) belongs to the mother alone;
or, between the parents, it belongs to the mother alone—this is the option regarding the father.
"Having touched water and bathed, one becomes pure"—this is merely an introductory statement; by the verse to be cited next, even for a father, the period is indeed only three days.
But having emitted semen, a man becomes pure simply by touching water;
however, due to the connection arising from the seed, he should observe impurity for three days.
By teaching that [impurity] lasts for three days when there is a cause, he approves of the aforementioned purification through touching water (*apasparśana*).

If one asks for what purpose this is stated, it is for the sake of an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) as a rule of similar form, not as something to be enjoined, like the statement "one may offer oblations of wild sesame gruel.
However, having emitted semen by engaging in sexual intercourse, immediately after the emission of semen, one becomes pure by touching water—that is, by bathing.
Therefore, from this "seed-related connection" (*baijika-abhisaṃbandha*): "seed-related" (*baijika*) means caused by the seed;
"connection" (*abhisaṃbandha*) means the production of offspring.
Therefore, in that case, why should one not conform to or follow [the rule]?
Impurity (*agha*) consists of ritual impurity (*āśauca*) for three days.
And the kind of impurity that results from the emission of semen when one has not bathed is not the same as that which occurs at birth; rather, in the latter case, it lasts for three days.
This is restated as being part of the latter half of the preceding verse.

For this very reason, the term *upaspṛśya* refers to bathing (*snāna*), not sipping water (*ācamana*), according to the statement: "Bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse.
However, some maintain that when a son is born, one may indeed touch [others] on that very day.

And so Śaṅkha says: "Upon the birth of a son, while the umbilical cord is still uncut, there is no fault in accepting gifts of molasses, sesame, gold, clothing, upper garments, cows, or grain; some say this applies to that very day.
Therefore, that day is auspicious for the ancestors and increases their satisfaction; by the mere remembrance of one's forefathers, that day does not become defiled. Thus [it is said].
Likewise, there is the statement, "some also perform the *śrāddha*";
by this, it is established that for the father there is an absolute absence of impurity (*āśauca*).
In that regard, these two *smṛti* texts are to be understood as optional alternatives (*vikalpyete*), depending on whether his livelihood was previously virtuous or non-virtuous.
Those who touch a corpse are purified in one day and night, or indeed in three periods of three nights; those who offer water for the deceased are purified after three days.
Three periods of three nights make nine days;
together with one day and one night, this constitutes a full day and night (*ahorātra*). Thus, ten days are taught in this manner for the sake of metrical conformity.
Regarding those who touch a corpse— those who perform its bathing, decoration, and so forth— for them,
as well as for others who carry it out, he will prescribe merely bathing;
and he will clarify this in the passage concerning "those who eat with the deceased."
And this [applies] to those who are *samānodaka* (sapindas), or to those who carry out the removal [of the body] for payment;
however, regarding the removal of one who has no protector, another *Smṛti* states:
"For those of virtuous deeds who perform such a removal, there is no impurity whatsoever, nor any ritual impurity (*aśauca*)."
For them, purification is ordained immediately by immersion in water.
As for the phrase "a twice-born who is not a sapinda," we shall explain that later.
Those who offer water are the *samānodaka*s;
regarding them, it will also be stated that when the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) is offered separately, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*).
In that regard, there is an alternative view:
this [period of impurity] applies to those who share the funeral rice-ball offerings (sapinda), with respect to the suspension of Vedic study and other such matters.
A disciple, performing the funeral rites for his deceased preceptor,
becomes pure after ten nights, together with those who partake in the offerings for the deceased.
The Pitṛmedha is the final sacrifice;
others, however, say that it refers to all ritual action.
By performing that, the disciple becomes pure after ten nights.
This rule applies even to those practicing the student's life (brahmacārin).
It is equal to that of those who carry out the deceased;
for them, the period of impurity lasts ten days, as they carry and escort the dead.
The meaning is that it is the same for the disciple as well.
In the case of a miscarriage, a woman is purified in as many nights as there were months of pregnancy;
when her menstrual flow has ceased, a virtuous woman who is menstruating becomes pure by means of a bath.

In the case of a miscarriage, it is proper that the purification for the woman alone lasts for as many nights as there have been months of pregnancy, because she is the one mentioned in this specific statement;
however, for the sapindas, the rules must be sought from other Smritis and established practice.

Vasiṣṭha, moreover, has prescribed three days for the sapindas: "When a child dies before reaching its first birthday, or in the event of a miscarriage, the impurity for the sapindas lasts for three nights."
"Miscarriage" (srāva), however, refers to the falling out of the fetus after three months but before the tenth month;
some, however, say it occurs before the ninth month.
The premature falling out of one whose time has not yet arrived is called miscarriage.
But it is not only for that which is liquid in form;
likewise, Gautama has stated regarding miscarriage that the nights are equal in number to the months of gestation,
and those in the seventh month also survive.

Therefore, in the seventh month, the period of impurity (āśauca) is complete. This, however, is appropriate for one born alive; otherwise, it is simply equal to the number of months of gestation. In this context, it is traditionally taught that for a menstruating woman, purification occurs through bathing once her menstrual flow has ceased.
In another Smṛti, it is stated that purification occurs after three days.
Regarding this, the established rule is as follows:
before the three days have elapsed, there is no purity even if the menstrual flow has ceased; after the three days, purity occurs even if the flow has not yet stopped.

However, regarding the statement "she becomes pure," since it is said here that she is "virtuous" (sādhvī), this implies that as long as her menses have not ceased, she has no entitlement to participate in Vedic rituals; it does not, however, mean there is a prohibition against physical contact and the like.
For it has been stated: "The first four days are censured."
The construction of the words is as follows: a menstruating woman becomes virtuous, pure, and fit for ritual action once her menses have ceased through bathing.
The inclusion of the word "woman" (strī) is intended to include women of all castes;
however, since the preceding verses were explained as referring specifically to Brāhmaṇas, the word "woman" is used here to remove any such doubt.
Even further on, wherever there is no specific evidence [to the contrary], it refers only to the mere class [of people], as in the example: "among men whose heads have not been shaved."
For men who have not yet had their heads shaved, purification is prescribed as lasting one night;
however, for those whose heads have been shaved, purification is held to occur after three nights.
Some explain these genitive endings according to the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti*, as characterizing the agent; for example:
"One whose tonsure has not been performed is purified in one day.
Likewise, the opinion of certain authorities has been stated that there is also an option depending on the stage of life.
These two [verses] belong to the explanatory statement (*vyavasthāvākya*) of that very verse.
Others, however, say that they are characterized by a connection through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*): "Of those who have died without having had their heads shaved, those who are their *sapiṇḍas*.
Among these, the latter position is intended according to established practice (*samācāra*).

Immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is also prescribed in another Smṛti; the scope for this is shown in that very same text: "Until the eruption of teeth, purification is immediate; until the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*), it lasts one night; for those whose tonsure has been performed, it lasts three nights."
Relatives should place a deceased child less than two years old outside the village,
having adorned it, upon pure ground, except for the collection of bones.
When two years have passed since the birth of one who has not yet reached the full age, he is called "one less than two years old" (*ūnadvivārṣika*).
His corpse, the kinsmen should place outside the village; they should set it down in a pit dug in the ground.
In another *Smṛti*, it is read: "One should bury [it]."
Having adorned [the body] with the ornaments of a deceased person—

even if the deceased is less than two years old, the practice of adorning should be understood to apply according to custom even in cases such as those who have undergone the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).
"In a pure place" means a spot of ground where there are no bones.

It should be buried and established in that which is pure by virtue of being devoid of an accumulation of bones; for it is said that bones are accumulated in the cremation ground. Therefore, by this statement, its placement elsewhere than there is prescribed.
Furthermore, the meaning of the statement is not that a collection of bones should not be made for such a person;
for that [collection] is simply not applicable because of the absence of cremation rites (*agnisaṃskāra*).
No funeral rites with fire should be performed for him, nor should the water-libation ceremony be performed;
having abandoned him like a log in the forest, one should pass three days in mourning.
By the phrase "like a log," he expresses indifference.
One should not perform even a *śrāddha* rite, nor offer water;
for by the prohibition of the water-rite (*udakakriyā*), the prohibition of the *śrāddha* is established, because of their relationship as primary and subordinate acts (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*).
Therefore, the prohibition of the *śrāddha* rite, which is established by customary practice, must be proven by means of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
Others, however, explain it as being for the purpose of prohibiting the burying [of the body] seen in other Smṛtis;
and from that, there is an option (*vikalpa*).
One should neglect it; one should disregard it and fail to perform the activity enjoined by the treatise.
The ritual offering of water should not be performed by relatives for one who has not reached three years of age;
however, they may perform it once his teeth have appeared, or even when his name has been given.
"Up to three years" means a prohibition until the third year, and not from the fourth year onwards.

It is for this very purpose that some read the word "ādi" (etcetera), [interpreting it as]: "The initiation should not be performed for one under three years, but for those aged three years and so forth."
And the traditional practice is exactly like this;
or they may perform it for one whose teeth have appeared.
Because of its association with the water-rite (*udakakriyā*), the cremation rite (*agnisaṃskāra*) is thereby permitted.
But surely, there is freedom of choice regarding conceptual construction;

in that case, why would anyone resort to a course of practice that is achieved through great effort and causes the depletion of wealth? Therefore, instruction on that [conceptual construction] is useless.
It is said:
this authority of the parents is entirely distinct from all others;
it is performed for the sake of benefiting the deceased.
It has already been stated previously that because [the rite] is occasional (*naimittika*), it must necessarily be performed;
however, it is determined here that there exists a prohibition regarding its mandatory performance. That it serves the purpose of benefiting the deceased is made known through permission.
In that case, there is no transgression of the injunction by its non-performance;
however, since the benefit to the preta arises from the performance, there is no inconsistency between the injunction and the prohibition.
If a fellow religious student dies, purification is prescribed after one day has passed;
however, for those who share the same funeral water (sapindas), purification is held to occur after three nights from the time of birth [of the deceased].

Fellow religious practitioners (*sabrahmacārī*) who share the same observances (*samānavrata*) are included by extension as those connected by water (*ekodaka*), up to and including those related by the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*).
Among them, in the event of a birth or a death-impurity (*sūtaka*), there is a period of three nights.
Furthermore, based on other Smṛtis, it should be understood that immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is also an optional alternative for those who offer the water libations.
In the case of women who have not undergone the sacramental rites, the kinsmen on the husband's side become pure after three days;
however, those of the same lineage (the father's kin) become pure according to the very rule already stated.
In the case of the death of those women who have not been formally married but have been accepted by mere word, their husbands' kinsmen are purified after three nights;

however, their own paternal kinsmen, the *sapiṇḍas*, are purified according to the previously stated rule for those whose tonsure ceremony (*cauḍaka*) has been performed—since the qualification here refers to the caste, it is three nights.
Others, however, have stated that uterine brothers are purified after ten nights.
And their intention is as follows:

the giving away of an eight-year-old girl is prescribed; and since she has not been given away, there is an absence of the designation "one whose tonsure ceremony is completed" (*nirvṛttacauḍaka*), just as there is for a boy who has been initiated (*upanīta*). At that time, because no other ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is prescribed, a period of ten days alone is appropriate.
However, others have read: "But on the day [of the marriage], for unmarried girls and for children, there is purification.
Regarding this, the commentators state that even if a girl who has reached the age of fifteen remains unmarried, the impurity lasts for that very day;
for there is no authority for allowing time to pass by bypassing the primary scriptural injunction.
To this it is replied:
what is the meaning of the phrase "and among the ignorant" (*bāleṣu ca*)?
For it has already been stated in the analysis of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) that "until the eruption of teeth, [impurity lasts] for one day" (*ādantajamanah sadyah*).
And it is not proper for this [general rule] to sublate that [specific rule], because the former is of a general nature while the latter consists in the establishment of a specific determination.
Therefore, although this single-day [rite] is mentioned separately, it remains fixed from the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) onwards, since a general rule depends upon its particulars.
Consequently, it is understood that this half-verse is indeed non-Vedic (*anārṣa*); it should be interpreted as having contact (*sparśa*) as its object.

For indeed, the prohibition of physical contact would apply to both those affected by death-impurity (*mṛtaka*) and birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), even in the case of a child, just as it does for an adult;
it is for this purpose that it was stated: "But for unmarried girls and children, purification occurs after a day.
And thus, the locative case is understood as denoting the scope (*viṣaya*).
And that [interpretation] is correct because it is a case of an agentive case-ending (*kāraka-vibhakti*);

otherwise, one would have to explain it by supplying an ellipsis and interpreting it as a locative of characteristic (*bhāva-lakṣaṇā saptamī*), meaning "the purification of those who live occurs when children have died. Nor is it established by this [text] that impurity (*āśauca*) results from touching them.
Because its purpose has been fulfilled in another context, because it is surrounded by the ground, and because contact is possible for that which is surrounded by the ground.
If it is asked, "How is a specific meaning understood when there is no specific statement?
[the answer is: because the rule regarding sipping water (ācamana) exists, and such a contact is perceived in the proximity of that very rule.
And likewise, they do not desire the touch of a child who has touched a menstruating woman; thus, there must be a qualification for this. To that effect, Gautama has stated it in his own Smṛti:
It is indeed proper to establish this;
therefore, the definition of the time for establishing the fires is entirely appropriate.
They should eat food that is neither pungent nor salty, they should immerse themselves in water for three days,
they should not consume meat, and they should sleep separately on the ground.
Alkali and salt:
"alkali" refers to barley-ash and the like;
"salt" refers to rock salt and the like.
They should not eat that;
or rather, the inclusion of the term "alkaline" (kṣāra) serves as a qualification for "salt," whereby rock salt (*saindhava*) is excluded.

Furthermore, "immersion" refers to bathing in rivers, ponds, and so forth, provided it is not at a designated bathing place (*tīrtha*), and involves the avoidance of rubbing the limbs with scrubbers and the like.
Furthermore, the consumption of meat is prohibited for as long as the period of impurity lasts according to another Smṛti;
thus it is recited: "They should not approach women, they should not perform purificatory rites, and they should not eat meat.
However, the author of the Gṛhyasūtra says: "They should remain for three days without eating, or subsist on what is purchased or produced [by others]."
And they should sleep on the bare ground, avoiding contact with others;
even during the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka), celibacy is demonstrated in another Smṛti.
This rule for impurity due to death has indeed been proclaimed for when one is present;
this procedure is to be understood as applying to relatives and kinsmen when one is absent.
It is placed there where he died, in that person's presence;
others, however, say that this rule applies only to those who were present at the time of departure.
"Relatives" refers to the *samānodaka* kinsmen.
"Relatives" refers to those who are *sapiṇḍas*;
others, however, consider "absence" to mean residing in another village or another city.
And among them,
if one hears that someone who was abroad has died within ten days of their departure,
he shall remain impure only for whatever portion of those ten days remains.
"Foreign country" (*videśa*) refers to another village and so forth, as previously explained.
"Passed away" (*vigata*) means deceased.
"Less than ten days" (*anirdaśa*).
This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*):
whatever the period of impurity (*āśauca*) is for anyone, the remainder of that [period] constitutes their impurity.
The repeated mention of "ten nights" (*daśarātra*) is for the purpose of completing the verse.
With regard to the origin [of the impurity], the period of impurity for birth and death must necessarily be determined by its commencement;
that is, when the *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) and so forth arise, the rule of ten days and so on begins from that point, not from when it is known by the *sapiṇḍas*.
Consequently, even if the *sūtaka* and so forth are known by a guest but not by the householder, the food is still unfit to be eaten.
In the same way, in both cases, this [impurity] is merely the occasion for the arising [of purification]:
for those subject to ten days of impurity, it lasts beyond that; but for those subject to three nights or one day of impurity, they become pure immediately upon bathing with their clothes on.
When ten days have passed, one shall remain impure for three nights;
but when a year has elapsed, one becomes pure simply by touching water.
For whoever has a period of impurity (āśauca) fixed at ten days or more, for him there is a three-night [period] after that;
but for whoever has a period of three days, one day, or the like, for him there is merely bathing with one's clothes on after that.
Thus, as he will state further on: "with one's clothes on," and so forth.
The meaning is that when a year has passed and elapsed, one becomes pure simply by touching water— that is, by bathing—
because from such statements as "with the hand and with the foot," contact with all parts of the body is understood, and that [contact] is indeed bathing itself.
Upon hearing of the death of a relative beyond the ten-day period, as well as the birth of a son,
a person becomes pure by immersing himself in water along with his clothes.
This rule applies to those who share the same water (samānodaka);
it also applies to sapindas in the case of the three-day or one-day periods.
"With his clothes" means together with his garment.
"Having plunged into the water" means having bathed.
If a child, one residing in another country, or a person belonging to a different lineage (pṛthakpiṇḍa) has died,
one becomes pure immediately by immersing oneself in water along with one's clothes.
"When the son is a child who has not yet cut his teeth," "when he is staying in another country," and "when one of a different *piṇḍa* has died"— these phrases have the same meaning.
"One of a different *piṇḍa*" means, in short, one who is a *samānodaka* (a sapinda beyond the seventh degree).
When he has departed for another country, purification is immediate;
however, when he is nearby, it is said that for those who offer water, purification occurs after three days.
If death or birth should occur again within ten days,
the Brahmin shall remain impure for as long as that period has not yet passed ten days.
Here too, the mention of "ten days" is intended to indicate the period of impurity (*āśauca*).

If another cause for impurity arises while the period of impurity belonging to a particular person has not yet expired, then purification occurs by means of the remainder of the first [period] alone; one must not, however, count ten days or more starting from the day that the intervening [impurity] occurred.
Thus says Gautama: "If that [impurity] should occur again within [the existing period], they shall be purified by the remainder of that [first period]."

In the compound *maraṇajanmanī* ("death and birth"), since the sequence cannot be understood without effort and because there is a possibility of their occurrence even out of order, it should be understood—based on established usage—that they refer specifically to those of the same kind (*samānajātīya*).
Furthermore, the word *punaḥ* ("again") is more effective when referring to things of the same kind.
The mention of *vipra* ("Brahmin") is also intended as an illustration for all those subject to ritual impurity (*āśaucin*).
In another Smṛti, however, it is prescribed: "At the remainder of the night with two [verses], and at dawn with three.

Having established that for this Brāhmaṇa there is ten nights of impurity upon touching a corpse, it states: "If someone else should die or be born in the interval, he becomes pure by the remaining days alone. This Smṛti does not admit a distinction between those of the same caste and those of a different caste.
When an Ācārya has passed away, they say that impurity lasts for three nights;
likewise for his son and his wife, it lasts for a day and a night—this is the settled rule.
The teacher is the one who initiates [the student].
Upon his death, the student must observe impurity for three nights.
Upon the death of that teacher’s son or wife, it lasts for a day and a night.

Upon the death of a learned Śrotriya who has been initiated, one shall remain impure for three nights; for a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, or a kinsman, one shall remain impure for a period of two days and the intervening night.
A *śrotriya* is one who studies a branch of the Veda.
"Endowed" (*upasaṃpanna*) means either associated with someone for the sake of friendship or some other purpose, or endowed with virtuous conduct (*śīla*).
Previously, however, it was observed that in the case of a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*), [the impurity lasts] for one day if he has not yet mastered the Veda.
In the *Abhidhānakośa*, however, "upasaṃpanna" is a synonym for "dead.
Because the period of impurity lasts for a long time, the former explanation is superior.

Others, however, connect [the rule] "three nights for a Vedic scholar who is a maternal uncle" specifically with that [maternal uncle], while [the rule regarding] "a night with the two wings" (pakṣiṇī rātri) is connected with disciples and others.

"Relatives" (bāndhavāḥ) refers to the brother-in-law, the maternal uncle's sister's son, and so forth. However, when there is a connection such as "for a maternal uncle, [one observes] a pakṣiṇī," then the pakṣiṇī period is already established for the maternal uncle by virtue of his being a relative;
the repetition is for the sake of making it obligatory.
Therefore, one may act as one desires toward other kinsmen.
When the king has died, one who resides within his realm remains impure for as long as the light [of the sun or moon] lasts;
however, if the king is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*), the impurity lasts for a full day, as does the case when a teacher (*guru*) who is well-versed in the scriptures (*anūcāna*) has died.
This word "rājan" (king) functions through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote the mere caste-class (*varṇa*) when that class possesses qualities such as consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

For it has been said: "In whose territory he resides... [and so forth]. If the word were to denote the sovereign of a territory delimited by a specific caste, that would be a case of metaphorical indication, and not the primary meaning of the word.
"With light" means it exists together with light. If one dies during the day, [the cremation] takes place during the day itself; however, at night, that [light] is absent.
Thus, at night, it is only night and not day.
This itself is the indicator that, in other instances where "night" is mentioned, there is an understanding of "day and night" even when "day" is not explicitly mentioned;
as in the expressions "by nights equal to a month," "three days," or "one day."
In the phrase "and by one day," however, the mention of "night" is for the sake of completing the meter.
At night, fire is the light;
for thus it is said in the *Agnihotra-brāhmaṇa*: "By means of fire as luster, she becomes possessed of luster; by means of the sun as luster, she does not [become so]."
In the case of one who is not a *śrotriya*—that is, one who does not study the Veda—the [impurity lasts] for a full day;
it does not occur at all during the night, even if the occasion (*nimitta*) arises during the night.
But how can one be an *anūcāna* and yet not a *śrotriya*?

For it is thus remembered in the scripture (*pravacana*) that one who has studied [the Veda] along with its limbs (*sāṅga*) is called an *anūcāna*. It is true that even a teacher (*pravaktṛ*) is called an *anūcāna*; however, this rule for the day applies to one who, in some way, expounds the meaning of the texts of the limbs and so forth.
And when the guru has been initiated, he is the primary object of honor; or [the rule applies] to the *ācārya*, because of the existence of other injunctions.

Some, however, connect the negative particle (*nañ*) with the word "non-Vedic scholar" (*aśrotriya*). Here, by the elision of the negative particle, they say that for one who is the teacher (*upādhyāya*) of others, no one at all prescribes this rule in that case.
A Brahmin is purified in ten days, a Kṣatriya in twelve days,
a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified in a month.

This [text] is intended to exclude the alternative options of three or four days and so forth, which depend on the previously mentioned modes of livelihood (*vṛtta*) for Kṣatriyas and others; however, the ten-day period for a Brāhmaṇa is merely restated here. In this regard, it must be asked: by what means is the fixed duration of time not already established for Kṣatriyas and others, such that this [text] is understood as being for the purpose of excluding other alternatives?
For this very [period] is what establishes the duration for them;
since this exists, the ten-day period is understood there as being for the purpose of indicating that [impurity].
And even though this exists, its status as an indicator of that [period] does not cease.
Even though the eligibility for the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*) is established, those other options belong only to that person for whom the ten-day period has been prescribed.

Furthermore, in another Smṛti, it is stated with reference specifically to the Brāhmaṇa: "For a Brāhmaṇa, the Vedic study may resume after one day," and so forth. However, regarding those other options mentioned in other Smṛtis, they are to be treated as alternatives (*vikalpyante*).

Regarding the eleventh day, a certain commentator says: "A Brahmin is purified after ten days. In this context, the mention of "days" (ahar) is intended to be significant; therefore, on the night of the tenth day, there is no impurity (*āśauca*).
Consequently, it is appropriate to perform the invitation (*nimantraṇa*) and other rites on the preceding day.
For one who is about to establish the sacred fires (*agny-ādheya*), the onset of impurity (*āśauca*) would occur through the morning vigil and other such rites;
that is incorrect. For if the day were intended [as the period for impurity], there would be no impurity even during the initial nights.
Now, it might be argued that [the rule] "the impurity for a death lasts ten days" will apply there;
however, what is the authority for not intending that meaning here?
Therefore, it has been demonstrated that this word *ahaḥ* denotes a full day-and-night (*ahorātra*).
And likewise, in the preceding verse, the inclusion of the word "entire" (*kṛtsna*) in the phrase "the entire day" is for the purpose of excluding the night.
One should not prolong the days of impurity, nor should one obstruct the ritual acts performed with the sacred fires;
furthermore, while performing that rite, even a kinsman does not become impure.

If someone holds the view that these aforementioned ritual options (*kalpa*) of three days and so forth are alternatives to the ten-day period based on equality, rather than being determined by distinctions such as one's conduct (*vṛtta*), and consequently thinks: "Since another [longer period] is possible for a much longer time, why should I adopt the one-day option which causes hardship to one's daily Vedic study? I shall resort to the ten-day period and remain in the ease of inactivity"—then, out of kindness toward such a person, that settled rule (*vyavasthā*) is clarified:
these are not equal, but are indeed fixed;
and the settled rule has already been shown previously.
Otherwise, for one for whom a specific period of impurity has been prescribed, how could there be an extension of that period, such that this [rule] would have meaning?
What fault is there in taking it in its clear sense?
Others, however, say that even when the days have passed, purification does not occur at all as long as the acts such as bathing have not been performed.
The author will later state, "A Brahmin is purified by water," and so forth.
In that regard, one might think, "I am not defiled because of non-performance [of rites] due to impurity," and thus fail to engage in bathing and other acts for the sake of purification.
To this, it is said: "One should not let time pass"—one must not delay while external impurity persists, even when the days have already elapsed.
As for those who claim that there is no impurity on the night belonging to the tenth day, it has been stated that they do not think correctly.

Likewise, Gautama, having stated that "when another period of impurity arises during an existing period of impurity, purification occurs by the remainder of the first," and considering that purification occurs by that very [remainder] when one night remains, said: "If one night remains, [purification is] by two [days].
One should not interrupt the rites performed with the sacred fires.
Since all rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti would otherwise have to cease due to impurity, this is stated:

those rites performed with the sacred fires, such as the evening oblation (sāyaṃ-homa) and others, one should not obstruct—that is, one should not omit or neglect them. "Obstruction" (pratyūha) means reduction or non-performance.

And one should not perform [the rite] oneself, since it is said: "Even a close relative (sanābhya) should not do that act. Even a close relative would not become impure; how much less so anyone else? Likewise, having stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*: "The obligatory rites should be suspended, except for those performed on the sacred fire-altars (vaitāna); some say they may be performed in the domestic fire (śālāgni)," it further says: "Others should perform these."

Furthermore, the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) is not performed as a mere oblation (*homa*); rather, it is a ritual performance consisting of all its constituent parts (*sāṅgaprayoga*), because it is only there that the agency of the person is possible. Since the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*), however, consists in the renunciation of a substance (*dravyatyāga*), it must necessarily be performed by oneself.
Therefore, the *homa*, the *vaiśvadeva*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, and so forth, are suspended.
However, the suspension of other acts such as silent recitation (*japa*) and the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) has not been indicated.
And these [rites] are obligatory;
therefore, permission is granted only for others, since it is prohibited in another Smṛti that "the fire-oblation and Vedic study are suspended.
Thus, there is a systematic distinction based on the difference between the obligatory and the optional.

But optional rites (kāmya) must certainly not be performed because of impurity, since one’s eligibility [for them] has lapsed. Now, one might object: even in the case of obligatory rites (nitya), there is no eligibility for one who is impure, nor is ritual purity (śauca) an auxiliary factor [of those rites].
If it is argued that what is performed constantly with deficient qualities is not called "optional" (*kāmya*),
but rather [optional] arises from this very statement—
do not say so.
In this context, even that which is a means of measurement (māna) allows for the agency of another—namely, that others may perform these [rites] for him;
and because that [agency of another] is defective, it is applicable to obligatory (nitya) rites, but not to optional (kāmya) ones.
However, regarding the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, there is a dispute.
And they cite another Smṛti:
"One should not perform a fire-oblation there, even with dry grain or fruits;
likewise, one should not perform the ritual of sacrifice during death and birth."
Therefore, the twilight oblations (*saṃdhyāhoma*), the new- and full-moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), and the annual rites beginning with those of the month of Āśvayuja must be performed;
however, the commencement of Vedic study (*upākaraṇa*) depends solely upon the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), not upon the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*).
Having touched a divākīrti, a woman in her courses, an outcaste, a woman who has recently given birth,
a corpse, or one who has touched a corpse, one becomes pure by bathing.
A *divākīrti* is a *caṇḍāla*, because of his association with extreme impurity and because he is seen used in that sense in the *Mārjāramūṣika-saṃvāda* of the *Mahābhārata*:
"And even at that time, there was a *divākīrti* afflicted by fear."
Nor [is this rule] for the barber, because he is touchable and his food is fit to be eaten.
As for the claim that this bath is required for him when performing the work of shaving, that too need not be stated, since it is already established.
For one who necessarily has the work of shaving performed, the body hairs touch the limbs; since those [hairs], having fallen from the body, are impure, bathing is already established as necessary.
*Tatspṛṣṭinam* means "one who has touched that which was touched by him" (*tasya spṛṣṭam*); one who possesses such [contact] is *tatspṛṣṭī*.
That by which these [others] were touched is also indeed subject to bathing.
Since there is no proximity for anyone else here, some say that the connection with the term *tatspṛṣṭinam* applies to the corpse alone, and not to those such as the *divākīrti* (the executioner).

Others, however, maintain that because they occur within a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*), and because they are heard at the end [of the compound], all [the members] are present in the intellect; therefore, there is a reference by means of the pronoun *tat*.
For here, having formed a copulative compound (*dvandva*) of everything up to "corpse" (*śava*), it is connected with the word *spṛṣṭi* ("touching").
In that case, since the meaning of the compound—namely, "those touched by them"—is present in the intellect, there is a reference by means of the pronoun *tat*.
For the connection with the word "touch" (*spṛṣṭi*) is not indicated for the corpse alone, because it is mutually connected with the "outcastes" (*patita*) and others;
rather, there is a connection of the word alone with the following word. For in a copulative compound (*dvandva*), each individual word denotes the entire meaning.

Consequently, all [the terms] would be proximate [to that word]. Furthermore, if one were to establish a connection between the word *śavaspṛṣṭi* (contact with a corpse) and the word *tatspṛṣṭi* (contact with that), and then connect it with the others, in that case, there would be no connection for the words *patita* (outcaste) and so forth with the word *spṛṣṭi*.
Therefore, the determination is made solely on the basis of customary practice.
Having sipped water and being constantly pure, one should recite, upon seeing something impure, solar mantras according to one's enthusiasm and the *pāvamānī* verses according to one's ability.
The impure substances are those previously mentioned due to their proximity.
The solar mantras are those dedicated to the Sun, such as "ud u tyaṃ jātavedasam" and others.
The Pāvamānī verses are those recited in the ninth maṇḍala of the ten books of the Ṛgveda, beginning with "svādiṣṭhayā" and so forth.
"According to one's enthusiasm" (*yathotsāham*) and "according to one's capacity" (*śaktitaḥ*) have the same meaning;
two words are recited due to the requirements of the meter.
Because of the use of the plural number, the count of three must necessarily be observed.
However, if there is no failure of a more important duty, then the recitation (japa) must indeed be performed.
Because of the mention of "mantras" and the citation of the *pāvamānī* verses from the Ṛgveda, purification occurs even before a hymn (*sūkta*) is completed, provided it exceeds three [verses].
A dog should also be included here [among those requiring purification].
That too is indeed impure; for it is recited in the Gautama-sūtra regarding this very category: "And [the food] of a dog—if some say that one should avoid what has been struck by it."
"Prayataḥ" means one who is self-restrained, focused on nothing else, and intent on the meditation upon the deity of the mantra and so forth;
or alternatively, "prayataḥ" means one who has engaged in the worship of the deity and so forth—when he sees [the desired object], he should act at that very moment and not otherwise.
Having touched a human corpse that is still moist with fat, a Brahmin becomes pure by bathing;
however, if it is no longer moist, he is purified simply by sipping water (ācamana) and then either touching a cow or looking at the sun.
A *nara* is a human being; this [body] belongs to him, thus it is *nāra*.
It is smeared with affection, flesh, marrow, and so forth.
The touching (*ālabhana*) of the cow is the act of contact.
The visual perception of the sun and the mental support of the cow are conceptualized.
One who has been formally initiated (ādiṣṭī) shall not perform the water-libation rite until the completion of his vow;
but once it is completed, having performed the water-libation, he becomes pure after three nights alone.
