*Ādeśa* means "instruction. Due to its connection with the instruction for the observance of vows (*vratādeśana*), one who is in that state is conventionally called a *brahmacārin*.

For such a person residing in the stage of studentship (*brahmacaryāśrama*), this is a prohibition against performing the offering of water, which is otherwise undesirable [for the deceased], in the case of those sapinda relatives who have died.
"But for those who have died previously, one should perform the daily offering (anvāhika) consisting of libations to the gods and ancestors.
The phrase "until the vow" means until the completion of the student's formal return (samāvartana);
it does not mean until the end of any intermediate period of hardship.
Upon the completion of his observances, having returned home, he shall offer water for each of all [the relatives] on a single day and observe impurity for three nights.
However, the offering of water for his mother is required even for one who is under a vow, and there is no violation of the vow thereby.
They cite another Smṛti text: "One who has committed an offense and has been sentenced does not offer water."
The water libation ceremony shall be withheld for those born of illicit unions, for those who have failed in their religious vows,
and for those who commit suicide.
The word "born" (jāta) is connected with each [term]:
one is "born in vain" who does not worship the gods, nor the ancestors, nor men.

For even when there is a qualification [for dharma], one who belongs to no stage of life (anāśramī)—having abandoned both the offered and the unoffered [sacrificial food]—is subject to great fault for remaining in that state for a long time, as heard in such passages as, "having remained without a stage of life for a year," and so forth.
For anyone other than a student (*brahmacārin*) or a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), eating food cooked by another is permissible;
however, cooking for one's own sake is prohibited.
Those born of a mixture [of castes] are those born from the intermixture of different castes in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), such as the *āyogava* and others.
Because they are censured, they are categorized by their association with those born in vain (*vṛthājāta*).

However, although *anuloma* offspring possess a mixed origin (*saṃkīrṇayoni*), they are not included here because they belong to the caste of their mother and possess [Vedic] eligibility (*adhikāritva*).
Furthermore, the designation "mixed origin" is not applied to *anuloma* offspring.
"These mixed castes (*saṃkīrṇayoni*), however, are those born from inverse (*pratiloma*) and natural (*anuloma*) unions;

they include sons born of women not authorized [for intercourse], those born from contact with multiple men, and those born of prostitutes. Furthermore, *pārastraiṇeya*s are those born of others' wives who, even in the absence of contact with multiple men, are born of a mixed union."
Some maintain that this prohibition applies to the sapindas and not to their sons;
however, others hold that it applies even to the sons of those who have committed suicide.
That is incorrect, because the scriptural injunction is heard without distinction.

Because they lack authority in the non-Buddhist forms of renunciation— such as those of the Bhāgala, Raktapaṭa, and others— and because they are indicated by a plural designation, these "outsiders" (bāhya) are so called due to differences in their vows,
philosophical views, and so forth. For those persons who have renounced the self, it is indeed permitted to abandon the body at will when their lifespan has not yet expired,
provided they are elderly or afflicted with incurable, grave diseases that have been rejected by physicians.
As it has been said:
"An old man who, having lost his memory of purity and having rejected medical treatment,
should kill himself by means of Bhṛgu (a precipice), fire, fasting, or water..."
"For him, there is impurity for three nights; on the second day, the collection of bones [is performed];
on the third, having offered water, one should perform the *śrāddha* on the fourth.
This rule applies even to those afflicted by diseases such as leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), for it is indeed intended for them.
As it has been said regarding one whose activity has ceased:
even while in the stage of a householder,
those setting out on the Great Departure do not wish to live in vain.

One whose faculties are impaired is said to be incapable of such acts as ritual purification (*śauca*) and the performance of twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*). Alternatively, one who, though his body is not yet decayed, brings himself to ruin—or one whose faculties are not impaired—is likewise mentioned. Therefore, permission is granted for the opposite case.
In other Smṛtis, the prohibition of water-libations for others is also prescribed,
as it has been said:
"And for those slain by kings, or by horned animals, fanged beasts, or reptiles..."
One should not perform a śrāddha for those who have abandoned their own selves.
Whatever water, offerings of food, or anything else that is given to the departed spirits—all that does not reach them; it perishes in mid-air.
Out of fear of public reproach, men should perform the Nārāyaṇabali;
therefore, food together with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) must be given even to these [outcastes].
Likewise, it is stated elsewhere:
"Death from a Caṇḍāla, water, a snake, a Brāhmaṇa, lightning, or even from fanged beasts, occurs for those whose karma has ripened."
And so it has been said:
"For those who set fire to the pyre, those who bathe and adorn the deceased,
and those who follow as mourners shedding tears, purification occurs through two *taptakṛcchra* penances."
Therefore, his funeral rites must not be performed by others,
nor should even the name of his lineage be used by them.
For that most wicked one dwelling in the ultimate hell, the cause is even greater:
his very name and everything about him is terrifying.
In these very same actions, Saṃvarta has prescribed the Sāntapana penance, Parāśara the Taptakṛcchra, and Vasiṣṭha the Cāndrāyaṇa together with the Taptakṛcchra.
In this regard, specific distinctions such as whether the act is unprecedented (*apūrva*) and so forth may be disregarded.
Regarding what was stated, beginning with "from a Caṇḍāla, from water," and so on, up to "death for those of sinful deeds," a doubt arises therein.

Does this rule—concerning the non-performance of funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) and the performance of penance (*prāyaścitta*)—apply to one such as a *caṇḍāla* who intentionally causes his own death, or rather to one who has fallen by accident and did not intend it?
Why is there this doubt?
Because Gautama stated here: "If [they die] by fasting, weapons, fire, poison, water, hanging, or falling [from a precipice], provided they were desirous [of death]."
And here, it is heard without qualification that [one becomes pure] "from a Caṇḍāla or from water.
In that regard, because there is a single treatise [with other Smṛtis], the phrase "from water" must necessarily be connected with the word "intentionally" according to another Smṛti;
and by association, the suspicion arises that the same applies elsewhere as well.
Furthermore, it is heard [in scripture]: "of those who perform evil deeds.
And an evil deed is that which is prohibited.
In this context, it is logical that one who performs what is prohibited is a performer of evil deeds.
And the state of being an agent consists in performing one's own activity and in being an instigator of another;
in that regard, lightning, fanged creatures, horned animals, and the like are not [agents],
nor are they instigators.
Nor are those [causes of death] like a pit, water, or a sword,
such that by taking them up one would be an independent agent who kills oneself.
Rather, it is made known by the scripture that he for whom such a death has befallen was one who committed evil deeds in a previous birth.
As in the case of those with black teeth and so forth. Even there, what is the point of this being made known?
It is intended to indicate that those with missing limbs and the like are connected to past sins.

An expiation (prāyaścitta) should be performed as stated by Vasiṣṭha; for some it consists of performing two *kṛcchra* penances, while for others it may be even more extensive. However, since the responsibility for the funeral rites has been taken away by death in this case, there is no purpose in this [penance].
If it were determined that he has committed a sin,
then anyone who has entered into matrimonial, friendly, or sacrificial relations with him would also become a wrongdoer;
yet such is not the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭas*).
For those who have entered into such a relationship are not questioned by anyone,
nor do they perform penance;
therefore, it is inferred that they desire [it].
However, since some read "of those killed by cows or Brahmins" in another Smṛti and then read "of those who abandon themselves" separately, it appears that this is a specific (exceptional) rule.
Therefore, a doubt arises: what is appropriate here? [The answer is: "for those who desire [to die]."
Why?
Because of the mention of "evil action.

For he who, by his own will, engages in an activity that causes his own destruction, thereby transgresses the scriptural injunction: "One who desires heaven should not depart before the end of his natural lifespan."
And he is rightly designated as one who performs evil deeds.
But was it not said that those [faculties] are not like swords and such, whereby killing would occur by mere intention? It is replied:
He who does not guard against negligence has indeed committed that [transgression].

Therefore, even if a person goes alone into a forest abounding in outcasts and robbers, although he may have no desire such as "May the outcasts kill me," nevertheless, because he has not avoided negligence through his engagement in activities conducive to that [danger], there is certainly a transgression of the scripture.

In this way, for one who crosses a river with his own arms or boards a doubtful boat under the command of an unskilled helmsman, if he perishes due to the loss of momentum or because the boat turns over, it is indeed appropriate that he be held responsible for his misdeed.
Likewise, if bathers were to be carried away after failing to ascertain the depth with their staffs or the presence of crocodiles and sharks, they would not be at fault.

Likewise, one who has boarded a boat that is firmly moored yet lacks oars, and which is being propelled by a skillful, attentive, and capable steersman through turbulent waters, might—if a sudden, swift wind arises as a whirlwind and the boat encounters a whirlpool—perish due to the failure of the raft; yet he would not be transgressing the scripture.
Similarly, if one does not avoid a region infested with snakes and is bitten and dies, he would indeed incur guilt, and not otherwise.
Likewise, having seen a cow with sharp horns or an elephant, if one does not retreat to a distance and is killed, a transgression is appropriate in this case.
Thus, when lightning flashes during the rains in the forest, it is indeed a fault not to enter a village or town.
If lightning should somehow strike someone staying in a village, then he is not at all at fault.
Therefore, it is proper to perform such actions exactly as prescribed.
In that context, the prohibition of water-libations is intended to illustrate the exclusion of all post-mortem rites (*aurdhvadehika*), as this has been cited in another Smṛti.
And for women who have resorted to heretical sects, those who act according to their lust, those who harm the fetus or their husband, and those who drink liquor.

Heresy (*pāṣaṇḍa*) consists in abandoning the scriptures and resorting to external doctrines, such as wearing a human skull, red garments, and so forth; those who rely on it are those who have adopted its specific emblems and are subject to the authority of that doctrine. And "acting according to desire" (*kāmacāra*) refers to the practice of sexual union with one or many other men, following mere whim by abandoning the conduct and family traditions of her own community.
Treason consists of administering poison, [noxious] substances, and the like to one's husband, as well as causing the abortion of a fetus.
Regarding the drinking of liquor (*surā*), it is by the consumption of that which is prohibited according to its respective prohibition.

On this point, someone says: although there is no distinction in the meaning of the genus (*jāti*) in the rule "A Brāhmaṇa shall not drink *surā*," because of the grammatical gender (*liṅga*), the prohibition applies only to the male Brāhmaṇa and not to the female.
Even though the genus (*jāti*) of woman and man is one, nevertheless their gender-marks (*liṅga*), namely femininity and masculinity, are distinct.
And here, since the word "Brāhmaṇa" is heard in the masculine gender, what occasion is there for the unmentioned [feminine]?

Just as in the case of the injunction "one should have the Brāhmaṇī drink [the mixture] for the sake of a son," it does not mean that one should have the man drink; likewise, when the masculine gender is heard, women are not included.

In some cases, gender is not intended to be significant; for example, in the injunction "A Brāhmaṇa is not to be killed," it is understood that the prohibition applies to a woman as well. In such instances, because the Brāhmaṇa is the most desired object (īpsitatama) according to the accusative case-ending, he possesses primacy.
And when there is primacy, other factors such as gender and number beyond the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadika) are not intended to be significant.
For instance, in the rule "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), the cleansing does not apply to only one cup.

In this case, however, because of the instruction regarding the action by way of the agent as an instrumental factor—namely, "surā is not to be drunk by a Brāhmaṇa"—even though the Brāhmaṇa is expressed by the verbal suffix in the form "a Brāhmaṇa should not drink surā," the nominative case is consistent with the third case (instrumental) due to the occurrence of those meanings within the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Thus, there is a state of being subordinate (*guṇībhāva*), and in the case of a subordinate element, everything that is heard is intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*).
For example, in the rule "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), a male animal is sacrificed and it must be one.
To this, it is replied:

In this case, the reason for the non-intentional or intentional inclusion of the second and third [factors] is not their status as subordinate or primary, but rather their attainment or non-attainment.
That which is not already attained and is logically possible as the object of an injunction is intended [to be enjoined], because it is understood from a word that has no other purpose.

However, when a different matter already known from another source is taken up for the sake of an injunction, it is presented by the word precisely as it was understood through that other means of knowledge, insofar as it is connected to the distinct function of the thing to be enjoined.
In the sentence "A Brahmin must not be killed," the injunction results in a prohibition alone; whatever else [is expressed] is understood from other sources.
However, the intention to express the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadika) arises because otherwise the Vedic revelation (śruti) would be rendered purposeless.
As for the gender, number, and so forth, which are the meanings of the suffixes, since they can be included as necessary adjuncts even if unintended, their expression or non-expression is discussed.

In this context, a person is not to be impelled toward [the act] by a Brāhmaṇa or others through an injunction, because such activity proceeds spontaneously due to aversion to it; and since everything here would follow of its own accord, a prohibition that is not itself enjoined is in no way capable of being connected. This is because there is no attainment [of the act] from any other source, because it is not an agent, and because as a qualification of a non-agent, it does not obtain a connection even by entering into the very nature [of the act].

Therefore, for the sake of establishing its positive concomitance (anvaya), its status as an object must be accepted. And when that [object] has been made an object by means of a positive injunction, the meaning of the verbal root (bhāvārtha) is required as its objective correlate.

Furthermore, since the objective portion [of the action] has been grasped by the negation, the meaning of the verbal root (bhāvārtha) has deviated from that [negation]. Having its performance established through worldly activity, it does not even desire to enter [the sentence] for the sake of establishing an injunction regarding itself. Rather, in an injunction that requires only a qualified subject (adhikāra), it establishes the status of the person who—having understood from another means of knowledge that he is the agent of killing—as the qualified subject; thus, it attains syntactic connection (anvaya) by way of its qualification. Therefore, the theory of "expression of the related" (anvitābhidhāna) is established. Consequently, because the verbal root's meaning, along with its qualification, cannot be the object of an injunction, worldly activity must be accepted [as the basis for its performance].
Furthermore, there is an activity characterized by passion (*rāga*), and for that [activity], as well as for hatred (*dveṣa*) and so forth, there is no restriction regarding gender or number.

Therefore, a word whose meaning is not subject to injunction, because its purpose is the communication of an already understood object, relinquishes its denotative power (*abhidhāna-śakti*) and indicates (*lakṣayati*) an object whose nature has been determined through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
In that case, since gender and number are not denoted by the word through its primary intention (*tātparya*), how could there be any intention to express them (*vivakṣā*)?
Since a noun stem must be expressed by some form of word, and a bare stem alone is not to be used, the gender and number are employed for that purpose.
Therefore, this is the understanding here:
the agent who has resolved upon the act of killing is enjoined to the meaning of the negative particle.
Therefore, in a prohibitive sentence, the hearing of the accusative case is not a restrictive factor when there is no intention to express it as such.

For even where the instrumental or the nominative is heard—as in "A Brāhmaṇa should not drink" (*brāhmaṇena na pātavyā*) or "A Brāhmaṇa should not drink" (*brāhmaṇo na pibet*)—there too, that [agent] is restated (*anūdyate*) because it is not something to be enjoined, since its status is already established by another source.
In those cases, the nominative and instrumental are connected precisely as qualifiers of the subject (*adhikāra*). Thus, they are equivalent to the accusative in that specific context.

Moreover, even when a second [accusative] case-ending is heard, that which is not already established is intended to be enjoined because it is the object of an injunction, as in the cases: "one should approach his wife" (*bhāryām upagacchet*) or "one should procreate offspring" (*apatyam utpādayet*).

For the worldly purpose of a "wife" is not [the object here], since that is already accomplished by the very act of marriage (*upayamana*). Nor is it something taken up by an injunction in another sentence such that it could be referred to according to its comprehension, as in: "He takes the Āśvina cup," "He takes the Maitrāvaruṇa cup," or "The Adhvaryu takes these ten"; in these cases, the cups (*graha*) are indeed taken up as qualified by a specific number.
Therefore, because the number is already determined, it is indicated in the injunction for sweeping according to that understood number.

Here, however, since there is no other sentence and this very [sentence] is the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), there is no authority for abandoning the number heard in the text. Consequently, the abandonment of the single [sweeping] presented by the independent expressive power of the word would arise solely from human intellect.

In the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal," because the injunction has the sacrifice as its object and because that [sacrifice] is by nature something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), there arises an expectancy for the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). When that which is to be enjoined is presented together with its specific qualifications and the action, if the operation of the injunction is not fully completed by the mere object, why would those words—which express their own meanings and depend upon other required meanings—not convey those meanings?
Those who know the science of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) state the injunction themselves and immerse themselves in what has been said by others;
however, what we have stated is easy to grasp through a simple means.
An excessively vast proficiency of learning is not required here;
indeed, this alone is its essence.
To that extent, such knowledge is useful for the practice [of the teachings]; whatever exceeds that is merely boasterism and is nothing but explanatory praise (arthavāda).
For in that case, a specific determination arises from the *arthavāda* where the requirement of the injunction remains unfulfilled.

As it has been said: when there are many means of food present, such as ghee, oil, salt, and so forth, and there is uncertainty as to "with what [one should offer]," it is understood to be "with ghee.
However, since no performance is heard of regarding the nights, the *arthavāda* "they become established" serves to fulfill that requirement.
Therefore, it is understood that [the injunction] is for one who desires consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).

Here, however, because the meaning of the word "Brāhmaṇas" is already complete and thus has no further expectancy (*nivṛttākāṅkṣā*), it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) depending merely on praise.
Now, it is presented merely as an indication of a sign (*liṅgadarśana*): "of the gods eating the oblation."

Therefore, just as it is said that "the more wicked follows after the excellence [of another]," that [prohibition] also, because it applies to men, is not meaningless as a restatement based on a partial [occurrence].

For women, too, there certainly exists the consumption of the remnants of the gods' food, such as clarified butter (*ājya*) and so forth; and the Vedic citation is seen in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* and other rites in the passage: "O sacrificial vessel, you are the seat of the Vedas."

Nor can the drinking of those [liquors] be inferred from the injunction, "One should not cause a faithful performer [of a rite] to drink surā," because that [prohibition] is already encompassed by the prohibition of killing a Brahmin. Therefore, the prohibition applies to the mere caste; this is the resolution regarding this point of contention.
Having carried out the funeral rites for one's own teacher, sub-teacher, father, mother, or preceptor who has passed away, one who is under a vow is not released from that vow.

He considers the term *sva* (one's own) to be an adjective qualifying the teacher; since the rule "when the teacher's teacher is present" extends [the requirement of permission] to that teacher as well, this is a prohibition [of saluting] even in his case. Others, however, explain the word *sva* as signifying a kinsman.
In that case, however, it would not be necessary to mention "father" and "mother."
Regarding the statement "the designation [of the term] has the sense of 'perpetual'":
by the words "whether little or much," the Teacher shows—
through the force of what was heard— that there is no loss of the vow for one who removes these [impurities].
The establishment of the meaning of the words is as follows: having removed others, one is separated from this [object].
One should carry out a deceased Śūdra through the southern city gate;
however, for the twice-born, one should do so through the western, northern, or eastern gates as appropriate.
Regarding the phrase "through the city gate," the mention of the "city" is intended as an illustration for villages and other settlements as well.
This rule applies where there is the possibility of multiple gates; it is an instruction for whoever has authority over a particular gate.
And because it is inauspicious, [the practice] is taught starting from the Śūdra by means of his occupation;
therefore, the phrase "according to what is appropriate" should be connected respectively with the Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, and Brāhmaṇa, beginning with the western direction and so forth.
There is no fault of sin for kings, nor for those observing vows or performing sacrificial sessions; for they always occupy the station of Indra and have become one with Brahman.

Although the word *rāja* refers to the Kṣatriya caste, nevertheless, because the reason "occupying the station of Indra" is provided here, it is understood through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as denoting the lord of a realm.
We shall explain this more precisely in the following verse.
*Vratinaḥ* means those who observe vows, such as those engaged in the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances.
The *sattrins* (those engaged in a sacrificial session) are those performing the *gavāmayana*, or those consecrated (*dīkṣita*) in another sacrifice.
Thus Gautama says: "For those who are not officiating priests, for the consecrated, and for celibate students.

Here is the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): Kings, while occupying and exercising the station of Indra, the sovereignty, the rank, and the lordship over progeny, attained the status of the *brahman*; they were observers of vows and performers of sacrificial sessions.
*Āśauca* refers to the impurity resulting from sin.
Others, however, consider it to apply to those who perform perpetual sacrifices (*sattrins*) who are constantly engaged in giving.
In its primary sense, it pertains to a specific type of sacrifice.
Immediate purification is ordained for a king in his position of high office;
the reason for this is his seat [of authority], for the sake of protecting his subjects.
That place whose nature is great is "māhātmaka. That very greatness is said to be that state in which, when a person is situated, there is the complete protection of all creatures.
And that sovereignty over subjects is what is meant by the statement, "the seat [of authority] is the cause here.
Thus it has been said: it is not mere birth that matters here, but rather the right to protect the subjects.
Furthermore, the word *āsana* here does not refer to a seat or a bed; rather, it denotes that which must be performed by one who has attained that station.

Therefore, even for one who is not a Kṣatriya, if he is capable of protecting the subjects, the absence of impurity (*āśauca*) has been explained by the ancients on the grounds that "it is for the sake of the complete protection of the subjects."
It is not that all forms of impurity cease entirely; rather, that maintenance of impurity which is incompatible with the protection of subjects is what ceases.

For example, in times of famine and the like, the support of the subjects is achieved by giving food from one's own treasury; likewise, during celestial, atmospheric, or terrestrial portents, there must be propitiatory rites. This is a duty to be performed by the King, or else because of the existence of doubts regarding Dharma among the twice-born in their hermitages, or even in the first sacrifice and so forth, where there is the role of the expounder—that too is a purpose [for the King].
And for those killed in a riot or battle, by lightning or by a sovereign,
or for the sake of a cow or a Brahmin, or for whomever the king so desires.
A *ḍimba* is a tumultuous crowd or a fight without weapons;
an *āhava*, *saṃgrāma*, or *yuddha* is a battle.
In those cases, there is immediate purification for those who have been killed.
"Lightning" and "thunderbolt"—this has been explained. "The earthly one" refers to any lord of the earth over the four castes.
For the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of a cow, even other than in battle, he who is killed by water, fire, or fanged creatures [is considered to have died a hero's death].
And whomsoever the king desires [to appoint], for the purpose of protecting and accomplishing his own affairs.
Whence is this [conclusion]?
Because for kings, the cessation of impurity occurs precisely through the act of protection; in that case, how could there be a cessation for anyone else simply by their will, without distinction?
[As it is said: "Of Soma, Agni, Arka, Anila, Indra, of Vitta and Appati, and of Yama..."
The king assumes the form of the eight world-protectors.
Vapu is a portion of Tejas;
Vaiśravaṇa is the lord of wealth;
Varuṇa is the lord of the waters.
In this very context, there is a second explanatory passage (arthavāda):
"A king who is empowered by Lokeśa is not subject to ritual impurity (aśauca).
For the purity and impurity of mortals arise from and dissolve back into the worlds."
The king is presided over by these lords of the worlds;
for him there is neither purity nor impurity, since mortals—that is, human beings—have authority regarding these two.
And the origin and dissolution of those two—their engagement and withdrawal from the worlds—belong to mortals, but not to the lords of the worlds themselves.
When weapons are raised in battle for one who has the duty of a Kshatriya in his hand, the sacrifice is immediately completed, and likewise the period of impurity; such is the established rule.
That by which one is praised or slain is a weapon (*śastra*).
Therefore, even when someone is struck with stones, clubs, or the like, the sacrificial rite (*yajñasaṃsthā*) is accomplished; it is not only by means of weapons such as swords and the like.
A battle (*saṃgrāma*) is called *āvaha* where those competing with one another are summoned for combat.
The duty of a Kṣatriya—namely, not turning one's back in battle and being employed by a lord for the sake of the subjects—is immediately established; that is, it reaches completion.
So too does the sacrifice, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others.
The meaning is that he becomes endowed with that merit;
likewise, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) is also immediate.
On this point, some connect the word "immediate" (*sadyaḥ*) with the phrase "one slain in accordance with the duty of a Kṣatriya."
Therefore, this rule applies only to one who has died on the battlefield, and not to one who has gone elsewhere from there on another day;
this point must be investigated.
A Brahmin becomes pure by touching water; a Kṣatriya, by touching his mount or weapon;
a Vaiśya, by touching his goad or reins; and a Śūdra who has performed his duties, by touching a staff.
When the period of impurity (*āśauca*) for the ten-day and other such durations has been completed, this following [rite] must be performed.
It was explained previously that "having touched water" (*apaḥ spṛṣṭvā*) prescribes bathing.
The phrase "one who has performed the rites" (*kṛtakriyaḥ*) is connected with the Kṣatriyas and the other castes.
And the ritual action is indeed bathing, since no other is mentioned;
having bathed, they should touch the boat and so forth.
Others, however, say it refers to the performance of the *śrāddha* rite.
By performing the *śrāddha* and other rites, everyone becomes completely purified;
even in that regard, a Brāhmaṇa is purified by touching water with his hand, whereas Kṣatriyas and others are purified by their vehicles and so forth.
O best of the twice-born, this purification regarding sapinda relatives has been declared to you;
now learn the purification for the deceased concerning all those who are not sapindas.
The first and second half-verses are intended to present the connection and the logical consistency between the preceding and the subsequent subject matter.
Having carried out the corpse of a deceased twice-born man who is not a sapinda, a Brahmin becomes pure after three nights, as does one who carries out the kinsmen on his mother's side.
"Like a kinsman" means according to dharma, not by means of a price. And "those who are related to the mother":
the inclusion of the word "related" (āpta) is for the purpose of including close kinsmen such as maternal uncles and others.
And from this it is inferred that one who is not a *sapiṇḍa* is not a *samānodaka*, nor is he anyone other than a *sapiṇḍa*.
If one eats their food, however, one becomes pure after ten days;
but if one does not eat their food and does not dwell in that house, one is purified in a single day.
For one who neither eats nor stays [at home], it is exactly three nights as previously stated;
for one who does not eat but stays [at home], it is exactly one day;
and for one who both eats and stays [at home], it is exactly ten days.
If one follows out of desire a deceased person, whether they be a relative or even a stranger,
one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter.

Following behind means pursuing with conscious intent; it does not apply if one follows by mere chance. Bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter are prescribed as the means for purification.
While his own kinsmen are present, he must not have a deceased Brahmin carried by a Śūdra;
for that offering, defiled by the touch of a Śūdra, would not lead to heaven.
One should not cause [the body] to be led away, nor should one have it carried out,
while those of one's own kin and of the same caste remain present;
because of the mention of the "offering" (*āhuti*), one should not burn [the body].
The mention of a "Brahmin" is not restrictive;

rather, based on the explanatory passage (arthavāda), it is understood that the touch of a Śūdra is indeed a fault for both Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas as well, and thus there is a prohibition [against such contact].
Knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind, water, smearing [with ashes],
wind, ritual action, the sun, and time are the agents that purify embodied beings.
Knowledge and the other factors are cited as examples for the purification of time;
likewise, these are the causes of purification within their own respective domains.
In the same way, time also should not be suspected [of being impure] in this context.

Among these, the specific cause of purification for each will be explained right here in this section; for others, it will be explained in their respective places. Among those, knowledge is internal, as taught in Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
Therefore, by the removal of the latent impressions of ignorance (*avidyāvāsanā*), one attains faultless knowledge upon the destruction of passion and other defilements;
and it will be stated that "the intellect is purified by knowledge.
Austerity (*tapas*) refers to the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other such practices.
That is the cause of purification for major and minor sins.
Regarding earthenware and similar items, fire [is the purifier] by means of re-firing;
food is the purifier of pure substances such as milk and roots.
That [truth] also purifies like austerity;
for it is well known that soft water is a cause of purification.
Regarding the mind, it will be said: "The mind [is purified] by truth."
*Upāñjana* refers to the whitewashing of monasteries and the like with lime, cow dung, and so forth, as well as sweeping and smearing.
*Vāyu* refers to wind [as a purifier] when grass, wood, and the like have been touched by outcasts (*caṇḍāla*) or have fallen onto a chariot.
*Karmāṇi* refers to rituals such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*).
And it has been said: "Standing while reciting [the prayers] during the morning twilight, one removes the sin of the night.
This has been explained in the second [book].
Although austerity is indeed an action, it is taught separately for the purpose of indicating its preeminence.
Moreover, in the scripture, austerity is generally taught as distinct from action, as in the expressions "those devoted to action" and "those devoted to austerity."
Of all forms of purity, purity in wealth is declared to be the highest;
for he who is pure in wealth is truly pure, not he who is purified by clay and water.
What is the relevance of this?

Just as one who has voided excrement upon earth, water, or clean ground proceeds without delay, so too, when one stumbles through negligence by seizing the property of others and so forth, a penance must be undertaken without delay for the sake of purification.
This will be explained in the eleventh chapter.
The wise are purified by patience; those who have committed forbidden acts by giving;
those whose sins are concealed by recitation; and those most learned in the Vedas by austerity.
Those who are wise are purified by patience alone;
for they are not afflicted by hatred, envy, or avarice.
Thus, even when evil deeds arise, they remain eternally pure.
Patience (*kṣānti*) is a mental quality consisting of equanimity toward all things.
Even regarding generosity (*dāna*), success in performing what was not previously undertaken has been taught in such passages as "by giving, one purifies [the stain of] killing.
Furthermore, for those whose sins are concealed, recitation (*japa*) has indeed been prescribed in the section on secret practices.
For those who know the Vedas, austerity consists precisely in the study of the Vedas and in knowledge;
as it has been said, "The austerity of a Brāhmaṇa is knowledge.
However, penances such as the Kṛcchra are the cause of purification for all people, not only for those who know the Vedas.
That which is to be purified is cleansed by earth and water; a river is purified by its current;
a woman defiled in mind is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born are purified by renunciation.

In the case of rivers where the water on both banks has become exhausted and is defiled by impurity, the water of that very river becomes pure through its own current as it flows with force and erodes its banks.
This is not like other ground, which is purified by the five [means] according to the rule for purification; such a conviction does not apply to the riverbanks.
Alternatively, this statement—"by the force of the river"—is said when there is a suspicion of impurity due to contact with an impure flow in a swift current.
It should not be thought that she is not purified because she has been touched by streams of impurity from here and there.
When no physical transgression is observed, a woman whose mind is defiled by contemplating the form and qualities of another man is purified by the menstrual flow of blood during her period.
Renunciation will be discussed in the sixth [chapter].
By that, O best of the twice-born, they become pure;
not at all [purified] by a mental transgression.
Whatever was thought by the ignorant, such as the killing of subtle living beings and so forth, that is removed from them.
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the elemental self is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom.

The person who is both the qualified agent and the performer is precisely this internal self; the internal organ consists of the mind (*manas*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and the body, which is the locus of experience.
Since the sense organs are composed of the elements, they are not distinct [from the body].
Herein, one thing is purified by another.
"But everything [is purified] by time" is intended as a praise. By the word "limbs," he indicates the whole through its parts.
Through water and bathing, the body is purified.
The mind, however, consists of both the real and the unreal; its impurity arises from unreal intention (*asaṃkalpa*) and is removed by truth through virtuous intention (*sādhu-saṃkalpa*).
It was previously stated that the mind is the cause of purity; therefore, this [truth] does not effect the purification of the mind through speech, but rather by supplying that [prior statement].
Thus says the Śruti: "Speech speaks as impelled by the mind; for that speech which one speaks while having another mind in view is indeed demonic (*asuryā*), not pleasing to the Vedas."
Endowed with knowledge—produced by the study of Sāṅkhya and Vedānta—and with austerity such as the Kṛcchra penance, the elemental self (bhūtātman) is purified.
The word "bhūta" here denotes a fundamental principle (tattva).
This is the ultimate self, known through the non-reified notion of "I," and it should not be understood as the elemental self consisting of the body.

The intellect (*buddhi*) is corrupted by its perception of the forms of non-existent objects, as seen in dreams and the like, through an adherence to objects imagined according to false doctrines; it is further impaired by the determination of a distinction between the reality of the self and the form of objects, where no such distinction exists. Alternatively, that intellect which arises from unexpiated evil karma from previous births, or from each individual misdeed—namely, the innate ignorance (*avidyā*) characterized by the grasping of non-difference [between the self and the not-self], or characterized by the absence of discrimination between the qualities (*guṇas*) and the self, or taking the form of attachment to wealth, sons, and so forth, and being the cause of excessive craving—that intellect is purified by knowledge (*jñāna*), which consists in the cultivation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) based upon its own self-luminous substrate.

Because of the difference between the intellect (*buddhi*) and its object, and because the object possesses form while the transformation [of the intellect] into the form of the object is unestablished due to the certainty of its changelessness, there is purity of the intellect.
Furthermore, in the former case, "knowledge" (*vidyā*) is simply the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas;
and its causality is like that of fire [acting] upon fuel by means of heat.
"Thus, pure and purified, one attains the world of Brahman"—this is that fourfold purification.
This is a praise [of the lineage], stating that since these purifications are the causes for the supreme human goal, such is the case in the procreation and other rites performed by them.
This decision regarding the purification of the body has been declared to you;
now hear the decision concerning the purification of various kinds of objects.

"Of various kinds of substances" refers to the many types of substances—whether luminous, earthen, liquid, solid, separate, combined, or composite—which serve as the instruments [of action]. By this, he states the distinction from the previous type of purity:
therein, for the self consisting of intellect (*buddhyātman*), purity is predominance;
for material objects, however, it is [purity] through their being fully mastered.
But here it is the reverse; hear the definitive conclusion.
This verse is intended to prevent confusion with the preceding matter.
The purification of luminous gems, as well as of all things made of stone,
has been declared by the wise to be by means of ashes, water, and earth.
Those things which become liquid through contact with fire are called taijasa (fiery), such as silver, gold, copper, iron, tin, lead, and so forth.
*Maṇi* refers to gems resembling crystal.
*Aśman* refers to stone.
The vessel made of stone is a modification of that [earth].
The word "of all" is for the purpose of completing the meter.
The objects of focus are the stones on the mountains and those situated in the rivers.
Since ashes and earth have a single function, they are treated as alternatives; water, however, is to be combined with both. But what, then, is the function here?
Regarding the removal of stains and odors:

it has been stated that purification for an impure substance consists in the removal of its stains and odors, as in the rule, "as long as the stain does not depart from that which is smeared with the impurity.
In this regard, the roughness of the substance is the same for both earth and ashes; purification occurs through a difference in the effect caused by oiliness.
The purification of the impure consists in making it fit for social intercourse by removing its taint of sin.
If this is so, then impurity itself must be defined as: "this thing, being in contact with that, is impure.
But surely worldly objects are understood in that regard by the world itself.
It is not so;
only the general category is known from common worldly usage. That which is loathsome due to contact with urine, feces, and blood, such a thing the world calls "impure."
That which is unfit for actions such as touching and so forth is impure (*aśuci*). How this unfitness arises must be discerned from the scriptures alone.
Furthermore, one who does not stumble over the property of others and the like is called pure (*śuci*).
Therefore, nothing is established here by this establishment of the meaning of words.
Even though it is established that "it is impure and has been removed," the fact that "this [impurity] is removed by this [substance]" is not established without a specific treatise (*śāstra*).

But how can the determination of a specific meaning of a word come from a treatise, given that a treatise is an authority (*pramāṇa*) only with respect to what ought to be done (*kartavyatā*), and not for the establishment of the meaning of words—as in the case of Pāṇini? This is because the *smṛtis* of Manu and others are accepted as being rooted in the Veda.
It is said:
there certainly exists an inference based on a positive injunction (vidhi-anumāna) to the effect that "one should not engage in transaction with that which is defiled by this substance.
There is no contradiction in the understanding that "that [substance] by contact with which the prohibition of transaction occurs is the cause of corruption."

Thus, even when pure, if a substance has been defiled, it must be used after having undergone the prescribed actions such as washing; in this way, its basis in an injunction can be established. Furthermore, the meaning of the injunction is not that "purity must be produced," for if that were the case, one would incur sin by failing to do so.

However, in worldly transactions concerning perceptible objects—which must be carried out using any vessel whatsoever, whether pure or otherwise—since the requirement arises from a general need, there is a scriptural restriction: "When there is a need, one should transact in this manner, and not in any other manner.

But surely, under the view that this is a restrictive rule (*niyama*), only one who seeks spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*) has the entitlement; for anyone else, however, it would follow that the act is performed merely for the sake of desire (*kāma*).
Just as in the consideration of grammatical correctness, although there is no difference in their capacity to convey meaning (*vācakatva*), there is a restriction regarding merit and demerit;

this is true, provided that there were no prohibition against an impure recipient (*aśuddhapātra*). But since such a prohibition exists, how could one engage in transactions with someone who has not performed purification?
The rule for purification, however, is merely a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*). In the case of a counter-exception, how can there be spiritual merit (*abhyudaya*)?
It simply means that there is no transgression of the prohibition.
Or rather, let this recollection be solely intent upon the comprehension of the meaning of the words, like the discrimination between what is correct and incorrect, or like a very brief memory.
As for the claim that the statements of Manu and others must have a basis in some practical action—who has said this?
In whatever case a certain kind of source can be understood to exist, that very thing is accepted as the basis.

In the case of the Aṣṭakā and similar rites, which are of the nature of things to be accomplished (*kārya*), such a sentence is the source; however, regarding an already established matter (*siddha-artha*), it concerns only an established object.

In the determination of word-meanings (*padārtha-vyavasthā*), this [sentence] is for the first time the basis of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra-mūla*), and thus it never constitutes an injunction (*kṛti*).
But here, it is not possible in any way for it to be the basis of linguistic usage.
Furthermore, regarding purity achieved through Vedic mantras, what basis in worldly usage could possibly exist?
Moreover, the injunction would be purposeless.
But is it not the case that Pāṇini also has an injunction, namely: "One should speak with correct words, not with incorrect ones"?
This is not a traditional teaching (smṛti) of Pāṇini;
for his work concludes merely with "this is correct" and "this is not.
However, this is indeed the recollection (smaraṇa) of the authors of the Dharma-sūtras, even if it exists.
This should be understood precisely from the *Abhidhānasāra*. But is it not the case that even in the *Smṛti* a rule is heard?
"The heirs shall divide [the estate] in this manner; the eldest shall take four shares," and "the eldest alone shall take [the whole]."
Is it that the injunctive sense (*vidhy-artha*) alone is traditionally taught (*smṛta*) for other optative suffixes (*liṅg-antara*) such as commands (*praiṣa*) and the like?

If you argue that the meanings of words are of the nature of injunctions (*vidhi-rūpa*), and that commands and so forth are merely supplements to the injunction because an instigation (*pravartanā*) is understood everywhere, then what kind of instigation is there in cases of cause and effect, blessings (*āśis*), or [the suffixes] used for established time (*prāpta-kāla*) and the like?
Furthermore, the act of grasping (*grahaṇa*) cannot be enjoined, because it is already obtained through one's own desire (*arthitā*).

If it is argued that the injunction is for the sake of restriction since the desire [for property] is common to both one's own and others' shares, this is not so; for a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi) is untenable unless there is a surplus over what is prescribed by the assumption of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*).
If it is argued that this is a preclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) termed a prohibition, that is correct;

however, at the very time of partition, whoever among the brothers should take an additional share with the consent of the others would incur sin even if such consent were given, and ownership would not be made known in respect to a portion of a single object.
For in the act of taking possession, the acquisition of ownership is implied; since that which is other than this is understood to be "non-property," it constitutes a prohibition.
Furthermore, even if one takes possession by transgressing that prohibition, ownership would indeed still arise.
And for this reason, it is also accepted [as the purpose] even in cases such as theft;
for at that time, apart from possession (*parigraha*), it cannot be determined whether "this is his property" or "this is not.

Therefore, since injunction (*vidhi*), restrictive rule (*niyama*), and exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) are impossible, the meaning of the distribution is simply this: "He is the owner of this much portion, and he is the owner of that much portion."
Therefore, in this context, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used in the sense of "the arrival of the proper time" (prāptakālatā), as in the expressions "they should take" (*hareyuḥ*) and so forth;
these are restatements of worldly practice, such as "one who is hungry should eat" or "one should approach the Lord for the sake of security and prosperity.
And Gautama has stated this quite explicitly in the passage beginning with "inheritance and purchase" (*rikthakraya*).

Therefore, regarding the Smṛti concerning the Aṣṭakā and other rites, the statement on purity and impurity remains as nothing other than an injunction for a purificatory rite (saṃskāra-vidhi); since it is rooted in an injunction, it is indeed enjoined by an injunction.
Consequently, both purity and impurity are to be understood through the scripture;
thus, purity must also be stated.
It is said:
"In that case, it has already been stated that 'fat' and 'semen' [are included].
Furthermore, the mention of "man" (*nṛ*) there is for the purpose of illustration, based on the observation of another Smṛti text.
Regarding dogs, cats, donkeys, camels, monkeys, crows, village pigs, domestic cocks, rats, jackals, carnivorous animals, wild beasts, birds, and mongooses—
the taking up of their fat and so forth, as well as their hair and flesh,

implies that this purification process must be performed for those things that are impure due to being defiled by urine and the like, according to the statement on purification; however, it does not apply to those [substances] that are used in their natural state.
For substances such as gold are not impure by their very nature, such that they would require purification at the time of ritual application.
Alternatively, a refinement based on visible practice is prescribed for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*),
just as eating while facing east is prescribed.
In that regard, the statement concerning purification would be contradicted.
As for the wiping and washing of vessels at the commencement of a meal, those are due to established custom (*samācāra*), and not from this Smṛti rule on purification.
Furthermore, whatever else is untouchable for a person—such as outcasts (*patita*), Cāṇḍālas, and so forth, as well as garlic, onions, liquor, meat, and the like—that too is a defiler of substances.
In this regard, as to what constitutes a defilement and what constitutes purification, one must consult other Smṛtis and established custom;
moreover, specific details have been stated by the sages Hārīta, Āpastamba, and Parāśara.
However, we have not set forth all those statements here.
This is by way of the specific context of the author, just as in the case of the author of the *Candragomītantra*.
An unblemished golden vessel, as well as one made of stone or silver that has not been chemically treated, is purified by water alone.
This rule applies to gold and silver, which are specific types of luminous substances and are free from stains.
However, for other materials such as copper and the like, purification occurs through scrubbing with brick-dust and other agents when they are touched by food remnants.
Where milk or water has been drunk, no stain remains there.

Regarding those parts of the body that become adhered to by remnants of food, ghee, milk, and so forth, the author will state later: "Therefore, for those two [hands and feet], by their own source alone.

Furthermore, because of the injunction to remove stains and odors, whatever substance is capable of removing a particular stain should be employed in that case; it is not restricted solely to ashes and water.
Thus, Hārīta recites: "With the powders of wheat, kuṣṭha, kalāya, barley, mung beans, and black gram," and so on.
Hārīta states that upon contact with a dog, a *caṇḍāla*, a woman in her courses, and so forth, even for objects free from visible stains, there shall be scrubbing twenty-one times with ashes.
Śaṅkha, however, says that for metallic objects defiled by a corpse, blood, semen, urine, or feces, there shall be turning over, scraping, or scrubbing twenty-one times with ashes;
among these, turning over applies to those that have been permeated by urine and the like for a long time.
*Āvartana* is the reshaping of a gem by removing its name and form according to one's desire to produce a different form.
*Ullekhanam* is the rubbing [of the stone] with a sharp instrument or a touchstone.
However, in another Smṛti, *ākara*, *dāha*, and *avacūlana* are prescribed.
In that regard, the "mine" (*ākara*) is the purification of gold that has been colored by goldsmiths.
"Burning" (*dāha*) is the finalizing of it by goldsmiths in the fire.
"Shaking off" (*avacūlana*) is the striking of it on all sides with a solid golden vessel by the goldsmiths when it has risen up during burning within that mine of color.
And so it has been said: "All sources [of water] are pure.
This includes that which arises from water, such as conch shells, crystal, and the like.
However, a conch shell that is stained should be cleaned with a paste of white mustard seeds, cow's urine, water, and milk.

For it is recited in another Smṛti: "With water for a conch-shell," and "with milk and water, and with a paste of white mustard seeds, for one who has become impure through contact with oily food-remnants.
*Anupaskṛta* means not dug up and filled [again], or else, entirely unimpaired.
And this applies as a supplement to all [the preceding rules].

Therefore, even when there is contact with dry impurities, Cāṇḍālas, and so forth, the purification prescribed in another Vedic branch (śākhā), which was previously demonstrated, remains applicable because of the state of being unsullied.
Through the combination of water and fire, gold and silver emerged; therefore, their purification by means of their own respective origins is more effective.
This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

Beginning with "Agni [desired] the wives of Varuṇa," and continuing through the explanatory passages such as "he desired," the origin of gold, fine gold, and silver is heard. By means of the human faculty, Agni desired the waters, the wives of Varuṇa; he united with them through the act of sexual intercourse, and from that, these two things emerged and were produced.
Therefore, for those two, there is extreme damage caused by their own source—that is, by fire, which is their own cause of origin—and also by water.
If the reading is *sayonyā*, it should be explained as "by ash," which has a common origin with them.
And because of that observation, earth is also sometimes permitted.
Purification is cleansing; it is more excellent.
The purification of copper, iron, bronze, brass, tin,
and lead should be performed as appropriate with alkaline substances, acids, and water.
"According to what is appropriate" (yathārham) means that for each person, whatever is suitable, by which means their impurity can be removed; this is the meaning.
For this very reason, what is stated in another Smṛti is also applicable: "Objects made of tin and lead should be cleaned with cow-dung and husks."

"Just as bell-metal vessels smelled by a cow, those defiled by the remnants of a Śūdra's meal, and those struck by a dog-cooker (śvapāka), are purified by ten applications of alkaline substances. Thus it is said.
For this very reason, various types of alkaline preparations combined with sour gruel, pomegranate, and so forth, become effective.
For all liquid substances, purification is traditionally held to be straining;
for solid masses, it is sprinkling with water; and for wooden objects, it is planing.
Substances subject to decay and having a liquid nature include ghee, oil, milk-whey, and so forth.

Regarding these, when they have been defiled by the remnants of crows and other such creatures, "purification" (*utpavana*) consists in the removal of a certain portion remaining at the front part [of the vessel].
However, in another *Smṛti*, it is prescribed as follows: with the hymn beginning, "The purifying one, the son of the Sun, with the tips of *kuśa* grass... [the purification is performed].

Others, however, say that *plāvana* (overflowing) is *utpavana* (purification by straining): as much of another substance of the same kind is poured in until, the vessel being full, some small amount overflows. This refers to direct defilement;
in the case of very small quantities, there is simply abandonment.
In the case of damage to the vessel, however, one should transfer the contents to another vessel.
But in the case of contact with what has been tasted by others (ucchiṣṭa), it is stated that one should place the oil or ghee into water and recite mantras;
in that instance, the removal of the vessel follows as a matter of course.
For indeed, it is not possible to use oil that has been poured into water without a vessel;
by association, the same applies to ghee. And this [process] of clarifying pertains to liquids.
Where the odor and color produced by contact with intoxicants or impure substances are not perceived, [the vessel may be used]; however, if those two are present, it must be discarded.
All of this is adopted from the Baudhāyana-smṛti.
Furthermore, Śaṅkha has prescribed re-cooking even for cooked substances;
this same purification applies even to all those impure things such as liquor and the like when they belong to Śūdras and others.
In this case, however, *utpavana* means simply pouring [the liquid] out.
As stated by Vasiṣṭha: "For things situated on the ground, it is like water;
those that are compact and solid—such as cold butter, *āmikṣā*, molasses, *parpaṭaka*, and so forth—if a portion of them is defiled, that portion should be removed, and the remainder is pure."
And it has been stated by Śaṅkha: "Of dried [substances] whose defects have been removed.
Alternatively, they are "assembled" from a whole composed of parts; that is, beds, seats, vehicles, and so forth, which consist of an aggregate of substances both of the same and different classes.
The phrase "whose defects have been removed" is to be understood in every instance.
In cases of contact with a corpse, dried excrement, or impure substances, that portion which has come into direct contact should be washed, while the remainder should be sprinkled with water.
Wooden objects made solely of wood, such as mats, wooden planks, and the like, when in contact with a corpse, a *caṇḍāla*, or feces, should be planed;
others, however, maintain that this applies only in the case of contact with feces.
By scraping, the application of perfumes and the like should be removed;
for what remains, there should be washing with earth and water or sprinkling.
However, in the case of contamination by a dog or similar animal, there must be washing alone, just as in the case of feces.
And for items such as beds and couches, which are constructed from wood, leather, and cords, purification is achieved through scrubbing due to their composite nature.
In the performance of a sacrifice, the cleansing of the sacrificial vessels is done with the hand,
whereas the purification of the *camasa* and *graha* vessels is by means of washing.
The purification of the *caru* vessels, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, as well as the *sphya* knife, the winnowing basket, the cart, the pestle, and the mortar, is by means of hot water.
These two verses are to be understood as illustrations by way of restating a meaning established in the Vedas.

Regarding sacrificial vessels such as the *graha* and *camasa*, when they are being used for a subsequent performance, the removal of smears of clarified butter (*ājya*), oblation (*havis*), and so forth adhering from the previous performance must be carried out with hot water.
Thereafter, according to the scriptural injunctions, the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) must be performed in some cases with the hand, in some with *darbha* grass, and in others with the *daśāpavitra*.
This is the purification resulting from formal application (*prāyogikī śuddhi*).
However, in the case of defilement by food-leavings and the like, it is like an ordinary worldly vessel;

for there is a specific scriptural injunction stating, "They do not become defiled by Soma," from which it is understood that in cases of defilement other than that, the general rule of purification applies.
The sacrificial ladles, cups, and wooden splinters are to be distinguished from the ritualists by their specific shapes.
The purification of large quantities of grain and clothing is performed by sprinkling them with water;
however, for small quantities, purification by washing with water is prescribed.
The abundance of grain is traditionally recorded as exceeding one *droṇa*;
however, others explain it in relation to the person and in relation to place and time—
for someone in a state of poverty, even half a *kuḍava* may be considered much.
Likewise, in a certain state, one whose treasury has increased reaches a state of abundance;
thus Baudhāyana said:
"The place, the time, as well as oneself, the substance, and the purpose of the substance..."
Having understood the rebirth and the state [of the disciple], one should apply the purification.
Likewise, regarding garments as well, some say there may be many beyond three;
even though the term "plurality" (*bahutva*) applies from three onwards, since the plural form "of the few" (*alpānām*) is heard in the text, therefore those up to three are considered "few.
The mention of "with water" (*adbhiḥ*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, it should also be observed that whichever garment has its contamination removed by whichever specific means, that [means] is to be applied;
and this has been shown previously.
The connection with sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is for the purpose of restricting the use of water.
The sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) must be performed with water alone;
the repetition [of the rule] is due to this very distinction.
And this applies in the case of a major defilement, such as contact with a corpse, excrement, a Caṇḍāla, or similar things.
Otherwise, however, for small quantities, only sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is prescribed.
If, even after washing, stains and the like do not depart from the cloth, then Gautama has stated that one should cut off only that portion or discard it entirely.
The purification of skins is like that of cloth, and the same applies to articles made of split cane;
however, the purification of vegetables, roots, and fruits is held to be like that of grain.
[This refers to] hides and leather straps that are touchable, but not those naturally impure [leathers] belonging to dogs, jackals, and the like.
This same rule applies even to their derivatives, such as shoes, armor, and so forth;
for in this context, the derivative is understood by means of the primary material, and the primary material is understood by means of the derivative.
And likewise, in the rule "of wooden [objects]," this same purification applies even to wood.
For Vasiṣṭha, after prescribing the purification for wooden objects, stated: "wood, bone, and earth.

If the original material were not included by means of the modification, how could there be an extension (atideśa) of the purification to wooden objects through that rule which prescribes a purification not previously mentioned?
However, it is indeed logical that there should be the acceptance of modifications of primary materials, provided that the perception of them as such does not cease.
"Woven from split bamboo" refers to items made from tree bark and the like.
In another Smṛti, this very same purification is prescribed for wings, strainers, skins, chowries, grass, cane, hair, bark, and garments made of bark.

In this context, "feathers" refers to those of peacocks and the like, as well as the chowries and other items fashioned from them; "pavitra" refers to *darbha* grass and to garments made of that *darbha*;
and by the word "grass," palm leaves are meant.
The "king of grasses" is known as the *tāla* tree; this is recorded in traditional lore (*smṛta*).
In that case, the designation of the whole is understood from a single part, just as Devadatta is referred to by the word "given" (*datta*) and so forth.
This applies to children of cows, horses, and goats, but not to humans, because when they die, [their bodies] are not to be touched.

All this purification is said to occur upon the destruction of a different substance (*dravyāntara*), not upon the destruction of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) [of the object], because the purification of cloth and grain is of one and the same form.
The mention of vegetables and so forth is like that of grain;

just as for grains in their state as grain, sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and washing (*prakṣālana*)—without other refinements such as threshing—are the causes of purification, so it is for vegetables and the like as well.

Therefore, this rule applies to those that are uncooked; however, for cooked items, even though they may be designated by terms such as "vegetables" (śāka) and so forth, another method of purification must be sought, as it has been stated:
"with golden water and with the flame of fire," and so on.

However, for vegetables and the like brought from a mine, as well as for buttermilk, curds, milk, and so forth, *prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling) and *paryagnikaraṇa* (circling with fire) are specifically prescribed by Hārīta.
Likewise, for leguminous grains, there is rubbing, splitting, grinding, and so on.
And this is for the purpose of removing doubt regarding contact with the feet.
Thus it has been said: "All sources [of gems] are pure."
Silk and woolen cloth are purified with saline earth; blankets of Kutapa wool with ariṣṭaka fruits; fine linen cloth with bilva fruits; and linen with white mustard seeds.
*Ūṣāḥ* refers to golden earth;
*ariṣṭaka* and the others are well known.
When there is an application of oil or similar substances, one should perform the removal of that application by means of water mixed with the powder of those materials.
*Kauśeya* is a specific kind of silk cloth.
Likewise, *aṃśupaṭṭa* is woolen cloth made of sheep’s wool; regarding these, Hārīta has stated that among items made of wool, the sun [is the purifier].
This should be understood to apply to those items that are constantly worn and have been touched by the bodies of many people, and not in the case of any other kind of defilement.
Since sprinkling and washing would otherwise apply to those [cloths] only in their pure forms, the rules for removing stains such as oil are extended to them.
The mention of "linen" (kṣauma) is intended to indicate other materials such as hemp-cloth (śāṇa) and the like.
For conch shells, horns, and objects made of bone or ivory,
purification should be performed by one who knows the rules using either cow’s urine or water, just as with linen cloth.
The bones, horns, and teeth of animals such as cows, sheep, and elephants—those that are touchable—are [the means of purification], but not those of dogs, donkeys, and the like.
There is an option between cow urine and water;
however, a paste of white mustard seeds is to be used in combination with both.
Grass, wood, and straw are purified by sprinkling;
a house by sweeping and smearing with cow-dung; and an earthen vessel by being fired again.
The stalks of rice and other grains are the straw used for such purposes as bedding.

"Grasses" refers to *kuśa*, *śādvala*, and so forth. Now, it was previously stated that in the expression "of wooden [objects]," the derivative form (*vikṛti*) implies the original material (*prakṛti*).
For what purpose is the taking of wood?
It is for the sake of a restrictive rule; it is specifically for sprinkling. Therefore, as long as there is no great injury [to the tree], the wood is not to be carved.

In the case of contact with a Caṇḍāla or similar outcastes, purification occurs by means of the rays of the moon and sun and the wind, according to this very rule. However, for items made from those materials, such as ladles and the like, when there is only slight defilement, washing and scraping must be performed; this applies to objects used for food and other purposes.
"Mārjana" refers to cleansing, specifically the removal of smoke, darkness, and so forth from a house.
*Upāñjana* refers to the smearing of the ground with lime, cow dung, and so forth.
This should be understood to apply when there is pervasive contact with a corpse, a *caṇḍāla*, a woman in her courses (*udakyā*), or similar entities;
however, in the case of non-pervasion, it applies only to that specific portion.
But when there is defilement by a corpse above [the ground], the purification prescribed consists of scraping the wall, allowing the rays of the sun to enter, touching with flames of fire,
and in some cases, re-plastering;
for earthenware vessels, it is re-firing.
The rite of circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) is to be understood as applying to cases such as contact with a person who has consumed leftovers;
however, re-cooking (*punaḥpāka*) is to be understood as applying to contact with vessels that held liquor and the like.
But in the case of direct contact [with such substances], there is simply abandonment (*tyāga*).
As it has been said:
"An earthen vessel that has come into contact with intoxicants, urine, feces, spittle, pus, or blood is not purified even by re-firing."
The ground is purified by these five means: sweeping, smearing with cow dung, sprinkling water, scraping, and the dwelling of cows.
Irrigation is performed with cow urine or water;
in some cases, it is said to be done even with milk.
Scratching is the making of incisions with a blade or similar instrument, and sowing is the act of planting.
And "sowing on the ground" follows precisely from the injunction of Gautama.
The repetition of the word "with five," however, is for the purpose of showing the application [of these acts] both individually and collectively with respect to striking.
Among those, purification devoid of sweeping consists of cleansing; whereas smearing, however, may be performed even alone on ground that is free from refuse.
In the case of contamination by urine, feces, and so forth, there shall be scraping and sweeping;
in the case of rivers, sandbanks, forests, and the like, there shall be sprinkling;
and for cattle, "dwelling" means keeping them penned for the duration of one day.

And all this must be done on the ground of the cremation ground (*śmaśānabhū*). However, as for the sowing (*āvapana*): where there were previously bone fragments, potsherds, and so forth, one should remove them and scatter other earth; and likewise in a place where [the remains] are hidden, such that their existence might be suspected after some time has passed. It is the same in such cases.
Food that has been pecked by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, sneezed at,
or defiled by hair or insects, becomes pure by the scattering of earth over it.
Here, from the word *jagdhi* (eating), it is understood that this verse refers to food;

for it concerns food rendered impure by being left over by birds such as parrots and others, but not by crows, *kaṅkas*, vultures, and the like—for in the case of the latter, there is a heavy penance prescribed in the rule "that which has been licked by a bird. Thus, this has been stated as the penance for eating food that was pure in its original state.
And thus, for one who has been smelled by a cow and whose penance is equivalent to that [of an outcaste], there would be no purification at all;
such would be the logical conclusion.
Nevertheless, other Smṛti texts and established custom must also be investigated.

For in this way, cultured people, having removed from ten *śarāva* measures of food that excess which has been defiled by crows or other carnivorous scavengers—only that much—and having purified the remainder, they consume it; however, they discard it if the amount is less than that.
In this case as well, a specific circumstance must be taken into account.
Moreover, in another *Smṛti*, even food defiled by a black bird is prohibited.
*Avadhūtam* is that which has been shaken by the breath from the mouth;
or that over which an action such as lifting is performed from the space of the air for the purpose of removing dust from a garment;
*avakṣutam* is that very thing over which one has sneezed.
The hair that falls from human beings becomes insects,
minute creatures, and worms; some of these, born from the sweat and food within the house, do not cause harm while alive, just like flies.
This is the purification for those who have died upon contact with food;

however, those born from contact with impure substances and those that feed on feces—these are unfit to be eaten even while living, according to the rule of Gautama: "That which has fallen into it [the food] by way of hair or insects is always unfit to be eaten."
In cases of extensive contamination, there is a total abandonment of the object;
however, when a large quantity is contaminated by contact with impure insects, one should remove only that small portion, while the remainder is purified.
According to another Smṛti, touching gold, silver, Darbha grass, and gems that are accompanied by water is prescribed even when they are defiled by hair and the like.
In some cases, even burning [the ground] is prescribed;
however, those who claim that this purification of the earth is sufficient have abandoned both the practice of other Smṛtis and the actual meaning of the scriptural statement.
In all purifications of objects, earth and water should be applied as long as the odor and the stain caused by contact with impure matter do not depart.
"Unclean" means untouchable;
and whatever is unfit to be eaten by a particular person, that is the cause of impurity for him—for example, *surā* liquor and intoxicants for a Brāhmaṇa, but not for a Śūdra.
That [argument] is incorrect.
Before the *gharma* offering, sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) are unfit for consumption, yet they are not untouchable.
However, substances such as *surā* and other intoxicants are forbidden for a Brāhmaṇa even by touch.
Therefore, it is only that whose touch is forbidden which, through contact, brings about impurity.
Therefore, this is not an absolute rule that whatever is unfit to be eaten is untouchable, or that whatever is untouchable is unfit to be eaten.
"Āktam" means smeared or anointed;
"tāvat" indicates the prescription of repetition.
Earth and water [are to be used] when there is a purpose;
and the purpose is the removal of odor and stain.
Even in the case of contact with dry impurity or contact that has persisted for a long time, the cleansing of those two—odor and stain—is performed only once with earth and water over time.

[Objection: But surely, the taking up of earth, water, and so forth for the sake of purification serves a visible purpose, since one becomes pure at that very spot once the smear has been removed; what then is the point of [the rule] "as long as it does not depart"?
[Response: It is said:
[it is] for the purpose of exceeding the number [prescribed] in such rules as "one [application] on the penis," and so forth.
When the removal of stains such as feces is impossible by the stated number [of applications], one should disregard that scriptural number and adopt a higher one;
however, the mention of the specific number is for the purpose of ensuring that the number is fulfilled even if the stain is removed with fewer than that.
Commentators explain that the mention of "earth and water" is intended to indicate any means of purification.

And therefore, even if that which has become a cause of impurity has been washed with water, it must still be scrubbed with alkaline substances and the like; otherwise, it would not be seen to "depart"—that is, to go away or cease to exist. "Caused by that" means produced by that impure substance.
And for this reason, the fragrance of musk and the like on a garment does not depart, nor indeed is it defiled.
