If a portion of a body smeared with saffron and the like should come into contact with an impure substance (amedhya), then even the saffron and such must be wiped away there, because that [portion] is indeed in contact with the impure; for in that case too, the rule regarding the removal of odor and smear applies.
If saffron-colored [stains] were grown upon the body and could not be removed even by rubbing, there would indeed be purification.
The gods ordained three purifiers for Brahmins:
that which is unseen, that which is washed with water, and that which is commended by word.
"Purified" means pure. The mention of "gods" is for the sake of praise.
The mention of "Brāhmaṇas" also includes all castes according to established custom.
That substance which is unseen— situated in a place not subject to protection and untouched by the contact of dogs, crows, and the like—

does not warrant a groundless suspicion of defilement based merely on its existence. Likewise, it is not a fault to consume food that has been prepared in a kitchen or similar place where cooks and others who have not performed purification are working, provided it remains unseen.
Furthermore, one should not entertain the suspicion that there might be no fault in a case where, at a later time, a previously unknown impairment is discovered;
for if that were so, it would contradict such statements as "these [scriptures] are [valid] even without [explicit] authority" and so forth.
Thus, first of all, that [scripture] is pure in which no connection with a fault is perceived by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, where even in the absence of a definitive means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), something is suspected through fallacious reasoning (*kutarka*), there it must be purified with water.

For example, when vessels, cooking pots, and the like situated in the same place are seen to be defiled by dogs, crows, and so forth, other items—though not seen [to be defiled]—must likewise be purified with water.
In the same way, such things alone are to be praised with words.
The learned should be made to recite, "May this be pure";
they say that purity comes from the word of a Brahmin.
The present tense (*laṭ*) in the word "is praised" (*praśasyate*) should be understood here as having the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*).

As for those who say that when a visible injury has occurred, and while the purification of the transgressor is being performed directly yet remains unseen, if the learned (śiṣṭas) declare, "His purification is accomplished," then it should be accepted—this is the meaning of the praise of speech.
That is incorrect;
because the unreliability of the word of an authoritative person (āpta) is not admitted in any case whatsoever, there would be the consequence of redundancy (paunaruktya).
Others, however, explain "cleansed by water" as an illustration:
that which is unseen and praised by speech is prescribed;
just as something cleansed by water is pure, so too is that which is unseen and praised by speech prescribed.
But if that which is pure—being free from perceived defects—is established by perception, inference, and scripture, then how [can it be said] "not even for a single day of the year"?
That [previous statement] refers to the subject of food;
this purity, however, refers to the subject of touch.
Or it is established by way of relative gravity or lightness, or by the distinction between times of distress and non-distress.
Water that has reached the ground is pure if it satisfies the thirst of a cow,
provided it is not contaminated by impurities and possesses its natural fragrance, color, and taste.
The mention of "ground" is for the purpose of illustration;
by this, even water that has entered into conduits is indeed pure.
For water is pure by its very nature, whether it is situated on the ground or in the sky.
However, the ground becomes somewhat impure due to contact with unclean substances.

For those who have gone there, this [rule] regarding the cessation of thirst—namely, "in how many [of these] the cow's thirst would cease"—is intended for the purpose of purification from whatever degree of impurity has been incurred through that contact.
"Cessation of thirst" (*vaitṛṣṇya*) means the ending of the desire to drink.
And this is for the purpose of indicating the measure.
Regarding this, it has been explained by the ancient commentators through the observation of a sign (*liṅga*), as in the passage: "Just as the dewlap of a cow, having been submerged in water...
That amount [of water] by which the cow's dewlap and so forth are submerged and its thirst is severed is the measure.
However, those that have come from pure ground are pure even if they are very small.
But how is it to be understood that they are pervaded by impurity? [The answer is: "endowed with smell, color, and taste.
The word "amedhyena" (by impurity), which ends in the instrumental case, is changed to the genitive case.
If they are endowed with—that is, joined to—odors and other qualities associated with impurity, then they are said to be "pervaded.
And this being the case, if in a pond or similar body of water impurity is seen in one spot, yet another part is devoid of such odors and the like, that [other part] shall indeed be pure.
The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise spread out for sale;
almsfood received by a student of sacred knowledge is always pure—this is the established rule.
Artisans, craftsmen, and those such as leather-workers, dyers, and weavers—their hands are always pure.
Consequently, they may be touched during the periods of impurity caused by birth or death;
however, when visible smearing with feces or other filth is present, their purity is not to be understood.

That which was stated as "they are proclaimed to be immediately pure" (sadyaḥ śaucāḥ prakīrtitāḥ) is precisely this; and there is no tautology here, because this has not been taught in the treatise of Manu.
Furthermore, there is another subject matter [as well].

Weavers weave cloth without having sipped water; for the purpose of separating the fibers of the threads, a mixture of flour and water and so forth is applied, and the vessel containing it is placed here and there on the ground. Whatever impurity arises from that is removed by this [washing].
However, one should not understand its purity to result from contact with those things that are inherently impure, for such contact is not prescribed as part of the weaver's craft.

And since this is the logical justification, even items handled by Mlecchas are not impure; in their case, purification is achieved through sprinkling and washing, according to the statement of Śaṅkha.
For it is stated therein: "The hand of an artisan is pure, as are commodities in their raw state.
A commodity (*paṇya*) is that object intended for trade which is sold for coins or measured by another substance; such a commodity is pure when displayed on the floor of a marketplace.

Although it may be defiled by contact with numerous buyers and by being placed on ground lacking plaster or other coatings, it is not thereby impure, provided that no visible damage is observed upon repeated inspection.
Because of the mention of "what is spread out," there is no purification even if the merchandise remains in the intellect of one staying at home;

however, regarding prepared foods such as groats and cakes, despite their purity, they are unfit for consumption precisely because of the statement of Śaṅkha: "Things from a marketplace are unfit for consumption.
From this very [text] and by association with it, the previously mentioned purification for a religious student (brahmacārin) is understood to apply in the case of such a defilement.
For one who is begging, there is the possibility of defilement such as walking along a street, seeing impure things, sneezing, spitting, and the contact of many hands with the alms-food;
thus, he states that [the food] is impure despite its being considered pure.
The mouth of women is always pure; a bird is pure when causing fruit to fall;
a calf is pure while discharging milk; and a dog is pure when seizing game.
"The mouth of all women is pure for the purpose of kissing and so forth,
and women are [pure] in connection with sexual intercourse," according to another Smṛti; this applies only to those connected with sexual intercourse, not to mothers, sisters, and the like.
In this context, it should not be thought that this prohibition against eating leavings applies to a woman;

for although she is connected with sexual pleasure, it has been established in the fourth chapter that one should not eat together with one's wife because of the scriptural injunction, "he shall not eat with his wife.

Furthermore, because of the inclusion of the word "always" (nitya), it does not apply only at the time of sexual union, but rather when there is a failure to engage in that very purpose [of procreation].
The term *śakuni* refers to the causing of fruit to fall.
Although the word *śakuni* denotes birds in general, based on established usage (*samācāra*), it is not intended here for crows, herons, and other scavengers.
Because of the inclusion of the word "falling," this rule applies specifically to fruit situated upon a tree.
When a cow is being milked, the calf clings to her udders for the purpose of causing the milk to flow.

Now, since it might follow from the statement, "Cows are pure except for their mouths," that they are otherwise impure, this [present] statement is intended to preclude that; thus, it refers to contact with their mouth.
But a dog is not pure.
But when one seizes a deer in order to kill it during a hunt or similar activity, then one is pure.
Manu has declared that the flesh of an animal killed by dogs is pure,
as is the flesh of one killed by other carnivorous beasts, or by outcasts such as Caṇḍālas, or by robbers.
Previously, in the context of "the dog is pure when seizing game," the intended meaning was simply that the dog is pure upon the killing of game;
here, however, the distinction is that it has been seized by him or by others through the striking of sticks and so forth.
The meaning of the second half of the verse is now being prescribed.
"By carnivorous animals" refers to hawks, jackals, and the like;
"by Caṇḍālas and others"—the inclusion of "others" is for the purpose of including beasts of prey and so forth;
"bandits" refers to Niṣādas, hunters, and others who make a living by killing living beings.
Those apertures of the body that are above the navel are entirely pure;
those below it are impure, as are the excretions that fall from the body.
This word "mouth" (kha) denotes a sense organ (*indriya*).
Therefore, when referring to the two feet, the plural form implies that those organs which are below are impure (*amedhya*).
This is incorrect, because it contradicts the statement that [the body] above the navel is pure.
In that context, it has been stated that the region above the navel is more pure (*medhyatara*) and superior;
this is only logical if there is purity below as well,
for it is not the case that something white can be "more black."
And this term "indriya" does not refer to the sense-faculties; rather, it has the meaning of "aperture. As it is said: "There are seven vital breaths in the head," and there are two apertures below.
The plural number is used because of the distinction between the female and male organs.
This being so, even when there is contact with the interior of the mouth, the hands and other parts remain pure provided there is no contact with the phlegm located therein;
likewise, they remain pure from the impurity of tears provided there is no further contact.
One should specify that flies, droplets, a shadow, a cow, a horse, the rays of the sun,
dust, the earth, wind, and fire are pure to the touch.
The mention of flies includes those born of sweat;
the mention of cows includes goats and sheep;
and the mention of horses includes elephants and mules.
The eclipse of the sun is among the luminaries;
droplets are water-drops whose specific forms are invisible through the mere experience of touch;
and shadow is that of outcastes (caṇḍāla) and others.
Earth touched by Caṇḍālas and others is purified by being stepped upon with the feet;
for other [types of soil], however, sweeping and so forth are prescribed.
These [beings], such as flies and the like, do not cause defilement even when touching excrement and similar substances.
A goat and a horse are pure from the mouth; cows are pure except for the mouth;
cats and mongooses may be touched; and well-behaved wild animals and birds are likewise pure.
Thus it is stated in another Smṛti.
For the purpose of purifying the discharge of feces and urine, earth and water should be taken as required;
likewise for the purification of the twelve bodily impurities.
And because impurities issue from the body, this is stated regarding its impurity:
for the purpose of purifying that which is the organ of excretion—the anus and so forth—by means of which feces and urine are discharged—one should take earth and water as required.
Disregarding any fixed number, one should take as much water and earth as is necessary until the odor and the smear are removed.
The bodily impurities (*daihika-mala*) are those residing in the body that cause impurity;
for the sake of cleansing even those [impurities], both earth and water are to be accepted as meaningful.
It is recited in another *Smṛti*:
One should take earth and water for purification during the first six [actions];
however, during the latter six, one becomes pure by means of water alone.
Regarding pure phlegm and the like, another Smṛti text states: "The application of nasal drops for the discharge of phlegm is permissible when there is an injury caused by phlegm.
Even though these belong to the latter group of six [impure substances], earth must certainly not be used as a purifier for them.
Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, earwax, nasal mucus, tears, rheum of the eyes, and sweat— these twelve are the impurities of human beings.
Regarding these twelve impurities that have been shown,
the mention of "man" is for the purpose of illustrating the case of five-toed animals;
as for dogs, jackals, and the like, their status is established simply by their being untouchable.
But regarding feces and urine, this applies to everyone except for goats, sheep, cows, and horses.
One application of earth should be given to the penis, three to the anus, ten to one hand,
and seven to both hands by one desiring purification.

After the voiding of feces and urine, one application of earth mixed with water should be made to the left hand for the sake of purifying the penis. According to the prescription for purification in another Smṛti, as much earth as can be held in that hand should be taken.
However, I say that the measure has already been stated by the word "as much as is necessary" (*arthavat*).
Some read as follows:
"The first handful is to be known [as the measure]; the second is half of that;
the third is to be known as the clay for filling three parts of the palm."
And this measurement applies only to the *pāda*;
however, elsewhere it is "according to the sense.
Even when there is a single elision (*utsarga*), the number remains exactly the same.
And this is an injunction for repetition;
there is a distinction between clods of earth, just as there is between cows and other animals.
Thus it is said here: "Other than one from an anthill, one from a distant place, one from a stable for horses," and so forth.
Thus, in this context, even [the distinctions] such as "white," "black," or "red" are not to be taken into account;
rather, one should desire it by wishing for it.
This is the purification for householders; it is twofold for students, threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics.

The rule for purification varies according to the specific stage of life (*āśrama*); however, for those who do not belong to a stage of life, it is simply this: "earth, water, and what is fit to be accepted [as alms]—this much is sufficient. Furthermore, even a Śūdra has the right to the householder’s stage; such is the enumeration.
Having voided urine or feces, one who has sipped water for purification should touch the cavities of the head;
likewise always when about to study the Veda or when eating food.
Having relieved himself in a place suitable for urination and having purified it according to the prescribed rule,
he should sip water and touch the apertures— the sense organs—
when about to study the Veda, as described in the second section on the rules for private recitation (svādhyāya).
Because the root *kṛ* has its primary meaning [of "making"], it is understood as "having performed" and then "having discarded.
Having wiped away urine and feces and having washed the anus and the generative organ, one should sip water (*ācāmet*).
And one who is about to study the Veda—since it is stated as a duty within the rule for private Vedic recitation that "one who is about to study must have sipped water"—[should do so].
But this [rule] applies to one who is teaching or about to study;
otherwise, those who recite the Veda are said to be like commoners.
Having performed various other worldly activities, one should not pronounce the syllables of the Veda without having sipped water (ācamana).
And while eating food.
One desiring bodily purity should first sip water three times and then wipe the mouth twice; however, a woman or a Śūdra should do so once each.
This restatement is for the sake of women and Śūdras;
although this has already been stated, it is repeated for the sake of women and Śūdras.
Some explain that the rule "a Śūdra [is purified] by touched waters" means that a Śūdra need only perform the mere touching of water.

Therefore, wiping or touching the ears and other parts, which might otherwise be applicable, is prescribed here as pertaining specifically to *śūdras*. As for women, since the rule "a Brahmin is purified by [water] reaching the heart" specifies caste (*jāti*), they would be expected to follow the same procedure as men; however, this [present rule] is stated [to modify that]. By the force of the expression "seeking bodily purity," if one engages in study or eating while already pure, then a triple repetition is not necessarily required.
Nor is there wiping.
What then? There is sipping water (ācamana) and the touching of the sense organs with as much water as is required.
There is no other rule for sipping water prescribed among the duties of a religious student (brahmacārin).
For Śūdras who live according to the law, a shaving of the head should be performed monthly;
their rules for purification are like those of Vaiśyas, and they may eat the remnants of the food of the twice-born.
This duty, which was mentioned in general for *śūdras*, is here stated in detail:
those who live according to justice, who serve the twice-born, and who perform the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*),
must undergo shaving— the tonsure— every month.
The genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental;
or alternatively, [the brahmins] are dependent upon them, being under their control; thus, "the task is to be done by the brahmins."
Because the root *kṛ* has multiple meanings, it must be explained; this is the understanding.
Like a Vaiśya, there are specific rules for purification, such as regarding birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and the like, as well as for sipping water (*ācamana*).
And eating the remnants of the food of the twice-born—this has been explained previously.
The principal [limbs] do not become defiled by food remnants, nor do droplets that fall upon the body;
nor do the beard hairs that enter the mouth, nor what remains stuck between the teeth.
Because the rule for sipping water (*ācamana*) is prescribed following the act of spitting and speaking untruths, it is made known that one who has not sipped water is impure.
Since even droplets (*vipruṣaḥ*) are emitted from the mouth, they constitute nothing other than spitting;
therefore, since the requirement to sip water would apply to droplets as well—given that spitting consists of the expulsion of phlegm—the author says this [to address that point].
The term *mukhya* refers to those things which exist in the mouth or have emerged from the mouth;
namely, droplets (*vipruṣaḥ*), provided they do not fall upon the body, as they do not cause one to become ritually impure (*anucchiṣṭa*).
But was it not already stated in the passage "droplets born from the mouth" that such droplets are pure?
It is elsewhere than apart from the bodily lotus;
this itself is the indicator.
Not every object has been shown.
"Beards" refers to the hair of the mustache;
"entered into the mouth" means having gone inside. The phrase "they do not make one impure by food remnants" is to be supplied as a continuation.
Therefore, other things such as betel nut (pūgaphala) certainly produce [the same result];
likewise, that which remains stuck between the teeth.
There is a specific rule in another Smṛti: "But regarding what adheres to the teeth, it is like the teeth themselves, except when touched by the tongue."
"Before falling," say some;
"one should know that among those things that have fallen, it is like [the case of] the outflows (āsrava); one becomes pure even while swallowing them.
Regarding "among those that have fallen," one should know it means "without the tongue," because purity is prohibited when there is contact with the tongue.
Drops that touch the feet of one who is giving water for rinsing to others should be known as equal to those on the ground; one does not become impure because of them.
"Causing others to sip water" means giving water for sipping to others;
this is what is intended:

when one gives water for sipping to another, if the feet of the giver of the water are touched by drops of water falling from the fingers of the hand of the person who caused the sipping—drops which arise from their impact with the ground—then he does not become impure because of them.

Just as certain drops of water that fall from the hand onto ground that is not defiled by earthly impurities remain pure, so too are those drops of water falling from the hand after one has sipped; one who is touched by them is neither *aprayata* (impure) nor *aśuci* (unclean).
Because of the mention of "another," both the person who performs the sipping (*ācamana*) must guard against contact with those drops, as must anyone else standing nearby.
And because of the rule regarding grasping the feet, touching as far as the shins and so forth is indeed improper.
If one who holds a substance in his hand is somehow touched by something defiled by food remnants,
he shall attain purity by sipping water (ācamana) without first setting that substance down.
A person who has incurred the need for expiation by means of sipping water (ācamana) is called "impure" (ucchiṣṭa).

For example, one who has discharged urine or other excretions but has not yet performed purification and sipping water, or one who is defiled by contact with impure substances and the like—if such a person has an object in hand; that is, one by whom food, drink, or objects such as clothing are held in the hand, he is called "one with an object in hand" (dravyahasta).
This usage is established according to conventional application, as in the case of "Vajrahasta" (the Thunderbolt-handed one) and similar terms.

If he has touched [something impure], then, without setting that object down and without removing it, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) while still holding the object in his hand.
But how is the sipping of water possible when an object is held in the hand? The rule for this is: "One should wash the hands up to the wrist."
Some say:

what is intended is merely contact with the body by means of the substance, not specifically by the hand; likewise, even in the case of impurity, when a substance is placed upon the *skandha* (shoulder) or other parts, the impurity belongs only to that which is defiled (*ucchiṣṭa*), and purification occurs in the same way once one has sipped water (*ācānta*).
Therefore, having taken the substance from the hand onto another part of the body, such as the forearm or the lap, one should sip water.
The intention is that just as a person becomes impure through contact with impurity, so too does one become pure through purification.
However, Gautama has stated: "One who is defiled while holding an object in the hand should set it down and then sip water.
Regarding this, they provide the following explanation:
Even though they are equally accompanied [by the rule], it is specifically the depositing (*nidhāna*) that is intended here.
Otherwise, when both purification and the holding of the object must be performed by one who possesses the substance, what occasion would there be for the depositing of the substance?
Therefore, since depositing would not otherwise be established, this statement is solely for the purpose of enjoining depositing.

How, then, is the purification of a substance achieved? By being taken up by a person with care, or by sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) as prescribed in another Smṛti. If, while dealing with food and drink, one should happen to touch something impure (ucchiṣṭa):
"One should sip water after sprinkling the substance; in this way, one does not incur fault.
If the act of setting [the substance] down were understood here even without an explicit statement, then the expression "even without having set it down" would be redundant.
Since the *smṛtis* form a single coherent body of doctrine, it is nevertheless understood here through the established rule that such is the case.
Now, however, a difference of opinion is perceived;
from that arises conceptual construction,
and its systematic establishment follows.
A more valuable substance is deposited [in the mouth], while another, remaining on the limbs, is understood [to be touched] after being placed there;

even when one eats food oneself, or touches a large amount of leavings, or is touched by one who is fit for sipping water but has not yet sipped, all such contact with the leavings of a substance constitutes impurity.
One who has vomited or been purged should bathe and then consume clarified butter;
one who has eaten food should simply sip water, while bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse.
Vamana (emesis) and virecana (purgation) are well known.
A man who has vomited up food that he had eaten through his mouth is one who has undergone emesis (*vānta*).
One for whom the urges to defecate have arisen more than eight times—either by consuming *harītakī* and similar substances or due to disease—is one who has undergone purgation (*virikta*).
The two of them should first perform their bath;
then, at the end, having consumed ghee, they may eat this other food.
And by this consumption of ghee, there is no exclusion of other meals.
Regarding the purification of substances in expiatory rites, this consumption of clarified butter is like cleansing with ashes or water;
one should simply sip water after eating food.
If, on the very day after eating that food, vomiting or purging should occur, then there is only the sipping of water, not bathing or the consumption of clarified butter.
Others, however, explain it independently:
"Having eaten, one should indeed sip water.
This is an exception to that very rule which prescribes sipping water immediately after eating.
Regarding those who engage in sexual intercourse:
one who has discharged semen during intercourse with a woman becomes pure by bathing.
Having slept, having sneezed, having eaten, having spat, having spoken untruths,
and after drinking water— even if already pure— one who intends to study should sip water (ācamana).
Having sneezed— the sound that arises from the nostrils of one who, though unwilling, is impelled by the wind—
one should do so even while being pure (*prayata*).
This [term "pure"] is connected precisely with the word "about to study" (*adhyeṣyamāṇa*).
Even when purified, one who is about to study should sip water and then study; the meaning is that he should perform the sipping of water as an ancillary part of the injunction for study.
However, after bathing and other such acts, he should do so only once.
As for what was further stated:

"Having slept, having sneezed, having eaten, and likewise having drunk water, the sage, as well as one who has sipped water (ācānta), should sip water again after spitting or speaking a false word. Thus, the connection here should be made as follows: "Having sipped water after eating, he should sip water again."
Furthermore, where it is recited that "one should sip water twice," there the repetition refers to a single action occurring consecutively.
This entire rule for purification, as well as the purification of objects, has been declared to you for all social classes; now learn the duties of women.
The first three words conclude the section on purification, while the fourth provides a summary of what is about to be said.

Although the term *śaucavidhi* (rules of purification) is a general term, because of its proximity to "purification of substances" (*dravyaśuddhi*), it comes to refer specifically to the other [types of] purification, like the expression "cattle and bulls" (*gobalīvarda*).
The duties of women (*strīṇāṃ dharmāḥ*) refer exclusively to those whose performance is uniquely female.
But that which is common, such as sacrifice and the like, is not mentioned here.
Whether she be a child, a young woman, or even an aged woman,
a female must not perform any action independently, even within her own home.

The purpose of the instruction is that independence for women does not exist in any state whatsoever. However, the statement regarding the division of ages is intended merely to demonstrate the circumstances under which her dependence occurs; its literal form is not what is intended to be emphasized.
"In childhood she shall remain under the control of her father, and under the control of her husband in youth."
When her husband has died, a woman should not exercise independence with respect to her sons.
And so it has been said:
"While her paternal kinsmen (sapindas) exist, the husband is the master of the woman;
but at the end of both sides [of the family], the king is considered the husband of the woman."
And by the words "among his sapindas," etc., it is indicated that [the rite] must be performed even when the owner is absent.
A woman should not desire separation from her father, her husband, or her sons;
for by separation from these, she brings reproach upon both families.
It is stated that instability is the cause for being subject to censure; one should act [in such a way] regarding what is blameworthy.
For, in the absence of these [causes], she lives or goes to another village—this is to be supplied [as the ellipsis].
She should always remain cheerful, be skillful in domestic duties, keep the household utensils well-maintained, and be not wasteful in her expenditures.

The word *sadā* (always) expresses frequency, just like the word *nitya*. Regarding the phrase "with a constantly smiling [face]," even when there is otherwise an impulse of anger or grief, one should display joy upon seeing her husband through a brightening of the face, a smile, playful speech, and so forth.
This instruction applies both to a maiden and to a married woman; it concerns her skill in domestic duties,
the accumulation and expenditure of wealth, religious observances such as ritual bathing, and so forth.

By the passage beginning with "and for the accumulation of wealth," the duties of the household have been described; therein, she must be skillful and clever. In this regard, tasks such as refinement and preparation must be accomplished swiftly.
She should have her household utensils well-maintained; "utensils" refers to items used in the home, such as bowls, jars, and so forth, which should be kept well-cleaned and beautiful.
Furthermore, regarding wealth spent on the food for friends, kinsmen, and guests, she should not be "open-handed"—that is, she should not be extravagant.
The meaning is that one should not spend excessively.
"One whose utensils are well-prepared" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound;
likewise, the analysis of the compound is "one whose hand is thus released."
Subsequently, there is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*);
by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), the word *muktahasta* signifies "generous."
To whomsoever her father or her brother— having obtained the father’s consent—
may give her, she shall serve him while he lives, and once he has passed away, she must not transgress against him.
Or, with the father’s permission, [the brother may give].

Just as a brother has the right to give when authorized by the father, so too, even when the father is independent [of authorization], it should be understood that the giving occurs when there is the consent of the wife,
because of their joint authority in all matters and because both possess ownership over the daughter.

That even when the father is absent, the mother may give [the daughter] away was shown in the ninth [chapter]. Since offspring belongs to both the mother and the father, and ownership arises on that account, mutual dependence is logical. "He should serve" means he should propitiate [her].
One should not step over that which is stationary or dead;
"stepping over" means transgressing.
The meaning is that one should not sit independently [upon it].
Just as she is dependent on him while her husband is alive, so too, even when he is dead, she must remain dependent on him at that very time;
for it is said: "The act of giving effects ownership.
As soon as she is given by the father, the father's ownership ceases and ownership arises in him to whom she is given.
And for this reason, the giving does not occur only at the time of marriage; rather, there is also a giving prior to the marriage at the time of the formal selection of the bridegroom.
What, then, is the purpose of marriage?
For their sake, auspicious rites, benedictions, and sacrifices are performed for Prajāpati at the wedding;
however, the formal giving away of the bride is the cause of [the husband's] ownership.

The accomplishment of a desired object is *maṅgala* (auspiciousness); that which brings about such accomplishment is employed for that purpose. In this context, the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) [in the phrase] "the sacrifice of Prajāpati" is neuter because it functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). That by which one goes toward or attains well-being (*svasti*) is called *svastyayana*.
The meaning is that whatever beloved object he possesses does not perish;
[this applies] to these women and in those marriages.

The sacrifice is performed for the deity Prajāpati with the mantra, "O Prajāpati, these [offerings] are not [for anyone] other than you. Such clarified butter oblations (*ājyahoma*) are prescribed by some for the marriage ceremony;
this is also an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other deities as well, such as Pūṣan, Varuṇa, and Aryaman. For thus are the words of the mantras in that regard:
Verses such as "Pūṣan the god" and "Varuṇa the god" are intended to reveal other deities.
What is made known here is that ownership arises from the very act of giving, even in the absence of a marriage ceremony;
the marriage sacrifice, however, is for the sake of auspiciousness, and so forth, is not the intended meaning here.
It is recorded in the Smṛtis that "making a wife" means marriage;
for even though ownership exists, one does not become a wife without marriage.
A husband who has performed the sacramental rite with mantras is the constant bestower of happiness upon his wife, both in this world and in the next, whether she is in her season or not.
"In all cases, except when prohibited"—thus he is a giver of pleasure even outside the proper season.
One who performs the consecration by means of mantras, namely the marriage rite, is a "performer of the mantra-consecration.
And [he is so] in the next world as well.
And because she has the right to practice dharma together with her husband and thereby attains its fruit, she is called the "giver of happiness in the next world."
Whether he is devoid of virtue, given over to lust, or entirely lacking in good qualities,
a husband must always be attended upon by a virtuous wife like a god.
One who is excessively addicted to gambling is "lacking in virtue" (viśīla).
One whose conduct is dominated by sensual desire is "one of lustful conduct" (kāmavṛtta),
or one who is devoid of [excellent] qualities.
One who is devoid of qualities such as learning and wealth;
"upacārya" means one who is to be propitiated or served.
For women there is no separate sacrifice, nor a vow, nor even a fast;
by that service which she renders to her husband, she is exalted in heaven.
It has been established more than once that those who have been separated from their husband have no entitlement to perform sacrifices;
therefore, even when performing vows and fasts, she should obtain his permission.
A "vow" (vrata) refers here to the resolve to abstain from liquor, meat, and so forth, but not to the *kṛcchra* penances.
In that regard, since recitation (*japa*) and burnt offerings (*homa*) are auxiliary elements (*aṅga*), and because these are absent for a woman,
it is not proper to say that her performance of the *kṛcchra* penance will be deficient in recitation and burnt offerings;
for it is not proper to abandon auxiliary elements at one's own will.
Because it is understood that a ritual action endowed with all its constituent parts (*aṅga*) is the means for attaining prosperity (*abhyudaya*),
the increase or decrease of those parts does not occur in dependence upon the varying capacities of individuals.
Furthermore, there exist members of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) who are capable of performing the ritual application by incorporating all the constituent parts.

Therefore, a woman or a Śūdra who desires spiritual prosperity has no entitlement to perform the Kṛcchra penances. We shall explain the specific rules regarding expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) later. "Upoṣita" refers to fasting; it is the cessation of food for one night, two nights, and so forth.
He desires to hear and attends upon [the teacher].
A virtuous wife, desiring the world of her husband, whether he be living or dead, should never do anything displeasing to him who took her hand in marriage.

The "world of the husband" (patiloka) is that world, such as heaven and so forth, which is acquired through the performance of dharma together with her husband. Desiring—that is, wishing to attain—that world, she should not perform anything unpleasant, such as association with other men, which is prohibited by the scriptures.
For it is impossible to determine what is pleasant or unpleasant for one who is dead;
nor is that which is pleasant while living necessarily pleasant for the deceased, because the nature of pleasure differs for those who have been reborn in another state of existence.
Therefore, that very independence which is prohibited is what is unpleasant;
one should not practice that.
She may indeed emaciate her body with pure flowers, roots, and fruits;
but she must not even utter the name of another man once her husband has died.
He shows that very point with its specific qualification:
suicide is forbidden for women just as it is for men.
As for what was stated in the *Āṅgirasa* [Smṛti] that "they should die after their husband," even that is not something that must necessarily be performed as an obligatory duty.
In that case, there is praise of the result;
and when one who desires the result is the qualified agent, there is an equality with the Śyena sacrifice.

For likewise, in the case of the qualification "one should harm living beings by means of the Śyena," even though there is engagement due to being blinded by an excessively intensified hatred, there is no quality of dharma.

Likewise here, for a woman whose desire for the fruit [of following her husband] has become excessively intense, even though there is a prohibition, it is possible for her to engage in dying by transgressing that prohibition; therefore, it lacks scriptural authority.

Consequently, there certainly exists a prohibition against a woman following her husband in death. Furthermore, because this Smṛti rule contradicts the direct Vedic revelation (Śruti), "Therefore, one should not depart before the end of one's lifespan," this Smṛti cannot even be so interpreted.
Just as the rule "having studied the Veda, one should perform the ceremonial bath" (snāna) prescribes bathing immediately after study for one who has not yet understood the meaning of the text,

so too, in the case of a woman whose husband is dead and who is childless— provided she possesses no husband's wealth or other heirs and subsists by some means such as spinning— it is stated [in this verse] because life is so dear to her that neglecting it would be contrary to the scriptures and is forbidden, and because, in times of distress, all forms of deviation (vyabhicāra) are permitted by such texts as "the *jāghanī* of Viśvāmitra," which would otherwise lead to her resorting to a livelihood based on sexual misconduct.
Granted, in this state she may emaciate her body, bring it to exhaustion, and maintain her livelihood with flowers, roots, and fruits as they happen to be available;
yet she must not even mention the name of another man, saying, "You alone are my husband from this day forward.
As for that which...
"When the husband is lost, dead, has renounced the world, is impotent, or has fallen from his caste—
under these five calamities, another husband is ordained for women.
In this context, because he is her protector, she may resort to another husband for the sake of her own livelihood through such work as that of a *sairandhrī*.
And this will be determined precisely in the ninth [chapter];
and that rule applies to a woman whose husband is away.
The use of the word "kāmam" (at will) is for the purpose of indicating a lack of approval.
Even the emaciation of the body is an improper act, but this other thing is even more improper: namely, union with another man.
Until death she remained patient, steadfast, and chaste,
longing for that supreme dharma which belongs to women who have but one husband.
This very point is made explicit:
until death one should remain a celibate student;
in this time of distress, one must not sustain oneself through sexual misconduct.
Patient,
she disregarded the suffering caused by that [fasting];
she did not let her celibate life be impaired by hunger, lest her mind be shattered by the waves of agitation.

Those women who have one husband, or those who are the wives of one man, are called *ekapatnyaḥ*. Desiring—that is, longing for—that dharma of theirs, beginning with the *Sāvitrī* vow, which consists of the power to grant boons, to utter curses, and so forth, she should not abandon her celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
In this state, if death should occur while she is subsisting on roots and fruits, there is no fault.
Many thousands of brahmins who practiced celibacy from their youth have gone to heaven without producing offspring for the continuation of their lineage.
In the preceding verse, intercourse with another man for the sake of livelihood was forbidden; by this [verse], however, the engagement for the sake of obtaining a son is prohibited.

For it is indeed heard [in scripture]: "There is no world for one who has no son. And in that context, the gender [of the word "son"] is not intended to be restrictive; therefore, this is stated to preclude such an engagement even for the purpose of obtaining a son.

Many thousands of youths, being celibate students (*brahmacārin*) who have not taken wives and are lifelong practitioners (*naiṣṭhika*), have gone to heaven; many thousands of them attain the celestial realm.
As for the practice of *niyoga*, it was ordained in the ninth [chapter] at the wish of the teacher's wife, and not by her own independent will when she desired a son.
"Without having established the lineage" means without having produced offspring for the sake of the increase of the family—that is, without having begotten sons.

Regarding the term *anekāni*: since a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) has the meaning of its final member as predominant, the use of the plural number is to be considered [problematic]. Even though there is a negation of oneness, it is difficult to find an expression for numbers such as two and so forth.

For in this way, although this [term] has its own form obscured by being deprived of its own referent through the imposition of its own property [negation], it nevertheless denotes specific very large numbers.
Just as in the expression "the village of Moda.
And the author of the *Cūrṇikā* stated that [the rule] is established by the word "from many" (*anekasmāt*);
he demonstrated the establishment of the prescribed usage of the singular number.
Alternatively, this word *aneka* expresses the meaning of "without a companion. The phrase "they went without companions" means that a wife had not served as their companion.
When her husband has died, a virtuous woman who remains steadfast in celibacy goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those who practice lifelong celibacy.
This very same point is stated further for the sake of strengthening one's practice.
But that woman who, out of greed for offspring, transgresses against her husband,
incurs reproach in this world and is excluded from the next world.

"The desire 'May a son be born to me' is the longing for offspring; because of that [desire], she who acts transgressing her husband and would unite with another incurs censure and reproach in this world and does not attain heaven."
No offspring born here belongs to anyone else, nor does it fall under the guardianship of another;
for virtuous women, a second husband is nowhere prescribed.
The offspring produced by another husband does not belong to that [man] at all;
and likewise, that which is produced by a man upon the wives of another does not belong to him either.
She who, abandoning her own inferior husband, serves one who is superior,
becomes indeed contemptible in the world and is called "one who has had a previous husband."
Not only does she incur reproach for this, but when there is infidelity toward her husband, a woman incurs censure in the world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by foul diseases.
Therefore, out of desire for rewards both seen and unseen, she must not transgress against her husband.
She who does not deceive her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body,
attains the world of her husband and is called "virtuous" by the righteous.
By this conduct, a woman who is restrained in mind, speech,
and body attains supreme fame in this world and the world of her husband in the hereafter.
Since the verses summarizing the duties of women are straightforward, I have not applied great effort to their explanation here;
such is the extent of the purpose of the instruction therein.

Just as, by the principle that "the act of resuming sexual union with another woman does not abide here and one must not transgress [this rule]," there is no further engagement together; likewise, by the statement "even a childless woman goes to heaven," the procreation of offspring is prohibited in times of distress—yet that same act will be permitted again by the Smṛti rules on *niyoga*. Thus, this procreation of offspring is subject to option (*vikalpyate*) because it is both enjoined and prohibited.

Regarding these two traditions, it is not possible to determine which tradition is superior by establishing a distinction such that in one case there is offspring and in the other case there is restraint;
for the purpose of both is accomplished.
A twice-born man who knows the law should cause his wife— who is of the same caste, of virtuous conduct, and who dies before him— to be cremated with the Agnihotra fire and the sacrificial vessels.
This verse is a restatement of what is established by logic:

thus, the consecration (*saṃskāra*) for the fire-maintainer (*agnihotrin*) has already been stated here by the words "she is a virtuous wife" and so forth; for it is said, "Indeed, these fires are not maintained when the wife has died."
Having given the sacred fires to a wife who has died first during the funeral rites,
one may again perform the act of taking a wife and likewise the re-establishment of the fires.
This is cited again for the sake of further qualification.
This too is a restoration of eligibility along with another [rule].

However, when it concerns wealth, a purpose, or the performance of dharma-actions, then even due to the state of being without assistance, there is no prohibition of eligibility for the forest-dweller's life or the life of a wandering mendicant.
And thus says the Śruti: "By old age, indeed, one is released from this," or else by the loss of purpose. Others, however, say:
In this context, the word "when" (yadā) will be supplied;
by this, the lack of contradiction with the scriptural injunction regarding the lifelong performance of oblations (yāvajjīvahomīya-śruti) will be established.
By this method, one should never neglect the five great sacrifices;
having taken a wife, one should dwell in the household during the second stage of life.
The concluding verse:
"And the mention of the five sacrifices is for the sake of establishing everything."
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the Commentary on Manu, composed by Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi Svāmin, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Vīrasvāmin.
Now begins the sixth chapter:
Having thus remained in the householder stage of life according to the rules, the twice-born graduate (snātaka),
with his senses subdued and self-restrained, shall dwell in the forest in the prescribed manner.
The stage of life characterized by the house is the "householder's stage" (gṛhāśrama).
"House" (gṛha) refers to a wife.
Having stayed there and performed its duties, one should dwell in the forest; such is the injunction.

By the use of the suffix *ktvā* in the word "having lived" (*sthitvā*), [the text] indicates that the stage of the householder precedes that of forest-dwelling. The stages of life must be undertaken in sequence;
one who has fulfilled the duties of the householder is then qualified for forest-dwelling.

This was stated by relying on the position of cumulative practice (*samuccaya*); otherwise, it will also be explained that forest-dwelling exists even for one whose celibacy (*brahmacarya*) has not been violated.
"One who has conquered the senses" means one whose impurities (*kaṣāya*) have ripened away and whose passion (*rāga*) has been exhausted.
Thus, the words *vidhivat* (according to rule), *yathāvat* (as it is), and *iti* (thus) are for the purpose of completing the meter;
they have been explained previously in their respective places.
This much is prescribed.
Having fulfilled the duties of the householder stage, one should take recourse to the forest-dwelling stage.
But when a householder sees his own wrinkles and grey hair,
and indeed the offspring of his offspring, then he should take refuge in the forest.
He demonstrates that very point which was stated: "One who has abandoned craving for the enjoyment of sense objects is qualified [for this practice].
*Valī* is the wrinkling of the skin;
*palitam* is the graying of the hair.
They say that "the offspring of an offspring" means "the son of a son.
Even though there is an offspring of a daughter in the form of a grandson (dauhitra), the learned do not accept this rule when a daughter is born to a son.
Others, however, state that the greying of the head and the birth of a grandson are intended to indicate specific stages of age.
Even one for whom graying hair might not occur in any way should resort to the forest in old age.
Just as one who has fathered a son and possesses black hair is entitled to the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires), so too is one who has fathered a grandson and has gray hair.
Even then, both the birth of a son and the state of having black hair serve solely as indicators of a particular stage of life.
If "neither too quickly nor too long" is intended as an illustration of the meaning, then an authoritative source (pramāṇa) must be stated.
Having abandoned village food and all personal belongings,
and having entrusted his wife to his sons, he should go to the forest, either alone or with her.
"Having completely renounced" means that from that time forward one should not eat food consisting of rice or barley;
this is what is expressed by the phrase "one who eats roots," and so forth.
"Appurtenances" (paricchada) refers to cattle, horses, clothing, ornaments, beds, and the like.
If the wife desires it, then she may accompany him; otherwise, he goes alone.

Others, however, describe that he should leave behind his young wife and go with his aged one. This rule applies when a wife exists; in the case of sons, there is either their entrustment [to care for her] or his departure for the forest.

Even when his wife has died, the forest-dwelling stage is prescribed by Āpastamba and others, stating that there is a re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punar-ādhāna*) in this regard. The settled rule is: he who lacks fickleness of the senses is a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*); the other, however, may take another wife.
Having taken up the Agnihotra sacrifice and the domestic implements for the sacred fires,
he should depart from the village to the forest and dwell there with his senses restrained.
The fires themselves are denoted by the term *agnihotra*.
Having taken up— that is, having grasped— the Śrauta fires as well as the domestic (*gṛhya*) equipment for the Agnihotra, such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles,
this [text] constitutes a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) regarding those items connected to the fire, since there is a rule for the relinquishment of domestic equipment.
With various kinds of pure food fit for sages, or with vegetables, roots, and fruits,
he should perform these very great sacrifices according to the prescribed rule.
One should offer— that is, perform— these very [oblations] which are prescribed for the householder;
the phrase "in accordance with the rule" is a restatement (anuvāda) intended to complete the verse.
He should wear either a skin or a garment of bark; he should bathe in the evening as well as in the morning;
and he should always maintain his matted hair, beard, and nails.
*Carman* refers to the hides of wild oxen and other animals;
*cīra* is a fragment of cloth;
*sāyam* is the time at the conclusion of the day.
"At dawn" means at the first rising of the day.
Thus, because of the prescription for bathing in the evening, they say that his meal is at night, since bathing is prohibited after eating.
Others, however, say that this is incorrect.
Since this is a vow for a *snātaka*, one should perform the bath after eating;
however, in the *Mahābhārata* it is recorded as a duty for all men.
Thus, bathing three times a day will also be an optional alternative for him.
One should not have one's matted hair, beard, body hair, or nails cut.
From whatever he may eat, he should offer a portion as a bali-oblation and give alms according to his ability;
he should honor those who have come to his hermitage with offerings of water, roots, fruits, and alms-food.
It has been stated, "with the food of sages" (*munyannaiḥ*). These consist of wild grains such as *nīvāra* and the like, as well as wild vegetables and the like.
The word *anna* is generally used for preparations of grain, such as boiled rice, flour-meal, and parched flour.
Therefore, although vegetables and the like are also food fit for sages (*munyanna*), they are mentioned separately.
Sages (*munayaḥ*) are ascetics (*tāpasāḥ*); their food is *munyanna*.
One should offer the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*), which have the nature of being cooked in fire.
To address the concern that one should not perform the *nirvapaṇa* (offering) when eating fruits ripened by time, he says: "Whatever may be his food.
Whatever he eats—be it flour or other substances according to his capacity—he should offer that as the *bali*.
This refers to what has been prescribed for Indra and Indra’s attendants (*indrāyendrapuruṣebhyaḥ*) and so forth, even in the absence of the *agnihotra*.

However, on this view, there is no oblation in the fire; that is incorrect. Since the word *bali* denotes sacrifice (*ijyā*) in general, this applies equally whether the offering is made in the fire or not.

Furthermore, even if this position were held—that whatever one might eat, it must be cooked on the fire and the oblation (homa) offered into the fire—nevertheless, he will state that vegetables and the like serve that specific purpose alone; one will eat what has ripened naturally over time. In any case, for one who eats what is ripened by time, the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is still performed on the fire.
This is a copulative compound (dvandva) consisting of *agni* and the others.
One should honor a traveler who has arrived at one's hermitage with water, roots, fruits, alms, and wild rice (nīvāra) and the like.
One should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Veda, self-controlled, friendly, and composed;
one should always be a giver and never a taker, showing compassion toward all living beings.

Anticipating the objection that one might cease the study of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*) and other duties under the impression that this is a different stage of life (*āśrama*), he says "constantly disciplined" (*nityayuktaḥ*) to show that there is no such cessation here.
This is not as it is in the householder’s stage (*gārhasthya*);
for in that stage, there are activities intended for household affairs, and while those are being performed, there is no time for Vedic study.
Self-controlled, endowed with self-discipline, and free from intoxication;
friendly, preeminent in acts of friendship, and speaking what is pleasant and beneficial;
intent on conforming to the minds of those nearby—he is one who is concentrated.
Even when dependent on others, one should not speak what is irrelevant or off-topic; nor should one speak excessively.
A donor [should give] water and alms-food.
One who does not receive [such gifts] should not beg from another stage of life for the sake of medicine or other necessities when they have arrived.
He is compassionate toward all beings;
compassion is pity.
Even though he possesses compassion, he would not beg from another for the sake of someone else's benefit.
He should offer the Agnihotra sacrifice pertaining to the three sacred fires according to the rules,
not omitting the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices through the practice of yoga.
A *vitāna* is a sacrificial hall; that which occurs therein is *vaitānika*.
One should offer—that is, perform—the *śrauta* rite pertaining to the three sacred fires (*tretāgni*).
The word *agnihotra* refers to the substance used for the oblation, such as barley gruel (*yavāgū*) and so forth, and is not the name of the ritual itself.

And consequently, the meaning that one should offer that [oblation] into the *āhavanīya* fire by means of the *agnihotra* and other rites becomes established; in the first case, the word *agnihotra* has the same referent as the verb *juhoti*.
But surely, another position was stated: "having entrusted his wife to his sons. In that case, how can there be eligibility for the Vedic rites (*śrauta*) without her?

If it is argued that this is "as in the case of one who has gone abroad"—that is, just as a sacrificer who has gone abroad is still qualified for the performance of the rite through his prior arrangements even while remaining at a distance, and thus remains the agent—so too the wife will grant permission to him departing for the forest, and thus their joint qualification (*sahādhikāra*) will not be contradicted. That too is untenable;
for such a performance would be appropriate only if the husband's departure were necessitated by some divine or human obstacle, and not by his own free will.
If [the wife] were capable, many auxiliary elements would be omitted;

for it has been stated that "in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, one should cause the wife to recite 'Veda'si, Vittirasi,' and so forth," and that would be lost. If it were argued that this injunction would apply to the case of departing together, that too is not correct, because no specific distinction is heard in the text.
Furthermore, in the case of depositing [the fires], no other method of disposal for those fires has been prescribed.
Moreover, this also contradicts the position that they should be maintained together:
"With pure forest foods fit for sages, gathered by himself during the spring and autumn seasons..."
"One should offer the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) and the cooked rice-offerings (carus) separately according to the rule.
By this, wild grains such as nīvāra and other foods fit for sages are intended,
because of the injunction to renounce domestic utensils.

Furthermore, sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) are prescribed in the Veda with rice and other grains, and these are cultivated; nor can the performance of the rite be completed by substituting some other pure wild food— neither by the principle of "that which arises [in its place]" (utpannanyāya) nor by the principle of the injunction regarding rice (vrīhiśāstravidhinyāya)— because such a substitution would constitute a dereliction of duty, and those [grains] are difficult for a wife to procure.
How can there be the abandonment of the sacred fires or of one's wife when there is an injunction for lifelong [observance]?
Therefore, the prescription of other stages of life (āśramas) and the performance of rituals involving the sacrificial fires would not be consistent;
effort must be made on this point.
Some say that the term *vaitānika* is applied by way of praise specifically to the rites prescribed in the Smṛtis;
and in the case of the Smṛti rites, there is no restrictive rule regarding rice and other grains.
For it is therein recorded:
"O King, whatever food a person eats, his deities eat that same food.
Therefore, the performance [of rites] with the food of ascetics would not be contradictory, and the conflict with the scriptural injunction regarding rice and other grains would be resolved.
The same authority exists there as well;
what is the resolution for that?
Since both are based on Smṛti, it will be sublated in this state.
As for the Vedic injunction that "one should sacrifice together with one's wife," that applies only to the Śrauta rites.
Alternatively, this rule does not pertain to the domestic fire at all;
rather, it was stated by Gautama that [this applies] after one has established the fire according to the Śrāvaṇika rite.
Here too, he will state that "one should abide by the Vaikhānasa doctrine. Therefore, these are indeed other ritual acts prescribed by the scriptures;
the terms such as *darśapūrṇamāsa* and so forth are applied there only figuratively.

Therefore, in that case, the establishment of those fires belongs only to one who is without a wife; for it has been stated that the disposal of the fires acquired through the householder stage occurs by merging them into oneself as "the Vaitāna fires. As for the objection—"Since there is a scriptural injunction for lifelong [performance], how can there be an abandonment of the fires?"—this will be examined in the section concerning the sequential order of the four stages of life (āśramas).
Others, however, say:
the offering (*homa*) of village-grown foods is prohibited, but not their use for the sake of the deities and so forth.
But surely, since it is said that "the five, including the sacrificer, consume the *iḍā*," there is consumption even in that case.
True;
however, that [abandonment] is scriptural, not worldly.
And it is the worldly [abandonment] that is prohibited by the word "having completely abandoned."
And his entering the village for that purpose is not contradictory;
for he will state later: "Or, having brought [food] from the village, he may eat.
This [objection] is incorrect.
This is because of the injunction, "with the food of sages.
Thus, everything beginning with "having established the fire according to the Śrāvaṇika rite" is logically consistent;
for indeed, it is recited: "having taken up the Agnihotra."
But it is not by "abandoning" [the fire];
for even the installation [of the fires] for one who is about to die or for one who has performed arduous penance will be mentioned in the context of the first departure.
Furthermore, there is no way to justify the application of terms such as *turāyaṇa* and so forth to the *śravaṇikā* fire.
In the case of one whose wife has died, that kindling of the fires shall be based on scriptural injunction;
or, when one desires forest-dwelling from the very state of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), then there is the kindling of the fires according to the *Śrāvaṇika* rite.
Therefore, the departure for the forest-dweller's stage (*vanaprastha*) occurs together with the fires and accompanied by one's wife for one who has already established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*).
And in that regard, the performance of Vedic rites with rice and other grains should be carried out according to the prescribed rules.
It must be explained in some way how even rice and other such grains constitute the food of sages;
for rice and barley are indeed purifying.

Furthermore, the entrusting of the wife belongs to one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*); in some way, there is recourse to the Smārta fire because both [the wife and the fire] are governed by the Smṛti.
And for one who has two wives, of whom one has taken the fires [with her], there is the rule stating that he should entrust his second wife [to the first].
*Skandayan*: *skandana* means transgression; it is the failure to accomplish the performance exactly as prescribed.
And this [suffix] is for the purpose of filling out the meter.
This "by way of yoga" also means:
by way of yoga, not skipping over [the stages], not destroying [them] through improper reasoning;
for "reasoning" (yukti) is simply the prescribed method (vidhi).
One should perform the New Moon sacrifice (darśeṣṭi), the Āgrayaṇa, and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices;
and likewise, in due order, the Turāyaṇa and the Dākṣāyaṇa.
The term *darśeṣiś ca āgrayaṇaṃ ca* is a collective dvandva compound.
The terms *cāturmāsya*, *turāyaṇa*, and *dākṣāyaṇa* denote specific Śrauta rituals;
for some, the *turāyaṇa* and others are indeed obligatory (*nitya*).

One should separately prepare sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) and cooked oblations (caru) according to the rules, using pure forest foods fit for sages, gathered by oneself during the spring and autumn seasons.

When the phrase "with the food of sages" (*munyannaiḥ*) is not connected with what precedes it, then there is no objection as to how the *vaitānika* rites—which are enjoined to be performed with rice (*vrīhi*) and other grains—should be carried out.
In this context, the *caru* and *puroḍāśa* offerings are to be understood as those prescribed specifically in the *vaikhānasa* scriptures.
Those that are born or ripen in the spring are called *vāsantāni*.
The phrase "thus with autumnal and pure [grains]" is a restatement;
by the words "brought by oneself," occupations such as receiving gifts and so forth are prohibited.
For the sake of performing the Smārta rites already mentioned, there is the taking back [of the property] by means of seizure and so forth;
the word "separately" (*pṛthak*) is used in the sense of completion, as in "according to rule."
Having offered that most pure forest produce as an oblation to the deities,
he should consume the remainder himself, along with salt prepared by his own hand.

On the sacred festival days (parvan), one should consume only what remains after offerings have been made to the deities, and not vegetables, roots, fruits, and the like. One should apply the remainder to oneself—that is, one should utilize it for one's own sake, meaning for the purpose of maintaining the body.
Furthermore, one should not consume salt prepared by oneself, such as rock salt (saindhava) and other varieties.
One should eat vegetables grown on land or in water, as well as flowers, roots, and fruits produced from pure trees, and oils derived from fruits.
One should eat things grown on land and those born in water,
as well as flowers, roots, and fruits.
One should avoid honey, meat, mushrooms growing from the earth,
bhūstṛṇa grass, śigruka, and the fruits of the śleṣmātaka tree.
"Bhūmāni kavakāni" refers to mushrooms;
the word *kavaka* has been explained previously as a synonym for the word *chatrāka*.
And those *kavakas* grow on the ground, as well as in tree hollows and so forth.
Therefore, the mention of "earth-born" (bhauma) is for the purpose of specification.
There is a contradiction with established custom, as mushrooms are prohibited without distinction among the duties of householders;
yet, it is appropriate that there be an exceeding of restrictive rules for the forest-dweller (vānaprastha).
Therefore, "bhaumāni" (earthly) is an independent term.
In this context, it should be understood as referring to a certain substance known among forest-dwellers by the name *gojihvikā*,
and not to anything merely born from the earth.
Since mushrooms have already been prohibited, the repeated prohibition of *bhūstṛṇa* and other such plants is for the purpose of prescribing the same penance as that [for mushrooms].
The words *bhūstṛṇa* and *śigruka* denote specific types of leafy vegetables (*śāka*) and are well-known among the inhabitants of the Vāhika country.
In the month of Āśvayuja, one should discard the sage’s food previously stored,
as well as worn-out garments and vegetables, roots, and fruits.
Regarding the two positions of accumulating for six months or accumulating for a year, the relinquishment occurs in the month of Āśvayuja.
Now, the food of a sage is indeed only that which is sufficient for his work;
there is nothing more than that.
Of what is there renunciation?
It is said:
it is not possible to grasp the scale at the time of acquisition.
Therefore, whatever remains should be relinquished in the month of Āśvayuja,
as well as worn-out garments; there is no relinquishing of those that are not yet worn out.
One should not eat what has been ploughed by a plowshare, even if it has been discarded by someone; nor should one eat flowers or fruits grown in a village, even when distressed.
There is a prohibition even against forest-grown [food] that has been ploughed.
By the phrase "village food," there is a prohibition even of village-grown items that have not been ploughed.

Even for one who is distressed, and even when other options are unavailable, because the worship of deities and so forth must necessarily be performed, such [food] is not to be accepted even under the alternative of using a substitute; this is the meaning.
The word "api" (even) should be understood as displaced in its position; for even flowers are not to be accepted, let alone grains.
He may eat food cooked by fire, or he may eat only what is ripened by time;
he may be one who grinds with a stone, or even one who uses his teeth as a mortar.

That which is cooked by fire, such as vegetables, boiled rice, and so forth—eating that is "eating what is cooked by fire. Or he should eat only that which has ripened naturally in its own time, such as the fruit of trees;
or else, this eating consists of grinding grains such as *nīvāra* and the like.
Having crushed [the food] with stones—that is, with rocks—and having reduced it to the form of flour, he should eat it.

Or else, whatever is available according to the season, such as gourds and the like, from which the outer husk or shell has been removed by means of stones, he should eat the inner fruit. One whose teeth serve as a mortar is called *dantolūkhalika*.
Having removed the husks with his teeth, he should eat;
even though there is no formal preparation (*saṃskāra*), that [preparation] need not be performed.
Or rather, as before, it is a characteristic mark of a specific kind of food: he should eat such food that his teeth alone accomplish the function of the mortar, namely the threshing.
He may be one who washes [his bowl] immediately after a meal, or one who accumulates food for a month; he may be one who stores food for six months, or even one who stores it for a year.
Regarding that which was previously mentioned as "food," one should acquire only what is sufficient for a single day's meal;

or, "accumulation for a month" (*māsa-saṃcaya*) refers to a store sufficient for a month, or a collection used over the course of a month. The suffix *ṭhan* should be applied [to form the word *māsaṃcayika*] because he possesses such a store.
Alternatively, the term *māsasaṃcayaka* should be understood here as a bahuvrīhi compound, meaning "one who has a store sufficient for a month" (*māsaparyāptaḥ saṃcayaḥ asya*).
The same applies to the two following terms as well.
One should eat food at night or by day, having gathered it according to one's ability; or one may eat only every fourth mealtime, or even every eighth mealtime.

Since eating twice a day is prescribed for the sake of human necessity, the cessation of one of those times is enjoined. Just as one's age advances, so should one abandon meal-times; even the fourth meal-time should be observed only up to the eighth part of the day.
Having passed three days and nights, one who eats on the evening of the fourth day becomes an "eater at the eighth meal-time" (*aṣṭamakālika*).
Since eating is the subject under discussion, it is understood that the connection with the fourth time-period refers specifically to that [act of eating].
Or he should pass through the bright and dark fortnights according to the rules of the Cāndrāyaṇa;
or else, at the ends of the two fortnights, he should eat boiled barley-gruel only once.
At the two ends of the fortnight— on the full moon day and on the new moon day—
one should eat the gruel prepared therein;
"once" means either in the evening or in the morning.
Abiding by the doctrine of the Vaikhānasas, he should always subsist solely on flowers, roots, and fruits that have ripened in their due time and fallen of their own accord.
"Ripened by time":
this is for the purpose of excluding the cooking of jackfruit and similar fruits even by fire;
such food cooked by fire is not forbidden for a householder.

There is a scripture named Vaikhānasa, in which the duties of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) are prescribed; abiding by their opinion, he should also learn the other conduct ordained in that scripture.
He should roll about on the ground or stand on his tiptoes for a day; he should pass his time by alternating between standing and sitting, approaching water at the three ritual libations.
"Turning about" means sitting on one side on the bare ground and then remaining on the other side.

Except for the times of eating and moving about, one should conduct oneself in this manner; that is to say, one should not sit down, nor walk about, nor sit upon a bed, nor a seat, nor against a wall.
One should stand on the balls of the feet or on the tips of the toes.
During the day, he should remain standing and sitting; however, for the night, he will prescribe sleeping on the bare ground alone.
At the three *savanas*—namely, morning, midday, and afternoon—he should recite "upa yann apaḥ."
In the absence of rivers and the like, he shows that bathing may be performed even with water drawn up from them.
In summer he should practice the penance of the five fires; during the rains, he should live under the open sky;
and in winter, he should wear wet clothes, thus gradually increasing his austerity.
One should subject oneself to the five fires:
having placed fires in the four directions, one should stand in the middle and endure the heat of the sun from above.

During the rainy season, one should take shelter in the open air under the clouds; in whatever place it rains, one should resort to that very spot, and for the sake of warding off the rain, one should not take up an umbrella, a garment, or similar items.
"In winter" is intended as an indicator for the cold season;
by this, the same rule applies to the cool season as well: wearing wet clothes.
"Gradually" means step by step.
Performing ablutions at the three sessions of the day, he should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
practicing even more rigorous austerity, he should wither his own body.
*Upasparśana* means bathing.
Other forms of austerity (*tapas*) as well—such as keeping the arms raised, fasting for a month, or observing the twelve-night vow—should be performed;
by practicing that which is more intense, more excellent, and productive of bodily pain, one should wither the body.
Having duly internalized the sacrificial fires within himself,
he should become a sage without fire or fixed abode, subsisting on roots and fruits.
The *vaitāna* rites are those pertaining to the sacrificial canopy; that is, the Śrauta rituals.
One should consign them into oneself according to the procedure for consuming ashes and so forth. Furthermore, the ritual for consignment into oneself is to be understood from the *Śravaṇaka*.

When a long period of austerity has been practiced and one has reached the age of seventy, then, while still remaining a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), one should abandon the fire and the dwelling, leaving behind the leaf-hut for the sake of residence. Where, then, should he dwell?
As will be stated later: "having the root of a tree as his abode."
The word "muni" (sage) is to be connected [with the preceding].
By this, the following meaning is expressed:
one should exercise restraint over speech.
One who observes the vow of silence is called "one of restrained speech" in the world;
[the phrase] "subsisting on roots and fruits" is intended to exclude other food.
One should not eat even wild grains such as nīvāra and other forest products.
Exerting no effort for the sake of pleasures, practicing celibacy, sleeping on the ground, having no sense of ownership over shelters, and making his dwelling at the foot of trees;
One should not exert effort toward objects that serve the purpose of pleasure;
one oppressed by heat should not approach the shade;
and one afflicted by cold should not kindle a fire.
If, however, the cessation of suffering such as cold occurs through the heat of the sun provided by fate, and the removal of that suffering is performed right there, it is not prohibited;
for this is prescribed at a time other than the rainy season and so forth, since it is the prescription of a dharma already undertaken.
Alternatively, the effort toward medicine is forbidden for one who is ill.
The cessation of disease is also called happiness;
therefore, one should not exert effort for the sake of its prevention. Sleeping on the ground, he should lie upon a bare patch of earth covered only with grass.
One should not form the notion of "mine" or the attachment of ownership toward shelters and dwellings, such as the roots of trees and so forth;
one should take the roots of trees as one's abode in place of a house.
In the absence of those, stone slabs, caves, and the like are also prescribed.
He should obtain alms for his sustenance only from Brahmins who are ascetics,
