or from other twice-born householders living in the forest.
The locative case is used in the sense of the ablative:
in the absence of fruits and roots from ascetics,
he should collect alms from householders, that is, from those living as forest-dwellers.
The sustenance is that by which satiety is achieved.
But in the event of impossibility,
one living in the forest may eat eight mouthfuls after bringing them from a village,
having received them either in a leaf-cup, with the hand, or with a potsherd.

Because it specifies "taking mouthfuls," this does not refer merely to begging for roots and fruits; rather, when other food is unavailable, the consumption of village-grown grain is permitted by this rule. Having taken [the food] with the hand alone—meaning without a vessel—one should eat from a "fragment," that is, a broken piece such as a shard of a bowl or similar object.
A Brahmin living in the forest should practice these and other initiations,
as well as various Upanishadic scriptures, for the sake of self-perfection.
One should practice these initiatory observances (*dīkṣā-niyama*) as well as others, such as staying within water and closing the eyes;
one should study, reflect upon, and meditate on the *śrutis*— the Upaniṣadic Vedic passages recited in the section concerning secret doctrines—
for the sake of self-perfection, or for the purpose of attaining Brahman, as the meditations (*upāsanā*) have been described.
"Various" is a restatement.
These [waters] have been resorted to by sages and Brahmins who are householders for the sake of increasing knowledge and austerity, and for the purification of the body.

Since it was stated without qualification that one should practice other [observances] as well, the possibility of practicing the initiations (*dīkṣā*) and so forth of the Śākyas, Pāśupatas, and others would also follow; he therefore prohibits that.
In the *Mahābhārata*, these are described as having been practiced by the Ṛṣis when they were suffering from great heat and other afflictions.
And those [virtues] which have been practiced by brahmins and householders—this has been stated [in the scripture]: "And this is not in conflict with the subsequent [stages of life].
Knowledge (*vidyā*) is the realization of the oneness of the Self; one should lead that to growth—that is, make it firm—by the study of the revealed scriptures (*śruti*).
And for the purification of the body, one should observe the initiation of dietary restrictions.
Or, having taken recourse to Aparājitā, he should go straight toward that direction, disciplined,
subsisting on water and air, until the fall of his body.
The intermediate direction between the eastern and northern quarters is called Aparājita (Unconquered) in the worlds; it is also known as Aiśānī.
Having taken his stand in that direction and resolved in his mind, "I must go toward this," he should then proceed toward it alone, moving straight and not in a crooked manner.

One should not avoid the currents of chasms or rivers; disciplined, subsisting on water and air, one should remain until the body falls. This is the procedure for traveling toward the east and the north.
As long as he does not fall [from his path], he should subsist on air and water;
being disciplined, having disciplined himself according to the Yoga-shastras,
this is called the Great Departure (mahāprasthāna).
Having cast off his body by means of any one of these practices of the great seers,
the Brahmin, freed from sorrow and fear, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.

One should cast off the body by means of one of these: the austerities previously mentioned, the great departure (mahāprasthāna) just described, or the conduct of the great seers; specifically, by entering a river, by leaping from a precipice, by entering the fire, or by abstaining from food. The fruit for such a person, who is free from sorrow and fear, is the attainment of the world of Brahmā.
Sorrow is the experience of suffering in the hells and other realms;
fear is the thought, "I shall go to hell.
That [sorrow and fear] departs from him.
He reaches the world of Brahman (brahmaloka) without any interval, not by way of the sequence beginning with light;
here, "the world of Brahman" refers to a particular location that is superior even to heaven, where he is magnified—that is, he remains being honored.
However, he does not attain the sovereign rule of Brahman itself, because of the use of the term "world" (loka).
For he will speak of liberation in the fourth stage of life (āśrama).
They say that liberation is not produced by ritual action alone.
But has it not also been stated for this [fourth stage]: "And various Upaniṣadic scriptures for the sake of the self's perfection"?
And self-perfection (*ātmasaṃsiddhi*) is the attainment of that state through the worship of the Self;
for no other meaning of the word "perfection" is logically tenable.
This is because in the Upaniṣadic scriptures, that which is to be realized by yogins is the Self, as it is said: "Established in Brahman, he attains immortality."
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "then he attains union" (sāyujyaṃ gacchati) and so forth,
it is said:
other perfections resulting from austerity (tapaḥ-siddhi) are also heard of in scripture.

If it is argued that, through such passages as "if he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers," there will result for the person a state of equality in power (*sārṣṭitā*) and residence in the same world (*sālokya*) as brought about by his intended objects,
but not liberation (*mokṣa*),
that is incorrect because there is no distinction [between the two cases].
Just as one is qualified for meditations (*upāsanā*) that yield limited results, so too is one qualified for the attainment of immortality.
Nowhere is it heard that meditations concerning non-duality must be performed by a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) alone.
But is it not the case that, having introduced the topic with "There are three branches of duty," the duties of the householder are stated by the passage beginning, "sacrifice, study, and charity"?
By the phrase "only austerity," the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) is indicated;
by the phrase "the student who dwells in the teacher's family," the lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) is indicated;
and by the phrase "one firmly established in Brahman," the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka) is indicated.
The worlds of merit have been described for these three;
by the principle of remainder, immortality belongs to that which is distinct from these.
This is not so.
One who is intent upon that [Brahman] abides in Brahman and strives toward it; for this word "brahmasaṃstha" (one established in Brahman) is used in its etymological sense.
Now, if all were eligible [for this practice], then it would have been sufficient merely to say, "One established in Brahman attains immortality.
It is not so.

The fruit of the stages of life (āśramas), as understood from their own scriptural injunctions, consists in attaining worlds of merit that are subject to decay; however, for one who is established in Brahman—even while remaining within those very stages of life—immortality characterized by non-return is ordained.
Now, it may be objected: "But for the knower of the Self, Brahman is of the nature of non-duality, and he is one whose actions have ceased. To this we reply: [it is true].

Furthermore, the stages of life (*āśrama*) are designated as the path of active engagement (*pravṛttamārga*); they consist of the performance of rituals characterized by distinctions among actions, agents, and results.

In that regard, there is a mutual contradiction between the realization of the non-dual Self (*advaitātma-vijñāna*) and the duties of householders and others, such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice, which rely upon those very same distinctions.
To this, it is replied:
This is the same even in the case of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*), because restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) are prescribed there, and these depend upon distinctions.
Now, it might be argued that for one who has renounced action (*karmasaṃnyāsī*) and stands on the path of cessation (*nivṛttimārga*), there are no injunctions of the scriptures at all;
but this is not the meaning of the scriptures.

It will be explained that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is precisely the abandonment of the notions of "I" and "mine," not the abandonment of the entire meaning of the scriptures. Even for such a person, when afflicted by hunger and the like and engaged in activities such as begging for alms, there certainly exists a relationship between action and its factors (*kriyā-kāraka*). In that regard, for one engaged in worldly activities whose purpose is visible, the cultivation of the realization of the non-dual Self (*advaitātma-vijñāna-bhāvanā*) is not contradictory; however, regarding scriptural duties such as the *agnihotra*, it is contradictory. Who, then, being a reasonable person, would speak thus?
Now it is said:

even for one afflicted by hunger and the like, the abandonment of non-duality lasts only so long as the opposing factor of eating persists. It is just as when a traveler walking in dense darkness places his foot upon a thorny spot, yet once the sun has risen and light is regained, he stands again rightly upon the thornless path.

Likewise, when one’s self-consciousness is interrupted by the affliction of hunger and the like, upon the cessation of that hunger—which serves as a locus of illumination—one again abides in non-duality alone by virtue of firm latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
This is not contradictory even for an ascetic;
nor is it contradictory for a householder to practice worship in the form of [identifying with] his sons, wife, and so forth.
But for one who has become habituated to duality through manifold activities, how can there arise the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of non-duality?
And it is said among the duties of a householder: "One should reflect alone," and likewise, "Having entrusted everything to one's son."
But surely there is the Śruti text: "Therefore, one who desires heaven should not depart before the end of his lifespan.
In that case, how can there be the renunciation of the body by a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*)?
For that Śruti cannot be made applicable to anyone other than the forest-dweller by this Smṛti.
For scripture is more powerful; and it ought not to be restricted in accordance with a Smṛti text.
It is replied:
When death is known to be imminent—either due to being worn out by old age or through the sight of undesirable portents—and one is about to die, there is no contradiction with the Śruti.
For it is heard there: "Not before the end of one's lifespan.
Indeed, if death were intended in an undesired state, the text would have simply said, "One who desires heaven should not depart [before that]."
Furthermore, the instruction on *ariṣṭas* (signs of death) found in the Upaniṣads becomes meaningful only for one whose death does not have this [specific] cause.
Having thus spent the third part of his life wandering in the forests,
he should renounce all attachments and wander as a mendicant during the fourth part of his life.
From this point forward, the intention is for the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśrama*). "The third part" means having remained for some period of time.
It takes as much time as is required for austerity to be well-performed and all desire for sense-objects to cease;
for it is not possible to know this by means of the primary third part of one's lifespan alone.
Indeed, the stages of life do not depend on a hundred years, since the onset of wrinkles, gray hair, and the birth of offspring is stated to be the time for entering the third stage of life.
Furthermore, that [knowledge] does not arise for everyone who is about fifty years of age;
and it is stated elsewhere that one should renounce when austerity has reached perfection.

Now, while for other stages of life there is a defined period—such as studenthood (*brahmacarya*) ending with the completion of Vedic study, and the householder stage (*gārhasthya*) lasting until the appearance of wrinkles and grey hair—here, in this case, there is no such limiting cause.
If the third part were relied upon exactly as it was heard—namely, "and when asceticism has become perfected"—then even there, a dependence on time would indeed be appropriate.
It is not known by how much asceticism perfection is attained;
therefore, a limitation of time is not fit to be stated.
It has been stated here that it is not possible to determine the third part of the lifespan in relation to a hundred years;
rather, the time for renunciation has been specified as occurring when the body is ripe.
One should go forth at such a stage of austerity and such an age that no further increase in intoxication is to be feared.
"Having dwelt" means having remained after performing the prescribed rule;
"renunciation of attachment" refers to the relinquishing of the sense of "mine" and delighting in solitude.
Having gone from stage to stage of life, having offered oblations, having conquered the senses,
and being weary from the practice of begging and making offerings, one who renounces increases after death.
He supports the position of cumulative practice with the phrase "from one stage to another.

Having gone from the householder stage to the forest-dweller stage, when one has performed the fire-sacrifices and has conquered the senses in both stages, then one should go forth as a wandering mendicant.
"Having died, he prospers," meaning that after death he attains a state of supreme magnificence.
"Exhausted for a long time by the giving of alms and offerings"—
this is a restatement of the duties pertaining to the stages of life (āśrama-dharma).
Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation;
but he who pursues liberation without having discharged them goes downward.
"Discharge" means the complete clearing of debts.
One should direct the mind toward liberation (*mokṣa*).
By the word "liberation," the stage of wandering mendicancy (*pravrajyāśrama*) is indicated.
In that state, the fruit of liberation alone is said to be predominant,
whereas it is not so in the other stages of life;
therefore, liberation results from the life of a wandering mendicant.
What, then, are those three debts? To this he says:

"Having studied the Vedas according to rule, having procreated sons in accordance with dharma, and having sacrificed with sacrifices according to one's ability, one should direct the mind toward liberation."

"One is born burdened with three debts: to the gods by means of sacrifice, to the ancestors by means of progeny, and to the seers by means of Vedic study"—this is a Smṛti text that restates the Śruti. But is there not the Jābāla-Śruti which says: "Having become a householder, one should renounce; or else, otherwise, one may renounce even from the stage of the student"?
It is said:
this was stated based merely on the fact of arising; it provides an illustration, but in that regard, the following is contradicted: "having thus not produced offspring."
If this scriptural authority exists, what then? This is stated:
"Because the householder's state is directly enjoined."

Regarding the injunction "one should go forth," there is no such rule as that "once gone forth, these specific acts must be performed by him in this particular manner. However, for the householder, the Agnihotra and other rites are prescribed with their full constituent parts and procedures; it is with this intention that [the text] speaks.

As for those lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika) and others who, not seeing this Vedic text, follow only the Smṛti rules, they are set aside by the householder stage of life, which is established by direct Vedic injunction.
And as for those who explain the meaningfulness of the Smṛti statements by claiming they refer to those disqualified, such as eunuchs and others—we do not understand their intention.

For if it be the case that one is not entitled to Śrauta rites due to incapacity regarding subsidiary elements (aṅga) such as the inspection of the clarified butter (ājyāvekṣaṇa) or the Viṣṇu-steps (viṣṇukrama), then since the scriptural injunctions regarding entitlement (adhikāra-śruti) have achieved their purpose by applying to one capable of performing the rite as endowed with such subsidiaries, one should not perform it even if one is incapable [of those specific parts].

If this is so, then even for those following the Smṛti rules, there is the fetching of water-jars and other items for the sake of the teacher, as well as the service of begging alms, for the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*); and even in the state of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*), it is said that "one should not dwell in a village for a second night. How then could the lame and the blind have the qualification for the sequence of Smṛti rituals? Furthermore, they possess the mark (*liṅga*) of initiation (*upanayana*).
From that [initiation], there is the request for marriage for them, according to the rule: "But if there is a desire for wives..."

Although the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), the beholding of the sun, the circumambulation of the fire, and the act of going around it have been prescribed—since marriage is impossible for one who has not been initiated because of his status as a *vrātya*—therefore, as far as possible, service to the teacher and even a defective state of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) still exist [for him].
However, for the eunuch (*klība*), there is simply no possibility of initiation due to his nature; and he is not authorized for anything whatsoever, whether by his father or otherwise.
Therefore, the view that renunciation (*pārivrājya*) and lifelong studenthood (*naiṣṭhikatā*) concern those who are not qualified [for Vedic rites] does not satisfy the mind.
It is true that this will be like the censure of the *uditahoma* sacrifice;
the statement of censure, "without having discharged [the debts]," is made by resorting to the position of their combination (*samuccaya*), and is not an absolute prohibition.
Alternatively, this should be understood as follows: that one who has not yet taken a wife is eligible for the life of renunciation.
A twice-born man who, without having studied the Vedas, without having procreated offspring,
and without having performed sacrifices, desires liberation, goes downward.
One who has established the sacred fires with sacrifices, including the regular animal and Soma offerings.
Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice, in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee,
and having internalized the sacred fires within himself, a Brāhmaṇa may renounce his home and go forth.
The Prājāpatya sacrifice is prescribed in the Adhvaryu Veda,
and in it the giving away of all one's possessions is ordained. Having performed that sacrifice, the sacred fires are consigned within oneself.
The procedure for the formal assignment (*samāropaṇa*) should also be understood from that very same source.
The compound *sārvavedasadakṣiṇā* has as its referent [the word] "one who has" (*asyāsti*). *Veda* means wealth; all of that is to be given.

This [suffix] is prescribed in the sense of "for the sake of" (*arthe*) as a self-applicative (*svārthika*), because *prajñā* and others belong to the class of words formed according to their general form (*ākṛtigaṇa*).

Others, however, say that the *puruṣamedha* is a sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) dedicated to Prajāpati. In that context, the first animal is the Brahmin whom one sacrifices for Brahmā; and since Brahmā is Prajāpati, and because designations proceed by way of the primary [referent], the *puruṣamedha* is [thus] called *prājāpatya*.

The gift of all one's possessions (*sarvasvadāna*), the internalizing of the fires (*agnisamāropaṇa*), and renunciation (*pravrajyā*) are prescribed in that very context. For thus is the scriptural tradition (*śruti*) there: "Now, having internalized the fires within oneself, by means of that internalization, and no longer looking back from the worship of the sun, one who has set out for the forest becomes firm toward gods and men at that very moment. As for the fact that renunciation is designated after one has internalized the fires within oneself—according to the statement, "These indeed are the sacrifices of the self"—therefore, because of his death, those [fires] which were given to her become internalized within the self alone.
Therefore, [the argument that] in the event of a wife's death one may renounce the world and need not necessarily take a wife again—this is not correct.
Rather, it must be stated that since it is recited [in the texts], "having given the fires to his wife, he performs the funeral rites," this applies when she dies first.
For this text is of human origin and not the Veda; thus, the rebuttal would be that we may indeed criticize what has been so stated.
For that teacher of Brahman who, having granted fearlessness to all beings, goes forth from his home, there are worlds consisting of splendor.
The praise of the fourth stage of life through the censure of the householder's life:
for in sacrifice animals are slain;
and according to the view that plants possess consciousness and the nature of growth, the cutting of grasses and herbs constitutes this "fear for living beings."
It has been stated that for one who has gone forth from the home and maintained the sacred fire, there is no [such thing as taking];
by saying "having granted fearlessness to all beings," this expresses the non-appropriation of green grass and leaves.
It consists of light and is eternally luminous;
there, the rising and setting of the sun are not perceived.
As it is said in the Upaniṣads: "Beyond this, the sun neither rises nor sets"—such are the words they speak.
Since not even the slightest fear arises for the twice-born from any living beings,
there is no fear whatsoever for him who has been liberated from the body.
This very point is stated again:
the meaning is that for one who is liberated from the body, the present physical frame falls away.
Having gone forth from the home, the sage, purified by his observances,
should wander as a mendicant, indifferent even when sensual pleasures are presented to him.

A sage is one who is endowed with purifying mantra-recitations, *darbha* grass, water-pots, and black antelope skins; or else, one who is purified by ascetic penances (*kṛcchra*) and is a speaker of nothing at all.

When desirable objects such as fine food and the like have been brought forth by someone, or when sounds such as songs and the like have appeared by chance, or when sons and others have come into his presence, he should remain indifferent;
he should not look upon them for long with an affectionate eye, nor listen to them, nor sit together with them.
As it has been said:
"One should always wander alone, without companions, for the sake of accomplishment;
seeing that what is accomplished belongs to the solitary one, he neither abandons [the path] nor is he abandoned."
By this, delighting in solitude is enjoined;
by the phrase "all alone," the abandonment of former acquaintances is expressed;
and by the term "without companions," it is meant that one should not even maintain the previous acceptance of servants and the like.
For one who is completely free from attachment and aversion toward consciousness, there arises this very equanimity toward all things.
Otherwise, regarding someone such as a servant who stands nearby, the thought would arise: "This one is mine, but that one is not.
This very attachment is the cause of limitation; for instance, it persists as long as one does not abandon it, and thus one is never truly abandoned by sons or others.

Therefore, he is not diminished and is not separated from his sons and others; he does not experience the suffering of separation from them. Otherwise, there would be great suffering when one must relinquish what has been attached to. For him, no one dies, nor does he belong to anyone.
He should be without fire and without a dwelling; he may resort to a village for the sake of food.
Indifferent, free from accumulation, a sage whose being is concentrated in meditative absorption.
The prior absence of the Vedic fires (*śrauta-agni*) has already been stated; by this [verse], the absence of the domestic fire (*gārhasthya*) is expressed.
Alternatively, this is a prohibition against cooking and against fuel for the fire intended for the purpose of warding off cold and so forth.
*Niketa* means a house.
For the sake of food, he may stay in a village for one night;
having accomplished his purpose, he should spend the remainder of his time in the forest.
And this single night in the village has been prescribed by Gautama.
In that regard, if he reaches the village at the same time [as the others], then his entry is solely for the sake of food; but if it is from afar, then he may stay for one night,
and consider the second night to be spent in the forest.
He should be equanimous even toward insentient objects such as a water-pot and the like, and he should not make them subject to his own will;
or alternatively, he should not perform medical treatment for the body.
Others, however, read the word as *asaṃkasukaḥ*.
Unsteady and wavering—by negating these, he teaches steadiness of mental activity.
A sage (*muni*) is one whose faculty of speech is restrained;
being concentrated (*samāhita*) in his disposition (*bhāva*), that is, in his mind, he should abandon conceptual constructions with his intellect (*manas*).
One is truly concentrated through one's very being, not by mere words alone.
A skull, the roots of trees, ragged clothing, solitude,
and equanimity toward all things— these are the characteristics of one who is liberated.
The bowl for eating alms is a skull or a potsherd;
the dwelling is at the roots of trees;
and the ragged garment is a piece of coarse, worn-out cloth.
Equanimity toward enemy, friend, those who are neither, and one's own self is the characteristic of the liberated one.
It is said that liberation is soon to be attained; however, one does not become liberated by this alone.
One should not rejoice in death, nor should one rejoice in life;
one should simply await the time, just as a hired laborer awaits his wages.
By this, she has stated that she is free from affliction:
she would not desire death,
nor would she seek life for the sake of attaining superior knowledge.
One should simply wait for the right time, thinking: "Whatever will come to pass,
let it be then," just as a laborer awaits his wages.

Having accepted wages, one maintains the duration of the contract, thinking, "This much time must be served by me for him"; there is no gain for the price if there is an interruption in the interim. Likewise, through this method, liberation occurs upon the fall of the body due to the exhaustion of *saṃsāra*, not through acting according to one's own whims.
One should place one's foot down purified by sight; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should speak words purified by truth; and one should act with a mind that is purified.
Having examined the path with his eyes, he should place his foot in a place where living beings do not suffer harm.
Since it would have been sufficient simply to say "one should speak true speech," the inclusion of the word *pūta* (pure) indicates that the word *satya* (true) is used figuratively;
by this, [the rule] becomes more comprehensive.
One who is purified by the mind should always be pure in mind;
one should not engage in coveting the property of others and so forth.
One should endure harsh words and should not despise anyone;
nor, depending upon this body, should one harbor enmity toward anyone.
When anyone speaks in transgression of the scriptures, that is *ativāda*, or offensive abuse.

One should endure it—that is, one should be patient—and should not respond with abuse; nor should one become angry in the mind. Therefore, he will say: "When reviled, one should speak what is wholesome."
By this, the agitation of the mind is restrained; it does not enjoin the utterance of virtuous words.
For at that time, one would be a speaker of falsehood, saying one thing with the voice while intending another in the heart.
[The phrase] "one should not despise" means:
One should not show contempt toward anyone.
One should not transgress in the honoring of teachers and others.
Nor should one harbor enmity even if someone were to strike this body.
One should meditate thus: "What is the use of this body of mine, whether it perishes or does not perish? May my body become composed of radiant energy."
One should not return anger to one who is angry; when reviled, one should speak kindly;
and one should not utter false speech scattered through the seven gates.
There are seven pairs: dharma and artha, dharma and kāma, artha and kāma, kāma and artha, kāma and dharma, artha and dharma, and dharma and artha—this is the *trivarga*.
In this regard, one should not utter false speech that is confused or distracted concerning these objects.
Because these are based on differentiation (*bheda*), and because all differentiation is unreal, it is said to be "false" (*anṛta*).
What then? One should speak only of that which is the basis for liberation.
Or else, there are the seven vital breaths located in the head; these are the doors of speech.
Or else, there are the six sense organs, with the intellect as the seventh.
Speech proceeds with respect to objects grasped by these [senses];
others say that these are the case-endings (sub-vibhaktis).
Delighting in the inner self, seated, indifferent to external things, and free from worldly desires,
one who seeks happiness should wander about in this world with oneself alone as a companion.
One-pointedness that culminates in the attainment of the penetration of the reality of the self is "internal.
One should remain intent on reflecting upon its meaning and finding delight therein.
The phrase "without regard" is a restatement of what was previously said for the purpose of practicing [this state] apart from those other objects and phenomena.

"Free from worldly gain" (nirāmiṣa) means devoid of craving. "Flesh" (māṃsa) is "worldly gain" (āmiṣa); having identified craving by means of that term, there is a prohibition [of it]. In this regard, living beings possess an excessive craving for it.
The rest has already been explained previously.
He should never seek alms by means of portents or omens, nor by the science of astrology and bodily marks, nor by instructions or discourses.

He should not, out of a desire for alms, speak of the results of portents—whether celestial, atmospheric, or terrestrial—such as eclipses, the rising of planets, the appearance of comets, fires in the quarters of the sky, earthquakes, and so forth; nor of omens such as the misfortunes of a household;
nor of the science of constellations, such as "Today is the constellation Kṛttikā, suitable for work," or "Today is the constellation for a journey," and so on.
*Āṅgavidyā* is the science of bodily marks, such as the characteristics of palmistry and so forth.

*Anuśāsana* is the instruction for a king regarding his subjects, such as: "One should conduct oneself in this manner; there should be peace with this person and war with that; why have you done this? Why do you not do that?
*Vāda* is a debate rooted in pride, consisting of the presentation of arguments and refutations when there is disagreement regarding the meaning of the scriptures.
One should not approach a house that is crowded with ascetics, Brahmins, birds, dogs, or other mendicants.
"Congested":
one should avoid that place for the purpose of alms where many people have gathered together to obtain food.
With his hair, nails, and beard trimmed, carrying a bowl, a staff, and a water-pot,
he should wander constantly with self-restraint, not causing pain to any living beings.
He will describe the vessels;
there are three staffs,
for he is indeed a triple-staffed ascetic (tridaṇḍin).
*Kusumbha* refers to a water-pot, not the safflower (*mahārajana*).
The meaning of the second half of the subsequent verse has already been established.
His vessels should be non-metallic and free from flaws;
their purification with water is prescribed, just as that of the *camasa* cups in a sacrifice.

The vessels for alms and water are non-metallic, meaning they are not made of gold or other metals; they are without cracks and without holes. They are to be free from stains by means of water alone, like sacrificial ladles (*camasa*).
However, it should be understood that when a stain occurs, its removal must also be accomplished by means of another substance.
A gourd, a wooden bowl, one made of clay, and likewise one made of split bamboo—
these, Svāyambhuva Manu declared, are the vessels for ascetics.
"Vaidala" refers to that which is made from split bamboo and the like;
these are the vessels for an ascetic, intended for alms and for water.
One should wander for alms at a single time and not seek an abundance;
for an ascetic who is attached to alms becomes attached even to sense-objects.
The rule that eating from alms-gathering must occur at a single time is prescribed, but this does not apply to the act of wandering for alms itself.
What is intended here is the prohibition against eating twice.
In that regard, having gone out once and then, at a second time, eating what was left over, one should not do so; it is for that purpose that the prohibition against eating is established.
For this very reason, he said, "One should not engage in elaboration.
For it is through the desire for a second meal that elaboration occurs;
for one who delights in solitude, there is no elaboration of alms-seeking for the sake of servants.
By stating the reason, he also prohibits satiety even in the case of eating only once.
When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle lies still, when the embers are extinguished, when the people have finished their meal,
and when the removal of the dishes has taken place, the ascetic should always go forth for alms.
The time when people have finished eating is "bhuktavajjanaḥ. Similarly, there are also [the times] such as "vidhūma" (when the smoke has ceased).
"Saṃpāta of bowls" refers to the discarding of the remains on the ground;
when that has passed, by all this he says that one should beg for alms at that time when the opportunity for giving alms has ceased during the first period of cooking.
With the verse beginning "vidhūma" (smokeless), he describes the commencement of the second cooking; "sannā musalāḥ" means the pestles have ceased from threshing and have been set aside.

One should not be despondent in the absence of gain, nor should one rejoice in its presence; one should take only what is necessary for the maintenance of life, being free from attachment to material requisites.
If, at such a time, nothing can be obtained from anywhere, then one should not succumb to despondency or mental exhaustion.
One should not harbor joy or dejection regarding gain or loss.
The measure of alms is that amount which is sufficient for the maintenance of life.
By this he shows the following:
in the absence of alms, the maintenance of life may be carried out even with unclaimed fruits, roots, water, and so forth.
"Possessions" refers to the bowl, staff, and other such items; "attachment" to them means striving to acquire them; one who has gone away from that is "withdrawn" (nivṛtta).
"Without desire" means as far as [that point].
One should utterly detest gains obtained through being honored;
for even a liberated ascetic is bound by gains obtained through being honored.
That which one gives after having honored someone is "gain obtained through honor. One should "despise" that— meaning one should censure or reproach it—
and for this reason, one should not practice what is censured.
In every way and at all times,
he should not accept alms for even a single day of such a kind;
the subsequent passage is an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*).
For bondage is not possible for one who is liberated.
By consuming little food and by staying and sitting in solitude,
one should withdraw the senses that are being carried away by their objects.
A secluded place is one devoid of people; there, standing and sitting should be practiced.
By this, the conquest of the senses as the fruit of delighting in solitude is demonstrated.
Alternatively, freedom from curiosity is expressed by this.
Where large crowds of people, consisting of both men and women and adorned with various ornaments, are seen, one should not remain there even for a moment.
Through the restraint of the senses, through the destruction of passion and hatred,
and through non-violence toward living beings, one becomes fit for immortality.
Cessation (nirodha) is the obstruction of the functioning toward its own objects.
"It conduces to immortality" means it becomes capable of, or fit for, immortality.
This shows that this [cessation] is just like the knowledge of the Self (ātmajñāna).
One should contemplate the destinies of men arising from the defects of their actions,
as well as their falling into hell and the torments in the abode of Yama.
This analytical contemplation on the ultimate truth is called the investigation into the true nature of saṃsāra, which is essentially suffering.

How indeed might this person transform the bodily affliction of wandering forth, the practice of begging, and so forth—which are causes of suffering consisting in the renunciation of friends, kinsmen, children, wife, wealth, and power—into something that is practiced without flaw, whether through necessity or by one's own will?

The destinies of human beings abound in suffering; they arise from the defects of karma resulting from the performance of prohibited acts, such as violence, theft, adultery, harsh speech, calumny, and evil intentions.
In this very world of the living, there are destinies such as poverty, the affliction of disease, humiliation, and physical deficiencies, as well as the experience of their fruits.
In the hereafter, there is falling into hell or the abyss, birth as worms or insects in impure places filled with urine, feces, and the like,
and torments in the abode of Yama such as being boiled in cauldrons.
Likewise, this other [point] should be considered:
separation from those who are dear, as well as union with those who are not dear,
being overcome by old age, and being tormented by diseases.
The accusative case is used because of the presence of the verbal action "one should observe" (*avekṣeta*).

"Beloved ones" refers to kinsmen such as sons; "separation from them" means being parted from those who have died before their time. "Union with the unpleasant" refers to union with enemies through battles and the like.
By old age:

old age is a specific state in the fourth stage of life; by it there is overwhelming, which consists of the destruction of the body's form, incapacity, impairment of the sense faculties, an abundance of diseases such as cough and asthma, being undesirable to all, and being an object of ridicule—by such things as these comes the overcoming by old age.
Furthermore, for some, there is affliction by diseases even prior to old age.

Furthermore, even for one who remains in such a state, great craving arises. If that is so, then this [craving] occurs even against the will of one who does not desire it; it brings about the departure from the body and again birth in a womb.
And the paths of this inner self through thousands of millions of wombs.
The departure of the vital breaths is an internal severance;
that pain is unbearable,
as is birth within the womb.

Therein, various kinds of suffering arise from the non-emergence of the sense faculties, resulting in a state of darkness for the one dwelling in the womb; there is also the pain described by physicians caused by the mother’s food—whether excessively cold or hot, or deficient or excessive.

Furthermore, the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) has undergone migrations and wanderings through thousands of millions of wombs as animals, hungry ghosts, worms, insects, moths, dogs, and so forth.
But is it not the case that the inner self is held to be all-pervading and eternal?
For him who pervades the entire world, from where could there be departure, and where could there be entry into a womb?
Furthermore, birth within a womb is impossible for that which is eternal. To this it is replied:

There is the view of some that this person (puruṣa), the size of a thumb, resides within the body; consisting of the subtle elements, mind, intellect, and ego, he undergoes the states of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) as long as it lasts. And when his [subtle] qualities have been accumulated, the power of consciousness (caitanya-śakti) becomes manifest.
Therefore, the attributes of that [subtle body] are figuratively attributed to the inner self (antarātman).
Alternatively, when those vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth—which constitute its functional states—depart, it is said that "he departs."
In this same way, its arising should also be understood;
furthermore, we shall explain this again in the twelfth [chapter]. What need is there for more?
He understands the connection with suffering for embodied beings arising from unrighteousness,
as well as the inexhaustible union with happiness arising from righteousness and purpose.
From *adharma* arises production, which is birth;
union with suffering is the experience of affliction.
*Dharma* is the category whose characteristic has been described; from that comes union with inexhaustible happiness.
This also must be considered;
the intention is that the life of a wandering mendicant (pārivrājya) is the primary duty (dharma).
And by means of yoga, one should contemplate the subtlety of the Supreme Self,
as well as its manifestation within bodies, both high and low.
Yoga is the steadiness of the fluctuations of the mind, as demonstrated by Patañjali.
Through that, one should contemplate the subtlety of the Self, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).

One should not form the notion of "Self" with respect to the body and so forth, or the vital breaths and so forth; rather, the intent of this is that, by means of the excellence of knowledge born of yoga, one must understand [the Self] as distinct from all these internal and external principles.
However, conceptual constructions such as "gross" and so forth do not belong to the self.

Just as its rebirth occurs in the superior bodies of gods and others, and there is the enjoyment of fruits through presiding over the body even though it is omnipresent, so too is it with respect to inferior beings such as animals, pretas, and piśācas.
In the view that [the self] is one, the established position is that the individual knowers (kṣetrajña) are indeed the manifestations of the Supreme Self.
Therefore, it has been stated that one should contemplate the courses of the Supreme Self.
Even if adorned, one should practice the Dharma, devoted to whichever stage of life one finds pleasure in; being equal toward all beings, the external mark is not the cause of Dharma.
Adorned with ornaments such as flowers and bracelets,

he should diligently perform the duties prescribed for a wandering mendicant, such as the meditation upon the Self; he should practice whatever is ordained for whichever stage of life (*āśrama*) he occupies.
One should not consider oneself a yogi merely by wearing the external marks such as the triple staff;
rather, one should be equal toward all beings.
The essential meaning is that one must strive to avoid passion, hatred, and greed.
The permission for ornaments is not granted by the abandonment of gender signs.
Although the fruit of the *kataka* tree clarifies water,
the water does not become clear merely by uttering its name.
When turbid water has the fruit of the *kataka* tree placed within it, it becomes clear and attains a state of transparent purity;
however, that water does not become stainless merely by uttering the name of that fruit,
but rather depends upon its actual application.
Thus, the wearing of the *liṅga* is like the name of the fruit;

accomplishment does not come from that alone, as long as the practices such as delighting in solitude (*ekārāmatā*), meditative worship (*upāsana*), and equanimity toward all things (*sarvasamatā*) have not been performed.
This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) supplementary to what precedes.
For the sake of protecting living beings, whether by night or by day,
and even when his own body is in distress, he should always walk upon the earth after carefully inspecting it.
Regarding what was stated—that one should place [the foot] purified by sight—this is the verse demonstrating its purpose:

even upon the exhaustion of the body, that is, even when there is bodily suffering, whether by night or by day, one must not, without looking or seeing, allow the body to come into contact with a grass mat spread out for the purpose of lying down.
For this transgression, there is an expiation.
Alternatively, there are certain extremely minute small creatures that perish by the mere contact with the various parts of the body; it is for their sake that this [precept] exists.
Whatever living beings a mendicant unintentionally injures by day or by night,
for the sake of their purification he should perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) after bathing.
"Jantūn" should be understood as "small creatures.
The syntactical connection is: "for the sake of purifying that sin which arises from their injury."
Even three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) performed according to rule by a Brāhmaṇa,
joined with the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava, should be known as the highest austerity.
By the word "brāhmaṇa," he states that this is a rule pertaining to the dharma of the caste;
it is not a rule for the wandering mendicant alone, but applies to all three as well.

Beyond three [repetitions], there is an increase in the fruit; however, three must necessarily be performed—those which were mentioned in the passage beginning "The *vyāhṛtis* preceded by the syllable *oṃ*. Here, *praṇava* refers to the syllable *oṃ*.
Endowed with these,
one should meditate on this during the time of breath control (prāṇāyāma). These are of three kinds, known as kumbhaka, recaka, and pūraka.

In that state, by restraining the outward exit of both the primary and the nasal breaths, there arise the practices known as *kumbhaka* (retention) and *pūraka* (inhalation); through the continuous expulsion of air from without without inhaling, *recaka* (exhalation) occurs.
The limit for this is shown in the second chapter, or alternatively, it is reached when, through austerity (*tapas*), no pain arises within that duration of time.
Just as the impurities of metallic ores are burned away when they are being smelted,
so too are the defects of the senses burned away through the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa).
The elements are gold and so forth; when they are smelted, only the gold remains.
Likewise, when the sense organs perceive their objects, joy and distress arise; the burning away of the evil associated with those two occurs through the cessation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The arising of joy and distress is forbidden for one who seeks liberation.

However, that [distraction] arises even for an embodied being who has abandoned attachment and whose senses are restrained by the power of reality, when forms, sounds, and so forth are presented by chance;
therefore, breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is for the purpose of removing those defects.
One should burn away defects by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma), and sin by means of concentration (dhāraṇā);
one should burn away attachments by means of withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and non-divine qualities by means of meditation (dhyāna).

The phrase "by means of breath-restraints" (prāṇāyāmaiḥ) has been demonstrated by the preceding verse. Others, however, say: "defects" (doṣāḥ) refers to passion and so forth; one should burn them away.
How can these [impurities] be burnt away by breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*)?
It is logical that sin is burnt by them;
for its arising is characterized as being imperceptible according to the scriptures, and its cessation is likewise.
Passion and the like, however, are known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
It is therefore logical that their relationship as the abandoned and the abandoner should be known through direct perception and the like alone, not through scripture (*śāstra*).
If the scripture were to say, "One should cause that which has the nature of desisting to desist," what would its authority be?
Therefore, unwholesome conduct caused by passion and so forth is designated by the term "defilement" (*doṣa*).
Its "burning" (*dāha*) results from the burning away of its effects.
For, by their very nature and inherent character, actions perish due to their momentariness.
And this alone is "burning," not, as in other cases, the state of being reduced to ashes;
and thus it is a restatement of the meaning of the preceding verse,
[as well as] by means of the concentrations (dhāraṇās).

Now, [it might be argued]: "Kilbiṣa" is indeed sin (*pāpa*) and that very same thing is a fault (*doṣa*). In that case, one should have said simply, "one should burn away faults by means of breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and concentrations (*dhāraṇā*). What is the purpose of using the word "kilbiṣa"? Or, even if it were "kilbiṣa," what is the point of including the term "fault" (*doṣa*)?
It is said:
the mention of "fault" (doṣa) must necessarily be made so that it may be understood that the burning away of specific sins occurs through breath-control (prāṇāyāma), and not of everything.
For by the word "fault," passion and the like are meant.
Therefore, the metaphorical designation of "sin" (pāpa) for that very cause has been stated as above.
If that is so, then let that alone be done; what is the use of this word "kilbiṣam"?
There is no fault, as it is for the purpose of completing the meter.

In that regard, breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) are said to be the burners of evil that has already arisen, whereas the concentrations (dhāraṇā) prevent the arising of faults altogether. What, then, are these concentrations?
By means of tranquility (*śamatha*) and the other [aids], the mind—which is being drawn away by the desire to see sense objects—is restrained; it is fixed upon that very same object.
And those contemplations on the defects inherent in sense objects consist of [meditations] such as "the skeleton-pillar" and so forth.
The causes of desire seen in women—such as their radiance, charm, youth, physical form, and valor—are [the objects to be countered].
And those [objects] are to be grasped by perception accompanied by conceptual construction (*savikalpa-pratyakṣa*), while conceptual constructions are streams of the mental faculty (*manodhārā*).

Therefore, through other conceptual constructions—such as "space is filled with urine and excrement" regarding that state of perceiving defects inherent in the object; or "this so-called female substance is merely a collection of bones and rags"; or "that which living beings have desired since of old must be avoided at all costs"; or "this delusion of a mere fragment of pleasure is momentary, and its indulgence leads to terrible and long-lasting torments of Yama"—it is possible to suppress [the attachment].
This very thing is called its thorough discernment (*tat-prasaṃkhyāna*). In this same way, it should be cultivated regarding food and other things as well.

Whether it be these [delicacies] such as sugar, ghee-filled cakes, fresh butter, and milk-rice, or alms-food consisting of coarse grain and the like—since there is no difference in their function of merely sustaining the body—any distinction that might appear due to a particular nature [of the food], existing for only a moment or an instant upon the tip of the tongue, is a momentary appearance resembling a city of Gandharvas. Thus it should be contemplated.
Thus he teaches that the fault of contact (*sparśadoṣa*) is to be meditated upon in other cases as well.
Others, however, say:
*dhāraṇā* is the retention, through the power of practice, of the abdominal air moving through the mouth and nose within the space of the heart, which is a specific part of the body.
Now, one might ask: what is the distinction between these common [meditations] and the breath-controls (prāṇāyāma)?

The distinction is that *dhāraṇā* consists of fixing the mind as desired on the arms, forehead, or other locations, devoid of the meditation on the *vyāhṛtis* and so forth; whereas the breath-controls are characterized by exhalation (*recana*).
Others, however, consider that friendliness (*maitrī*), joy (*muditā*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are these *dhāraṇās*.
Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, established toward all living beings—
these concentrations quickly lead the meditator to the Brahma-world.
In this context, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the absence of hatred, but not affection for a friend, because the latter is of the nature of bondage.

Compassion (*kṛpā*, *karuṇā*) is a mental state (*cittadharma*); it is the desire to deliver a suffering person from their pain upon seeing them, thinking, "How might this person be raised up from this suffering?
It has been stated that it is not merely the non-commencement of non-violence and favoring others.
Therefore, this is said as follows: this mental quality must be practiced.

It is sympathetic joy (*muditā*), which is the turning away from sorrow—whether that sorrow arises from causes such as illness or from the fear of hell and so forth—and not mere exhilaration, because the latter is a cause of attachment (*rāga*).
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is well known [to apply] toward sense objects, toward those who benefit one, and toward those who cause harm.
Dhāraṇā is the immobility of the mind within the space of the heart through devotion to the contemplation of Brahman.
Pratyāhāra burns away *saṃsarga*, which is the association of the senses with their objects—that is, their engagement therein; this is what pratyāhāra destroys.
Then, one should either withdraw the sense faculties or create an obstruction for them.
When confronted with a wondrous form, such as a sight of a beautiful woman in a bangle or similar object, the eyes should be closed, or the gaze should be directed elsewhere;
the same applies to all the sense faculties.
And thus, the yogin’s concentration becomes unimpeded regarding the qualities that are not the Lord— namely,
the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
And they [the qualities] are not independent; they are dependent on another, their forms being subject to consciousness.

For the Puruṣa—who is inactive, devoid of pleasure and so forth, and free from attributes—the conceit "I am happy," "I am miserable" arises. This conceit, which consists in identifying with the qualities despite being devoid of them, must be burned away by meditation on the discrimination between the qualities and the Puruṣa.
One must effect the discrimination between the qualities and the Puruṣa thus: "The Puruṣa is of the nature of consciousness and devoid of qualities; Prakṛti consists of the qualities."
How is that to be performed? And what, moreover, is to be meditated upon through meditation? To this he says:
Among beings, high and low, it is difficult to be known by those of unrefined self.
Through the yoga of meditation, one should perceive the destiny of this inner self.
The inner self is the inner controller (antaryāmī) Puruṣa; its course, that is, its true nature, must be understood as it really is.

The conceit of pleasure and pain is not restricted to human birth alone; rather, the notion of "I" and "mine" regarding various high and low beings—such as animals, pretas, piśācas, and so forth—is produced by ignorance and must be removed.

Or rather, how is it that this all-pervading one—who is greater than the intermediate space, greater than heaven, and greater than these worlds; who possesses all desires, all tastes, all smells, and all touches—yet, while practicing this [meditation], remains free from hunger and thirst even amidst such pleasure and pain of the body, because the body does not experience all enjoyments within its various forms? "Who am I? he asks. "Oh, the majesty of karma! That this one, who is the self of all and independent, is made dependent by karmas. I shall no longer perform these [actions] which stand in the place of a wicked master; like a hired servant, I shall merely carry out my duties."

Just as a certain hired laborer, having entered service to please his master out of necessity, might think: "As long as he is difficult to approach, prone to punishment, intent on threats, and harsh in speech, I will not serve him further; I shall merely repay what I have received from him, such as wages and so forth, by performing this work"—thus he should remain reflecting.
He should contemplate: "I shall reach the end of the fruits of the deeds already committed by experiencing them, and I shall not perform others," and so forth.

Likewise, one should meditate after having ascertained— through the study of the Vedānta and other means— that these individual souls (kṣetrajñas) are manifestations of the Supreme Self (paramātman) and not independent entities, for there exists nothing whatsoever other than the Supreme Self.
Others, however, say that "dhyānayoga" refers to both meditation (dhyāna) and yoga.
Therefore, one should perceive the course of the inner self; having examined it, one should remain seated, perceiving its course through meditation (*dhyāna*) and yoga.

Alternatively, yoga is for the sake of meditation—that is, having achieved steadiness of mind, one should perceive the course of the self. Through acts of worship, one should bring face-to-face that stainless form described in the Vedāntas, which is distinguished by qualities such as being undecaying and immortal.
It cannot be known by those whose selves are unrefined—that is, not prepared by the scriptures.
One endowed with right vision is not bound by actions;
however, one devoid of such vision enters into the cycle of transmigration.
He states the result of the immediately preceding injunction:
"Right vision" (samyagdarśana) is the knowledge of the self as it truly is, just described; one who is "endowed with that" has achieved direct realization. Such a person is "not bound by actions."
He does not follow the cycle of existence because of the exhaustion of performed actions through their fruition and because of the non-performance of others;
however, by this it is not said that liberation results from knowledge alone.
He who is devoid of the internal vision taught in the Vedānta and performs only ritual action goes to the cycle of rebirth.
Through non-violence, detachment of the senses, Vedic rituals, and the practice of severe austerities, they attain that state in this world.
However, these two verses serve as evidence that liberation results from the combination of knowledge and action:
by the former, knowledge was stated;
by this [latter], actions are now stated.
Which, then, are those Vedic rites whose fruit is the attainment of that state? It is said:
first, there are those rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), the fruits of which—such as heaven and so forth—are explicitly heard within their own injunctive statements (*vidhi-vākya*).
To postulate any other fruit besides those would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the principle.
Alternatively, resorting to a mixed result would be purposeless;

and since the meaning of the sentence is completed by that much, how could it be connected with a result characterized by the attainment of that [heavenly world] which is not required by the injunction? When the purpose of the injunction is fulfilled through a directly stated and syntactically connected element, the injunction does not require anything else.
To this it is replied:
there is indeed another sentence on this point, namely "by sacrifice he attains that," which occurs in the section concerning secret rites (*rahasya*).
Consequently, due to the principle of the distinctness of connection (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), two separate results are appropriate.

Consequently, for all optional (kāmya) rites, there will be no contradiction in their being connected with uninterrupted fruits and their having the attainment of the supreme state as their purpose. In that regard, through two sacrifices performed as distinct applications, both heaven and liberation (apavarga) come to pass.
Furthermore, no specific sacrifice is heard of here [in the text] by which this fruit would belong to the obligatory (nitya) rites rather than the optional ones.

Now, it might be argued: "Because the delimitation of the fruit is not heard of in the case of the obligatory rites (*nitya*), there is no contradiction [in their being included], and thus it is logical that they are the subject matter [of the statement]; this is not the case for the optional rites (*kāmya*).
For by that much alone, the phrase 'by that sacrifice' (*tāvataiva yajñena*) attains a universal scope. If this is said:
What is the use here of hearing about a fruit?
Vedic sentences culminate in an injunction to act (*kartavyatā*),
and that injunction is understood through words such as "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*) even without a Vedic word for a fruit.
Even there, a connection with a fruit is certainly not required; if one were to assume such a connection, it would be redundant and thus fail to achieve its singular purpose.
Therefore, the statement "by sacrifice" (yajñena), finding no other basis, refers to the distinct domain of everything denoted by the word "sacrifice"—both the obligatory and the optional.
And this fruit does not belong to those actions performed out of desire, because it is not heard [in scripture] that one "desires liberation" (*apavargakāma*).
It was with this very intention that it was said: "Being of the nature of desire is not praised.
And in the *Mahābhārata* as well: "Let not the fruit of action be your motive; let there be no attachment to inaction for you."

Therefore, for one whose internal organ is enveloped by the grasping of difference, who possesses craving and ignorance, and who is not liberated from the notions of "I" and "mine," there is the attainment of a limited fruit intended [by such action].

But for the other, because he is impelled toward a specific fruit without intending it, and acts with the understanding that "this must be done," there is the attainment of Brahman, which consists of immeasurable and unsurpassed bliss.

Nor should this be questioned: that since it is impossible to perform all the sacrifices—whether they be one hundred and seven or however many there may be—the teaching would result in non-commencement.
Since the perfection of performance here is achieved through the perfection of vision alone,
it is for this very reason that it is said, "endowed with right vision.
And all ritual sacrifices (kratavaḥ) are to be accomplished by means of vision.
And so it has been said: "Other Brahmins worship by means of knowledge alone.
Alternatively, the phrase "to whatever worlds one goes" is a restrictive specification, as in [the injunctions] "one desiring heaven" or "one desiring a son.

Those whose inner selves are permeated by the grasping of distinctions such as past and beginningless [time], proceed toward the primary human goal through mere untruth, out of greed for visible results.

Some say that just as a child is induced to take medicine for the sake of nourishment by the false promise that "your crest-lock will grow," so too [is one induced by the false prospect of rebirth]. Another opinion holds that "eternal" here refers to ritual actions (*karma*).
If those [obligatory duties] are not performed, they act as obstacles by being causes of transgression;
therefore, when they are performed, there being no obstacle, it is said that [liberation is attained] "by means of Vedic rites alone.
Even though these rites are not enjoined for the purpose of liberation, [they nevertheless contribute to it].
By means of those extremely fierce causes of bodily torment,
he [attains] the station, the place, the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka).
They accomplish and appropriate it;
or rather, they attain that state of his which is his prerogative—namely, universal sovereignty and autonomy—which is to say, they attain his very form.
It has bones for its pillars, is bound together by tendons, plastered with flesh and blood,
covered with skin, foul-smelling, and filled with urine and excrement.
This is for the purpose of generating dispassion:
let alone the bodies of worms, insects, moths, and the like, or those born from water, mud, and sweat;
even this human body, which is intended as something desirable, is like a small hut of urine and excrement, for humans are constantly afraid of it, fearing its fall.
Now he describes it by means of the small hut:
the bones are like pillars; it is supported by them.
It is bound together by sinews;
it is smeared and plastered over with flesh and blood;
and it is covered on the outside by the skin of the body.
Alternatively, it is covered above that [surface];
it is full of urine and feces.
The genitive case is used here as in the expression "full of rice" (*odanasya pūrṇa*).
One should abandon this abode of the elements, which is possessed by old age and grief, a dwelling place for disease, afflicted, full of passion, and impermanent.
Old age is a particular state [of existence] that causes the deterioration of the body in the final stage of life;
it is afflicted, constantly seized by diseases;
it is full of passion, longing for all objects, and when these are not attained, there is great suffering which, even if endured, is without remedy and irreversible.
Therefore, having reflected on this, one should abandon this body.

It is the dwelling place of the elements—the modifications of the primary matter consisting of fat, marrow, phlegm, urine, semen, and blood—for they dwell here; it is not the dwelling of the Self, because the Self is omnipresent.
Therefore, no craving for the body should be formed.
Just as a tree leaves the riverbank, or as a bird leaves a tree,
so too, by casting off this body, one is liberated from the crocodile of suffering.
Regarding this body, which is like a small hut, its analogies are the riverbank and the tree.
It should not be abandoned by one's own will through such means as entering fire; rather, no craving for it should be formed.
Its eventual collapse will occur spontaneously through the exhaustion of karma, just like that of a tree standing on a riverbank.
Regarding what was said— that one should not rejoice in death—

for one who has attained the light (*jyotis*), has mastered the movement of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and has restrained the mind from the transformations of delusion, he should effect his departure beforehand,
just as a bird leaves a tree.
It is like a crocodile; it is called a "grasper" because it shares the common characteristic of being a cause of suffering.
Thus it is said: even for that which was obtained with great difficulty, as long as the body exists, suffering inevitably arises through the power of the object itself.
This is stated in reference to the aforementioned misconception.
Having relinquished both good deeds toward those dear to oneself and evil deeds toward those who are disliked through the practice of meditative concentration, one attains the eternal Brahman.

The agitation of the mind caused by joy and distress, characterized by elation, grief, and so forth, should be avoided by this means: one should reflect and cultivate within the mind through the practice of meditation that "whatever someone does that is pleasing is distinguished as the result of my own past merit; this agent does not act kindly toward me out of affection, nor is he able to inflict upon me the harm of enmity or painful wrongdoing. By reflecting in this way, neither attachment toward the one who acts kindly nor aversion toward the one who acts unkindly arises in him.

Acting in this way, one approaches—that is, attains face-to-face—the eternal and perpetual Brahman; one is not obstructed by the path beginning with light (*arcis*). From the inclusion of the term "perpetual," non-return is understood.
When one becomes free from longing for all things through one's state of being,
then one attains eternal happiness both in this world and after death.

This is an instruction regarding the nature of the mind (*cittadharma*). Desirelessness (*niḥspṛhatva*) does not consist in the abandonment of the objects of desire, but rather in the relinquishing of their cause. "State" (*bhāva*) refers to a mental quality or a characteristic of the self (*ātman*) defined by longing.

Regarding "in all things" (*sarvabhāveṣu*): the second word, *bhāva*, signifies "objects. By the inclusion of the term "all," attachment even to those things necessary for the maintenance of the body—such as food and drink—is prohibited; however, desire itself is not [prohibited].
For his hunger and thirst are indeed destined to arise from the inherent power of things;
moreover, desire (*icchā*) is distinct from longing (*spṛhā*),
for longing is that which is connected with passion (*rāga*) and has dejection as its cause.
Desire, however, regarding food and so forth, arises spontaneously immediately after the digestion of the food and drink that has been consumed.
By this method, having gradually abandoned all attachments,
one who is completely liberated from all dualities abides in Brahman alone.
"Having abandoned all attachments":
attachment (*saṅga*) is the notion "this is mine" regarding cows, horses, elephants, gold, slaves, wives, fields, dwellings, and so forth;
it is through the abandonment of that, and by embracing the state of delighting in solitude.

Having first resorted to this as the primary means, and then by means of this aforementioned method through the performance of the external and internal collection of rites, one abides in Brahman, whose nature is consciousness.
Actions do not bind him;
he becomes liberated from all dualities consisting of the results of auspicious and inauspicious actions, namely pleasure and pain.
All this that has been described here is indeed meditative;
for no one who is not a knower of the inner self ever enjoys the fruit of ritual action.
When meditation exists, that which pertains to meditation comes to be;
it is obtained when meditation is practiced.
What is that?
That which has just been declared— that is, spoken of directly, but not established as the primary purport—
is the presentation of good and evil deeds as the causes of the pleasant and the unpleasant for those two [the doer and the experiencer].
A person's state of being an agent of what is unpleasant is like the cause of pain in a fever, or like the burning power of fire when approached incautiously.

Just as one who has been burned by fire does not hate the fire, so too should one regard even a person who acts unkindly; one should not seek to prevent them. And this occurs when there is meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the mind is one-pointed.
This should be practiced with the heart at all times:
that these two, pleasure and pain, are the fruit of karma.
The king is not the giver of happiness, such as a village or other possessions; rather, the acquisition of these upon my first approach is due to my own exertion.
It is previously performed meritorious karma that is the giver, not the king.
Likewise, it is not the king who causes me distress through punishment; it is my own actions that distress me, not the king, nor is anyone else capable of doing so.
This must always be meditated upon and reflected upon;
even that which was taught for the sake of generating detachment from cyclic existence—such as the "skeleton-pillar" and so forth—that too must be cultivated constantly.
For one who does not know the inner self [cannot achieve this].
In this context, "the internal mind" is what is being spoken of.
He who does not understand what has been thus declared, does not ascertain it, and does not cultivate it through practice,
does not partake in the fruit of action.
The practice of a wandering mendicant—such as the act of begging for alms and staying for only one night in a village—and so forth, does not attain that fruit called liberation.

This is the meaning: [liberation is not attained] as long as a state of desirelessness toward everything has not arisen through the very cultivation of [the contemplation of] the skeleton-pillar and so on, and as long as the abandonment of passion and hatred has not been achieved by relinquishing the fruits of actions.
And that [liberation] occurs only when the mind is thus constantly purified; it does not happen spontaneously.
Alternatively, the phrase "he remains established in Brahman alone" is a reference to that which has been designated as such;
this abiding in Brahman is achieved through meditation (*dhyānika*), and is not obtainable merely by the performance of ritual actions.
To the question "What is that object of meditation?", he says: "For one who does not know the inner self (*anadhyātmavid*)."

That treatise which deals with the self, such as the Vedānta and so forth, is "adhyātma"; it does not mean the Veda itself. Alternatively, that which is established regarding the self is "adhyātma," such as: this self is distinct from the body, senses, mind, intellect, vital breath, and so on; it does not perish when these perish; it is the agent of actions and the enjoyer of their fruits—all of this occurs for one who is drawn by the perception of duality.
But when this [self] is one whose impurities are destroyed, it is untouched by defects or by effects; because of its unity, this very self is all this, and there exists nothing else distinct from it.
Difference is merely a manifestation of light.

He who does not know the Upaniṣads concerning the color of Hari, the water, and so forth, and who does not produce firmness through meditation with one-pointed and continuous intelligence, does not obtain the fruit of action as described.
Therefore, the meaning of the verse is that the Self, whose nature is declared in the Vedānta, should be meditated upon constantly, except for the time spent on eating and recreation.

Alternatively, although the context concerns those who have gone forth (pravrajita), there is nevertheless a mention of the householder as well, by virtue of his partaking in the fruits of ritual action, provided that action is predominant.
Therefore, this is what is meant:

even if householders perform rituals such as the Agnihotra, yet they do not know the secret sciences (*rahasyavidyā*)—namely, those sciences embedded within the rituals, such as the *udgītha* or whatever else follows the *udgītha*, as stated in passages like "those skilled in the section on rituals"—nevertheless, they do not obtain from that a full fruit which persists for a long time.
This meaning is demonstrated in two scriptural passages, the Vājasaneyaka and the Chāndogya:

"O Gārgī, he who performs sacrifices, offers oblations, and practices austerities without knowing this Imperishable (akṣara), even for many thousands of years, that [action] becomes merely finite"; likewise, it is stated in the Chāndogya: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the Upaniṣadic insight—that alone becomes more powerful.
Thus, the excellence of the fruit belongs only to him who acts after having known the aforementioned knowledge taught regarding the self (adhyātma).

And this has been stated: "Those who know thus, and those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity"—the Śruti declares that for these performers of action who possess such knowledge, there is attainment of the world of Brahman by way of the path beginning with light (*arcis*).

Thus, since meditation on the object of contemplation for the sake of self-knowledge has been prescribed, the recitation of the Vedas was not previously established as its means; therefore, he now prescribes it:

"One should constantly recite the Brahman pertaining to the sacrifice (adhiyajña), that which pertains to the deities (ādhidaivika), that which pertains to the self (ādhyātmika), and that which is declared in the Vedānta."

Only the recitation (*japa*) of this is permitted for him, and not the study for the sake of practice as is the case for householders and others. Regarding sacrifices (*yajña*), "pertaining to sacrifice" (*adhiyajña*) refers to the Brāhmaṇa portion that prescribes them.
"Pertaining to the divine" (*ādhidaivika*) refers to that which pertains to the gods (*adhidaiva*), namely the mantras that reveal the deities.
The distinction among those very [Vedic texts] is that they are "internal" (ādhyātmika),
as in "I was Manu, I was with the Rudras," and so forth.
Furthermore, that which is stated in the Vedānta also demonstrates the combination of ritual action and knowledge for the sake of attaining Brahmanhood.
This is the refuge for the ignorant; this indeed is for those who possess knowledge;
this is for those seeking heaven; this is for those seeking the infinite.
He designates that which is called the Veda as "this," and that too is indeed Brahman;
and so it has been said:
"Two Brahmans are to be known: the Brahman of Sound (śabdabrahman) and that which is the Supreme (paraṃ brahma).
One who is proficient in the Brahman of Sound attains the Supreme Brahman. Here, "study" refers to knowledge, and "proficiency" results from the practice of its meaning.
This is an explanatory supplement (arthavāda) to the preceding injunction;
it concerns those who are ignorant and do not understand its meaning, who are nonetheless entitled to recitation (japa) and other such practices.
Accordingly, the venerable Vyāsa has demonstrated that spiritual perfection (siddhi) is attained by those who perform recitation.

Alternatively, for those who are ignorant— those who do not know the self and have not understood the reality of the self through the scriptures, yet are devoted to its meditation but have not attained stability of mind— the Veda is their refuge; for by means of recitation (*japa*), the performance of rituals, and that much knowledge, they do not fall into hells or births as insects, moths, and the like.
This is precisely what those who understand [should know].
But how is this a refuge for the wise? To this he says: "For those seeking this heaven."
Thus, for those who know only the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) and have not attained mental stability in the Self, the fruit of heaven and so forth is obtained through the performance of rituals.

Others, however, having abandoned attachment and whose defects such as passion have been destroyed, are devoted to the meditation on the reality of the Self through knowledge; for them, there is infinity, which is non-return [to saṃsāra].
The meaning is that for all of them, the Veda alone is the refuge; there is no other path.
The twice-born man who wanders forth as a mendicant by means of this sequential method shakes off all evil in this world and attains the supreme Brahman.
"Gradually" means the performance of yoga.
The meaning is: having discharged the debts by means of that sequence which was stated regarding the combination of self-knowledge and ritual action (*karma*), [one should proceed].
