"Having shaken off evil, like a horse shakes off the dust from its hair," in the same way, by means of the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*).
As it has been said: "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, so evil action does not cling to one who knows this.
He attains the Supreme Brahman;
he becomes of that very nature, with the grasping of duality ceased. This is the injunction regarding the fruit of knowledge and the stages of life (āśrama).
This dharma has been taught to you for ascetics of restrained self who have renounced the Vedas; now learn the yoga of action.
The renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) of the Veda means its abandonment; those who possess this are called *vedasaṃnyāsikas*.
By the word "Veda," the abandonment of ritual acts such as sacrifices and oblations is intended, but not the abandonment of recitation (*japa*).
However, reflection on the Self (*ātmacintana*) is indeed enjoined.
Only those activities such as pilgrimages and fasts that are accomplished solely through wealth or through bodily affliction are prohibited;
however, there is no prohibition against those rites such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) and recitations (*japa*), which are accomplished by means of the self alone.
We shall demonstrate this very point in its proper place.
By the first half [of the verse], there is the conclusion of the stage of renunciation (pravrajyā-āśrama);
by the latter, there is the promise to teach the duties of one who has renounced the Vedas (veda-saṃnyāsika).
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—
these four distinct stages of life originate from the householder.
All these, when practiced in due order according to the scriptures,
lead a Brahmin who acts as prescribed to the supreme goal.
But surely, given the promise "I shall declare the duties of the renunciant," the enumeration of the stages of life (āśramas) is irrelevant to the subject at hand.
Some say this is not so; it is intended to show that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is not a separate stage of life, but is included within these very ones.
And in which [stage] is it included?
He is included within the householder,
for he indeed dwells in a house;
others, however, include him among those who have gone forth (pravrajyā), because of the commonality of having abandoned attachments.

Therefore, there is no purpose in its inclusion [among the stages of life], for one will not be qualified for sacrifices and the like by means of the duties of a person (*puruṣadharma*) or the duties of an ascetic (*yatidharma*), since these are prescribed by specific words [in the texts]. If it is argued that this is because he lacks a stage of life (*anāśramitva*), and that there would be the contingency of penance according to the rule "one who remains without a stage of life for a year [must perform penance]," we reply: since this very regulation is known through the scriptural statement itself, how can there be any application of penance? Therefore, the mention of other stages of life is intended to praise the renunciant (*saṃnyāsika*) by way of comparison with the householder and others.
And this is in order to strengthen the collective sense;
the meaning is that these [stages] have their basis in householders.
The analysis of the compound is: "the householder is the source (*prabhava*), the cause of their subsistence."
And among all these, according to the injunctions of Vedic revelation,
the householder is said to be the best, for he indeed supports these other three.
This is improper:
by the scriptural revelation of the Vedic treatises, the establishment of the householder stage is affirmed, as is the obligation to support the others;
yet the existence of the other stages of life follows precisely from the direct scriptural injunction for the householder stage.
Direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*) is more powerful than proximate Smṛti texts on austerity.
Now, it might be argued that this connection is not made because it is not enjoined by Vedic revelation;
however, this is indeed the connection.

Even though this injunction exists, the superiority of the householder for the purpose of supporting those [others] is established by the statement "he [should support] these three"; however, it must be explained how this is so, given that the other stages of life (*āśrama*) are also based on *śruti*—for if they were based on *śruti*, this *smṛti* would clearly be contradicted by the direct injunction of the householder stage, and so forth—and furthermore, no other possible connection [between the householder and the others] is feasible.

Now, if it be argued that all [stages] are indeed prescribed by the scriptures, with reference to the *Jābāla-śruti* which states, "Having become a householder, one should become a forest-dweller; having become a forest-dweller, one should renounce," then the contradiction with the *smṛtis* remains entirely unresolved.
Furthermore, this *śruti* is not prescriptive;

for it is not heard there that "one must dwell thus in the forest" or "these specific rites are to be performed by the forest-dweller alone, and these by the renunciant," in the same way that every rite of the householder—from the initial *ādhāna* sacrifice up to the final *iṣṭi*—is explicitly stated. Such is not the case regarding the other stages of life (*āśramas*).

It is heard that he was merely a name, having been a householder, and so forth. Therefore, the state of being a householder is taught as the root of the stages of life (āśrama), which is contradictory from beginning to end.
To this, it is replied:

It is true that from the time of the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) onwards, household duties are explicitly heard in the Śruti for one who has taken a wife. In that regard, since the purpose (*prayukti*) must be determined, which rite is enjoined by the Śrutis?

Is it the entitlement to the *svāhā* [offerings] through the *agnihotra* and other rites as heard in the Śruti; or rather, by the injunction for the procreation of offspring; or else, by a visible human purpose?
But surely, passion impels one toward a woman in general, not specifically toward marriage;
for there is a logical principle that "that without which something cannot be accomplished is the motivator of that thing.
And for those possessed by passion, the performance of domestic rites is accomplished by means of a woman in general.
Why, then, would they require marriage?
True;
this would be so if, in another scriptural statement, intercourse with any woman whatsoever were forbidden.
Even when the acquisition of the Vedas is equal for all, the distinction between what is permissible and what is forbidden is understood through the scriptures;
therefore, since those of a steadfast nature cannot achieve their own welfare without marriage, it is indeed appropriate to suspect that the Veda is the motivating factor.
If this is so, then there are no motivating factors for everyone.
Since the cessation of [all] purposes occurs for everyone when that [truth] exists, what is the use of defining it?
Let that which serves as the motivator for marriage be so.

But how can the other stages of life (āśramas) be justified when the householder stage is established by direct injunction? Furthermore, in what respect does this inquiry into the motivation for marriage fall within the scope of the present topic?
It is said:
"It is true that it has been stated that the purpose of all is accomplished.
This is true.

When the assistance [of one thing] for another is accomplished through the application of the former, there is no need to postulate a separate application [for the latter], as it follows by implication (*prasaṅga*).
For example, rice grains, being applied for the purpose of human life—namely, sustenance—are employed in ritual acts;
however, the acquisition of wealth is not applied for the sake of the ritual act itself.

Or, just as knowledge is not employed even when one possesses the status of a Vaidya (one learned in the Vedas), because that [status] is already established by the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*),

so too here, since activity is established through desire (*kāma*), the scriptural injunctions regarding ritual action (*karma-śruti*) need not be applied. Therefore, the injunctions for obligatory rites will apply even to one who has not yet married.
And therefore, one who has somehow become matured in his impurities (*kaṣāya*) while still in the stage of studenthood (*brahmacarya*) does not desire [to marry].
Consequently, because of the absence of a second [partner], he will not be eligible [for ritual action].
And thus, due to the lack of eligibility for the Vedic rites (*śrauta*), such a person would fall into another stage of life (*āśrama*).
Others think:

"This marriage is not like a transaction involving wealth; for while life is impossible without wealth—since one indeed lives by means of wealth—it is not the case that there is an absence of life without a woman. Therefore, since no visible purpose for a self-restrained person is possible [in this case], marriage is undertaken even for the sake of eligibility for religious duty (*dharma*)."
This must necessarily be understood in this way: that an effort must be made for the purpose of generating the qualification [for ritual action].

Otherwise, since one who has performed an emission (utsarga) is impure, if the qualification were removed, then even one who performs the purification at the proper time following birth and so forth would not be guilty of transgressing the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*).
And if that were the case, for what purpose would one undergo the hardship of purification after death and other such events?
If it is argued that even this [effort] is indeed enjoined, then there is only the transgression of that much, and not of a thousand injunctions.

Now, if it should be asked: "Of which injunction is this the operation, such that it teaches that a person must exert effort so as to become qualified for the sake of accomplishing qualification?"—the answer is:

the injunctions regarding the Agnihotra and so forth, whose traditional scripture (āmnāya) he possesses, lead him to understand the duty (*kartavyatā*) pertaining to those [rites]; they do not, however, enjoin the production of the sacred fires (*agni*).
The sacred fires (*agni*) are also studied by one who proceeds with the desire for the rites performed for specific wishes (*kāmya*), in order to establish his qualification for them;
for when those [fires] have been produced, there are scriptural injunctions regarding lifelong maintenance for one who has established the fires (*āhitāgni*).
Furthermore, only one who possesses a wife is qualified for the establishment of the fires (*ādheya*).
Just as one establishes the sacred fires (*agnīn ādhatte*) in order to make oneself eligible (*adhikārin*), so too does one marry a wife.
Therefore, no purpose for any injunction is established if eligibility for the *agnihotra* and other rites is not to be produced.

Nor does the injunction for marriage itself convey that it must be performed for its own sake, because—like the scriptural texts on the obligatory *agnihotra* and so forth—it is a sacramental rite (*saṃskārakarma*) and lacks any mention of an [independent] entitlement (*adhikāra*).
On this point, the predecessors say:
there is a scriptural text concerning the discharge of the three debts, beginning with, "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is indeed born burdened with three debts," and so forth.
This scriptural text refers to the state of being bound from the very moment of birth.
And here, the second birth known as the *upanayana* (initiation) is not intended, because prior to that, one possesses the same status as animals.
That very period of time during which the comprehension of one's entitlement (*adhikāra*) occurs once birth has taken place is what is grasped by the scriptural statement regarding the debt (*ṛṇa*).

Consequently, for a learned man who possesses the entitlement, if he should seek a maiden in marriage and not obtain her, his entitlement to the forest-dweller’s stage (*vānaprastha*) and so forth arises only when he is completely grey-haired.

For he determines this: that a maiden indeed solicits [the rite] at the very time of youth; others say—explaining the meaning of the Vedic text—that the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is prescribed only for one with black hair, and that it should not be performed by one who is entirely grey-haired, except in the event of his wife's death.
Because of his connection with ritual action, the householder is the best;
thus, the superiority of that very stage of life (*āśrama*) is what is being stated.
"Regarding these three":
this is another reason for its preeminence, namely that it supports the other stages of life (āśramas).
This has been stated [in the verse]: "by means of knowledge and by means of food."
This very point is confirmed by means of an illustration:
Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean,
even so do all those in the [other] stages of life find their resting place in the householder.

The rivers are the Gaṅgā and others; the streams are the Bhidya and others. The distinction in the designation of "river" and "stream" is due to a certain difference in the configuration of their channels and a difference in their flow.
The prescription of singularity, however, is by way of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). The difference in gender is like that between the words *bhāryā* and *dāra*.
"Abiding" (*saṃsthiti*) means the substratum (*āśraya*).
Just as the ocean is the locus of all waters, so the householder has authority over all dharmas.
Moreover, by these four classes of twice-born men belonging to the various stages of life,
the tenfold dharma must always be practiced with diligent effort.
This verse is intended as an introduction to what is about to be explained.
The term *daśalakṣaṇa* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has ten characteristics.
Here, *lakṣaṇa* refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*).
It is to be served at all times and practiced;

these are mentioned again for the sake of emphasizing their preeminence among those already stated. Furthermore, by this repetition, the position that there is a synthesis of knowledge and action is reinforced.
Fortitude, forgiveness, self-restraint, non-stealing, purity, control of the senses, wisdom, learning, truthfulness, and freedom from anger— this is the tenfold characteristic of dharma.
Fortitude and the others are qualities of the self.
Among them, fortitude (dhṛti) is the reliance on one's inner being when wealth and such are exhausted;
if they have perished, what of it?
"It is possible to acquire [merit]"—
thus, when there is separation from the beloved and so forth, one steadies the agitated mind as before, reflecting that "the course of saṃsāra is like this.
Patience (*kṣamā*) is the endurance of offenses.
The absence of any impulse toward provocation when someone has committed an offense is self-restraint (*dama*). This consists of the abandonment of arrogance born of learning and the like.
Non-stealing (*asteya*) is well known.
Purity (*śauca*) is the cleanliness of food and so forth. Restraint of the senses (*indriyasaṃyama*) is non-attachment toward objects that are not forbidden.
Intellect (*dhī*) is right knowledge, which consists in the removal of opposing views, doubt, and the like.
*Vidyā* is knowledge of the self (*ātman*).
There is a distinction between *dhī* and *vidyā* based on the division between knowledge of ritual action (*karma*) and knowledge of the inner self (*adhyātma*).
To avoid this tautology, some read it as *dhīvidyā*.
That is not correct, because a distinction has been shown.
"Other" is well-known.
Non-anger is the non-arising of that which would otherwise arise.
Forgiveness is the refraining from inflicting harm even when harm has been committed against one.
Those brahmins who thoroughly study the ten characteristics of dharma,
and having studied them, live in accordance with them, go to the supreme goal.
This is a statement of the fruit of the preceding injunction;
the mention of the fruit resulting from study is intended to encourage the performance of the injunction.
Practicing the Dharma characterized by the ten marks and remaining composed,
a twice-born man, having heard the Vedānta according to the injunctions, should renounce his worldly life free from debt.
"One should renounce while free from debt.
This means that renunciation occurs only when the three debts have been discharged;
one is not entitled to the life of a wandering mendicant at any other time.
The same applies to renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*):
one must study the Vedāntas according to the prescribed rule;
for one who has not understood the meaning of the Vedāntas, there is no renunciation.

Although knowledge of the Vedānta, like the ritual scriptures, is implied by the performance of the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*)—since there is no difference in their being denoted by the term *svādhyāya*—nevertheless, the Vedāntas are mentioned again for a specific purpose: one must be intent upon them. Now, what is the meaning of the scriptural injunction, "Then he should renounce"?
What is this so-called renunciation?
It is the relinquishing of the sense of possession, such as "this is mine.
But has it not already been stated that they are "those who have renounced the Vedas"?

In this regard, what is understood here is the renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) of the Veda or the meaning of the Veda, and not the renunciation of those acts such as receiving gifts which are for the sake of accomplishing Vedic rituals.
This is because [the scripture] says "for those desiring this infinity," since study is prescribed even when knowledge is the primary aim.

As for the *agnihotra* and other rites, however, because they are accomplished by means of material substances, their abandonment occurs simply through the absence of the sense of "mine-ness" (*mamakāra*).
And this practice of taking up the sacred fires (*dharmāpādaka*) applies to one whose wife has died, who has reached the end [of his life], or who has made provision for another;
for it is recited in the *Vājasaneyaka*: "When he thinks he is about to depart, then he says to his son," and so forth.
Furthermore, the consigning of the fires (*agnisamāropaṇa*) is prescribed at that time, and they declare: "By old age, indeed, he is released from this [body] when it is no longer fresh."

Furthermore, regarding those rites that cannot be accomplished by material substances—such as the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and the obligatory fire-sacrifices (*nityāgnihotra*)—since these are not prohibited, one has the entitlement to perform them until the very last breath.
Having renounced all actions and cast off the defects of action,
he should dwell happily in the sovereignty of his sons, self-restrained and practicing the Veda.
"Let him study the Veda"—this expresses the non-abandonment of the Veda;
this has already been demonstrated.
Alternatively, there is a reading ending in the present participle suffix *śatṛ*: "studying."
One should dwell happily in the sovereignty of one's sons.
The mention of "sons" refers to a son who has been born;
however, they say that even for another person in his place, such as a citizen or similar official, the entrustment of the household to him is likewise appropriate.
Having thus renounced actions, intent upon his own duty and free from longing,
he destroys sin through such renunciation and attains the supreme goal.
One for whom his own duty—namely, the supreme worship of the Self—is the primary concern is "one whose supreme concern is his own duty" (*svakāryaparamaḥ*).
Being free from longing (*aspṛhaḥ*), he should not entertain desire for anything whatsoever, even in his mind.
This fourfold dharma of the Brahmin has been declared to you; it is meritorious and yields imperishable fruit after death. Now learn the dharma of kings.
The Dharma is fourfold, consisting of the four stages of life (āśrama);
all of this is prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa.
But surely, since the term "twice-born" (dvija) was heard at the outset in the passage, "Having thus remained in the householder stage, the twice-born graduate (snātaka)..."?
And because no contradiction has yet arisen [regarding that], the desire of the three castes is certain;
therefore, it is proper that this mention of "Brāhmaṇas" is intended solely to indicate the three castes.
This would not be the case if there were not a single syntactical unity between the opening and the conclusion.
But when there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), the meaning of the opening statement can be understood as being more powerful;
the meaning determined by a thorough consideration of the entire sentence is what is ascertained.
Therefore, the mention of "twice-born" (*dvija*) must be restricted to the Brahmin.
A Brāhmaṇa possesses the status of being twice-born (*dvijāti*), but not all who are twice-born possess Brāhmaṇahood.

Furthermore, since the primary meaning of the word *dvija* is applicable here, it is not proper to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for something that is not connected [to the primary sense].

Likewise, in the Mahābhārata, the three stages of life (*āśrama*) are heard of even for a Śūdra; having begun with the statement, "For one who has fulfilled his duty through service," the stages of life are prescribed for all, excluding only the meatless [stage].
The meaning is "the life of a wandering mendicant.
It does not mean that he should not perform any of the stages of life (*āśrama*) at all.
Rather, by means of service and the procreation of offspring, he obtains the fruit of all the stages of life.

By serving the twice-born while living the life of a householder, one obtains the fruit of all the stages of life (āśramas), with the exception of liberation, which is the fruit of the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka).
Therefore, it is established that the system of the four stages of life is indeed a duty of the Brāhmaṇa alone.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Thus ends the sixth chapter of the Commentary on Manu, composed by Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi, son of Bhaṭṭa Vīrasvāmin.
Now begins the seventh chapter: I shall proclaim the duties of kings, how a monarch should conduct himself,
how his origin comes about, and how his supreme success is achieved.
It has been stated that the word *dharma* denotes what ought to be done (*kartavyatā*).

The present declaration is that what must be performed by the king shall now be described. Furthermore, that which is to be performed is twofold: that which has a visible purpose, such as the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) and so forth, and that which has an invisible purpose, such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice and so forth.
In this context, that which has visible results is taught as the primary subject;
it is precisely therein that the established rules for the duties of kings (rājadharma) are found.
Furthermore, the word "king" (rājan) here does not denote the Kṣatriya caste, but rather refers to a person endowed with qualities such as consecration and sovereignty.
For this very reason, he says: "In whatever manner the king may conduct himself.
By the mention of the "king," he indicates that the authority here pertains to one who possesses sovereignty over a realm;
for the duties mentioned here are said to have other means of valid knowledge as their source, and are not all rooted in the Veda.
And since it has another source, that which is not contradicted by the *Dharmaśāstra* is stated here;
and so Kātyāyana says:
"Having set aside what is declared in the *Arthaśāstra*, one should follow what is declared in the *Dharmaśāstra*."
*Yathāvṛttaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose conduct (*vṛtta*) is such as this" or "one whose manner (*prakāra*) is such as this.
The referent of the other member of the compound (*anyapadārtha*) is the king.
If the primary emphasis were on the object itself (*yathārtha-prādhānya*), it would be an *avyayībhāva* compound.
*Vṛtta* is activity for the purpose of protection and for the sake of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*).
*Saṃbhava* is origination;
that has been described [in the passage] beginning with "The Lord created the King."
The supreme and most excellent accomplishment for one desiring victory is universal sovereignty;
this is the promised fruit of the conduct of a king.
Having duly received the Vedic consecration, the Kṣatriya must,
according to the law, provide protection for all of this in the proper manner.
"Brahman" refers to the Veda. The refinement (saṃskāra) pertaining to that is "brahmic.

This means that the injunction for private Vedic study (svādhyāya-vidhi) is to be accomplished as that which produces from the Veda both its literal apprehension and its characteristic meaning for one who possesses such apprehension.
However, because its purpose is the acquisition of the Veda (*brahman*), it is proper to call the *upanayana* "Brahmic" (*brāhma*).
And so he will state later: "From those learned in the three Vedas, [he should learn] the triple knowledge (*trayī vidyā*).
Otherwise, it would be a teaching of what has already been known.
"By a Kṣatriya" refers to the forty-eight sacraments beginning with *garbhādāna* according to the Smṛti scriptures;
by this, it is indicated that only a Kṣatriya is entitled to the sovereignty of a kingdom.

In the absence of a Kṣatriya, the extension of that [rule] to him should also be understood; the intention is that otherwise there would be a failure of progeny. This applies to everyone who pays taxes, as well as to the poor and the helpless.
The phrase "of these" refers to the inhabitants of his own territory, with specific mention of their respective provinces and cities;
"according to rule" means not transgressing the rule, which is the treatise in the form of a Dharmaśāstra, and not the Arthaśāstra composed by Uśanas and others.
Protection (*parirakṣaṇa*) means preservation (*paripālana*).
It consists of avoiding states of woe (*apāya*), not being overwhelmed by the powerful when one is weak, and not transgressing the boundaries of the scriptures (*śāstra-maryādā*).
Protection is the safeguarding against suffering (*duḥkha*).
Furthermore, by transgressing the treatises, one incurs invisible suffering;
therefore, by not transgressing them, people are protected through fear of the king.
If it is argued that there is suffering in royal punishment, [we reply that] compared to the great suffering of hell and other realms, royal punishment is quite minor.
The injunction is "it must be performed," and the qualification [for such performance] has been defined in the eighth [chapter].
For when this world was without a king and everyone fled in fear from all sides,
the Lord created a king for the protection of all this.
When [the world] has fled, been afflicted, or become unstable,
Prajāpati is the Lord.
This is a hymn of praise.
Having extracted the eternal portions from Indra, Anila, Yama, and Arka; from Agni and Varuṇa; and from Candra and Vitteśa.
Anila is Vāyu;
Vitteśa is Dhanapati, Vaiśravaṇa;
and mātrās are the constituent parts.
Eternal and substantial;
having extracted and drawn out.
Since the king was fashioned from portions of these lords of the gods,
he therefore surpasses all beings in splendor.

Because he was fashioned from the portions—the particles of splendor—of these foremost gods, Indra and the others, for that reason he overcomes [all] and his face becomes difficult to behold. He was extracted and produced by means of their splendor; for the verbal root *kṛṣ* is used in the sense of "producing."
Therefore, because it has "down to the lower realms" as its limit, the word *mātrabhyaḥ* should be read with either the ablative or the instrumental case ending.
Like the sun, he scorches both eyes and minds;
and no one at all on earth is able even to look upon him.
"He shines as if burning";
he is described thus because he cannot be seen face-to-face. As it is said: "And one is not able to behold him on earth."
Even Brahmins, though superior by birth and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*), are unable to look him directly in the face.
Thus it has been said: "They should sit below while he sits above."
By his own power, he becomes fire and wind; he is the sun, the moon, and the King of Dharma (Yama); he is Kubera, Varuṇa, and Indra.
Because the deities beginning with Agni are the substratum of the *mātrās*, they are described in this way by virtue of being endowed with their power;
"prabhāva" refers to that power which is supramundane (*alaukikī*).
A ruler of the earth must not be despised even if he is a child, for thinking "he is merely a human being";
indeed, he is a great deity dwelling in human form.
A king, even if he is a ruler of the earth, should not be despised by a fool simply because he is "this man. Rather, one should consider that he is some great deity abiding in human form.
Therefore, it is improper to show contempt toward a king, even if no fault has been seen.
Ordinary fire burns only the man who approaches it carelessly;
but the fire of a king burns the entire family, along with its livestock and accumulated wealth.
These are explanatory verses (arthavāda) for this injunction.
Although it concerns the duty of a king, this applies to every person's purpose:
the man who touches fire with his hand or the like, or who stays near it even when it is blazing, is one who approaches it improperly; if he stumbles through negligence, he is burned.
But a king, when enraged, consumes his family along with his sons, wealth, wives, and kinsmen;
whoever among them are relatives or one's own people,
he destroys them as well, together with their livestock and stores of wealth, on account of their connection to the offense.
Having truly considered the task at hand, as well as his own power, place, and time,
he repeatedly assumes various forms for the sake of accomplishing dharma.
One should not think, "The king is my kinsman" or "the king is my friend.
Whose friend could a king ever be? And who are the friends of a king?
Out of self-interest, people behave like friends toward an enemy and like enemies toward a friend.
Likewise, those who are powerless may forgive some offense, but once they have gained power, they uproot it;
so too with place and time.
Therefore, for the sake of establishing dharma and for the sake of accomplishing his purpose, he assumes a universal form.
In one moment he is a friend, in another moment an enemy; a king does not remain of a single nature.

Therefore, one must not place trust in a king. One should not behave toward him with affection, favoritism, or kindness based on the perception that his age is equal to one's own; rather, he should always be regarded through the lens of political prudence (*naya*).
In whose favor dwells the lotus-born Śrī, in whose prowess dwells victory,
and in whose anger dwells death— for he is composed of all splendor.
When pleased, he bestows prosperity through his propitiation;
when angry, he joins one with death.
Therefore, he who desires prosperity should propitiate him.
He does not merely endow one with prosperity; rather, even those who are his enemies, he overcomes and slays when satisfied.
Therefore, by one desiring the destruction of enemies, he should be served properly.
[This is] Padmā.
The word *padmā* is used as a synonym for *śrī* (fortune) for the purpose of expressing greatness; the meaning is that she bestows great fortune.
And these benefits are obtained by the king, because he, being composed of all splendors, bears the radiance of fire, the sun, and the moon.
But whoever hates him out of delusion will undoubtedly perish;
for the king sets his mind upon that person's swift destruction.
People do not perish so readily from transgression as they do through greed for desired objects; therefore, he says it again and again:
"He who hates that king or behaves with hostility toward him will undoubtedly perish;
indeed, his destruction is swift."
Someone else might forgive an offense by not reporting it to the king when it is impossible to do so;

for in that case, there would be a loss of wealth for the litigant, and even a fact established [in court] may turn out otherwise due to the variability of the witnesses' minds—anticipating this, someone might indeed forgive it.
Yet, because the king intends to destroy that [forgiveness], the person is surely afflicted by the offense held in the king's mind.
Because the king possesses power, when he exerts himself, a contradiction with independence arises.
Therefore, that king should determine what is right for those he holds dear,
and he should not deviate from that dharma even regarding those who are not dear.

Since the king is composed of all splendor, for that reason, among those who are dear and beloved—such as ministers, priests, and others—he should, according to the requirements of the matter, determine and establish the law, that is, the settled course of action not contrary to the scriptures or custom; he should not deviate from it.
Such an order of the king must not be transgressed—for example: "Today, a festival must be celebrated by everyone in the city";
"A wedding is taking place at the minister's house; everyone must assemble there."
Likewise, cattle must not be killed by soldiers today;
birds must not be captured;
and courtesans must be entertained by wealthy patrons for these many days.
Likewise regarding those who are undesirable: one must not associate with them;
entry into their house must not be granted.
Such a law, proclaimed here by the king through the sounding of drums and other means, is not to be transgressed.

But the king does not have the power to establish the religious duties of those belonging to the castes and stages of life, such as the Agnihotra and so forth, because that would entail a contradiction with other Smṛtis; and since there is no contradiction in this regard, the statement [of Manu] remains meaningful in its own domain.
For that purpose, the Lord formerly created Dharma, his own son, the protector of all beings, the staff consisting of the splendor of Brahman.
The origin of the king has been described;
now the origin of the rod of punishment is being stated.
For his sake—that is, for the purpose of the king—to accomplish his objective, the Lord Prajāpati created the rod of punishment.
What is the king’s purpose in wielding the rod of punishment?
It is said:
he is the protector of all living beings.
The protector and guardian is indeed punishment;
without punishment, a king is unable to protect.
Therefore, punishment was created solely for the purpose of establishing kingship.
"Dharma is his own son, consisting of the splendor of Brahman"—this is a praise of the rod (*daṇḍa*).
Dharma is not merely sacrifice, giving, and so forth; rather, it is the rod itself.
Nor should this be understood as unrighteousness (*adharma*) because it involves the taking away of life and wealth; on the contrary, it is indeed dharma.
The son was born from the very body of Prajāpati;
he was not composed of the five elements, but rather was fashioned from that pure radiance which belongs to Brahman,
prior to the creation of the Rajas.
Out of fear of him, all beings, both stationary and moving, become intent on their livelihoods and do not deviate from their own duties.
Out of fear of that rod,

when there is a desire to express merely a relationship [between the rod and the beings], the sixth case is used because the state of being a cause of fear does not exist [in the relationship itself].
Out of fear of the rod, stationary beings become fit for enjoyment— that is, they become capable of providing enjoyment— by means of fruits, flowers, shade, and so forth.

For that stationary tree which does not bear fruit is withered; if it does not wither, because its roots extend everywhere, it is cut down and made into a building material. By this analogy of the tree, such should be done to the person who is to be punished for acting against the king's interests: punishment should be administered by means of cutting, uprooting, and so forth.
The mention of "stationary beings" (sthāvara) is for the purpose of praise by way of illustration: such is this punishment that even stationary beings are punished, how much more so those that move?
However, stationary beings have no such thought as "this is our punishment";
they do not deviate from their own nature, they do not flower out of season, nor do they bear fruit.
Having accurately considered the place, the time, the power, and the learning [of the offender],
he should appropriately apply [punishment] toward men who act unjustly.
This punishment is prescribed for those high ministers and others who act unjustly and commit acts harmful to the king;
however, regarding others who engage in mutual transactions, it is stated here that [the king] should act after fully ascertaining the circumstances.
This very verse has been explained in that same context.
Knowledge is superior, and that concerns the subject matter of the Vedas.
"According to what is fitting" means according to what is appropriate for each individual;
that is to say, he should cause it to be imparted, set in motion, or performed.
Having considered all this and having examined it, punishment should be administered according to the specific requirements of each case;
otherwise, a punishment improperly meted out would bring visible harm to the king.

The distinction between the seventh and eighth memorial verses concerning the matrix of punishments lies in their division into the visible and invisible [consequences], and the division into one's own subjects and the people of the realm.
That king is the personification of punishment; he is the leader and the ruler, and he is traditionally held to be the guarantor of the dharma of the four stages of life.
In reality, he alone is the king;
when he exists, there is royal power;
he alone is the person.
He by whom even powerful men are humbled like women and brought under control is the leader;
by him all affairs are led forward.
The ruler is the one who possesses the command; "command" (śāsana) means the king's order, and its state of being a command exists when there is punishment.
Thus, agency [in the case of the king] is metaphorical, based on the nature of things (dharmataḥ).
Whatever dharma belongs to the four stages of life (āśrama), punishment stands as its guarantor;
just as a guarantor does not allow one to deviate, so too does punishment.
The rod of punishment governs all subjects; the rod alone protects them.
The rod remains awake while others sleep; the wise know the rod to be Dharma itself.
The king does not govern through the treatises regarding what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, nor through injunctions and prohibitions; rather, it is punishment alone that does so.
Punishment alone protects the weak from the powerful.
Even when the king’s officers are asleep, it is only out of fear of punishment that the world does not behave according to its own whims.
Punishment is of two kinds: royal punishment and the punishment of Yama.
When properly maintained through careful deliberation, he delights all his subjects;
but when applied without deliberation, he brings about destruction on every side.
It was maintained, brought forth, and set in motion;
"having observed" means having observed with regard to the previously mentioned place, time, and so forth.
It delights the people and engenders affection among them;
when applied in a contrary manner, not only does it fail to accomplish its own purpose, but being misapplied, it destroys the welfare of the people like poison.
If the king were not vigilant in inflicting punishment upon those deserving of it,
the stronger would roast the weaker like fish on a spit.

Because punishment is not administered, those who are stronger—superior in strength, possessing greater physical power, having men with weapons in their hands, or being more numerous—will devour the weak like fish on a spit.
Just as fish are impaled on spits for the sake of food, so too would a powerless person be preyed upon by those of superior power through the seizure of wealth, body, wife, and so forth.
Therefore, one should punish those deserving of punishment without negligence or laziness.
"How can I possibly exercise discernment? I shall simply not inflict punishment"—such a thought must not be entertained.
A crow might eat the sacrificial cake, and a dog might lick the oblation;
furthermore, there would be no sense of ownership over anything, and the social order would be overturned, with the low rising above the high.
Even dogs, crows, and other such most base creatures would vie with the gods;
they would consume the sacrificial offerings such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa* cakes intended for the gods, were it not for their being restrained by punishment.
Furthermore, no other form of ownership—the relationship between owner and owned—would exist, nor that between husband and wife, or father and son.
The husband would not exist for the wife; women would act with independence.
There would be an inversion of high and low:
that which is low, such as the *vṛṣala* and others, would become high and predominant.
That which is superior, such as the Brāhmaṇas and others, would fall into inferiority and degradation;
Śūdras would teach the Dharma,
and Vedic Dharma would not be practiced.
The entire world is subdued by punishment, for a pure man is indeed rare;
through fear of punishment, the whole world is fit for the enjoyment of life.
One who is pure and clean by very nature and by very essence regarding virtue, wealth, and pleasure—such a person is difficult to find; he can only be obtained with great hardship.
However, one who is conquered by punishment is subdued by that punishment and is established on the right path;
consequently, he does not act according to his own whims.
It has already been stated previously that [this is] for the enjoyment of the world.
Even the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, birds,
and serpents are made to serve for the enjoyment [of others] only when oppressed by the rod of punishment.

Those deities such as Parjanya, Vāyu, Āditya, and so forth, who serve for the sake of enjoyment by ripening plants through fixed cold, heat, and rain—[this is so] because they fear the threat of his punishment.
Otherwise, why would the sun and moon, or Dhātṛ and Parjanya, not deviate from their own fixed times of activity?
For if they possessed independence, perhaps the sun might not rise for two or three days at some point.
But fearing punishment, one does not transgress the boundary;
and thus says the Śruti:
"Out of fear the sun shines, out of fear the moon gives heat."
"Out of fear, both fire and wind [do not destroy the world].
And the fact that the Dānavas and others do not annihilate this entire world day and night is due to the majesty of the rod of punishment.

That birds such as parrots and mynas, which serve as ornaments for the home, do not pluck out the eyes of children; and that hawks, crows, herons, vultures, and the like do not devour those who are still alive—all this is likewise due to the power of the rod.
Furthermore, that all serpents and snakes, though their very nature consists of wrathful venom, do not collectively bite every living creature, is the efficacy of the rod.
Therefore, this is spoken as a praise.
Therefore, even gods and others of great supernatural power, or even insentient things, do not deviate from their own boundaries out of fear; how much more so, then, human beings?
Regarding this, a verse was recited by the ancients:
"But having seen the wretchedness of the forest *pāṭala* trees..."
"The *kuṭaja* flower laughs boldly with its blossoms; even a lowly person laughs by offering a connection. Indeed, one who finds a vulnerability will surely strike at it. Thus it was said.
All social classes would become corrupted, all boundaries would be broken,
and there would be universal upheaval in the world through the misapplication of punishment.
The perversion of punishment consists in its non-application or its application unjustly.
When that occurs, all social classes (varṇas) would become corrupted, because the intermingling of castes (saṃkara) proceeds through illicit intercourse with one another's women.
The "dams" are the boundaries [of conduct]; they would all be broken.
The meaning is that there would be a total destruction of all social boundaries (*maryādā*):
Brahmins would behave like Śūdras, and Śūdras would behave like Brahmins;
consequently, there would be universal disorder in the world.
Even the three worlds would not benefit one another through rain, heat, and so forth.
Where the dark-complexioned, red-eyed Punishment stalks about, destroying evil,
there the subjects do not go astray, provided that the leader perceives rightly.
These two are most highly praised among men;
therefore, he praises them by means of a metaphorical description of punishment as being non-existent:
"Punishment is twofold, bestowing both suffering and fear."
The state of being a cause for fear arises from its dark color, and the state of being a cause for suffering arises from having red eyes.
The praise of the rod is thus completed:
the rod must necessarily be employed.
And that [distinction] depends on place and so forth;
all other [statements] are explanatory praise (arthavāda),
provided they are intended as such.
The leader is the master of the rod of punishment. If he perceives rightly, having carefully considered the place, time, and other factors, he protects [his subjects];
therein the people do not become deluded and are not afflicted by any fault.
They say that the king who is a speaker of truth,
who acts with circumspection, who is wise, and who is skilled in the matters of dharma, kama, and artha, is the one who should be appointed as its administrator.
This is the excellent vision of the legislator: truthfulness, acting with circumspection, wisdom, and skill in the three aims of life (*trivarga*).

He is a speaker of truth who, by following the scriptures in administering punishment, does not increase it upon learning of someone’s great wealth, nor does he diminish it out of affection for a favorite.
He is wise, meaning he knows the specific circumstances regarding the relationship between the oppressor and the oppressed in various regions and so forth.
Sometimes space is sublated by time, or time by space;
or both of them are sublated by the power of knowledge. And one who understands the relationship of mutual exception and non-exception between these two [is wise].
Since a matter may be set aside simply because it is obstructed by the requirements of practical necessity, wisdom is of use here.
Furthermore, there exists a relative weight among dharma and the other goals;
when the practice of dharma is so slight that its pursuit results in great harm, then that dharma is abandoned.
It should be understood that [the text] beginning with "he will settle [it] by means of expiation" refers to this.
A king who administers that [punishment] properly prospers through the three aims of life;
but one who is blinded by passion, unjust, or base, is destroyed by that very punishment.
One who acts with impartiality increases [in merit] by inflicting punishment equally upon both enemy and friend;
one blinded by desire is dominated by passion;
one who is uneven is prone to anger.
A base person, because he seeks out deceptions,
is destroyed by punishment alone, or by the anger of the subjects, or by some unseen fault.
For punishment is indeed a very great power, difficult to be wielded by those of undisciplined soul;
it destroys the king himself, along with his kinsmen, if he deviates from righteousness.
That which is his supreme majesty is the *daṇḍa*.

It is difficult to be wielded by those of undisciplined soul—those who have not been properly trained through the scriptures, through service to their teachers, or through innate humility; it cannot be rightly administered by them.
One should not think: "The *daṇḍa* is administered merely by command; what is so difficult about it?"
Therefore, the king’s punishment strikes down that negligent man, along with his kinsmen, who does not remain vigilant and who lacks effort in that regard;
for the king is not destroyed by the body alone, but together with his lineage of sons, grandsons, and so forth.
Then he would afflict the fortress, the kingdom, and the world with all its moving and unmoving beings, as well as the sages dwelling in the intermediate space and the gods.
Where punishment is inflicted regardless of the location and other factors, there occurs the destruction of the kingdom along with its king, including its animals and stationary beings.
Therefore, the king should be petitioned by the ministers and the people, or such a region should be abandoned;
for the gods and sages are thereby afflicted.
The gods subsist on offerings from this world;
and because [the practice] such as ritual performance has been cut off in this [age], the divine sages have indeed perished.
And so it was said by the authors of the Purāṇas:
"He who, abiding by the [duties of] the castes and stages of life, conducts himself in this world, is indeed remembered as the cause of stability for the divine births in heaven and other realms.
From the first verse up to this verse, the summary of the meaning is as follows: the protection of the realm must be performed by a Kṣatriya who maintains impartiality.

And since that [dharma] does not exist without punishment, it must necessarily be determined with precision in consideration of place and other factors; it should be administered according to the scriptures, whether within one's own kingdom or in another's kingdom.
Otherwise, if it is applied incorrectly, there will be destruction in both worlds.
All other [statements regarding its nature] are merely explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
He cannot be led by the right path by one who is without a companion, who is deluded, greedy, of unrefined intellect, and attached to sense objects.

Now this chapter is commenced for the purpose of gathering assistants. For one who lacks those endowed with the qualities of assistants and so forth—namely, noble, refined, and capable ministers, generals, and judicial officers—it is not possible to administer justice according to principle, even if he himself is free from fear and fully possessed of the qualities of leadership and the [proper] time.
"Justice" (*nyāya*) is a determination that follows the scriptures and takes into account the specific place and other such factors.
Therefore, excellent companions should be sought.

The point is this: just as one who is himself deluded, distracted, and of unrefined intellect; who is attached to sense-objects and greedy, and thus fails to employ his wealth properly; and who, being possessed of such defects, cannot maintain himself correctly—even so it is for one who is without a companion.
However, by one who is the opposite of this, it can be accomplished.
This same point is stated by way of its opposite:
"Punishment can be successfully administered by one who is pure, true to his word, follows the scriptures, possesses good assistants, and is wise."
Pure and free from greed,
faithful to his word and devoted to truth,
he proceeds in all his actions placing truth alone at the forefront; such a person has conquered his senses.
How can there be truth for one whose senses are unsubdued?
He follows and acts according to the scriptures;
he has good companions, meaning his associates are excellent.
He is joined by assistants who are not foolish and are devoted through faith;
he is wise and intelligent.
This [person] is described as the opposite of that "fool" mentioned previously.

Therefore, the meaning of these two verses is that one who is free from the five defects and endowed with those very same virtues is authorized to administer punishment and becomes a partaker of excellence in both seen and unseen rewards.
He should conduct himself with justice within his own kingdom, be severe in punishment toward enemies,
straightforward toward friends, and endowed with patience toward Brahmins.
A country inherited through the succession of fathers, grandfathers, and so forth, is the basis for one's designation;
for a Kashmiri, it is Kashmir, and for a Pāñcāla, it is the Pāñcālas—this is one's own kingdom. Therein, one who conducts himself according to justice should act with justice.
Conduct (*vṛtta*) arises from right reasoning (*nyāya*); therefore, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Alternatively, the reading may be *nyāyavṛtti*.
Having restated this which was already established previously, the infliction of severe punishment upon enemies is now enjoined.
One should further afflict the kingdoms of others; in that regard, neither obstacles nor the obstruction of one's own kingdom should be overlooked.
For one who acts in this manner, majesty arises.
The enemies of one whose wealth is majesty bow down;
he is endowed with patience toward all Brahmins.
Even in the face of offenses, punishment should be administered with conciliation, not with anger.
Even those residing in a foreign kingdom, if they can be protected at the time of an attack on one's own country, should not be killed.
Toward affectionate friends, he should be straightforward, meaning his intellect should be free from crookedness;
he should be one who accomplishes the task, making that objective his primary concern.
Affectionate friends share both prosperity and adversity.
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he lives by gleaning ears of grain,
his fame spreads throughout the world like a drop of oil upon water.
This is a praise of one whose conduct has been previously described:
even for one who lives by gleaning ears of grain and whose treasury is utterly depleted, his fame expands and spreads;
consequently, foreign kingdoms submit of their own accord, and the people of his own kingdom remain steadfast out of affection.
But for a king who is the opposite of this, whose self is unconquered,
his fame in the world diminishes like a drop of clarified butter upon water.
Thus, for one who has deviated from this conduct,
the cause is the lack of self-mastery;
that is, one whose self is not restrained according to the scriptures.
The king was created as the protector of all the social classes and stages of life, who are each established in their respective duties in due order.
The king was created as the protector of those who abide by their own duties;
for a king, there is sin in failing to protect those established in their own duties.
However, if those fallen from dharma should be harmed by someone, the king is not excessively at fault in that matter—this is what he shows by the phrase "in their respective duties."

Alternatively, it is not applicable to those who are "unattached," meaning those who are not dependent on their own duties due to the instructions of the scriptures or the counsel of friends and others; toward such people, the king should not employ duplicity. The mention of "caste" (varṇa) is for the purpose of protecting women, children, and the elderly.
For they are not merely those who dwell in hermitages.
Then for what purpose is the mention of "hermitage" (āśrama)?
It is for the sake of indicating preeminence, as in the case of the expression "Brāhmaṇa-Vasiṣṭha."
Or rather, this is a statement of the purpose:
they must not be allowed to deviate from their duties, such as the observances of their stage of life (*āśrama*) and the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*);
nor should they be subjected to injury by means of punishment or the like.
Otherwise, there would be no avoidance of contradiction;
thus is protection to be understood.
In cases such as the non-performance of the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*), [the recitation of] another's name occurs.
The duties of the king are twofold; this is indicated by the mention of the castes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*).
This very point has been stated [in the verse]: "He shall protect the castes and the stages of life according to justice."
Therefore, whatever must be done by one who protects his subjects along with his attendants,
all that I shall declare to you correctly and in due order.
This verse is intended to introduce what is about to be explained.
Now, that which must be done by the king, together with his servants and his own assistants, for the sake of protecting the subjects, is being stated.
Having risen early in the morning, the king should attend upon the Brahmins who are learned and advanced in the knowledge of the three Vedas, and he should abide by their instruction.

Having risen in the morning, left his bed, and performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana) according to the prescribed rule, he should first grant an audience to the Brāhmaṇas. "Upāsana" means sitting near them and engaging in inquiries regarding their welfare and so forth.
The prefix "pari-" is used here for the sake of completing the meter.
One should abide by their teaching;
their teaching consists in the carrying out of their commands.
If they should give an instruction for the sake of someone's benefit, one should not suspect it to be contrary [to the Dharma], nor should one perform it if it is purposeless.
"Those advanced in the three Vedas" (*traividyavṛddhān*):

the collection of the three sciences is "the triple knowledge" (*traividyam*); those who have studied that are "those versed in the triple knowledge" (*traividyāḥ*). By conventional usage, these refer to students of the three Vedas, beginning with the *Ṛgveda*; they are both learned in the texts and knowers of their meaning.
One should attend upon such Brahmins and carry out their instructions;
they are the elders, the best among those learned in the three Vedas, preeminent in both study and realization.
One should always serve elderly Brahmins who are pure and learned in the Vedas;
for one who constantly serves the elderly is honored even by the Rākṣasas.

"Vṛddhān" refers to elderly Brahmins of established age; this is something not previously mentioned, whereas other qualities such as being "viprān" (learned) and so forth were already established. "Śucīn" means those who are free from defects or impurities.
This too is unprecedented:
just as the reason for being an object of meditation lies in the knowledge of the study [of the Veda], so too does purity.
The second half-verse is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
As for the *rakṣasas*:
though they are merciless, possess great strength, and are devoid of all virtue, even they honor one who serves his elders.
He states the purpose of serving the elderly:
"From them he should constantly acquire discipline, even though his own self is already disciplined;
for a king whose self is disciplined never perishes."

From those learned and aged Brahmins, he should acquire and learn discipline and the conduct of kings. Even if he is disciplined by his own intelligence or through treatises on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*), he should nevertheless exert effort in the instruction of the elders.
Those who have observed practical experience are more skillful than those who merely know the treatises.
Alternatively, for the sake of generating an excellence of proficiency, even one who is already disciplined must train himself before elders and noble persons by his very nature.
Just as gold that is pure by nature is seen to possess an even more refined form when it undergoes refinement through contact with fire and other such means.
The fruit of that application of discipline does not perish.
Many kings, together with their retinues, have perished through lack of discipline;
yet even those dwelling in the forest have attained kingdoms through discipline.
The very meaning previously stated is further confirmed by these three verses:
those who are undisciplined and possess worldly attachments are ruined.
"Possession" (parigraha) refers to the abundance of children, wife, elephants, horses, and so forth.
But those who are disciplined do not lose their kingdom upon obtaining it;
even when they are far away, dwelling in the forest, or devoid of a treasury, they have attained and secured the sovereignty.
Vena was ruined through lack of discipline, as were King Nahuṣa,
Sudās Paijavana, Sumukha, and Nimi.
In both cases, they describe examples well-known in the world;
these are to be understood as narratives from the Mahābhārata.
Pṛthu indeed obtained his kingdom through discipline, as did Manu;
Kubera obtained mastery over wealth, and the son of Gādhi obtained the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
"And Gādhi’s son [Vasiṣṭha] attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
But surely, what occasion is there for mentioning the attainment of Brāhmaṇahood when the context concerns the right to rule? One should have described only the acquisition of the kingdom, as before.
It is said:
even compared to wealth and power, excellence of birth is difficult to attain, because it is the cause of all authority.
But how can discipline be its cause?
The application of the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*), vigilance, avoidance of excessive expenditure, lack of greed, refraining from vices—such as these constitute discipline (*vinaya*).
Yet even all this is not the sole cause of Brahminhood;
for austerity (*tapas*) is heard of as the cause in that regard, as in such passages as: "Viśvāmitra performed austerities, [thinking], 'May I not be the son of a non-seer'."

It is said: policy (*naya*) is not merely the doctrine taught in the treatises on worldly affairs (*arthaśāstra*). What then? It is both the scriptural injunction (*śāstrīya-vidhi*) and worldly custom (*lokācāra*).
Furthermore, in the treatises it is indeed ordained that an elevation of birth through austerity is attained in another life;
however, the case of Viśvāmitra’s attainment of Brahminhood while still being a Kṣatriya in that very same birth is merely a legendary account.

From those learned in the three Vedas, he should learn the triple Veda, the eternal science of government, the science of inquiry, and the knowledge of the self; and from the people, he should learn the various undertakings of commerce and agriculture.
In the reading where "vidyām" ends in the accusative case, the word "adhigacchet" (should master) must be supplied.

Since the instruction regarding kingship is given for one who has completed his period of Vedic studentship (*brahmacarya*), and since that [kingship] is accomplished through the mastery of the meaning of the three Vedas (*trayi*), this instruction is for the purpose of practice.
*Trividyā* means knowledge consisting of three parts; those who study that are *traividyāḥ*. From them, one should learn the *trayī*, the triad of Vedas beginning with the Ṛgveda.
He should reach a definitive conclusion regarding doubtful matters from the Vedas;
that is to say, he should deliberate upon the meaning of the Vedas together with them.
Out of pride born of his royal status, or through the arrogance of thinking "I am omniscient," he must not neglect matters that are being questioned.
And *daṇḍanīti* (the science of government). *Nīti* is that which pertains to *daṇḍa*.

They say that *daṇḍa* means "subduing" (*damana*). That by which enemies, one's own subjects, and the inhabitants of the realm who act unjustly are subdued is *daṇḍa*; this consists in the excellence of ministers and other [officials].

Political science (*nīti*) is its purpose; therein lies the rule, which one should learn from those who know it, such as the authors of works by Cāṇakya and others. The word "eternal" (*śāśvatīm*) is a praise.

Although the entire world can be understood through the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*) because this subject matter is rooted in positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), nevertheless, those treatises are intended for the instruction of the ignorant and for the mutual confirmation of the wise; thus, the mastery of the science of government is appropriate.
Likewise, *ānvīkṣikī* consists of logic (*tarka*), the science of statecraft (*arthaśāstra*), and so forth.
*Ātmavidyā* is the science of the inner self (*adhyātmavidyā*).
Or rather, it refers to the two words "viśeṣaṇa" (qualifier) and "viśeṣya" (qualified).
That *anvīkṣikī* which is beneficial for oneself is based on logic (*tarka*); one should study that.
For that [scriptural knowledge] is indeed employed for the cessation of calamities and prosperity, and for the pacification of mental agitation;
whereas the science of logic belonging to the Buddhists, Cārvākas, and others, is of little utility anywhere.
On the contrary, it destroys faith in those whose intellects are not particularly sharp.
But when he knows Ānvīkṣikī as an independent discipline, then his proficiency in the clarity of speech during dialogues with envoys and the like does not become an object of ridicule.
And [he understands] the undertakings of economic activity (vārtā):
the thorough knowledge of the value of commodities and skill in trade constitute vārtā, the mastery of which is achieved through the Bārhaspatya manual.
"Undertakings caused by that" refers to undertakings concerning livelihood (*vārtā*).
Having understood the nature of livelihood, the engagement in activity directed toward it is an "undertaking.
This one should learn from the world.
In this context, "the world" refers to those who live by trade,
for they are indeed skilled in that regard;
furthermore, the phrase "from the perspective of the world" should be applied as a supplement to the two preceding cases.
Therefore, in all cases, the phrase "from those who know it" is understood.
One should apply oneself day and night to the conquest of the senses;
for one who has conquered the senses is able to keep the subjects under control.

The reiteration here of the conquest of the senses—which was already taught among the duties of a religious student (*brahmacārin*) as being essential for all human goals—is intended to make known that this discipline is the foremost among the duties of a king.
To this effect, he says "one who has conquered his senses," and so forth.
This is well known to everyone: the subjects of one whose senses are unconquered do not remain under his control.
Yoga is the essential intent;
day and night means throughout the twenty-four hours.
One should diligently avoid the ten calamities arising from desire and the eight born of anger, which have miserable ends.
This is another purpose for the instruction on the conquest of the senses:
for one whose senses are unconquered, calamities are difficult to avoid;
they have a miserable end—that is, their conclusion or finality is characterized by suffering.

Calamities bring pleasure at the time they first occur, but later they produce bitterness; therefore, they are called "ending badly" (*durantāni*). Alternatively, their end (*anta*) is difficult to reach.
For those whose birth has its origin in desire are unable to turn back from that addiction.
He states the purpose for avoiding these, as well as their relative gravity:
"For a lord of the earth who is addicted to vices born of desire is deprived of both wealth and dharma; but one addicted to those born of anger is deprived of his very self."
Through the loss of wealth and virtue, one is separated from oneself;
however, the distinction regarding those [karmas] born of anger is that one is separated from everything.
He now shows those vices by their own names:
hunting, gambling, sleeping during the day, slander, women, intoxication, the triple symphony [of song, dance, and instrumental music], and idle wandering— this is the tenfold group born of desire.
Hunting is the killing of wild animals;
gambling is play centered on dice.
The harmful nature of these two is well known.
"Sleeping by day" (*divāsvapna*) means not engaging in one's duties at the time for performing those duties. By the word "day," it is not intended that only the daytime is meant;
as it has been said: "Those who are fast asleep when they ought to be awake."
Alternatively, it is daytime sleep itself that is primary;
for it is forbidden and obstructs all undertakings. Moreover, because others who desire to see [the king] do not achieve that [audience], it generates resentment among the subjects.
Slander is the concealment of another's faults in private;
by it, all subjects become alienated.
Furthermore, when those who ought not to be slandered are slandered, unrighteousness is established as a certainty.
The harmful nature of women and intoxication is well known. The triple symphony (*tauryatrika*) consists of dancing, singing, and instrumental music.
Idle wandering (*vṛthāṭyā*) is roaming here and there for no purpose or for a trivial purpose.
"Tenfold" means having the measure of ten. "Born of desire" (*kāmaja*): *kāma* is longing; that from which [the suffering] arises is "born of desire.
Alternatively, it is "born of desire" because it arises for the sake of enjoying distinguished pleasures or from a particularity of what has been previously experienced.
Slander, violence, malice, envy, jealousy, and the spoiling of wealth, as well as verbal and physical harshness— this is the eightfold group born of anger.
Slander (*paiśunya*) is the disclosure of that which ought to be concealed regarding those who are well-disposed toward one, such as ministers and other kinsmen.
Violence (*sāhasa*) is the employment of a superior person in a lowly task, or the imposition of taxes or imprisonment for even a minor offense.
Malice (*droha*) is silent assassination, or the infliction of injury upon a person while they are still alive.
Envy (*īrṣyā*) is the exclusion of the commonality of an object that is shared by all, or the inability to endure it.
Envy (*asūyā*) is the revelation of faults in the virtues of those possessed of virtue.
Malice (*arthadūṣaṇa*) is the spoiling of wealth, or the non-giving or seizing away of riches.
Harshness of speech and harshness of punishment are well known; "anger" means hatred,
and those dominated by it perform these acts.
One should strive to conquer that greed which all poets know to be the root of both these [vices]; for both these groups arise from it.
It has already been stated that greed (*lobha*) is the root of the group of vices born of desire (*kāmajavyasana*).
Since desire (*kāma*), longing for the enjoyment of sense objects, and greed—whether termed *icchā*, *abhilāṣa*, or *lobha*—are not different in meaning, one might ask:
how can greed be the root of the group born of anger (*krodhaja*), given that it is said, "Both these groups arise from that [greed]"?
It is said:
here, it is not intended that greed is the cause of those two groups;
rather, greed is [intended] as being equal to the two groups.
That which all these calamities produce as harm, that alone does greed produce even for one who is otherwise free from calamities.
Thus it has been said: "Greed [destroys] all virtues.
Therefore, this was stated figuratively: "these two arise from that."
If greed were not to arise, how could there be equal fruits?
For it is the defect in the cause that makes manifest the defect in the effect.
Therefore, if there is a fault in the calamities because they are its effects, then certainly that same fault is said to belong to the cause as well.
Alternatively, it is the greedy person alone who develops an attachment to those things that should be avoided, such as backbiting;
the other, however, is appeased by conciliation even regarding a very minor object.
Thus, this two-fold category of vices is said to have its root in greed through figurative usage.
Drinking, dice, women, and hunting— one should know this tetrad, in their respective order, to be the most grievous among the group of vices born of desire.
It is well known that this group of four, beginning with sleeping during the day, possesses a far greater degree of fault.
One should always know that this triad— inflicting physical punishment, verbal abuse, and the violation of property— is always grievous, even within the category of offenses born of anger.
It is well known that this triad is even more evil than slander and the like.
A self-possessed person should know that among this group of seven vices which are everywhere interconnected, each preceding one is more grievous than the next.

Between drinking and gambling, drinking is the more serious vice. For in it there is the loss of consciousness; the sane become insane, the living become like the dead; one's private parts are exposed, and one's learning and wisdom are lost. There is the loss of friends and separation from the virtuous, while association with the wicked ensues. One becomes addicted to singing and other pursuits that destroy wealth, and one reveals secrets of pleasure and counsel. Even the proud become objects of ridicule, and even those of profound nature speak nonsense through the force of intoxication—such are the faults of drinking. In gambling, however, one who knows the dice certainly wins, while even for one ignorant of the game, defeat is only a matter of chance.
Between the two vices of women and gambling, the vice of gambling is more serious;
for even that wealth which has been won by it becomes poison to the winner.
Likewise, the resulting persistence of enmity is common to both sides, while victory alone results in the loss of what was enjoyed.

Furthermore, the suppression of the urges of urine and feces causes a looseness in the body that is indeed the primary cause of disease; for this reason, even when afflicted by minor ailments and the like, he does not suffer excessively from his own pain.
Even when his mother has died, he continues to play;
and when his tasks are accomplished, he is not drawn away even by his friends.

One who avoids the property of others as if it were a red-hot iron ball incurs no blame; yet, for one who neglects the provision of food and other necessities to the hungry and the destitute, even if they are endowed with every virtue, they are to be disregarded like a blade of grass. Such are the evils of gambling.

In the vice of women, however, there is the procreation of offspring, the experience of abundant grooming and food, and the acquisition of merit and wealth. Furthermore, a woman can be employed for the king's benefit or used to carry out secret missions.
Between the vices of women and hunting, the vice of women is more serious.

The neglect of duties, indifference toward royal affairs due to attachment to the vice of women, the wasting of time, the abandonment of dharma, the persistence of the faults of drinking, and addiction to falsehoods and other vices that destroy wealth—these are the consequences.

In hunting, however, there is physical exercise, the binding of bile and phlegm, the reduction of fat and other humors, proficiency in aiming at moving or stationary targets, the development of skill in weaponry, and mastery over rustic people.
Thus, within this group of four vices born of desire, each preceding one is more evil than the next.
Furthermore, for one born of anger, there is a continuous sequence of faults resulting from the infliction of punishment, as well as attachment to falsehood and other vices that destroy wealth.
Between the infliction of physical punishment and verbal abuse, the infliction of physical punishment is more serious;
for while the destruction of the body and such consequences resulting from physical punishment can be remedied, [the harm of verbal abuse cannot].
In the case of verbal abuse, however, the fire of anger born of intolerance can be extinguished by the waters of gifts and honors.
Between verbal abuse and the defilement of wealth, verbal abuse is more serious;
for those possessed of brilliance do not fall into fear when their minds are agitated by harsh words.
And thus runs the proverb:
"Having pierced a firm, well-aimed arrow that has entered deep into the bone, they extract the shaft and leave the limb free of the barb;
but words cannot be removed even from the heart."
A forest pierced by arrows or struck down by an axe grows back;
but the wound caused by speech, O loathsome one, from a harsh word spoken, never heals.
Since wealth depends upon fortune, those possessed of splendor do not take account of the impairment of that wealth;
thus, the greater importance of each preceding category over the subsequent one within these two groups has been demonstrated.
Between calamity and death, calamity is said to be the more grievous;
one who suffers calamity sinks lower and lower, while one who dies free from calamity goes to heaven.
Although both death and calamity may take away everything, there is nevertheless this distinction:
death takes all in this world alone, whereas calamity does so both here and in the next.
Thus it is said: "The man beset by calamity sinks lower and lower."
The meaning is that one goes to hell. By the word *vyasani*, extreme addiction to this class of objects is expressed; therefore, such addiction is prohibited, but not a slight indulgence.
For these [vices] are indeed calamities that snatch away virtue, wealth, pleasure, and life, not only for another man but especially for a king.
Furthermore, the non-indulgence in drinking and the like is both improper and impossible;
therefore, their habitual practice is what is prohibited.
He should appoint seven or eight ministers who are hereditary, learned in the scriptures, heroic, skilled in hitting the mark, of noble birth, and thoroughly tested.

Those who have descended through the lineage of fathers and grandfathers, possessing many sons, wealth, and kinsmen, with cattle, land, and riches manifest, residing in that country as original inhabitants—
*mūla* meaning foundation or established status, and those existing therein being *maula*; they are knowers of the scriptures.
"Śāstra" means instruction or the knowledge of servants;
by this, other qualities are also included.

Namely: being wise, firm in action, retentive, skillful, eloquent, powerful, possessed of practical discernment, endowed with energy and majesty, enduring of hardship, pure, generous in character, possessed of a suitable nature, free from arrogance and fickleness, beloved, and one who does not act as an enemy.
By the word "hero" (*śūra*), one who is indifferent even toward body, wife, children, wealth, and so forth in the service of the king is meant.
Likewise, he is fearless in the face of death, possesses zeal for battle, and, being alone, opposes many out of fear of humiliation; he is a firm striker, powerful, and one who has attained his mark.
By this, he speaks of their proven capacity for action:
those who have witnessed the workings of the sword, who have fulfilled their duties and offices, and who have experienced the stages of counsel;
for those born of noble lineage, restrained by the goad of their family, do not engage in what ought not to be done.
Ministers and assistants—
these should always remain by the king's side,
numbering seven or eight.
This is the rule:
by which they become few and of one mind,
and consequently, the king's counsel shall remain unexposed.
There is also a breach of secrecy among many;
therefore, only this many [ministers] should be appointed,
having been thoroughly tested by means of trials involving dharma, artha, kāma, and fear.
This examination is now described.
