The domestic priest, having been falsely accused by the king on a minor matter, should, through trusted men and with the gift of much wealth, instigate each individual minister toward the destruction of the king, saying: "This [plan] for the king's ruin is pleasing to all the ministers; what do you think of it?
If he rejects it, he is proven pure by the test of dharma.

The commander-in-chief, having been insulted as before by someone with some pretext, should have trusted men secretly instigate each minister one by one toward the destruction of the king, saying: "This [plan] is approved by all the ministers; what do you think of it? If he rejects it, he is proven pure by the test of wealth. A female ascetic who has gained confidence within the harem should instigate each minister one by one, saying: "The queen desires you and has already arranged a meeting."

Regarding the test of refusal: he is pure in the trial of desire when certain men employed by the king, acting in concert with ministers who have made an agreement, spread a rumor that "the king is being killed. Having learned of this rumor, a certain trusted man of the domestic priest should inform the ministers of the secret plan, saying: "Having overheard this rumor, the king is going to carry out your suppression."

And one among those very persons, having previously made a secret agreement, should incite each of the king’s ministers individually. Those who refuse are purified by the test of fear. Alternatively, he should first appoint hereditary officials as collectors of revenue and treasurers.

Those who collect wealth from the villages, protect what has been collected, and employ it [properly]— it is said that such original members of the council, who deal with all matters of financial affairs, should be appointed.
Those learned in the treatises are the ministers who serve as counselors for the intellect.
"Brave," "superintendents of the army," and "those who have hit the mark"— these and other such terms are qualifiers for all [the ministers].

Furthermore, they consider that the previously mentioned examination of each one individually and collectively, as well as the encouragement of the king's ministers regarding matters pertaining to the king, is not appropriate.
For this indeed would be the cause of dissension among the ministers;
therefore, some other virtuous woman should be employed, and another matter concerning destruction should be cited as an example.
Even an action that is easy to perform is difficult for one person alone, especially so without assistance; how much more so is sovereignty, which brings such great results?
It is established that the common household duties of a householder, such as the easy task of tending cattle, horses, and so forth,
are performed by one person who tends the cow and another who milks it;
this cannot be accomplished by a single individual alone.
Even that is difficult for one person to accomplish, especially without assistance;
what is difficult cannot be achieved by one who lacks the capacity.
For how can one person alone tend cattle, and how can he protect a wife?
A kingdom, however, involves great undertakings and the activity of prosperity; its application is fruitful. For one who observes [these factors], great fruit arises.
Moreover, it is not possible for a single person to understand the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) in its entirety.
Therefore, companions who have been examined and found to be equal to oneself should be employed in various undertakings.
Together with them, he should constantly deliberate upon common matters: peace and war, stability, the collection of revenue, protection, and the consolidation of what has been acquired.

Together with those chief ministers of counsel and officials in charge of affairs, he should deliberate upon peace and war—matters that are not excessively secret—considering whether peace is appropriate at this time or whether war is; he should examine the merits and defects in both cases.
However, he should determine what must be done by his own intelligence so that he does not become subject to the influence of others.
Furthermore, he should consider this other matter: the strategic position (*sthāna*).
That [kingdom] is fourfold: the army, the treasury, the city, and the realm.
Among these, the army consists of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
Their maintenance, nourishment, protection, and so forth must be attended to.
For lack of concentration is not the primary concern.
Likewise, regarding the treasury, there is the abundance of gold and silver, the prevalence of silver, and the characteristics of income and expenditure.
Whatever sources of income the treasury possesses, those must not be squandered nor delayed for the sake of the servants.

Likewise, the livelihood (*svājīva*) of the realm—which is synonymous with the country—consists of means for sustaining oneself and others, such as rivers, trees, pastures suitable for cattle, abundance of enemies, hatred, and the frequent presence of those who have fled; it should also be protected, possess livestock, not depend on rain for its crops (*adevamātṛka*), and be capable of enduring fines and taxes in times of distress, and so forth.
Regarding the city, he will state later that "it should be well-equipped with weapons.
Alternatively, "place" (*sthāna*) refers to not being displaced from one's own territory.
In this way, the aggregate [of royal duties] is also to be considered;
therein, agriculture, cattle-rearing, and the establishment of forts, as well as trade, tolls, and fines, and so forth [are included].
He will explain protection pertaining to one's own kingdom later on.

It involves the pacification of those who have attained [power], as well as the practice of honor, charity, and renunciation toward righteous ones who possess divine power and knowledge; the granting of permission to those who are worthy;
the liberation from all bonds;
and the bestowing of favor upon the distressed and the diseased.

He shall initiate unprecedented festivals and continue those already established. Having eliminated any unrighteous conduct that undermines the treasury and the army, he shall establish righteous legal proceedings.
He shall cause unrighteous practices—whether previously non-existent or practiced by others—to cease, and promote righteousness.
Nor should one cause another to revoke what has been performed for the sake of the Dharma;
in this manner, the locations and other factors are to be considered.
Having ascertained each of their individual intentions, he should act for his own welfare regarding the affairs of both the individuals and the collective.

Having ascertained the secret intention and the state of mind harbored in the hearts of each of them individually, he should consider the reason why, when they are all gathered together, one man may be lacking in eloquence in an assembly yet bold in private, while another has acquired wisdom in an assembly.
Then he should question them all collectively;
thereafter, he himself should determine and carry out that which is more appropriate and beneficial for his own purpose.
Its authority is that which has been taught by one of those very [teachers], being uncontradicted and faultless.
But the king should deliberate upon the supreme counsel concerning the sixfold policy with a distinguished, wise Brahmin among all his advisors.

A wise person— one who is learned and knowledgeable in the treatises on statecraft— should deliberate upon a supreme counsel, one that is strictly to be kept secret and endowed with the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*). For a Brahmin possesses superior wisdom, and because of his righteousness, he is trustworthy.
Always placing his trust in him, he should entrust all affairs to him;
having reached a decision together with him, he should then begin the work.

Having entrusted the entire circle of the kingdom to such a brahmin, he should enjoy the pleasures of sovereignty with full confidence; having deliberated with him, he should carry out activities such as marching and sitting in camp, as well as judicial proceedings and the administration of the realm.
He should also appoint other ministers who are pure, wise, steadfast, thoroughly tested, and capable of properly collecting revenue.
Regarding what was stated—that there should be seven or eight—this is an exception to that rule:
he should appoint collectors of revenue and storekeepers who have been thoroughly tested by means of secret trials (*upadhā*).
He should appoint as many diligent, capable, and discerning men as are required for the performance of his duties.
All these should be appointed as experts in mantras, discerning, learned, and qualified;
they should be skillful, possessing great perseverance even in the presence of fear or when faced with causes for despondency; and they should be untiring and free from laziness.
And it is said in the *Adhyakṣapracāra*:
"He whose minister is intelligent, loyal, diligent, skilled in matters of dharma and artha, pure, capable, and of noble birth, shall possess the kingdom."
Having entrusted all affairs to him, one who is attached to enjoyments does not perish;
by means of gifts and favors, he brings the king under his influence.
For their sake, he should employ those who are brave, capable, and of noble birth at the mines and in the workshops;
and those who are timid within the inner apartments.
Regarding wealth—that is, in the administration of income and expenditure—one should employ those who are pure and free from greed over financial matters.
He illustrates these financial positions with examples, namely: mines and industrial enterprises.
Mines are the locations for the extraction and processing of gold, silver, and so forth. Occupations include the cultivation of food crops, cotton planting, and the like.
The inner quarters consist of the harem, the dining hall, the bedchamber, and the women's apartments.
The timid should be appointed there;

for the brave, if incited, might kill the king when he is alone. Moreover, all who are capable, by virtue of their energetic nature, do not neglect their master’s business at the proper time, disregarding the risk of falling into conflict.
And he should appoint as a messenger one who is learned in all the scriptures,
who understands gestures, facial expressions, and conduct, and who is pure, capable, and of noble birth.
This is the preeminent quality of an envoy: the knowledge of gestures, facial expressions, and physical movements.

When a king or his ministers desire to form an alliance with another state, they should attentively observe the envoy's gestures, place their full confidence in him, and repeatedly welcome and praise his complete statements.
One should disregard these qualities if they are the opposite.
Physical appearance refers to deformity of the body, pallor of the face, change in complexion, silence, and long, hot sighs.
Through such transformations as these, one indicates wretchedness, thinking: "He has met with some calamity; that is why he is discolored.
Confidence of speech, refinement of the body, and a serene countenance—such things indicate joy.
One is pure regarding matters concerning women through specific modes of approach,
because in connection with women there is neither the disclosure of secrets nor humiliation.
A messenger who is loyal, pure, skillful, mindful, knowledgeable of place and time, handsome, fearless, and eloquent is praised by kings.
Being devoted, he is incorruptible; being skillful, he does not transgress the requirements of place and time;
and being mindful, through the continuity of his unimpaired memory, he recounts the master’s praise.
Knowing place and time, he speaks even that which was not specifically instructed if it is appropriate for that occasion.
Being well-built and handsome, he speaks skillfully and appropriately because of his pleasing appearance. By the term "free from fear," it is meant that he speaks with proficiency.
Being eloquent, he is capable of providing a reply in response to a message.
He states the purpose for the effort to accomplish the qualities of an envoy that have been mentioned:
"The army depends upon the minister; the administration of justice depends upon the army; the treasury and the kingdom depend upon the king; and peace and its opposite depend upon the envoy."

The power of punishment (*daṇḍa*)— namely the force consisting of elephants and so forth— rests with the minister and the commander-in-chief, because it is by their will that action is undertaken in affairs. The power of discipline (*vainayikī*) rests with the power of punishment,
because whoever is to be disciplined, whether residing in one's own kingdom or in a foreign realm, must be punished.
That which relies on discipline is "disciplined";
it is an action or a duty;
[it occurs] when the treasury and the kingdom are under the control of the king.
The treasury is the place of accumulation;
the kingdom is the realm.
These two must not be left dependent on others, nor should one personally consume the fruit of the harvest before it has ripened.
Peace and its opposite depend upon the messenger.
Peace is achieved through pleasant speech and the demonstration of the master’s interests; war results from the reverse of these.
Both of these are dependent on the messenger.
Such is the messenger’s restatement of the matter;
this very point is stated again:
for it is the messenger alone who unites those who are divided and indeed breaks apart those who are united.
The messenger performs that action by which men are divided.
The messenger effects a reconciliation as instructed; he likewise causes those who have been reconciled and united to fall apart.
He conveys pleasant messages even when not requested, as well as disagreeable or improper ones, and so forth.
He says that gold and other such goods have not been promised;
thus the messenger creates a rift. This is the specific stratagem taught by which kings are divided.
Those who have committed verbal abuse arise in this manner.
He also shows another duty of a messenger:
"Through secret hints, gestures, and movements, he should discern the facial expression, the hint, and the gesture in this person's affairs, as well as what is intended among his servants."
Having understood in truth everything intended by the enemy king,
one should apply such effort as will not cause oneself suffering.
That messenger [was engaged] in the duties and affairs of King Yātavya.
He should dwell in a region that is arid yet rich in crops, predominantly inhabited by noble people, free from turmoil, delightful, with submissive vassals, and providing a means of self-sustenance.
One should establish a city by taking refuge in a desert fort, an earth fort, a water fort, a forest fort, a human fort, or a mountain fort.

A land-fort (*mahīdurga*) is one surrounded by a strong water-channel, raised twelve cubits or more with bricks or stone in the manner described above—having a height twice its width—with a base like a palm tree and a top built with *kapīśīrṣa* (beehive) masonry.
A water-fort (*abdurga*) is one encircled by unfathomable and accessible water.
A forest-fort (*vārkṣadurga*) is one covered on all sides for about half a *yojana* with dense, great trees.
A human fort supported by a fourfold army, consisting mostly of heroic men with excellent weapons,
situated on a mountain ridge that is difficult to ascend and accessible by only a single path, with water from internal rivers and springs— this is a mountain fort.
But with every effort, one should take refuge in a mountain fortress;
for, by virtue of its many advantages, the mountain fortress is distinguished above all others.
Among these, the first three are inhabited by wild animals, creatures dwelling in holes, and apsarases;
the latter three are inhabited, respectively, by monkeys, humans, and gods.
The first three are the fortresses of the bow and so forth; "resorted" means they have made them their refuge; "deer" refers to wild animals.
The *gartāśrayas* are those such as crocodiles and mongooses;
the *apsarās* are those such as crocodiles and tortoises.
This is for the purpose of demonstrating that whatever qualities and defects belong to these fortresses and the creatures inhabiting them, the same apply to kings as well.
The next three are:
monkeys, apes, and langurs.
Just as enemies do not harm those who have taken refuge in a fortress,
so too do foes not harm a king who has taken refuge in a fortress.
This verse concerns the purpose of constructing fortifications.
Even those with very little strength, if they take refuge in a fortress, cannot be easily overcome by enemies of great power; therefore, it is appropriate to take refuge in a fortress.
A single archer standing upon a rampart can fight a hundred; a hundred can fight ten thousand. Therefore, a fortress is established.
This purpose of a fort is well known:
by the analogy of a wall, it is said that this refers to the strength of a mountain fort (*giridurga*).
That is incorrect, because walls are also possible in the case of an earth fort (*mahīdurga*).
Therefore, the purpose of all difficult tasks is conceptualized by one's own intellect.
That [city] should be well-equipped with weapons, wealth, grain, and vehicles; it should also be provided with Brahmins, artisans, machines, fodder, and water.
"Equipped with weapons" means provided with swords, spears, and the like.
The mention of "weapons" is intended to indicate other implements of war as well, such as armor, helmets, and equipment.
"Wealth" refers to silver, gold, and so forth.
Vehicles are chariots, horses, and so forth;
by artisans such as those who operate machines, carpenters, and the like; and by means of fodder.
[They may be carried] by Brāhmaṇas, ministers, domestic priests, or others.
Sometimes they proceed with the assistance of royal authority, under the guise of a staff-bearing ascetic or out of fear of the royal standard.
Furthermore, because this is intended as an illustration, one should also consider physicians, medicines, and so forth.
One should cause to be kept ready whatever is useful for healing and other such purposes.
In its center, he should have his own house constructed—
spacious, well-protected, suitable for all seasons, bright, and provided with water and trees.
It was fully supplied,
being used for the king’s own royal treasury, armory, stables, and so forth;
it was well-guarded and possessed many chambers.
One should have a house built,
suitable for all seasons and adorned with flowers and fruits of every season— that is, a place where all seasons are present.
By the word *ṛtu* (season), its effects such as flowers, fruits, and so forth are indicated.
In the reading *sarvartuga*, the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) is "that which goes to or reaches all seasons" (*sarvān ṛtūn gacchati prāpnoti*);
however, the meaning remains the same.
Whatever exists in a certain place is said to be pervaded by that [place]. "Bright" means whitened with lime. "Endowed with water and trees" means provided with shower-houses, gardens, and groves.
Having occupied that [seat], he should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks,
born of a noble family, pleasing, and endowed with beauty and virtue.
Having taken possession of that house, a wife should be wedded from a great family for the sake of assistance therein;
this is for the purpose of protection through such a connection.
That [rule] beginning with "of the same class" (savarṇām) has already been shown previously.
"Charming" means delightful; "endowed with radiance and beauty" refers to form, which is the physical configuration;
"qualities" refers to speech, conduct, and so forth.
Endowed with, or joined to, those.
He should appoint a domestic priest and indeed choose officiating priests;
they shall perform for him the domestic rites as well as those pertaining to the sacrificial fires.

Even though there is an indication of the accusative case, the singular number is intended to be significant despite the lack of explicit emphasis on primacy, because it is specifically prescribed elsewhere, as in the cases "he cuts the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ chinatti*) and "he should take a wife" (*bhāryāṃ vindeta*).
One should choose the officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*).
And their number is to be understood from the scriptural text itself.
And as for the qualities [of the officiant]: he should be neither too stout nor too thin, neither too tall nor too short, neither too old nor too young;
he should have seven generations on both sides of his lineage established through learning, austerity, and meritorious deeds.
With regard to such persons, no suspicion of non-Brahminhood arises, as in the case of the rule "a learned man performs the sacrifice," and so forth.
The domestic rites are those such as propitiatory and auspicious ceremonies;
the sacrificial rites are those pertaining to the three sacred fires, which relate to the maintenance of the household fire.
The king should sacrifice with various kinds of rituals accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees;
and for the sake of dharma, he should bestow enjoyments and wealth upon the brahmins.
By means of the Pauṇḍarīka and other sacrifices characterized by abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*),
he [obtained] enjoyments (*bhoga*) and wealth (*dhana*).
"Enjoyments" refers to garments, perfumes, ointments, and so forth, as well as various kinds of food.
Wealth refers to gold and the like;
they desire that gift to be given constantly,
specifically for the sake of the Dharma and for the very purpose of its arising.
He should cause the annual tax to be collected from the kingdom by trustworthy men;
he should be devoted to the traditional rules in the world and behave toward his subjects like a father.
He should collect taxes, such as the sixth or eighth part of grain and other produce,
through trustworthy officials who have been proven pure by tests of wealth and other means;
and, as it has been stated, he should be devoted to the sacred tradition.
One should rely on treatises of logic that prioritize the sacred scriptures;
or else, one should accept only that portion which has come down through tradition and nothing more.
One should behave toward people as one would toward one's own father.
One should behave with a sense of affection toward other kings as well.
He should appoint various learned supervisors in their respective places;
they shall oversee all the affairs of the men as they carry out their work.
He should appoint superintendents—those authorized and overseers—who are of various kinds and many types: mild, fierce, righteous, and intent on the acquisition of wealth.

In those respective places, such as the treasury, the storehouse, and the various commercial and industrial works, he should station wise men as authorized overseers for the collection of customs duties, ships, elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, and so forth.

All these should be understood as being endowed with the qualities of a minister, as stated in the *Adhyakṣapracāra*. Those superintendents should oversee all the affairs of other men who perform duties pertaining to their respective positions: elephant-keepers by the Superintendent of Elephants, horses and the like by the Superintendent of Horses, and cultivation and so forth by the Superintendent of Cattle.
One should be a worshiper of those Brahmins who have returned from the teacher's house;
for this is called the imperishable Brahminic treasure of kings.
Those who have studied and understood the meaning of the Vedas in the teacher's household (gurukula) and desire to enter the state of a householder (gārhasthya) should be honored with wealth;
this too is a "regular gift" (naiyyamikadāna).
For this very reason, it is said that for kings, [such merit] is inexhaustible.
Because it is eternal, it is inexhaustible and lasts as long as life;
and because it is desired, it ceases when no fruit remains.
That which was described as "pertaining to the lineage" and "intended for sacrifice" is precisely this.
But others say:

in that [other context], giving is prescribed for those who request it; here, however, because the qualification applies even to those who do not request it, the honoring of men must be performed by means of the mere act of prescription and by the gift of pairs of garments and so forth.
Thus it is said: "He should be a worshiper of the Brahmins."
It is a treasure like a treasure because it yields the highest fruit;
it is "Brahmic" because it is in close proximity to Brahman.
Neither thieves nor enemies can carry it off, nor does it perish;
therefore, the king should deposit this inexhaustible treasure with the Brahmins.
Whatever wealth is given to brahmins, neither thieves such as forest-dwellers and the like, nor enemies and adversaries, can seize it;
nor does it perish through being forgotten or lost on account of a suretyship, as might happen with wealth kept in the ground.
It does not overflow, it does not fall away, and it never perishes;
that which is offered into the mouth of a Brahmin is superior to the Agnihotra sacrifices.
This very same point, which must necessarily be carried out, is stated again by way of another method:
that which is offered into the fire sometimes spills—that is, it falls down while being offered—or likewise the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and so forth may fall away due to being overcooked;
and consequently, through such deficiency in the ritual action, it perishes for the learned (*śiṣṭas*).
But as for this gift to Brahmins, these faults do not exist in it;
therefore he says it is "superior to the Agnihotras," meaning superior to the offerings made into the fire.
Since the word *agnihotra* here functions in its primary sense as the name of the ritual itself, the mention of "etc. (*ādi*) must then be explained accordingly.
"Offered in the mouth" (*mukhe huta*):
for the hand alone is the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa, according to the scriptural statement, "The twice-born is indeed remembered as having his mouth in his hands.
*Variṣṭha* means most excellent or supreme.
And this is a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda), not a censure of the oblation itself.

A gift given to one who is not a Brahmin yields an equal reward; to one who merely calls himself a Brahmin, it yields a twofold reward; to a teacher, a hundred-thousandfold reward; and to one who has mastered the Vedas, an infinite reward.
And "to the Brahmins" is the subject under discussion;
likewise, it was stated previously: "to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the true meaning of the Veda.
Furthermore, the attainment of the fruit of giving as heard in the scriptures would not otherwise be possible.
For what kind of similarity could there be—whether in terms of genus (*jāti*), quantity (*parimāṇa*), or utility (*upakāra*)?
If it were first in terms of genus, then food given to the gods with the intent of providing medicine would result only in suffering;
for medicines are generally bitter, pungent, and astringent, being purgatives rather than producers of pleasure.

Now, if it were by way of the atom, even there, if it were merely an equality of measure regardless of the substance, then if gold were given, one might receive copper of that same measure, or something else such as earth or wood.
Or, if it were by way of both genus and measure, the very same faults mentioned previously would apply.
Or, if it were by way of utility, even there, if the utility must be of that same genus—such as the utility of medicine being the cessation of disease—[then the same problems follow].
And since there is no fruit when there is no disease, the disease must be brought about by the giving of medicine which has the cessation of disease as its fruit;
or else, it follows that [the result] is simply another equal suffering.

Therefore, just as in the case of the rules "the *nivīta* is for humans, the *upavīta* is for the gods; he wears it over the shoulder, for he thereby makes it a mark of the gods," where the specific modes of wearing (*upavyāna*) do not constitute separate sentences from the *nivīta* and so forth, so too should this [present case] be understood.
To this it is replied:
there is no hearing of a verbal suffix here, because all [the words] are equal.
In that case, if it is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), let the phrase "a thousand [cows] to one who has mastered the Vedas" be that explanatory praise.
Now, as for this injunction: because it is supplementary to other injunctions, an injunction must be accepted everywhere, since there is no distinction [in that regard].

However, in the case of the *nivīta* and others, because the verb "he wears" (*upavyayate*) is observed here, and because its meaning lacks the fitness to be the object of an injunction, and because singularity is understood, it is just like the word *yukta*. Thus, no specific [rule] has been stated.
As for the claim that "there is no giving to non-Brāhmaṇas," that must have been forgotten, since giving to the poor, the helpless, and so forth from all social classes (*varṇa*) is ordained.
And these very sentences are the injunctions for the king’s giving to Brahmins.
As for what was said— that the attainment of the fruit as heard in scripture is untenable because it is accepted in every respect— it is replied to as follows:
This linguistic usage is worldly; that which is not exceedingly superior in the world is called "equal," as in the expression, "the barley meal is equal to salt.
And the mention of the number "double" is with reference to benefit: to whatever extent there is benefit for him, it becomes double.
It is not the attainment of that very substance, nor is it a benefit of that same kind; rather, it is the production of an excellence of joy.
Furthermore, there is no mention here of a specific fruit such that even this doubt might arise: "Is that very substance to be attained, or is it that very benefit?
In cases where no specific fruit is mentioned, heaven (*svarga*) is the fruit.
Furthermore, it is heard in scripture that the fruit of giving sesame seeds and other such items is [merely] a worldly acquisition (*prāpti*);
what room, then, is there for any suspicion regarding the equality of the substance?
Therefore, this point is also established: here, through the excellence of the recipient (*pātra*), an excellence of the fruit is achieved in each successive case.
And thus it is said: "Indeed, specifically regarding the recipient.
[The term] *brāhmaṇabruve* [is used];
the word *bruva* is used in the sense of contempt.
The meaning is that a "brāhmaṇa by birth alone" is one devoid of qualities such as Vedic study and so forth.
An "ācārya" is one who initiates [the student].
One who has "gone to the end of the Veda" (vedapāraga) is one who has reached the conclusion of the Veda through both study and hearing.
Indeed, depending specifically on the recipient and through the very nature of one's faith,
one enjoys the fruit of giving— whether it be small or great— after passing away.
A *pātra* (recipient) is so called because it causes one to fall away from unrighteous action (*adharmakarman*), or because it protects one who is falling; thus, it is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).

Alternatively, a *pātra* is a vessel for ghee, oil, and so forth; by metaphorical extension (*upacāra*), this [recipient] is also called a *pātra*, for in this case as well, a substance (*dravya*) is deposited within it.
And it is said: "This inexhaustible treasure of kings is indeed called the Brahman-treasure.
Its distinction (*viśeṣa*) or differentiation consists in its being with qualities (*saguṇa*) or without qualities (*nirguṇa*), and so forth;
by that cause, the fruit of giving is obtained.
Or, even if it is small:
what is given to one who possesses virtues and is endowed with good conduct and Vedic study is great, whereas what is given to one devoid of virtues is small;
likewise, it depends upon the degree of faith as well.
Whatever substance, endowed with faith, is given to a worthy recipient according to the rules of place and time— that is the means for accomplishing dharma.
In this context, "place" refers to a provincial region other than one's own place of residence.
Because she has departed for a distant land, his being nearby is the cause for giving;
it is the impairment [of the ritual] consisting in some deficiency of limb on the part of one engaged in a sacrifice.
The eclipse of a planet and so forth;
the ritual procedure;
the excellence of the purificatory rite consisting of the recitation of auspicious verses preceded by the offering of water; and the clarity of one's disposition, and so forth.
*Dravya* refers to cattle, land, gold, and so forth.

*Śraddhā* is an intense longing for attainment; it is a continuum of cognition (*buddhi-saṃtāna*) characterized by the thought, "How might this be removed from me? *Pretya* means "after passing away."

He states that there is no fixed rule regarding the arising of the fruit immediately after the action, but not because the fruit belongs exclusively to another birth; for in the case of Vedic rites, it is understood that the desire itself is restricted to the fruit [of this very life].
When challenged by those who are equal, superior, or inferior while protecting his subjects,
a king should not retreat from battle, mindful of the duty of a Kshatriya.
When all other means have been exhausted, war is ordained for a king.

In that context, this verse is intended to prohibit indifference on the part of one who has gone to the battlefield and has not been summoned, even if his own force is equal, inferior, or superior [to the enemy's].
He must not think, "I will not strike those of inferior strength."

Alternatively, when enemies such as forest-dwellers (*āṭavika*) and others, having transgressed the previously established boundaries, invade the country, or when they enter into an alliance with the king's enemies—if they cannot be restrained without war—then one must indeed fight them, even if their forces are inferior. Even if they have not been formally challenged by word, in reality they are indeed challenged;
for this is the duty (*dharma*) of Kṣatriyas: that when challenged by those who constitute the constituent elements of the state, one must fight against all of them in battle.
One should not take into account birth, age, training, personal effort, and so forth;
this is the Dharma that should be remembered.
Not retreating in battles, the protection of subjects,
and service toward Brahmins— this is the supreme means for the welfare of kings.
This verse is for the purpose of showing that these three factors have an equal result.
In battles, kings who desire to slay one another and fight with their utmost strength, never turning their backs, go to heaven.
Where other heroes are summoned for the sake of battle, that is an *āhava*, a conflict;
they are competing with one another, desiring to kill each other— that is, wishing to slay one another.
"Engaging in battle" means striking;
"with supreme power" (paraṃ śaktyā) means with the highest possible strength, that is, according to one's capacity. Due to Vedic usage, the form *param* occurs in place of *parayā*.
The connection is: "fighting without turning their backs, they go to heaven.
Now, one might object: since those who have engaged in battle do so out of greed for sovereignty, and since a visible result is possible [in that case], how can there be heaven?
It is said:
heaven is dependent upon the rules of combat to be described by the words "not with deceptive weapons" and so forth;
for those rules have no other purpose.

Alternatively, if defeat is certain, one who has lost all hope may still enter into battle; that too leads only to heaven, because even for one who has lost his kingdom, it is possible to survive by surrendering to a more powerful foe.
Therefore, the attainment of that fruit (heaven) is appropriate.
For this very reason, this case does not fall within the scope of the prohibition against self-surrender.
The rulers of the earth are lords of their respective mandalas, not, however, their dependents;
for the activity of the latter is solely for the sake of their master, not for their own sake.
Consequently, how could there be any possibility of fruit for them, being like officiating priests who have been hired for a fee?
In this way, how can there be the production of fruits such as heaven for these [kṣatriyas] who have been hired for wages?
But has it not been stated without distinction:
"For one slain in battle with uplifted weapons, and for one killed while following the duty of a kṣatriya..."?
"The sacrifice is immediately completed.
Likewise:
"There are these two persons in the world who pierce the solar orb:"
"A wandering ascetic engaged in yoga, and a hero slain while facing the enemy"—thus it is said. Likewise, in the *Mahābhārata*, heaven is shown even for those who merely witness the battle.
Furthermore, there are indicative marks within the mantras [to this effect].
Those who fight in the great battles, those heroes who abandon their bodies,
or those who give away thousands as sacrificial fees— may he go even to them.
Those who fight demonstrate the great fruitfulness for sacrificers who give a thousand-fold dakṣiṇā and for heroes who have surrendered their lives at the front of battle;
yet they do not act solely for the sake of death.

For at the time of formal selection (*saṃparigraha*), there is no such agreement as there is in the case of the *hotṛ*, *udgātṛ*, and others, whose selection is restricted solely to the performance of the priestly functions designated by their own specific titles.
Therefore, death that occurs for the sake of one's master’s business leads precisely to the aforementioned result;
nor is there an absence of fruit for another from an action instigated by someone else.
For, indeed, at the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), even one who is not the sacrificer is purified by bathing, even if he is a slayer of a Brahmin.
To this it is replied:
In a war for the sake of the subjects, the sacrifice of one's life is indeed for the sake of dharma.

As for what was said regarding those "with weapons raised in battle," that refers to one who is not independent because he has been hired for wages, or to one who has girded his loins with the thought, "O Kuru, set forth for the fray"—it is with reference to such a person that this statement concerning the sacrificial rite is made.
And being thus situated, he is "slain while facing the enemy.
Alternatively, for one who fights, the very absence of hell will be his "piercing of the solar disk.

In that case where the territory of another king is struck down, broken, or its people plundered by a king who is the lord of another realm, the sacrifice of life in battle for that purpose is for the sake of Dharma.
For there is blinding darkness in hell; because that [darkness] is absent, when there is light, there is the statement regarding the piercing of the solar orb.

"He pierces the solar orb" means that he reaches the worlds above and does not fall downward. For one who has been hired for wages, if he abandons his master when battle is at hand, there is a falling into hell. However, for one who fights for that purpose, having discharged his debt for his master's sustenance and being unimpeded by his own evil deeds, the attainment of heaven and other realms is indeed certain through his own merits.
Therefore it is said, "The sacrifice is completed immediately.
This means that without any interval, one attains heaven as the fruit of the sacrifice, according to the unqualified scriptural statement.
In this way, even in the *Mahābhārata*, the statement regarding the attainment of the fruit of heaven by those hired for wages becomes logically consistent.
As for the attainment of heaven for those who witness a battle, that is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
Alternatively, since there are many means of livelihood, heaven results as a necessary consequence specifically from living by the sword.

As for the claim that they are not hired for the sake of death: when wages are paid to those who bear arms, there is no purpose other than war, since no specific instruction to the contrary is given—they are hired with the understanding that "being prepared for all tasks, my purpose must be accomplished in every way. Therefore, when war presents itself, the master’s interest must be served even unto the fall of the body; in this way, one becomes free from debt. But if death occurs for the servant while war has not yet presented itself, then all are indeed free from debt.
For when he is engaged in that task, his agreement with it is exactly of that nature;
moreover, the observation of the indicative mark—that "at the time of battle, one must fight"—is indeed appropriate.

However, regarding the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), there is an explicit statement: "Therefore, at their meeting... Thus, [the rule applies] to the encounter.
But here, the distinction is that it is to be accomplished through battle.
He now demonstrates those rules whose purpose is transcendental (adṛṣṭārtha):
"While fighting his enemies in battle, he shall not strike them with deceptive weapons;
nor with barbed ones, nor with poisoned ones, nor with those having points blazing with fire."
*Kūṭas* are those which are made of wood on the outside but contain sharpened weapons within.
*Karṇins* are arrows whose tips are fashioned with ear-shaped blades at their base or middle.
For once they have entered, they become difficult to extract; when being pulled out, they pierce even that part of the body which was not already pierced by blows.
They are smeared with poison, meaning they are coated with venom. Their lances are made of fiery material, blazing and set ablaze with fire.
One must not fight with these.
One should not strike one who has mounted a vehicle, nor a eunuch, nor one with palms joined in reverence;
nor one with disheveled hair, nor one who is seated, nor one who says, "I am yours."
One standing in a chariot must strike only one who is mounted on a chariot; one standing on the ground must not be struck.
A *klība* is a eunuch or one devoid of manliness.
"Elsewhere" refers to one who is firmly seated, whether sitting upon the back of a chariot or on the ground.
One should not kill even that person who says, "I am yours.
Here, the specific word used is not intended to be restrictive;
one who speaks submissively—even with words of this kind such as "I am yours" or "I have taken refuge in you"—must not be killed.
One should not strike one who is asleep, nor one who is unarmored, nor one who is naked, nor one who is unarmed,
nor one who is not looking on, nor one who is engaged with another.
The reading is either "not naked" (na nagnam) or "not broken" (na bhagnam).
Since there is a prohibition against one who has cast off his armor, the case of one who is naked does not even arise.
Because he lacks a helmet and other such gear, and is naked in part, he should be regarded as "naked.

Furthermore, because even one who has turned away from his genitals is prohibited [from being attacked], if he says, "Even though I am facing you, I will not fight with you," he is not to be pursued with the thought that he must certainly be fought.
This applies to one who is not fighting while being watched.
He who is merely a spectator should not be killed;
however, there is no prohibition against one who both observes and fights,
having encountered an opponent.
One who is fighting with one person must not be struck down by another.

Recalling the dharma of the virtuous, one should not strike one who is suffering from the loss of weapons, nor one who is distressed, nor one who is severely wounded, nor one who is terrified, nor one who has turned away.

"Calamity regarding weapons" refers to distress caused by weapons, such as the breaking of a weapon, the warping of a sword into a ring-shape, the snapping of a bowstring, and so forth; having encountered such [a situation], one who is "distressed" (ārta) is one whose sons, brothers, or others have been slain.
Having recognized through the color of the face and other signs that [the enemy] is "frightened," even if he is facing him with his weapon raised—
"Parāvṛttam" means having turned back and standing [there].
These are the rules.
In the case of non-compliance, there is transgression.

And in that case, the statement regarding the attainment of heaven is a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). What, then, is the correct view here? That the prohibition is for the sake of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), as in the injunction: "One should not eat *kalañja*."
For in this way, the negative particle (*nañ*) functions in its primary sense:
"the dharma of the virtuous" means "this is the conduct of the learned," as he says by employing the word "remembering."
But he who, out of fear, turns his back in battle and is slain by enemies,
incurs all whatever evil deeds were committed by his master.
One should not think thus: "If one who has turned away is killed, then he is a wrongdoer, but if he is not killed, he is not.
What then? The statement regarding fault is based solely on the fact of having turned away.
Furthermore, one who has turned away and been killed should not entertain this thought: "I have experienced the blow of the sword; I am free from debt; I have fulfilled my duty to my master."
He demonstrates through the observation of an extreme fault that such blows are for no purpose whatsoever by stating, "the evil deed belonging to the master.
As for the statement later regarding the appropriation of his merit, that is a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*);
for good or evil performed by one person cannot possibly belong to another.
And there is no destruction of the well-performed deed;
rather, it is said that the fruit of the well-performed deed is delayed for a long time due to its being obstructed by a great evil deed.
Furthermore, whatever merit he has acquired for the sake of the next world,
his master takes all of that from one who is killed while retreating.
And whatever merit he has earned, his master takes it all away.
"For the sake of the hereafter" means that which is acquired for the purpose of the next world; one who possesses wealth (artha) is called "wealthy" (artha).
The suffix *ac* is applied because it belongs to the *arśas*-class [of nominal stems].

That purpose which was acquired for that world—that is, for "yonder" (*amutra*) or "in yonder world" (*amuṣmin loke*)—becomes fruitless for him; or rather, *amutrārtham* means "that which has its purpose in yonder world."
This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with different case-relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*), because it is intelligible and serves a specific purpose.
Chariots, horses, elephants, umbrellas, wealth, grain, livestock, women,
all types of property, and base metals— whatever one wins belongs to him.
Base metals, beds, seats, copper vessels, and so forth—
whatever anyone wins belongs to him.
Since it might follow from the king's ownership that he should take these, this [rule] is stated as an exception to that.
Residences on grounds of gold and silver, and so forth, belong to the king alone;
this is the enumeration for that purpose.
Weapons, vehicles, and so forth, also belong to the king alone.

Because grains and other such items are mentioned separately, the word "wealth" (dhana) refers here to cattle, buffaloes, and the like; likewise, people employ the expression "half of the king's wealth."
And they shall give a share to the king; such is the Vedic revelation.
And the king must give to all the warriors that which was not won individually.
Regarding the principle that "whatever has been won by someone should be taken by him," this specific rule is stated:

they should give the *uddhāra* (the share) to the king; the meaning is that having set aside the best portion of the goods, they should give it [to the king]. They must not take everything for themselves.
Thus says this Vedic revelation (*śruti*):

beginning with "Indra, having slain Vṛtra," and so forth, it continues, "Having become great, he said to the deities, 'Grant me a share'. Or, in the case of a king, when there is a separate victory or a self-acquired victory where such a division does not exist—wherein this village was conquered by one person and that neighbor or other belonged to another, and everything has been completely uprooted at once—in such a case, the servants are to be shared out by the king according to the principle of pacifying those who have obtained [booty].
This eternal warrior-dharma has been declared as unadorned;
a Kṣatriya, while slaying his enemies in battle, should not deviate from this dharma.
This is a summary:
"yodha" means warriors; their duty is "yodhadharma.
It is "anupaskṛta," meaning unblemished or irreproachable, or alternatively, unaltered.
Therefore Sanātana said:
"If it were set in motion by its own will, it would be subject to modification;
it would not fall away, nor would it move, but would persist at all times."
The mention of the Kṣatriya is intended to show that he is the primary person entitled to this [rite], and not to imply that this duty does not apply to anyone else who occupies his position.
One should seek to acquire what has not been acquired, protect with effort what has been acquired,
increase what has been protected, and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients.
A Kṣatriya should not be content like a Brāhmaṇa; rather, he should exert effort in acquiring what has not yet been acquired,
protect the wealth that has been acquired, and increase the wealth that has been protected.
One should accumulate a store of wealth;
from that, one should give to those who are worthy recipients,
rather than spending it in such a manner.
Thus it has been said: "Expenditure should be less than income."
One should know that this fourfold [dharma] has human purpose as its aim;
one should always perform its practice correctly and without sloth.
Whatever objects belong to a person, their purpose is fourfold;
in that regard, these four activities are to be employed: acquisition, preservation, increase, and giving.
The word *artha* denotes that which is beneficial.
This is the purpose for the sake of accomplishing the goals of human life;
one should perform the constant practice of those four types [of duties] as they have been set forth.
One should seek what is not yet obtained by means of force; protect what has been obtained with vigilance;
increase what has been protected through growth; and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients.
He should always have his rod of punishment raised, always display his prowess, always keep his secrets concealed, and always seek out the vulnerabilities of his enemy.
"One who has raised the rod" (*udyatadaṇḍa*) means one by whom the rod has been raised;
"raised" (*udyata*) means exerted, that is to say, engaged in activity.
In that regard, he should constantly discipline the force consisting of elephants and so forth through training exercises.
Training should be administered through riding, breaking, and so forth;
likewise, there should be practices for making [the animal] fit for work.
Furthermore, regarding such riding and activities, there is the application of dress, ornaments, grooming, and so on, as well as the readiness to wield the whip.
For one acting in this manner, his possession of the power of energy (*utsāha-śakti*) becomes manifest within the circle [of vassals].
Likewise, he is one whose manly effort (*pauruṣa*) is constantly displayed; "displayed" means that his duty has come to be manifest, having attained visibility.

At border passes, forest regions, and other such places, trustworthy men should be stationed; armored guards should be appointed there to remain constantly on watch. One must always keep oneself concealed and guarded.
Having kept one's own secrets hidden, that location must be made secure through both the winning over of others and the protection against the intrigues of enemies.
By constantly seeking out vulnerabilities and ascertaining the entire faction of the enemy's activities, one should immediately sow dissension among them.
The entire world trembles before one who constantly holds up the rod of punishment;
therefore, he should subdue all beings by means of that very rod.
The fruit of the immediate [action] is that the entire world trembles and fears,
and one becomes renowned for one's majesty.
Therefore, one should subdue all beings—both those of one's own nature and others—by means of punishment alone;
for when one exerts such effort, enemies, being terrified, submit without even further effort.
One should always conduct oneself with sincerity alone and never with deceit; remaining ever well-guarded, one should also recognize the deception employed by the enemy.
*Māyā* is deception; one should not act with it, for one would thus become untrustworthy. Nor should one instigate those who are of alien nature and whose true character is unknown.
One should understand, as it truly is, the deception employed by the enemy;
having understood it through discernment, one should carry out subversion.
In that regard, the faction of those who must be dealt with is fourfold.
By those who are angry, greedy, fearful, or insulted;
in that context, whoever has performed some craft or shown some service, those two [the employer and the employee] are deceived, or they are employed with favor, or they are insulted.
For that purpose, one who performs similar craft or service becomes angry, thinking: "This person's craft or service is not being utilized by us. Such people are susceptible to instigation.

Likewise, one who has been favored with affection but later fallen from honor and office; one whose kinsmen and favorites have been exiled while he himself was forcibly honored and accepted [into favor]; one who has been superseded by his own relatives; one whose entire property has been confiscated while another of equal conduct and learning is being honored and he is treated with contempt—such as these are the "angry" (kruddha) group. The "greedy" (lubdha) group consists of those such as: one against whom slander has been made by someone else; one punished for offenses similar to those of others; those stationed in all offices of authority who suffer the fall of their staff while wandering within [the palace]; and those whose wealth was suddenly accumulated [only to be lost]. These and others constitute the greedy class.
The "fearful class" consists of those who are impoverished, miserly, addicted to vices, heavily indebted, and so forth.

The "insulted class" consists of those who are self-important, those who have been denied honor due to their enemies, those humiliated by inferiors, the fierce, the reckless, those dissatisfied with their enjoyments, and so forth.
One should win over such people from the enemy's side and protect them for one's own.
An enemy should not discover one's own vulnerability, but one should discover the vulnerability of the enemy;
like a tortoise, one should withdraw one's limbs and guard one's own weak points.
This very point is stated again:
one should exert such extraordinary effort that one seeks out the vulnerabilities of the enemy while protecting one's own.
For if someone who is angry or otherwise compromised is discovered by spies such as fraudulent ascetics (*kāpaṭika*), he will be won over by his own side.
"One should hide one's limbs like a tortoise and protect one's own vulnerabilities;
guarding one's own weak points against the incitements of others is of great importance"—this is what he expresses by this [verse].
One should contemplate one's goals like a crane, display valor like a lion,
snatch away like a wolf, and flee like a hare.

Just as a crane, through the application of meditation and other yogic methods, attains a means to capture a school of fish—even those naturally residing in difficult-to-reach waters—by being intent on excluding them; so too, one should not fall into despondency, realizing that even goals extremely difficult to attain are reached through an exceptional application of effort in contemplating their purpose.

Just as a hare, because of its small body, is able to leap out even from atop a herd, so too a king, though alone and without allies, unable to remain when provoked by an uprising of neighbors on all sides, should escape from his fortress after inflicting a blow upon the enemy, seeking refuge with one who possesses virtuous qualities.

And just as a wolf, intent on seizing livestock, pounces upon them upon finding the keeper's negligence, so too, thinking "he is preoccupied with guarding himself," one must not abandon the effort to seize him; for that time will come when he will be pounced upon like a wolf.

Just as a lion kills even large-bodied creatures such as elephants through its possession of prowess, energy, and power, so too one should not fear a great force of enemies; for even one of little strength, if possessed of zeal, may sometimes slay one of great strength.
Thus, while he is victorious, whatever adversaries he may have,
he should bring them all under his control through the expedients beginning with conciliation.

Those who act as obstacles by way of opposition must be brought under control; however, those who act with favor should first be dealt with through conciliation and other such means, and not by force from the very outset.
If, however, they do not abide by it through the first three expedients,
he should gradually bring them under control by force alone, using punishment.
Regarding what was stated—that those who cannot be subdued by conciliation and the other [means] must be brought under control by force—it is this:
they are to be overcome by force, having been subdued gradually through such an application of punishment, and not through reckless violence.
Regarding the four means of policy beginning with conciliation, the wise always praise both conciliation and force for the perpetual prosperity of the kingdom.
Among the means of policy—conciliation and the others—to be described hereafter, conciliation and force are praised as being superior.
When conciliation is employed, there is no immediate upheaval; through force, however, all objectives are achieved.
Just as a reaper pulls out the weeds while protecting the grain,
so should the king protect his kingdom and slay those who stand as obstacles.
Those who plot against the king—their friends, kinsmen, or those who approach them through connection—should not be destroyed, provided they are not involved in that criminal act.
Only those who are actually wicked should be punished, not their associates; this is demonstrated by the analogy of the milkman.

Just as when grain and weeds grow together and are extremely intertwined, one carefully preserves the grain and removes the weeds, so too in one's own kingdom, even between those who are most intimate friends, only the one who possesses faults should be restrained, not the one who is well-disposed.
Therefore, through the discernment of the virtuous and the non-virtuous, the virtuous should be encouraged and the non-virtuous should be restrained.
The king who, out of delusion and through lack of foresight, oppresses his own kingdom,
shall soon be deprived of both his kingdom and his life, along with his kinsmen.

But that king who, failing to exercise the aforementioned discernment, out of delusion or negligence oppresses his own kingdom, shall soon fall from both his sovereignty and his life— due to the lack of affection among the people and the wrath of the subjects—
and he will be slain even by reckless individuals acting alone, regardless of their own lives.
Just as the vital breaths of living beings diminish through the emaciation of the body,
so too do the vital breaths of kings diminish through the emaciation of the kingdom.
One must generate intense affection within one’s own kingdom by being extremely vigilant;
for that [kingdom] stands in the place of the body.
Just as the life-breaths depart when the body is emaciated by unwholesome food, parching food, and so forth, so too do they depart from the emaciation of the kingdom.
He should always carry out this regulation for the consolidation of the kingdom;
for a king whose kingdom is well-consolidated prospers in happiness.
Gathering is the method of protection.
That king by whom his own kingdom is well-gathered—meaning brought under control or protected through the method of protection—thrives in happiness.
He should establish a *gulma* (military outpost) in the midst of two, three, or five [villages],
and likewise he should organize the collection of taxes for hundreds of villages throughout the kingdom.
Between two villages, one should establish a *gulma* (military outpost). A *gulma* is a group of men for protection; one should establish a station (*saṃgraha*) presided over by that very [outpost].
It is appropriate that one should make the person the presiding authority;
here, the "possessor of authority" (adhikārī) is what is meant by "collection" (saṃgraha).
This applies likewise to groups of three and five.
Alternatively, *saṃgraha* is the place where objects intended for the king are collected.
He should appoint a lord of a village, as well as a lord of ten villages, a lord of twenty, a lord of a hundred, and likewise a lord of a thousand.
In each individual village, one should appoint a headman;
above him, a lord of ten villages;
and so it should be everywhere.
The village headman himself should gradually report any faults that have arisen in the village to the leader of ten villages;
the leader of ten should report them to the leader of twenty.
The lord of twenty should report all of that to the lord of a hundred;
the lord of a hundred villages, in turn, should personally announce it to the lord of a thousand.
Those village faults which cannot be remedied by the official in charge of a single village should be reported to the lord of ten villages (*daśeśa*).
If he is likewise unable [to resolve them], it should be notified up to the lord of a thousand (*sahasrapati*).
Whatever items are to be paid daily by the village dwellers to the king,
such as food, drink, fuel, and so forth, the village headman shall receive those.

This is the livelihood for one appointed over a village. The village headman (*grāmika*), being the official in charge of the village, shall receive those [shares]; that is, he shall take them for his own maintenance from what must be given to the king by the villagers, such as food and so forth, consisting of the sixth or eighth part of the grain and other produce.
As he will say: "One-eighth [of the tax] on grain," and so forth.
The superintendent of ten should enjoy the family of one; the superintendent of twenty, five families; the superintendent of a village, a village; and the lord of a thousand villages, a city.
One who is appointed over ten villages is a *daśī*;
likewise a *viṃśī*. This is a Vedic formation of the word.
A *kula* is a portion of a village, known in some places as a *haṭṭa* and in others as an *uṣṭa*. One who is appointed over twenty villages has these five units as his jurisdiction;
one who is the superintendent of a hundred villages has authority over all of them.
"The Lord of a Thousand shall provide sustenance for the city and the town according to their respective positions and duties; this is the truth."
Indeed, another minister of the king— one who is learned, affectionate, and vigilant— should oversee their village affairs as well as their individual matters.

When they disagree with one another regarding village affairs, another person— someone who is capable in his own work, a trusted advisor, most eminent, affectionate, and free from passion and hatred— should be appointed to oversee the matter.
And in every city, one should appoint a single overseer of all affairs,
stationed in a high place, formidable in appearance, like a planet among the stars.
"High station" means preeminent;
"of terrible form" means majestic.
Like Mars among the stars, he was endowed with a force consisting of elephants, horses, and so forth.
He himself should always personally inspect them all;
he should thoroughly ascertain their conduct in the realms through spies who move among them.
That city official should patrol all those districts with his own force and fill them [with his men] when there is a need;
he should thoroughly oversee the conduct of all those chiefs and correctly understand their true nature.
By whom?
By royal spies, such as fraudulent ascetics and others.
For the king's appointed guardians are generally deceitful servants who seize the property of others; therefore, he should protect these subjects from them.
Those whose character is to take the property of others are "appropriators of others' wealth"—deceitful and acting improperly; they generally become persons in positions of authority.
Even those who were previously pure protect their own riches;
therefore, one should not overlook them merely by inferring their prior purity, but should instead watch over them with great effort.
He should protect these subjects from them;
for by such negligence, not only is the king's wealth destroyed, but he even reduces the subjects to poverty.
Those of evil intent who should take only wealth from litigants,
the king shall confiscate their entire property and carry out their banishment.

Those appointed as guardians who, under the pretext of a mere trifle, inflict fines upon the subjects from litigants, litigants themselves, or businesspeople, the king shall subject them to confiscation of all property and banishment.
He should provide daily maintenance for women and servants engaged in royal service, according to their rank and the nature of their work.
He should provide daily maintenance for those women employed in the inner apartments, such as maidservants,
and for the class of servants, such as palanquin-bearers;
he should not give them a village or a portion thereof once a year.
"According to the position and the work":
"Position" refers to the primary assignment, such as guarding the bed and so forth; "work" refers to physical activity. The livelihood should be granted in accordance with these two.
In a primary position, even if the work is small, the livelihood should be large; in a low position, even if the work is great, it should be small. This is what is appropriate for both.
A paṇa shall be given as wages for a low-ranking servant, and six for a high-ranking one;
likewise, clothing shall be provided every six months, and a droṇa of grain every month.

The *avakṛṣṭa* (lowest class) is one employed in sweeping and cleaning; for his food, one *paṇa* shall be given. For the *utkṛṣṭa* (highest class), after every six months have passed, clothing shall be provided, and one *droṇa* of grain shall be given monthly.
Four āḍhakas make one droṇa.
He will state the measure of a paṇa later;
these [measures] are for the purpose of determining a livelihood.

Having carefully considered the buying and selling, the distance traveled, the food along with its incidental expenses, and the security of the goods, the king should cause the merchants to pay taxes.
The procedure for seizing property:

an examination of purchase and sale such as—"For what price was this bought? What does it fetch when sold? In what length of time is it sold? To what extent is it lost through negligence, or not?"—as well as the distance and whether it is reachable by travel in a long or short time.
Food refers to the root [of sustenance], such as parched grain, boiled rice, and so forth.
"Expenditure" (*parivyaya*) refers to the requisites for that food, such as clarified butter, soup, vegetables, wealth, and so on.
"Security" (*yogakṣema*) refers to the absence of fear of kings or thieves, or the presence of safety from thieves, for one traveling through a forest or a wilderness.
With reference to this, taxes should be collected from the merchants;

the reading "vaṇigbhir dāpayet karān" (he should cause the merchants to pay the taxes) is appropriate, because the designation of the object (*karmasaṃjñā*) does not apply due to the restriction [of the rule] regarding verbs of motion and the like.
Alternatively, the verbal root has the meaning of "punishing"; in that case, it possesses two objects, just as the verb "to punish" (*daṇḍ*) does.
Just as water-creatures, young calves, and bees consume their food little by little,
so should the king take from his kingdom an annual tax that is small and small.
This is for the purpose that a reduced tax should be collected from one whose cultivation has been exhausted;
"vāryokas" means leeches;
"ṣaṭpadāḥ" means bees.
Just as they become well-nourished by taking only a small amount, so too the king must not cut off their very roots.
Having considered how both the king and the performers of actions may be joined with their respective fruits,
the monarch should always determine the taxes in his realm accordingly.
He says this very thing:
the agent of actions—whether a merchant or a king—should be joined with the fruit; likewise, he should establish taxes.
There is no cause for a restriction on their amount.
Where there is a great gain, one should take even more than that, even by exceeding the stated limit.
The king shall take a fiftieth part of livestock and gold;
of grain, an eighth, a sixth, or even a twelfth part.
A fiftieth part should be taken from cattle and gold of high value.
Regarding grains, the specific share should be understood in consideration of whether they are easy or difficult to process.
"Fifty" means that which completes fifty.
In the case of the rule "from twenty and so forth," the suffix *tamaṭ* is applied;
however, if the reading is *pañcaśadbhāgaḥ*, it is a different number, like *dvibhāga* and others.
Furthermore, he may take a sixth part of trees, meat, honey, and clarified butter,
as well as of perfumes, medicinal herbs, juices, flowers, roots, and fruits.
By the word *druma*, trees are meant;
the rest is well known.
One-sixth part of these should be taken from the profit.
Of leaf-vegetables, grasses, skins, split-bamboo articles, earthenware vessels, and everything made of stone;
Even when dying, a king shall not take a tax from a Śrotriya;
nor shall a Śrotriya dwelling in his kingdom perish from hunger.
He should act in such a way that a learned Brahmin does not suffer from hunger within his realm.
In whose kingdom a learned scholar perishes from hunger,
his kingdom likewise perishes from that same hunger before long.
This is the fruit of transgressing the immediate injunction.
Having ascertained his learning and conduct, he should provide him with a livelihood in accordance with dharma;
and he should protect him in every way, like a father protects his own biological son.
A righteous livelihood— that by which the duty of maintaining the family is not undermined—
having arranged such a livelihood, he should protect it from all sides against thieves and others, as well as from his own excessive expenditure.
Whatever dharma he performs daily while being protected by the king,
by that the king’s lifespan, wealth, and kingdom increase.
This is the fruit of protecting those who follow the Dharma and the Vedic tradition: the increase of lifespan, wealth, and the kingdom.
Whatever little the king may cause to be paid by commoners in his realm who live by trade, even if it is designated as "tax" (kara), it is known as the annual tribute.

One should cause a tax to be paid to a *brāhmaṇa* who is a learned *śrotriya* from a commoner (*pṛthagjana*)—that is, one other than such a *brāhmaṇa*—who lives by means of worldly activities such as agriculture, the investment of wealth, buying, and selling.
Because the designation "tax" (*kara*) has arisen for him, he is called "one characterized by tax" (*karasaṃjñita*).
The lord of the earth should cause artisans, craftsmen, and Śūdras who subsist by their own labor to perform work for one day each month.
He shall compel those who subsist solely by their craft,
as well as Śūdras who support themselves [by manual labor], such as porters and carriers, to perform work for one day every month.
One should not cut off one's own root nor that of others through excessive greed;
for by cutting off one's own root, one afflicts both oneself and them.
The non-collection of taxes such as the hand-fee (*kara*) results in the cutting off of one's own root; the collection of excessive amounts results in [the cutting off] of others' roots.
And that [occurrence] arises from craving; this is a restatement.
Through the cutting off of one's own root, self-affliction occurs due to the depletion of the treasury.
Therefore, they too are afflicted;
when war has arisen, one whose treasury and power are exhausted will inevitably be overpowered by enemies during the effort to extricate himself,
and that constitutes a great affliction for them.
However, for one who ensures the collection of taxes at all times, there is no distress caused by them.
A lord of the earth should be both severe and mild after considering the task at hand;
a king who is both severe and mild becomes esteemed.
Sharpness and gentleness must be constantly practiced;
such a king becomes esteemed and beloved by his subjects.
When exhausted by overseeing the affairs of men, the king should appoint a chief minister— one who knows the Dharma, is wise, self-controlled, and of noble birth— to that seat.
Wearied by observing the affairs pertaining to his subjects, he should remain tranquil;
he should appoint a minister endowed with qualities such as knowledge of dharma and the like— one who endures all burdens— to oversee those affairs,
and not [himself] upon that very throne.
Having thus performed all these duties incumbent upon himself,
he should protect these subjects, remaining both disciplined and vigilant.
The term "thus" (*evam*) refers back to the meaning previously stated, beginning with the gathering of companions.

Having performed (*vidhāya*) or having done (*kṛtvā*) that which is to be done—the helpful act—is what is called "that which is to be done. One who is "engaged" (*yukta*) is one who is devoted to that.
For this very reason, he should be vigilant;
or rather, vigilance at all times consists in the non-lapsing of his intellect.
In this manner, he should protect his subjects.
He from whose kingdom the subjects are being carried away by bandits while they cry out for help— even though he watches with his servants— he is dead and does not truly live.
He states the fault in the failure of the two aforementioned forms of vigilance:
if he does not remain alert toward the various vulnerable points (*gulma-sthāna*), then the subjects will be carried off by bandits and thieves who seek out such weaknesses;
what will he do for them?
Therefore, such a king is as good as dead;
life itself is death.
For this reason, one must remain vigilant.
Crying out and wailing,
they are being carried away while he watches; though it has been pointed out that he will see it,
his servants merely look on, they do not run after him nor do they rescue them.
They are all as if dead.
The supreme duty of a Kṣatriya is indeed the protection of his subjects;
for a king who enjoys the prescribed fruits of his office is joined with righteousness through that very act.
The king enjoys the fruit he has obtained; he is joined with righteousness. Otherwise, by merely providing protection for those who favor him, he incurs guilt.
Having risen during the final watch of the night, having performed his purifications with a concentrated mind,
and having offered oblations into the fire and honored the Brahmins, he should enter the auspicious assembly hall.
The final watch [of the night] is the Brāhma-muhūrta;
therefore, he says: "having performed purification, being composed in mind, and having offered oblations into the fire."
Furthermore, there is no injunction for the fire-oblation (homa) during the Brāhma-muhūrta;
for at that time, four muhūrtas still remain of the night,
and the oblation must be performed after the night has dawned, by omitting the portion corresponding to the break of dawn.
Having honored and worshipped the Brahmins, he should enter the auspicious and blessed assembly hall.
Remaining there, he should bid farewell to all his subjects with joyful greetings;
and having dismissed all his subjects, he should deliberate together with his ministers.

Remaining there in that assembly hall, he should greet the subjects who have come for an audience, gladden them with appropriate conversation, looking upon them, rising from his seat, and salutation, and then dismiss them, granting them leave to depart as they came.
Then, when they have been dismissed, he should deliberate with his ministers on what ought to be done.
The fivefold nature of counsel, which consists in determining the duties pertaining to one's own kingdom and those of foreign kingdoms, will now be shown.
Having ascended a mountain ridge or a palace, or having gone to a secluded place,
or in a forest free from undergrowth, he should deliberate unobserved.
The procedure for teaching the mantra:
Having gone into seclusion and staying in a solitary, uninhabited place,
one should act in such a way that one remains unobserved— even by inference— so that people do not know, "This thing exists."
"Niḥśalākam":
*śalākā* means reeds or stalks;
that place where there is not even a blade of grass, such that there is no possibility of anyone staying there, is *niḥśalākam*.

These are the constituent elements of undertakings: the means of commencement, the excellence of personnel and materials, the division of place and time, the remedy for setbacks, and the accomplishment of the task.
Alternatively, one should not let the time for action pass by, for in that case the deliberation would be protracted.
One should not disclose these [elements] to others, and thus the counsel remains secret.
That king who, even if devoid of treasury, is not known by ordinary people when they have assembled [to oppose him], enjoys the entire earth.
This verse is for the purpose of excluding those who reveal mantras;
ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are those who do not possess mantras and are outside the knowledge of mantras.

At the time of reciting the mantra, one should purify those who are dull-witted, mute, blind, or deaf; those born as animals; those past their youth; women; barbarians; the diseased; and the deformed.
Whatever living beings there may be, he should purify them while reciting the mantra; he should remove them from that location for fear of the disclosure of the mantra.
For even among animals, such as parrots and mainas, they too disclose the mantra.
Even cows, horses, and other such creatures who have ascended to yoga and changed their class (*nikāya*) become carriers of news, whether true or false.
Likewise, other royal sciences such as invisibility and so forth are also heard of.

Since their inclusion is already established by the term "deficient" (*vyaṅga*) itself, the mention of the others is like the expression "cattle and bulls" (where the bulls are mentioned despite being included in "cattle").

One need not entertain the concern that a mantra might fail for one who is not deficient if his hands, feet, or other limbs are severed—thinking, "He is unable to go anywhere; he remains confined right here, so how could he break the mantras?"—for [the rule applies to those who are otherwise whole].
