Alternatively, such ministers should not be appointed because of the possibility of delusion of intellect;
therefore, they are not even trustworthy, and for that reason, one must keep them at a distance.
Those who are despised, as well as animals and especially women, betray a secret; therefore, one should be careful in that regard.

Those who are devoid of pride and have been humiliated—such as the lowly and others—are sometimes capable of hearing something when there is a lack of respect, and sometimes they may be able to utter syllables; from that, there could be a breach of the mantra.
Furthermore, those who are clever are able to infer something from the scriptures (*āgama*).
At midday or at midnight, being rested and free from fatigue,
one should contemplate the goals of dharma, kama, and artha, either together with others or alone.
One should contemplate the mutual opposition among the factors beginning with dharma;
when any one of them increases, it will overcome all others.
The acquisition of those things that are mutually contradictory,
the giving away of daughters in marriage, and the protection of sons.
The acquisition and gathering of those who pursue dharma, artha, and kāma, or of ministers;

the giving away of daughters in marriage according to the requirements for accomplishing one's own objectives; and the protection of princes, that is, the sons of the king—these matters are to be considered.
By means of such expressions as "We are yours," you should cause them to grasp both the Dharma and its purpose.
For a new substance, whatever kind of object it is smeared with, that very thing it absorbs;
likewise, those whose minds are unconditioned first grasp whatever is said to them.
If they associate with the wicked, then their own nature becomes like that of those [wicked ones].

And being smeared with the impressions of evil conditioning (*duḥsaṃskāra*), they cannot be turned back from calamities. As it has been said: "Upon a garment dyed blue, a cosmetic of saffron is difficult to apply."
Therefore, they should be constantly instructed. Among them, those who possess virtues he should cause to increase;
the others he should provide with a small share.
One should consecrate the eldest son, who possesses great virtues and is free from envy, as the crown prince;
thus, one must always be diligent in the protection of the prince.
The dispatching of messengers, as well as the remaining tasks to be performed,
the conduct within the inner apartments, and the activities of the secret agents.
He should consider by whom reconciliation or even war should be undertaken, and by whom the dispatch of an envoy should be planned;
he should deliberate on the connection with the enterprise already begun for the sake of its stabilization.
Guarded by the troops of the inner court (*antaḥvaṃśika*), he should enter the inner apartments (*antaḥpura*) from the various enclosures (*kakṣā*).
In that regard, the Elder should observe whether the queen is pure or impure.
For a brother, while hidden within the queen’s chamber, killed King Bhadrasena; and a son, remaining inside his mother’s bedchamber, killed the Karūṣa king.
With an anklet smeared with poison, the queen killed Vairantya; with a girdle, she killed the Sauvīra king; and with a weapon concealed in her braid of hair, she killed Vidūratha.

Therefore, one should diligently examine these points of vulnerability. One should prohibit the association of the women of the inner apartments with shaven-headed ascetics, those with matted hair, and sorcerers, as well as with outside female slaves.
Furthermore, one should deliberate upon the activities of spies, mendicants, and others through a succession of secret reports.
He should understand in truth the entire eightfold business and the five classes [of officials],
as well as loyalty and disloyalty, and the conduct of the circle of states.

Undertaking what has not been begun, the performance of what has been begun, the excellence of the performance, and the non-accumulation of the fruits of action; likewise, conciliation, sowing dissension, bribery, and force—this is the eightfold action. Alternatively, it consists of trade routes, the building of waterworks and embankments, the construction of fortresses, the maintenance and repair of those already built, the capture of elephants, the digging of mines, the settlement of uninhabited lands, and the clearing of timber forests.
Others, however, say:
In taking and in giving, likewise in commanding and in forbidding,
in the fifth [matter] regarding the expression of meaning, and in the observation of legal proceedings;
Constantly engaged in the purification of punishment, that king who possesses the eightfold course and performs the eight duties goes to heaven, honored by his enemies.
These are the two verses of Auśanasa.
In this context, "appropriation" (*svīkaraṇa*) refers to the taking of taxes;
"bestowal" (*visarga*) refers to the giving of wealth to servants.
An *praiṣa* is the abandonment of what is harmful.
A *niṣedha* is the restraint of excessive activity among those entrusted with affairs.
And a *arthavacana* is the prohibition of improper activity.
The supervision of legal proceedings when there is doubt regarding the specific duties of the social classes (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas);
the infliction of punishment upon those who mutually accuse one another and upon those who have been defeated;
and the performance of penance for errors committed through negligence—this constitutes the eightfold duty.

The group of five consists of spies disguised as fraudulent scholars (*kāpaṭika*), ascetics who have renounced worldly life (*udāsthitaka*), householders (*gṛhapati*), merchants (*vaidehika*), and forest-dwellers (*tāpasa*).
Fraudulent scholars are students who are bold and well-versed in the secrets of others.
Having won them over with wealth and honor, the minister should say to them: "Taking both the king and me as your authority, you must report immediately whatever is unwholesome wherever it occurs."
One who has returned from the life of renunciation is called an *udāsthita*.
Being endowed with wisdom and purity, he should cause work to be performed on land capable of providing all kinds of food, provided with abundant gold and disciples.
And from the fruits of the agricultural labor, he should provide food, clothing, and shelter for all renunciants.

Among them, those who desire a livelihood, he should instigate with these words: "In this very manner, the king’s business must be carried out by you; and at the time for food and wages, you must present yourselves.
All renunciants should likewise instigate their respective groups.
A farmer whose livelihood is exhausted, yet endowed with wisdom and purity, is one who bears the guise of a householder (*gṛhapati-vyañjana*).
He should perform agricultural work on the land as previously described.
One whose livelihood is exhausted who engages in trade, being endowed with wisdom and purity, is a spy in the guise of a merchant (*vaidehika-vyañjana*).
He should perform the work of a merchant on the designated land; the rest is the same.
A shaven-headed man or one with matted hair, desiring a livelihood, should assume the guise of an ascetic.

Near a city, having many disciples with matted hair and shaven heads, he should publicly eat a handful of vegetables or barley once a month under the pretext of religious duty, while secretly consuming food as he pleases.
His disciples, also disguised as ascetics, should honor him with well-known yogic practices.

The disciples should first announce the acquisition of wealth, and then predict a fire, danger from thieves, the execution of a wicked person, or news from abroad, saying: "This will happen today or tomorrow," or "The king will do this.
His secret agents, dispatched for that purpose, should bring those things to pass.

Furthermore, there are spies among his subjects who must necessarily be supported, who study the science of marks (*lakṣaṇavidyā*), the science of limbs (*aṅgavidyā*), the science of sorcery (*jaṃbhakavidyā*), the art of illusion (*māyāgata*), the duties of the religious orders (*āśramadharma*), and the knowledge of omens (*nimittajñāna*).
In that regard, the king should establish these five types of persons within his own territory with the assistance of these ministers.

Among the ministers, chaplains, generals, crown princes, gatekeepers, chamberlains, and others, he should dispatch secret agents (*sattrins*) who are experts in correct designations, dress, crafts, and languages, under the pretext of being commoners.

Likewise, hunchbacks, dwarfs, Kirātas, the mute, the dull-witted, the deaf, the blind, actors, dancers, singers, and so forth, as well as women who move about in the inner apartments, forest-dwellers in the wilderness, and villagers in the countryside, should be employed for the purpose of male activities, each engaged in their own respective series of tasks.
These [five types of spies] should recognize one another as such;
they are established as moving and non-moving, secret and openly designated.
Having thus organized the fivefold group, one should ascertain the loyalty or disloyalty of the enemy and of oneself through this very fivefold group consisting of ministers, priests, and others.
In that manner, the conduct within the royal circle should proceed; [the king should determine] which vassal is concerned with peace, war, and so forth, and in what specific activity each is engaged.
One should diligently investigate the conduct of the middle king, the activities of the conqueror,
the movements of the neutral king, and those of the enemy as well.

In this circle of kings (*rājamaṇḍala*), these four primary royal constituents (*rājaprakṛti*) are principal: the seeker of conquest (*vijigīṣu*), the enemy (*ari*), the middle king (*madhyama*), and the neutral king (*udāsīna*).

Among them, that king who is endowed with the constituent elements and has risen up, thinking "I shall conquer such a world," is the seeker of conquest (*vijigīṣu*) by virtue of his possession of the power of energy (*utsāhaśakti*).
The enemy is of three kinds: natural (*sahaja*), ordinary (*prākṛta*), and artificial (*kṛttrima*).
The "intermediate" (madhyama) is one who is capable of suppressing both the enemy and the conqueror when they are not united, but not when they are united.
The "neutral" (udāsīna) is one who is capable of suppressing the enemy, the conqueror, and the intermediate king when they are not united, but not when they are united.
In brief, these are the constituent elements that form the root of the circle of states;
eight others are likewise enumerated, and thus they are traditionally remembered as twelve.
These are remembered;
these root natures (mūlaprakṛti) of the maṇḍala have been explained,
as well as eight others.
Of these four constituent elements, each single element has two [related] elements—namely, a friend and an enemy.
These eight, together with the original four, thus become twelve on both sides.
There are five others known as the minister, the kingdom, the fortress, the treasury, and the army;
these are each described briefly, totaling seventy-two.
The five constituents, beginning with the ministers, belong to each one of the twelve constituents.
Therefore, six times twelve makes seventy-two.
Immediately after [the conqueror], one should know the enemy and likewise the one who serves the enemy; next to the enemy is the friend, and beyond those two is the neutral party.
One should know the enemy to be separated from the territory of the seeker of victory by one intervening state, as well as the enemy’s friend and the friend of that friend.
In this way, the territory separated from the enemy by one intervening state becomes the friend of the seeker of victory;
the neutral power is beyond those two.
And the characteristics of enemies and friends should be observed in both the innate and the acquired types.
He should win over all of them by means of conciliation and other such measures,
whether employed individually or collectively, as well as through personal prowess and statesmanship.
He should reconcile and bring [the enemy] under control;
the two human methods are indeed conciliation (*sāma*) and force (*daṇḍa*).
And regarding this, it has been said: "They praise conciliation and force."
One should always deliberate upon the six measures of policy: peace, war, marching, halting, dividing the army, and seeking refuge.

In this regard, peace (*saṃdhi*) is for the purpose of benefiting both [parties] through the giving of gold and other gifts; war (*vigraha*) is its opposite; marching (*yāna*) is the act of going toward a single objective; staying quiet (*āsana*) is indifference; double-dealing (*dvaidhībhāva*) is the simultaneous adoption of both peace and war; and seeking refuge (*saṃśraya*) is surrendering oneself to another. These are the six measures of policy (*ṣadguṇāḥ*).

Among these, whichever quality he considers himself capable of employing—such as building fortifications, capturing female elephants, excavating mines, establishing trade routes, felling the Jatuvana forest, or reclaiming lands in regions not dependent on rain—he should adopt that quality for the purpose of seizing the enemy's wealth and for the sake of frustrating the enemy's intellect.
This being the case,
having carefully considered the task at hand, one should employ sitting encampment, marching, alliance, and war, as well as double-dealing and seeking protection.
Having made an alliance with one [king], he should falsely dispute with another who is capable [of providing aid].
Likewise, having both allied and disputed,
he should employ all these actions after having carefully considered the task at hand.
There is no fixed time for this;
whenever one considers it appropriate, at that very moment one should perform it.
If a restriction of time cannot be determined, what is the purpose of the instruction?
He spoke thus: "A distinction is difficult to perceive, whereas a generality is easy to perceive;
even this is useful for the ignorant."
A king should know that alliance and war are each of two kinds;
likewise, marching and sitting encamped are both twofold, as is the practice of seeking refuge.
When the undertaking of the journey is common to both parties, and likewise when it is the opposite,
that peace should be known as having two characteristics and being connected to the future.

We share the same vehicle; we shall go together as equals toward the fruit of that vehicle, sharing in its results equally, and you must not overstep me. Whatever is gained from that shall belong to both you and me.
Alternatively, "You go one way, and I shall go another"—thus, when the action of traveling together is not shared, it is the opposite case.

War is traditionally held to be of two kinds: that waged by oneself for the sake of one's own purpose, either at the improper time or at the proper time, and that waged because of an injury inflicted upon a friend.

The time for a personal war (*svayaṃ-vigraha*) is when one is necessarily able to draw out the enemy by means of one's own strength; when one is endowed with energy, one’s subjects are united and prosperous, successful in their respective tasks such as agriculture and the like, and will thus deprive the enemy of his undertakings; when the enemy’s subjects have lost their livelihoods and can be turned to one’s own side through instigation—this is the time for a personal war. The opposite of this is the wrong time.
Even in that case, war may be undertaken for the sake of harming an ally.
If one's ally has been harmed by the enemy, then, having reflected upon that, war should be waged even at an improper time.
Even if one is oneself the immediate neighbor of the enemy, nevertheless, with that ally as a helper, it is possible to repel the enemy.
One who is the immediate neighbor of the enemy is an ally, whereas the enemy of the enemy is the one whose territory is adjacent to the enemy's.
According to another reading, "and when an injury is done by a friend": if he (the king) is oppressed by that [enemy] because of it, then war should be waged even out of season.
This twofold nature of war is for the sake of one's own purpose and for the sake of a friend's purpose.
Alternatively, one type [of policy] arises from one's own prosperity, while the second occurs when a friend has been wronged and is in distress.
When an urgent matter arises by chance,
marching alone or in alliance with a friend is said to be the two-fold way of marching.
Traveling either alone or in a group constitutes the two-fold nature of travel.
One should travel alone when one has the capacity; otherwise, one should travel in a group.
An urgent matter refers to the occurrence of a calamity for another.
For at that time he becomes most worthy of being approached;
but later, once he has attained some elevation, he becomes difficult to bring down.
When one's power has gradually diminished due to fate or past actions,
or out of regard for a friend, neutrality (āsana) is said to be of two kinds.
The seat is self-restraint.
That too is twofold:
for one who has declined, it consists in providing strength and resources; for one who has prospered, it consists in maintaining vigilance toward the enemy.
And he should wait upon his seat out of consideration for his friend.

If a friend who has been depleted by an enemy does not enter into such an alliance, and [the king thinks], "This [enemy] should not be encouraged by my friend," then he should remain there in accordance with that [friend's] conduct.
And that depletion—whether caused by fate or by past deeds—is merely a restatement.
By this cause, the increase and decrease of everything occur.
In that regard, "fate" consists of one's own past negligence, a habit of excessive expenditure, a lack of vigilance regarding one's own strength,
and even previously committed unwholesome karma.
Or rather, this should be explained by way of inversion;
"from delusion" (mohāt) is an alternative reading,
but its meaning has already been explained by the word *daiva*.
The dual state of both the army and the lord for the sake of accomplishing the objective is proclaimed as "duplicity" (dvaidhībhāva) by those who know the qualities of the sixfold policy.
The maintenance of the army and that of the master are distinct:
the master of the fort [is maintained] with a small force, while the commander-in-chief is joined with a large force elsewhere.

Alternatively, some measure should be taken to favor the army by means of oaths and so forth, in consideration of obtaining gold and other wealth; however, the other [the master] should act quickly with greater [resources].
This means known as *dvaidhībhāva* (duplicity) has this very nature: that both the power and the master remain in a two-fold state. In this regard, another form of such duplicity must be explained.
And nothing specific is being said by this;
rather, it is simply that the state of both the army and the master is twofold.
In that regard, it should be stated that there is a "double-dealing" (*dvaidhībhāva*) regarding *māyā*, and this constitutes its twofold nature.
It is said:
this is to be understood through implication—that this must be done for the sake of favoring others and for the sake of one's own business.
This is the "twofold division" (dvaidhībhāva) of the state of being divided (dvidhābhāva).
Seeking refuge with the virtuous is traditionally recorded as being of two kinds: for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose, and when one is being oppressed by enemies.

When one is being oppressed by enemies, seeking refuge elsewhere for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose (*artha*)—where "purpose" means the cessation of oppression—one may resort to another who is capable of achieving that end; having abandoned one's own country, one should go there.
Furthermore, even when not currently oppressed, one may seek refuge with another for the sake of a pretext (*vyapadeśa*), in order to avoid future oppression.
"This person is his companion; he cannot be harmed"—such an establishment of designation (*vyapadeśasiddhi*) is not brought about by anyone.
By the word "designation" (*vyapadeśa*), that which relies on the purpose of designation is expressed through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
There is an alternative reading: *vyapadeśārtham* ("for the sake of designation").
Where, then, should one take refuge?
To this he says: "Among the virtuous.
One should resort to whichever among those kings are virtuous, from whom no misconduct is to be feared.
By the word "sādhu," qualities such as the capacity to protect one from humiliation and so forth are expressed.
When one perceives that one's own superiority in the future is certain,
while the suffering in the present is slight, then one should resort to peace.
The future is the time yet to come.

If he should think, "This [rival] is equal in strength to me, or perhaps even weaker, but because of the time, I am able to overcome him through instigation once my purpose is achieved, or by winning over his allies," then he should make peace.
Superiority is the state of possessing greater strength.
*Dhruvam* means "certainly. *Tadātve* refers to the present time; this is a word denoting the current moment.
When he considers all his subjects to be exceedingly well-pleased,
and likewise himself to be highly exalted, then he should wage war.
When he considers his own subjects, such as the ministers and others, to be joyful, filled with enthusiasm and loyalty, and won over by gifts and honors;

and when he considers himself to be exceedingly exalted due to the abundance of his treasury, elephants, horses, and so forth— then, under some pretext, having caused a breach in the treaty, he should resort to war.
When he perceives his own army to be joyful and well-nourished in spirit,
while that of the enemy is the opposite, then he should march against the foe.
Prosperity (*bhāva*) is the cause for the nourishment of joy.

Sharing with abundant wealth, the fact that their agricultural and other labors have borne fruit, and so forth, are the causes for the nourishment of joy. Power (*bala*) consists of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
When the opposite is true for the enemy, then one should march against the enemy; that is to say, one should lead an expedition against him.
The causes for marching are not merely the causes for war; rather, they include those as well as the decline of the enemy's prosperity and the nourishment of one's own subjects.
But when he is completely depleted of both mounts and forces,
then he should sit with diligence, gradually conciliating his enemies.
The mounts consist of elephants, horses, and chariots; the army consists of infantry. The distinction between them is like that between "cattle" and "bull."
When one's own strength is exhausted, one should remain conciliatory toward the enemy;
conciliation consists of winning him over through peaceful words and the bestowal of gifts.
When the king considers his enemy to be stronger in every respect,
he should then divide his army into two parts and accomplish his own purpose.

It is impossible for one who is besieged by a powerful enemy to maintain a reconciliation; therefore, taking refuge in a fort is beneficial. Furthermore, establishing oneself within a fort constitutes a state of double-dealing (*dvaidhībhāva*), as has been explained previously. For it is observed that it is precisely the stronger party who, when in calamity, divides their forces into two.
But when he becomes most vulnerable to attack by the forces of his enemies,
then he should quickly seek refuge with a righteous and powerful king.

When one considers oneself most vulnerable to attack, most easily overcome, and situated in a fortress, then one should quickly abandon that fortress and take refuge with another who is righteous, from whom no treachery is to be feared, and whose nature is firm and composed of glory. By the term "the powerful," this is clearly demonstrated.
One should constantly serve with all efforts that person who effects the suppression of both the subjects and the enemy's forces, just as one would a teacher.
It has been stated that [the king] must be powerful. To explain by what measure of power one becomes powerful, this is said:
he should seek the support of whichever of his own subjects are wicked and whichever enemy is capable of suppressing both.
He should be served like a guru, having abandoned pride.
O Great King, one should not think, "This person too is merely conducting himself with equanimity. He should be served as if he were a lord.
By all efforts, by means, by pleasant words, at the proper time, and by remaining close at hand.
If he should perceive even there a fault arising from taking refuge, he should engage in fair combat without hesitation.
If, even in that very refuge, one were to perceive or somehow recognize a fault caused by taking refuge,
as well as the signs indicating the presence of such faults—
namely, regret after giving, showing contempt for the fire-offerings previously performed, and the public recital of one's misdeeds.
Not giving what has been seen [to the teacher], speaking with hostility—these are the modes of conduct of the wicked.
Then, even when that refuge is known to be harmful— and by the word "even," when there is no faultless refuge—
one should, remaining unperturbed, engage in fair combat at that time as well.
For there is no destruction in taking refuge;
indeed, one of great strength is seen being conquered even by one of little strength.
Moreover, in the final state, there is merit in either case: in victory, sovereignty; in defeat, certain heaven.
We shall, however, demonstrate the excellence of war:
one who possesses the power should march for the conquest of the circle [of kings] by relying upon each individual quality.
A king who understands statecraft should employ every possible means such that his allies,
neutrals, and enemies do not become superior to him.
By means of skillful speech— whether through conciliation and the other methods individually or collectively—
and by including "all," even through means such as making a formal agreement (*saṃdhi*) and so forth;
one should act accordingly and strive in that manner.

A king who is knowledgeable in ethics (*nīti*), conversant with the science of polity (*arthaśāstra*), possessed of innate wisdom, or skilled in policy (*naya*) and other such arts, should ensure that his three powers (*śakti-traya*) do not fall short of those of his allies and others; likewise, in the performance of duties assigned to the constituent elements of the state (*prakṛti*) and so forth, he should make himself superior to them. The mention of the "middling" [king] was omitted for the sake of metrical requirements.
However, he too should be viewed as such; one should not regard him as a friend and remain indifferent toward him.
For there is no such thing as a "friend" apart from one's own self-interest;
indeed, friendship is established [only] on that basis.
Even a friend becomes an enemy due to the influence of one's own self-interest when it reaches a state of excess;
as Vyāsa has said:
"No one is anyone's friend, and no one is anyone's enemy."
"Friends and likewise enemies are to be understood through the application of their capacities.
Thus, one should deliberate upon the circle [of kings] by means of these expedients.
One should examine all future undertakings as well as their immediate consequences, and one should also truly evaluate the merits and faults of all past actions.

"Tasks" refers to actions and purposes; he should examine all of them as they are about to be undertaken— their future, which is their subsequent transformation in the coming time, and their present, which is the state at the moment of commencement— and he should examine them in reality, according to their true nature.

For tasks have many facets and can change in an instant; therefore, this instruction is for the purpose of deliberating on how one should undertake those tasks for which neither of the two times [past and future] is pure. One should examine, according to reality, the merits and defects of all past and transcended matters.

In this context as well, having examined the merits and defects of past actions, one should consider how to undertake again those very past actions that possess merit; such is the purpose of the instruction on investigating the reality of the merits and defects of past deeds.
One who knows the merits and defects regarding the future, who makes swift decisions in the present,
and who understands the remaining consequences of past actions, is not overcome by enemies.
For indeed, he who understands the merits and defects of actions in the future, that is to come, is necessarily one who acts with deliberation; he undertakes them himself and does not incur fault.
Such is the purpose of knowledge.

Furthermore, he who quickly discerns what is present in the current moment does not delay in action; being one who reaches quick certainty in the present, he becomes one who acts swiftly, performing what is meritorious and not what is faulty.

When a task has been completed in the past, he who understands that there is still further work to be done—and does not consider it finished—obtains a connection with the fruits of all meritorious undertakings; thus, being superior, he shall not be overcome by his enemies.
Indeed, it is impossible to provide a complete instruction on the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) within the treatises on Dharma; therefore, only a mere indication has been stated.
He should arrange everything in such a way that friends, neutrals, and enemies do not gain the upper hand over him; this is the summary of political strategy.

One should act in such a way that others do not outmaneuver one through various stratagems, whether by means of those already acquired or by other methods; this is the summary principle (*saṃkṣepika-nyāya*) for the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*).
Furthermore, in this way, there is no contradiction regarding the prevention of being outwitted.

This should be understood as follows: through the protection against instigation (*upajāpa*) regarding vulnerable points (*kṛtya*), through remedial action during calamities (*vyasana*), through the consolidation of one's own circle (*svamaṇḍala*), and through the correct application of the qualities and means (*guṇopāya*), there is success in undertakings. Thus it is to be viewed.
Now he describes the action of one about to march forth:
"But when the lord sets out on his vehicle toward the enemy's kingdom,
then he should proceed slowly toward the enemy's city according to this rule."
When he intends to attack the enemy's kingdom, he should then proceed toward it in this manner, without haste;
the introduction of what is about to be said is for the sake of easy understanding.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the lord of the earth should set out on his expedition,
or else toward the months of Phālguna or Caitra, according to his strength.

Desiring to wage a long war depending on the enemy to be attacked and his own strength, one who possesses abundant forces should march against an enemy kingdom rich in autumn and spring crops during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.

For by marching at this time, one secures the autumn harvest already present in the home and other places, brings in the spring crops, and possesses great capacity for tasks such as besieging a fort; moreover, the roads are free from the usual obstacles of winding paths, marshy waters, and thickets; the season is neither too hot nor too cold; and even if the crops have ripened, they are not yet fully harvested, which is favorable because it allows time to wait out the period when the three types of crops might otherwise be destroyed. Furthermore, the enemy is forced to rely on another's support, ensuring that the depletion of both parties' crops is effectively achieved while one’s own strength remains undiminished.

If he intends merely to inflict injury, or if the march can be accomplished in a short time, he should march with his forces during the months of Phālguna or Caitra toward a region where spring crops predominate;
for even then, he possesses fodder and other supplies for himself, while the enemy's crops in the fields are damaged by his passage.
"According to his strength" means that he should march in such a manner as is consistent with his available forces.
This is an exception:
however, at other times also, when he perceives certain victory,
he should march forth even after declaring war, or when a calamity has arisen for the enemy.
Apart from this, during other seasons such as the rainy season and so forth,
he should march when he considers his own victory to be certain.

For when the army consists primarily of elephants and horses— specifically when there is horse-force in the rains and elephant-force [in other seasons]— then victory is absolute due to the power of the season favorable to one's own forces.

When a calamity has befallen an enemy concerning his own army, treasury, or other resources, one should march against him regardless of the condition of one's own forces or the timing; for an enemy afflicted by such a calamity becomes easy to overcome.
Like a piece of wood, it perishes merely through its connection with those employed for their respective qualities.
"Having seized" means that one should march after having hemmed in the enemy to be attacked and having summoned them;
in this very [context], a great [principle] is understood.
Having performed the ritual at the root according to the rules, as well as the preparatory rites for the journey, and having secured a dwelling place and properly stationed spies;

At the outset, one should secure one's own fortress and kingdom; furthermore, having established countermeasures against the rear-enemy (*pārṣṇigrāha*), one should ensure that the fortress is well-provided with abundant grain and the like, and equipped with excellent machines, walls, and moats. Regarding the kingdom as well, one should provide protection for one's own forces from the guild-armies (*śreṇībala*).

Having restrained those who are inclined toward giving and honor, they should be stationed along the frontiers against the rear-attacker (*pārṣṇigrāha*); and a capable portion of the army should be maintained within one's own kingdom. Furthermore, the equipment necessary for an expedition—such as elephants, horses, and other forces, as well as weapons and armor—should be kept ready.
Having thus provided instruction to others according to the prescribed rule:
"Āspada" means a foundation or support.

What then? One should regard others—those who are angry and so forth—as not belonging to oneself; having grasped them and taken them under one's wing, one should apply oneself correctly and appropriately for the sake of knowing [the enemy's] disposition, since that disposition has ceased to concern the territory of another.

Whether he has begun to gather visible resources, or intends to provoke the circle of enemies, or whether he wishes to seek refuge with a neutral or intermediate power, or whether he desires to destroy the root of his journey, or intends to effect a formal severance, and so forth—one should act in accordance with how these things truly are.
Having cleared the threefold path and his own sixfold power,
he should march toward the enemy's city according to the rules for a protracted campaign.
The path is of three kinds: the desert (*jāṅgala*), the sunny (*ātapa*), and the forest (*āṭavika*).
Some say it is of three kinds because they substitute "forest" (*vana*) for "wilderness" (*āṭavika*). Others say it is [of three kinds]: elevated (*unnata*), depressed (*nimna*), and level (*sama*).

Having thus purified the threefold [obstacles], one should cut down the trees, shrubs, and creepers that block the path; level the high and low ground; create fords across rivers and ravines; eliminate predatory beasts that obstruct the way; win over those who incite opposition; and ensure an abundance of fodder, fuel, and other necessities.
This constitutes the sixfold army.
According to some, the sixfold army consists of elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, the treasury, and laborers.
Others say it is the casting [of the enemy] into a treasury;
others say it is by means of the division of the forces of primary servants, guilds, friends, enemies, and forest-dwellers,
according to the rules for future contingencies.
"Sāmparāyika" refers to the hardship encountered in battle; that for which this is the purpose is "sāmparāyika.
Alternatively, he may march against the enemy by way of a fortified position (*durga*).

Furthermore, the encampment of the army in various locations—consisting of stationary and mobile forces, with ramparts made of many openings, enclosures, wooden planks, and branches, and so forth—is established in such a manner.
But especially so for one who has come on a journey.
One should be especially vigilant regarding a hidden enemy who serves as a friend, as well as one who has gone away and returned; for such a person is an enemy intent on causing hardship.

One should be more cautious regarding a secret, hidden friend who serves the enemy, as well as one who has gone and returned; one should be more diligent and more attentive toward him, meaning that one should not trust him.
For he is a more dangerous enemy than others, such as those who are merely angry and so forth.
Thus, from both the expression "more cautious" and the expression "more dangerous," it is understood that one who has gone and returned is not to be trusted by anyone else.
He is of four kinds:
one who has departed for a reason and returned from the opposite reason—such as one who went away because of a fault and returns again having abandoned both [faults and virtues];
and one who has returned for a reason, who is to be abandoned because of his shallow intellect and his tendency to act impulsively.
Furthermore, no further deliberation is required in this case.

One who has "gone from a cause" (*kāraṇāgata*)—meaning one who went away due to the fault of his master and has returned from another [place] due to his own fault—is to be treated with respect; if he has come because of attachment [to the community], then he should be accepted. However, if he was sent by another or desires to cause harm due to that same fault, then he should not be accepted.
Setting out against a foreign kingdom,

he should march along that route in either the staff-array (*daṇḍavyūha*), or the wagon-array (*śakaṭavyūha*), or the boar-array (*varāhavyūha*), the crocodile-array (*makaravyūha*), the needle-array (*sūcīvyūha*), or the eagle-array (*garuḍavyūha*).
In this context, an array in the shape of a staff is a *daṇḍavyūha*. Similarly, it should be applied that an array in the form of a cart is a *śakaṭavyūha*, and so forth.

With the commander-in-chief at the front, the king in the middle, and the general at the rear; with elephants on the flanks, horses near them, and foot-soldiers beyond those—this all-around formation is the *daṇḍavyūha*, which is not oblique and is intended for use when there is danger from all directions.

The *sūcīvyūha* (needle-array) has its troops stationed on level ground, with brave men at the front; it is extremely long and upright, such that while engaging others, the enemy's flank is exposed. The *makaravyūha* (crocodile-array), however, is broad at the head and the flanks and is praised for being symmetrical on both sides; yet it does not achieve all objectives nor secure the goal.
For when it is struck by the brave, it leads to the collapse of even the other [troops].
He should station the remainder of his force, having determined that other tasks are contained within its end; however, he should cast the rest of the army into the interior of the formation.
Thus, by means of the specific arrangements mentioned, or specifically with respect to the stated purposes, he should advance on level ground using the *daṇḍa*, *garuḍa*, or *sūci* formations.
In uneven and perilous terrain, [one should proceed] with carts, crocodiles, and boars.
From whichever direction he anticipates danger, in that direction he should extend his forces;
and he himself should always take up his position in the lotus formation (*padmavyūha*).

On that route, from whichever place there might be apprehension of danger from those who act as obstructors, the army should be extended from the previous encampment by that distance—either for a *gavyūti* or more.

Therein, the forces of infantry, cavalry, chariot-riders, and elephants should be stationed attentively, provided with abundant fodder, capable of delivering firm blows, spread out, well-nourished, mutually supportive, and with their chariots, horsemen, and elephant troops held in check.
This is the *padmavyūha* (lotus array), circular in its distribution on all sides, with the one seeking victory stationed in the center.
In this manner, he should always enter a city or depart from a village.
The commander-in-chief and the army supervisor should station themselves in all directions;
and whichever direction one suspects danger from, that one should designate as the east.

The *senāpati* is the lord of the entire wealth and the commander of the forces; since there cannot be two of them and because they are designated by a dual number, their presence in all directions is impossible. Therefore, it is their subordinates who are referred to by that term. And due to the arrangement of those men, those two [the *senāpati* and the *balādhyakṣa*] themselves are considered to be stationed in all directions.

Thus, having stationed various horses, elephants, and so forth, which are connected to them, on all sides for the purpose of engaging in battle, one should place a mountain, a forest, or a pit behind as a supervisor (*adhyakṣa*).
In whatever direction one might fear danger, as that would be the eastern quarter,
so should the wise construct the settlement, as if for the purpose of exiting toward the front.
And he should station trusted men as outposts on all sides—
men who are skilled in both their positions and in combat, fearless and steadfast.
He saw military camps and assemblies of men; some were directly all around him with conchs and drums, while others were the opposite.
And therein arose a malady difficult to cure, leading to great misfortune.
He distinguishes them by their qualities;
"reliable ones" and "those resembling reliable ones" is for the purpose of showing there is no difference between them.
"Those who have formed the perception [of the goal]."
Those by whom a signal was made for the purpose of communication are "those who have made a signal" (*kṛtasaṃjñās*); to them [the author says]:

"In the opportune moment of battles, we shall indeed raise musical instruments (*tūrya*) such as the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, banners, and so forth; and when there is apprehension regarding their disappearance, one should act in this very same way.

It is established that when the conch is sounded or the banner raised, one should stand separately; likewise, "in this manner they should strike together," "in this manner they should retreat," and so on.
"Expert in their positions, they can be approached by other heroes; when gathered together, they can be overcome. 'In this situation we are not separate, while the others are separate,' and so forth.

You who are skilled in pursuing [the enemy] in battle and similar maneuvers, having entered after forming a compact array and preventing their expansion, you must strike from the rear and employ various tactics. One must seize the rear of those who have broken and fled through hundreds of different paths," and so on.
"Fearless ones, they have advanced in a wide formation."
One should station many such detachments, which consist of unchanging units characterized by non-differentiation,
extending for a distance of one *gavyūti* in all three directions, with their locations varying daily;
he should remain vigilant for the purpose of instilling fear in the enemy.
People become confident through the observation of acts such as giving gifts and showing honor.

When the battle has commenced, the conflict for all is for their own self-interest; they have come together with the ministers and others thinking, "The king is my name only," "We are all equal in wealth and enjoyment," and "In victory there is the kingdom, and in defeat there is heaven."
One should make a small number of troops fight in close formation, while one may extend a large number at will;
having arrayed them in the *sūcī* (needle) or *vajra* (thunderbolt) formations, one should cause them to fight.

For when a force that is not consolidated encounters a powerful and extensive army, it is destroyed by the blows of the enemy's mounts as its individual components are shattered; and since these [individual units] are produced for that very destruction, one should therefore cause one's own few men to fight while remaining consolidated.
Fighting with mutual regard and striking one another, they become capable of withstanding the enemy's consolidated forces through mutual assistance, mutual affection, and rivalry.
One might think: "One may, at will and as desired, expand them for the sake of the task and cause many scattered men to fight," and so forth.
When these [arrays] are broken, fear will come; seeing many enemies or even one's own men, there may be terror.
The "needle" (*sūcī*) is the previously mentioned breaking of the "axle-array" (*akṣavyūha*), arranged three-fold in front and behind, and breaking through the two flanks.
Having thus divided oneself into a needle-array, one should fight.
For this reason, these two are accepted as being capable of establishing and arraying all the arrays of the virtuous.
However, when these two belong to the enemy's force, then the opposite must be applied to one's own force.

But when they are equal, [the distinction is made] on account of being nourished, being devoted, being honored by the virtuous, and being abundant and acting toward a single goal; thus, the distinction is made according to the circumstances through the appropriate statements.

From the statement "he should cause them to fight," it follows that the king himself, for the sake of coordinating that [battle], should remain as a reserve (*pratigraha*) by taking refuge in battle arrays, fortresses, and the like.
As stated in the *Samānatantre*:
"Having advanced two hundred bow-lengths, the king should stand as a reserve."
However, one who does not accept gifts should not fight for the purpose of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.

One should fight with chariots and horses on level ground; likewise, with boats and elephants in marshy terrain; with bows in places covered by trees and shrubs; and with swords, shields, and other weapons on firm ground.
He speaks for the purpose of arranging the army and the terrain:
one should fight with chariots and horses on level ground,
for there they meet with no obstruction.
A marshy region (*anūpa*) is one where water predominates.
Even there, in places with little water, [elephants move] by means of their trunks, while in deep water they use boats;
for it is in those [latter cases] that their movement is easy.
[The terrain] covered with trees and shrubs [is understood] by the mention of "bows" (*dhanurbhiḥ*);
and because they serve the same purpose, that which is cluttered with pits for cattle and the like is also included.
"Dry land" (*sthalam*) refers to a place free from stones, trees, creepers, pits, and so forth; success is achieved on such ground.
One should fight with handheld weapons such as arrows and missiles such as *śaktis*, because of the nature of close-quarters combat;
for this [verse] is intended to demonstrate such capability.
Furthermore:
He should station the men from Kuru-kṣetra, Matsya, Pañcāla, and Śūrasena— both tall and short— in the vanguard ranks.
Kurukṣetra is well known.
The region of Virāṭa is designated as Matsya.
In Nāgapura are both the Pañcālas, as well as the Kānyakubjas and the Āhicchatras.
The Māthuras are born in Śūrasena;
in this instance, the suffix indicating the abstract sense (bhāvārtha) is indicated as elided.

For those born in this region are generally large-bodied, powerful, broad-chested, heroic, proud, and difficult to withstand—those who, standing at the front, become a cause of fear for their enemies.
Those with long bodies, though occupying a small space, produce long breaths due to their great stature;
however, those who are light cannot cause death, and being hidden by fearless people, they strike while being unable to inflict harm.
Furthermore, these serve as mirrors for others.
Having arrayed his forces, he should encourage them and examine them thoroughly;
he should also discern their movements even as they are fighting the enemies.

Having formed a battle array and displaying his own forces vigorously, he should gladden them by saying, "Will these be conquered? These have already been defeated by your prowess! He should also provide instruction based on omens, such as: "In victory there is great gain of wealth and happiness for those who depend on you and their dependents; in death, there is heaven and the repayment of the master's wages; in defeat, there is the absence of all three," and so forth.

Respect such rules regarding the causes [of war]; for if the primary person (the king) is inevitably compelled by force, yet—out of cowardice—remains under the pretext of not accepting the slaughter of his own people and does not desire battle himself, and so forth;
in that case, those who might say: "This is not so;

this slaughter of ours here is for our own sake, for we are those who live by the sword, and the immutability (*avyayībhāva*) of the specific duty of battle is the exertion of one's own dharma; the king, who is a cause of misfortune, must be protected in every way."
He should specifically take note of those who think, "He remains here for this purpose: to grant us, who are exhausted, the favor of rest and freedom from fatigue.

He should win them over with conciliatory measures, such as embracing, gifts of ornaments, and other rewards; he should cause the victor, the one who praises him, or the one who causes the expenditure of others to treat them thus, and he should observe the movements of the enemies as they fight.

"How will the treasury or the army act in battle? Some have double-dealing hearts, while others favor the enemy side"—because of such constant anxieties regarding men, even those who provide assistance do so only for the sake of their own interests; therefore, one should place the wicked among the strength of trusted allies.
Just as an enemy takes refuge in a fortress, he states the means for seizing that fortress:
"One should sit besieging the enemy and afflict his kingdom;
one should constantly spoil his fodder, food, water, and fuel."
A siege should be conducted in such a way that no one can exit and nothing can enter.
The "realm" (rāṣṭra) refers to the territory outside the fort. Its "affliction" consists of the destruction of its own local supplies, the crushing of its resources, and so forth.
The spoiling and destruction of fodder and other such items by means of mixing them with inferior substances and the like.
He should break down the tanks as well as the walls and moats;
he should launch a surprise assault upon him at night and likewise cause terror.
The mention of "tanks" is intended to represent all types of water reservoirs.
In that regard, the purpose regarding a tank is the destruction of its embankment by means of a dam;
as for a wall, it is the breaching by means of siege engines or its demolition through a tunnel.
By filling the moat or by breaking down its sides,
one should cause brave men to storm through the breaches; and at night, one should terrify the enemy within the fort.
By men who carry jars of fire upon their heads and utter the cries of jackals,
those people who themselves remain awake at night due to the sighting of portents become easy to subdue, for a population exhausted by staying awake is easily conquered.
And at that time,
he should repeatedly instigate those who can be won over, and he should recognize when that has been accomplished;
then, when fate is favorable, he should fight, free from fear and desiring victory.
Those who should be instigated are the angry enemies who are of noble birth and desire their own kingdom; the reason is that one should instigate them.
The meaning of "one should instigate" (upajapet) is that one should cause [them] to designate [the enemy] as something to be done by the agent.
The meaning of "one should instigate" is that one should cause [them] to accept [the proposal].
Sowing dissension (*upajāpa*) consists of causing a rift by means of providing instruction on one's own welfare based on [the enemy's] reliance [on others].

By that means, one should discern whether the enemy, though acting well, has begun something while stationed in a fort for the purpose of provoking the forest tribes (*āṭavika*), the rear-attacker (*pārṣṇigrāha*), and so forth; or whether he has entered into an alliance with either the middle king (*madhyama*) or the neutral king (*udāsīna*), and so on.
Furthermore, when fate is favorable—that is, when the fate of the seeker of victory (*vijigīṣu*) is propitious—[one should act].

When the constellations, planets, deities, and auspicious moments are favorable, when the practitioner has seen auspicious dreams and omens, and when the winds and other elements are propitious, one desiring victory and free from fear should first proceed to the fortified positions to engage in battle.
One should strive to conquer the enemy through conciliation, bribery, or sowing dissension— either collectively or individually— and never by means of war.
One should not fight impulsively.

First, there is the instruction on establishing a distinguished status, which includes being pleasant-faced toward one another, sitting together, conversing, and seeing each other's wives and so forth.
The "bestowal of gifts" refers to the presentation of goods such as gold and other items for the purpose of generating affection.
Distinction refers to the inclusion of those born into that lineage and so forth;
from that qualification follows the absence of fear and the like, which serves as the cause for [the practice].
Since victory is seen to be uncertain for two who fight,
and defeat likewise occurs in battle, one should therefore avoid war.
Since this rule is not observed—that he who conquers must necessarily be exceedingly strong, and he who is defeated must necessarily be exceedingly weak—victory is impermanent.
If even the three previously mentioned expedients are not possible,
one should fight in such a manner that, being well-equipped, one may conquer the enemies.

Even when the outcome is uncertain and victory is equally possible through conciliation and other means, how much more so should one fight with formality and according to that proper manner by which one's own victory may be secured?
For in victory there is a kingdom, and even in death there is heaven; thus, victory is gained in both ways.
The plotting of obstacles against the enemy—such as treacherous warfare and other such methods—is to be immediately abandoned, as it involves excessive destruction and the infliction of suffering.
And so Vyāsa said:
"O Dhanañjaya, even Śakra himself would not be able to stand before those who return again and those living beings who are devoid of hope."
When defeat is uncertain, then withdrawal is appropriate;
for once life has departed, one does not accomplish any purpose by which one might behold auspicious things or attain heaven when dead.
Having conquered, he should worship the gods and righteous Brahmins;
he should grant exemptions and proclaim amnesties of safety.

Having conquered the enemy by whatever means possible and attained this state of tranquility, one should therefore, within this city and its countryside, honor the righteous gods and Brahmins who perform their prescribed duties according to their capacity— avoiding what is forbidden— and having conquered the enemies through self-mastery over desire, one should worship them as is appropriate with substances such as perfumes, incense, and flowers, by means of rituals including the distribution of offerings and the clapping of hands, beginning with the performance of the *sādhya* rites.

For the sake of exempting the householders, he should grant them a status characterized by the suspension of extraordinary taxes, heavy levies, and tolls, or provide them with land; or alternatively, he should grant them one or two years' worth of revenue.

He should also proclaim this to the elite citizens and country-folk by means of drums, cymbals, and the striking of maces, declaring: "Let those who, out of devotion to their sovereign, have suffered an unwarranted loss, continue to perform their respective duties until the end of the protection [granted]."

Even when such favor is being shown, if he should think that because of his subjects' devotion to their lord, or others, "I am highly esteemed due to my eloquence and majestic nature," and thus his own power of punishment would be unable to prevail,
then— having ascertained the intentions of all these people in brief—
he should install someone of their own lineage there and establish a formal covenant.

Having understood in brief that this is the intention of the citizens and others, [the king] should think: "He does not desire this; he wishes to make one born of his own lineage the ruler. In that region, he should enter into an agreement with that very person of his own lineage—who is mild, pure, and has a beloved and happy wife—as well as with the principal officials and the assembled subjects. The terms should include the sharing of the treasury, gifts, and a fixed limit, such as: "By your divine grace, you must act on my behalf even in times of misfortune; you must personally attend to what ought and ought not to be done at the proper time; and you must provide both military force and financial resources," and so forth.
And one should establish for them the righteous legal procedures as they have been declared;
and one should honor him with precious gems along with the principal men.

Whatever types of established conditions they have—whether accumulated, previously initiated, or consisting of grants to Brahmins, livelihoods for gods, the management of temple property, and so forth—the king should authorize them and treat them as authoritative; for in this way, their loyalty toward him is secured.

Furthermore, the king should honor those who are the leading men there—with weapons, wealth, grain, ornaments, vehicles, umbrellas, thrones, and the binding of the ceremonial cloth—by virtue of their promises, the large number of their kinsmen, and other such qualities.
Why, then, is the giving of jewels and such things prescribed for one's kinsmen? It is said:
"Taking away is unpleasant, while giving is a source of pleasure;
therefore, the timely bestowing of desired objects is highly praised."
The failure to bestow what is worthy of being given is an act displeasing to a new king or anyone else, and it is the cause and reason for their dissatisfaction.

Conversely, giving and returning a gift are acts that produce pleasure; although both are well known to be so in many instances, when performed [only] thus, they bring happiness regarding desired objects, whereas otherwise they cause suffering—this is the meaning.
That which is joined with the proper time, occurring at the right moment, is praised.
Furthermore, even when something at some time produces pleasure, it does not produce pleasure that is slight or unwholesome;
therefore, giving and taking should be performed with regard to the proper time.
Whatever has passed and whatever is yet to be told—
all this activity is dependent upon both divine and human ordinances.
Of these two, the divine is indeed inconceivable, whereas action exists within the human.
By implication, "karma" here refers to the fruit of the action that is to be performed;
all of that, without exception, is "dependent" (āyatta), meaning subservient to something. It is a "disposer" (vidhāna) because it ordains—that is, it assigns—the fruit of the action.
He specifies that [result] as being divine or human.

Regarding the divine—namely, dharma and so forth, which concern what was previously performed as enjoined or prohibited—the fruit of one's own action is the result; if the fruit is the performance of the action, it pertains to the visible purpose of right and wrong conduct.
And thus says the Śruti:
Fate, ordainment, necessity, inherent nature, time, Brahmā, Īśvara, karma, destiny, fortune, merit, and the inner conjunction of beings— these are synonyms for that which was performed in the past.
Smṛti also [states this].
"One should know that destiny (daiva) is what was performed by oneself in a previous body, like karma;
whereas human effort (puruṣakāra) is said to be that which is performed here in this life.
Although the phrase "of the divine and the human" (daivamānuṣasya) might have been expected, because [the victim] has died, the intention is to express that both the divine and the human are causes.
In this undertaking, this fruit of action depends [on human effort].
Destiny does not bestow its fruit when devoid of human exertion;
for it necessarily requires human effort.
Nor is it the case that human effort [is effective] independently of fate.
For even from fate alone, independent of human effort, there might occur the union of a person with the fruit, such as a fetus;
yet when no fetus exists, the production of the fruit must be inferred from the conjunction of fate with the restrictive factors.
In this way, even from human effort, if it were independent of destiny,
then when exertion is present, it would always belong to everyone;
but this is not the case.
Therefore, both are causes.
And so Vyāsa said:
"All human undertakings are the primary cause of two kinds of actions."

"Beyond destiny (daiva) and human effort (puruṣakāra), nothing else exists. Thus it is said. In the *Samānatantro* as well, it is stated: "Destiny protects the world through right and wrong policy, while human action [protects] through deeds.
Regarding this, those who hold destiny to be the cause say:
In this matter, destiny alone is the cause.

For we see those who are dull-witted, impotent, lame, and the like—crippled and devoid of human effort—who, being unable to provide a remedy, yet obtain the fruits of karma through other conditions and are happy;
likewise, those who are capable of providing a remedy, yet are healthy, brave, proficient in the sciences, and skillful, remain miserable despite their exertions.

Likewise, they observe that results, whether desired or undesired, are produced through the mere operation of destiny (*daiva*) independent of human effort (*puruṣakāra*), such as the acquisition of wealth or the falling of a thunderbolt.
And by accepting this, the instructions for undertaking actions that have the other world as their purpose become all the more meaningful.
Thus, knowing that "we enjoy here the fruits of what was done previously with effort, and we shall enjoy in the future what is done here," people remain free from doubt.
One should strive in this way for the Dharma;
as they say in illustration:
"I know the Dharma, yet I do not practice it."
"I do not know evil, nor do I have any active engagement in it; I have been released by the Creator exactly as I am, and there is no one else beyond this who can command me. Thus [he spoke].
For those who maintain that human effort is paramount say:

"In this case, human effort alone is the cause; by being diligent and performing his own activity, one obtains the fruit of the agent's operation—the result of the action such as agriculture—just as in the acts of farming and so forth.
And thus it has been said:
In this world, action alone is to be grasped and practiced by those who are not wicked;
for having performed an action, a person experiences its result, and neither eats it nor does not eat it.
Moreover, even when food is available, those who do not eat are not satisfied;
therefore, the principle is that the result which follows immediately after the act of ingestion is the production of a result caused by that [act].
Consequently, in this case, there is no operation of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
And by acting thus, the instructions for undertaking actions become meaningful;
as they have said:
"The Sage strikes down even destiny when it has encountered him at some point."
Likewise, it brings forth cold, heat, and rain, and it destroys them as well.
When both are thus established, both are the cause, because in the absence of either one, the result does not occur.

However, in some cases, certain factors operate with predominance, and thus that [predominant factor] is grasped. Even an exertion of human effort, when overwhelmed by powerful destiny (*daiva*), falls apart.
Just as wet wood thrown into a small fire does not burn,
so too, if destiny is weak, it bears fruit when preceded by great effort and human exertion— just as even wet wood, when thrown into a great mass of fire,
does not cause the fire to go out.
Indeed, destiny that is weak is overcome by human effort;
and conscious action is overcome by superior destiny.
Having thus reflected, he said:
"Of those two, fate and human effort, fate alone is inconceivable";
the word "but" (tu) serves the purpose of restriction.
Its essential nature is unknown;
it is inconceivable as to at what time it will yield its fruit by means of that [action].
Furthermore, because it cannot be fully understood except through the treatises, and because it is impossible to apply it without such investigation, it is said to be "infeasible."
In that regard, destiny is fruitless.
Among humans, human effort—meaning action—is what will be discussed, because it is the subject at hand;
and wealth is also action among humans.

Some knowledge regarding agriculture and such activities can be deliberated upon, such as: "I must perform this kind of agriculture and so forth with these means, including fate and other factors, and its result will be such. When one has thus commenced an undertaking and desires to persist through its beginnings and its conclusions, then fate must be taken into account; it is not the case that one should act in this manner even when things have gone wrong.
Up until the experience of the fruit, because destiny is inconceivable, one should not be anxious about that;
rather, having reflected upon human action, whatever task is to be done should be performed. For he who acts haphazardly perishes.
An expedition endowed with both divine and human factors accomplishes all objectives;
in such an undertaking, the divine factor prevails in its excellence, while the human factor remains equal.

(a) When one who possesses the three powers and is joined with human exertion desires to conquer a foreign kingdom, that very expedition which is endowed with both divine and human factors becomes the accomplisher of all goals.
Nevertheless, destiny exerts its influence with excellence in that situation;
the meaning is that human effort alone becomes superior.
For, without destiny, there can be no misfortune for the one to be attacked (the enemy) at that time, whether it be caused by destiny or by human agency, for one who desires victory.
Human effort is equal to destiny when it is not overextended; or rather, the two are equal and identical. (a)
Furthermore:
Human existence, as it proceeds according to the divine law, is joined with great affliction; yet it is the means for accomplishing its purpose. (b)

That is improper; for when destiny and human effort are turned away, it is through the ordainment of destiny that human exertion proceeds toward the eightfold action. That [exertion] achieves its purpose and fruit with great hardship, or it becomes fruitless.
Therefore, even if it is not accomplished despite the hardship, one should not be dissatisfied by depending on destiny. (b)
But that human effort which proceeds when conjoined with destiny accomplishes all the purposes of the mantras without difficulty. (c)
Human effort is human exertion (*puruṣakara*).

When that very effort is applied toward a destiny (*daiva*) that is exceedingly virtuous, it then becomes a means for accomplishing the complete fruit without difficulty and with absolute certainty. (c)
To confirm this point, there is an illustration in two verses:
"Some maintain that even battle is a field [of action] joined with human effort, yet it yields fruit only to one who is devoid of destiny. (d)
Some say that the field is "nourished" by human effort. (e)

Furthermore, when [the teaching] has been seen again and again and explained correctly as purified, it does not grant its fruit to one who is devoid of the divine [fortune] characterized by such helpful qualities. Thus it is said.
Even when joined with destiny, if it is devoid of human effort, the field yields fruit only through human effort. (f)
"Even for one who is joined [with effort], it is by means of destiny (*daiva*). The conjunction with destiny, moreover, is inferred from that granting of the fruit;
and thus, the absence of that [effort] in the prior case is the state of destiny.

But others say: since fate, being sufficient when its time has arrived, is accomplished simply through the perception of results such as rain and so forth, it is said to be "done"; thus, by the phrase "devoid of seed," it demonstrates the absence of human effort (*puruṣakāra*). (f)
The moon, the sun, and other planets, as well as wind, fire, and water—these are accomplished here through divine power and through human effort. (g)
The planets, beginning with the moon and the sun, are brought about by destiny—known as the natural merit and demerit of men—as the cause for the experience of pleasure and pain.
When they reach undesirable positions, they are brought to equilibrium through human effort by means of pacification rites and other such methods;
while remaining in their current positions, they are made to act in accordance with their non-deviating nature. (g)
Or he may march together with him, having carefully made a treaty, while keeping in view the threefold fruit: a friend, gold, or land.
Having carefully considered the rear-attacker and the ally within the circle of states,
one may obtain the fruit of an expedition from either a friend or even an enemy.
A king does not prosper so much by the acquisition of gold and land as he does by gaining a firm friend who, though currently weak, is capable of future endurance.
A light friend who knows the dharma, is grateful, has a contented nature, is loyal, and is steadfast in his undertakings is highly praised.
The wise say it is difficult to find an enemy who is wise, of noble birth, brave, skillful, generous, grateful, and steadfast.
Nobility, knowledge of men, heroism, and compassion; constant magnanimity and the arising of the qualities of one who remains impartial.
Knowledge of persons is knowledge of the world.
One who knows the distinctions among persons becomes a benefactor in accordance with their needs;
he follows them appropriately and becomes capable of accomplishing what must be done.
Out of the pride of his compassionate virtues, the merciful one, whose mind is full of pity, protects them from greed;
being of great vision, he always forgives their faults even when they involve abundant wealth.
A king should, without hesitation, abandon even land that is secure, always productive of crops, and conducive to the increase of cattle, for the sake of his own self.
Even such a territory he should abandon without delay,
provided it is secure and cannot be overcome by forest tribes and the like;
for him, both [the treasury and the army] must always be preeminent.
It has abundant crops, is well-watered by rain, and promotes the increase of livestock because it is of a *jāṅgala* nature and possesses many fruits, leaves, and grasses.
Indeed, land with such qualities abounds in merchants and farmers; it is free from famine and disease, and its inhabitants are capable of sustaining themselves even in the wilderness.
In the fourth case, both [the abandonment of the natural state and the acquisition of the new] apply.

He does not indicate that one should abandon the natural state of the armed forces all at once in that situation; rather, one should abandon that [state] which one considers possible to recover from by means of the remaining constituent elements (*prakṛti*).

Just as there is no distinction in the abandonment of allies, treasury, and army, so too one should abandon even a land possessed of excellent qualities at that moment when one considers it [recoverable].
One should save wealth for times of misfortune; one should protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth;
but one should always protect oneself, even at the cost of both wife and wealth.
This observance is to be accomplished through difficult means;
it is for the sake of an emergency.
Just as smoke is known to be for the sake of mosquitoes—to drive away mosquitoes—one should protect wealth for that purpose; there is no other purpose for the protection of wealth.
For wealth indeed has its fruit both in being given and in being enjoyed.
Thus, by means of it, one provides vehicles, seats, and staffs, and wins over those who can be won over by intrigue.
Furthermore, even with wealth, one's wives must be protected.
The mention of "taking a wife" is intended to include those connected by vows and relatives.
However, one's own self must be protected.

If one is unable to protect oneself by any other means, one should give away all possessions, even abandon one's wife at the proper time, remain restrained in speech, and—having renounced wife, wealth, and so forth—practice the Dharma.
But for those who perish out of attachment to wealth and wife, neither that wealth, wife, and so forth is seen, nor is the unseen merit gained, because they do not practice dharma and adharma;
nor is there the abandonment of a wife from childhood,
nor does this [prohibition] against abandoning her prevail.
This [rule] has been stated even in the section on the duties of kings (*rājadharma-prakaraṇa*); because its purpose is visible, it should be understood as applying to others as well.

Now, one might object: "Once a king has obtained a kingdom and possesses great wealth, he will perform the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and other rites, and he will enjoy incomparable happiness; therefore, what can the world do about such a grievance?
This is not a valid objection.

There are purifying acts even for one who possesses little, and practices such as *japa* and the like even for one who is destitute; wealth is merely a cause for specific [results]. Furthermore, this is not something censured by the world in this particular situation.
And this must not be done hastily.
For this reason:
"Having thoroughly observed that all calamities arise together,
a wise person should employ every means, both those already combined and those yet to be applied."
Calamities are divine and human misfortunes;

these, occurring simultaneously within the realm of the constituent elements (*prakṛti*), however excessively they may arise, the wise man should employ all means—such as conciliation preceded by gifts, sowing dissension preceded by conciliation, conciliation accompanied by gifts and dissension, or even force alone, or gifts alone—and so forth. Thus should the wise man release [the situation].
The meaning is that one should employ whatever has been obtained after examining and deliberating upon it; however, one should not remain despondent.

In response to the inquiry "How so?", he says: "Relying upon these three— the practitioner, the goal to be attained, and all the means in their entirety— one should strive for the accomplishment of the purpose."
"one should accomplish one's own purpose"—this is an alternative reading.
In that case, having approached oneself as the seeker (*upetāra*), one should accomplish the task like a friend;
all means, whether combined or separate.
This also states the general indication of the goal to be attained (*upeya*):
by relying upon and accepting [the means],
this becomes encompassed through the contemplation of their efficacy.
For what purpose are means approved by one who is capable? One should investigate whether that which is capable is appropriate, considering by what means this [goal] of theirs might be attained.
"In its entirety" (*kṛtsnaśas*) is a qualification of the triad; the meaning is "entirely.

And thus, for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose, one should employ the means at the proper time and in the proper manner, according to whatever is to be accomplished by a particular means and as is appropriate therein.

Because these states are infinite, it is impossible to describe them all in detail within this treatise; therefore, they have been stated in brief. Consequently, one should apply the method of examination. Having approached [the subject], he speaks also by way of its specific nature: "For he who is disciplined succeeds; disciplined, he possesses self-mastery."
Both of them were endowed with statesmanship; even the thief was possessed of wisdom.
Having thus deliberated on all this with his ministers, the king,
after exercising himself and bathing at midday, should enter the inner apartments to eat.

Thus, having deliberated with his ministers on all this conduct as it has been described—whether in times of calamity or in times of peace—and having considered what ought to be done in which situation according to his own capacity, the king, at the time specified for midday, should perform physical exercise and then the prescribed bath.
Although bathing was mentioned out of sequence earlier, it is stated again here for the sake of the kingdom, as it is appropriate for those engaged in auspicious customs.

This concluding summary is intended to specify that, for the purpose of undertaking the bath, the king should first go to the inner apartments (antahpura) equipped with food and other necessaries, rather than [going directly] to the bath.
In a secluded place.
There, one should eat food that has been thoroughly examined by attendants who are like his own self, who know the proper time, who are incorruptible, and who have neutralized poison with mantras.

There, within the inner chamber, were those who acted as his personal protectors, being equal to himself; they were knowers of the proper time, understanding the specific times determined by age, particular states, and so forth, as well as the specific requirements for the offering of various foods, drinks, and other provisions.
Those who are unassailable, indivisible, and trustworthy—
such as attendants, physicians, and the like—
should eat all the food and other edibles that have been taken up and examined by them.
An examination should be conducted by skilled physicians using the fire-wheel and other such methods.

When food is contaminated with poison and has dried, impurity is indicated by discoloration and the loss of its natural fragrance; when thrown into the fire, it becomes excessively withered, emits a "veti-veti" sound, and the flames take on a discolored hue.
Furthermore, when observed, there occurs the death of birds [hovering over it].
