Where the cuckoo dies at the mere sight [of it], the jīvañjīvaka bird withers, and the eyes of the cakora bird perish even when poison is merely shown, and where there occurs the obstruction of the testicles and perspiration,
and so forth— in such cases of female sorceresses, one should recite over them mantras that remove poison.
One should mix all his substances with water that destroys poison, and,
being self-controlled, he should always wear gems that counteract poison.
One should purify all the king’s articles of use, such as garments and so forth, with anti-poisonous waters.

One should also employ anti-poisonous gems, such as the *garuḍodīrṇa* and the *nāgadamaṇi*. Out of constant concern for safety, one should always wear these at all times, even apart from the time of eating.
And women who have been thoroughly examined, whose dress and ornaments are pure, and who are well-composed, should attend upon him with fans, water, and incense.

Women who have been examined and scrutinized through tests (*upadhā*) regarding their character, purity, and conduct—such as female slaves or attendants—should touch or serve [the king] by means of fans, water, and incense; they should be well-dressed, having bathed and assumed appropriate attire, and remain composed with undistracted minds.
Having thus investigated their dress, ornaments, and even their hair and nails for signs of deceitful appearance, [they may approach].
Perhaps they might kill them there with weapons after gaining their confidence,
or they might touch them with ornaments smeared with poison.
One should exert effort in this manner regarding vehicles, beds, seats, and food,
as well as in bathing, grooming, and all forms of personal adornment.
In this way, one should exert effort regarding poison, water, gold, and so forth at the beginning;
"bath" refers to bathing the head,
and "fragrance" refers to yellow pigment (rocanā) and the like.
The mention of "seating" here is for the sake of illustration;
for just as great care is exercised there when one is seated, so too should it be exercised regarding vehicles and the like.
Having eaten, he should indeed enjoy himself with the women in the inner apartments;
but having enjoyed himself at the proper time, he should again reflect upon his duties.
In that very inner apartment, for his own diversion, he should sport at his pleasure with women, such as his newly married wives and others.
The phrase "at the proper time" should be connected with the subsequent clause "as long as it is the time for recreation.
Having thus enjoyed himself and being rested, he should again deliberate alone or with his ministers upon the affairs that have arisen at the appropriate time.
Adorned with ornaments, he should inspect the armed troops once more,
as well as all the mounts, weapons, and accoutrements.
Having emerged from the inner apartments, he, being adorned, should inspect the armed forces and grant them an audience;
because of the repetition of the word "again," he must see them constantly, even if they were seen earlier in the forenoon.
Effort should be exerted by those who live by arms regarding their weapons and equipment.
And all the mounts [should be inspected];
even their mere inspection is for the purpose of ensuring their growth and for the purpose of instilling excellence in those assigned to them.
Furthermore, the supervision of staff and servants, who are primarily dependent on wages, should be performed frequently from both sides.
Having performed the twilight devotions, he should, while bearing his weapon, listen within his inner apartments to the reports of those who disclose secrets and to the activities of his spies.
Although the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) has already been prescribed for the three castes,
it is mentioned again here so that the duty toward one's progeny might not be neglected for some time, or to indicate the immediate sequence of the subsequent rites;
[this is to be performed] within the house.
That which occurs in secret, such as in palaces and similar places; those who report it, whether they be citizens or certain recruited spies;
and their activities—activity meaning conduct—as well as what has been seen, heard, or done by them, and the observation of them at this particular time, are all required.
He should act so as not to be discovered by others, remaining composed and adhering to the fixed timing for accomplishing his objectives;
and he should observe the task once it has been undertaken so as not to cause distress, lest it become difficult to accomplish, or pass away, or even become impossible to achieve. Thus it is said.
Having gone to another chamber and dismissed those people,
he should enter the inner apartments again, surrounded by women, for the purpose of eating.
Therefore, having gone from the house to another chamber and having dismissed that confidant who revealed the secret, he should re-enter the inner apartments surrounded by his women attendants.
Having eaten there again a little, gladdened by the sounds of musical instruments,
he should go to rest at the proper time and rise with his fatigue dispelled.
*Kiṃcit* is an indeclinable. *Tūryāṇi* refers to musical instruments such as the flute, lute, small drum, clay drum, kettledrum, conch, and so forth.
Delighted by their soft sounds, which are pleasing to the ear, one should go to bed at the appropriate time—that is, one should pass that specific time which is suitable for sleep.
Free from fatigue and with all suffering entirely vanished, he should rise to attend to his duties.
A healthy lord of the earth should observe this rule;
however, when he is unwell, he should entrust all of this to his servants.

"Regarding this"—namely, that which was mentioned as occurring at midday or at midnight—"his conduct" refers to his activity; by means of that, he should personally attend to it. "He should station" means he should employ or assign it among his servants.
For as long as he is able, he should do so;
thus, having arranged for the performance of self-protection through independent means, he carries out his duties toward both his subjects and himself.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Duties of Kings," in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu within the Mānava Dharmaśāstra.
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the Commentary on Manu, composed by Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi, son of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Vīrasvāmin.
Now begins the eighth chapter: But the king, desiring to inspect legal cases, should enter the court modestly, together with Brāhmaṇas and with ministers who are experts in counsel.
The protection of the subjects is ordained as the livelihood of the king, and that [is established] here:
the bearing of weapons and missiles is for the Kṣatriya; trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture for the Vaiśya.
For the livelihood of a Śūdra, it is the service of the twice-born.
"A king who conducts himself in this manner attains unsurpassed worlds.
Thus, righteousness increases in the world;
furthermore, there is indeed the right to sovereignty even for members of other castes who live by the occupation of a Kṣatriya.
Whoever is known as the protector of all the worlds is considered a king;
and the fulfillment of duty is ordained for the common welfare of the world.
And protection consists in the removal of suffering;
suffering is twofold: visible and invisible.
Among these, the visible suffering is that which afflicts a weak person by the stronger through the seizure of wealth and so forth.
But for the other [the king], there is suffering in the hereafter produced by the demerit (*pratyavāya*) born from the transgression of his duty; this is "invisible affliction" (*adṛṣṭapīḍā*).
For when subjects behave improperly toward one another due to hatred, envy, and the like, they follow a wrong path and would be afflicted by the fault of their unseen karma (*adṛṣṭadoṣa*).
And from that, the kingdom is destroyed.
For sovereignty over subjects is called "kingdom";

when they perish, whose kingdom would it be? Therefore, legal proceedings and other matters, being regulated by the rod of the scriptures, do not deviate from their course out of fear; thus, in both ways, they are protected.

The king’s power of punishment consists of fines, taxes, duties, and so forth; there is no other righteous means of livelihood for him. Thus, even through the exhaustion of his resources, the kingdom would fall into ruin.
Therefore, for the sake of maintaining the kingdom, he must attend to the administration of justice.
This is now stated:
here, "legal procedure" (*vyavahāra*) refers to the process by which the plaintiff and defendant mutually refute and establish their respective positions;

or alternatively, it refers to the fact that the subject matters themselves, such as the non-payment of debts and so forth, being points of dispute, must be made the object of investigation because they are capable of being scrutinized.

Having said "desiring to see," the coreferentiality [is expressed] as "he shall look upon the legal matters. Furthermore, there is a subsequent reference: "of these, the first is the non-payment of debts. The connection is that "he shall investigate those subjects."
The assembly hall (*sabhā*) is a place presided over by the person to be discussed who is about to be mentioned;
"entry" (*praveśa*) is the act of entering its interior.
Should one enter alone?
"No," he says, "together with Brāhmaṇas.
Now, to whom does the qualification "those who know the mantras" (mantrajña) apply?
It cannot apply to the ministers (mantrin), because their status as ministers is already established by that very title.
For one who does not know the mantra cannot be called a *mantrin*.
Nor would the knowledge of it by Brahmins—who are authorized to oversee legal proceedings—be for the sake of some unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
To this, it is replied:
This is indeed a qualification of the Brahmins;
for they, being ignorant of the mantras, might act with reckless determination and thus bring misfortune upon the king. Otherwise, they would cause harm to the king.

For instance, if someone who has relied upon a high minister while conducting business with the people is suddenly defeated in a legal dispute, and yet is neither punished nor compelled to pay a fine by the seizure of his wealth, then the administration of justice would not have been carried out with impartiality; the people would suspect him of partiality or incompetence.
On the other hand, if he is punished, there may be a disturbance of the state due to the agitation caused by the high minister.

But virtuous experts in the *mantras*, being doubtful, if they create an obstruction to the legal proceeding by some pretext so that they may inform the king in secret, saying, "Of these two litigants, this one loses and this one wins; however, the case has not been decided by us at that very moment—the Sovereign is the final authority," then the king, having understood this, instructs the chief minister: "Your man is losing; let there be no ruin for me. Thus, the decision is postponed for the time being.
"You yourself must act in such a way that this man is reconciled and his affliction is removed.
These ministers, whose words are authoritative, prevent all people from engaging in harmful activities.

Others, however, consider the term *mantrajña* (knower of counsel) to apply to both [the king and the ministers] through a distinction in meaning, like the eye of a crow [which serves both functions].
When the ministers are specified, "knowledge of the mantra" refers to the thorough knowledge of the respective elements (*dhātu*).
In the case of the Brahmins, however, it also includes the state of equilibrium regarding the purpose of the task.

It is not merely the entry of the ministers and Brahmins; rather, according to the subsequent statement, "one should observe the decision," they must enter as appropriate. Otherwise, their entry would be for the sake of some unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Therefore, one should not make a decision alone; rather, one should deliberate together with them.
"Disciplined" means free from the fickleness of speech, hands, and feet, for from such instability, misfortune may arise.

Because of the inclusion of the term "pārthiva" (king), this instruction is not intended for the Kṣatriya alone; rather, it applies to any other lord of the earth, a ruler of a region, for otherwise the kingdom would not remain stable.
Seated there or even standing, having raised his right hand and wearing modest dress and ornaments, he should examine the legal cases of the litigants.

"Sitting" means seated upon the seat of justice (*dharmāsana*); "standing" means remaining upright without sitting, as movement is prohibited. Furthermore, the distinction between standing and sitting is determined by the specific requirements of the case at hand.
In a matter of greater importance requiring much to be said, he should be seated; in a matter of lesser importance requiring little to be said, he should stand.
Walking is to be prohibited in every respect, for one who is intent on looking at the path would not be able to attentively grasp the precise statements of the plaintiff and the defendant.
Others, however, consider it to have an invisible purpose (adṛṣṭārtha): that one should stand when ascetics, Brahmins, and others are standing; sit when they are sitting;
and raise one's hand [when they raise theirs].
"Having raised the left hand" means having performed the act of rising;
this deviation from the rule of the Sūtra author is because it is prescribed for all occasions, and thus this is the "under-garment" (upavyāna) in times of distress.
Therefore, the meaning is that the hand should be lifted up, and not kept in contact with what is nearby.
And at the time of prohibiting a question, he should indicate this through his demeanor, but not by the act of departing and so forth.
By this observation of his conduct, his underlying intention (*tātparya*) is made known;
for generally, men who are intent upon their tasks raise their hands in effort.
Then, as the judge departs while seated at his ease, the king does not fix his mind upon the retinue, thinking, "We have been defeated by these fearless courtiers.
The mention of the "grasping of the hand" is intended to indicate the arm;
for the employment of the mere hand throughout the administration of justice would cause distress.
And this instruction is not for an unseen purpose;
namely, that one should be "without ornaments or finery.
In the preceding verse, it was stated for the sake of withdrawing the attention from the objects of both the external and internal senses.
This, first of all, is for the sake of allowing people to approach him with ease due to his modesty;
for if his dress were ostentatious, those of such a character would fail to recognize him.
Therefore, he should never wear ostentatious dress or ornaments.
"Attire" (*veṣa*) refers to specific features such as the arrangement of hair and clothing;
"ornament" (*ābharaṇa*) refers to earrings and the like.
Among these, "haughty attire" (*uddhataveṣa*) includes wearing garments with the upper body exposed, wearing bright red clothes, and so forth.

With his ornaments raised high, adorned with many brilliant jewels and numerous necklaces, he was indeed as difficult for ordinary people— and especially for those who were hostile— to look upon as the sun. "He should look [at them]"— this states the purpose of entering the assembly hall.

The discerning king should observe this. And this instruction regarding the audience with the king shall extend up to the application of punishment and the delivery of justice according to the facts of each case; its essential purpose is that his authority over protection alone remains duly exercised.
Furthermore, because such a vision [of dharma] is impossible for others, they lack the qualification [for it].
However, the examination of legal cases—which has as its sole fruit the severing of doubts for all—is indeed available to a learned Brāhmaṇa, just like the instruction on penances;
for it has been said: "In matters of legal difficulty, he should speak."

Likewise, when there is a disagreement among members of a single group—such as merchants, farmers, cattle-herders, and so forth—concerning matters pertaining to their own group's customs or other matters, prosperity results from a superior decision; therefore, the king is enjoined to oversee such legal proceedings.
For it has been stated:
"Families, guilds, assemblies, and the authorized king..."
"The basis of worldly transactions is the family, and from these [families], it proceeds further and further to the teacher.
In this context, "families" refers to a group of kinsmen;
one must not deviate from the established rule set by them.
If, however, they do not trust you there, saying, "These are your more distant relatives," then it should be reported to the guilds (*śreṇi*).
Guilds consist of merchants and others who live by similar occupations;
among them, [the claim] has greater weight than that of kinsmen.

For kinsmen do not restrain one who has deviated from the duty of his kin out of fear; however, guilds—fearing that the guild's integrity would perish through approaching the king and being subjected to humiliation by royal officers upon their entry—investigate the matter after first taking a surety so that no one may deviate from it, declaring:
"A fine must be paid in the assembly, or you must not deviate at all."
The *gaṇas*— those who move about in groups, those who build houses, palaces, and so forth, as well as monastery-dwelling Brahmins and others—
should oversee the legal proceedings of their own members.
In that regard, *upasadas* (formal assemblies) must be held for the sake of ensuring stability.
The distinction is that while those previously mentioned lived by their own individual labor, these, however, act collectively.
Because they act collectively, the members of the guilds (*śreṇi*) are more knowledgeable about the facts of the case than others; thus, they are the ones to adjudicate disputes.
Others, however, say that "families" (*kulāni*) refers to neutral persons.
For they, being internal to the matter and not having formed a formal assembly (*śreṇi*), are the judges.
An appointed official is a learned Brāhmaṇa versed in the three Vedas;
for it is ordained that he possesses the authority to speak in matters of legal difficulty.
His authority over the former [the king] is due to his learning;

the king’s authority, too, is due to his superior power. Therefore, when a decision has been made by a learned king himself, this [objection] does not apply: "He who thinks 'I am not defeated,' even though he has been defeated according to justice."
"Having imposed double the fine, he should restore that work once more. Thus [it is said].
This applies to other judicial procedures;

for in those cases, there is an occasion for speech, as one might ask what the king will say when the matter has not been correctly decided by the officials but has been investigated by the king himself. There is another meaning: the person appointed by the kings is the *rājasthānīya* Brāhmaṇa.

Likewise, for another householder, there certainly exists a judicial proceeding extending even to punishment, because of the traditional rule that "the householder is independent in his own home. This is well-examined for the sake of disciplining latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) regarding those such as disciples or sons who are attached to what is to be learned from scripture; however, this applies except in cases of corporal punishment or acts leading to loss of caste (*patanīya*).
The meaning is this: in the case of a minor offense, the householder himself acts like a king, but when there is a major transgression, it is proper to report it to the king alone.

Therefore, the objection raised by some—having attributed the status of an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) to the phrase "he shall see," and thus suspected that only Brāhmaṇas and others possess the qualification [to adjudicate], and having subsequently supported this with great effort—is incorrect; for there is a difference in scope and a difference in qualification.

For the king’s own domain extends up to the infliction of punishment, whereas for Brāhmaṇas and others, it extends only up to the final decision (*nirṇaya*). Furthermore, their respective qualifications (*adhikāra*) are distinct.

The purpose of the king is the maintenance of the kingdom, while for others, it consists of benefiting others through the removal of doubts and so forth; therefore, there is no concern whatsoever regarding a confusion of their functions. What must be done is the elimination of any disagreement on this point.
For when two litigants are in conflict, the king must establish equality in the administration of justice;
otherwise, if they have reached an agreement, what obstacle would there be for the king to accept it?
For we shall explain later that one who possesses purity of body is free from the obstruction of dogs.
Day by day, they were compiled separately according to eighteen categories, based on reasons observed in local custom as well as those found in the scriptures.
By the first half [of the verse], the grounds for a legal decision are stated;
by the second half, there is the specification of the number of titles of dispute (*vivādapada*).
The verb "he should examine" (*paśyet*) is supplied from the preceding verse, as is the word "matters" (*kāryāṇi*).
"Every day he should look after the affairs": as each day passes, the determination of legal cases must be carried out.
Regarding the word "by means of reasons" (*hetubhiḥ*):
a reason (*hetu*) is the instrument for reaching a decision.
And that [means of knowledge] is twofold:
consisting of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and consisting of formal determination (*vyavasthā*).
Among these, that which consists of valid cognition is the cause for the ascertainment of an object, such as witnesses and so forth.
Since conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) is established upon a determination of an object even when it is unreal, [the means of knowledge] takes the form of a formal arrangement (*vyavasthārūpa*).

For example, in the case of an oath of truth, a single witness agreed upon by both parties—if his status as an authority has been accepted by the plaintiff and the defendant—attains the state of being a cause for a decision even if he has not been examined by the members of the court.
However, there can be no determination of an object based on the word of an unexamined person when his reliability (*āptatva*) is not known to be true.
Even when there is agreement among the judges, it serves as the basis for a formal determination (*vyavasthā*).
And that determination is of two kinds: common and uncommon.
Due to differences in location and differences in the substratum, it is also of two kinds: non-contradictory and contradictory.

Non-contradictory (*aviruddhā*): for example, among certain Southerners, when a husband has died, a sonless woman ascends the family pillar (*sabhāsthāṇu*). Having ascended it and been examined by the officials, and having performed the prescribed rites (*kṛtalakṣaṇā*), she immediately thereafter receives the inheritance from the sapindas. Likewise, among the Northerners, if food is given to one who asks for a girl being sought in marriage, then even if it is not explicitly said, "She is given to you," she becomes betrothed (*pratiśrutā*).
And contradictory (*viruddhā*): in some regions, grain is lent in the spring and is to be repaid double in the autumn.
Likewise, when a pledge has been used with permission, even if the interest on the resulting wealth has doubled, it continues to be used until the principal gold is repaid;
for the rule stating that "one may take an eightieth part as interest on a loan, but the interest shall not exceed double [the principal]" is contradicted in this case.
In that regard, the distinctions based on local usage are expressed by the term "reasons observed in the country."
The reasons seen in the treatises are those recited in the treatises;
some of these have their status established by the authors of the treatises, while others are restated as they actually exist in reality.
Among these, those whose status is established by the treatises are, for example, documentary evidence, possession, and witnesses.
Inference, however, is restricted to real entities, just as a hunter tracks the path of a deer by means of drops of blood.
Although not everything worldly obtains its authority from the words of a treatise-author, nevertheless, that which is purely worldly must in some instances rely upon the treatise.

And as for such worldly matters as "if there is such an offense, this is the ordeal" and "possession for such a length of time is proof," it is said that even those, though worldly, are seen in the treatises.
And within that established system, whatever is possible at the root of the treatise authors is authoritative;
however, that which lacks such a possible root is not to be respected,
as is the case with the recitation of the *lekhyakarman*.
"Thus, requested by both parties, this has been written by me, the son of so-and-so; let the scribe, so-and-so, write it according to the truth.
If the scribe were to enter his own name at the very beginning, saying, "I, named so-and-so, the son of such-a-one, am writing this," there would be no fault whatsoever.
For he designates his name for this purpose so that the scribe may be identified by the statement, "This was written by him.
If that scribe is verified by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then what he has written is authoritative.
And if he were not to identify himself by his own family name, then whose reliability would be sought through other means of knowledge?

However, if through the examination of another document or by some other means there should be recognition that "this is the work of a distinguished scribe," then even if he is not personally identified, there is no fault whatsoever.
In that case, even if the scribe does not write, "This was written by me," such a document would indeed possess all its required characteristics.
And this examination of the scribe is useful in that regard.
In this case, the inclusion of the scribe within the category of witnesses is due to the small number of other witnesses;
however, where there are many other trustworthy witnesses who have signed with their own hands, the trustworthiness of the scribe is of no consequence.
Such is another established rule.
A document is [validated] by a document itself, and one with witnesses by witnesses;
however, a document is superior to witnesses, and witnesses are [superior] to a document.
There is no basis whatsoever for this arrangement;
for documents are of two kinds: those written by one's own hand and those written by another's hand.
Those written by another's hand are also of two kinds: those written by a scribe who writes by his own hand and those written by an authorized scribe.
This document, executed by the hand of another, is in every respect nothing but a form of testimony; for in that case, the distinction between "testimony" and "writing" is untenable.
Indeed, its definition is as follows: "The witnesses, with their own hands, preceded by the names of their fathers and so forth..."
"In this matter, such-and-such persons shall write as witnesses together"—thus it is stated.
Nor is the validity of a document written by a single hand accepted, just as [the testimony] of a single witness [is not accepted].

Now, if the reason for this distinction is that "those very witnesses who have set their hands [to the document] are the ones who wrote it," then no superiority is established by this specific qualification.
For trustworthiness is the cause of superiority, and that must be examined in both cases.
Therefore, in such a written document, the principle of the conflict between witnesses applies: one should accept the majority.

Being authorized (*adhikṛtatva*) is also not a distinguishing factor; for in that context, the distinction lies in the fact that one who has been thoroughly examined is authorized. And not all those authorized by the king are necessarily well-examined.
If, however, such a person were free from defects due to being endowed with supreme virtues, he alone would indeed attain the status of a corroborative authority.
For instance, royal land-grant charters, even when written by the hand of a single scribe, become authoritative.
This is because they contain the donor's "signature" (*svāhastakya*), which is his own admission: "This much has been received by me from him," and "This must be given to him."
In that case, if he later says, "It was not received," then those who state what was previously recorded win the case;
there is no occasion at all for witnesses there.

Now, if it is understood from a document belonging to the other party that "this was accepted by him," yet at a later time he himself says, "It was not received," then between these two admissions, for what reason would the latter be sublated by the former, and not the former by the latter?
Because they are equal, there is doubt regarding contradiction;
therefore, it is proper to employ another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This would indeed be so if equality were established.
For the admission that "it was not received" can occur even due to greed and other such motives;
however, no sane person would say "it was received" without having actually received it.

Even in that case, if he should say, "It was returned, but no document was executed because of absence, and a counter-document was not obtained because the scribe was absent due to the urgency of another pressing matter," then there is simply no occasion for other means of proof, such as witnesses and the like.

As for the rule that "what is written [is valid] by what is written," this technical convention cannot override the understanding derived from the inherent capacity of the facts themselves. Indeed, we see creditors gradually clearing a debt held in their hands; they do not record on the back of the document that the money has been cleared, saying, "This much has been paid today," or "I will bring more tomorrow morning and, having combined it, I shall credit it to the account," or "Having cleared everything within a few days, I shall tear up the document.
This is because there is no connection between the document and the actual state of affairs.

Furthermore, when a debtor is constrained by a creditor and is unable to pay the principal, interest, and profit, yet is given only a portion for the sake of clearing the debt, how can it be said that he is not entitled to it as long as a written receipt has not been delivered?
Moreover, if this rule—that "a document is [cancelled] only by a document"—is accepted, then how can the fact of its being executed through force or fraud be investigated?
For in such a case, the possibility of another document does not exist.

Therefore, just as in this case where a document exists but another means of proof (*pramāṇa*) is employed to ascertain its validity, so too should it be employed in other cases. For example, someone might report: "Having gained confidence in him, I executed a document; he said to me, 'Take this amount of wealth for the sake of an immediate auspicious occasion (*puṇyāha*), and tomorrow I will give you everything,' and having said that, he gave only that amount of wealth and did not give the remainder. In such a case, there is indeed an occasion to employ another means of proof.

In that case, if the debtor has witnesses for this matter, then once the document has been presented and rendered suspect, the creditor must prove his claim by means of "delivery on the following day" (*śvodāna*). If, however, the agreement between those two was made in secret, then there is occasion for divine proof (*daivī kriyā*).
But if even in that case there is no confidence due to the possibility of error, a settlement must be reached through an oath of truth (*satya-śapatha*).
But if this were so, a document written in one's own hand would be invalid because it depends on the perception of other means of proof;
thus, there would be a contradiction with the rule that "that which is marked by one's own hand is established even without witnesses.
By this same logic, one would not see the object being given in person.
Having received it solely in his presence, one declares: "This much has been received by me from him.
Those [others] would also be witnesses;
in that case too, it can be said: "Having gained confidence in him, I accepted it."

It has been said in this regard that the actual state of things cannot be subverted by a contradiction with scripture (*smṛti*). Furthermore, this statement will serve as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only where it finds its proper scope; in some cases, however, such a scope does not exist.
If a document remains in the hands of a creditor for a long time, then if the debt has indeed been paid by him, how is it that he neither requested the document nor had it surrendered?
For such neglect of a matter as this for a long duration is impossible;
rather, his practice of speaking falsely is inferred from it.
And so it has been said:
"In matters requiring action, one should report the king's strength either immediately or within three days."

Furthermore, where there is a bond for enjoyment but no enjoyment is recorded, or where the time of forfeiture is not specified, in such a case of dispute—even without witnesses—a document in one's own hand is decisive; for debtors cannot claim, "This was said by you out of affection; now abandon it," nor is there an opportunity for the previously stated words, "I will give it after the document has been made. Thus, having said, "I shall give it," he does not give it.
If it was not given, how was the enjoyment of the property tolerated?
For if this were the case, enjoyment accompanied by a document would be the proof;
yet they declare that mere enjoyment alone is authoritative.
"Written documents, witnesses, and possession"—to this we reply:
what are we being questioned about?
Possession that has lasted for a specific period is the means of proof, not mere possession.
For it is recited thus: "Whatever [period] of ten years, likewise for one who sees but does not speak, there is loss of land after twenty years.
What, then, is the meaning of this [saying], "a written document by a written document alone"?
It has been explained by others.

When there is doubt regarding a specific author—such as whether this was written by this person or not—it is resolved by means of a document whose authorship is certain through its own characteristics. However, in a case where a transaction was made in the presence of witnesses, any doubt as to whether it was performed or not is removed by those witnesses;
they alone are the authority in that matter.

In that case, the examination of another document prepared by the same party is not required. Furthermore, in matters involving deliberate intent, such as the non-payment of debts and the like, a written document is superior to witnesses alone.
For witnesses might forget, or they might enter into a relationship with one of the parties, or they might encounter some other ground for disqualification as witnesses due to sin.
However, because a written document is well-protected by being under one's own control, it is superior to witnesses;
this very point is expressed by the words "but [witnesses are superseded] by a written document.
By means of a document established by one's own hand, one considers even a forgotten matter to have occurred.
Or, even if the witnesses are deceased, they become authoritative through the recognition of their handwriting;
other interpretations have been correctly formulated by Bhartṛyajña himself, and thus they should be understood from him alone as being in every respect rooted in authoritative sources.
One must follow the established rules regarding the causes for the composition of Smṛtis.
Nor is it reasonable to conceive of memory itself as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For it cannot be said that the memory of worldly conventions is rooted in the Veda, because the modes of victory and defeat are of the nature of established facts and are cognizable through perception and other means;
for this matter is already established.
Thus, in common usage, one person is said to "win" while the other "loses.
Furthermore, as for the mention of a gender here, that too should be understood as being like the injunction, "One desiring health should eat the *harītakī* fruit.
Since the purpose regarding the purification of substances has already been analyzed in connection with such cognitions whose nature is that of an injunction, we shall not exert further effort here.
Among the eighteen paths of discourse,
the path is the object of dispute;
it is with reference to these matters that people generally engage in disputes.
"Bound tasks" refers to purposes, that is to say, the accomplishment of goals;
we shall demonstrate these later.
He states their individual importance separately.
These are each distinct purposes and do not, moreover, subsume one another;
whereas other [purposes] are subsumed within the "consequential" (anuṣaṅga) and so forth,
these are not like that.
But there are thousands more [verses] that follow in succession.
Of these, the first is non-payment of debt; then deposit, sale without ownership, partnership, and the non-delivery of what has been given.
Non-payment of wages, breach of contract,
rescission of purchase and sale, and disputes between owners and herdsmen;
The law concerning boundary disputes, verbal and physical assault,
theft, violence, and the abduction of women;
The duties of women and men, partition of inheritance, gambling, and betting—
these eighteen topics constitute the foundation of legal procedure here.
The status of "first" (*ādyatva*) or "primacy" (*prāthamya*) regarding the non-payment of debts (*ṛṇādāna*) is either relative to the order of recitation,
or it is primary (*mukhya*);
for by this [latter sense], even forest-dwellers are included.

That which is connected with the non-payment of debt, as well as the non-payment of debt itself—such as "I have given this debt to you; give me a document of clearance," and so forth—is not [strictly] the non-payment of debt; however, because it is mentioned therein, it should be designated by that term.
Likewise, [the section on] debt: what is to be paid and what is not to be paid, by whom, where, and in what manner, as well as that which [is due],
and the rules for giving and receiving.
Thus it is said:
In that regard, the debt to be paid is that which was contracted by oneself and that contracted by the father, provided one inherits the estate.

That which is not to be paid is a debt contracted by oneself that exceeds double the principal, and that contracted by the father incurred through gambling and the like; this applies to the son, the husband, and the father respectively.
Likewise,
a woman shall not pay a debt contracted by her husband, nor one contracted by her son,
except for what she has promised herself or what was contracted jointly with her husband.

Although this is included within the term "that which is to be paid" (*deyam*), nevertheless, there is a distinction: that which is incurred through gambling and the like is payable by its very nature regardless of specific circumstances, whereas this [present case] is payable due to a restriction on the agent; thus, there is a difference as between a cow and a bull (*gobalīvardavat*). Furthermore, regarding the phrase "up to" (*yāvat*), there is a distinction up to the point of doubling [the debt], as explained previously. In the reading "where" (*yatra*), there is the inclusion of place and time:
where it was received, there it must be returned.
If the creditor so desires, [the debt may be paid] even in another country;
if possible, time [for payment] is also permitted;
it has been stated that one need not desire [payment] in the autumn.
"Or in summer when the crops are ripe, or whenever he thinks there will be an influx of wealth for him.
This means that if possible, everything [should be paid];
if not, some portion, until it has been cleared off in due order.
"By all means, even by the exhaustion of one's entire being, it is equal to [the exhaustion of] karma.
"The dharmas of giving and receiving" refers to witnesses, written documents, and so forth.
"Harshness" refers to verbal punishment.

*Daṇḍa* and *vāk* form the compound *daṇḍavācam*; by the rule "after a *dvandva* ending in *c*, *ṣ*, or *h*, [the suffix] *a* is added," the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) *a* is applied. Then, from the sense "one who possesses that," the suffix *ṭhan* is applied according to the rule "after [a word ending in] *at*, the suffixes *ini* or *ṭhan* [are used]. Regarding the term *strīpuṃdharma*: it is a compound like *śākapārthiva* and others, meaning "a man together with a woman."
In the analysis of the compound as "a woman and a man" (*strī ca pumāṃś ca*), it would result in *strīpuṃsaśabha*.
In these matters, for men who are mostly engaged in disputes,
he should determine the legal case by relying upon the eternal Dharma.
The inclusion of the word "mostly" (*bhūyiṣṭha*) is for the purpose of indicating preeminence;
there are other grounds for legal transaction as well.
For example: "You gave me this house for the purpose of dwelling; why then do you give it to another before the year has passed?"
And this is not the revocation of a gift, for there is no cessation of ownership here; it is merely a permission for the enjoyment of one who dwells [there].
Likewise, as in the case of: "A window has been made by you in my house facing my courtyard.
Regarding the phrase "resorting to eternal dharma": [it means] relying upon the eternal law.
Wealth and desire are impermanent.

Alternatively, the Dharma is eternal; one should uphold that established order which has existed from time immemorial. However, that which has been introduced by those of the present day is not to be respected because of its impermanence.
But when the king himself does not personally conduct the investigation of legal cases,
then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to investigate those cases.
One who is proficient in the eighteen branches of knowledge, designated as a judge (*prāḍvivāka*),
skilled in the science of inquiry (*ānvīkṣikī*), and devoted to the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*.
If, due to preoccupation with some other urgent matter or through lack of proficiency, he does not see [the document] himself, then a learned Brāhmaṇa should be appointed.
And that "learnedness" which pertains to the subject matter of legal proceedings is already implied by the very fact of his eligibility for that office;
for one who does not know something is not entitled to authority in that regard.
However, the thorough knowledge of the *dharmaśāstra* serves the purpose of preventing the determination of a contrary meaning through the fault of passion and hatred.
For one who knows the *dharma*, even when passion and hatred are present, he does not err due to the fear of the scripture; thus, the thorough knowledge of the *dharmaśāstra* is useful.
The examination of legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*), moreover, is undertaken for the sake of that [knowledge].
That knowledge without which it is impossible to reach a legal decision is implied by the authority [of the office];
however, that which is done otherwise after having known [the law] is a cessation [of duty] falling within the scope of other instructions.
And he will state this very point with another effort: "The three who know the Veda and the learned man appointed by the king."
However, the thorough knowledge of other treatises would serve for the sake of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) for one who is authorized in worldly practice (*vyavahāra*).
It should be read as "the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) should be learned.

[Regarding the form *niyuñjyāt*,] the followers of Kātyāyana record the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the rule: "one should employ [the suffix] after a root preceded by *svar* etc., ending in a vowel" (*niyuñjīta svarādyantopasṛṣṭāt*).
Surrounded by exactly three members of the court, he should examine his judicial duties,
having entered the foremost assembly hall while either seated or standing.

By the term "by the members of the assembly" (sabhyaiḥ), although no specific caste is mentioned, they are understood to be Brāhmaṇas alone; this is because of the mention of "Brāhmaṇas" later on, and because of the mention of "together with Brāhmaṇas" earlier.
However, the mention of "three" is for the purpose of excluding one or two;
indeed, three or more are intended.
We shall explain this further in the section on witnesses (*sākṣiprakaraṇa*). Regarding the phrase "having entered the court itself at the very front":

having entered the court by virtue of occupying the king's position, the repetition of the mention of standing and sitting—along with their respective duties—is intended either for the sake of illustration or to exclude other [specific] rules.
Therefore, he does not sit upon the royal throne.
In whatever place three Brahmins learned in the Vedas sit together,
along with a learned official of the king, they know that assembly to be a court of Brahmā.
It has been stated that "having entered the court (*sabhā*), he shall examine legal cases.
Now, in common usage, the word *sabhā* refers to a particular type of house or palace, as in the expression, "The divine court fashioned by Maya, adorned with gold.
In some instances, it refers to an assembly of specific persons. To exclude these meanings, [the author] states the definition of the court.
Where three Brāhmaṇas learned in the Vedas are present, as well as a relative of the king who is appointed and qualified— and who,
alternatively, is the one mentioned immediately in the preceding verse—
it is this assembly that is intended here.
The mention of Brahmā is for the purpose of praise;
just as the assembly of Brahmā is faultless, so too is this one.
When dharma, pierced by adharma, enters an assembly,
and the members of that assembly do not extract the dart, they themselves are pierced.
One should either not enter an assembly or speak what is correct;
for a man who remains silent or speaks falsely becomes a sinner.
In this sense, two things are prohibited:
one should not engage in false views under the authority of having entered the path, nor should one neglect false views when they are being committed by another.
In both cases, there is a fault.

They say that when an opposing party acts erroneously, one who remains silent or who speaks in a manner contrary to the scriptures and logic by interposing his hand becomes a sinner and a partaker of guilt.
Therefore, he must not entertain this hope:
"The second judge perceives falsely; he alone is implicated, while I, remaining silent and indifferent, why should I be joined with sin?"
By the prohibition against entering the court, the undertaking of the authority to preside over legal proceedings is here prohibited;
that is to say, one should not enter the court,
meaning that the office of overseeing judicial affairs must not be assumed.
If he has been appointed, it should be stated that this is appropriate;
however, they do not accept the silence of a learned man who, though not appointed and merely present by chance, witnesses the members of the court holding false views.
Thus, whether appointed or unappointed, one who knows the Dharma ought to speak.
Now, an objection might be raised by royal officials: "Why does this unauthorized person speak? and consequently, one must depart from that place.
This is what is meant by the statement: "And when there is injury to the weak, if one is capable [of preventing it, one must intervene]."
Where dharma is slain by adharma, and truth by falsehood, while the members of the assembly look on, there the members of the assembly are themselves slain.
Dharma is the established order determined by scripture, logic, and local custom.
If that is destroyed—that is, ruined—by the plaintiff or the defendant through adharma, which consists of its transgression;
likewise, truth is destroyed by witnesses through falsehood.
If the judges and others merely look on and do not extract the truth, then they are "slain," becoming like corpses; thus they are censured.
Therefore, when the plaintiff and defendant act perversely, the members of the court must not remain indifferent, nor should the witnesses.
Whether it is established by the mention of dharma and adharma or by the mention of truth and falsehood, both are included here for the sake of completing the verse.
Therefore, it has been explained by way of the distinction between objects.
Dharma, when violated, destroys; Dharma, when preserved, protects.
Therefore, Dharma must not be violated, lest violated Dharma slay us.
One must not, out of fear, act otherwise than according to the truth; for when dharma is transgressed, it is dharma that destroys, not the seeker of wealth nor the king who assists him.
Likewise, dharma alone, when protected, dispels all fear;
neither the seeker of wealth nor others, even when enraged, are able to cause harm.
Therefore, one who understands that pleasure and pain depend upon *dharma* should not destroy *dharma*.
If we destroy *dharma*, then it strikes back at us like an enraged serpent; thus, lest *dharma*, once destroyed, slay us, *dharma* must be protected for the sake of self-preservation.
For the Blessed One, Dharma, is indeed the Bull (vṛṣa); the gods know him who treats that Dharma with contempt as a Vṛṣala (outcaste). Therefore, one should not violate Dharma.
By means of the etymological derivation of the word *vṛṣala*, the one with false vision is censured.
One is not a *vṛṣala* by birth; rather, he is so called because he obstructs (*alaṃkurute*) the rain of desire (*vṛṣa*)—that is, Dharma. The word *alam* here signifies cessation.
The gods have understood this meaning as "vṛṣala";
as for humans, if they consider it merely a word for a caste, let them so consider it at their pleasure, but the gods are more authoritative.
And they consider the application of the word *vṛṣala* to be based on this ground for its usage (*pravṛttinimitta*).
The mention of "devas" (gods) is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).

Therefore, in such actions as "at the time of a *śrāddha* ceremony, a *vṛṣala* must not be admitted" or "a *vṛṣala* who is a thief should be killed," it is a Brāhmaṇa who holds false views who is to be understood by the word *vṛṣala*.
Consequently, thinking "may I not incur the state of a *vṛṣala*," one should not neglect nor destroy the Dharma.
The attribution of the status of a *vṛṣala* is a form of censure.
Dharma alone is the true friend who follows one even unto death;
for all else, like worldly prosperity, goes to destruction along with the body.

The teaching that "one must not transgress the Dharma out of fear" was already taught by the statement, "Dharma itself, when violated, destroys"; what is taught here is that [it] must not be transgressed out of affection.
Since Dharma is one's sole true friend, one should cultivate affection for it.
Even another person who is a friend abandons his life out of regard for some task.
Even for one who may be an ultimate friend, that friendship lasts only until death;
but the Dharma follows a person even after they have died.
Therefore, out of regard for a friend, one must not practice false views or remain indifferent.
Wife, son, friend, wealth, and inheritance—
these perish with the destruction of a man's body;
but dharma alone never abandons him.
Therefore, one should abandon wife and children, but not dharma.
Whatever else there is besides dharma, such as a wife and so forth, all that goes to destruction along with the body.
Since no one other than dharma is capable of protecting one after death, dharma must not be abandoned even out of consideration for friends or kinsmen.
One quarter of the guilt reaches the perpetrator, one quarter reaches the witness,
one quarter reaches all the members of the court, and one quarter reaches the king.
Nor should this thought be entertained by either the plaintiff or the defendant: "The land or other property of one party is being seized;
he alone shall bear the fault of the seizure of land, while we, not having committed that act, why should we be guilty, since that sin is divided fourfold"?
For this is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda).
For there is no transfer of sin committed by one person to another.

Nevertheless, because they have transgressed the prohibition against false views, sin arises for them as well, having a false object; even though the king himself does not see it, he becomes possessed of fault due to the fault of his appointed officials, such as the judges.
Or, if the king’s official, having been informed of misconduct, fails to restrain the defeated wrongdoer and does not again provide a correct judgment, then he too becomes a partaker of sin.
Alternatively, the mention of the "king" is intended as an illustration for those in authority;
the meaning is that when the king himself perceives falsely, he incurs fault, and when one acting in the king's stead does so, then that person incurs the fault.
The king becomes [sinless] by this, and the members of the assembly are released from guilt;
the sin goes to the perpetrator where one who deserves censure is censured.
This very same point is stated by way of its opposite:
where one who possesses faults is not permitted to conceal them, but rather his fault is made manifest, there everything turns out well.

From the words "where there is Dharma" onwards, these are *arthavādas* intended to show the results of good and evil through censure and praise, for the purpose of forbidding indifference toward false views.
One who merely lives by his birth may indeed be called a "pseudo-Brahmin" (brāhmaṇabruva),
but a Śūdra can never be the expounder of dharma to a king.
It has been stated that one should carry out the determination of dharma together with Brāhmaṇas and with ministers who are experts in counsel (*mantra*).

Since the caste of the ministers is not specified therein, even Śūdras who have entered the assembly might—by virtue of being ministers—be authorized to determine legal proceedings; being devoted to those matters and possessing some degree of refined intellect, they might express the established rules of dharma.

Furthermore, a thorough knowledge of the *Smṛti* scriptures is not required for every legal proceeding, such that the prohibition of Śūdras would be suspected of being useless on the grounds that it is rendered purposeless by their absence.

For the causes of victory and defeat are indeed those things cognizable by worldly means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), such as witnesses and the like; for instance, that "this witness is righteous and has no connection to this person through any relationship," whereas "this one is not a witness because his falsehood has been observed repeatedly"—such matters can be inferred by oneself by one whose intellect is cultivated, and they do not fall solely within the scope of the Smṛti scriptures. Therefore, this is a prohibition of what would otherwise be applicable.
Furthermore, there is no restriction of caste regarding the office of minister as there is for the domestic priest (*purohita*).
For, after stating that "he should deliberate together with them," it is subsequently said that "he should deliberate with a Brāhmaṇa.

Therefore, the meaning is this: even if a Śūdra should somehow attain a partial understanding of justice, nevertheless, when litigants dispute in the royal court, the minister or the official in charge of punishment must not say anything [on his behalf].
The first half of the preceding verse is to be explained as a supplement to the prohibition.

For it is impossible to assert that one who lives solely by his caste, devoid of qualities such as learning and the like, is appointed as a teacher of Dharma; since his very nature has been examined [in the previous passage], this permission is a supplement to the prohibition—like the saying, "Eat poison, but do not eat in his house"—and is not a mere permission in itself.
For this very reason, he says "if you so desire" (*kāmam*).
For if the word "kāma" (at will) were employed, its status as an injunction would be contradicted.
Others, however, say:

since the Brāhmaṇa is enjoined as the speaker, it follows that at that time the qualified person (niyojya) must be a learned Brāhmaṇa; thus, the three other castes—the Kṣatriyas and so forth—are excluded there. Here, moreover, the prohibition of the Śūdra is for the purpose of permitting the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya in the absence of a learned Brāhmaṇa.
The rest is the same.
In the phrase "he subsists on mere birth," the word *mātra* is used for the sake of restriction;
he lives by relying solely (*kevalam*) on the Brāhmaṇa caste itself, and not on specific qualities such as Vedic study and so forth, because he is devoid of such qualities.
The word *bruva* is used in the sense of contempt.
The kingdom of that king for whom a Śūdra performs the discernment of dharma perishes, like a cow in the mud, even as he looks on.
This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) supplementary to the preceding rule:
the kingdom and the subjects of that king for whom a Śūdra performs the discernment of dharma—that is, the determination of legal matters—perish and decay, like a cow in the mud.
That kingdom which consists mostly of Śūdras, which is overrun by atheists and devoid of the twice-born,
quickly perishes entirely, afflicted by famine and disease.

This also is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda) as before. Furthermore, by virtue of the context, the predominance of Śūdras should be understood as referring to those who decide legal disputes;
where Śūdras are the majority among those who determine legal disputes, that kingdom quickly perishes due to afflictions such as famine and disease.
It is said that upon the destruction of the kingdom, there is the destruction of the king;
"overrun by nihilists" is the illustrative example. Just as [a land] is overrun—that is, occupied—by nihilists such as the Lokāyatikas who deny the existence of the next world, and therefore...
"Without twice-born status":
for among nihilists (*nāstika*), the distinction between Brāhmaṇas and the other classes is not real, because of their intermixture.
As it has been said: "Brāhmaṇas and the others are like the designations 'physician' or 'merchant,' and so forth."
Or, in a situation where there is a conflict regarding the Dharma, that place where the twice-born are not accepted as authorities is "advija."
Having occupied the seat of justice, with his body properly covered and his mind composed,
he should pay homage to the world-protectors and then begin the examination of legal cases.

That seat upon which Dharma is primary is the *dharmāsana*. For on the royal throne (*rājāsana*), one makes material wealth (*artha*) alone the primary concern, even by subordinating Dharma in accordance with the requirements of maintaining the kingdom. However, the meaning here is that in the adjudication of legal disputes, one must rely solely upon Dharma as the primary factor; it does not, however, indicate a difference in the physical seat itself.
"With covered limbs" means having the body concealed by clothing and so forth.

"Having bowed to the world-protectors"—that is, having paid homage to the eight world-protectors, Indra and the others—one should begin the examination of the case. These two acts, the covering of the limbs and the bowing to the world-protectors, serve an invisible (transcendental) purpose. "Composed" means having a mind focused on nothing else during the examination of the case.
For in this way, the purpose is clearly seen; or rather, the inclusion of the term "composed" (*samāhita*) serves as a qualification for the salutation.
Even though it may appear that something has already been stated here, there is nevertheless no excessive redundancy because this is a metrical work.
The dative case in *lokapālebhyaḥ* is used in the sense of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
How so?

Because the inclusion of the action itself (*kriyāgrahaṇa*) was enjoined in the rule for the recipient, for the sake of examples such as *śrāddhāya nigṛhṇate* ("he restrains himself for the sake of the ancestral rite") and *patye śete* ("she lies down for her husband").
Furthermore, the mention of "action" (kriyā) does not refer exclusively to the domain of [roots] such as *gṛhṇāti* and so forth, because it is not stated so in the Bhāṣya.
Having understood both benefit and harm, as well as merit and demerit in their entirety, he should examine all the legal cases of the litigants according to the order of their castes.
Virtue (*dharma*) and vice (*adharma*) alone are what constitute benefit (*artha*) and harm (*anartha*); the acquisition of cattle, gold, and so forth is not "benefit," nor is its opposite "harm.
Rather, having understood that virtue alone is benefit and vice alone is harm, and having resolved this firmly in one's heart, one should view all actions accordingly.
Alternatively, both benefit and harm must be understood, as well as virtue and vice.
One must understand the essential nature of Dharma and the triviality of worldly objects;

or rather, in a situation where there is great harm but only a small amount of unrighteousness (adharma), one should avoid that harm. For a slight transgression can be dispelled by means of a great benefit, such as through acts of giving or ritual expiation.
In an assembly of many litigants, the order of castes (varṇa) should be followed.
This is the sequence for the viewing of cases when all are equally afflicted.

However, when even a person of the lowest caste has urgent business or a great matter at stake, then by the principle that "he whose affliction is urgent [must be seen first]," one should look after that very case first and not respect the prescribed order.
For it has been stated that the determination of legal disputes is for the sake of maintaining the stability of the kingdom; therefore, one must not rely on the literal meaning alone.
One should discern the internal disposition of men by external signs:
through their voice, complexion, gestures, facial expression, gaze, and movements.
And thus he says this:
the meaning of the verse is that both truthfulness and falsehood must be determined by inference from the conduct of witnesses as well.
Therefore, the mention of voice and so forth is for the sake of illustration.
What is meant is that one should determine [the truth] by whatever sign is certain, and not by voice and so forth alone, because those are subject to deviation.
For those unaccustomed to entering the court may, upon seeing the high-ranking officials, undergo a natural transformation even if they are telling the truth;
whereas those who are bold may conceal their true appearance.
Voice, complexion, and gesture constitute "voice, complexion, and gesture"; their manifestations are "the manifestations of voice, complexion, and gesture.
Manifestation (*ākāra*) means transformation (*vikāra*).
For it is the alteration of the natural state of the voice and so forth that constitutes a manifestation.
By means of these, one should discern— that is, determine—
the internal disposition or intention of men, such as litigants and witnesses. In this context, a modification of the voice refers to stammering, weeping, and so forth in speech.
The change in complexion refers to the alteration of the body's form and so forth;
the gesture refers to perspiration, trembling, horripilation, and so forth;
and by the eyes refers to the casting of glances characterized by agitation or anger.

This is self-evident through gestures such as the movement of the hands or the twitching of the eyebrows; for even when an intention is being concealed, the tone of voice and other such cues reveal it when observed with skill. For it is well known that these possess the power to manifest a hidden intention.
By means of physical forms, gestures, gait, movements, and speech,
as well as by changes in the eyes and face, the internal mind is perceived.
For instance, by this verse he demonstrates that the power of accents and so forth—which were previously mentioned—is observed in the world; thus, there is no redundancy.
In this context, "modes" (*ākāra*) are those things such as gestures (*iṅgita*) which are performed or manifested.
"Gestures" (*iṅgita*) has already been explained.

The plural number is used because of the distinction between individual instances. The term "movement" (*gati*) is carried over from the preceding verse; it is "stumbling," meaning it has become otherwise by its very nature.
"Speech" refers to words that are contradictory in their preceding and succeeding parts. "Distortion of the speaker" refers to specific changes in the mouth and so forth.
The remainder has already been explained in the previous verse.
The summarized meaning is that by means of these worldly transformations, the internal mind is perceived even elsewhere.
The king shall protect the inheritance of a minor heir until he has returned from his teacher's house or until he has passed his childhood.
But surely, the administration of justice has been introduced as the subject to be discussed;
in that context, what relevance does the protection of a child’s property have?
It is said in reply:
This [section] is commenced in order to remove this very matter from the scope of legal dispute:
the property of a minor must be protected by the king as if it were his own property;
otherwise, paternal uncles and other relatives would fall into dispute, each claiming, "I must protect this," or "I must protect that."
Nor is there any other occasion [for this discussion],
as it is mentioned in connection with the conventional usage being anticipated;
furthermore, since it is not taught among the exclusive duties of a king (*rājadharma*), it must be stated at this very juncture.
The heir of this [minor] is a child; thus, it is "the property of a minor's heir.
Here, the term "heir" (dāyāda) is used in the sense of an owner (svāmin).
The king shall protect the wealth belonging to a minor until he has returned from his teacher’s house—that is, until he has passed beyond childhood and transcended the state of being a child.
And this is the distinction:
for one who remains a householder from childhood, the period "past childhood" is mentioned for his sake;
however, for one who is a religious student (vrataka), even though childhood has ended, he must maintain his wealth until his return home (samāvartana).
Alternatively, for the twice-born, the limit is the return from studentship (samāvartana); for others, it is the passing of childhood.
The same protection should be afforded to women who have sons by barren wives,
to those whose families have been destroyed, to women devoted to their husbands, and to widows who are afflicted by illness.
The king shall properly protect the property of anyone who is destitute;
likewise, those such as wives and so forth are mentioned merely as examples.
In this way, the protection of the subjects is fulfilled.
The preceding verse, however, is for the purpose of defining the time limit.
*Vaśā* means a barren woman.
*Aputrā* means one whose sons are incapable, or who has no sons at all, or whose sons are destitute.
"Barren women and those without sons" is a copulative compound (*dvandva*).
But is it not the case that a barren woman is also one without a son?
True.
The mention of both [the mother and the father] is for the purpose of protecting her even while the husband is still alive;
for once she has been superseded by another wife, the husband becomes indifferent toward her. The inclusion of the term "destitute of family" (niṣkulā) serves as a qualification of those women.
This is said for those women who have no protector such as a husband, paternal uncle, or maternal uncle, who are themselves incapable due to their female nature, and whose kinsmen are envious.
For it is the kinsmen who must protect the character, the person, and the wealth of women.
Thus it has been said:
He is the lord over protection and maintenance;
when the husband's family is exhausted, devoid of men, and without refuge, he is the authority.
While her paternal kinsmen (sapiṇḍas) are present, the father’s side has authority over the woman;
but when both sides have failed, the king is the husband and the master of the woman.
But if she herself is somehow capable [of performing the rite], there is no role for her relatives therein;
for this very reason, he says "among those who are afflicted," by which incapacity is indicated.
Others, however, have explained that "afflicted" refers to those whose husbands are ill;
even if she is not a widow, she should be protected by the king himself due to her husband's incapacity.
This applies to women who are without male protectors.
Those women who have no family or kin are called *niṣkulā*.
Others, however, say that a *niṣkulā* is an unchaste woman (*kulaṭā*).
Even for them, wealth acquired through prostitution and other such means must be protected by the king, provided they have not fallen from their caste.
And in this view, there is the inclusion of independent *niṣkulā* women; that is, among widows who are devoted to their husbands—
where a "widow" (*vidhavā*) is one whose husband has died.
*Dhava* is a name for a husband; one who is deprived of him is a *vidhavā* (widow). If she remains devoted to her husband (*pativratā*), [she is not truly widowed].

In that case, she is one whose wealth must be protected; however, regarding those women who are addicted to adultery, their unfitness to possess woman's property is recited in another Smṛti: "One who is intent on doing harm, shameless, and a destroyer of wealth..."
"And a woman who is addicted to adultery does not deserve her woman's property.
Thus, her expulsion is ordained;
and "expulsion" means placing her outside the main residence, not necessarily banishment itself.
Since even for those women who have fallen, residence near the home and the provision of mere food and clothing are ordained,
one should follow this very rule even regarding women who have fallen:
"Food, clothing, and drink should be given, and they should dwell near the house."

Therefore, whatever rule regarding the banishment of women is heard in connection with [the forfeiture of] their woman's property (*strīdhana*), their wealth, their entire estate, and so forth, that must be understood as referring to such a specific case.
Nevertheless, whatever has been earned by her through begging for alms or similar means, she alone is entitled to that; her relatives shall not seize it.
In this present context, however, it is the taking of a second wife (*ādhivedana*) that is prescribed on this very ground, and not the seizure of the woman's property.
For thus it has been said:
"A woman who is a drunkard, of bad conduct, or hostile;
one who is diseased, harmful, or always wasteful of wealth—she may indeed be superseded by taking another wife."

And therefore, by the authority of the *Mānava-smṛti* stating that "she does not deserve [to receive] woman's property (*strīdhana*)," this very Smṛti is explained as follows: she does not deserve the woman's property given for supersession (*ādhivedanika*); the meaning is that nothing already given to her should be taken away from her. As for what was stated—"one should give equal [wealth] for supersession to a superseded wife"—it does not mean that what was previously given to her must be confiscated.
We, however, say this:
the confiscation of the property of a woman who hates her husband and is devoted to adultery is indeed proper;
for it has been stated even here [in this very text]:
She who transgresses against one who is negligent, intoxicated, or afflicted by disease shall be abandoned for three months, deprived of her ornaments and belongings.
The meaning is that she should be deprived of her ornaments and finery.
But those kinsmen who should seize the property of those women while they are still living,
a righteous lord of the earth should punish them with the punishment prescribed for thieves.

This penalty for a thief applies to those kinsmen who misappropriate the woman's property; for they seize it by means of many fraudulent devices, thinking, "This woman is not her own mistress; what can she give, or what can she enjoy? We are the masters here. Thus, out of suspicion that they are thieves, the penalty for a thief is ordained even though they may not actually be thieves.
The lord of the earth should punish those kinsmen, such as brothers-in-law and others, who might seize the property of those women while they are still alive;
he should restrain them with the punishment for theft, which will be described later:
"With whatever limb a thief commits an offense against men..."
"That which is to be cut off must indeed be cut off; that is the instruction of Manu.
Thus, this [protection] must be especially guarded by the king against his own kinsmen, whereas the protection against thieves is prescribed as pertaining to his own kingdom.
The king shall cause property whose owner has disappeared to be kept in custody for three years;
within three years the owner may take it, but after that period the king may take it himself.

If a certain object belonging to an owner has been lost through negligence while he was traveling on a road, or has fallen off [his vehicle] in a forest or wilderness, and is found by forest guards or other royal officials and brought into the presence of the king, the king, having secured it, should place it publicly at the palace gate or on the main highway. Alternatively, it should be announced by the sounding of a drum, proclaiming whose property and what exactly has been lost. It must then be kept in the very place where it was found, under the supervision of a guard.

In this manner, it should be kept for three years. Within those three years, if someone should claim ownership on some ground, then that person must be handed over a share consisting of the aforementioned sixteenth part and so forth, once the property has been cleared; after that period, it is to be entered into the king's own treasury. That wealth whose owner has disappeared is "ownerless" (*pranaṣṭasvāmika*).
"Pranaṣṭa" means unknown;
"riktha" means wealth;
the collection of three years is "tryabdam."
As in the case of *trivarṣā*, there is an absence of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* when the word *abda* occurs;
the word *abda* is a synonym for *saṃvatsara*.
One should cause [it] to be placed, that is, one should establish it.
"Arvāk" means prior to three years; "haret" means the owner should take possession.
The word "arvāk" denotes a limit, signifying "before" in terms of direction, place, and so forth.
Others, however, say that the phrase "the king should take" is a permission for enjoyment rather than an act of seizure.
Indeed, it is not proper to seize the property of another even after three years have passed;
therefore, if the owner does not appear after three years, the king may take possession of it himself.
How, then, are they to explain this verse: "whatever [property] for ten years"?
If it is argued that the seizure of another's property is improper, then its enjoyment is likewise improper;

for another's property, when being enjoyed, is simply destroyed, just like clothing and other such items. In that case, the figurative designation of "seizure" is appropriate, because the very act of enjoyment possesses the same result as seizure.
But it must be stated what kind of enjoyment there is in the case of elephants, horses, and so forth;
therefore, there is no reason to abandon the literal meaning of the text.
Furthermore, the verb *harati* is frequently seen used in the sense of "to take" (or "to receive"), as in such expressions as "he shall take the inheritance" (*ṛkthaṃ haret*).
Therefore, the meaning is this: the king should take—that is, appropriate—for himself.
But how, then, can an owner demonstrate his ownership when the property has been lost?
To this he says:
"He who says, 'This is mine,' shall be questioned according to the prescribed rule."
Having verified the form, number, and other characteristics, the owner is entitled to that property.
Whoever comes and says, "This is my own property," he should be interrogated according to the prescribed rule. "To be interrogated" means to be questioned. What is this method of interrogation?

One should interrogate him as follows: "Who are you? What substance was lost? Of what form, what dimension, and what number? Did it fall or not fall? If it fell, in which place? Furthermore, from where did you obtain it? If he corroborates the form, number, and so forth—where "form" refers to the nature of living beings, clothing, and the like, such as "a white cloth" or "a cow"—[then he may be trusted].
Likewise, "number" refers to ten cows or ten yokes;
by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," it includes measurements such as cubits and so forth, quantities such as gold and so forth, or miscellaneous forms of property.
He becomes the owner when he has verified all of this.
Therefore, one deserves to take possession of that property.
"Correspondence" (saṃvāda) is said to mean that if what was determined by one means of proof is determined by this very same [means] in exactly the same way.
And the mention of form, number, and so forth is for the sake of illustration, as it applies to other grounds for ownership such as witnesses and the like.
One who fails to report the location, time,
color, appearance, and size of the lost object accurately deserves a fine equal to the value of that object.
This penalty is prescribed for one who acts falsely:

he who does not declare the place and time of the lost property—stating whether it was lost in this place or at this time; nor its true nature or ultimate reality, such as its color being white and so forth; nor its form, such as whether it is a cloth, a garment, or a pair of clothes; nor its measurement, such as five cubits in length or seven cubits in measure—if he fails to report these, then he deserves a fine equal to that, commensurate with the amount of wealth regarding which he acted falsely.
Then, remembering the duty of the virtuous, the king should take a sixth, a tenth, or even a twelfth part of what has been lost and found.
One should take—that is, seize—a sixth, tenth, or twelfth part of the property found after it was lost;
the remainder should be restored to the owner.
In this regard, a twelfth part is taken in the first year, a tenth in the second, and a sixth in the third.
Alternatively, the distinction of parts is made with regard to protection and the destruction of afflictions;
that is, by recollecting the Dharma of the virtuous and knowing that "this is the proper conduct for disciples."
Property that has been lost and subsequently found shall remain under the supervision of appointed officials;
any thieves the king may catch therein, he shall cause to be executed by means of an elephant.

"Recovered after being lost" means recovered after having been previously lost; it refers to what was first lost and later found again.
