It should be kept under the supervision of capable and devoted guards. Even if it is thus guarded, if some thieves should seize it, the king shall have them executed by an elephant.
The seizing of the elephant is for the sake of an unseen result.
If a man should truthfully declare, "This treasure is mine," the king shall take a sixth or even a twelfth part of it.

Wealth that is secretly deposited in the ground after it has been dug up is called a *nidhi* (treasure). Such treasures may be several hundred or even several thousand years old. In that regard, if a treasure is somehow discovered by someone while the earth is being excavated, it belongs to the king.
And so Gautama says: "The discovery of a treasure-trove is the property of the king. This should be understood to apply to a treasure whose depositor is not remembered;
for it has been stated that "the one who reports it shall receive a sixth part."
However, this verse should be understood as referring to a case where the depositor is indeed known, or where the person is a *tatpuruṣa* compound such as "the father or grandfather" and so forth.
The meaning is: "He who should say, 'This treasure is mine,' must establish it by means of truth and proof. From him, one should take a sixth part.
Once its ownership by that [person] has been determined, the king takes a sixth part or other portion;
and this alternative depends on the qualities of the informant.
But one who speaks falsely shall be fined an eighth part of his own wealth,
or a smaller fraction calculated according to the value of that very treasure [in dispute].
He who fails to prove his claim— saying, "This was deposited by me, or by my ancestor"— is a liar and must be punished.
As much wealth as he possesses, from that [the king] shall cause him to pay an eighth part; or rather, a smaller fraction, measure, or portion of that very treasure—this is the meaning.

However, he should not cause that specific substance, such as gold and so forth, to be paid; rather, another substance of equal quantity or equal value, by means of which amount of wealth the punished person does not go to ruin or is made to accept discipline. A choice between these options should be adopted depending on specific circumstances such as the consequences of the act, and depending on the qualities of the individual.
This indicates that the fine shall be smaller than the previous extraordinary fine.
Therefore, in a case where one possesses great wealth but the treasure found is small, he should be fined an eighth part of the value of the property relative to the treasure;
for that [eighth part] will indeed be very small.
But a learned Brāhmaṇa, having discovered a treasure previously deposited,
may take it entirely, for he is the master of all.
When a learned Brāhmaṇa discovers a treasure deposited by his ancestors, such as his father and so forth, he may take it all; he need not give the previously mentioned share to the king.
This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda): for he is the lord of everything.
Thus it has been said: "All this is the property of the Brāhmaṇa."
And this complete appropriation applies only to a treasure whose owner is a Brāhmaṇa.

However, in the case of a treasure whose owner is unknown, the king's share certainly exists even when it has been found by a learned Brāhmaṇa; for the author will later state: "But of ancient treasures... and so forth.
If a king should discover an ancient treasure buried in the earth,
he should give half of it to the twice-born and deposit the other half in the treasury.
This is the king's rule for the distribution of gifts from that treasure which was discovered by the king himself.
By the word "treasury" (kośa), the place where the accumulation of wealth is kept is meant.
The phrase "anciently deposited in the earth" is a restatement of its nature as a treasure (nidhi).
Since he is the lord of the earth, the king receives half the share from ancient treasures and minerals found in the ground for protecting them.

This statement, "For of ancient treasures," is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to the rule that even when a treasure is found by someone else, the king must take the previously mentioned share.
Furthermore, this is a rule regarding minerals (*dhātu*) found in the earth that was not previously established.
Gold, silver, and the like are the seeds [of minerals], while red lead, black ointment, and so forth are the minerals themselves.
He who digs for gold mines and the like, or he who subsists on minerals such as red chalk (gairika) found in mountains and so forth, must likewise give a share to the king as previously stated.

Regarding the term "half-share" (*ardhabhāga*), the word *ardha* here denotes a mere portion because it is used in a compound construction, as in the expressions "half a village" (*grāmārdha*) or "half a city" (*nagarārdha*). However, the neuter gender of the word indicates an equal division.

But here, in this compound, because there is no perception of a specific gender and because the preceding word—by virtue of the particle *ca*—refers to the portion consisting of six, ten, twelve, and so forth which has been previously mentioned, it is understood as denoting that [portion].
The meaning is: "it takes a half," that is, it takes a single part.
The reason for this is stated: "because of protection."
Even though the royal protection may not be applied to something deposited in the earth because of someone's ignorance, nevertheless, its forcible seizure by a powerful person is possible;
therefore, protection indeed has its purpose. It is for this very reason that he says: "For he is the lord of the earth."
He is the lord of the earth;
therefore, it is proper that he receive his share of whatever is obtained from his land.
The king must restore to all castes the wealth stolen by thieves;
by using that for himself, the king incurs the guilt of the thief.

Whatever wealth has been taken by thieves, the king, having recovered it, shall not appropriate for himself; rather, it must be restored to those very persons who were robbed. By the use of the word "all," it is indicated that it should be given even to those of the lowest caste (caṇḍālas).
In another reading, *caurāhṛtam*, the analysis is *cauraiḥ āhṛtam* (brought by thieves), and the compound is formed according to the rule *sādhanaṃ kṛtā*.

In yet another reading, *caurahṛtam*, the compound is formed either by the application of the rule regarding the third case (*tṛtīyā*) or by a formal division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), as previously explained.
The meaning here, however, is this: whatever has been stolen by thieves and is impossible to recover must be given by the king from his own treasury.
The second half of the verse should be construed as follows: "the king, utilizing that [wealth].
Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *yuj* preceded by the prefix *upa* should be understood here in its figurative sense (*lakṣaṇayā*) as "appropriating" rather than "joining.

For when someone does not give wealth to another when the time for it has arrived, but instead employs it for his own purposes, he is said to have "utilized" that very wealth belonging to the other; thus it is rightly said: "The king, by utilizing that, incurs the guilt of the thief."
*Kilbiṣam* means sin.
One who knows the law, having carefully examined the laws of castes and regions, the laws of guilds,
and the laws of families, should establish his own duty.
Countries such as Kuru, Kāpiśa, and Kaśmīra, having fixed boundaries, constitute a *janapada*.
The phenomena (*dharma*) existing therein are called *jānapada*;
these are certain things that exist there and are practiced under the designations of those respective regions.
Alternatively, the people residing there are designated by the term "janapada," as in the expression "the platforms are shouting. That which is to be performed by them is "jānapada";
this is a secondary derivative (taddhita) formed with the sense of "belonging to that" (tasyedam).
The term *jātijānapadāḥ* is a genitive compound meaning "local customs of castes. Local customs pertaining solely to specific castes must be protected by the king.

Having reflected and deliberated—namely, whether they are contrary to the sacred scriptures (*āmnāya*) or not, and likewise whether they cause harm to anyone or not—the king should establish and cause those that are not contrary to be practiced; this is the meaning.
And so he will say later: "that which has been practiced by the virtuous.
Alternatively, it is a descriptive compound (viśeṣaṇasamāsa) meaning "those who are both [members of] castes and inhabitants of the countryside";
and by the word "caste" (jāti), permanence is indicated.
This is merely a praise of local customs (*deśadharma*). Just as birth is eternal, so too are local customs that do not contradict the scriptures eternal.
Those whose purposes are visible, such as the grazing of cattle and the draining of water, should be practiced as if they were eternal.
Just as villagers in this region establish a convention that "cows must not be grazed here" for the sake of accomplishing some purpose, and whoever violates it is punished by the king;
or alternatively, *jānapada* refers to those born in the countryside (*janapada*), meaning inhabitants of the land. Those who are *jānapada* by birth are *jātijānapada*.
"Birth" (*jāti*) means birth or origination;
by this, the permanence of men's connection to a place is indicated.

Those who are born in that region, those whose ancestors originated in that region, and those who reside there—those qualities belonging to them, distinguished by all these qualifiers, which have arisen from time immemorial, are expressed by the term *jātijānapada*.

Since the suffix *cha* would have been applicable according to the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ* in the context of a *taddhita* derivative, the suffix *aṇ* was used instead because of its Vedic character (*chāndasatva*).
Alternatively, through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), the word "person" (*puruṣa*) is applied to the duties (*dharma*) associated with him.
Therefore, this restriction of place regarding duties is to be understood as being observed by such a person.
For these are indeed the local customs of the Mlecchas, and not those of the Āryas.

Since they possess characteristics similar to animals and are not entitled to [the Vedic] authority elsewhere, they practice a dharma established by their own traditional conduct, such as marrying their mothers and so forth;
this is not to be prohibited by a sovereign ruler.

For those who follow the customs of their own country, this is a duty of their caste (*jātidharma*), because it is permitted by virtue of their connection with residence in that region; furthermore, there is no contradiction here with the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). Any contradiction exists only regarding those for whom [the rules] are specifically intended, not regarding animals. But was it not stated, under the section concerning those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), that "non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, purity, and restraint of the senses" [apply to them]?
And the Mlecchas are indeed those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*).

In that regard, if one is not defiled by marrying a mother or by voiding urine when there is an absence of purification with water, what kind of restraint of the senses could there be, or what sort of purity?
This has already been stated.
These practices, such as purity and the rest, belong to those residing in the middle of Āryāvarta;
however, among the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*), there is no restriction of duties to specific regions.
We shall explain that some regional customs (*deśadharma*) have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
Those who have entered into a common undertaking—such as merchants, artisans, usurers, and *cāturika*s—their rules are called *śreṇīdharma*.

For example, certain merchant leaders, by their word, determine the king’s share and present it, saying: "We live by this trade; this is your royal share, while whatever profit remains shall be ours, whether it be less or more."

In that regard, once trade has been authorized by the king, merchants establish mutual regulations for the sake of obtaining superior profit—such as: "This commodity shall not be sold for such a length of time," or "This fine shall be imposed under the king's authority," or "It is for the purpose of a festival for the deity.
In this matter, if anyone transgresses, he is to be punished for violating the guild law (*śreṇīdharma*).
These are called "family laws" (*kuladharma*).
"Family" (*kula*) refers to the lineage (*vaṃśa*).

Within that, there exists a duty established by an ancestor of renowned greatness, such as: "Whoever born in our lineage obtains wealth from any source shall not employ it for any purpose other than giving it to Brahmins.

Likewise, provided there is suitability, those very same persons who were the officiating priests (*yājaka*) of one's ancestors, or those who were the recipients of gifts such as daughters in marriage, are the ones to be employed.
One who transgresses this must be compelled by the king to perform it.
This is stated again because, since these [acts] involve a collective assembly, there might be a suspicion that they are contrary to dharma;
furthermore, we shall explain later that this is not a case of "breach of agreement" (*saṃvidvyatikrama*).
Performing their own duties and remaining established in their respective tasks, men become dear to the world even when they are far away.
By this, the visible and invisible nature of the aforementioned dharma of the local people and others is demonstrated.
Those who perform their own duties in accordance with the stability of their family become dear even when they are far away;
whereas everyone else becomes dear by being nearby due to the intensity of association.
But one who performs his own duty is dear even from afar;
by the phrase "established in their respective duties," he speaks of the non-performance of another's work.
The meaning of the verse is that those who do not perform the works of others become dear to everyone.
The king himself should not initiate a legal case, nor should his official;
nor should he ever swallow up a matter brought forward by another.
A legal matter refers to the subject of a dispute;
the king himself should not initiate such a case.

For the sake of harming some seditious person, or for the sake of seizing the wealth of a wealthy man, he should not cause distress to that person’s debtor or anyone else who has committed an offense by saying, "Why do you not bring him before me, saying 'He owes this to you'? or "This man has committed such an offense that I shall first have him executed"—the king must not act in this way, even if he feels hatred or greed for wealth.

And one should not "swallow" (graset) that which has been brought forward and reported by another claimant; that is to say, one should not suppress it. The verb *nigirati* is used in the sense of contemptuous disregard, and the verb *grasati* has the same meaning.
And thus people say: "Whatever is said to him, he swallows it all; he does not offer any reply.
Others, however, explain the second half of the verse as follows:
"Nor should one seize—that is, take possession of—the wealth or property that has been obtained through legal proceedings by any other means."
For if a king were to proceed with the imposition of monetary fines based on even a slight pretext or deception, then a fault would be seen in the next world,
and there would be ruin within his own kingdom.
Now, this is another explanation offered by some.

The king should not initiate a legal proceeding on his own initiative; even upon directly perceiving someone committing an improper act, he should not say anything himself until that person has been drawn into the judicial process by the action of another party. It is through the very sight of the judicial proceeding that the defeated party is brought under restraint, not by the king.
And this should be understood as applying only to matters such as the non-payment of debts;
however, those who are like thorns—such as thieves, violent assailants, and the like—the king himself, having discovered them, should seize them.
The rest is the same.
Nor is he a "puruṣa" of this [king]; that is, he is not a person (puruṣa) authorized by this king.
Just as a hunter traces the track of a deer by drops of blood,
so should a king trace the path of dharma through inference.
As it has been said: "Even though he has seen [the offense] himself, the king should not suddenly attack or seize anyone; for even this may occur through mere jest.
But how is this to be understood—whether this was done in jest or whether it was caused by an underlying impulse such as anger?
To this, he says: "This is to be known through inference."

Just as a hunter or deer-trapper, having struck a deer that has vanished from his sight, tracks and reaches its location by following the drops of blood flowing out from the wound, even so should a king determine the cause of a matter—whether it be out of his sight or within his sight—by means of inference. Furthermore, *dharma* is the comprehension of the truth regarding the subject matter of legal proceedings.
The repetition of what was already stated concerning inference is for the purpose of strengthening the memory.
Established in the procedure for legal proceedings, one should examine the truth, the matter, oneself as the witness,
the place, the form, and the time.

Established—that is, engaged—in the procedure of legal proceedings (*vyavahāravidhi*), he should not merely examine the words of the lawsuit, but also this other [set of criteria] beginning with truth. Regarding that, the examination of truth is as follows: even if one or the other of the plaintiff or defendant, out of modesty, has not stated the matter in its full detail, if the king is somehow able to determine "this is the nature of the case" through other means of proof or through the aforementioned inference, then he should rely upon that and not neglect it, thinking, "By this person, not all of this has been stated."
Thus it has been said: "Having set aside deception, the king should conduct legal proceedings among living beings. Regarding the term *artha*: the word *artha* denotes either wealth or a purpose.
In this context, if he should obtain a great *artha*, then even by abandoning other royal duties, he should not be distressed; he must indeed attend to the investigation of legal cases.

Alternatively, if someone should say, "This matter was taken from him by the witnesses or by another member of the court," then it must be investigated whether this subject of litigation is so slight that the seizure of wealth is not possible. If, however, the matter is significant and the members of the court and the witnesses have fallen into distress, then it should be considered probable and ascertained through other means of proof.
And this should be sought out by making oneself the witness.
This is what is meant:
he should employ spies according to the method of clearing out thorns;
or else, he should examine himself—that is, he should examine his own condition, whether there is a depletion of the treasury or an abundance of it.

In this view, "witnesses" (*sākṣiṇaḥ*) is an independent word. Regarding the observation of place: in some instances even a small matter attains greatness, while that which is great elsewhere may become minor in certain cases;
such is the observation of place.
In this same way, time should also be viewed.
Form has the nature of being an object of conventional usage;
one should perceive its heaviness or lightness.
Others, however, have explained it as follows:
one should perceive the essence and the fruit of truth and its opposite, making oneself the witness.
This is what is meant.
That is to say, truth should be resorted to because of its gravity and great purpose, as it serves as the means for achieving both worlds;
whereas wealth should be abandoned because of its lack of essence.
Heaven and other such realms constitute the "place" that is attained by resorting to truth.
The time is long; the dwelling is there;
the form is beautiful, handsome, and captivating.
This very same [set of qualities] is reversed when one abandons truth and relies solely upon material gain.
One should establish as law that which has been practiced by the virtuous and by righteous twice-born men, provided it is not in conflict with the customs of the country, the family, or the caste.
The "virtuous" (*santaḥ*) are those who avoid what is prohibited; the "righteous" (*dhārmikāḥ*) are those who perform what is enjoined.

Although a single word is capable of conveying both meanings, nevertheless, because they are presented as distinct, they are explained in this way according to the division of their respective domains.
Whatever they practice that is not found in the words of the *Śruti* or *Smṛti*, one should establish—that is, cause to be performed—for the regions, families, and castes.

"Not contradicted" means not in conflict with the Śruti and Smṛti as they are found in their extant forms. Regarding the authority of local and family customs mentioned in the verse beginning "the laws of castes and regions," this [present verse] specifies its qualification:
that is authoritative when there is no contradiction with the sacred tradition (āmnāya), but it is not authoritative when there is such a contradiction.

Therefore, even those matters concerning villages, districts, and royal affairs which are based on observed practice (*dṛṣṭārtha*) should be respected only if they are not contrary to the *Śāstra*, not if they are contrary to it.
For example, in some regions, a debtor is made to pay his debt by selling himself;
yet that practice is contradicted by the rule: "And that [debt] may also be paid through labor" (YDh 2.41).
Furthermore, this is shown by the verse.
As for other conduct, its authority is stated precisely through its connection with the learned (*śiṣṭa*), as in the phrase "and the conduct of the virtuous.
And the status of being "virtuous" is not tenable by practicing that which contradicts such [scriptural] meaning.
Therefore, this instruction does not concern that which is not for the sake of the unseen (adṛṣṭa).
But another says:
whatever is practiced in another region by righteous, virtuous twice-born men, provided it is not contradicted by Śruti or another Smṛti, the king should establish that as law even in other regions.
Just as the *udvṛṣabha-yajña* and other such rites, well-known among the Northerners (*udīcya*), ought to be performed by those of the East, the South, and the West;
why?
Because from custom (*ācāra*) a traditional law (*smṛti*) must be inferred, and from traditional law, the revealed scripture (*śruti*).

And if it were inferred in this way—that "this must be performed by the Northerners"—then, since the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is traditionally taught to have many meanings, such as "born there," "existing there," "come from there," "set out toward that," and "in the remaining cases" (*śeṣe*), and because these suffixes take the form of both characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and modification (*vikāra*), there would be no such person as a "Northerner" (*udīcya*) who could be excluded by the word "Northerner" (*udīcya*), since the suffix would apply to other meanings as well, even those not explicitly mentioned.

Consequently, it follows that this [act] must be performed by any person whatsoever; for the designation of a region (*deśasamākhyā*) cannot serve as a restrictive factor, as it lacks a fixed causal basis.
Now, if one were to infer a specific scriptural injunction (*vākya*) to the effect that "it is to be done by one born in the North, or by a resident of that region," even that would be fallacious.
For one born there might not perform it elsewhere, and likewise, a resident of that region who was born elsewhere certainly does not perform it.
Furthermore, the claim that [the dharma] belongs to one born in the northern region (*udagdeśa*) and residing there is also untenable because of the impermanence of both birthplace and residence;
for neither birthplace nor residence are eternal, unlike caste (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), or lineage (*gotra*).
Therefore, since no eternal restrictor of performers can be established, *dharma*s have as their scope all people.
There are no such things as "local customs" (*deśadharma*);
by this same reasoning, there are likewise no "family customs" (*kuladharma*).
How then is it that the authors of the *Smṛtis* designate them separately as "local customs" and "family customs"?
It has been stated that the established order has a perceptible purpose and is fixed;
therein it was said that the Dharma and its restriction are logically consistent. Furthermore, the family is a portion of the lineage (*gotra*).

But as for that which pertains to the dharma of an entire lineage—such as the rule that the Vāsiṣṭhas should not intermarry with the Vaiśvāmitras—that is indeed eternal because the designation of the lineage is eternal; thus, we desist from further discussion.
That which is common to all titles of legal procedure has been stated;
now, with the intention of specifying a particular case, he says this:
"Urged by the creditor for the sake of recovering the debt from the debtor..."
He shall cause the debtor to pay the amount established as due to the creditor.

He who receives wealth from another with the understanding, "I shall repay it with interest at a later time," is the debtor (*adharmarṇa*). He who lends it with the understanding, "I shall receive it back with interest," is the creditor (*uttamarṇa*).
These two are relative terms.
The "object" (artha) refers to the debtor's property.
Since the context concerns wealth, it is specifically that which must be given to the creditor which is meant here. Its "accomplishment" (siddhi) is its delivery to the creditor.
The second word, *artha*, signifies "purpose. This is the collective meaning:

when the creditor is urged by the king, saying, "May that wealth which was borrowed from me by the debtor be realized for me; may you, O King, cause it to be paid," then the king shall cause the creditor's wealth to be paid by the debtor.
One who possesses wealth is a *dhanika*;
moreover, by common usage, it is the creditor (*uttamarṇa*) alone who is called *dhanika*.
Because of the connection with the verb "should cause to pay" (*dāpayet*), the dative case would have been expected.
However, because the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is incomplete, it is not treated as such;
for example, in the expressions "he gives the back to the one who strikes" (*ghnataḥ pṛṣṭhaṃ dadāti*) or "he gives the garment to the washerman" (*rajakasya vastraṃ dadāti*),
the primary meaning of the root *dā* (to give) is not present here.
In this case as well, because ownership belongs to both [parties] and yet ownership is absent for both, the meaning is that he gives while the matter is incomplete.
Is he to be made to pay solely by the word of the creditor?
No; the author says "when it has been proved."
When it is understood that he maintains [the debt] by means of a certain means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
or alternatively, when it has been manifested and he has personally admitted it—
since the author will later state regarding one who denies what was admitted, "in the case of denial by the debtor" (*apahnave 'dhamarṇasya*).
But how is it said that one who has personally admitted [the debt] is "one who has cleared it"?
This is not a fault; for even in the case of forgetfulness, one becomes "one who has personally admitted" it by means of a handwritten document or the like.
One who has cultivated [the path] but has not entered it, and one who, despite knowing, practices erroneously.
By whatever means a creditor may recover his own wealth,
by those very means he should secure the debtor and compel him to pay.
In this world, a creditor would not have to pay a share to the king for a debt not yet recovered, nor would he be subject to a fine from the king for failing to collect;
however, out of a desire for their own share, kings might cause creditors to seek wealth through improper means. Therefore, to prevent this, it is said here:
by whichever of the methods to be described below the creditor may recover his own previously advanced wealth, by those very means he shall compel the debtor to pay.

"Having gathered" means having made firm; that is to say, having ascertained that "by this very means, this is obtained from this. Alternatively, "gathering" (*saṃgraha*) refers to conciliation that is favorable.
*Uttamarṇika* means one who is a creditor (*uttamarṇa*). That which is both supreme (*uttama*) and a debt (*ṛṇa*) is *uttamarṇa*;
one who possesses that is *uttamarṇika*.
The form [is derived] by the rule *ata ini-ṭhanau*;
the other two [suffixes, *ini* and *ṭhan*,] are treated in the same way.

These should be inserted among the *sarvadhana*-type compounds; otherwise, as in the case of "a village with brave men" (*vīrapuruṣakaḥ grāmaḥ*), the compound is formed by a *bahuvrīhi* itself, because the coreferentiality is already expressed and there is no difference in meaning when the sense of possession (*matvartha*) is already stated.
Furthermore, the possessive suffix (*matvarīya*) is difficult to justify here;
for "debt" (*ṛṇa*) refers to wealth that is the object of a transaction for the purpose of gaining interest, and it has two related parties:
the lender and the borrower.
And for the instigator, that [debt] is the most excellent,
as he is independent in both the giving and the reclaiming of the wealth;
whereas for the other, it is inferior because of the giving with interest and the great amount of effort required.
This, however, is merely for the sake of etymological derivation;
in fact, these two [words] are denotative for both the speaker and the listener solely by virtue of conventional usage (rūḍhi).
The following verse is intended to demonstrate what the means (upāya) for that [conventional usage] are.
One should recover a debt through legal process, through artifice, through customary conduct,
and by force as the fifth means.

In this regard, according to the method of the *dharmaskandhas*, there is a gradual taking [of property]: "This today, this tomorrow, this the day after tomorrow; just as the management of his household is thus, so too are we members of your household, worthy of a share"—such is the application of the recited rule regarding *dharma*.
However, one who is destitute should be made to pay through legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*);
otherwise, having given wealth like water poured into the ear, he should be made to engage in trade, agriculture, and so forth.

In that case, the wealth produced therefrom should be taken from him. However, as for a legal dispute that must be reported to the king, since it involves the application of all possible means when other resources are exhausted, and because it has already been encompassed by the taking of force (*bala*),
one who does not pay directly— even if he possesses wealth— should be made to pay through stratagem (*chala*).
Under some pretext, such as a marriage festival or the like, one should take an ornament such as a bracelet and not return it until that person has paid the debt.
Customary practices include fasting or sitting at the door of the debtor's house.
Force consists of presenting the matter before the king’s court.

In this context, it is said that the king, having restrained one who does not pay through conciliation and having oppressed him, causes [the debt] to be paid; however, the "force" refers to the wealth and so forth belonging to his own household, for it is stated by Uśanas in this very same passage that "the force of the subjects belongs to the king.
Others, however, describe this as an instruction specifically for the king, because it occurs within the section on the duties of kings (*rājadharma*).
The king, having been informed through various means, should cause the defeated debtor to pay, as well as one who has admitted the debt himself;
however, his entire property must not be seized by force and handed over to the creditor.
For the king must act in a way that benefits both parties.
Furthermore, if one who is not indebted were to give away all his possessions, it would lead to the ruin of his family; that too is not proper.
For it has been said:
"One should not be pressured, but should be made to pay gradually, from time to time, according to his income."
"But a Brāhmaṇa especially [is not to be punished] when the king is righteous.
Therefore, he should be made to pay something by way of interest;
however, if there is an abundance of wealth beyond what is required for his family, he should be made to pay everything.
And when all [other means] are impossible, one should act equally even by means of legal action;
according to another interpretation, deceit and improper conduct must not be employed without having informed the king.
A creditor who recovers his own wealth from a debtor by his own means must not be prosecuted by the king for recovering what is his own.
This verse is intended to clarify the very point already stated:

when a creditor recovers his wealth from a debtor by means such as *chala* (fraud) according to his own will, he must not be addressed by the king with any such words as: "Why have you taken this jewelry and other property from him under a pretext or deception without informing me for the purpose of clearing your own debt? or "Having taken it, why do you not restore it to him?"

But when the debtor is found to have misappropriated the wealth and the matter has been proven by evidence, the judge shall cause him to pay the debt to the creditor and a small fine according to his capacity.

Even when there exists a means of proof that establishes the truth, one should not employ deceptive tactics against a person who does not admit it of his own accord. Rather, the king himself must be informed of the matter.

When the case has been brought before the king, if a debtor denies the debt—saying, "I owe him nothing"—and is subsequently proven by means of evidence consisting of witnesses, documents, or possession, the king should compel him to pay the money to the creditor.
"A mere fraction of a fine" (*daṇḍaleśa*) means a very small fine, that is to say, just a fine;
elsewhere, he will state that the tenth part [of the property] is the fine.
However, one who is unable to pay even that much should be made to pay a fine, even if it is less than the tenth part.
Alternatively, this fine—ranging from one-tenth up to the maximum according to capacity—is for one who, through negligence, somehow forgets and denies [the debt].
The means of proof (*kāraṇa* or *pramāṇa*) is threefold;
it has been enumerated here as that which is possible in these cases by others.
And so they have said:
"Where there is no written document, nor is a witness found, and where the aforementioned means of proof are absent, there the divine method of proof (*daivī kriyā*) shall be employed."
When a debtor, upon being told "Pay! in the presence of an assembly, denies the debt, the plaintiff must point out a location or cite another reason for his claim.

When, in an assembly or at a place of legal proceedings such as a court, a debtor—having been told by the king or the judge, "Give the money to the creditor"—denies it through unrighteousness (apalāpa), then the plaintiff, the creditor who advanced the funds, shall "indicate the place" (*diśet*); that is, he shall point out a witness who serves as proof.
Alternatively, he may indicate another means of proof, such as a written document (*lekhyādi*).

Since the word "place" (*deśa*) is used figuratively to include witnesses residing in the location where the loan was made, the word "means" (*kāraṇa*), though a general term, refers specifically to means other than witnesses, such as documents, according to the maxim of "the cows and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*).
And therefore, there is another reading: "or he may point out the cause.
The meaning of this is also the same. Alternatively, there is this other reading: "the accused shall indicate the place."
This is the meaning:

when the debtor, being told "Give!", admits, "It is true that the wealth was indeed returned," he who was previously the plaintiff has become the defendant. And that defendant may point out the place, saying, "In which place was it returned by you to me?"
And one should specify the time, since the mention of "place" is intended as an illustration;
or one should point out the reason.
One should say: "Sir, there is [a reason]; what is the reason for your teaching? Point that out."
Alternatively, one may indicate that which is to be shown—that at that time there was no grounds for producing witnesses and so forth, nor any other cause;
the word "vā" (or) is used in place of the word "ca" (and).
He who points out an incorrect place, he who, having pointed it out, denies it,
and he who does not understand the contradictory meanings of what precedes and follows;
It has already been stated that when a debtor denies a debt, the creditor must inform the king; and the notification should be made in this manner:
"In this place and at this time, this much wealth was received from me by him.
If, when questioned, he claims, "I was not in this place at the time of the receipt indicated by him," he points to a different location.
Alternatively, the witnesses of place have been explained; he now points out those witnesses as being impossible with respect to time and place.
Having pointed out the place and so forth, he denies it, saying, "This was not pointed out by me.
And he is one who does not comprehend the preceding and subsequent matters—the earlier and later points—which have been stated as discordant and contradictory.

Or, he says what should have been said later before what should have been said first; and he does not attend to the disorder of sequence in his own speech. "One should designate him as inferior"—the verb will be supplied everywhere [in the subsequent cases].
Furthermore, he who, having pointed out what was to be pointed out, subsequently evades it, and when questioned about a matter that has been correctly proposed, does not accept it; |||
The first half [of the verse] provides the conclusion of the matter already stated;
the second half states the matter not yet mentioned.
That which was said—“he who points out a place that is no place, and he who, having pointed it out, denies it”—is precisely the meaning of the term *apadiśya*.

A non-place (*adeśa*) is indeed a false pretext (*apadeśa*). Having cited that as a pretext—that is, having spoken it—and then subsequently running away or withdrawing, he says: "These two, place and time, were not determined by me; only so much place and time as you have fixed upon belongs to me.
He, too, is deprived of that object.

When he has correctly formulated his point, which is coherent and certain, and it is stated, yet when questioned—"What do you say to this? or "By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do you establish your own position?"—he does not respond coherently but instead initiates another topic of conversation, thinking, "I will lose by the conclusion of the deliberation; therefore, I shall waste time. For him too, there is indeed defeat.

Alternatively, "apadeśa" means a pretext; he who, having made such a pretext—that is, having put forward an excuse—withdraws, saying, "Now a great pain has arisen for me, I am unable to reply," or who departs under false pretenses and the like, he too is defeated.
He who converses secretly with witnesses in a place where conversation is forbidden,
he who does not wish to answer when a question is being put to him, and he who walks away— these are also [to be considered as defeated].
In a place unfit for conversation, such as a secluded spot or the like, he converses with the witnesses alone, fearing that they might break ranks.

When being interrogated, questioned, or examined, he refuses to address the inquiry or the matter under investigation; he gains time by citing some royal business or by seeking the favor of princes, ministers, and others.
And he who should likewise flee; [these are grounds for suspicion].
The verb to be expressed is precisely "he is defeated" (*sa hīyate*);
the meaning is the same as what was stated previously in "but he who runs away" (*yas tv apadhāvati*) and also in "and he who flees" (*yaś cāpi niṣpatet*).
The purpose for this repetition has already been explained.
To avoid excessive redundancy, some distinction must be adopted.
If, when told "speak," he does not speak, or if he fails to clarify what has been said,
or if he cannot discern the consistency between what precedes and what follows, he is defeated on that account.
This verse, whose meaning has already been stated, is seen again through other verses;
and the purpose of this repetition has been explained by the principle that "wholesome advice should be understood even when repeated many times.

As for the literal meaning: when the proponent has exhausted his position, the opponent, being asked, "Speak on this matter," if he does not speak—even though being questioned again and again—[he incurs a penalty].

For he who, because there is no correct reply and due to his habit of offering false replies, thinks, "By this very fact my defeat occurs; but if I remain silent, my defeat would be merely uncertain," and thus fails to provide a reply—he too is defeated.
And regarding this, the author will state the limitation of time: "If he does not speak within three fortnights.

For in the case of one who is immediately summoned, a delay is appropriate only because of a failure to understand the meaning of the plaintiff's claim and a consequent inability to formulate a reply.

And in this case, for one who speaks only very gradually, the completion of the three-fortnight period may take five, ten, or twelve days; however, silence must not be maintained for such a long duration.

As for the further time mentioned—namely, that "even when the matter is settled, one might wait for a year in case of a lack of readiness to respond"—this is not to be respected as a rule. For if a lack of readiness is the cause for waiting, why would it cease to be a cause once it occurs after a year?
Furthermore, this rule—that eloquence (*pratibhā*) arises after one year—is not understood to hold true in every case.

Therefore, it is appropriate to grant a period of deliberation for only as many days as are required to ascertain the meaning of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) and for the rejoinder (*uttara*) to become manifest.
And since even a person of dull intellect achieves this in just that many days, no further time should be granted for deliberation.
But for the plaintiff, it is appropriate to lodge his own claim on that very day;
for he has reached a certainty, thinking, "This person owes this to me," or "This person has done me this injury.
Indeed, he acts according to his own will.
How could his own interest remain undetermined when he merely informs [the court] of his own position?

But as for the defendant, who is unaware of the connection [to the case] and is being brought at that very moment by the king’s officers, how indeed could he determine his own or the opponent’s position?
For the investigation of both sides falls upon him at that very instant.
Otherwise, one does not become the respondent (*uttarapākṣika*).
Therefore, regarding the matter to be proven by the proponent (*pūrvapākṣika*), there is either the completion of the preliminary motion on that very day or the acquisition of two days.
Both of these positions are also supported by other Smṛti texts.
For thus it has been said:
"The proponent, having established a firm conviction, should always remain steadfast;
he should refine his own position for ten days or twelve days."
Likewise, for this other reason, one who seeks [the fulfillment of] a claim should have it documented immediately to establish the matter as promised;
whereas an examination over the course of a year is invalid due to the impossibility of its basis.

For it cannot be said that the legal tradition (*vyavahāra-smṛti*) has its root in the Veda in the same way as the Aṣṭakā rites and so forth, because the subject matter is not of the nature of a ritual act (*kārya*).
Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that [the self] cannot be the object of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This indifference toward the three positions is not universal;
as it has been said:
"In cases of violence, theft, verbal abuse, false accusations, and the loss of a woman, one should litigate immediately; in other matters, the time is said to depend on the will [of the parties].
For in cases such as violence and the like, if they are neglected for a long time, the opponent might win over others.
Therefore, an immediate trial is prescribed;
nor do reasons such as forgetfulness or the like apply here, as they have not been mentioned. For in cases involving violence and similar offenses, one must inform the king at that very moment.
For in that case there is intense urgency;
when clothing and such are being taken away, there arises the apprehension of passion toward that indifference. Furthermore, witnesses may happen to be present there by chance.
For when they have gone to another country, they are not recognized by their name, caste, and so forth;
consequently, there is an absence of any inherent means of proof.
Furthermore, in matters such as the recovery of debts, they sometimes reach a mutual agreement with one another.
In that case, there is no room for the king's intervention. Generally, when the matter is already cleared, the recollection of how much was given is of no use;
however, one who acts with violence must certainly be punished by the king, even if he is being reconciled by the other party.
Therefore, it is established that in cases such as debts and the like, there may be a delay, whereas in cases such as acts of violence (*sāhasa*), judgment must be immediate.
As it has been said:
"Because of the complexity of legal disputes and because of the potential incapacity of even the traditional law (*smṛti*)."
In matters such as debts and the like, one may take time at will out of a desire to know the truth.
When a plaint is confused, it cannot be grasped due to its complexity;

even when a plaint is unconfused, though its sequence may have been omitted, it cannot be remembered in its entirety by everyone at the time of the response because of its great length—this is the meaning of "another's memory" (smṛtyantara).
And it has been said: "One should not fail to establish [the case]."
Having pointed out the object to be proven, one does not establish it because of the absence of a means of proof, or because [the reason] exists in the dissimilar case (vipakṣa).
Furthermore, one would not know what precedes or follows;
this has already been stated.
Therefore, he loses—that is, he becomes defeated—with respect to that matter, which is the subject of the legal proceeding; such is the meaning.

Having said, "There are witnesses who know [the facts] concerning me," if one who is established in dharma does not point them out when asked to do so, one should declare him to be defeated on these grounds.

When one says, "I have witnesses who know [the facts]," and when it is said, "Let them be named," he remains silent—failing to specify them by their country, name, caste, or distinguishing attributes—then, for each of these previously stated reasons, the judge (*dharmastha*), that is, the presiding officer (*prāḍvivāka*) seated in the court of justice, shall declare with certainty: "This man is defeated; he has lost the legal proceeding. Just as defeat occurs through the non-occurrence of evidence that subverts the opponent's position, so too does it occur through the absence of proof for one's own position.

Furthermore, the certainty of non-existence [is established] because it is not introduced again and again at the appropriate occasion, and because it does not exist when another cause is not introduced.
The word *jñātāraḥ* ends in the suffix *tṛn*;
in that context, the form *idam* is correctly used with the accusative ending, because the sixth case (genitive) is prohibited by the rule *khalarthāṭṭaṅām*.
The reading "hīnaṃ tat" ends in the accusative case.
The word "iti" should be understood as having the sense of "in this manner. One should point out that [the object] is inferior by means of these aforementioned modes and other such similar ones.
But when there is a reflection upon the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), then the reading is *hīno 'sau* (he is defeated);
because the meaning of the sentence functions as the object (*karman*), there is an absence of the accusative case ending.
These are the grounds for defeat (*parājaya-hetu*).
But these [signs] are not fallible like facial expressions, gestures, and so forth.
For when someone does not present himself on successive occasions for deliberation, or being present, does not offer a reply, it becomes certain in that case: "He has no ground for victory.
Moreover, if the king were never to defeat one who consistently fails to provide an answer, then the established legal order would be undermined.
However, the failure to perceive the sequence of what precedes and what follows should be understood as being like [the inconsistency of] gestures and so forth.

When a person who is at all times eloquent, bold, and possessed of presence of mind exhibits gestures and the like that become otherwise, these serve as corroborative factors—standing in the place of the observation of a logical mark—even when the cause of defeat has not yet been determined by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If the plaintiff does not speak, he shall be bound and punished according to the law;
if he does not speak within three fortnights regarding the matter of justice, he is defeated.

If the plaintiff (the claimant) does not state the subject matter of the legal dispute after having summoned some person to the presence of the king, then he shall be bound and punished for being purposeless.

Regarding the type of punishment, the duration of imprisonment, the amount of the fine, and the summons of the defendant, these should be determined by considering his merit and the loss incurred by the summons.
Therefore, the plaintiff must litigate on that very day.
The meaning is that if the defendant does not speak within three fortnights, then he is neither to be fined nor imprisoned.
Rather, after this period of time has elapsed, if there is no further response, he is simply not defeated with respect to the legal matter.
The meaning is that this defeat is due to the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), not through deception.
The term "tripakṣāt" should be understood according to the rule for words beginning with *pātra* (i.e., as *tri-pakṣāt*), and thus there is no elision of the vowel *ī*.
The true reality of this world has been previously determined by us.
Whatever amount of wealth one may conceal, or whatever amount one may speak falsely regarding,
those two— being ignorant of the Dharma— must be made by the king to pay a fine double that amount.

If one has determined through other means of proof that five thousand [coins] were given, yet ten have been entered in the document and so forth—having determined that another means of proof, namely time in the form of years, is required—one who proceeds everywhere relying solely on the authority of the document is a litigant engaged in deception and shall be fined double.
However, for one whose conduct might be suspected of being otherwise even due to forgetfulness, the fine is ten percent;
the same applies to the other party as well.
It is not the case that when the whole [debt] is denied the fine is one-tenth, whereas when only a portion is denied the fine is double;
rather, those two who act otherwise than the truth out of deceit should be fined double.
In cases of forgetfulness or poverty, the subsequent fine [is applied].

Whoever denies or disclaims whatever amount of wealth [is owed]—the debtor being one who knows not the law—and whoever, as a creditor, speaks falsely regarding the amount of wealth, namely, states it to be the opposite of what it is; both that creditor and that debtor are ignorant of the law (adharma-jña).
The fine is double that amount. The word "that" (tat) refers to the wealth being denied.
The fine or punishment shall be double the amount that was denied.

Furthermore, because of the mention of one who "does not know the law" (adharmajña) as a sign, it is stated that this punishment applies specifically to cases where fraud has been definitively established.
But one who, having been questioned by a seeker of wealth while remaining steadfast, denies the charge,
must be judged by at least three witnesses in the presence of the king and Brahmins.

When one who has reached the stage of being a defendant— having been summoned, charged, and provided with a surety— is questioned in the presence of the king by the judge or others, asking "Do you owe this to him or not," and being thus asked, he denies it or conceals it; then, by one seeking wealth who desires to recover his own previously advanced property, the defendant in dispute must be examined through witnesses and compelled to pay.
"By those having at least three" (*tryavaraiḥ*):
[the compound] *tryavara* means "those for whom three are the minimum. By the word *avara*, he expresses the sense of a lower limit or a minimum degree.
If they are extremely few, then there should be three;
otherwise, more than three.
"In the presence of the king and the Brahmins" means:
But surely, for those very individuals by whom the legal proceeding has been initiated, the interrogation of witnesses should take place in their presence alone;
what is the point of this requirement that it be conducted "in the presence of the king and the Brahmins"?
It is not so.
Since the interrogation of witnesses is also appropriate by means of dispatching a person of authority,
the statement "he should be questioned directly" is a reiterative injunction.
I shall now fully describe the kind of witnesses who ought to be appointed by wealthy men in legal proceedings, as well as how the truth must be spoken by them.
This verse introduces the characteristics of witnesses:

I shall describe, as they are about to be stated, what kind of witnesses—of what sort and endowed with what qualities—should be employed by creditors (dhanins) in legal proceedings concerning the lending of money and the like;
and I shall also explain the manner in which truth (ṛtam) or reality (satyam) must be spoken by those who are questioned, beginning with the rule that it should be done in the forenoon and so forth.

Householders who have sons, who are native-born, and who belong to the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes— when summoned by the plaintiff— are fit to give testimony, but not just anyone, except in times of emergency.
Householders are those who have taken a wife;
the word "house" (gṛha) refers here to a wife,
for they do not practice fraud out of fear of being surpassed by their own wives.

Some individuals, though indifferent to their own selves, speak even falsehoods with the thought: "We shall protect ourselves by going to another country, or we shall remain hidden right here, and we shall acquire wealth or friends.

Householders, however, out of fear for their family, think, "Where would we not protect ourselves? and thus, having set themselves far aside, they do not act otherwise due to their concern for their family and the fear of royal punishment.
Regarding the term "those with sons": they are called "those with sons" because of their affection for their children.
Furthermore, one who has neither son nor wife may, at the time of questioning witnesses, even if he is of good conduct, sometimes not be present.
For he does not have a fixed residence in any single place;
the same should be explained for the *maula* [villagers] as well.
The *maula* are the local people, those born in that region.
For they do not speak falsely among their own kinsmen and relatives out of fear of evil.
"Mūla" means foundation; those who possess it are "maula.
This is an explanation of the term's meaning.
The secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix, however, must be applied in the sense of "being" (*bhāva*) alone;
for it is not contradictory that whatever exists in something also belongs to it.
[Thus, they are called] those born from the *kṣatriya*, *vaiśya*, and *śūdra* wombs.
He is not a Brāhmaṇa;
for his study and teaching are prescribed at all times, or else the daily Agnihotra sacrifice is required.
In that case, lest there be an obstruction to his religious duty (dharma) while the king is far away, he is not enjoined to perform [the visit].
However, one who has learned the matter by chance is the most preeminent witness in the absence of other witnesses when the legal matter is of great importance;
and thus there will be an interrogation of the witness according to the rule: "One should question a Brāhmaṇa with the words, 'Speak!
The word *yoni* (source/origin) is connected with each [of the preceding terms].
The *kṣatra* is its source, origin, or cause; thus it is "of *kṣatra* origin" (*kṣatrayoni*).
The meaning is that he belongs to the *kṣatriya* caste.
Alternatively, the compound is also explained by the rule regarding the fifth case (*pañcamī*), based on the analysis: "his birth (*yoni*) or origin is from the *kṣatra*."
When it is stated by the plaintiff, "These are my witnesses," then they become fit for the function of witnesses;
however, those who come of their own accord and give testimony are not [legally valid] witnesses,
except in cases of emergency.
Some say that the absence of other witnesses constitutes an emergency; that is incorrect,
for the cause of being disqualified from testifying is the tendency toward contradiction.
It does not depart [from its validity] in the absence of another corroborating witness.

We do not say that those causes for speaking falsehood—which exist even when witnesses have been disqualified—such as personal interest in the matter and so forth, are permitted in this situation. What then? This is an authorization for those who have experienced the facts themselves, such as Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) and others, when no other witnesses are available and summoning whom would result in a conflict with *dharma*; it is not, however, for those who speak untruths.

Trustworthy persons from all castes, who are knowledgeable in all matters of dharma and free from greed, should be appointed as witnesses for legal cases; however, those who are the opposite should be avoided.

The authoritative persons (*āpta*) are those who are non-deceptive, who speak of things exactly as they have perceived them, and whom the world does not suspect of being deceivers; they are renowned for being devoted to the practice of dharma.

They are knowers of all dharmas—namely, all dharma whether based on revelation (*śrauta*), tradition (*smārta*), or established in custom (*ācāranirūḍha*)—knowing them without exception, such that they understand: "In this world is hell as a result; in this world is heaven. For they fear speaking untruth, seeing hell [as its consequence].
They are free from greed and noble-minded, not regarding even a small amount of wealth as much.

All the qualifiers apply to each individual [person], because they are subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to the act of witnessing, and because in the case of a subordinate element, their collective application (*sāhitya*) is intended.
By the phrase "among all castes," it is meant that there is no restriction based on birth (*jāti*) regarding all such duties.
As for the statement regarding the classification by birth, we shall explain that further on.
This is what is meant:
all castes may be made witnesses by all litigants, as far as possible.
In legal matters such as the non-payment of debts and so forth,
one should avoid those who possess characteristics contrary to what has been stated.
Although there is no possibility of such contrary persons being included when specific individuals have already been mentioned, this exclusion is nevertheless of a worldly (conventional) nature.
For generally, worldly people, having enjoined one thing, prohibit another that is its opposite;
thus speakers say: "Action disciplines a substance, not a non-substance.

Furthermore, in this context, the primary characteristic of a witness is non-contradiction, and that cannot be determined through the mode of affirmation, but rather through the absence of the causes of contradiction.
For non-contradictoriness is not visible through direct perception;
for that consists in the designation of things as they truly are.
And in the case of an object apprehended by the sense of hearing, how could there be a perceptual determination of its being true to reality?
For when a matter is perceptible, no investigation into witnesses is required;
nor is it possible for there to be corroboration by other means of knowledge in every case where the object is beyond the senses and accessible only through verbal testimony.
Therefore, since those [causes] are frequently observed to produce false statements, the absence of such causes leads to the inference of non-contradiction.
Therefore, this introductory statement, "but one should avoid those that are contrary," is intended to demonstrate that.
One should not employ those who have a financial interest, nor those who are trustworthy, nor companions, nor enemies;
nor those whose faults are evident, nor those afflicted by disease, nor those who are corrupt.
These are recited as being the instruments for making false statements that are likely to occur.
Among them, those connected with the subject matter are the creditor, the debtor, and so forth.
For when a creditor is defeated by the words of a debtor, he may, at that very moment, overcome by a fit of rage, cause the debtor to be paralyzed from paying the debt.
Therefore, such a person, conforming to the mind of the wealthy creditor, is able to speak in accordance with it;

for that reason, he is not a witness. Furthermore, even the creditor, when the debtor is destitute and has obtained wealth through a legal victory, might sometimes speak in favor of the debtor's side with the thought, "He will repay me"; thus, he too is not a witness.

Alternatively, "artha" means purpose; one who has some purpose to be accomplished for the litigants through being a witness, or by whom those two [litigants] have something to be accomplished, is not a witness because he possesses even a trace of self-interest. Or, one who shares the same result as the matter involved in the lawsuit—such persons are those related to the matter in this manner.

Trusted persons are paternal uncles, maternal uncles, and others who, by virtue of being friends or kinsmen, are intimately involved in one's affairs; allies include sureties and the like; and enemies are well known.
Those whose faults have been observed include those who have given false testimony on other occasions,
or those who have practiced other prohibited acts;
as well as those afflicted by disease, being tormented by illness.
The term "afflicted" (*ārta*) is used [in the sūtra] not merely for those who are slightly ill;
for in one who is suffering, anger, forgetfulness, and so forth may lead to false testimony.
"Corrupted persons" (*dūṣitāḥ*) refers to those who have committed mortal sins (*pātakinah*) as well as those who have habitually committed minor offenses (*upapātakāḥ*).
The mention of "those whose faults have been seen," however, is for the purpose of including those very individuals who have already undergone punishment;
for, since they have been made to accept discipline through the imposition of punishment by kings, they do not become corrupt at present.
The king shall not be made a witness, nor artisans or actors;
nor one learned in the Vedas, nor one dwelling in a religious order, nor one who has renounced all worldly attachments.
At the time of the disposal of wealth or other matters by a litigant, saying "you shall be my witness," the king must not be requested to serve as a witness;
for if he were to give testimony, people might suspect him of partiality,
or because of his sovereign power, his giving [testimony] might lead to the ruin of one of the parties' cases.
Furthermore, it is not proper to question [them] according to the rules for witnesses (*sākṣidharma*).

Even if an inhabitant of that region might corroborate [the facts] by means of documents and the like, he would nevertheless not perform all the duties of a witness; thus, there is a prohibition against making inhabitants of that region witnesses.
This is because, in the case of artisans and others, there is the apprehension that their own work would be obstructed.
Moreover, they live by means of social cohesion;
and it is the very nature of country folk that even when they have themselves determined, "We are living," they become angry with witnesses and others once they are defeated.
Consequently, the universal social cohesion of artisans and the like is destroyed.
Furthermore, because of their naturally fickle nature, they can even be swayed from their conduct;
thus, they might succumb to partiality.
However, in the case of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), his obligation to serve as a witness is prohibited just as it is for a king—not because of a lack of trustworthiness, but for other reasons.
For being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyatva*) does not destroy authority; rather, it produces it, especially so.
Indeed, being learned in the Vedas has never been observed to be a cause of contradiction.
The same applies to what follows as well.
Artisans are those who live by their crafts, such as cooks, blacksmiths, and the like;
performers are actors, dancers, singers, and so forth;
a *śrotriya* is one who recites the Vedas.
However, he who is intent upon Vedic study is what is understood here;
or alternatively, being "learned in the Vedas" (śrotriya) is intended as an indicator of the performance of ritual acts.
Therefore, for one intent on such performance, there is a prohibition because [study] would be in conflict with it.
The celibate student (brahmacārī) is one who dwells in the [proper] marks.

However, those who bear the marks of wandering mendicants (parivrājaka) or heretics (pākhaṇḍa) are excluded precisely because they follow false scriptures. Householders who have renounced the Vedas are those who have emerged from worldly attachments.
Attachment is the enjoyment of sense objects through habituation, or the undertaking of actions for the sake of visible results.
Neither one who is dependent on another, nor one who is censurable, nor a thief, nor one who performs forbidden acts;
neither an elderly man, nor a child, nor one alone, nor an outcaste, nor one with impaired faculties.
The word *adhyadhīna* is conventionally used for those who are entirely dependent, such as a slave born in the house (*garbhadāsa*) and others;
however, others read it as *adhyādhīna* because the phonetic combination is identical.
*Adhyādhīna* means one who has been made a pledge (*bandhakīkṛta*).
One who is to be spoken to and instructed refers to a disciple, a son, or the like, because they are dependent upon the teacher;
or alternatively, it refers to one whose body is loathsome due to leprosy or other diseases.
A *dasyu* is a hired servant or wage-earner, for according to etymological science (*nirukta*), he is so called because he "performs tasks" (*upādāsayati*).
And because such a person is paid by the day, he does not possess absolute dependence [on others]; thus, a separate instruction is given.

Since he has fallen into a livelihood based on labor, there is a destruction of his means of subsistence for those of that sort; furthermore, because his mode of life is meager, there is also a lack of trustworthiness due to the possibility of greed and other vices.
As for the thief (*caura*), however, because a different word is employed, he is not included under the term *dasyu*.
Or a bandit with a hard heart and cruel conduct;
or one who performs forbidden acts (*vikarmakṛt*), that is, one who performs actions contrary to the scriptures,
such as a Brāhmaṇa following the occupation of a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya, and so forth.
An "old man" is one who, due to the decline of age, lacks memory;
a "child" is a minor who has not yet attained legal capacity.

Since the rule regarding "at least three" would otherwise preclude a single witness, this prohibition is intended to permit two witnesses under certain circumstances, as in the case of a document executed by three hands.

Even though there is no third scribe in that case, someone might have the suspicion that the mere act of writing does not constitute witness-status. The "last" refers to one such as a barbarian or a caṇḍāla; this is a prohibition against those who, by virtue of being born from a Śūdra womb, would otherwise be eligible [to serve].
One with impaired faculties refers to those who are blind, deaf, and so forth; their perception occurs through bodily affliction and due to the impairment of the senses.

Neither one who is distressed, nor intoxicated, nor insane; neither one afflicted by hunger or thirst, nor one oppressed by fatigue, nor one tormented by desire, nor one who is angry, nor even a thief.
One who is afflicted is one whose kinsmen, wealth, and so forth have been destroyed; one who is intoxicated is one made drunk by liquor;
one seized by epilepsy is a madman or a demon-possessed person.
"Afflicted by hunger and thirst" means distressed by hunger and thirst.
"Fatigue" is that which arises from excessive physical exertion, such as traveling long distances or fighting; one is "tormented" (ārta) by that.

"Lust" is the desire for sexual union with women; one is "afflicted" by that. Both "separation" (vipralambha)—meaning the lack of union—and "extreme union" are conditions because they cause agitation of the mind, as well as through the apprehension of separation regarding the means to achieve those [objects].
One who is angry has even greater anger toward another;
for because his mind is pervaded by anger, he neither experiences [the object] nor remembers what has been experienced.
A "taskara" is a thief.

Even though he is a performer of improper acts (*vikarmakṛt*), nevertheless, because of the mention of distinct categories, the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*) should be understood to apply here.
Women shall give testimony for women; twice-born men of similar status for twice-born men;
virtuous Śūdras for Śūdras; and those of the lowest birth for those of the lowest castes.
Where the two parties, plaintiff and defendant, are both men, there women cannot serve as witnesses.
However, where a man has a legal matter with a woman, or where women have a minor mutual matter among themselves, women certainly may be witnesses.
Nor is this a restrictive rule that women must give testimony only for women and not for men.
In legal proceedings concerning men alone, the reason given for admitting women as witnesses only in certain instances is their instability;
yet, there are some women who, like the female exponents of the Veda (*brahmavādinī*), are speakers of truth and possess steady intellects.
"Twice-born" (*dvija*) refers to those who are equal to the [actual] twice-born.
A twice-born man who is more authoritative, even when giving testimony that is dissimilar and whose status as an authority is suspected, does not become one whose word is trustworthy;
for such a person must be regarded as an authority itself,
since he is indeed similar to it.
For among similar things, it is possible for them to occupy the same location and to possess mutual knowledge of one another's effects;
however, for the other [the dissimilar], proximity to that location must be achieved through effort,
whereas for two similar things, it is established by its very nature.
Thus, even from an inferior person, an inferior quality may be accepted if it is similar [to one's own];
however, it is not the case that a superior quality should not be accepted.
Similarity exists through caste, craft and so forth, or through qualities such as action—namely, hearing, study, and the like—as well as through commonality of character.
And this should not be understood as applying to very great matters;
for trustworthiness is not determined among those of inferior qualities.
And for the lowest castes, such as the Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas, there are likewise only those born of the lowest wombs.
"Antya" means those that are at the end;
the analysis of the compound is "those for whom that source is the cause of arising.
This is merely an illustration.

Those who are equal in terms of birth, craft, character, and so forth—even those such as merchants, artisans, and musicians who are not explicitly mentioned here—their [status] is determined by the equality of their cause.
However, whoever may be an eyewitness should give testimony for litigants in the case of occurrences within a house, in a forest, or even when there is danger to life.

In cases where an act occurs within a house that arises unexpectedly—such as verbal or physical assault, abduction, theft, or violence—or where such an act occurs in the forest; or when the body is being tormented at that moment by bandits or others and something has been seized from anywhere; or when someone has been appointed as a guarantor for the sake of wealth, yet witnesses cannot be found or do not wait for that duration; or when a matter is discussed in secret and they take back the wealth without public disclosure—in such circumstances, anyone who is an eyewitness should be accepted as a witness.
"Anubhāvī" means one who has directly perceived it.

The phrase "anyone whatsoever" indicates that there is no restriction regarding caste or class; furthermore, he says "and at that time there was no similar person" to indicate that there was no one else like him.
The expression "inside the house" is intended to signify that the place was secluded from people.
By this, even deserted temples and the like, where people are sparse, are included;
thus, the mention of "the wilderness" (*araṇya*) is for the purpose of demonstrating this very point.
Others, however, explain it differently, [stating] that there is also the passing away (*atyaya*) of the body.
Regarding any witness in the case of the lapse of a legal proceeding (*kāryaśarīra*):

when a matter being carried out lapses and becomes impossible to perform at a later time, there is no restriction regarding the witnesses based on caste, gender, age, similarity, or the presence of a relationship and so forth.
This very point is demonstrated by the following [verse].
In the absence of a woman, the rite may be performed by a child, an elderly person, a disciple, a relative, a slave, or even a hired servant.
The change of gender is stated by the word "striyā" (by a woman);
the change of age is indicated by "bālena vā sthavireṇa vā" (by a child or by an old man);
and the exception regarding relatives is established by the phrase beginning with "śiṣyeṇa" (by a pupil).
And this is merely an illustration for the purpose of showing the deviation of such rules;
therefore, they are not strictly observed even when there is similarity of genus.
However, [factors] such as being seen as a friend or an enemy, or the presence of defects, are not accepted [as exceptions].
Those for whom the capacity to utter some falsehood is observed, yet not as a pervasive trait, do not incur censure.

However, those for whom it is a widespread characteristic, occurring only in certain instances due to a particular excellence of quality, may deviate from truth; therefore, they are witnesses only in specific cases.
And it has been said:
"A single person may be found among a thousand— neither from friendship, nor from enmity, nor even from a connection of wealth— such a person should not practice falsehood.
Thus, in the absence of other witnesses, the task may be performed even by a woman.
"What?"— the word "testimony" (sākṣyam) is supplied from the preceding verse.
The mention of "by the pupil" (śiṣyeṇa) is intended to demonstrate the relationship of the teacher and the disciple.
The term "kinsman" (bandhu) is a restatement of the relationship by birth that is not subject to removal;
even though such a relationship exists, one who is not too closely related is included.
Therefore, a brother-in-law, a maternal uncle, a brother-in-law by marriage, and others are not witnesses.
For the term "kinsman" (bandhu) is conventionally established in such a sense;
by the word "servant" (dāsa), the relationship between master and servant is indicated.
Neither the master, nor the teacher, nor the officiating priest are witnesses in every kind of matter.
A slave is one born into slavery;
a hired laborer is one who works for wages.
Now, it may be objected that children and others have already been excluded from serving as witnesses due to their incapacity.

For these [senses] are not capable of determining testimony because of the instability of the intellect due to defects such as its immaturity; thus, that which was set aside in times of adversity is being reconsidered. For its capacity does not manifest in times of adversity.
It would be like one who might say: "Fresh rice need not be cooked; however, if there is fire, it must be cooked. This is not a fault.
Thus, for this very purpose, the subsequent verse is commenced.
One should recognize that the speech of children, the elderly, and the sick who testify falsely is unstable, as is the speech of those whose minds are agitated.
This is its meaning:
here, "fools" and the like are not intended to refer to those whose minds are entirely unattained, unbound, or deluded, such that the subject matter would have to be taught from the very beginning;
rather, it is permitted for those who are capable of comprehension but whose minds are not yet perfectly stable.

Their words should be examined by means of inference. If they speak coherently, do not falter, and are not associated with any suspected defect, then they are authoritative. Regarding this, it is said: one should recognize the speech of those who speak falsely as unstable.
This is what is meant:
one should determine the falsity of speech by its instability.
In this context, the instability of speech consists of the mutual incoherence of words and the lack of clarity and completeness of the syllables.
And this is intended as an illustration of the various conditions of children and others;
those who, due to age or disease, have reached such a state that they utter something else when intending to say something else, and whose speech is indistinct—they are not witnesses.
This ground for disqualification from being a witness is to be understood through direct perception.
But other [causes], such as passion, hatred, wealth, greed, and so forth, which are common to all, are to be examined through inference;
and these have already been mentioned:
those whose minds are arrogant, who are by nature afflicted, and whose intellects are lacking in firmness.
In all cases of violence, theft,
