and adultery, as well as in verbal and physical assault, one should not examine the witnesses too closely.
Force (*saha*) is strength; that which is done by relying upon it is *sāhasa* (recklessness).

That which is the performance of an improper act through the king's favor, by virtue of having a great faction, by the strength of one’s own body, or by relying on the powerful—that is *sāhasa*, such as tearing clothes, setting fire [to property], cutting hair, and so forth.
The rest is well known.
In this case, the witnesses are not to be examined;
that is, the examination consisting of such criteria as being householders, having sons, and so forth, is here prohibited.
However, that which is suspected of being a cause for deviation—consisting of passion, hatred, greed for wealth, and the like—must certainly be performed.
It has been stated that this tradition (smṛti) is based on a visible foundation.

In the event of a conflict between witnesses, the lord of men should accept the majority; but when the numbers are equal, he should accept those distinguished by their virtues; and when there is a conflict between virtuous witnesses, he should accept the best among the twice-born.
In a case concerning a plot of land or similar property where there is a dispute, and both parties have cited witnesses as proof of possession—
where some claimants assert possession while others, the defendants,
deny it— the testimony of the majority should be accepted.
But among those who are equal in number, those who are superior by virtue of their qualities— meaning those possessing many qualities—
or those endowed with even a single quality that is preeminent and beneficial for the goals of man;
when there is a distinction among such virtuous persons of equal merit, caste (jāti) must be taken into account.
If all are equal, there shall be an oath;
or else, something else equivalent to that.
One should accept the majority.
One should accept the testimony of many as authoritative.
"Duality" refers to the statement of mutually contradictory meanings.
Testimony is established through seeing or hearing in the presence [of the event];
by speaking the truth therein, a witness does not fall away from dharma or worldly prosperity.

But has this not already been stated by the words, "Whoever is an eyewitness"? How then can an alternative proof be suspected, such that it is said here that "the establishment of the witness is through seeing and hearing"?
To this it is replied:
A witness must be appointed by one who intends to engage in legal proceedings, being told, "You shall be my witness."
In that regard, one who has not been addressed in such a manner would not [otherwise] attain the status of a witness;
for this reason, the following is stated:
even if it is not said, "Whosoever was present there and somehow an experiencer, you ought to remember this matter between us," one indeed becomes a witness.

"From direct seeing" means from immediate experience and from hearing; the word "direct" (*samakṣa*) must be understood as applying to both. When something is heard by one person from someone else, and then heard by another from that person, it is "heard through tradition" (*paraṃparāśruta*); therefore, one who hears through such tradition is not a witness (*sākṣin*).
This is established by worldly convention—such as "this improper act was done by him" or "he owes this to him"—but not by means of formal proof (*pramāṇa*).

In that context, "direct perception" (*samakṣadarśana*) refers to the immediate experience of an object. Regarding matters such as the lending of debt, physical assault, or verbal abuse, "directly seen" means perceived through the operation of the eyes; likewise, regarding matters such as "this was taken from me by him," it refers to the hearing of words. Although the root *dṛś* (to see) denotes mere apprehension in general, nevertheless, for the sake of following the meter, auditory cognition (*śrotrajñāna*) is mentioned separately as "hearing" (*śravaṇa*).
This much is intended here:
one by whom something has been experienced through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is a witness.
The inclusion of the word "in the presence of" (*samakṣa*) is for the purpose of indicating any means of valid cognition whatsoever.
Therefore, even that which is experienced through inference and so forth is indeed "experienced.
Consequently, what is heard from the scripture of a reliable person (*āptāgama*), though not perceived directly, is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The latter half of the verse, however, is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*); for speaking the truth has been enjoined, and it is understood through other means of knowledge that one who speaks untruth suffers a loss of merit (*dharma*) and wealth (*artha*).
A witness who gives testimony in an assembly of noble men that differs from what was seen or heard goes headfirst to hell after death and is excluded from heaven.
This [verse] is intended to show the consequences for witnesses who speak untruthfully.
It has been stated that the word *dṛṣṭa-śruta* is a synonym for *upalabdhi* (perception);
therefore, anything other than that is *anupalabdha* (unperceived).
If he says this: "Noble ones, members of the assembly, you who act rightly—
in their presence, in that assembly, one goes with face cast down, head bowed, to hell, to the place of torment."

After dying, he falls away and is deprived of heaven; for even the merit he has performed for ascending to heaven is obstructed by the gravity of the sin of giving false testimony. However, it is not that the karma leading to heaven is destroyed by some other sin.
Because actions produce their own respective fruits, except in the case of expiatory rites (prāyaścitta).
Even where one might see or hear something without being formally appointed as a witness,
if questioned there, one should state it exactly as seen and exactly as heard.
But was it not already stated under the rule "because of seeing in person" that there is testimony even for one who has experienced [the matter] in some way, even if not appointed?
In that case, what is the purpose of this [rule], "even where one is not recorded"?
Or what is the distinction?
It is said:
it is appropriate for one who has been entered into a document to serve as a witness due to his specific involvement in the transaction, but not for one who has not been so entered;
for if both were witnesses, the act of entering [the name] into the document would result in futility.
Therefore, in order to dispel this doubt, this is stated:
the previous verse [applies] where witnesses have been enumerated,
but this one [applies] where there is a written document accompanied by witnesses.
"Unbound" means not even recorded in writing;
"seeing" and "hearing" have already been explained;
the rest is easily understood.
A single person who is greedy shall not be a witness, nor shall women, even if they are many and pure;
this is because the intellect of women is unstable, and others also who are possessed by defects [are excluded].
Furthermore, the prohibition of a single witness applies to one who is devoid of greed and other such vices;
by this, even a single witness who is certain of the truth through his veracity is indeed admissible.
Women, however, are not eligible to give testimony under any circumstances, whether they be few or many.
"Even though they are pure" means even though they possess virtuous qualities.
The reason for this is that "the intellect of women is unstable.
This fickleness of intellect is the very nature of women.
However, even if virtues are acquired through effort, they may perish due to negligence, laziness, and the like; therefore, their inherent instability will surely persist.
Just as in the case of a sick person, even if the digestive fire has been restored by means of ghee and other remedies, the natural state of illness recurs with even the slightest negligence.
For this reason, one cannot place full confidence in those [women], even if they possess virtues.
As for the statement that women may also serve as witnesses when others are unavailable,
this applies only where they are questioned at that very moment and where there is no suspicion that their minds have been influenced by anyone;
however, where there is an interval of time, the losing party might sometimes win them over, and thus they are never to be admitted as witnesses in such cases.
"And others who are also enveloped by defects":
the meaning is that other men besides women who are enveloped or overcome by defects such as diseases and the like, being possessed of many defects.
But what, indeed, are these so-called defects?
And it has been said:
"Lust and the other [defilements] are prohibited by the treatise; they are suspected of being causes of deviation [from the path].

Even though these faults have been stated by their own specific names alone, this [present statement] is not redundant, as it is for the purpose of including those that were not explicitly mentioned."
For authors everywhere agree that a term may express both a general and a specific meaning.
Others, however, by eliding the vowel *a*—reading "alubdho 'py ekaḥ" (even one who is not greedy is not a witness, how much less one who is greedy)—explain it in this way;
thus, there is permission for two [types of witnesses].
The long vowel *ī* in *śucyā* is difficult to justify, because of the rule *voto guṇavacanāt*;
however, some support its formation by the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ*.
Whatever they might say by its very nature should be accepted as conventional;
therefore, whatever else they might speak for the sake of dharma is meaningless.

The meaning is this: whatever witnesses state in accordance with their own nature regarding a legal matter is to be accepted; however, if they speak for the sake of dharma with a perverted sense of duty that deviates from their true nature, that is useless and not to be accepted. Speaking of a matter exactly as it was seen is what constitutes testimony according to one's nature.
However, if [you say] this was done with the thought, "Let there not be any distress for this ascetic on account of my words," that is pointless.
It is like when someone reports, "I have been insulted by this man," and the other person denies it.

The witnesses say, "He was reviled truthfully, but in jest, not out of anger. In that case, the statement of the witnesses, "he was reviled," is to be accepted; however, the phrase "in jest" is not to be accepted because it was not stated by the defendant, and thus, even though spoken, it is an answer to what was not asked.
"Relating to worldly convention" means pertaining to conventional usage;
"devoid of purpose" means meaningless.
Others explain it as follows:

When people cite a passage with faltering words due to lack of confidence or similar reasons, it does not follow that it is therefore unacceptable; rather, their disposition must be discerned through inference—whether they falter due to timidity or because they are speakers of untruth.
This has already been stated previously, and one should not disregard the literal meaning of the text.
When the witnesses have arrived in the assembly hall in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant,
the judge shall interrogate them, consoling them with this procedure.
"In the assembly" means within the assembly;
this is a compound formed according to the *śauṇḍādi* group.
Those who have gone to the place of legal proceedings must be questioned, in the presence of both the plaintiff and the defendant, according to the procedure to be described hereafter.
He should console them by speaking gently;

for through harshness, those who are afraid of the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) would not remain in their natural state and might fail to remember everything, since fear is a cause for the loss of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). The term *prāḍvivāka* is used conventionally to refer to the person appointed by the king to oversee the administration of justice.

Although the etymological meaning of the parts—namely, "one who asks" (*pṛcchati*) and "one who discriminates" (*vivicati*)—is possible even for a king, nevertheless, we observe the usage of the term in its distinct sense [as applied to others]: "The minister or the judge (*prāḍvivākaḥ*) who might decide a case otherwise.
Thus, one who asks is *prāṭ*; according to the rule *kvib-vaci-pracchi-śri-dru-śru-pruvāṃ dīrgho 'saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca*, the suffix *kvip* is added to *pracch*, resulting in *prāṭ*.
One who discriminates specifically in matters of legal difficulty is *vivāṭaḥ*.
According to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*,
the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
By the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*, the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *ka*) occurs for the letters *ca* and *ja*.
He who is both a questioner (prāṭ) and a judge (vivāka) is a prāḍvivāka.
Whatever you two know of each other's conduct regarding this matter, tell it all in truth, for you two possess the status of witnesses here.

Whatever you know regarding this matter of legal dispute— whether it be their mutual conduct or behavior, whether witnessed publicly or in private— all that speak truly and accurately; for your testimony is required here,
and your authority in this matter depends upon your words, whether they be true or false.
By this [statement], they are encouraged.
Although there is a general indication that "you are witnesses in this matter," the hearing of all relevant facts must be understood by implication;
for those who have not heard the particulars are not capable of knowing the subject of the inquiry.
A witness who speaks the truth in testimony attains irreproachable worlds;
and in this world, he gains unsurpassed fame—this speech is honored by Brahmā.
From this point forward is the rule for the interrogation of witnesses concerning truthful speech.
By speaking the truth, a witness attains worlds characterized by heaven and the like—worlds that are blameless, beyond reproach, and the cause for the enjoyment of desired fruits.
Alternatively, the word *loka* may be understood as referring to [rebirth in] a particular caste.

The meaning is that he is born into an auspicious birth. And in this birth, he obtains unsurpassed fame and renown— of which there is nothing else more excellent or superior— and the people offer him words of praise.
For this speech is true, and Sarasvatī has been honored by Brahmā Prajāpati.
Speaking falsehood in testimony, one is bound tightly with the nooses of Varuṇa for a hundred lifetimes, rendered powerless; therefore, one should speak the truth in testimony.
By the preceding demonstration of the seen and the unseen, as well as the auspicious and the inauspicious, witnesses were encouraged to speak the truth;
by this [verse], the arising of suffering in the case of false testimony is shown.
This is solely for the sake of truthful speech.
The act of a witness is testimony.
Speaking untruth therein, one is bound and tormented by the nooses of Varuṇa;
"bhṛśam" means excessively.

Helpless and made dependent in all his movements—even those of speech and sight—for as long as a hundred births, there are the terrible nooses of Varuṇa, with ropes of serpents, or the afflictions of dropsy.
As a means to avoid this fault, the injunction is: "One should speak the truth."
In the expression *ājātīḥ*, this prefix *āṅ* does not signify either a limit (*maryādā*) or inclusion (*abhividhi*);
for if that were the case, the ablative case would be required.
Therefore, this prefix is meaningless, just as in the word *pralambate*.
And here, a second repetition is also understood:
"He who is seized by the belly undergoes a hundred births."
A witness is purified by truth; dharma increases through truth.
Therefore, truth must indeed be spoken by witnesses among all social classes.
It is purified, that is, it becomes clean; it is liberated from other sins as well—this is the meaning. The rest has already been explained.
For the self alone is the witness of the self, and the self is likewise the refuge of the self;
do not despise your own self, the supreme witness of men.
This very point is made clear by the following verse.
Evil-doers indeed think, "No one sees us";
yet the gods see them, as does the inner person within their own selves.
The word "not" is displaced [in the sentence].
Those who commit evil deeds, such as those who practice fraud and the like, think:
"No one sees us."
By the particle *iti*, it is established that the meaning of the sentence is the object of the verb "to think.
The sentence-meaning is not "no one sees us," but rather "those gods who are about to be mentioned do see us."
It is one's own inner self.
As it has been said: "For the self alone is the witness of the self.
Now, who indeed is this evildoer, and who else could be his witness?
To the extent that the Self alone is the agent of both auspicious and inauspicious deeds, and the inner person is the witness—
this is true.
However, by superimposing the status of a deity upon that very Self, the designation of "action" and "agent" as distinct entities is for the purpose of removing falsehood.
You recognize the form of the deity;
yet you do not [recognize] your own true, internal, and bodily form, nor the external, non-self, and insubstantial [form]. Thus, one is exhorted: "Do not commit evil for the sake of enjoying these.
Therefore, do not despise yourself; do not disregard your own self, the unsurpassed witness of men.
For while another witness bears testimony only in this world, this one gives testimony even for one who has died;
therefore, one must fear it.
A speaker of untruth might sometimes think: "What can this witness do to me when I have entered into another body?"
That is not so;
the self is the movement of the self,
for there is no movement other than that which exists apart from the self.
For there cannot be two selves for a single person;
however, others hold that the distinction lies in this: the Supreme Self is the witness, while the transmigrating selves are those who are subject to injunctions.
Who, then, are those gods who perceive even one practicing secret, hidden sin? To this he says:
"The sky, the earth, the waters, the heart, the moon, the sun, fire, Yama, the wind, night, the two twilights, and Dharma know the conduct of all embodied beings."
By the word "heart" (hṛdaya), the subtle person (liṅgapuruṣa) residing in the heart is denoted.

The capacity to see heaven and so forth is superimposed upon the insentient as consciousness. However, in another philosophical system, the great elements themselves are sentient by virtue of having the nature of deities.
And so it is described that the Earth approached Brahmā for the sake of removing her burden;

because they are omnipresent, there is nothing that is beyond their perception, and thus they know the conduct and character of all embodied beings, as well as the auspicious and inauspicious deeds residing within their own bodies.

In the presence of the gods and Brahmins, the judge, being himself pure, should question the pure twice-born men regarding the truth in the forenoon, while they are facing either northward or eastward.
The deities, such as Durgā, Mārtaṇḍa, and others, are represented by images;
[he should approach them] who have performed the rites of bathing, sipping water (ācamana), and so forth, being pure.
The questioner himself should likewise be in such a state of purity.
The word "ṛtam" is used solely for the purpose of completing the verse;
the rest is well known.
One should ask the Brāhmaṇa, "Speak"; the king, "Speak the truth";
the Vaiśya, with [threats of] cattle, grain, and gold; but the Śūdra, with these [grave] sins.
But where does this third [instrumental case] in the phrase "by means of cows, seeds, and gold" come from?
If it is argued that it is called the instrument because of its connection with the action expressed by the word *pṛcchet* ("if one should ask"), that is untenable;
for in that context, it is the word (*śabda*) that is the instrument, not the object (*artha*).
This is not a fault;
it should be explained in such a way that [the items] like cows and so forth function as the instruments of the question.
It should be understood that "by sins" (*pātakaiḥ*) is a remainder for both [phrases], namely: "by the sins consisting of cows, seed, and gold."
Therefore, this is the meaning:
one should question [the accused] by means of examples of heinous crimes involving a cow, seed, or gold.
The interrogative statement should be recited as follows: "If you speak falsely, that same sin which results from stealing or killing a cow shall be yours."
In this manner, one should question the Śūdra regarding the offenses (pātaka) that are about to be mentioned.
It has been stated, however, that the word "pātaka" should be understood as referring to designations that indicate offenses, because the primary [offenses] cannot be the subject of such questioning.

Whatever worlds are ordained for the slayer of a Brahmin, for the killer of women and children, for the betrayer of friends, and for the ungrateful— those same worlds shall be the lot of one who speaks falsely.

The worlds characterized by hell and other such states that are attained by those who commit the murder of a Brahmin shall belong to you if you speak falsely; therefore, speak the truth—such is the exhortation.

Furthermore, he who betrays a friend, or destroys Brahmins and others by seizing their wives, all their property, and so forth; and he who, forgetting a favor received, harms that very benefactor—that ungrateful person attains whatever suffering awaits him in the hereafter.
O Bhadra, whatever merit you have accumulated since birth—
all of that would go to a dog if you were to speak otherwise.
The meaning is that [your effort] would be as fruitless as going after a dog.
Others, however, maintain that the mention of "going after a dog" is intended to illustrate the fault;
just as if one were to acquire a superior object such as gold with great difficulty and then cast it away into a flow of impurity, such is the nature of that meritorious deed.
Furthermore, it has been stated more than once that there is no transfer of a well-performed deed committed by one person to another.
O virtuous one, as for you who think of yourself, "I am alone," this sage who observes merit and demerit is ever-present within your heart.
The sage, who is the observer and seer of merit and demerit, remains silent.
But who is this sage?
To demonstrate the extreme nature of fear, he says:
"Yama, the son of Vivasvat, the god who resides here in your heart."
If you have no dispute with that, then do not go to the Gaṅgā, nor to the Kurus.

This Yama, who has come to your ears as the one who severs the bodies, wealth, and possessions of all living beings and restrains them with torments—he dwells right here in your heart, not at a distance.
And he punishes the offender this very moment.
Do not think in your mind: "This Self of mine will neglect me."
For he has nothing that belongs to himself;

if there is no dispute with him, and if he is serene and trustworthy, what is the use of going to the Ganges for one desiring to bathe for the purification of sin, or what purpose is served by going to Kurukṣetra?
Whatever fruit characterized by liberation from sin is obtained from those places, that is obtained right here in this non-deceptive Supreme Self.
For the self of an evildoer does not become free from apprehension,
thinking, "What might come of this for me?
Even for an atheist, some form of doubt certainly arises at times.
The river Gaṅgā purifies,
but the region of Kurukṣetra is itself purifying.
Naked, shaven-headed, carrying a skull-bowl, hungry and thirsty,
and blind, he who gives false testimony shall go to the house of his enemy as a beggar.
*Kapāla* refers to a fragment of a vessel such as a shallow bowl (*śarāva*) or the like; this is easily understood.
Headlong into blind darkness shall the sinner go to hell—
he who, when questioned during a legal determination of dharma, speaks falsely in response.

The meaning is this: he who, when questioned about a sign (*nimitta*), speaks what is false and untrue, is seized by that sin and evil; with his feet upward and his face downward, he reaches that hell—a place of torment—in a great, dense darkness.
The term "blind" (*andha*) is used because in other forms of darkness something may still be seen, but there, nothing at all can be perceived.
Like a blind man eating fish along with their bones,
is that man who, having entered the assembly, speaks what is inconsistent with the facts and not based on direct perception.
One speaks that which is devoid of meaning and contrary to truth;
for example, as thorns, when eaten or consumed, do not produce such pleasure as fish do.
Even when there is a mere measure of pleasure through greed for wealth, it results in great suffering—thus is the analogy of eating too much food containing thorns.
Indeed, when the wise Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) has no misgivings regarding one who speaks,
the gods know no other person in this world to be more excellent than him.

When a witness speaks, the Knower—the Kṣetrajña, the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī) Puruṣa who knows both truth and falsehood—does not entertain doubt as to whether he will speak the truth or the untruth; He does not suspect him thus, but is certain that "he speaks only the truth. Since his own Self is free from suspicion, the gods know no man to be more excellent, superior, or most praiseworthy than that man. Who, then, is this Knower? And who else is there to be suspected?
For there is indeed only one Self; setting speech in motion by means of its own effort, it becomes the knower.
That very same [Self] is joined with that attribute through the expression of doubt in the form, "What might this be? How might it be?
In that case, the occurrence of any differentiation is untenable.
This is true;
it was stated thus by means of an imagined distinction,
just as one says, "the self kills itself by means of the self."
Listen, gentle one, to the number of kinsmen he slays by speaking falsely in testimony, categorized in their proper order.
This section is commenced for the purpose of demonstrating that false witnesses are a specific kind of sin based on a specific kind of falsehood regarding material things.

In this regard, this verse, being taught by way of an address, serves to inspire respect. It is understood that what is taught in secret between two parties may be taken lightly as being of little consequence; however, this matter is of extremely great importance and must be heard with full attention.
The singular form "O gentle one" (*saumya*) is intended to refer specifically to Bhṛgu, even though many disciples are present.
In the phrase "in which testimony," the locative case is used with a different grammatical subject (*vyadhikaraṇa-saptamī*).

This is a locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*), meaning: "in whatever legal proceeding—which is distinguished by various objects—there is testimony, [if] therein [one speaks] a falsehood caused by that [testimony]."
And [the rule] "of another, by whose state" (Pāṇini 1.1.39) applies.
Alternatively, there is a distinction of witnesses due to a distinction of substances; in that case, it is indeed a grammatical coreferential construction (samānādhikaraṇa).
The word "tāvataḥ" is derived in the sense of measure (parimāṇa).
In that context, since even a large number of individuals might be conceived as a mere quantity—such as children, women, or the elderly—he specifies them "by number.
The phrase "in successive order" (*anupūrvaśas*) is for the sake of easy comprehension, for what is expressed in a sequential manner is easily understood.
And here, the intended sequence is that which pertains to numerical order.
Because that very [point] will be explained later, [it says] "the five sacrificial animals," and so forth.
One kills five by lying about cattle, one kills ten by lying about cows;
one kills a hundred by lying about horses, and one kills a thousand by lying about men.
"Falsehood for the sake of an animal":
this is a compound (samāsa) like "vegetable-king" (śākapārthiva). Falsehood also destroys the five kinsmen.
And consequently, they fall into hell.
[The five are: mother, father, wife, male child, and offspring.
But how can there be a result for one person through a transgression committed by another?
We maintain that another person attains heaven, hell, and so forth through the merit, demerit, and the like performed by someone else due to association;
what is meant is that this person is abandoned by them.
Alternatively, the sin resulting from their being killed accrues to him; thus, even though he does not kill, he is said to "kill" because the resulting unseen effect (adṛṣṭa) is identical.
And this is a commendatory statement (arthavāda), not an injunction regarding its performance;
for if it were an injunction regarding its performance, one would incur the penance for violence.
This becomes the penance for giving false testimony.
The progressive increase in the number of counts and so forth is intended to signify the gravity of the expiation, rather than being meant as a literal enumeration;
thus, it is stated that the expiation for each subsequent offense is more severe.
When there is doubt as to whose slave this man is, any falsehood spoken therein is called "falsehood regarding persons."
One who speaks falsehood for the sake of gold destroys both those already born and those yet unborn;
one destroys everything by speaking falsehood regarding land. Therefore, do not speak falsehood regarding land.

But how can there be a conjunction with what belongs to another when there is no contact with those who are unborn, such that it is said, "He kills both the born and the unborn"? It has been stated: this is a mere explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding one who speaks every falsehood concerning land.
"Do not speak an untruth concerning the earth;
[this is because of the rule] *smottare laṅ ca*.
This address "mā vādīḥ" (do not speak) is also a direct exhortation for the sake of emphasis.
What, then, is this so-called "earth"? It is that which is well known as the terrestrial globe, supported by mountains and bounded by the oceans.
But who is the master of such a thing, or who is its taker away?
For there is no such thing as a sovereign of the entire earth;
thus, the verse says: "No mortal whatsoever is worthy to give [the whole] of the earth. The intended meaning is that there is no one who is a universal monarch.

"O Viśvakarman Bhauvana, you wish to give me away. He heard the king addressing him by his own name and by the title of his paternal uncle, "O Viśvakarman Bhauvana," thinking, "He wishes to give me away.
"He will deceive me; I shall sink into the midst of the waters, into the middle of the water."
"Since you have thus made this resolve in vain, I shall immerse myself in the water. By this immersion in water, he declares the fruitlessness of his vow for giving;
just as something cast into the water is useless, so too is this [vow].
"This agreement with Kaśyapa is false.
Let this agreement of yours—the promise, the vow, 'I give [myself] to Kaśyapa'—be in vain; I am to be killed. I belong to all in common, to be enjoyed by all people.
Kings merely possess the right to insist upon protection"—this is the intended meaning.
Therefore, since the possibility of seizing land by means of such a small amount does not exist, how could there be a dispute?
True;
just as this word "land" (*bhūmi*) is used here, it is likewise used for fields, villages, sacrificial grounds, and so forth.
And in that case, ownership certainly exists;

since giving and taking away apply only to what is perceptible, there is nothing inconsistent here. Furthermore, as for its "taking away," it refers to a form of removal such as occurs with a house and so forth, not like the cutting down of a creeper.

Consequently, one who might walk upon another's field or someone who might take some soil would not be a thief of land. The Mīmāṃsakas have stated: "Land [cannot be stolen] because it is common to all.
And with reference to the word "land" as denoting only a portion [of the whole], the venerable Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana has recited [this verse] among the duties of giving (*dānadharmas*):

"Even others on earth, including kings, must approve of the dharma of giving; for this inexhaustible treasure of Brahman has been ordained for rulers. Thus, the Mīmāṃsakas have stated that the non-giftability of land in the Viśvajit sacrifice refers only to the entire globe, saying: "Land shall not be given, because it is common to all."
The meaning is: since all persons are indistinguishable in their fitness for walking about and so forth, the earth cannot be made one's own; how, then, can it be given?
However, according to this view, villages, cities, and the like should be given in the Viśvajit sacrifice.

Others, however, read: "They lead the sacrificial fee between the Sadas and the Patnīśālā"; since a rule regarding a quality [such as walking] is impossible in the case of the earth, fields and other such things may also be given here.
Because of the use of the singular number in the expression "speaking," the address "Listen, gentle one" (*śṛṇu saumya*) refers specifically to the witness and not to the disciple.

From the verse beginning with "But a Śūdra by these sins," all instances of the second person (*madhyama-puruṣa*) refer to the interrogation of the Śūdra, because they form a single syntactical unit characterized by a common verbal suffix denoting a greater degree of sin.
From the verse beginning with "Blind, he may go to the house of an enemy," all interrogations refer to the witness.

Because the section is interrupted by the change in verbal form, and because the second person maintains the same sequence of meaning, the designation in the third person—"one should go" (*gantavyaḥ*)—is intended to terminate the previous topic.
They say that [the law regarding] women's enjoyment and sexual intercourse is like that regarding water;
and likewise for aquatic gems and all those made of stone.
In the case of water situated in wells, ponds, and the like—whether it be great or small—there is no fault, just as there is none regarding the earth.
Likewise, regarding the enjoyment of women, which is called sexual intercourse, there is no fault such as "By whom was this woman enjoyed through the act of sexual intercourse?
As for gems produced from water, these are the *manaya* gems, pearls, and so forth.
"In gemstones made of stone" refers to those such as lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*) and the like; it is connected with the word "gems.
Gems are indeed of two kinds: those born of water and those made of stone.
Therefore, since the act of taking the jewels was already established, the inclusion of the two qualifiers is for the purpose of completing the verse.
"Water-born" (*abja*) means those produced from water;
"made of stone" (*aśmamaya*) means modifications of stone.
Having considered all these faults in speaking untruth,
speak everything exactly as it was heard and as it was seen, straightforwardly.
Setting aside conjecture and refutation, speak according to what has been seen and heard as it truly is, without distortion.
One should treat Brahmins who are cattle-herders, merchants, artisans, actors, servants, or usurers as one would Śūdras.
Artisans (*kāravaḥ*) are craftsmen such as carpenters, blacksmiths, cooks, and so forth;
*kuśīlavas* are dancers, singers, and the like;
and servants (*preṣyāḥ*) are those known as slaves who carry out the orders of another for the sake of their livelihood.
Moneylenders are those who subsist on interest;
even though they are Brāhmaṇas, according to the context, they are to be regarded like Śūdras regarding testimony and oaths, but not in other matters.

Just as a Śūdra is not questioned regarding testimony on the basis of the merit of his gifts and so forth, and is purified by means of the fire-ordeal and the like in an oath, so too is this oath; even though it was not previously introduced, nevertheless, because of its immediate sequence [to the preceding], because it possesses a fault, and because of its being a preparatory act—since immediate sequence is a cause for connection even when there is a preparatory act—and because of the proximity of what is about to be stated, which results in a convergence of age as before, it is equal [in application] to the oath as well.
A man who speaks thus regarding matters of dharma, even if he knows otherwise, does not fall from heaven; they call that the speech of the gods.
The meaning is that even one who knows otherwise but speaks otherwise does not fall from heaven; even by speaking falsely, he is not defiled. Is this always the case?
"No," he says;
"in matters according to dharma.
That is, in transactions concerning objects by means of dharma, such as compassion and so forth, as the cause.
Furthermore, the fact that dharma serves as the cause will be demonstrated in the following verse;
and this is not stated according to my own whim,
but rather, the traditionalists (smṛtikāras) who preceded me have also uttered these words.
What, then, is the "divine speech"?

It is that speech belonging to the gods by which one thinks, "In this particular circumstance, untruth must be spoken"; having heard this, Manu and others speak it—this is the praise of untruth in a specific context.
However, others have explained this verse as being supplementary to the preceding injunction.
Therefore, this [rule] must apply to Brāhmaṇas such as cowherds and others in the context of interrogative statements;

otherwise, since there are Brāhmaṇas, how could these [others] be interrogated like Śūdras—as in the command "Speak the truth"—without even those who know the law being at fault? For Manu and others speak such words as "these are to be treated like Śūdras," and they are the authority regarding dharma and adharma.
And they must speak the truth; and that [truth] should be as prescribed therein, for where that very dharma exists, or where falsehood exists, there the speaking of falsehood itself is the dharma.
In cases where telling the truth regarding a Śūdra, Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, or Brāhmaṇa would result in their death, a falsehood must be spoken; for that is superior to the truth.

In this context, what is stated by the phrase "one should not speak untruth" is that the prohibition has as its scope persons other than Śūdras and the like; it does not, however, enjoin the speaking of untruth.
For if that were the case, the syntactic unity with the prohibition would be subverted.
What, then, is the scriptural mention of the occasion (*nimitta*) here?
Regarding the word *tatra*:

since that [word *tatra*] is a qualifier of the killing (*vadha*), it does not denote the killing itself; for it is impossible for that which is non-existent to serve as a causal condition (*nimitta*).
Consequently, the following meaning results: once the killing has been performed, one must subsequently speak a falsehood concerning either that [killing] or something other than that.
It is established in reality.

Now, one might object: since "wherein" (*yatra*) indicates the basis of worldly convention (*vyavahāra-vastu*), and "therein" (*tatra*) subsequently refers back to that very same thing, it follows that for that conventional practice wherein those who have been defeated become liable to execution, its status as a cause (*nimitta-bhāva*) would be inappropriate.
Regarding this, they say:
"In this case, a falsehood is not forbidden even toward those deserving of death,
because the life of a more wicked person is unworthy."

However, as for the argument that since kings might not execute someone who is unworthy of death due to a minor offense—such as a slip of the tongue regarding a lie told out of fear of public exposure—there is no certainty because the king's nature and the punishment of anger are unscriptural and lack fixed limits, this too cannot be established as a valid cause [for the rule].
Therefore, it is logical that [the prohibition] is merely a supplement to the prohibition [of lying].
In the text of Gautama, moreover, there is not even the suspicion of an injunction to lie.

It is logical that one resorts to untruth when there is a prohibition such as "there is no fault in speaking falsehood if one's livelihood depends upon it," which would otherwise lead to acting according to one's whims regarding both truth and falsehood; for in the case of a killing, while the truthfulness of one's speech might serve as a causal factor, one nevertheless resorts to untruth out of fear of transgressing the prohibition, "One must not harm any living beings.
Therefore, this [untruth] has been committed: if he does not speak when questioned, he does not kill; and since he does not kill, how could he be tainted by the fault of harming?

If it is argued that even though he possesses independence, because he is being killed by the king at the latter's command, he incurs the status of being the cause for that act and thus constitutes the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*), we say no; not every cause is an instigator, as in the cases "one's lineage [is established] by wealth" or "fame by learning.
In these instances, learning and fame possess the causal status of being instigators.

Furthermore, this causal state—characterized by the suitability for the production of worldly results—is not something entirely different from substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*); rather, it is simply those very substances and qualities.
Even where an action is heard, as in "cooking with fire" (*agninā pākaḥ*), that too is expressed by *kṛt*-suffixes as an established state of being (*bhāva*) in its own form.

Furthermore, this causal factor (*hetu*) which prompts the agent's activity according to the technical treatises is not such that its causality consists merely in being a prompter; this is the meaning.

If, for instance, causality were restricted to the forms of commanding or entreating—namely, orders and requests—then the derivation of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) would be impossible in cases such as "he causes rice to dry in the sun" (*śoṣayate vrīhīn ātape*), because [the sun] is insentient.

But has this not already been answered by the commentators? [They argue: "In the case of metaphorical action (*upacarita-kriyā*), it refers to an insentient entity, as in 'the alms lodge' (*bhikṣā vāsayati*) or 'the cow-dung fuel teaches' (*kārīṣo 'dhyāpayati*).
For in these cases, there is no assistance (*upakāra*) produced by consciousness; rather, because another motivator (*prayojaka*) is certain, [the action is attributed to the object].
Indeed, for the student who performs the study impelled by the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), [the words] restate the obstacles characterized by cold and so forth.
In the case of cow-dung (kārīṣa), there is the superimposition of being a prompter;
for it is called a "prompter" because of its capacity to impel.
And this [capacity] is seen even more clearly in non-conscious things such as wind and water with respect to fire and wood.

In that case, because there would be an absence of commanding and so forth by those who enjoin, motivate, or praise the ritual procedure, the words would have to be used in a figurative sense. Alternatively, this "motivating" (prayojakatva) consists in the performance of the action on behalf of another; and since that must conform to the activity of the motivator, it is the undertaking of another action distinct from commanding and so forth, known as "arrangement" (saṃvidhāna).
For it is precisely in the act of arranging that one is said to "cause to do."

Just as for one who desires to eat, one person brings a vessel while another serves the food; or for someone intent on killing, one person hands over a weapon while another inflames his fury by exposing the victim's faults— such a person, though devoid of the form of an actual instigator (*preṣitr*) and so forth, is an "instigator" (*prayojaka*) in the sense of performing actions conducive to the accomplishment of the result for the one being employed, provided he acts in a manner that facilitates it.
In this view, the cow-dung fuel (*kārīṣa*) and the teacher (*upādhyāya*) would both be considered equal [as agents].

Here too, that without whom the action does not come to completion, and for whom the specific designation of a *kāraka* would otherwise not apply, is the primary instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*).
And without the student (*adhyāyitr*), the cow-dung fuel cannot assume its status as the cause of the act of studying.
The teacher, however, is capable even without that [fuel], and thus the cow-dung fuel (*kārīṣa*) is used in a figurative sense.
Furthermore, wherever the status of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth is established by the observation of an affix denoting a cause (*hetumat*), there too it is merely figurative.
For example, seeing someone who has gone repeatedly to a distant village even for a very small purpose, one says: "The horse causes Devadatta to go."

But where neither proximity nor distance, nor the status of being internal (*antaraṅga*) or external (*bahiraṅga*), is perceived for anyone, there all those who contribute toward that suitability are instigators (*prayojaka*).

Now, one might object: "In the technical designation of a *kāraka*, there is no application of the 'internal' principle; so what is the distinction between the cow-dung fire (*kārīṣa*) and the teacher (*upādhyāya*)?
That is merely the internal system of those venerable ones.
They do not have real entities as their basis, for affirmation and negation both have real entities as their basis.
Furthermore, it is recited there: "The grammatical factors (kārakas) exist according to the speaker's intention."
This being the case, wherever someone might intend to express the agency of one who is actually not the agent, there both the prescription and the prohibition of the agentive suffix would apply;
as for example, in the enumeration of sins, it is recited: "the buyer, the seller, the preparer, and the server.
Therefore, that grammatical convention of yours, intended merely to establish a formal analysis (*anvākhyāna*), does not override the actual state of affairs (*vastu*).
For this very reason, the commentators have stated: "If the performance of a capable act were the cause [of death], it would follow that even a mere cause is a cause;
consequently, if someone gives food to another and that person dies from gluttony due to overeating, the giver would incur the status of being the killer.
And yet, that [death] is not brought about by that [act of giving].
For this instigator, known as one who provides food, is determined by another action; thus, neither the killing nor the envy and so forth constitute the cause [of the death] in any way.
Or, even if that were the cause, we maintain that there is no agency [in the sense of being a doer] because of the absence of the status of an instigator.

However, in a case where someone is wronged by the theft of land, gold, or the like, and he should somehow die from the resentment over that theft, it must be considered whether there is only the fault of the theft for the thief, or whether he also possesses the status of a causal agent (*nimittibhāva*) with respect to the killing.
What is there to be considered here?

Since the relationship between cause and effect is understood through its non-deviation, it is not possible for the seizure of land and so forth to have a fixed cause [for death] in the same way that the stroke of a sword or the act of eating has a fixed cause [for death].
What kind of restriction is intended here?
Indeed, it is not a fixed rule that some die while others do not;
because of the differences in the individual nature of persons, the very same medicine is beneficial for one with a phlegmatic constitution but has the opposite effect for another.
Furthermore, for all entities, the manifestation of a different capacity depends upon the distinctions of place, time, and nature, as well as auxiliary causes.
That very same characteristic, depending on the person's wealth and lineage, and depending on other living beings who are the cause of one's thirst, becomes the cause for its cessation.
Thus, for one who is utterly intolerant and full of resentment, the seizure of his property, humiliation, and so forth, lead to death.
In that case, how can the status of these factors as causes be denied?

But for one whose mind is gentle, there is indeed only indifference in that regard. Furthermore, as for those who, overcome by anger, might die by means of fasting, falling into a chasm, consuming poison, or the like, with the intent of taking revenge upon an offender—the same principle applies there as well.
Now, one might object: since in such cases one observes other well-known causes, such as the consumption of poison, the offense of seizing land and so forth cannot be considered the cause of death.

If it is argued that anger is produced by this [object] and thus proceeds toward the cause of death, such that it constitutes a causal condition (*nimitta*) through a traditional succession (*pāraṃparya*), then in that case, some people, being distressed even by wholesome advice, might commit suicide; consequently, the advisors in those instances would be murderers.
Likewise, the envious, withering away out of jealousy over the property of others, would attribute fault to the wealthy.
Likewise, other deluded minds follow after their beloved sons or masters; in that case, the status of being a killer would accrue to those beloved ones and others.

Furthermore, others, upon seeing a beautiful woman, become envious with fragile minds, their hearts breaking and their souls devoid of discernment; in that situation, virtuous women would be rendered culpable.
Thus, this very consequence has arisen: that for one who is dead, there is the sin of killing a Brahmin.
This is indeed true, provided there were no distinction between injunctions and prohibitions;
for beneficial instruction is enjoined, while the seizing of one's own property and so forth are prohibited.
And thus they have said:
If, for some reason, a reversal occurs for those who have acted with a desire to help, no fault attaches to them; it is like a medicinal herb that acts as a counteragent to poison.

In this regard, it is not only the case that there is no fault when a physician or the like, seeking to benefit a patient, administers medicine that somehow results in an adverse outcome; rather, it is stated that even in the case of another, such as a cow or other animal sinking in deep mud, if its death occurs despite the rescuer’s exertion in pulling it out with his arms, the rescuer is not at fault.
This applies everywhere.

Furthermore, when someone is seen performing their own duty and possessing an excellence of wealth, if another person burns with envy toward them, no one has transgressed the meaning of the scriptures on account of that person.
For a determinate state of being must be the object of negation;
however, regarding mental factors residing in other living beings which undergo change at every moment, it is impossible to ascertain their specific intrinsic natures.
Indeed, it is not possible to determine that "this person is afflicted by her excellence of form."
Furthermore, when the object of negation has been ascertained, it is not logical for it to be treated as an unascertained object.

In that case, where there might be some cognition of a cause—such as a reversal of syllables, emaciation of the body, and so forth—due to being overwhelmed by a fallacious logician, what is the use of associating with such a person who is prone to error? Or let her be a woman who kills men!
This is not so.
For even such a state of being a cause is not the object of a prohibition, because it would contradict another injunction;
for in this case, there exists an injunction prohibiting deviation.
Nor can injunctions, which have found their scope in a domain not already occupied by another injunction, be expected to encroach upon the domain of a contradictory injunction.

Even those who think that the instruction on the preservation of moral conduct prohibits activity characterized by passion (*rāga-lakṣaṇā pravṛtti*) but not that characterized by scriptural injunction (*śāstra-lakṣaṇā*), [argue as follows]: "By virtue of his great majesty, let there be no cutting off of this ascetic's life. Thus, through the desire to save his life, one who is about to die engages in union; he would not transgress the prohibition against sexual misconduct. As for the principle that one injunction does not apply within the scope of another injunction, this case is not actually within the scope of another injunction, because it is characterized by passion.

But surely, even regarding engagement [in action], there is no scriptural injunction, because—as in the case of a mandatory command (*niyoga*)—there is an absence of any traditional rule permitting transgression. Now, if it is argued that one engages in it out of fear of the prohibition—"one should desire killing" [if one does not engage]—that prohibition itself prohibits only violence characterized by passion (*rāga*).
And it is not that he does not engage out of passion; rather, he engages out of fear of the prohibition.
Furthermore, even that activity which proceeds from the desire to benefit others occurs by way of avoiding what is prohibited.

Even if someone were to beg for something and say, "I shall kill myself," one would not be a killer toward him by not giving it; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the collapse of all worldly conventions.
And they should worship Sarasvatī with sacrificial oblations (caru) dedicated to Speech as the deity,
effecting the supreme expiation for that sin of untruth.
Speech (*vāk*) and that which is a deity (*devatā*)—that is "speech-deity" (*vāgdevatā*).
And the sacrificial porridges (*caru*) intended for that purpose have speech as their deity;
*carus* are grains of rice that are not overcooked.

Because of the use of the plural number in the injunction "they should sacrifice with them," the word *carubhiḥ* is plural. It does not mean that there are many individual *caru* offerings, nor that they are combined as in the case of the *vrātyastoma* sacrifice. Rather, the plural is used because if the god rains, many Brāhmaṇas should perform the sacrifice;
it is not like the rule "one should sacrifice with three *kapiñjala* birds."
Thus, this [act] becomes a falsehood spoken for the sake of favoring Brāhmaṇas and others. "Falsehood" (*anṛtam*) refers to the sinful act characterized by the speaking of untruth.
Just as with a religious act (*dharmakriyā*), the genitive case is used here in apposition.

However, for those who hold that merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are produced by action rather than being the action itself, in their view the expression "the sin of falsehood" (*anṛtasya yat enaḥ*)—though involving different grammatical cases—is a case of metaphorical coordination; that is, because the sin is caused by falsehood, the sin is [metaphorically] called "falsehood.
Its *niṣkṛti* means its removal, purification, or sanctification, which is to say, its expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
It is *parā*, meaning preeminent or excellent.
But surely, how can there be sin here, since it has been stated that there is no fault in speaking untruth under such circumstances?
Some say that "abstention [from speech], however, yields great fruit.

But according to this scripture, for one who has made the resolve, "I must not speak untruth for as long as I live," this expiation is prescribed so that the fault of a false resolve does not accrue to him.
Even regarding the prohibition of house-burning and killing, there is an occasional injunction (*naimittika-vidhāna*).
The phrase "for the expiation of sin" (*enaso niṣkṛtim*) is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
How, then, should they worship Sarasvatī with oblations dedicated to Speech (*vāg-daivatyaiḥ*)?
If Sarasvatī is the deity of speech (*vāk*), how is she worshipped?
Or, if the deity exists as the identity of speech and Sarasvatī, then since the nature of a deity is understood through words, these two terms "speech" and "Sarasvatī" would be distinct.

Just as when one is enjoined with "one offers to Agni," the offering is made with "svāhā to Kṛśānu, the flaming one," and even though it is said, "one should offer having prepared [the oblation] for Vāyu; Vāyu is indeed breath (*prāṇa*)," the offering is not made with "to Prāṇa."
True;
speech itself is the deity.
Because of their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) has the sense of "deity."

Because of the use of the accusative case in the expression "Sarasvatīm," [the word cannot refer to the deity]. For a deity is not that which is designated by the accusative; the accusative is used for the object (*karman*), whereas the deity is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), not the object.
How, then, is there the connection of the word *sarasvatī*?
This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
[For example: "One offers to Agni; Agni, indeed, is all the deities."
Speech itself is Sarasvatī; by that sacrifice, she too becomes sacrificed to. Through the ritual act, the deity is made known.
How so?
Some say: "Agni is to be sacrificed to; Prajāpati is to be sacrificed to; likewise, one sacrifices to Agni," and so forth, because the deities are worshipped there and there in their own right.

In this context, the root *yaji* (to sacrifice) signifies the worship of a deity; and worship has as its object that which is being worshipped. Therefore, the use of the accusative case there is appropriate.
And thus it is recorded in the Smṛti that "the deity is to be worshipped," and so forth;
yet this is not tenable,
for under this view, the status of being a deity would have to be sought from elsewhere.
In that regard, there is a contradiction with the traditional legal authority (smṛti) which states that "the deity is the recipient of the sacrifice.
And this smṛti is more authoritative because it is independent.
The aforementioned deity is both the one to whom the offering is directed and the one to be meditated upon.

"One should meditate mentally upon that deity for whom the oblation has been taken"—since this refers to the object of that action, this accusative case ending is used in the sense of the *karman* (object).
Or one should offer clarified butter into the fire according to the prescribed rule with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras,
or with the verse beginning "ud," which is addressed to Varuṇa, or with the three verses whose deity is the Waters.
The mantras called *kūṣmāṇḍas* are recited in the Yajurveda;
with them, one should offer clarified butter (*ghṛta*) into the fire.
And "offering" (*juhoti*) is the relinquishment of a substance while designating a deity.

Regarding the specification of the *āghāra* oblation, since the locus is indicated here by the words "in this fire," the deity should be understood as that which is indicated by the wording of the mantra (*mantravarṇika*).

In those mantras where no specific mark (*liṅga*) of a particular deity is seen—as, for example, in "Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against the gods" (*devakṛtasyainaso 'vayajanam asi*) and so forth—the ritualists (*yājñikāḥ*) hold that Prajāpati is the deity.
Alternatively, it means that whichever deity is seen elsewhere to possess the status of a deity, that one is connected here as well.
And likewise, the authors of the *Nirukta* also state: "Or rather, that deity might be Kāma.

Even though the deity of one oblation is never the deity of another, nevertheless, the act of sacrificing (*yajati*) is heard [in the scripture], as are the materials and the mantras; since the deity is absent here, the form [of the injunction] must be explained as "he offers" (*juhoti*), meaning "he should offer with what follows.
And that is incorrect.
In that case, one should have said, "one should sprinkle [the water] in such a manner.
However, we maintain that in the formula, "Thou art the expiation for sin committed against the gods," the word *avayajana* itself means the act of expiation (*avayājana*);
therefore, that [act] is the deity.

And since the object denoted by a mantra must exist everywhere, there is no absence of the description of the deity in the mantra. Regarding the statement "with the verse beginning with *ud* [addressed] to Varuṇa," this refers to the verse *ud uttamaṃ varuṇapāśam asmat*; it is indicated by the opening word *ud*, which has Varuṇa as its deity.

The mention of *vāruṇī* is for the purpose of excluding other verses that begin with the word *ud*, such as *u tvā madantu stomāḥ*. Regarding the phrase "with a triplet having the waters as its deity" (*abdaivatenārcā*): here, *daivatam* is simply *devatā*; since the waters are the deity (*daivatam*) of this triplet, one should recite it with the verse beginning *āpo hi ṣṭhā*.
And for this reason, there is one oblation for each [verse] individually, like the word "each," and one collective oblation for the whole set.
The phrase "ghee in the fire" is to be supplied everywhere.
According to the rule.
The meaning is: "of whatever kind is the conduct of the learned.

And by that [conduct], since the sacrificial oblation (havis) exists, even though the specific procedure (itikartavyatā) has not been prescribed, he permits only this much: sweeping the ground, sprinkling water around the fire, looking at the oblation, the ladle-offering (sruvahoma), and so forth.
Because of the word "or" (vā), all these [acts] are indeed optional.
If a man who is not ill fails to give testimony regarding a debt or other matters within three fortnights,
he shall be liable for that entire debt and a fine of one-tenth from all sources.
Fifteen days and nights constitute a *pakṣa* (fortnight).
The collection of three *pakṣas* is *tripakṣam*.

Although the feminine gender would have applied here because it is a *dvigu* compound with a final member ending in the vowel *a*, there is a prohibition [of the feminine suffix] based on the observation of examples such as *pātra*.
If this were so, the term "tripakṣī" would not be applicable; however,
there is a change of gender in that Vedic usage,
and the ablative case is used for the object when a gerund (*lyap*) is elided.
The meaning is that if one fails to give testimony for up to three fortnights,
even if he is healthy and his body is unafflicted, he shall incur that debt;
and furthermore, a fine of ten percent (daśabandha).
A tenth part of that debt shall be imposed as a fine.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" in the phrase "in cases such as debts," the commencement of all legal proceedings is indicated.
The second mention of the word "debt" is for the purpose of illustration.

In whatever legal proceeding testimony has not been given for such a length of time, it is implied that the witnesses of the losing party are the ones responsible. The term *gada* (disease) is used to indicate by synecdoche any cause for a similar inability to appear;
therefore, in this context, one must also examine whether there have been family calamities, pressure from creditors, or other such obstacles.
The word *bandha* refers to a specific quantity and so forth; in the context of fines, it denotes ten *māṣas*.
The inclusion of the word "man" (*nara*) and the phrase "from all [sides]" (*sarvataḥ*) are for the purpose of completing the verse.
Others, however, say that the meaning of the statement "he shall incur that debt" is as follows:
He would incur the sin characterized by the non-payment of debt;
or, for one being defeated by the king, he should pay a tenth part of whatever fine is imposed—thus, having already been punished, he is punished again.
If, within seven days of the testimony being given,
a witness suffers from disease, fire, or the death of a kinsman, he shall be compelled to pay the debt and a fine.
Regarding the phrase "within seven days," because of the ablative case, the word "before" (*arvāk*) is to be supplied.
On any one of the seven days, if a witness is seen to suffer from illness or the like, he is proven a liar by divine means and must be made to pay according to the previously stated rule.
Illness that causes extreme suffering, fire that burns cattle or vehicles, and the death of a close relative such as a son or wife—these are the signs of his being a false witness.
But in matters where there are no witnesses, when two parties are disputing with one another,
if he cannot ascertain the truth in reality, he should cause it to be established even by means of an oath.

Those legal proceedings in which witnesses are non-existent are "without witnesses. In such cases, the king, not knowing the truth, should ascertain it— meaning he should discover it through both worldly inference and, as will be described, through divine inference consisting of an oath.
Although the root *labh* signifies "attainment," by implication it has the sense of "knowing," for there is no other way to attain the Truth.
Even if the reading were *na vindan*, it should be explained in exactly the same way.

"In cases lacking witnesses, one should cause [the matter] to be obtained by means of an oath"—this much is the conclusion of the injunctive statement; the word "mutually" (*mithaḥ*) is for the purpose of completing the verse.
"Mutually" means with one another.
Great seers and gods have taken oaths for the sake of a particular purpose;
even Vasiṣṭha swore an oath before King Paijavana.
This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) concerning the previously mentioned rule regarding oaths.
For the sake of their business—that is, for the purpose of deciding doubtful matters—the great seers, beginning with the Seven Seers (Saptarṣis), took oaths.
And in this regard, the narrative of the venerable Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana should be cited as an illustration.

When those lotuses had been stolen, the Seven Sages swore among themselves: "Whoever steals this lotus shall go to that destination of evildoers," and so forth. By the gods, headed by Indra—Indra, indeed, having been cursed by Ahalyā, made various oaths out of fear of the curse.

The separate mention of Vasiṣṭha is for the purpose of indicating his preeminence. The meaning is that he "caused [them] to swear. Since the specific sense is understood from the accompanying word (*upapada*) itself, the root *śap* (to swear) functions here in the general sense of "doing" or "performing."
Just as "yajñaṃ yajate" [means] "he performs a sacrifice" and "puṣṭaḥ" [means] "he has nourished his own prosperity," so too should "śepe" in "śapathaṃ śepe" be understood.
From the root *śap* in the sense of "obtaining" (*upalambhane*), the form "śepe" arises in the third person singular middle voice of the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
There was once a king named Paijavana.
At that time, having been reviled by Viśvāmitra, Aghāsura entered the sacrificial circle; his conduct agitated by desire and anger, he took an oath, saying, "I am a Yātudhāna.
Viśvāmitra said in the presence of that king, "By this very [act], his hundred sons have been devoured; for he is a Rākṣasa.
Thereupon, he (Aghāsura) replied:
"May I die this very day if I am a *rākṣasa*": such is an oath consisting of the wishing of an undesirable thing upon oneself.
When touching the head of one's son, wife, or others, this wishing of an undesirable thing should be understood as an oath.
A wise man should not take a false oath even for a trivial matter;
for by taking a false oath, one perishes both in this world and in the next.
This is the declaration of the consequences for a false oath.
"Vṛthā" means otherwise, that is to say, untruthful.

In that regard, the fault of a false oath depends on the type of substance being withheld, such as gold and so forth; while the fault is minor in the case of a small matter, there is certainly a greater fault in a more serious matter due to its gravity.
After death there is destruction and hell; in this world, great infamy;
but if it is known by other means of proof, there is punishment by the king.
In matters concerning women, at weddings, regarding the fodder for cows, as well as for fuel,
in assisting a Brāhmaṇa, and in taking an oath, there is no sin.

*Kāma* (desire) is a specific kind of pleasure produced by a particular contact of the sense organs; those women in whom such desire arises for a man—such as wives, courtesans, and so forth—are called *kāminīs*.

In that context, an oath taken for the sake of fulfilling a desire—such as "I desire no other woman, you are the mistress of my life"—is permissible. However, regarding an oath such as "Unite with me," "This must be given by you," or "I shall give it," there is indeed the fault of a false oath (*vṛthā-śapatha*).

This is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*) and not a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*). Therefore, there is no fault in the aforementioned form of oath when it is administered to that very woman alone; for if it were a locative of cause, there would be a fault in the cause itself—the seizure of another's property.
Consequently, the prescription of punishment—beginning with "ten times more than for desire" and so forth—is not appropriate.
Nevertheless, in a dispute arising immediately after the occasion [of the offense], the fault of taking a vain oath certainly exists;
thus it is in all cases.

In marriages— such as when one says, "You must not marry another woman, nor may another marry her"— this kind of falsehood for the sake of a friend or similar person regarding a marriage is not a fault; however,
it is not so in cases such as the concealment of caste.
Regarding fodder for cattle:
"I must take this for the sake of providing grass for the cows; there is no fault in me for taking it from another who is unrelated to them and who, while giving false testimony, swears an oath.
The same applies to firewood.
Providing assistance to Brahmins is an act of favor; since providing favor to all social classes is already permitted, what is the purpose of this specific statement?
Some say:
"An oath is permitted for a Brāhmaṇa, whereas for Śūdras and others, it is indeed a falsehood;
yet, because of the statement, 'For this [oath] is superior to truth,' this is not a falsehood."
Therefore, there is no prohibition in that case;
for this is a prohibition against a false oath.
This is a restorative rule (*pratiprasava-śāstra*) for that which was previously prohibited.
Therefore, there is no fault in cursing one who seeks to favor all social classes.
For what purpose, then, is this [curse] uttered?
It is said:
In that regard, protection from execution has been stated as applicable to all social classes (*varṇa*);
however, assistance (*abhyupapatti*) is for the Brāhmaṇa alone,
for that indeed occurs through the acquisition of wealth and the like.
And in all such cases involving actions related to others, the permission for an oath should be understood as applicable only when success through other means is impossible.
One should cause a Brahmin to swear by truth; a Kṣatriya, by his vehicle and weapons; a Vaiśya, by his cattle, grain, and gold; and a Śūdra, by all the heinous sins.

Now, if one were to cause another to perform an oath consisting of the act of proclamation—thinking, "If I were to do this, I would incur this undesirable consequence"—then he is said to be "swearing.
[One might say: "I swear by truth," meaning, "By truth and so forth, may this dharma of mine, which is based on truth and the like, become fruitless.
In this way, weapons as well as vehicles serve as instruments [of the oath].
If one swears an oath by these [objects], they shall not be fruitless.
A Vaiśya, having touched cows, seeds, and gold with his hand, should swear: "May these become fruitless for me," as before.
But a Śūdra is told to swear by all sins: "May the sins that are about to be described be mine."
One should cause him to carry fire, or immerse him in water;
or else, one should have him touch the heads of his sons and wife individually.

One should cause him to fetch fire with his hand shielded by an *aśvattha* leaf; the specific details regarding the distance between those two points being seven steps and so forth should be investigated thoroughly from other *smṛti* texts.
This very point is stated because of its well-established traditional transmission.
The meaning is that the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) should immerse him in water.
One should touch the heads of one's son and wife.
This means touching the head of the son or the wife with the hand, or even by means of speech through the performance of an oath, since an oath is of such a nature;
this is stated to be done separately for each individual.
He whom kindled fire does not burn, whom water does not cause to float,
and who does not quickly meet with misfortune— such a person should be known as pure in his oath.
This heated iron ball, when taken by one who is blameless, does not burn;
nor do the waters cause him to float upward;
and in the ordeal of the oath or the sacred water (kośa) and so forth, he does not meet with misfortune—that is, he does not suffer affliction.
"Fire is disease"—this has been stated here.
He is pure, clean, and faultless.
The limit is fourteen days, according to another Smṛti.
For in the past, when Vatsa was accused by his younger brother,
the fire— the witness of the world— did not burn even a single hair of his because of his truthfulness.
But how is it that fire will not burn and water will not drown?

Anticipating the objection that "the great elements do not deviate from their own nature because they are insentient," he confirms the meaning stated by means of an explanatory illustration (*arthavāda*). Even though this matter is to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) or is perceptible to the senses, one might think that swearing oaths and threats are merely intended to produce a fierce terror, like a magic trick devised by a rogue; thinking thus, he sets forth a Vedic example.
Practitioners become firm in their practice through the attainment of the goal by seeing what occurred previously.
There was a seer named Vatsa of the Kaṇva lineage.
He was accused and reviled by his younger half-brother, who said: "You are not a Brahmin; you are the son of a Śūdra woman."
He replied to him, "I enter the fire by truth if I am not a Brahmin.
When he had spoken thus and entered, the fire did not burn even a single hair of his.
How so?

If it is asked how fire knows truth by means of truth as its cause, he says in response: "The spy of the world. One who is hidden in nature and who knows what has been done and left undone by others is called a spy (*spaś*).
And that "spy" (cāra) is also known as "the vow" (praṇidhi).
For the Blessed One is Agni, who moves within all beings and is the knower of what has been done and what has not been done.

Accordingly, there is a usage in the *Chāndogya* and *Tāṇḍaka*: "The fire which is between the armies of the gods and the asuras"—having approached that fire, Gautama said, "May your honor move about here as our spy," and so forth.
Alternatively, even as an illustration of a specific case, the *Pañcaviṃśa-brāhmaṇa* should be cited: "Vatsa and Medhātithi were both Kaṇvas.
Medhātithi reviled Vatsa, saying, 'You are no Brāhmaṇa,' and so forth, ending with 'his hair did not even burn.
But surely even thieves are not burned?
Even virtuous people are seen being burned; so how can there be confidence in an oath? It is said in reply:
This established rule cannot be set aside by an observed deviation, because such deviation is merely occasional.
Indeed, such deviation is observed even in the case of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) such as perception; yet these are not thereby rendered non-authoritative.
If it is argued that those which possess deviation are not actually denotable by the term "perception" and so forth—
Because of the statement that "that which deviates is not perception, and that which is perception does not deviate," it can likewise be said here:
"That which deviates is not an oath; that which is an oath does not deviate."
What, then, is an oath?
It is that which lacks the deceptive power of paralyzing [the opponent], as determined by the mere performance of the ritual procedure and so forth.
Its opposite is a non-oath.
For such a person, there is no deviation [from the result].
Nevertheless, even in that case, the ripening of the fruit of previously performed karma occurs because it serves as the causal condition;
even one who has committed an offense is released by virtue of a more weighty unwholesome deed performed in the past.
One who has committed no offense is seized due to a fault from a previous birth;
for the causes that manifest the ripening of the fruits of karmas are indeed diverse.
Out of a thousand, only one is falsely accused.
But the general rule is that [an oath] is not false;
this is the same even in the case of the Putreṣṭi, Kārīrī, and other such rites.
Therefore, it should be understood that an oath is to be accepted as valid just like a witness.
For they too sometimes speak falsely;
this is not merely a display of fear.
Oaths uttered according to established custom are said to be grounded in truth.
In whatever marriage false testimony has been given, that very transaction shall be annulled; though performed, it shall be as if unperformed.
In whatever legal proceeding a case has been conducted by means of false witnesses, that proceeding must be set aside;
what has been done shall be as if undone.
Even if he has received the money, the creditor must be made to restore it, and any fine already collected must be relinquished.

It is said that when it is determined, "You have been defeated by mere words," the legal proceeding ceases; however, the distinction is that this applies even if the punishment has already been carried out to its conclusion. The repetition [of the phrase] is for the purpose of completing the verse.
Testimony is declared to be false due to greed, delusion, fear, friendship, lust, anger, as well as ignorance and childishness.
False testimony is that which is caused by greed and other such motives.
The mention of the subject matter is for the purpose of determining the specific nature of the punishment.
"Vitatha" means untrue.
In all instances, the fifth case ending has the sense of cause.
I shall now declare, in due order, the specific punishments for anyone who gives false testimony in any one of these cases.

For taking [something] out of greed, one should be fined a thousand; for out of delusion, the first *sāhasa* fine; for out of fear, two middle *sāhasa* fines; and for out of friendship, four times the first *sāhasa*.
The construction of the sentence should be as follows: "He who speaks falsely out of greed shall be fined one thousand [paṇas].
In this context, greed is the cause for one who, having taken wealth from another, speaks deceptively;
[the phrase] "out of delusion" refers to mental confusion.

One who speaks according to the facts and speaks of things as they have been seen might, at the time of questioning, speak otherwise due to some cause of mental agitation—either being deluded and failing to grasp the correct meaning of the question, or because of forgetfulness; this is said to be "due to delusion" (*moha*).
