Fear (*bhaya*) is terror. It is the apprehension: "If he should defeat me on account of my truthful speech, he might perhaps kill me by harming my kinsmen, wealth, or other interests."
The understanding that "one thousand" refers to a specific number is derived from another sentence, namely "of paṇas.
However, in the earlier passage— "the first *sāhasa* is two hundred and fifty paṇas," and so forth—
the term "two middle *sāhasas*" undergoes a grammatical modification (*vipariṇāma*).
The meaning is that it was previously four thousand;
that same meaning is expressed here through a varied mode of expression in accordance with the requirements of the meter.
Ten times more [sinful] than desire is the former [anger], but three times more than that is anger itself;
from ignorance there are two full hundreds, but from childishness there are exactly one hundred.
*Manmatha* means desire (*kāma*).
When women are disputing, if a person, desiring one of them, speaks falsely, he shall be fined two thousand five hundred [paṇas].
If it is due to anger, the fine is tripled; since the first *sāhasa* (fine) is the subject under discussion, that which follows it is the middle *sāhasa*.
Or, at the very end, from worldly consciousness; thus, the supreme [enemy] is indeed hatred, which is anger. "From ignorance" means:
If one should state something contrary to the facts due to error, but not at the time of the questioning,
the fine shall be two hundred [paṇas]. It is the demonstration itself that is contrary, not the verbal expression.
Childishness (*bāliśya*) is the state of being a child, the lack of legal capacity.

This punishment for childishness applies to one who has slightly departed from childhood but has not yet attained stability of intellect; for any other, however, there is simply the status of being incompetent as a witness.
The wise have declared these punishments for false testimony to be proclaimed for the sake of ensuring that dharma does not deviate and for the restraint of unrighteousness.
He shows that punishment serves both purposes in order to demonstrate its necessity for implementation.
Dharma is the established order rooted in the scriptures and traditional practice; its non-deviation is called non-cessation.
A righteous king, having punished the three social orders who give false testimony, should banish them; however, he should only exile a Brāhmaṇa.
For those who have committed an offense once, the former punishment applies.

For those who persist in it through repetition, after having been punished, there shall be banishment—expulsion from the kingdom—or death, as seen in the application of the *Arthaśāstra* and because the nature of the system of punishment is such.
However, a Brāhmaṇa one should only exile.

"Deprivation of clothing" (*vivāsana*) means the removal of clothes or the demolition of a house. The form [of the word] is derived from the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the sense of "he causes to be deprived of clothing" or "he causes to be deprived of a dwelling," with the elision of the suffix according to the rule *ṇāviṣṭavat*.
"The three castes" refers to the three beginning with the Kṣatriya, since a different punishment has been prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa.
Manu, the son of the Self-existent, has declared ten places for punishment;
in these three castes they may exist, but a Brāhmaṇa should depart unhurt.
The word *sthāna* is a synonym for *viṣaya* (object).
By these [specified] locations, he who has committed an offense is to be punished.

Since the infliction of a monetary fine is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa by means of the word [in the text], the instruction regarding his remaining unhurt is understood as being for the purpose of avoiding physical injury, even though the number ten is included within the category of wealth.
We, however, say that by the phrase "with his entire wealth intact," even the infliction of a fine on the property of a Brāhmaṇa is indeed prohibited.
Therefore, for one who has somehow committed an offense only once and is endowed with learning, good character, and noble birth, there is no punishment involving the seizure of wealth.

And so Gautama, referring to such a Brāhmaṇa, begins with the words, "Two in this world are firm in their vows," and continues with, "and he is to be exempted from [punishment] in six cases," and so forth.
The genitals, the belly, the tongue, the hands, and the feet as the fifth;
the eyes, the nose, the ears, wealth, and likewise the body.
The organ of procreation is the [limb] for the act of generation for both men and women.
This is merely a general enumeration; its specific application will be explained later.
Furthermore, in cases where no specific punishment has been prescribed, that person by whichever limb he committed the offense must be afflicted in that very same limb.
In that regard, sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached is the restraint of the genitals; theft is [restrained] by the cessation of food from the stomach and so forth;
and verbal and physical violence are [restrained] by the tongue and the hands.
Transgressing with the strength of his feet, he stepped over their feet; turning around, he looked confidently at the king's wives with his eyes;
and he smelled the fragrance of their ointments with his nose.
Hearing from behind a wall or a curtain a king deliberating in secret, one should report it to the ears [of the authorities]:
"A punishment well-known for wealth [is prescribed];
for the body, there is execution for a great sinner."
Having fully understood the consequences, as well as the place and time in their true nature,
and having considered both the capacity [of the offender] and the gravity of the offense, he should inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment.
This is the *mātṛkā-śloka* concerning offenses for which punishments have been stated or not yet stated;
the determination of punishment in all cases should be made by following its meaning.

In this context, "concomitance" (*anubandha*) refers either to repeated engagement [in the offense] or to the cause of such engagement—that is, that by which one is bound to or employed in that action.

Having fully understood that [the offense], one should examine the subsequent circumstances (*anubandha*): whether it was committed for the sake of sustaining oneself and one's family, or through preoccupation with religious duties (*dharmatantra*); or whether it was due to addiction to intoxicants, gambling, and the like; and likewise, whether it was done out of negligence, intentionally, at the instigation of another, or by one's own will.
One should also consider the location (*deśa*), such as a village, a forest, a house, water, a place of birth, or a place of delivery.
Time refers to night, day, and so forth, or to times of plenty, famine, childhood, youth, and so on.
Capacity refers to power and lack of power, or wealth and poverty.
Offense refers to any one of the eighteen grounds [of defeat].
Having examined all of this in its proper sequence, he should inflict punishment or act in such a way that the worldly order does not fall into ruin.
Unjust punishment in this world destroys one's reputation and ruins one's fame;
it also prevents access to heaven in the next life. Therefore, one should avoid it entirely.

Unjust punishment is punishment that is primarily characterized by unrighteousness; it is administered either by disregarding what was previously stated, or merely on the basis of the recitation of this treatise, or by the king’s own will, or through passion, hatred, and so forth. Such punishment destroys one's reputation and cuts short one's fame.
Fame (*yaśas*) is the renown of one's virtues within one's own country, while glory (*kīrti*) is [such renown] in another country.
Alternatively, fame is the reputation for merit during one's lifetime, whereas glory is [reputation] pertaining to future times.
Fame and glory consist of being endowed with faultless virtues.
Or another distinction may be inferred, since this is an explanatory passage (arthavāda).
It is "not conducive to heaven" because it acts as an obstacle to the attainment of heaven produced by other rituals.
The phrase "also in the next world" is for the purpose of completing the verse, since heaven belongs to the hereafter.
A king who punishes those who do not deserve punishment, and fails to punish those who do deserve it,
incurs great infamy and goes to hell.
In the preceding verse, there was a specific rule for determining the circumstances such as the motive and so forth;
by this [verse], however, the punishment of those who are innocent is prohibited, while its application to those who are guilty is enjoined.
This is intended to prevent the king from abandoning [the duty] out of favor, considering punishment merely as a means of livelihood.
One should first impose the punishment of verbal censure, followed by the punishment of "fie" (reproach).
Third is the punishment of fines, and after that, the punishment of corporal chastisement.
If one who possesses good qualities has committed even a slight offense for the first time, he should be rebuked with words such as, "You have not acted rightly; do not do so again.

If, while being thus disciplined, he does not desist, one may declare, "What fault is there in this? and then he should be censured with harsh words and insults, such as "Fie! Fie! and the like. If he still does not desist even after that, he should be punished with a fine according to the scriptures.
Disregarding even that, he should be punished for his overbearing power and so forth;
and the punishment of death consists of beating, mutilation of limbs, and the like, not necessarily execution itself.
As it is said:
"But when one is unable to restrain these [enemies] even by execution,
then one may employ all these four methods against them."

If killing is considered execution, what else could there be by which [the offender] can be restrained? And how can one restrain this evil? Preceded by such harsh words as these, both fines and execution should be combined against those who are incorrigible. Even when corporal punishment has been inflicted, if the person does not desist, then he has not been truly restrained; therefore, one should not simply release him, but rather that penalty of execution must be carried out.
Furthermore, this undertaking is for the purpose of the renewed application of fines and corporal punishment.

Since verbal punishment is mild, who would question it? And it is observed that one who has been punished with a fine may be subjected to corporal punishment again, as in the case of a finger amputation for a pickpocket.
I shall explain in their entirety those designations for copper, silver, and gold that are well-known on earth for the purpose of worldly transaction.
The designations such as *likṣā* and so forth for copper and other substances are well known in common worldly usage; what is the need for technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*) in the treatises?
In this regard, the usage of elders is like that of words such as "cow" (*go*).
Therefore, he says: "for the sake of worldly convention. The word *artha* signifies an object;
by this, the establishment of conventional usage is relied upon.
And since it is established through common usage, being equivalent to words such as "cow" and so forth,
what is the use of instruction from a treatise?
It is said in reply:
The instruction is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).
Since these names also apply to other measurable things such as iron, bronze, gold, and so forth, it is intended to exclude those.
Furthermore, since there is also variation regarding measurement in certain regions, it is intended to exclude that as well.
In some cases, it is restricted by way of a specific relationship;
thus, in one instance, the binding is with forty-eight māṣas, in another with sixty-four, and in another with one hundred and eight. All of this is so restricted.
And furthermore, the connection is made in this way:

"I shall declare those designations well-known on earth for the purpose of worldly transaction, so that the entire world may conduct its affairs by means of these alone; otherwise, even the established application of punishments and the like would not be possible."
That subtle particle of dust which is seen when the sun shines through a lattice opening is called the *trasareṇu*, the first of all measures.
Some do not recite this verse, because there is no disagreement regarding the *trasareṇu*.
That particle of dust which is seen when the sun has entered through the opening of a window-lattice is the *trasareṇu*.
The word *antara* is a synonym for "opening" (*vivara*).
First, [it concerns] those means of valid cognition.
Eight trasareṇus should be known as one *likṣā* by measure;
three of those are a *rājasarṣapa*, and three of those are a *gaurasarṣapa*.
In that context, the measurements have been accumulated;
furthermore, this word "līkṣā" does not refer to a tiny sweat-born insect.
Three of those *līkṣās* constitute one unit of measurement known as a *rājasarṣapa*.
It should be applied in this manner.
Consequently, those who argue that objects such as barley and so forth do not possess the dimensions as previously stated are refuted;
for there is no fixed dimension for objects such as barley.
How, then, is the meaning of the aforementioned measurement established?
And how shall I explain the measurement according to the designations already introduced?
Since a *trasareṇu* (a mote of dust) has a fixed measurement, all of this must be determined by means of it.

Furthermore, skilled people are able to combine *trasareṇu* particles; thus, this is not an instruction on a matter that cannot be undertaken. This [calculation] remains uncontradicted as a traditional recollection (*smṛti*) of the number of goldsmiths' measures.
Therefore, the object itself must be determined with precision and in its entirety.
Six mustard seeds make one medium-sized barley grain; three barley grains make one *kṛṣṇala*;
five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*; and sixteen of those make one *suvarṇa*.

The word "middle" (*madhyama*) serves as a cause for non-confusion when it refers to measurement; for instance, [the term] "neither too small nor too large, but the size of a mustard seed" makes the use of the word "middle" meaningful. However, if it were intended to refer to a technical name (*saṃjñā*), there would be no purpose served by the word "middle," since the word "barley" (*yava*) itself functions as the name.
That [objection] is incorrect.
This composition is not one in which the purpose is stated for every individual section;
it is a work in verse.
In such a case, even though the meaning is already connected [to the context], something is said here in accordance with the requirements of the meter.
And it possesses a logical connection;
for an expression lacking such connection is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it contradicts the meaning of the sentence, nor is one that expresses what has already been understood.

The specific measure called a *yava* is "intermediate" because it is situated between the beginning and the end, namely the various measures starting from a hundred *trasareṇus* and so forth. It is "five-kr̥ṣṇala" (*pañcakr̥ṣṇalika*) because five *kr̥ṣṇalas* are contained within it;
therefore, the suffix *ṭhan* (which becomes *-ika*) should be applied according to the rule *ata iniṭhanau*.
In the reading *pañcakṛṣṇalakaḥ*, it is a bahuvrīhi compound ending in the suffix *kap*;
sixteen of those *kṛṣṇalas* constitute one *suvarṇa*.
Four *suvarṇas* make one *pala*, and ten *palas* make one *dharaṇa*.
Two *kṛṣṇalas* weighed together are to be known as one *rūpyamāṣaka*.
"Palam" is the indication of the name;
"gold" is the named object;
"four" is the qualifier.
"Dharaṇa" is the designation; "ten palas" is the designated object. "Two kṛṣṇalas" is the designation.
They consider "rūpyamāṣaka" to be a collective designation. But surely, in the explanation of the māṣaka as a unit of silver, he asserts that two *kṛṣṇalas* are to be understood;
and from that, there is uncertainty.
If the two balance-strings are held equally balanced and devoid of any excess weight,
it serves the same purpose as the term "middle" (*madhya*); for, by being held in an even state, there is no uncertainty regarding the measurement.
Sixteen of those silver *dharaṇas* constitute one *purāṇa*;
furthermore, a copper *kārṣika* coin weighing one *karṣa* is to be known as a *kārṣāpaṇa* or a *paṇa*.
Sixteen silver māṣakas constitute one *dharaṇa* of silver;
"purāṇa" is another name for it.
Both "kārṣāpaṇa" and "paṇa" are two names for a copper *karṣa*.

And the word *karṣa*, whose meaning is well-established in common worldly usage, is understood here [in its conventional sense]; it is not defined [technically] like the *kṛṣṇala* and other such terms by means of a statement of non-deviation from reality.
Ten *dharaṇas* should be known as one *śatamāna* of silver;
a *niṣka* should be understood by its measure as consisting of four *sauvarṇikas*.
*Śatamāna* is the designation for ten *dharaṇas*.
Since the word *rajata* (silver) is also used to denote gold,
this designation applies to both silver and gold.
The measurement of gold, however, should be determined from another treatise;
and accordingly, he will specify later that "the silver [coin] is a śatamāna."
Two hundred and fifty paṇas are declared to be the first amercement;
five hundred should be known as the middle, and one thousand as the highest.
In the phrase "middling and highest," the term *sāhasa* (violence/fine for violence) must be supplied.
Although the words "middling" and "highest" appear here alone, they are seen in other legal texts [in the context of] "the highest punishment by these two.
There, by virtue of established scriptural usage and association, *sāhasa* is understood.
The members [of the syllogism] are clear.
When a debt that is admitted is due for payment, one deserves a fine of five percent;
if it is denied, the fine is double that—this is the ordinance of Manu.
When one who has been brought before the royal court admits, in accordance with the law, that a debt is indeed due and says, "I truly owe this to him," he deserves a fine of five percent;
the remainder [of the claim] is fined at the twentieth part by virtue of this admission.
Why is this so?
"Why was the creditor not satisfied right there outside, instead of being sent to my presence?"—for this transgression of the rule, he deserves punishment.
But he who commits another offense by denying the debt, saying "I do not owe him anything," and is proven by those witnesses, must pay double that amount;
that is to say, double the five percent, which makes ten percent.
This is the instruction of Manu Prajāpati; that is to say, the established rule or policy beginning from the time of creation.
Others, however, interpret the word "that" as referring specifically to what is to be given;
thus, whatever is to be given to him, double that amount [is to be paid].
Therefore, this forms a single syntactical unit with the phrase "as long as the debt exists";
otherwise, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Since no specific scope is indicated, if they were to share a single subject matter, an option (*vikalpa*) would result.
And that is not logical, because doubling [the number] results in an excessive abundance.

Even in the absence of an explicit mention, its referent must be shown; since the "group of five" (pañcaka) is proximate to it, it is logically appropriate to understand it as a reflection upon that very same [number].
A moneylender may employ the rate of interest prescribed by Vasiṣṭha for the increase of wealth;
he may take one-eightieth part of a hundred per month.
"Eighty" is the specification of the rule;
"ordained by Vasiṣṭha," and so forth, is the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
Because Vasiṣṭha—the venerable one who knows the three periods of time and is free from defects such as greed—took that interest, it is therefore praiseworthy.
Through that [interest], the wealth increases, and there is no fault of greed.
He should release it; he should employ it.
When the wealth is [lent], he should specify that interest to the debtor at the time of the loaning of the wealth.
This same limit for interest applies to all goods, such as clothing, grain, gold, and so forth.
Regarding items that are counted or measured, such as liquids where the interest is eightfold, we shall explain that these are exceptions to the rule of doubling [the principal].
Remembering the dharma of the virtuous, one may take two per cent interest;
for by taking two per cent, one does not become a sinner regarding wealth.
Two percent interest is given on this hundred;
thus it is "two per hundred. This rule of two per hundred applies to one who has many dependents and was previously a sacrificer, and it persists for a month.

The passage beginning with "of the good" (satām) is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) here. As for the phrase "the dharma of the good," this [grammatical] increase (vṛddhi) is also the dharma of the virtuous;
by means of this, their status as virtuous persons is not lost.
He is not said to be excessively intent on wealth.

This is shown by the statement: "he does not become a sinner regarding wealth. Sin regarding wealth (*arthakilbiṣa*) consists in the wrongful appropriation of another's property; one who possesses that is a "sinner regarding wealth" (*arthakilbiṣī*).
One may take interest at the rate of two, three, four, five,
or ten percent per month, according to the order of the social classes.
From the four castes in the order beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, four [types of] portions— starting from two— are permitted to be accepted respectively;
they must be equal,
neither less by a quarter nor more by a half.

The inclusion of the word "entire" (*samagra*) is for the purpose of removing the doubt that even when there is an excess over that amount, the designation of "two-fold," "two and a quarter," or "two and a half" would not cease; it functions just as [the word "entire"] precludes the application of another name despite a difference in quantity.
This is also an alternative method for one who cannot subsist by the previous rule.

Or rather, this rule applies where one's wealth is small for a great religious purpose and the recipients are not exceedingly virtuous, according to the principle: "those who take wealth from the wicked... and so forth.
"Samām" is an alternative reading;
this interest is [to be paid] for the duration of one year and not beyond that, otherwise, due to its magnitude, it would result in doubling [the principal].
But one shall not obtain interest on a secured loan if it is used for the debtor's benefit;
nor, due to the lapse of time, can there be a transfer or sale of the pledge.
The application [of a pledge] is manifold, being taken either as a deposit or otherwise. A pledge (*ādhi*) is also of two kinds: to be guarded (*gopya*) and to be used (*bhogya*).
The one to be used is also of two kinds: that whose use is determined by agreement, or that which is used in its own form.
A pledge (ādhi) is a milch cow or concealed gold and the like;
with reference to such a pledge that is to be used, this is stated, and not regarding a pledge "with profit" (sopakāra).
Various things that provide benefit include a milch cow, fields, gardens, and so forth.
While such property is being used—interest arising from a loan (*kausīdī*), as just mentioned, shall not be obtained;
however, one who uses a pledge (*ādhi*) shall not receive any other interest.

In the case of a pledge (ādhi) that is secret, even when it has doubled in value due to long-term retention over time, there is neither relinquishment (nisarga) nor sale if the debtor refuses to redeem it;
"relinquishment" here refers to its transfer according to the prescribed rule.
Furthermore, if it has been transferred elsewhere, it continues to accrue interest even after it has doubled.
Likewise, he will recite later the words "once brought back";
sale is well known,
and that too must not be performed.
What, then, should be done in this situation?
One should enjoy the pledge for as long as the debt has doubled;
after that—
The pledge shall be released when the money arising from it has entered [the creditor's possession] and become double its original amount;
such is the case for a pledge for use (*bhogya*).
However, a pledge for use where the profit is exhausted remains in place until the pledgor returns.

But if a creditor somehow falls into poverty and has only that much wealth remaining, he may wait for some time and then, having informed the king, sell the pledge; having taken for himself twice as much of his own wealth as was produced from the sale, he should hand over the remainder into the hands of a neutral intermediary for the sake of the debtor. [Objection: Is it not the case that "the pledge shall be forfeited when the debt has doubled, if he does not release it"?
Thus it is recited.
We shall explain this later.
Because it is subject to destruction, there is no loss of ownership for the former owner, nor does the transferor acquire ownership.
And if there were neither gift nor sale, what kind of ownership could be said to belong to him?
Therefore, by the force of the prohibition, the statement regarding "loss" is explained as being for the purpose of permitting the enjoyment of that which was prohibited from being enjoyed;
or else, it refers to objects such as clothing.
For when that [wealth] is being consumed, it indeed perishes;
its status as an object of enjoyment cannot exist in the same way as that of fields and the like, which remain without falling away from their essential nature.
Therefore, this must be explained according to the established rule of the Smṛti.
In this context, "destruction" and "renunciation" are used in a figurative sense,
whereas the prohibition of "sale" is used in its primary sense;
for that [prohibition] cannot be understood as being figurative.
Introducing this very point, another Smṛti text states: "The two [pledges] would not be dependent on sale.
Therefore, in this context, *nisarga* (alienation) means pledging elsewhere, because of its association with "sale"; for the two are similar in certain respects.
A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it shall forfeit the interest.
He should satisfy the owner with its value; otherwise, he becomes a thief of the pledge.
But was this not already stated previously in the words "but never on a pledge"?
True;
however, that case where the enjoyment is exactly equal to the interest constitutes the scope of the former rule.
But where there is great interest and only slight enjoyment—such as when one enjoys [the property] by force—the entire interest shall be forfeited.

Where land, cattle, or the like is pledged, and its enjoyment is not commensurate with the interest, and the debtor does not pay even the accumulated interest, nor has the principal doubled, then in such a case, some extraordinary means must be employed to determine the exact amount of interest due.
However, if clothing or similar items being enjoyed should perish, the debtor should satisfy the pledgor with their value.
The other [the debtor] also gains interest.
Therefore, if he does not give [the interest] otherwise, he becomes a thief of the pledge.
For whatever kind of pledge he has used, the same punishment that applies to the theft of that [item] shall be imposed upon him.
A thief is a robber;
others explain that when [a debt] is consumed by force, there is a loss of interest.
Or he may consume it for its value alone;
that is, for the price of the debtor, which is the gold representing the value.

This case concerns one who, while consuming, is told: "Do not destroy my security; do not consume it; I will release you after a few days," yet even when told this, he continues to consume it. That is the scope of this rule.
Both an open pledge (*ādhi*) and a sealed deposit (*upanidhi*) ought not to suffer the lapse of time;
if they remain for an excessively long duration, both shall be forfeited.
*Ādhi* has its meaning already explained.
*Upanidhi*, however, is a deposit placed within a garment and enjoyed out of friendship;
these two must not be kept for a long period of time.
What then? They must be released when the time for release has arrived.
The time for the release of a pledge is when the debt has doubled;
its transgression is the failure to release it even at that time.

Even in the case of a deposit (*upanidhi*), as long as there is no occasion for [the owner] to think, "This is mine; I shall enjoy it," that is the time for its recovery. Any time longer than that is "excessive time" (*kālātyaya*).
They do not deserve that; the meaning is that it should not be done.
He states the reason: "Those two would become unenforceable.
For it is established that if those two remain for a long time without being reclaimed, they become unenforceable.
Therefore, one should strive to secure a pledge while the wealth has only doubled.

This is friendly advice; for even over a long period of time, there can be no forfeiture of either a pledge (*ādhi*) or a boundary (*sīman*), as the author will later state: "A pledge, a boundary, and the property of a minor.
Therefore, this is merely a restatement of that very point.
Others, however, maintain that this instruction refers to the subject of a pledge (*ādhi*).

When one, out of malice, lets time pass while the debt has doubled, that money—though it would have reached a threefold profit—does not increase further; nor does he now have the right to pledge or sell it elsewhere. Out of such envy, thinking "may he not obtain interest here," it is said in that case: "the two [pledges] shall be forfeited. By relinquishing them with this intention, his ownership ceases.
However, for one who somehow does not release [the slave] due to a lack of wealth, there can be neither abandonment nor sale.

Alternatively, another meaning is that he "overlooks" [the matter] by way of his mouth; it is said with the suspicion that [the slave] has already passed into the hands of another: "The two [abandonment and sale] would be subject to forfeiture."
When used with mutual affection, these never perish:
a milch cow, a camel, a draft horse, and any animal being tamed for work.
*Saṃprīti* is simply *prīti* (affection).
By means of that [affection] acting as the cause, cows and other such things are enjoyed; they do not perish.

Perishing consists in the loss of the previous owner's connection and the arising of ownership for the enjoyer; that perishing does not occur in the case of cows and other such things being enjoyed through affection.
But surely, there is no deprivation by enjoyment in the case of any *upanidhi* at all;
for it will be stated that "deposits and *upanidhis*, as well as women [are not lost by enjoyment].
What, then, is the distinction regarding cows and other such items?
It is said:

where there has been possession for ten years and there is no destruction of the thing's essential nature, a prohibition regarding deposits applies to the seizure that would otherwise be obtained by virtue of the general statement "whatever [property].

However, one might raise the objection that since items such as [the contents of] a box (*denu*) and so forth do not even possess the status of a deposit, they cannot be the subject of this prohibition.

For the word "cow" (dhenu) is based on the act of conception; if it were to become a cow (*dhenu*) in the following year, that is, if she were to conceive after being covered by a bull, she would attain the status of a "cow," and then one might suspect: "This belongs to him alone, not to Devadatta.
Since a four-year-old heifer (*praṣṭhauhī*) is not to be used [for pleasure], and a pledge (*upanidhi*) is to be enjoyed with affection;
for it is observed that what is to be enjoyed by oneself is returned after having been protected and then used again.
Furthermore, this is not the nature of a pledge (*upanidhi*), for a pledge is something to be enjoyed;
since that which is to be enjoyed does not exist [in this case], what kind of quality could constitute its status as a pledge?
And this is a prohibition regarding deposit (*upanidhi*);
therefore, since that [specific] prohibition does not apply because the nature of a deposit has been transcended, another effort [of a rule] has been stated.
For camels and other such animals as well, when they are used for ten years, they undergo a change of state.
Therefore, even in that case, there is no status as a pledge (*upanidhi*).
Some consider the word "vahant" (carrying) to be an epithet of the horse;
this rule does not apply to a bull.
Others, however, consider it to mean a donkey or a mule;
"damya" refers to a young ox,
which is employed for the purpose of being yoked as a beast of burden.
Others, however, consider the negation to have the sense of an alternative:
apart from this [case], there is occasional misappropriation of other deposits;
therefore, in the case of clothing and so forth that is used out of affection, as well as that which has been completely worn out, there is indeed misappropriation.

For when a garment has been taken out of affection and subsequently worn out, the owner does not disregard it; rather, he says, "There is still an opportunity: give me back the garment! You have destroyed it; therefore, settle the matter with its equivalent value."
Whatever property an owner observes being enjoyed by others for ten years while remaining silent in its presence, he does not deserve to recover it.
The phrase "whatever is being enjoyed" is to be construed with the term "established.
Although there is a general reference due to the proximity of the word "wealth-owner" (*dhanī*), it is understood here as the neglect of wealth that is currently being enjoyed.
The expression "whatever" includes everything, such as female and male slaves, raw materials, household utensils, and so forth.
For that [property] is not universally recognized in the world as "wealth"; rather, it is well known that only cows, land, gold, and the like constitute highly valuable wealth.
Therefore, this is the meaning of the sentence here:

whatever property is being enjoyed by another, if the owner of the wealth—the master of the property—looks on for ten years, says nothing, does not bring the matter before the king, and does not say to the enjoyer in the presence of his family, "This is mine; why is it being enjoyed by you yourself?", then after those ten years, he is not entitled to recover or claim it.
The meaning is that his ownership ceases.
By the term "perception," mere knowability is expressed, not necessarily direct perception;
we shall explain this under the word "in the presence of" (*saṃnidhau*).
By others, not by kinsmen or relatives; and so another Smṛti states: "Except for kinsmen and relatives," and likewise:
"That which is eaten by relatives, kinsmen, and those of the same caste."
That enjoyment does not cease; one should conceive of that enjoyment as being elsewhere.
That is incorrect;
for if that were the case, there would be no fixed determination as to who are kinsmen and who are relatives.
If one were to grasp merely the relationship [of ownership], there would be nothing to be excluded.
Therefore, it is only he by whom another's property is enjoyed who becomes such [a wrongdoer].
However, that being the case, the word "another" (para) would be a mere restatement and thus devoid of purpose, for there is no designation of "another" with respect to anything at all.
That [objection] is refuted by the examples of "husband and wife" or "father and son.
For in those cases, there is indeed a designation [of identity] even with respect to the self: "She, the wife, is indeed half of one's own self," and "The son is indeed called one's own self.
Therefore, for husband and wife, or father and son, the presence or absence of enjoyment is not the cause [for their being considered a single entity].
Even for those whose property has been divided, when the time for enjoyment arrives, non-enjoyment is indeed an obstacle [to ownership].
Furthermore, regarding the wife’s separate property (strīdhana) that was taken from the husband, there is no lack of proof of the husband’s enjoyment if it is secured by a pledge;
for she is entirely dependent on him.
There is no distinction between the two;
even her property (strīdhana) must be protected by him alone.
Furthermore, it is recited [in the legal texts]: "Except for the property of the king, of women, and of a Śrotriya."
Thus, by this, it is stated that there is a loss of ownership for the owner who remains indifferent.
The following verse is intended to show for whom that [possession] is possible;
it is a supplement to the statement "he does not deserve to obtain it," namely: "if he is not dull-witted and not a child.
If he is not dull-witted and not a child, and his property is enjoyed by another...
That [claim] is defeated by legal procedure; the possessor deserves that wealth.
A *jaḍa* is one who lacks comprehension;
a *pogaṇḍa* is a child.
One under sixteen years of age is called a *bāla*, while one [between sixteen and twenty] is called a *pogaṇḍa*.
And this is intended as an illustration of other causes for the incapacity to protect one's own property as well:

addiction to liquor and gambling, being afflicted by a chronic disease, being solely intent on asceticism and Vedic study, lack of skill in legal transactions, deficiency of the organ of speech, and deafness. When these causes of incapacity exist for someone, ownership over his property does not accrue to the enjoyer even after a very long time;
rather, it is enjoyed [by him] over that object.
The word "asya" (of this) refers to the creditor.
The *viṣaya* (territory) is Kaśmīra for the inhabitants of Kaśmīra, and Pañcāla for those of Pañcāla.
Even if the debtor and the creditor were to reside in the very same country, this legal procedure applies to one who is devoid of power.

Even in this interpretation, this is merely an elaboration (*prapañca*), because it has been explained as being for the purpose of demonstrating the inclusion of even those who are not idiots (*ajaḍāpogaṇḍa*).

Therefore, it should be understood that if one enjoys another's property for ten years, and no cause for neglect on the part of the owner—who is aware of it—is conceivable, then the enjoyer alone deserves that wealth; it belongs to him.
But surely, ownership cannot rightly arise from mere enjoyment.
Possession is logical only when ownership exists;
for if ownership were derived from possession alone, there would be a lack of stability regarding ownership.
Furthermore, this limit of ten years is not intended to apply to all types of property according to other legal codes (*smṛti*).
What then? [The rule is]: "For one who sees [the possession] but does not speak, there is the loss of land after twenty years.
Others, however, do not accept the forfeiture of land even by means of twenty years of possession, asserting that possession for three generations alone is authoritative.
Still others, however, do not at all admit ownership through possession that is devoid of a title of acquisition (*āgama*).
For thus they say:
"He who enjoys [property] that has not been acquired, even for many hundreds of years;
likewise..."
Where enjoyment is perceived but no scriptural authority is seen anywhere, there the scriptural authority is the cause, not the enjoyment; such is the established rule.
Those who maintain that possession by three generations is sufficient recite as follows:
"That which has been possessed for a very long time without a title by three preceding ancestors cannot be taken away, having come down through the succession of three generations."

This is its meaning: "tradition" (*āgama*) refers to gifts and so forth. In the absence of such tradition, what was enjoyed by the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather belongs to the fourth generation; it is not established merely by twenty years [of possession].
Regarding this, it has been stated elsewhere:
In the beginning, however, the cause is the gift; in the middle, possession accompanied by title;
but in the end, possession alone shall be the proof in regard to immovable property.
Success [in ownership] arises from possession for three generations, not from possession by the father and grandfather alone.
Even in this case, possession for twenty years is not a valid proof.
Others, however, maintain that possession—even if it lasts for a hundred years—is invalid if it is devoid of a legal title (āgama).
And so they have said:
"But he who enjoys property without title, even for many hundreds of years,
the lord of the earth should punish that sinner with the punishment due to a thief."
But he who asserts possession alone and never the title—there, the title is the cause, not the possession; such is the settled rule.

As for the phrase "many hundreds of years," that refers to the possessor himself and states his own enjoyment as the reason for the long duration; the meaning is that it cannot be established without the enjoyment of his father and grandfather.
But how can one person have enjoyment for many hundreds of years?
This is not a fault.
Words such as "hundred," "thousand," and so forth, which denote plurality, are intended to express a long duration of time.
For example: "Man indeed has a lifespan of a hundred years, a hundredfold vigor, and a hundredfold sensory power.
What is meant by this is that ownership is not established for the first possessor merely through possession, even if that possession exceeds twenty years.

The meaning is that [the rule] would not even apply to a son; thus it remains exactly as it was heard [in the text]. For indeed, the memory of a tradition (āgama) over many hundreds of years is impossible.
Consequently, ancient temples of the gods, Brahmin monasteries, and villages would be seized by kings.
Even a written edict, being inscribed by a scribe appointed by the king, would not be recognized as such in ancient times;
furthermore, it might even be suspected of being a forged document.

Therefore, long-standing possession serves as a cause that indicates the possibility of acquisition through gift and other means for the purpose of establishing ownership, but it is not the actual creator of ownership itself.
For this very reason, possession is enumerated among the means of proof:
"Written documents, witnesses, and possession— these are remembered as the threefold means of proof."
But [this does not apply] to the seven sources of wealth (*vittāgama*) being included among the causes of ownership, nor in cases such as "learning, heroism, austerity, and a maiden," and so forth.
Alternatively, this rule regarding "without title" (*anāgama*) and so on refers to those cases where force (*bala*) and the like are suspected to be the cause of enjoyment;
this has been recited in this very section.
"What is deposited, what is taken away, what is placed down, what is obtained by force, what is begged, and what is enjoyed in the owner's absence—these six [cases] are without legal title.
Now, one might object: "Is this point not already established by the rule concerning pledges (*ādhi*) and boundaries (*sīmā*)?"
No; the meaning is simply that he eats for as long as the aforementioned period lasts for three generations.
However, this [present rule] is undertaken to exclude [eating] even beyond that time.
Thus, there is the statement: "for many hundreds of years."
*Anvāhita* is that which is openly entrusted; otherwise, it refers to when one thing is shown and another is secretly substituted.
*Hṛta* means stolen at night by means of breaking through walls, deceit, and so forth.
*Balāvaṣṭabdha* means seized by force; "by force" (*prasahya*) is the understood sense.
The rest is well known.
If possession for three generations is the means of proof, then what is the meaning of the rule: "There is loss of land for one who sees [the taking] and does not speak for twenty years"?
Some say:

If, while one has been enjoying [the property] for such a length of time, there exists a defect in the document—such as it being produced by a powerful person or a partisan, or due to the loss of sequence or letters caused by negligence—the debtor is declared [guilty] by these two means: falsehood and improper conduct.
Even a document of doubtful form is determined [as authentic] by this duration of enjoyment.
Others, however, say:
In a case where one person offers that very same plot of land as a pledge to one party, and that same plot to another,
and while for the first it is the initial period of validity and for the second it is the subsequent period,
there— despite the initial nature of the validity— the twenty-year possession of the latter is stronger.
And this is incorrect, because of the statement: "He by whom the pledge has been accepted, for him it is established [as a debt] through the acceptance of the deposit.
Furthermore, the acceptance of land is simply the desire for its enjoyment; therefore, in such a case, the establishment of the pledge occurs even in a short time.
It is with this very intention that it was said:
"Even when a document exists and witnesses are living,
that which is not enjoyed— especially in the case of immovable property— is not secure.

The use of the word "especially" (*viśeṣa*) indicates that there is no failure of proof in the case of cattle, horses, and the like, even if they are not being enjoyed, because they are not necessarily objects of enjoyment [in the same way as land].
For instance, a cow might not conceive; what kind of enjoyment (*bhoga*) could she have then?
Land, however, always yields fruit; thus, without the acquisition of enjoyment, the establishment of ownership (*bandhatva*) is not achieved.

Even in that case, if one who has somehow neglected or abandoned [the land] should have it taken over by a second acquirer through proximity or other means, or if it is not taken over by the other [original owner] due to distance or preoccupation with other affairs—lacking the aforementioned proof—then it is considered that ownership is not established by that much alone.

But when one who has indeed taken a pledge is immediately thereafter ordained as a monk and contracts a severe illness, or when he has no one else authorized for the protection of the property and so forth, then even if he returns after a long time, he recovers his property—even if it has been appropriated by another—provided that at the time [of appropriation] there was no fixed period for its recovery.
Others, however, say that this [rule] is intended to mean: "The redistribution of brothers who have divided their inheritance unequally is prescribed for the purpose of equalization;
that [redistribution] does not take place after twenty years. Thus they interpret this [text].
If the fruit were merely this much, it would have been appropriate to state it right there;
however, the general statement, by way of elevating the context, makes known that its scope extends to other subjects as well.
Others, however, say that where land that had become fallow has been brought under cultivation, the enjoyment of that specific plot of land is what is intended.
If they say, "The master has been restrained for so many years by means of boundary-markers and field-fences, and both the land and that territory [belong to him]," then those venerable ones reply:

"In this world, if two persons occupy the same place, possess equal capacity, share the same nature, have equal wealth, pursue identical purposes, and are not related to one another, then for the one who neglects the other's enjoyment of property for such a long duration while standing by and watching, there is no ownership whatsoever over immovable things;
rather, [ownership is lost] entirely due to the contradiction posed by possession for three generations."
For these two Smṛtis are contradictory;
they do not admit of any interpretation by which ownership both exists and does not exist at the same time.
Therefore, this [following] arrangement is logical.

Although there are many grounds for the acquisition of ownership, such as gift, sale, or mortgage, nevertheless, when no specific ground is perceived, it is proper to accept the nature of a mortgage in the case of possession for twenty years in the matter just mentioned;
for ownership is both unstable and subject to enjoyment,
and when the substance is diminished, it may be recovered from that [mortgage].
Consequently, possession by three generations establishes ownership for everyone;
as for the possibility of gift or sale, that will apply only to the duration of one year.
There is nothing inconsistent in possession lasting twenty years.

Where both parties have proceeded by the force of possession alone, without any traditional title (*āgama*), there the prior possession, even if long-standing, is sublated by a present possession of twenty years that is free from defects.
It is thus stated that possession for a certain period acquired through legal proceedings (*daṇḍapūrvikā*) sublates possession that has descended through three generations;
that [prior possession] is "sublated" by means of legal process.
The inclusion of the term "transaction" (*vyavahāra*) is for the purpose of excluding [mere] possession (*dharma*).
Therefore, if one somehow knows [the deposit], then he would lose the case.

However, even then, there is no proof for this person's claim of having used the deposit; thus, those who transact [on his behalf] would lose, because that is not the rule, and one is defeated by such possession alone. Let this matter rest.
A mortgage, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, an open deposit, women, royal property, and the property of one learned in the Vedas do not perish through adverse possession.

That which is placed [as security] is called *ādhi*; it refers to a pledged substance such as cattle, land, gold, and so forth, as well as the money that is taken from a creditor. *Upanidhi* is described by another treatise as a concealed deposit (*antarhito nyāsaḥ*), which is deposited with its form not revealed, covered by cloth or other items bearing marks.
However, that which is to be enjoyed out of affection is appropriately denoted by the term *upanidhi*, since it is already included by the mention of *nikṣepa* (deposit).
A boundary (*sīmā*) is the demarcation of villages and the like;
for because it is common to many, negligence regarding it is possible.

In the case of houses and the like, however, those consisting of walls, moats, and so forth, measuring two or three cubits in size, are common to both [parties]; they may be utilized by either one in some way.
Because they are of small value, one might even neglect them for some time;
yet, even in such cases, one considers the possibility of a cause for the departure of the owner, such as the giving away of the property or other circumstances.
Therefore, his sons or grandsons, because the boundary has been clearly indicated by secret marks and the like, certainly do take it away.

The mention of "the property of a minor" is for the sake of illustration, as it was stated that the term *pogaṇḍa* (minor) had already been shown [to apply here]. "Women" refers to female slaves or wives.
The seizure of property other than wealth has not been mentioned; for it was stated that "the [limit] for wealth is ten years.
But surely there is no wealth here;
this phrase "whatever it may be" is a reference to material objects in general.
It is not so;

for by virtue of the connection [with the word "wealth"], the general term "anything whatsoever" (yatkiṃcit) is understood to have wealth as its object in the phrase "one who possesses wealth" (dhanī).
Who says that women are not wealth?
The word *dhana* (wealth) is applied to a substance that can be so employed.
Now, from this very context of a woman’s property (*strīdhana*), there is an indication of ownership in general;
for by the analogy of "wealth," even men are indeed acquired as slaves through enjoyment.
"Royal property" refers to the wealth of kings, who are the lords of the land.

For they, because of their great wealth, seek out treasures of noble lineage; yet, by means of various secret methods employed by officials, they are brought to ruin, even while looking down upon those who are less than themselves.
The property of a *śrotriya* refers to the seizure of the wealth of a *śrotriya*.
The foolish man who enjoys a pledge without the permission of the owner must pay half the interest as compensation for that enjoyment.
It has been stated: "A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it shall forfeit the interest.
For this refers to the seizure of the entire [pledge].
In that case, when its use is forbidden, one who uses the pledge by force shall forfeit the interest; he loses the interest in its entirety.
Prohibition applies when permission has not been granted.

When an object of enjoyment is being used in secret, the pledge does not perish; in that case, this verse states that for items such as ornaments made of silver or gold, there is a forfeiture of half the interest.

However, regarding new and highly valuable items such as ornaments or clothing that are worn out, it is explained by the great commentators that not only is the interest lost, but the principal itself is forfeited and enters [the creditor's possession] after the debtor has been pressed.

But Yājñavalkya has explained it as follows: where both the master and the subordinate (adhyadhīna) are transacting, and a pledge has been given by the subordinate and witnessed by the master; and there, on a certain occasion, the debtor asks the subordinate, "I have a need for this pledge"; and having been authorized by him according to the logic of a deposit (upanidhi), he uses it at another time; if the master, seeing him using it, [is aware that] he has exhausted the pledge authorized by him—in such a case, there is the abandonment of half the interest. That is incorrect.
Since the conventional usage between master and servant is mutually dependent,
when one of them has been authorized in each respective case, this [transaction] is employed according to dharma as being authorized.
In such a context, ownership constitutes the meaning of the word "master."
Otherwise, he who grants bondage must necessarily be endowed with ownership;
however, one who is under another's authority is not an owner.
If this is so, then [the master] would be a thief.
Therefore, there is a superimposition of ownership;
or rather, since the utilization [of the body] is dependent on another, the conventional usage of "ownership" occurs because of permission from that other, as in the case of Brahmadatta.
Thus, the meaning remains exactly as stated before.
The inclusion of the word *svāmin* is for the purpose of completing the meter.
In the phrase "the unwise man enjoys" (*bhuṅkte 'vicakṣaṇaḥ*), the vowel *a* should be understood as being joined [to the following consonant] according to the rules of *saṃhitā*.
For he who possesses the notion, "I certainly have growth; there is an additional profit in the enjoyment of material things," he is the unwise man.
For the established rule is not something to be discarded by worldly treatises, such that both profit and enjoyment would constitute an increase.
Therefore, that increase must be enjoyed;
"expiation" (niṣkṛti) means supreme purification, which is to say, a restrictive regulation.
Others, however, maintain that this prohibition applies even when the debt has doubled but the pledge is not being released, asserting that his offense is indeed slight;
first of all, they must state the scope of Yājñavalkya’s statement: "the pledge shall perish."
Interest on a loan, once stipulated, shall not exceed double the principal;
for grain, fruit, wool, and beasts of burden, it shall not exceed five times the original amount.
*Lusīda* (interest) is the investment of wealth for the sake of profit; therein lies the interest (*vṛddhi*).
Alternatively, *kusīda* is the very wealth belonging to the lender that is being employed [for profit].
When wealth is given with the thought, "Having given my own small amount, I shall receive more," that is *kusīda*.
In that regard, interest does not exceed the doubling [of the principal].
The creditor who has lent money for the sake of interest may receive from the debtor only so much as until the principal has become twofold.
Is it not the case that a doubling of interest is prescribed by scripture?
[If so,] together with the principal, the total would amount to threefold.
It is not so.
A quality (guṇa) is said to be a constituent part (avayava); it necessarily depends upon a whole (avayavin), and in this context, that whole is wealth (dhana).
Therefore, it is stated that the capital which is the object of the transaction becomes doubled by this method.
Accordingly, another Smṛti states: "In a long-term loan, there is doubling of the principal; the pledge must be released when the capital has become doubled through the profits accruing from it.
Furthermore, interest is of various forms.
When kārṣāpaṇas are employed [as capital], it is the kārṣāpaṇa itself that increases;
in some cases,
it is offspring— meaning the offspring of women or cattle.
In some cases, there is interest on the use of objects such as cattle or land;
regarding this, some say that the doubling [of the debt] applies specifically to interest of the same kind (*sarūpavṛddhi*),
for in that case, the doubling of the interest is understood in its primary sense.
It is not understood whether this doubling refers to number, or to size, or to weight;

thus, there is uncertainty as to which it might be. For indeed, a high value based on the price of animals is clearly observed in the case of elephants, horses, and so forth, in transactions involving purchase and sale.
For those of great magnitude are indeed of great value.
But is it not the case that there is indeed similarity within a continuum? The continuum of a cow is indeed a cow.
In that case, the presentation of these distinctions—namely, "growth," "similarity," and "continuity"—is not tenable.
It is said in reply:
similarity does not arise merely from being of the same kind, but rather from the equality of age, size, and so forth.
Therefore, the presentation of a distinction is appropriate.
Even regarding the acquisition of enjoyment, how is a doubling understood?
Cows are employed in order to produce things that provide benefit.
Cows, land, and so forth, as well as milk, fodder, and so forth, are enjoyed according to their availability;
in that regard, what kind of doubling [of interest] could there be? Furthermore, such a practice is observed in some places.
Land is enjoyed for hundreds of years until the principal and interest are repaid;
and Yājñavalkya recites: "And a pledge is enjoyed as long as it has not been returned.
To this, it is replied:
When only "increase" is heard, how can it be restricted to the specific case of "doubling"?
For a general understanding arising from a direct scriptural statement (śruti) cannot be established in a specific instance without further evidence.
As for the objection that doubling is impossible in the case of continuous interest, let an effort be made to understand [the meaning].
Since increase occurs for those things born from that very source which has been determined by its root-price (*mūlamarṣa*),
it is possible to determine equality even regarding the enjoyment of land, such as barley and wheat, by means of the price of what is being harvested therefrom.
Furthermore, the word *guṇa* is also used in the sense of "benefit" (*upakāra*).
When this is the case, how is it understood who possesses equal merit and who is the benefactor?

If the interest arising from that [loan] is exactly equal to the value produced by the exchange of cattle or grain, then there is equality of merit, even in the absence of equality in quantity and so forth.
As for the common practice in some places, you yourself have already refuted it by employing the term "in some cases" (*kvacit*).
When a lapse in proper conduct occurs, the *smṛtis* (traditional law codes) serve a meaningful purpose as restrictive rules.
Just as one might say, "My eyes are beautiful" or "My feet are very delicate," the grammatical treatise is initiated on the principle that the plural number is used for many things.
However, when such a lack of connection [to actual usage] is observed, the rule is rejected.
This was stated for the purpose of establishing the correct usage of the priority and posteriority of subordinate elements (*upasarjana*) and prefixes (*upasarga*).
For no one, when they ought to use the form *prapacati*, uses *pacati prete*.

Furthermore, even the scriptural statement—"The pledge (*ādhi*) is enjoyed as long as it is not returned; until its double has entered [as interest] from the time of the loan"—can also be interpreted in this way.
And because it forms a syntactical unity with another *smṛti*, this alone is rightly determined; and this has been established in detail elsewhere as being "once deposited."
By the word "once" (*sakṛt*), that which is established or accepted is meant; that is to say, repeated application.
"Placing" (*ādhāna*) is said to mean "establishing" (*sthāpana*);
and by way of verbal determination, "ascertainment" (*nirūpaṇa*) is indeed the same as "establishing."
Furthermore, a renewal of the contract (*prayoga*) occurs when the doubled amount of money is being taken back.

When the creditor, for the sake of doubling the interest, and the debtor, intending to accomplish a great purpose with that wealth, perform a renewal of the instrument (*karaṇaparivṛtti*), declaring, "The previous interest, or this [new] interest, shall begin to accrue from today onwards," then even though it has already become double, it continues to increase further.

Or, if through the transfer to another person the debt becomes doubled and is useful to the creditor, then the debtor, being urged, hands over another man who is giving [the money], saying, "He will give this to you after so many days. In that case, the amount being given by his own hand increases again.
And this person is not a surety for the payment, but rather a depositor and the giver himself.
This, however, has been explained as not having been transferred to another person by an honest man.

Alternatively, even before doubling [of the debt], when the debtor hands over the pledge to another person once the coins have doubled along with the interest, the release of that pledge alone is lawful.
While the pledge remains prior to the doubling of the interest, from that day forward it begins to accrue doubling again.
When the creditor, with the debtor's permission, pledges that same collateral elsewhere and receives his own wealth, then [the original debt] continues to increase.
This is the transfer to another person.
When the debt has doubled in both cases, the debtor may, by whatever means possible, obtain permission from the creditor to take it from someone else;
or, if something else is taken from him, the borrower transfers it elsewhere because he is about to go to another country or due to some other business.
But the straightforward [author] does not desire an interest exceeding double the principal from that same debtor when the loan has not been renewed;
therefore he says: "When the debt has not passed to another person, there is a renewal of the transaction," and we shall explain the purpose of this later.

However, as for those who explain that this rule applies where the entire accumulated interest of one year is taken all at once, whereas in cases where even though it has reached the time for payment, not all of it is paid, there may be the taking of more than double— on their view, the word *na* (not) would not be literal, nor would *āhita* (placed/deposited) have its intended meaning. For if only the interest accumulated over one year were to be taken, and there were a further taking [of interest] in the second year, then the restriction to doubling would never apply anywhere.
Now, as for one who brings back wealth together with interest that has doubled, let there be a prohibition against anything exceeding that;
prior to doubling, he gives only the interest he is capable of giving,
while the principal may be taken by him in unlimited measure.
This too is of no consequence:
it is just that one who carries [the goods] should receive a gratuity, not an excessive amount;
however, for one from whom the king somehow obtains even a doubled amount, the release of an excess is unjust.
Furthermore, this is not the meaning of the word *ahitā*.

Alternatively, there is a variant reading, *āhṛtāḥ*; even so, the word *sakṛt* would have its meaning rendered uncertain, and the logical principle (*nyāya*) would be abandoned. Moreover, one's own reading would be established rather than the *Smṛti* of Manu; thus, the very arrangement [of the text] already stated is the correct one.
In the case of grains and the like, one does not exceed the fivefold rate—that is, the increase is five times the principal.
In another Smṛti, however, a fourfold rate is stated for grain, according to the rule: "The interest on gold, clothing, and grain is twofold, threefold, and fourfold, respectively.

In this regard, the settled rule is as follows: if the lender is poor while the borrower is endowed with great wealth and has used that grain to generate a large profit, then the interest is fivefold; otherwise, it is fourfold.
*Sada* refers to the autumn harvest, because grain (*dhānya*) is mentioned separately.
A *lava* is well known among the northerners as a measure for wool.
*Vāhya* refers to draft animals such as donkeys, camels, oxen, and so forth.
An interest rate higher than the established rate is not permitted;
they say that such a path is usury, for [the law] allows only five percent per hundred.
"Anusāra" (conformity) means that all matters follow, pursue, and accord with this;
it refers to the conduct prescribed by the Teacher.
And that is manifold, ranging from the eighty parts and so forth up to the five hundred.

Therefore, the interest that has been stipulated as excessive is not valid for the creditor from the debtor; why? Because it is "excessive," meaning it is outside the scope of the sacred scriptures (śāstra). He states another explanatory passage (arthavāda):
They call that the path of the indolent,
where base men sink; through such indolence,
they are marked as wealthy only by name.

"This is the path, the way, and the practice of the lazy, not of the virtuous"—this is the censure [of usury], which must necessarily be imposed upon those who, with the thought that "he will accomplish a great task by means of my wealth," desire to take five percent, regardless of the distinction of social classes (*varṇa*). To this end, it is said: "But [if] it is done out of necessity, [it may be more than that]. An alternative reading is: "But [if] it is done out of necessity, [it may be] more than the essence."

For one who is truly nothing, even a small gift bestowed by him may attain great significance through that very wealth or otherwise; yet for such a person, no excellence beyond the worth of a man is achieved, as he is only worthy of five hundred [pieces].
One should not collect interest exceeding that of a year, nor that which is unapproved;
namely, compound interest, periodical interest, stipulated interest, and bodily interest.
That which occurs in a year is "annual" (*sāṃvatsarī*).
That which has passed beyond that is "post-annual" (*atīsāṃvatsarī*).
The sense of the suffix *bhava* (denoting occurrence) is included by implication.

Alternatively, although the form *atisaṃvatsarā* would be expected when [the word] *saṃvatsaram* has passed, the suffixes *vṛddhi* and *īkāra* must be applied because of the similarity to Vedic usage.
For those for whom interest is five percent per month, that interest applicable to all castes should be collected up to one year, but not after the year has elapsed.
Or else, it means "as long as the year."
A year is a full year;
interest should not be sought for longer than that.
Even by the debtor, there should be no delay beyond one year.
The meaning is that one should extract [the interest] by drawing it out from one's own capital and bring it forward.
Even that which is paid before the lapse of a year is considered as having already exceeded a year.
Alternatively, starting from a month up to a year, the amount of interest must be determined according to its measure.

The application [of the interest] should be made such that it increases by the month or by the year; however, one who desires the profit for two years does not sometimes cause [the debt] to be held for a long time [thinking], "What is the use of my profit for a few months if you take it for two years or more? In that case, if he takes it, this interest is for such a length of time; even if he gives it back earlier than that, the debtor should be made to pay the two-yearly interest as determined by the time. One should neither give nor cause to be given an interest that is not to be taken.

Just as monthly interest (*māsikī vṛddhi*) is made payable when one clears the debt on the very second day of the first month, so too, when one agrees that "it shall increase by the year," it is then made payable in that same manner, and not according to a period longer than that.
Nor should one collect what is not seen [in the scriptures]:
that which is not seen in the *śāstra*, such as the ten-and-one rule (*daśaikādaśikā*) or anything exceeding five percent, one should not accept.
Some say that this is merely a restatement of the point that [an entity] is not established as distinct;
however, this [following interpretation] is more logical:
the meaning is "unseen" and "unaccumulated."
As long as [the interest] has not accumulated over many months, so long the daily interest or monthly interest is not to be taken.
But was it not said that one "should take the interest of a month"?
That refers to the measure of the monthly [interest], not to its actual taking at that time.

The phrase "he shall not even recover" applies by extension to interest on a revolving loan (*cakravṛddhi*), interest according to the time (*kālavṛddhi*), contractual interest (*kārikā*), and corporeal interest (*kāyikā*).
"He shall not take at all":
although this is a prohibition directed at the debtor, it should nevertheless be understood by implication as applying to the creditor alone.
For what would a debtor, when distressed, not do?
Alternatively, "vinirhāra" means simply taking;
thus, the prohibition is expressed verbally as applying only to the creditor.
But surely, since the rules for double and other increments have been prescribed, there is no possibility at all of "wheel-increment" (*cakravṛddhi*) and the like;
so what is the point of appending this prohibition?
It is said in reply:
A prohibition that has not been previously established implies an optional alternative;

for example, in the injunction "one should not sing the Brahmasāman at the fire-consecration," the prohibition makes known that the singing of the Sāman exists even though it was not specifically prescribed.
By this means, these [other options] are also permitted by way of prohibition.
For some who engage in long-distance trade, there are also forms of interest such as *cakravṛddhi* (compound interest) and others.
Therefore, for merchants traveling by land or water, it is said: "Those traveling through wildernesses [take] ten percent, while those traveling by sea take twenty percent per hundred."
"Or they may pay the interest agreed upon by themselves in all cases among all classes of people.
Thus, the interest agreed upon by the parties themselves applies universally to all classes of people specifically for those traveling through wildernesses and the like, but not for others.
In that regard, *cakravṛddhi* (compound interest) is mentioned in another Smṛti: "Interest on interest is *cakravṛddhi*."
Others, however, hold that a "wheel" refers to a vehicle such as a cart, and the "increase of the wheel" (cakravṛddhi) is the interest accruing on it.
For them, interest accrues only on the day the wheel moves;
but when there is no movement due to crossing a river or because of bad weather and the like, there is no interest.
In this same way, for others who employ draft animals such as oxen, such an increase is called *cakravṛddhi* (wheel-interest).
*Kālavṛddhi* (time-interest), however, is that which accrues month by month;
the mention of "month" is intended as an illustration.

Interest that is not accumulated, but is taken day by day or month by month, for which no specific time limit is awaited, and which then becomes double the principal if not paid at that time— this is interest of a single form known as *kālavṛddhi*.
*Kāritā* is that which is agreed upon in this manner, or whatever amount the creditor and debtor settle between themselves in consideration of their mutual benefit.
This rule also applies only to merchants traveling in various directions;
for others, however, it has been stated that a separate rate is not established, namely, "one deserves five percent per hundred.

Alternatively, when gold is lent and clothes are received as interest, there the property serves as collateral (*ādhi*); that is *kāritā*, which would apply both in the case of receiving the benefit of use and regarding matters involving the form of a deposit (*nyāsa*).
Physical [misconduct] is to be purified by physical action;
and physical livelihood [is to be purified]—in due order—for those who live as camel-drivers and so forth.
He who, being unable to pay the debt, wishes to enter into a new transaction, shall,
after paying the interest that has accrued, renew the bond.
If one who has become unable to pay a debt that has doubled through interest due to the exhaustion of his wealth, he should be made to undergo a new transaction;
that is, the instrument—such as a written document or witnesses—should be renewed.
However, he must pay the interest that has been won, meaning the amount that results from calculation.
Regarding what was stated—that more than double [the principal] should not be accepted—this is an exception to that rule: "for this is a new transaction.
But why does it have the purpose of being an exception to the doubling [of the debt]?
To the extent that there is no such statement here as "the wealth together with the interest increases" or "the principal capital increases," but rather only an action is heard;
and that [action] has been explained by another interpretation as "it should cause the instrument to be exchanged."
If it does not increase, for what purpose then is there a change of the instrument (the medium of exchange)?
It is said:
when wealth is obtained through peaceful means but is not being given away, there is the possibility of laziness and the like; furthermore, as time passes, witnesses might forget.
As it has been said:
"In whatever matter a ten-year period of neglect has occurred by the party who caused it,
there shall be no dispute at all in that case, especially in matters of violence."
Likewise, a debt neglected for ten years becomes irrecoverable;
and thus the ancients have explained it:
this is an instruction for the king and a favor toward one who is oppressed.
If, by renewing a doubled loan, there is a new transaction involving interest on the total—including the previous interest—and this constitutes a favor for one who is greatly oppressed;
or if, having seized all of it at that time, he is not made to pay [the full amount], such a favor is granted to the indigent.
Such a favor has indeed been ordained by fate itself.
And likewise, this has been ordained in all the Smṛtis regarding this state: "Now,
if a debtor should become incapacitated due to the lapse of time,
he shall be made to pay the debt when his capacity is observed, at the proper place and time, according to his means."
If the debtor has become impoverished due to misfortune from the gods, he must not be oppressed by the king through imprisonment or other such means.
What, then, should be done?
When he somehow acquires wealth, he should be made to pay it back gradually, as far as possible.
"Having observed his power" means having ascertained his wealth;
he is to be made to pay what is appropriate.
As the author will state later: "He should also make him perform labor accordingly."
Therefore, when the cause has been transformed, that which we have stated is precisely the purpose.
Without having shown the gold there, he may exchange it;
he ought to pay back as much interest as has accrued.

Without having displayed the gold and without having paid the interest on the gold due to his poverty, he should again renew the transaction right there. In the presence of witnesses, he should say: "I owe him this much principal, and this much interest," and he should record this in a document.
They explain that the interest should be stated as much as may be possible for it to grow;
furthermore, when the principal is renewed, a smaller rate of interest must be applied— one by which the debtor is not excessively oppressed,
meaning it is less than what it previously was.

According to the opinion of Yājñavalkya, Sahāya, and Nārada, however, even one capable of paying as little as a single *kākiṇī* must be made to pay at the time of the transfer of the instrument of proof.
This is so that the witnesses do not merely witness by hearing; rather, the debtor’s connection to the matter becomes directly perceived before them.

For, through both hearing and seeing, the witnesses will have fulfilled their duty, and [the debtor’s thought] that "the wealth has been neglected for ten years" and so forth—which otherwise remains in his mind—will become subject to destruction.
One who has ascended to the increase of the wheel, being established in the proper place and time,
will not obtain that fruit if he transgresses the requirements of place and time.
"I shall go to Vārāṇasī; let your draft animals and my goods be taken [there], and this shall be your interest.

In that case, if he does not reach that place due to a wilderness, crossing a river, civil unrest in the kingdom, or other such obstacles, and returns from some intermediate location with a certain profit, then the stipulated interest is not to be paid. For how could there be interest for those who carried [the goods] as far as that destination but did not reach it?

For draft animals carrying loads over a long distance, there is great hardship; for the owner as well, the benefit derived from the use of the draft animal is effectively realized over that same period of time.
However, when they return quickly, the owner is indeed able to employ them elsewhere again. This very circumstance constitutes the transgression.
Thus, there is a lapse of time, such as: "Let my oxen carry [the load] for a month; this much shall be your interest.
In that case, if he returns after a fortnight, the debtor has "entered into" (samārūḍha)—meaning accepted or agreed to—the compound interest (cakravṛddhi).
