Regarding that interest, place and time are established; since he has resorted to a specific place or a specific time in the manner previously described, and has not done so without qualification, such a debtor, by transgressing those [specified] place and time, shall not obtain—that is, shall not receive, shall not partake of, and shall not have to pay—that fruit called interest. This is the meaning.
Is there no profit at all there, or is it five percent?
He said: "No;
those skilled in sea-voyages perceive the place, the time, and the purpose."
But whatever rate of interest they establish, that applies to the realization of the debt there.
The mention of "undertaking sea voyages" is intended as an illustration for any journey in general.
Whatever interest merchants—whether traveling by land or by water—establish, that is the fixed rate regarding the acquisition of profit in that case;
the meaning is that it is precisely that which must be determined.

Those who perceive and know the place and time, seeing that "in this region there is such an amount of profit," and "in that [region] there is such an amount"—but not merely those skilled in sea-voyages, such as the helmsmen and others—others explain the preceding verse in this way by supplying words according to their own whim: regarding that debt which depends upon place and time, if one has reached that [place] but does not obtain from that region the fruit arising from that place, known as profit, then what kind of interest applies there? In response to this inquiry, the following verse [is spoken].
The mention of "increase" (vṛddhi) is intended to indicate interest as well.

The king should recognize as authoritative that rate of increase which merchants—who possess an excess of greed—may mutually establish, being experts in the calculation of loss, expenditure, and effort. In this context, "therein" refers to the acquisition [of the loan].

The prefix *prati* is a *karmapravacanīya* because it serves as the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) of attainment (*adhigama*); therefore, by the rule "the second case ending is used after a word joined with that [indicator] when expressing an indicator (*lakṣaṇa*), a state of being so (*itthaṃbhūta-ākhyāna*), or a companion (*tadyukta*"), the accusative case is employed.
If a man stands here as a surety for another's appearance,
failing to produce that person, he shall pay the debt from his own property.
In the lending of money, there are two kinds of security: a surety or a pledge.
Regarding that, this is said concerning the category of the surety:
a surety is of three types—of appearance, of confidence, and of payment.

In this context, with reference to the guarantor for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*), he says this: "He for whose appearance the guarantor stands, [thinking] 'In such-and-such a place, this person must be shown to you by me,' while acting thus, should strive—that is, he should make an effort—from his own property to pay that man's debt;
the word 'should pay' is the sense."
The mention of "taking a loan" is intended as an illustration for all matters of legal dispute (*vyavahāra*).
Therefore, whatever subject matter is enumerated in legal proceedings, that object must be delivered by one party when charged by the other, through the production of proof (*darśana*).
In cases such as verbal abuse or adultery, a stipulation regarding the wager (*paṇa*) must be made.

If it has not been shown [to have been paid], then I must pay it; however, if no agreement was made, he shall be made to pay only the royal fine. But in the case of corporal punishment, the ransom for that is one *suvarṇa*.
A son is not liable to pay for a guarantee, a frivolous debt, what is due from gambling or liquor, nor the remainder of a fine or a tax.

*Prātibhāvya* is the function of a surety (*pratibhū*). That which must be performed by a surety, such as the clearing of another's debt and so forth, is *prātibhāvya*. *Arhattā* is fitness or capability.
This is prohibited by this [text].
And when that [authorization] is prohibited, there is a prohibition of the authority [to give].
Since one who lacks authority does not give, it is thus stated that "it should not be given."
In all cases, the action and the word must be explained and understood as referring to the Arhat.
But how, then, can a son incur a liability such as becoming a guarantor (*prātibhāvya*)? For he has not taken on that debt himself.
This is not a fault.

Whatever has been accepted by someone as something to be given is indeed considered "given," because its fruit is equal to that which has been received. Having thus attained a determined nature, it is therefore prohibited [to retract]. A "vain promise" (*vṛthādāna*) is a pledge made for the sake of jest or similar motives, such as saying, "Perform this task for me; once it is completed, I shall give this. When the task has been accomplished and the father has accepted the pledge, the son cannot be made to pay it in any way, even if he was not the one who originally promised.
In this manner, [the rule applies] to rewards and the like, as well as to matters concerning the jesting of bards.

Or, for example, if one thinks, "I shall cause this much to be paid to such-and-such a merchant," and a messenger is sent for that purpose, but it somehow fails to be paid because the merchant is absent or due to some other reason, then if the father dies after the payment has been made to another, the son is not liable to pay. Regarding gambling: "gambling-related" (*ākṣika*) refers to what is owed to the master of the gaming house (*sabhika*), or whatever was taken for the purpose of another; thus it can be known [that the debt exists].
This is its refutation:
it can be determined that the debt of one who has abandoned his kin, who sleeps, sits, and dwells only among rosaries, and whose well-known pastime is [counting] them, is "due to dice" (ākṣika);
that which is caused by the drinking of liquor is "due to liquor" (saurika).
The mention of *surā* is intended as an illustration for all types of intoxicants (*madya*).
Therefore, this prohibition of debt applies to one who is addicted to drinking and a habitual drunkard;
however, there is no such prohibition regarding fines or taxes.
This is a prohibition regarding a case where some portion of the fine and some portion of the toll were paid by the father, but the full fine and toll were not paid;
however, in a case where nothing was paid by the father, he is made to pay it.
It has also been stated without qualification in another Smṛti: "Suretyship, commercial tolls, liquor, gambling, and fines shall not devolve upon the sons."
In this regard, there is an alternative view:
when the offense is great and the paternal wealth is large, the prohibition applies to the remainder;
the same applies to the marriage-fee (*śulka*).
But when it is very slight, [the transgression] pertains to everyone.
But in the case of a surety for appearance, the previously mentioned injunction shall apply;
if the surety for payment has died, the court shall cause even his heirs to pay.

The rule that was enjoined and stated by me in the preceding verse—namely, that sons are not liable for their father’s suretyship, which refers to suretyship for appearance (*darśana-prātibhāvya*)—is as follows:

if it were the case that the sons of a surety for confidence (*pratyaya-pratibhū*) must be made to pay, [the author] says: "When a surety for payment (*dāna-pratibhū*) has died, the heirs, i.e., the sons, are made to pay; not in the case of any other.
If this is so, then the first half-verse is redundant.

When it is stated that the sons of a surety for a gift (*dānapratibhū*) are liable [for the debt], it is understood by implication that there is no connection with the sons of any other kind of surety.
Now, for the sake of clarity, it is said:
"The mention of the word 'surety' (*pratyaya*) must also be made."

Otherwise, since "seeing" (darśana) is mentioned in the prohibition and "giving" (dāna) is mentioned in the injunction, there would be a doubt as to whether the rule applies or the prohibition applies to one who has fallen away from both.
There is no such doubt, because it has been clearly stated in another Smṛti:
"Where a surety for appearance (darśana-pratibhū) or a surety for payment (prātyayika) has died..."

"His sons shall not pay that debt, except those who stand ready to give. Here too, because the phrase "the surety for payment" (dāna-pratibhū) functions as a restrictive injunction (vidhi), it does not apply elsewhere.
The mention of "appearance" (darśana) is intended as an illustration (upalakṣaṇa).
Furthermore, being illustrative in a restatement is not a fault.
If one asks what the purpose is, it is that the composition of the verses by Manu is diverse.
Furthermore, when the debtor has not paid and the guarantor— who was known for his character—
has subsequently died, by what means may the creditor seek to recover the debt?

With this verse, the author, being in doubt, poses a question and resolves it with the answer. The cause of the doubt lies in two words: "adātari" (toward one who does not give) and "vijñātaprakṛtau" (toward one whose nature is known). These words ending in the locative case are explained as being in apposition: "adātari" means toward a surety (*pratibhū*), and "pratijñātaprakṛtau" means toward one whose nature has been declared.
For what reason would a creditor seek to recover a debt, or desire to obtain it? Would he do so by his own efforts alone, or does he involve even the son of the surety?
Why is there doubt?
It has been stated [in the preceding verse] that "when the surety for payment is dead," therefore, when someone other than him has died, what connection could there be for his sons?

Since it is certain that one who knows the nature [of the debt] and knows the cause [of the obligation] has stood as a surety (*pratibhū*) after receiving wealth, from this arises the understanding that there is a connection with his sons, because he released [the debt] for the sake of clearing this [surety's] liability.
The word "again" (*punaḥ*) expresses a distinction from the preceding case:
that the sons of a surety for payment (*dāna-pratibhū*) are connected [with the debt].
In that case, when the non-payer has died,
the creditor— the one who is to give—
is the one who subsequently, that is, at a later time, [receives the debt]. This is the meaning.
The remainder has been explained.
*Parīpsā* is the desire for acquisition.

But if the surety has been designated as having sufficient wealth and possesses adequate funds, he shall pay that from his own property; such is the settled rule regarding one who has been designated.

"Nirādiṣṭa" means assigned; "nisṛṣṭa" means entrusted from one's own wealth. [The meaning is: "Become a guarantor (lagnaka) for this money; you must recover this money from me if I do not pay it. "Alaṃdhanaḥ" means having sufficient wealth.
It refers to that which has been fully released, being as much as is required to be paid to the creditor.
However, if only a small amount has been released while a large amount remains to be cleared, he should not be made to pay.
This is the answer to the previous question:
even if the surety for payment has not been designated today, his son shall be made to pay from his own property alone.

In the same way, it should be understood that [the rule applies] to one who has been "designated" (*nirādiṣṭa*) as a son; for he alone is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*). If it is argued that the liability of an actual surety (*sākṣāt-pratibhū*) follows simply from being a surety, this is not so. The established position is that [the term] is used in the sense of "designation," according to the limits of the treatise (*śāstra-maryādā*).

Since it is already established through deliberation that [the son] is the basis of reliance (*avalambana*), the expression "designated as the basis" (*nirādiṣṭo 'lambana*) is stated merely to conform to the requirements of the metrical composition (*padya-grantha*).
A legal transaction entered into by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted, or dependent, or by a child, or an elderly person, or one who is incoherent, is not valid.
The word *vyavahāra* (legal procedure) is a synonym for *kārya* (legal action).

Whatever action there may be—such as giving, mortgaging, or selling—and whatever evidence there may be, such as written documents, that which is performed by these [persons] is not established; even though it has been done, it is considered as not done.
Those who are intoxicated or insane are well known [as incapable].
One who is "afflicted" (ārta) is one tormented by the loss of wealth, kinsmen, and so forth, as well as one for whom fear has arisen.

Because words such as "intoxicated" (*matta*) are used in their etymological sense (*yaugikatva*), this prohibition indicates the absence of legal capacity only for as long as one is possessed by intoxication and the like.
This is mentioned merely as an illustration for the state of being "not in one's natural condition" (*aprakṛtisthatva*).
"Even if one who has entered [the ritual] performs what was prescribed,
they say that it is as if unperformed; for he is not independent by reason of his cause."
And one who is not abiding in their natural state is said to be one whose intellect is overwhelmed and thus incapable of discerning their own task.
And it has been said:
"Those possessed by desire and anger, those afflicted by distress, fear, or calamity..."
"And those overwhelmed by passion and hatred should be known as having fallen into a state contrary to their nature.

Thus, having formed a *dvandva* compound of "passion" (*kāma*) and so forth, [the term] "afflicted" (*pīḍita*) is used; the instrumental compound (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*) "afflicted by them" (*taiḥ pīḍitāḥ*) is formed according to the rule for instruments (*sādhana*).
By that, there is a prohibition of one who is afflicted.
And this person, being currently possessed by passion, desires such things as embracing women;
those engaged in other activities such as gambling are likewise intent upon them.
For these people, being so distracted, are not authoritative, because they lack attention to the determination of transactions such as acting as a guarantor even for their own master.

For, being preoccupied with another task when questioned by another, they do not carefully discern such things as: "Let this be given to him," or "Surety has been accepted," or "In regard to such an object, in such a manner, he says this," and so forth;
or they accept the intention that "let there be no obstacle to his natural activity while he remains here," saying, "Go, everything you say shall be carried out"; or they accept dependence.
As it has been said: "He is independent because of the cause."
The very reason by which one who lacks autonomy is not an authority—that same reason exists for this person, even though he possesses autonomy.

Just as one lacking autonomy cannot direct even his own affairs, so too this person, being enslaved by desire and the like, fails to discern the purpose [of things] or the merits and defects of actions as they are being performed; thus, he becomes equal to one who lacks autonomy.
The "afflicted" (ārta) has been explained.

The words *abhiyukta* (accused) and *ārta* (afflicted), though denoting the substratum (*dharmin*), should be understood through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as referring to the qualities (*dharma*):
namely, being accused (*abhiyoga*) and being afflicted (*āturatā*).
"Calamities" (*vyasana*) are those arising from desire and anger, such as hunting and the like.
One who is occupied with a task, even if distracted, is said to be performing some action with intent;
likewise, one who is engaged in that [action] even while not actively occupied is "delighting in its meditation.
Alternatively, the words *kāma* and *krodha* refer to the one who desires and the one who is angry.
And in this interpretation, the words *bhaya* (fear) and *vyasana* (calamity), forming a *dvandva* compound and ending in the third case, are connected with the word *pīḍita* (afflicted).
Others, however, [interpret them] as entirely independent;
[they mean those] who are "enveloped," that is, pervaded, by passion (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*).

Attachment (*rāga*) is, in some cases, an infatuation with things regarded as one's own; or, for one who meditates, it is the satisfaction of the mind upon the accomplishment of a desired object belonging even to someone else. Its opposite is the object of aversion (*dveṣa*). When an adversary is perceived as not belonging to oneself, there arises a state of satisfaction resulting from the discomfort caused by that person or its reverse; such are the forms of attachment and aversion.
In every respect, his conviction regarding the reality of these [objects] wavers, and he does not remain steady for even a moment in the task intended to be performed.
One says one thing but acts another;
such a person is "not abiding in their natural state" (*aprakṛtistha*).
Otherwise, all persons would be "not abiding in their natural state," being possessed by desire and the like, and afflicted by old age, decrepitude, eye diseases, and ailments of the head.
But this is not the case;
for the *garbhadāsa* (slave from birth), the son, the pupil, and the wife are *adhyadhīna* (dependent).

Even though, by conventional usage, only the *garbhadāsa* is [specifically] *adhyadhīna*, nevertheless, because the term is intended to indicate those who lack independence (*asvatantra*), all of them are included.
Whatever they do regarding their own property, such as giving it away and so forth, succeeds only after having obtained the permission of the owner;
and thus Nārada says:
"Whatever act a minor performs, and whatever is done by one who is not independent..."
"They say that what has not been done [by the teacher] is as if undone.
Thus the disciple is considered dependent, while the teacher possesses independence.
Women, sons, slaves, and other dependents are likewise without independence.
But that which belongs to one who is an independent householder shall be his own, having been inherited in due succession.

Now, if it is said that women lack independence while men possess independence, this is untenable; for wealth is common to both. How could a man, being alone and without his wife's permission, have the power to give away, sell, or otherwise dispose of property?
Regarding this, it has been said:
"They say that transactions entered into by women are invalid, except in times of distress."
Likewise, beginning with the statement "the eldest in the family," it is said: "What he has done shall be considered done; a task is not considered done if performed by one who is not independent.
For when wealth is held in common, a man is just as dependent as a woman.

While the terms "ownership" (*svāmyam*) and "dependence" (*pāratantryam*) appear to be contradictory, they must be understood here in this specific arrangement: that ownership exists [in the head of the household], while these [other members] remain under such a regulation.

Dependence (*pāratantrya*) is the state of being subject to another, which consists in following their will. And if one who is dependent does not obtain the power to employ [the object] without the will of another, what kind of ownership (*svāmya*) can he have? Now, regarding giving, pledging, and selling, they are powerless because of the context.

One's own wealth may be employed for the enjoyment of one's body and other such purposes as long as one desires; however, for twice-born men who possess great wealth dependent on others and whose selves are restrained by the scriptures, it is so that they may have personal enjoyment. This is appropriate when the child is under the dependence of his master; when he has attained legal capacity (*vyavahāra*), then he shall be the master.
The same applies to sons and others.
However, for a woman there is never independence;
whether she be a child, a young woman, or even an old woman.
It is an established principle that no action whatsoever should be performed independently.

The inclusion of women within the state of non-independence from their master is stated here. By the mention of this dependence, however, no prohibition is made regarding the disposal of women's own property.
Rather, what is prevented is giving, pledging, selling, and so forth, in an improper manner.

They are dependent; their status must be determined, for they themselves are not capable of discerning such matters—namely, that "this person is worthy to receive gifts of land, gold, and so forth," "one should form a marriage alliance with this man," or "this property is fit to be bought or sold from him.
Therefore, at the time of executing a document or similar act, the consent of the husband and others is required.
This is because once the deed has been completed, there would be an opportunity for her to say, "I knew nothing of this; I have been deceived by you."
But if she has the consent of her husband and others, what will she say?
As it has been said:
"Even these means of proof are valid if the husband approves."
In the absence of a husband, the son [is the protector], or the king is the protector in the absence of both husband and son.
Lack of independence has also been restricted:
"They are instructed that they are considered masters in regard to giving away and selling";
yet even in the case of a deliberate error by a child, the wife and others may be directed by the master through means such as reprimands, but not [so] regarding the disposal of property.

"She must be restrained immediately, or she may be abandoned in the presence of the family"—thus, this dependence belongs to women alone and not to men; for even in the case of one who has fallen from his status (*patita*), there is an instruction to wait until the completion of his penance.
Therefore, even in the most extreme emergency, there is no sale whatsoever of slaves and the like.
In these cases, with reference to the phrase "of the master," the wives,
disciples, and female slaves possess dependence according to their respective status.
However, because wealth is held in common, it is established that a wife has no entitlement to perform sacrifices or other rites anywhere without the husband's permission.
And as for this:
"When her sons' husband has died, she should likewise remain under their control;
while both [parents] are alive, she shall be dependent, even if she is advanced in age."
Of these two as well, the father is superior; it is held that in his absence, the progenitor is the authority.

Thus, by this [statement], the dependence of sons [is established]; as for the objection that "this contradicts [the previous statement]," there is no contradiction. In the case of a son who is a minor and lacks legal capacity, there is dependence on the mother.
However, a son’s dependence upon his mother consists in the protection of the mother’s wealth from dangers such as thieves;
likewise, a son’s dependence upon his father applies to one who has not been separated [from the family estate] and resides in that father’s house.
But when one has been divided from his father and has acquired wealth by himself, then, "after the sixteenth year, he should behave toward his son like a friend"—
this indeed constitutes independence.
A child is one who has not attained legal capacity, being under sixteen years of age.
An elder is one whose memory is impaired, overcome by old age, and past his legal capacity.
Even if such a person should at some time be in his natural state, he is nonetheless not an authority, because he lacks reliability.

However, in the case of a husband whose wife acts as an obstacle to the affairs of people, this [legal proceeding] is permitted with her consent; otherwise, it is "unrelated" (*asaṃbaddha*). One who conducts a legal transaction for the sake of another without being authorized—neither a brother nor a father—is not entitled to say such things as, "I owe a hundred to Devadatta," and so forth.

However, in the case of brothers who share a common purpose and all conduct their affairs equally, the sale of cattle, goats, and so forth, as well as the pledging of houses and the like, performed by even one of them, is valid because of their mutual connection.
The word *vyavahāra* (transaction) is intended to include all types of transactions;
otherwise, due to the context, it would refer only to transactions concerning debts.
A speech does not become true even if it is well-established,
if it speaks of phenomena that are external to the fixed conventional [truth].
Speech is generally that word which conveys some object to be performed;
whatever object is conveyed by it is that which is to be performed.
Is not all speech, then, untrue?
He says: "No.

If [the transaction] is outside of the law—that which is called 'outside the law' being that which contradicts the scriptures and established conduct—such as interest exceeding five percent, the sale of a wife or children, or the giving away of one's entire estate by an heir, and so forth;
even if these matters were established, recorded on a document, or for which sureties were given, they do not hold valid.
Conventional dharma is that which is established by custom;
it is fixed and beginningless, not something created in the present.
And this is a continuation of what preceded.
An act such as giving performed by those who are not independent or who abide in an unnatural state is indeterminate; thus, it is not authoritative.
Whatever has been mortgaged, sold, given, or received through fraud,
or wherein one perceives deceit— that entire transaction he shall annul.
Yoga means deception;
whatever pledge or mortgage has been made by such means is known to have been done through fraudulent intent,
and the king shall annul that.
A certain man, being pressured by a creditor, says, "I have nothing.
To the objection, "But you do have a field, a plot of ground, or a garment; give those up," he, out of this apprehension, makes a secret pledge of something to some relative.
Then he says, "That has already been made a mortgage by me to another."
And this is understood:
because even though there is a manifest document, it is impossible for that [document] to be the basis of the pledge (*ādhātṛtā*).
For if it were established as a pledge in the ultimate sense, how could the pledgor himself enjoy [the property]?
Having rendered such a fraudulent mortgage invalid, the debtor must be made to pay the field and other property to the creditor.

Furthermore, when one who possesses ownership through another title makes a formal transaction at the time of paying the debt by means of a different title, that too constitutes a fraudulent mortgage.
In that case, the debtor—or whoever has been made to appear as the owner through that fraudulent title—must be compelled to produce the true title.
The same applies to sale and other transactions.

If one sells an item of great value for a small price, or if one does not even take payment from the buyer, or says, "This has been sold by me to you here; this is yours," then at a later time he cannot say, "It was sold by you, it is mine; take back the price. Nor can this rescission of a sale be revoked after ten days have passed.

Or, when the previously mentioned cause exists, or another cause exists, he causes [the property] to be bought by one who has acquired it, or he sells it; and neither is the purchase seen in legal proceedings for the purpose of embezzlement through coins and the like, nor is he one habitually accumulating coins and the like—by such means, there is the acquisition through fraudulent sale (*yogavikraya*).
Regarding fraudulent gift and acceptance (*yogadānapratigraha*):
that which is owned by both parties is given after an agreement has been made with the recipient; such is fraudulent gift and acceptance.

The expression "giving and receiving" is a *dvandva* compound analyzed as such, even though the mention of either the act of giving or the act of receiving necessarily implies the other, since one cannot be established in its own nature without the other. Nevertheless, the mention of both acts is for the purpose of completing the meter. Alternatively, if only one act were mentioned, the punishment would apply only to the perpetrator of that act and not to the second party, because—even though the second party is a means (*sādhana*) for that act—they are not explicitly mentioned by the word.
Therefore, the separate mention of both the giver and the receiver is for the purpose of imposing punishment on both.
If that were the case, then in the phrase "what is acquired through connection, mortgage, or sale," one would also have to include the second action, such as "purchase" and so forth.
It need not be included; for even without its inclusion, punishment would follow either from another Smṛti text or from a general rule of law.
"Or where one might perceive a pretext (upadhi)"— a pretext is a deception. By this very [rule], a pretext should be excluded from these actions even in other cases.
For example, someone was told by a wealthy man: "I will not release you until you provide a guarantor who states that the debt shall be paid within this many days."

When he has become silent, someone makes an agreement with the creditor, saying: "Accept me as his guarantor while I press him; he has done me much wrong, and I am becoming a guarantor solely for the purpose of afflicting him—I shall not have to pay anything myself. Then the creditor says openly: "If you have no other guarantor and do not seek [payment through] labor and the like, surely you wish to seize his wealth. Being thus pressed, he replies: "I have never before engaged in such a transaction with this man."
The guarantor, however, says: "I am your guarantor.
If he does not wish to do so, out of distress or constraint, he says: "Do as you wish.
This is not included among the previous types of transactions.
In this same manner, activities such as agriculture, trade, and the commencement of crafts—being distinct from these [three]—should be illustrated.
Giving, mortgaging, and selling are merely examples.
Whatever action whatsoever is performed through these means, the king shall cause all of that to cease.
Even if a deed has been performed, the king may declare it unperformed and shall not accept it as valid;
he should punish both the doer and the one who caused it to be done.
If the borrower should perish and the expenditure has been made for the family,
that debt must be paid by the kinsmen from their own property, even if they have already divided it.

It has been stated that the debt must be repaid by the one who received it; in his absence, by his son or grandson; and in their absence, by the heir to his estate. Apart from these, the repayment of the debt to another is not intended to be required.
In this regard, concerning a certain matter, this is stated for that purpose:

if the one who received the wealth has perished, died, or gone to another country—and expenses have been incurred by the family—then that debt must be paid by the kinsmen, namely the brothers, their sons, paternal uncles, and so forth; even if they are divided and have separated their property, the meaning is that it must be paid from their own respective wealth.
As long as the brothers live together, whatever debt arises among them is to be paid from the household assets themselves.
The division of what remains from that is as it has been stated:
"Whatever debt has been contracted by an undivided paternal uncle or by a brother..."
"Or whatever they may give for the sake of the family, all that [must be paid] from the inheritance.

This means that when a debt has been contracted by any one of those who are undivided for the sake of the family, all—the brothers, paternal uncles, their sons, and so forth—must pay it, but not if it was not for the sake of the family; such is the meaning.
Because of the mention of "undivided," it is likely that such a debt would occur primarily among them alone.
For it is not observed that those who have divided their property take on debt for the sake of maintaining the family of another;
therefore, he says "even by those who are divided. By the word "even" (api), it is implied "and also by those who are undivided.

If, among brothers who are divided, one should depart abroad without having provided for the maintenance of his own family, and the other, out of great magnanimity (*mahāsattvatā*), should maintain that person's family, then the latter must indeed pay the debt contracted by the former—whether it be a brother or a paternal uncle—even though they are divided, once he has returned from abroad.
Whatever legal transaction a dependent person may carry out for the sake of the family,
whether in his own country or abroad, the head of the household shall not annul it.
Let brothers and the like be set aside for now.

Even a household servant or a domestic employee who is under the authority of the master, if he should carry out a transaction—such as the sale of cattle or livestock, or the utilization of fields, threshing floors, and so forth—for the sake of the family, whether by way of debt or a commercial contract, in his own country or abroad, while the master is present or absent, the senior householder shall not rescind it; rather, without further deliberation, he should approve it, saying, "Well done.
Others, however, say that this is a commendatory statement (arthavāda) supplementary to what precedes, and not an injunction (vidhi).
Thus it has been said:
"Indeed, there is no seed for [interpreting this as] an explanatory passage (arthavāda),
because when analyzed, it remains expectant [of further connection], due to the relation between the words 'yat' and 'tat' regarding the debt."

Now, regarding the phrase "by one intoxicated, insane, afflicted, or dependent," because a dependent person lacks independence, what is done by such a person is not authoritative. Furthermore, it is not reasonable to assume that [a transaction] made for the sake of the family while the master is present is invalid;
otherwise, there would be the ruin of the family.
Therefore, one who is dependent on fate becomes authoritative regarding the activity whose nature consists in supporting that [being].
Manu has declared that all matters performed by force— whether given by force, enjoyed by force, or even recorded by force— are as if not done at all.

Just as that which is done by children, by those who are not independent, by those remaining in their natural state, or by those acting under duress is not authoritative, so too is that which is done by force.
The rule is that all matters effected by force are to be set aside;
"enjoyed," "given," and "recorded" are merely examples.

In this context, "given by force" refers to when land, gardens, or the like that are not being used are given for the purpose of transport; or when one desiring interest forcibly imposes money upon those unwilling to carry a load; or when one consumes merchandise after depositing the principal in their houses.
"Written" means the preparation of a document.
"All" means other such matters as well; the sense is that these are legal transactions (*kāryāṇi*).

Regarding the phrase "a fraudulent mortgage," it has been explained in detail here; yet, even though it could have been included within this very verse by means of the power of its composition (*yogabala*), Manu composed two separate verses.
The composition of Manu’s verses is diverse.
[A transaction] made by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted, or dependent, or by a minor or an elderly person, if done by force—[is void].
"And because of connection with the unconnected, conventional practice is not established.
[This means] it is simply not established; it does not come to be like a means of valid cognition (*māna*).
Three suffer for the sake of others: witnesses, a guarantor, and a family;
whereas four prosper: a Brahmin, a wealthy man, a merchant, and a king.

When requested by another, testimony, acting as a guarantor, and overseeing legal proceedings must be performed by means of one's family and so forth, not by approaching of one's own accord through force.
Therefore, those who act on their own initiative do not become authoritative.
Alternatively, by acting for the sake of another, they incur hardship.
For these [servants] have not even a scent of self-interest;
therefore, they should not be made to work by force.
As for the family, there are elder men.
When requested by another, Brahmins and others accumulate [wealth];

therefore, a Brahmin should not be made to accept [gifts] by force against his will. Alternatively, if the accumulation is for the sake of property belonging to another—since his own activity is thus for his own benefit and not solely for the sake of another—that Brahmin must not be compelled by force to engage in the giving or receiving of that.
The common worldly saying that "giving is to be accomplished by force" does not prohibit one from making someone give; rather, it means one should make him give if he so desires.
However, in the case of begging, force is required.
Thus, a wealthy man who lives on usury should not be treated like a person of substance who is merely indifferent to his obligations.

Why is it considered *kusīda* (usury)? Because one gives [the loan] to another for trade, thinking, "Not to me," or because one forcibly causes another—who does not desire it—to incur that expenditure without having the wealth deposited. For one increases through being requested by another, not by employing force, due to the prohibition in the scriptures.
In this way, a merchant who is a moneylender engages in trade solely out of a desire for the increase of wealth;
a merchant is one who lives by his wares.
Even a king, a ruler, prospers by collecting the royal fines that have been imposed.
But he should not engage in legal proceedings by instigating [parties] through force and the like;
thus it has been said: "He should not himself initiate a lawsuit.
The rule concerning Brahmins and others is a restatement (anuvāda) intended as an illustration for the king.
Alternatively, this is an elaboration of examples for everything; likewise, the subsequent [section] as well.
A king, even when impoverished, should not take what ought not to be taken;
nor should he, even when prosperous, relinquish what ought to be taken, however small the matter may be.
Apart from taxes, fines, duties, and so forth prescribed by the scriptures, no other wealth of the citizens is to be taken by the king, even if his treasury is depleted.
However, that wealth which comes through scriptural injunction and legal justice as a fee for protection, he must not relinquish, even if it is as small as a single *kārṣāpaṇa*.
Thus it has been said:
"A king should cause his treasury to increase like the path of an anthill.
Thus it is said.
By seizing what should not be seized and by abandoning what should be seized, the weakness of the king is made manifest; he perishes both in this world and after death.
It is "not to be taken" (anādeya) because it is unworthy of being taken;
the suffix -ya is used here in the sense of fitness (arhe kṛtyaḥ),
and this has already been demonstrated.
Weakness is made known by the subjects [through rumors] such as, "He punishes us, yet he is unable to conquer thieves, forest-dwellers, vassals, and the like.
Thus, the citizens proclaim his incapacity against enemies;
consequently, when attacked by them, one whose subjects are disaffected perishes here.
Because of seizing [wealth] here, and because of inflicting unjust punishment after death.
Through the collection of tributes, through the mixing of castes, and through the protection of the weak, the power of the king is generated; thus he prospers both in this world and after death.
The non-taking of what belongs to oneself by right, or rather, the taking of what is excellent;
"excellent" (śobhana) means precisely that which is auspicious (bhavya).
The conjunction of two letters is the conjunction of letters with those of the same class.

Since a conjunction resides in two things and since the two related entities have not been mentioned, it is logical that the expectation [of what those entities are] refers only to the phonemes (*varṇa*), as they are the subject under discussion.
As for the conjunction of the phonemes with their intermediate productions (*avāntaraprabhava*), that cannot be designated as a relation belonging to the phonemes alone.
However, some read "na" [in the text], [interpreting it as] "because of the non-conjunction of the phonemes."
In every respect, this is a restatement of the prohibition against the intermixture of castes;
for it is because of protecting those who are weak and being oppressed by powerful enemies that the king's power is generated.

The correct administration of justice must be carried out and the infliction of unjust punishment must not be carried out; these specific points will be recited as explanatory statements (*arthavāda*) of the verses.

Therefore, like Yama himself, the master should personally abandon both the pleasant and the unpleasant, and conduct himself with the impartiality of Yama, having conquered anger and subdued his senses.
And thus he elaborates on this very point:
"This servant is my own, therefore he is dear; and this one is merely a resident of the kingdom, who remains loyal only to that whose kingdom he inhabits, and for that reason is not dear.
Abandoning such partiality, he should be equal toward all subjects in both protection and legal administration, like Yama.
For such indeed is the conduct of Yama that has been observed.
Regarding the word "of Yama" (*yamasya*), they maintain that the suffix *ya*—which is prescribed as an addition (*aupasaṃkhyānika*)—supersedes the suffix *aṇ*.
But who, then, partakes in a state equal to that of Yama? One who has conquered anger and conquered the senses.
One should conquer passion and hatred by means of what is called detachment.
But that evil-minded king who, out of delusion, performs his duties unrighteously,
will soon bring himself under the control of his enemies.
He who performs his duties through unrighteousness abandons *dharma* out of sheer delusion and becomes utterly bewildered in this world.
This is the fruit born of unrighteousness for him: his enemies bring him under their control by causing his subjects to become disaffected.
For when subjects are disaffected—being provoked, greedy, fearful, or insulted—they may be incited by others to turn against him.
And then they repeatedly bring [them] under their control;
they punish, bind, kill, and seize the kingdom—this is subjugation.
But he who, having restrained desire and anger, perceives matters according to dharma—
toward him the subjects turn, as rivers flow toward the ocean.

Just as rivers flow toward the ocean, and having reached it, remain devoted to it, becoming one with it and never turning back from it, so too, through the conquest of desire and anger, the subjects—possessing security and prosperity—become one with the king.
If someone reports to the king that a creditor is recovering his debt by his own will,
he shall be made to pay a fourth part of that amount to the king, and the creditor's debt shall be paid by him.
*Chanda* means desire.

When a person, having not obtained permission from the king, proceeds by his own will through the aforementioned four methods to acquire wealth, or when such a person has been so engaged, the king’s officers shall summon him, saying: "I am blocking this place; give me the wealth!
If, upon being questioned, he admits, "I owe it," he should be made by the king to pay a fine equal to one-fourth of that amount.
As long as he holds [the debt] for him, the debtor must be made to pay his entire debt therefrom. If he holds a hundred, he is to be fined twenty-five and made to pay that hundred to him.
Thus, it is twenty-five [percent].
However, one must not mistakenly think that out of a hundred [coins] belonging to the king, twenty-five remain for the creditor;
for in that case, the creditor would be the one punished, not the debtor.
A debtor of equal caste to his creditor may discharge the debt by means of labor;
one of lower caste must pay it immediately, while one of higher caste should pay it gradually.
A debtor who is penniless is not released from his debt simply because of his poverty; rather,
he must be made to perform labor or enter into a state of servitude.
Whatever wealth a laborer uses to perform that work must be accounted as having entered his share even if the total yield is not yet realized; furthermore,
if he performs the work and the wealth along with the profit has entered [the common fund], there shall be liberation from servitude.
The creditor shall make [the debt] equal;
subsequently, when the wealth has been cleared, there is no longer the relationship of creditor and debtor.
Otherwise, one remains a creditor and the other a debtor, and this state continues to be maintained.
A person of the Brāhmaṇa caste is equal; one of the same caste is of equal birth; one of lower birth is of inferior caste;
whereas one who is superior is of higher caste or possesses greater qualities.
One should give gradually, in due order, according to their arising.
In the *Nārada-smṛti*, it is recited: "But a Brāhmaṇa who is impoverished should pay gradually according to his means.
Therefore, for the sake of clearing the creditor's wealth, the king must not oppress an impoverished Brāhmaṇa, and the creditor must be protected.
By this procedure, the king shall bring to a state of justice those legal matters of disputing men that are established by the evidence of witnesses.
"By this" is a reference back to the previously mentioned manner;
"by the method" means by the procedure;
"established through the testimony of witnesses."
The word *siddha* is connected with each [term] individually. *Siddhāni* means established or determined by witnesses.
*Prayayaḥ* means inference or divine procedure (*daivī kriyā*).
He should bring all matters to a state of equality— not only those concerning the non-payment of debts, but others as well;
he should remove the disputes between plaintiff and defendant and produce a consensus.
The non-payment of debt has been concluded; the legal procedure is finished, because in all cases the modes of victory and defeat are of this nature.
Indeed, apart from witnesses and the like, there is no other means for resolving the determination of the case in subsequent disputes.
The subsequent elaboration must state only the specific punishments and the nature of those offenses;
thus, the nature of "sale without ownership" and "repentance" (rescission) is established as to what they are like.
A wise man should deposit a trust with one who is of noble birth, endowed with good conduct, knowledgeable in dharma, truthful, possessed of a large following, wealthy, and honorable.

One of renowned lineage is one born of a noble family, whose father and grandfather were learned, righteous, and possessed of great possessions; who, being restrained by the traditions of their own family, do not engage in improper acts;
for such a person is indeed unable to endure even the slightest reproach.
People do not at all censure him;
for his conduct, character, and behavior— his natural fear of public reproach—
are fully perfected and he is endowed with them.
One who knows the Dharma is one who has attained an understanding of its meaning through the study of the Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas.
A speaker of truth is one who has repeatedly been observed in his actions to speak the truth.
One of great lineage is one whose prestige is supported by friends, kinsmen, the king, ministers, and others, such that he cannot be easily approached by corrupt royal officials.

A wealthy person, for the sake of protecting his own property and out of fear of the unseen (karmic consequences), does not engage in the seizure of another's goods, thinking: "I have sufficient wealth; what need is there for that which belongs to another? If it were somehow discovered, I would be punished.
A noble person is one who practices righteousness or is upright by nature.
[This applies to] a deposit.
The term *nikṣepa* (deposit), denoting gold and other valuables being deposited, is expressed by means of the suffix *ghañ* as an instrument of action (*karaṇa*).
A wise person should deposit—that is, place—for the sake of protection;
thus, one who deposits in this manner becomes a wise man (*prājña*).
Otherwise, he becomes a fool;
having become a friend, he teaches what is perceived, for this instruction does not concern an unseen purpose like that of the *aṣṭakā* and other such rites.
When a deposit is placed with such a person, there is no loss; in such a case, there arises no suspicion that "it was not deposited by him.

However, one who is a naked mendicant, a gambler, a drunkard, or the like—even if drawn into the matter by someone—is not a fit object for suspicion, even if it were said, "My father deposited this in his hand," regarding a large amount of wealth such as gold;
yet, when the deposit consists of only a few cowries, suspicion certainly does arise.
Whatever object a person deposits in another's hand in whatever manner, that must be received back in exactly that same way; as was the delivery, so shall be the receipt.

"Yathā" (as): in whatever manner [the deposit was made], whether the ocean [of wealth] was sealed or unsealed, with witnesses or without witnesses, and so forth—in that very same way [it must be returned].
That object deposited must be received back exactly as it was;
just as the gift was given or deposited, so it is taken back.

In a case where it is certain that [the debtor] always places the sealed document in the creditor's hand, if there is a dispute and the unsealed document is produced, and the debtor says, "He did not seal it; he took it from me by force and departed," then in such a situation of doubt, the debtor loses the case. For the sealing is generally established by other means of proof.
On other occasions, however, when a seal has been destroyed, the king must employ another means of proof to determine the specific quantity of what was stolen;
he should be punished with the general penalty for denial alone,
whereas the penalty for misappropriation of a deposit applies only once the value of the property has been ascertained.
But surely, when a total denial has been proven, it is only right that the defendant be considered defeated.
True;

however, this applies where the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is established—for example, when Devadatta is accused after a village has been plundered, saying, "On such-and-such a day, that village was destroyed by you along with other thieves."

He said, "I did not go to that village on that very day. There, the witnesses stated: "On that day, we saw what was stolen there, but we did not see [the thief]. In that case, Devadatta also denied the theft, since his presence in the village on that day was established.
When another evident cause is present and yet not perceived, it is indeed reasonable to infer that even theft is occurring due to the proximity of the location;
however, in this case, the sealed deposit of men who have lost it through negligence is taken away while remaining unsealed.
As the giving was, so too is the taking.
The denial [of the deposit] may arise from the thought, "What opportunity do I have for being accused?
For one cannot infer [the existence of the deposit];

even if one could somehow infer it, its specific quantity cannot be established by the mere statement of the deposit without another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, a determination through ordeal (*divya*) and so forth is appropriate.
In every case, the certainty is that one who cannot establish [his position] by means of another part of the argument is indeed "defeated on a single point."
If one who has been asked for a deposit does not return it to the depositor,
he shall be summoned by the judge in the absence of that depositor.
This verse is recited in the traditional collection with its sequence inverted;
having first recited the first half-verse, one should then recite "in the absence of witnesses," and after that, "he should be entreated.
Such is the proper reading.
For such is the connection of the meaning:

when ordeals (*divya*) are applicable due to the absence of witnesses, this statement [is made]. It is not as in cases such as the non-payment of debts, where ordeals are administered immediately after the absence of witnesses; it is not like that here.
Rather, one should have his conduct investigated by spies.
If, when being investigated thoroughly, he does not stumble in any part of his conduct, then he should not be harassed with oaths.
But if he falters in this regard, then even the suspicion that he might have misappropriated a deposit is entirely justified.
Therefore, this must be purified by divine means;
for the theft of another deposit is not established merely by the theft of multiple deposits.
It may happen that, having stolen one [deposit] for some weighty purpose, once that purpose is accomplished—or if remorse has arisen—one returns the other.

Therefore, this collection of verses is intended for the immediate cessation of the oath of one who has deposited [the object] and intends to reclaim it; it is not, however, a formal presentation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Nor is it appropriate to compel the first plaintiff to pay a fine—even if the theft of another deposit remains unproven—just as a royal punishment is imposed for the theft of a deposit by a judge.

For if one were to be made to pay when the theft is unproven, then the treatise on legal procedure (*vyavahāra-śāstra*) would exist merely for the sake of a formal decision rather than for the purpose of reaching a true determination.
Consequently, it would contradict the principle that a determination must be made by means of logical reasons (*hetu*).
Therefore, this matter is neither scriptural nor a worldly convention;
rather, it should be interpreted as having another purpose, according to the manner stated in the passage beginning with "in the absence of witnesses."
In the absence of witnesses, having truly deposited gold with him through spies endowed with [appropriate] age and appearance, and by means of pretexts;
Now we shall proceed to the application of the meaning of the terms.
That [deposit] must be requested by the judge in the presence of the depositor.

If the depositary denies it—saying "nothing was deposited by you"—to that requester by whom it was placed in secret in the absence of witnesses, then once the depositor has informed the king, he should not reveal the facial expression of the holder of the deposit.
What, then, should he do?

By means of secret agents and stratagems, having deposited his own gold, bullion, silver, or other property with another person, he should request or demand it from that second depositary through the judge (*prāḍvivāka*).
The mention of the "judge" is intended to indicate any official authorized to render a legal decision.
Should he be requested directly?
No, it is said;
rather, through the medium of those who have made vows, by those endowed with youth and beauty.

By virtue of which they are endowed with age such that they do not become children— for it is suspected that the deposit of those who have been incited by others is for the purpose of deceiving me— there is no suspicion regarding those of mature age.
In this same manner, the endowment with physical form is to be explained.
The form itself of a certain person becomes such that from its very sight, fickleness appears;
and thus he explains this form as "freedom from passion," O Blessed One.
By this it is meant that one should make such vows that the holder does not suspect: "This undertaking is for the purpose of deceiving me."
"By pretexts," "with frauds," and "by means of reasons for depositing":

these refer to the statement of a reason—such as "I am depositing this with you now for this purpose"—which arises from falsehood, such as fleeing to another village due to royal harassment and the like.
And all of this must be done before the depositor is present.
If he should act according to what was entrusted and as it was done,
there would be nothing therein by which he could be accused by others.

If the holder of the deposit should admit, "Certainly, it is here; take it," and then deliver it— just as it was deposited, whether sealed or unsealed, in its original state such as cloth and so forth, or rolled up, or otherwise unmarked, such as an ornament that has not been used and is free from scent, having been placed there with the house-seal or his own mark— if he delivers it exactly in that manner, then there is no truth whatsoever in what others who were previously present allege, namely, that "this man denies our deposit due to a lack of witnesses."
The distinction between "as deposited" (*yathānyasta*) and "as made" (*yathākṛta*) is based on whether the deposit was made with hidden or unhidden marks;
or alternatively, the distinction is based on the difference in the actions of the receiver and the depositor.

"As made" means that whatever was received—whether without conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*) or with support (*sāvalamba*)—must be returned exactly as it was received; the meaning is that no time limit should be set for its return.
If, however, he does not pay that gold to them according to the rule, he shall be seized and compelled to pay both; such is the established principle of the law.
If those depositors employed by the judge do not return the deposited property, it is explained by the phrase "according to the rule" (*yathāvidhi*) as being "according to what was done.
That custodian, being restrained by the king's officers, shall be compelled to pay both—the claimant's dues and the king's fine.
This is the established legal principle (*dharmasya dhāraṇā*).
The intended meaning here has been explained.
A deposit (*nikṣepa*) and a sealed deposit (*upanidhi*) must never be handed over to a next-of-kin;
they are lost if [the depositary] perishes, but they are not lost if he does not perish.

Regarding the immediate successor, "immediate after arising" refers to the depositor’s son, brother, or wife—whomever possesses ownership over the depositor’s property. Ownership for the wife has already been stated; likewise for the son regarding ancestral property, and for the brother regarding joint property.

In that situation, one of them might beg [the deposit] from the depositor while he is absent, saying, "Give this to us; it belongs to us. Then someone might give it with the thought: "This is common property; one deposited it and another took it away, so what is the harm?"
Therefore it is said: "A deposit (*nikṣepa*) and a sealed deposit (*upanidhi*) must not be returned to another person.
He states an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) in the form of a reason: "In the event of a mishap, those two perish.
A "mishap" (*vinipāta*) is a change of state (*anyathātva*), such as the recipient's departure for another country and so forth.
In that case, both of them lose [their claim].
If he did not return the money to the depositor after taking it away, then what answer can the debtor give when questioned by him?
To say, "This wealth was taken by your brother, who is a joint owner," is no valid answer.
It has been stated that "as the gift, so the acceptance.
This is an elaboration of that very point: the object must be returned to the same person from whom it was received, whether he be the owner or not the owner.
However, if the immediate neighbor does not undergo a change of heart (or objection), then there is no fault even in giving it to him.
Regarding this, he says: "But in the case of non-delivery, they are not lost;
for in that case there is a means of proof, therefore I entrust it.
The meaning of the verse is that when delivery has been made to the immediate neighbor, even if a mishap occurs, the owner must give his own property to the depositor who requests it.
But he who should himself deliver [the deposit] to the next-of-kin of the deceased must not be prosecuted by the king, nor by the kinsmen of the depositor.
Therefore, it has been stated that there is no obligation for the depositary to give [the deposit] back while the depositor is still alive.

However, in the case of one who is dead, if someone gives the property himself without knowing that "this wealth belongs to him," he should not be subjected to the hardship of legal documentation and the like, nor asked, "Do you know of anything else?
or "If he had possessed more than this, would he have given that too? Thus, he is not to be troubled.
If even here a doubt does not cease—thinking that he was very wealthy and yet does not employ [the debt] with anyone else—then another means of proof must be examined for the sake of certainty.
He should not be harassed by oaths involving poison, fire, and so forth;
however, the water-jar ordeal (*ghaṭa*), the *kośa* ordeal, and the *satyataṇḍula* ordeal are not prohibited.
For they do not cause excessive affliction;
this is the second application regarding the absence of witnesses. And whatever application was made for those two should also be understood here.
One should seek that object with sincerity and with affection;
having investigated his conduct, one should settle the matter through conciliation alone.
In all these cases of deposits, this rule shall apply regarding their recovery;
however, if [the depositary] does not withdraw anything from the ocean, he shall not incur any penalty.

Regarding deposits that have been increased [in value], the procedure just mentioned—beginning with "in the absence of witnesses," and so forth—is to be understood as the means for establishing the truth.

In the case of a deposit placed in the ocean, the holder of the deposit shall not be subject to such questioning from the depositor as, "There was another substance in this vessel which has been destroyed by worms," and so on. The same should be understood regarding destruction by rats and other such causes.
If clothing or other items placed in a wooden container are eaten by mice with sharp teeth after they have gnawed through the wood, there is no fault on the part of the depositary.

Furthermore, if a large bundle wrapped in cloth and sealed is deposited, and it cannot fit inside that wooden container, then even if it is eaten by mice or other creatures outside, there is indeed no fault.
And if this knowledge belongs to the depositor—that the holder has reviled him, saying "I have no other goods"—or if his depositor is someone who knows his character and is perhaps nearby.
If he does not give [the value of what was lost], provided that it has been stolen by thieves, carried away by water, or consumed by fire, and he has not taken anything from it for himself.

If thieves, whether known or unknown, should plunder [the goods] by means of breaking through a tunnel or other such methods, the loss falls upon the owner alone, provided that the depositary had taken precautions for protection. If it is carried away by water, meaning transported to another region by water; [in this case, the loss is also the responsibility of the owner].
One should seek out the thief of a deposit and likewise the person who did not entrust it by all means possible, and even by means of Vedic oaths.
One who takes back what was deposited without witnesses, or one who, having not deposited anything, demands it after taking it away, shall be investigated.

Investigation is the effort toward the full ascertainment of the truth through the operation of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The "means" (*upāya*) are the instruments of knowledge or the methods such as conciliation (*sāma*) and so forth.

Therefore, for one whose conduct has lapsed and who does not admit [the truth], even flogging, imprisonment, and so forth may be employed—just as in the case of a thief regarding great wealth—for the purpose of making him realize the truth.
Punishment is not [to be applied] when the truth is not determined.
The mention of "Vedic" is for the sake of praise.
He who does not return a deposit and he who demands it without having made a deposit— both of these should be punished like thieves, or made to pay a fine equal to the value of the object.
This is the punishment for one who denies having deposited what was actually deposited, and for one who demands what was never deposited:
he is fined an amount equal to the wealth regarding which he acts fraudulently.
The king shall cause the one who misappropriates a deposit to pay a fine equal to its value;
likewise, he shall do so for the one who misappropriates a sealed deposit (upanidhi), without distinction.
The punishment for a thief was stated previously;

by that, corporal restraint or the confiscation of property equal to the value of the theft was prescribed as an alternative depending on the distinction of caste, except in the case of a Brāhmaṇa. This [present rule] sets aside that [corporal punishment]. By this re-enactment, the punishment for a thief is restated as consisting only of verbal censure, fines, and so forth, and is combined with the monetary fine, but not with forms such as the amputation of limbs.

Nor is it appropriate to say that this repeated statement is intended to preclude corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa—which might otherwise have been applicable under the preceding rule as an alternative—since corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa is prohibited in general by the injunction: "One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa.
*Upanidhi* refers to that which is enjoyed through friendship;
in such a case, one should not take account of either the specific nature of the object or the caste of the person.
However, another [author] has defined *upanidhi* [as a specific legal deposit];
that [definition] applies only there and not here. Since no such technical definition is provided here, it is logical to accept the term in its ordinary, worldly sense.
And he will say: "and of that which is presented out of affection."
Any man who, by means of fraudulent tests, should seize the property of another,
must be executed publicly with various forms of capital punishment along with his accomplices.
*Upadhā* means deceit;
it is synonymous with *chadma*.
And these [deceits] are of many kinds.
The exchange of goods— such as showing saffron and giving safflower and so forth,
or the reduction of weights and measures, and so on— in that regard he will state another rule, beginning with "one thing should not be mixed with another," and so forth.
But here, what is intended are things such as causing alarm, demonstrating a benefit received from the king, and describing the girl's affection, and so on.

They say such falsehoods as: "Thieves will rob you if I do not protect you; the king is extremely angry with you, but I have interceded much on your behalf; I shall cause the king to grant you the office of city magistrate or provide you with a primary favor; the daughter of Puṣpamitra is deeply in love with you and has sent this gift through my hand"—having spoken thus, they attach their own gifts and return many things in exchange.

Having observed this, they report other matters in secret to the king or to someone equal to him, saying, "Your business has been commenced," and so forth; through such deceptions (*upadhā*), they consume the property of others.
For them, this public execution on the royal highway—accomplished by various means such as being impaled on a stake, decapitation with an axe, or trampled by elephants—is prescribed.
Others, however, based on the context, say that this refers specifically to the subject of deposits (*nikṣepa*).

For in that case, having promised, one takes [the object] by not handing it over, thinking, "I have deposited it elsewhere; he is not present now, but will come tomorrow or the day after. Thus, one steals by failing to deliver it.
Whatever deposit was made by someone, and of whatever amount, in the presence of witnesses—that same amount it must be recognized as; one who declares otherwise deserves punishment.
The word "ya" (who) is a designation for the type of substance being deposited;

"yāvān" (as much as) refers to the quantity. For example: "He who says, 'Gold was deposited by me in his hand,' yet gives bell-metal; or he who says, 'A hundred [coins] were placed [with him],' yet gives half."
He is asked whether [the offense] was committed in secret or in the presence of someone;
if he says, "in the presence of a family," then the family members are the witnesses.
In that case, what they say when questioned is indeed the truth;
one who speaks falsely, speaking in contradiction, is punished.
Even then, if he should say in the presence of the witnesses, "Silver was deposited by them, but something else was established [as collateral] without them," [he is liable].
There is here an occasion for the operation of another means of valid cognition;
this verse, moreover, does not have the purpose of enjoining something additional.
If a gift was made privately by someone, or received privately, it must be returned privately; as the giving was, so must be the taking back.
By the phrase "in whatever manner one deposits," this rule for depositing is stated;

by means of this, one proceeds in other matters as well. Even in cases such as the non-payment of debt, bailments, and sales, that which was made by someone in a particular manner must be returned in that very same manner.
One must not disclose what was done in secret by seeking a share [of the debt] in the royal court and so forth.
Therefore, when a debt is taken on the basis of a handwritten document (svahastalekhya), the debtor is not made to pay a share in the royal court;
rather, the creditor's wealth must be fully discharged.
Since this very [rule] already establishes the case of deposit (*nikṣepa*), the repetition there is for the sake of indicating its permanence.

Therefore, in cases other than deposit, even if something was done in secret, there may occasionally be a public restitution when there is a suspicion of misconduct. Alternatively, what is prohibited here is the making public of that which was done in private.
In that context, however, the meaning is different—such as "the ocean" and "not the ocean"—and thus there is no tautology.
The word *mithas* should be understood as "in secret";
or alternatively, *mithas* means "mutually."
Every task is to be accomplished by two [parties]; thus, acts such as giving and so forth are performed between one another.
The repetition [of the word] is for the purpose of excluding a third party.
The word *dāya* (gift/transaction) is a general term that includes not only deposits but also other transactions such as sales and the like.
In such cases, the king should reach a decision regarding deposited wealth as well as that which was entrusted out of friendship, without causing hardship to the holder of the deposit.
By this, the conclusion of the section is made:

regarding a deposit (*nyāsa*) or a pledge (*nikṣepa*) offered out of affection and given for a short time for the purpose of enjoyment, a decision must be rendered in such a way that the holder of it is not oppressed— meaning,
without causing him harm or distress.
Two or three verses regarding the making of a deposit (nikṣepa) contain injunctive meaning;
everything else has been stated out of friendliness, being established from other sources.
One who sells another's property as his own, being neither the owner nor authorized by the owner, should not be admitted as a witness; he is a thief who considers himself no thief.
This legal title known as "Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner" is now introduced.

If another person—such as a son or someone else who is not the owner—sells property or the like belonging to another without the permission of the owner, one should recognize him as a thief or a robber.
Even though he who purchases it from him considers that seller to be no thief, [the law regards him otherwise].

"One should not lead him as a witness" means that one should not lead—that is, bring—that man forward; one should not cause him to act as a witness; he should not be appointed to the office of a witness. For such a person is exactly like a thief.
And because of being a thief, one is not qualified to be a witness;
it is not only the status of being a witness that is prohibited,
but rather [the eligibility] for all activities that must be accomplished by virtuous people.

Since it is already established that property sold by one who lacks authorization over another's goods does not become the property of the buyer, this prohibition—stated by way of forbidding the act in the presence of witnesses—is intended for the sake of variety.
He shall be liable for restitution along with his family and fined six hundred panas;
if he has no family ties and offers no excuse, he shall incur the guilt of a thief.
By the preceding [verse], it was stated that those who perform actions on behalf of others—such as acting as witnesses in deeds performed by virtuous persons—are unworthy [of the reward].
By this [verse], a fine of six hundred is prescribed;
that is to say, one who takes [property] should be made to pay and be punished with six hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*.

"With lineage" (*sānvayaḥ*): "lineage" (*anvaya*) refers to a connection characterized by following after. One who has such [a lineage], such as a son, a brother, or others who follow the master, is "with lineage."

For even though he sells it without authorization, he is not an overt thief; because he possesses the thought, "This is indeed mine, as it belongs to my father," this same presumption arises regarding him. He gives the price after selling it to that very person.
However, one who has no connection whatsoever is "without trace" (niranvaya).
He has undoubtedly incurred the punishment for the sin of theft;
he is without recourse. If that house has not been vacated by him, then, being without recourse, he shall be punished like a thief.
If, however, it was given or sold to him by someone from that very house, and he accepted it because of his ignorance, or sold it through an open purchase, then he is not to be punished like a thief;
he should merely be made to pay six hundred [paṇas].

Alternatively, "connection" (*anvaya*) refers to the sale; "purchase" (*kraya*) refers to the acquisition of that sellable object from another source; "removal" (*apasara*) refers to something other than purchase, such as acceptance as a gift (*pratigraha*) or other means of acquisition.
This is what is meant:
if he has neither purchased it from anyone nor obtained it through acceptance or other such means, then he is a thief.
But whatever gift or sale is made by one who is not the owner is to be known as invalid; such is the established rule in legal proceedings.
It is not only that which is purchased from one who is not the owner that fails to be established; rather, even that which is received [as a gift] does not succeed.
"Dāya" refers to a gift given through acceptance or out of affection; that too does not succeed.
By the phrase "he sells for another," the lack of ownership on the part of both the seller and the receiver is expressed.

This prohibition is established because ownership might otherwise be suspected on the grounds that "one becomes an owner through inheritance, purchase," and so forth; this is the settled rule regarding legal transactions and must not be transgressed.
Where enjoyment is perceived but no scripture is seen anywhere, scripture is the cause there, not enjoyment; such is the established rule.

In a matter such as cattle, gold, or land, where the enjoyment of one person is observed while another possesses a title—such as inheritance or a gift—that establishes ownership, the title (*āgama*) is stronger than the enjoyment (*bhoga*).
Enjoyment itself is *saṃbhoga*;
it is the cause for ownership.
"In that case" refers to the established state.
Thus, ownership is not established by mere possession alone;
rather, the specific nature of that which constitutes ownership has been explained previously.
Whatever contradiction there might be with the statement "for ten years" has been resolved right there.
Whoever receives any wealth from a sale in the presence of the family members indeed acquires that wealth lawfully through purchase, for it is thus purified.
He demonstrates the kind of purchase by which ownership arises:

"market" (*vikraya*) refers to the marketplace where merchants sell; whoever there takes the wealth—whether it be cattle or other goods being purchased, or the price paid—obtains it through a lawful purchase, provided it is pure and in the presence of witnesses from a reputable family.
If it is purchased according to the rule at an appropriate price,
in the presence of a multitude of other traders and brokers who are not suspected of being persons of sinful character, one acquires ownership and does not forfeit it;
otherwise, if the sale is by the owner himself, the goods must be returned, but the price is received.
Therefore, he who sells it is punished for buying it improperly and must forfeit its value.
This has been stated:
"Purity [of title] comes from the production of the seller; the owner recovers the property, and the king receives the fine."
The buyer receives the price; therefore, he who sells it is the one [responsible].
This very point is established by this verse.

Now, if the original owner cannot produce the root evidence but has cleared his title by means of a public sale, he shall not be punished by the king and is released; the original claimant does not recover the property.
The purchase from a person whose wickedness is improbable has been declared according to the rule beginning with "But from a man...";
if that seller can be produced, then the previously stated procedure applies, namely, "the owner [recovers] the property," and so forth.
However, if that seller has departed, and the buyer cannot produce the original seller who sold it to him—nor the owner by whom it was marked—[then the following applies].

When a purchase is made openly in the presence of people at a well-known marketplace, the buyer is purified by such a transaction; thus, once the property has been cleared through this kind of purchase, the buyer is released without penalty.
As for the wealth, the original owner—or one who has proven his ownership—recovers it. One who seeks what has been lost is called a *nāṣṭika*.

In the case of the form *naṣṭika*, when the suffix *ṭhan* is applied in the sense that "this person has something lost," the suffix *aṇ* must be added as a pleonastic (*svārthika*) because it belongs to the *prajñādi* group; or alternatively, it means "one for whom the lost object is the motive.
Thus, the summary is this: in the sale of a revealed [lost] item, there should be no punishment, but the loss of the wealth remains certain.
An object whose form is mixed with another is not fit for sale;
nor is that which is defective, nor that which is deficient, nor that which is far away, nor that which is concealed.
In connection with the topic of selling what does not belong to oneself, another rule regarding sale is stated:
one must not sell other substances such as saffron mixed with inferior substances that merely resemble them, such as safflower.
