Furthermore, one must not sell anything that is "blameworthy" (*asāvadya*), meaning clothing or similar items that have become degraded through long storage in a container, having lost their value and appearing worn out despite seeming new.
Nor should one sell anything that is deficient in weight, measure, and so forth;

or that which is far away, situated at a distance in another village; or clothing, molasses, or other goods; or that which is concealed, covered, or hidden by cloth and the like; or that whose true nature is obscured by some coloring substance such that an old object appears as if new—that which is thus concealed must not be sold.
Having displayed the substance and its specific qualities, the sale must be concluded;
otherwise, if it is done differently, the transaction is not valid, and there is no fault even if the item is returned after ten days.
Since no other penalty is prescribed here, this penalty for "fraudulent practices" applies.
Others say that because it is recited under a different heading, this is the punishment for selling what one does not own.
If, after showing one girl, another is given to the groom,
Manu has declared that he may marry both for the price of a single bride-price.
Since the giving of a maiden for a fee (*śulka*) and so forth constitutes a form of sale, the law (*dharma*) regarding this matter is stated here.

At the time of receiving the fee, if one who has accepted the fee shows a beautiful girl but then gives one who is deficient in beauty, deficient in age, or deficient in qualities, both of them must be taken back by the payer of the fee with that same single fee.
This rule applies specifically to maidens.
However, regarding substances such as cattle, horses, and so forth, another rule will be stated for this transgression.

A giver does not deserve punishment if he has previously declared the defects [of the girl], provided she is not intoxicated, not afflicted with leprosy, and has not already engaged in sexual intercourse.
Having stated that there is no punishment for one who gives [a maiden] after declaring defects such as insanity, he states the punishment for one who does not declare them by way of prohibition:

she is not only to be given away at the bride-price (*śulka*); even if she has been given away, she remains "not given" if she was intended to be married by another through a *brāhma* or other form of marriage. For one who knows this, he shall incur the guilt of a thief; for one who does not know it, the fine is six hundred, as that is the subject under discussion.

The purpose [of this rule] is that there is no punishment for one who gives a girl after first declaring and making public the defects—such as being insane or afflicted with leprosy—and specifically the defect of having engaged in sexual intercourse by saying, "This girl has such-and-such a defect. This applies to those who are insane or leprous, as well as the fault of sexual contact belonging to her who has already experienced intercourse. Having proclaimed these faults beforehand through verbal disclosure, there is no penalty for the giver. Thus is the meaning.
If an officiating priest (ṛtvij) chosen for a sacrifice should abandon his own duty,
a share proportional to that work must be given to him by the other performers together.
This is the introduction to the topic of collective enterprise (*saṃbhūyasamutthāna*).
In this regard, he first cites a Vedic example of collective work:
the *yajña*, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others.

In that regard, for the purpose of accomplishing the various constituent parts of the ritual act in the form of a sacrifice, a priest is chosen by you with the agreement: "You must perform this office of the *hotṛ*, the *adhvaryu*, or the *udgātṛ*," and it is to be carried out according to the Vedic injunction. If, due to some incapacity or the like, one should abandon or fail to complete what was half-done, then a portion of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) must be given to him in proportion to the work performed.
Having determined the total fee for that sacrifice, a fourth part is due when a fourth of the rite is completed, a third when a third is completed; such is the proportionality.

Together with the performers: the performers are the subordinate priests (tatpuruṣa) of the principal officiating priests (pradhānartvij), such as the Hotṛ, Udgātṛ, and others, including the Prastotṛ, Maitrāvaruṇa, and so forth.
And when the sacrificial fees have been given, if he causes his own work to be neglected,
he shall receive his entire share even if he has it performed by another.

"At the midday pressing, the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) are given. Therefore, after that point, those who abandon the ritual act shall receive the fee that cannot be reclaimed; the word "fee" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence], meaning one should not cause it to be abandoned in opposition.
Having paid another wage, the sacrificer should have that ritual completed by another person.

The ritual action must be performed by officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and they become officiating priests through the act of selection (*varaṇa*). Furthermore, that selection occurs at a fixed time prior to the commencement of the rite.

Therefore, if the sacrifice were to be performed with defective rites, it would be flawed; yet, since the completion must also be achieved, one might think, "If it is to be completed even if defective, I shall perform the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) with other agents. To prevent such a thought, it is stated: "by another [agent] alone."
Only that which is impossible is defective; however, everything possible must be performed.
Some authorities state that the term "should cause to be done" refers to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) as well.
If he is unable to do it himself, he should take the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and give more to them.
Prior to the southern offerings, the sacrificer alone is authorized for the completion of the remaining rites.
In whatever ritual those specific fees for individual components have been prescribed,
he alone shall receive them, or alternatively, all [the officiants] may share them together.
Furthermore, another Vedic passage relevant to the present topic is stated:

in Vedic ritual, sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are prescribed in their entirety; they are not assigned by division to each individual participant, as in the rule, "Its sacrificial fee consists of one hundred and twelve [cows].
And that rule follows other sacrifices, such as the *rājasūya*, which are modifications of it, through the principle of extension (*atideśa*).

In that regard, with respect to certain subsidiary rites (*aṅgakarma*), another sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is prescribed for each step in connection with specific persons, such as "two golden *prākāśa* vessels for the Adhvaryu," and so forth. These constitute the subsidiary fees (*pratyaṅgadakṣiṇā*).

This verse is intended to present the doubt: Is the connection with the verb "he gives" (*dadāti*) for the Adhvaryu like that of the four classes of priests (*cāturvidya*) and others—meaning these are the fees for all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), while the Adhvaryu is merely the recipient—or rather, do they belong to him alone, while for the others they are merely their allotted shares?
In each step, there are sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) based on specific persons regarding the limbs; these are the "fees for each limb" (*pratyaṅgadakṣiṇā*).
Alternatively, the word *pratyaṅga* is used in the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*):
those which depend upon limb after limb are the "limb-by-limb" ones (*pratyaṅga*).

He [the opponent] says: "The primary person alone should receive those [gifts]. This is stated as a question based on the premise that since there is no distinction in their status as agents (*kartṛtva*), others too should participate—that is, they should obtain them—just like the principal sacrificial fee (*pradhānadakṣiṇā*).
The conclusion (*nirṇaya*) is that, having been declared for the sake of a specific person, they are intended solely for his purpose.
In this way, the primary meaning of "gives" is preserved,
and the connection with the person is not for the sake of an unseen result (adṛṣṭa).
The Adhvaryu should take the chariot, and the Brahman the horse at the time of the gift;
or the Hotṛ may take the horse, and the Udgātṛ the cart at the purchase.
At the establishment of the fires, the Adhvaryu should lead forth the chariot,
and the Brahman, a swift horse;
or the Hotṛ may lead forth either a stallion or another horse.
In certain branches of the tradition, these are the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Therefore, regarding the cart used for the purchase of Soma, that belongs to the Udgātṛ.
It is also recorded that on that cart, one ox should be yoked and the other unyoked.
And by that [purchase], the Soma is bought and brought forward;
others, however, say it is for a transcendental result (*apūrva*) and not for the purpose of bringing forward the Soma, for it cannot be qualified by the act of purchase.
Thus far, the rule regarding the subsidiary sacrificial fees (aṅgadākṣiṇā) associated with specific persons has been stated.
Now he explains the distribution of the principal sacrificial fees (pradhānadākṣiṇā), which are prescribed in general terms:
"The primary priests are entitled to half [of the fee]; others are entitled to half of that [half]."
Those entitled to a third share receive a third part, and those entitled to a quarter receive a fourth part.

Among all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), those who are the principal ones are the "half-sharers" (*ardhin*). Whatever total sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is prescribed for that sacrifice as a whole, they are the recipients of half of it; that is, they take the half.
For in Soma sacrifices there are sixteen officiating priests, among whom four are the principal ones: the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, the Brahman, and the Udgātṛ.
Half of those—namely twelve hundred—is his *dakṣiṇā*; half of that is fifty-six.

With half of that again, namely twenty-eight, there are others who possess [that share], for whom the selection immediately following him is prescribed: the Maitrāvaruṇa, Pratiprasthātṛ, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and Prastotṛ.
"Tṛtīyins" means those who have a third part.

The word *aṃśa* (part) has the same meaning as the word *ardha* (half), and the word *ardha* does not necessarily refer only to an equal division; it also applies by way of proximity to what is slightly less or more.
Therefore, sixteen are taken from fifty-six as the third part;
thus, there are four for each.
They give an equal third part [of the fee] to each; and from the fifty-six [parts], the Acchāvāka receives a third for the Hotṛ,
the Neṣṭṛ for the Adhvaryu,
the Agnīdh for the Brahman, and the Pratihartṛ for the Udgātṛ.
And those who perform a quarter-part of the ritual action are called *pādinas*;
and in the fourth position, at the end of the station of the Maitrāvaruṇa,
they constitute the fourth parts.
In the case of the group of twelve, it is as previously stated; likewise,

in the passage "they initiate him with a hundred," the same application (*klpti*) must be made through such expressions as "he initiates the half-sharers" (*ardhinaḥ*) and "he initiates the quarter-sharers" (*pādinaḥ*).
In that regard, it is precisely the procedure of the twelve stages; the legal practice heard elsewhere has been performed here as well according to that very same method.
When men here perform their respective duties in association with one another,
the apportionment of their respective shares must be carried out according to this application of the rule.

Just as in a sacrifice, he who is appointed to many tasks—tasks that cause bodily hardship and require a superior degree of expertise—receives a larger sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), whereas one who performs fewer tasks receives less; likewise, among those engaged in worldly undertakings such as building a house or a temple, acting together and in concert—among carpenters, master builders, architects, and so forth—the share belonging to the architect (*sūtradhāra*) and the share belonging to the master builder (*sthapati*) are determined by this application of rule (*vidhiyogena*). "Rule" (*vidhi*) here means the Vedic sense; "application of rule" (*vidhiyogena*) means by the established order well-known from that [Veda], namely the order pertaining to the sacrifice.
Likewise, in the viewing of a drama and similar performances, there is an apportionment of shares among the dancers, singers, and instrumentalists.

Although all of them are learned and capable of performing every task, nevertheless, the share is according to the nature of the work and not according to the person; such is the principle of collective enterprise (*saṃbhūyasamutthāna*).
If wealth has been given by someone to anyone who asks for it for the sake of Dharma,
and subsequently that wealth does not turn out to be so [for that purpose], then that wealth should not have been given to him.

If someone says, "I am a householder," or "I wish to perform a sacrifice," and says, "Give me something," and if it should be given to him, he might not perform a sacrifice nor engage in the rites of marriage;
he might squander that wealth on gambling or with courtesans, or employ it elsewhere for interest, profit, agriculture, and so forth. To such a person, [the gift] must not be given.
The prohibition against giving what has been given is not tenable;
therefore, the meaning of the sentence is that it must be taken back.
Alternatively, the term *dattam* (given) should be explained figuratively as referring to what was promised (*pratiśrutam*), meaning that which was promised should not be given.
And so Gautama says: "Even after having promised, one should not give to one who is joined with unrighteousness;
how much more so in this case?
He states that both are [equally forbidden]: the taking back of what has been given, or the non-giving of what was promised.
And thus both [cases] are recited in another Smṛti.
For Nārada says, beginning with "I am the doer of this deed," that "what is given through ignorance is also considered as not given.
That which is given for the sake of a specific purpose must be recovered from the house of the recipient even if it has been settled, provided that purpose is not fulfilled.
According to the opinion of Nārada, at that time there is merely the commencement of the gift and its formal delivery; however, the completion occurs when the purpose has been fulfilled.
If, however, he should accomplish it out of pride or greed,
he shall be made to pay one suvarṇa by the king as atonement for that theft.

"Recovery" (*saṃsādhana*) means the pursuit of what was promised like a debt through reporting to the king and so forth; it is the reporting to the king of what was accepted but is now being denied, saying, "He intends to take back what he gave me"—this is "recovery," which serves to confirm what has been established.
The phrase "out of pride or greed" is a restatement of the cause.
For one who acts in this manner, the fine shall be gold; this is the expiation for that theft.
Fearing the punishment for theft, he provides gold;
and because it was given by him without suspicion of being a thief, the word "theft" (steya) is employed to dispel the doubt as to how this man—who did not take it himself—could be a thief.
Even though he possesses the status of a thief, the scriptural penalty for stealing gold applies, and he should be treated like a thief in other legal proceedings.
Thus has been declared the lawful manner of non-repayment for what has been given;
hereafter, I shall explain the non-payment of wages.
The first half concludes the preceding discussion on disputes;
the second half introduces what is to be explained hereafter:
this has been declared as the non-reversal of what has been given.
Apakriyā is the failure of action;
its negation is expressed by the negative particle *nañ*.
Thus, giving does not become wavering.
This is precisely what constitutes steadfastness in giving;
it is "dharmya," meaning not departing from the Dharma.
One should not entertain the doubt: "How can the Dharma not be seen when, having given one's word, the gift is not delivered?"
This indeed is the dharma here: that which is not given, and that which has been given is taken back. It is stated as such.
The compound word *yathāvat* functions in the sense of "according to reality" (*yāthātathye*).
The meaning is "properly determined.
Alternatively, the word *yathā* functions in the sense of fitness (*yogyatā*); thus, the suffix *-vat* should be applied in the sense of "deserving that," [yielding *yathāvat*].
*Vetana* means wages; its *anapakriyā* is the non-neglect thereof.
The proposition is that the dharma pertaining to those who perform their own work for wages is now being stated.
If a hired servant, though not ill, should out of pride fail to perform the work as prescribed,
he shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas*, and his wages shall not be paid.

One who performs the work for the price specified is intended here as a "hired laborer" (*bhṛta*). A "hired laborer" is one who has entered into a contract based on the specific nature of the work to be performed. Having agreed, saying, "Give me five *rūpakas*; I will perform this work for you within such a time," if he does not complete the work, he is to be fined gold *kṛṣṇalas* or [coins] of copper or silver, after taking into account the nature of the work and the circumstances.
And if those images assigned for wages are not obtained, [the artisan shall pay].
If one who is not ill does not perform the work as prescribed out of pride,
there shall be a loss of wages and punishment for him who, though afflicted by disease or other causes, fails to work out of pride.

Therefore, he is not permitted to say: "Give me a portion of the fruit corresponding to the share of the ritual act performed by me. Some maintain that this same penalty applies even to officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who abandon their duties of their own accord;
however, that is incorrect.
For here there is great loss for the sacrificer due to his partial performance; therefore, a heavy fine is appropriate in this case.
Furthermore, they should be made to pay whatever the sacrificer has lost.
They must restore the physical depletion caused by the consecration (dīkṣā), the Upasads, and the Devavratas.

If another craftsman initiates any work—such as digging a tank or building a temple for a deity—and says, "I shall complete it for you; proceed," and then subsequently withdraws, he must bear all the loss, expense, and labor of his employer, according to the principle of the merchant and the carrier of goods.
For this principle has been extended by Kātyāyana to all cases:
if a merchant's goods should be lost through the fault of the carrier, the carrier shall bear that loss.

Or, as stated in the Sūtra of Kātyāyana: "If another person, having pledged wealth for someone's work, should turn back halfway through, he too must bear that [debt]"; the connection is that having pledged—that is, attached—the wealth and caused its expenditure, if he turns back when half the work is done, he must pay it.
This same principle applies even to one who works for six months or a year, or to a *bhaktadāsa* (slave for food) who performs work as it arises.
And Nārada says:
One who, having promised to perform work, does not do it; or one who, having received wages, performs work by force;
or one who, having received wages, does not perform the work, shall pay double the wages as a fine.
One who abandons his work before the time is completed deserves the forfeiture of his wages.
Punishment and the forfeiture of wages have been declared for one who is not ill;
now, that which pertains to one who is ill is being stated:
"But the one who was ill, once recovered, shall perform [the work] from the beginning exactly as it was stipulated."
Even after a long period of time, he would surely receive that wage.

If a laborer who has been hired while afflicted by illness should abandon the work half-finished and depart, he, having recovered his health, must return and perform that work as originally stipulated from the beginning.
Even after a long time, once freed from affliction and returned, he shall indeed receive his wages for the remainder of the work performed.
As it has been said: "Whether he be distressed or healthy, if one does not have him perform that work, his wages must not be paid, even for a small amount of work left undone."

Alternatively, if the master does not prevent it, and the person who was made to perform that work has paid his own wages, then he should be made to perform an equivalent amount of work while in good health.
Even if the master should say, "I have nothing further to be done by you," in that case too,
the afflicted person shall certainly receive what was stated according to the work performed.
This law regarding the non-payment of wages has been declared in its entirety;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the law concerning those who violate agreements.
This is indeed the name of this legal head (vivādapada) concerning the non-payment of wages;
therefore, this objection is not valid:
"How can it be called the act of non-payment of wages when it is also described as the act of payment, given that [the employer] would simply not receive the wages at all?"
For the status of being a name is not contradicted by its connection with any associated object whatsoever.
Indeed, not all the meanings of a word are simultaneously active;
thus, even though in the Agnihotra both Agni and Prajāpati are offered oblations, the name "Agnihotra" nevertheless continues to apply.
This has been stated in that very same place regarding the pillar-reflection: "and that which is level or low.

*Samaya* means agreement, understanding, or convention—the undertaking that "this must certainly be done by me with your consent. Those who break or transgress that are the "breakers of convention" (*samayabhedin*).
Now that which was indicated as "the transgression of agreements" is being explained.
With the first half [of the verse], there is a summary by way of the previous method; with the latter half, there is an indication of another section as previously announced.
If a man, having made a formal agreement with truth regarding a village, a district, or a guild,
should break that agreement out of greed, the king shall banish him from the realm.
A village is a collection of houses;
it refers to the people residing therein,
because it is only among them that mutual agreements can occur.
In this way, a collection of villages is a country (*deśa*).
A community (*saṃgha*) is an assembly of living beings who follow a single dharma, even if they reside in various countries and belong to various species;
for example, the community of monks, the community of merchants, and the community of those possessing the fourfold knowledge.

Regarding the affairs of villages and the like: for example, if the villagers from another village are mostly plundering our village, grazing their cattle in our pasture grounds, and leading away water by breaking the embankments—if it is your opinion that we should not allow them to do this today, then if, while we are thus obstructing them, a physical conflict arises with them or a legal dispute occurs in the royal court, in that case we shall all act with one purpose; otherwise, we shall remain indifferent.

In that regard, those who agree, saying "Certainly," yet subsequently violate the established custom of the village—having thus encouraged [the breach] and then deceived them, or having joined with those very people by force, or not remaining among his own kin—he should be banished from the king's realm and expelled;
he must not be allowed to dwell within his own territory.
Likewise, in matters concerning merchants' guilds, monasteries, Brahmins, and so forth, once an agreement has been made, it must not be transgressed by him.

This is the penalty for the violation of an agreement concerning a task that benefits a village and the like, which is well-known according to the scriptures and established custom, and which does not conflict with the interests of the city or the kingdom.
Regarding the term "through greed":
greed is the lack of independence caused by one's own desire for some scent of personal benefit, induced by the leader of another village.
But for one who maintains that there is no contradiction [between scripture and perception] due to ignorance, another alternative is possible.
Having restrained him, the king should compel that violator of the compact to pay four suvarṇas, six niṣkas, and one silver śatamāna.
Having seized, restrained, and oppressed [the offender], and having not allowed him to obtain the opportunity for death, he should be fined.
"Catuḥsuvarṇāḥ" refers to those *niṣkas* whose measure is four *suvarṇas*.

Although it has been stated here that a *niṣka* consists of four *suvarṇas*, nevertheless, observing other measures such as "the wise say a *niṣka* consists of one hundred and eight *suvarṇas*" from other treatises, [the author] specifies [the term].
If it is argued that this is understood solely through the force of the name and its etymological derivation, there is no fault, as it is a metrical composition (*padyagrantha*).
Others, however, having formed a *bahuvrīhi* compound for the sake of the great meaning, speak of three staffs:
one who is to be punished should be fined six *niṣkas* together with four *suvarṇas*.
Ten *niṣkas* are thereby conveyed [as the meaning].
For the sake of establishing the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the sense of possession (*matvartha*) must somehow be applied in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*).
For it is not the case that Devadatta is called "Citragu" (possessor of brindled cows) merely because he is accompanied by brindled cows.
And these three punishments may be combined as one with respect to the offense;
this punishment is optionally commuted by the penalty of banishment.
A righteous lord of the earth should apply this rule of punishment to those who violate their agreements within villages, castes, and assemblies.
And in the case of collections of castes—namely, assemblies of various castes or of those belonging to the same caste—the meaning is: "those for whom there is deviation regarding that object.
This is the conclusion of the section.
If, after having purchased or sold anything in this world, one should have cause for regret,
he may return that object or take it back within ten days.

Regarding goods that are frequently bought and sold, which remain intact during the course of trade and do not diminish in value from their original state—such as vessels made of tin or copper, which possess a stable price—the rescission of a sale or purchase may occur within ten days, provided they have not been used. However, for items that have few buyers and are sold on occasions such as divine processions or festivals, where the price is uncertain, rescission may take place on that very day or the following day. In the case of fruits, flowers, and the like, rescission must occur at that very moment.
Even after having purchased it, if one has regret, thinking, "This is not useful to me," he should return it within ten days;
the seller should take it back.
If the seller regrets it, thinking, "I did not do well in selling this," then the buyer must restore it to him.
And this rule applies to those residing in the same place;
for those residing in different regions, there is a temporary return [to their home].
Some maintain that this procedure concerns objects such as cattle and land, not clothing and the like.
For in another Smṛti, a different rule is prescribed regarding merchandise for sale;
thus Nārada recites:
"He who, having purchased a commodity for its price, considers it a bad purchase..."
That [article] must be returned by the seller to the buyer on that very same day, provided it remains undamaged.
"On the second day, the buyer, by taking possession, incurs a third part of the price;

on the third day, it is double that; after that, it belongs to the buyer alone. Regarding this: "merchandise" (*paṇya*) is that object intended for sale, by selling which a person engages in transactions—such as purchasing other goods with the proceeds—to earn a livelihood. It is thus either displayed or not displayed in the marketplace by merchants. In this context, by the use of the term "merchandise," a specific distinction is intended to be expressed.
Otherwise, only "having purchased for a price" would need to be considered.
What, then, is this distinction?
It is said:
If even that which has been purchased is sold by merchants without relinquishing its character as merchandise, then they purchase it solely for the purpose of resale.
Regarding these merchants who buy from and sell to one another, some say the rule of Nārada applies, while for others it is that of Manu.
What, then, is correct in this case?
Alternatively, one should follow the established conventions regarding commodities and the like.
Thus, for those commodities, commercial practice is established through such things as the shifting of horses' strength, the mounting of elephants with hooks, and the demonstration of their sale.

In the case of deposits and the like, if cloth or other items remain unexamined and undamaged, then as long as there is no loss, the full value is returned to the depositor, while [the bailee] retains the object itself.
But in this case, even if there is only slight damage, the buyer must pay the full price.
But after ten days, one should neither give nor cause to be given;
both he who takes it and he who gives it shall be fined six hundred by the king.

Beyond ten days, there is no rescission of a purchase; nor, even if a rescission has arisen, if either the buyer or the seller disputes it before the king, they both shall be fined six hundred [paṇas]. The prohibition "he shall not give" is not for the sake of some unseen spiritual result (adṛṣṭārtha).
What, then, is known?
Such is the established rule:
after ten days, even if the buyer does not wish to keep it, he must not be forced to relinquish it, nor may the seller be compelled to take it back.
And therefore, if both giving and taking were to occur through mutual consent, there would be no fault in that case.
But for one who gives away a girl who has defects without disclosing them,
the king himself shall impose a fine of ninety-six paṇas.

If a maiden is possessed of defects, yet she is neither disclosed nor made known to the suitor by her giver, but is given away in this very manner, then a punishment for the giver must be inflicted by the King once the matter is known.
The mention of "taking [the girl] oneself" is for the sake of emphasis.
And the defects of a maiden are those which cause the obstruction of religious merit, progeny, and capability; namely, consumption, disease, and sexual intercourse.
"Against one who is not intoxicated"—this refers either to the penalty mentioned in this specific context or to this [present] punishment.
But that man who, out of malice, declares a maiden to be "not a virgin" without demonstrating her fault, shall incur a fine of one hundred [paṇas].

If one says of a girl that she is "not a virgin" (*akanyā*) because of her conduct, sexual intercourse, or marriage relations, and does not substantiate that charge with evidence of such a fault, then he shall be fined one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*.

Others, however, hold that because the fine is small while the insult is great, and because the suffix *-tva* is seen to denote a state rather than a single action, the actual form of the word "not a virgin" is intended here.
Thus, if one insults her using this very expression, "She is not a virgin," his fine shall be one hundred [kārṣāpaṇas].
What, then, is the distinction here?
It is said:
that proponent of this view is asked, "How is it that she is not a maiden?"
If he should say, "She is shameless, cruel, and speaks indecently; this is not the conduct of maidens,
and she does not establish this [claim]," then this punishment applies when the denial of the maiden's virtues has been stated.

Alternatively, relying on the word "maiden" (*kanyā*) as denoting the first stage of life, one might say to a suitor who has made his request in absentia: "Is she not indeed a maiden? Is she too young or too old? If, when the maiden has been given away, she should inform the king, saying, "My daughter was most beautiful; this man, while making his request, had a longing for her," and having spoken thus, he is defeated—then, if this was said at the appropriate time, this is the penalty for the defeated party.
The mantras of marriage are established for maidens alone;
they never apply to non-maidens among men, for such women have lost their eligibility for religious rites.

The taking of the hand is marriage, the act of taking a wife, because the mantras are present therein; moreover, through the connection with these two [mantras], "He sacrificed to Agni" and "She sacrificed to Agni," they demonstrate their agency in the marriage.
However, in reality, what is enjoined in the rule for marriage is that one should approach the maiden; the mantras express precisely that same meaning.
Furthermore, marriage with virgins does not occur simply because the word "virgin" (kanyā) is heard in the mantras, for mantras do not possess injunctive force (*avidhāyakatva*).
This very point is reinforced by means of a prohibition of the opposite:
"Nowhere among men [is there marriage] with those who are not virgins."

In no branch of the Veda is a marriage of men with a woman who is not a maiden (akanyā) heard of. Those whose sacred rites have been suspended have no entitlement to dharma, such as the Agnihotra, nor to the injunction for procreating offspring; therefore, they are not to be married.
Consequently, it is stated immediately after the preceding verse that one who calls a maiden "not a maiden" should be subjected to a heavy penalty.
A girl who has not attained sexual intercourse is called a maiden (*kanyā*).
The mantras of the taking of the hand are the definitive mark of a wife;
their completion, however, should be understood by the wise to occur at the seventh step.
*Dāra* means wife; its characteristic mark is the *nimitta*, namely the marriage mantras. By their employment therein, the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) called marriage is accomplished.
For the twice-born (*dvijāti*), however, there are [specific] mantras.
In that regard, there is the occasion for a Śūdra to take a wife, yet he has no mantras; with the exception of the mantras, all other procedural requirements (*itikartavyatā*) exist for him as well.
Therefore, the mantras are indicative of the sacramental rite known as marriage.
The completion (*niṣṭhā*) of those mantras should be understood to occur at the seventh step.

Having performed the oblation of fried grain (*lājāhoma*) and having circumambulated the fire three times to the right, the woman takes seven steps, beginning with "Become one-footed," and so on, up to "Become a companion at the seventh step."
Once he has departed, there is no cause for regret on the part of the girl’s father or the bridegroom;
even Unmādinī remains his wife and must not be abandoned.
However, this is not at all a marriage in the case of a woman who has already had sexual intercourse;
even though the nature of the ritual procedure—such as the offering of parched grain and so forth—is present, she does not become a wife.
Therefore, in that case, there is a right of rescission (anuśaya) just as with other commodities.

Just as the *āhavanīya* fire is not produced by an *ādheya* rite performed by a *śūdra*, so too, even if the fire-consecration (*agnisaṃskāra*) is performed for a woman who is a *sapiṇḍa*, it does not constitute the essential nature of marriage (*vivāhasvarūpa*). In that case, however, it is well known from the words of Vasiṣṭha that because of performing such a consecration, one man incurs the need for penance (*prāyaścitta*), and the girl remains ineligible for marriage even with another man.

If one has married a woman afflicted by a disease that prevents procreation and does not abandon her, what then is the recourse? As long as he possesses the capacity [to marry again], he shall marry another; however, this is like the case of a wife who speaks unpleasantly, where the rule applies immediately. But once the *ādhāna* (consecration of the fires) has been performed and she has borne a son, even if she should suffer from a wasting disease, he must not supersede her, because the grounds for supersession are specifically enumerated.
Even in that case, if this [rule] "but for those who have proceeded out of desire" is accepted as the governing principle, we do not object;
by that very [principle], the law regarding a maiden is stated in brief.
Just as for other goods there may be a peaceful restitution even after ten days have passed, it is not so for maidens who have already been married.

Even for those who are to be given as a bride-price (*śulka*), the same legal principle regarding other property applies prior to the marriage; however, because of the scriptural statement that "for her who is given for the sake of dharma, there is no rescission at all," even in that case, there is indeed the possibility of taking back the girl up until the seventh step, according to the rule: "One may take back even a girl already given if a superior suitor arrives."
But in the seventh step, because the giving has not ceased—as in the case of giving material objects such as cows—there is no taking away.

Furthermore, when a cow has been given by one person to another, there is no subsequent regret regarding the giving or the receiving due to a mutual desire between the two, because the act of giving has ceased at that very moment.
If, however, the recipient were to give it back to the donor, that would constitute a new act of giving; it would not be a cessation of the previous gift.
Thus, there is no mutual renunciation by a bride and groom who possess their respective qualities, even prior to the marriage;
nor, once the marriage has been performed, is there any renunciation of the bride even if she is found to have defects.
A girl who has experienced sexual intercourse is no longer a maiden and is therefore abandoned, because the marriage of a maiden is what constitutes her being married.
And marriage is equivalent to "use.
Just as a garment that has been worn is not returned to the seller even within ten days, so too is a maiden once married.
Furthermore, this matter will be determined later in the section concerning the rule that "a maiden is given only once."
In whatever matter one may have a cause for regret after it has been performed,
one should establish that person on the path of righteousness by means of this procedure.

This ten-day period of legal uncertainty (*anuśaya*) is not only the rule for the merchandise of merchants; rather, by means of this repetition—"in whatever [transaction]"—all undertakings, such as wages, agreements, interest, and loans, are encompassed by this ten-day procedure.
"Lawful" (*dharmya*) means not departing from the Dharma. "Path" (*panthā*) means a way.
The king should establish and settle [the matter];
this is an extension of the rule "when the task has been performed," because when the matter has already begun,
everything ceases to apply.
For where there is a latent liability (*anuśaya*), and that liability has been determined or established internally, there is a ten-day waiting period. However,

some maintain that this rule does not apply where money has been taken for the purpose of interest, or where a priest has been chosen and his fee paid, and a dispute has begun once the agreement was made.
For what has been done does not become undone;
and this [action] is said to be "ceased" because it was not performed, not because it had begun. For this suffix *kta* is not used here in the sense of the inception of an action (*ādikarman*).
For there is no reason to abandon the primary meaning.
As for the statement that "what has been done does not become undone," even though it has been done, it is as good as undone because its intended effect has been negated,
just like food that has been eaten and then vomited.
Even regarding worldly objects, there is a systematic order to be understood through the treatises (*śāstra*).
In some cases, engagement and non-engagement are to be known solely from the treatises;
even though these matters have already been established, their withdrawal is nevertheless prescribed.
Even when the investment of wealth has been completed and the coins have been brought to their proper place, they must be returned due to the lingering resentment of one party.
Losses and expenses incurred while the coins were being transported according to the rules of the treatises must be borne;
likewise, they desire a monthly interest on the coins as soon as they are received.
In this regard, the notion that "this bond must be enjoyed for such a length of time" and so forth is revoked within ten days by means of *anuśaya* (repentance).
However, the selection of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is like the marriage of maidens;
even though this rule exists in the scripture, the formal agreement (*saṃvid*) may proceed after ten days have passed.
I shall now duly declare, according to the principles of dharma, the legal dispute arising from the transgressions of both owners and herdsmen regarding livestock.

Regarding disputes between owners and herdsmen—such as cowherds and the like—concerning cattle and other livestock, when there is a conflict such as "My cow was destroyed by you; give it back to me," and the herdsman likewise contradicts this, saying "It was not my fault," I shall hereafter explain precisely and skillfully the true nature of the law and the legal settlement regarding this subject of litigation. This introductory summary of the section is intended to focus the attention of the audience.
If during the day the responsibility for loss falls on the keeper, and at night on the owner within his own house,
but if it be otherwise regarding the security of the property, then the keeper shall incur the responsibility for the loss.

During the day, when a fault arises regarding the acquisition and preservation of cattle—such as those things to be mentioned later, including their being lost or destroyed—the blame and censure fall upon the herdsman; therefore, he must bear that liability. At night, however, the fault lies with the owner in the case of animals that have died by hanging or other such means.
If they have been brought into the owner's house by the keeper, that is one case;
otherwise, however, if they have not been brought in by the keeper even at night and remain in the forest itself, then the keeper shall be liable for the loss.
This is what is meant.
When cows under the care of a herdsman eat the crop of someone’s field or are killed by someone, then [the responsibility] lies with the herdsman;
but if they have been entrusted to him by the herdsman, then it lies with the owner.
Here, the term *yogakṣema* is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) for what is not actually *yogakṣema*.
Just as one with sight [is distinguished] from the blind.
What is this "security and well-being" (yogakṣema)?
Therefore, he elaborates:
"A cowherd who is paid with milk may milk at most ten cows."
That [fee] shall be the wages for a servant with the master's consent; it shall be the wages for a herdsman when he is not otherwise paid.
A cowherd is one who protects cows;
he is sometimes supported by food and the like, and sometimes by milk.
Among these, one supported by milk [receives] from ten cows either the best (*varām*) or the worst (*avarām*), due to the elision of the vowel *a* in the *saṃhitā* text.

Regarding protection, there must be proportionality. He who has no other food should take the milk of a single cow from ten [cows]. According to this principle, wages should be calculated for the protection of fewer or more animals.

In this manner, when driving out cows that are either milkable or non-milkable, as well as heifers, young oxen, or calves, the owners should determine whether one-third or one-fourth of the milk is to be given [to the herdsman].
This verse is intended merely to provide a general indication; however, the specific local regulations of the region must be followed.
If the village cowherd, thinking "I shall determine the wages," abandons the cows, he must not milk a tenth cow without having obtained the permission of the owner.
Even one who is paid with food might milk [the cows] with the intention of exchanging them for milk; to prevent that, it is stated that he must have the consent of the owner of the cows.
One who proceeds without the consent of the owner is liable to punishment.
That which was just mentioned:
if one has not been supported by food and so forth, there should be support;
or this mode of livelihood may consist of being supported by milk.
A servant engaged in cow-herding for the sake of maintenance and not for the sake of religious duty,
or one who takes the milk of a tenth cow by his own will, would be a thief; however,
since this [taking] is permitted in this case with the thought, "this is his wages," there is no fault.
If it is argued that even here there is certainly a fault due to acting without the owner's consent, that is true; however, some measure of punishment must be devised.
Yet, such a person does not become a thief;
rather, in this case, he would be a misappropriator of a deposit.
This verse should be stated at the beginning;
therefore, it is recited in some places immediately following that.
If an animal is lost, destroyed by worms, killed by a dog, or dies in a dangerous place,
the keeper alone shall make restitution if it was due to a lack of human effort.
"Lost" means having departed from the range of vision; it is not known where it has gone.
"Destroyed" means by worms.
Worms named *ārohaka* enter through the cow's birth canal and cause its destruction.
"Killed by dogs"—
this is stated for the sake of illustration;
therefore, this same rule applies to those killed by jackals, tigers, and other such animals.
If an animal dies in a dangerous place such as a precipice, a cave, or among rocks,
the keeper alone shall pay compensation for the loss,
provided that the death was due to a lack of human effort on his part.
Human effort (*puruṣakāra*) is human activity.
In this case, it refers to the presence of the guardian and his engagement in warding off wolves by means of sticks and other such tools;
[the fruit] is "separated" from that.

If, while making an effort to ward off a tiger or similar threat, he is simply not capable, or if some animal suddenly springs up and rushes into a pit with such speed that even one pursuing it cannot turn it back, there is no fault on the part of the keeper.
If cattle have been stolen by thieves after being publicly proclaimed, the herdsman is not liable to pay,
provided he reports it to his own master at the proper place and time.
If cattle have been stolen by thieves after the drums have been beaten and proclaimed, the herdsman is not made to pay for the animal.
The proclamation is intended to indicate the herdsman's incapacity [to prevent the theft];
if many thieves plunder by force, then the herdsman is released from liability.
If he, when the time is right, reports it to his master at that very moment—
whether in the region where the master is present,
or how he knows it to be there, or else in the master’s place of residence.
In that case, even if the owner is not present, he is nevertheless represented by one who, having informed the king or an official, attacks the thieves;
the word "his own" (*svasya*) is used to exclude the king.
For a master makes an effort to recover his own property, whereas a king, even when informed by a guardian, does not do so to the same extent.
And it is difficult for a guardian to report [the theft] to the king;
furthermore, if he were to report it after the thieves have already fled, he would indeed be guilty of an offense.
One should give the ears, hide, tail-hairs, bladder, sinews, and bile to the owners of the animals; when they have died, one should show them the identifying marks.
When the animals have died due to the exhaustion of their lifespan, the ears and other parts should be offered to the owner.
*Gorocanā* is the powder found within the horns of cows.
A *basti* is a specific part of the body.
The marks are signs such as the ear-cuts and so forth, intended for the purpose of identifying the specific owner;
he should also display these.
In this manner, the keeper is cleared of liability.
For through the sight of a mark, recognition occurs, such as: "This is that same animal."
But when goats and sheep are hemmed in by wolves and the herdsman does not come to their aid,
whatever wolf may forcibly kill shall be the fault of the herdsman.
The goat and the sheep are "goats and sheep" (*ajāvikau*);
the ewe is "ewe and ram" (*avikaiḍakā*).
These, when hemmed in or besieged by wolves, jackals, and the like, are not killed at the very first attack.

In this interval, because he has not been released until his liberation and the herdsman has not come to set him free, if the wolf should kill [the animal] there by force, having overcome it, while the herdsman does not come— that is the fault of the herdsman. He must cause the master to pay [compensation],
and he himself must perform an expiation.
Because of the cow's great importance, it cannot be obstructed by a jackal; therefore, the term "goat and sheep" is used, but not because they possess that [jackal-like] nature.
Consequently, this same principle applies to young calves as well.
If, among those cows being grazed together in the forest,
a wolf should spring upon and kill one of them while they are penned, the herdsman is not at fault in that matter.
In the preceding verse, the dual number (*dvivacana*) in *ajāvike* is used with respect to the species;
because it is a *dvandva* compound of animals and birds, its singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) is optional.
Here, however, the reference in the plural as *tāsām* (of them) is made with respect to the individual instances.

When animals have been corralled, placed together in one location, gathered into a herd, their movement restricted from the cardinal and intermediate directions, and they are grazing in the forest within the range of sight—if a wolf should emerge from some thicket and kill one through the sequence of moving and leaping, the keeper is not liable for the fault; for it is impossible to make a forest dense with many trees, shrubs, reeds, and creepers free of gaps, and wolves follow such openings. Furthermore, because of the mention of "together," if a killing occurs when the animals are scattered at a very great distance, there is indeed fault.

When animals have fallen into the hands of a keeper, if they should incur a loss through his negligence, it must be rectified by that very keeper; this detailed exposition is provided for the sake of easy understanding, even though the principle is already established.
The common land surrounding a village shall be one hundred bows on all sides, or else three throws of a yoke-pin; for a city, however, it shall be three times that amount.
A bow of theirs is four cubits; a hundred [bows] is four hundred cubits;
[this is measured] all around in the four directions.
An exemption from taxes must be granted to the village. Land that has not been sown with crops should be set aside for the cattle to graze upon comfortably.

A *śamyā* is a wooden staff; having been propelled by the force of an arm, the area from which it is lifted and thrown again until it lands for the third time constitutes its measurement, or the exemption (*parihāra*) is the space covered by such a throw of the *śamyā*.
Three times that is the measure for a city.

A village and a city are well known. The "falling of a *śamyā*" refers to the cessation of the velocity-impetus (*vega-saṃskāra*) of a *śamyā* that has been projected, resulting in its coming to rest upon the ground.
If cattle should destroy unenclosed grain there,
the king shall not inflict punishment upon the keepers of the animals.

In that case, no field should be cultivated on land subject to such exemptions; if it has been cultivated, then the livelihood derived from it is forfeited. Therefore, the fault lies solely with the owners of the field, not with the cattle-herders.
For indeed, Pāla, one cannot lead each individual animal away by binding it with the hand,
nor is there any other exit for the animals.
One should construct a fence there such that a camel cannot look over it,
and one should block every opening through which the face of a dog or a pig could pass.
The arrangement of thorny branches and the like as a fence around fields, gardens, and so forth, for the purpose of preventing the entry of livestock, is called a *vṛti*.
That which is commonly known in some places as a *parṇikā* is a *vāraṇā-vṛti* (a fence for warding off). Its height should be made such that a camel cannot look over it.
Is this [word] "camel" used in the second case in the sense of the third case? [That is, does it mean "by means of a camel" or "from the perspective of a camel"?]
We say: "No.
How then does the camel not see the enclosure?
Because it does not see the second side, which is at a great height, the enclosure remains unseen.
One should block every hole and opening;
whatever can be entered by the snout of a dog or a pig should be made the size of that snout, so that even the snout of a dog cannot fit.
The meaning is that even from its opening there is only a small aperture.
When an enclosure has been made in this manner,
if cattle enter a fenced field on the road or one situated near a village,
the keeper is liable to a fine of one hundred [paṇas]; however, he should drive away the animals if they are unattended.
On a road that is enclosed, in a field situated near a village, and within the area designated for exemption (*parīhāra*),
the word "end" (*anta*) signifies proximity.

If an animal should eat [the crops] while it has a keeper— that is, when a keeper is present— the keeper shall be subject to a fine of one hundred [paṇas], since a fine cannot be imposed upon the animal itself.
Even when the keeper is not present at home,
if that keeper is not well-known [to the owner], nor is there a watchman sent by him whose wages consist merely of a coin (rūpaka),
then the cattle, being without a keeper, must be warded off with sticks and the like, but they are not to be punished.
And [this applies to] those that are without a keeper, such as bulls that have been set loose; however, for other animals that are without a keeper, the fine falls upon the owner.
Alternatively, there is a *praśleṣa* (elision) of the word "unfenced" (*aparivṛte*).

And because of the connection with the field, the owner of the field, being understood [as present], is connected as the referent of the other member of the compound in the phrase "together with the keeper" (*sahapālena*), meaning that the owner of the field is "with the keeper.
Who is to be punished regarding the field?
Both are to be punished.
The owner of the field and the herdsman.
First, it is said, why did the owner of the field not construct a fence around his field on the path?
And by the herdsman as well, while the fence exists, why should the field be grazed upon?
One should restrain cattle that are without a keeper or have strayed from the herd due to negligence;
likewise, Gautama states: "On a path or in an unenclosed field, [the responsibility lies] with both the keeper and the owner of the field."
In other fields, however, the animal deserves a fine of one paṇa and a quarter;
but in all cases, it is the settled rule that a sixth part must be given to the owner of the field.
Fields other than those belonging to highways, fields for cultivation, or the outskirts of a village—when [cattle] graze upon these, the fine is one *paṇa* and a quarter.
Now, it might be argued that in this case there ought to be a small fine, since the field is near compared to a distant field;
however, when the field crosses the highway or is outside the village, a heavy fine is appropriate.
"Why does the cowherd permit them to go there?
This is not a fault;
for if a heavy penalty were not prescribed here, then through their daily entering and exiting, the fields of neighboring villages would be ruined by the grazing cattle.
Out of fear of severe punishment, they protect [the cattle] with great effort;
otherwise, for one who leads the cows somewhere for the sake of specific grass, the punishment is slight.
Even in this case, there must be a prohibition against those who are without a herdsman.
In all cases, the field-owner is entitled to a good fruit when it is given;
and those [fruits] have been determined by the experts according to measure for the cultivator.
"Because he has a field," [the suffix] *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *vrīhi*;
this is "dhāraṇā," meaning this is the settled conclusion.
And because of the inclusion of the word "all," the owner of the field obtains compensation even when the animal is without a keeper.

Although the word *paśu* (beast) is a general term applicable to buffaloes, goats, sheep, camels, donkeys, and so forth, nevertheless, based on the observation of other Smṛtis, it is understood that this penalty applies specifically to cows.
Accordingly, Gautama states elsewhere regarding other calculations: "Ten [paṇas] for a horse or a buffalo; two for goats or sheep," and so forth.
In this regard, there is an exception:
"Manu has declared that one should not be punished for killing a cow within ten days of calving, nor bulls, nor animals dedicated to the gods, whether they have a keeper or are without a keeper."
From the mention of "cows," there is an implication of faults regarding buffaloes and the like. "Vṛṣas" refers to bulls.
"Deva-paśus" (sacrificial animals for the gods) are those prepared by the sacrificer for the purpose of a divine sacrifice, with the ritual imminent.
Furthermore, images of lions, elephants, and so forth, established upon mounds of bricks and the like, are called "deities";
their "animals" are those which have been released by someone for their sake.

For at that time, because a relationship of owner and owned exists between the gods and the animals, and because a relationship of master and servant is impossible for a human, this rule applies to those who serve as ornaments in the temples of the gods; it does not, however, apply to those kept in the temples by their guardians for the purpose of carrying loads,
milking, and so forth, since it is those very guardians who employ them for the sake of the gods.
Therefore, in that case, only the keepers are the owners;
hence, whatever duty belongs to others who possess ownership is applicable there.
However, unappropriated objects used for the adornment of sacred sites produce the purity of a divine animal without any intervening obstacle.
Bulls released according to the ritual procedures for the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) and other such rites may be taken up by some;
whether they are subsequently accompanied by a keeper or, if not taken up, become unattended, there is no punishment for either case.
In the event of a transgression by the landowner, the fine shall be ten times his share;
however, if it occurs through the negligence of the servants, the fine for the landowner shall be half of that.

If there should be a transgression, violation, or offense committed by the owner of the field on his own field—such as sowing at the wrong time, sowing unsuitable seeds during the summer heat, having his own cattle graze there, or entering his house with fruit unbeknownst to him—then he should be fined ten times the amount of the share that would otherwise go to the king.

Now, if this was done without his knowledge by servants employed for the protection of the field, then the fine for the servants is half; the connection [of the rule] is that "in the case of an offense by the servants, the fine for the field-owner is [half]."
This has been stated here in connection with the topic of the field (*kṣetra*).
A righteous lord of the earth should observe this rule in cases of transgression involving owners of livestock, the animals themselves, and the herders.
This verse is easy to understand.
When a dispute has arisen concerning a boundary between two villages,
one should determine the boundary in the month of Jyeṣṭha when the landmarks are clearly visible.

In the phrase "regarding the boundary" (*sīmāṃ prati vivāde*), the word *sīmā* functions as the cause for the boundary. Because the prefix *prati* is a *karmapravacanīya* when used in the sense of a "mark" (*lakṣaṇa*) or "being in such a state" (*itthaṃbhūta*), it can be said that the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is also [used] on account of the mark.
"Boundary" (*sīmā*) means the limit (*maryādā*), the division of villages and so forth, the measure, the extent, or, in short, the delimitation.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, the determination must be carried out.

He states the reason for specifying this particular month: "When the boundary markers are clearly visible. By "markers" (setavaḥ) are meant the boundary signs to be described later—specific types of boundaries such as clods of earth, stones, and so forth. This is because prior to this time, when grasses like *tṛṇa* and *guñjā* have grown up, no distinction can be perceived between the clods and stones and other parts of the ground.
When grasses are no longer visible there because it has been marked by stones, then that is determined to be the boundary;
the same applies to places where creepers grow and so forth.
Prior to spring, no distinction is perceived in the springtime burning.
And because the reason has been stated, one must not grant a delay of time beyond the month in which [the symptoms] are manifested in a particular place;
however, at other times, there may be a requirement for time in order to recognize the signs—this is the sole purpose of mentioning the "elder" (jyeṣṭha).
And he should establish boundary trees— *nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*, *kiṃśuka*, *śālmalī*,
*sāla*, *tāla*, and indeed milk-exuding trees.
"Pādapas" are trees;
"milky-sapped" refers to those such as the *arka* and *udumbara*.
Because these are long-lived, they should be planted only at the boundary location, not in the middle of the village.
If performed outside the designated boundary, they would not be determinative.
Bushes, various types of bamboos, śamī trees, creepers, and level ground,
as well as reeds and kubjaka thickets— in this manner, the boundary is not lost.
Stones, bones, cow-hair, husks, ashes,
potsherds, dried cow-dung, bricks, charcoal, gravel, and likewise sand;
And he should cause other boundary markers to be concealed,
having observed that in the world there is constant confusion among men regarding the knowledge of boundaries.
Shrubs (*vīrudhaḥ*) are those with compact trunks; thickets (*gulmāni*) are bamboos, *āragvadha* trees, and so forth.
The term "various" (*vividha*) is used because of their great number.
Vallis (creepers), *vratatī* (twining plants), long sprouts, types of grasses, artificial grounds, and mounds covered with young grass and the like;
the separate mention of the *kubjaka* (the *Arjuna* tree) is for the sake of emphasis, as it is classified as a shrub (*gulma*).
Karīṣa is dried cow dung.
Aṅgāra refers to pieces of wood burnt by fire.
Śarkarā refers to earth hardened like stone.
A skull-shaped fragment shall be one part of the boundary;
the king should cause other [markers] to be concealed for the sake of a final determination once a new village has been settled.
In this way, the boundary shall never perish.
Otherwise, someone might destroy that area by plowing it.
Reservoirs, wells, ponds, and springs,
as well as temples, should be constructed at the junctions of boundaries.
Large bodies of water are ponds; *vāpīs* are lotus-pools;
and *udapānas* are wells and the like.
Springs are flows of water; places where water trickles slightly are regions of the earth.
Sanctuaries of deities are the abodes of yakṣas and so forth.
These are illuminating factors.
For these [boundary markers] cannot be destroyed with little effort, and if they were destroyed, there would be great transgression. Furthermore,
because everyone seeking water and everyone seeking a vision of the deity is present there, the junction of the boundary becomes easily known by the witnesses.
Furthermore, those of this kind which the earth would not consume due to their age,
he should cause to be placed inconspicuously at junctions and boundaries.
The instruction regarding *gulma* and the others is for the purpose of illustration, not for the purpose of exhaustive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*).
Such types include the essence of *khadira*, black collyrium, and so forth, which are similar to sugar and the like.
What constitutes this "being of such a type"?
Therefore, he says: "The earth shall not consume [the sinner] because of time.
The consumption by the earth is used as a metaphor to indicate its essential nature;
just as that which has been consumed is no longer perceived as a distinct entity, in that same way, one should make it appear as if it has become one with the earth.
By these signs, as well as by long-standing possession and the constant flow of water, the king shall determine the boundary between two disputing parties.

When both villages are empty, [the boundary] is to be determined by signs; or by the continuous and uninterrupted prior possession of those residing there, provided its limit is not forgotten— not merely by possession for three generations, for that is prohibited as a means of proof in the case of "a pledge or a boundary," since neglect is possible there because a boundary is common to many.
However, for those who do not recite the word *sīma* (boundary) there, the authority of possession (*bhukti*) is already established;
since the authority of indicative marks (*liṅga*) has already been stated, one might suspect the exclusion of other means of proof, and thus it is stated again:
"What is this 'arrival of water' that is mentioned as a means of proof?"
Just as other boundary markers are established at the time of a new settlement, so too must the flow of water be established.
Alternatively, in the case of two villages where that same arrival of water is the cause of division in one area while there is a dispute in another area, that very water is the authority.
Or rather, this refers to the case of a large village.
Or, if there is another village on the opposite bank of a river, one should not say of that [river] "our land exists even here";
for even if some land is separated from a certain village by such a current, that very [river] remains the cause of demarcation in the case of a small-scale encroachment.
If doubt were to persist even upon seeing the marks,
then the determination of the boundary dispute would depend solely on the testimony of witnesses.
But how can there be doubt when the characteristic marks are present?
As for those that are concealed, if they were somehow brought from one place to another in concealment by someone, there would be no certainty at all.

Even those that are visible, such as the *nyagrodha* trees and others, do not grow only within a boundary; they are born elsewhere as well. Therefore, because they appear [only] as such, there is doubt.

Furthermore, where this kind of estimation does not exist, there the means of proof (*pramāṇa*) itself consists of the indicative signs (*liṅga*). "Reliance on witnesses" (*sākṣipratyaya*) means having witnesses as its cause; it refers to that case wherein the conviction rests upon the witnesses.
Certainty (*viniścaya*) is the realization of reality (*tattvādhigama*).
The intended meaning is that in a dispute over boundaries, where the evidence is doubtful or non-existent, the determination is based on witnesses.
In the presence of the villagers' families and the witnesses at the boundary,
the markers of the boundary should be questioned by both of those disputants.

Even if a village consists of countless people, nevertheless, when two litigants from two villages are at issue, witnesses regarding the boundary must be questioned in the presence of those two, as well as other local families and the assembled multitude of villagers.

At the time of questioning the witnesses, all the villagers—even those engaged in legal business—must remain present; neither the plaintiff nor the defendant is permitted to say, "Why are these people standing by in a dispute concerning a matter that concerns only us?"
Alternatively, if certain very elderly persons from neighboring villages are designated as witnesses, other inhabitants of those villages should be present;
for they have heard [the facts] from those elders, and when questioned in their presence, the elders will not deviate from the truth regarding the boundary markers.
Where there are signs of both kinds, the determination of the boundary is made after ascertaining them from the elders;
where such signs are absent, witnesses are questioned regarding the boundary itself, asking, "What is the boundary here?"
Once they have been questioned, he should fix the boundary exactly according to the decision they all unanimously declare, recording the names of all of them as well.
Whatever determination those witnesses may declare, all of them [should be recorded];
however, the rule regarding the statement of conflicting testimonies—namely, that when there is a division, the majority prevails—does not apply here.
He should fix it in writing, that is, he should inscribe it upon a document.
And as for witnesses, they are so called by way of distinction.
Bearing the earth upon their heads, wearing garlands and red garments, they—
having been made to swear by their own meritorious deeds— shall lead you with justice.

Having taken clods of earth from the broad earth with their heads, the witnesses— wearing garlands, bearing wreaths as appropriate, wearing red-colored flowers, dressed in red garments, and having red coverings—
even though the root *rañj* also functions in the sense of producing a different color from white, its usage is most frequent for red, as in "a red cow" or "red [color]";
and this is intended to produce fear.
And those wearing red garments become agitated;
they are made to say, "Let whatever merit we have acquired be rendered fruitless.
They should each recount their own good deeds by means of their respective specific names, using the distributive repetition "each by their own."
The giving away of a daughter in marriage, bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha), and so forth—
these are specific ritual acts.
They should lead [the deceased] by means of that path which is upright and righteous, being not devoid of truth.
*Samañjasam* is an adverbial modifier. They should lead [the litigants] by means of that path which is not departed from truth (*satya*), which is straight (*ṛju*), and righteous (*dhārmika*).
*Samañjasam*, *ṛju*, and *spaṣṭam* have one and the same meaning. And since truthful conduct is said to be clear (*spaṣṭa*), it is called *samañjasam*.
Those who lead [the case] according to what has been stated are purified as truthful witnesses;
but those who lead it contrarily shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas].

When falsehood is determined through other means of proof, through signs that are otherwise inexplicable, or from more trustworthy persons, the fine for each of the two hundred [coins] shall be imposed.
This is because each one acts as a witness, and witnesses are subject to punishment; for they do not testify collectively.
Witnesses who are devoted to truth—truthful witnesses—are purified; they are not bound by the sin of speaking untruth.
According to what has been stated, by way of reality as it truly is (*yāthātathya*);
for there is no occasion here for speech consisting of mere words.
By this, only the correspondence with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indicated.
Alternatively, "by the truth" means by that which has been stated according to the scriptures;
for it is said in the scriptures that one must speak the truth, and therefore it is expressed as "by the truth as it has been stated."
In the absence of witnesses, however, four inhabitants living on the outskirts of the village boundary shall,
being purified, determine the boundary in the presence of the king.
The neighbors of the village and those living on the borders should be questioned; one should reach a decision based on their testimony,
according to the rules for witnesses, and not otherwise.
The phrase "in the presence of the king" is for the purpose of completing the verse;
it does not mean that the neighbors determine [the matter] according to their own will as if they were the king.
But in the absence of neighboring villagers, he should also interrogate these men who dwell in the forest and live within the boundaries of the original inhabitants.
The relationship between the qualifier and the qualified in the phrase "of the primary neighboring [elements]" is for the sake of praise.
Those that arise at the time of the establishment of the village and coexist with its origination are called "primary" (*maula*).
And these neighbors are eternal, because they are eternally present.
Their non-existence as well follows from their having been somehow eradicated;
what then is the recourse?
At that time, one should also inquire about these [points] which are about to be explained.
Alternatively, the original witnesses (*maula*) have been explained; the neighbors (*sāmantas*) are those who should be interrogated.
In the absence of the aforementioned original witnesses, the neighbors are the authority.
In their absence, one should employ forest-dwellers and question them skillfully.
Hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers,
snake-catchers, gleaners, and other forest-dwellers.
These [ascetics] wander through the forests;
while traveling through the midst of a village, they might perhaps learn of that event.
For, as they travel along that path, having previously seen some men plowing a disputed area, they would ask: "What is this village that is being plowed by you?"
In this way, prior experience is possible; for example,
hunters who live by hunting—
even when they are pursuing a deer that has escaped from the forest— have a connection with villages.
Likewise, there are fowlers who live by catching birds;
they roam through all the villages in search of them. There are also cowherds who wander here and there to identify various types of grass for their cattle.
Fishermen (*kaivarta*) and boatmen (*dāśa*), who subsist by digging ponds and other such works, go here and there; where would our labor be of use?
Root-diggers (*mūlakhānaka*) dig for the roots of trees and thick *kāśa* grass and the like.
Snake-catchers (*vyālagraha*) are those who seize serpents; for the sake of their livelihood, they too search for snakes in various locations.
Therefore, they too have many connections with those belonging to surrounding villages;
even those who live by gleaning, though poor, sustain themselves merely for their livelihood by wandering through many villages,
as do others seeking fruits, flowers, and firewood.
Whatever marks for the boundary junctions those witnesses may declare when questioned,
the king shall establish that according to the law for both villages.
The construction is: "they were questioned according to the Dharma. "Sīmāsandhayaḥ" means those boundaries and the junctions;
a junction is the meeting point of two villages.
And that is indeed the boundary;
the characteristic is the indicator.
The determination of boundaries for fields, wells, tanks, groves, and houses is to be understood as depending upon the testimony of the neighbors.
An *ārāma* is a grove or garden, as well as a vegetable patch;
the determination regarding its extent is based on its surrounding area.
This is stated for the purpose of excluding hunters and the like.
The boundary-mark is the boundary-binding;
it is that which is tied down or established for the purpose of defining the limits of a boundary.
If the neighbors should speak falsely when men are disputing over a boundary,
they shall all be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement.
The punishment for neighbors is greater than that for previous [categories of persons].
The phrase "separately, separately" is a restatement (anuvāda), as the underlying principle has already been stated.
Those living near a field and so forth are necessarily aware [of what occurs there].
The severity of the punishment for these [witnesses] increases according to their proximity.
However, since it is not mandatory for neighbors to know the boundaries belonging to others, the fine of two hundred [paṇas] should be applied to them as well;
thus, for witnesses and neighbors at a village boundary, the fine is two hundred.

However, those who, relying on the term "neighbor" (*sāmanta*), claim that there should be equal punishment because of the neighborly status of both village and field boundaries, are to be disregarded due to their contradiction with logic.
One who seizes a house, a pond, a garden, or a field by means of intimidation shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; if it was done through ignorance, the fine shall be two hundred.

This is stated because of the context concerning fields and so forth. The mention of "fear" is intended to illustrate the underlying motive. For one who steals while knowing that "this belongs definitively to this person," the fine is five hundred.

When the "middle-level violence" (*madhyama-sāhasa*) has been established, the mention of the "five-hundred [paṇas]" is for the purpose of adjusting the punishment upward or downward according to specific circumstances.
Alternatively, some consider that the specific number mentioned previously was not intended to be definitive;
thus, one seizes property by instilling fear, saying: "I shall cause this to be recorded in legal proceedings," "I shall have the king punish you," or "I shall have you harmed by thieves."
In that case, the infliction of punishment is an alternative provision for other intervening circumstances.
When a boundary cannot be determined, the king himself, knowing the law, shall assign land to some based on their relative benefit; such is the established rule.
"Inconceivable" means impossible to determine, due to the absence of indicative marks or witnesses.
The king alone, by his own will, should assign—that is, grant—the land, saying, "This land is yours, this is yours.
One who knows the Dharma must not show partiality toward anyone at all.
This is what he says: by reason of mutual benefit.

By whatever boundary both villages become equally beneficial, by that [boundary], even if the land of one should be smaller—if the field be of good quality and highly productive—that location is to be considered in relation to it.
The fifth case [is used] in the sense of *lyablopa* (the elision of a gerund);
that is, with reference to assistance.
Alternatively, one might bestow [wealth] upon some, while taking it away from others in an uncertain manner.
