If the group of disputants is unable to define that boundary while others are capable of doing so, then he should assign it to others;
in this way, benefit is secured for himself as well as for many of the villagers.
Thus has the law regarding the determination of boundaries been declared in its entirety;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the determination of verbal abuse.
The meaning of the verse is a prior summary, which introduces a subsequent concise statement.

Having stated "in the case of physical assault (*daṇḍa*) and verbal abuse (*vācika*)," there would be a change in sequence for the sake of brevity: verbal abuse first, and then the application of physical force.

However, since in a *dvandva* compound the sense of the individual members is understood through their mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), and because each member conveys both meanings, the word "assault" (*daṇḍa*) also includes the meaning of speech; thus, what change in sequence is there?

And thus, the commencement of the *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence of order) sūtra was justified by the author of the *Mahābhāṣya*, relying on this very view [in the statement]: "Because of the indication of technical terms (*saṃjñā*) and compounds (*samāsa*)."
A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred [paṇas];
a Vaiśya deserves either fifty or two hundred; but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment.

Harsh speech is abuse (*ākrośa*). It is of many kinds: speaking cruelly or indecently; piercing the vital points (*marma*); cursing (*abhiśāpa*), such as "May you become a low-born outcaste (*vṛṣala*)"; causing pain through falsehood, such as saying "Your daughter is pregnant"; and associating one with major or minor sins (*pātaka-upapātaka*).
In that regard, this is the punishment for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who abuses a Brāhmaṇa.
In other cases, such as when an accusation involving a *pātayitavya* offense has been made, the punishment is the middle amercement (*madhyama-sāhasa*), as stated in other Smṛtis.
For a Śūdra, "killing" (or corporal punishment) should be understood according to the specific nature of the verbal abuse, taking the form of beating, cutting off the tongue, execution, and so forth.
A Brāhmaṇa should be fined fifty [paṇas] for defaming a Kṣatriya;
for a Vaiśya, the fine should be twenty-five; and for a Śūdra, the punishment is twelve.

*Abhiśaṃsana* refers to every form of verbal abuse other than that which constitutes a *pātaka* (a sin causing loss of caste), because a different punishment is prescribed for the latter. Furthermore,
this [term] is used with the locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*),
whereas *vaiśye* is used with the locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*).
The punishment for a Brāhmaṇa who reviles and for one who is reviled has been stated.
However, regarding Kṣatriyas and others [reviling one another], the specific rule must be sought in other Smṛtis.
Thus says Gautama: "A Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya are treated like a Brāhmaṇa and a Rājanya."
In the case of mutual abuse, if a Kṣatriya should revile a Vaiśya, he shall be fined fifty [paṇas]; a Vaiśya who reviles a Kṣatriya shall be fined one hundred.
Likewise, if a Kṣatriya reviles a Śūdra, he shall be fined twenty-five; a Vaiśya [reviling a Śūdra] shall be fined fifty.
However, for a Śūdra reviling others, the fine will be stated according to their respective qualities.
In the case of an equal-caste offense among the twice-born, the fine shall be exactly twelve;
in the case of unspeakable disputes, that same amount shall be doubled.
The mention of "twice-born" (dvijāti) is not restrictive.
When there is mutual abuse between persons of equal caste, the fine is twelve [paṇas].
Equality is determined by birth, wealth, kinship, age, occupation, and learning, since no specific distinction has been taught.

In that regard, if the offender is of the same caste but superior in wealth, the fine is double; if he is of the same caste and superior in kinship, it is triple; and so on, up to sixfold for one who is destitute of all virtues against one possessing every virtue.
"Slanderous words" (*vādāḥ*), "abusive words" (*ākroṣāḥ*), and "unspeakable words" (*avacanīyāḥ*) are those directed toward an extremely cruel mother, sister, wife, and so forth.
The measure of the fine in such cases is double that [standard amount].
Because it is in the neuter gender, this "all" (sarva) is a remainder [referring to the entire category], and not restricted solely to the case of equal castes (*samavarṇa*).
Alternatively, the construction is "that very hundred," since the neuter gender has such force and because "hundred" was heard in the first verse.
Therefore, even in the case of unutterable offenses among those of equal caste, the fine is two hundred.

For the sake of establishing the indicative mark (liṅga), the word "measure" (parimāṇa), though not explicitly heard in the text, must be supplied; however, it is better to assume a word that is merely separated [from its context] than to supply one that is entirely absent.
But a once-born man who insults twice-born men with harsh speech shall suffer the cutting off of his tongue, for he is of low origin.

A Śūdra is of a single birth. If he reviles or insults members of the three higher castes with harsh speech associated with mortal sins (pātaka) and the like, or with speech of a cruel nature, he deserves the cutting off of his tongue.

The statement "born from the lowest" (jaghanyaprabhava)—meaning a Brāhmaṇa was produced from the feet—is an expression of the reason intended to include those born in the inverse order (pratiloma) as well.
They too are indeed of low origin, because there is a prohibition against any other caste [than these four], stating that "there is no fifth."
But for one who pronounces their name or caste with malice,
a glowing iron spike ten fingers long shall be thrust into his mouth.
*Abhidroha* means reviling, contempt, or the thought of disparagement, O Brāhmaṇa; "do not compete with me.
The same should be applied to other cases as well.
*Grahaṇa* means seizing (*graha*).
One utters a name without an honorific suffix, or with the addition of a contemptuous suffix, such as "Devadattaka.
This is done with malice—that is, anger; malice here means anger, reproach, or censure—and not out of jest.
"Niḥkṣepyaḥ" means to be thrown down; "prakṣepyaḥ" means to be cast [into]. "Śaṅkuḥ" means a stake or wedge. "Jvalan" means blazing, being set on fire; "ayomayaḥ" means made of iron or metal.
If he should out of pride give instruction in the Dharma to Brahmins,
the king shall cause hot oil to be poured into his mouth and his ears.

"This is your own duty; this is the procedure here; do not act thus; you are a follower of the Vedic tradition"—those who, out of pride born from knowing even a fragment of grammar, instruct Śūdras with such words as these, are subject to this punishment. However, there is no fault if one, out of affection or simply because he is a Brāhmaṇa, reminds someone who has forgotten due to some lapse regarding the distinction of place and time, saying: "Do not let the forenoon pass; perform the rites for the gods; satisfy the gods; wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder (upavītin); do not wear it over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta)."
"Scalded" means causing pain due to contact with fire; "one should pour" means one should sprinkle. It is appropriate for the mouth, because [the teacher] instructs by means of the mouth.
What is the fault of the ear?
It is the prior hearing of false reasoning and the like.
One who, out of pride, speaks falsely regarding another's learning, country, caste, or even their physical body, shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas].
Regarding what has been heard, he says, "This was not correctly heard by him";
he thus rejects even that which was heard, saying, "What he has heard is not purifying.
Regarding one who prides himself on his noble lineage from Brahmāvarta, he says, "He is a mere outsider."
Thus, one might call a Brahmin by birth a "Kṣatriya," or a Kṣatriya out of contempt a "Brahmin";
one might call a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) a "graduate" (snātaka);
or one might call a person with a bodily limb a "bodily being" (śārīra), or a person without a physical defect a "leper" (duścarmā).
"Vitathena" means "by the false" or "by the untrue"; the third case ending is used according to the rule *prakṛtyādibhya upasaṃkhyānam*.
Alternatively, "vaitathya" (falsity) is non-dharma (*adharma*), and its causality with respect to what is expressed is indeed logical.
Arrogance (*darpa*) is the contempt for others arising from pride in one's own qualities.
There is no fault if it occurs through ignorance or in jest.
But for whom is this punishment intended?
We say it applies to all;
others, however, hold that because of the context concerning Śūdras, it refers only to a Śūdra, while in the case of the twice-born, it refers to falsehood.
Whether one is one-eyed, lame, or otherwise similarly deformed,
even if speaking the truth, one shall be made to pay a fine of at least one *kārṣāpaṇa*.
One who is deficient in one eye is called *kāṇa* (one-eyed);
one who is deficient in a foot is *khañja* (lame).

Likewise, one who is *kuṇi* (crippled) or *cipaṭa* (flat-nosed), whether by truth or untruth—and by the word "api" (even), even by falsehood—if one says "he is one-eyed" when he is not one-eyed, or says "he is one-eyed" when he is indeed one-eyed, the fine shall be at least one *kārṣāpaṇa*.
If, for some reason, he is to be shown favor and the punishment is to be extremely slight, then the minimum fine is one *kārṣāpaṇa*.
Otherwise, depending on the specific status of the person, the Śūdra may be fined two, three, or five [kārṣāpaṇas], or all [the fines] may apply as previously stated.
One who defames his mother, father, wife, brother, son, or teacher shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who does not yield the path to his teacher.
Sowing discord by means of falsehood consists of causing estrangement and generating hatred.
For example, one causes division by saying such things as: "This mother of yours is not affectionate; she is excessively greedy for her second son and gave him a golden ring in secret.
In this way, one divides father and son, husband and wife, brothers, or teacher and disciple.
The mention of "the son" is for the purpose of indicating the second relative involved.
Otherwise, if only "the mother" were mentioned, the punishment would apply to one who alienates the mother from her son, but not to one who alienates the son from his mother.
Even though alienation has both as its substratum, in common practice, the person through whose agency the act is performed is the one who is to be considered the alienator.

In that context, since the term "son" is used for illustrative purposes, the offense occurs precisely when one reviles the mother by saying such things as, "This is not your son; he is ungrateful and ill-behaved," and so forth, and not toward the son as previously shown.
Others, however, define *ākṣāraṇa* (reviling) as the production of mental distress.

For instance, [if one says], "I shall explain wealth or sacred learning," or "I am going to frequent holy places," or "I am going on a journey"—if, through such words, the mother suffers mental anguish out of fear of his departure, she should not act in such a way.
"As long as those gurus live, one should not perform any other [duty] nor act without their permission.

However, regarding the production of distress in the mind through acts such as inciting hatred, one is not released from the hundredfold [penalty], because the fault is great, as it constitutes an opposition to the guru. To marry another woman when one's wife is compliant and has sons is "slander" (*ākṣāraṇa*).
If one treats a virtuous son otherwise than he deserves without cause,
or if one does not yield the path in every way to a teacher, the fine shall be one hundred [paṇas].
A wise king should inflict punishment upon both Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas:
for a Brāhmaṇa, the first amercement; but for a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement.
When a Brahmin and a Kṣatriya have mutually insulted each other, the construction [of the sentence] is to be understood by supplying the words: "this is the punishment for those two.
Alternatively, the dative case is used in the sense of purpose;
thus, the punishment must be inflicted for the sake of their discipline.
This punishment applies when an accusation of a mortal sin is made in the form of causing suffering.

In the case of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, it is likewise determined that, with respect to their own respective castes, the application of punishment shall be exactly as prescribed, with the exception of corporal mutilation.
In the same way, the first and middle [fines] for the two [lower] castes are extended by analogy;
thus, in that very order, for a Vaiśya's abuse of a Śūdra, the first fine applies,
and for a Śūdra's abuse of a Vaiśya, the middle fine applies.

"The infliction of punishment, with the exception of cutting off [the tongue]," means that by the phrase "a once-born man against a twice-born man," the [penalty of] cutting off the tongue was prescribed; this [present rule] sets that aside. "Against his own caste" refers to this.

One should not think that "similar class" (samānajātīya) refers to [any] similar caste; rather, the inclusion of the word "one's own" (*sva*) here— referring to the Vaiśya and Śūdra— is intended to mean,
according to the intent of the verse, as far as mutual verbal abuse is concerned.
The phrase "one's own caste" should be connected to the preceding [verses] as well. "Leading forth" means setting into motion.
For a Kṣatriya who incites a Vaiśya or a Śūdra [to commit an offense], the fine is half of the first *sāhasa*.
In this same manner, the rule applies to the Vaiśya and the Śūdra as well.
This rule for punishment regarding verbal abuse has been declared according to the truth;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the determination of punishment for physical assault.

*Daṇḍapāruṣya* (assault) is the infliction of suffering by means of a staff; just as the touch of a thorn or similar object causes pain to a person, the term *pāruṣya* is applied here because of this common quality of causing pain. In that context, "determination" refers to the determination of the specific punishment.
This verse is intended to serve as a summary and introduction to the preceding section.
If a person of the lowest caste should injure the highest caste with any limb whatsoever, that very limb of his must be cut off; such is the ordinance of Manu.
The *antyaja* refers to those starting from the Śūdra down to the Caṇḍāla;
the *śreṣṭha* refers to one belonging to the three higher castes.
If one should injure such a person with any limb—whether directly or by means of an intervening weapon such as a staff or a sword—that limb of his must be cut off.
Violence (*hiṃsā*) consists of striking with anger, raising the hand or another limb with the intent to strike and forcefully bringing it down—that is, killing itself.

The repetition "that... that" (*tad tad*) is used for distributive emphasis; the singular forms "limb" (*aṅga*) and "to be cut" (*chettavya*) are intended not to be understood as referring to a single part.
Therefore, when one strikes with multiple limbs, there must be a severing of each and every one.
"Instruction" (anuśāsana) means teaching; this is the boundary established by Manu. The mention of "instruction" is for the purpose of engaging a compassionate king [in this duty].
Raising his hand or his staff, he deserves the cutting off of his hand;
striking with his foot out of anger, he deserves the cutting off of his foot.
If, having raised and lifted up [the hand] out of anger with the intent to strike that limb, he does not let it fall, his hand shall be cut off.
The mention of a "staff" is intended as an illustration for any instrument of injury that causes similar pain;
therefore, in the case of a soft hoof or the like, another punishment applies.
Regarding the phrase "striking with the foot," here too it should be understood that "having raised [the foot]" is implied; this same [penance] applies even to one who merely threatens to strike.
One born of a lower caste who seeks to sit on the same seat as one of superior caste shall be branded on the hip and banished, or his buttock shall be cut off.
A Brāhmaṇa is superior by birth, even if he is inferior due to immoral conduct; the other castes are superior or inferior to one another in their respective order.
In this context, the term "born of an inferior [caste]" (*avakṛṣṭaja*) denotes an inferiority of birth (*janman*); because of its proximity, superiority is also understood as being by birth alone.
And for a Brāhmaṇa, there is absolute superiority by birth, not inferiority.
Therefore, this is the punishment for a Śūdra who has ascended the same seat as a Brāhmaṇa:
his hip— that is, his buttocks—
shall be marked there with a brand.

Furthermore, marking with nectar, saffron, and so forth in the rite of branding (*aṅkavidhi*) is not merely for the purpose of making a sign; rather, it is for the purpose of proclaiming the punishment, so that people might fear transgression. Therefore, that mark which remains indelible even in another country is taught as being produced by means of an iron stylus.
And so he will say later: "having branded them with punishments that cause terror.
He should also be expelled from the kingdom.
*Sphik* refers to a specific part of the buttocks.
The left and the right [buttocks]; and one should mark that with a sign. Because of the rule of optionality, there is a cutting off of only that much, not of the entire buttock.
And by the phrase "desiring to obtain," it is not meant merely by the presence of desire;
rather, it refers to one who has actually attained [the state].
This is because desire can easily be denied, whereas the punishment is severe.
The king shall cut off both lips of one who spits out of arrogance;
he shall cut off the penis of one who urinates [upon him], and the anus of one who passes wind [upon him].
If one sprinkles urine upon another, or throws it toward them for the purpose of insulting them—even if there is no physical contact—he insults them with urine and must be punished;
this same penalty applies to him as well because the result is identical.
Spitting refers to the discharge from the nose or the mouth.
If one emits [wind] from his nose with that [hand], his nostril is to be cut off, because it was stated [in the rule] "by whichever limb";
belching is a contemptuous sound from the anus;
this is done out of arrogance, not out of negligence.
If someone seizes him by the hair, one should cut off both his hands without hesitation; likewise for seizing him by the feet, the beard, the neck, or the testicles.
The word "out of pride" (darpāt) is understood to carry over.
One should have the hands of a Śūdra cut off if he seizes a Brāhmaṇa by the hair with the intent to insult him.
Although the dual number is used, both hands are to be cut off even if only one causes pain equal to that of two, not just one hand alone.
The beard is the facial hair.
Furthermore, for any other limb that, when seized, causes pain equal to that of seizing the neck and so forth, this same punishment applies in every case;
without hesitation.
The deliberation—attained through the subsequent verse—as to whether the suffering produced for one who has been seized is great or small, is hereby precluded;
the punishment applies to the mere act of seizing.
One who breaks the skin shall be fined one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who causes blood to flow;
but one who cuts the flesh shall be fined six niṣkas, while one who breaks a bone shall be banished.
This is stated regarding mutual offenses among the twice-born, as well as regarding the offense of a Śūdra against another Śūdra:
he who merely pierces or tears the skin but does not cause blood to appear shall be fined one hundred;
the same fine applies when blood is seen.

Although blood is not seen without piercing the skin, nevertheless, since a heavier punishment would apply due to the greater offense, the mention of "one hundred" is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*).
Others, however, say that this is stated for the sake of cases where blood flows from the ears, nose, and so forth, even when there is no external breach of the skin;
but that is incorrect.
For since the injury is greater when there is an internal breach, a heavy fine is appropriate; therefore, where blood flows even slightly, the fine is one hundred [paṇas],
but for a fracture of the skull, it is as in the case of [a wound to] the flesh.
It has been stated that the word *niṣka* denotes a specific measure of gold.

Regarding the phrase "one who causes the bones to be split is to be banished," one should read it as *asthibhedakṛt*, forming a compound with the word ending in the suffix *ghañ* and then adding the suffix *kvip* to express "one who performs that [action]. Thus, it means "one who effects the splitting of bones."
Exile (*pravāsana*) means execution according to the application of the *Arthaśāstra*, or it means banishment;
for the study of the *Arthaśāstra* is observed in the rules regarding punishments.
For instance, the usage "tenfold fine" (*daśabandha*) is found in the works of Bārhaspatya and Auśanasa.
The state of being free from latent tendencies belongs to the Brahmin alone, and not to others.
It is the established rule that the punishment for injuring any of the forest trees must be proportional to the degree of their utility.
The mention of "vanaspati" (trees) is for the purpose of illustrating all types of immobile beings (*sthāvara*).

Regarding the injury or destruction of a tree that provides great utility through its fruit, flowers, leaves, shade, and so forth, the punishment is the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*); for one of medium utility, the middle fine; and for one of low utility, the first fine.
Likewise, the specific location must be taken into account, as well as whether it involves the cutting of leaves, the cutting of fruit, or the cutting of branches.
There is also a distinction among fruits: their great value and their difficulty of attainment.
Likewise, one should observe the distinction of location as well—whether at a boundary, at a crossroads, or in a forest of asceticism.
When a blow is struck against humans or animals for the sake of causing pain,
one should inflict a punishment in proportion to the extent of that great suffering.
Regarding what was stated as "one who pierces the skin," this is its specific qualification.

If the term "human" were not included, and this verse were to apply to the injury of any living being whatsoever, there would be an equal penalty for large animals and small animals, such as beasts, birds, and wild animals; it is for that purpose [the term "human"] is used.
This is so that the punishment may correspond to the degree of suffering, as in the phrase "according as the pain is great."

In the case of a slight wound or a small amount of blood from living beings, because of the [relative] insignificance of the blow, one deserves a fine of less than a hundred [paṇas], even if it is more than a hundred; whereas if the wound is great, the fine is more than a hundred, even if it is less. Others, however, hold that because of the mention of "greatness," this refers to the increase of the fine when there is great suffering, not for the purpose of reduction in the case of a slight [wound]; thus, it remains exactly as stated in the text. In that context, "struck for the sake of pain" means a blow intended to produce pain.
But there is no increase [of merit] through negligence.
Having fully understood the consequence, these two verses themselves should be explained by way of illustration.
In the case of crushing a limb, as well as in the case of vital breath or blood,
he shall be made to pay the expenses of recovery or even the full penalty.
The "crushing" (*avapīḍanā*) of limbs occurs through the binding with firm ropes and the like, or by the dislocation of joints and so forth.

In such cases, the person who caused the injury must pay to the victim an amount of wealth sufficient for the restoration [of the limb], namely the cost of wholesome food, a physician, medicine, and the like. This same principle should be applied in full to the crushing of vital organs (*prāṇa*) and blood (*śoṇita*).

Alternatively, the connection is that he shall be made to pay for the restoration and the loss of the vital breath and the blood; by implication, it is understood as "of those [two] which have been diminished. Restoration (*samutthāna*) means returning to the natural state. Vital breath (*prāṇa*) means strength.
When one who has become unwell due to a blow recovers from emaciation and the like through food, his strength diminishes;
therefore, as long as that strength has not yet returned to the body, whatever is beneficial for it—such as ghee, oil, and so forth—should be made available to him.

Likewise, when blood or other fluids have been lost, or when he has become weakened by it or afflicted by another disease, he is to be made to pay the expenses of recovery until he returns to his natural state of bodily health.
If he does not recover it, then he shall pay back both that object and the fine, returning everything to the king.
If anyone should damage the property of another, whether intentionally or unintentionally,
he shall provide satisfaction to the owner and pay an equivalent amount to the king.

"Goods" refers to household utensils such as winnowing baskets, mortars, jars, pots, cauldrons, and so forth, or others for which no specific fine has been mentioned; "damage" to these means their destruction of original form, even while they remain functional.

Whether done intentionally or unintentionally—that is, whether caused by negligence or deliberately—because there is no distinction in the act of damaging, one must produce satisfaction for the owner of the goods by giving another object of the same kind, by its value, or by conciliation.
To the king, however, one should pay the value of the goods or the goods themselves.
There is an exception to this in certain cases.
For leather goods, leather articles, and items made of wood or clay,
as well as for flowers, roots, and fruits, the fine shall be five times their value.
Having formed a *dvandva* compound of "leather" (*carman*) and "leather articles" (*cārmika*), there is a compound with the word "articles" (*bhāṇḍa*) as the head noun (*viśeṣya*).
Alternatively, having formed a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) of "leather" and "articles," there is a *dvandva* with the word "leather.
Leather articles are those items made from leather, such as waist-bands, thongs, and so forth.
Unprocessed hides of cows and other animals;
or alternatively, leather vessels made entirely of leather, as well as items covered with leather, which are "leathern" (cārmika);
and wooden vessels such as mortars, pestles, planks, and so forth.
A *loṣṭha* is a product of clay, a lump of earth shaped like a stone;
it refers to vessels for cooking small amounts of food and the like made from that material.
For its destruction, the fine shall be five times the value.
And the arising of satisfaction on the part of the master remains a certainty.
They declare that there are ten exemptions for the vehicle, the driver, and the owner of the vehicle; in any other case, a punishment is ordained.
By this section it is demonstrated that even when injury is present, in certain cases there is no fault.
"Vehicles" refers to carts and the like, mounting which they travel along a path;
and those carts and so forth are drawn by oxen, donkeys, buffaloes, and other such animals.
Or rather, those very [animals] such as donkeys and so forth are the vehicles (yāna) to be mounted by those who ride upon them; the traveler (yātṛ) is one who has mounted it;
the owner of the vehicle (yānasvāmī) is the one to whom that vehicle belongs.

In that context, when there is the destruction of some property or death caused by these [animals] such as the *cakravega* and others, or by horses and so forth engaged in pulling a chariot, the rule regarding the transgression between the owner of the animal and the herdsman (*paśusvāmipālavyatikrama*) would apply; however, the specific distinction therein—which determines whether the fault sometimes lies with the driver, sometimes with the owner, sometimes with both, and sometimes with neither—is not stated there and is intended here. That is now stated: "Exemptions" (*ativartanāni*), meaning they proceed beyond the punishment for injury; that is to say, no punishment applies here, as the circumstances that would constitute grounds for punishment do not exist.
The punishment for the remainder is [to be applied] in cases other than the causes already mentioned;
those [other causes] shall also be explained later.
First, he states those cases where there is no fault:
when the nose-rope is severed, when the yoke is broken, when the animal turns sideways or faces the opposite direction,
and likewise when the axle or the wheel of the vehicle breaks.
Manu has declared that there is no punishment for the breaking of a yoke, nor likewise for the snapping of a thong or a rein, nor when one cries out "Get away! while being struck.
That which pertains to the nose is "nāsyam"; this is formed with the suffix *yat* according to the rule for body parts (*śarīrāvayavāt*).
It refers to the rope attached to the nostrils of oxen, the bit of horses, or the goad of elephants.
When that [yoke] was cut and broken,
and the yoke—
the wooden shaft of the chariot— was shattered.

The term *chinna-nābhi* (with its navel severed) refers to either a chariot or an animal by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, because both are connected [to the driver] either directly or through a lineage.

When a vehicle approaches from the side or from the front—whether moving sideways or backwards due to some irregularity of the ground or out of fear of the animal—the driver would not be at fault even if he somehow commits an offense.
For a driver is capable of protecting those facing him; however, when [the vehicle] is situated sideways or behind, how could he protect that which is not visible?
"Facing toward" means returning back.
Others, however, say there is no fault when a vehicle is moving straight ahead while an animal is being struck as it passes transversely;
they consider "facing toward" to mean facing directly forward.
Why has he come face-to-face and, upon seeing the wielder of the discus, does not yield the path?
The terms *akṣa* and *cakra* are well known as the axle and the wheel, respectively;
*yantrāṇi* refers to the leather lashings for the wooden parts of the chariot.
The *yoktra* is the wooden collar for the neck of an animal. The *raśmi* is the rein or hand-strap used for the purpose of controlling the movement of draft animals.
*Ākranda* is a loud cry meaning "go away" or "move aside";
the particle *iti* is used here to indicate the utterance of words well-known in common speech to convey that meaning, rather than implying that this specific word must be employed.
If, while shouting "Move aside! Move aside! to draft animals that are not obedient, the driver does not swerve from the path and an accident occurs, there is no fault.
If a vehicle turns off course due to the driver's negligence,
the owner shall be liable for the damage and must pay a fine of two hundred panas.
If the driver is trustworthy, the driver alone deserves the fine;
if the driver is untrustworthy, all those seated in the vehicle shall each be fined one hundred [paṇas].
The *prājaka* is the driver of the vehicle; his deficiency consists in being untrained, not in negligence.
For if there is negligence on the part of a trained driver, the master is not at fault.

Therefore, for that reason, if the draft animal or the vehicle should turn off course together—leaving the clear path and going sideways or backwards—and should thereby destroy anything, the master shall be fined.
"Why was an untrained driver appointed?"— regarding this,

because other punishments are prescribed according to the specific type of living being and the specific nature of the object involved, as will be stated later in the passage beginning with "in the case of killing a human, [the fine is] immediate," the phrase "two hundred" is not intended [as a fixed rule].

Since the purpose of the sentence is merely to indicate that this is the occasion for the punishment, no further meaning is heard in the subsequent text by which one could say that the sentence therein prescribes a specific number.
But if, while obstructed on the road by cattle or by a chariot,
he should cause the death of living beings, the punishment there shall be without hesitation.
The punishment for injury has been stated;
now, in order to specify the particulars therein, he says this:

If that charioteer is obstructed on the road by another vehicle approaching from behind, and his progress is blocked by one standing behind him—whether because of lack of training or through negligence—he urges the draft animals forward with speed; yet, if while attempting to steady them again, a nearby chariot causes a sudden check to that momentum, and consequently, due to the forceful impact of the front chariot, living beings such as humans or the draft animals (horses and so forth) yoked to the chariot, or the chariot itself, or parts of the chariot, should kill other creatures, then there is no deliberation regarding punishment.
The punishment remains the same.

Alternatively, suppose horses that have galloped at speed, upon seeing a chariot coming head-on as an obstacle on the road, are forcibly restrained and go sideways; because they are positioned to the side [of the driver], they might strike those nearby. In that case, no specific punishment has been prescribed, because there is no fault on the part of the charioteer (*prājaka*).
Or else, "standing on the road" means being present there; "obstructed" means not being restrained; "specified" (*vicārita*) means specifically ordained or distinguished.
In the case of killing a human being, one quickly incurs a guilt equal to that of a thief;
for large living beings such as cows, elephants, camels, horses, and so forth, the guilt is half [of that].
If a human being is killed by the chariot or the animals while such a driver is in charge, then his guilt and punishment are like those of a thief.

Although for a thief there are punishments such as execution or the confiscation of all property, here only a monetary fine is intended and not death, because the rule "half in the case of great [animals]" applies only where a half is possible. Furthermore, since some authorities accept that this is the *uttamasāhasa* (highest fine), and since a fine of two hundred is prescribed for minor animals—which occupy the third rank when injured—it follows that for the primary [animals] occupying the first rank, the highest fine is appropriate.

"Living beings" refers to those possessing vital breath, such as humans, animals, birds, and so forth. "Greatness in the great" consists of the power of cows and the physical size of elephants and the like;
by the inclusion of the word "and so forth," donkeys, mules, tigers, and others are also somehow included.

We, however, say that he would have stated "a thousand" [if] other punishments like those for a thief had not been intended. Therefore, because of the mention of "half," let there be no death penalty; rather, all the punishments for a thief mentioned previously—such as the confiscation of all property and so forth—are extended by analogy to these persons with respect to their status.
But is it not the case that the extension of another thief's punishment for the killing of a human being is improper?
That [punishment] was prescribed specifically for the slaying of a human,
and that consists of death itself for men of noble birth.
In this regard, why is it explained in such a way merely out of deference to the word "half" occurring in another sentence?
It would be better to simply resort to the occasional figurative application of the word "half" itself.
True, if the word "half," when connected with "killing," could be justified otherwise.

Nor is it possible for the phrase "and not like a thief," which has arrived here by way of syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*), to function with a different meaning in the preceding and following sentences.
For the killing of small animals, the fine shall be two hundred;
however, for auspicious beasts and birds, the punishment shall be fifty.
Those of diminished size are the small ones;
some of them are small by age, such as calves, colts, and young elephants; others are small by their very nature of birth, such as goats and sheep.
In that regard, he will state five *māṣas* for goats and sheep;
this penalty applies to the remaining small-sized animals, such as cows and so forth.
"Auspicious deer" refers to those such as the *pṛṣat* (spotted deer), both by their appearance and their characteristics.
"Birds" refers to swans, parrots, mainas, and so forth;
"inauspicious" refers to crows, owls, jackals, and so forth;
and the word "beast" denotes the class of four-footed animals.
They desire this punishment for mere violence alone;

they do not state that it is the cause for the procedure regarding vehicles under discussion. By the very statement "the punishment therein has been deliberated," the section on vehicles is thereby concluded.
"Deliberated upon" means that the deliberation is complete;
now this is stated independently of the present context.

However, regarding the phrase "in the case of large living beings, half," the word "half" should be understood—based on another Smṛti—as meaning that the cutting off of hands and so forth constitutes the offense, but not killing.
For donkeys, goats, and sheep, the fine shall be five māṣas;
however, for killing a dog or a pig, the fine shall be one māṣa.

"Pāñcamāṣika" means that whose measure is five māṣas. Since it is not established that *māṣa* refers to a specific class of substance, and because the middle interpretation is more reasonable, they say this is a designation for silver;
however, gold would also be appropriate.
Thus, it is equal to that and does not exceed it;
however, the established doctrine (siddhānta) is that the category of substance (dravyajāti) is to be postulated in consideration of the subsequent factors (anubandha) and so forth.
A wife, a son, a slave, a servant, and a uterine brother—
when they have committed an offense, they may be beaten with a rope or a split bamboo cane.
"Having incurred an offense" means those who have committed an offense;
an "offense" (*aparādha*) is a transgression or a deviation from proper conduct. When such an offense has been committed by them, they should then be beaten.

For even beating is said to be violence, and that is prohibited by the injunction "one should not harm living beings"; however, it is here permitted as an exception (*pratiprasava*) for wives and others when there is the occasion of an offense. Furthermore, these terms are relative (*saṃbandhi-śabda*).
Whomever's wife she may be, and whomever's servant he may be, he must be disciplined by him;
this is primarily a rule concerning the method for establishing [the person] on the right path, not merely a rule regarding corporal punishment.
Therefore, verbal censure and other such measures should also be employed.

Sometimes there may be a beating in accordance with the offense. The term "younger brother" (kanīyān) should be read as standing in the place of "uterine brother" (sodara); likewise for "brother" (bhrātā) and "younger one" (anuja).
For he is worthy of being beaten by the elder like a son.
Even if he is a half-brother, fatherless, virtuous, and dependent on his elder brother—
if he goes astray, he must be restrained by means ranging from verbal correction to physical punishment.
"Veṇudala" refers to bamboo bark.
This is also an illustration [of the rule] regarding such mild instruments of affliction as creepers and the like.
But one must strike on the back of the body and never on the head;
for striking otherwise than this, one incurs the guilt of a thief.
If one strikes in a manner other than the prescribed places or with the prescribed instruments, or if one strikes dice and the like with clubs and such, one incurs the punishment for a thief;
this is a censure,
but it is not the actual penalty itself.
What is intended by this is that the punishment which applies elsewhere for violence applies here as well.
Thus has been declared in its entirety the determination of punishment for assault;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule for the determination of punishment for a thief.
This determination of assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*)—that is, the legal settlement of punishment (*daṇḍavyavasthā*)—has been stated in its entirety.
For in this title of litigation (*vivādapada*), the word "punishment" (*daṇḍa*) signifies the means of proof by implication;
thus, the first member of the compound constitutes the name [of the title].
This verse serves the purpose of introducing the conclusion, stating: "Henceforth, I shall describe the various types of punishment for the thief and the robber."
A king should exert the utmost effort in the suppression of thieves;
through the suppression of thieves, his fame and kingdom increase.
A certain compassionate person, considering cruel action to be violence, does not engage in it;
therefore, for the sake of inducing such engagement, a commendatory statement (arthavāda) praising the suppression of thieves is commenced.
For there is no fault of violence here; on the contrary, because it is a cause of visible benefit, the very act of harming a thief is conducive to the highest good.

Furthermore, many explanatory passages (arthavādas) are included in order to proclaim the equivalence [of this work] to the Vedas; for therein, the injunctive statements (vidhyuddeśa) are generally accompanied by such explanatory passages. By following that understanding, the established conviction arises that "this is a Vedic matter."
In this regard, there are some practitioners who proceed excessively with praises;
they should apply themselves with supreme effort, with excellence, and with extraordinary intent. They should cause [the practice] to circulate both secretly and openly with the utmost diligence.
Thieves are robbers; restraint consists of punishment, execution, imprisonment, and so forth. When this is done, fame—that is, renown—arises.
This king’s country is free from calamity; thieves do not prevail there, and the nights are equal to the day—thus it remains established everywhere.
The kingdom prospers.
The kingdom—the inhabited territory—and the men dwelling therein flourish, being unharmed by robbers.
Rejoicing in prosperity, even those residing in many distant border regions take refuge in the kingdom free from affliction;
consequently, it prospers.
For that king who is the giver of fearlessness is always worthy of honor;
indeed, his sacrificial session (sattra) is ever-increasing, with the gift of fearlessness as its fee.

He who grants freedom from fear—by preventing unjust punishment—to those in authority, such as thieves and others, is always worthy of honor, even when he has fallen from his kingdom and dwells in the forest, even in casual conversation.
A *sattra* is a specific type of sacrifice, such as the *Gavām-ayana*;
that [merit] of his increases and comes to fruition.
By the phrase "it increases," he means that [the gift] which has arisen with all its limbs and such qualities thus grows;
the meaning is that one obtains the fruit of a sacrificial session (sattra) day by day.
Wherein the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consists of fearlessness.
In other sacrificial sessions (*satra*), there is no sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*);
however, this [session] is distinguished from all others in that it possesses a sacrificial fee.
And since that fee is of a nature distinct from the fees of cows, horses, and so forth, the distinction from the *satra* is meaningful.
A sixth part of all righteousness accrues to the king who protects;
likewise, a sixth part of unrighteousness accrues to him who does not protect.
From all forms of religious merit such as sacrifices performed by village-dwellers and forest-dwellers alike, the king receives a sixth part of that *dharma*.
Likewise, even from unrighteousness (*adharma*) committed secretly by thieves, a sixth part accrues to the king.

It is not only through the failure to protect those who are robbed that unrighteousness falls upon kings; rather, even for those who commit the theft, there arises unrighteousness by virtue of their act of stealing, and the kings become connected with even a portion of that through their failure to suppress them.
Furthermore, preventing those who are to be protected from being connected with unseen faults (adṛṣṭadoṣa) is indeed their protection;
therefore, it is appropriate that a king authorized in this matter incurs sin by failing to perform it.
But is it not improper for him to receive a sixth part of the merit (dharma), since he has been hired for wages?
It has been stated that the poor, the helpless, renunciants, and others do not pay taxes;
what inconsistency is there in this regarding the full protection of one's own duty?
Whatever one studies, whatever one sacrifices, whatever one gives, and whatever one worships—
the king becomes a sharer of a sixth part of that through his proper protection.
Regarding what was stated as "from all [sources]," this is its detailed exposition:
study and the other duties have been made known elsewhere for the sake of dharma and are well-established in form;
worship is the honoring of gods and gurus.
The phrase "of that" (tasya) should be construed as "of that object [consisting of] action," such as study and so forth, because the word *kriyā* (action) is feminine.
Regarding the term "one-sixth part":

it does not mean that the king receives a sixth portion from the five parts of the fruit of the action belonging to the agent; for it is understood from the context of entitlement (*adhikāra*) that the agent alone is the enjoyer of the entire fruit of the action.

Rather, because of the correct apprehension [of duty] and the performance of one's own actions, only that much fruit arises for the king. There is no transfer of merit or demerit performed by one person to another; it is established that there is no fruit for one who has not acted.
Protecting all beings according to dharma and executing those deserving of death, the king performs sacrifices every day with hundreds and thousands of sacrificial fees.

Protecting all beings, both stationary and moving, from thieves, and executing those deserving of death according to the scriptures—by doing so, the king daily obtains the fruit of sacrifices such as the Pauṇḍarīka, for which hundreds of thousands are given as sacrificial fees; this is a praise [of the king's duty].
That king who, failing to provide protection, takes tribute, taxes, tolls,
the share of produce, and fines, shall immediately go to hell.
Terms such as *bali* and others are names for taxes to be collected by the king, well-known in various regions like the word *sūpa-māṇavaka*.
Among them, *bali* is one-sixth of the grain and other produce;
*kara* is the collection of wealth.
*Tulka* is the share obtained by a merchant;
*pratibhāga* is an offering such as a portion of the fruit or a tribute.
If a king takes these but does not protect [his subjects] from thieves, he shall immediately go to hell upon the exhaustion of his life.
Having taken the king's share, protection must be provided out of fear of the exhaustion of one's lifespan in hell; such is the purport of the verse.
They say that one who does not protect, but consumes [the people] while taking a sixth part as tax,
is the remover of all the impurities of the entire world.

This is a supplementary deprecatory explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) for the preceding [verse]. He does not protect; he is a devourer because he subsists by taking the king’s share from the subjects. He clarifies this very point with the phrase "one who takes a sixth part as tribute" (*baliṣaḍbhāgahārin*).
The learned call such a king the remover—that is, the appropriator—of the entire stain and evil of all the world and of all his subjects;
the meaning is that he is defiled by every sin of his subjects.
One should know that a king who disregards the bounds of propriety, who is an atheist, a plunderer, who fails to protect his subjects, and who devours them instead, is destined for a downward path.
*Maryādā* is the established order of *dharma* rooted in the scriptures and the conduct of the learned; he by whom this has not been observed—that is, has been transgressed—is a *nāstika*.
A *nāstika* is one who holds that "there is no world beyond, there is no gift, and there is no oblation.
The first [type] is one who has abandoned *dharma* due to passion and other afflictions; the second is one who possesses a perverse dogmatic adherence, thinking that such things do not exist.
One who plunders and seizes the wealth of his subjects by unjust punishments is equal to such a robber; one should know that he, being a non-protector,
goes to a downward state— he should know that he has fallen into hell and will soon be gone to a downward state, having fallen into hell indeed.
There is another reading: "One should abandon a king who is untruthful.
One should abandon him who says one thing but does another; one should not remain in his domain.
One should diligently restrain the unrighteous by three means:
by confinement, by imprisonment, and by various forms of corporal punishment.
Having strengthened [the rule] with explanatory statements (arthavādas), he now introduces the procedure for punishment:
"The unrighteous one"— and from the context, this refers to a thief—
"he shall punish," that is, restrain him, by means of three methods of restraint.
*Nyāya* means restraint. *Nirodhana* is confinement in a royal fortress or a prison house.
*Bandha* is the production of a state of lack of independence by means of ropes, shackles, and so forth, in that very same place.
Various forms of killing range from beating up to the destruction of the body and ending with the relinquishment of life.
Although the number three is already established by the very mention [of the three types], the explicit statement "by three" is for the purpose of including other methods of restraint;
by this, pouring hot oil and so forth are also included.
For by the suppression of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous,
kings are constantly purified, just as the twice-born are purified by sacrifices.
Men joined with evil are wicked; their restraint has been described previously. Those who act according to the scriptures are virtuous.
Their "gathering" (*saṃgraha*) means favoring them and assisting them according to one's ability.
By that, they are purified and become free from sin; this is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), meaning they become as if purified by a rite of atonement (*prāyaścitta*).
Alternatively, "purification" (*pūtatva*) may simply mean the non-arising of sin.
Just like Brahmins, they are constantly engaged in sacrifices through the performance of the five great daily sacrifices and other regular rites.
A lord who seeks his own welfare should always forgive those litigants who revile him,
as well as children, the elderly, and the sick.
The parties involved are the plaintiff, the defendant, and their relatives or friends.
If, while someone is being punished, his father, mother, or another relative should revile, abuse, or curse the king, then forgiveness must be granted;
this applies even to children and others who are parties to the case.
In this way, one's own welfare is accomplished;
for the very fruit of the injunction "one must be patient" is one's own benefit.
He who endures being reviled by those in distress is exalted in heaven because of that;
but he who does not endure it out of pride goes to hell because of that.

When one who is reviled or abused by those who are distressed and who do not deserve such treatment endures it and does not become angry, he is exalted in heaven by that very act of forbearance; for by means of this *kṣamaṇa*, he attains greatness in heaven.
[The suffix] *ya* is applied here because the root belongs to the *kaṇḍv-ādi* class.
He attains magnificence in the celestial realm.
Therefore, forgiveness should be practiced without anger.
Since one who is free from desire acts according to his will, he says:
"But because of the conceit that 'I am the master,' if one does not endure [insult], one attains hell."
The mention of "the afflicted" (ārta) is for the purpose of indicating children and the elderly as well, since this [statement] is a supplement to what preceded.
A wise thief should go before the king with disheveled hair, confessing that theft: "I am a man of such deeds; punish me."
When no specific qualification is mentioned, the stealer of gold should be understood as a thief, because for that very person, the act of returning [the property] is prescribed in another scripture.
Nor is this injunctive rule intended merely to bring about such a return, since it is a rule prescribing punishment;
for it has been stated: "Therefore, I shall proclaim the rule for a thief regarding the determination of punishment."
Therefore, this is a restatement regarding the journey:
"The gold thief must go into the presence of the king with disheveled hair, being wise and courageous."
"Running"—this is an alternative reading.
By proclaiming or declaring on the road that very sin, saying, "I am a man of such deeds; so much gold was stolen by me from a Brahmin," you must effect my restraint.
Taking up a club, or a staff made of khadira wood,
or a spear sharp at both ends, or even an iron rod.
Some maintain that there is a sequential instruction of the pestle and so forth according to the order of the castes;
that is incorrect, for the word "or" (vā) would not be justified.
Furthermore, they do not accept this as an expiation for a Brāhmaṇa;
we shall determine that in the section on expiations.
The staff must be made of Khadira wood; he is not to be struck with a club.
Whether through punishment or through release, the thief is freed from his theft;
but by failing to punish him, the king incurs the guilt of the thief.
By following the teaching and by striking with pestles and other weapons, a Kṣatriya and others are released from sin;
this is because of liberation through renunciation. "Go, you have been forgiven"—thus it is said that for a Brāhmaṇa, penance alone [is prescribed]; thus, killing and penance are both ordained.
In that regard, there is first of all no execution for a Brāhmaṇa;
rather, asceticism is his expiation.
Furthermore, there is no approaching the king at will regarding asceticism.
Therefore, this liberation belongs to the Kṣatriyas and others; and that occurs after he has taken monetary fines,
since it says, "without having punished," and so forth.
Furthermore, even when liberation has been achieved through purification, no fault accrues to the king because he did not issue the command;
nor was the command itself mandatory, for liberation was also mandated. In that regard, the statement regarding the fault is contingent upon the alternative where the command was issued.
For such a conceptualization is indeed conditional.
Furthermore, it is not reasonable to assume that what is heard as an obligatory rule is merely optional;
thus, Vasiṣṭha and others have stated in general terms:
"Sin falls upon the king who releases a criminal."
If the king should have him executed, he incurs no fault by killing in accordance with dharma.
This alternative is not tenable.

For in some cases this injury is prohibited—as in "one should not harm living beings"—where it is undertaken for the sake of human ends through passion and so forth; while in other cases it is enjoined as being for the sake of the sacrifice—as in "the initiated one [should sacrifice] that which belongs to Agni and Soma."

However, this statement regarding the release from the teaching is not indeed a prohibition when there is a positive injunction. How so? It is not a prohibition; for the general prohibition, "One should not harm living beings," cannot be sublated without a specific injunction. Now, it might be argued:
This is not the object of a prohibition, because it has the purpose of [establishing] ritual action (*karman*).
But how can the purpose of ritual action be understood without an injunction (*vidhi*)?
If you say "from worldly experience," then it is merely a worldly activity.
How, then, could a prohibition apply there?
Should one not rather determine the scope of activity with respect to the primary act?
If the activity is indeed Vedic, then it follows from that very source even for the violence which is a subordinate part of it.
For there is indeed a single performance regarding both the subsidiary and the principal acts.
Now, if it is argued that activity toward the subsidiary arises from a desire for gain, then this act of killing is all the more worldly;
for one who seeks a livelihood is restricted by the duty of protecting subjects, not by the injunction [to kill].
Therefore, even this violence that is an auxiliary [to the king's duty] falls within the scope of prohibition because it is equal to the *śyena* sacrifice;
nor is its status as an auxiliary fixed by worldly convention,
for the protection of subjects cannot be accomplished without violence, since it can also be accomplished through restraint and other such means.
This is not a fixed rule that the performance of the subsidiary and the principal must be of a single form; otherwise, there would be no distinction between the Agniṣomīya and this [case].
Therefore, even when the principal is characterized by desire (lipsā), it must be admitted that the subsidiary is characterized by an injunction (vidhi).

Furthermore, it is not possible to accept that their killing is characterized by scriptural injunction (*vidhi-lakṣaṇā*), because both its essential nature and its purpose are worldly, as are the act of protecting [the victim] and the act of killing itself.

If, however, it were characterized by scriptural injunction, it would have to be subject to option (*vikalpa*)—like the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup—and thus would be prohibited by the words of the teaching.
Others, however, think as follows:

These are two sentences. By the words "because of the command," the intention of the thief is stated; by the subsequent half-verse, the fault incurred by the king for failing to issue that command is expressed.

In that case, if the king were to release [the offender] by taking the fault of his own failure to punish upon himself, he would indeed be freed from that sin. Likewise, for a Brāhmaṇa as well, killing one who has come of his own accord is a cause of purification, according to the statement: "He is the target of those who bear arms. Since it is said that "there is no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa," if the king should kill him by transgressing this prohibition, the Brāhmaṇa would indeed be purified.
Without having punished him with clubs and other such means, and without having killed him,
one becomes joined with whatever evil belongs to that thief.

The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the one who eats his food; an unfaithful wife transfers hers to her husband; a pupil and a sacrificer transfer theirs to their teacher; and a thief transfers his guilt to the king.
One who eats food is an "annāda.
A *bhrūṇahan* is a slayer of a Brahmin. He who eats the food belonging to such a person "mārṣṭi"—that is, he wipes away, casts off, or adheres to—that sin of Brahmin-slaughter upon himself.
Just as a soiled garment is wiped in water and that dirt is transferred to it, so it is here.
And this is a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda):
that sin arises for him,
but the slayer of a Brahmin is not thereby destroyed.

When a wife is unfaithful toward her husband—that is, when she has a paramour—if he forgives her, sin is produced for the husband even in this case; it does not depart from him. Likewise, regarding the teacher and the pupil, and the sacrificer and the pupil: if the pupil commits an offense against the teacher by rising before the sun or other such transgressions, yet the teacher forgives him, that sin is cast upon the teacher.
In the same way, the sacrificer stands in relation to the officiating priest;
since the latter is also indeed a guru, the term "officiating priest" was not explicitly mentioned.
Likewise, the thief stands in relation to the king, provided he is not restrained by the king.

Even a patron (yājya), once the ritual has commenced, must not disregard the injunction if he fails to abide by the words of the officiating priest (yājaka); in that case, he is to be abandoned, but one must not subject him to beating and the like as one would a disciple.
Since there is no injunction regarding all other matters such as food and so forth, this [statement] is merely an explanatory praise (arthavāda).
But men who have committed sins, having been punished by kings,
go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed meritorious deeds.
This clarifies what was said regarding how those who perform the punishment of evildoers protect themselves from [the consequences of] their actions:
those by whom the rod of punishment has been wielded and inflicted by kings—having committed sins—become stainless and cast off of sin through that royal punishment.
And when the sin has departed, they attain heaven by means of that karma of theirs which leads to the ascent to heaven.
For great indeed is the evil that obstructs the fruit of pure action;
[it affects] the doer of good deeds, who constantly performs virtuous acts,
just as it does for the righteous and holy.

Unrighteousness does not arise for those who are non-existent; rather, it is destroyed by suppression once it has arisen in them—this is the distinction between prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*).

Because of the mention of "men" (*mānava*), and not because of the context, this refers to men in general and not only to thieves. Furthermore, the word "punishment" (*daṇḍa*) pertains to physical restraint and does not overstep the context.
For a monetary fine is for the sake of the king;
it is indeed the king’s livelihood.
But in the case of corporal punishment, its purpose being for the benefit of the person being punished cannot be denied, for it is a refinement of the body itself.

Now, if this thought is that protection itself cannot be accomplished without violence, and since that [protection] is for the sake of the king, how can it be said that the killing is for the sake of those being killed?
Furthermore, is it denied that protection is seen to be for the sake of those being protected?
For that kingdom is not to be acquired by the king solely for his own self-preservation; rather, servants such as tax-collectors and tribute-gatherers are employed for that purpose.

Therefore, since violence is even more useful for protection, it cannot be established that the purpose of the one being harmed is served by such violence. Or how could protection not be accomplished without violence? If they are restrained for this very purpose [of protection], they will simply return to their misconduct; they can be restrained even by means of imprisonment and the like. Furthermore, if others, seeing those who have been restrained, will refrain from acting out of fear, then they can be made to suffer even by means of a monetary fine.
Even when thousands are being slain, [acts of protection] continue to proceed;
therefore, this violence, while being an act of protection, must be understood as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) for the one being harmed.
Consequently, there is a restrictive rule regarding the amputation of limbs and the like.
Furthermore, the procedure involving elephants and the like will produce only invisible (adṛṣṭa) merit for those deserving punishment; it will not serve the king's material interest.
Therefore, it is established that liberation from sin occurs through corporal punishment, not through monetary fines.

Accordingly, the author will later state that branding is to be applied to those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin), whose entire property has been confiscated and whose punishment has been cast into the waters, for the purpose of excluding them from social intercourse.

And if they could be purified by a monetary fine, then branding again would be useless. Furthermore, regarding the distinction between one who comes of his own accord and one who is brought [as a prisoner], let that distinction belong to the thief himself alone.
All of this, however, pertains to the subject of corporal punishment.
But he who takes a rope or a water-pot from a well, or who breaks a water-trough,
shall incur a fine of one māṣa and shall restore that [item] to its place.
A *prapā* is so called because people drink there; it is a place for holding water or a reservoir from which water has been drawn.
The specific variety of bean (*māṣa*) is not specified here; it should be understood as belonging to the categories of desert (*maru*), arid upland (*jaṅgala*), or marshy (*anūpa*) regions.
And one should collect that rope or other object and return it to that place, not to the king.
For one who steals more than ten jars of grain, the punishment is death;
for stealing less than that, he shall be made to pay eleven times the amount, and that property must be restored to its owner.
The word *kumbha* refers to a specific measure and not to every jar;
its determination varies by region, being twenty *prasthas* in some places and twenty-two in others.
Regarding the rule prescribing the death penalty for one who steals more than ten [units], the stated meaning is further regulated by the attendant circumstances (*anubandha*) and other factors.
In the remaining ten cases, the fine is eleven times the ordinary amount;
"that [stolen object] and its value" is to be applied everywhere in cases of theft.
It is recorded in the Smṛtis that grain consists of seventeen types, beginning with rice (vrīhi) and barley (yava).
Likewise, for goods measured by weight, such as gold, silver, and the like, as well as for the finest garments, there shall be the death penalty if the amount exceeds one hundred.
*Dharaṇa* means weight (*dharimā*), which is a scale (*tulā*); those things measured or delimited by it are *dharmameya*.

Since liquids such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*) have their measure determined by *prastha* and other units, whereas solids have their measure determined by weight, he says "of gold, silver, and so forth" (*suvarṇarajatādīnām*).

Although silver is already included by the use of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is mentioned again for the purpose of specifically including [precious substances] like coral (*pravāla*) through the inclusion of "scale," and not copper, iron, and the like.
If one steals more than a hundred of these, there is the death penalty.
But what does this "hundred" refer to—is it palas, or indeed karṣas, or perhaps kārṣāpaṇas? Some say it refers to palas.

But there is no reason for a distinction here; therefore, in whatever place, at the time of measuring wealth, the transaction occurs according to a certain number— such as "this is a hundred of gold," whether measured in *tolakas* or *palas*— the determination is according to the local custom,
as is the case with the garments of the wealthy, such as silk (*kauśeya*) and brocade (*paṭṭa*).
The phrase "punishment is death for more than one hundred" is to be supplied here as well.
In this case too, a pair of garments is counted as one;
however, a bed-cover such as a flower-patterned cloth and so forth is counted as only one.
But surely, since the rule would already be established by the words "gold, silver, and so forth," the inclusion of the term *parimeya* (measurable) is redundant.
It is not redundant, for its purpose is to include highly valuable items such as camphor, aloe-wood, musk, and the like.
Indeed, by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), metallic objects are included, or those things designated by measures such as the *niṣka*.
For there is no designation of "karṣa" and so forth for camphor and the like.

Even though the number "one hundred" applies to silver just as it does to gold, nevertheless, just as there is a difference in penance, a difference in punishment is also appropriate, because it is unjust to equate what is unequal.
Therefore, death [as the penalty] applies when an amount of silver equal to the value of the gold taken is seized.
But for camphor and the other substances, the number is indeed one hundred palas.
If the value exceeds fifty [paṇas], the cutting off of a hand is prescribed;
for the remainder, however, one should determine a fine eleven times the value.
This is easily understood.
Regarding the phrase "from the price," it is not that the stolen object itself must be returned; for in some cases, an item of that same kind may simply not be available.
Therefore, restitution may be made by means of coins or grain and the like.
One deserves the death penalty for stealing men of noble birth, women especially, and the most precious of gems.
Those born into noble families who possess qualities such as learning are "well-born" (kulīna).
And by the word "and" (ca), it is implied that they are specifically those well-born men endowed with virtue, beauty, and good fortune among women. Thus is the meaning.
The attributes of women are mutually dependent;
the primary and most excellent jewels, such as diamonds, lapis lazuli, emeralds, and so forth,
should also be understood here as being equal to a hundred pieces of gold.
Otherwise, since superiority would be merely relative, the application of punishment would not be established.

[The phrase] "deserves death" (vadham arhati) should be understood everywhere as meaning "deserves [punishment]," with the sense of the verb *arhati* being applied in consideration of the attendant circumstances (*anubandha*) and other factors.
But for those who are of low birth, remaining [debtors], and non-principal [servants], the interest at the end shall be elevenfold.
In cases of the theft of large animals, weapons, or medicinal herbs,
the king shall determine the punishment after considering the time and the specific circumstances of the act.

Large animals refer to elephants, horses, and the like; the determination of the punishment for their theft takes into account the time and other circumstances. But is it not the case that consideration of time and so forth has been stated to apply everywhere?
And likewise: "One should consider time, place, age, and capacity when determining acts of punishment.
This is true;
once the essential nature of the punishment has been ascertained, its degree—whether it be less or more—depends upon the attendant circumstances and other such factors.

Just as in the case of a judicial execution, where the punishment consists of considerations such as beating or killing, here the penalty is of an entirely different nature. For instance, even a sword worth twenty *paṇas*, if it is seized from an enemy who has raised his weapon, constitutes the death penalty because of that extraordinary act and the timing of it.

At other times, it is double or elevenfold. Likewise, when medicine—which is of great necessity due to its being unobtainable—is stolen at the time of its administration, even if it were merely being moved about, it causes great suffering to the patient through the lapse of time as it requires decoctions and so forth; therefore, there is a heavy penalty in that case. But at other times, it is small.
For no such disparity is found elsewhere;
otherwise, that very same single verse would have been recited in the section on punishments.
Therefore, this must be explained.
During a time of war, the punishment for horses and other such animals depends on the needs of the state;
as for weapons used by the king, there may sometimes be forgiveness and sometimes severe punishment.
However, in the case of cattle, buffaloes, and so forth belonging to the subjects, the king must not show leniency.
Furthermore, whatever task is to be accomplished by means of horses and the like must also be taken into account.

Even as for military engagement (*vigraha*), if it takes place in a mountainous region or similar terrain where there is no great need for horses, there should indeed be a reduction in the army's strength.
Having waited for the right time, having understood the situation, and having carefully examined it, one should determine the appropriate force.
In this matter, that alone prevails, not the treatise.
In the case of cows belonging to Brahmins, for breaking a fence,
and likewise for the theft of livestock, one must immediately undergo the punishment of having half a foot cut off.
"Established among Brahmins" means dependent upon Brahmins or having Brahmins as their owners;
[the locative case] "in the taking of these" is used in the sense of the genitive.
And of animals such as goats, sheep, and so forth—
the plural number is not intended to be significant in every case—
immediately, at that very moment, without deliberation.
Half of a foot is a half-foot (*ardhapāda*); one who possesses that is a "half-footed" person (*ardhapādika*).
And this is possible only if half of a foot is cut off by him;
therefore, the meaning of the sentence is that "the cutting off of half a foot must be performed."

A *kharikā* is that by which a bull is driven to a cow-pen, a field, or similar places. Regarding "causing pain" (*bhedane*), the ancient commentators explain it as the production of suffering by means of a goad while the animal is being driven; they state that "driving" (*vāhana*) is intended as an illustration for all such acts of urging animals.

Others read that he causes suffering by driving [the ox] necessarily; they say this punishment applies specifically to the act of driving with a goad. Still others, however, call the fourth part of the hind leg the *kharikā*.
A *kharikā* is that which is well known as being prone to running away; one who pierces such an animal, whether it be a keeper or another person, shall be made to pay half a *pāda*.
Others, however, taking the locative case to signify "in relation to" (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*), supply words such as "curd and so forth contained in a cow.
That is incorrect.
When it is possible to connect the words as they are heard, why should there be an insertion (adhyāhāra)?
Of thread, cotton, and fermenting agent; of cow dung and molasses; of curd, milk, buttermilk, water, and grass.
Likewise, for the theft of vessels made of bamboo or split cane, of salts,
of earthenware, and of clay or ashes;
Of fish, of birds, of oil, of clarified butter,
of meat, of honey, and whatever else originates from animals.
For other such items as these, for raw grain,
for cooked rice, and for all kinds of prepared foods, the fine shall be double their value.
Wool refers to woolen cloth and the like;
salts refer to rock salt, biḍa salt, and so forth;
and whatever else originates from animals, such as meat and the like.
"Of others" refers to cakes, sweetmeats, and so forth;
the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) indicates a category (*prakāra*).
A category consists of similarity (*sādṛśya*), which is equivalence (*tulyatā*), taking the form of performing similar functions, utility, and so on.

And likewise, by the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), items such as clarified butter-scum (*sarpirmaṇḍa*), sugarcane pieces, sugar-candy, inspissated milk (*kilāṭa*), honey-comb (*kūrcikā*), and cakes (*apūpa*) are included.
Some also maintain that what originates from animals includes the wool of the *rāṅkava* goat and the like;
by the inclusion of "and so forth," both the primary form (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*) are intended.
And the mention of both—curd and milk—is for the sake of illustration.
Likewise, by the inclusion of the term "thread" (*sūtra*), cloth made of thread is also included.

Although items such as reed-mats (*nalikā*) are made of thread, because they originate from animals and are considered inferior, they fall under the scope of the exception to the rule "and [the gifts] of the most excellent."
The word "oil" (taila) denotes viscidity by its very nature, not exclusively a product of sesame;
therefore, oils such as those from linseed, priyaṅgu, and pañcāṅgula are also included.
For flowers, green grain, shrubs, creepers, trees,
and other unhusked plants, the fine shall be five *kṛṣṇalas*.
Navamālikā and other such flowers;
green grain standing in the field that is unripe;
and *naga*, meaning trees.
Regarding "others" [meaning] those that have not been winnowed:

because of the use of the plural number, and because the act of winnowing—which consists of the removal of husks, straw, and so forth—is possible only in the case of grains, the term "grains" is specifically drawn forward from the following verse.
For even though shrubs and the like possess leaves and flowers, there is no conventional usage of the term "winnowed" when they are mixed together.
The expectation of the removal of spittle follows from the preceding [rule]. In this case,
the fine is five *kṛṣṇalas*.
The *kṛṣṇala* weights are produced from various substances;
they depend on the requirements of smallness or largeness [of the object].
"Of gold," say the predecessors.
When grain, vegetables, roots, or fruits have been cleaned,
the fine shall be one hundred panas for theft from one who has no kinship ties, and fifty panas as a penalty for theft from one who has such ties.
The "root" refers to sugarcane, grapes, and so forth.
Regarding "theft without connection" (*niranvaya*):

"connection" (*anvaya*) means conciliation, such as employing affection toward the owner with the thought, "What is yours is indeed mine," and acting on that basis; or using words such as, "If this is not so, then please take it. Where such [acts of conciliation] are not performed, that is "without connection."
The punishment is increased because it constitutes a form of violence (*sāhasa*).
"With kin" (*sānvaya*) means together with his relatives;
alternatively, "without kin" (*niranvaya*) refers to one with whom there is no connection whatsoever, such as residing in the same village and so forth.
In that case, he should be fined one hundred [paṇas].
Alternatively, if it was unguarded and without witnesses,
but there was a guardian present, the fine shall be small due to the fault of both parties.
This penalty applies to grains situated in a threshing floor,
for it is there that they are fully ripened;
however, in the case of those situated in a house, the eleven-fold fine previously mentioned applies.

An act committed by force, provided it is accompanied by a claim of ownership, is *sāhasa* (violence); however, that which is done without such a claim is *steya* (theft), as is the case when one takes property and then denies it.
The taking away of another's property is called theft (*steya*);
