by virtue of the well-known meaning of the verbal root, its perpetrator alone is a thief (*stena*). However, in this context, a specific legal usage is intended; for that purpose, this verse is composed.

Theft is not merely the taking of another's property, for if it were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of applying the punishment for theft even in cases such as the non-payment of debts or the misappropriation of deposits.
The distinction in terminology is intended to distinguish between different types of punishments.
An action (*karman*) is that which, when performed, causes suffering to others, such as tearing clothes, setting fires, or the seizing of goods.
In the case of arson, although there is no actual taking away of property, they nevertheless consider it to be theft because it is committed in secret and involves concealment.
For in the case of theft, the punishment depends on the specific nature of the property;
that [specificity] would not exist here [in the case of arson].
It is for this very purpose that the section on theft has been displaced [to this point].

Because of the inclusion of the word "act" in the phrase "an act committed by force," even something other than the actual seizure of property—such as an improper act done in this manner—is indeed *sāhasa* (violence).
What, then, is the punishment when an act like setting fire is committed without force?
We shall explain this under the section on the purification of thorns (*kaṇṭakaśuddhi*).
For this very reason, they prescribe a punishment for the breaking of a wall even when there is no actual taking of property, within the context of the purification of thorns;
otherwise, it would have been mentioned simply as theft (*steya*).
But the king shall fine that man who steals these prepared articles one hundred [paṇas], as well as whoever would steal the fire from the house.

These items, such as thread and the like, are "prepared" (*upakḷpta*) when they are ready for the time of their intended use, such as being given away or enjoyed; or alternatively, they are "refined" (*saṃskṛta*), meaning their functional capacity has been enhanced.

For example, that very same thread, when placed in the hands of a weaver for the purpose of weaving, is sometimes doubled and sometimes twisted. Similarly, there is the refinement of curd by churning with black pepper, sugar, and so forth, or the refinement of milk into ghee, and so on.
In such cases, the fine is one hundred [paṇas].
In the reading "ādyam" (the first), it refers to the first *sāhasa* fine.

Regarding the phrase "taken from the fire-sanctuary," this is for the purpose of the *śālāgnihotra* and so forth; or else, in winter, for the poor who are afflicted by the cold, it refers to the provision of fire—even if not formally established—for the sake of warding off the cold at the time of cooking, or for warming at the time of heating.
This penalty for fire applies without distinction to a small or large amount, whether the fire was formally prepared or not.

Even though the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is included in the phrase "the staff and so forth," a fine equal to the value of fire is not possible, because the practice of buying and selling it is not established.

Rather, the fine equal to twice the value of that fuel by which the fire is produced in its measured quantity, or twice the value of those sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) [by which it is maintained], is possible and can be designated; moreover, the satisfaction of the owner remains certain.

Therefore, in the case of stealing the three sacred fires (*tretāgni*), the owner must be given as much wealth as would be required for the rite of re-consecration (*punar-ādheya*) and the expiatory sacrifice (*prāyaścittīṣṭi*).
Therefore, this punishment for fire applies only to the case of the *śālāpraṇītāgni* (the fire brought forth for the hall), because it is of small value;
however, in the case of the *tretā* fires, it is double that value.

Likewise, Śaṅkha states that when sacrificial materials—which are easily available and do not cease to serve their purpose—are stolen, there shall be amputation of a limb for one who steals *kuśa* grass, water-pots, or the materials for the *agnihotra*.
But when the sacred fires have been taken away, one's entitlement [to perform rites] ceases altogether;
how then could there not be a great punishment in that case?
With whichever limb a thief commits an offense against men,
that very limb the king shall remove as a deterrent.
This is the punishment for one who persists in the offense again and again.

For one who, even when punished with a fine, does not abide by the path, and who—having been punished three or four times—still does not desist, there shall be the amputation of limbs; this is independent of the value or quantity of the goods and independent of whether it was a breaking of a wall or other such acts, being based solely on the act of theft itself.
Whatever limb the thief relies upon for strength while persisting in the act of theft, that very limb the king shall take away—that is, he shall cut off.

For one who, relying upon and seizing someone's feet, flees while thinking, "No one at all can follow me," his feet shall be cut off. For another who thinks, "I am an expert in breaking locks," his hands shall be cut off.
This is for the purpose of reprimand and to show a corresponding result.
*Pratyādeśa* is a rejection characterized by self-assertion, pride, anger, and contempt, or it is an act of humiliation;
it is the making known that "I shall do this very thing to whosoever acts in such a manner. This is *pratyādeśa*.
Neither father, teacher, friend, mother, wife, son, nor domestic priest—
none is exempt from punishment by the king who does not abide by his own duty.
"Wife" and "son" refer to one's own body, that is, one's own physical frame.
Furthermore, what constitutes punishment for oneself?
It refers to the intended performance of expiatory rites, ascetic penances, giving of gifts, and so forth.
He has deviated from his own duty;
whoever does not perform his own duty is all such a person who deserves punishment.
Where an ordinary person would be fined one kārṣāpaṇa, the king should be fined one thousand; such is the established rule.
An ordinary person is a common man who is not endowed with exceptional virtues.

For whatever offense such a person commits, the king’s fine shall be a thousandfold that of the commoner; this is because the mention of the *kārṣāpaṇa* is intended to illustrate the scale of the punishment, and because punishment serves a visible purpose.
Furthermore, since it is impossible to restrain another without first restraining oneself, it is logical that the king deserves a proportionate punishment for his own transgressions.
Because of their great wealth, one should not disregard even a small fine.
By this same principle, the degree of deficiency or excess [in punishment] applies to those authorized by the king, such as ministers, domestic priests, and others.
Furthermore, a monetary fine for Brahmins may be disposed of by casting it into the water or offering it to Varuṇa.
For it will be said: "He is indeed the wielder of the rod of punishment for kings."
In the case of theft, the sin of a Śūdra becomes eightfold;
that of a Vaiśya is sixteenfold, and that of a Kṣatriya is thirty-twofold.
For a Brahmin, it may be sixty-four, or even a full hundred, or twice sixty-four; for he is indeed one who knows both the faults and the virtues thereof.
Because it is stated as a reason that "he indeed knows its faults and virtues," this punishment is for the learned.
Where a base person is made to pay one *kārṣāpaṇa*, there a learned Śūdra is made to pay eightfold.
That sin or evil which is incurred—that is what is expressed by the term "eightfold. It is connected with, or brought about by, the number eight.

It is "multiplied by eight" (*aṣṭāpadya*), meaning it is multiplied; thus, the word *aṣṭāpadya* denotes that which is eightfold in both ways. Likewise, that same [fine] is doubled for a Vaiśya, for he is directly entitled to study and knowledge.
A Śūdra, however, might somehow acquire some knowledge through his reliance on and association with Brāhmaṇas;
yet a Kṣatriya, due to the fault of his office of protection, is punished twice as much as him even though their learning is equal.
As for the Brāhmaṇa, the lawgiver never tires of imposing punishment upon him.
"Whether it be sixty-four, or one hundred and twenty-eight;
for his teaching or his role as instructor is superior, and from that, protection would arise.
What offense has an ordinary person, who is like an animal?"
The ignorant, being unaware of virtues and faults, engage in what ought not to be done.
If even the wise were to act in the same way, alas, the world would be destroyed, for there would be no third person to provide instruction.
Thus it has been said: "In this world, two uphold the vow of righteousness: the king and the learned Brāhmaṇa."
By this [verse], there is an increase in the punishment for a Brāhmaṇa compared to that of a king;

and this is a prescription for the mere degree of increase, not a prescription for the specific numbers as they are literally heard, because regarding the punishment for a Brāhmaṇa, we hear of no fixed limit such as "this" or "that.
Nor is an option (vikalpa) appropriate, because there is no basis for establishing a settled rule.
For an option between two things of equal strength is untenable if it relies upon a different subject matter;
for what king would abandon the sixty-four [arts] belonging to the qualities of a Brahmin to adopt [only] the [punishment] consisting of the twice-born's merit?
An option would only be possible if the punishment had an invisible (transcendental) purpose.

And it has been stated that this [Smṛti] does not have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Likewise, Gautama says: "In the case of a transgression by one who knows [the law], the punishment is more severe. Therefore, they declare that its status as an injunction (*vidhitva*) is not subject to infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Furthermore, an option (*vikalpa*) based on [the presence of] qualities is not logical, because it has already been refuted by the verse beginning with "naṣṭa" (the lost, etc.).
Moreover, since this [passage] possesses a purposeful meaning, an injunction is understood here;
and since that [injunction] finds its basis in the prescription of an addition, it is not capable of being construed as a mere option according to the literal wording.
Manu has declared that taking roots and fruits from trees, wood for the purpose of fire, and grass for the fodder of cows, does not constitute theft.

The term *vānaspatya* refers to forest trees (*vanaspati*); the suffix is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). Bamboo shoots and the like, when taken for the purpose of food, constitute what is not theft (*asteya*).

The roots and fruits of trees, as well as other items such as lotus stalks and grain, are included in the list beginning with "roots and so forth" for the purpose of a single mouthful; a punishment is prescribed for taking roots and fruits beyond that amount. The statement regarding non-stealing refers to taking for the sake of a meal; however, according to another Smṛti, there is a punishment even for one whose livelihood is not diminished, if he somehow becomes greedy or takes what is not his own.
And so Gautama says: "One may take flowers as one would for oneself, and fruits from trees that have not yet ripened.

Wood for the sake of fire—for one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), when no tree is at hand and the fire is about to go out—wood for the purpose of maintaining it is faultless; or one should lay down fuel-sticks (*samidh*) made of *palāśa* wood.
And if there is a village where *palāśa* is not abundant, how should it be done? If they were to be gathered [from elsewhere], there is no fault.
"And grass for the cows":
the dative case is used here in the sense of "for the purpose of" (tādarthye).
Because of the mention of "cows," it is indeed a fault [to offer grass] for the purpose of making a mat.
However, for those who desire the connection of "cows" with the word "grāsārtha," the form *gobhyaḥ* would not be appropriate;
for in that case, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would be required.
A Brahmin who seeks to obtain wealth from the hand of one who takes what is not given—
even by means of officiating at sacrifices or teaching— is exactly like a thief.
This is an extended application (atideśa):
a Brāhmaṇa who lives off thieves is to be punished like a thief,
even by means of officiating at their sacrifices or teaching them.
The particle *api* indicates another action;
by it, receiving as a gift, out of affection, and so forth, are included.
This refers to Kṣatriyas and others who, through their own duties such as trade and the like, otherwise acquire the wealth of thieves.
The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa," however, is for the purpose of removing the conceit that [the king] thinks, "I have indeed acquired this through dharma by officiating at his sacrifice.
One who takes what is not given—that is, seizes it—is a thief (*adattādāyī*).

If he should desire to obtain it (*lipseta*), meaning he wishes to acquire it even before the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) have been received, the suppression of the thief occurs precisely because of that connection.
A twice-born man traveling on a journey whose provisions are exhausted, taking two stalks of sugarcane and two roots from another's field, does not deserve to be punished.

The mention of the "twice-born" (dvija) is for the purpose of excluding the Śūdra. A traveler is one who does not reside in a single village; even among such travelers, it refers specifically to one whose means of subsistence are exhausted and whose provisions for the journey have run out.
Two stalks of sugarcane, one radish—this is for illustrative purposes regarding limited quantities of *harītakī*, mung beans, and other pulses or grains.
Accordingly, another Smṛti states: "There is no prohibition regarding *śamī* pods, cucumbers, fodder for a team of oxen, or grass.
"From another's field" means from a place belonging to another; this includes even an enclosed field.
One who binds those already bound, one who releases those already bound,
and one who seizes slaves, horses, and chariots, shall incur the guilt of a thief.
Horses and other animals whose fetters and bonds have been loosened are kept away from secluded places abounding in *mustā* grass, barley, and the like.

If, while the owner or keeper is asleep, someone should tether them with a halter or bind them with a bit and so forth, he should be punished like a thief on the suspicion that "surely this man intends to lead them away.
However, there is no fault for one who binds them solely for the purpose of protecting them, such as when they have strayed from the owner's house or arrived after being separated from the herd.
In the same way, this very act constitutes "taming" (*dama*) when one binds cattle and other animals with halters and the like around their necks;
and it is the "liberator" (*mokṣaka*) of those who have been bound by chains on their feet and so forth.
Furthermore, having secretly incited the masters of the halters, he carries off bonded servants and others, saying: "I will give you much; why do you serve him?"

In this context, where it was stated that "the death penalty is prescribed for the abduction of men of noble birth," by this [verse], the case of slaves is being addressed. Just as in that very instance regarding a man of noble birth, so too here, one must not carry out the act of seizing or taking them away after having incited them.
In that context, [the phrase] "by force or by theft" refers to the taking of horses and chariots; "one who steals horses and chariots" means one who takes away horses and chariots.

Regarding the phrase "of large animals," in that [other case] the horses belong to the king, whereas these [animals] belong to the local districts. In that case, the punishment is at the king's discretion, but here the execution is mandatory. Even though there are many punishments for thieves, nevertheless, according to another Smṛti:
"Those who seize bandits, as well as those who carry off horses and elephants,
and those who kill by force— such men he shall impale upon a stake.
Likewise, in this [text] as well, having begun with the words "by whatever means," it concludes with "he shall take away that very thing."
Others, however, consider "a chariot yoked with horses" to be a generic category, since it serves as an illustration for horses, oxen, chariots, and so forth.
In that case, the punishment must be considered for horses alone and for the chariot separately;
for while the punishment for theft has been declared in another Smṛti for horses alone, it is thereby established for horses when they are yoked to a chariot as well.
However, for those who consider "taking" to mean abducting [the victim] after instigating them, the term "horse-chariot" indicates a chariot-maker—
that is, a maker of chariots— and this applies to all crafts.
In the case of the abduction of artisans, the punishment is that of a thief.
Even for horses, there is encouragement by the sight of a mare.
By suppressing thieves according to this rule,
a king shall obtain fame in this world and unsurpassed happiness after death.

By following this aforementioned path while suppressing thieves, one attains fame—consisting of the praise of all people—for as long as one lives in this world; and after death, having passed away, one enjoys the unsurpassed happiness known as heaven.
This is the conclusion of the section.
A king who desires to attain the station of Indra and imperishable, undecaying glory should not overlook a reckless man even for a moment.
Force (*sahas*) is power; one who acts by means of that is a perpetrator of violence (*sāhasika*).

A person who, disregarding faults both seen and unseen, relies solely on force and openly engages in acts such as theft, injury, and abduction—all of which cause suffering to others—is a *sāhasika*. That is what is meant by the term "violence" (*sahasa*).

Sāhasa (violent crime) is not a category of offense distinct from theft and the like; rather, those very acts become *sāhasa* because they are committed by force (*prasahya*). Even though acts such as arson or the tearing of clothes are already established as offenses due to their nature of destroying property, one must not overlook them nor delay even for a moment in suppressing them; once the perpetrator is caught, he must be punished at that very instant. He does so desiring to attain directly the station known as Indra’s heaven, which has Indra as its lord.

Alternatively, desiring his own royal station to be like that of Indra, on account of their common quality of immovability—for subjects follow him through both punishment and favor, by means of suppressing those who deserve suppression—it has been said: "as rivers flow toward the ocean";
[he attains] imperishable and undecaying fame.
There are two objects qualified and two qualifiers: "position" (*sthāna*) and "imperishable glory" (*akṣaya-yaśas*).
Alternatively, glory itself is qualified by both; "decay" (*kṣaya*) is a reduction in measure, while "expenditure" (*vyaya*) is destruction without remainder.
Neither of these two applies to it.
Fame does not become soiled, nor is it ever severed;
this is a praise consisting of a statement of the actual facts.
A man who commits an act of violence— whether through foul speech, theft, or indeed by means of physical punishment— is to be known as the worst among evildoers.
This is a figurative statement (arthavāda) intended to praise the method of punishment.
One who is wicked in speech is "vāgduṣṭa," meaning a thief or robber;
and one who commits violence with a staff is "daṇḍenaiva."
The word "staff" (daṇḍa) is intended as an illustration for any weapon;
compared to these three preceding wrongdoers, this one is the most excessive wrongdoer of all.
But that king who tolerates one engaged in violence quickly goes to destruction and incurs hatred.
This too is an explanatory statement (arthavāda). The causative suffix (ṇic) is used here in its primary sense with respect to the root *mṛṣ*, meaning "he who tolerates a man intent on violence."
He who endures and forgives meets with ruin and incurs the hatred of his subjects, and he is overcome by those whom he hates.
A king should not, for the sake of a friend or from the acquisition of vast wealth,
release those who act with violence and bring fear to all living beings.
Therefore, it is said: one should not disregard a person from the side who is being entreated by a minister or others for some reason of affection;
nor should one neglect him thinking, "He himself will give very much wealth.
Those who act with reckless violence bring fear to all living beings.
This, too, is an explanatory statement (arthavāda).
The twice-born may take up arms when their dharma is obstructed,
or during a upheaval of the twice-born and the social orders caused by the exigencies of time.
One who kills in self-defense, in a conflict over sacrificial fees, or in order to protect a woman or a Brahmin, does not incur sin if he acts according to dharma.
Because of the injunction, "One should carry a bamboo staff," it is inferred that Vedic scholars (śrotriya) may take up weapons.
Furthermore, a weapon provides an excess of force to one who possesses superior strength, which is characteristic of a violent person (sāhasika).
Therefore, fearing such violence, the taking up of weapons—which was otherwise not permitted—is prescribed for the twice-born with the rule: "Weapons should be carried by the twice-born."
The sentence is interrupted by this much;
however, the remainder is connected with the phrase "killing according to dharma" (dharmeṇa ghnan). Therefore, there are these two sentences.

As for those who maintain that the killing is permitted only under these specific circumstances and not otherwise—for them, what would be the fate of one who, having fallen unexpectedly into the presence of an assassin, is himself unarmed?
For they do not expect him to take up weapons.
Alternatively, it is explained thus: when the Dharma is obstructed due to a disorder caused by time, and when the king has transgressed and the established order has ceased, one may take up arms;
otherwise, however, during a period of good governance, the king himself provides protection.

For a king cannot possibly remain with his hands outstretched toward every individual. There are some wicked persons who even harass royal officers, despite those officers being most heroic and diligent; yet they fear those who carry weapons. Therefore, the constant carrying of arms is appropriate.
Moreover, what is the point of merely seizing them? It would merely produce a sense of intimidation.

"No," he says, "one who kills according to dharma does not incur sin. This instruction extends even to the limit of violence. As for what Āpastamba stated—"A Brāhmaṇa shall not take up a weapon even for the sake of examination"—this is a prohibition against drawing it when the aforementioned cause is absent, not a prohibition against possessing it.
For those who have cast off their armor are examined [for faults]:
when there is an obstruction of Dharma, such as the destruction of sacrifices and other rites by certain individuals;
and when there is a confusion of the social classes (*varṇa*), meaning their lack of stability through the intermixture of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*) and so forth.
In a situation caused by time, such as the death of a king and so forth,
one may take up a weapon for the sake of protecting one's own wealth and family;
others, however, maintain that on this occasion it may even be taken for the sake of others.

And so Gautama says: "Also in the case of harming the weak, if one is capable of rescuing them. It has been stated that taking up a weapon is for the purpose of averting the fear of the destruction of a sacrifice; he now states another occasion: "and for one's own protection."
The prefix *pari-* signifies "on all sides.

One who kills for the sake of protecting his body, wife, wealth, and sons does not incur sin, provided he acts according to the Dharma; furthermore, there is no contradiction with the commitment regarding sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
If sacrificial fees intended for a sacrifice were to be stolen by some, then one must fight on that account.
Others, however, connect it thus:

"If an obstruction has arisen in battle for the sake of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), when the [performance of] dharma has not proceeded—that is, when there is a failure to fulfill the agreement regarding the sacrificial fees."
The "affront" (*abhyavapatti*) to women and Brahmins refers to humiliation; that is,
where virtuous women are approached by force by someone or even killed, or likewise, where Brahmins are killed by someone.

In that case, by killing with a sword or similar weapon, one does not incur fault; the meaning is that no transgression of the prohibition against violence is committed. Since there is no prohibition [against such killing] and the possibility of acting according to one's own will (*kāmacāra*) arises, one must necessarily proceed to kill after reflecting upon other injunctions and contemplating the statement of Gautama: "If one is capable of releasing [the victim] from harm caused by a weaker [assailant]."
Now, if there arises the apprehension of an assailant, then one should protect oneself from all sides; this is indifference (upekṣā).
One must fight without hesitation for the sake of self-preservation.
He demonstrates this:
whether it be a teacher, or a child or an elder, or a Brahmin of great learning.
One should indeed slay an approaching assassin without hesitation.
An "assassin" (ātatāyin) is said to be one who is prepared in every way to destroy one's body, wealth, wife, or sons;
one may kill such a person without hesitation.
The mention of the teacher and others is merely a commendatory statement (arthavāda).
"These too are to be slain, how much more so others"—
yet even though these [others] may be *ātatāyin* (aggressors), there is no killing of them.
By the rule "the teacher and the expounder," the killing of even those who have done harm is prohibited.
The connection can be made as "the guru who is an *ātatāyin*";
this being the case, this is a qualification of the *ātatāyin*.
Consequently, how could there be a prohibition against an *ātatāyin* other than the guru and the rest?
Because there is no other sentence [to the contrary].
If it is argued that the sentence "there is no fault in killing an *ātatāyin*" is another statement that generally permits [such an act], that too is not correct;
for no injunction (*vidhi*) is heard therein, and since it functions as an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to the preceding [text], it merely restates what has already been established.

In this regard, however, you say: even if the rule is simply "one who attacks" (*ātatāyin*) and the remainder is a mere explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), nevertheless, there is the permission for the killing of teachers and others.
For being harmful (*apakāritva*) is one thing, while being an *ātatāyin* is another.
For one who inflicts some kind of injury but not by means of his entire body and so forth is merely harmful; distinct from him is the *ātatāyin*.
And thus it is recited:
"One with a raised sword, one with poison or fire, one with hands raised for a curse,
a slayer by means of the Atharvaveda, and a slanderer against the king."
One who violates his wife's fidelity and one who is intent on seeking out her vulnerabilities—
one should recognize all such persons as *ātatāyin* (assassins).
Based on the statement "one who is coming," it is said that one who rushes forward with a weapon to kill, or who desires to seize the wives [of another], must be killed;
however, they argue that once the offense has been committed, one should remain indifferent, thinking, "What else will he do?
That is incorrect.
For he will later state, "whether manifest or unmanifest," intending to treat these two as equal both in what is yet to be done and in what has been done.
Therefore, the phrase "as he approaches" is a restatement (anuvāda) made by treating him as one who has come to act or has gone after having acted.

Furthermore, he is killed because he is an *ātatāyin* (an aggressor); however, one who has performed his duty does not become an *ātatāyin*. It has been stated by this [verse] that killing for the sake of protecting oneself, as in "protecting oneself," is not permitted.
No guilt whatsoever attaches to the slayer for killing an assassin, whether done openly or in secret; it is simply fury meeting fury.

"None at all" means there is neither unrighteousness (*adharma*), nor punishment, nor expiation. "Publicly" means in the presence of people; "secretly" means by the administration of poison or by any other such means.
*Manyu* is the deity presiding over anger; he encounters that *manyu*.
In this case, there is no relationship of killer and killed.
When it is said that "the purpose of two men is destroyed by the anger of an assailant," this is a figurative statement (*arthavāda*).
Just as one desiring to receive a gift might say, "Who shall give to me? I am not the receiver, nor are you the giver; therefore, how can there be the fault of receiving?"—so it is here as well.
In this case, no specific punishment has been prescribed for the perpetrator of violence; that [punishment] is to be found in the section on assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*).
However, in this instance, it is even greater, since it has been stated: "he should be known as the worst evildoer."
The king, having branded those men who have set out to violate another's wife with terrifying punishments, shall banish them.
The word *dāra* (wife) applies to a woman who has been consecrated through marriage. "Another" means someone other than oneself.

"Touching" (*abhimarśa*) refers to sexual enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*), beginning with embracing; embracing is the coming together of two persons. "Commencement" (*pravṛtti*) refers to the initiation of the pleasure born of enjoyment. For the purpose of desisting from that, there is encouragement by means such as sending a female messenger (*dūtī*).
Moreover, they declare *saṃgrahaṇa* to be "touching.

Therefore, the meaning is this: having identified a man engaged in approaching another's wife, one should brand him with sharp-pointed spears, tridents, or similar weapons that cause terror, and then banish him by means of cutting off the nose and other such punishments.
Since specific punishments have been prescribed for all these cases here, this is not a general punishment applicable to the subject matter at hand.
What then? It refers to repeated occurrence.
However, this is logical:
for one who does not obtain another object, there is a combination [of exile and a monetary fine] due to the difference in the nature of the offense.
We shall demonstrate it accordingly.
For from that arises the intermixture of castes among the people,
by which unrighteousness, which destroys the very root, leads to total destruction.
"Origination" means arising.
From that act of approaching another's wife, a "mixture" (*saṃkara*) arises in the form of an intermediate caste;
by the birth of which unrighteousness (*adharma*) takes away from the root of the world—that rain which has fallen from heaven. Unrighteousness [thereby] seizes it.

For when righteousness (*dharma*) exists, rain is produced from the sun; yet, when there is confusion of castes (*saṃkara*), neither the *Kārīrī* sacrifice nor the giving of gifts to worthy recipients occurs. Consequently, due to the absence of these acts—giving, sacrifice, and oblation—which are the causes for the production of crops, it becomes capable of destroying the entire world.

Therefore, one should banish those who violate another's wife, lest there be a confusion of castes which is the root of unrighteousness, or else, protecting the rain that is the root of the production of crops and so forth.
A man who engages in private conversation with another's wife,
having been previously accused of such offenses, shall incur the first amercement.

"Conversation" means talking; engaging in such talk—meaning initiating conversation—while being previously accused or charged with offenses such as adultery, including soliciting her woman, is what is meant. One who has been seen committing such an offense elsewhere, or whose guilt is suspected, is "fickle. According to some, this refers to one for whom conversation is forbidden in private places such as a well or a pond. Even if he engages in conversation with another's wife for a specific reason, he shall incur the first *sāhasa* fine; the meaning is that he must be made to pay it.
But he who, having previously been unaccused, speaks out for a valid reason,
shall incur no fault whatsoever, for there is no transgression on his part.
This is a counter-example to the preceding rule:
even if one has not been accused, by conversing with or mixing with [a sinner] without cause, one incurs the same punishment as before.
He who addresses another's wife at a sacred bathing place, in a wilderness, or even in a forest,
or at the confluence of rivers, shall be guilty of adultery.

Although "another's wife" (*parasya patnyāḥ*) was already established in the context, the explicit mention of "another's woman" (*parastrī*) is for the purpose of not excluding the mother, sister, the teacher’s wife, and so forth;
for although they are indeed related to another, they are not designated as "another's woman.
A *tīrtha* is said to be that path by which people descend to fetch water from rivers, ponds, and the like.
For that place is generally devoid of people;
one does not stay there for the purpose of water.

Such a place is designated as a meeting spot, and when it is so arranged, one must certainly go there. [He thinks: "Even though I am staying here, I shall not be suspected. People will think that he is either seeking water, performing his daily purification rites during the day, or waiting for someone.
In another passage, however, there might be the suspicion: "Why is he waiting here?
Therefore, the prohibition applies specifically to a *tīrtha*.
For an *araṇya* is a place devoid of people beyond the village, dense with thickets, trees, creepers, and the like.
In the forest, where trees are densely clustered;
the confluence of rivers is their meeting place,
for that too is a location for making appointments.
He shall incur the offense of *saṃgrahaṇa*. *Saṃgrahaṇa* consists in the desire for another's wife;
therefore, it is implied that whatever punishment is prescribed for that [offense] shall apply to him as well.
This prohibition applies even to one who has not been accused, even when the grounds for accusation exist.

As for what Āpastamba stated—"one should not pass by a woman without speaking"—that refers to the situation where other persons knowledgeable in this scripture are present; in such a public setting, one should perform the salutation, such as "Sister, homage to you," without delay.
Acts of assistance, dalliance, touching her ornaments and garments,
and even sitting together on a bed or a seat— all this is declared to be *saṃgrahaṇa* (adultery).
To one who is not related by any kinship tie, one performs a service by giving gifts such as clothing and garlands;
likewise, by providing food, drink, and so forth;
and through play, jesting, and the use of indirect speech and the like.
Touching ornaments and clothes:

touching ornaments such as necklaces, bracelets, and so forth that have come into contact with her body; knowing them to be hers, one touches them even when they are held by another, despite there being no purpose for doing so.
Likewise, sitting together on a single bed, even when their bodies are not actually touching.
All of this is subject to the same punishment.
If a man touches a woman in an improper place, or if he, being touched by her, consents to it,
it is all recorded in the legal tradition as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse), provided there is mutual consent between them.
However, where movement such as coming and going is accomplished even without touching that place,
there is no fault in a crowded public area;
likewise, a part of the body is also considered a "place."
In that regard, there is no fault in touching a vessel held by her hand or shoulder when setting it down;
however, there is a fault regarding the lips, chin, breasts, and so forth.
Or, if he is pressed by her while she touches his breast or other parts, and he endures it without forbidding her by saying, "Do not do that," and so on, [he incurs a fault].
If this occurs with mutual consent and intentionally, there is no fault in it when it remains unfulfilled;
however, this does not apply to the initial stage of the act.

If a woman, while stumbling, clings to a man’s neck, or a man clings to a woman between her breasts, or if they proceed to take an object held in the other's hand—like one who intends to fall on dry ground but falls instead into mud—neither of them would be at fault.
A non-Brahmin deserves the death penalty for adultery;
the wives of all four castes must always be protected with the utmost care.
The nature of *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse) has been stated.
The punishment is now described here:

a non-Brāhmaṇa, such as a Kṣatriya or others, having committed *saṃgrahaṇa*, deserves a punishment ending in life—the forfeiture of life, that is, execution—regardless of the distinction between low and high castes among all four *varṇas*.
But how is it that there is an equal punishment for one who has sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Śūdra woman?
Regarding this, he states the meaning of the underlying reason: "Wives must always be protected.
A king must protect the wives of anyone whatsoever more than his own wealth or body.
For if there were an equal degree of mixture, even a Śūdra’s family would be destroyed.
This is what is meant:
this matter is based on scriptural authority; the reason for it must be stated here, and that has already been stated.
Regarding this, earlier commentators have explained:
"This previously mentioned punishment does not apply to every instance of sexual intercourse (*saṃgrahaṇa*).
What then? It applies specifically to the primary act of sexual union (*gamana*), which consists of a particular pleasure produced by a particular kind of touch."
For how else could greeting and traveling together with [such persons] at sacred fords and other places result in equal punishment?
Therefore, it is the non-Brāhmaṇa Śūdra who deserves the loss of life when approaching a twice-born man, and no one else;
for it is not right to treat those who are unequal as equals.

Therefore, regarding the previously mentioned acts of sexual intercourse (*saṃgrahaṇa*), the punishment should be determined in consideration of the attendant circumstances (*anubandha*) and other factors.
Where it is certain that this undertaking—consisting of acts such as providing assistance—is for the sole purpose of sexual intercourse, the primary punishment alone is appropriate;
for there is no inconsistency in this case.

And this is observed in both cases as well; thus it was said: "If this punishment applies here to the primary act of sexual intercourse (*saṃgrahaṇa*), what will it do? For there is no other [act] that constitutes primary sexual intercourse.
For no worldly object has been definitively established for him by which he would be impelled toward acts such as assisting another's wife;
and as for that which you consider to be primary sexual intercourse (*saṃgrahaṇa*), there is a heavy punishment for it.
If it is argued that "approaching another's wife is prohibited and thus subject to the authority of the scriptures," [we reply:]...
Know that there is also a prohibition regarding acts of assistance and the like.
If it is argued that, just as with the prohibition, the penance would likewise follow as being equal [to the original offense],
what kind of undesirable consequence (aniṣṭāpatti) is this?
However, this would follow as an undesirable consequence (*prasajyeta*) if that were expressed by the term "embracing" (*saṃgrahaṇa*);
for it is when semen has been emitted that the act of sexual intercourse and so forth is designated.
Wherever such a punishment exists, there a corresponding suffering is incurred.

Therefore, in this contrary case, the penance for the emission of semen must be inferred to apply to [acts such as] "assisting" (upakāra) and so forth, because it is designated by that term [in the rule].
Furthermore, if there were only a slight punishment for conversation and the like, people would engage in them;

consequently, those who have been overcome by another through conversation with another's wife and so forth—having their passion ignited and being drawn by the arrows of Love—would disregard their bodies and pay no heed to royal punishment.
However, it is possible to avoid [the offense] only at the very first engagement, provided that the passion is not maintained as a continuous process.
Therefore, a heavy penalty is appropriate for one who actually approaches another's wife;
but in this case, because of the mention of the "end," there ought to be another, initial penalty.
For they do not become speakers of untruth.
"Prāṇānta" means that which has the end of life as its limit; he must be caused to fall [into punishment] until it falls upon his vital breaths.
By this, even the seizure of all property, the cutting off of limbs, and so forth, are also implied.

Furthermore, the status of being a "punishment" (daṇḍatva) is known for each individual case elsewhere, but one is not punished for a collective aggregate when many punishments are prescribed; thus, that [penalty] which applies to a non-Brāhmaṇa for violating a woman of the twice-born classes is the greatest.
Therefore, this specific interpretation is indeed appropriate, and not applicable everywhere.
In that regard, for one who has sexual intercourse with women of good family who are unwilling and have husbands, the penalty is the taking of life, even if they are of low caste.
Beggars, bards, those initiated for sacrifice,
and artisans may converse with women without being forbidden.
Beggars who live by alms may engage in conversation consisting of requests for alms without being forbidden, provided they have not been prohibited by the master;
or rather, they should not be prevented at all.
So too with bards and panegyrists.

Those initiated for a sacrifice may converse for the purpose of stating their wages; so too craftsmen, such as cooks and others. These are not to be prohibited even at sacred bathing places and similar locations.
One who has been forbidden should not engage in conversation with the wives of others;
however, one who converses despite being forbidden deserves a fine of one suvarṇa.
Some think that this is a penalty for conversing with those who have been forbidden, such as mendicants and others; that is incorrect,
for it has already been stated that they are not to be forbidden at all.
And why should there be a fine of gold for mendicants?
Therefore, anyone who, even if not publicly accused, somehow practices what has been forbidden by his master, shall be fined gold.
This rule does not apply to the wives of wandering performers nor to those who live off their own labor;
for they entice women and keep them hidden away.
The prohibition against conversing and the prohibition against performing services for them do not apply to the wives of *cāraṇas*.
*Cāraṇas* are actors, singers, and others who perform for public spectacles;
likewise, this refers to those wives who live by their own appearance, subsisting through their own dress.

Alternatively, [the term] refers to one's own daughter; for it is said that "this very self is half [of oneself]. Those who live off her are those who tolerate her paramours. They entice and unite her with another man.
Being hidden means being concealed; they do not stand openly in the marketplace.
Precisely because they wear the dress of householders, they differ from well-known courtesans.
They "cause to move" (cārayanti), meaning they incite sexual intercourse; they attract men through the play of their eyes and eyebrows, jesting, and so forth.
Their permission for this is virtuous conduct (*sajjana*), while "causing to move" is the actual union itself (*saṃprayoga*).

Alternatively, the meaning is that they cause their own women to be "fitted" or employed [for prostitution], and they cause other women to be sent forth by means of [their own] women, making their own female attendants act as courtesans and procuresses.
However, he who engages in conversation with such women,
or with female slaves who eat only a single meal a day, or with female ascetics in secret, shall be made to pay a small fine.

If he converses with wandering women in secret, in private, or in a secluded place, he shall be fined a very small amount of gold— such as one-thirtieth part or similar— taking into account his caste and social standing; for their status as courtesans is not complete,
since they consort with men only when permitted by their husbands.
In that regard, one should interact with the husband through the medium of a female messenger, and not directly, because they lack independence.
However, when women are dancing or singing openly, conversation by way of questions such as "What is this? during the occasion of observing their gestures, rhythm, and so forth, is not prohibited.
The female servants and slave-girls, brought from the seven origins of slavery, share a single master; they have one meal and are confined by one man.
Even in that situation, there is yet another slight degree of restraint.

Furthermore, is this word *dāsī* (slave-girl) a relative term such that she is the slave only of him who is her master, or is it based on the nature of the work—like the words *sūpakāra* (cook) and so forth?
In this case, the first position alone holds, because [the other] would lack semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*) when a qualification is employed.
Whosoever is someone's slave, even if she associates with others like a courtesan, whether she be a royal slave or a common slave, she is to be restrained.
If she has not been taken as a concubine, there is no offense in having sexual intercourse with her; however, if she has been taken as a concubine, the punishment for this has already been stated.
We shall explain this matter more precisely in the section on the partition of inheritance.
Those who have gone forth [into homelessness] but lack protection are those such as Śīlamitra;
for they are like lustful men concealed by their outward signs.
He who violates an unwilling maiden deserves immediate execution;
however, a man who violates one who is willing, being of equal status, shall not suffer execution.
This is an incidental point:
"equal" means of the same class.
He who should defile a maiden who does not consent—that is, deprive her of her virginity through sexual intercourse with a male—must be executed immediately on that very day, without delay.
There is no offense against one who is willing; how, then, could there be the attainment of the death penalty?
And whatever may occur in this regard, we shall explain it later.
Even though it is heard here that "the killing is equal," when the consideration of caste necessarily arises even in the case of killing, the rule is restricted by proximity.
One should not cause a maiden who is pursuing a superior man to pay anything at all;
however, one who is serving an inferior man should be kept confined in the house.

One shall not inflict any punishment upon a girl who has engaged in sexual intercourse with a man who is superior to her father’s family in even one of the following: birth, wealth, character, or learning.
Since a maiden lacks independence, a punishment would otherwise have been due for those authorized to protect her, such as her father and others; this verse is a prohibition against that.

However, if she consorts with a man of inferior birth and so forth, or shows a longing for sexual union, she should be kept confined—her play and diversions ceased, and supervised by female attendants—or she should be made to dwell within her father’s house itself until her desire has subsided.
Then, having produced a particular state of joy toward one of low birth, she would remain restrained until her very last breath.
A man of lower caste who has sexual intercourse with a woman of the highest caste deserves death;
however, if her father consents, he may have intercourse with a woman of equal caste upon paying a bride-price.

It has been stated that for the violation of an unwilling maiden, the punishment is death for all—without distinction between those of lower or higher status—with the exception of a Brāhmaṇa. However, regarding the violation of a willing maiden, they say this:
[if she is] superior in beauty, youth, and caste...
The "lowest" (jaghanya) is one who is extremely base;
he should not be killed even if there is no great disparity in their qualities.
However, if he approaches a willing woman, he should pay a bride-price to her father, as in the Āsura form of marriage.
If the father does not consent, then a corresponding fine should be imposed upon the king. But is this not a *gāndharva* marriage—a union through mutual desire?
In that case, a fine is not appropriate.
It has been said that in the Gāndharva form of marriage there is no legal penalty;
for this very reason, this is not the duty of a virtuous wife (*satī*), nor is it a formal marriage, due to the absence of the consecration by fire (*agni-saṃskāra*).
As for the statement attributed to Vyāsa in the *Śākuntala*—that it is "without mantras and without fire"—that was done in such a manner by Duṣyanta because he was tormented by desire.
Marriage is not merely the union through desire;
rather, there are eight types of marriage due to the different means of formal acceptance (*svīkaraṇa*), and not because of a difference in the act of marrying itself.
In that regard, the selection of the groom (*varaṇa*) must be performed again in this manner.
Alternatively, the *gāndharva* form occurs after the appearance of menses;
before the menses, there is either a bride-price (*śulka*) or a fine (*daṇḍa*).
Now, what is the course of action for the maiden?
She should be given to him alone;

however, if her desire has ceased, she may, at will, go elsewhere. Furthermore, even in this case, there is indeed the taking of a fee for the purpose of compensating for the single act of sexual enjoyment.
If the suitor has ceased his desire, he should be made to accept [the bride] by force.
But that man who, out of arrogance, should violate a maiden by force,
his two fingers shall be immediately cut off, and he deserves a fine of six hundred [paṇas].

Even if the maiden is willing, if her father or other guardians are present, he who— disregarding their wishes and by means of arrogance or force— overpowers them, thinking "Who is capable of doing anything to me?", and out of mere passion for the maiden should defile her (the root *kṛ* has multiple meanings here), his half-fingers should be immediately cut off, or he should be fined six hundred [paṇas].

Others, however, maintain that this is a summary of the very meaning of "one who would violate an unwilling woman," which refers to the range of offenses from beating up to killing. In this context, one who violates a woman of inferior caste is not killed; rather, his finger shall be cut off.
One who defiles a willing woman shall not suffer the same punishment as one who cuts off her finger;
rather, he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas] in order to prevent a recurrence of such conduct.
The phrase "with her consent" (*sakāmām*) is a restatement, as the preceding rule also pertains to cases involving a willing woman.
When the act is committed by force, the previous punishment applies; however, when done secretly like a theft, the fine is two hundred [paṇas], excluding the amputation of the fingers.
Now, if a maiden who is already in love with a certain man is deflowered by him during their union—thereby terminating her maidenhood—the punishment for that man is this one.
Alternatively, the fault here is merely the touching of the hand;
for once he knows that the maiden to be sought has been touched by me, no other man will seek her, thinking her to be already in love with another.
If a maiden should defile another maiden, she shall be fined two hundred panas;
she shall also pay double the bride-price and receive ten lashes with a rod.
If a maiden, out of childishness or out of aversion to [another] form and so forth, should defile another maiden, she shall be made to pay two hundred [paṇas];
and the bride-price (śulka) shall be tripled. What, then, is the measure of the bride-price?
This depends on the beauty of form and so forth of any one of these [individuals], as well as their good fortune.
*Śiphā* refers to blows with ropes, creepers, or whips.
But a woman who violates a maiden deserves immediate shaving of the head,
or else the cutting off of two fingers, as well as being drawn by a donkey.
For a woman who destroys the female characteristics of virgins, the punishment is shaving the head—that is, the cutting off of the hair—or the amputation of a finger;
in the case of cutting the hair, she must be led away on a donkey.

Depending on the distinctions of caste and so forth among the virgins, and the distinctions of the offenders to be punished, they desire this punishment for women of the three higher castes according to the sequence starting with Brahmins, and they prescribe various marks [of infamy].
Since they lack any means of valid cognition, they are to be disregarded.
But that woman who, arrogant because of her kinsmen or her own virtues, violates her husband,
the king shall have her devoured by dogs in a public place where many people are gathered.

*Laṅghana* is going elsewhere after transgressing against one's husband. If a woman does this out of pride—thinking, "I have many kinsmen who are powerful and wealthy; I possess the excellence of feminine qualities, such as beauty and good fortune; what is the use of this [husband] with his mere character and appearance?"—then she should be devoured by dogs until she dies.
"Configuration" (saṃsthāna) refers to a place;
it is where many people are gathered together, such as at a crossroads and the like.
They should cause the sinful man to be burned on a heated iron bed;
they should pile wood upon him, and there the evildoer shall be consumed by fire.
That man who is the paramour of the wife shall be burned on a red-hot iron bed made like fire.
While he lies there upon the bed, the executioners shall pile wood over him and cast it on top;
until, by the blows of the wood, the flames of the fire, and the heat of the bed, he has died.
For a wicked man who has been accused for a year, the fine shall be double;
likewise, for cohabiting with a *vrātyā* woman or a *caṇḍālī* woman, the fine is exactly that much.

"Accused" (*abhiśasta*) means one who is proclaimed as a perpetrator of that [crime]. He who has been apprehended with a woman is "accused" and punished. If, after having waited for a year, he is apprehended again with that same woman once the year has passed, then for him—having been accused once—the punishment for being a wrongdoer again after a year has elapsed is double.
In the compound reading *saṃvatsarābhiśastasya*, some kind of interpretation must be made; [the penance lasts] for that same duration as when one has cohabited with a *vrātyā*— that is,
for as long as the man remains defiled.
We say: no;
for even there, punishment is of many kinds according to whether the individuals are superior, inferior, or middling. Which of those applies here?

It is not known what "twofold" means. Rather, it should be understood in some way as follows: for cohabiting with a Cāṇḍālī woman, the penalty is exactly the same as for a Vrātyā woman; however, for stealing from an Antyaja, the fine is one thousand [paṇas].
A *vrāta* is a multitude, a crowd, or a group; a *puṃścalī* is a harlot who moves about with such a group. Thus it must be construed.
Alternatively, let it be that one who deserves a *vrāta* (multitude) is a *vrātyā*; the letter *y* is for the sake of the meter (*daṇḍādi*).
And who deserves a *vrāta*?
A harlot (*puṃścalī*), for she is one to be enjoyed by many men; she indeed deserves a multitude of men.
Alternatively, the female slaves belonging to many masters in a village are *vrātyas*.
As for those who consider a woman who has not been married to be a *vrātyā*, in their view, this is not the primary meaning of the word;
for this term *vrātya* is employed by the authors of the *Smṛtis* to refer to those who have fallen away from the *Sāvitrī*.
And that [initiation] is not possible for women.

Now, if one argues that for women there is an initiation in the form of marriage because of the scriptural statement regarding its attainment, then—like a man who lacks that [initiation]—she would be a *vrātyā*; thus, it would be figurative rather than primary.

Even if the word "initiation" (*upanayana*) is applied to marriage which is not actually an initiation, nevertheless, when it is said "one devoid of initiation is a *vrātyā*," one does not understand it to mean "one devoid of marriage."
Likewise, when it is said, "This region is a lion," even though the word "lion" is applied to the region, one does not perceive that the region is non-human (amāṇavaka).

If you argue that while the primary sense exists there, it is impossible here, we reply: figurative cognition is not based on mere impossibility; rather, what is it based on? It is based on another relationship, disregarding [the primary sense].
The term *upanayana* might be used figuratively for marriage;
but what is the reason that the term *vrātya* is considered figurative?
Even if it were figurative, to claim it is based on the absence of marriage is difficult to establish.

Regarding the term *vrātyajā*: just as one born from a crow is a crow and one born from a hawk is a hawk, it is suspected that [the offspring] is a *vrātya* because of the close connection with many relations, through which there is an understanding of the extension of the form [of the word]. However, even though a connection exists, a *vrātya* woman (*vrātyabhāryā*) cannot be denoted by the word *vrātya*.
For when there is a connection expressed as "this is he," the feminine form must occur according to the rule *puṃyogād ākhyāyām* ("in the case of a name [derived] from connection with a male").
And to that extent, this [word] would be formed by a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) when there is an intention to express a distinction.
Therefore, if the word *vrātya* is to be understood in a figurative sense, then one who is born of that [caste] should be understood.
Now, regarding the meaning of the word: [one who is] "worthy of a group" (vrātam arhati) [is a vrātya].
However, a woman who has fallen from marriage is neither the primary nor the secondary [meaning];
furthermore, there is no fixed time for the marriage of women such that those who fall from it at that specific time would become vrātyas.

Even regarding those who are to be married before the onset of puberty, in the absence of a *svayaṃvara*, a maiden may remain in her father's house at her own will until death, provided she has been permitted by her guardian beyond that time.
A Śūdra who cohabits with a woman of the twice-born castes— whether she be guarded or unguarded—
is deprived of a limb if she was unguarded, and deprived of his entire property if she was guarded.

From a Śūdra down to a Caṇḍāla, if one approaches women of the twice-born castes who are protected—meaning those belonging to the twice-born classes who are guarded by their husbands and others while living within their own caste—he shall be punished according to the rule.
If it is asked what the punishment is: "If he approaches one who is unprotected, he is deprived of a limb and of his entire property";
that is, he possesses both a limb and his whole wealth.
By what is it diminished?
By those two alone, because they are the subject under discussion, because nothing else is specified, and because no particular distinction is mentioned;
thus, the auxiliary factor itself is at fault.
If one goes [to the teacher] in secret, one is deprived of everything—
not by a single limb alone, but even by the body itself.
With the aim of such deprivation, the cutting off of limbs, the seizure of all property, and death are taught as the consequences.
The meaning is that his degradation must be effected.
And so Gautama says: "In the case of approaching an Arya woman, there shall be the excision of the organ and the confiscation of all property; and likewise if she is protected."
A Vaiśya shall be punished with the forfeiture of all his property after being imprisoned for one year;
a Kṣatriya shall be fined one thousand [paṇas] and deserves to have his head shaved with urine.
For a Vaiśya, the punishment of forfeiture of all property has been prescribed.

However, here, due to association, even though he possesses the status of a twice-born, this punishment does not apply to a Vaiśya in the case of approaching a woman of his own caste; rather, it applies only to a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya.
Likewise, for a Kṣatriya who approaches a Brāhmaṇa woman, the punishment is one thousand [paṇas] and the shaving of the head with urine.
Donkey urine should be taken in place of water.
Others explain that because no other substance is prescribed, the increase in punishment results from the suppression [of the offense] for a year within the same category [of substances].
If he causes [the offense] to persist for a year, then this punishment applies;
however, the first explanation alone is the correct one.
Nor should it be asked how there can be equal punishment for those who are equal, inferior, or superior.
For it has been said: "The wives of all social classes must always be protected most carefully."
If a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya should have intercourse with an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman,
the king should fine the Vaiśya five hundred [paṇas] and the Kṣatriya one thousand.
The "unprotected" woman has already been explained; she is one whose virtue has lapsed and who is without a protector.
For approaching her, one should impose a fine of five hundred [paṇas] on the Vaiśya. The root *kṛ* (to do) here functions, by virtue of the context, in the sense of "inflicting punishment."
The meaning is "he should punish.
"Pañcaśataḥ" means "one who has five hundred," a *bahuvrīhi* compound with a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*).
It should be done in such a way that he comes to possess five hundred.
Does this mean that whatever is in excess must be confiscated from him? We say, no;
for if that were the case, no punishment would have been prescribed for one whose wealth consists of five hundred [paṇas] or less.

What, then, is the meaning of "he shall inflict five hundred"? Since the context concerns punishment, it means he shall inflict a punishment connected with the amount of five hundred. Likewise, "a Kṣatriya who possesses a thousand" [means he shall be fined one thousand].
He possesses a fine of one thousand [paṇas], but no wealth in his house.
He should be explained as "one whose limbs and entire property" (*aṅgasarvasvī*); it should be carried out in such a way that both his limb and his entire property become his punishment.
For a Kṣatriya who is authorized for protection, the punishment is greater; he protects, yet he himself commits the offense again.
But both of them, having violated that protected Brahmin woman, should be punished like Shudras or burned in a fire of straw.

Those same two, a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, who have violated a protected Brāhmaṇa woman—that is, having had sexual intercourse with her or being in the very act of engaging in intercourse—shall be punished like a Śūdra; for it is said, "By all means, she is lost [to him]. Or they may be burned by a fire of straw.
The word "or" (*vā*) is used to indicate an alternative regarding the manner of execution, not an alternative regarding the execution itself.
For no punishment other than death is prescribed for a Śūdra who acts in secret.
A Brahmin who approaches a protected Brahmin woman by force shall be fined one thousand [paṇas];
he who has sexual union with one who consents shall be fined five hundred.

If a guarded woman, even if she has fallen from her virtue, is protected by someone—whether by her father, brother, or kinsmen—and a Brāhmaṇa approaches her by force, he shall be made to pay one thousand [paṇas].
If she is both guarded and virtuous, there shall be banishment and branding as additional punishments.
Furthermore, even if she is virtuous, she is still referred to by the term "guarded"; nevertheless, the Brāhmaṇa is released from liability beyond the mere payment of one thousand.
In all cases of branding and banishment, these two [punishments] are applied; however, in the case of violating another's wife, they are applied face-to-face.
Shaving the head is ordained as the punishment for a Brāhmaṇa;
however, for the other castes, the punishment shall be one that ends in death.

Where the execution of Kṣatriyas and others is prescribed, there the shaving of the head applies to a Brāhmaṇa. For example, as it is said: "A non-Brāhmaṇa deserves the death penalty for adultery; however, one should burn the man.
That which goes to the end of life, or brings about the end of life, is "prāṇāntaka" (fatal).
The suffix *ṇvul* is applied because it is seen in other instances as well.
Others, however, read "prāṇāntika" as an alternative reading;
that which exists at the end of life (*prāṇānte bhavaḥ*) is "prāṇāntika," formed with the suffix *ṭhañ* according to the rule for words beginning with *adhyātma*.
For others—meaning for the castes other than Brāhmaṇas, such as Kṣatriyas and so forth—the [penalty] is heard to be "ending only with life," meaning preceded by execution and the like.
Immediately after that, this is stated:
they consider that the shaving of the head (mauṇḍya) being mentioned is prescribed as a fine of one thousand [paṇas] as a supplementary measure to that [death penalty].
Otherwise, since the death penalty is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa, what occasion would there be for a Brāhmaṇa such that it is stated: "Shaving [the head] is the end of life"?

If it is argued that this follows from the general rule "one should burn a man," then that [penalty] should apply only to that [general case]; for in that way, its applicability to that specific subject would be clearly understood.
One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is situated in every kind of sin;
rather, one should banish him from the kingdom, leaving him with all his wealth and unhurt.
Regarding the phrase "in all sins," this rule of the context applies not only to the case of sexual intercourse with a protected woman (*saṃgrahaṇa*), but to other offenses as well.
The word "even" (*api*) indicates that even if a Brāhmaṇa has committed every possible sinful act simultaneously, he must never, at any time, be killed.
What, then, should be done for that sinner?

One should expel this Brāhmaṇa from the kingdom and the territory; one should banish him with his entire wealth—that is, together with all his possessions—and unharmed, meaning with his body uninjured. Even his wealth must not be confiscated.
How, then, is there corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa?
Some say:
"But when exile is being imposed, it prohibits a monetary fine in addition to the property that is being exiled."
Others, however, think that he should be banished after having his entire wealth confiscated and all his property taken away.
No greater unrighteousness exists on earth than the killing of a brahmin;
therefore, a king should not even contemplate his execution in his mind.
This is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) supplementary to what precedes:
there is no unrighteousness (*adharma*) other than the killing of a Brahmin that has a more abundant fruit of suffering.
The ablative case is used by supplying the word "other" (*anya*).
For that reason, a king should not even in his mind desire the execution or the mutilation of this brahmin.
If a Vaiśya should approach a protected Kṣatriya woman, or a Kṣatriya a protected Vaiśya woman,
both of them deserve the same punishment as one who approaches an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman.
"In the case of approaching an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman, one should impose a fine of five hundred on a Vaiśya and a thousand on a Kṣatriya.
In this context, the fine of five hundred applies to the Vaiśya.
If he who is himself the protector causes the very thing he was meant to guard to be lost, it is appropriate that his punishment be severe.
A Brāhmaṇa should be made to pay a fine of one thousand [paṇas] for approaching those two when they are protected;
however, for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya approaching a Śūdra woman, the fine shall indeed be one thousand.
A Brāhmaṇa who has sexual intercourse with a concealed Kṣatriya or Vaiśya woman shall be fined one thousand [paṇas];
this applies even when the punishment of banishment and branding remains in force.
For a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya having intercourse with a Śūdra woman, the fine is one thousand [paṇas].

*Sāhasra* means "consisting of a thousand" (*sahasram eva sāhasram*), with the suffix *aṇ* used in its own sense (*svārthika*). Alternatively, it means "that which has a thousand," referring to the punishment (*daṇḍa*) as the external referent (*anyapadārtha*),
with the possessive suffix *aṇ*.
If a Kṣatriya has intercourse with an unprotected Vaiśya woman, his fine shall be five hundred [paṇas];
he shall undergo tonsure with urine, or the Kṣatriya may instead receive the same punishment as a Śūdra.
The fine for a Vaiśya who has intercourse with an unprotected Kṣatriya woman is five hundred [paṇas]. For a Kṣatriya [who does the same], the penalty is the same;
or else he shall undergo the shaving of his head by means of donkey urine.
This same punishment applies to both parties in the case of approaching a Vaiśya woman.

A Brāhmaṇa who approaches an unprotected Kṣatriya woman, a Vaiśya woman, or a Śūdra woman shall be fined five hundred; however, he shall be fined one thousand if he approaches a woman of the lowest castes (antyaja).
If a Brāhmaṇa has sexual intercourse with an unprotected woman of the Kṣatriya or other castes, there is punishment for both parties.
An Antyaja refers to a Caṇḍāla, Śvapaca, and so forth;
in that case, the fine is one thousand [paṇas].
In this regard, the summary of the punishment of one thousand [paṇas] is as follows:
for a Brāhmaṇa who has sexual intercourse with guarded women of any of the four castes, the fine is one thousand;
for having intercourse with the wives of a Śrotriya, there shall be banishment and branding.
Except in the case of those who have gone abroad;
however, in the case of the wives of *śrotriyas*, it is prescribed on account of the great severity of the penance.
For approaching an unprotected woman, there shall be five hundred [strokes] and branding, followed by banishment.

Even though she may not be designated as another's wife because she is unprotected when the sacrament of marriage has taken place, she is nonetheless an unchaste woman who has transgressed her husband’s ownership; for a non-Brāhmaṇa, the penalty for approaching her by force is the death sentence if she is protected.
If she consents, the penalty is a fine of one thousand, along with banishment and branding.
For approaching a protected woman, one should impose a fine of five hundred on a Vaiśya and one thousand on a Kṣatriya.
That king in whose city there is no thief, no adulterer, no one of evil speech, no perpetrator of violence, and no one who strikes with impunity, shares in the world of Śakra.
That king in whose city, district, or kingdom there is no thief or robber attains the world and station of Śakra, the Lord; he reaches heaven.

"Not one who goes to another’s wife"—meaning a woman who is the wife of another, or a kept mistress, or a remarried woman; the mention of "woman" is for the purpose of prohibiting even those who are not wives or are unrelated.
"A speaker of evil"—one who commits the three kinds of verbal abuse.

The perpetrator of violence is so called; the one who strikes with a staff is the perpetrator of physical assault. The phrase "shares in the world of Śakra" is to be understood as applying in all cases.
This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) supplementary to the section on the seduction of women by thieves and others.
The suppression of these five within his own realm by a king brings him imperial power over his kinsmen and confers glory upon him in the world.
Sovereignty (*sāmrājya*) is the state of being the life-giver to others; it is independence among one's own kin (*sajāti*). By "one's own kin," kings who are equal rivals are intended.
He presides over them as their sovereign; the meaning is that they become his executors of commands.
And in the world, they produce fame and renown for him.
In both cases, it is precisely punishment that acts as the cause.
People say, "This one is wrathful and a bringer of death," yet they actually praise him.
If a sacrificer should abandon an officiating priest, or if an officiating priest should abandon a sacrificer—
provided that the other is capable of the rite and free from fault— the punishment for both of them shall be one hundred panas.
The officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is the performer of ritual acts at a sacrifice, such as the *hotṛ*, *udgātṛ*, and others.

Although that designation applies from the time after the formal selection (*varaṇa*) until the completion of the performance, nevertheless, this rule does not concern the mutual abandonment of those who have already commenced their ritual duties; rather, it concerns the period prior to the selection.
The usage of the term "officiating priest" (*ṛtvij*) is based on the status they previously held.
He who has been chosen in one marriage ceremony must be chosen again even in another ceremony.
This is not merely a non-abandonment of one previously chosen; rather, it applies to his father and others as well.
For Nārada says: "One previously enjoyed [as a son-in-law] is one chosen by oneself."
Moreover, this restriction does not apply to a single individual alone;
rather, it is a family tradition (*kuladharma*).
This has been explained in detail in the *Mahābhārata* regarding the *Saṃvarta-Maruttīya* [episode].
Therefore, those same families from whom the officiating priests were chosen by one's father and ancestors should be chosen;
this same rule applies even to those who perform sacrifices for others,
and they too should engage those very same families.
If one desiring to sacrifice does not choose a priest who has already performed the office of priesthood, or another of that same lineage, but instead solicits some other officiant—
one who is capable in the performance of the sacrifice, skilled in its application, and free from defects such as moral blemish or physical deficiency—

then if such a priest, being thus solicited, should refuse to accept the office of officiating, provided he is free from these very defects and the patron is capable and learned; [in that case, the following applies].
For such abandonment by those two, the fine is one hundred [paṇas].
A priest who abandons his patron (yājya) shall be made to pay one hundred; likewise, a patron who abandons his priest.
This rule regarding priests and patrons applies not only to them, but also to pupils and teachers.

And so Gautama says: "Furthermore, a priest who does not perform sacrifices and a teacher [who fails in his duty] are to be abandoned; likewise, those who serve those whose conduct leads to a fall from caste are to be abandoned.
One falls [from caste] by abandoning [a teacher] except in the case of a formal renunciation.
Some also maintain this rule regarding the recipient of a gift even in the act of accepting it.
Neither mother, nor father, nor wife, nor son deserves to be abandoned.
One who abandons these, provided they have not fallen from their status, shall be fined six hundred by the king.
A mother does not deserve abandonment;
she is not to be cast off.

Abandonment—meaning expulsion from one's own home—is [only justified] when a mother’s conduct has faltered, or when she fails to provide assistance despite being called upon to do so for a service rendered.
The same should be explained for the father and others as well.
Due to the association with the term "relation" (*saṃbandha*), the word "woman" (*strī*) is intended here specifically as a wife.
There is no abandonment of these [relatives] as long as they have not fallen from their caste.

Regarding the mother, however, Śātātapa states that "some say she does not fall [from her status] with respect to her son. Furthermore, the abandonment of a wife consists of ceasing sexual intercourse and forbidding her from domestic duties;
however, the provision of food, clothing, and so forth is not forbidden.
It is stated: "Even when women have fallen [from virtue], clothing, food, and drink should be given to them, and they should dwell near their own homes."
When twice-born men in their hermitages dispute with one another regarding their duties,
a king who desires his own welfare and seeks to act righteously should not issue a contrary judgment.

Regarding those dwelling in forest hermitages, such as forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) and others, when they dispute among themselves within their hermitages concerning a duty or *dharma* that has become a point of contention—arguing, "This is the meaning of the scripture; this is not"—he should not hastily pronounce a settlement of the *dharma*, nor should he issue a verdict by his own authority as if he were a sovereign over others.
How then?
In the manner that will be described below.
In this way, one's own welfare is accomplished;
the meaning is that there is no abandonment of the purpose of the scripture.
And even though householders belong to a stage of life (āśrama), the method of determination is exactly as has been stated.
The subject matter (*kārya*) consists of the points of dispute characterized by doubt regarding the Dharma;
and by the mention of the "stages of life" (*āśrama*), it is explained that the scope [of the treatise] is restricted to specific subjects.
Having honored these men as is appropriate together with the Brahmins, the king, having first pacified them with gentle words, should restore them to their own duty.

He now states how that should be performed: having honored in exactly the same manner each person who deserves a particular kind of worship according to their qualities— by means of Brahmins such as ministers, domestic priests, and so forth—
whether through collaboration in the act of worship or in the proclamation of the Dharma.
And at that time, those Brahmins should be known as truthful.
Together with them, he should explain his own duty, what is just, and the matter at hand.
Once his greatness is established, the instruction to the members of the assembly serves the purpose of securing preeminence.
One should place them at the forefront;
for in this way,
people do not become angry with the king because of his instruction.
