Having first pacified them with words of affection and praise, and having made them free from anger, one should then speak.
If a Brāhmaṇa fails to feed his neighbor and next-door neighbor at a festive meal for twenty twice-born men who are worthy, he deserves a fine of one māṣaka.
"Veśa" means a dwelling, that in which one enters; "prativeśa" is that which faces it, namely the house facing [one's own]; one who resides there is a "prativeśya" (neighbor).
In the reading with the initial long vowel (*prātiveśya*), the suffix *aṇ* is used in its own sense.
Similarly, an "anuveśya" is said to be one who dwells behind [one's house].
If he does not feed those two— if,

having brought them to his own house on an auspicious occasion such as a wedding or other festival, twenty or so other twice-born men are fed there— then he shall be made to pay a fine of one *māṣaka* of gold.
This is understood from the qualification "gold" (*hiraṇyam*) used later [in the text], which applies here as well.
If those two neighbors, the neighbor and the next-door neighbor, are worthy—being neither hostile nor utterly devoid of merit—then [they are fit].
If those learned in the Vedas do not feed a virtuous fellow-student during auspicious rites,
they shall be made to pay double the value of that food and one *māṣaka* of gold.
This undertaking is for the sake of those who are not neighbors;
this is a rule for fellow students of the Veda (*sabrahmacārin*).

A learned scholar (*śrotriya*) [should invite] another such learned scholar endowed with good qualities to "prosperous rites" (*bhūtikṛtya*)—where "prosperity" (*bhūti*) means wealth, and "rites" refers to activities performed when there is abundance of wealth, such as communal feasts and the like.
Alternatively, the term *bhūti* (prosperity) is an adjective qualifying *kṛtya* (rites).
Those rites characterized by prosperity (*bhūtimanti*) are those such as weddings and the like that are performed with abundance and profusion, wherein more than twenty men are fed.

At such festive occasions, if one does not feed [the guest], one should cause him to give twice as much food for the sake of that rite; that is, he should be made to pay a fine of food equivalent to twice the amount required for those rites of prosperity.
Or both [the fine] to the king, namely gold or a māṣaka coin.
One who is blind, mentally disabled, a cripple, or seventy years of age and infirm,
as well as one who renders service to those learned in the Vedas, shall not be made to pay any tax by anyone.

The instrumental case in *saptatyā* is used in the sense of "by nature," as in the expression *prakṛtyā virūpaḥ* ("deformed by nature"). One who has been born for seventy years is thus called [a "seventy-year-old"].
By serving those who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyas*)— that is, those engaged in Vedic study— either through personal attendance such as massaging their feet or by performing manual labor,
these artisans shall not be made to pay [the tax] month after month by anyone;
the phrase "by anyone" implies that they must not be made to pay even by one whose treasury is depleted.
The king should always honor one learned in the Vedas, those afflicted by illness or pain, children, the elderly, the destitute, those of noble lineage, and the virtuous.
"Veneration" (*saṃpūjana*) means "favor" (*anugraha*), because verbal roots have multiple meanings;
for no other form of veneration is possible for children and the like.
They record in their tradition that the term *śrotriya* here refers specifically to a Brāhmaṇa.
One who is afflicted by separation from loved ones and the like;
one who is destitute and impoverished; and one born of a great family.
One born into a family distinguished by reputation, wealth, learning, valor, and other such qualities is of noble lineage (*mahākulīna*).
One who is noble (*ārya*) is of upright nature and free from crookedness.
Toward these individuals, one should extend favor through gifts, honors, and the like.
Some explain "possessing nothing" as a specific qualification of one born of a noble family.
On a smooth board made of *śālmalī* wood, a washerman should wash clothes slowly;
he should neither carry away clothes with other clothes nor store them together.
There is a tree named śālmalī; a board made from its product is used here,
for it is smooth by its very nature,
and even by the strokes of a garment, no parts of it are worn away.
For those [spirits], having passed away, might tear one's clothes;
yet this restriction to a specific species of wood is not for the sake of some unseen merit (adṛṣṭa).
Therefore, there is no fault in using any other wood that possesses such a nature on its surface.
Regarding smooth and non-rough [clothing]:
one should not carry away another's garments in exchange for one's own garments;
having tied them up or wrapped them over [one's head], one should not take them to a bathing place to wash them.
Let there be no destruction of the garments by binding them; for they become excessively compressed when so pressed. Nor should one wear them while they are still wet.

One should not give clothes belonging to one person to another; that is, one should not give them for the purpose of wearing, even for a price. For it is another who wears these clothes, and the washerman merely causes him to wear them.
Since no specific punishment has been mentioned, the previously established fine of māṣakas should be applied.
A weaver shall give ten palas [of thread] and receive one pala more;
if he acts otherwise than this, he shall be made to pay a fine of twelve [paṇas].
A weaver, a *kuvinda*, weaves cloth;
he is the maker of garments such as those for carts and the like.
Taking ten *palas* of thread, while weaving a cloth, he would give back a garment weighing one *pala* more.
One should pay everything according to this rate of increase.
An assessment must be made for coarse and fine garments, as well as for those with fur;
otherwise, there shall be a fine of twelve paṇas.
This penalty applies when interest is not paid;
however, in the case of forfeiture of the principal, that which was stated by the *gaṇa* applies.
Thus, if one does not pay the interest on twenty *palas*, the fine shall be double.
In this manner, the calculation should be made as "threefold," "fourfold," and so forth;
others, however, say that the staff [fine] is the king's share.
Those skilled in customs houses and expert in evaluating all types of merchandise shall determine the price according to the goods; from that, the king shall take one-twentieth as tax.
Those places where tolls are collected are called toll-stations (*śulkasthāna*), established by kings or merchants as fixed for their respective regions.

At those stations, those who are skilled toll-collectors (*śaulkika*)—who cannot be deceived by rogues, and who are discerning experts knowing the methods regarding the arrival, purchase, sale, loss, expenditure, quality, and worthlessness of all merchandise—should determine the price of the goods that have arrived from another country or are being taken away.
From that, the king shall take a twentieth part.
But what is the use of calculating the value? It should simply be stated that "one-twentieth of the merchandise [is the tax].
True, this applies when the king takes the goods according to their actual form.
Garments such as cloths are used for their own inherent form;
in that regard, since a twentieth part [as a tax] prior to the twentieth [unit] is not possible without cutting, the assessment of value is for this purpose.
This is stated "according to the merchandise" in order to make known that there is no customs duty (*śulka*) on items that are not for sale but are for one's own personal use.
Thus, in accordance with the time, not every commodity is sold at all times for a single fixed price.
Therefore, the determination of the price of commodities depends upon place and time; there is no fixed price.
If one, out of greed, exports those goods that are the king’s own famous wares or those which have been prohibited, the king shall confiscate his entire property.

Those commodities renowned for their association with a king because of their utility to royalty—such as elephants, saffron in Kashmir, silk and wool in the eastern regions, horses in the western regions, and gems and pearls in the southern regions—their renown arises from the fact that they are easily obtained within the territory of a particular king but difficult to find elsewhere.
For by means of these, kings enter into mutual alliances.

Those items which have been prohibited by the king—such as "this [commodity] must not be taken from my territory elsewhere, or it must be sold only here, as in the case of grain during a famine"—if one, out of greed, exports them to another country or sells them, the king shall confiscate everything; "sarvahāra" means the seizure of all property. This is the punishment for one who takes them away out of avarice for wealth.
But for the purpose of paying tribute to another king, even physical hardship such as being besieged in a fortress and so forth is greater.
One who evades a customs station, one who buys or sells at an improper time,
or one who gives false accounts in the reckoning of goods, shall be made to pay a fine eight times the amount of the loss.
A merchant is one who buys and sells.

He avoids the customs station by taking a detour, or he travels at an improper time, such as at night when the customs officials have departed. Or, being dishonest in enumeration, he states a lower amount during the counting.
This enumeration is illustrative;
therefore, this same rule applies even in the case of concealing [the offense].
The fine is a penalty consisting of an eightfold multiplication of the transgression.
As long as he conceals it, for that duration [the fine] is eightfold; or rather, he should be made to pay eight times the appropriate duty (śulka) on that which was concealed.
The first interpretation alone is logical, for the word *atyaya* (transgression/fine) is applicable there, and it is applied to the object because it is the cause of that [fine].
Others, however, connect the phrase as "those who buy and sell at an improper time"; and this prohibition applies when the customs duty has not been paid or when the transaction occurs in secret.
Having investigated the importation, exportation, and storage, as well as both the increase and decrease of all commodities, he should regulate their purchase and sale.
Those who are sellers in the marketplace shall not be permitted to set the price according to their own will, nor shall the king purchase at a price fixed by his own preference.
How then?
This and that must be determined.
Regarding the arrival: does it return from another country or not? Likewise, does it come from such a great distance?
Similarly, regarding the place of departure: is it transformed right now, or does it remain?

For a commodity departing at this very moment, even a small profit is of great fruit; furthermore, there is profit through buying and selling other goods with the price generated from that [initial] profit.

Having examined all this— including the increase and decrease resulting from location, how much its price increases, and what kind of decrease occurs— he should arrange the purchase and sale within his own territory in such a way that there is no hardship for either the merchants or the buyers, and thus establish the market price.
Every five nights, or else every fortnight when it has passed,
the king should perform the formal offering of the guest-water (argha) for these [deities] in their presence.
Because substances undergo increase and decrease due to their coming and going and other factors, the value of goods takes on many forms.
Therefore, the fixing of prices must be verified every five nights; it should not be considered as having been established once and for all, nor should one place trust in merchants.
Rather, one must personally remain vigilant.
Regarding a commodity that takes a long time to be exported, the search for its price should be conducted over a fortnight; in other cases, it should be conducted over five nights.
All weights, measures, and balances shall be well-marked;
they must be re-examined every six months.
The balance (*tulā*) is well known. Measurement (*māna*) refers to the *prastha*, the *droṇa*, and so forth.
A counter-measure (*pratīmāna*) is that which is made for the purpose of determining the weight of gold and other such items.
It should be well-marked on all sides and stamped with the royal insignia.
Having personally ascertained it through direct observation, he should seal it with his own seal;
every six months, he should have it re-examined by trustworthy officials so that no one may tamper with it.
A vehicle shall be made to pay one paṇa at the ferry; a man, half a paṇa;
an animal and a woman, a quarter paṇa; and an empty-handed man, half of a quarter paṇa.
A vehicle, such as a cart or the like, crossing over a riverbank must pay a *paṇa* as a ferry toll.
Since it will be taught later that this applies to vehicles filled with goods, this royal share refers to empty-vehicle conveyances being brought across for the purpose of fetching goods.
A load carried by men, when being brought for the purpose of fetching goods, must pay half a *paṇa*.
Livestock, such as cows, buffaloes, and the like, as well as a woman, constitute one quarter (pāda).
A "void" (riktaka) means nothing at all.
He who has taken [the goods] for the second time, that man shall be made to pay half of a quarter (pādārdha).
Because it is possible for an empty man to cross a river by means of his own agility, he is made to pay a small amount;
however, because a woman lacks such capacity for crossing by herself, she is made to pay much. This applies to the ferry and the cause for the ferry fee.
Vehicles filled with goods shall be made to pay ferry-toll according to their value;
those with empty containers, as well as men without luggage, shall pay whatever is appropriate.
"Goods" (*bhāṇḍa*) refers to items such as clothing, grain, and so forth.
Vehicles filled with these, according to their value, must be made to pay for the crossing when they are being ferried across.

If a great quantity of highly valuable items such as clothing has been loaded there, then they must be made to pay a large amount; however, if it is not excessively heavy, consisting of grain and the like, then they must pay a small amount.
In this way, the river should be conceived of as being easy or difficult to cross.
"Vessels" refers to vehicles carrying whatever small amount of goods there may be;
here, the word *bhāṇḍa* denotes wealth.
And those who have no other possessions do not give even half a foot-measure; rather, they give whatever is available, whether more or less than that.
In this matter, no fixed rule can be established; therefore, the meaning of the scripture is simply that one should act according to one's own discretion.
On a long journey, one should know that a crossing may be found according to the location and the time, such as on the banks of rivers; however, there is no such sign in the ocean.
First, there is the gift for crossing from this shore to the other;
this refers to traveling by boat between villages,
or on a long journey to be covered by a distance measured in *yojanas* and so forth.
"According to the place":
that very ferry-fee which has been established by the ferrymen at whichever location;
"according to the time."
"Time" refers to the rainy season and so forth, when there is abundant water; in such a case, the fare is one thing.
When a river has little water and it takes a long time to reach a village, the ferrymen undergo greater exertion, and thus the fare is higher.
Regarding the term for the fare (*tara*), the word *tara* is used here in the sense of the cause [of crossing] for the effect [the act of crossing].
To whatever extent the distance is long, to that same extent the ferry fare increases;
this should be understood to apply to riverbanks.
On the ocean or the great sea, there is no fixed characteristic for a ferry fare.
It is not possible to determine how many *yojanas* the boat has been carried so that the price may be calculated accordingly; however,
on rivers and streams, it is possible to know whether this path is one *yojana* or two *yojanas* long,
for in those places, villages serve as markers of measurement.
In that regard, whatever the price is for a distance of one *yojana*, it is doubled for two *yojanas*.
However, on the ocean, the ship carries many goods, and it is not possible to accurately determine the measurement in *yojanas* and so forth;
for this very reason, it is said that "there is no fixed standard on the ocean."
A pregnant woman in her second month or beyond, as well as a renunciant,
a sage, Brāhmaṇas, and those bearing religious marks, shall not be made to pay the ferry-toll when crossing.
After two months, a woman whose menstrual period has begun becomes one who has manifested pregnancy;
because she is to be favored, the ferry-toll should not be taken from her. A renunciant is one belonging to the fourth stage of life (āśrama).
The sages are ascetics;
the Brahmins are those who bear the marks [of their stage] and are students of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*).
The mention of "Brahmins" is a qualification.

Therefore, this rule does not apply to those who merely bear the external marks of renunciation. They should not be made to pay a ferry-toll (*tārika*) or a fare (*paṇa*) and so forth for the purpose of crossing.
Although the term *tārika* alone would have sufficed according to the requirements of the meter, the word *tara* is included for the sake of clarity.
Whatever on a ship may be damaged through the fault of the boatmen,
that must be paid by the boatmen themselves, having assembled together from their own respective shares.

If goods not loaded onto a boat are lost due to the fault of ferrymen or sailors who—either by steering through a whirlpool or by knowing the location and failing to secure it with firm lashings—allow water to enter the vessel, or if the wind is let loose by means of iron pins, leather thongs, or cord lashings, and consequently the goods are shattered or destroyed, then those very ferrymen must pay compensation from their own respective shares to the owner of the goods; all the ferrymen who were on board shall assemble and pay together.
This decision regarding legal procedure for those traveling by boat has been declared:
in the event of an injury on the water caused by the fault of the boatmen, there is no punishment if it was due to an act of God.
Those whose livelihood is by boat travel by means of ships; for them, this rule is declared: whatever is lost in the water due to the fault of the boatmen, that they shall pay.
In the case of a divine calamity or an accident, such as the breaking of the ship due to wind and so forth, there is no punishment for the sailors for the loss of goods.
This same principle applies to carriers of goods or porters on land.

If a porter proceeds with diligence, holding onto his staff for support, with the upper part of the load firmly tied, and by chance the merchandise of one who has fallen on a muddy path is destroyed due to his sight [failing], there shall be no fault on the part of the porter.
One should cause the Vaiśya to practice trade, money-lending, and agriculture, as well as the tending of cattle; and the Śūdra [should perform] service for the twice-born.
On this point, some explain as follows:
even if they are unwilling, the Vaiśya and the Śūdra must be made to perform those duties by force, because this is their own specific duty (svadharma).
Even though there is a visible purpose, an invisible purpose also exists, because it is a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi).
And this being the case, it follows that even a Brahmin must be made to accept [a gift] by force.
If it is argued that this has been stated as a fault only with respect to the [opposing] position, then this very same position applies here as well;
therefore, that is incorrect.
When there is a desire for wealth, the restriction is based on the scripture;
however, activity is not necessarily bound by an injunction. Where there is a personal motive, the injunction does not function as the instigator.
But the function of the injunction pertains to the restrictive portion (*niyamāṃśa*).
Such is this restriction:
one should cause only a Vaiśya to engage in trade; if he should do anything else when no calamity exists, he should be punished.

In this way, [the rule] applies specifically to the acceptance of gifts from a Brahmin; likewise, it follows that even one who is capable of accepting gifts should remain devoted to contentment. As for what is heard in the scripture—that [one may take] "even against his will"—that is a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
A Śūdra alone is for servitude; in this way, the nature of restriction should be understood to apply everywhere.
A Brāhmaṇa should support a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who are distressed for a livelihood out of compassion, making them perform their own respective duties.
A Brāhmaṇa who has been emaciated by his mode of livelihood should support them with gifts of food and the like; he should provide for the maintenance of both Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.

Out of compassion—that is, with sympathy—he should cause them to perform their own respective duties: those which are the specific duties of a Brāhmaṇa, such as fetching sacrificial fuel, *kuśa* grass, and water-jars, or else those which are the specific duties of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.
A Kṣatriya should be appointed to protect the village and similar duties; a Vaiśya to his own tasks such as agriculture and the rearing of cattle.
This rule applies by implication to a Brāhmaṇa who possesses great wealth and extensive retinues.
Because of the statement "his own duties," he must not be made to perform servile labor, such as cleaning away contemptible leavings and the like.
If a Brāhmaṇa, out of greed and by virtue of his superior power, compels initiated twice-born men to perform servitude against their will,
he shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king.
They have been refined and initiated.
Although this is understood from the mention of the "twice-born" (*dvija*) alone, it is nevertheless stated so that it may not be perceived as merely indicating the three castes (*traivarṇika*).
It refers to a Brāhmaṇa who makes those of his own caste perform servitude—consisting of washing feet, clearing away food-remnants, sweeping, and so forth—even though they are unwilling.
The state of being a master is "prābhavyam," which means lordship.
One who causes [another] to act by virtue of an excellence of capability—such as strength and so forth—is to be fined six hundred [paṇas].
This is on account of greed.
However, one who acts out of hatred and so forth should be punished more severely.
The form *prābhavatyāt* is derived from the present participle (*śatṛ*) of the root *bhū*, with the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*).
Because of the statement "by virtue of authority" (*prabhutvena*), there is no fault on the part of the teacher.
From the statement "if unwilling," it follows that for those who are willing, there is another punishment.
But one may cause a Śūdra to perform service, whether he has been purchased or not;
for he was created by the Self-existent One solely for the service of the Brāhmaṇa.
"Acquired" means purchased; "unacquired" means obtained as alms-food and so forth.
This is a restatement of the rule that will be explained hereafter.
The phrase "only for the purpose of service" is an explanatory praise (arthavāda).
Even if released by his master, a Śūdra is not freed from servitude;
for that is innate to him, so who can remove it from him?

One who has relied upon [a master] through the seven modes of servitude remains so even if released by him or even if liberated from him; however, who can remove that innate, natural, and co-existent state of servitude from such a Śūdra? Just as the Śūdra caste cannot be removed from him, so too servitude cannot be removed.
This is a commendatory statement (arthavāda),
since he will later state that a Śūdra is released from slavery upon a specific cause.

One captured under a banner, one who is a slave by food, one born in the house, one purchased, one inherited, one given as a gift, and one enslaved by way of punishment— these seven are the origins of slavery.
The mention of the "banner" (dhvaja) is for the purpose of indicating the vehicle;
an army is called "possessing banners" (dhvajinī).
It was brought from there.

"Having been defeated in battle, he is made a slave. But what is the meaning of this statement regarding a Kṣatriya—that a Kṣatriya, when defeated in war, becomes a slave? We say: "No," because it is the Śūdra who is the subject under discussion, as it is said, "He was created for servitude alone."
Having conquered his master, the latter's slave is brought away;
he enters into slavery for the one who has brought him.
But has it not been stated that slavery is specifically prescribed for the Śūdra, as it is innate to him?
It is not so;
for if that were the case, there would be no fixed rule, as it would not be known whose slave he is. Indeed, all members of the three higher castes would then be his slaves.
For one who follows his own specific duty (*svadharma*), there is no such lack of restriction, because [the latter] is not a prescribed rule (*avidhi*).
Others, however, maintain that since it is said "all should serve each subsequent [higher caste]," servitude exists even for Kṣatriyas and the rest;
but that is incorrect.
Servitude is one thing, and service is another;
even performing lowly tasks constitutes servitude for one who is unknown. There is no restriction on anything commanded by the master.
Service (*paricaryā*), however, consists of massaging the body and being entrusted with the protection of wealth, the wife, and so forth;
this has been elaborated upon by Nārada.
One who enters into servitude for the sake of obtaining food is a *bhaktadāsa* (slave for food).
One born in the house is "born-in-the-house" (gṛhaja);
one produced from a female slave is a "slave by birth" (garbhadāsa);
one purchased with wealth is [a slave] obtained from the presence of his master.
An adopted son (*datrima*) is one given [in adoption] out of affection or for some unseen spiritual purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
An inherited son (*kramāgata*) is one who comes from the father’s lineage.
Now, what is the distinction between this [inherited son] and one born in the house (*gṛhaja*)?
The "born-in-the-house" (*gṛhaja*) is one born of that very master's female slave; the other, however, is "succession-arrived" (*kramāgata*).
A "debt-slave" (*daṇḍadāsa*) is one who, being unable to pay a fine to the king, is made a slave.
They also maintain that slavery exists even for those of low caste, according to the rule: "One should perform [labor] equally through work."
That is incorrect;
servitude is one thing, and the performance of its duties is another,
and this punishment is not such that it would be included within the former.
Nor has the maintenance of a man born into the state of slavery been mentioned; it is said that [slavery] occurs solely through action.
Likewise, there is also slavery by means of labor.
But is it not the case that even a Śūdra who has come under one's power through dharma is considered a slave?
In that regard, how can there be seven origins of slavery?
This is not a fault;
for his status as a slave is not innate.

Because one who seeks merit (dharma) is subject to desire, the acts of giving and lending are not appropriate for him, just like a slave born in the house or purchased. For it has been said: "In whatever way [one follows] virtuous conduct... and so forth.

By saying this, the following is demonstrated: his servitude is not permanent; rather, it pertains to one who seeks a specific reward. Consequently, there is no servitude for one who does not desire it.
Therefore, if a Śūdra possesses wealth and lives independently without depending on Brāhmaṇas and others, he would never be at fault.
A wife, a son, and a slave—these three alone are declared to be without property;
whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong.
These three, though they have acquired wealth, are yet without property;
for whatever wealth they acquire belongs to their master— that is, it is the property of him to whom they have become subject.
The wife’s property belongs to the husband; the son’s to the father; the slave’s to the master.
But if these [wives, sons, and slaves] are destitute of wealth, how can they have the entitlement to perform ritual acts?

In that regard, this [scriptural injunction] would not be applicable: "If the two sons should be maintainers of the sacred fires (āhitāgni), then the son should give to those same persons to whom the father gave."
"The natural duty (*sahaja-dharma*) must also be practiced by both husband and wife; you must not transgress [your duty] regarding *dharma*, *artha*, and *kāma*.
If she were destitute of wealth, what other non-transgression could there be regarding *artha*?
Furthermore, the rule that 'even a Śūdra may sacrifice for himself with *pākayajñas*' would be contradicted if he were destitute of wealth."
There would be no contradiction [in the rule] if it were intended to apply specifically to Śūdras who act according to their own will.
For slaves indeed possess ownership over their own property, insofar as they are designated as having "their own property.
Indeed, such a designation cannot exist in the absence of a relationship [of ownership].
It is a contradiction to say that acquisition does not produce ownership;
therefore, this which you maintain—that what they acquire is not their own—is inconsistent.
It is just as if someone were to say, "She, of whom I am the son, is not my mother. Such is this [position].

Or, if women had no ownership, then the enjoyment of pleasure with the wife alone, which is permitted [by the husband], would be rendered without basis by such scriptural texts as, "The wife indeed has authority over the household goods.
To this, it is replied:
this is a prescription of dependence.
In the absence of her husband’s permission, a woman must not independently expend wealth anywhere at will;
the same should be understood to apply to sons and slaves as well.
Others, however, believe that the mention of "wife and son" is intended to include the slave.
And this statement of his is for the sake of a further point:
in times of distress, one should have no hesitation regarding their taking of wealth, for that is indeed the property of the husband alone.
A Brāhmaṇa may confidently take property from a Śūdra;
for he has nothing that is his own, as his wealth is to be taken by his master.
And thus someone has said: "This refers to the case of a Śūdra who has attained the Dharma.
For it has been stated that there is no evidence for such a distinction.
Therefore, the Śūdra is the slave of everyone, and it is he alone who is declared to be a fit recipient of gifts.
"Confidently" means without hesitation.

One should not entertain the doubt, "How can one accept the wealth of a Śūdra, for that is prohibited? because it has been stated that he possesses no property whatsoever over which he could have an accumulation.

His wealth is taken by his master; this alone is the purpose of its acquisition, for the master takes it. Therefore, one may confidently undertake the acquisition of goods—that is, the taking of property.
Thus, even if it is not being brought [to him], he should employ it as if it were situated in his own house.
This is appropriate when there is a specific purpose:
for one who possesses no wealth, there is no fault in accepting [gifts] from a Śūdra slave.
One should diligently cause the Vaiśyas and Śūdras to perform their own respective duties; for if they deviate from their own duties, they would throw this entire world into turmoil.

If they were to transgress their duties, they would agitate and throw the world into confusion; therefore, they must not be permitted to deviate from their respective occupations with ease. Even Vaiśyas, upon committing even a slight transgression, should indeed be subjected to a heavy punishment.
There is no bondage;
even wealth is capable of fulfilling one's own dharma.
Day by day he should inspect his works and vehicles, as well as his fixed income and expenditure, his mines, and his treasury.
For the purpose of maintaining the duties of kingship:
"economic activities" refers to agriculture, tax stations, and so forth;
"vehicles" refers to elephants and the like.
One must constantly investigate his income and expenditure: "This has been entered [into the treasury], this has been disbursed.
Mines are lands where ores such as gold and other minerals are produced;
the treasury is the place where stores of wealth are kept.
Thus, by settling all these legal cases, the king,
having cast off all sin, attains the supreme goal.

By settling legal disputes, such as those concerning debts and the like, in the manner described—that is, by bringing them to a conclusion through a formal decision—he casts off and removes whatever sin there may be, provided it is of an unknowable nature; thus, he attains and reaches the supreme goal, the desired state of heaven or liberation.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "General Judicial Procedure," within the section on the Duties of Kings in the Saṃhitā of Manu’s Dharmaśāstra as proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Thus ends the eighth chapter of the Commentary on Manu, composed by Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi, son of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Vīrasvāmin.
Now begins the ninth chapter: I shall declare the eternal duties of a man and a woman who abide in the path of righteousness, both in their union and in their separation.

Following the section on adultery (*strīsaṃgrahaṇa*), there is the indication of the legal titles (*vivādapada*) beginning with "the duties of husband and wife" (*strīpuṃdharma*) and "partition" (*vibhāga*).
That is now being stated:

if a wife is somehow oppressed by a husband who is excessively afflicted [by passion], she should litigate against him before the king; this is indeed the rule for one who follows justice, provided the wife is not possessed of hatred, envy, or similar motives. Thus, the conduct toward such a husband is described as being [proper] even toward one who is devoid of virtue (*viśīla*).
There is no sovereignty over the wife;
rather, there is service toward her, such as attending to her feet and so forth, just like that of a servant.

Although the words *strī* (woman) and *puruṣa* (man) denote the human species as qualified by specific genders, nevertheless, in this context, they refer to the relationship of husband and wife. This is indicated by the inclusion of the word *svaiḥ* ("by their own [husbands]") in the verse: "Women, being dependent, should be kept under control day and night by their own men. Thus, it points to the state of being related.

The purpose of the statement of the present proposition is as follows: I shall describe the conduct, the adornment, and the protection of the body regarding the union of a husband and his wife—that is, their dwelling together in one place—as well as their conduct during separation, such as when traveling abroad, in accordance with dharma.
The inclusion of the word "eternal" (śāśvata) is for the sake of praise;
[it refers to] those two who abide on the path of dharma.
This is an explanatory restatement;
it is the proper path, established by the legal treatises and traditional practice.
Women must be kept under dependence by their own men day and night; and if they become attached to sensual objects, they must be established under one's own control.
Women should not be permitted to act according to their own will in matters of dharma, artha, and kāma.
Whatever wealth is to be employed for dharma and other such purposes, in that regard, one’s own male relatives—such as the husband and others—must be consulted according to their seniority.
"One's own male relatives" refers to those authorized for protection, as specified in the passage beginning, "The father protects [her]," and so forth.
For women who become attached to sense objects such as songs and the like, forming a habit of indulgence in them, must be kept under one's own control and restrained from them.

Although the cessation of independence regarding all activities has already been taught by the phrase "being dependent," the repeated mention of turning away from sense objects is intended to ensure that this is avoided with diligent effort.

Let it not be understood that they are to be restrained only from contact with other men and similar acts, while remaining at home and addicted to drinking liquor and so forth—[in which case] they would incur no fault.
By the word "and" (ca), this duty is first stated for men;
[it follows that] independence should not be granted to women, which implies that they too must not act independently.
And thus, by the word "and" in the phrase "of the man and of the woman," those duties belonging to both the woman and the man with respect to each other are expressed.
But it is not the case that sacrifices and the like [are so]; thus there is a consistent application [of the term].
The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the sons protect her in old age; a woman does not deserve independence.

Protection (*rakṣā*) is the warding off of misfortune (*anartha*). Misfortune, however, consists of humiliation through the transgression of improper conduct, through non-engagement [in duty], or through the unjust seizure of wealth and so forth. Its warding off is its prevention.
That [protection] must be performed by his father and others. The verb *rakṣati* (he protects) is used in the sense of the optative (*liṅ*) due to its Vedic character;
hence, the suffix is prescribed in the sense of "one should protect" (*rakṣet*).
The mention of the division of age is for the purpose of indicating that there are greater faults [in failing to protect them];
however, all persons at all times are authorized for the sake of protection.
The inclusion of the term "childhood" (kaumāra) is intended as an indication of the period prior to marriage.
Thus, the display of youthfulness by a woman whose husband is alive is merely a constant restatement (nityānuvāda).
For whenever she is dependent upon someone, at that time she must necessarily be protected by him.
And likewise, even while the husband is alive, the father and the son have the right [to the property];
this has been shown in the Mānava [Dharmaśāstra]:
"All these [relatives] should always provide for his protection."
If this were explained in detail, it would result in excessive prolixity.
But has this not already been stated by the words "by a girl or by a young woman"?
Not so.
Lack of autonomy is one thing, and protection is another.
In that context, lack of autonomy was taught; here, however, protection is being discussed.
Even for one who is dependent on another, it is possible to ward off misfortune.
But is it not also recited here that "a woman does not deserve independence"?
It is said in reply:
by this, independence is not prescribed [as forbidden] with respect to all activities.
What then? One who is not independent and whose mind is distracted is not capable of protecting oneself, due to being naturally devoid of power.
However, the statement regarding the fifth [case] is for the sake of indicating lack of independence, because another meaning has been stated there.
A father who does not give [a daughter] in marriage at the proper time is censurable; a husband who does not approach his wife is censurable;
and when the husband has died, a son who does not protect his mother is censurable.

If the father does not give [the daughter] when the time for giving has arrived, who then determines the time for giving a girl? It is recorded in the Smṛti that it is from the eighth year onwards, prior to puberty.
There is also an indicative mark here:
"Not approaching, not having intercourse, not sporting with his wives, being dependent.
Regarding the time for approaching, it has been stated that the fertile period (*ṛtu*) is the time, excluding the forbidden days (*parvan*).
A woman must be protected especially from even the slightest of attachments;
for if she is not guarded, she will bring grief to both families.
"Prasaṅga" means improper association.
This refers to such things as being occasionally in the company of a woman of unvirtuous character, or a child, or the sight of men in bright attire standing at the door of one's house;
for by their very nature, these lead to the wavering of the mind and its susceptibility to harm.
These, it is said, are not directly of the nature of faults;
for direct contact with women does not itself constitute a fault in women. It is said [to be a fault] because of its subtle [consequences]; therefore, they must be guarded against and restrained.
It is established that she must be protected with particular effort by all those of her own family— such as brothers, paternal uncles, and brothers-in-law—
and not by anyone else.
For seeing this supreme dharma common to all social classes,
husbands strive to protect their wives, even if they themselves are weak.

This is the highest duty for the four castes; seeing and knowing this, even those who are weak should strive—that is, they should make an effort—to protect their wives. Since the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used here, it implies that because the protection of property is the most important matter, the wife’s body—which is like a jewel wrapped in cloth yet exposed on the outside—must be protected from the assault of the day and night through excessive passion. To prevent her from falling into the power of others, she must be guarded by some means, such as by residing within the royal family or under their supervision.
For by protecting his wife with diligence, he indeed protects his offspring, his conduct, his lineage, himself, and his own dharma.
The protection of women must be carried out not only because of the instructions of the scriptures,
but also because of these many practical purposes:
namely, procreation, which consists of offspring in the form of sons and daughters.
The meaning is that there is no confusion.
*Caritra* refers to the conduct of the learned;
*kula* has been explained previously.
The fault of a wife who has fallen from her virtue attaches itself to the entire family of any noble lineage; thus, women are not considered virtuous for them.
Alternatively, protection [is required] because, due to the lack of purity in the lineage of fathers, grandfathers, and so forth, the funeral rites (*aurdhvadaihika*) have not been performed;
[he protects] himself.

It is well known that [a husband] is inevitably killed by his paramour, or even by his wife herself using poison and the like; and he loses his own dharma as well, because an unchaste woman has no entitlement to religious duty (*dharma*).
Therefore, when the wife is protected, all this is protected.
The husband, having entered his wife and become an embryo, is born here;
for that is the "wifehood" (jāyātva) of the wife, because he is born again from her.
This is a figurative statement (arthavāda).
For there is no observation of the husband entering the wife's womb;
therefore, this "entry" is spoken of figuratively by way of the semen, which is the essence of the body.
"You are indeed the self (ātman) named son"— this very [etymology] is the basis for the application of the word *jāyā* in the sense of "wife," since the husband is born (*jāyate*) from her.
If the word *jāyā* were based solely on the birth of offspring, then even a paramour would be called a *jāyā*.
For whatever kind of man a woman associates with, she gives birth to a son of that same kind;
therefore, for the sake of the purity of offspring, one should guard a woman with great effort.
He demonstrates what was stated in the phrase "one's own offspring":
it should not be thought that a woman gives birth to a son of such a kind as the second man she serves;
nor is similarity of qualities intended here.
For [if that were so], one born from a Śūdra or similar caste would attain the status of a Caṇḍāla or similar caste;
and even for one born of a woman of the same caste, that very caste-status would not exist, because of the scriptural statement: "among wives whose wombs are unconsecrated.
Furthermore, even if there were a similarity of qualities, it would follow that a woman whose husband is of bad character or impoverished would be permitted to go to a superior man.
But when this is an explanatory passage (arthavāda), then it is interpreted as "of such a kind" meaning "in accordance with one's family."
No one is able to guard women by force;
however, they can be guarded through the application of these strategic means.
This verse is intended to praise the method that will be explained hereafter.
Women cannot be protected by force—that is, by means of physical power such as confining them within the inner apartments or expelling other men from them;
rather, they can be protected through the application of these aforementioned methods.
"Yogas" means applications;
the sense is: by means of methods being employed.
He should employ her in the collection and expenditure of wealth,
as well as in cleanliness, religious duties, the cooking of food, and the supervision of household utensils.
Wealth (*artha*) means riches.

Their accumulation (*saṃgraha*) consists of determining their quantity through counting and so forth, and then placing them in the house for the sake of protection—storing them by binding them with ropes, iron chains, and the like, or marking them with seals, and so on.
Expenditure (*vyaya*) is the distribution of that very wealth, such as: "this much is for the sake of food," and "this is for the sake of soup," and "this much is for the sake of vegetables."
Purity (*śauca*) consists of the cleansing of ladles, pots, and so forth, as well as the smearing of the ground and similar acts.

Dharma consists of the giving of water for sipping (*ācamana*) and water-libations (*tarpaṇa*), and the worship of the gods with offerings of food, flowers, and various articles in the women's quarters, the dwelling, and other such places.
The cooking of food is well known.
Whatever may be her personal property, such as a throne, a couch, and so forth,
she should be appointed to oversee that.
Those women who, though confined at home by trustworthy male guardians,
protect themselves by their own efforts, are truly well-protected.

Those who perform what is appropriate at the proper time are called "attentive"; these are the chamberlains who serve in the inner apartments. Those who are confined in their own homes by them and rendered dependent—being guarded by the prohibition against wandering at will—are not truly protected;
rather, they protect themselves by their own efforts.
How do they protect [the teachings]?
By being appointed to these tasks.
This is a praise of the aforementioned method; it is not a prohibition of other methods.
Drinking, association with wicked people, separation from her husband, wandering about, sleeping [inappropriately], and dwelling in another's house— these six are the vices that corrupt women.
Wandering through marketplaces for the purpose of purchasing food, vegetables, and the like, as well as visiting temples;
staying for many days in the family home of relatives rather than living in one's own house;
and the seduction of women.
These are the causes of agitation for the minds of women;
for they abandon the fear of their fathers-in-law and others, as well as the fear of public censure.
They do not examine form, nor is there any regard for their age; whether he is handsome or ugly, they enjoy him simply because he is a man.
One should not entertain this conceit: "I am fortunate, handsome, and young; how could she desire another after abandoning me?
For they do not consider whether he is handsome or of heroic form;
they simply perceive that he is a man, and with that alone they enjoy him and unite with him.
Due to their proclivity for men, their fickle minds, and their natural lack of affection,
these women act perversely toward their husbands even when guarded with great effort in this world.
When any man whatsoever is seen, the agitation of the minds of women—thinking, "How might I be united with him?"—is *pauṃścalya* (unchastity).
Furthermore, there is instability even regarding other matters such as religious duty (*dharma*) and so forth, due to their fickle-mindedness;
for instance, they desire precisely that person who is hateful, and they lustfully long for whichever brother, son, or other relative they have seen.
Affection, passion, and craving for a husband, son, or others cause their hearts to be bound by pride;
through association with these defects, they become corrupted and undergo transformation toward their husbands.
Therefore,
having thus understood their nature as born from the creation of Prajāpati,
a man should exert the greatest effort toward their protection.
Prajāpati is Hiraṇyagarbha. He was born at the time of his own manifestation, that is, at the time of creation.
The rest is clear.
Manu assigned to women the bed, the seat, ornaments, lust, anger, ignobility, treacherous intent, and misconduct.
Lying down is reclining, characterized by a habit of sleeping; sitting is characterized by a habit of not rising;
adornment is the embellishment of the body.
Desire is the longing for the enjoyment of sensual pleasures;
anger is hatred;
ignobility is affection toward one who is loathsome and hatred toward one who is beloved, as well as the concealment of outward appearance and a lack of moral integrity.

The state of being a hater (*drogdhṛbhāvaḥ*), or the quality of being a hater (*drogdhṛtvaṃ*) toward one's husband, father, and so forth; that is, the unrighteous nature of husbands and others due to their being objects of a person's vices.
This is a compound consisting of the word *bhāva* joined with the agentive suffix *tṛc* from the root *druh*.
Improper conduct and service to base men—
this is the nature of women ordained by Manu at the beginning of the creation. Beds, seats, and ornaments are presented as illustrations for [their] malice and improper conduct.
Just as these entities exist by their very nature and are unshakable, so too are misconduct and the like.
"There is no ritual efficacy for women through mantras; such is the established rule in the Dharma.
For women are without [Vedic] authority and devoid of mantras; they are falsehood—this is the settled conclusion."
Some maintain this view:
"Even if there is deviation from chastity, they will attain purity through Vedic recitation, secret penances, and so forth; therefore, there is no fault.
This is not correct.
For women do not have ritual acts or even the recitation of mantras by which they might attain purification through their own learning when a transgression of conduct remains unexposed; therefore,
this [statement] is merely a supplement to the rule that they must be protected with effort.

Therefore, those who describe this as a general prohibition of mantras, and who—considering it a prohibition—maintain that whatever rite connected with women is performed by anyone whatsoever—whether women are involved as agents, as in the evening *bali*-offering and so forth; or as objects of refinement (*saṃskārya*), as in the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) and so forth; or as recipients (*saṃpradāna*), as in the *śrāddha* and so forth—in all such cases, because of the prohibition of mantras, rites such as the *śrāddha* for women must be performed without mantras:
they are speakers of what is incorrect, because this [text] has another purpose.

This should be explained as an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), according to the principle of having that [which exists] as its object; it depends upon the consecrations of the *cūḍā* and the mantras associated with prescribed prohibitions.
Furthermore, due to the absence of formal study, there is—by implication—the absence of penance and the recitation of mantras. They are devoid of sense organs.
They lack the faculties of vigor, steadfastness, wisdom, and so forth; therefore, even against their will, they are sometimes overcome by force through evil conduct.
Thus, it is proper to protect them.
The statement that "women are untruthful" is a reproach based on their untruthful speech, due to their instability in both moral discipline and affection.
And likewise, many scriptural passages have been chanted even in the Vedas for the purpose of examining specific characteristics; hear their expiations.
Regarding the point that women are by nature impure in heart, he cites Vedic statements in the form of mantras and arthavādas as witnesses.
And so:
"Just as I have stated that women are falsehood, even so there are scriptural revelations (śrutis) in the Nigamas, the Vedas."
The word *nigama* is a synonym for the Veda and its usage is observed in such passages as "babhūtha," "ātatantha," and so forth;
it also has the meaning of a term denoting a commentary on the meaning of the Vedas.

"Nigama, Nirukta, and Vyākaraṇa are the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas). For in the Nirukta, there is indeed usage such as "these are the nigamas. However, here [in this context], that is impossible because of the mention of *śruti* and because of the examples to be stated later.
Therefore, the word *nigama* is understood here as a synonym for the Veda.
The relationship of container and contained exists due to the distinction between the whole and its parts.

Within those *nigamas*, the *śrutis*—which are constituent portions, sentences that have been chanted (*nigīta*), studied (*adhīta*), and proclaimed (*saṃśabdita*)—are what are recited; such is the meaning.
And regarding the eternally occurring [recitation], the absence of division of time and so forth has already been explained. There is an alternative reading, "nigadas.
Nigadas are specific types of mantras.
The *śrutis* are the statements of the Brāhmaṇas.
This matter—that women are untruthful—is shown in both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas.
In the view that there are many such [statements], the word "are" (*santi*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
Listen to those among those scriptures which take the form of expiation—that is, which serve as atonement for transgressions.
If it is asked for what purpose they are cited, it is for the sake of examining their specific characteristics (*svālakṣaṇya*).
A "specific characteristic" is an inherent nature that is eternally present; [these citations are] for the purpose of demonstrating that.
That which is characterized by armlets, earrings, and so forth is here sublated; this "own-characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa) means "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva).
This is their own-characteristic, namely, that which consists of deviation.
"Whatever my mother, wandering about unfaithful to her husband, lusted after,
may my father take that seed of mine"— this is the illustration of that [Vedic verse].
By the three quarters ending with the word *itikāraṇāt*, a portion of the mantra is imitated:
"That my mother was unfaithful (*apativratā*)—meaning she whose vow (*vrata*) or rule (*niyama*) was that she had no desire for another man than her husband even in her mind;
the opposite of that is *apativratā*."
While wandering and going to the houses of others,
she saw a man there dressed in brilliant attire and became lustful;
she conceived a greedy longing for that other man.
May that evil arising from my birth—the semen belonging to my father—be removed;
may that defect be wiped away by that semen.
The nominative case is used here in place of the genitive for the sake of metrical variation.
Alternatively, semen itself is conceived as the father;
even while not relinquishing its own characteristic, it enters into grammatical coordination with [the word for] semen,
just as in the expression, "The sky is my father."
Alternatively, semen is also called the "seed of the mother.
May that semen—the progenitor, the father—purify it;
the meaning is: "May the defect of the mother be removed by the power of the seed born of the father."
This is an illustration—that is, an example—of this [logical reason] which is of a deviant nature:
all those who recite do so with this mantra.
If all women were by nature corrupt, then the application of the mantra would be established as a rule; otherwise, it would be merely occasional.
This mantra is employed during the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, as well as for the consecration of the water for washing the feet (pādya) at a Śrāddha ceremony.
Whatever undesirable thing she contemplates in her mind for her husband,
this is rightly called the concealment of that transgression.
The "grasper of the hand" (pāṇigrāha) is the husband.

Whatever undesirable or unpleasant thing a woman thinks of in her mind—such as contact with another man—the concealment and purification of that mental transgression is declared by this mantra when it is employed in the ritual.
Incidentally, the purpose of the mantra has thus been shown.

Although the purpose of employing a mantra as a subsidiary element of a ritual action is indeed its ritual quality (*karmaguṇatā*), nevertheless, because it is applied to recitation (*japa*) and so forth, it is also said to serve the purpose of preventing mental transgression (*mānasavyabhicāra*).
Whatever the qualities of the husband with whom a woman is united according to the prescribed rule,
such qualities she acquires, just as a river does from the ocean.
One who desires to protect his wife must protect himself from immorality;
nor can this be accomplished by that alone,
because the wife of one who is immoral becomes likewise [immoral], whereas the wife of one who possesses virtue remains virtuous.
Just as a river flowing downward, though its water is sweet, becomes saltwater when it joins with the ocean.
Akṣamālā, though born of a low womb, attained honor through her union with Vasiṣṭha; and Śāraṅgī reached a state of venerability through Mandapāla.
Even Akṣamālā, though of low birth, attained a state of being worthy of honor through her union with Vasiṣṭha;

and Śāraṅgī, though an animal, was likewise honored when united with the sage Mandapāla, who was like a sparrow. Therefore, even those of low birth and younger age are to be honored more highly than their husbands.
And so it has been said: "Women [are to be guarded] according to their age."
These and other women in this world, though born of lowly origin,
have attained eminence through their own respective auspicious qualities as wives.
Those whose birth or origin (*prasūti*) is inferior or low-born are "those of low birth" (*avakṛṣṭaprasūtayaḥ*).
Others include Gaṅgā, Kālī, and so forth.
Because two [categories] are under discussion, the plural form "these" (*etāḥ*) implies a third [category] by means of the word "and" (*ca*).
And these two also undergo reduplication.
Thus has been declared the auspicious conduct for men and women in worldly life, which brings about pleasant results both in this world and after death; now learn the duties concerning progeny.
The journey of the world, the conduct of the world, and the custom of the world—
this is established by worldly consensus.
This matter is not defined by scriptural injunction such that it could be protected in this way and not otherwise.
And because they are not protected, defects such as those arising from childbirth occur;
therefore, now learn the laws concerning progeny:
to whom does the offspring belong—to the seed-giver or to the owner of the field?
The future time is the *udarka*; those for whom that is pleasant are praised, for all things indeed come to an end at their conclusion, but these do not do so. This is the praise.
But one might ask: what is the "resulting in happiness" (*sukhodarkatā*) of the duty toward offspring?
For offspring depend upon [the father], and women, being shrouded by many defects, are fit for abandonment.
To prevent such a conclusion—that "who indeed could support everyone in the household?"—he says:
For the sake of procreation, these highly fortunate women are worthy of honor and are the lights of the home;
between women and the goddesses of fortune (Śrī) in households, there is no distinction whatsoever.
Because their faults can be remedied, they are worthy of honor.
This detailed exposition of their faults is not for the purpose of contempt or avoidance, as one might treat those who are falsely accused or outcasts;
rather, it is for the purpose of protection from those very faults.
For the cooking pot is not set on the fire because there are beggars,
nor are barley seeds sown because there are deer.
By "procreation" (prajana), what is intended is the entire process beginning from conception up to the nurturing of offspring.
And so he will say: "The procreation of offspring and the protection of those born.
[Women are] like lamps in the home;
for it is well known that there is no service whatsoever in the household without women.
Even when there is abundant wealth, if the wife is absent, householders are unable to satisfy each guest with food and other offerings when friends, kinsmen, and others arrive;
just as there is no power in one who is poor, therefore there is no difference between a woman and wealth in the home.
The procreation of offspring, the nurturing of those born,
and the conduct of worldly affairs for every purpose— woman is visibly the foundation of these.
A woman is the cause, the instrumental condition (*nimitta*).
This is evident in matters such as the procreation of offspring.
"Worldly conduct" (*lokayātrā*) refers to the winning over of those who have come to one's home by giving food and other gifts, as well as invitations, formal requests, and so forth.
For every single object, a woman is the cause of bondage for him;
"daily" (*pratyaham*) is the reading. The word *pratyakṣa* here signifies that which is internal.
The meaning is "internal."
Offspring, religious duties, service, and supreme delight depend upon the wife;
likewise, heaven for one's ancestors and for oneself is dependent on her.
The meaning of this verse has already been shown previously.
She who does not deceive her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body,
attains the worlds of her husband and is called "virtuous" by the righteous.
But through infidelity to her husband, a woman incurs reproach in this world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by foul diseases.
In the fifth [chapter], both verses have been explained.
Listen to this meritorious discourse, beneficial to all people, which was uttered by the virtuous and by the great sages of old concerning a son.
An "introduction" (upanyāsa) is the presentation of a subject for investigation, or the investigation itself;
learn that [which has been] spoken—
uttered— with respect to a son, concerning a son, by the virtuous, the learned, and the great seers.
"Beneficial to all people" (*viśvajanyam*) means conducive to the welfare of all persons;
"meritorious" (*puṇyam*) means producing auspiciousness.

Because this was interrupted by the praise of women, the phrase "learn the duty regarding progeny" (*prajādharmaṃ nibodhata*) is restated for the sake of renewed emphasis: "learn [this] instruction" (*upanyāsaṃ nibodhata*).

They recognize the son as belonging to the husband; however, there is a conflict in the sacred texts regarding the progenitor: some say he is the one who produces the child, while others know him to be the owner of the field.
The husband is the one who marries; all learned men recognize and accept as his son that child born of a woman who has been consecrated by him through the sacrament of marriage—
there is no disagreement on this point.

This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). However, regarding the conflict of scriptural statements (*śrutidvaidha*) concerning the progenitor: where there is one who is solely the producer in the field of another, but not the husband, there is a conflict of scriptural statements—that is, a difference of opinion.
He shows this:
some say the progenitor is the one who possesses offspring; others say it is the owner of the field—that is, the husband—even if he is not the biological father of the child born of that wife.
Having thus presented doubt arising from the teacher's erroneous practice, he supports that very doubt by stating the reason.
The woman is considered to be the field, and the man is considered to be the seed;
from the union of the field and the seed, there is the birth of all embodied beings.
A woman is like a field;

a field is a portion of ground that is the site for the production of rice and other crops, and a woman is similar to that. Just as seed sown in a field grows when it is held there, so too does the semen [sown] in a woman.
The person is indeed [only] the seed;
here too, the word "become" (*bhūta*) is used in a figurative sense.
His semen is the seed, not the person directly; however, because it is the substratum for that [semen], the person is designated as such.
The conjunction (*samāyoga*) is the relationship characterized by the nature of the substratum and the dependent;
from that arises the birth or production of all embodied beings—that is, of the fourfold collection of living creatures. Even for those born from sweat, space is the field and sweat is the seed.
Therefore, doubt is appropriate, because it is impossible for [the result] to occur in the absence of both;
for in the production of offspring, there is an operation by both.
Since there is no reason for a definitive determination (*vinigamana*), there is a doubt as to whose [the child] it is: whether it belongs to both or to one of the two.
And this is the meaning of the entire section: the relationship between offspring and progenitor is not to be determined by inference;
and we shall explain this in the verse on partition.
In some cases the seed is superior, while in others it is the female womb;
but where both are equal, that offspring is highly praised.
The excellence of the seed was indeed observed by great sages such as Vyāsa and Ṛṣyaśṛṅga;
for even among sons born from the wombs of women— such as Dhṛtarāṣṭra and others who were "field-born" (kṣetraja) sons—
they were Kṣatriyas, despite being born from Brāhmaṇas, because they belonged to the caste of their mothers.
But when both are equal—meaning they have the same owner and belong to the same caste—that offspring is praised because there is no conflict;
for it has already been stated: "They recognize the son as belonging to the husband."
Between the seed and the womb, the seed is said to be superior;
for the procreation of all beings is indeed characterized by the nature of the seed.
When doubt has been thus established, he first adopts the position that the seed is primary:
because of its primacy, offspring belongs to the one whose seed it is.
And its primacy is established because, although substances such as rice have many causes such as soil and so forth, they are observed to conform to the specific qualities of that [seed].
Therefore, it is clearly logical to accept that offspring—which follows the unperceived seed—is an effect, and like rice and other grains, it must conform to the properties of that [seed];
for in every case, the uniformity of the effect is not abandoned.
Thus, he demonstrates the primacy of the seed: "For [the seed] is the source of all beings."
The procreation, that is, the birth, of all beings is characterized by the characteristics of the seed;
it is marked—that is, distinguished—by whatever characteristics the seed possesses, such as its form, color, and configuration, meaning that it conforms to the nature of that [seed].
Whatever kind of seed is sown in a field prepared at the proper time,
that very kind of seed grows therein, manifested by its own inherent qualities.
This verse is provided as an expansion of the meaning of the immediately preceding [statement], demonstrating the connection with the speaker;

it will explain the meaning of the word *yādṛśa* (of such a kind) through the passage beginning with "rice, *śāli* grains," and so forth. "At the appropriate time" means when the sowing season—such as the rainy season—has arrived, and the ground has been prepared by plowing, leveling, and other such treatments.
Such [a seed] grows and is born;
it manifests as a visible form characterized by its own qualities, such as color, configuration, taste, and potency.
For this ground is called the eternal womb of all beings;
yet the seed does not nourish any qualities of the womb during its growth.
The persistence of the qualities of the seed was stated previously;
by this [verse], he speaks of the absence of the qualities of the field.
This earth is called the womb and the field for living beings—the immovable ones, as well as herbs, grasses, shrubs, and creepers.
Furthermore, none of the qualities of those [elements] are observed within them;
neither earth nor dust is perceived there.
It is the seed that nourishes during the stages of growth.

In this context, the word "seed" (*bīja*) refers to rice and the like from which a sprout has emerged, not to the root itself; for even that [root], when sown again after being partially consumed, indeed becomes a seed in another year. It does not "thrive" (*puṣyati*) nor does it "persist" (*anuvartate*). The verb *puṣ* is used here in the sense of persisting, which constitutes a factor for thriving.
The state of having an object (*sakarmakatva*) is the cause for the second case ending (*dvitīyā*).
He either attains or partakes of the qualities of the womb;
he does not nourish nor does he conform to those [qualities] in their growth or their constituent parts.
If the persistence of the root *puṣ* (to nourish) were expressed by the verb, then [the word] "in nourishments" (*puṣṭiṣu*) would be redundant.
Therefore, because roots have multiple meanings, only the other [meaning] should be explained by the verb;
or else, the phrase "in nourishments" is for the purpose of completing the verse.
In some way, the redundancy must be avoided;
or else, the logical connection (anvaya) should be stated by means of the relationship between the general and the particular,
as in the expression "he has nourished his own nourishment."
Even in a single field on the earth, seeds sown by farmers at the proper time arise in various forms here according to their own nature.
The meaning just mentioned is explained by means of an illustration.
The word "even" (*api*) is to be supplied here as well.

The meaning is that even in a single field—that is, in a single plot of earth—at whatever specific time a particular seed is sown by farmers, seeds of diverse forms arise, because they conform to their own inherent natures (*svabhāva*).
And if the field were predominant, then because the field is one, all [results] would be of a single form.
Rice, śāli rice, mung beans, sesame seeds, masha beans, as well as barley,
garlic, and sugarcane— these all sprout according to their respective seeds.
He shows those seeds as having various forms,
according to the nature of each seed;
in all cases, the plural is used when referring to a genus.
That one thing is sown and another is born—this is not tenable;
for whatever seed is sown, that very same thing sprouts forth.
This very same point is concluded by means of different words:
"When mung beans are sown, rice does not grow"—this is impossible.
What was stated by way of negation is now restated by way of affirmation: for whatever is the seed [of something], [that alone arises].
Therefore, a wise and disciplined man, who understands both theoretical knowledge and practical wisdom and desires long life, must never sow his seed in another's wife.
Thus, having presented the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
By this [verse], the preeminence of the field (*kṣetra*) is expressed.

But is it not the case that there is no word here signifying the preeminence of the field; rather, only a prohibition against approaching another's field is heard: "One must never sow in another's wife"?
The meaning of this is that one must not sow seed in another's wife;
it does not, however, mean to say that "the offspring belongs to the owner of the field.
This is true.

This is because it forms a single syntactical unit with the statement, "Likewise, a seed sown in another's field perishes"; thus, this prohibition is caused by the visible defect characterized by the seizure of offspring, and is not a prohibition of sexual intercourse for the sake of some invisible (transcendental) purpose.
For that [latter] has already been refuted in the fourth [chapter] by such statements as, "For such a thing is not conducive to long life.

Therefore, since the scriptural prohibition is subordinate to something else and forms a single unit with what follows immediately after, and lacks independence, it is logical that its purpose is to establish the primacy of the field (*kṣetra*).
"With one who is wise" means with innate wisdom;
"disciplined" means instructed by his father and others;
"one who knows knowledge and realization"—here, the words *jñāna* (knowledge) and *vijñāna* (realization) function as instrumental nouns.
Knowledge refers to the Vedas and the auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*); specialized knowledge refers to the domain of logic, arts, and so forth.
This is what is meant.
Whoever possesses any intelligence at all should not act in this manner, for such is the established rule in all the scriptures.
As for the fool who is like an animal, he is simply not qualified for this; thus, this is a restatement [of what is already known].
Furthermore, the phrase "by one desiring long life" is intended to serve as a recognition of the prohibition found in the fourth chapter.
And thus, the suspicion that there might be a separate negation is dispelled.
Regarding this, those who know the past recite verses sung by Vāyu:
"Just as a seed should not be sown by a man in what belongs to another."

The word *gāthā* denotes a specific type of metrical composition; as Piṅgala has stated: "In this [treatise], what is unestablished is called *gāthā*. Furthermore, verses (*śloka*) that have been handed down through tradition without dispute are also called *gāthā*. For instance, after saying, "This sacrificial *gāthā* is sung," *gāthā* verses are recited later in the Veda, such as: "That which was his before, that is his after."
"Chanted by Vāyu" means recited by Vāyu; "proclaimed by Vāyu" means taught by him. "Knowers of antiquity" refers to those who understand other ancient kalpas.
"In the possession of another" means in the field of another.
Just as an arrow, once shot, vanishes from the sight of one who continues to shoot at the mark it has already pierced in the sky,
so too does a seed sown in another's possession quickly perish.
He now shows those verses:
"The arrow, the shaft—it perishes. When one person pierces a deer already struck by another archer through a gap in the sky, ownership of the kill belongs here to the first archer.
Just as an arrow shot into the open sky vanishes without reaching its mark and becomes fruitless for one who intends to pierce what has already been pierced,
so too is the seed cast upon another's wife:
the offspring belongs to the owner of the field.
Those who know the past recognize this earth as the wife of Pṛthu; they call a field of sthāṇu-grass the "cleaver of stumps" and a deer with a thorn the "thorny deer."
Such is this relationship between husband and wife established by the ancient sages, that even though they are distinct, they appear as if unified.
For instance, the Earth—whose vast connection [to him] dates back many thousands of years—is designated by that very name, "Pṛthivī.
Therefore, even if born by another man, a son belongs to him whose wife she is.
They say that the field belongs to the one who clears away the stumps, because there is no other relationship [between them].
The genitive case-ending expresses the relationship between owner and owned.
One who cuts down where stumps—meaning the growth of shrubs, bushes, creepers, and so forth—are located is called "the stump-clearer."
That field belongs to him by whom the ground was cleared of sprouted shrubs, creepers, and climbing plants and made into a field;
the fruit produced there from plowing and sowing belongs to him alone.
The phrase "they call [the hunter] the owner of the deer with the arrow" is to be supplied here as well.

When many people are pursuing a deer for the sake of hunting, they say that the deer belongs to him whose arrow-head is seen in the animal; and it has been stated in the passage "the arrow perishes" (*naśyatīṣu*) that he who was the first to strike it is the owner.
"The person is only this much: wife, self, and offspring—so the wise have declared; likewise, he who is the husband is remembered as the woman."
And it is logical that the offspring belongs to him whose wife she is, because there is indeed oneness between the wife and the husband; for even progeny is one's own self.
How else could the self of one person belong to another?
Thus, this is first of all observed in the world.
"Even those Brahmins who are experts in the scriptures speak in this very way."
A wife is not released from her husband by means of a ransom or by abandonment;
thus we know the law established of old by Prajāpati.

Now, one might think that by purchasing them with the gift of wealth and so forth, the wives of others will be made one's own; and once the other’s ownership has ceased, the son born from her becomes the son of the progenitor.
This is not so, because it is impossible to bring another’s women into one’s own ownership as wives, even for thousands of gold coins.
Nor does a woman abandoned by her husband acquire ownership for a recipient simply because he has discarded his property;

for, based on the grammatical indication of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the word "udvaheta" (he should marry), which refers to the fruit of the action intended for the agent, a woman consecrated by one man cannot become the wife of another.
This is just as the *Āhavanīya* and other sacrificial fires, once established by one person, cannot be designated as *Āhavanīya* and so forth for another through ritual actions or similar means.
Purchase, sale, and exchange;
relinquishment is abandonment.
By these two [acts], one is not released [from her]; her status as a wife does not depart.
A share of inheritance falls but once; a daughter is given in marriage but once;
and one says "I give" but once—these three things happen only once among the virtuous.
This has been explained in the eighth section on the rules for inheritance.
For at the time of partition, the division must be carried out by those entitled to equal or unequal shares among the portions that are equal or unequal.
This [verse] is intended to prohibit anyone from contesting once that [partition] has been performed.
Even in that case, if he were to point out at the outset that some portion was not as it should be, then there would indeed be a subsequent partition.
