However, if after a long time he should declare it to have been improperly made—by which time others may have performed repairs on their respective portions for other purposes, or cloth, gold, and so forth may have been consumed—then he is only capable of effecting an equalization; he cannot, however, bring about a complete redistribution of the entire property.

Others, however, state that the purpose of the rule regarding "once-and-for-all settlement" (sakṛt-nipāta) is this: for those such as eunuchs who are ineligible for a share, once it is subsequently discovered that they are eunuchs or otherwise disqualified—which is the cause for not receiving a share—there is no taking away of their share.

Likewise, if those entitled to two, three, or four shares should by chance agree among themselves to an equal distribution, they shall not, upon later regret, be permitted to take back [the shares] by overstepping the previous arrangement.
As for one who has become an outcast (patita), however, I shall explain the forfeiture of even a share already received.
"A maiden is given [in marriage] only once.

Although by this [rule], ownership of the husband is stated even before the wedding following the formal betrothal (*vāgdāna*), nevertheless, upon considering such passages as "one may take back even a given maiden" and "the wise should know that their finality [of the marriage] occurs at the seventh step," it is established that [the rule regarding the once-only giving] applies only to specific cases;
and this has already been explained.
He says once, "I give.
For cows and the like pass to another in the very same form in which they are one's own property;
however, a maiden, while being one's own as a daughter, is given away as a wife without her own status as a relative being revoked—thus she is mentioned separately.
But surely, if the father’s own connection [to the girl] does not cease, how can the giving of the maiden be accomplished?
For this is the nature of giving: that the connection of one ceases while that of another arises.
This is not a fault.
In this context, there are two types of relationships: that of offspring and progenitor, and that of owner and owned.
Of these, the relationship of offspring and progenitor does not cease, whereas the other does cease.

Thus, by stating "in childhood she shall remain under the control of her father," the text indicates the non-cessation of the father's ownership here; and by stating "of the one who takes her hand," it indicates the arising of that [ownership] in the husband.

Just as one who begets offspring does not share in the ownership of the progeny when it concerns cows, horses, camels, female slaves, buffaloes, goats, or sheep, so it is likewise with the wives of others.
Those who possess seeds but have no field, and who sow them in another's field,
never obtain the fruit of the crop that has grown.
This is indeed well known:

those who possess the seed but do not own the field—the owners of seeds such as rice and so forth—do not obtain the fruit of the crop that has grown, such as mung beans or black gram, if its production occurs in another's field.
If a bull were to sire a hundred calves upon the cows of others, those calves belong only to the owners of the cows; the bull's emission was in vain.
By the preceding [verse], the law regarding stationary objects was declared or made known as a well-established principle;
by this [verse], it is illustrated with respect to domesticated animals such as cows and the like.

Even if a bull belonging to one person were to sire many calves upon the cows of another, the owner of the bull would not receive even a single calf; all those calves belong to the owners of the cows, that is, the cowherds.
The *ārṣabha*—that which pertains to a bull—is "skandita," meaning the emission of semen; it is "moghā" or "vṛthā," that is, fruitless and in vain.
In the same way, those who possess no field but sow their seed in another's field benefit the owner of the field; the owner of the seed does not receive the fruit.
This is an instruction regarding the former [case]:
just as they do with cattle and other such things, as well as with stationary objects, so too do they act among humans;
they accomplish the purpose, the requirement, and the work of the seed for the sake of the owners of the field.
But when no reward is intended for either the owner of the field or the sower, the benefit belongs visibly to the owner of the field; for the womb is more powerful than the seed.

The fruit for those who provide the field has been stated without distinction, not for the one who provides the seed. He states that this [rule] applies to the remaining cases by saying "without prior agreement" (*anabhisaṃdhāya*).

"Prior agreement" (*abhisaṃdhāna*) refers to the establishment of a mutual understanding between the provider of the seed and the provider of the field, like the proverb of the lost horse and the burnt chariot.

Where there is no formal agreement stating, "Let the fruit belong to both of us," in that case, the manifest benefit—the certain fruit—belongs to the owner of the field alone. By the word "manifest" (pratyakṣa), he expresses its indisputable nature;
for the soil is more powerful than the seed.
The field is of superior power.
But when there is mutual agreement,
because of the undertaking of the act, that which is given for the sake of the seed—
both the owner of the seed and the owner of the field are seen here as sharers in it.

It has been stated that when there is no intention [to benefit] the owner of the field, the fruit belongs to the owner of the seed. But when there is such an intention, does the fruit belong to the owner of the seed, or to both?
He says: "To both."

The acceptance of an action—its formal acknowledgment as "this is exactly so"—is the certainty characterized by consciousness; that is what is intended here by "action. Having caused such an action to be accepted, whatever is given for the sake of the seed—that is, for the purpose of producing the fruit which is the effect of the seed—is understood by implication to be the "seed.
In this case, both [the giver and the recipient] are sharers in its result.
If seed carried by the current of a flood sprouts in someone's field, that seed belongs to the owner of the field alone;
the owner of the seed does not receive the fruit.

It has been stated that when a seed is sown in another's field, the loss belongs to the sower. In this regard, one might think: "Surely this [theft] is appropriate for him because of his own human error; he certainly desires to seize the field. Otherwise, why would he sow in another's field?"
But as for one by whom [seed] was sown in his own field, yet carried elsewhere by a flood or the wind—if he loses his own property, what fault is there on his part?
To address this, it says:
"Seed carried away by a flood or the wind."
A flood is a pouring of water; that which is brought or carried by that wind and sprouts in someone's field belongs to that person alone.
Since this is already established, the statement "the sower does not receive the fruit" is for the sake of clarity;
the meaning is that in all cases, the field is predominant.
This law regarding the procreation of cows, horses, female slaves, camels, goats, sheep, birds, and buffaloes should be understood.
Because the context concerns offspring, one might think that this rule applies only to them; therefore, the mention of cows, horses, and so forth is made.
Alternatively, since the terminology of "seed" and "fruit" is more commonly established as referring to crops and the like, he speaks in order to exclude that [narrower sense]:
"This is the law everywhere for bipeds, quadrupeds, birds, and stationary beings."
The word "this" refers back to the two [cases] mentioned.
When there is no intention [to harm], the fruit belongs to the owner of the field; when there is an intention, it belongs to both.
Furthermore, since the mention of cows, horses, and so forth is for the sake of illustration, this same principle applies even to dogs, cats, and the like.
If that is so, for what purpose is it said "if among the cattle of others"?
This is a restatement of a well-known fact: generally, cows belong to men, whereas birds and the like do not.
"Female slaves" refers to those obtained through the seven sources of slavery.
"Birth" (prasava) refers to the arising of the body; the meaning is "with respect to that" or "therein."
Thus has been proclaimed to you the essential and the worthless nature of both seed and womb;
hereafter, I shall declare the duty of women in times of distress.
"Sāra" means the essential or primary; "phalgu" means the non-essential.
"Upasaṃhāra" refers to the conclusion of the preceding section. The latter half [of the verse] provides an indication of what is about to be stated.
Calamity consists in the absence of food and clothing necessary for the maintenance of life, as well as the interruption of one's lineage.
The wife of an elder brother is the teacher's wife for the younger;
however, the wife of the younger brother is considered the daughter-in-law for the elder.
With these two verses, he restates the established rule for ordinary circumstances in order to prescribe *niyoga* (authorization for levirate) in times of distress:
"The elder (*jyeṣṭha*) is one born first; the younger (*anuja*) is one born later; the youngest (*kanīyān*) or junior (*yavīyān*) is indeed the younger brother."

An elder brother who approaches the wife of a younger brother, or a younger brother who approaches the wife of an elder brother— even if they are authorized [to do so]— become outcasts, unless there is a state of distress.
In the case of approaching each other's wives, there is loss of caste for both the elder and the younger brother when no emergency exists, even if a formal authorization (niyoga) has been granted.
When the lineage is on the verge of extinction, a woman who has been duly authorized by her husband or by a sapinda relative may obtain the desired offspring.
By this, an injunction distinguished by all particulars is prescribed:
"Upon the extinction of the lineage, a woman duly appointed must procreate offspring from a brother-in-law or others.
That which was stated as "the duty of women in times of distress"—this very extinction of the lineage constitutes such a time of distress.
By the word "lineage" (*saṃtāna*), a son is meant, as well as a daughter who is an appointed daughter (*putrikā*);
for she alone continues the paternal lineage, and no other does.
Its "destruction" (*parikṣaya*) means non-arising, the destruction of what has arisen, or the failure to appoint an appointed daughter.
For we shall explain that a woman alone has no authority over a daughter or any other substitute for a son. "The appointed woman, authorized by her elders, may procreate.
But why "by her elders"? [This is because] she is under their guardianship.
Because of the illustration from another Smṛti;
or else, simply from the word *niyoga* itself,
for even in common worldly usage, *niyoga* is said to be that which pertains to a teacher (*guru*).
For one who teaches because he has been commissioned by a student is not said to be "reciting";
rather, it is one commissioned by a teacher who acts and recites.

Furthermore, "elders" (guru) should be understood as those of the husband's lineage, such as the mother-in-law, father-in-law, and brother-in-law, and not [the elders] beginning with one's own father.
By means of this offspring, those for whom a funeral rite (*aurdhvadehika*) performed by it serves as a benefit are said to possess offspring.
If this is so, then since there is also a benefit to the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) through the grandson (*dauhitra*),
it follows that the father must appoint his daughter [to produce such an offspring].

It has been stated by whom those who possess offspring are defined; by the mention of the *devara* (husband’s brother) and the *sapiṇḍa*, it is understood that only those belonging to the husband's lineage come to mind. Furthermore, in various passages of the Mahābhārata, the role of the appointer (*niyoktṛ*) is shown to belong exclusively to members of the husband's side.

For this very reason, when a brother's son exists, the practice of *niyoga* (authorization for procreation) must not be performed. For the benefit to the lineage belongs only to those who have been authorized; they are the ones entitled [to act] because they seek the benefit of the offspring through the affection generated by a son.
The deceased has no entitlement [to ritual acts].
How, then, is he designated as "one's offspring"?
In some way, he benefits [the lineage] through the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
We say "because of the scriptural statement.

For although there is no injunction that "one must procreate offspring" which was carried out by him [the deceased], nevertheless, the meaning of the scripture is that the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and so forth must be performed for him by one born through the *niyoga* injunction upon his field (*kṣetra*).
And thus, it is understood that [the son] is a benefactor to him.
We shall explain this in detail further on.
A *devara* is the husband’s brother;
a *sapiṇḍa* is one belonging to the husband's lineage.
That same [penance] applies to a woman;
it is stated in another Smṛti that it applies even from mere birth.
The word "properly" (samyak) reiterates the upcoming rule regarding being smeared with ghee and so forth.
The term *īpsita* (desired) is used in the sense of that which is to be attained through a ritual act (*vidhi-kṛtya*). By the word *īpsita*, he expresses the capacity for performing the task.
Therefore, if a daughter is born who is blind, deaf, or otherwise impaired, the *niyoga* (authorization for procreation) must be performed once again.
But one appointed to a widow, being anointed with clarified butter and remaining silent, may procreate a single son at night; by no means a second.
The mention of "widow" is not restrictive;
this same rule applies even while the husband is alive, provided he is impotent or otherwise incapable, because the author will later state: "those two who, being appointed, disregard the rule..."
This alone is its purpose:

here there is a restriction regarding the objects [of sexual intercourse], not a restriction regarding the rules themselves; for if it were understood otherwise, because they would not be relevant to the context, they would apply only to a widow.
This is intended to prevent looking at lamps and such during the night, since approaching [the husband] during the day is already prohibited by another scriptural statement.
But others say: that prohibition concerns the purpose of the person (the spiritual goal), whereas this [rule] concerns ritual action.
Therefore, by traveling during the day, one may procreate a son born in the field;
one may procreate a single son, but not a second.
The counter-exception to this is as follows:
some who know the [Vedic] lore consider a second procreation with women to be permissible,
seeing that the purpose of the *niyoga* (authorization for procreation) between those two has not yet been fulfilled according to the law.
The opinion of some is that he is the second son; these are those who know the matter— that is, those who understand the rules for the procreation of a *kṣetraja* son—
and who perceive that the purpose of the appointment (*niyoga*) has not been fulfilled.
Regarding the injunction that "a son must be procreated by the appointed woman," they consider this rule to be unfulfilled by the procreation of only one son;
they hold that the singular number is not intended to be significant.
What is their intention?
They consider the singular number to be unintended (*avivakṣita*).
Because the substance is primary and the action is subordinate, there is non-intentionality, as in the case of the singularity of the cup (*grahaikatva*).

But surely, even when there is no explicit teaching, once the primacy of the substance is understood through the accusative case, the intentionality regarding specific qualities such as number remains established.

From the indicative force (*liṅga*) of the injunction "a twice-born man should marry a wife," there is a transgression of the singular number in the rule regarding offspring, as seen in the mantra: "Beget ten sons upon her.
If this were so, one would not remain restricted to exactly two wives.
It is precisely in anticipation of this doubt that the statement "a second" is made for the purpose of excluding others.
The meaningfulness of that [term] also has this intended meaning:
in the section on marriage, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) applies to the legitimate son (*aurasa*), because of the recitation of the mantra;
however, here there is a departure from the singular number, based on the common usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) who say, "one who has no son" or "one who has only one son."
Or rather, it is because this very tradition (smṛti) conceives of the praise of a second son as being in accordance with dharma and the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra).
When the purpose of the appointment regarding the widow has been accomplished according to the rule,
the two should behave toward each other like a father-in-law and a daughter-in-law.

But here, the object of the injunction is that toward which one is enjoined; and that [act] is characterized by approaching [the husband], culminating in sexual union and physical contact. Once that has been completed, the previous mode of conduct applies—just as toward a teacher or a daughter-in-law.
Toward the wife of the elder brother, the younger brother should behave as toward a guru; and toward the husband of the younger sister, the elder brother should behave as toward a daughter-in-law.
Because of their mutual relationship, the woman should behave toward the elder man as toward a daughter-in-law, and the man toward the elder brother’s wife as toward a guru.

If those two, being appointed [to the task], should act according to their own desire, disregarding the prescribed rule, they would both become outcasts, like one who violates his daughter-in-law or one who violates the bed of his teacher.
The procedure begins with "anointed with clarified butter" and so forth;
by transgressing this, one incurs loss of caste (*pātitya*).
The elder brother who is thus appointed, the man who violates his daughter-in-law, and the younger brother who violates his elder's bed are all considered violators of the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpaga*).
A widow must not be appointed to another [man] by the twice-born;
for those who appoint her to another would destroy the eternal Dharma.
This is a prohibition of the appointment (*niyoga*) previously ordained.

Regarding this, some maintain that because of the mention of a "widow" (*vidhavā*), the prohibition applies specifically to one whose husband is dead; thus, they hold that the injunction and the prohibition have distinct scopes, [the former] being "she should be appointed by a husband who is impotent" (*klība*). Others, however, argue that since the scriptural injunction mentions the "interruption of lineage" as the occasion for the act, and such an interruption can occur even when a husband is impotent, diseased, or deceased.
And likewise, prohibition is no less distinct from injunction;
for one who has lost her connection with a husband is called "widow" (*vidhavā*),
and that [logical structure] is identical in both cases.
And this must necessarily be understood in this way;
otherwise, even the rule regarding being anointed with ghee and so forth would not apply to a woman who is appointed by a eunuch.
For in that case as well, they prescribe: "And he who is appointed to a widow shall be anointed with ghee."
Therefore, since there is no distinction in what is enjoined, the prohibition is likewise without distinction;
and thus, when the scope of both injunction and prohibition is equal, there is an option between them.
And this mandatory injunction for procreating offspring is understood to be indeed optional, like the taking up or not taking up of the Soma cups.

But when there is an injunction for the production of a result such as "one conquers through a son," then, since in the absence of offspring there is an absence of that benefit consisting of the funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) which are its effect, how could there be an option between two distinct results?
An injunction and a prohibition are optionally combined when they have the same scope and refer to a single purpose,
as in the case of the taking or not taking of the *ṣoḍaśī* cup— so say some.
It has been stated that when there is an abundance of auxiliary factors (*aṅga*), there is an abundance of the fruit;
however, regarding the accomplishment of the primary task (*pradhānakārya*), there is no distinction.
Therefore, in this view, he states that there is an absence of benefit to the son.
If this [action] proceeds for the sake of a specific benefit, then by transgressing the prohibition, it is equivalent to the Śyena sacrifice.
However, this point must be examined here:
why does that person who is enjoined proceed to act?
For there is no injunction for him [the husband] stating that he must go when commissioned; however, such an injunction exists for the woman, namely, "by a woman who is properly commissioned.
And the meaning is that the fulfillment of the commission for the woman does not occur while the brother-in-law and others are engaged in the act.
It must be stated that their activity also proceeds according to that same rule, for it is the *kṣetraja* son who is desired; since activity arises from passion (*rāga*),
[the objection] that the injunction of rules such as being anointed with ghee would be purposeless is not valid— it is not purposeless.
Thus, when [an offspring] is born according to these rules, he receives the designation "kṣetraja" (born of the wife) and no other;

as for the statement that "the word of the guru must be carried out," which some cite as a basis for action— this being the case, it would follow that one might engage in drinking liquor and similar acts by the will of the guru.
Nor is he a guru who incites one to what should not be done;
even for a guru, if he is arrogant, ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done,
and has set out upon a wrong path, his abandonment is ordained.
This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa).
Furthermore, "abandonment" means desisting from the duties of one's teacher.

By this, the following argument is also refuted: that the statement regarding the fall from one's status (pātitya) due to the transgression of a rule implies permission for a mode of life preceded by such a rule, [and thus] "both of them would become fallen."
Otherwise, for one who engages in intercourse in every manner, there would be a fall from caste; thus, a specific fall [from caste] would be untenable.
For that [fall] is not heard of in the case of a man alone, but rather in the case of a woman. And for her, when desiring a son, *niyoga* is prescribed.
For it is with reference to that [transgression] that the statement regarding "one who has fallen" occurs, namely, "both of them would become fallen.
In the absence of transgression, only the man is fallen; but upon transgression, both are fallen—thus, even by this indication, [the fact of her being a wife] emerges clearly.
Therefore, it must be explained how there can be such activity characterized by the injunctions concerning the husband's younger brother (*devara*) and so forth.
It is said:

Just as there is no sin in offering the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) to one's offspring when following the example of Vyāsa and others, so too, for the purpose of procreating a son through a wife (*kṣetraja*), there is a requirement for the authorization of the elders (*guru-niyoga*).
Therefore, it must be understood that there is no transgression (*cyuti*) in approaching [the woman] under such circumstances.
Indeed, it is not logical to admit that great souls can have an active engagement characterized by passion.
Furthermore, as for the argument that the statement regarding one’s fallen status (*patitatva*) upon transgressing a rule serves as a sign [of such engagement], that is incorrect;
because if a man were fallen, he would lack the qualification for procreation, and thus the act of producing offspring would be purposeless.
Therefore, this is merely a semblance of the injunction regarding the divine king and so forth.
Nowhere in the mantras pertaining to marriage is "authorization" (niyoga) mentioned;
nor, furthermore, is the remarriage of a widow prescribed in the rules for wedding ceremonies.

Regarding the rite of marriage (*udvāhana*), those mantras which are employed there—such as "The maidens have worshipped the god Aryaman and Agni," and others connected with it, such as "With me as husband, may you reach old age" and "With me as husband, may you be blessed with offspring"—in all these cases they say that the child belongs to the one who carries [the bride] away, the suitor. It is not heard therein [in the Veda] that "beget from him with whom you are joined by me. By the mention of the mantras, he demonstrates this.
Even among the *mantras* and *arthavādas*, there are none of this kind; he shows this from afar: "The remarriage of a widow is not mentioned in the rules for marriage.
Here, "remarriage" (*āvedana*) is intended to mean "union" (*gamana*).

Alternatively, this woman is united [in marriage] at the very time of the wedding; the brother-in-law will marry his brother's wife, and therefore this *niyoga* is indeed prescribed within the context of marriage.
It is not, however, that there is a separate rite of marriage here.
This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) supplementary to what precedes.
This practice, condemned as a mere bestial custom by the ignorant twice-born,
was declared even for human beings while Vena was ruling the kingdom.
This too is merely an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) supplementary to the prohibition of the injunction.

Those who are ignorant and do not correctly understand the scripture, and who, as practitioners of worldly affairs, do not know that the indicative suffixes (*liṅga*) and so forth have another purpose—by them that which is a "beastly practice" (*paśudharma*), which is utterly censurable even for humans, was proclaimed and set in motion. That [practice] belongs to the present time and is not beginningless; it occurred while King Vena was ruling and protecting the kingdom.
But has it not been stated that there are no indicative marks at all? It is not so; it was stated that they do not exist in the marriage mantras, but they are seen elsewhere.
"Who, like a widow [seeking] her brother-in-law, brings you two together in the dwelling-place, as a young woman [brings] a man? and so forth.

Just as a widow makes a man her husband, her brother-in-law, in a common bed, who indeed makes the two of you mindful [of each other], by which you do not depart? What is the distinction in the marriage mantras? The intention is that this [mantra] is indeed of the nature of a sequence for the rite of procreating offspring.
"By other learned men" is how it has been read.
This practice known as approaching a brother's wife has been declared censurable among humans; it is the law of beasts,
yet it prevailed during the reign of King Vena.
In ancient times, while enjoying the entire earth as the most eminent of royal sages,
his consciousness was so overcome by desire that he caused the intermixture of the social orders.
While enjoying and protecting [the earth],
how indeed could he, being the most eminent of royal sages (*rājarṣi*), cause the intermixture of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*)?
It has been said that he who enjoys the entire earth does so by virtue of his status as a great king (*mahārāja*).
He is one whose consciousness—that is, the stability of the mind—is afflicted and destroyed by desire, characterized by passion and so forth.
From that time forward, the virtuous censure anyone who, out of delusion, employs a woman whose husband has died for the sake of offspring.
The explanatory passage has a clear meaning.
If the husband of a maiden should die after the verbal betrothal has been made true,
her own brother-in-law shall marry her according to this following rule.
Because it takes the form of a formal commission (*niyoga*), this practice is said to pertain to a maiden.
When the verbal betrothal has been made true— that is, when the gift of the bride by one party has been completed and accepted by the other—
the husband's own brother, his *devara*, shall take her, meaning he shall marry her, according to the procedure that will be described hereafter.
Having approached her according to the prescribed rule— she being clad in white garments and pure in her vows—
he shall unite with her in private once each season until she gives birth.
"According to rule" means according to the scriptures; "having obtained her" means having married her in the manner prescribed for marriage. This marriage is one based on verbal declaration.
She is likewise called a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman);
even though she has been wedded, she does not become a wife,
for her marriage is merely a formal rite intended for the sake of another.
And thus he shows: "Having given a daughter to one, she is not given again to another.
The meaning is that she is not to be given to a brother-in-law (devara). And how could she, being ungiven and not having become his own property, become a wife [dressed] in white garments?
This rule applies to sexual intercourse; this same dharma is also intended for other types of engagement.
A wise man, having given his daughter to one, should not give her again to another;
for by giving her once more after she has been given, he incurs the sin of lying regarding a human being.

"Their completion, however, should be known by the wise at the seventh step"—this is a prohibition against the apprehension that even a girl who has been given [in marriage] might be given again if the groom dies before the wedding;
for there is a specific restatement regarding a particular case, whereby such a woman is called a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman).
One should not give her to another after having given her to one man and then that man having died.
Acting in such a manner, he incurs the falsehood of a person; whatever sin exists in the abduction of a human being, that becomes his.
Even after accepting her according to the prescribed rites, one may abandon a girl who is blameworthy,
diseased, severely corrupted, or one who was offered through deception.
*Vidhi* means the scripture; that which is worthy of it is *vidhivat*.

Whatever rule (*vidhi*) has been stated by the scripture—namely, "for the foremost of the twice-born, [the funeral rite] is with water alone"—that very authority regarding water is recorded by some in relation to the subject of a maiden.
Even after having accepted her, he may abandon the girl before the marriage ceremony.

He should abandon one who is censurable, one with ill-omened marks, or even one previously accepted who has not yet lost her virginity; likewise, one who is shameless, one who speaks excessively to many men, one who is diseased—specifically afflicted by consumption (kṣaya)—one who is corrupted, one designated as "sickly" and the like, and one whose affection is fixed on another.
Others explain that "corrupted" (*vipraduṣṭā*) refers to one whose virginity has been violated (*kṣatayoni*).
They do not think correctly.
If a woman who has not been enjoyed by a man is a maiden and remains unaltered, then she is indeed not defiled.
But if she has been united with a man, then she is no longer a maiden.
In that context, the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of the phrase "one should abandon the girl" is untenable;
yet her abandonment has already been mentioned.
Furthermore, she who is presented through deception—whether possessing deficient or redundant limbs—and she who is joined for a specific motive [are also to be abandoned].
Even if she has been chosen, she must be abandoned if even minor faults have been mentioned.
But if one should bestow a girl who has defects without having disclosed them,
he should render that gift void for that evil-minded giver of the bride.
The defects of a maiden have been stated;
if one gives her away—that is, bestows her—without having declared or mentioned them, that gift shall be rendered void and fruitless by her being returned.
This very point, already stated, has been made exceedingly clear by the preceding verse.
A man who has business to attend to should depart after providing for his wife's livelihood;
for a woman, even one of steadfast character, may fall into corruption when distressed by a lack of means.

When he is about to go abroad, he should provide for his wife's maintenance before departing; this is how the injunction "having provided" (vidhāya) is to be understood, meaning that while traveling he must arrange for her livelihood. He should act in such a way that she has a means of subsistence for the duration of his absence, consisting of food, clothing, household utensils, and other necessities for the maintenance of the body.
Having made such an arrangement, he may travel from his own country to another country;
being "one who has business," meaning one who has a purpose consisting of the human goals (puruṣārtha), both seen and unseen.
The unseen is dharma, while the seen consists of wealth and pleasure.
Thus he will say later with the words, "one who has gone abroad for the sake of religious duties," and so forth;
by these causes, staying away from home while abandoning one's wife is forbidden,
for [the wife] may indeed be emaciated by lack of livelihood.
The demonstration of the faults [of such behavior] is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).
Even one who is established [in virtue] might become corrupted through contact with another man and the like, being emaciated and afflicted by lack of livelihood and poverty.
"Staying" refers to the conduct of one's family; it is considered that a woman endowed with such [conduct] might incur blame if, at the time of hunger, she lives by resorting to another husband.
The suffix *liṅ* is used here in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*).
If her husband has gone abroad after providing for her maintenance, she should live observing her religious observances;
but if he has gone abroad without providing for it, she may live by means of blameless crafts.

The restriction is as follows: just as when the husband is present there is a prohibition against traveling abroad or leaving the house, so too when he has gone abroad, she remains steadfast, relying upon and maintaining [the household] as if he were there.
However, if he has gone abroad and she lacks a means of subsistence, she may live by crafts such as carding wool or making nets;
likewise, she may use even censurable items such as fans and the like.
This alone is the means of livelihood for widows and others, produced by their own labor.
A man who has gone abroad for the sake of dharma should be awaited for eight years;
for the sake of knowledge or fame, for six years; but for the sake of pleasure, for three years.
Regarding what was stated—that one should travel abroad for the sake of business—he now demonstrates those specific tasks;
the difference in the duration of waiting depends on the particular nature of those tasks. However, it has not been stated that "after this time, she must perform this [specific act]."
Regarding this, some say that on account of the context, one should live by means of blameless [means].
That is incorrect;
for prior to this time, what would have happened to her if she were to die by means of blameless [means]?
For her abandonment is not permitted, as it is forbidden for a man;
therefore, even before this rule regarding waiting, she who cannot subsist by irreproachable crafts may live by reproachable ones.
Others, however, allow for adultery.
And likewise, another Smṛti states:
"When her husband is lost, dead, has renounced the world, is impotent, or has fallen from his caste—
in these five calamities, another husband is ordained for women."
Others also say:
"Her vow of celibacy can never be removed;
for that [practice] was ordained for her among the duties of women even by Manu, who stated: 'But when her husband has died, she shall not take the name of another.'"
When the husband is dead, there is no transgression [of duty], how much less so when he has gone abroad?
For the word "husband" (pati) is based on the act of protecting, as in "village chief" or "lord of the army.
And therefore, by virtue of this statement, she would not be dependent upon her husband.

However, for the sake of his own livelihood, he may resort to another by performing tasks such as working as a *sairandhrī* (a female servant). If, while he is supported by someone else for a period of six months or a year, his husband should arrive and be able to win her over, saying, "Abandon your wife," then as long as the time [of the contract] is not yet full, she belongs to the husband alone; the rest has been chewed over in the fifth [chapter].
Others also state this same point.
The ancients, however, maintain that there is the status of a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman).

She who has been abandoned by her husband, or she whose husband—allegedly—does not return for such a length of time because his livelihood is withheld, is considered as good as abandoned by him. Consequently, if she should be married again according to the law of the *punarbhū*, then when her [first] husband returns, he should say nothing.
Furthermore, the claim that "this [woman] is the wife of one who seeks rebirth" is incorrect;
we shall demonstrate the meaningfulness of that verse by means of the arguments regarding purchase and relinquishment.
"Dharmakārya" means both dharma and its effect;
it is for the sake of that purpose or objective of the journey.
Why?
For a householder, there is no purpose in a long-term absence from home for the sake of dharma;
for he must necessarily tend to the sacred fires and perform the five great sacrifices.
Whence is it that one must go? [The answer is: "Every spring, one must sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Ritual acts such as bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), which are prescribed by the Smṛtis, should also be performed provided they do not conflict with the Śruti.

Nor does the rule apply that "for one who has gone abroad after making arrangements, [the rites] do not bear fruit," because it is stated that even when one has gone abroad after making arrangements, [the duty remains] until the next *parvan*; for it is said that one should personally offer the oblation on the *parvan* day, while the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) may perform it at any other time.

Even though the pilgrimage of one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) is equal in its status as a *smārta* (tradition-based) duty to that of one who performs the five sacrifices (*pāñcayajñika*), it is not proper for him to go on a pilgrimage if he abandons his wife, since such a journey is only appropriate when undertaken together with her.

It is said in reply: by the command of a guru; when gurus send someone forth for the sake of their own business—whether for the acquisition of merit or for service to the king—that is a journey abroad for the sake of dharma.
Or [the purpose may be] expiation by wandering through the regions of ascetic groves;
or else, for the sake of acquiring wealth intended for religious duties, thinking, "I am poor; I shall acquire wealth from somewhere"; or for the sake of learning.
Now, it is said that the acquisition of a wife occurs after one has bathed,
and the bath occurs for one who has completed his studies;
therefore, how can there be a desire for knowledge on the part of one who has already married?
This has been shown:
one who has slightly understood the meaning of the Vedas is qualified for marriage, while the bath and other rites are prescribed once [the meaning] is ascertained.
This is not tenable.

When the inquiry into Dharma has been completed, the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) follows; and this inquiry consists in the ascertainment of the truth through the removal of doubt preceded by investigation.
True.
This is not an injunction for the purpose of seeking knowledge.
And this being the case, [the purpose] would already be understood by the phrase "for the sake of the duties of dharma.
Even when there has arisen an understanding applicable to one's qualification, [one studies] other sciences for the sake of excellence in practice,
for the sake of distinction, for the sake of quickly proclaiming valor and fame, and for the sake of proclaiming externally a state of being a distinguished scholar.
Traveling abroad for the sake of fame is one reason for exile;
following courtesans for the sake of pleasure is another, as is going to marry a more desirable wife.
Furthermore, in another Smṛti text, a distinction regarding the time [of impurity] is recorded based on whether a child has been born or not.
And likewise Viṣṇu says: "Eight [sons] may be born of a Brāhmaṇa woman, six of a Kṣatriya woman, and four of a Vaiśya woman; for each subsequent caste, the number of sons born is doubled.
There is no restriction of time regarding a Śūdra woman;
some say it should be for one year.
A husband who hates his wife should wait for one year;
but after a year has passed, he may take away her property and no longer cohabit with her.
"Her husband is hateful" means she hates him;
however, one should not expel her on this account.

This is because the accusative case in the word "enām" (her) would be untenable with the prefix *sam* in the verb *vāsayet*; rather, "he should cause her to dwell [there]" means he should keep her there by means of reprimand.

Even in the case of a grave offense, there is no expulsion from her [the teacher's] presence, according to the statement: "One should restrain her within a single dwelling. Even regarding this specific cause for penance, the removal of the pupil is intended for the purpose of instilling discipline;
it is not an absolute and total deprivation in every respect.
She who transgresses against one who is negligent, intoxicated, or afflicted by disease shall be abandoned for three months, divested of her ornaments and belongings.
Transgression consists in showing contempt for her service and being indifferent toward what is beneficial, such as medicine and the like; it does not consist in approaching another man.
Furthermore, there must be a renunciation of sexual enjoyment for three months for the same reason as before.
She should be deprived of ornaments such as necklaces and bracelets.
By means of personal belongings, such as vessels, bowls, and the like, or by means of female and male servants.
There is no abandonment of a wife who is insane, fallen [from caste], impotent, barren, or afflicted with a foul disease; nor is there any revocation of the inheritance for one who hates [her].

The words *klība* (impotent) and *abīja* (seedless) denote a eunuch (*napuṃsaka*). However, there is a distinction: one is one whose semen is wind-like (*vātaretas*), while the other is one whose sexual organs are inactive.
For one who hates such a man, the previously mentioned punishment does not apply.
"Apavartana" means embezzlement; "proṣita," "pratiṣiddha," "anna," and so forth are prohibited by other Smṛti texts.
A wife who drinks liquor, is untruthful in conduct, or is hostile,
as well as one who is diseased, harmful, or always wasteful of wealth, may indeed be superseded by another marriage.

A woman who drinks liquor—that is, one who is devoted to drinking intoxicants—is unfit for the duties of the household, such as cooking and preparing food, because she is occupied with that [drinking]; therefore, she deserves to be superseded by another wife.
As for her whose drinking of liquor has been forbidden by her elders, the author will state her punishment in the verse beginning with "if she should drink despite the prohibition."

In the case of a woman herself violating a rule, it is appropriate that she should restore her status through penance—just as one restores oneself after transgressing another's rule—and furthermore, she may be superseded by another wife. Accordingly, the grounds for supersession are enumerated as causes for the obstruction of religious duties, the procreation of offspring, and household management, such as being "contrary," "diseased," or "wasting wealth. However, regarding a Brāhmaṇa woman, since the consumption of liquor is prohibited by scripture, the penance for drinking it applies only to prevent its recurrence; yet, there is no loss of caste (*pātitya*) from drinking liquor, because the scripture enumerates specific causes for loss of caste, stating: "A woman falls [from her caste] through abortion or service to a low-caste man. Thus, there is no loss of caste from drinking liquor.
We shall explain that in the eleventh [chapter], and it has also been stated in the fifth:

she is of untruthful conduct and improper behavior; she speaks harsh and false words to her servants; she eats even before the performance of the *balikarma* offerings; and she lacks faith in the feeding of Brahmins during rites for the gods (*daiva*) and ancestors (*pitrya*).
One who destroys wealth is characterized by excessive spending and fails to protect household utensils and furnishings, purchasing them for an exorbitant price.
One who is harmful has a habit of excessively beating servants and others out of groundless suspicion.
She is one who embezzles the daily expenses.
Supersession is the marrying of another woman over her.
He states that supersession may apply to other wives as well:
"A barren wife may be superseded in the eighth year; one whose children have died, in the tenth;
one who gives birth only to daughters, in the eleventh; but one who speaks unpleasantly, immediately."
In that regard, a barren wife should be superseded in the eighth year, but one whose children have died in the tenth;

for by superseding her, there would be a failure in the performance of the rites due to the absence of the birth of offspring, because of both the injunction for the procreation of offspring and the injunction for the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*).
Indeed, the establishment of the sacred fires is not prescribed for one who has no son.
The same applies to a woman whose children have died or who gives birth to daughters.
However, in the case of a woman who speaks unpleasantly, there is no supersession because of the absence of fault; this rule does not apply when she is capable of forbearance.
But a wife who is sickly yet beneficial and endowed with good character may be superseded after she has been informed; she must never be treated with contempt.
Devoted to her husband and intent on service,
she is here subject to the rules regarding permission and humiliation, because the previous [wives] possess these qualities.
By the mention of the "sick woman," the barren woman and the mother of female children are also indicated.

Since there is no distinction regarding what is under discussion and because there is no cause for actual contempt, "contempt" (avamānana) refers here to occasional instances such as reprimanding and so forth for the purpose of instruction.
But a woman who, having been given in marriage, should depart from the house in anger,
she must be restrained immediately or abandoned in the presence of the family.
For a woman who has departed due to anger caused by a lack of affection, both abandonment (*tyāga*) and confinement (*saṃnirodha*) are prescribed according to the specific circumstances;

however, this does not apply when she has left for reasons such as food or clothing, where there is satisfaction [with her departure]. In such cases, the removal of anger consists of being reprimanded by mother-in-law, father-in-law, or others, while confinement (*saṃnirodha*) consists of being placed under the supervision of guards.
Renunciation has been explained as non-enjoyment and the avoidance of sharing a bed.
"Family" refers to kinsmen, both those on the father's side and those on one's own side.
She who drinks liquor even on prohibited occasions or during festive celebrations,
or goes to a theater or a social assembly, shall be fined six *kṛṣṇalas*.
In the case of a prohibition, this punishment applies to women of the Kṣatriya and other castes who have relations with their teacher;
it does not apply to Brāhmaṇa women according to the scriptures.
For in that case, liberation is not attained by punishment alone; rather, it is by great [punishment]. Furthermore, there is no fear of addiction to drink among those who seek prosperity therein.
However, among those for whom drinking is not prohibited, a respectful practice is observed when they have gathered for festivals;
this is what [the author] properly forbids even on occasions of prosperity.
And this punishment is to be administered by the husband.
Even though the duty of kingship exists, it is understood that for women, the husband is the master.
Furthermore, other masters of dependents also possess independence regarding punishments to a certain extent in matters concerning their servants and others.
Prosperity refers to festivals such as the birth of a son, marriage, and so forth.
"Spectacle" refers to the viewing of actors and the like;
"assembly" refers even to a vast gathering of people.
This penalty applies to one who is curious about such an assembly.
If twice-born men should marry women both of their own class and of other classes,
seniority, honor, and the right to the household shall belong to them according to the order of their castes.

If those who have married out of desire should take wives both of their own caste and of other castes, then among them seniority shall be according to the order of their castes and in accordance with their birth, neither according to age nor according to the order of marriage.
Regarding the offering of fruits and other honors, the precedence belongs first to the Brāhmaṇī wife, then to the Kṣatriyā and Vaiśyā wives; such is the order of castes.
The principal residence, the main house, belongs to the Brāhmaṇī.
The order of marriage among those of the same caste is recorded as the determining factor.
The wife alone, and no one of a different caste under any circumstances, shall perform the service of her husband’s body and his daily religious duties for all [the deceased].
The wife herself should perform the service of the husband's body, characterized by cooking and other such necessities, as well as giving, feeding, and tending to him;
however, there is no fixed rule regarding the massaging, washing, and so forth of his back and feet.
But when they are present together, the order of attending to the limbs of the body follows the order of their castes.

The daily religious duty (*naityaka-dharmakārya*) consists of the evening meal and so forth, as well as the smearing of the fire-sanctuary, sipping water (*ācamana*), and the offering of water-libations (*tarpaṇa*).
This is a deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*):
"But he who, out of delusion, should have that performed by another woman while his own wife of the same caste is present..."
Just as a brahmin-cāṇḍāla was seen before, so indeed is he now.

But he who causes this rite to be performed by another woman of a different caste, while a woman of the same caste is available, is a Brāhmaṇa indeed, yet he is regarded as a Caṇḍāla on account of his former [act].
To one who is distinguished, handsome, excellent, and suitable,
one should give that maiden according to the prescribed rite, even if she has not yet reached marriageable age.

The relationship between the qualifier and the qualified in the phrase "to one who is excellent and handsome" (*utkṛṣṭāyābhirūpāya*) is as follows: the meaning is "to one who is excellent and more handsome.
Alternatively, "excellent" due to [superiority in] birth and so forth, and "handsome" are two distinct qualifiers.

One who has attained beauty (*abhirūpa*) by facing toward form (*rūpa*) and shape (*ākṛti*) is "handsome. Alternatively, it is a word denoting essential nature (*svabhāva*); thus, one who possesses an excellent nature is called handsome even if he is learned.
[He gives] to one who is similar in terms of birth and other such factors.
The *vara* is the groom or son-in-law.

Even though she has not reached [the marriageable age] and is unfit, because she is under the sway of passion, she is a "girl" (*bālā*) who has not yet attained the age of maidenhood; in another Smṛti, she is called *nagnikā*.
She is one in whom desire—that is, longing—has not arisen, and she is eight or six years old, but not merely an infant.
For thus [it is said]: "the indicative mark is an eight-year-old girl.
This very mark applies even to a marriage performed for the sake of dharma.
Otherwise, if passion alone were the motivating factor, they ask: how could there be a marriage of one who has not yet reached [puberty]? Thus they say.
That is incorrect;
for even those seeking wealth marry a young girl.
Not every application [of a rule] has been set forth in the third book.
A maiden, even if she has reached puberty, may remain in her father's house until death;
however, he must never give her in marriage to one who is devoid of good qualities.

The giving away of a maiden should take place before her first menses. Even when the menses have appeared, one should not give her away as long as a bridegroom endowed with good qualities has not been found.

"Good qualities" include excellence in learning and valor, a handsome appearance, being of mature age, avoidance of what is forbidden by worldly custom and scripture, affection for the maiden, and so forth.
A maiden who has reached puberty should wait for three years;
but after this period, she may seek a suitable husband.
"Seminal fluid" refers to the period of fertility; even if she possesses it, he should remain in her house for three years.
Beyond that, in the absence of a superior [husband], she may choose for herself a suitable man of the same caste.
If she should approach a husband of her own accord when she is not being given away,
she incurs no sin whatsoever, nor does he whom she approaches.
After three years have passed, if she chooses a husband who does not give her away, there is no fault on his part.

Since the absence of fault for the maiden was already stated by the preceding rule, this [verse] is intended to address the fault of the one being chosen. Furthermore, it is recorded in the Smṛti that the appearance of menses occurs at twelve years of age.

A maiden choosing her own husband (svayaṃvarā) shall not take for herself the ornaments belonging to her father, nor those belonging to her mother, nor those given by her brother; if she were to take them, she would be a thief.

If the brothers and others initially gave her ornaments with the intention that she should choose [her husband] herself, but did so without knowing her true intent, she should return those ornaments to them alone.
However, if they give them to her while she is already in such a state [of having chosen], then there is no forfeiture.
Therefore, it is not proper for an ornament given with the specific intention, "We will not give her to him," to remain with him once that intention has changed.
There is an alternative reading in the masculine gender, "stenaḥ syāt" (he would be a thief);
they say that this implies the groom's thievery.
Therefore, he must be made to relinquish the ornament.
One who takes a girl who has reached puberty should not pay a bride-price to her father;
for by obstructing her menses, he would be overstepping his authority as master.
This is the prohibition of the bride-price for a woman who has reached puberty and is to be given with a price;
and that [prohibition] would override ownership.
It has been stated that "in childhood, she shall remain under the control of her father."
Furthermore, when she has reached another [family], the father no longer possesses ownership over her even if he does not take [the bride-price];
for the reason—that she is to be given the *śulka* and so forth—is the same, and thus the father's ownership ceases.
"Departure" (*apakramaṇa*) means cessation.
Obstructing means the act of obstructing the production of offspring;
some say that this verse is not of human origin.
A thirty-year-old man should marry a charming twelve-year-old girl,
or a twenty-four-year-old man an eight-year-old girl, if he is one who is diligent in his religious duty.

The intended instruction is that a girl should be married after such a period of time has elapsed, and not that marriage must take place at exactly this specific age. Furthermore, the number of years is not to be taken literally; rather, she should be married after a long period of time has passed so that she is quite young.
For this [restriction] is not heard in the context of marriage (*vivāha-prakaraṇa*),

such that, as a qualification of the person to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*), it would exclude the time— whether ten years or twenty-five years— as being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that rite. But surely, even that which resides in another sentence can indeed be an injunction of an auxiliary?

True; here, due to the excellence of the context and its placement in the text, another intention of the Teacher is inferred. Likewise, there is the practice of the learned. Furthermore, since this time is not possible for a son who is already married to take a wife again, the injunction "he should take a wife again" would otherwise be untenable.
A husband obtains his wife as a gift from the gods, not by his own will;
doing what is pleasing to the gods, he should always support her if she is virtuous.
The meaning of the verse is that a virtuous wife must not be abandoned by her husband even if she is possessed of faults such as opposition or speaking unpleasantly;
the remainder of the verse is a praise.
As for the rule "but he may confine her in a single room," that is prescribed even for an unvirtuous wife, provided she has committed adultery only once.
But in the case of repeated practice, there must indeed be abandonment;
otherwise, nothing would have been accomplished by the injunction that "one should not maintain such a virtuous woman.
Furthermore, as for that which...
One should cause an unfaithful wife to live deprived of her authority, in a state of impurity, subsisting on mere alms, humiliated, and sleeping on the ground.
And that [provision] depends on the husband's will when there is the capacity [to give];
however, in the absence of his will, there is simply abandonment.

Furthermore, regarding what will be stated later—that "even for those who have fallen from their caste (patita), clothing, food, and drink must be given," and so forth—we shall explain that this is a statement of prohibition concerning the commencement of eating alms-food and the acquisition of a dwelling during penances for such acts as the killing of a Brahmin.
In any case, however, there is no provision for the maintenance of an unfaithful wife;
nor is any abandonment mentioned here that could lead one to assume [her exclusion] as being within the scope of shared enjoyment.
From the meaning of mantras and explanatory passages (arthavādas) such as "Soma gave her," the status of the deities as givers is understood.
Alternatively, because she becomes the wife of the deity at the marriage ceremony, it is said that "she is given by the gods.
One should not obtain her according to one's own desire;
for unlike other things such as cattle or gold which are obtained in the marketplace, this wife is not to be acquired in that manner.

Therefore it is said: "not according to one's own will. [The term] *devānāṃ priya* means "beneficial to the gods"—for when the wife has been abandoned, there is no benefit to the gods because the rites such as the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice cannot be performed.
Therefore, one should support her even if she is hostile.
If she has fallen [from her status], the husband may take another wife who possesses the required qualifications.
Women were created for the purpose of procreation, and men for the purpose of continuing the lineage;
therefore, the sacred scripture declares that religious duty is common to both, performed together with the wife.
Procreation (*prajana*) is the taking of a conception;
lineage (*saṃtāna*) is the implantation of the embryo.
For that reason, because the production of offspring depends upon both, the Veda declares the duty common to both woman and man as belonging to the man together with his wife.
Therefore, because there is no authority for [the husband] alone, women must not be abandoned even if they are hateful.
If the giver of the bride-price dies after the bride-price has been paid for the maiden,
she should be given to the husband's brother, provided the maiden consents.

In the case where the bride-price (*śulka*) has been received by her father or others, but she has not yet been given away, and she is established as to be given solely by word of mouth—should he die in the interim, then she would, like other property, fall to the brothers-in-law (*devara*), or to all of them together as in the case of Yudhiṣṭhira and others, or in their absence, to the *sapiṇḍa* relatives. To specify the particular rule for this situation, it is stated that "she must be given to the brother-in-law"; she is not to be given to all the husband's brothers, nor to the *sapiṇḍas*, but rather to one brother-in-law alone—and even then, only with the consent of the maiden.
Now, what is the course of action if the girl is no longer available?

If the girl prefers a life of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), then the bride-price (*śulka*) belongs solely to the girl’s paternal kin. If, however, she seeks another husband, then having relinquished the previously received bride-price, she is given after receiving it from another.
Even a Śūdra, when giving away his daughter, must not accept a bride-price;
for by accepting a bride-price, one performs a disguised sale of the daughter.
Regarding the taking of a bride-price (*śulka*) by mutual consent, the rule has already been stated previously.

Someone might have this doubt: "The taking of a bride-price is not a fault, since a specific status is mentioned in the scripture for one whose price has been taken. To dispel this doubt, he says: "Even a Śūdra shall not take a bride-price.
When there is engagement by mutual consent, it is a scriptural restriction; it is not that the scripture declares the act itself to be something that ought to be done.
Just as the drinking of liquor is not authorized by the scripture merely because an expiation is prescribed for one who has drunk it;
and as for that which was stated under the name of "toll" (śulka)— namely, "for he takes the toll out of greed"—
the specific distinction for which this [separate] reading is shown has already been demonstrated.
But this is what neither others nor any other virtuous men have ever done:
that having promised something to one person, it is then given to another.

This prohibits what was stated previously—that once the bride-price (*śulka*) has been received, if the giver of the price dies while the maiden’s own desire remains, she may be given to another. [The verse] says:
"If, having promised her to one who gave the bride-price, she is again given to another after receiving the bride-price once more, then the maiden herself should exercise her choice (*svayaṃvara*).
This is the very meaning.
Indeed, we have never heard of such a thing, even in previous births:
the sale of a daughter concealed under the name of a "bride-price" (śulka).
The meaning is: "We have not heard this from anyone before, in previous births or in other eons."
Mutual fidelity until death—
this should be known as the supreme duty of husband and wife in brief.
Through the expression of speech without distinction, there is non-deviation in all actions.
Thus Āpastamba says: "She must not be transgressed in matters of dharma, artha, and kāma.
And these alone constitute the highest good: dharma, artha, and kāma.

And so it has been said: "The established rule is that [the pursuit of] the three aims (trivarga) [is to be practiced]. As for what they say—that non-abandonment [of one's wife] constitutes non-deviation [from fidelity], otherwise a man, like a woman, would not be permitted to marry more than one wife—that is incorrect.
There is a scriptural statement regarding men who act according to their desire: "A barren woman may be superseded by another wife in the eighth year," but this does not apply to women.
Furthermore, there would be another indicative mark [of this distinction]: "One man may have many wives, but one woman does not have many husbands simultaneously."
That which exists until the end of death is "until-death-end" (*āmaraṇāntika*). The meaning is that even upon any one of the two deaths, there is an end to it.
This should be understood briefly as the excellent dharma of women and men.
Likewise, once they have performed the prescribed rites, the woman and man should always strive so that,
even when separated from one another, they do not transgress their mutual fidelity.
They should strive with great effort so that they do not transgress one another;
"transgression" means overstepping, which is the failure to remain together in the pursuit of dharma, artha, and kāma.
Having performed their rites—that is, having undergone the sacraments such as marriage—they should remain inseparable from that point forward.
This concluding verse does not teach any meaning that has not already been stated.
This is the transitional verse connecting the preceding and following sections:

"This law concerning men and women, together with the rules for sexual pleasure, has been declared to you; as well as the acquisition of offspring in times of distress. Now learn the law of inheritance."
Once the duties of husband and wife and the procreation of offspring have been discussed, the occasion for the partition of inheritance arises.
After the father and the mother have passed away, the brothers, having assembled, shall divide the paternal inheritance equally; for they have no power over it while the two are alive.
The optative suffix (*liṅ*) in "they should divide" (*bhajeran*) indicates that the time for it has arrived;
this has been explained in detail in the fifth [chapter].
Alternatively, it means "at whatever time it has been transferred."
The eldest alone shall take the paternal wealth in its entirety;
the rest shall depend upon him, just as they did upon their father.
By the mere birth of an eldest son, a man becomes a father of a daughter and is freed from his debt to the ancestors; therefore, he deserves everything.
He upon whom one pays off a debt, and through whom one attains infinity—he alone is known as the son born of dharma; the others are known as born of desire.
The phrase "the others" is an explanatory statement (arthavāda);
for if one were to grasp the intended meaning exactly as it is heard [literally], the younger brothers would simply be unworthy of a share,
which would contradict what is to be stated later.
The eldest brother should protect his younger brothers like a father protects his sons; and they, in accordance with dharma, should behave toward their eldest brother as sons do toward their father.

They are to be protected like sons, but they are not to be treated with contempt by being deprived of wealth and other necessities on the grounds that they are "merely children. They, too, should cultivate the thought, "This man is our father.
Thus it is said: "And they should behave toward him as toward a son."
Another praise:
"The eldest son causes the family to prosper or, conversely, brings it to ruin;
the eldest is most worthy of honor in the world, and the eldest is not censured by the virtuous."
He alone who is preeminent in virtue causes the family to prosper;
this very one, being devoid of virtue, brings that family to ruin. When the eldest brother is possessed of virtuous conduct, even the younger brothers behave likewise.
They, too, dispute with one who is devoid of virtue.
He who is the eldest and behaves as an elder should be honored like a mother and like a father; but he who does not behave as an elder should be respected merely as a kinsman.

The conduct toward the eldest [brother] is like affection toward a son: protection, non-neglect regarding his body and wealth as if they were one's own, and turning him away from improper acts. However, toward one who behaves otherwise, one should show respect through rising to greet him and saluting him, as one would for a kinsman, or like a maternal uncle or paternal uncle. If he acts otherwise, his subordination ceases.
Thus they may dwell together or separately out of a desire for dharma; dharma increases through separation, therefore separation is consistent with dharma.

Because one lacks the power to act according to one's own will, it is impossible to perform sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma independently with one’s own property; therefore, for the sake of accomplishing those rites, this partition—which is established by reason—is prescribed by the rule: "or separately, out of a desire for merit.
It is not, however, that non-partition constitutes demerit; rather, partition itself is a meritorious act, like the Agnihotra and other rites.
But surely, since non-partition is a cause for obstructing the performance of dharma, it must indeed be demerit?
This is not a fault.
Transgression occurs upon the non-performance of what one is authorized to do;

however, one whose wealth is undivided has no such authorization because he lacks the possession of the sacred fires (*agnimat*), since the formal taking of the fires is prescribed precisely at the time of partition.

However, for one who has married while his father is still living and has at that very time taken up the sacred fires (*parigṛhītāgni*), there is no non-division because he is already authorized [in the rites].
Even he, if he has fallen away from his commitment or otherwise possesses sufficient wealth for the performance of prescribed duties, would not incur sin by living together [with his father].
For it has been stated that the status of being righteous or unrighteous does not exist in division or non-division by their own nature.

But surely, since there is the statement that "for brothers who are undivided, a single religious duty (dharma) prevails," there is indeed the manifestation of dharma prior to partition through joint performance, just as between husband and wife;
for because the property is common, it must be performed by all together.
This is not so in the case of the *agnihotra* and similar rites.
For the Agnihotra and other rites are performed in the Āhavanīya and other fires;

and since the Āhavanīya and others are designated by their consecration (*saṃskāra*), they do not attain the status of being connected to either [the sacrificer or another] because of the observation of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
Furthermore, there is a prohibition seen against one who offers oblations in a fire belonging to another: "One does not sacrifice in the fires of another."
For there is no injunction regarding the Smārta fire even in the domestic (gṛhya) fire;
because the word "house" (gṛha) is used in its specific sense and denotes the fire, this same principle applies.
This is because [the rites] such as the feeding of guests are recited among the Great Sacrifices (mahāyajña).
"One should perform the domestic rites (*gṛhya-karma*) according to the rule in the nuptial fire,
as well as the performance of the five sacrifices (*pañca-yajña*). Thus, the authority for these rites resides solely in the *Gṛhyasūtras*.
Therefore, this statement "a single dharma" should be understood as referring merely to faith, meritorious works, food offerings, and so forth.
The eldest shall receive a twentieth part as his preferential share, as well as the best of all the property;
half of that shall be the share of the middle son, and a fourth for the youngest.
Some maintain that this Smṛti rule regarding the distribution of shares pertains to a time long past and is not to be practiced today,
because Smṛtis are restricted to specific times.

They argue that the designation of it as something to be practiced is for the sake of attaining spiritual merit through knowledge, similar to the case of long-duration sacrificial sessions (dīrghasattra).
For indeed, nowadays no one is seen performing long-duration sacrifices (*dīrghasatra*);
however, Brahmins do study the instructions for them.
And thus it has been said that other duties belong to the Kṛta Age.
Therefore, just as there is a restriction of place, a restriction of time for phenomena (*dharma*) should also be understood.
For a phenomenon that has been taught is not practiced in every location;
thus, local customs (*deśadharma*) are said to be established within specific regions.
Otherwise, if all [acts] were to be performed, there would be no designation of specific regions for the *dharmas*.
Thus he recites: "This [dharma] is indeed for the learned twice-born," and so forth.
Therefore, the Smṛti texts concerning the *uddhāra* (expiation), the *niyoga* (appointment of a widow), and the slaughter of cows, though taught, are not to be practiced.
This is not well-founded;

for such a restriction of time is nowhere heard of, except in the case of specific rules regarding evening, morning, festival days, and so forth. As for the claim that "the duties in other [ages] were different in the Kṛta Yuga," that has already been explained in the very first [section].
For this [difference in practice] is not the cause for the establishment of Dharma according to the division of Yugas.

It has already been stated that there is no restriction of place either—such as being made by the Middle Country or the Eastern Country—other than [the requirement of] inclining toward the east and so forth, in the context of the passage: "The laws of castes and regions, and those practiced by the virtuous.
Furthermore, the performance of long-duration sacrifices (*dīrghasatra*) is possible even in the present day.

The word "year" (*saṃvatsara*), however, has already been shown to refer primarily to days. As for the fact that nowadays no one is seen performing it, this is due to the inability of many to accomplish the performance of the enjoined matter—despite its being prescribed as an obligatory duty—in various ways, or due to a lack of desire for the result, or due to atheism (*nāstikatā*). As for the statement regarding King Vena, it shows a performance from that time onwards as belonging to a very remote antiquity; thus, it is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) and not an instruction regarding time.
The twentieth part belongs to the eldest;
having set aside the twentieth part from all the property, it must indeed be given to the eldest.
For the middle son, half of that, which is the fortieth part.
Thus, the youngest brother receives a fourth part, which is an eightieth part relative to the eldest.
Once this has been set aside, the remainder must be divided into three parts.
Of these, whatever is the best and most excellent among all the goods belongs to the eldest alone.
Alternatively, there is also the reading "paraṃ varam" even in the case of material objects (*dravya*).
This means that among those things—whether superior, inferior, or middling—that exist as objects and so forth, whichever one is the most excellent, that alone is what is prescribed for him.
Where cows or horses are present, the single best one should be given to the eldest; it must not be accepted in exchange for another object or by means of its price.
This is the rule for the extraction of all three types of virtuous persons, because the extraction of those possessing virtues is observed [to apply to all].
The eldest and the youngest shall take [their shares] as prescribed;
those who are other than the eldest and the youngest shall have the middlemost wealth.

In the case of one who has more than three sons, having set aside for the eldest and the youngest as prescribed if they possess merit, that which was stated in the immediately preceding verse as the fortieth part of the middle son—if he too possesses merit—must be shared among even many such middling sons. However, in the case of middling sons who are all of equal merit, according to the previous statement, a fortieth part of each individual's share is declared to be set aside.
Thus, the statement "their middle wealth shall be [theirs]" is expressed in both ways.
That which is designated as "middle wealth" in the subsequent verse should be given by all together in a collective assembly,
or alternatively, it may be given to each individual according to their seniority or juniority.
Of these two options, the first is appropriate for those who are devoid of merit.
They are not worthy of much wealth;
the second [category] is for those who possess virtuous qualities alone.
The eldest son shall take the best of all kinds of wealth, as well as whatever is particularly excellent; furthermore, he shall receive one choice item from every ten.
With the first half-verse, he restates what was said [in the previous verse]: "that which is the best among all substances.
The word *jāta* is a synonym for *jāti* (genus) or denotes a variety (*prakāra*).
*Agraja* means the eldest (*jyeṣṭha*).
"Foremost" means the best;
even if it is only a single garment or ornament that is superior,
one should take that one rather than ten, or rather than ten parts.
If there are ten cows or horses, then one should take the best single one; or if one does not obtain [the whole group], it is from a portion of ten. The word "ten" (daśa) refers to a group.
Others, however, explain that the suffix *tasi* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*).
They read the plural form as "ten excellent [gifts] from each ten," meaning that one should accept ten excellent gifts.
Another remembers them as distinguished by their number: "a hundred of the single-hoofed and the two-footed animals."
There is no deduction for those who have successfully performed their own duties;
however, something whatsoever should be given to the elder as a means of increasing his honor.
The preferential share (*uddhāra*) mentioned previously regarding ten head of cattle does not apply here.
As for those brothers who are accomplished and distinguished in their respective duties, such as Vedic study and the like—
the term "in ten" is explained as being merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*).
In the ten [verses], that which was stated as the extraction of the verse is entirely absent due to the connection with ritual action;
however, even by those [means], whatever slight additional method for increasing manhood and performing worship there may be, that should be given to the eldest.
In this way, when the preferential shares have been set aside, one should allot equal portions;
but if no preferential shares have been set aside, the allotment of shares for them shall be as follows.
When the *uddhāra*—the additional share—has been extracted and set aside, one should assign equal shares to the remaining wealth;
when it has not been extracted, the distribution of shares will be as described below.
