The eldest son shall take one share in excess; the one born after him, one and a half shares; and the younger brothers, one share each—thus is the law established.
"With one part more" means he should take his own share increased by one part; that is to say, he should receive two parts.
"Then the younger brother" means immediately after him, he receives one and a half (half of two).
"The youngest," those born after him—all these [younger brothers] shall have an equal share, meaning neither more nor less.
The brothers shall each separately give to their own respective sisters a fourth part from their own respective shares; those who are unwilling to give would become outcasts.
The word *kanyā* is generally used for unmarried girls;
furthermore, in another Smṛti, it is stated that "the son of an unmarried girl" (*kānīna*) belongs to those who are *aprattāḥ* (unbestowed).
Therefore, this share is declared to belong to one who is unmarried.
From their own shares, brothers should give a fourth part of their respective portions to their sisters, having regard for their own caste.
Where there are many sisters, the allotment of a fourth part must be made in relation to the brother of the same caste. And thus is the meaning: [the brothers shall give from their own shares].

The son shall take three shares and the daughter a fourth; as for what has been said by some— that there is a great benefit in the father’s act regarding unmarried daughters, since while the father lives they are consecrated through his will even with wealth [given] as a price, whereas upon his death they become heirs to shares—
that is equal in the case of the son as well, and what kind of objection can there be against a matter that is expressly stated in the sacred word?
Now, if the intention is that the practice consists of giving solely for the purpose of marriage, then such practice is weaker than the Smṛti;
moreover, it is not absolute.
And since it is not absolute, this restriction is properly based on the Smṛti.
As for what has been said by someone— that only that which is necessary for the marriage itself should be given, and not a fourth part as literally stated—
he should be told this:
there is no fixed amount of wealth to be given at a marriage.
Just as it is said, "He should give her twelve hundred [cows] as a sacrificial fee," so too he should simply clothe and adorn her and marry her;
or it is heard in the scriptures that he should give her a *saudāyika* (marriage-endowment).
Furthermore, ornaments consist of gold, gems, pearls, coral, and so forth, and are divided into many kinds.

In that case, it is not known how much wealth should be given or what kind of ornament [should be provided]; therefore, for the sake of the highest purpose, it is proper that this be one-fourth of one's own share.
Nor is there any contradiction with the scriptures or with logic regarding this matter;
other Smṛtis likewise support this very position.
"But those who have not been consecrated should be consecrated by the brothers who have already been consecrated;
and the sisters, having given a fourth part from their own shares," so it is said.
Likewise:
"Until her initiation, she shall take a share; thereafter, the husband shall maintain her.
This is the meaning of this [text]:

where there is only a small amount of wealth belonging to the brother and the sister such that the maintenance of the girl cannot be provided from a one-fourth share, in that case the girl shall take an equal share until her initiation.
But beyond that, one should take even a small fourth part according to another Smṛti.
How then is mere maintenance to be ensured? To this it is said: "The husband should maintain [the wife] beyond that.
They explain the mention of "brother" as referring to a uterine brother.
What is the intended meaning?
The word "brother" (bhrātṛ), when used without a qualifying prefix, functions in its primary sense only for a uterine brother;
furthermore, the separate mention [of the uterine brother] serves as an indicative mark (liṅga).

For she who has no uterine brother, her inheritance or her *saudāyika* property does not accrue [to anyone else]. If it is argued that a half-brother will give it, he does not give it in the absence of another scriptural statement. By the word "brother" (*bhrātṛ*), those who have the same father but different mothers are included.
However, it is logical that [the term] applies to the daughter of one's father's sister and others through figurative usage (*upacāra*).
In this way, the fact that the word "one" (*eka*) has multiple meanings is not accepted;
furthermore, the practice of other *smṛtis* is superior to this.
For it is recited therein: "That which remains after the paternal inheritance has been given, as well as the debt inherited from the father—that must be divided by the brothers.
The meaning is that they should divide the remainder after setting aside what must necessarily be paid by the father from that [inheritance].

And just as the repayment of debts and so forth is declared [to be obligatory], so too is the giving away of a daughter, because it is a necessary duty; for it is said, "and from daughters, that which pertains to the giving [of them]. In this context, neither the word "sister" nor the word "brother" is heard.

Since this doubt might arise—that what is called "separately" means that each individual share of the collection belongs to all [the creditors]—it is also appropriate [to interpret it thus]. This is stated [in response]: because there is demerit for those who do not give, they are not made to pay by force.
For this reason it is said that those who do not wish to give would become outcasts.

Indeed, it is stated that whoever is the owner of a certain portion in a given matter should take it; it is not, however, stated by this that he must give it to him. Just as it is not said that "a brother should give to his brother."
And that which is said [to be given] is further [given] to those who have no owner.
One should never divide goats, sheep, and single-hoofed animals unequally;
however, it is ordained that goats and sheep may be divided unequally, with the share going to the eldest alone.
"One-hoofed animals" refers to horses, mules, donkeys, and the like.

At the time of partition, if goats and sheep cannot be divided into equal numbers, they shall belong to the eldest alone; one should not seek to achieve equality by deducting them from the shares of the other property, nor should one sell them and compel the others to pay the proceeds.
In the term "goats and sheep" (*ajāvikam*), the singular form is used optionally according to the rule for the optional singular of a copulative compound of animals.
If a younger brother should beget a son upon the wife of the elder brother, the division of property in that case shall be equal; such is the established law.
Since it might follow from the rule of the elder brother's appointment (*niyoga*) that the same entitlement as a father extends to the uterine brother, this is stated to preclude that:
"In that case, the division shall be equal;
there shall be no preferential share (*uddhāra*), nor shall the eldest take one part more than the others," nor indeed should anything at all be given [to him as a special portion].
He should be impartial.
Toward whom?
Toward his biological father, his paternal uncle, and his younger brother.
However, it will be stated later that the son of an unauthorized woman is indeed unworthy of a share.

Furthermore, this indicative mark—namely, "the brothers having assembled"—shows that even though the word "brothers" (bhrātṛ) is used, the division must be made together with the brother's son when no [actual] brother is present.
Subordination of the principal is not tenable according to the law;
the father is the principal in procreation, therefore one should honor him in accordance with dharma.
The secondary son (kṣetraja) is subordinate;
[this statement] that he is equal to the primary son (aurasa)—having supplied this ellipsis—is not consistent with dharma, that is, with the scriptures.
For the *aurasa* son, it is said, receives the entire senior share like his father.
But this son born of the field (kṣetraja) is secondary; therefore, one should treat him according to the law.
"The law" refers to the previously mentioned arrangement of shares.
Now, since he too is an eldest son, why does he not receive a share like that of the legitimate son (aurasa)?
Therefore he says: "The father is primary in procreation. Here, "father" is intended to mean the progenitor;
he is primary in the production of offspring.
And this [son] is secondary, being begotten by the younger [brother].
The verse is understood only by supplying the words "the subordinate is equal to the principal.

This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and since it serves as an explanatory passage for the preceding prohibition of the eldest's share, an interpretation must be made by resorting to some basis for the terms "principal" and "subordinate."
Others read: "Therefore, one should abandon him by means of the Dharma.
That is incorrect, because it has been stated that [the rule] applies equally in all cases;
furthermore, since this is an explanatory statement (arthavāda), no suspicion of an alternative option (vikalpa) should be entertained.
If a doubt should arise as to how the division of property should be made in a case where there is a younger son born of an elder wife and an elder son born of a younger wife:
The elder (*jyeṣṭhā*) is the one married first;
the younger (*kaniṣṭhā*) is the one married later.

Regarding the children born of these two, a doubt is raised as to whether seniority should be determined by the order of their mothers' marriages or by the order of their own births; this will be resolved later for the sake of reaching a consensus.
The eldest son shall take one bull as his preferential share;
the others shall have bulls inferior to that, according to their respective mothers.
One born first is "pūrvaja"; he is declared to be the junior [in age] who receives the share of the bull.

Therefore, those other bulls besides that one which are not the eldest should be given to the many, one by one. And thus, for the son of the eldest (*jyaiṣṭhineya*), this much has been stated as the additional portion: namely, the best bull; its superiority is merely in quality, not in number. [The phrase] "of those inferior to that pūrvaja" means those who are fewer than that first-born.
To the question "Of how many? he says:
"Since the mother is primarily the source of one's own self, therefore in this context seniority is based on the mother, not on birth."
But the son born of the eldest wife, though not the eldest [by birth], shall take a bull and sixteen [cows];
the remaining sons shall divide [the rest] according to their mothers—this is the settled rule.
An alternative supplementary portion for these is stated as optional:
"If a first-born son is born to a non-first wife, he shall take fifteen cows;
'sixteenth' refers to a bull, and by virtue of the connection with the bull, the cows are thereby obtained."

Just as for this [owner] there is no interest in the second cow, so the other cows—the remaining ones—should be taken by [the sons] from their respective mothers; for just as their mother is more important, he whose mother is senior should take the senior [cow], and he whose mother is junior should take the junior one. Alternatively, this additional preferential share (*uddhāra*) is prescribed for the eldest son, while the previous [share] remains as it was.
There is no elision (praśleṣa) of the vowel 'a' here.
The remaining [sons] who are younger shall take [the estate] according to their mother;
this is what is distinguished by the phrase "according to their mother" (svamātṛtaḥ).
Since these two verses are merely explanatory (arthavāda), no effort is made toward their analytical distinction; this is just a preliminary introduction.
This is the established conclusion:
among sons born of wives of equal status, there is no seniority according to the mother; rather, seniority is said to be according to birth.
"Similar" means belonging to the same class.
Even in the Subrahmaṇyā invocations, it is recorded that the address is made according to birth-order;
and among twins conceived together, seniority is recorded as being determined by birth.
This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) that establishes birth-order seniority.

There is a mantra called *subrahmaṇyā* used by the *chandoga*s in the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice, beginning with "O Subrahmaṇyā, for the summoning of Indra; O Indra, come! and so forth. Because of the multiplicity of its applications, the plural form is used.
Regarding this, the following is said:
By designating the father through the first-born son, it is said: "The father of Devadatta sacrifices. Primacy by birth is primary;
any other [primacy] derived from the connection to the mother's marriage is secondary.
Between twins conceived at the same time, seniority is determined by birth.
A sonless man may, by this rite, make a daughter his "appointed daughter" (putrikā), with the agreement:
"Whatever offspring may be born of her shall be the performer of my funeral rites."
"Whatever offspring may be born of her shall be my *svadhākara*.
The word *svadhā* refers to the purpose characterized by the duties of a son, such as the *śrāddha* and other rites for the sake of the deceased (*aurdhvadehika*).
However, this specific word [the entire compound] is not to be uttered.

And so Gautama says: "A childless father may designate a daughter as an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) after performing sacrifices to Agni and Prajāpati, having made an agreement that 'this offspring is for my sake.

According to some, she becomes an appointed daughter by mere intention alone; thus, even without the application of mantras and the like, she becomes an appointed daughter, but not in the absence of the agreement."

Even if the intention has been formed in the heart, it is said that as long as it is not made known by speech, the son-in-law might act contrary to one's wishes; therefore, one should designate her as a "putrikā" (appointed daughter). This is the designation for her.
In former times, Dakṣa himself, the lord of progeny, created these daughters according to this very method for the sake of increasing his own lineage.
Dakṣa, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), who knows the method for procreating offspring, is cited as the example;
this is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) known as "the action of another" (parakṛti).
With a joyful heart, he respectfully gave ten daughters to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
and twenty-seven to King Soma.
"Having honored [them]"—
this is what is prescribed here.
Based on the indicative mark of the word "ten" and so forth, they also maintain that one may fashion many putrikās.
Just as one's own self, so is a son; a daughter is equal to a son.
While she remains as one's very self, how could another take the wealth?
It has been stated, "Whatever offspring may be born of her, that shall be mine. Since offspring is the inheritor of the estate,

it is hereby ordained by way of an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) that, upon the death of the father, the daughter appointed as a son (*putrikā*) who has not yet produced a son is entitled to inherit the wealth, which would otherwise not have been obtained.
While she remains as his very self for the sake of obtaining a son, wealth belongs to her alone; therefore, the birth of a son belonging to him [the father] is not appropriate here.
Alternatively, it means "while she, who is like his own self, exists in the form of a father.
The word "daughter" (*duhitṛ*), though a general term, should be understood from the context as referring specifically to an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), as she is equated with a son.
Whatever may be the mother's separate property (yautaka), that shall indeed be the share of the unmarried daughter;
and the daughter’s son alone shall take the entire estate of one who dies without a son.
The term *yautaka* refers to the separate property of a woman;
for in that case, she alone possesses exclusive ownership.
Others, however, maintain that it refers only to the *saudāyika* (gift from the husband's family) and not to the general property of a woman related by kinship.
For in that regard, her independence is established upon obtaining the *saudāyika* (marriage dowry) wealth; women are held to possess independence with respect to that.

However, as for other [wealth], such as daily provisions for food, ornaments, and so forth, given by the husband, she has only the remainder after what has been used. That which is accepted by a young woman is called *yautaka*.
It belongs exclusively to the maiden (*kumārī*).

Because of the mention of "maiden," it does not belong to one who is no longer a maiden. Furthermore, since the particle *eva* (exclusively) functions as a restatement of what is already established, it overrides the context.
And for this reason, the *yautaka* (marital gift) pertains even to the case of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) and an unmarried girl (*kumārī*).
Thus, Gautama, having stated that "the woman's property belongs to her offspring," further says: "to the daughters who are unmarried and unsettled.
In this context, "unsettled" refers to those who, though married, are childless and have been expelled from their husband's house, and by whom no firm establishment has been gained.
And the daughter’s son alone shall take the entire wealth of one who has no son and no legitimate (aurasa) son;

however, when a legitimate son exists, he will declare what share he is entitled to. Here too, it is specifically the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*) who is the "daughter’s son" (*dauhitra*), not every such son, because—as in the previous case—there is evidence that the departure from the general context applies only to the domain of *yautaka* (separate property).
For the daughter's son shall take the entire inheritance of his father who has no [other] son;
he alone shall offer two funeral cakes, one to his father and one to his maternal grandfather.
"To the maternal grandfather and great-grandfather who are without sons.

Some have explained that since the fact that the son of an appointed daughter (*pautrika*) and the daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) inherit the entire estate was already stated by the preceding [verse], this verse is intended as a restatement for the purpose of prescribing the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*).
They also read the text as "yadi haret" (if he should take).
In whichever share one might take everything, in that very same share he should give [the funeral cake];

however, when the position is that the division there should be equal, then he need not give it. Otherwise, since the giving of the *piṇḍa* would already be established by the rule "whosoever takes from whom, he shall give to him," this repeated statement would be purposeless;
and the restatement of the taking of the entire inheritance would likewise be purposeless.
That is incorrect;
for the long-established reading is precisely this: "the sonless father's [son] shall take," and the word *pitṛ* is more commonly known to denote a biological father than a maternal grandfather.

And for this reason, if the husband of the appointed daughter (*putrikā*) has no son by his other wives, while the appointed daughter herself has a son, then by the birth of that very son, both the father and the grandfather are to be understood as having sons.

But when the progenitor (*bījī*) has a son born of other women, then the son of the appointed daughter—even if born of a married wife of the same caste—shall neither inherit the property of the progenitor nor offer the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*).
For the relationship of procreator and procreated is one thing, and the relationship of offspring and ancestor is another.

Even those who are not biological progenitors possess offspring through sons such as the *kṣetraja* (son born of the wife), while biological progenitors such as Nīpa, Ajīgarta, and others possess sons through those who are sold or abandoned. Furthermore, in the definition of the legitimate (*aurasa*) son, the phrase "in one's own field" (*svakṣetre*) includes the word "own" (*sva*); for the daughter appointed as a son (*putrikā*) belongs to the father alone, since her husband is merely a suitor to be obeyed and the master in her maternal family remains the father.
Therefore, it should be stated in this manner.

In that case where the husband of the appointed daughter (*putrikā*) has no other son, and the son of the appointed daughter is the sole heir to the entire estate, in that case he must perform the offering of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*). However, when the biological father (*bījī*) comes to have a son, then that son of the appointed daughter need not offer the funeral cake to the biological father; for is it not said that he is a daughter’s son (*dauhitra*)?
The meaning is "the son of an appointed daughter" (pautrikeya).
Just as it is heard in scripture that he who inherits even from the father on the maternal grandfather's side must also give [the funeral offerings] there,
yet one need not give on other sides merely because of being on another side.

Furthermore, the injunction "one should give" in the context of the view that [the term] refers to all [ancestors] does not imply a prohibition regarding other alternatives, because giving to both the father and the grandfather is otherwise unestablished. Since it is said that "indicating" (*dyotana*) constitutes an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) by means of which, while indicating what is being restated, one avoids the implication that one should give to someone else instead, and rather ensures that [the gift] is given to both simultaneously.
Just as for the father and the maternal grandfather, so it is for the paternal grandfather and the great-grandfather;
and likewise for the two ancestors beyond them.
In this world, according to the law of dharma, there is no distinction between a son’s son and a daughter’s son;
for both of them were produced from the bodies of their respective parents.
This is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) supplementary to what precedes.
How so? Because there is no distinction between those two, namely the mother and the father.
But if, after a daughter has been appointed, a son is subsequently born, the division of the estate shall be equal; for there is no right of primogeniture for a woman.

In that case, the division is equal; there is no senior share for a son born [to her]. For a woman has no seniority; it is only the share of the inheritance that is denied to her seniority, but not her respectful conduct toward him.
But if an appointed daughter (putrikā) should somehow die without having borne a son,
her husband shall take that wealth without hesitation.
However, because the appointed daughter (*putrikā*) has no owner of her own, it is stated that she does not acquire a connection to the husband's property.
Now, is the appointed daughter consecrated by marriage, or is she not consecrated at all?
If she is consecrated by a sacramental rite (*saṃskriyate*), she becomes his wife;
for marriage is the act that makes one a wife.
Consequently, if her wealth is not so consecrated, it would amount to approaching a maiden (*kanyāgamana*), which is a transgression of the rule that "one should always be devoted to one's own wife."
"Let it be as you wish.
[Objection: "But in this case, is not this verse useless?
[Response: "This is not a fault."

The commencement of this verse is indeed appropriate for the purpose of completing the explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) and for dispelling the doubt that "just as this offspring does not belong to the husband, so too does the wealth [not belong to him].
Furthermore, there are many verses of Manu that are explanatory statements.
Alternatively, let it be that she is not consecrated (*saṃskriyate*).

However, under this view, it does not follow that there is sexual intercourse with a maiden. Why? Because once it is established that one born of such a woman is the son of the maternal grandfather, the subject at hand is determined by defining the transgression of the injunction for the man who approaches her.
And these [acts] are not indeed non-falling [offenses].
Furthermore, on what grounds do you object by considering the meaning of the word "maiden" (kanyā), claiming that the designation of "maiden" would apply?
For there are three kinds of maidens.
First, there is the woman who has not yet had sexual intercourse with a man;
likewise, there is one consecrated to the gods (*devahitā*), and one who is still in her first youth.

In that regard, if it were argued that she who has not been united with a man [is *anūḍhā*] simply because she has not yet engaged in intercourse, then even for a married woman (*ūḍhā*), the status of *anūḍhā* would continue to apply as long as she has not yet experienced her first sexual union.
For in this treatise, the word *kanyā* generally denotes one who has not had sexual intercourse with a man.
Now, as for the phrase "devoid of sacraments" (*saṃskārahīnā*),
that too is not correct.

For, from the very first, the word itself is understood there—by means of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) due to the force of other possible means of knowledge—to have the intention of recollection (*smaraṇa*), as in the case of [the rule] "beneficial" (*hita*).
As it has been said:
"The mantras pertaining to the taking of the hand are established only in the case of maidens."
"Men [should not marry] those who are not virgins (akanyāsu) anywhere, for they have lost their capacity for dharma-acts.

Here, because of the indicative mark of the mention of the "loss of dharma," a woman previously enjoyed by a man is called "non-virgin" (akanyā). By contrast, in its opposite case, a woman not so enjoyed is called a "virgin" (kanyā). Thus, in all instances, the religious acts (dharmāḥ) being performed are understood by following the primary meaning of the term.
And not all of them [are included];
rather, only as many as for which there is evidence.
For instance, in the case of the term *kānīna*, both the father’s ownership and the absence of sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) are understood.
For indeed, when there is merely an absence of formal rites (*saṃskāra*), the sons of a woman who has married by her own will or of one who is unmarried are called *kānīna*.
And when there is merely the father's ownership as the defining characteristic, even the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) is designated as *kānīna*.
As for what was said—that a transgression of the rule would result from [intercourse] with one's own wife—[that objection is refuted].

For this does not mean that one should go to others than one's own wife; rather, it means that one does not desire another's wife nor another's wife. If that were the case, since the prohibition against another's wife would already be covered by this [rule], the specific prohibition of another's wife would be redundant.
What then? One should maintain delight in one's own wife through the practice of cultivating that delight, because an excellence of affection arises from such habituation.
And since he neither desires another woman nor the wives of others, he does not fall away from the dharmas; this is a restatement (anuvāda).
Alternatively, even for one devoted to his own wife, they might approach her on prohibited days; [therefore, the following rule is given].
Thus, by means of deep sleep itself, he remains without offspring;
furthermore, there is no prohibition against another's wife,
because, not having married, there is for him no designation of a "wife" by anyone.
What, then, is the correct position here regarding [the girl] being "unfit for marriage"?
For there are eight forms of marriage,
and they receive their distinct designations as Brāhma and so forth based on the specific manner of acceptance.
Furthermore, she has no power over her own disposal since the father’s ownership has not yet ceased;

moreover, by prohibiting the marriage of a girl who has no brothers, [the text] indicates that a *putrikā* (appointed daughter) is not to be married, just as it says: "One should not marry a girl who has no brothers, for her offspring becomes his."

This prohibition is contextual; if it is transgressed, the very status of marriage as a *saṃskāra* (sacramental rite) does not exist, just as the capacity for the *āhavanīya* fire and other such functions is absent in the case of establishing a fire with a *śūdra* woman and so forth. Since its basis is found even within the prohibitions against marrying one's sister and others, this [prohibition], though dependent on the context, precludes the status of being a *saṃskāra*. Accordingly, when a maiden worthy of being seen is unavailable, the learned (*śiṣṭas*) marry one who has a tawny complexion (*kapilā*) and the like, and they likewise practice the performance of joint religious duties (*sahadharmānuṣṭhāna*).

In this context, the absence of a violated womb (*kṣatayoni*) or having had another [husband] before is such that even if one has married a woman with the same *pravara* and so forth, they do not perform the duties of a wife under any circumstances.

It is for this very purpose that some authorities describe the visible defects in the rule "one should not marry a *kapilā*," lest it be understood as being of the same nature as the prohibition against marrying a *sapiṇḍa* and others, even though that prohibition belongs to the general topic. Furthermore, how could there be any suspicion regarding marriage in the case of one who marries a brother’s widow, given that she is explicitly prohibited?
It is said:
the remainder of this prohibition is heard in the words, "for that becomes his offspring.
Consequently, it is only for the purpose of producing offspring that a *putrikā* is not a wife for religious duties (*dharma*).
"But let there indeed be joint entitlement for wealth and pleasure.
Let this be so; however, marriage is precluded because of the absence of one's own [male] organ.
[Objection: But on that view, would not the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*) be merely a maiden-born son (*kānīna*)?
For he would not belong to the father, nor would he be the offspring of two unconsecrated [parents].

However, according to the view that consecration is required, one who possesses both characteristics—the state of belonging to the father and the presence of consecration—is distinguished from the *kānīna* son when either one of these attributes is absent due to direct perception; this is logical.
To this, it is replied:
We do not say that the characteristic of a son born of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*) does not belong to him;
rather, this indeed is his characteristic:
"The son whom a maiden may secretly bear in her father's house..."
"One should call him by the name *kānīna*, born of a maiden from her husband.
This is its meaning:
he who possesses such characteristics is to be understood here in this treatise under the designation *kānīna*.

And when the question arises as to whose offspring he is, the second statement, "born of the maiden from her husband," [provides the answer]. Alternatively, it is not the meaning of the individual words that is being indicated here; rather, the relationship is being regulated.
"One who is of such a kind as this *kānīna* should be called a relative of the husband"—thus there is indeed a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*).

And this relationship, even when there is a difference in the referent (*padārtha*), is indeed differentiated by the difference in limiting conditions (*upādhi*), through the distinction between secrecy and publicity.
Others, however, say: if the referent is that very same one, then the relationship between the word and its meaning for the term *kānīna* must be understood as being entirely uncontradicted.
If they consider the term *kānīna* to apply to any offspring whatsoever, let the designation *kānīna* be used for the son of the father;
however, others maintain that the Smṛti itself is restricted to a specific sense,
for the word *kānīna* is not employed everywhere for the mere offspring of an unmarried girl (*kanyā*).
Rather, we also accept this in cases characterized by the *Mānava-smṛti*:

even when the specific application is not determined and only a general remembrance remains, the understanding of the particularities— such as the attainment of merit— is indeed logical based on the actual performance.

Whether she was not formally appointed or was so appointed, the mother becomes the grandmother through the son whom she obtains from a suitable man; by him she shall offer the funeral cake and inherit the wealth.
Upon considering the preceding and following statements, this [text] is understood through hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) to refer specifically to the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*).

It has been stated that even the son of an unappointed daughter is an heir to her maternal grandfather’s wealth; how much more so, then, the son of an appointed daughter? Thus, because [the statement] is supplementary to another [rule], it would result in the injunction regarding the appointed daughter being purposeless; therefore, it does not aim at the inheritance rights of the daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) in general. But surely, in another Smṛti, the entitlement of the daughter’s son alone to offer the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) is heard: "The same applies to the maternal grandfathers."

Even here, setting aside the immediate context, it is more logical to understand that the statement refers exclusively to the daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) by the force of the scriptural sentence itself, namely: "He should offer the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) and take the wealth.
Likewise, another [text] has stated: "For the daughter’s son [inherits] the entire inheritance," and so forth.
To this, it is replied:

Regarding what was stated concerning "the maternal grandfathers" (*mātāmahānām*), is that plural number intended with reference to individual persons, or is it used figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) to include the maternal great-grandfather and others? If the view of individual persons is adopted, it would follow that the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) is due to only one maternal grandfather, just as in the case of the *śrāddha* and other rites;
and that [single offering] is contradicted once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed.
For thus they say: "From this point forward, one should give [the offerings] to three [ancestors].
Furthermore, even if it is argued that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for anyone other than the father will not be performed, that too is not correct, because there is no prohibition against it.

Since there is no distinction in the proximity of the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇā*), if the specific defining characteristic is not fully understood, there would be a lack of comprehension; furthermore, by the force of memory and so forth, there would be the abandonment of the context (*prakaraṇa*), which results in the contingency of contradiction. For it is that specific [meaning] which is extracted from the context, just as in the case of "there are twelve *upasads* for the *ahīna* sacrifice.
Moreover, it has been stated that the phrase "or those not performed" (*akṛtā vā*) is intended for something else.
Therefore, this refers to the *pautrikeya* (the son of an appointed daughter).
Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains immortality;
and through the grandson of a son, one reaches the realm of the Sun.
By the service rendered through the birth of a son, one conquers—that is, attains—the ten worlds free from sorrow, such as heaven and the rest;
that is to say, one is reborn there.
Likewise, through a grandson, one obtains infinity, which is to say, a long-lasting residence in those very same realms.
Through the son of his grandson, he reaches the realm of the sun, the world of the Ādityas;
he attains luminosity and is no longer obscured by any darkness.
Because a son saves his father from the hell named Put,
he was therefore called "putra" by the Self-Existent One himself.
This is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) supplementary to the rules for procreating offspring.
It is designated that there is a hell called "Punnāman" (named after men) consisting of fourfold births on earth;
a son who is born saves one from that, meaning he is born into a divine womb.
For that reason, he is designated as "son."
In this world, no distinction is established between a son’s son and a daughter’s son;
for even a daughter’s son delivers him to the next world just like a son’s son.
In this case as well, the *dauhitra* should be understood as being precisely the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*).
For even a *dauhitra* rescues his maternal grandfather in the hereafter, just like a grandson (*pautra*).
This too is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), since the matter has already been prescribed by rule.
There is no difference between these two:
in one case it is the mother who belongs to another family, and in the other it is the father.
Therefore, even a daughter’s son constantly delivers this deceased person from the aforementioned hell in the world beyond.
The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā) should first offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his mother;
the second to her father, and the third to that father’s father.

In the passage, "He himself should offer two pindas, one to his father and one to his maternal grandfather," the offering of pindas by the son of an appointed daughter (putrikāputra) is stated with the maternal grandfather as the starting point.
Therefore, this is another sequence for the offering of pindas by the son of an appointed daughter:
he should first offer a pinda to his mother, and so forth.
The second [offering], however, belongs to the father;
it should be understood as belonging to the father of that very [daughter].
As for those who read "pitus tasya," they, having first set aside [the portion] for the appointed daughter (*putrikā*), offer it to her progenitor.
And "of his father's father" refers to the third [offering] for the father of the progenitor himself;
however, in this view, the offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍa) to the maternal grandfather would not have been mentioned.
But he who has an adopted son endowed with all good qualities shall indeed inherit that estate, even though he has come from another lineage.

It has been stated that "neither brothers nor fathers, but sons are the heirs of the father," thus declaring the right of all sons to inherit. However, when a legitimate son (aurasa) exists, those such as the son born of the wife (kṣetraja) and others are entitled only to subsistence. "The legitimate son alone is the master of the paternal wealth."
"But for the sake of compassion toward the rest, one should provide a livelihood.
From this, it is established that the son given in adoption (datrima) indeed inherits the estate.
However, this statement is intended to establish his right even when a legitimate son (aurasa) exists; otherwise, nothing would be accomplished by this [text].
"But what is his share?
Some say it is equal to that of the legitimate son (*aurasa*), because there is no specific instruction [to the contrary].
That is incorrect.

For if equality were being asserted, then just as it was recited in the section concerning the appointed daughter (*putrikā*), it would have been recited here as well: "the division there shall be equal.
Therefore, it is said that a calculation of shares—such as a sixth or an eighth part—must be made, just as in the case of the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*).
To this, too, something must be said.
Just as the specific share for the *kṣetraja* son was stated as "the sixth part, however, belongs to the *kṣetraja*," so too will [the author] state it for the *dattima* (adopted) son.
Therefore, the purpose of this repeated mention must be considered.

But the Teacher says: because of the repetition and the absence of a specification of distinction, a calculation inferior to that of the *kṣetraja* is appropriate; yet it is not a case of having no share, nor is it an equal share, nor is it equality with the *kṣetraja*.
An adopted son shall never take the family name or the inheritance of his biological father;
for the funeral cake follows the family name and inheritance, and the ancestral offering (svadhā) ceases for one who gives it away [to another].

Furthermore, the fact that the adopted son does not take the lineage or the wealth from his biological father has already been stated; because he has departed from that lineage, he does not inherit the family name or the estate.
And in the absence of inheriting the lineage and the estate, he does not offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his biological father either.
For the funeral cake follows the lineage and the inheritance; it goes to the lineage and the inheritance.
To him whose lineage and inheritance are taken, the post-mortem rites such as the offering of the funeral cake and water are performed.
From him [who is excluded], they depart—that is, they cease.
The performance of the *svadhākāra*—such as the *piṇḍaśrāddha* and other rites—is indicated here;
this [duty] ceases for one who gives his own son to another.
The meaning is that he need not perform it.

This same principle applies to the *kṛtrima* (artificially begotten) and the others—the *sahoḍha* (born together), the *apaviddha* (cast off), and the *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* (belonging to two lineages)—in that they provide benefit to both [fathers].
Others, however, explain the phrase "he shall not take" (*na haret*) and "he shall not cause to be taken" (*na hārayet*) as containing an implied causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*).
On this basis, they say that he must benefit both [fathers] just like the *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*.
But the latter is a method of assistance; they explain it thus:
if a son does not take the family lineage or the inheritance, then it should be explained accordingly.
And this is not tenable;
for no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) can be stated regarding the existence of a separate entity.

Both the son born of an unauthorized woman and the son obtained from the husband's younger brother by a wife who already has sons are unworthy of a share, being respectively born of an adulterer and born of lust.
It has been stated that when a husband dies without a son, a woman must seek the authorization of her elders for the procreation of a son;
this [present verse] is a restatement of that very point.

If a woman, desiring a son, should procreate a son without being authorized by her elders—acting under the delusion that "I am indeed my husband's field (*kṣetra*), and the son born of the field (*kṣetraja*) is the heir to his property"—that son, though begotten upon her, is not an heir to the inheritance.
For since one born according to the specific procedure beginning with [the husband being] the *kṣetraja* is designated as *kṣetraja* in the scripture,
it is by that very designation that the right to inherit the estate (*rikthaharatva*) of this *kṣetraja* son is here precluded;
however, the offering of the funeral cake (*piṇḍadāna*) is not forbidden, even if he were born of an outcast (*patita*).
Nārada, however, records a specific rule:
"Those who are born of a woman not authorized [to bear children], whether by one man or by many, are all non-partakers of the inheritance; they are the sons of the seeders alone."
"They shall give the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to the progenitor if the mother was taken for a price;

but in the case of one who has approached him without a price, the givers of the cake belong to the husband alone"— from this statement regarding the son, because there is no injunction for his production as there is for the *kṛtrima* and other types of sons, and because he is not enumerated among the [twelve] kinds of sons, those born from the seed of men of the three higher castes are entitled only to subsistence, not to the inheritance of the estate.
Since it is traditionally taught that, without distinction, all sons [are entitled to maintenance] when the father has died,
they shall indeed receive a livelihood, because even after the father's death, the remaining wealth intended for the son's benefit remains subject to partition.

In this very same way, the sapinda-bījakas (those related by both blood and seed) of a son born of the legitimate womb (aurasa) and others must be provided with a share sufficient merely for their subsistence.
However, there is no right to inherit [for them], because the right to inherit is heard of only with reference to specific enumerated types of sons.
And this has been stated: "If those mentioned should have a single heir...

By this view, it follows that those born of an unauthorized woman (*aniyuktāsūta*) and others do not receive a share in the other case, but rather the seed-owner (*bījin*) shall obtain the inheritance.
This inheritance should be understood as sufficient for her maintenance.
Because she has been mentioned [in that context], she is spoken of here for the sake of determining her share, just like the female slave.
She is one among those seven sources of slavery previously defined, for whose employment it is understood that this [share] is provided.
One born of her is not a slave; there is an absence of the designation "son. Even for a Śūdra, those born of such [a woman] are entitled to subsistence, just like Brāhmaṇas and others.
But another says:
even those who perform fixed labor are slaves.
Just as there are those designated as bath-attendants, decorators, cooks, or purifiers,
so too women who have been restrained by desire and are maintained with food and clothing become slaves.
Likewise, when a man has sons but no son is present, a woman may be authorized by her husband's brother even if she is already authorized [by him].
How, then, can there be a *niyoga* for a woman who already has sons?
The intention is that it is the brother-in-law himself who is appointed for the sake of desire under the pretext of procreating a son.
Thus, both would be born of an adulterer (*jāra*), but the one born of the woman who already has sons would specifically be born of lust.
In the case of the first purpose, the engagement is solely for the sake of a son, not out of lust or greed.

Even if a man has intercourse with an appointed woman, a son born contrary to the prescribed rule is not entitled to his father’s inheritance, for he was procreated by one who has fallen from his status.
"Non-observance" refers to the abandonment of the rule regarding white garments and so forth;
the meaning is that such a person does not deserve the inheritance, nor is he a *kṣetraja* son.

Since the husband and the brother’s wife were authorized by the scripture to procreate a son through the observance of the rule, it is only logical that they become outcastes (*patita*) by abandoning that rule.
A son born to a woman appointed for that purpose is, in law, just like a legitimate son of the body; however, that seed belongs to the owner of the field, and so does the offspring.
The phrase "as if legitimate" (*yathaurasa*) is prescribed here for the purpose of securing the eldest son's share; otherwise, it would not be stated.
By this rule, the *uddhāra* (extra portion) of the eldest share is obtained by the *kṣetraja* son born of the eldest wife.
Therefore, this is an exception to the principle that "the subsidiary [son] shares an equal portion with the primary [legitimate son]."
Since both [the field and the seed] possess authority, the determination [of ownership] depends upon their respective qualities.
Indeed, there is no other purpose for this verse, as everything has already been stated previously.
That seed is spoken of in this way by way of praise for the *kṣetrika*—the owner of the field—because it produces its specific result.
For this very reason, he says "by way of *dharmatā*," that is, by means of the scriptural arrangement (*dharma*).
In this context, "another means of knowledge" refers to the production of offspring in a visible form.
This verse is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).
He who takes charge of the wealth and the wife of his deceased brother shall procreate offspring for that brother and hand over that very wealth to him.
This rule is stated for the case where there is no brother whose property has been partitioned;
however, the previous rule applies to those living together.
This much is the distinction between the preceding and the subsequent rules.
This should be explained as meaning that he, having procreated offspring for his brother according to the law of *niyoga*,
should give it to that [brother] alone, and not to his [the brother's] mother.
And by this very principle, women are entitled to maintenance.
But it is not [given] because of her husband's wealth or power, since it will be explained otherwise later.
That is his property;
one should give that property to him whose wealth has been partitioned.
If a woman, being authorized by her husband, obtains a son from a brother-in-law or another [relative],
they declare that son to be born of lust, excluded from inheritance, and illegitimately begotten.
The term "aniyuktā" should be understood as a compound with the prefix *pra* (i.e., *praniyuktā*).

If it is argued that this contradicts what was stated previously—since, if that were the case, [the term] would be redundant—it has been stated in various places that the avoidance of redundancy [is achieved by reading it as *praniyuktā*]. However, the predecessors do not accept that interpretation.
Therefore, this is the explanation:
even when [the woman] has been duly appointed, a son born [to her] does not deserve the paternal inheritance;
[this is because he is considered] "born of lust."

As for the further argument that, although one proceeds from a mandate (*niyoga*) and not from desire (*kāma*), nevertheless desire is necessarily present therein; therefore it is said to be "born of desire" (*kāmajam*).
That which has arisen falsely is so called because it is unfit for the purpose for which it was produced.
And thus, this is a prohibition of the previously mentioned "unfitness for a share" (*bhāgārhatva*); consequently, it is considered optional (*vikalpita*).
Furthermore, the teacher [Upādhyāya] maintains that if the reading were *aniyuktā*, it would not at all be consistent with the subsequent reading.
This rule for the division [of inheritance] among those born of a single womb from one man should be understood;
now learn that which applies to those born of many women of various kinds from one man.
In the case of those born of a single womb and of the same caste, there is indeed the taking of everything.
Now, they explain the case of various women of different castes;
the word "many" (*bahvīṣu*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Others, however, consider this to be intended:

the rule for the distribution of shares—such as "one born of many wives of various castes shall take four parts," and so forth—applies to those born of multiple wives of different classes; but for those born of a single wife of a different class, there is simply the taking of the entire inheritance.
If a Brāhmaṇa has four wives in the proper order [of castes],
this rule for partition is prescribed when sons have been born to them.
The mention of "successive" (*anupūrva*) is a restatement of the sequence shown in the third [chapter];
this also serves the purpose of announcing the summary that is about to be explained.
The plowman, the breeding bull, a vehicle, an ornament, and a dwelling—
these should be given as a special portion to the Brahmin, along with the best one share from the principal estate.
*Kīnāśa* means a ploughman; it is also used for a miser. Since that [meaning] is impossible here, it is not accepted.
And so says the mantra: "Indra was the lord of the plough, the Maruts were the *kīnāśas*; let the *kīnāśas* come to the pressed juice with their draft-animals."
A vehicle is a cart and so forth;
an ornament is a ring worn by one's father and so forth;
a residence is the principal dwelling.
And as for the single share, out of all the shares, one should be given as the principal portion;
having set this aside from the common property for the eldest, the remainder is to be divided according to the method to be described hereafter.
From the inheritance, the son of a Brāhmaṇa shall take three shares; the son of a Kṣatriya woman two shares;
the son born of a Vaiśya woman one and a half shares; and the son of a Śūdra woman shall take one share.

Even though it is heard that there is oneness [of the inheritance], this same method of calculation has been shown for two or many heirs when their shares are equal; however, the calculation is different when the numbers are unequal.
Or, having divided the entire collection of inherited property into ten parts,
one who knows the Dharma should make a righteous partition according to this rule.
"Inherited" means that which has taken the form of wealth.
It is "righteous" because it is spoken of as dharma.
This does not agree with what was stated previously, because of the verse containing the formal proposition that is about to be stated.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman shall take four shares; the son of a Kṣatriya woman, three shares;
the son of a Vaiśya woman shall take two shares; and the son of a Śūdra woman shall take one share.

Although here [in this text] no distinction is made regarding the shares of sons born of Kṣatriya wives and others, another specific rule concerning their shares is heard in another Smṛti through two particular traditional authorities:
"Land acquired by gift should not be given to a son of a Kṣatriya wife;
even if the father should give it, upon his death the son of the Brāhmaṇa wife shall take it. Thus it is said.
The land acquired by acceptance is "land obtained through acceptance";
there is no prohibition regarding land acquired by purchase and other such means.

Thus, it is stated elsewhere: "But one born of a Śūdra woman from a twice-born man does not deserve a share of land"; this indicates that the prohibition applies to land in general for the son of a Śūdra woman.
And this [rule] should be understood as referring to cases where other wealth exists;
otherwise, the rule regarding the tenth part would apply.
Furthermore, in the absence of other wealth, there would be no means of livelihood at all.

I, however, say that while the giving of a share is prohibited, the provision [of maintenance] for the sake of livelihood is certainly not barred. If it is asked what the distinction is: in the case of the "share" view, when one's own inheritance arises, it applies to everyone and everywhere, even in matters such as giving and selling.
In other cases, however, there is subsistence from what has been produced by that [master].
A Śūdra obtains rice and food for his livelihood from the son of a Brāhmaṇī alone; what is the use of imagining a share of the land?
And so it has been said: "He receives the basis of that livelihood according to the rule for a resident pupil."
This is true;
however, his livelihood must be provided for on account of the paternal estate.

And if it were not provided at the time of partition, then the twice-born brothers—perhaps being of improper conduct or due to some other cause—might seize it through giving, selling, or other such means.
In that case, his livelihood would be destroyed;
however, when there is a deliberation [on the matter], he does not obtain it elsewhere than where he is appointed, without having received his authorization.
Whether there be a legitimate son or even no son at all,
one shall not, according to the law, give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra woman.

A "virtuous son" (*satputra*) refers specifically to one who exists, namely a son of a Brāhmaṇa woman; he alone is intended here, not merely any son of a twice-born man. Consequently, even if sons of Kṣatriyas or Vaiśyas exist, if there is no son of a Brāhmaṇa, [the heir] receives one-eighth; and if there is only a son of a Vaiśya, he receives one-third.
Others, however, say that the term "sonless" (*aputra*) denotes the absence of any son of a twice-born man without distinction.
In this view, the remaining wealth after the tenth part goes to the sapinda relatives;
however, this is a faultless arrangement.
When there is a plurality [of servants] regarding the acquisition and preservation of property, then the Shudra takes the tenth part.
Now, if the property is sufficient for the livelihood of only a few people, then it belongs exclusively to the son of the Śūdra wife.

Regarding the sons of Kṣatriyas and others born of wives of both their own and other castes, the rule is shown in another Smṛti: "Sons born of a Kṣatriya from wives of his own caste and those of other castes down to the Śūdra shall receive three, two, and one shares respectively.
Sons born of a Kṣatriya from wives of his own caste and those of other castes, ending with the Śūdra, are entitled to take three and so forth shares according to the order of the castes.
Then, from his own property, the Śūdra sons receive a sixth part, and the Vaiśya sons a third.
Others, however, explain the force of this verse as follows:
when he gives to a son of a Śūdra woman, then having calculated the total wealth, a tenth part must be given by him, and not more than that, even though [the father] possesses independence.
As he will state later: "whatever his father might give";
in this view, the words "saputra" (with son) and "dadyāt" (should give) are more appropriately construed as being in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
Otherwise, the connection—"he whose father has a son, whether living or not, should give"—would be awkwardly constructed.
The phrase "with his sons and their portions" refers to the designation of the sons and others; "he should give" refers to those who are living, such as the son or the *sapinda* relatives.

Consequently, if there are no sons of the Kṣatriya or Vaiśya castes, but only Brāhmaṇa and Śūdra sons, then the Śūdra does not receive exactly a tenth share; rather, he receives only a very small amount of wealth, not more. Where there are ten cows, four belong to the Brāhmaṇa, one to the Śūdra, and five to the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya.
When those two are absent, then the five cows are to be divided between the Brāhmaṇa and the Śūdra according to that same arrangement.
If the Brāhmaṇa were to take all of them, he would neither be a "taker of a share" nor a "taker of four shares.
Therefore, the rule "he should take four shares" is an arrangement applicable when there are four brothers.
Even for a Śūdra, the entitlement to take a tenth part applies only when there are four [sons];
in the cases of two, three, or four [sons], there is an increase in the share for both [the father and the Śūdra].
The son of a Śūdra woman by a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya father does not inherit the estate;
whatever his father may give to him, that alone shall be his wealth.
The son of a Śūdra woman does not inherit the property of the twice-born.
Is this always the case?
No, he says; rather, he receives only that which his father may give him.
The allotment of a tenth part made by his father is indeed his; he does not obtain anything more than that paternal share from others.
Regarding this, Śaṅkha has also stated: "A son of a Śūdra is not a sharer of the wealth;
whatever his father may give him, that alone is his share, though they should give him another pair of cattle."
The words "the brothers" are the ellipsis for the phrase "at the time of partition.
Others, however, maintain that this rule applies to the son of an unmarried Śūdra woman,
asserting that there is no indication here of a marriage.
The word *śūdra* denotes a specific caste.
Therefore, whatever his father may give him—that is, whatever means of subsistence has been given to him by his father—that alone should be given [to his son].
If, however, he has made some arrangement for his lifelong maintenance, then that alone is his wealth, and nothing at all need be given to him by his brothers.

As Gautama states in the very section concerning the sons of Śūdra women: "Even in the case of those not formally wedded, if he serves them, he may obtain the means of subsistence according to the rule for a pupil.
According to their view, those born of unmarried Kṣatriya and Vaiśya women would be entitled to inherit the estate;
however, it is not known what share they should receive therein.

If it is argued that "the share is according to the status of those who have been married," even there, the mention of "those not married" is neither an indicative mark (*liṅga*) nor is there a scriptural statement (*vacana*).
How is there no such statement?

Because it is said, "The legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*) alone [is the heir]," the *aurasa* son is defined in relation to wives lawfully wedded; furthermore, the characteristics of a *aurasa* son do not apply to those born of women who were not lawfully wedded.
And it has been stated: "the son of one not authorized," and so forth.
Now, this refers to the case of a brother's wife.
For even when authorization (*niyoga*) is prohibited—and thus there is a prohibition against him being called "the son of one not authorized"—the notion that he belongs to that category still arises.

If it is argued that "in this case too, there is [the rule] regarding those born [of a widow] immediately upon her conception," then [it follows that] for all of them, sons born of another's wife without formal authorization (aniyuktāsutāḥ) are provided for their livelihood, even in the absence of such authorization. Thus, the maintenance of all of them has been declared.
Or, sons born of wives of equal caste for twice-born men shall,
after giving a preferential share to the eldest, divide the remainder equally among themselves.

The word "or" (*vā*), being unintelligible without a second alternative, becomes complete in its sense by referring back to the subject at hand. Since the prohibition against a Śūdra inheriting the entire estate applies only when wives of equal or unequal caste are excluded, it is understood to concern only the twice-born castes.
Consequently, it is stated that in the case of a Brāhmaṇa who has no son by a Brāhmaṇī wife, sons born of Kṣatriyā or other wives shall inherit the entire estate.

In this same manner, the son of a Kṣatriya by a Vaiśya wife [is treated]. However, this is not the intended meaning: that after giving a preferential share (*uddhāra*) to the elder brother, all those born of women of different castes (*asavarṇā*) should share equally with the sons of women of the same caste (*savarṇā*), because this would contradict the previously stated reduction of one share.
Even if it were argued that equality is indeed appropriate when the sons of the same caste are devoid of qualities while the others possess them, [this is not so].
And so it has been said: "The son of a wife of the same caste who behaves improperly does not inherit, according to some.
This is incorrect, because caste is of paramount importance;
for the teachers have stated that "the ownership of the property belongs to the one who is born [in that status]."
Therefore, this is the explanation here:

those born even from women who are not of the same caste (asavarṇā), provided they are born when [the father] has no wives of the same caste (savarṇā), shall divide the share of the wife with the preferential portion (uddhāra) in the same manner as those born of wives of the same caste.
For a Śūdra, however, only a wife of his own caste is ordained, and no other;
those born of her shall share equal portions, even if there should be a hundred sons.
A marriage in the inverse order is not permitted for a Śūdra;
this is a restatement of what has already been said [regarding the other castes]:
"Those born of her shall have equal shares."
This was stated because there is no fifth distinct caste;
for him, only a wife of his own caste exists, and no other.
Of the twelve sons whom Svāyambhuva Manu has named for men,
six are kinsmen and heirs, while six are kinsmen but not heirs.
This is the section on the Sūtra-sthāna that is about to be explained.
The word *bandhu* is a synonym for *bāndhava*.
There are six who take the lineage and inherit the estate, while the others are the opposite.
Whatever the reality is in this matter, that will be demonstrated further below.
The legitimate son of the body, the son begotten on the wife, the adopted son, the made son, the son secretly born, and the cast-off son— these six are both heirs and kinsmen.
The son of an unmarried girl, the son received with a bride, the bought son, the son of a remarried woman,
the self-given son, and the Śūdra son— these six are non-heirs and not kinsmen.
The indication of the number by means of two verses is for the purpose of demonstrating the two groups.
Just as one obtains a certain result when crossing water with a poor boat,
so too does one obtain a similar result when crossing over darkness by means of bad sons.
Because the *kṣetraja* and other sons are mentioned together with the *aurasa* (legitimate son), there arises a suspicion of their equality;
this [verse] is intended to preclude that.
Bad sons such as the *kṣetraja* and others are not capable of providing the same benefit as an *aurasa* son.
Even though no specific distinction is heard [in the text], they explain it thus because of the context.
Others, however, consider them to be "bad sons," meaning those who are not authorized heirs.
This is what is intended.
While these [sons] exist, one should not consider oneself successful by thinking, "I have a son.
Rather, one must again exert effort toward procreating a legitimate (aurasa) son.
For the suffering born of evil deeds in the next world is darkness; it is said that one discharges this debt to the ancestors through progeny.
If there should be two sons, one legitimate (aurasa) and one born of the wife (kṣetraja), who are co-heirs,
each shall take that paternal inheritance which belongs to his own biological father, and not the other.

In the case of a eunuch who has previously taken a wife, regarding the son born of that wife (*kṣetraja*)—whether the husband subsequently dies or becomes diseased—it is possible for both the *kṣetraja* and the *aurasa* (legitimate) sons to exist simultaneously once his eunuchism is somehow cured by medicine.

However, the principle that "whatever belongs to the father [belongs] to whichever of the two" does not apply here; for the owner of the field alone is his father, and he shall receive only that man's inheritance.

Even if the biological progenitor were to be designated as "father" on account of the act of procreation, the son is still called *kṣetraja* figuratively, because he is the son of the one who possesses the field.
In that case, when the wealth has been taken by the mother of an illegitimate son (*aurasa*) who, for some reason, acted improperly, a male child is subsequently produced;
and by him, the wealth is made dependent solely upon her through affection and so forth, and he has no *sapiṇḍa* relatives.
In this situation, if the paternal inheritance accrues to him, this very fact serves as the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
"Those such as the son of an unauthorized woman and others become heirs to the estate of their progenitor when there are no sapinda relatives [of that progenitor].
Others, however, explain:

"When an heir exists, the kṣetraja son born [to another] receives the inheritance from his progenitor, and not from the owner of the field (the biological father), provided there is a legitimate son (aurasa)."

And it has been stated that when a legitimate son of the body exists, there is a share for him; [it is also said] that "the two sons, the son of the body and the son begotten on the wife, are sharers of the father's wealth," and likewise, "but the son begotten on the wife shall have a sixth share.
He demonstrates how those two become co-heirs, possessing wealth held in a single hand.
The legitimate son of the body alone is the master of the paternal wealth;
however, for the sake of kindness toward the others, he should provide them with a livelihood.

When there is a legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*), all others, such as the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) and the rest, are non-heirs; they shall receive only a maintenance from the *aurasa* son.
This is out of compassion and is blameless;
one who does not give [this] incurs sin.
When the legitimate son (aurasa) divides the paternal inheritance, he should give a sixth share of the father’s wealth to the son born of the wife (kṣetraja), or even a fifth share.
Since only the mere right to subsistence is obtained—as in the case of sons such as the purchased (krīta) and others—this alternative regarding the share of the *kṣetraja* son is now stated;
and that [share] depends upon his qualities.
The two sons, the aurasa (legitimate) and the kṣetraja (son born of the wife), are sharers in the paternal inheritance;
but ten others, in their respective order, are sharers in the family name and a portion of the inheritance.

The first half-verse is merely a restatement of the previously mentioned rule, and not a separate injunction. It is intended to show that the status of the *kṣetraja* son is not considered equal to that of the *aurasa* (legitimate) son in terms of being a sharer of the family lineage (*gotra*) and a sharer of the portion of the inheritance (*riktha*).
It has been stated that "the share of the inheritance is commensurate with his maintenance.
Regarding the adopted son (*dattaka*), they cite another Smṛti text as being like that of the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*):
[in] due order.

The son of the body (aurasa) and the son of the wife (kṣetraja) are co-heirs simultaneously; for the others, however, the latter inherits only in the absence of the former. If it is said that "of these there are six heirs and six non-heirs," then the mention of inheritance by these two groups—divided into heirs and non-heirs—is untenable, since they are called "non-heirs" only when the son of the body exists.
[This implies] that the first six provide great assistance, while the other six are inferior.
The first [son] is the legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*); the others have equal fruits.
Likewise, the six subsequent ones are inferior to him;
yet, with respect to their own respective categories, they are indeed equal.
There is no difference between those recited previously and those recited subsequently.
One should know that son whom he himself begets upon his own consecrated wife to be the legitimate (aurasa) son, the first in rank.
The word *sva* (one's own) expresses "belonging to oneself" (*ātmīya*) and does not denote "being of the same class.

By this [explanation], it is understood that an *aurasa* son is one born from a woman who has been consecrated (*saṃskṛtā*) by the man himself; otherwise, the word *saṃskṛtā* would have to be taken as intended to exclude [sons born of] one unconsecrated.
Consequently, even in the case of a woman consecrated by another, he would still be an *aurasa* son.
And since the term *aurasa* (legitimate son) has already been explained in its primary sense, even the sons of Kṣatriyas and others are *aurasas*;
for they possess no other characteristic of a son [than that].

Others, however, considering the qualification "belonging to the first age" (*prāthamakalpika*) as a specific attribute of the *aurasa*, regard the sons of Kṣatriyas and others as *aurasas* who do not possess the complete characteristics.

But if it is explained in this way, then just as one who lacks the full characteristics [of an *aurasa*] is still an *aurasa* son when born from a consecrated wife of his own caste (*svakṣetra*), so too would that status apply to one born from an unconsecrated wife of his own caste; how much more so, then, for those born from wives of the Kṣatriya and other castes? For they are indeed sons and are entitled to a limited share. Now, it might be argued: "In the absence of the defining characteristics of the *aurasa*, the *kṣetraja*, and so forth, how can there be the status of a son, given the restriction to twelve types?"
To this it is replied:
what is the use of a definition? Because worldly convention is well-established.
For instance, people in the world conventionally designate that which is born from someone as "that person's son."
Likewise, when someone applies the conventional designation "father" to one who is not the progenitor, he is corrected by another, saying: "This is not your father; for you were not born by him.
Through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), it is understood that the progenitor is the father and the one born is the son.
However, the formulation of a definition is intended for the purpose of specifying particular cases.

As for the claim that sonship belongs to the progenitor of the *kṣetraja* and other types of sons, that sonship is based on function (*kāryanibandhana*), because sonship is established even for one who has no [biological] son through the prescription of a specific function; yet, since the status of being a biological son (*jātatva*) is excluded by that [functional definition], it is not [merely] the state of being born.

Thus, these are called "substitutes" (*pratinidhi*) by them. For if sonship were based solely on birth, there would be no distinction between the *aurasa*, the *punarbhava*, and the son of an appointed woman (*niyuktāsuta*), as their birth would be equal.
Furthermore, because the causal relationship [of producing] a son exists, no one could truly be without a son.
As for worldly convention (*laukika-vyavahāra*), it is inconsistent, since the term "father" is seen to apply even to the progenitor.

Therefore, even though the word is employed, the convention of "son" should be understood—just like the conventions of "wife" and so forth—as being based on a specific meaning derived from common usage (like the words *indra* and others) and by the rules of origin (*utpatti-vidhi*) in the scriptures.

And regarding that statement concerning the biological son (*aurasa*) being "primary" (*prāthamakalpika*), it should be understood as referring to legal procedure (*vyavahāra*). It is not only in legal procedure, but also with respect to benefit (*upakāra*); for it is observed through the father's own experience that the biological son is capable of providing greater benefit, and thus [the text] makes known that he is "primary. Furthermore, the designation of a substitute (*pratinidhi*) is intended to indicate a reduction in the degree of benefit.
For a substitute is not possible for these [sons], because a substitute is only applicable to the performance of auxiliary rites (*aṅga-upacāra*) for an action already commenced.
Furthermore, a son is not an auxiliary part of the rite, since the act of procreating offspring is a secondary (*guṇa*) action.
Therefore, even though the status of being a son exists in the case of the *kṣetraja* and others, the mention of them as substitutes is intended to praise the status of the legitimate (*aurasa*) son.

Just as the statement "others are indeed non-animals compared to cows and horses; cows and horses are the animals" is a way of speaking of other animals as "non-animals" in order to praise cows and horses;

and just as it is said that whoever is born from someone's seed is his son, as demonstrated in the Mahābhārata—where Pāṇḍu, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Vidura, and others, though born from Dvaipāyana, are not designated as "the sons of Vyāsa."

And just as it has been demonstrated that the status of being a legitimate son (*aurasa*) for the sons of Kṣatriyas and others is purposeful, so too [the case] of the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) results in an excess over the number twelve when counting sons. Let it be so; what is the fault?
"Let this son be the thirteenth; for he is included because his fruit is equal to that of a legitimate son (aurasa), owing to his similarity to him.
And so it is said in another Smṛti: 'The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā) is equal to him.'"
A son born on the bed of a man who has died, is impotent, or is diseased, from a woman duly appointed according to the sacred law, is known as the *kṣetraja* (son of the wife).
"Of one who is diseased" refers to one afflicted by diseases such as consumption (rājayakṣmā) for which there is no remedy;
the remainder is clear.
If the mother or the father should give a son with water in times of distress—
one who is similar [to themselves] and given with affection— he is to be known as a son given in adoption (datrima).
The word "ca" (and) is appropriate to be read as "vā" (or), as in "the mother or the father. For it is not proper for the offspring of both to be given away if either one does not consent.
Alternatively, the word "vā" may indeed be read.

And so it has been said: "Either the mother or the father may give; of these two, the father is the superior. This refers to the context of assigning [the child] to other duties. Now, one might object: "If ownership has already been acquired, then since [the child] is 'the mother's own,' the father has no status as a giver with respect to the son.

True. However, because the statement "from the father" applies specifically to cases where there is no [other progenitor], and because the rule "the mother belongs to the seed-owner" applies to specific cases of assignment, it is stated that [the two rules] are consistent.

And Vasiṣṭha says: "A woman shall neither give nor receive a son. [The term] "similar" does not refer to caste; rather, it refers to qualities corresponding to the family. Thus, even a Kṣatriya or others may be suitable as an adopted son for a Brāhmaṇa.
The mention of "joy" (prīti) is for the purpose of excluding greed and other such [afflictions].
But he whom one may make similar to oneself, who is discerning of virtues and faults,
and who is endowed with the qualities of a son— he is to be known as the "adopted" (kṛtrima) son.
In this case as well, "similar" should be understood as similar only in terms of qualities (*guṇa*).
As for those who explain it as "of the same class" (*savarṇa*), the reading *sajātīya* would be appropriate for them if that were the intended meaning;
however, similarity is not by way of caste (*jāti*), but rather as has already been stated.
Regarding one who is discerning of virtues and faults:
some say that [the initiation] is not performed as long as he has not attained legal capacity (*vyavahāra*),
for such a person does not know virtues and faults.
At that time, he knows: "He by whom I was born, and by whom my maintenance is now performed as a son—I too am his son.
Because the status of being an adopted son has been accepted, he is to be regarded in exactly that manner.
However, there is no distinction between the two cases.
He who is born in a house but whose father is not known is one born secretly in the house; he belongs to him whose wife gave birth to him.

Furthermore, if the mother is not known because she has gone out many times due to confusion, then her caste is not known; for it has been stated by the ancients that "the caste of one whose seed is unknown is determined from the mother.
And this applies where there is no suspicion that the man belongs to a lower caste;
