for if such a suspicion exists, there is the possibility of a *pratiloma* (inverse-caste) birth.
Because he was born in the inverse order, he has no authority anywhere to perform the duties of a son.
A son whom one may adopt after he has been abandoned by both his parents or by either of them is called an *apaviddha*.

By a mother who has given birth many times, who is unable to support [the child], who is in extreme poverty, or due to some defect such as a lack of devotion to her parents— and not on account of her being an outcaste (pātitya), for it is shown that such a person has no entitlement whatsoever to perform rites for a son—
this too is an abandonment by one or the other. The adoption is with the intent of regarding him as a son, and not merely out of a desire for his livelihood.
If a maiden, in her father's house, should secretly give birth to a son, one should call him by the name Kānīna; he is born from a maiden and belongs to the man who marries her.
This verse has been explained previously.
Furthermore, the determination of shares for those sons who are *svayandatta*, *kṛtrima*, and *apaviddha* has already been established;
likewise, the prohibition against accepting land as a gift applies only when other wealth is available.
If a woman who is pregnant is married, whether her condition be known or unknown, the child belongs to the husband;
such a son is called *sahoḍha* (one taken with the bride).
If one should purchase from his mother and father a son for the sake of offspring,
that son is his "bought" (krītaka) son, whether he be similar or dissimilar [to him].
He who, having been abandoned by his husband or being a widow, produces offspring again by his own will after marrying once more, is called *paunarbhava*.
If she is still a virgin, or even if she has returned from another,
she deserves to undergo the sacramental rite again with a husband taken from a second marriage.
One who is bereft of parents, or has been abandoned by them without cause,
and offers himself to another, is known as a self-given son (svayaṃdatta).
The son whom a Brāhmaṇa may father out of lust upon a Śūdra woman is called a Pāraśava, because he is born as a corpse (śava) while still being carried across (pārayan).
The phrase "out of desire" is a restatement of the expression "for those who have proceeded out of desire.
Even one who assists by providing funeral offerings and the like is equal to a corpse; he is non-beneficial because his assistance is incomplete.
Whether born of a female slave or the female slave of a male slave, whatever son may be born to a Śūdra, he shall, with permission, take a share; thus the law is established.
A son born even to a Śūdra from an unmarried woman who has not been authorized [for intercourse] is indeed a legitimate son (*suta*).
Thus, although the meaning is that she is the slave-girl of the slave, nevertheless, by virtue of this scriptural statement, one born of her belongs not to the slave, but to the master of the slave.

If permitted by his father, he shall receive an equal share with the legitimate son (*aurasa*) when the division of the estate for life is being made; otherwise, if the father should say, "This one is to have an equal share with you."
But when the father does not grant permission, it is stated in another Smṛti: "Even one born to a Śūdra from a female slave shall be a sharer of the inheritance by the father's will;
by his will, he shall receive as much a share as the father permits. When the father has died, the brothers shall make him a half-sharer."
They should do so in proportion to their own shares; they themselves should take two shares each and give one share to him.

One who has no brothers shall take everything, except for the son of a daughter. In the absence of legitimate sons (aurasa), he alone shall take the entire inheritance, provided there is no daughter’s son (dauhitra).
When that [son] exists, the daughter's son is considered as one's own son (*aurasa*), because no other is mentioned and he is established in the mind due to being the subject under discussion.
However, the established rule is that the sons of female slaves belonging to Brahmins and others are entitled only to subsistence, not to inheritance.
The wise declare that these eleven sons, beginning with the son of the field (kṣetraja) as previously described, are substitutes for a son, intended to prevent the failure of religious rites.

In the absence of the primary [son], there is a substitute; therefore, it is stated that these [other sons] are to be appointed when the legitimate son (*aurasa*) does not exist. Regarding these, in another Smṛti:
A different sequence has been stated;
for example, one who is born in secret is called the fifth by some and the sixth by others.
In that regard, the order of recitation is not a factor here, precisely because there is no fixed rule for the recitation.
And we shall demonstrate later that this purpose serves to show that [the rule] is not a subordinate element (*anaṅga*).
It is performed so that there may be no omission of the injunction— "one must procreate offspring"—
for this injunction is indeed obligatory (*nitya*).

That [debt] must be discharged by a householder in whatever manner possible. In this regard, the primary method is through one's own biological son (*aurasa*); in the absence of that, these secondary methods (*anukalpa*) should be resorted to.
These sons born from the seeds of others who have been mentioned incidentally belong to him from whose seed they were born, and not to the other.
They explain that in the absence of what was previously mentioned, this is a prohibition of an injunction:
"Those substitutes which were stated as being to be made in the absence of a legitimate son (aurasa) are not to be made;
because, since they are born from the seed of another, they are the sons of that [other man] alone, and not of this [man]."
The meaning is that those [shares] do not belong to the one by whom they are made.
Consequently, there is an option (vikalpa) between the injunction provided by the preceding [text] and this prohibition;
and that [option] is established with respect to the taking of the inheritance.

The son born of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*), the son received with a bride (*sahoḍha*), the son of a remarried woman (*punarbhava*), and the son secretly born (*gūḍhotpanna*) do not inherit property;
however, the adopted son (*dattaka*) and others do inherit, provided there is no legitimate son (*aurasa*).
Furthermore, the *kānīna* and the others do not take the paternal wealth even when there is no legitimate son; they receive only food and clothing, whether a legitimate son exists or not.
For it has been said:
"It is right for a wise man to give to all [dependents] as much as he is able—namely, food and clothing for life; for by not giving, he would become fallen."
Manu has declared that among brothers born of the same father, if even one should have a son, they all become possessed of sons through that son.
If among all those women who have but one husband, one should have a son,
Manu has declared that they are all possessed of sons by virtue of that son.
In the absence of a superior [heir], one who is inferior is entitled to the inheritance;
however, if there are many of equal status, all are sharers of the estate.
Neither brothers nor fathers, nor sons are the heirs to the father's estate;
rather, the father shall take the inheritance of one who dies without a son, and the brothers as well.
Water should be offered to three; the funeral cake proceeds for three;
the fourth is the one who bestows these; a fifth is not assigned.
The wealth of each person shall belong to his nearest sapinda;
after him, it shall go to a sakulya, or else to the teacher or the pupil.
But in the absence of all these, Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas, pure, and self-controlled shall be the heirs; thus the Dharma is not lost.
The property of a Brāhmaṇa is always inviolable by the king; this is the settled rule. However, in the absence of all [other heirs], the king may take the property of the other castes.
For one who has died without offspring, one should procure a son from a member of the same lineage;
whatever collection of property there may be, that one should bestow upon him.
But if two [sons] should dispute over the wealth of their mother, both of whom were born from her,
each shall take that which was his father's property, and not the other.
When the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers and the uterine sisters shall divide the maternal estate equally.
Whatever daughters they may have, to them also something should be given from the maternal grandmother's wealth, according to their merit and with affection.

That which is given before the nuptial fire, that which is received from the father's house, that which is given as a token of affection, and that which is obtained from a brother, a mother, or a father— this is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman.

Furthermore, that which was given as a post-nuptial gift (anvādheya) and that which was given by a husband out of affection shall belong to the offspring of a woman who has passed away while her husband is still living.

Whatever property was acquired during marriages of the Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Gāndharva, or Prājāpatya types, it is ordained that upon the death of the wife without issue, it belongs to the husband alone.
Whatever wealth may have been given to her in marriages such as the Āsura and others,
it is ordained that upon her death without offspring, it shall belong to her mother and father.
Whatever property may belong to a woman, however given by her father, that a Brāhmaṇī wife shall take; or it shall belong to her daughter, or to her offspring.
Women should not effect a withdrawal from the household or from its midst,
nor even from their own wealth, without the permission of their own husband.
Whatever ornaments may have been worn by women while their husband was alive, the heirs shall not divide them; those who do divide them fall from their status.
Those who have no share are the impotent, the outcaste, those born blind or deaf,
as well as the insane, the idiotic, the mute, and whoever else is devoid of sense organs.
However, it is right for a wise person to provide food and clothing to all of them according to his ability; for one who does not give would indeed become an outcast.
It has been shown that all [categories], including eunuchs and others, are included by virtue of being under discussion;
"extremely" means for as long as one lives.
Since food and clothing are for the purpose of maintaining the body, it should be understood that wages must also be given to servants and other attendants who are useful for that purpose.
For indeed, it is not possible for the blind and others to live without an attendant.
For those who hold that marriage is obligatory, one must provide maintenance for them along with their wives.
According to one's capacity and in proportion to one's wealth, food, clothing, and other necessities should be given.
"He has fallen" is an explanatory statement (arthavāda).
If, however, eunuchs and others should somehow have a desire for wives,
their offspring— provided they have produced progeny— are entitled to the inheritance.
Desire is the longing for union, which is the cause of sexual pleasure;
when that exists, one should marry.
In that case, offspring—whether a son or a daughter—born into that lineage is entitled to the inheritance, the partition of the estate.
Whatever share was previously stated for a daughter,

that indeed belongs to one who is impotent yet has wind-semen (*vātaretas*), for he certainly possesses the desire for sexual intercourse; but how, moreover, can there be the production of offspring for him?
And it has been said: "He who is born on the bed [of another], or the son of one deceased, of one impotent, or of one diseased.
Furthermore, by this verse, the marriage is shown to be motivated by passion (*rāga*);
for if it were motivated by duty (*dharma*), how could there be marriage for those who are ineligible for ritual acts?
Furthermore, the incapacity for being led [to the altar] has been shown to apply to those born blind, the lame, those with wind-semen (impotent), and eunuchs;
however, the insane and others are ineligible for initiation—how then could they have marriage?
And the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) serves its purpose within the scope already mentioned.
For if all [those previously mentioned] were to be included by the force of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), then even one who has fallen from his caste (*patita*) would be included;
and that is not desired, as it would contradict the Smṛti.
Alternatively, this rule should be understood to apply when those who have completed their Vedic studies and performed their marriages become insane or otherwise afflicted.
But surely, for those who have already performed a marriage, the statement "if there is a desire for wives" would not be appropriate?
This is not so, because the desire for a wife is possible even for those who have already married;
however, the ancients saw a purpose for this [rule] even in the case of a marriage performed for the sake of dharma.
Consequently, since a eunuch has the right to perform Smārta rites, marriage for his sake is indeed appropriate even in the absence of a desire [for offspring].
However, regarding Śrauta rites, because the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) occurs only after one has fathered a son, a eunuch has no right to them.
Furthermore, that which is logically the motivating cause (*prayojaka*) must be demonstrated.
Whatever property the eldest son acquires after the father has died belongs to the younger brothers as well,
provided they are devoted to learning.

If one should produce an increased yield from a field through some clever means—whether inherited from one's father, or obtained from a friend, a king, a minister, a priest, or others—that belongs to all [the co-owners] in common.
One must not think, "This was not acquired by my father in the past; it was obtained by me through my own intelligence; therefore, this is mine alone.

Because of the statement "those who maintain their learning," this rule applies to those who live by their knowledge, such as artisans, craftsmen, and the like, as well as physicians, actors, singers, and so forth.
But if wealth should accrue through the efforts of all the sons, including those born of ignorance,
the rule is that there should be an equal division of it, as it is not ancestral property.
Non-earning [of wealth] consists of agriculture, trade, service to kings, and so forth;

in this regard, slight variations in degree should not be taken into account. Even in that case, if something has been acquired by anyone to a great extent, there is indeed non-division [of the property].
This statement is intended to prohibit the granting of a special share (*jyeṣṭhāṃśa*) to the eldest son.
However, if there is only a slight excess [of wealth], an equal distribution of shares for all is prescribed.
Because the phrase "not belonging to the father" (*apitrya*) is used as a reason, this same rule applies even to the property of one who has no offspring.
But whatever is his wealth acquired through learning, that shall belong to him alone;
as shall that obtained through friendship, that received at marriage, and that received with the honey-mixture offering (madhuparka).

That which is acquired through learning—such as teaching and the like—or through skill in crafts; likewise, that obtained from a friend; that received on account of marriage; that obtained for the sake of progeny; and that received as a madhuparka offering for officiating at a sacrifice.

Although this too constitutes wealth acquired through learning (*vidyādhanam*), nevertheless, because it is obtained on the occasion of officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*), it is designated separately.
Others consider what is obtained from the father-in-law’s house to be *audvāhika* (nuptial property), since it is obtained on the occasion of the wedding (*udvāha*).
But he among brothers who, though capable of supporting himself by his own labor, does not desire wealth [from the inheritance],
shall be excluded from his share after being given something for his subsistence.

When brothers live together and manage their affairs through agriculture and other means while the paternal wealth still exists, if one among them does not participate in those affairs, this exclusion from the inheritance is prescribed for him:
"He is to be excluded from his own share.
He is to be deprived of his portion; he is to be set aside.

Whatever has been acquired through business from his own share or from his wealth exceeding that [share] shall not be given to him; however, this is not a prohibition regarding the ancestral principal. Even in that case, he is not to be entirely excluded from participation; rather, having taken for himself whatever portion results in hardship for his livelihood, the remainder should be given to him. Alternatively, "he should be excluded" (nirbhājya) means he should be made separate; he should not be allowed to live together [with the others].
In some cases, because the property was acquired through wealth that is common to the powers of subsequent time, there is equality of shares.
In that regard, Nārada has shown the determination of shares:
according to his statement, one who emerges [from the household] or departs [from it] takes a larger share, while one who remains unmentioned takes a small share.
That which has been acquired through one's own labor without depleting the paternal estate,
being obtained by one's own effort, he is not obliged to give it away unless he so desires.
The non-giving of knowledge that has been acquired by oneself is already stated;
by this [verse], it is declared that what is distinct from that—namely, what is obtained through agriculture and so forth—is not to be given.
But surely, this very verse need not have been spoken?

It is said that what has been obtained by one's own effort and by one's own exertion, one ought not to give away if one is unwilling; what then is the point of the verse concerning wealth acquired through learning and so forth? To this it is replied: The meaning is as follows: even if one has acquired property through one's own effort and exertion, one must still give it to those who are worthy of receiving gifts, such as the blind, the lame, and the like. This is because there is no distinction between property acquired through effort and property acquired through inheritance. Furthermore, since the scriptures enjoin giving to the blind and others, and since it is impossible for them to acquire property through their own effort, it follows that one must give to them from whatever property one possesses. Therefore, the verse concerning wealth acquired through learning and so forth is stated in order to indicate that one should give even from property acquired through effort when it is given to those who are worthy of receiving gifts. Thus, the sense is that one should give even from property acquired through effort to those who are worthy of receiving gifts. Alternatively, the meaning may be that one should give even from property acquired through effort to those who are not worthy of receiving gifts, provided they are in distress. For it is said: "One should give even to those who are not worthy of receiving gifts when they are in distress. Thus, the sense is that one should give even from property acquired through effort to those who are not worthy of receiving gifts when they are in distress. In the case of mantras, marriage, and so forth, since the undertaking does not originate from oneself in every instance, they are designated as distinct.
But whatever paternal property a father may acquire that was not previously obtained,
he need not share that with his sons unless he so desires, as it was acquired by himself.

If a father seeks property other than what was acquired by himself, that which he has acquired [for his own sake] shall not be divided against his will, even by sons who have attained their rights of inheritance.
What, then, is the time for partition among sons while the father is still living? It is said: [as follows].
When the father himself divides his sons, it has been stated that [the mother's share is determined] "when her menses have ceased" or "while she is living and desires [it].
Likewise, [it is said] "when the father’s desire has departed" or "when his passion has ceased.
Otherwise, however, as soon as the sons are born, they immediately become the masters of their grandfather’s wealth.
And so it has been said:
"Regarding land acquired by the grandfather, whether as a hereditary holding or as physical property,
the ownership therein belongs equally to both the father and the son."
And even though the son possesses ownership, as long as [the other sons] have not yet arrived,
all [the sons] are entitled to share the grandfather’s wealth without distinction, because partition is preceded by [the establishment of] ownership.
Furthermore, in transactions such as pledges or sales, the father’s wealth must not be employed by one who has a son already born.
However, the application [of the property] is shown to be for the maintenance of the family of the practitioner (*yogin*) and so forth.

Even though ownership belongs to the sons in this state according to established practice (*ācāra*), since a censure is observed stating that "those who divide [the estate] by force against the father's will are blameworthy," it is inferred that those who divide it by force are sinful.
Just as ownership arises through the acceptance of an improper gift (*asat-pratigraha*), yet the fault lies with the person, so too that which is inherited through such a lineage is indeed impure.
Therefore, when another means is available, the father should not be petitioned;
for in that case, it would constitute unrighteousness (*adharma*).
Even wealth acquired by oneself must certainly be divided once one recognizes that the sons have attained their rightful status and possess merit.
And it has been stated: "A father established in old age shall divide his sons;
he shall give the eldest an excellent share and the others equal shares. Nor does this refer to the property of a grandfather.
For in that case, the father has no power to grant a larger share to the eldest son, because the ownership of both is equal.

As for the rule that "the unequal distribution among those who have been divided is declared lawful when made by the father," they maintain that this applies only to a very small degree even in the case of the grandfather;
for where two full shares have not been taken [by the father], there would indeed be an exception in the case of property acquired by himself.
If those who were divided while living together should divide again, the division in that case shall be equal; there is no right of primogeniture in that instance.
The meaning of this verse is clear.

Regarding the rule of partition, it is intended to eliminate any expectation of a preferential share (*uddhāra*), because of the statement: "the rule is that [the share] shall not include the paternal property. Thus, the preferential share consists of all the paternal wealth.
In this case, however, the statement is made because of the apprehension that, due to past circumstances, there may be no paternal wealth.
If among them the eldest or the youngest should be deprived of his share at the time of distribution,
or if either one should die, his portion is not lost.
Among those brothers, if the eldest or the youngest brother is excluded from the distribution of shares—
the term "distribution of shares" meaning the time of partition—

and if he incurs a ground for exclusion such as falling from his caste (pātitya) or the like, which renders him ineligible for a share; [then the property shall be divided among the remaining brothers].
Or he might die;
his share is not lost.
This is the procedure for it.
The uterine brothers, having assembled together, shall divide that property equally,
as shall the brothers who are reunited and the uterine sisters.
Those uterine brothers whose assets are commingled shall take [the inheritance],
as well as the uterine sisters;
for those who are unmarried are designated as "uterine" (sanābhi).
Furthermore, those who have been given away (prattāḥ) undergo the status of another family; thus, they are not uterine siblings of their brothers.
As for the phrase "and those who are reunited" (ye ca saṃsṛṣṭāḥ), the word "and" (ca) includes the sister.
However, one should not entertain this doubt: "The uterine brothers and those brothers who are reunited shall take [the share].
For if that were so, it would follow that even non-uterine brothers who are reunited would be entitled to a share.
Indeed, there are both uterine brothers who are not reunited and uterine brothers who are reunited; where both exist, they should take their respective shares through a partition between the two.
And this would not contradict [the following rule]:
"But a uterine brother who is a co-resident shall take the wealth, not one who is not uterine;
even if he is not a co-resident, a uterine brother shall take it, but not one from a different mother."
This is its meaning:
a stepbrother does not take [the inheritance], even if he is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* (one who has lived in partnership), provided that a uterine brother exists, even if he is not a *saṃsṛṣṭin*.
Among the uterine brothers, only he with whom [the deceased] was a *saṃsṛṣṭin* takes it, and no other, even though the others are also uterine.
Thus it has been said: "But a reunited coparcener [inherits from] a reunited coparcener, and a uterine brother [inherits from] a uterine brother.
However, when there are no uterine brothers at all, then only those uterine half-brothers with whom he was reunited shall take the property, and not others.

For they say that among uterine brothers who are divided but living together, even though they dwell in great proximity, their presence is understood to have a specific effect regarding matters arising from common property, even for those who are divided.
Therefore, even among those who have already divided their inheritance, if one of them dies, the uterine brother alone shall take [the share]; his portion is not lost.
Nor should it be objected that at that time no share had arisen for him such that its loss would need to be considered;
for it has been stated: "When [the right] has arisen, he is to be called the owner."
"For they have no authority over those two while they are alive."
In that regard, [the text] shows that immediately after the father’s death, ownership belongs to the sons: "If an eldest brother, out of greed, should defraud his younger brothers,
he shall lose his status as the eldest, receive no share, and be restrained by the kings."
"Insult" refers to contempt shown during royal ceremonies and the like, or deceiving others by means of wealth.
It has been stated that "one who is not the eldest is to be honored like a kinsman";
this is not a prohibition of all conduct toward an elder in every respect.
And "non-participation" means the unfitness to receive the eldest son's share.

He should be restrained—since no specific method is prescribed—by means of verbal censure and the threat of punishment, and by the infliction of a monetary fine in the case of an offense commensurate with its gravity.

All brothers who are engaged in improper occupations do not deserve a share of the wealth; nor should an elder brother make a separate acquisition for himself without giving a portion to the younger brothers.

Those engaged in improper occupations, those who practice forbidden acts, those who act without instruction, those who have not taken a wife, and those whose wives are slave-girls—since there is a separate prohibition regarding the outcaste, this prohibition applies to those among these who persist in such conduct. Furthermore, one should not take from their wealth what has been used without being given; having acknowledged it as such, if one should carry away their separate property (*yautaka*) or any interest thereon.

If he deposits it with other brothers who are managing the family estate, and when they ask, "Where is that wealth? he replies, "I shall show you the principal," then he should cause them to pay even the interest along with the principal. However, if at that very time he shows it to the brothers, saying, "This surplus is seen; take it according to your shares, and I too shall set it aside from my own portion and not let it accrue interest," then there is no share for them; that belongs exclusively to him as his separate property (*yautaka*).
If brothers who have not yet divided their inheritance should rise up together [in business],
the father must by no means give unequal shares to their sons.

Regarding the statement, "The partition made by the father is declared lawful for those who have divided [the estate] unequally," that is prohibited in this specific case. "Joint effort" (sahotthāna) means that all of them acquire wealth;

for instance, one through agriculture and the like, another through receiving gifts, another through service, and another by protecting what has been acquired and employing it as needed when they are not present.
All of that, having been brought together, should be divided equally;
nothing more than the father's share should be given to anyone out of affection or similar motives.
But one born after the partition shall inherit the father's wealth alone;
or, those who may have reunited with him, he shall divide it together with them.

Regarding the two shares that the father took for himself at the time of partition, which were designated as "he shall receive two parts" after the division: those very shares must be accepted by him if the father so desires, either during his lifetime or after his death.
In that matter, the brothers may not say, "Why does he take two shares?"
But if there is no wish of the father, then an equal share, equivalent to his own, must be set aside for him.
As for those who were reunited with the father after his death, that paternal portion belongs to them alone.
Thus it has been said: "One should give a share, or take back a share, for one who is born and for one who has died."
Those who were reunited shall give [the share] to the one born [after reunion]; and after the father's death, they shall give his share equally,
with the understanding that they are "divided together."
Vasiṣṭha has shown that for a sister, there is no division [of the inheritance] until she gives birth.
The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies without offspring;
and when the mother has also passed away, the father’s mother shall take the wealth.
This verse has been explained.
When all debts and assets have been distributed according to the rule,
whatever may subsequently be discovered, all of that should be divided equally.
If, due to ignorance, a portion is divided as either less or more than it should be, and it is subsequently discovered by another, it must be made into equal shares.
Furthermore, after the time of partition has passed, there is no "extra share" (uddhāra) for the eldest.
Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women,
security and welfare, and pasture land are declared to be indivisible.
The intention here is to express the unity of clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, and water.
"Vehicles" (*patra*) refers to means of transport such as carts, wagons, and so forth.
"Ornaments" (*alaṃkāra*) refers to items such as rings and the like.
Clothing of equal value, but not of great price;
water from wells, tanks, and the like;
and women who are female slaves.

Regarding "security" (*yogakṣema*): because security arises from yoga, there is protection from thieves and others by means of ministers, domestic priests, counselors, elders, and the site itself. Furthermore, it is recited in another *Smṛti*: "In the case of the site, no partition [of ownership] exists."
"Where cattle graze, there is pasture," he says; by this,
he demonstrates that what was stated by the father— namely, "for here there is no transgression of dharma"— is untenable.
For those prohibitions apply only to things not previously seen; therefore, by transgressing them, there would be no demerit.
This division of property for you and the ritual procedure for sons—beginning with those born of the wife’s field (kṣetraja) and others—has been declared; now learn the law concerning gambling.
The king should prohibit gambling and betting within his realm;
these two vices bring about the end of kings who rule the earth.
Gambling and betting are open forms of theft;
therefore, the king should always exert effort to suppress them.
That which is performed with inanimate objects is called "gambling" (dyūta) in the world;
that which is performed with animate beings is to be known as "betting" (samāhvaya).
The king shall execute all those who engage in gambling or betting, whether they do so themselves or cause others to do so, as well as Śūdras who assume the marks of the twice-born.
He shall quickly banish from the city gamblers, actors, cruel men, those belonging to heretical sects, those engaged in forbidden occupations, and liquor-sellers.
These, existing in the kingdom as secret thieves of the king,
constantly afflict the virtuous subjects through their improper occupations.
In ancient times, this gambling was seen to cause great enmity;
therefore, a wise person should not indulge in gambling, even for the sake of amusement.
Whosoever man should practice that [prohibited act], whether secretly or openly,
there shall be a discretionary punishment for him according to the king's will.

The various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are explained as being exactly the same as those stated by the King: "Learn the law of gambling"— starting from that point, two or three verses are prescriptive.
Every [such statement] is also an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).
But a member of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes who is unable to pay a fine shall discharge the debt through labor; a Brāhmaṇa, however, shall pay it gradually, little by little.

Kṣatriyas and others who are destitute of wealth must not be brought to ruin by means of confiscation of their property. Rather, they should be made to pay the fine through labor—that work which is appropriate for them and useful to the king. A Brāhmaṇa, however, should be made to pay gradually, without causing hardship to his family.
The acts of binding and beating are forbidden for him.
The previous verse concerned the creditor;
this one concerns the punishment.
Non-redundancy.
For women, children, the insane, the elderly, the poor, and the sick,
the king should administer punishment using whips, split bamboo, ropes, and the like.
Regarding "damam" (punishment):
even when it comes to performing labor, only those who are poor and incapable are taken [as subjects];
they are to be beaten with whips and the like because of their equality with those who have committed great sins (*mahāpātakin*).
Śiphā is a creeper;
vidala is tree bark.
But those who, having been appointed to official duties, ruin the affairs of the litigants while being consumed by the heat of wealth— those the king shall render destitute.

Those officials, such as the royal representatives (*rājasthānīya*) and others, who are appointed and authorized to oversee the legal proceedings and other matters of litigants (*arthin*) and defendants (*pratyarthin*), might—being scorched by the heat of wealth—seize money from one of the parties and thereby ruin the cases. The king should strip them of their property; confiscation of all their assets is the punishment to be imposed upon them.

Even though there exists another provision for punishment to be mentioned later regarding those who act out of habitual partiality, this very punishment is the more appropriate one for members of the court (*sabhyas*).
Furthermore, those others such as generals who, when appointed to assist someone, take the property and then cause its destruction, they too are to be punished in this very same manner.
Others, however, read the text with the elision of the vowel *a* (i.e., *aniyuktāḥ*), meaning those who are not appointed;
for those who, out of favoritism toward the king or through superior force, provide assistance to one person while intending to ruin the task of the second, this is the punishment.
The phrase "by the heat of wealth" is not intended to be emphasized;
rather, the term "unappointed" is the primary factor.
He shall put to death those who forge royal edicts, those who corrupt the subjects,
those who kill women, children, or Brahmins, and likewise those who serve his enemies.
Those who forge official decrees (*kūṭaśāsana*) claim that even what has not been commanded by the king was "done by the king.

A decree (*śāsana*) is a royal edict. An official document (*patraka*) written by a scribe authorized by the king—stating such things as "one must not eat in this person's house," "this favor has been granted to him by command," or "this regulation has been established by the king"—is called a decree; it is a decree because it is constrained by the king's command.
They form factions and protect them;
they are corrupters and sowers of dissension among subjects who are angry or greedy;
and they are killers of women, children, and even Brahmins.
Those who serve enemies, those who serve the king's foes, and those who move secretly back and forth.
Whatever has been decided and adjudicated anywhere, one should know that it is done according to dharma; one who has come into existence [as a successor] shall not set it aside.
In whatever royal court a legal matter has been adjudicated— that is, decided upon the completion of the proceedings and the determination of the case—
the king should recognize that as indeed accomplished, provided it was not merely stated with truthful words but was also formally decreed and a punishment was imposed;
he must not reverse such a decision except in the event of a double fine being required.
As it has been said: "Having imposed a double fine, one should restore that transaction.
In the previous case, the nullification was due to the taking of wealth;
this case, however, is due to another cause, such as ignorance and so forth.
Whatever legal matter the ministers or the judge might decide incorrectly,
the king himself shall settle that case and fine them one thousand [paṇas].
The "minister" refers to one who holds the position of a royal official and so forth;
he, along with the [other] thousand, shall be punished.
Just as in the case of the punishment of the hundred Gargas, the completion of the sentence occurs by means of the collective group.
The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—
all these men are to be known individually as perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin).
A Brahmin who drinks liquor is indeed a perpetrator of a mortal sin;
a thief is one who steals the gold of a Brahmin,
not just anyone.
The restatement of what has already been said is for the sake of what follows.
And for these four who do not perform expiation,
he shall prescribe a lawful punishment consisting of both corporal and monetary fines.
But surely, it is only a Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor who is a sinner;
and for him, there is no corporal punishment, according to the rule that "there is no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa.
In that case, how can it be said that [the penalty applies] to all four castes?
Some say that what has fallen [into the water] is grasped even if it was not previously held, because of the force of the number "four.
Others, however, say that the marking is conjoined with the body.
And that [quality] belongs to the Brahmin as well;
however, others say that by the word "also" (api), this punishment applies to all five,
or even to all four.

By the force of the word "api" (also), the corporal punishment for the killing of even a fifth person associated with them— a Brāhmaṇa— has already been stated in the preceding [text]: "And one should kill those who kill women, children, or Brāhmaṇas."
By this, branding itself is meant as something applied to the interior of the body;
"in accordance with the law" (dharmyam) means that greater or lesser severity should be inflicted according to the nature of the offense.
For violating the teacher’s bed, the mark of a female organ should be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern banner;
for theft, the foot of a dog; and for killing a Brahmin, the figure of a headless man.
The mark on the forehead is for the purpose of non-prohibition, because one hears it said: "Kings shall not brand [criminals] on their foreheads."
Indeed, being unfit to eat with, unfit to sacrifice with, unfit to study with, and unfit to marry with,
they shall wander the earth in misery, excluded from all religious duties.

Since the prohibition of eating together (*saṃbhojana*) and so forth is already established by the inclusion of "all things" (*sarvadharma*), their specific mention here is for the purpose of making known the gravity of the fault.
Eating together means consuming food in one place and listening to songs and the like;
sacrificing together (*saṃyājana*) means performing sacrifices for those very people, or performing sacrifices along with them.
The reading should be understood in this way:
"asaṃpāṭhyāvivāhinaḥ. This is a dvandva compound meaning "those with whom one does not recite together and those with whom one does not intermarry."
Regarding the term "miserable" (*dīnā*):

even though they possess their own property, due to the prohibition of using things related to that [property], as well as by eating alms-food and so forth, and by the extreme contempt of others, there is the discarding of rags of cloth and the like.
"However, these persons who bear the marks [of their crimes] must be abandoned by their kinsmen and relatives;
they are to be without compassion and without salutation—this is the instruction of Manu."
"Those whose characteristics have been established" means that when the relationship of cause and effect has been determined.
Even if they are afflicted by disease and other such conditions, one should not show compassion toward them;
and even if they possess qualities such as seniority, they are not to be saluted with rising from one's seat and other such gestures.
This very [definition] is to be understood as the dharma by virtue of the force of the statement itself.
But those of the higher castes who perform the prescribed penance as declared shall not be branded on the forehead by the king; rather, they should be made to pay the highest fine.
For the other castes besides the Śūdra who perform penance, there is no branding;
however, as punishment, they shall be made to pay the highest fine of one thousand paṇas.
For offenses against a Brāhmaṇa, the middle amercement shall be imposed;
or he may be banished from the kingdom, along with his wealth and his belongings.
The phrase "but those performing penance" is not required here;
in these offenses such as the killing of a Brahmin, a Brāhmaṇa is to be fined the middle amercement.
The word "unintentionally" is drawn from the subsequent verse [and applies here].
Having been punished, he should be made to perform penance along with his belongings;
this applies to a virtuous Brāhmaṇa who is worthy of favor.
Or, if he does not wish to do so, he shall not be banished.
However, those others who have committed these sins unintentionally deserve the forfeiture of all their property; but if they did so intentionally, they deserve banishment.
Other castes, such as Kṣatriyas and others, who have committed these sins—the great crimes (mahāpātakas)—unintentionally and without desire, shall be deprived of all their property.
Some authorities maintain that for those who perform penance, this punishment is optional in relation to the previous one; however, for intentional acts, death is prescribed for them.
For a Śūdra, if the act was unintentional, there is branding and confiscation of all property; if intentional, there is death.
A righteous king must not take the wealth of one who has committed a mortal sin;
for by taking it out of greed, he becomes tainted by that very guilt.
But has it not been established that punishment by means of wealth is the king’s mode of livelihood? How, then, is that wealth not included here?
It was stated in the passage beginning with "those whose punishment has been removed by the king."
Having cast that staff into the waters, he should offer it to Varuṇa;
or he should present it to a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct.
Mentally reflecting, "This is for Varuṇa," one should give it into the waters— that is, throw it into the waters—
or one should give it to a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct.
Varuṇa is the lord of punishment, for he is the wielder of the rod over kings;
the Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas is the lord of the entire world.
This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for the preceding injunction regarding the performance [of penance]:
Varuṇa rules over the punishment of those who have committed great sins (*mahāpātakin*);
for he is the wielder of the rod of punishment for kings, meaning he is their leader and sovereign.
In the same way, it should be understood that the Brahmin is also the owner of that wealth by virtue of this [scriptural authority].
Wherever a king avoids acquiring wealth from evildoers,
there men are born in due time with long lives.
And the crops of the people ripen individually according to how they were sown;
children do not die prematurely, and nothing deformed is born.
These two verses are also well-known explanatory statements (*arthavāda*).

In the phrase "they are born by time," the present birth is not intended; rather, it refers to those already born and those yet to be born. "Deformed" means being devoid of hands, feet, eyes, and so forth.
But a king should slay with various terrifying means of execution that person of inferior caste who, out of lust, oppresses Brahmins.
One born of the lowest caste is a *śūdra*.
"Oppression" (*bādhana*) consists of the seizure of wealth and other possessions, as well as physical torment.
"Varied" (*citrā*) refers to diverse methods, such as impalement on a stake, bloodletting, mutilation of limbs, or being struck with a sword, and so forth.
Causing agitation and bringing suffering for a long period of time.
As much demerit is seen for a king in killing one who should not be killed, so much is seen in releasing one who deserves to be killed; however, merit accrues to him who exercises restraint.

Whatever fault there is in executing one who should not be executed, an equal fault exists in releasing one who deserves execution. For a king as described above—one who takes a sixth part [of the produce]—if he fails to perform his own duty, he must necessarily incur sin; however, for one who performs it, there is never the attainment of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
As for this traditional teaching on dharma, such as "But dharma belongs to him who administers justice," all of it is merely an *arthavāda* intended to praise the performance of one's own duty.
This instruction regarding execution, however, is intended for the purpose of subduing and bringing [the enemy] under control;
therefore, it should be carried out by means of various methods of killing as they have been heard [in the scriptures].
In instructions concerning visible worldly matters for the sake of achieving success in statecraft (*rājyatantra*), the teaching is that one should kill warriors according to what has been observed.
In that case, because the instruction has a visible purpose, killing is not mandatory;
and this being so, there is no fault for one who restrains [the offender] by other means such as imprisonment.
Thus has been declared in detail the determination of legal procedure for two parties disputing with one another regarding the eighteen grounds of litigation.
This verse is for the purpose of concluding all conventional discourse.
Thus, performing his duties in accordance with the Dharma correctly, the lord of the earth should seek to acquire territories not yet obtained and protect those already acquired.
The meaning is that one who is intent on contentment should not think, "I shall desire what has not yet been obtained."
Having settled in a properly chosen location and having constructed a fortress according to the treatises,
he should constantly exert the greatest effort in the removal of thorns.

Having carried out the settlement of the country and the construction of fortresses as described in the seventh chapter, one should perform the removal of thorns (*kaṇṭakoddharaṇa*). By that means also, the protection of the realm is accomplished.
The word "thorn" (*kaṇṭaka*) is applied to thieves and others because they share the common quality of being causes of affliction.
He demonstrates this very point:
"By protecting those of noble conduct and by clearing away thorns,
kings who are devoted to the protection of their subjects go to the third heaven."
What is enjoined by the noble scriptures must be performed; this is a prohibition against the practice of other [customs].
The compound "tadvṛtta" is a *bahuvrīhi* with the elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*), meaning "those whose conduct is that [of the scriptures].
By this, the poor, the helpless, and the *śrotriya* who pay neither taxes nor tolls are included.
For it is logical that by protecting them, one goes to the third heaven;
however, for others, because they have been purchased through their service, there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) if they do not perform it, as will be stated later: "and he falls from heaven.
By paying the price for the continuation of protection, there is merely an absence of transgression, but no heaven.
Alternatively, the statement regarding the attainment of heaven is dependent upon the restriction of one's mode of livelihood, as was stated previously; however,
the observation that for others [the king] is purchased by his livelihood means that the king’s mention of heaven is merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).
Even the protection of those who do not follow the prescribed occupations (*avṛtti*) is prompted by the king’s own occupation, for that king stands in the place of a share of his own kingdom.

Just as artisans living by their crafts are made to perform work by the king month after month—one task each—in order to collect taxes while they are already practicing their craft for the sake of their livelihood, so too the king, being engaged in his own occupation and intent on protecting the subjects, is made by the scripture to protect the noble ones as if it were a compulsory duty (*nityakarman*).

For just as one who has consecrated the sacred fires (*agnyāhita*) performs the obligatory rites according to the injunctions of desire, and not for the sake of attaining heaven or other rewards; [so it is here].
For those [rites] are not enjoined for the sake of a fruit, and yet they are performed;
this case should be viewed in the same way.
Therefore, whatever mention of a fruit there may be, it is all merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*); thus says the learned Viṣṇusvāmin.
Whatever the reality is in this matter, that has been shown below.
But that king who takes tribute while failing to punish thieves—
his kingdom becomes agitated and he falls away from heaven.
The governance of the kingdom, according to the scriptures, cannot be accomplished without the restraint and punishment of thieves through execution and other means.

Therefore, for one who accepts his livelihood yet recoils from the execution of thieves, there is a twofold fault: in this world, it is a transgression against the state; in the next, it is the loss of heaven.
And it is logical that one who has accepted the sacrificial offering (*bali*) but fails to perform the corresponding expiation (*niṣkṛti*) is indeed guilty of a fault.
But that kingdom which is fearless and relies upon the strength of its arms increases constantly, like a tree being watered.
This very well-known fact is restated here as a supplementary detail to the rule for the execution of thieves.
A king, whose eyes are his spies, should recognize two kinds of thieves who steal the property of others: those who are open and those who are secret.

Spies who are concealed within the kingdom and who possess knowledge of the king's affairs are like eyes for him; thus he is "one whose eyes are his spies. For those who are open thieves, there is no legal status as "thieves" in the world, unlike others such as forest-dwellers or night-prowlers.
By means of these, a general undertaking is made for the purpose of refuting that [position].
Those who live by various wares are "open deceivers," while those such as thieves and forest-dwellers are "concealed deceivers."

Among them, those who deceive for the sake of trade by using specific weights and measures, and who manipulate the entry and exit of goods from their place of business, are merchants who are open cheats (*prakāśavañcaka*).

Those who steal at night are thieves (*stena*); forest-dwellers (*āṭavika*) live in desolate regions. Furthermore, there are those who seize by force; these are not the only ones, but rather these and others whom we shall describe hereafter.
Bribe-takers, those who practice fraud, deceivers, gamblers, those who live by predicting auspicious events, and fortune-tellers, together with diviners;

*Utkocakas* are those who, for the sake of someone's business, engage in the accomplishment of that task by receiving wealth from a king, a minister, or others. *Aupadhikas* are those who act with deceit; they say one thing while doing another.
Having displayed visible affection, they proceed to act with forced assistance.

Even without receiving any actual benefit, they perceive through some other sign that another person’s purpose will certainly be accomplished, and they seize upon the other, thinking, "I am doing this for you. Or, deception (*upadhi*) consists in the display of intimidation.
"Deceivers" (vañcakāḥ) refers to gamblers who always play for the sake of seizing wealth;
or the word may have a distinct meaning: "deceivers" (vipralambhakāḥ) are those who, having said, "We ourselves will do this work for you, we shall not remain elsewhere," fail to carry it out.
Having approached, they rob the villagers by means of various forms and diverse methods;
those such as the Śivamādhavas subsist upon Śiva and the Sun;
and those such as astrologers, who live by predicting auspiciousness and instructing on pacification rituals.
Or else, they say, "I propitiate this deity for your sake—Durgā and Mārtaṇḍa"—just as those who live off the wealth of the wealthy do.
Or again, those whose livelihood consists of pronouncing blessings are those who say, "May there be auspiciousness for you," though they themselves are inauspicious. They are auspicious only by name.
Spectators praise the characteristics of men for everyone by examining their hands.
Likewise, high officials who act improperly, physicians,
those skilled in the practice of crafts, and clever courtesans [should be avoided].
The high officials (*mahāmātra*) are those such as ministers and domestic chaplains who are in close attendance upon the king; they would be those acting improperly.
The physicians (*cikitsaka*) are medical practitioners.
Those engaged in the practice of crafts (*śilpopacāra*) include painters, leaf-cutters, image-makers, and so forth.
"Service" (upacāra) means bringing wealth after performing and displaying one's own craft and skill that is not currently being utilized;
likewise, courtesans and those skilled in service [bring wealth] by showing affection that is not genuine.
The term "those who act improperly" (asamyakkāriṇaḥ) is to be applied everywhere [in this context].
One should recognize such people as manifest thorns in the world,
as well as others who move in secret— ignoble men wearing the outward marks of the noble.
The inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is used because it is impossible to enumerate all the varieties of rogues who steal the property of others, such as those mentioned above.

For instance, they describe a woman who is actually indifferent as one who is full of passion and contemptuous; likewise, a servant, presenting himself as a devoted follower, leads away the gold of a simple-natured man, yet he is not a servant for the sake of wealth. Saying "You are Brahmā, you are Bṛhaspati," they lead away those rich in ignorance with the words, "Give [this] by your favor; I shall return it in a few days. Once the purpose is accomplished, the sweet-talker becomes very thin and turns into a speaker of unpleasant things; such are those who move in secret.

Having identified them through secret agents who have conducted themselves well and performed their duties, and through spies in various disguises, he should incite them and bring them under his control.
By those who perform that work— those who perform similar tasks and have previously performed that work with knowledge—
or else by those who are currently being made to perform that work, having gained an opportunity for the sake of accomplishing their inclusion, they will come and speak;
likewise by other spies of various disguises.

Having publicly proclaimed their faults according to the truth in relation to each of their respective duties, the king should administer punishment properly, taking into account both the strength of the offender and the nature of the offense.
For indeed, without punishment,
it is impossible to restrain the wickedness of thieves who possess evil intentions and move about secretly upon the earth.
Assembly halls, water-stations, bakeries, taverns, and shops selling cooked food; crossroads, sacred trees, public gatherings, and places of spectacle.
Dilapidated gardens, forests, the workshops of artisans,
as well as empty houses, groves, and pleasure parks.
The king should cause such regions to be patrolled by both stationary and mobile military units, as well as by spies, for the purpose of suppressing thieves.
He should recognize them through their companions who follow them and understand their various activities,
and he should encourage them by means of clever former thieves.
By means of instructions regarding food and drink, by visiting with Brahmins,
and by discussions of heroic deeds, they should bring about their meeting.
Those who do not approach him there, and those who are rooted in enmity, the king should forcibly slay along with their friends, kinsmen, and relatives.
A righteous king shall not execute a thief without proof of the stolen goods;
however, he may execute one caught with the stolen goods along with the implements [of theft] without hesitation.
Moreover, whoever in the villages provide food to thieves, or even give them space for their goods— all of them he should have executed as well.
He should swiftly punish those appointed to protect the realms and the vassal lords who have been exhorted [to act], if they remain neutral during attacks, just as one punishes thieves.
Furthermore, even one who lives by the Dharma but has fallen away from the commitment to the Dharma should be scorched with punishment alone, for he has strayed from his own duty.

Those who, despite having the capacity, do not rush to the aid of others during a village raid, the destruction of a sanctuary, or when seeing a robbery on the road, shall be banished along with their belongings.

If they have the capacity [to resist] but fail to do so due to laziness or other such reasons, they are to be banished. However, as for those who have made a secret agreement with thieves, their execution was previously prescribed; thus, "he shall cause them to be put to death."
"Paricchada" refers to cattle, horses, and so forth;
even that must be provided [to the debtor] and not confiscated, for he must not be rendered destitute of his basic necessities, though his wealth may be seized.
He should execute with various punishments those who misappropriate the king's treasury, those who stand in opposition to him, and those who instigate enemies.

The treasury (*kośa*) is the place where kings store their accumulated wealth; those who steal from it are to be executed regardless of the type or quantity of the goods. This also applies to those who act with hostility toward it. Furthermore, this includes those who obstruct the importation of what the king intends to bring from other lands—such as noble horses and the like that are rare in the eastern regions for easterners, or elephants originating from the Kalinga region and so forth for northerners.
Likewise, those who turn friends into enemies and, having done so, unite them with enemies;
those who are instigators and inciters of foes—
one should have them executed.
It has been stated that because [the act] serves its own independent purpose, killing is not necessarily required.
But those thieves who commit robbery at night by breaking into a house,
the king should have their hands cut off and impale them upon a sharp stake.
In the first offense, one should have the fingers of a housebreaker cut off;
in the second, his hands and feet; in the third, he deserves the death penalty.
"Granthibheda" means one who cuts a knot (*granthiṃ bhinatti*).
"Cutting" (*bheda*) refers to the loosening or release of a knot; a "knot" (*granthi*) is found at the end of a garment or similar object.
Alternatively, those who, by some trick, loosen the knot of whatever property has been seized and wish to carry it away are called *granthibhedas*.

For those [offenses], in the first instance of proceeding, there shall be the cutting off of the fingers; in the second instance of proceeding, the cutting off of the hands and feet; and in the third instance, execution.
The king should punish like a thief those who provide fire, food, weapons, or shelter [to criminals], as well as those who facilitate the theft.
"Setters of fire" refers to those who provide fire for the purpose of removing cold and so forth.
"Weapons" refers to instruments such as knives and the like. "Plunderers" refers to those who are the agents who lay hold of stolen goods.
All of them should be understood as being like thieves.
Although the granting of an opportunity for weapons was mentioned previously, it is stated here again for the sake of summary.
One who destroys a tank should be executed by drowning in water or by some other form of pure execution;
or, if he repairs it, he should be made to pay the highest fine.
The mention of a pond (*taḍāga*) is for the purpose of illustration;
some maintain that this same fault applies even to taking water from a river,
but that is incorrect.
For the offense in the case of damming a large reservoir is great, whereas it is slight in the case of damming a river; indeed,
this same rule applies even when water is diverted by breaching the embankment of a reservoir.
One should indeed put to death those who break into granaries, armories, or temples, as well as those who steal elephants, horses, or chariots, without hesitation.
But he who diverts the water of a tank already established,
or cuts off the inflow of waters, shall be made to pay the first amercement.
He who, except in an emergency, should discharge impurity upon the royal highway,
shall pay two kārṣāpaṇas and must immediately clean away that impurity.

On a royal road, in a village, a city, or on a street, one should not discharge impure urine or feces; nor should a Caṇḍāla or similar person be made to deposit them there after being brought from elsewhere.
This is stated as an absolute prohibition except in times of distress.
In an emergency, one may have a Caṇḍāla or the like remove it by paying him a fee, or do so oneself if no other person is available.
Furthermore, one who has fallen into calamity, an elderly person, a pregnant woman, or even a child deserve only a reprimand, and that [offense] must be purified; such is the established rule.
"One who has met with misfortune" refers to those previously mentioned;
"the elderly and others" includes those who are unable to go outside the village.
Regarding the phrase "even to shed blood," it is suspected that they might even designate something impure [as blood].
This must not be done again;
if it is done again, there will be great retribution from the king. Such speech, containing anger and constituting an insult, must be expiated—this is the instruction of the king.
If the throwers are not known, then the road must likewise be cleared by the *caṇḍālas* and others.
For all physicians who practice falsely, there shall be punishment:
the first amercement for non-human beings, but the middle amercement for human beings.
Physicians are healers.
The administration of medicine by those who practice wrongly occurs in two ways:
either through ignorance of the application of the treatises, or even when the treatises are familiar, through lack of dedication due to a desire for gain.
In the case of non-human animals such as cows, horses, elephants, and so forth, the first *sāhasa* (lowest fine) should be applied;
likewise, in the case of humans, the middle *sāhasa* applies.
Furthermore, if through such improper conduct the animal should perish quickly, then a heavy punishment must be prescribed.
One who breaks the crossing-bridges, flagstaffs, or images shall repair all of that and pay five hundred [paṇas].
The "crossing" (*saṃkrama*) is the path by which they cross over, descending [into the water] by means of such signs as touching water and so forth.
A bright garment, a banner, or a mark belongs to kings, ministers, and others;
likewise, a staff is found in the temples of the gods, and it has been explained that such things belong to images.
One should remedy it, restore it to equilibrium, and bring it back to its original state.
For the adulteration of unadulterated goods,
as well as for their breaking or the false piercing of gems, the punishment is the first amercement.

When one who seeks profit defiles substances that are themselves non-defiled—such as when a grain-seller mixes excellent, faultless grain in the field with straw and chaff; or when saffron and the like are mixed with other substances such as non-saffron;
or when gems and pearls are split, meaning they are divided into two parts;
or when they are pierced in a place where they should not be pierced, which is called *apavedha* (improper piercing).
In this context, the root *vedhati* is used in the sense of "piercing," because roots have multiple meanings;
this is a form derived from the root *vidh*.
Gems are indeed classified as inferior, mediocre, or superior.
In those cases, the imposition of punishment must be carried out:
for middling offenses, a middling punishment; for superior offenses, a superior punishment.
But he who deals unequally with equals, whether by measure or by price,
shall incur the first or indeed the middle amercement.

Regarding those goods for which an exchange on the basis of equality is prescribed—such as "sesame seeds [are exchanged] for grain, being equal to them"—if one acts unfairly therein, one might give sesame seeds for trade and receive a large quantity of grain such as rice (*vrīhi*) and so forth; or, in the absence of an exchange, one purchases from such grains at a price higher than their value through a commercial transaction. Alternatively, suppose one person has an upper garment or a pillow to sell, while another has various cloths; in that case, the latter are of use to the one who possesses the pillow.
And [the case] with Upabarhaṇa is similar:
having learned that the goods there belong to him, he gives them at an equal price and takes back a higher value;
he is said to "deal unequally with equals" by means of the price.
These two punishments apply to both the buyer and the seller.
The term "carati" (moves/circulates) has the same meaning as "mūlyataḥ" (by way of price); likewise, in this view, the word "vā" (or) serves merely to complete the meter.
The first and middle [fines] for buying and selling are prescribed according to the value of the object.
And he should place all the prisoners along the royal highway,
so that those miserable, deformed evildoers may be seen there.

One should establish or construct prisons in well-known areas along the royal roads, so that those who are suffering may be seen there; by this, he indicates that they may be established elsewhere as well, showing that they should be situated where people frequent such places.
By this, he states that other forms of affliction for those held in confinement should also be carried out.
They are "distorted" by the attainment of another state, such as extreme emaciation of the body, through fasting or eating only a little;
the rest is clear.
One should immediately banish anyone who breaks down a wall, fills up a moat, or destroys a gate.
The punishment for the destruction of fortifications such as walls and the like is exile;
moats are excavated portions of the ground.
In all cases of malevolent magic, a fine of two hundred [paṇas] shall be imposed;
likewise for those uninitiated persons who perform root-rites (mūlakarman) or various kinds of sorcery (kṛtyā).

*Abhicāra* is the act of killing by means of unseen methods, such as the power of mantras and the like. This punishment applies to those engaged in it when the victim is not fit for *abhicāra*. In cases of *abhicāra* against those who are not fit for it, one is not released by this much alone.
In that regard, that should be understood as the punishment for killing a human being.
The inclusion of the term "all" is for the purpose of applying the punishment without distinction to both worldly and Vedic [acts].
The Vedic [examples] include the Śyena sacrifice and others.
Worldly [actions] include picking up dust from under a tree, piercing with a needle, and so forth;
*mūlakarma* refers to subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) and the like. "Trustworthy" refers to one's son, wife, and others; those other than these are "untrustworthy."

*Kṛtyās* are indeed types of malevolent sorcery (*abhicāra*), being powers inherent in mantras and the like; they are well known among spirits and other beings as the causes for expulsion, creating enmity with friends, inciting hatred toward one's family, causing mental derangement, and so forth.
One who sells seeds unfit for sowing, one who steals such seeds,
and likewise one who destroys boundaries, shall undergo the punishment of mutilation or death.
Having declared what is seedless to be seed, one sells it by concealing its true nature.
For instance, seeds of grain, vegetables, and the like that have been soaked for a long time sprout in the field, yet they cannot be called sterile.
Furthermore, one extracts the seed from the field; having extracted the excellent seed that sprouts quickly and substituting it with something resembling it, such as inferior grain, one sells it.
Alternatively, they carry away the sown seed after uprooting it from the very field.
A boundary (*maryādā*) is a settled rule established by scripture, local custom, and tradition. "Deformed" refers to the mutilation of ears, nose, and so forth.
But a king should have a goldsmith, who is the most wicked of all thorns and who acts unjustly, cut into pieces with razors.
Among all those thorns previously mentioned, the goldsmith is the most sinful.
If the genitive case is used here in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*),
how is it that there is no absence of compounding according to the rule *na nirdhāraṇe*?
And its extreme wickedness consists in the fact that even by a very small act of taking, a great sin arises; furthermore, the theft of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold is a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*).
Therefore, one should have him cut into pieces if he persists in such injustice.
They steal by means of exchanging [weights], using false scales, heating [the metal], cutting it, and so forth; they take [it].
In this case, there is no consideration for the quantity of the property being stolen, nor any consideration for the caste of the owner;
rather, repetition is taken into account because of the severity of the punishment.
However, in the first instance of the offense, the cutting off of a piece of flesh with a razor should be substituted for a monetary fine.
It has been established that for those being restrained through physical punishment, their evil departs.
In cases of the theft of Sītā-crops, weapons, or medicine,
the king shall determine the punishment after considering the time and the specific circumstances of the act.
The earth being ploughed is *sītā*; the implements for that work are the plough, the spade, and so forth; a punishment shall be prescribed for the theft of these.
Is it by mere wish?
No, he says; rather, it depends upon the time and the task.
When the time for plowing has arrived, the punishment is great.
And when that [destruction] occurs in what has not been cultivated, then the destruction of the great fruit is indeed even greater;
"having encountered" means having recognized it as imminent.
At other times, however, it is in accordance with the nature of the substance and so forth.
Likewise, regarding weapons such as swords and the like at the time of battle,
or medicine at the time of its administration for therapeutic purposes:

if, because that medicine has been stolen and not administered, great suffering arises for the patient, and no other [medicine] is available at that time— or even if another is available, it would take a long time to administer due to requirements such as preparation by a physician and so forth— such considerations may justify the imposition of a royal penalty.
Regarding weapons and the king's regalia:
otherwise, if the people are apprehensive of enemies or thieves, then a heavy fine is imposed;
if [the apprehension] is slight, the fine is slight.
The sovereign, the minister, the capital, the realm, the treasury, the army, and likewise the ally—these are the seven constituent elements; thus the kingdom is said to have seven limbs.
Once the removal of thorns (*kaṇṭakaśuddhi*) is completed, the duties of a king (*rājadharma*) useful solely for the administration of the kingdom are now described.

Just as the non-destruction of the kingdom occurs when these [duties] are performed, so too does the non-destruction of the kingdom occur equally when judicial proceedings (*vyavahāradarśana*) or the removal of thorns are carried out.
Furthermore, "thorns" generally consist of those who depend upon the queen, the princes, the king's favorites, and the military commanders.

One should not, at any time, release them with such a thought, out of fear of a disturbance in the constituent elements (*prakṛti*), for there is a most important purpose served by the commander-in-chief and the feudal lord.

What is the use of imprisoning this offender against the realm? For that reason it is said: "The realm is equal [to the king] through its master and so forth," because it is a constituent element of the kingdom.
And the relative weight or lightness of these constituent elements is stated for this very purpose.
If there is great unrest caused by a minister, it must be averted;
however, one should not act impulsively with the thought, "The kingdom is weak because of him, so I will purify the state of its thorns [enemies] by some means after awakening [the people].
Therefore, even setting aside the instructions of the seventh chapter, this should be understood in this context.
The master is the king himself;
the minister is the counselor, the chaplain, and the commander-in-chief;
the city is the residential capital.
The realm (*rāṣṭra*) refers to the provinces (*janapada*).
The treasury (*kośa*) is the accumulation of wealth such as silver, gold, and bullion.
The army (*daṇḍa*) consists of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, or alternatively, it refers to legal punishment and the like.
The friend is one who shares the same purpose, as it has been said: "Therefore, the friend follows immediately after that.
These are the constituent elements (*prakṛti*) of the kingdom—the causes and components—just as the potsherds are to a jar.
Alternatively, the word *prakṛti* denotes intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Thus, the entire kingdom, being of that very nature, has been cast aside.
The detailed expansion of its divisions consists of seventy-two; furthermore, whatever other division exists therein has already been explained.
Among these seven constituent elements of sovereignty, one should know that, in their respective order, each preceding one constitutes a more serious calamity than the one following it.
The misfortune of one's own forces is more serious than the misfortune of an ally;
for one who possesses his own forces is able to favor an ally.
The same applies to the army and the treasury.
For when the treasury is destroyed, the punishment itself is surely destroyed;
such is the relationship between the treasury and the kingdom.
Indeed, if the kingdom is destroyed, from where can the treasury arise?
Furthermore, when there is a threat of the destruction of the kingdom, the city must be protected with great effort;
for it is there that all constituent parts, means, and resources are available. Among these, the minister is the most important.
For when the chief minister is destroyed, the entire force is shattered;
it is well known that when one's own self is destroyed, everything is destroyed. Thus it has been said: "But the self must be protected above all else."
And thus there is an illustration:
"In this world, of the seven-limbed kingdom which is supported like a triple staff,
nothing excels anything else due to the specific excellence of their mutual qualities."
"Of one who is supported like a triple staff": this means that for one who is supported, there is a state of mutual dependence.
He says this very thing:

Because of the excellence of their mutual qualities, they stand in a relationship of mutual assistance toward one another, and because each arises and perishes [in dependence on the others], just as the collection of earth, seed, and water produces a sprout;
therefore, the worshipfulness of all of them is taught here.
Indeed, there exists in this case a distinction between what is weightier and what is lighter.
As for the statement that "nothing [else] is superior," this is intended to mean that one must act with great care in protecting friends and others;

for when there is an obstruction by a powerful force, the destruction of the kingdom follows the loss of a friend only after a long time, and not immediately—this is the basis for [the claim of] its lesser importance.
In various specific tasks, however, this or that particular factor is distinguished; whichever factor accomplishes a given purpose is said to be the most excellent in that context.
There is no object that is not of use to a king;
for there exists a task that is accomplished by a lowly person and not by one of high status.

Therefore, all subjects must be protected with diligence; the kingdom must not be oppressed through unjust punishments and the like, and it must be guarded with effort against disturbances such as thieves—this is the essential meaning.
Therefore, this is merely a remnant of the "removal of thorns."
