Through one's conduct, through the application of energy, and through the very performance of actions,
one should constantly know one's own power and the power of others, as well as that of oneself and the Supreme.
One should constantly know the capacity of both the other person and oneself.
One must always understand this: "What does he intend to undertake? What can he do to me? And what can I do to him?
How, then, is this possible to know?
By means of "conduct" as described in the seventh chapter;

by means of "the application of enthusiasm," those who have been satisfied by giving and so forth are joined with enthusiasm, as are those who have attained the fruits of agriculture and other labors;
and by means of "action" itself regarding karmas.
"Works" refers to activities such as fortification; by undertaking them, an enemy is understood to be powerful, for those works bring about the attainment of wealth, from which power arises.
Having reflected upon all oppressions as well as calamities,
and having considered their relative weight and lightness, one should then undertake the task.

Afflictions (*pīḍanāni*) include the torments of hell, famine, falling [into lower realms], and so forth; likewise, droughts, excessive rains, alternating cycles of calamities, rats, locusts, thunderbolts, and the like.
Misfortunes (*vyasanāni*) arise from desire and anger, or are presented as the failure of destiny resulting in the loss of one's own son.
Nevertheless, one must always maintain perseverance.

Alternatively, one should not remain merely contented. Rather, one must consider the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*), the daily income and expenditure, and ascertain, through some means, the conduct of the kingdom and the desires of the subjects from the mouths of spies. Or else, these matters should be understood through activities other than the pursuit of pleasures such as dance and song.
One should indeed undertake actions again and again, even when exhausted;
for prosperity attends the man who perseveres in his undertakings.
"A man intent on action is joined with prosperity"—this is a restatement of an established fact.
Even if, due to some performed action, a result has not been obtained in some way, one should nevertheless not become discouraged;
or rather, one should not become complacent.

Now, first of all, reflection on the six measures of policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) has been undertaken; the daily income and expenditure have been understood to some extent; and the condition of the kingdom, as desired by its constituent elements (*prakṛti*), has been ascertained through the reports of spies. Alternatively, other duties are to be known through activities such as the enjoyment of pleasure from dance, song, and so forth. Regarding the mention of "the person" (*puruṣa*): let alone the king, even another person from the countryside prospers through the glory of exertion.
Thus it is said: "One should seek prosperity until death."
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages are all the conduct of the king; for the king is said to be the age itself.
For this reason as well, one must be intent upon the commencement of action;
for one who does not initiate action would be a person of the Kali age,
and that is a great fault.
And the king should not think, "Kali is a specific period of time well-known from the Itihāsas; how could I be that?
For all these ages are the very conduct of the king.
This will be demonstrated hereafter.
When Kali is asleep, it is the Dvāpara age; when awake, it is the Tretā age;
when intent upon actions, it is the Tretā; but while moving about, it is the Kṛta age.
One who is habitually inactive and asleep becomes Kali;
one who knows the means for advancement and practices them becomes Dvāpara while awake;
and one who applies himself to determined action becomes Tretā.
When all forms of the universe are endowed with the fruits of action according to the scriptures, it becomes the Kṛta Yuga.
O King, a ruler should conduct himself with the splendor and conduct of Indra, Arka, Vāyu, Yama, Varuṇa, Candra, Agni, and Pṛthivī.
The meaning is that *tejas* (vitality) is the semen, the effect, which is to say, the capacity.
Just as Indra pours down rain during the four months of the rainy season,
so should one practicing the vow of Indra shower his own kingdom with the objects of desire.
In this context, a restriction to a specific month is not intended;
rather, it means that for four months the rain-cloud rains continuously.
Therefore, what is being stated is that one should constantly, at all times, fill one's own kingdom with objects of desire.
One should act in such a way that those within one's own kingdom become devoted.
Just as the sun draws up water with its rays for eight months, so should he take taxes from the kingdom; for that is indeed the vow of the sun.
Just as the sun takes up even a small amount of water through its gentle heat, so too should [the king] take taxes; this is the meaning of the simile.
Just as the wind enters all beings and moves through them, so too should one enter by means of spies; for this indeed is the "Wind-like" vow.
Just as Yama restrains both the beloved and the hated when their time has come, so too must subjects be restrained by the king; for that indeed is the vow of Yama.
In the case of an offense, one should act with impartiality toward both a beloved and a hated person when exercising restraint.
Just as one who is bound by Varuṇa with his nooses is clearly seen, so should he restrain the wicked; for this is indeed the vow of Varuṇa.
Those who do not perform their duties should be restrained without exception, so that they do not flee.
Just as men rejoice upon seeing the full moon, so do the subjects rejoice in that king who observes the lunar vow (cāndravratika).
At the time of appearing before the subjects, one should be free from anger, adorned with ornaments, and have a joyful countenance;
the meaning is that one should be devoid of the distress caused by heat.
One who is endowed with majesty, radiant, always intent upon evil deeds,
and a destroyer of wicked vassals— that is remembered as the Agneya vow.
One who is extremely provocative and wicked is subject to the *āgneya* vow;
likewise are neighboring kings and ministers who are equipped with many means of action.
Just as the earth supports all beings equally,
so too is the vow of a king who sustains all beings.
The earth is the ground;
likewise, the poor, the helpless, and the lineage members are to be supported.
Employing these and other means, always vigilant,
the king should suppress thieves both within his own kingdom and in that of others.
The concluding verse:
By these divine observances,
and by others understood from worldly custom.
Even when fallen into the greatest calamity, one should not provoke the Brahmins;
for if they are angered, they can instantly destroy him along with his army and his mounts.
Even if one whose treasury is exhausted is punished by a more powerful king, he must nevertheless not seize the property of a Brāhmaṇa even in times of distress,
nor should they be provoked to anger through contempt and the like.
By whom fire was made to consume all things, the great ocean rendered undrinkable,
and the waning moon made to wax— who would not perish by provoking them?
To establish the meaning previously stated, he reiterates a world-renowned historical narrative concerning the greatness of the Brāhmaṇas;
regarding these matters, the traditional accounts (ākhyānas) are to be understood from the Mahābhārata.
Who could prosper by harming those who, when provoked, might create other worlds and world-protectors,
or turn gods into non-gods?
It destroys and obscures;

because there is no distinction among memories, even the destruction of the best ones constitutes a contraction, as was demonstrated by the sage Vyāsa when the Gāṇḍīva bow was cast aside by Yudhiṣṭhira.
Upon whom the worlds and the gods always depend,
and for whom Brahman itself is wealth— who, desiring to live, would harm them?
The three worlds are the earth and the others.
The gods depend upon the Brāhmaṇa by means of oblations;
because of his preeminence in teaching and the abundance of his ritual duties, the Brāhmaṇa is the refuge of the gods, whereas the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya are not so.
Whether ignorant or learned, a Brāhmaṇa is a great deity;
whether consecrated or unconsecrated, he is like the fire, which is a great deity.
One should not show contempt toward those who rely on their birth alone, without regard for their learning, just as one does not disregard them in acts such as giving;
and just as one would not place this [fire] at the feet, so it is with respect to the sacred fire.
Even in cremation grounds, the radiant fire is not defiled;
when offered oblations in sacrifices, it increases all the more.
The meaning of this is clear: even one of evil conduct is not to be despised; such is the sense.
Thus, even if they engage in all kinds of undesirable actions,
Brahmins are to be honored in every way, for they are the supreme divinity.
Those who persist in undesirable or forbidden acts should be punished according to the scriptures by means of mild measures, rather than by attacking them suddenly as one would other castes.
When the Kṣatriya power has become excessively overbearing in every respect toward the Brāhmaṇas, the Brāhmaṇical power alone must be its restrainer; for the Kṣatriya is born from the Brāhmaṇa.

When a Kṣatriya proceeds to oppress Brāhmaṇas, the Brāhmaṇas alone are their restrainers. When Kṣatriyas, intoxicated by the pride of wealth, act by violating the established order, they are set back onto the right path by the Brāhmaṇas through means such as prayers, burnt offerings, and curses. The reason for this is that the Kṣatra is born from the Brahman.
The origin of the Kṣatriyas from the Brāhmaṇa caste:
this is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda).
Now, it might be argued that whatever is the cause of the arising of something cannot be its destroyer;
but this is not so.
For fire arises from water, the Kṣatriya from the Brāhmaṇa, and iron from stone.
Their all-pervading fire is extinguished within their own sources.
"It is born from the waters and from the herbs and trees"—thus fire is produced from the waters alone.
Its all-pervading heat burns everything that can be burned and overcomes with its brilliance;
yet, upon reaching the waters, that heat of his is extinguished.

From stone comes iron, such as swords and the like; by it everything is pierced, yet it itself bursts apart upon contact with stone. In the same way, Kṣatriyas who desire victory everywhere are victorious, but if they behave with arrogance toward Brāhmaṇas, then they perish.
The Kṣatriya power does not prosper without the Brahmanical power, nor does the Brahmanical power increase without the Kṣatriya power;
when the Brahmanical and Kṣatriya powers are joined together, they flourish both in this world and in the next.
As for that sovereignty which is devoid of Brahmins—a kingdom where the ministers, domestic priests, and others are not Brahmins—how can there be prosperity therein?
Likewise, how can even the Brahmins, when dependent upon the king, obtain success?
Only when both are joined together do they conquer the world.
The words *brahman* and *kṣatra* denote the castes (*jāti*) of Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya respectively.
Having bestowed upon the Brahmins all the wealth arising from fines,
and having established his son in the kingdom, he should seek his end in battle.
But when he is overcome by old age, having accomplished all his duties, then, provided there is wealth or property, he should give to the Brahmins the entire amount arising from fines.
It has been stated that the wealth of those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin) is to be offered to Varuṇa;
it must not be seized by the king.
But other fines belong to the king.
Since there are many purposes for visible and invisible matters, and since it is the time of departure, all this [wealth] is to be employed [for that purpose].
Others, however, explain that the mention of "fines" (daṇḍa) is intended to indicate taxes, tolls, and so forth as well.
That being the case, it would mean that "he should give away his entire property.
This implies that everything except vehicles, weapons, land, and servants must be given.
However, if this were the interpretation, the statement "having secured the kingdom for his son" would not be consistent.
For it is not possible for one who lacks a treasury to exercise royal authority;
he should seek his end in battle. He should engage in combat by sacrificing his own life.
If, by some chance, he should not encounter battle in his final state, then he should abandon his body by means of fire, water, or other such methods;
however, the attainment of the excellence of the fruit occurs in battle.
*Samāsañjanam* means mounting or placing upon.
Acting thus and ever intent upon the duties of kingship, the monarch should employ all his servants in deeds that are beneficial to the worlds.

Conducting himself and dwelling thus, always disciplined and devoted to the duties of a king as taught in the scriptures, he should employ all his servants in what is beneficial for the various worlds—that is, for those within his own kingdom.
This eternal rule of action for the king has been declared in its entirety;
one should likewise know this rule of action for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra in due order.
By this first verse, the duties of the king are summarized as ending with the purification of thorns;
by the second, they cause one to recall what was stated regarding the treatment of Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
But a Vaiśya, having undergone the purificatory rites and taken a wife,
should be constantly engaged in agriculture and the like, as well as in the protection of cattle.
One who has undergone the purificatory rites, been initiated, and performed marriage;
"vārtā" refers to the collection of activities at the times to be described hereafter;
he should be appointed to that.
Just as the science of economics was taught in the work of Bṛhaspati.
For Prajāpati, having created cattle, entrusted them to the Vaiśya;
and he entrusted all subjects to the Brāhmaṇa and the King.
The explanatory passage (arthavāda) shows that the protection of cattle by a Vaiśya is not merely for the sake of livelihood, but also for the sake of dharma.
But how can the unseen (adṛṣṭa) be mentioned when the seen (dṛṣṭa) is present?
It is because it is a formal entrustment (niyogaparidāna), meaning: "Just as you must protect the subjects, so too must you protect [the cattle] by way of this rule."
The authority of the Kṣatriya has been established as consisting in the protection of the subjects;

that of the Brāhmaṇa consists in the universal authority [to act] through the instruction of penances and so forth, and through recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth, based on the principle that "from the Sun rain is born.
This is stated for the sake of illustration.
In the same way, for the Vaiśya, his duty consists precisely of cattle-rearing and so forth.
A Vaiśya should have no desire [to think], "I shall not tend cattle";
if the Vaiśya so desires, they must by no means be tended by anyone else.
But surely, what desire is there for the sake of life?
As it has been said: "Even if it is unseen, it is nevertheless dependent upon the seen, just as facing east is [dependent] upon eating.
In that case, how can it be said that "there should be no desire on the part of a Vaiśya"?
For one who does not desire to eat does not incur transgression.
This is true; however, it is stated in order to make known that animal husbandry is superior to agriculture and the like.
Some believe that all these [occupations] are restrictive in nature and yield equal results.
In that case, if the results were equal, even one who lacks desire for it would have to perform another action while desiring yet another.
However, when [the former] is more excellent in quality than others, then one should subsist by means of that; there is no engagement in another action.
Therefore, one should live depending upon that alone.
One should know the relative value and worth of gems, pearls, corals, metals, woven textiles, perfumes, and liquids.

By the word "loha" (metal), he means copper, iron, and bell-metal. Regarding the strength or weakness of the price—that is, the deficiency or excess of the price—it depends on place and time: in what place is this highly valued, or in what [place] is it of low value?
The same applies to time as well.
One should know the method of sowing seeds, as well as the defects and virtues of the soil; one should also understand the application of measures and all the applications of the balance.
One should understand this sowing: "this seed is sown extensively," "this is sown densely," and so forth.
These are the qualities and defects such as: "this seed sprouts in this field," "this does not," or "this bears fruit abundantly.
*Droṇa*, *śūrpa*, *āḍhaka*, and so on are specific measures; those [measures] which are measured by hand are their applications.
He should consider the worth and worthlessness of merchandise, the merits and defects of various regions,
the profit and loss on commodities, and the breeding of livestock.

By the word *bhāṇḍa*, saleable goods such as cloth and skins are meant. Regarding their quality or lack thereof: that which remains undeteriorated over time is "substantial" (*sāra*), while the opposite is "insubstantial" (*asāra*). Furthermore, there are the merits and defects of regions, such as: "In this region rice is abundant; in this region barley [is abundant]; in this region such is the custom; such is the character of the local people," and so forth.
"And by using this kind of fodder and this kind of salt at this time, the cattle will thrive."
He should know the wages of servants, the various languages of men, the methods of storing goods, and their purchase and sale.
He should know the wages for servants, slaves, messengers, and so forth, including cowherds, shepherds, high officials, and others— specifically, how much their pay is—
and he should understand the dialects of regions such as Mālava, Magadha, and Draviḍa, knowing that in these countries people pronounce things in this manner for such meanings.
"This substance is to be stored in this way; it transforms in this way; it is covered in this way; it is joined with this; it is sold for this much.
And he should exert the utmost effort to increase his wealth through righteous means, and he should diligently provide food for all living beings.
The meaning is that much food must be given;
otherwise, one would be punished by the king.
It is for this purpose that it is stated here.
And this belongs to one who possesses great wealth.
For a Śūdra, however, the supreme dharma for attaining the highest good is indeed the service of illustrious householders who are Brahmins learned in the Vedas.
By the term "of the illustrious," virtuous conduct is indicated; service indeed means personal attendance,
and its practice brings about the highest good.
Pure, devoted to excellent service, gentle in speech, free from egoism,
and always taking refuge in Brahmins and the like, one attains a superior birth.
By means of purity through water and clay, by the restraint of the senses,
and by serving the superior members of the three castes with gentle speech— meaning one who does not speak harshly due to being tainted by the study of logic and other such treatises—
one attains a superior birth as a Brāhmaṇa or the like; this is the meaning.
The purpose has been clearly stated.

Furthermore, by the mention of "resorting to a Brāhmaṇa," it follows that for one who has resorted to another and serves others as well, this [practice] is indeed *dharma*, provided it is not in contradiction with that [primary duty].
This auspicious rule of action for the social classes in times of non-distress has been declared;
now learn, in due order, that which pertains to them in times of distress.
And the purpose has been clearly stated.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Thus ends the ninth chapter of the Commentary on Manu, composed by Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi, son of Bhaṭṭa Vīrasvāmin.
Now begins the tenth chapter: The three twice-born castes, remaining steadfast in their own duties, may study [this law];
however, it is the settled rule that among them, only the Brāhmaṇa may expound it, and not the other two.

"The entire Veda, along with its secret portions, must be mastered by the twice-born"—thus is the rule for self-study (*svādhyāya*) prescribed for the three castes for the purpose of acquisition. Furthermore, the non-forgetting of what has been acquired is also prescribed for those in all stages of life (*āśrama*):
"One should be constantly devoted to self-study, and likewise one should constantly examine the scriptures."

The *śāstra* is indeed the Veda alone, for it is called *śāstra* primarily because it instructs (*śāsana*) and because it propounds injunctions not known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
That alone is the *śāstra*;
elsewhere, the term *śāstra* is used due to a commonality with the composition of a literary work.
Likewise, one should study the Veda regularly; [for] "neglecting the Veda" (*brahmojjhatā*) means reviling the Veda.

As for the *brahmayajña* (sacrifice to Brahman), it is accomplished by studying even a single *sūkta*, a *sāman*, an *anuvāka*, a *khaṇḍa*, or a single *kāṇḍikā* throughout one's life. By that, the constant recollection of the Veda (*brahmasmaraṇa*) is not required.
Thus, because this injunction lacks a [previously established] object, its purpose is merely to provide a restatement (*anuvāda*).

The phrase "a Brāhmaṇa should teach them, not the other two" is intended to exclude the teaching of the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya. But is it not the case that, by the rule "teaching belongs to the Brāhmaṇa," etc., teaching is already unattainable for those two?
This is not a fault;
since the act of providing a livelihood is explicitly stated in the scripture, it is understood that the cessation [of teaching] applies only for that purpose.

However, this [verse] removes the doubt that the gift of knowledge for the sake of dharma might still exist even for those two [the king and the Vaiśya], as such a gift certainly does exist for them as well.
Now, if there is a general prohibition,
then this is stated as something already established for the purpose of generating the application of the definition of a "kinsman" (*jñāti*).

And by doing so, the connection that should be followed— namely, that "this [definition] must not be abandoned"— will be maintained, as well as the conventional usage regarding Vaiśyas and Śūdras and the possibility of mixed castes.
Someone says:
"Teaching (*adhyāpana*) is the instruction in the pronunciation of words, whereas exposition (*pravacana*) is also the explanation of their meaning.
Therefore, because they are distinct, the cessation of teaching does not entail the cessation of explaining its meaning; hence, there is a separate mention of 'instruction' (*upadeśa*)."
But surely, the word "Veda" does not occur here;
how then can the act of recitation have that as its object? Or perhaps this term "recitation" is said to refer even to secular prose and verse.
It is said:
if that were so, the injunction would have an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha);
consequently, it would follow that one must postulate a qualified subject (adhikāra), and there would be a postulation of a fundamental basis (mūlakalpanā).
However, since this Smṛti has been explained as having its source in perception, there is no risk of the undesirable consequence of postulating an unseen source.
Although "the twice-born" already establishes that there are three castes, the phrase "three castes" is used merely to fill out the meter.
The same applies to the expression "established in their own duties."
A Brāhmaṇa should know the means of livelihood for all according to the rule;
he should declare them to others and should himself likewise abide by them.

"And one should not teach him the Dharma"—this means that no instruction on the Dharma should be given to a Śūdra; this is the general rule. The exception to this is that the duties regarding his livelihood (*vṛttidharma*) should be taught. "Livelihood" refers to the maintenance of the body and the family; one should know the means for that purpose.
"He should teach them to all others"—
the plural number is used for the purpose of including Śūdras;
and he himself should likewise behave in that same manner.
The meaning is that the rules of conduct thus taught are to be practiced.
Due to his distinctiveness, the excellence of his origin, his observance of restrictive rules,
and the distinction of his refinement, the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of the social classes.
But what is the reason that only the Brāhmaṇa is authorized by virtue of being the subject under discussion, and not the Kṣatriyas and others as well?
Because [the author] recites this encouragement as a supplement [to the rule]:
"On account of his preeminence" (vaiśeṣyāt), meaning because of his distinction, that is to say, because of his superiority in qualities.
Now he states the superiority [of Brahmins]: "Because of the excellence of their origin" (*prakṛti-śraiṣṭhyāt*).
This is said because they are born from the highest limb.
"Origin" (*prakṛti*) means the cause.

And because of the maintenance of a restrictive rule (*niyama*)— namely, the prohibition against drinking intoxicants— it is this very restriction that is intended. Alternatively, the *snātaka* vows, such as the carrying of a bamboo staff and so forth, belong to the Brāhmaṇa alone.

Furthermore, a "distinction" (viśeṣa) regarding ritual refinement (saṃskāra) is intended as a restriction; the vows of a *snātaka* constitute such a distinction, as seen in passages such as "with [mantras] that reach the heart," and because initiation (*upanayana*) and other rites are prescribed for the child alone.
However, for the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya, this occurs after childhood, at the ages of eleven and twelve respectively.
For this reason, the Brāhmaṇa is the lord and ruler of the social classes (*varṇas*).
What, then, are these so-called *varṇas*?
Is the word *varṇa* a term denoting human caste (*jāti*)?
He says: No.
The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya are the three twice-born castes;
the fourth is the once-born Śūdra, and there is no fifth.
The four castes (*varṇas*) range from the Brāhmaṇas down to the Śūdras.
Others, however, such as the Barbaras, Kaivartas, and so forth, are of mixed origin (*saṃkīrṇayoni*), as will be described later.
Among these, three of the four are twice-born (*dvijāti*), because the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) is prescribed for them.
The Śūdra is of one birth (*ekajāti*).

For he has no initiation (*upanayana*), because the rule for initiation specifies the connection with particular castes, stating: "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year, a Kṣatriya in the eleventh, and a Vaiśya in the twelfth.
They do not mention the Śūdra at any time.

Now, one might argue that since no specific time is mentioned, let the initiation of a Śūdra be considered to occur at an indefinite time. This would be the case if the originative injunction for initiation were stated independently and in a general sense. However, these [passages] are connected with specific castes and times; they must therefore be either statements of occasion (*nimitta*) or mere commendatory praises (*stuti*).
But it does not arise separately;
therefore, by the power of which means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) could its introduction be made at an indefinite time?
If this is so, then what is the point of this [statement] that "the fourth is of one birth" (*ekajāti*)?
True.

This is for the purpose of dispelling a mere doubt; for it is suspected that there might be the application of [the rite] without mantras and without a fixed time, based on the statement "it is not faulty if [done] without mantras.
But surely this sentence belongs to the procedure for the *pākayajña* sacrifices, since it is heard in their proximity; having fulfilled its purpose there, it ought not to apply elsewhere.
For this very reason, it was stated that [the objection] is merely a doubt;
however, from the perspective of ultimate reality, the verse is intended solely for the purpose of establishing the rules of conventional usage.
Among wives of equal caste who have not lost their virginity,
those born in the direct order [of castes] should be known as belonging to that same caste.

Furthermore, what indeed are these so-called Brahmins and the rest? For their mutual distinction cannot be ascertained; for universals (jāti) are understood only through dependence upon individuals (vyakti).
Furthermore, individual instances (*vyakti*) are not capable of communicating their mutual distinctions unless they are perceived as having specific configurations of their own parts.

Nor is there a difference in vocal form (*vāk-ākāra-bheda*) among Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and so forth, comparable to that between a cow and a horse, by which they might become objects of sight through inherence in a visible form (*rūpa-samavāya*).
Nor are they accessible to other types of action through differences in smell, taste, and so forth, such as those found in melted ghee or oil.
Nor can distinctions be determined by such attributes as purity of conduct or tawny hair, because these are observed to be intermingled everywhere; furthermore,
social convention depends upon individuals,
and since individuals are prone to deception, no ultimate establishment of reality can be reached through them.
Therefore, the definition of caste (jāti) is stated:
among all social classes (varṇas), this is the characteristic of caste—that those born of wives who are equal and of the same caste, having been duly wedded, are to be known by that very caste.
Generally, whatever the caste of the mother and father may be, that same caste is to be understood for the offspring born of a wedded wife.

Because the term "wife" (*patnī*) is a relative word, the one who has married her—the father—is thereby understood. Consequently, he who is born from that very man by that very woman becomes a member of that same caste.

Furthermore, the inclusion of the phrase "one whose womb is unimpaired" (*akṣatayoni*) excludes the status of being a wife (*patnītva*) on account of a remarriage sacrament (*punarvivāhasaṃskāra*), as well as [the status of being a wife] for the mothers of the *sahoḍha* and *kānīna* sons.
But is it not the case that these women have no marriage sacrament (*saṃskāra*) at all, because of the statement: "The mantras pertaining to the taking of the hand [are used] for maidens"?

Even though one might infer a scriptural sacrament from hearing the word "marriage" in the phrase "that embryo belongs to the husband," since that term merely expresses the fact of acquisition, there is no recognition of a prescribed rite.
Therefore, the verbal root functions in the sense of mere acceptance; the meaning is "of the one who accepts."

The meaning is that she belongs to him alone by whom she was taken after deceiving her father and others, and from him comes the son; this is because there is no rite of consecration for a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman).
It is recited [in the texts] that "if she should be one whose virginity is intact";
and even in the case of a woman who has gone and returned (*gatapratyāgatā*), the husband is declared [as the owner] due to the recognition of the word "again" (*punaḥ*).
Nor is there any authority for them to perform [the rite] together with those [wives];
the term "patnī" (wife) applies only in connection with a sacrifice. Therefore, the expression "akṣatayoni" (one whose womb is unviolated) is redundant.
In this context, some earlier authorities read "among women" (*nārīṣu*) as a synonym for the word "wife" (*patnī*); however, that too is of no consequence.
For if only the term "one whose womb is intact" (*akṣatayoni*) were used, then those born even to women who have not undergone the sacramental rites would be considered members of that caste.

By the reading of the word "wife," which is sanctioned by scriptural injunction, it is understood that she who has been consecrated by the ritual procedure and brought to the state of being a wife is intended.

However, those who are approached while still virgins remain *akṣatayoni* (virgins with an intact womb), but they do not become wives (*patnī*). Therefore, the purpose of the term *akṣatayoni* must be stated.
It is said in reply:
As for what was stated— that they are not wives because of the absence of connection with a sacrifice— if they were to be married, that itself would constitute a sacrifice;
moreover, in that case as well, there is indeed a sacrifice involving Pūṣan, Varuṇa, and Aryaman,
and the words *yāga* and *yajña* have the same meaning.
Therefore, they must indeed be wives.

It is not logical to say that they are not wives simply because, being non-maidens, they are ineligible for marriage. Consequently, since [the rule] would otherwise be purposeless, the purpose of the term "one whose womb is unviolated" (*akṣatayoni*) is stated.
In common usage, the word *patnī* (wife) is seen to be applied even when there is no connection to a sacrifice through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as in "the washerman’s wife.
Similarly, elsewhere, the word *gṛhiṇī* (housewife) is used for women who are kept mistresses;
that term, too, refers specifically to a wife, yet it is applied there as well due to some similarity in their status.
Although it is not logical to resort to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) when a primary sense is available, nevertheless, acting as a friend to those of dull intellect, he dispels their mere doubt.
What indeed is not doubted by those of deluded minds?
The mention of "conformity" (ānulomya) is for the sake of what follows.
As for those who read "they are indeed those very same [beings]," their meaning is also that they belong to that same class (*tajjātīya*).
To this it is replied: what is the basis of authority for this recollection of the authors of the Smṛtis?
Because it does not have the nature of an action, it is not equivalent to the instruction on dharma and adharma;
furthermore, it has been stated that there is no other means of valid cognition [for it].
If it were based on another Smṛti, the consequence of a "blind tradition" (andhaparaṃparā) would follow, as shown in the *Pramāṇaśloka*.
It is said:
the very usage of the elders is the root, just like the traditional rules for grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*).
But has it not been stated that this [usage] is faulty?

For this very reason, the restrictive Smṛtis are fruitful; it cannot be said that the recollection of those who are highly proficient is otherwise. Those established in the Śāstras are well-known to be more authoritative.
And it is possible that their root is beginningless linguistic convention (*anādivyavahāra*).
According to the view of some, even direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is possible for those whose lineage and caste have been determined through such memory (*smṛti*).
This has been explained in detail in the *Smṛtiviveka*.
But is it not the case that in another Smṛti there is no such distinction?
For it says: "From men of the same caste, upon women of the same caste, are born those of the same lineage; through blameless marriages, sons are born who increase the progeny."
By the first half [of the verse], caste (*jāti*) is indicated; by the latter half, the capacity for increasing the lineage of those born from marriages such as the Brāhma and others is shown.
In that context, regarding the phrase "from men of the same class (*savarṇa*) upon women of the same class (*savarṇāsu*)," the word *patnī* (wife) does not occur here.
How is it that it does not occur?
"Whether this rule is intended to apply only to cognizable things or not— let it be so or not— the specific rule is stronger than a general rule;
moreover, direct perception is stronger than non-perception."
Since it is possible that a particular feature was not seen by one person but was seen by another,
the recollection of an authoritative person (*abhiyukta*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because its basis is possible.
But is this not a non-definition, as it lacks pervasion (*avyāpti*)?

For by this [definition], Brāhmaṇahood does not belong to those born of a pregnant bride (sahoḍha), the son of an unmarried girl (kānīna), the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava), and so forth, nor to the kuṇḍa and golaka, nor to the son begotten on another's wife (kṣetraja).
If it is argued that these [categories] are simply unintended [by the definition], then what is their caste?

Furthermore, since the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* lack Brahminhood, they would have no possibility of being invited to a *śrāddha*, making the prohibition [of them] redundant; moreover, it would contradict other Smṛti texts, such as: "This rule was declared by me for sons of the same caste."
Furthermore, that which is the definition is itself the defined.
The defined is that which is not yet known, while the definition is that which is already known.
For example, when there is doubt as to who Devadatta is, [one identifies him by saying: "He is the one with the armlet, the earring, the broad chest, and the rounded arms."

In this case, however, it would be just as if someone were to say, "What is a crow? and the answer given were, "One born from a crow. Similarly, [the question] "Who is a Brāhmaṇa? is answered by "One born from a Brāhmaṇa. For even in the case of the progenitor, Brāhmaṇahood is not established, and there is a contradiction with logic (*nyāya*);
for in the world, one born from a male of the same class and a female of the same class becomes a member of that same class.
Just as a cow [begets] a cow from a cow, or a horse [begets] a horse from a mare;
regarding this, it is said: as for what was asked, "What is their genus (jāti)?"—what need is there for another genus? They are, first of all, human beings.
And they are entitled to the duties of men by virtue of their unappropriated specific caste, as well as by virtue of being sons and so forth through ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and the like.
Furthermore, all have the entitlement to giving.
But surely, without the instruction of a distinction, practical usage cannot be established, since the human species is common to all?
This is incorrect.
Every individual possesses their own specific name according to each person, such as Devadatta or Yajñadatta.
Furthermore, if a designation based on a relationship must be made, one is designated precisely as "born of an unmarried woman" (kānīna) or "born of a pregnant bride" (sahoḍha).

If it is argued that this [caste] is merely a general form because it exists within the four varṇas, then the designation "Devadatta’s son by a maiden" and so forth will be made by means of the progenitor.
Therefore, it is irrelevant to say how the designation is made.
In that case, all dharmas are understood with respect to the four varṇas and those belonging to the intermediate castes.
In this context, "plurality" refers to the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa.
Nor is there even a single caste among these, because this definition applies to all castes.
Just as one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Brāhmaṇī mother who has been wedded by him is a Brāhmaṇa, so too are those born of Kṣatriya and other fathers and mothers of the same caste.
And in the absence of all particularities, how could there be a universal?
For indeed, in the absence of all particularities such as *śiṃśapā* and so forth, the possibility of "treeness" does not exist;
moreover, there are those born from within [the caste] through both direct and inverse unions.

Among them, those born in the natural order (*anuloma*) belong to the mother's caste, whereas those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*) are devoid of the [Vedic] Dharma, with the exception of non-violence and so forth.
And all of them are specifically designated by their own particular names;
yet even the name "caste" does not exist among them there.
In that regard, what are those factors by which these [persons] would be governed?
And where is that statement which would govern them?
For there exists no rule of Dharma based on a distinction of caste.
It is because they are authorized by the treatises as belonging to all castes and intermediate classes.

It is said in response: as for the mention of the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*) in relation to non-violence and the other virtues, that is intended merely as an illustration of human beings in general; for even though there is an authorization for those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), the term functions in its primary sense [of the four castes].
On the contrary, it is capable of indicating only the status of another species as a companion, and cannot remain in an intermediate state;
we shall explain this very point further on.
Furthermore, there is this [text]: "But all those born of transgression are recorded as having the same dharma as Śūdras."
Degradation (*apadhvaṃsa*) is the loss of ritual purity (*asaṃskāra*).
It is of eight kinds, as stated in the passage beginning with "by the transgression of the castes" (*varṇānām vyabhicāreṇa*).
Transgression (*vyabhicāra*) consists of approaching the wives of others among those of the same caste.
We shall state something else:
therefore, even though they do not possess the status of caste (varṇa), their entitlement [to the rites] is based solely on scriptural injunction (vācanika).
As for the Kṣatriya, however, his status is determined solely by the caste of his mother, because of the observation of indicative marks (liṅga).
Regarding the son of a *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*, the specific duty is heard [in the scripture] as "by agreement.
Furthermore, a different rule for him is seen in other Vedic texts as well.
Therefore, one of the same caste as the Brāhmaṇa and others shall receive an equal share from his paternal uncle; thus, one should deal with him according to that law.
And that is not appropriate in the rule as stated;
for then this [person] would be following the dharma of a Śūdra.
Since it has been stated that wealth is intended for sacrifice, how could he possibly have a share of it?
The *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* are indeed *kṣetraja* [sons];
and the conduct of the learned is likewise.
Pāṇḍu, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Vidura, being *kṣetraja*, belonged to the caste of their mothers.
Therefore, the prohibition regarding the *śrāddha* is appropriate.

Furthermore, even one who has fallen from his caste (*patita*) is prohibited therein, since, being excluded from all religious duties (*dharma*), there is no possibility whatsoever of his eligibility [for the rite].

As for the other *smṛti* text stating "among those of the same caste," that should be explained either as a restatement of what has already been said—applying it according to the circumstances—or as referring specifically to the *kāyaputra* (the son of the body).
And as for that characteristic which is well-known, is the meaning of "brahmin" not indeed established by worldly convention?
Wherever the word "brahmin" and so forth is employed, the statement is made there for the purpose of excluding [other] degraded states.
This alone is the defining characteristic of caste (jāti) with respect to mother and father.
Nor is there an infinite regress, because saṃsāra is beginningless.
However, a contradiction with the principle under discussion would arise if these classes were directly apprehended by perceptual determination;
rather, they must exist according to their characteristic of being remembered, as they are recalled.

Or, just as words such as "Vasiṣṭha" and others are employed with respect to those whose meanings are known through an uninterrupted tradition of memory even without a presently perceived property of lineage—serving as the basis for linguistic usage in such expressions as "the Brāhmaṇas who are Vasiṣṭhas" or "the Vāsiṣṭhas are listening"—so too should this be viewed.

Just as, while Brāhmaṇahood is common to all, specific distinctions such as "these are Bhṛgus," "these are Vatsas," or "these are Bhāradvājas" have memory as their sole authority, in the same way, while humanity is common to all, the linguistic usage that "these are Brāhmaṇas" and "these are Kṣatriyas" is likewise established.
Furthermore, those who have stated that the Jābāla Śruti constitutes an indicative mark (liṅga) cite it as follows: "Satyakāma Jābāla asked his mother, 'Of what lineage am I?
She replied to him thus: 'In my youth, while I was a wandering servant, I conceived you;
I do not know that [your lineage].'"
Having heard this, he went to Hāridrumata Gautama.
He said to him, "I wish to live the life of a religious student under you.
He replied as follows.
"What is your lineage?
He replied:
"I asked my mother, and that mother spoke to me, 'In your youth... and so forth.
"Gautama, no one who is not a Brahmin would be entitled to say this. Fetch the fuel, my dear; I shall lead you [to the teacher]."
This is its meaning:
"In my youth, I was united with many men;
I do not know by whom you were fathered."

Gautama, however, concluded from the truth of her words that he was born of a Brāhmaṇa woman; therefore, he initiated him. From this, we might think that even those born of unmarried women of the same caste are of that same caste. But this is of no consequence, because [the sage] said, "I took you [as my wife] in my youth."
It is said that in youth memory does not become firm, because the mind in youth is full of intense longing.

Furthermore, while I was serving as an attendant for the sake of my female attendants, being oppressed by hunger, I wandered about much and did not remain in one place; therefore, I have no memory of my husband’s clan name (*gotra*). Thus it is established that those born of a wife of the same caste belong to that same caste.
Even for Gautama, there was no realization that "this man is a Brāhmaṇa" based on those words;
rather, he already knew him to be a Brāhmaṇa,
though he did not know his lineage (gotra).
By means of the question regarding lineage (*gotra*), the question regarding conduct (*caraṇa*) is to be understood.
In that regard, there is a distinction in the initiation (*upanayana*);
however, there is no purpose for the initiation based on a distinction of lineage.

But it is not as some say: "This is a question about caste because of one's noble birth; I shall understand the caste from the lineage itself, for a direct question about caste would be impertinence."
Sons begotten by twice-born men on women born immediately after them in the social order are said to be similar [to their fathers], yet they are censured due to the defect of their mothers.

Those sons who are born in the immediate, uninterrupted [order] according to the natural sequence should be known as similar, but not of that same caste. For example, [a son born] from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother, or from a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother;
they are similar to them, but not those very [same castes].
The reason for this is that they are censured due to the defects of their mothers;
because they take after their mothers, they are superior to them on the mother's side but inferior to them on the father's side.
Since the term "by the twice-born" (*dvijaiḥ*) is used in the plural and the defect of the mother is specifically mentioned, this applies to those born in the direct order (*ānulomya*).
Since, in the case of inverse order (*prātilomya*), [the offspring] is taken from the father's side because [the mother] is of a lower caste than the father,
the mention of "in the direct order" (*ānulomya*) in the preceding verse— which was stated for the sake of what follows— is redundant here. Therefore, it is taught in the subsequent verses.
This is the eternal rule for those born of women one degree lower;
one should know this righteous rule to apply to those born of women two or three degrees lower.
He restates the meaning expressed by the first half-verse; by the second, he provides a summary of what is to be said.
"Separated by two or one":
for a Brāhmaṇa, a Śūdra woman is separated by two [classes], and a Vaiśya woman is separated by one.
The verse is not particularly purposeful.
From a Brāhmaṇa on a Vaiśya maiden is born one named Ambaṣṭha;
from a Śūdra maiden is born a Niṣāda, who is called a Pāraśava.

A Vaiśya woman is one degree removed from a Brāhmaṇa; the son born of her is an Ambaṣṭha, who in another Smṛti is called a Bhṛjjakaṇṭha. From a Śūdra maiden who is two degrees removed, [the sons] are a Niṣāda and a Pāraśava.
The word *niṣāda* also applies to one born of a *pratiloma* (inverse) caste. Commentators explain that the mention of "a maiden" (*kanyā*) is intended as an illustration for women in general;
the meaning is "in a Vaiśya woman."
In this way, it should be understood in all cases.
From a Kṣatriya father and a Śūdra mother is born a being named Ugra, who possesses the physical form of both a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra and whose conduct and pastimes are cruel.
Conduct and behavior consist of bodily activity and verbal engagement;
these two become cruel in his case.
This is a descriptive restatement of their inherent nature.
The word *vapuḥ* denotes intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) alone;
because it arises from both classes [of causes], it possesses the characteristics of both.
These six are recorded as base-born (apasada): those born from a Brahmin in the three [lower] castes, from a Kshatriya in two castes, and from a Vaishya in one caste.
In this context, the first three quarters [of the verse] are merely a restatement;
however, the fourth quarter is intended to designate the *apasadās* (outcasts).
These should be understood as the *apasadās* born from women of the next or the second lower caste among the members of the three *varṇas*.
The *apasadās* are censured because they have fallen short of the fruit expected from a son, in comparison with sons of the same caste.
From a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇa maiden is born a Sūta by birth;
from a Vaiśya father, sons known as Māgadha and Vaideha are born to the wives of kings and Brāhmaṇas respectively.
The previous rule applies to the direct order (ānulomya);
however, this one is stated for the inverse order (prātilomya).
The mention of "maiden" (kanyā) has its meaning already explained.
From a Vaiśya, the Māgadha and Vaideha [are born] according to their respective order: the Māgadha from a Kṣatriya woman and the Vaideha from a Brāhmaṇa woman.

From a Śūdra, on women of the Vaiśya, Rājanya, and Brāhmaṇa castes, are born the Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla— the lowest among men— through the intermixture of the social orders (varṇasaṃkara).
In this case as well, the correspondence is strictly according to the order of enumeration.

Although the designation "vaiśyarājanyā" (the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya woman) refers to the generic classes, the feminine gender is understood through the force of the context, just as in the expressions "deer's milk" (*mṛgakṣīram*) and "hen's egg" (*kukkuṭāṇḍam*). The feminine suffix was not employed here merely for the sake of metrical convenience.
But when there is an interval of one caste, as prescribed by tradition, the Ambaṣṭha and Ugra are born through natural order;
likewise, the Kṣattṛ and Vaidehaka are born through the inverse order.
From a Brāhmaṇa on a Vaiśya woman one step apart is born an Ambaṣṭha; from a Kṣatriya on a Śūdra woman is born an Ugra.
These two are born in the direct order (ānulomyena).
Likewise, in the inverse order (prātilomyena), from a Śūdra on a Kṣatriya woman is born a Kṣattṛ, and from a Vaiśya on a Brāhmaṇī woman is born a Vaideha.
The two are equal in activities such as dwelling and so forth,
but not in sacrifices and the like;
one is a Caṇḍāla, born in the inverse order, and untouchable.
And just as in the verse of Divākīrti, bathing occurs only upon touching him and not upon touching others who are of inverse birth (*pratiloma*);

so too, for the Sūta, Māgadha, and Āyogava—who are born from immediate unions—their connection with touch and other such acts is established by the maxim of "the stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpika*), just like that of the Caṇḍāla.
Those sons of the twice-born who are born of women immediately following [their own caste] in order are designated by the name "immediate" (anantara), on account of the defect of their mothers.

Just as [the offspring] of a Brāhmaṇa from a Kṣatriya woman and a Vaiśya woman [are so designated], likewise, those born of a Kṣatriya from both [of these two women] are called by the name of the next lower [caste]. "Next lower" (anantara) means a caste that follows in the natural order (anuloma); for them, it is the same as the mother's caste—this is the meaning.
The inclusion of the term "next lower" (anantara) is not intended to be restrictive.

For this very reason, he says "due to the mother's defect. They are not defiled by the superiority of the father's caste; therefore, even though there is a mixture of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*), they are recorded as belonging to the mother's caste according to the scriptural injunctions.
It is thus stated that the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) must be performed for them;
for, without this specific statement, the sacramental rites would not be obtained for them—just as in the case of a mule (*aśvatara*), because it belongs to a different species (*jātyantara*).
However, when the mother's caste is declared by this statement, there is no fault.
From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of an Ugra is born one named Āvṛta; from the daughter of an Ambaṣṭha is born an Ābhīra; and from the daughter of an Āyogava is born a Dhigvaṇa.
The Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla—the lowest of men—are born from a Śūdra in the reverse order; these are the three base-born (apasada) sons.
From a Vaiśya are born the Māgadha and the Vaideha; from a Kṣatriya is born the Sūta alone. These others are also born in the inverse order, and they are the three base-born (apasada) castes.
One born from a Niṣāda father and a Śūdra mother is by birth a Pukkasa;
however, one born from a Śūdra father and a Niṣāda mother is known as a Kukkuṭaka.

This Niṣāda mentioned in this verse is not the one born from a Brāhmaṇa and a Śūdra woman who was previously described; rather, it is the one born in the inverse order (pratiloma) who will be mentioned hereafter, for the context concerns those born in the inverse order, and the Niṣāda caste is well known as being born in such an inverse manner. Likewise, from a Śūdra and a Niṣāda woman, a Kukkuṭaka is born.
One born from a Kṣattṛ father and an Ugrā mother is known as a Śvapāka;
one begotten by a Vaidehaka on an Ambaṣṭhā woman is called a Veṇa.
Women are born in the natural order (anuloma), while men are born in the inverse order (pratiloma); when these two unite, the offspring are of the inverse castes, namely the Śvapāka and the Veṇa.
Those sons whom twice-born men beget on women of their own caste, but who are devoid of the sacred observances and excluded from the Sāvitrī, one should designate as Vrātyas.
These are not [the same as] those born from inverse unions of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*);
therefore, they are mentioned in this rule.

Those whom the twice-born (*dvijāti*) beget upon women of their own caste, yet who do not observe Vedic vows, are not students of sacred knowledge (*abrahmacārin*), have fallen away from the *Sāvitrī*, and are devoid of initiation (*upanayana*), they should then be designated as *vrātyas*.
The construction "they produce those who are without vows" is not intended here;
for neither those who observe vows nor those who do not produce [children], since the rite of initiation (upanayana) is prescribed for those who have already been born.
This is a restatement of the characteristics of the *vrātya* as previously mentioned, for the purpose of what is to be said next.

As for this reading, "One should designate those whom they procreate from a woman who has not observed her vows as Vrātyas," that is incorrect, because it contradicts the previously stated definition of a Vrātya.
From a Vratya Brahmin is born the evil-natured Bhṛjjakaṇṭaka,
as well as the Āvantya, the Vāṭadhāna, the Puṣpadha, and the Śaikha.

The phrase "in women of their own caste" (*svavarṇāsu*) is carried over from the preceding verse, because the female sex is not explicitly mentioned here and because its inclusion is necessarily implied.
In another *Smṛti*, one born to a Brāhmaṇa from a Vaiśya woman is recorded as a *Bhṛjjakaṇṭaka*;
therefore, [the author] specifies [the subject] as "one of sinful nature."
For he is not evil-minded because he is compliant;
whereas this one, born from a *vrātya* who is himself unrefined (*asaṃskṛta*), is rightly censured due to his lack of qualification.
Furthermore, synonymous terms do not differ in their usage merely because they are established in different regions.
But it has been explained by the ancients that these are the names of his sons and grandsons:
Bhṛjjakaṇṭaka was born of a Brāhmaṇī woman,
and Āvantya was born of an Āvantī woman.
In that very [lineage] was Vāṭadhāna; from Vāṭadhāna came Puṣpaśekhara;
and so it continued for those who followed.
From a Vratya of the Rajanya caste are born the Jhalla, the Malla, and the Licchivi;
as well as the Nata, the Karana, the Khasa, and the Dravidian.
From a Vrātya Vaiśya are born the Sudhanvan, the Ācārya, the Kāruṣa,
the Vijanman, the Maitra, and the Sātvata.
Those of such a kind are to be understood as being well-known by these very designations.
Through sexual misconduct, through marrying those who should not be married,
and through the abandonment of one's own duties, the intermixture of castes arises.

Adultery is sexual intercourse with the wife of another. That [occurs] with women of the same caste who belong to others—whether they are born in the direct (anuloma) or inverse (pratiloma) order—and whether they are married or unmarried, [if one acts] himself. Unlawful marriage is the marrying of a woman who should not be married.
Sisters, nephews, and others are ineligible for marriage because they are not born from the womb (*ayoni*).
The "abandonment of one's own duties" refers to the neglect of rites such as the initiation (*upanayana*) and the study of the Vedas.
Some maintain that even those who follow the profession of a Kṣatriya and so forth are described here as being excluded only if they lack sons or descendants.
I shall now describe in their entirety those of mixed birth who are born from inverse and natural orders, as well as those who are mutually intermingled.
*Vyatiṣaṅga* means connection.

It refers to the mutual intermingling of those born in the direct order (*anuloma*) with others of the direct order and of the inverse order (*pratiloma*), and likewise of those born in the inverse order with others of the inverse order and of the direct order.
This statement is made for the purpose of providing the designations that will be explained hereafter.
The Sūta, the Vaidehaka, and the Caṇḍāla— the lowest of men—
as well as the Māgadha, the Kṣattṛ caste, and likewise the Āyogava.
These, whose characteristics have already been stated, are presented again in reverse order for the sake of what follows.
These six produce offspring of similar caste within their own wombs;
they also procreate children belonging to their mother's caste when united with women of superior castes.

These, such as the Sūta and others born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), produce offspring similar to themselves when they procreate within their own wombs; the meaning is that they produce those belonging to their own caste.
For example:
a Sūta begets a Sūta upon a Sūta woman.
And likewise, a Caṇḍāla [begets] upon a Caṇḍāla woman.

Furthermore, those who are born from mothers of their own caste—the *anuloma* sons of the same caste as their mothers who were mentioned previously—are called *anantara*; they too produce offspring exactly similar to themselves when they procreate within their own wombs, just as an Ambaṣṭha [begets] upon an Ambaṣṭha woman.
Likewise, those who are inferior to themselves beget [sons] from a Vaiśya woman; for it has been stated that they possess the caste of the mother.
Others, however, read: "they are born into the mother's caste.
And the meaning of this is that, in their own wombs—such as the Ambaṣṭha and others—and in the mother's caste, namely the Vaiśya woman, they beget only similar [offspring].

Although the Ambaṣṭhas and others are superior to pure Vaiśyas, they are nevertheless said to be equal [to them], because both groups have the right to perform the duties of a Vaiśya. The inclusion of those born in the natural order (*anuloma*) is obtained through the force of the term "mother's caste" (*mātṛjāti*), even though the word "these" (*ete*) refers back to those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*). Furthermore, it should be understood that those who approach women of higher castes in the inverse order procreate offspring of even lower status, as will be seen from a consideration of what is stated below.
For those born to women of their own caste by Āyogavas and others do not receive the designation "Āyogava" and so forth;
rather, the inclusion of the term "similar" is based on the commonality of being born through the inverse order (prātilomya).
Furthermore, the state of being "lower" is employed without regard for internal subdivisions.
Therefore, this is the meaning of the sentence here:
from those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), whether to women of the same caste or to women of a higher caste, only those born in the inverse order (pratiloma) arise.
Just as for three castes, the offspring of two is born of this [mother],
so too among the outsiders, by way of immediate succession, [the offspring] is born from its own kind.
The self of this Brāhmaṇa is born from the three castes;
among the two castes of Kṣatriya and Vaiśya, the state of being twice-born (dvijatva) is produced, as well as in his own womb.
Thus, the Brāhmaṇa produces twice-born men from the three castes.

In the same way, among the outsiders as well, by means of the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya [in reverse order], the self of the Kṣatriya and the Brāhmaṇa attains the status of being twice-born (*dvijatva*). And when that status of being twice-born exists, the initiation (*upanayana*) must be performed.
For the author will state later: "These six possess the duties of the twice-born."
However, there is this distinction:
those born from a natural (anuloma) union belong to the caste of the mother; they are of the same class as the mother.
We shall now state this merely by way of praise.
And they also, being even more corrupted than those before, procreate upon one another's wives many outsiders who are likewise despised.
And those six, beginning with the Āyogava, also procreate many further outsiders among one another's wives.
For example: the Āyogava begets upon the wife of the Kṣattṛ, and the Kṣattṛ upon the wife of the Āyogava; thus they mutually procreate those who are despised relative to themselves.
For instance, the Āyogava begets upon the wife of the Kṣattṛ one who is even more outside than himself, and one who is even more outside than that upon a Caṇḍālī.
Thus it is everywhere.
Just as a Śūdra begets an outcaste being upon a Brāhmaṇī woman, so too does an outcaste beget one even more outcaste within the fourfold caste system.
Thus, regarding the mutual intermixture [of castes], the birth of those who are outside [the system] from women born in the reverse order has been described according to the previous rule.
Now, the fourfold caste system (cāturvarṇya) is being discussed.
In this context, the root *sūyati* is employed as having exactly the same meaning as *janiti*.
"Produces" means "generates";
this is indicated by the following verse.
Acting in opposition [to their duties], those of the outer castes further beget even more outward and inferior offspring; thus, they produce exactly fifteen distinct castes.
However, for each individual caste, there are those of mixed origin:
some are *anuloma* (born in the natural order), some are *pratiloma* (born in the inverse order), and some are both *anuloma* and *pratiloma*.
For a Brāhmaṇa, they are *anuloma*; for a Śūdra, they are only *pratiloma*; and for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, they are both *anuloma* and *pratiloma*.
For a Kṣatriya, there are two anulomas and one pratiloma;
for a Vaiśya, there is one anuloma and two pratilomas.
Thus, these constitute the twelve anuloma-pratiloma offspring.
For each one of these, as they proceed through the four stages, there are four varieties;
some of these are inferior and some are non-inferior,
while all others are even more external.
Being "more external" refers to the remoteness from the caste of one's mother and father, due to being inferior to [the standard] karmas.
This is clarified by means of examples;
first, we shall speak taking the *pratiloma* castes as our subject.

The Āyogava, born from a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya mother, produces four types of offspring—upon a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, and a Brāhmaṇa woman. Thus, including himself, this Āyogava constitutes five groups.
The same applies to the Kṣattṛ and the Caṇḍāla.
Thus, from a Śūdra, there are three groups of five, making fifteen types in total.
Likewise, there are two born from a Vaiśya in the inverse order (pratiloma): the Māgadha from a Kṣatriya woman and the Vaidehaka from a Brāhmaṇa woman;
and the [Ambaṣṭha] is born in the natural order (anuloma) from a Śūdra woman.
In that regard, when one born of a Śūdra woman procreates within the four castes, this same principle applies.
When he approaches a Śūdra woman, a lower caste is born in comparison to him;
likewise, approaching a Vaiśya woman, he procreates one who is even lower.

In this way, those born from a Kṣatriya or a Brāhmaṇa woman solely from a Śūdra father are superior; "in this way" means they are both inferior and non-inferior depending on the relative status [of the parents]. The same should be understood for a Kṣatriya or a Brāhmaṇa [father] [with respect to a Śūdra mother].
However, this is the distinction for the Brāhmaṇa: his [offspring] are only those born in the natural order (anuloma).
Thus, there are fifteen divisions for each of the four castes, which amount to sixty; together with the four primary castes, that total becomes sixty-four.
Through their mutual contact, other infinite varieties arise;
thus it is said: "And those many external [factors] as well.
This occurs in a contrary manner by transgressing the scriptures.
Existing as they couple together;
"inferior and non-inferior" is a single compound word.
Alternatively, the meaning is that being inferior, they give birth to—that is, produce—those who are inferior.

Regarding the statement "there are only fifteen phonemes," since there is no fifth [class]—meaning that the fifth lacks the status of being a phoneme—the status of being a phoneme among the fifteen must be understood as a figurative designation (*upacāra*).
From a Dasyu and an Āyogava woman is born a Sairandhra, who knows the art of personal adornment and service, is not a slave yet lives as one, and subsists by means of snares.
*Prasādhana* means adornment.
*Upacāra* means compliance.

She who knows the rules regarding the arrangement of hair, the application of saffron, sandalwood, and the like as decorative ointments, the massaging of hands and feet, and the timely performance of tasks for those seeking gain—such a woman is so described.
He who was not a slave lives by the life of a slave; he serves someone for a year's wage or for six months' wages,
or else, through knowledge of the rules, he becomes an attendant to all for the sake of his livelihood.
The livelihood of the hunter is considered [the first].
This second means of livelihood is the *vāgurā*,
which is the killing of wild animals in the forest.

And that [slaughter] by the noble ones is for the sake of offerings to the gods and ancestors, and for the sake of hunger; it is not, however, a livelihood through the sale of meat after killing animals like a hunter.
Killing many living beings for the sake of a livelihood occurs only by royal command.
He procreates one named Sairandhrī.
The term *dasyu* refers to one who will be described [later]. Regarding the specific caste (*jāti-viśeṣa*) called *ayogava*,
the female gender is understood by implication.
The Vaideha, however, procreates the Maitreyaka,
who praises men incessantly and strikes a bell at the break of dawn.
One named Maitreyaka is produced—that is, born—from an Āyogavī woman. He who is born from a Vaiśya father and a Brāhmaṇī mother is called a Vaideha;
there is an alternative reading, *maireyaka*.
*Mādhūka*:
this is a word used for comparison; it means "resembling the *madhūka* flower" because of its sweet speech.
Alternatively, according to the rule "the suffix *ḍa* is seen even after other [roots]," it is derived from the sense that it "acts like a *madhuka*."

The vowel lengthening [in *bandī*] occurs according to the rule "anyeṣām api"; furthermore, there is initial *vṛddhi* strengthening (*ādi-vṛddhi*) due to the suffix being used in its own sense (*svārthika*).
Its function is that which is called a *bandī*, who praises men—that is, human beings—unceasingly, at all times.
At dawn, at the time of awakening, they strike and beat the bell for the purpose of waking kings, lords, and others;
it produces only the *āyogavī* tone because that is the subject under discussion.
The Niṣāda begets the Mārgava, a slave who lives by the work of boats;
those dwelling in Āryāvarta call him a Kaivarta.

Because of the context of the inverse order (*pratiloma*), he who was previously mentioned as the *niṣāda* born from a *śūdrā* woman by a *brāhmaṇa* is not the one referred to here; rather, it is the *pratiloma* son specifically from an *āyogavī* woman, like a *dasyu*. This inverse-born son is named Mārgava;
he has two other names as well: *dāsa* and *kaivarta*.
Āryāvarta is well known; his livelihood consists of working on boats, that is, he lives by the operation of boats.
Among these Āyogavī women— who wear the clothes of the dead, are ignoble, and eat despised food—
there arise three distinct groups of those born of low caste.
The maternal origin of those three who were just mentioned, ending with the Mārgava, has not been stated; this verse is for the purpose of explaining that.
These [offspring] are born of Āyogava women;
and their qualification is "wearing dead clothes," which means they wear the garments of corpses.
They are ignoble and untouchable;
they eat food such as meat and leftovers, which is censured.
From a Niṣāda father and a Kārāvarī mother, a Carmakāra is born;
from a Vaidehika father, Andhra and Meda sons are born, whose dwellings are outside the village.

Because of the restrictive particle *eva* in the subsequent passage—"is born from a Vaideha woman alone"—the connection is understood here as well: "From a Niṣāda, a son named Kārāvara is born from a Vaideha woman.
From a Vaidehika, two [sons], the Āndhra and the Meda, are born;
from what woman?
Regarding the Kārāvara and Niṣāda: because of their proximity here, and because they arise from a Vaideha father and a Vaidehī mother of a different caste, they are explained in this way.
And due to the distinction of the female, these two castes arise from a single caste.
Those two whose dwelling and residence were outside the village.
From a Caṇḍāla and a Vaidehī woman is born a Pāṇḍusopāka, who deals in bamboo; he is also called an Āhiṇḍika. He is likewise born from a Niṣāda and a Vaidehī woman.
From a Cāṇḍāla father and a Vaidehī mother, a caste named Pāṇḍusopāka is born.
His livelihood consists of dealing in *tvaksāra*.
*Tvaksāra* is bamboo; he lives by its trade—by the buying and selling of bamboo, or by making mats and the like.
From a Niṣāda by that same woman is born an Āhiṇḍaka; his livelihood is this very one, or it may be sought elsewhere.
But from a Caṇḍāla, by a Pulkasī woman, is born a sinful Sopāka who lives by the occupation of root-thievery and is always censured by virtuous people.
Calamity is suffering; its root is killing, which is one's livelihood.

The means of living for those who kill the condemned consists of carrying the corpses of the helpless by order of the king, taking their clothes and other belongings, eating the funeral offerings (*piṇḍa*) for the deceased, and so forth.
Furthermore, from a *caṇḍāla* and a *pulkasī*, a [son] is born.

Alternatively, "that calamity" refers to the division [of property] among trees and the like starting from their roots; that is the livelihood. Among the trees that have been cut down, he lives by uprooting whatever root remains continuous and selling it or otherwise utilizing it for a living.
But from a Caṇḍāla, a Niṣāda woman gives birth to a son called an Antyāvasāyin,
who frequents cremation grounds and is despised even by those outside the caste system.
They call the *antyāvasāyin* a *caṇḍāla*;
or alternatively, one born from a *niṣāda* woman and a *caṇḍāla* man has the name *antyāvasāyin*.
His sphere of activity is the cremation ground, and his livelihood consists of burning corpses and similar tasks.
Therefore, he should be known as even more contemptible than a *caṇḍāla*.
This has been presented merely as an illustration, for the mixtures [of castes] are infinite.
These castes born of intermixture, as indicated by their fathers and mothers,
are to be known— whether hidden or manifest— by their own respective actions.

Those actions which were just mentioned, such as working with bamboo bark (*tvaksāra*) or trade (*vyavahāra*), by means of these, those who are not well-known should be understood as belonging to that same class [of persons] by virtue of names such as *sopāka* and so forth.
They have been shown by their father and mother through their specific distinction;
whether they are concealed or manifest, they should be understood as belonging to that same class.
In the case of the Āyogava woman, the division of shares is as shown by the father: from the Niṣāda comes the Vaidehika, and from the Vaidehika come the two types of Āndhra.
Sons born of women of the same caste or of intermediate castes possess the nature of twice-born men;
however, all those born of women of lower castes are recorded as being of the same nature as Śūdras, having fallen from their proper status.
Those born from members of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) to women of the same caste possess the duties of the twice-born (*dvija*); this is merely restated as an established fact.

The statement regarding the equality of those born in immediate succession (*anantaraja*) is for the purpose of their acquiring those same duties. Those born in the intermediate order (*antaraja*) are those born in the natural direction (*anuloma*).

Those born from a Brāhmaṇa to a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya woman, and those born from a Kṣatriya to a Vaiśya woman—they too possess the status of the twice-born (dvija) and are entitled to initiation; this is the meaning. Furthermore, once initiated, they are authorized in all the duties of the twice-born. But surely, by the rule "they are named after the [mother's] immediate [caste]," their belonging to the caste of the mother has already been stated?
And consequently, their entitlement to those duties that are common to that caste is indeed established.
True;

however, because of the mention of the name "immediately following" (*anantara-nāman*), someone might suspect that this is merely a designation for them and not an extension of the caste status. Therefore, for the sake of clarity, the statement begins: "The six sons possess the duties of the twice-born."

Furthermore, those who are born from degradation (*apadhvaṃsa*) or from the mixture of castes (*saṃkara*) share the same nature as Śūdras and possess the same conduct; the meaning is that they are entitled to the duties of Śūdras.
However, the specific details regarding those born in the reverse order (*pratiloma*) will be stated later.
The mention of "immediate" (*anantara*) is intended merely to indicate those born in the natural order (*anuloma*).
Therefore, even though he is separated by an intervening caste, the son born of a Brāhmaṇa from a Vaiśya woman is included;
however, the Pāraśava born of a Śūdra woman is not, because he exceeds the number six.
But by the power of the seeds of their asceticism, they undergo increase and decrease among human beings here, birth after birth, in age after age.
These aforementioned offspring born in immediate succession, through the power of their asceticism and the power of their seed, undergo progress and decline in every age and in every birth;
this we shall explain in the section concerning "one born from a Brāhmaṇa upon a Śūdra woman."
This is an elaboration of what was stated regarding the abandonment of one's own duties:
"But through the gradual neglect of their rites and by their transgression against Brahmins, these Kshatriya lineages have fallen to the state of Shudras in this world."

Where the omission of ritual acts (*kriyālopa*) is connected [to the individual] by way of being a sanctification (*saṃskāryatā*), as in the case of initiation (*upanayana*) and so forth; or where it is connected by way of being the agent (*kartṛtā*), as in the case of the obligatory *agnihotra* and the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and so forth—the omission of these refers to the non-performance of both types.

Consequently, loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśa*) occurs not only through the absence of the initiatory rite (*upanayana-saṃskāra*), but also through the abandonment of the prescribed rites for those who have been initiated.
And thus it says "gradually":
the status of a Śūdra applies to the lineage beginning with sons and grandsons, and not to the one who was born [as such] alone;
however, in the absence of initiation (upanayana), a different designation applies to that very person.

Even though that caste-status does not cease, for his sons and grandsons, it is precisely another caste, such as *bhṛjjakaṇṭaka* and so forth, that serves as the basis for designation; thus, "by the transgression of being a Brāhmaṇa" means by the transgression of the rules prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa.
Alternatively, it refers to the absence of approaching an assembly (*pariṣad*) when there is doubt regarding the meaning of the scriptures or concerning expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
The Pauṇḍrakas, Auḍras, Draviḍas, Kāmbojas, Yavanas, Śakas,
Pāradas, Pahlavas, Cīnas, Kirātas, Daradas, and Khaśas.

Words such as *puṇḍraka* and others are, in the ultimate sense, names of countries; however, in this context, the view is adopted that they primarily denote Kṣatriyas and, by association with them, are used for the countries themselves—just as in the rule for the elision (*lup*) of the suffix, "the elision occurs when [the suffix denotes] his residence in a country" (*tasya nivāso janapade lup*), and not according to the principle "because the connection is not perceived" (*lub yogāprakhyānāt*). The statement regarding their status as *vṛṣalas* (outcastes) is based on the fact that the four-fold caste system (*cāturvarṇya*) does not generally exist in these regions.
