Alternatively, if words such as "Puṇḍra" and others were somehow observed without a connection to a specific region, then they should be understood as belonging to this same class [of names].

Since Kṣatriyas are described in the Mahābhārata and elsewhere, someone might have the misconception that these people of today are also Kṣatriyas; for this very reason it is said, "these are Vṛṣalas.

Furthermore, regarding those inhabitants of the distant frontiers, such as the Kirātas, Venas, Daradas, and so forth, their non-attainment of the status [of Aryans] is restated by the Veda in the passage: "One should not go to such a person, nor should one go to the end [of the earth]."
Those castes in the world who are outside those born from the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet—
whether they speak the tongues of barbarians or the speech of the Aryans— are all traditionally known as Dasyus.
Speech that consists of improper words whose meanings are non-existent or unreal is called *mleccha*;
for example, that of the Śabaras, Kirātas, or other outcastes. Those who dwell in Āryāvarta speak the speech of the Āryas.
And those who are known as being of a caste other than the fourfold varṇa are then called *dasyus*.
This is what is meant:

residence in a particular country is not the cause of being a barbarian (*mleccha*) or of caste-mixture; rather, it is the well-known application of terms such as "Barbara" and so forth as previously described.
The meaning is that those born from the mouths and other [parts] who are not well-known by terms such as "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth are excluded;
all of them are called *dasyus*.
Those who are considered the outcasts among the twice-born, as well as those born of degraded unions,
should subsist by performing those very occupations of the twice-born that are held in contempt.

The *apasadās* (low-born) are those born in the natural order (*anuloma*) and the inverse order (*pratiloma*), as well as those born of degradation (*apadhvaṃsaja*); the distinction between them is like that between "cattle" and "bull.
They should maintain themselves by performing services suitable for the twice-born;
because they perform servile tasks that are censured, they themselves are censured.
And so it will be stated:
"The training of horses and charioteering for Sūtas; medical practice for Ambaṣṭhas;
service to women for Vaidehakas; and the trade of merchants for Māgadhas."
Women's work refers to the duty of guarding the inner apartments;
trade routes are well known as consisting of land and water paths, and so forth.
The killing of fish is the occupation of Niṣādas; that of the Āyogava is carpentry; and the slaughter of wild animals is the occupation of Medas, Andhras, Cuñcus, and Madgus.
Tvaṣṭṛ is the wood-cutter; his work is carpentry.
For the Kṣattrus, Ugras, and Pulkasas, their livelihood consists of dwelling in holes, killing, and binding;
for the Dhigvaṇas, it is working with leather; and for the Veṇas, it is playing musical instruments.
The *bilaukasas* are snakes, mongooses, cranes, and so forth;
their killing and capturing constitute the livelihood of the Kṣatriyas and others.
Leather work includes the sewing of armor and the like, as well as the stitching of sandals and so forth.
The playing of musical instruments refers to the drum (*muraja*), the half-drum (*ardhamuraja*), and so forth.
These learned ones should dwell at sacred shrines, by trees, in cremation grounds, on mountains, and in groves, subsisting by their own prescribed duties.
Those living outside the village should reside in regions characterized by mountains;
their caste marks should be known by the learned.
Whatever specific duty has been ordained for each person, he shall subsist by that alone.
One does not obtain the opportunity to perform either superior action or the act of mixing [the castes].
The dwellings of Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas shall be outside the village;
they must be provided with broken vessels, and their wealth shall consist of dogs and donkeys.
Their dwelling place, having departed from the villages, should be a shelter.

They are "those with discarded vessels" (apapātra), meaning those who must live for a long time [in such a state]; the vessels in which they have eaten are not to be purified, but are to be abandoned—[that is,] other than those made of gold and silver.
The specific types of purification for these two have been stated.
Alternatively, they are "those with unworthy vessels":
one should not give flour, cooked rice, or other such food into vessels that belong to them and are smeared [with impurities].
Having given [the food] into a vessel placed on the ground or held in another's hand, they should take that vessel once it has been set down on the ground.
Or, the vessel may be broken or unfit for use, as he will describe in the passage beginning with "eating from a broken vessel" and so forth.
Their wealth consists of dogs and donkeys.
They would not grasp cows, horses, gold, silver, and so forth as being "wealth."
His garments shall be the clothes of the dead, his food shall be from broken dishes,
his ornament shall be iron, and he must constantly wander about as a mendicant.
They should wander at all times; they must not dwell in a single place.
A man practicing dharma should not seek association with them;
their mutual dealings and marriages should be only with their own equals.
*Samaya* means a convention or a common purpose; it is synonymous with association (*saṃgati*).
The meaning is that one should not perform activities such as standing, sitting, or wandering in the same place together with them.
*Vivāha* refers to taking a wife and so forth.
He, too, is exactly like this.
Their food should be given by others in a broken vessel;
they must not wander through villages or cities at night.
That [gift] must not be given to them directly;
it should be caused to be given by some servants in the manner previously described.
There is a prohibition against wandering within villages or cities at night due to the fear of physical contact.
They may move about during the day for the sake of their business, marked by royal edicts; and they shall carry out the disposal of a corpse that has no kinsmen—such is the established rule.
They wander about during the day for the sake of business, for the purpose of accomplishing their own tasks such as buying and selling,

or they may travel for the sake of royal business, or on account of city festivals, spectacles, and the like. And even there, they are marked by royal edicts, distinguished by signs commanded by the king such as the *vajra* and so forth, or by execution decrees consisting of axes, hatchets, and other tools carried upon their shoulders.
And so it has been said:
"They shall constantly execute those condemned to death according to the scriptures by the king's command;
they shall take the garments, beds, and ornaments of the executed."
One should discern by their own actions a man who is devoid of caste, unknown, born of a defiled womb, and who, though appearing noble in form, is actually ignoble.
One who has departed from his caste and fallen away from the fourfold social order (cāturvarṇya),
being unrecognizable when suspicion arises, should be determined— by the actions to be described hereafter and by his exceptional natural traits—
to be born of an adulterer. When suspicion exists, one who delights in base acts and performs cruel deeds should be known as born of an adulterer and produced from a defiled womb.
Lack of nobility, harshness, cruelty,
and a disposition toward inaction reveal in this world a man born of a defiled womb.
The ignoble person is dominated by hatred and envy;
he is harsh, intent on his own self-interest,
cruel, and devoted to greed and violence.
The self is inactive and devoid of prescribed actions;
by these inherent natures, birth in a defiled womb is manifested.
He inherits the character of his father, or that of his mother, or indeed both;
for one born of a low womb can never suppress his own innate nature.
One of base birth is of mixed origin;
he does not invariably grasp his own nature, that is, his own cause.
Even for one born into a preeminent family, if there is a confusion of birth,
that person inevitably adopts the conduct of those [of mixed origin], whether to a small or great extent.
His morality is that by which he is born, not that of whose field [it is];
he is thus renowned in the world.
But in that country where these corrupters of the social orders are born through promiscuity,
that kingdom, along with its inhabitants, perishes very quickly.
Therefore, the king must avoid the intermixture of castes.
The kingdom consists of the inhabitants of the realm and the countryside;
the kingdom includes the ministers and other officials.
The self-sacrifice of one's body for the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow,
as well as the protection of women and children from those who are hostile, is the cause of success for outsiders.
"Unadorned" means not having accepted wealth;
"favor" means an act of kindness;
[this refers to] outsiders who are of inverse caste.
It is called the "cause of accomplishment" because birth in an excellent lineage is itself the cause for accomplishing success;
they obtain such a birth that they become qualified [for practice].
Alternatively, "accomplishment" refers to the attainment of heaven and so forth.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, and restraint of the senses—
Manu declared this to be the summary of dharma for the four castes.

Purity consisting of external means such as earth and water has been stated collectively for all the various classes of this [twice-born] category, not according to the specific divisions of caste such as Brāhmaṇa and so forth.
The rest has been explained.

If non-violence were the duty (*dharma*) of those who follow the inverse order (*pratiloma*), how then was it stated that "fishing is for the *niṣādas*, the killing and trapping of burrow-dwellers is for the *kṣatriyas* and others," and likewise that some say, "non-violence applies to anything other than those [animals] which are prescribed as fit to be killed for the sake of livelihood"?
Others consider that non-violence is their duty because it serves as a means for attaining prosperity (*abhyudaya*), but they do not accept that there is a prohibition against violence for them.
It is as if one were to say, "There is no fault in eating meat.
If non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is their dharma, how then are they to live?
If you argue that, based on some understanding, their abstention from violence is established as their dharma, then what is the means for their livelihood?
Furthermore, there are other modes of livelihood restricted to each specific caste.
Occupations such as teaching and the like are not applicable [to others] because they are absolutely impossible;
even occupations such as agriculture are restricted to the Vaiśya.
For a Śūdra, there is service or other common occupations,
as we shall demonstrate in the section on "how they should live" regarding learning and crafts.
As for what is said— that they should subsist by those acts of the twice-born which are censured— what could possibly be more censurable than violence?
Furthermore, the killing of fish is not utilized by the twice-born;
its utility is merely occasional, such as in *śrāddha* rites or when feeding guests, rather than being a constant means of livelihood.
Therefore, killing and the like are not independent [acts].
If one born of a Brāhmaṇa from a Śūdra woman procreates with someone of a superior caste,
he attains the caste of his superior up to the seventh generation.

Because he takes [the child] in the womb (*garbhe gṛhṇāti*) and because the embryo is born from hearing [the Veda], the connection with the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) should be understood in the masculine designation.
Therefore, this is what is meant:

if a maiden born of a Brāhmaṇa from a Śūdra woman is procreated by a superior Brāhmaṇa—one possessing excellence of caste—she enters into a relationship that serves as the cause for producing offspring through rites such as marriage and so forth.
If a girl is born even in that [lineage], she is to be married by a Brāhmaṇa alone.

Thus, through this succession, when the seventh person is reached, he who is born therein [attains the status]. Regarding the word "superior" (*śreyas*): although it refers merely to one of a higher caste, nevertheless, here, due to the proximity of the word "Brāhmaṇa" and because of the subsequent statement, "the Śūdra attains Brāhmaṇahood," it should be understood as the attainment of Brāhmaṇahood for the Śūdra caste.
By this same reasoning, for the caste born of a Vaiśya woman in the fifth generation, and for that born of a Kṣatriya woman in the third generation—
here too, there is an elevation from the female side.
Thus, for a Vaiśya, the status of a Kṣatriya is reached in the third generation.
When a maiden born of a Śūdra woman is united with a Vaiśya man, she attains the status of a Vaiśya in her third birth;
when born of a Śūdra woman by a Kṣatriya man, she attains it in her fifth birth. Here, the word *yuga* signifies "birth."
One who is inferior, belonging to a low caste, goes to—that is, attains—the superior, that is, the exalted caste.
The prefix *āṅ* is used in the sense of inclusive limit (*abhividhi*), meaning "pervasive" or "all-inclusive."
A Śūdra attains the state of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Brāhmaṇa likewise attains the state of a Śūdra;
one should know that this is exactly the same for those born from a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya.
The meaning of the statement "a Śūdra attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa" has been explained; likewise, "a Brāhmaṇa descends to the status of a Śūdra.
Here, the "Brāhmaṇa" should be understood as one born of a Brāhmaṇa father [from a Śūdra mother], namely a Pāraśava.
And if he marries a Śūdra woman possessing the characteristics already described, then he incurs a degradation in birth;
this they explain as being the third [birth].
Just as those who have attained elevation during the aforementioned cycle of ages (yuga-parivarta) become entitled to the sacraments (saṃskāra) and ritual acts (karma).
If it should be asked: "Wherein lies the superiority between one born by chance from a Brāhmaṇa father and a non-Aryan mother, and one born from a non-Aryan father and a Brāhmaṇī mother?"
The word *kim* is used here in the sense of censure.

If, due to the predominance of the seed, those born of women of a lower caste gradually attain the status of the father's caste—becoming superior to the mother's caste—then this same principle should be observed even when the field (the womb) is predominant, as in the case of the "field-born" (*kṣetraja*) son.

Therefore, just as one born from a Brāhmaṇa father upon a non-Aryan Śūdra woman—even if she is unmarried and by chance—is considered superior, so too is there superiority through the predominance of the field when [a child] is born from a non-Aryan Śūdra man upon a Brāhmaṇī woman.
As it has been said: "In some cases the seed [is primary], in others the womb."
One born of a noble man by a non-noble woman may become noble through his qualities;
however, one born even of a non-noble man by a noble woman is certain to be non-noble. This is the settled rule.
If one born from an Ārya—a Brāhmaṇa of superior caste—from a non-Āryan woman, that is, a woman of low birth, would indeed be an Ārya;
but what of his belonging to the Brāhmaṇa caste? No, he says: it is by means of qualities.

By virtue of his qualities—that is, through a secondary application (gauṇī vṛtti) based merely on his eligibility for the *pākayajña* and other such rites—he is called an "Ārya" in relation to those who will be described as Āryas. However, one born from a non-Ārya Śūdra father and an Ārya Brāhmaṇī mother is certainly a non-Ārya; this is the settled rule.
This is what is meant:
as long as the explicit statement itself maintains its primacy, it is not possible to suggest anything else by means of inference.
Therefore, it is logical that the offspring belongs only to those of the same caste; the field’s primacy results in an offspring born of the field (kṣetraja) only, and not elsewhere.

And having established this, the Dharma is settled thus: both of these [the first and the last] are not to be made [through ritual refinement], because of the deficiency of their birth; the former is so by its very origin, and the latter by being born in the inverse order.
Both the Caṇḍāla and the Pārāśava are ineligible for the sacraments and unfit for initiation;
regarding this, the explanatory statement (nigada) containing a reason is an arthavāda:
"The former [the Caṇḍāla] is so because of the deficiency of his birth."
He who is born to a Brāhmaṇa from a Śūdra woman has a defective birth because of the defect of the womb, even though the seed is predominant;

he is the next [in rank], the Caṇḍāla. He is a *pratiloma* (one born in the reverse order) because of extreme reversal, due to the defect of the father, even though the field (the mother) is predominant.
Just as good seed sown in a fertile field comes to fruition,
so too one born of a noble father from a noble mother is worthy of every refinement.

The two previously mentioned [types of offspring] are not to be consecrated, whereas those born of their own species are to be consecrated; this is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) applicable to both cases.
Therefore, this alone remains established:
that in some cases it is the seed and in some cases the womb, according to the traditional instruction.
However, an exclusive appropriation [of one side] is not tenable.
Some wise men praise the seed, others the field; still others praise both the seed and the field. In this matter, however, the established conclusion is as follows:
Just as there are these three positions,
one or another of these positions has been adopted by someone;
some say that the seed alone is superior.
And thus, one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and among the three [classes] beginning with the Kṣatriya mother is superior by virtue of the mother's caste.

Others, however, say that the field is preeminent, because a "field-born" (kṣetriya) person, being born in whatever field, becomes of that [field's] caste, and his offspring belongs to that very [field].
Still others consider both the seed and the field to be superior.
Thus it has been said: "The good seed in the good field. Not being satisfied with all of this, he says: "In this regard, however, the established conclusion is as follows;
this is what stands determined here."
Seed sown in a non-field perishes right there within;
likewise, a field without seed becomes merely a barren wasteland.
A seed sown even if planted in a non-field, such as saline soil (*ūṣara*), perishes right there in the interim without yielding fruit.
A field that is either seedless or possesses unsuitable seeds becomes merely a barren plot (*sthaṇḍila*) or a wasteland (*khila*);
the meaning is that no fruit is obtained from it.
Since sages born of animal species became honored and praised through the power of their seed, therefore the seed is praised.
Those who have been honored by anyone are saluted;
those who are praiseworthy are extolled with words of praise.
Therefore, the seed is distinguished—so say those who maintain the primacy of the seed.
It has been stated that this is incorrect, and in that regard, the established position is as follows.

Alternatively, by the phrase "by the power of the seed" (*bījaprabhāveṇa*), the primacy of the seed is not being demonstrated; rather, it is merely a refutation. For one might suspect that because the primacy of the seed is observed in cases such as Mandapāla and others—where their offspring were sages born of animal wombs—their status as sages was due to the primacy of the seed. However, in those cases, the status of sagehood for their offspring did not arise through the primacy of the seed, but rather through a specific quality of merit (*dharma*) produced by the power of austerity, sacred learning, and so forth.
Having carefully considered one who is ignoble yet performs noble deeds, and one who is noble yet performs ignoble deeds, the Creator declared: "They are neither equal nor unequal."

A non-noble (anārya) is a Śūdra. He is one who performs noble deeds, being devoted to the service of the twice-born and so forth, performing domestic sacrifices (pākayajña), and intent on bowing to the gods and the twice-born.
A noble (ārya) is a Brāhmaṇa or one of the other [higher castes].
He is one of ignoble conduct, practicing what is forbidden and abandoning prescribed duties.
Having thoroughly considered both of them and understood their respective qualities,
the Creator Manu, the son of Prajāpati, having deliberated with his intellect to determine which of the two possessed a superior quality or which was ultimately better, spoke as follows.
A Śūdra, even if possessed of superior qualities, would not be equal to one who is equal in caste, nor indeed superior;
yet it is further stated that he is not unequal either—
what then [is the point] of a caste that, though superior, is seized by many defects?
This is what is meant: a person is not to be honored by relying on the power of birth; rather, virtues are what are to be honored.
Birth is not able to protect one who is devoid of virtue, for that would lead to the absurd conclusion that the instruction on penance is useless.
This verse, beginning from the words "born of a non-Aryan woman," is intended to censure the mixing of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*) and to praise [the performance of] ritual action (*karman*).
Nothing is here enjoined or prohibited, nor is any previously unknown matter made known, as is the case with defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, these [passages] serve solely for the purpose of praise.
Those Brahmins who abide in the womb of Brahman and remain established in their own duty should properly subsist by means of the six duties in their proper order.
This is the introduction to the duties in times of distress.
The source is the cause.
Brāhmaṇas established in the source of Brahman should subsist by, that is, perform, the six duties.
Roots have multiple meanings;
they function according to their sequence and according to their specific application—
that is, according to which agent is authorized for which particular action.
Some have injunctions as their purpose, while others have perceptible purposes.
Teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices,
giving gifts, and receiving gifts— these six are the duties of the first-born (the Brāhmaṇa).
In the first chapter, their recitation was for the purpose of praising the scripture;
here, however, it is for the purpose of an injunction.
Although the injunction for them individually has already been stated, they are nevertheless mentioned here collectively out of kindness.
This form is indeed dependent upon other injunctions, as is the case with these ritual acts due to the scriptural statement;
therefore, having restated what has been prescribed, the matter about to be stated is enjoined.
Of his six duties, three are his means of livelihood:
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of gifts from pure persons.
The classification of the threefold karma has a clear purpose:
one set of three is taken as having a visible result by implication,
while the other has an invisible result.
One who is pure and free from evil deeds—
thus even a Śūdra who is pure attains [the goal]. What is your begrudging attitude?
A contradiction with another Smṛti would result [from your position], for it says: "A Brāhmaṇa may eat and receive gifts from twice-born men who are excellent in their own duties.
Therefore, it must be explained in such a way that there is no contradiction.
For when non-contradiction is possible, contradiction is not logical.
Alternatively, this is merely a restatement (anuvāda), because this very meaning has already been enjoined in such passages as "one should seek wealth from the king."
Three duties are withheld from a Kṣatriya by a Brāhmaṇa:
teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and thirdly, the acceptance of gifts.

These are not the livelihoods of a Kṣatriya; however, those acts which have an unseen purpose—such as sacrifices, Vedic study, and giving—are not prohibited. Furthermore, since the Veda is the subject under discussion, it is this teaching of the Veda that is forbidden, but not the science of archery, the arts, crafts, and sciences.
In the same way, these [prohibitions] should cease with respect to a Vaiśya;
such is the settled rule, for Prajāpati Manu did not prescribe those duties for them.
This has been explained previously.

These duties, such as teaching and so forth, were not stated by Manu Prajāpati with respect to those two, the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya; the meaning is that they were not recorded [as their duties] in the Smṛti.

The bearing of weapons and missiles is the livelihood of the Kṣatriya; trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture are those of the Vaiśya. However, the duty (dharma) consists of giving gifts, study, and sacrifice.
This is their livelihood:
weapons (*śastra*) such as swords and the like,
and missiles (*astra*), which are the mantras for them well-known in the science of archery (*dhanurveda*).
This too is merely a restatement of what has already been said.
The words "merchant" (*vaṇik*) and "livestock" (*paśu*) are used here with their respective occupations included—namely, trade and cattle-rearing.
Although all duties such as Vedic study and so forth belong to everyone, these [occupations] are nevertheless predominant for them.
The study of the Vedas for the Brāhmaṇa, protection for the Kṣatriya,
and the occupation of trade and agriculture for the Vaiśya are the most distinguished among their respective duties.
The study of the Vedas and teaching— these being specified because they constitute the primary mode of livelihood—
are thus distinguished among one's own duties;
within the scriptural modes of livelihood, these are more conducive to spiritual welfare than other means of subsistence.
But if he cannot subsist by his own prescribed duty as a Brāhmaṇa,
he may live by the dharma of a Kṣatriya, for that is the one immediately next to him.
When his body, family, and regular duties suffer from exhaustion, and he does not possess sufficient wealth for them, then he is said to be "not living" [by his own means]. At that time,
as previously described through teaching and other such means,
he may live like a Kṣatriya by protecting villages and cities, by bearing weapons and missiles, and, if possible, by exercising overall sovereignty.
The meaning of the root *jīv* has already been explained; it does not refer merely to the maintenance of the body.
What then? It indicates the performance of household duties and the persistence in obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), for that [the family] is his immediate concern.

The term *pratyanantara* means "immediately following. Because of the mention of the cause (*hetu*), there is an exclusion of anything separated [by time]. Even if one abandons one's own livelihood, one should not think that there is no distinction in the case of a Vaiśya or a Śūdra regarding the transgression of the scriptures committed therein.
And so it has been said:
"But if one cannot subsist by both [occupations], how should it be? One should live by adopting the livelihood of a Vaiśya, namely agriculture and cattle-rearing."
But if one cannot subsist by either of these two,
the sequence is demonstrated by this [rule]:
first the immediate mode of livelihood, and in its absence, the indirect one.
The mention of agriculture and cattle-rearing is intended merely to illustrate the occupations of a Vaiśya;
for he will later state that one may live by the livelihood of a Vaiśya, including trade, while prohibiting the sale of certain items.
The relationship between action as the means and its result as the end has already been established through the principle of the general and the particular.
In this context, agriculture, trade, and moneylending are mentioned as permissible even when not in times of distress, just like teaching and other such occupations.
Some say that agriculture is traditionally considered "falsehood" (pramṛta), while trade is "truth-and-falsehood" (satyānṛta).
Furthermore, it is stated here that agriculture and trade must not be performed by oneself, and the same applies to moneylending.
In this context, performing [the work] oneself is permitted.
As for the objection raised regarding equality—on the grounds that [these occupations] are like teaching and so forth—that has been refuted right here.

If agriculture and the like were common to all [classes], why would it be said that "agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade are for the livelihood of Vaiśyas," and that they are not for the livelihood of Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas? Therefore, [they are not equal].
Furthermore, regarding the statement, "Sacrificing for others, teaching, and receiving gifts from the pure," those [means of livelihood] will also be fully explained there.
Therefore, for one who lives by the rules of teaching and so forth, agriculture and similar activities are indeed prohibited.
As for the instruction of these [activities] elsewhere than in this specific context, its purpose has already been demonstrated in that very place.
Even if he must live by the occupation of a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should carefully avoid agriculture, which consists mostly of violence and depends upon others.
The censure of agriculture is for the purpose of praising the other occupations of the Vaiśya, and not for the purpose of prohibiting it;
for if that were the case, the instruction regarding it would be rendered meaningless.
They consider agriculture to be good, yet that livelihood is censured by the virtuous;
for the iron-tipped wood destroys both the earth and those who dwell within it.
People consider agriculture to be a virtuous action;
this is appropriate.
For a man who cultivates the land, much grain arises, and from that he benefits guests and others by giving them food; therefore, it is virtuous.
And so it has been said: "One who is fond of guests does not fail to plow;
one should perform agriculture with effort, everywhere with diligence. Likewise, [use] the plowshare, which is resonant, very auspicious, and well-handled."
"He plows the cow, the sheep, and the fat, swelling [cow]," and so forth;
they do not consider this correctly,
for that mode of livelihood is censured by the virtuous.
For what reason?
A plow with an iron mouth destroys the earth and those creatures that dwell within the earth.

He also kills those living beings on the earth, such as grass-leeches and the like. Now, one might ask: what kind of killing is there of the earth? For it does not experience pain from being struck by wood in the same way that a living being does.
However, everyone has experienced the tearing up of the earth; thus, [the author] makes it known that this constitutes a fault.

But for one who, due to a deficiency in livelihood, abandons skill in the Dharma, this is the merchandise of a merchant: it is to be sold for the increase of wealth, with the best portion already extracted.
The word "this" (idam) is a reference to that which is about to be stated.
"Merchandise of the Vaiśyas" (viṭpaṇya) refers to whatever is for sale by Vaiśyas; even that may be sold by a Brāhmaṇa due to a deficiency in livelihood or a lack of wealth.
"Items to be set aside" (uddhāryāṇi dravyāṇi) are denoted by the term *uddhāra*.
That in which a portion has been set aside is described in this way;
having extracted the items to be mentioned hereafter, other things are to be sold.
"The increase of wealth" is a restatement of its inherent nature.
For it is well known that in trade there is an increase of wealth;
however, for one who renounces [trade], there is the perfection of righteousness—that which is steadfastness in dharma.
Therefore, he makes it known that the selling of merchandise must not be performed by him.
From this it is understood that among all the occupations of Vaiśyas, agriculture is the most censured; trade is inferior to that, and cattle-rearing and so forth are inferior even to that.
One should exclude all liquids, prepared food along with sesame seeds,
stones, salt, and both domestic animals and humans.
The six tastes are sweet and so forth;
substances in which these predominate, such as molasses, pomegranate, and kirātatiktaka, are prohibited.
For indeed, tastes do not exist in isolation.

Although the word *rasa* (taste) does not itself denote a substance through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) like words such as "white," it nevertheless indicates the substance, just as in the expression "a hamlet on the Ganges.
"Should exclude" means he should abandon; that is to say, he should not sell it.
"Cooked food" refers to prepared food such as boiled rice and the like, but not raw grains such as rice in the husk.

"Along with sesame seeds" means that even sesame seeds themselves are not to be sold; however, this is not a prohibition against sesame and cooked food when used together, nor is it a permission for them alone. "Stones" refers to all types of rocks.
Salt, although not of the nature of stone,
is included under the term "stone" when referring to *saindhava* salt.
In the context of flavors, this mention of salt is for the sake of its permanence.
By him, the sale of honey and other such items is permitted on certain occasions.
Domestic animals are those belonging to villages; wild animals are those of the forest. Human beings are those of the human race.
And all woven cloth that is dyed, as well as hemp, linen, and wool—
even if they should be undyed— as also fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs.
*Tāntavam* refers to that which is made from threads, such as garments, cloths, or large wraps (*bṛhatikā*).
*Rakta* means red;
the word *rakta* is more commonly established in the sense of the color red.

For instance, one who is dyed is called "red" (*lohita*), even though the meaning of the root *rañj* (to dye) also includes the imparting of another color to something white; this is seen in the case of hemp, linen, and woolen cloth, which are [referred to as such] even when they are not dyed.
As it has been said: "Even if they should be undyed...
The rest is well known.
Water, weapons, poison, meat, Soma, and all kinds of perfumes;
milk, honey, curd, clarified butter, oil, liquor, molasses, and Kuśa grass.
"Arms" refers to swords, nooses, and so forth.
"Fragrances" refers to specific substances such as tagara, uśīra, sandalwood, and the like.
This is to be explained in the same manner as the word "flavors."

Milk along with its derivatives is well-known from other Smṛti texts; therefore, whey, inspissated milk, buttermilk, and so forth are also not to be sold. The mention of curd and ghee is made because they are the primary products.
"Madhu" refers to beeswax (madhūcchiṣṭa), following the principle of partial elision as in the case of "Devadatta" for "Datta.
For this is prohibited in another Smṛti;
furthermore, since honey produced by bees (*sāragha*) is already forbidden here by the word "kṣaudra," and since *mādhvīka* is prohibited later under the category of intoxicants (*madya*).

Others, however, explain that the word "madhu" is used for the sake of prohibiting *mādhvīka* (honey-wine) while it has not yet reached the state of being *madya* (intoxicant). That is incorrect; this word does not denote the juice extracted from crushed grapes.
What then? It exists precisely in the form of liquor (*madya*).
This is because we observe the usage "both [are] intoxicated by honey-liquor and milk-liquor" (*madhvāsavakṣībāv*), wherein intoxication (*kṣībatā*) is caused solely by liquor.
The mention [of *madya*] is for the purpose of precluding the denial that molasses (*guḍa*) possesses the nature of being a juice (*rasatva*).
Others, however, explain it for the purpose of permitting sugar-candy, molasses, and so forth.
All wild animals, fanged creatures, and birds;
liquor, indigo, lac, and likewise all one-hoofed animals.
The terms *āraṇya-paśu* (wild animal) and *śabda* (sound) have been explained by means of the analogy of molasses and salt;

this is for the purpose of permitting domestic animals (*grāmya-paśu*). For even domestic animals are included in the category of "contact" (*saṃyoga*) regarding violence, and thus [the mention of wild animals] serves to prohibit [the killing of] them.
Fanged animals include dogs, pigs, and the like; birds are winged creatures;
and single-hoofed animals include horses, mules, donkeys, and so forth.
Some read "bahūn" (many) in place of the word "tathā" (so);
thus, there is no fault in selling a single one.
Having personally undertaken agriculture with the necessary desire, a farmer may sell pure sesame seeds for the sake of dharma, provided they have not been kept for long.
Regarding the phrase "cooked food together with sesame seeds," this is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) based on the specific nature and purpose of the otherwise prohibited sesame seeds.
"Pure and not long kept" specifies their particular nature;
"for the sake of dharma" specifies their particular purpose.
"Pure" means unmixed with rice and other grains;
for those mixed [with other grains] for the purpose of *kṛsara* and the like, sale is impossible.
"Not long kept."
One should not wait with the expectation: "Disregarding profit such as wealth and so forth, I shall receive a small price today and a great price at a later time.
Alternatively, they are pure and not black;
this is a prohibition against black sesame seeds.
Or rather, the meaning is "not long-standing," for black [grain] becomes long-standing;
once black [grain] has been produced or purchased, it must not be sold.

The statement "the farmer himself [performs] the cultivation" is a common conventional description (*prāyika-anuvāda*); the individual words are not intended to be taken literally (*na vivakṣitāni padāni*).

There is no prohibition even against those [sesame seeds] acquired through acceptance of gifts and other means, provided they are used for a religious purpose (*dharma*)—that is, where sesame seeds are sold for such purposes.

In this context, when cows are purchased with coins for the sake of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and the like, or for the sake of Vedic study, the *agnihotra*, and so forth; or when rice and other grains are purchased for the sake of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices—that is a sale for the sake of dharma.
Likewise, it is the same case when the sesame seeds themselves are utilized by the purchaser for acts of charity and the like, or for the use of medicinal oil.
If one performs any act with sesame seeds other than giving them as food or as an ointment,
he becomes a worm in a dog's excrement and sinks there together with his ancestors.
This is a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding the prohibition of selling sesame, intended to distinguish it from the sale of other types of sesame that are under discussion.
Now, it was previously stated that the indication of a fault is invariably connected as the result of prohibitions.
Therefore, is this—"Becoming a worm, he eats and anoints himself with sesame, and gives them away"—merely a commendatory statement?
It is said:
this is stated because of hearing of results that are impossible and contradictory to other treatises;
for instance, it is said [in some texts] "together with the ancestors."
And they have committed no offense whatsoever;
for the fruit of good and evil deeds accrues to the doer,
and it has already been stated previously that the ancestors can in no way be considered the agents.
Furthermore, the statement that "one falls immediately by [eating] meat" refers to the status of being fallen (*pātitya*) according to the rule of others, not to actual loss of caste (*pātitya*).
Therefore, only the fact that "something undesirable exists" is connected with the prohibition;
it is not appropriate to take the expression exactly as it is literally heard.

Where there is an activity such as eating, or elsewhere than that—such as at a place of sale and so forth—whoever deals with sesame seeds there attains the state of a worm; he becomes joined with the aforementioned fault.
One falls immediately by selling meat, lac, or salt;
a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Śūdra within three days by selling milk.
The meaning has been explained.
But by intentionally selling other commodities here,
a Brāhmaṇa attains the status of a Vaiśya within seven nights.
From the expression "out of desire," it is inferred that this applies when there is no distress (*anāpadi*).
The observation regarding the gravity or lightness of meat and other substances is for the purpose of specifying particular penances;
we shall explain later that heavy [substances] require heavy [penances] and light [substances] require light [penances].
Flavors may be bartered for flavors, but salt must never be exchanged for flavors;
prepared food may be bartered for unprepared food, as may sesame seeds for grain, provided they are of equal value.
The tastes are those previously mentioned;
they are to be bartered for other tastes.
Having given sweet substances such as molasses and the like, one may take sour substances such as *āmalaka* and so forth.
One should not merely add salt and then take another flavor;
there is an alternative reading, "salt with sesame seeds.
In this reading, the prohibition applies to salt only when accompanied by sesame seeds, and not to other flavors.
Prepared food, such as groats or boiled rice, should be bartered for other food, such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and the like;
sesame seeds, however, may be exchanged for grain, such as rice and so forth, at equal value.
Having given a *prastha*, one should receive back exactly a *prastha*; one should not give more or less in consideration of its market price.
Exchange (*vinimaya*) is indeed nothing other than sale (*vikraya*). However, the root *krī* (to buy) is recited in the context of the exchange of goods;
yet that is not correct, for Gautama shows a distinction by stating "but exchange" when sale was the subject under discussion.
In that case, then, selling (*vikraya*) is the transfer of goods for a well-known price such as gold and so forth;
bartering (*vinimaya*) is the exchange for other goods different from that.
A Kṣatriya who has fallen into misfortune may live by all of this,
yet he must never at any time take pride in a higher mode of livelihood.
By all this,
this is a counter-exception for a Kṣatriya regarding prohibited merchandise;
nothing whatsoever is forbidden for him to sell, as it is for a Vaiśya.

However, even though he has abandoned his own livelihood, he should never think of the superior Brahminical livelihood as something to be desired, nor should he form the thought in his mind, "I shall adopt this. Adverse fate is a lack of policy;
this is intended as an indication of times of distress.
"Gone" means "attained";
that is to say, one who has fallen into calamity.
If one who is base by birth should live by superior occupations out of greed,
the king, having deprived him of his wealth, shall banish him immediately.

One who is lowest by birth and inferior, such as a Kṣatriya or others— even though the Kṣatriya is the subject under discussion— this prohibition against the livelihood of a Brāhmaṇa applies to all. This verse is exactly so.

The most excellent is the Brāhmaṇa who is indifferent [to worldly gain]; he lives by means of his duties, such as Vedic study and the like. This man is to be punished with the confiscation of all his property and banishment.
Better is one's own duty, though deficient, than the duty of another well-performed;
for by living according to the duty of another, one falls immediately from one's caste.
This is an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda) intended as a censure of the preceding injunction:

that which is the duty prescribed for someone based on their caste may be performed even if it is deficient—that is, even if its constituent parts are incomplete—whereas the duty of another, even if complete in all its parts, must not be performed.
In this context, the phrase "by the duty of another" constitutes the explanatory eulogy as a censure.
A Vaiśya who cannot subsist by his own duty may also live by the occupation of a Śūdra;
provided he does not perform forbidden acts and, when capable, desists from such conduct.
For a Vaiśya who cannot subsist by his own duty, the occupation of a Śūdra is permitted,
provided he performs service such as washing the feet and avoids improper acts.
Acts such as wiping away food-leavings and the like are improper; these must be avoided.
"One who is capable should desist" is the rule that applies to all cases.
On this point, it has been stated by someone that, by virtue of the underlying capacity, this [prohibition] is extended by analogy to Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas as well.
Regarding this, another person raises a doubt:
"How could a Brāhmaṇa perform the livelihood of a Śūdra?
For it is heard [in scripture] thus:"
"Superior and inferior actions exist for those two;
having excluded the intermediate actions, those [other two] are indeed common to all.
This is incorrect.
But this is not its meaning: that by implication, the Śūdra’s mode of livelihood is permitted for a Brāhmaṇa.
What then? It means "one who is capable should desist," which we have stated applies as a supplement to everything.
But a Śūdra who is unable to perform service for the twice-born and has fallen into distress regarding his wife and children may subsist by the work of craftsmen.
Artisans are craftsmen, such as cooks, weavers, and so forth; their occupations, such as cooking and weaving, are well known.
One should live by these.
The distress caused by one's wife and children, and the inability to support them—
by this failure of the foundation of wealth, since marriage and other rites are prescribed for him only in times of calamity, it is inferred that these actions are of an inferior nature.
Those crafts and various arts by which, when practiced, the twice-born are served— these are the works of artisans.
By means of those practices which have been performed and carried out,
they are served and attended upon;
these are the activities and crafts that are useful for that purpose.

Although craftsmanship (*śilpa*) is indeed nothing other than the work of artisans (*kārukarma*), it is nevertheless mentioned here separately; thus, "artisans" refers to carpenters, builders, and the like, while their activities consist of carving, building, and so forth.
"Crafts" (*śilpa*), however, refer to works such as leaf-cutting, image-making, and painting.
A Brāhmaṇa who does not follow the livelihood of a Vaiśya, yet remains on his own path and is suffering while distressed by a lack of subsistence, should practice this dharma.
"Not practicing" means not doing so out of one's own desire.
This is what is meant:
if the occupation of a Kṣatriya is impossible, one may either follow the occupation of a Vaiśya or accept gifts from unworthy persons.
These two modes of livelihood are equal;
however, the livelihood of a Kṣatriya is superior to accepting gifts from the unworthy.
Alternatively, in the absence of other means, one may not follow the livelihood of a Vaiśya.
Furthermore, accepting gifts from the unworthy is inferior even to the occupation of a Vaiśya;

by stating that one is "established on his own path," he indicates that there is a combination of occupations permitted in times of distress. "Emaciated by lack of livelihood" means being distressed, that is, falling into a state of despondency.
A Brāhmaṇa who has fallen into distress may accept gifts from anyone;
that a means of purification should become defiled—this is not tenable according to the Dharma.
"In every respect" means that no regard should be paid to the species or qualities of the recipient.
Here too, among those who are inferior, more inferior, and most inferior, there is indeed a sequential attainment of each subsequent one in the absence of each preceding one;
just as, for example, in the absence of the occupation of a Kṣatriya, the occupation of a Vaiśya [is permitted].
The stream of the Gaṅgā is pure;
it is said that it is not defiled by contact with impurities, for a river is purified by its own current.
So too is a Brāhmaṇa.
No fault accrues to Brahmins from teaching, from officiating at sacrifices, or from accepting gifts— even from those that are censured— for they are like fire and water.
The acceptance of gifts from improper persons was mentioned previously;
by this [verse], officiating at sacrifices and teaching are permitted.
The phrase "from one who is censured" (garhitāt) connects with the two preceding [prohibitions] as well, according to the maxim of the lion’s glance (siṃhāvalokita).
Just as fire and water are pure everywhere, so too are Brāhmaṇas; this is a praise.
Some say:
"Just like accepting gifts from the unworthy, performing sacrifices for the unworthy and teaching them are also not permitted."
If those two [the *dharma* and *adharma*] were to exist, they would have been recited in the preceding verse just like the *pratigraha*.
However, here, because there is an absence of an injunctive suffix (*vidhipratyaya*), the fault arises that "it belongs to the Brahmins.
This is because, through the use of the present tense suffix, it is understood as a mere explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) based on a description of an already established fact.

Furthermore, the statement regarding the acceptance of gifts is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), since it is already established by the preceding rule; and because they form a single syntactical unit, the same should apply to officiating at sacrifices and teaching as well. We, however, maintain that in the absence of [other means], such activity—even in those cases—is appropriate, because engagement is recorded in tradition: "In whatever way possible, he should rescue himself from transgressions."
But the recitation of the rules for times of distress is for the purpose of ritual action.
He who, having fallen into a life-threatening situation, eats food from whatever source it may come, is not smeared by sin, just as the sky is not defiled by mud.
Previously, the acceptance of gifts from improper persons was forbidden;
by this [verse], food corrupted by its source of acceptance is permitted.
The phrase "from here and there" refers to the owner of the food without regard for his caste or occupation.
The remainder is an explanatory passage (arthavāda).
Ajīgarta, being hungry, approached to kill his own son;
yet he was not tainted by sin, as he was merely acting to counteract his hunger.
There was a sage named Ajīgarta.
Tormented by hunger, he approached and prepared to kill his own son, named Śunaḥśepa;
yet it is not fitting to say that he was a meat-eater.
The narrative of Śunaḥśepa is well known in the Ṛgveda;
a detailed account of that scripture is not required here.
However, the ultimate meaning is the allegorical interpretation (arthavāda) which takes the form of primordial nature (prakṛti).
In this way, all these are to be viewed.
Desiring to eat dog-meat out of distress, Vāmadeva— who was discerning of dharma and adharma— did not become defiled, for the sake of preserving his life.
Thus there was a seer named Vāmadeva;
afflicted by hunger, he desired to eat—that is, to consume—the flesh of a dog.
But Bharadvāja, a man of great asceticism, being afflicted by hunger along with his sons in the lonely forest,
accepted many cows from the carpenter Vṛdhu.
Vṛdhu was my carpenter, one from whom gifts should not be accepted;
nevertheless, the seer named Bharadvāja accepted many cows from him.
Afflicted by hunger, Viśvāmitra— who was discerning in matters of dharma and adharma— approached to eat the haunch of a dog, having taken it from the hand of a Caṇḍāla.
The great sage named Viśvāmitra was world-renowned.
On one occasion, due to the suffering of hunger, he took a dog's haunch from the hand of a Caṇḍāla and approached it with the firm resolve to eat it.
The mention of the "dog's haunch" is intended to show that there is a fault not only in food that has been defiled by another, but also in that which is inherently impure by its very nature.
The intended meaning of the verse is that even food defiled by all kinds of faults may be eaten in times of distress.
Between receiving gifts, officiating at sacrifices, and likewise teaching,
receiving gifts is the lowest and is censured for a Brahmin after death.

The meaning of the verse is that when the possibility of officiating at sacrifices or teaching exists—both of which are slightly censured in times of distress—one should not resort to accepting gifts from censurable persons.
Sacrificing for others and teaching are always performed by those whose souls are refined;
however, the acceptance of gifts may be performed even from a Śūdra of the lowest birth.
In this very context, there is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) in the form of a reason:
it is simply the way of the world that those who have not been initiated do not study nor perform sacrifices;
therefore, even one who is greatly distressed will not officiate at a sacrifice for a Śūdra or teach him.
Giving, however, is established as being for all castes;
thus, it follows that one may accept gifts even from a Śūdra.
Therefore, that [acceptance] is inferior.
Sin committed through officiating at sacrifices or teaching is removed by recitation and burnt offerings;
however, that caused by accepting gifts is removed by renunciation and by austerity alone.
Through recitation (*japa*) and burnt offerings (*homa*), sin departs and is destroyed;
therefore, there is no harm [to the recipient].

As for the sin arising from acceptance (*pratigraha*), that is removed by the renunciation of that acceptance and by austerity (*tapas*)—which will be described as "drinking milk in a cow-pen for a month," and so forth.
A Brahmin who cannot subsist otherwise may gather grain, even by means of *śiloñcha* (gleaning ears and picking up single grains), from here and there;
gleaning (*śila*) is better than receiving gifts, and picking up grains (*uñcha*) is praised as even superior to that.
This restatement also expresses a mere explanatory praise (arthavāda):
"It is a great injustice that one should take another's property;
even though taking what is not heard of [in scripture] in such a case would be blameworthy, by this much it becomes praiseworthy."
In this context, moral conduct (*śīla*) belongs to the same category as receiving gifts (*pratigraha*);
it is precisely this [conduct] that becomes the cause for the suffix of excellence, as in the expression:
"moral conduct is superior to receiving gifts."
For excellence is experienced as a degree of superiority only in relation to something inferior;
indeed, it is never the case that a Brahmin is superior to a Caṇḍāla.
Therefore, even when gleaning ears of grain (*śila*) and picking up individual grains (*uñcha*) are included, the taking of food from one's own field is not [included].
Nevertheless, gleaning ears of corn and single grains is better.
Even though the livelihood of gleaning is said to be absolutely superior, it still bears some similarity to receiving gifts;
for in that case, there may be a deficiency in the ritual action due to the presence of presiding deities or the arrival of servants.
Even in the case of accepting what is improper, the notion that "this [acceptance] is not blameworthy because it is grasped within oneself" is untenable;
for in that context, the grasping occurs within oneself regarding material objects already present.
Therefore, even the livelihood of gleaning ears of grain and single grains is not free from fault.
Therefore, it is logical that "virtue is better than receiving gifts," and so forth.
If they are in distress, desiring base metals or wealth, the king should be petitioned by Snātaka Brahmins; however, if he is unwilling to give, he deserves to be abandoned.
In this context, three conditions for accepting gifts from a king are stated: "by those who are sinking" means by those who have reached the ruin of their household or are in distress;
"desiring base metals" refers to earrings, bracelets, and so forth, or turbans, seats, gold, or other wealth such as cattle, bullion, or other items suitable for sacrifice.
The lord of the earth should be entreated by Brahmins, and the ruler of the region should be petitioned.
Regarding the statement here that "one should not accept gifts from a king," that prohibition should be understood as referring to a wicked king;
for it has been said: "[from] one who is greedy and acts contrary to the scriptures."
He who, having been asked and desiring to give, nevertheless does not wish to give, deserves to be abandoned;
one should not dwell in his vicinity.
Alternatively, "tyāga" means loss;
and since nothing else is specified, it results in the loss of merit (dharma).
Cultivated land is better than uncultivated land; likewise, cattle, goats, and sheep, gold, grain, and cooked food—each preceding one is less blameworthy than the following.
A field that is unplowed and uncultivated is praiseworthy;
it also becomes suitable for goats and sheep.
The meaning of the verse regarding their mutual distinction is thus understood.
There are seven righteous means of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, conquest, investment, the application of labor, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous.
Inheritance (*dāya*) is wealth acquired through lineage;
gain (*lābha*) is [the acquisition of] treasure-troves and the like;
or it is the sharing of property acquired by a father or others.
Even if it has come down through the succession of one's father and so forth, it still cannot be designated by the term "inheritance" (*dāya*), because it is common to many.
Thus, it is stated in another Smṛti: "An *nibandha* is property.
Alternatively, that which is obtained out of affection from a friend or from the house of a father-in-law is "acquisition" (*lābha*).
Purchase is well known;
victory is [attained] in battle;
the application of labor refers to usury, agriculture, and trade.
And for this reason, these possess the nature of dharma according to the distinction of caste.
Among them, the first three are common to all;
victory belongs to the Kṣatriya.
For a Vaiśya, there are indeed the occupations of trade and agriculture;
for a Brāhmaṇa, the specific distinction is the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous. Even among all the social classes, the division follows the principle of priority as previously shown.
Some dispute over the purchase price; that is not correct, because it would entail the undesirable consequence of the collapse of all commercial transactions.
Some even desire that victory [in a lawsuit] be determined by a wager on every subject matter.
That is incorrect;
for in other Smṛtis, regarding the phrase "gambling with associates," it is stated that wealth obtained from gambling is impure.
Likewise, others say that *prayoga* refers to non-activity.
For instance, the usage "an application preceded by knowledge" (jñānapūrvaprayoga) is observed;
in that case, it is understood as "the application of a word.
Similarly, there are the expressions "application of action" (karmaprayoga) and "performance of action" (karmapracāra).
Knowledge, craftsmanship, wages, service, cattle-rearing, trade, agriculture, contentment, begging, and usury— these are the ten means of livelihood.

In times of distress, this mode of livelihood is permitted for all men. In that regard, knowledge—excluding the Vedic sciences—such as the science of medicine, logic, and the science of poisons and antidotes, is not blameworthy when pursued by anyone for the sake of subsistence.
Artisanal craft has already been explained.
Wages consist of servitude; service is the following of another's conduct;
contentment is satisfaction.
And this is for the sake of illustration;
therefore, these means of livelihood are intermingled according to the mode of conduct prescribed, because they pertain to human beings in general.
Neither a Brāhmaṇa nor even a Kṣatriya should ever practice usury;
however, for the sake of dharma, one may at will give a small amount to a more sinful person.
"For the sake of the Dharma" should be understood as referring to the aforementioned course of action in times of distress.
Because of the expression "from one who is more sinful," not even a small amount should be accepted from a righteous person.
As it has been said: "Agriculture, trade, and usury are equal to teaching [forbidden] when one has fallen into distress."
Even when taking a fourth part as his share during times of distress, a Kṣatriya who protects his subjects to the best of his ability is liberated from sin.
For a king whose treasury is depleted, an exception to the rule of taking a sixth part is permitted, whereby a fourth part is authorized;
the remainder is a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*). The word "param" is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), meaning "by means of supreme protection."
Victory belongs to him who follows his own duty; he should not turn his back in battle. Having protected the Vaiśyas with his weapon, he should collect the lawful tribute.

By the word "victory," that which is joined with the fruit of victory is enjoined as one's own duty (*svadharma*). Thus, one should not turn one's back in battle; the meaning is that when fear has arisen, one should not turn away from the fight.
Having protected the subjects in this manner, the king shall cause taxes to be levied from the Vaiśyas.
Since Vaiśyas possess great wealth,
those appointed to collect them in such a way are not killed even when they have committed an offense.
The toll on grain for the Vaiśyas shall be one-eighth; for other goods, it shall be one-twentieth, with a minimum of one kārṣāpaṇa.
Śūdras who provide services, artisans, and craftsmen [shall pay the same].
An eighth part of the profit of those dealing in grain should be taken;
the word *viṭ* here signifies "the people.
Of those dealing in gold, a twentieth part [should be taken].

Śūdras are those whose service is their means of livelihood; since their service is their instrument (upakaraṇa) or benefit (upakāra), they should not be made to pay anything. The same applies to artisans and craftsmen.
Thus, what was previously stated regarding artisans—namely, "month by month" and so forth—is for the purpose of taking an additional share; this verse [is intended] for that purpose.
But if a Śūdra, seeking a livelihood, should serve a Kṣatriya,
or if a Śūdra wishes to live, he may do so by serving a wealthy Vaiśya.
But when a Śūdra desires a livelihood, he should then serve a Kṣatriya;
because it is said that "taking up a livelihood" implies that service to a Kṣatriya is solely for the sake of subsistence and not for the sake of dharma.
It follows, therefore, that service to a Brāhmaṇa serves both purposes.
In this manner, one should live by pleasing a wealthy Vaiśya.
For the sake of heaven, or for the sake of both worlds, he should propitiate the Brahmins;
for one who has acquired the title of "Brahmin," that indeed constitutes the fulfillment of his duty.
It is said that he should "attain success.
Regarding this, he says:
when the word "brāhmaṇa" has arisen for him—that is, when this designation "this is a brāhmaṇa" applies to him—then he should be known as one who has accomplished his duty and achieved his purpose.
Alternatively, it should be explained as "of one who has acquired the designation of a Brāhmaṇa";
that is, when his designation arises as "this person is dependent upon a Brāhmaṇa."
Service to Brahmins alone is proclaimed as the distinguished duty of a Śūdra;
for whatever else he performs becomes fruitless for him.
Service to Brāhmaṇas alone is the primary duty of a Śūdra;
therefore, whatever else he performs, such as vows, fasting, and so forth, that is fruitless for him.
However, there is no prohibition against his performing acts such as giving gifts or *pākayajña* sacrifices, because these are directly enjoined by scripture.
The prohibition of other [occupations] is for the purpose of praising the service of Brāhmaṇas.
He should provide for his livelihood from his own family resources as is appropriate,
having considered their capacity, their skill, and the number of dependents they support.
This is the duty of the twice-born;
a means of livelihood must be provided for him as he performs service.
From one's own family, he is to be protected like a son.

Having considered his own capacity and his skill in performing duties, as well as the number of dependents he must support—namely, his servants and the wives and children belonging to them—he should provide for the maintenance of all of them.
Leftover food should be given, as well as worn-out garments,
the dregs of grain, and dilapidated household utensils.
The meaning of the word *ucchiṣṭa* has already been explained.
That which remains after guests and others have eaten should be given to a dependent Śūdra.
Likewise, worn-out garments that have been washed and are white [should be given]. *Pulākāḥ* are grains that lack substance.
In this way, the requisites such as beds, seats, and so forth [are also included].
For a Śūdra there is no sin whatsoever, nor does he deserve the sacramental rites;
he has no entitlement to dharma, yet there is no prohibition against him from dharma.
This entire verse is a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Whatever has not been specifically prohibited for him by way of direct mention—such as violence, theft, and so forth, which are prohibited by general injunctions regardless of one's specific caste—no sin arises from the transgression of those acts.
However, that which is explicitly heard through the word [of the Veda], such as violence, theft, and so forth, in that case he certainly incurs a fault.
Nor is he eligible for the sacrament characterized by the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*);
as it has been said, "The three castes are the twice-born.
Thus, he has no entitlement to *dharma*, such as ritual bathing, fasting, and the worship of deities; he possesses no obligatory duty (*nitya-adhikāra*) in these matters.
One does not incur sin by its non-performance;
it is not a prohibition from dharma.

Regarding those rites such as ritual bathing, fasting, and vows for which there is no mandatory performance and no sin in their non-performance—that is, where there is no prohibition—one does not face a prohibition regarding such dharmas.

If there were no such prohibition against this [practice], then, because it is prohibited by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), its performance would be appropriate for one desiring spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*).
In the same way, the abstention from eating garlic and so forth should also be understood as leading to his prosperity;
however, the abstention prescribed by the general scripture (*sāmānya-śāstra*) yields a great fruit.
Therefore, the undertaking [of this treatise] is based on the principle that there is no negation of the Dharma.
But those who desire dharma, who know dharma, and who practice the dharma of the virtuous, do not incur blame for [eating] except when it involves mantras; rather, they receive praise.

He says this very thing: "Desiring to attain the Dharma," meaning those who wish for spiritual prosperity; "having practiced the Dharma of the virtuous," meaning they have relied upon the Dharma of the noble ones.
Except for the recitation of mantras, they do not incur fault.
Therefore, by practicing the conduct of the virtuous—such as fasting for many days, worshipping deities, and paying homage to gurus and Brahmins—they do not incur fault;
rather, they obtain praise and its fruit.

Furthermore, one must not think that those rites of the Brāhmaṇas and others, such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa and so forth, which are accompanied by mantras, do not become faulty for a Śūdra when performed without the mantras.
For, when the rites have been prescribed with mantras, their performance devoid of mantras would be non-scriptural (*aśābda*).
Thus, the scope of the phrase "excluding the mantras" has been demonstrated.
And so the venerable Vyāsa has said:
"It is certain that a Śūdra does not fall here [in this world], nor is he eligible for the sacraments (saṃskāra) in this world.
However, he does not enjoy the dharma prescribed by the Smṛtis, nor is there a prohibition against him regarding dharma. Thus it is stated.
This too is merely a restatement of what has already been prescribed:
one does not fall [from caste] due to the consumption of garlic, liquor, and so forth;
it has already been stated that such acts render one unfit for the purificatory rites.

And it has been stated that, because he has not been initiated (*anupanīta*), in the absence of those duties prescribed by the *śruti*, the general duties prescribed in the *smṛti* according to the aforementioned manner are not prohibited for him.
Likewise, another *smṛti* states: "He may himself perform *pākayajña* sacrifices;
the *namaskāra* formula is permitted as his mantra."

Furthermore, as for those who say that Śūdras have an occasional entitlement to the establishment of the domestic fire (āvasathya-ādhāna), the pārvaṇa, the vaiśvadeva, the annapākayajña, and so forth,
we do not understand their intention;
for the establishment of the domestic fire has been prescribed by the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras specifically for the members of the three higher castes.
Furthermore, this has not been so ordained by Manu and others;
likewise, it is not ordained therein that one should perform the *gṛhya* rites solely in the nuptial fire.
How, then, could there be the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) for a Śūdra?
Now, if it is argued that the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna) is implied by the rules for the *pākayajña* sacrifices, that too is not correct;
the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice will take place in the common (laukika) fire. Indeed, what is explicitly stated in the text must be accepted as such; it is not possible to imply anything else.
This has already been demonstrated in the context of the phrase "in the marriage fire.
If by the word *pārvaṇa* the *āmāvāsya* (new moon) śrāddha is meant, we grant that; for the *aṣṭakā*, *pārvaṇa*, and *vaiśvadeva* śrāddhas have been prescribed.
However, if the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are meant, that has been refuted.
For in whatever measure one who is free from envy abides in virtuous conduct,
in that same measure he, being beyond reproach, attains both this world and the world beyond.
The meaning of this verse has already been explained.
For even a capable Śūdra should not amass wealth;
for a Śūdra, having acquired wealth, oppresses the Brāhmaṇas themselves.
Even though he is capable, a Śūdra must not accumulate wealth through activities such as agriculture;
regarding this, the author states an explanatory passage (arthavāda) concerning the nature of the reason:
having acquired—that is, taken possession of—great wealth, a Śūdra oppresses the Brāhmaṇas alone.
What, then, is the harm to the Brahmins?
Because of their great wealth, they might cause [the king] to accept excessive gifts from Brahmins;
yet, the acceptance of gifts from Śūdras is forbidden for them.
In that case, one would incur fault by becoming a cause [of harm];
and there is no suspicion of a karmic defect for one who performs what has not been prescribed.
Therefore, "one should not serve Brāhmaṇas"—this alone is the prohibition.
These duties for times of distress have been proclaimed for the four castes;
by properly performing them, they attain the supreme goal.
By correctly practicing the duties prescribed for times of distress, the supreme goal is attained.
Since there is no transgression of the ordained rules through the protection of the body, it is logical that one obtains auspicious results.
This is a restatement of the scriptural principle that one who has fallen into distress should not hesitate regarding the acceptance of improper gifts and the like.
This entire rule of dharma for the four castes has been proclaimed;
hereafter, I shall declare the auspicious rule for expiation.
This is established by the very reading [of the text].
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.

The *Manusmṛti* is venerable, and its appropriate commentary by Medhātithi has indeed vanished due to the power of fate, such that no manuscript of it can be found anywhere. Therefore, King Madana, along with his son Araṇasuta, had a restoration of this [work] undertaken from various regions by having manuscripts copied here and there.
Thus [ends the work] composed by Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi, the son of Bhaṭṭa Vīrasvāmin.
The tenth chapter in the Manu-bhāṣya.

Now begins the eleventh chapter: One seeking offspring, one intending to sacrifice, a traveler, one who has given away all his possessions, one seeking wealth for the sake of a teacher, for the sake of parents, one desiring to study the Vedas, and one who is afflicted by illness.
One should indeed know those Snātakas who are Brāhmaṇas seeking alms for the sake of dharma; gifts should be given to these, who possess nothing, according to the excellence of their learning.
The completion of the meaning of the sentence occurs with these two verses:
a donor characterized by many qualifications is enjoined;
that is, one should give according to the excellence of their knowledge to those who are destitute and who beg for the sake of Dharma from [the king] or others belonging to his lineage.
Now, when the word *dharmabhikṣuka* functions as a qualifier of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), it is understood to include the fulfillment of [the donor's] qualification (*adhikāra*).
Thus, it is said that the occasion for a specific [type of] gift is the cause (*nimitta*), and the entitlement to give (*dānādhikāra*) is contingent upon that cause (*naimittika*).
One whose life-continuum (*saṃtāna*) or progeny (*prajā*) is the purpose (*prayojana*) is called a *sāntānika*, meaning one who seeks marriage.
For in that case, wealth is utilized, and it serves the purpose of the lineage through successive generations. However,
because of the mention of "dharma," for those who proceed out of desire— namely, in the undertaking of a second or subsequent marriage— it need not necessarily be given.
Thus, one who makes a statement regarding his livelihood for the purpose of performing obligatory sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma should be understood [as follows]:
a traveler whose provisions for the journey are exhausted;

and a "possessor of all wealth" (sārvavedasaḥ), who has given away his entire property as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in the Viśvajit sacrifice, but not for the sake of expiation or similar purposes.
One who seeks the study of the Vedas:
although for a religious student (brahmacārin) both Vedic study and subsisting on alms-food have been prescribed, nevertheless, wealth sufficient for clothing should be given to him.
Alternatively, even for one who has mastered the Vedas and desires to know their meaning, [wealth should be given] even while he subsists on alms.
"Upatāpī" means one who is diseased.
The mention of the "snātaka" is for the sake of praise;
for it is generally in the case of a snātaka that [eating] for the sake of a guru or for the sake of Vedic study occurs.

It is prescribed that a student (brahmacārī) must perform service for the sake of his teacher. To those who are "niḥsva," meaning destitute or without wealth, [the gift] should be given according to the distinction of their learning: much to one with extensive knowledge, and little to one with little knowledge.
But is it not the case that all of this being introduced is irrelevant?
For it was promised: "Henceforth, I shall proclaim the auspicious rules for penance.
This is not a fault, because this section pertains to the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-dharma).

Because expiations (prāyaścitta) are of unequal nature, they are taught together; however, since this matter is the cause for the expiation, it is stated first. It was said that "a gift (dāna) should be given," and the word *dāna* here functions as a noun denoting the object of the action (*karmasādhana*).
In response to the expectation of what that which is to be given is, there is the following verse.
For food accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to these foremost of the twice-born;
for others, it is said that cooked food should be given outside the sacrificial altar (vedi).

Although the word *dakṣiṇā* refers to a gift bestowed in connection with a ritual officiant (*karmakara*), it nevertheless denotes a substance to be given other than cows, land, gold, vessels, and so forth.
For such is its common worldly usage; thus, "to others" means to those mendicants who are distinct from these [officiants].
Cooked food—that is, prepared food—should be given for the purpose of eating.
This very act of giving to guests outside the sacrificial altar—that is, elsewhere than at a sacrifice—is what is being restated here among the duties of a householder.
The king, however, should bestow all kinds of jewels upon those Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, as well as sacrificial fees for the sake of the sacrifice, according to their merit.
For all social classes, giving has been prescribed as a means to achieve human goals (puruṣārtha) for the sake of attaining fruits such as heaven;
however, this instruction is intended as a specific rule for the king.
A king possessing abundant wealth must bestow all kinds of jewels—such as gems, pearls, and so forth—upon the Brāhmaṇas according to their merit and in accordance with their learning and conduct.
And the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is for the sake of the sacrifice;
it is taught again [here] for the sake of accomplishing rites performed for specific desires (kāmyakarman).
"Should bestow" means he should cause [the recipient] to accept or cause him to take hold of it.
If one who has already taken a wife obtains another wife by begging for her, his fruit is merely pleasure; however, the continuity of the lineage belongs to the giver of the wealth.
This prohibition applies to one who, out of desire, seeks a second or subsequent marriage;
the statement that "mere pleasure is the fruit" and so forth is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), and should not be understood literally.
Others, however, explain [the matter] differently.
"That which is for the sake of the Dharma should be given to one who seeks the continuity [of the lineage], not to one engaged in sensual desire.

This same point is stated again in another way: "It should be given to one who seeks the continuity [of the lineage]; however, this person desires pleasure and is not one who seeks the continuity [of the lineage]. This is the meaning.
For that continuity belongs to the giver of the substance, not to him [the recipient].
One should bestow wealth upon Brahmins according to one's ability—those who are learned in the Vedas and live in seclusion; thus, after death, one enjoys heaven.
He who possesses food sufficient for three years to maintain his dependents,
or even more than that, is worthy to drink the Soma.
He who possesses wealth sufficient for the maintenance of his dependents for three years—that is, one who has a three-year supply—or more, is entitled to drink the Soma.
