Since the Śruti declares that the obligatory Soma sacrifice must necessarily be performed, this prohibition does not apply even when there is distress regarding the maintenance of dependents, because the authority of the Śruti is stronger.
Therefore, this prohibition concerns the optional (icchā) Soma sacrifice.
But is it not the case that wealth is employed for the purpose of hiring in the Soma sacrifice, since it is said, "Its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of one hundred and twelve [cows]"?
In that case, the livelihood increases, and therefore wealth is employed there in the Soma sacrifice.
It is not so stated: "He who possesses a three-year supply... and so forth.
But surely, since the wealth for the ritual function exists as a constant even when [other] wealth is absent, it is intended that this must indeed be performed even with wealth already available;
if the term "giving" (dāna) which effects excellence applies to mere food, then there would be the exclusion of such things as the giving of gold for the purchase of Soma and so forth.
Therefore, if a twice-born man drinks Soma when the substance is very small, even if he has previously drunk Soma, he does not obtain its fruit.
By this [verse], it is restated that for one who performs [an act] despite being ineligible by transgressing a prohibition, the absence of the result—which is established by logic—is indicated.
Furthermore, because of the mention of "the result" (phala), its scope as pertaining specifically to optional rites (kāmya) is perceived even more clearly.
This applies even to one who has previously drunk Soma.
By this, he shows the necessity of performing the first sacrifice;
this is an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda) regarding the drinking [of Soma] and so forth, and not a prohibition against one who has not drunk Soma.
One who is capable of giving to strangers while his own kin live in misery—this is a mere semblance of dharma; it is like the taste of honey at first, but bitter as poison in the end.
When one's own kin— servants, ministers, mother, father, children, wife, and so forth— are living in misery,
if one gives to those strangers for the sake of fame, that gift for him is like the taste of poison;
it is sweet at the onset and in its immediate impact.
Just as the taste of poison is sweet at the moment of contact but its ripening is bitter because its fruit is death, so too is such a gift.
Although it produces fame and happiness for the time being, it becomes equal to the taste of poison due to the arising of misfortune in the next world.
Thus he says: "That is a counterfeit of Dharma; it resembles Dharma but is not Dharma, just as mother-of-pearl is [the object] of the cognition of silver."
Whatever one performs for the sake of the afterlife by oppressing one's dependents results in unhappiness both while living and after death.
This is a deprecatory explanatory passage (arthavāda) regarding the preceding [rule]. Servants have already been explained.
"Impediment" (uparodha) refers to the taking of food, clothing, and so forth, according to their needs.

*Aurdhvadehika* refers to that which has the next world as its purpose. *Udarka* means the future time; since the result of this gift will have an unpleasant future, its purpose is already established [as being undesirable].
If a sacrifice of a sacrificer should be obstructed by the absence of even a single limb—
especially in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, while a righteous king is in power— then [the following applies].
If there should be a Vaiśya who possesses many cattle but performs no sacrifices and does not drink the Soma juice,
one may take that wealth from his household for the sake of completing a sacrifice.

In this context, because of the mention of "limbs" (*aṅga*), this act of taking gold is not prescribed solely for the failure of all other sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*); rather, it applies even in the case of those [gifts] such as animals and the like.
The expression "he should take" (*āharet*) denotes merely the origination of the act of appropriating it, not a specific means.
Consequently, it may be seized by begging, barter, or even by theft.
But has it not been stated that ownership does not arise through theft?
This is not a fault;
for here, by the very word "one's own" (sva), it is implied that it is to be taken away.
For it is thus said: "One may take [the property] of one who performs inferior rites.

And regarding this act of taking, there is no specific reason to distinguish whether it applies to one who has already commenced a sacrifice complete with all its constituent parts but lacks a single part, or to one who intends to commence it;
for since it is stated that this applies "especially to a Brāhmaṇa," the inclusion of even a single constituent part applies to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas as well under this same condition.
Now, it might be objected that since it is said "who is a Kṣatriya who would beg?", begging is forbidden for a Kṣatriya.
But this is saying too little;
even for a Brāhmaṇa, theft is prohibited.
Therefore, regarding that occasion, there is no restriction on the means of acquisition;
the statement "provided he is righteous" is merely a restatement (anuvāda),
for it implies that theft is prescribed for a king who knows the Dharma on that particular occasion.
But since everything else has been restrained, how could there be any activity?
The mention of "many cattle" is intended as an illustration for wealth in general.
One whose sacrifice is deficient does not perform even other acts such as giving and so forth, let alone the ritual itself.
Even though he is not a Soma-sacrificer;
"from the household" means from the family home.
For theft from one's own home is more blameworthy [than from elsewhere], and therefore that is permitted.
Furthermore, this restriction does not apply exclusively in this way;
rather, whatever is obtained from elsewhere, such as from a threshing floor and so forth, must certainly be used.
And he will say: "From a threshing floor, from a field, or from a house."
He may take three or two [grains] at will from the house of a Śūdra;
for the Śūdra has no proprietary right in sacrifices.
In the absence of a Vaiśya woman, [the milk] may be procured even from a Śūdra woman.
Regarding the phrase "three or two," it should be understood that these refer to the limbs (aṅga), based on the context of the limbs.
Here, the explanatory passage (arthavāda) states: "For there is no [impurity] for the Śūdra."

Although the acquisition [of wealth] through various means was previously prescribed, nevertheless, there is no begging for it here, according to the rule: "A Brahmin should not beg for wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice.
But is it not the case that in another Smṛti, the performance of a sacrifice with the wealth of a Śūdra is prohibited without distinction?
By the force of this instruction, it should be understood that one may accept [wealth] from a Śūdra.
But others say:
because it has been accepted by a Brāhmaṇa, that wealth does not belong to the Śūdra at all.
As for the prohibition, it should be understood as applying to that wealth with which the Śūdra performs rites for pacification, prosperity, and so forth, acting like a sacrificial priest.

In this case, however, the designation "wealth of a Śūdra" would apply to him by way of past history; and since there is no current status [as a Śūdra], the rule from the scripture remains "and that which belongs to her" (yā caiva).
If there is one who possesses a hundred cows but has not maintained the sacred fires, and another who possesses a thousand cows but does not perform sacrifices—
one may take [wealth] from the households of even these two without hesitation.

The meaning of the verse is that [the sacrifice] should be performed even by such Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas. The mention of "cows" is intended to indicate wealth of a corresponding measure. "One who does not sacrifice" means one who does not perform the Soma sacrifice.
If one takes back what was taken from a person who does not give it up because it is held as permanent,
then his fame spreads and his merit increases.
This verse applies to all social classes (*varṇa*).
One who is habitually acquisitive—meaning one who at all times earns wealth through agriculture, receiving gifts, usury, and so forth, yet does not give it away—must resort to other means.
The term "of the non-giver" (*adātuḥ*) should also be understood to include one whose character is devoid of sacrifice (*ayāga-śīla*).
In the same way, having fasted for six meals during the seventh meal-time,
one may take food from a person of low conduct according to the rule of not providing for the morrow.
Even when one's own family is in distress, one should take from others as previously described.
Because of the rule regarding taking only for the morrow (*aśvastana*), he permits [taking] only for the sake of sustenance for a single day, not more.
The phrase "of one of low occupation" refers to taking for the sake of work.
In another Smṛti it is said: "At first, one should accept [gifts] from an inferior; if that is not possible, even from an equal;
but if that is unavailable, one may take even from a superior, provided he is righteous."
Regarding the seventh meal:
when one has not eaten for three days, on the morning of the fourth day, he should proceed to take food for the purpose of eating;
thus, by the rule "one should eat in the evening and in the morning," two meals are prescribed for each day.
Whether from a threshing floor, a field, a house, or wherever it may be found,
that [stolen property] must be declared to the person who asks, provided he does indeed ask.
The phrase "or from where" refers even to groves and the like;
it means that [the teacher] must explain [the origin] to one who asks.
Regarding the statement "if he asks," he should not be made to ask by force through further sending [of messengers] or other such means.

Alternatively, if the owner of the property asks, or if the king asks, then having led him to the royal palace, the distinction between the regions must be shown. And thus Gautama says: "When questioned by the king, he shall declare [the facts]."
This rule is to be understood as applying in both cases—whether it concerns the interruption of food or the obstruction of a sacrifice—due to the specific context.
A Kṣatriya must never seize the property of a Brāhmaṇa;
however, he may take the property of a bandit or one who neglects his religious duties if he cannot otherwise subsist.
Regarding the phrase "by a Kṣatriya":
the mention of the Kṣatriya is intended to indicate the Vaiśya and the Śūdra as well.
The word "kadācana" (at any time) means "in times of great distress."
[This applies] specifically to two Brāhmaṇas who are, respectively, a Dasyu and one devoid of ritual action.
A Dasyu is a thief; one devoid of ritual action (niṣkriya), however, is one who does not perform his duties and lacks merit.
He who takes wealth from the wicked and bestows it upon the virtuous makes himself a boat and carries both across.
A *plava* is a boat for crossing the ocean;
it is that which carries away both [the giver] and [the recipient] to whom it is given—
this is a supplementary explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).
The wise know that the wealth of those who habitually perform sacrifices is the property of the gods;
but the wealth of those who do not sacrifice is said to be the property of asuras.
This is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda) for him:
one should not take [wealth] from those who possess virtues, but there is no fault in taking it from those devoid of virtues.
A righteous lord of the earth should not inflict punishment upon him;
for it is through the folly of a Kṣatriya that a Brāhmaṇa perishes from hunger.
In this circumstance, the king must not inflict punishment upon those brought before him as thieves;
for it is due to his own childishness and folly that they perish from hunger.
The word "hunger" here is used non-literally (as an *arthavāda*), since both factors are under discussion and because of the nature of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

Having ascertained his circle of servants and his own family members, and having understood their learning and character, the lord of the earth should provide them with a righteous means of livelihood.
A righteous mode of conduct is that by which even the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) are accomplished.
Even by one whose treasury is exhausted, something must be given by drawing from the inheritance assigned to the queen, the princes, and others, as well as from wealth prescribed for such purposes.
By the phrase "from his own family" and so forth, this rule applies specifically to a king of great wealth, because of the statement "all jewels."
Having provided for his livelihood, the king should protect him on all sides;
for from that protected person, the king obtains a sixth part of the merit of dharma.
The meaning of this verse is clear.
A Brahmin should never beg for wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice;
for a sacrificer who has begged [for such wealth] is born as a Caṇḍāla after death.
Begging for alms is prohibited here; however, there is no fault in obtaining what is offered unasked.
And so it has been said:
"One should know that the acceptance of goods obtained without being asked is not considered 'acceptance' (pratigraha) according to both distinguished worldly custom and the scriptures.
This prohibition concerns [wealth] not intended for sacrifice, but does not apply to the maintenance of dependents.
Some consider this to be merely a supplement to what preceded;
because they perceive faults in begging, they state that [the practice of] taking [alms] is taught as an alternative means.
That Brahmin who, having begged for wealth for the sake of a sacrifice, does not bestow it all,
goes to the state of a crane or that of a crow for a hundred years.
The fruit of using for another purpose that which was begged for and set aside for the sake of a sacrifice is the attainment of the state of being like a crow.
He who, out of greed, misappropriates the property of the gods or the property of Brahmins—
that evil-souled one lives in the next world on the leftovers of vultures.
The wealth belonging to the three social classes who are habituated to performing sacrifices is the property of the gods;
whereas the property belonging even to a Brāhmaṇa who is not habituated to sacrificing is the property of a Brāhmaṇa.
In this way, the verse remains consistent as well.

However, this verse beginning with "the wealth of those devoted to sacrifice" is an *arthavāda*; it is not intended as a technical definition of the meaning of words like "theft" and so forth. Therefore, it is explained otherwise.

Wealth that has been relinquished for the purpose of performing sacrifices and other rites dedicated to the gods is "divine property" (*devasva*), because a primary relationship of ownership is impossible for the gods;
for deities do not employ wealth according to their own will,
nor is any activity of guardianship observed on their part.

And that which is called "one's own" in the world is of such a nature. Therefore, that which is spoken of with reference to a deity—namely, "this is not mine, this belongs to the deity"—is *devasva* (property belonging to a deity).
And that is enjoined for the deities such as Agni in sacrifices like the Darśapūrṇamāsa.
This is established precisely by the conventional usage of the learned in the case of secondary means such as the worship of Durgā and so forth.
Now, it is said in the world that "the property of a deity" refers to images possessing four arms and the like;
and it is proper for the meaning of a word well-known in the world to be accepted in the treatise.
This might be so if the word *devasva* were established as being partless;
however, its collective meaning is superior because it is established through its parts, namely, "the property (*sva*) of the gods (*devānām*).
Furthermore, there is no basis in any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for postulating a separate sentence [to explain it].
The primary divinity of those with four arms and so forth has already been set aside by the conventional usage of "image" (pratimā).
Furthermore, there is no definition of a "destruction" (vyaya) here.
Even if it were considered "divine property" (devasva) based on common practice, there is nonetheless no relationship of owner and owned.
And in the manner already stated, the establishment of one's own conventional usage [is explained]; the remainder is in the second [chapter].
At the end of each year, one should regularly perform the Vaiśvānara-iṣṭi for the sake of expiating the failure to perform the prescribed animal and Soma sacrifices when they cannot be performed.
The nature of the Vaiśvānara sacrifice is to be understood from the Gṛhya-smṛtis.
"The change of the year" (*abdaparyaya*) refers to the commencement of the second year once the [first] year has concluded.

Regarding the prescribed and ordained animal and Soma sacrifices that are obligatory—such as the six-monthly or annual animal sacrifice, and the obligatory Soma sacrifice in the spring—[these must be performed].
In the event of their non-availability due to defects such as lack of wealth,
and for the sake of expiation— that is, to remove the fault incurred by the non-performance of an obligatory rite—
they prescribe another ritual act when this specific occasion arises.

In this regard, some maintain that there is a combination (samuccaya), even though the purpose is one and the same, because of the difference in the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and the injunctions here. That is incorrect;

for instance, regarding the expiation for killing a Brahmin, he will later state that there is an option (vikalpa) between the Vedic and Smṛti rites by the words "and by the Abhijit and Viśvajit sacrifices."
If a twice-born man performs a religious rite according to the rules for times of distress when he is not in distress,
it has been determined that he does not obtain its fruit in the hereafter.
For one who possesses wealth yet resorts to the secondary alternative—such as the Vaiśvānarī rite as a substitute for the rules of distress—that purpose is not accomplished.
By all the gods, the Sādhyas, the Brāhmaṇas, and the great ṛṣis,
fearing death in times of distress, a substitute for the sacred law was established.
This is precisely the meaning: a substitute should be resorted to in times of adversity, not in times of prosperity.
For that person of evil intellect who, though capable of following the primary rule, conducts himself according to a secondary alternative, there exists no fruit pertaining to the future life.
This too is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) supplementary to what precedes;
"sāmparāyika" means pertaining to the next world.
A Brahmin who knows the Dharma should not report anything to the king regarding those human disciples who have done him harm; he should deal with them by his own power alone.
The meaning of the verse is that there is no fault in the employment of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) when it serves as a sign; however, malevolent magic is not being enjoined here,
nor is the king's awareness [of the crime] being prohibited.
When the causal conditions are complete, one who proceeds to perform malevolent magic (abhicāra) should not be told anything by the king.
For it will be said: "The Ordainer, the Punisher, and the Speaker [is fate]"; therefore, one should not speak ill of him.
This is for the pleasure of the king.
Regarding the phrase "from the pupil":
even though there is a positive injunction [to report], one should inform the king; nor does the prohibition remain the primary intent upon considering the concluding verse.
Furthermore, the causes [for reporting] have been stated, such as "one who commits adultery with the wife," and so forth.

One who knows the Dharma and is skilled in the procedures for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) should inform the king, saying, "He has caused me some slight affliction," by means of his own power, through mantras and curses.
The meaning of the subsequent verse is precisely that.
Between one's own prowess and the prowess of a king, one's own prowess is more powerful;
therefore, a twice-born man should subdue his enemies by his own prowess alone.
A king might sometimes fail to act with restraint due to lack of skill, but he would never neglect his duty of his own accord; thus, his own effort is more powerful.
Without hesitation, one should employ the Atharva-Angirasa hymns;
for the weapon of a Brahmin is indeed speech, and with that, the twice-born may slay his enemies.
This verse is intended to dispel the doubt as to what that "one's own effort" (svavīrya) is. "Śrutayaḥ" means those things that are heard;
the meaning is that those methods of malevolent magic (abhicāra) which are heard in the Atharvaveda are to be performed.

Because the performance of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) is prescribed there in abundance, the term *Atharvāṅgirasa* is used; however, this does not mean that such acts are unauthorized in the other Vedas.
Alternatively, the scriptural injunctions regarding malevolent rites are designated by the word *Atharvāṅgirasa*.
Or else, the word *Ātharvaṇa* itself is employed in this very sense, as in the passage: "The sacrifice known to the Ātharvaṇas is for the fulfillment of desires."
A Kṣatriya should overcome his own misfortune through the strength of his arms;
a Vaiśya and a Śūdra through wealth; but the best of the twice-born through recitation and burnt offerings.
It is indeed a supplement to what precedes.
One who is a provider, a teacher, a speaker, and friendly is called a brahmin;
one should not speak what is unwholesome to him, nor should one utter harsh words.
This has been explained previously.
Toward a Brahmin who practices malevolent magic, one should not say "Let this man be subdued," nor should one utter unwholesome speech.
One should not let a harsh word escape.
There is also a prohibition against verbal censure and the punishment of "fie" (*adhigdaṇḍa*).

Alternatively, among all the social classes (*varṇas*), a Brāhmaṇa must not be provoked, for he is capable of restraining [others] by himself through the power of his knowledge of the three Vedas (*trayīvidyā*);
he is the ordainer and the creator.
He is the ruler and subduer of other kings;
he is the speaker of what is beneficial;
therefore, he is friendly.
Therefore, because he is endowed with all powers, he must not be disregarded as being weak.
Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one of little learning, nor a fool, nor one who is afflicted, nor likewise one who is uninitiated, should be the officiating priest for the Agnihotra.

Since the selection of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is prescribed for the *agnihotra*, and because the injunction "one should offer or cause [another] to offer" applies without distinction to both women and men, the possibility of women—whether maidens or young wives—acting as milk-offerers (*kṣīrahotṛ*) would otherwise arise; this is what is prohibited here.
Similarly, the possibility of one who knows only the rule for the two oblations, or one of little learning, or a fool, performing it is also prohibited.
"Afflicted" means suffering from disease.
"He is unconditioned and not initiated"—
but this is incorrect;

for regarding the *śrauta* Agnihotra, they follow the established practice that one should perform the sacrifice oneself on the *parvan* days, while at other times one of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should do so.

Furthermore, since the office of officiating priest (*ārtvijya*) is not possible for women, they explain that the prohibition regarding girls and young wives applies specifically to the *gṛhya* (domestic) fire, while its purpose is to permit it for a woman who has already borne a son.
Accordingly, other authors of *sūtras* also state: "If she so desires, the wife may herself offer the morning and evening oblations in the *gṛhya* fire.
Others, however, because of the statement "one who is skilled in the *vaitāna* [fires]," consider this to apply exclusively to the context of the three sacred fires (*tretāgni*).
The *vitāna* is the sacrificial hall (*vihāra*), and that is possible only in the case of the *śrauta* fires.
Furthermore, women and others do not have access there; nor is it for the ignorant, because the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*) is prescribed exclusively for distinguished men.
Therefore, the mention of the *agnihotra* is for the purpose of illustrating all ritual acts, and the mention of the *hotṛ* priest is for the purpose of illustrating all officiating priests;
thus, this *smṛti* is merely a restatement of the meaning of the *śruti*.

For these fall into hell, as do he who performs the sacrifice and he for whom it is performed; therefore, the officiating priest (hotṛ) should be skilled in the sacrificial rites and one who has mastered the Vedas.
These [persons], beginning with the maiden, go to hell when they offer oblations;
and so does the sacrificer who causes them to offer.
If a Brāhmaṇa, despite possessing the means, does not give a horse as the sacrificial fee for the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya),
he remains one who has not established the fires.
At the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), a horse should be given as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
The mention of the "Prājāpatya" [horse] is for the purpose of praise;
or alternatively, the Prājāpatya is neither too excellent nor too inferior.
Nevertheless, worldly people employ the term *prajāpati* with respect to such a matter;
because of the statement "provided there is wealth," even one who does not give when [wealth] is lacking certainly remains an *āhitāgni*.
One who is faithful and has conquered the senses should perform other meritorious deeds;
however, one should never, under any circumstances, perform sacrifices here with meager sacrificial fees.
A sacrifice where the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) given is less than what has been prescribed is called one with a "small fee. The fee is indeed for the purpose of hiring;
if a laborer can be obtained for a small wage, why should much be given, as is the case in the world with draft animals and the like?
For what wise person would buy for ten *paṇas* what can be obtained for one?
This prohibition is directed at one who thinks that the gift of twelve hundred [cows] is for the sake of increasing the fruit;
however, it does not prohibit those ritual systems which, by their very origin, have small sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) in the Soma sacrifice.
A sacrifice with meager sacrificial fees destroys one's senses, fame, heaven, longevity, renown, progeny, and cattle; therefore, one who possesses little wealth should not perform a sacrifice.
The statement of the result [arising] from the transgression of a previously mentioned injunction.
A Brāhmaṇa who, out of desire, neglects the sacred fires of the Agnihotra shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one month; for that act is equal to the killing of a hero.
"Having cast aside" means having abandoned. Abandonment consists of the non-performance and the cessation of obligatory rites such as the *agnihotra*.
Although this instruction on expiation (*prāyaścitta*) arises incidentally here, it is introduced because of the context.
Because of the use of the plural number in the word "agnīn" (the fires), one must infer that this refers to the abandonment of the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*).
The scriptural authority states, "He is indeed a slayer of heroes among the gods," and "He is a killer of heroes.
Since these words express intentional action, the same inference applies to intentional abandonment. However, in the case of unintentional abandonment, there is no such [sinful] consequence.
Those who, having obtained wealth from a Śūdra, maintain the Agnihotra sacrifice—
they are indeed the officiating priests of Śūdras and are censured among those who discourse on Brahman.

They explain that one should not perform the *ādhāna* (establishment of the sacred fires) with wealth obtained from a Śūdra out of favor or similar motives; however, the performance of obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) for one who has already commenced his religious life is not prohibited.
Thus it has been said: "One should not perform [ritual] practice after begging from a Śūdra."
However, there is no fault in obtaining what is not solicited for the sake of one who has already commenced a ritual act;
likewise, while sustaining oneself by accepting gifts from the unworthy is prohibited,
the performance of obligatory rites (nityakarman) is permitted.

Therefore, by the force of the statement that makes no distinction between wealth acquired through begging or obtained otherwise, this prohibition is understood to apply specifically to the *agnyādheya* (the consecration of the sacred fires).

If this prohibition were intended for all ritual acts, then since that would already be established, the specific prohibition against begging would not be stated; nor would it be said, "One should not [seek] wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of sacrifice."
Treading with his foot upon the heads of those who are constantly ignorant and who serve the fire of the low-born (vṛṣala), the giver shall cross over all difficulties.

The statement that the fires [of those who neglect their duties] become the fires of a *vṛṣala* is based on an indicative mark (*liṅga*); this entire section concerns the declaration of the fault incurred when one transgresses the preceding injunctions.
A man who fails to perform prescribed duties, practices what is censured,
and indulges in the objects of the senses becomes liable for penance.
Now the penances relevant to the present subject are being explained.
First, he defines the qualification for them:
what is the qualification here?

That which is prescribed as obligatory (*nitya*)—such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and the fire sacrifice (*agnihotra*)—is so because its obligatory nature is made known by such phrases as "one should perform the *agnihotra* as long as one lives.
Likewise, that which is prescribed for occasional causes (*aniyata-nimitta*), such as bathing after touching something impure, is also prescribed.
One who fails to perform these through negligence, laziness, or the like [incurs sin].
Likewise, one who, transgressing the scripture, indulges even in what is censured and prohibited, such as the drinking of liquor and so forth,
becomes liable to perform penance.
This is what is meant: this entitlement is contingent upon the performance of prescribed acts and the avoidance of prohibited ones; it is for this reason that there is expiation.
But is it not the case that the *sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice is prescribed for one who desires a village?
In that case, for one desiring a village, there would somehow be a transgression of the injunction in the event of non-performance.
Even if it were granted that the one desiring the village incurs sin, that [sin] would belong to him only when he has the desire for it;
for when he desires the village, then that [act] becomes enjoined for him.
If one does not proceed [to perform it], one would transgress what has been prescribed;
consequently, one would incur the need for penance.
To this, it is replied:
When one engages in an activity with the desire for a result, thinking "May I become the master of the village," that engagement is not characterized by an injunction (*vidhi*).
The scripture (*śāstra*), however, merely makes known the relationship between the sacrifice and the village as that which is to be accomplished and its means.

Although, in reality, even in that case the meaning of the sentence primarily establishes the necessity (*kartavyatā*) [of the action], nevertheless, the injunction makes that necessity understood solely for the sake of accomplishing the result.

Therefore, for one performing the sacrifice, the fruit is not produced, yet there is no transgression (*pratyavāya*). Where there is a transgression, there is expiation (*prāyaścitta*). But how is it known that a transgression occurs through the non-performance of obligatory rites (*nitya*)?
For it is not heard in the case of the Agnihotra and other such rites that "he who does not perform it shall incur sin.
However, it is heard in the supplementary passages (vākyaśeṣa) that "it becomes superior to the altars" and so forth;
in all such cases, these explanatory passages (arthavāda) exist for the purpose of demonstrating the transgression [of non-performance].

Furthermore, their objective basis (*ālambana*) must necessarily be stated; otherwise, they cannot form a single syntactical unit with the injunction (*vidhi*). Even where [an objective basis] is not explicitly heard, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are postulated for the sake of supporting the injunction.

Moreover, the capacity of the injunction to impel action is not established through the *arthavādas* alone; otherwise, it would be untenable as long as the avoidance of transgression (*pratyavāya*) resulting from non-performance is not postulated.

In such a matter, an injunction operates within the linguistic usage of the elders; however, it is understood as being directed toward the instigation of a person. And persons cannot be incited toward that which is not a human goal (apuruṣārtha).
Therefore, this conceptualization is for the purpose of establishing the Vedic revelation so that the injunction, which functions as an impeller, is not undermined.

Although such a result could be obtained even through the conceptualization of heaven and so forth, nevertheless, because it would contradict terms such as "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*), it must also have the purpose of avoiding transgression (*pratyavāya*).
This has been stated.
For the kind of activity that arises in men out of fear could not be produced here even by hundreds of millions of injunctions.
Therefore, it should be understood that "not performing what is prescribed" refers to obligatory (*nitya*) action.

But is there not any word [in the scripture] regarding the touching of impure things and so forth that indicates they are obligatory, such as [the word] "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*) and the like?
What is the purpose of another word here? It is because when a specific occasion (*nimitta*) is heard, it is understood that the duty must be performed by virtue of that occasion.
No dependence on another qualification arises;
for by the acceptance that "it must be performed whenever the causal conditions are present," its obligatory nature (*nityatva*) is established.

Even in the case of the *agnihotra* and other such rites, the word "obligatory" (*nitya*) is not used [in their primary sense], because their status as obligatory is due to the constancy of their causal conditions.

"Indulging in objects that are not well-known" means being devotedly attached to refined foods, the eating of cooked rice, the anointing with sandalwood paste, and so forth; that is to say, being intent on the longing for sense-objects.
[Objection: But has this not also been prohibited by the rule, "One should not indulge out of desire in any of the objects of the senses"?
[Response: He considers that this is not a prohibition, because it falls under the specific context of the *snātaka* vows.
For in that context, where the word *vrata* (vow) is the subject, it is a specific mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) that is taught as the prohibitor—the thought, "This must not be done by me.

Alternatively, someone might think that there is no parity [between the two] in the case of a minor prohibition, thinking that this particular thing is not being prohibited; therefore, they are made equal.
Alternatively, it is observed that even when a particular is already included within a general category, it is taught separately for the purpose of indicating its preeminence;
as in the example: "The Brāhmaṇas have arrived; Vasiṣṭha has also arrived.
[In this case,] one undergoes penance.
The word *prāyaścitta* (expiation) exists by way of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) in the sense of a specific occasional rite (*naimittika*).
Therefore, the exchange [of the order of words] in the phrase "or desires that" (*tad etīcchati vā*) must be made, according to the rule "transposition is frequent" (*vyatyayo bahulam*).
Furthermore, the mention of the word "man" (*nara*) is for the purpose of including all four castes (*cāturvarṇya*) within the scope of the injunction.
The wise know that expiation is prescribed for a sin committed unintentionally;
however, some say it is also required for a sin committed intentionally, based on the evidence of the revealed scriptures.
This is stated for the purpose of ensuring greater severity in penance even when a transgression is committed intentionally;
they say that penance is required for a sin committed unintentionally—that is, through negligence—which constitutes a violation of the scriptures.
For what reason, then?
"One who, transgressing the injunctions of each scripture, engages in what ought not to be done, will perform an expiation"—
what is the specific reason for this, since they consider that if an offense were committed intentionally, the expiation would render the scripture useless?
Thus he sets forth the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) by way of an objection.

The meaning of the scripture is that an expiation must be performed for a transgression committed both intentionally and unintentionally, because of the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even when done intentionally.
Regarding the phrase "on account of the indication of the Śruti," the *Upahavya-brāhmaṇa*—which contains a Vedic indicative mark (*liṅga*)—should be cited as an example:
"Indra gave the Yatis to the hyenas."
Furthermore, it is not possible for ascetics to give gifts to dogs unintentionally;
the meaning of the statement, "Prajāpati gave the Upahavya sacrifice to Indra for the sake of expiation," is clear.
A sin committed unintentionally is purified by the study of the Vedas;
however, that which is committed intentionally through delusion is purified by various kinds of expiatory rites.

Furthermore, do these penances terminate merely upon the occurrence of the cause—like the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and so forth—or do they extend until the effect is achieved—like physical purification (*śauca*), for the purpose of destroying the fault that has arisen?
Regarding this, some say:
"Indeed, action is not destroyed."
The very nature of dharma and adharma is that they cease only when their effect has been produced;
for actions do not perish without having bestowed their own fruit.
Thus it has been said: "Action is never exhausted."
Therefore, whoever commits a transgression necessarily experiences the fruit of hell resulting from it.
If one does not perform expiations, then from that transgression arises another sin (pratyavāya).
This is incorrect, for [sin] is not indeed karma.
"Therefore, for the sake of purification, one must always perform penance"—by these very words, the purpose of purification is prescribed.
And thus, by performing those [penances], one may remove the evil, because it was committed by oneself.
This is also stated: by the rule of prohibition, it is understood that the performer of the prohibited action incurs demerit (*pratyavāya*).
It is not possible to render that [falsehood] false by means of penances;
that too is incorrect, because he has understood it to be a cause of suffering,
and even in penances, there is indeed suffering such as austerity, charity, and so forth.

The cessation of a great future suffering that is anticipated through present suffering is indeed logical, just as [the cessation of] a disease is achieved by administering bitter and pungent medicines, light food, and so forth.
For example, if someone who has committed an offense comes of his own accord and informs the king, saying, "I am the one who did this deed," he receives only half the punishment;
however, he who is brought forcibly by the king's men is punished more severely.
Thus, the purposefulness of the instructions is established.
Therefore, because it is prescribed, its very nature is to counteract the effect [of the transgression].
Although it is designated by the term *niṣkṛti* (expiation) or *prāyaścitta* (atonement), it is also the removal (*niryātana*) of the fault committed.
Departure without cause is called "expiation" (*niṣkṛti*).
Likewise, even penance (*prāyaścitta*) is not for the purpose of restoring one's eligibility;
for it has been ordained that only for the five mortal sins (*pātaka*) does there occur a "falling away" (*patana*), which is the loss of the status and duties of the twice-born.

And in this context, one should not understand the division of subject matter as being "the study of the Vedas for unintentional acts and austerity for intentional acts," because both [remedies] are shown to serve both purposes, because they are recited under the heading of the instruction on causes [of sin], and because penances such as "the killer of a Brahmin [shall perform penance] for twelve years" are about to be introduced. Therefore, the purport of the verse is that the penance is light for an unintentional act and heavy for an intentional one.
But surely, one who acts unintentionally has no agency at all; it is only one who acts with prior deliberation (*buddhipūrva*) who is called an "agent.
And as in common worldly usage, when one is impelled by fate, people ask, "What is this person doing?
Furthermore, where an action proceeds from a desire for gain (*lipsā*), there a prohibition applies.

For one who desires intoxication does not wrong a thirsty person by saying, "Do not drink wine. However, for one who, seeking water and with the perception that it was water, has drunk wine, there is no fault, as he acted without knowledge; for his engagement in the act did not proceed from a desire for wine. Now, it might be argued that an engagement characterized by a scriptural injunction is not prohibited.
True.
However, among the characteristics of objects (*arthalakṣaṇa*), there is then a negation of every characteristic of an object by means of water.
Some say: [this is so].
A rule that culminates in a transgression has the same meaning as a prohibitive scripture, like the injunction to consume poison.
For them, this is not a matter for objection;
poison, when taken without distinction whether knowingly or unknowingly, invariably leads to death.
The same applies to such acts as the killing of a Brahmin and so forth.

Even for those who act because of the injunction "it must be done" and do not act because of the injunction "it must not be done," there is a prohibition regarding one who is engaged in worldly activity; and such a person is called an "engaged agent" (*pravṛtta-kartṛ*).
Agency exists even without prior conscious intention, as in the expression "the bank falls."
Nor is this absence of agency merely figurative;
for it is recorded in the traditional law (smṛti) that "the independent one is the agent," not that "he who acts by his own will is the agent.
Furthermore, from this very statement, it follows that there is a fault caused by negligence and that there is an expiation (prāyaścitta); what is the use of another speculative interpretation?
Having incurred the state of requiring expiation— whether by fate or by his own prior actions—
a twice-born man shall not associate with the virtuous as long as that expiation has not been performed.
"By fate" means by one's own negligence;
others, however, read "by delusion" (*mohāt*) in place of the word "fate," for it is only through delusion that an improper act is committed.
For what wise person would transgress the scripture?

[This applies] especially to action performed in a previous life—that is, action performed in another birth whose fruit has been experienced and which is inferred from signs such as having deformed nails—and likewise to that performed in this life, whether intentional or unintentional, as may be inferred from its signs.

What is meant is this: one must perform [the expiation] for a transgression committed in this life, whether done intentionally or unintentionally, and likewise for one committed in another life that is to be inferred from its signs.
Furthermore, what is the expiation for those with bad nails and so forth?
The *kṛcchra*, *atikṛcchra*, and *cāndrāyaṇa*—these are the general expiations.
However, Vasiṣṭha has stated that whichever mark a person possesses, that very same expiation must be performed by him in some measure.

And for this reason, all of them, having failed to perform expiation, should avoid association with the virtuous—by means of activities such as Vedic study, through sharing a single location, and so forth. Although association, being dependent on both parties, is effectively prohibited for both by the prohibition of one side, it is nevertheless prohibited again later on with the words "association with the virtuous [should not be done] by them," because the agents are different.
For if only one were prohibited, only that person would be subject to expiation, even though the association exists.
Therefore, for the sake of expiation for both parties, there is a prohibition in both cases;
consequently, one should not associate with those who have black teeth and so forth, provided they have not performed expiation, whether they be virtuous or non-virtuous.
In this world, certain evil-minded men undergo a transformation of their appearance due to their own misconduct, as well as by what they have done in the past.
He says this very thing:
"In this world, some [beings] are [afflicted] by misconduct— by the performance of prohibited actions in this life—
as well as by previously committed karmas, as was stated before."
Now, this conceptual proliferation regarding the transformation of form is set forth in sequence as the manifestation of the marks remaining from past misdeeds.
A thief of gold suffers from deformed nails; a drinker of liquor, black teeth;
a killer of a Brahmin, consumption; and one who violates the Guru’s bed, a skin disease.
An informer suffers from a foul-smelling nose; a slanderer, from a putrid mouth;
a stealer of grain, from a deficiency of limbs; and one who adulterates goods, from an excess of limbs.
One who steals food suffers from chronic illness; one who steals speech becomes mute;
one who steals clothing suffers from leucoderma; and one who steals a horse becomes lame.
Thus, by the distinction of their karma, they are born highly censured by the virtuous—
stupid, mute, blind, deaf, and likewise deformed in appearance.

The disease known as *kṣaya* is famous among physicians as *rājayakṣmā*; by that [sin], one becomes possessed of it through a particular kind of killing a Brahmin. One who approaches the wife of a guru becomes afflicted with a skin disease (*duścarmā*). A slanderer becomes possessed of a nose that carries a putrid odor.
Thus, the informer has a mouth that breathes out foul odors.
But is not the informer simply a slanderer?
True.
The distinction is this: one person, having imagined them, proclaims the faults of others, whereas another proclaims those that are real but unknown.
Excessive similarity consists in having too many limbs.
The "mixer" (*miśraka*) is one who adulterates substances with other things that merely resemble them,
such as mixing saffron with *kusumbha* dye or other items with others.
The "afflicted" (*āmayāvī*) is one whose consumed food does not digest properly.
Stuttering is a deficiency of speech wherein one is unable to respond; epilepsy is well known; the rest are of deformed appearance.
"Form" (*ākṛti*) means configuration; it is deformed and unattractive, resulting from their specific actions.

For those who have experienced the fruit of these actions in the hells of Kumbhīpāka and other places of Yama’s torment, when only a slight remainder of that karma remains and their accumulated merit (*sukṛta*), which had not yet yielded its fruit, becomes ready to bestow its own result, there arises the non-existence of evil karma (*duṣkṛta*); thus, the occurrence of a remainder of karma is established.
Therefore, one must always perform expiation for the sake of purification;
for those whose sins have not been atoned for are born endowed with censurable physical marks.
For one whose sins have not been expiated is characterized by blameworthy marks, such as deformed nails, black teeth, and so forth.
Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher's wife,
and association with those who commit such acts— these they call the great sins (mahāpātaka).
Approaching the wife of a guru, theft, and association with those who have fallen from their caste are the great sins (*mahāpātaka*) for all social classes (*varṇa*).
The drinking of intoxicants (*surāpāna*) is [a great sin] for the Brāhmaṇa alone.
Theft consists of the stealing of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold; for according to another Smṛti, "the theft of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold is a great sin."

The word *pātaka* (sin) applies to all transgressions—whether major sins (*mahāpātaka*) or minor sins (*upapātaka*)—based on its etymological derivation from the root *pat*, meaning "to cause to fall. The prefix *maha-* is used for the purpose of indicating gravity.
And [one should avoid] association with them, even with each one individually.
And he will say, "One falls [from one's caste] after a year," and so forth.
Falsehood regarding one's own excellence, backbiting directed toward the king,
and the persistent fabrication of falsehoods against a teacher are equal to the killing of a Brahmin.

The term "samutkarṣe" (for the sake of excellence) is a locative of purpose (*nimitta-saptamī*), as in the expression "one kills a tiger for its skin. That falsehood which is uttered with the thought, "I shall attain excellence"—whereby one attains an extraordinary degree of honor, wealth, or status through being a Brāhmaṇa, a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), or of noble lineage—is equal to the murder of a Brāhmaṇa. In such cases, one represents oneself as possessing qualities that one does not actually possess.

Alternatively, for one who desires to attain an excellence of the mass of merit through an exceptional recipient (*pātrātiśaya*), even an unworthy person (*apātra*) is called a "worthy recipient" (*pātra*). Such a designation of excellence (*samutkarṣa*) is false; however, this is not the case when there is a consideration of a minor matter, even if the term "excellence" is applied.
Slander is the disclosure of another's faults by speaking falsely;
it is the insistence on falsehood toward a teacher through the utterance of untruths that causes agitation of the mind,
such as saying "your daughter is pregnant" and so forth, out of groundless malice.
A dispute with him before the royal court, or persistent insistence, or the making of false accusations;
for Gautama likewise states: "False accusations against one's guru are equal to mortal sins (pātaka)."
Abandoning one's Veda, reviling the Vedas, giving false testimony, killing a friend,
eating forbidden food or what should not be eaten— these six are equal to the drinking of liquor.
For one who has studied his own Veda, forgetting it through lack of practice is "neglecting the Brahman" (*brahmojjhatā*);
or it is the abandonment of the injunction for daily Vedic study.
Giving false testimony, even in cases other than those involving self-elevation, is also [a sin].
The killing of a friend is the slaying of one who is a well-wisher.

Regarding "condemned food and that which is not to be eaten": "condemned" means prohibited by the scriptures, such as garlic and the like; "not to be eaten" refers to that which causes mental dissatisfaction, which one eats after resolving, "I shall not eat this."
The misappropriation of a deposit, as well as the theft of men, horses, silver, land, diamonds, and gems, is declared to be equal to the theft of gold.
This applies even to the deposit of worthless goods. The term "man" (*nara*) refers to the genus; thus, this same rule applies even in the case of abducting a woman.
For he who, having given his daughter in marriage, gives her again to another when no fault exists in the first man, for him also this same penalty applies.
Thus it is said: "One incurs the falsehood of a person."
They know that the emission of semen into women who are one's own kin, virgins, or those of the lowest castes, as well as into the wives of a friend or a son, is equal to violating the Guru's bed.
One's own sisters, those born from the same womb; maidens who have not yet been married; and women of the lowest castes, such as Barbaras and Caṇḍālas.
Of a friend (*sakhi*); a *sakhā* is a friend, [the genitive] is *tasya*. The mention of "woman" (*strī*) is not for the purpose of excluding [the prohibition] only in the case of a wife (*jāyā*).
In this way, there are other women of the son as well who are obstructed from the practice of sexual intercourse.

However, we say that although the term "woman" (*strī*) is used, the statement regarding their equality is made because it would be improper to treat the married and the unmarried as identical despite their difference.
This is not intended for the purpose of prescribing an expiation; rather, its primary aim is to demonstrate the gravity [of the offense].
Consequently, the expiation becomes more severe. As it has been said: "For sins that are grave, the expiations are grave; for those that are light, they are light."
For if this were intended for the purpose of prescribing expiations, it would have been stated in the very section on the prescription of expiations; furthermore,
the author would not later extend the expiation for killing a Brahmin to false testimony and the murder of a friend, which are here equated with drinking liquor,
nor would he again prescribe the expiation for killing a Brahmin for "false persistence against a teacher," which is here equated with killing a Brahmin.

Likewise, regarding the phrase "in the case of a maiden," since the emission of semen—which has been equated here with violating the Guru's bed—is further prescribed as having the same expiation as violating the Guru's bed, it is understood that this equation is not for the purpose of [the same] expiation.
Others, however, think that the equation will be stated separately even in the absence of actual gravity; this is not improper.

Therefore, the prescription of the expiation for killing a Brahmin for drinking liquor and for the two cases equated with it—false testimony and killing a friend—is for the purpose of expiation, as an alternative to the expiation for drinking liquor.
And for this [penance], only an extension (atideśa) is heard; however, there is no option regarding the equalization [of the penances],
as in the case of "having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown."
Now he states the minor offenses (upapātakas):
killing a cow, sacrificing for those unfit to sacrifice, adultery, selling oneself,
abandoning one's teacher, mother, father, or son, and neglecting the private Vedic recitation or the sacred fires.

Those who are unfit for sacrifice (ayājya) are Śūdras and others who have not committed a conflicting sin (aviruddhāpātakin). "Saṃyājyam" means the act of sacrificing for them; the suffix *ṇya* is used here in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*), which is a Vedic usage. "Selling oneself" means making oneself subject to the control of another, like a commodity such as cattle, by way of servitude.
Others, however, read "adultery" (*pāradārya*) and "selling [what should not be sold]" (*avikraya*).
Lack of enthusiasm and abstention from food refer to resorting to despondency even when faced with a very slight affliction. Abandoning the teacher means failing to attend upon him properly.
If the teacher is capable of teaching but fails to do so, one may resort to another teacher;
the same applies to the mother and father. Furthermore, the abandonment of these persons, provided they have not fallen from their status, leads to sin.
But for those who have fallen [from their caste], this is indeed intended:
"the abandonment of Vedic study and the sacred fires" is what is connected [to the rule].
And the abandonment of Vedic study consists in the non-performance of the injunction: "One should study the Veda every day."

Is this transgression [applicable] to the abandonment of [the practice] on a single day, or to that which lasts for a month or a year? Since there is no distinction specified, it would follow that it applies to the daily [practice]. That is incorrect, because this rule is obligatory (*nitya*).
Furthermore, he will state a different expiation for the transgression of obligatory duties;
therefore, what is intended here is abandonment up to the point of forgetfulness. That [abandonment] is equated with the drinking of liquor by means of the term *brahmohjhatā* (neglect of the Veda).
In this regard, the following is for the purpose of providing an alternative option.
Since this [latter] is light and that [former] is heavy, an alternative should be applied according to the specific situation.
In that context, if one who is already engaged in another Vedic rite abandons his Vedic study, that constitutes a minor offense (upapātaka).
However, for one who abandons [the fires] out of devotion to sensual enjoyments, attachment to wealth, or a habit of quarreling, it is equal to drinking liquor.
But because "fire" is mentioned here as characterized by singularity, it should be understood as referring to the domestic fire (*gṛhya*).
Since there was previously the plural form "fires" (*agnīn*), it follows that the Vedic fires (*śrauta*) are what is being referred to.
But surely, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance has been prescribed for that case as well; since this [act] is also a minor offense (upapātaka), the same should be stated here too.
This is not a fault, for among the minor offenses there are other penances as well.
The distinction between heavy and light, or lesser and greater, depends on one's capacity;
therefore, the mention of the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance there is for the purpose of establishing a rule.

"Abandoning a son" means failing to support him or expelling him from the home when he is no longer an infant and has attained adulthood; however, there is no fault in abandoning a son who is a sinner.
The elder brother remaining unmarried while the younger is married is *parivitti*, and the younger brother marrying before the elder is *parivettṛ*.
Furthermore, giving a daughter in marriage to either of them, or officiating as a priest for either of them in a sacrifice, [is likewise forbidden].
The younger brother is the *kanīyān* sibling.
The officiating for those two refers to performing the role of a priest (*ṛtvij*) at their weddings or at sacrifices such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.
Defiling a maiden, usury, the breaking of a vow, and the sale of a tank, a garden, a wife, or one's own offspring;
Defiling a maiden (*kanyādūṣaṇa*) is the act of representing her as having been enjoyed by a man through the determination that "this girl has been used by a man.

Alternatively, it is the insertion [of a finger] into the generative organ with the thumb and so forth; this constitutes a distinct category of *dharma* (offense), excluding the act of sexual intercourse itself.
For in that latter case, equality with violating the Guru's bed (*gurutalpa*) has been stated.

Usury (*vārdhuṣitvam*) is the adoption of a livelihood through the lending of wealth when there is no distress. However, in the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti* it is said: "The lending of grain for interest is called usury (*vārdhuṣitvam*).
And this is a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) of the scriptures.
Nor does it apply to worldly matters.

"Falling away from the vow" (*vratacyuti*) refers to a resolution (*saṃkalpa*) such as: "I shall not eat in that person's house which is forbidden by the learned; I must indeed fast. Falling away from that resolution constitutes one's falling away from the vow.
But is it not the case that "vow" (*vrata*) refers to a restriction (*niyama*) made by one's own will?

And if that resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is made by one's own will, then what transgression of scripture (*śāstrātikrama*) occurs upon its cessation? For it has been stated that one who fails to perform what is enjoined becomes subject to penance (*prāyaścitta*);
yet this [resolve] is not something enjoined.
It is said:
True, the undertaking is characterized by desire;
however, the completion is scriptural.
Just as there is engagement in optional rites such as the *saurya* sacrifice out of a desire for results, yet their completion is governed by the scripture;
so too, when the desire for the fruit has passed or the fruit has been obtained, they should avoid the remaining parts as prescribed, saying, "This man is a coward who merely started the work.
However, an extremely light expiation will be declared for the transgression of the *snātaka* vows.
Therefore, this may be considered as follows:
a grove consists of gardens, parks, and the like;
according to another Smṛti, all land is not to be sold.
The state of being a Vrātya, abandoning kinsmen, teaching for wages,
receiving instruction for a fee, and the sale of goods that should not be sold;
Relatives (*bāndhava*) are those other than uterine brothers and the like, such as maternal uncles, maternal cousins, and so forth;
even they, if not yet living, must be maintained when one has the means.
Thus it is said: "when one's own kin are living in misery."
If this is so, then the passage beginning with "of the son" (*sutasya*) and so forth is redundant.
No; the statement serves another purpose, just as the prohibition of the *haṃsa* follows from the prohibition of the *jālapāda*.
Therefore, the abandonment of one's mother and others constitutes a minor offense (*upapātaka*).
But here, however, it is lighter: teaching for wages. This refers to one who teaches while being a hired laborer, as well as one who studies from such a hired teacher.
The ten items that are not to be sold have been stated in the tenth [chapter].
Authority over all forms [of crafts], the operation of great machines,
the harming of medicinal plants, living off women, malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), and root-rites (*mūlakarman*).
"Mines" (*ākarāḥ*) refer to lands containing gold and other minerals; "authority over them" (*tatrādhikāraḥ*) means lordship by virtue of royal appointment.
By the inclusion of the word "all," other sources of revenue are also understood;
thus, this includes the administration of villages and cities, as well as the administration of judicial proceedings, the infliction of punishment, and the collection of taxes.
In the same way, there is the operation of great mechanical devices such as dams and embankments for the purpose of regulating the flow of water;
the injury and cutting down of unwithered medicinal plants;
and the livelihood of women.
Livelihood by means of a woman includes maintaining one's body and family with a woman's wealth, or treating a wife as a commodity for sale, or employing courtesans.
Sorcery (*abhicāra*) consists of killing an enemy through Vedic curses, the application of mantras, or sacrifices such as the *Śyena*.
Root-work (*mūlakarma*) is the act of subjugation performed solely through the application of mantras and similar rites.
Felling green trees for the sake of fuel,
undertaking activities for one's own sake, and likewise eating food while disparaging it.

However, there is no fault in using [fire] for purposes such as fuel, since it is purified by fire and all [substances] may become dry. The "undertaking of an action" refers to the undertaking of cooking; because of the prohibition that it should not be for one's own sake due to being afflicted, the undertaking of an action is explained in this manner.

For if the prohibition were inferred solely from the instruction regarding expiation at the commencement of an action, it would not be logical for there to be an expiation for what is not prohibited; this is because of the statement: "and one who practices what is censured [is subject to penance].
But now, since the prohibition is already established by what has been stated, the expiation is prescribed.
Therefore, there is no burden of conceptual construction [in this case].
[The objection is: "Is it not the case that [the rule] 'one should not eat food that is censured' refers to food and drink that are already condemned? From where does this [present case] arise?"
This is for the purpose of distinguishing [the cases]:
that penance applies to repeated practice, whereas this [present case] applies only once;
or else, there is a difference in the underlying cognition.
Not maintaining the sacred fires, theft, non-payment of debts,
studying heterodox scriptures, and the practice of acting as a professional actor.

The author of the Smṛti considers that for one who has performed marriage, possesses wealth, or has fathered a son, the state of not having established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgnitā*) is a transgression; because there is no distinction regarding their entitlement, the obligatory Vedic injunctions (*nitya-śruti*) serve as the motivators for the obligatory establishment of the fires (*nityādhāna*). But how, then, is the establishment of the fires enjoined by the Veda?
In a certain context, it is stated that by this [injunction], even the traditional scripture (*āgama*) would be sublated.

Furthermore, since its own subject matter is understood to be for the purpose of producing the fires—as in "one offers in the *āhavanīya*," and so forth—how could there be an application to another subject matter?
For the fires have already been enjoined by such passages as "one offers in the *āhavanīya*."
And since their accomplishment does not occur without the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*), it is said that when the fires are employed, that [establishment] is also employed.
If this is so, then the entitlement (*adhikāra*) for those who have established the fires exists for the purpose of accomplishing the fires; in the absence of the fires, one is not entitled.
Furthermore, the establishment of the fires is not obligatory (*nitya*) in the same manner as the injunctions for lifelong performance (*yāvajjīva*) and the like.
Therefore, how can there be the fault of not maintaining the sacred fires?
For it is prescribed that an expiation must be performed for the non-performance of what is enjoined, as in the injunction: "One should establish the fires.
True, it is indeed enjoined.
It is not for the sake of heaven, nor for the attainment of another qualification;
rather, it is for the production of fire.
And as for fire, one who knows its purpose and has need of it acquires it by that means, whereas another does not.
What suspicion could there be here of the non-performance of what was enjoined, such that one would have to undergo penance?
For how could he who does not acquire gold be considered at fault? It is replied:
From this very statement, it is understood that when one has the qualification [for Vedic study], the sacred fires must necessarily be acquired.
"Theft" refers to taking property other than those items already mentioned. "Of debts" means the performance [of the rites] according to the scriptural injunction "by four debts."
And false treatises are those of the Cārvākas and Nirgranthas, wherein neither valid means of knowledge nor Vedic action connected with its fruit is found;
as well as the state of being a professional actor, a wandering minstrel, a dancer, or a singer.

The theft of grain, base metals, or cattle; the consumption of intoxicants and consorting with forbidden women; the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; and atheism—these constitute secondary sins (upapātaka).
The seventeen types of grain include hemp and so forth;
base metals consist of items made of iron, copper, and the like, such as small pots and cauldrons.
But was it not already stated in the preceding verse that theft [in general] is [a sin]?
This has already been answered by the analogy of the prohibition against swans (*haṃsapratiṣedhavat*).

Alternatively, theft (*steya*) occurs when something is taken from another and, having been acquired, is not purified through its inherent nature; for it is not universally recognized as "theft" merely because of an act of taking away, such as [taking] through fortitude and so forth.
Regarding the term "drunkard" (*madyapa*): [it refers to one who drinks intoxicants].
A Brāhmaṇa’s consorting with women of the Kṣatriya or other castes—whether by sharing a bed or engaging in sexual intercourse;
the killing of a woman, even a Brāhmaṇī;
and atheism, which is the dogmatic adherence to such views as "there is no other world" and "there is no merit in giving."
Causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa, smelling things that should not be smelled or intoxicants, crookedness, and sexual intercourse with a male are recorded as acts that cause loss of caste for a Brāhmaṇa.
The function of causing bodily pain by means of a staff in hand and so forth is the activity of *ruj* (harming).
Why then [is it] "not to be smelled"? For there is no prohibition against smelling anywhere, as there is a prohibition against eating.
But it is not possible to understand that whatever is inedible is also untouchable;
for ghee and other substances taken for the purpose of sacrifice are inedible, yet they are not untouchable.
It is said in reply:
Because it is putrid and foul-smelling, garlic, onions, human excrement, and the like distort the sense of smell; these are what are intended here.
Furthermore, by association with intoxicants (*madya*), only that which is unfit to be eaten is understood, not rotten wood and such things.
Deceit is crookedness, a lack of clarity in the heart; one thing is said, another is done, and something else entirely is held within the heart.
The killing of donkeys, horses, camels, deer, and elephants, as well as goats,
sheep, fish, snakes, and buffaloes, should be known as acts that cause loss of caste (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*).
The deer—such as the *ruru*, the *pṛṣata*, and others—are wild animals.
The *ibha* is an elephant;
although it is also a type of deer, it is specifically mentioned here because it generally dwells in villages.
*Mīna* means a fish;
*ahi* means a serpent.
Accepting wealth from those who are censured, engaging in trade, serving Śūdras,
and speaking untruths should be known as acts that render one unworthy (apātrīkaraṇa).

Those Śūdras who are censurable and unworthy of receiving gifts because they perform evil deeds—from them, the taking of wealth by way of acceptance is forbidden, since accepting gifts from those whose acceptance has been repeatedly rejected is prohibited.
The killing of worms, insects, or birds; eating food mixed with liquor; stealing fruits, firewood, or flowers; and lack of fortitude—these bring about impurity.
Worms are small creatures that take refuge in the earth;
likewise, insects are those of similar nature whose bodies are somewhat more developed, including wingless and winged varieties such as flies, locusts, and the like;
and birds are winged creatures such as parrots, starlings, and so forth.
"Associated with intoxicants" means touched by intoxicants and permeated by their odor. "Lack of steadfastness" is the instability of the mind; it is a falling away even from a slight impairment.
Now, learn correctly those various vows by which all these aforementioned sins are respectively expiated.
The causes for expiation have been stated;
the distinction in terminology is for the purpose of distinguishing between types of expiation.
This is a summary statement of what is about to be explained.
A slayer of a Brahmin shall dwell in the forest for twelve years, having constructed a hut,
subsisting on alms for the sake of self-purification, and carrying the skull of a corpse as his banner.
A dwelling constructed of grass, leaves, and so forth, which serves as a protection against rain, heat, cold, and the like, is called a house or a hut (*kuṭī*).
"For years" means for equal years. "Subsisting on alms" means...

In another Smṛti, alms-gathering from seven houses without prior intention is prescribed. Regarding the phrase "the head of a corpse," it is understood that one should carry a raised representation of a head made of wood or similar material as a banner for one who has been killed or another [criminal].
Those who know the meaning of words do not hold this view;
for that [person] is not called "the corpse's head.
Furthermore, there will be another injunction here, such as "one who has had his hair shaved should dwell [there]," and so forth.
Or he may become a target for those who bear weapons, according to his own wish;
or he may cast himself headlong three times into a kindled fire.
Where archers aim and pierce a target in battle, one must become that very thing;
or else, in the midst of combat, one should receive the blows of weapons from others while fighting elsewhere,
according to one's own will.
If one who is included therein kills through negligence, there is no purification even though he has killed his own [son];
those who are learned understand that this is an instruction regarding expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Alternatively, it refers to knowledge of the science of archery (*dhanurveda*).
Or he should throw himself into a blazing fire, rising up three times and falling back in again.
Or he should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha, the Svarjit, or the Gosava;
or with the Abhijit and Viśvajit, or even with the Trivṛt-Agniṣṭut.
The ruler of a realm has the entitlement to perform the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
In that rite, the prescribed sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of wealth brought from the east and other directions, such as gold and so forth.
Furthermore, those who have not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) are not entitled to participate in these sacrifices.
Furthermore, the laying of the fires (ādhāna) need not be performed for that purpose alone;
for the ritual acts intended as expiations must be complete with all their constituent parts (sāṅga),
and the laying of the fires is not itself a constituent part.
Or one may travel seven hundred yojanas to Japan or any other [sacred land] for the sake of removing the sin of killing a Brahmin, eating sparingly and with senses restrained.
Eating moderately, he is not satisfied by more than necessary; his senses are restrained, he lives a life of celibacy, and he is without greed for sense-objects.
One should bestow one's entire property upon a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas;
for wealth sufficient for livelihood, a house, clothing, and household goods [should be given].
Whatever there may be, such as cattle, gold, and so forth—all that must be given.
Regarding this, there is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*): "For wealth is sufficient for life.
By giving that much wealth to another, one has effectively given life; thus lies the equality.
"House, dwelling, and household goods.

By the word "household goods" (paricchada), whatever implements for the house are included—such as clarified butter, oil, grain, and so forth; pots, pans, and the like; and base metals, beds, and seats—all that is understood.
Or, eating only sacrificial food, he should follow the Sarasvatī upstream;
or, with his diet restricted, he should recite the Saṃhitā of the Veda three times.

He should subsist on sacrificial food (haviṣya), the food of sages (munyanna) such as wild rice (nīvāra) and the like, as well as cultivated food (grāmya) such as water, milk, clarified butter, and so forth.
He should follow along as many streams as there are in the Sarasvatī, moving against the current;
being restricted in diet, he should practice the cessation of food.
One should recite the Vedic Saṃhitā, together with the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, three times.
Regarding these penances, the following is the settled rule here:
for the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa, the twelve-year penance is an alternative to this [target-shooting] for those who bear arms.

Even though the twelve-year penance does not end with death, nevertheless, if an intermediate death occurs by the decree of fate, the transgression is not averted because there is no purification until the penance has been completed.
In the case of the second [penance], however, one is freed from sin at that very moment;
or, one who is struck by a weapon might perhaps not die.
For this very reason, the penance previously mentioned should be given as an option according to one's preference;
however, entering the fire applies only to one endowed with qualities such as being a *śrotriya*,
and even then, only when that fire possesses the quality of having been used for a *savana* sacrifice.

There are three states for the slayer of a Brahmin; its conclusion is the tearing apart of the limbs with a weapon, as they read in the case of one who has entered the *savana*. Furthermore, a doubling [of the penance] is not possible in cases where death is the end, for it is not possible for death to occur twice in a single birth.
Because he experiences an equivalent amount of suffering, his [penance] is doubled;
however, it is not proper for the twelve-year penance to be doubled.
For who, even among those equal to the gods, would perform a penance for twenty-four years?
For if one dies with a year remaining [until the end of the penance], everything becomes fruitless.
As for the Aśvamedha sacrifice, it is an alternative to the previously mentioned rites for members of the three higher castes when possible.
However, the Gosava and other such sacrifices may apply in the case of an unintentional killing by one who possesses great virtues.
And for the killing of even a single member of the Brahmin caste, [the penance lasts] for a hundred *yojanas* by way of mental resolve;
the same applies to the subsequent cases as well.
In the phrase "with the *Trivṛt-agniṣṭut*," there is a grammatical coordination (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
In this way, with the Svarjit and Gosava [sacrifices], there are two expiations, namely the Abhijit and Viśvajit.
Having shaved his head, he should dwell at the edge of a village, or in a cow-pen, or in a hermitage,
or at the foot of a tree, devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins.
This is a certain optional rule taught as a specific feature of the twelve-year penance:
shaving the head is a new requirement;
furthermore, at the foot of a tree belonging to the hermitage, there may optionally be a hut.
Why, then, was it not stated right there?
The ancient commentators have explained that it was so that what is about to be taught regarding one who has already commenced the twelve-year penance might constitute a separate expiation;
for if it were independent, it would apply elsewhere when another [penance] has been commenced, since a fault is heard of in the case of failing to complete what has been commenced.
Because they are treated as distinct subjects, there is a separate application;
that is, one [application] belongs to the other.
For the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow, one should properly sacrifice one's life;
the protector of a cow or a Brahmin is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Even without providing protection, one is liberated by the complete renunciation of life; and even with providing protection, one is liberated without the renunciation of life.
