Whether he attempts to prevent it, or wins back all his property, or even loses his life for the sake of that [property] belonging to a Brahmin, he is released from sin.
One who has resisted, engaged [in combat], or been wounded by a weapon in the act of fighting— this applies to at least three [instances].
If it is fewer than that, then there must be three repetitions.
He is released if he engages in battle, even if he dies without having rescued [the victim];
or if he recovers the entire property—including what was stolen by thieves—from Brāhmaṇas and others;
or if he grants the gift of life to a Brāhmaṇa for that purpose.
But was it not said that "one who protects a cow and a Brāhmaṇa [is purified]"?
True;

it was stated that if one liberates a cow stuck in the mud or being carried off by bandits, or a Brāhmaṇa being carried away by enemies, thieves, or a river, through battle or some other physical exertion of the body, then he is purified.

In this case, however, because of the apprehension regarding that cause, if a Brāhmaṇa, while his wealth is being seized, kills himself out of confusion or fights recklessly with thieves, then by giving him an equivalent amount of wealth—consoling him by saying, "Do not die; I shall give you this much wealth"—and having given it, one is released from liability.
Thus, one who is firm in his vows, constantly practicing celibacy, and concentrated in mind,
removes the sin of killing a Brahmin upon the completion of the twelfth year.
From this statement, it is understood that the remainder from the beginning has been transcended.
The words "of firm vows" (*dṛḍhavratas*) and "composed" (*samāhitas*) are particles used for metrical completion.
This is the conclusion of what preceded.
Or, having confessed his own sin before the gods on earth assembled with the king of men, he is released from it after bathing in the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the horse sacrifice.
The final position is stated:
having confessed one's own fault to the brahmins who are the deities of the earth, in an assembly with the human kings, the kṣatriyas.
The officiating priests are Brāhmaṇas and the sacrificer is a Kṣatriya; thus, having performed the Aśvamedha and bathed at the concluding rite (*avabhṛtha*), he is liberated.
Because the twelve-year penance has been previously mentioned, this [Aśvamedha] is intended as an independent alternative.

Others, however, maintain that since it is taught among the alternatives, it serves as the limit for the completion of the commenced twelve-year penance itself—just like the rescue of a cow or a Brāhmaṇa.
"Just as, by means of the Sarasvata sacrifice, one attains either a fortnight or a springtime [of prosperity] upon rising";
however, we say:
because the first [alternative] has been withdrawn, there is an optional half-reading; thus it possesses both forms when it is possible for it to occur both at the commencement and at the conclusion.
The Brahmin is said to be the root of Dharma, and the Kshatriya its summit;
therefore, by confessing one's transgression in their assembly, one becomes purified.

The explanatory passage (arthavāda) here is that the sin of the sacrificer and the officiating priests—whether they be Brāhmaṇas or Kṣatriyas—must be made public at the assembly of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
By his very birth, the Brahmin is the deity even of the gods;
he is the authority for the world, for Brahmā alone is the cause in this matter.
One who has committed an offense must approach an assembly (*pariṣad*);
however, the procedure to be performed by that assembly must be one that honors the sacred law (*vidhi*).
Such is the nature of this assembly; to this effect is the following verse and the next.
By his very birth, a Brahmin is a god even among gods and an authoritative witness for the world, like one who perceives with direct vision;
no one doubts even his word.
The reason for this is the Veda, which is Brahman; for he who knows its meaning is accepted as an authority when he points out that which is unperceived.
Those three who are knowers of the Vedas shall declare for them a complete expiation for the offense;
that shall serve as their purification, for the speech of the learned is indeed purifying.
By this, the approach to the assembly (*pariṣad*) by one who is performing penance (*prāyaścittin*) is described; and its definition is: "Three Brāhmaṇas who know the Vedas constitute an assembly.
But will it not be stated later that "an assembly consists of at least ten members"?

Likewise, in the statement "even a single knower of the Veda [is qualified] regarding dharma," it is not the number ten that is prescribed for persons; rather, it is the qualities. And thus, in the passage "one who knows the three Vedas, a dialectician, a logician," it is indeed the qualities that are being specified.

By the phrase "even one who knows the Veda," he makes this clear: even in the absence of other qualities such as being a logician (*haituka*), the status of being a member of an assembly of those who know the Veda is attained by the knowledge of the Veda alone.

Thus, although the qualities such as being a logician were mentioned [previously], they are not required here; for otherwise, the mere state of knowing the Veda would not constitute the definition of an assembly of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).
This verse, however, is intended to specify the number.
In this context, although the term "knowers of the Veda" (*vedavid*) is employed, qualities such as being a rationalist (*haituka*) and so forth are also included;
for otherwise, the status of a knower of the Veda would not constitute the defining characteristic of an assembly of the learned (*śiṣṭapariṣad*).
We shall explain this very point later.
If being a knower of the Veda does not occur without [the possession of] rationality and so forth, then how is it that this was stated: "even one who knows the Veda"?
We shall explain right there that even in the absence of other qualities, this was said for the purpose of including one who knows the Veda.
Therefore, three persons who have performed penance must be questioned together.
At times, negligence or lack of attention may occur even for a single person;
likewise, even by one who is learned, this act of approaching the assembly must be performed for the sake of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
And thus, the speech of the learned is indeed purifying.
Nor does it follow that there would be an absence of secret penances;
for that is "secret" when it is unknown to anyone, whereas if it is known, one must go before the assembly.
And so it has been said: "By confession and by remorse.

This, however, is incorrect, because this [matter] falls within the domain of conceptual construction. For it is said: "Having considered the capacity [of the offender] and the nature of the sin, one should determine the penance"; thus, one should determine the penance for those cases where no specific expiation has been stated.
In that case, if a conceptual construction has been made by means of three [reasons], it is to be considered valid.
Therefore, by adhering to any one of these rules with a concentrated mind, a Brahmin,
through self-mastery, removes the sin committed by killing a Brahmin.
This verse serves as a summary of all the penances for the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*). The mention of the "Brahmin" here is intended to indicate all social classes (*varṇas*).
"He removes" means he takes away.
By "possessing a self" is meant possessing self-knowledge;
one who is intent upon the meaning of the treatise is called "one who possesses a self.
Such a person's determination does not deviate from the meaning of the treatise.
Having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown, one should observe this very same vow;
as should one who kills a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who knows [the Veda], or a woman who is an Ātreyī.
The fetus belongs specifically to the Brahmin caste.
By whom should the abortion be caused?
It is "unrecognized," meaning that the specific characteristics of the woman or man are unknown.
The designation [of the killer] is according to the respective cause of the woman or the man.
But how can there be the destruction of the fetus when the woman herself has not been killed?
It occurs through the administration of medicinal herbs and the like, resulting in the abortion of the fetus.
Because of the singular number in the phrase "this very [penance]," they say that only the twelve-year penance immediately preceding it is extended by analogy.
Others, however, hold that "this" refers to the cause of purification in its general sense; therefore, there is an extension of all penances.
This applies when a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya is the one who knows [the secret] and acts as the sacrificer.

The past tense is not intended [as significant here], as in the other Smṛti rule: "A Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya who have gone to the Soma sacrifice. Therefore, this injunction applies to those who have already begun the drinking of Soma, and not to the sacrificers of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other such rites.
But the observation of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is that [the text] causes the sacrificer and the wife to exist;
thus, "having become a Brāhmaṇa woman, she sacrifices. An *Ātreyī* is a woman born from the lineage of Atri.

Since there is no distinction in caste between women and men, Brahmin women would also be included [in the category of those whose killing constitutes a minor offense]; therefore, the mention of the *Ātreyī* is intended to exclude those of other lineages (*gotra*).
Consequently, the killing of any other Brahmin woman is indeed a minor offense (*upapātaka*), as stated in the rule:
"The killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya."
As for the phrase "friend of women," that refers to women of all four castes (*cāturvarṇya*).

Regarding women of lower status, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the penances for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) and major offenses (*mahāpātaka*). This option depends upon the qualities of the husband and whether the act was committed intentionally or unintentionally.

In the case of a nursing mother and her infant, or when the life of infants is difficult to sustain in their absence—even if they are of a different caste—the killing of a Brahmin’s wife who, though faultless, is being incited by her husband’s hatred or by some other cause, provided she maintains her virtue and does not engage in sexual intercourse; even so, because of the injunction that "the killing of a woman or a friend" is [a minor offense], this applies only in such a context. Otherwise, however, the rule is "women and Śūdras."
Regarding an *ātreyī*, however, there is no alternative [view].
Others, however, say that an *ātreyī* is a woman in her courses because of her association with pregnancy, based on the rule: "The killer of an embryo and the killer of an *ātreyī* shall be slain."

A "bhrūṇahā" is one who commits the killing of a Brāhmaṇa; and she must be a Brāhmaṇī woman herself. In this context, she is called an *ātreyī* because a fetus (*garbha*) is necessarily carried (*uhyate*) within her womb (*kukṣi*).
Although a secondary derivative suffix (taddhita) is not prescribed by traditional rule for such a formation, it nevertheless occurs in accordance with actual usage.
Having given false testimony, having reviled a teacher,
having embezzled a deposit, and having committed the murder of a woman or a friend;

However, this expiation applies when one speaks falsely regarding testimony concerning gold, land, and so forth, or when there is a doubt as to whether a killing or similar crime has occurred; for in these cases, an excess of fault is heard in the scriptures, as in the passage beginning with "of those who break [the law]," and so on. In other instances, the determination of the penance must be made according to the relative gravity or lightness of the offense.
"Pratirabhyeti": that which was called "stubborn adherence to falsehood" is precisely this *pratiraṃbha*—an undertaking of harm toward the teacher preceded by agitation (*saṃrambha*). *Nikṣepaḥ*.
In this case as well, there may be the assumption that [the person] is a poor man, a wealthy man, one of low status, or another member of the Brāhmaṇa caste, and so forth.

However, where only one [type of person] is heard mentioned, it must be according to what is explicitly stated; what occasion is there for such an assumption? Moreover, there is no light penance prescribed here for false testimony or for misappropriating a deposit.

Even that [penance] prescribed for drinking liquor is equal to this, and is even more severe, because it takes into account whether the subject has been heard or not heard [in the scriptures], as well as one's capacity—even though there is the scriptural statement, "for those for whom no expiation has been declared."
This purification has been declared for killing a twice-born man unintentionally;
for the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa, no atonement is prescribed.
"Having killed" means having slain.
"Expiation" (*niṣkṛti*)—the meaning of this has been explained previously; it is intended to teach the gravity of the penance (*prāyaścitta*).
If a twice-born man, out of delusion, drinks liquor, he should drink liquor that is red-hot like fire;
when his body has been consumed by it, he is then released from that sin.
The Vedic revelation regarding the twice-born is intended solely for the Brāhmaṇas;
and another Smṛti states: "They may drink hot *surā* [only] for a Brāhmaṇa. The phrase "out of delusion" refers to this.
The mention of the color "fire-colored" is for the purpose of indicating the general characteristic of perceiving colors and sounds;
for this very reason, it says that when the body is consumed by fire, one is liberated.
Or he should drink cow's urine that is fire-colored, or water alone;
or milk, or ghee, or even the liquid from cow dung, until death.
One of the prescribed penances indeed results in being turned into the color of fire.
The specific substances such as cow’s urine and others are intended to prevent death by other means.
And it should be understood that *surā* refers specifically to that made from flour (*paiṣṭī*).
They designate her as "the principal" (mukhyā);
however, in other instances, the usage is figurative (gauṇa).
And this [penance applies] to drinking [liquor] intentionally.
And so he will say:
"Having drunk *vāruṇī* out of ignorance, one is purified by the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) alone.
It should be understood that "fire-colored" means "touching fire."
And so he says, "until death.
Liquor is forbidden even for women;
for it is stated in the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti*: "Likewise, a Brāhmaṇī woman who drinks liquor becomes [degraded]."
The gods do not lead her to the world of her husband;
having exhausted her merit, she wanders right here in this world, and after death, she becomes a water-dweller among the waters.
Or, for the sake of removing the sin of drinking liquor, he should eat grain-husks or oil-cake once at night for a year,
wearing hair-cloth, with matted locks, and carrying a skull-topped staff.
This [consumption] is permitted when life is at risk for the sake of medicine,
even if it is something otherwise prohibited.
However, if it was done through ignorance, a re-consecration accompanied by the *taptakṛcchra* penance will be shown later.
Others, however, maintain that *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* possess a figurative status of being liquor;
thus it is stated in another *Smṛti*: "For the drinking of *asurā* and *madya*, the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance should be practiced.
The word "once" (*sakṛt*) applies as a remainder to both *kaṇa* and *piṇyāka*.
At night;
"clothing made of hair" refers to cloth made from cow-hair, goat-hair, and so forth; "wearing matted locks" means having them in a topknot or otherwise with the remaining hair.
"Having a banner" means by means of a jar of liquor and so forth.
Surā is indeed the dregs of food, and evil is called a dreg;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink surā.

Although the word *anna* is etymologically derived as the object of the act of eating, its most common usage nevertheless refers specifically to rice and the like, as well as cooked grains (*bhakta*), flour-meal (*saktu*), cakes (*apūpa*), and so forth.
Thus, the distinction made in the expression "condiments with food" (*annena vyañjanam*) is logically justified.

Therefore, since liquor produced from flour (*paiṣṭī surā*) is designated as "food" because it is a derivative of ground grain, this [scriptural statement]—namely, that it is "the dregs of foods"—provides the justification for its prohibition; this is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the prohibition of liquor made from flour.

The mark [of sin] accrues to the three castes; even by the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes, *peṣṭī* should not be drunk. Furthermore, that alone is the primary *surā*, [as compared to] the *gauḍī* and *mādhvī*.
Thus, just as the expiation for *sīdhu* and *mādhvīka* is heavy, it is not so for other intoxicants such as *ariṣṭa* and the like.
The word "impurity" (*mala*) is explained as "sin" (*pāpman*) for the purpose of showing an excess of censure.
Even though this occurs within the section on expiations, this is a prohibition against drinking *surā* based on the force of the sentence itself.
And because it constitutes a separate sentence, it is not an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).
Gauḍī, paiṣṭī, and mādhvī are to be known as the three kinds of *surā*;
just as each one is [forbidden], so are all of them; they must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born.
That which is a derivative of molasses is *gauḍī*.
Even for those for whom only sugarcane juice itself becomes intoxicating, the designation *gauḍī* is not contradictory, as it is a metaphorical application of the name of the cause to the effect.
That which is a derivative of honey is *mādhvī*.

*Madhu* and *mādhvīka* [are forbidden] by virtue of their state of transformation (*vikāra*). This shows that there is no prohibition for the fresh juice of the grape (*mṛdvīkā*) as long as it has not reached the stage of being intoxicating liquor (*madya*).
For the traditional law (*smṛti*) states: "Indeed, they consider untransformed *madhu* and *mādhvīka* [to be permissible]."

Even where there is a prohibition by means of the word *madya* (intoxicant), there is no prohibition at all for one who has not yet acquired the capacity for drinking intoxicants, because such a person is not denoted by the word *madya*.

Just as the word *śukta* (fermented sour liquid) applies to that which possesses a specific state and not indiscriminately— since that very same substance, when it has not yet attained acidity, is not called *śukta*.
Just as that very same cow is not a bull while it is in the state of a calf,

so too, through the mere mixture of a combination of flour, water, and so forth, there is no *surā* (fermented liquor) until, by means of a period of fermentation, it has acquired the power to intoxicate.
This should be understood to apply likewise to the transformations of sugarcane juice and *mṛdvīkā* (grapes).
In that case, it follows that there would be drinking of only a small amount— namely, that quantity which, when drunk, does not cause intoxication—
and also due to the contact with substances that act as an impediment.
This is not a fault.

This is not a prohibition against the arising of intoxication, such that one should act in a way that one does not become intoxicated or drunk; rather, it means that whatever possesses the capacity capable of producing intoxication must not be drunk,
for even a small amount possesses that power.
To the extent that even a small amount of dry wine with little potency causes intoxication, whereas a large amount of oily wine with great potency does not—
it cannot be asserted on this basis alone that the power of intoxication is absent [in the latter].
Furthermore, the non-existence of the cause [of intoxication] in wines is certainly not established by the absence of the effect.
For it is not inferred that fire lacks the power to burn simply because it is incapable of burning a large piece of wood, since such fire is observed to possess the power to burn dry grass.
Furthermore, as for the argument that if the capacity were obstructed by another substance, one would incur the sin of drinking [alcohol],
that too is not a valid objection.

For it is not that such a thing lacks the power to burn when burning with grass; rather, although that power exists, it is incapable of initiating the effect. Furthermore, for you, the presence of a counter-cause does not destroy the power, which is eternal, nor do other substances destroy the power, but rather they obstruct the initiation of the effect.

And likewise, even when there is contact with substances that produce that same quantity [of intoxicant], a person of bilious temperament (paittika) becomes intoxicated while one of phlegmatic temperament (ślaiṣmika) does not; therefore, it is inferred that there is no destruction of that [intoxicating power].

Consequently, this is neither a prohibition of the future state of being an intoxicant, nor is it a prohibition of the substance having reached a particular state—such as the absence of an obstructing factor—as in the case of saying, "That thief must be avoided."
This is not a negation of that which has not yet attained the state of being sour; [rather, it is a negation of what would otherwise follow].
As for the form *mādhvī*, since it is a quality, one might ask why it is not *mādhavī*;
the resolution is that "a rule conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not necessarily fixed."
And the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this *paribhāṣā* is the inclusion of the term "guṇa" in the rule *or guṇaḥ*, where one could have simply said *āroḥ*.
Furthermore, the mention of the "best of the twice-born" (*dvijottama*) here is for the purpose of permitting the drinking of wine for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.

Thus, the drinking of wine by the Bhāratas and Yādavas described in the *Mahābhārata*—as in the subsequent verse, "Both Keśava and Arjuna were seen by me intoxicated with honey-liquor and *āsava*"—is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
But then, how is the plural form "all" (*sarvāḥ*) justified, given that there is only one object of comparison (*upamāna*) and two objects being compared (*upameya*)?

Furthermore, here the statement regarding the impurity of food (*annamalatva*) is both a statement of reason (*hetunirdeśa*) and an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), where the impurity is the reason, just as in the case [of the injunction]: "One offers with a winnowing basket, for by it food is prepared."
Wine, meat, and spirits— food for Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas—
must not be consumed by a Brāhmaṇa who partakes of the sacrificial oblation (havis) of the gods.
Yakṣas and other censurable beings, devoid of discrimination between what is fit and unfit to be eaten, consumed meat.
*Surā* and *āsava* constitute *surāsavam*;
according to the rule "the singular form is used for classes of inanimate things," it is treated as a singular collective.

In this context, *āsava* refers specifically to a particular kind of intoxicant; it is mentioned here as being slightly distinct from ordinary liquor, much like the expression "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*).

For a Brahmin who partakes of the oblations due to the gods—such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa* cakes prescribed for the New and Full Moon sacrifices—it is proper to consume these, but not the food of Piśācas and the like, such as liquor and meat.
Intoxicated by liquor, a Brāhmaṇa might fall into impurity, or he might recite the Veda, or he might perform some other improper act, being deluded by intoxication.
Falling into impurity is an explanatory praise (arthavāda) similar to [the prohibition against] eating the food of gods.
But one might ask: how can a Vedic example be something that should not be done? To this it is replied:
In comparison to that, one might perform another improper act.
How is it improper? Because the utterance of the syllables of the Veda by an impure person is prohibited.
He whose Brahman residing in the body is once drenched with liquor loses his status as a Brahmin and becomes a Śūdra.
The heart, which exists in the form of refinement within the Veda that has been studied, is designated by the word "Brahman.
Therefore, when the heart is flooded with liquor, one attains the state of a Śūdra.
The mention of the Brāhmaṇa is for the purpose of prohibiting all types of intoxicants for the Brāhmaṇa.
This demonstrates that for both Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, the prohibition applies specifically to liquor distilled from flour (paiṣṭī).
This manifold expiation for the drinking of liquor has been declared;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the expiation for the theft of gold.
The preceding and following verses have their purpose already stated.
A Brahmin who has committed the theft of gold, having approached the king and made his own deed known, should say: "May your majesty punish me."

This is the expiation for stealing gold from a Brāhmaṇa. The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is intended to indicate all social classes (varṇas), because no other specific expiation has been prescribed for Kṣatriyas and the others. "Instruct me" means "restrain me."
And having gone, the king should be addressed;
furthermore, in this context, the word "king" (rājan) refers specifically to the ruler of a country and does not depend on the Kṣatriya caste.
Taking up a club, the king himself shall strike him once;
by this execution the thief is purified, but a Brāhmaṇa is purified by austerity alone.
A *muśala* is a particular kind of staff, made either of iron or wood;
it is intended that he himself [wield it] once.
He is purified by death.
Whether the killing by a single blow results in death or not,
one becomes pure by such a strike with a club;
however, a Brahmin becomes pure through the austerity that will be described hereafter.
Here too, the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is not intended to be restrictive;
likewise, the term "twice-born" (dvija) will be used later on.
And although the theft of even a *kṛṣṇala* constitutes a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), nevertheless, the penance ending in death should be understood to apply to the theft of a hundred *suvarṇas*.
The penance involving punishment has been stated in its corresponding form.
And here it has been said that "for more than one hundred [strokes], there is execution"; therefore, for cases below that, an appropriate determination must be made.

As for the other penance where "one becomes purified through death," in that case the king should take up an Udumbara weapon and cause him to die by it; for it is known from scripture that "one becomes purified through death."
When the killer is a Kṣatriya or similar person who is both a master and virtuous, this [penance] is understood to apply;

however, when he is intent on death, then it may be so—either for the sake of a specific purpose, or as an offering of that purpose, or then the remainder [of the penance] consists of being naked, smeared with ghee, and falling from a height onto cow-dung and the like.
But a twice-born man who, desiring to remove the impurity born of stealing gold through austerity,
shall wear rags and perform the penance for killing a Brahmin in the forest.

And because of this restatement of the twelve-year penance (*dvādaśavārṣika-dharma*), it is an extension (*atideśa*) of that very [penance], not of the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*); there is no other expiation (*prāyaścitta*). The construction is: "He shall perform that vow (*vrata*) which has been prescribed for the slayer of a Brahmin. *Apanunutsuḥ* means desiring to remove (*apanetum icchuḥ*).
That is to say, desiring purification.
By these vows, a twice-born man may remove the sin committed through theft;
however, he should expel the sin of approaching the teacher’s wife by means of these same vows.
But surely, since the two [penances]—"the thief is purified by execution" and "by austerity"—are mentioned earlier, the use of the plural "by these" (*etair*) is not correct.

This very fact is an indicator that one should prescribe even those [penances] not explicitly mentioned, including those already stated, depending on the circumstances such as the attendant factors (*anubandha*).
The term *gurustrīgamanīyam* means that which has sexual intercourse with the teacher's wife as its motive.
The "sign" (nimitta) is also called the "purpose" (prayojana), because it causes [the action] to be undertaken; that is, it impels one to act.
Having addressed the sin of violating the teacher's bed, he should lie upon an iron bed;
or he should embrace a blazing metal image (sūrmī); by death, he is purified.
"An adulterer of the guru's bed" (gurutalpagaḥ) or "one who has violated the guru's bed" (gurutalpī)— this is the reading.
By the suffix -in in the word *talpī*, which expresses possession, a specific kind of sexual union between a man and a woman is denoted.
The teacher (guru), the preceptor (ācārya), and the father— here the word *talpa* refers to a wife. Having approached the wife of a preceptor, one must perform this penance.
Another [penance] applies to approaching a woman of the same caste who is like one's own mother;
these three penances are prescribed for intentional acts after having publicly proclaimed the sin.
On a bed or couch made of iron that has been heated by fire, he should lie down, for there is a scriptural statement that "one is purified by death.
A *sūrmi* is a heated iron image in the form of a woman; he should embrace it, that is, he should hug it.
Or, having himself cut off his penis and testicles and placed them in his joined palms,
he should walk straight toward the direction of Nirṛti until they fall.
Purification occurs through the process of excision.
The power implied by the instrument is an auxiliary factor in all cases;
whatever is capable of cutting is obtained through that capacity.
The south-western direction is the *nairṛtī* quarter.
"Walking straight" means walking without crookedness;
the meaning is that one should not avoid chasms, pits, and the like.
For a reflection upon walls and such objects would indeed move as soon as it encounters them.
Carrying a skull-topped staff or clad in rags, with a beard and dwelling in a solitary forest,
he should perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year with a concentrated mind.
This expiation applies to approaching one's own wife under the delusion that she is another woman when it is not preceded by conscious intent;
it also applies to approaching a woman of a different caste even when done intentionally.
*Cīra* means a fragment of cloth.
"Bearded" means one whose beard has grown;
even in the case of approaching a woman of the same caste who is unchaste, the expiation is indeed light.
Or, with his senses restrained, he should practice the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for three months,
subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya) or barley gruel (yavāgū), in order to expiate the sin of violating the Guru’s bed.
This penance applies to approaching the wives of maternal uncles, paternal uncles, and others for whom the status of "guru" is extended by analogy.
*Haviṣya* refers to milk, roots, clarified butter, and the like;
*yavāgū* refers to liquid gruel and similar drinks.
By these vows, those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin) may remove their impurity;
likewise, those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) [may do so] by means of these various kinds of vows.
This is a concise statement of what has been said and what is yet to be said.
One who has committed the minor offense of killing a cow shall drink barley-gruel for a month;
having shaved his head, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, covered with the hide of that very cow.

"Goghna" means "one who kills a cow"; the suffix *ka* is applied here according to the rule for words such as *mūlavibhuja*. Regarding the phrase "he should drink barley," some say it refers to drinking barley-flour (*saktu*).

Others, however, maintain that the word denoting the raw material (*prakṛti*) is used here for its product (*kārya*), namely the barley-gruel (*yavāgū*); therefore, what is intended is that one should grind the barley and have [the sinner] drink it.
In the former position, there would be the assumption of unmentioned liquids such as water;
for barley cannot be consumed without water and the like.
Here, however, it is a mere indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and an indication is lighter than the assumption of what has not been mentioned.
"Having performed the shaving" means having shaved the head, or it refers to the cutting of the hair.
"In a cow-pen" (goṣṭha) is where the cows reside; [he should do so] with that hide.
It is not that the cow was killed, but rather that another [animal] was also [killed].
For two months, with his senses restrained, he should eat a limited amount of food, free from pungent seasonings and salt, at every fourth mealtime, and perform his bath with cow urine.
Having eaten a single meal every two months, one should eat in the evening on the second day.
Since "alkaline" (*kṣāra*) is mentioned as a specific type of salt, rock salt (*saindhava*) is not prohibited;
for if the prohibition of alkaline substances were independent, it would apply even when they appear in a copulative compound (*dvandva*).
In that regard, the application of the expression serves to indicate the meaning of two words.
When there is a simultaneous substratum, a *dvandva* compound is formed.
Once the *viśeṣaṇasamāsa* (descriptive compound) is established, there is no connection with the permission (*anujñā*) of a qualified object.
There is no brevity through compounds and the like; "measured" means very little.
It is not that much by which satiety occurs and the maintenance of the body is achieved.
"Bathing with cow urine at all three times [of the day];
for two months, at the fourth time"—this is the connection.
Thus it is stated in another Smṛti.
Having shaved his head, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, covered with a cow-hide;
for two months, even his bathing is prescribed to be performed with cow-urine.
One should perform the act of washing the feet using water alone.

Nor can this [rule] be connected with the phrase "two months," for the mention of bathing is merely for the purpose of completing the meter. At the time of bathing, if impurity of the feet or other parts occurs, then by implication they must be purified using that very water according to the rules for the purification of substances.
Therefore, even for the purpose of purification, the sipping of water (ācamana) is performed with water alone at the time of bathing;
at other times, purification is by means of earth.
That purification by earth and water must be performed in that specific sequence.
Since cow urine is prescribed for hearing during the ritual bath, what occasion is there for its use in sipping water (ācamana) and the like?
Even in the case of bathing, it is used as a constituent part of the expiation (prāyaścitta) for the sake of purification.
By day he should follow those cows, and while standing, he should inhale the dust rising from them;
having performed service and paid homage, he should remain in the vīrāsana posture at night.
He should follow behind those cows whose place he occupies as they go out to graze;
because of the reference by the word "those" (tāsām), it refers to those [cows] whose stall he is in.
There is no following behind other cows that are going out.
The dust raised by them, the *reṇu*, would rise upward and he would drink it.
Thus, having spent the day right there together with them, he would return again to the cow-pen together with them,
approaching them while serving them by scratching their itches and removing the dust.
Having paid homage by bowing with the head upon the knee,
one should dwell in the vīrāsana posture.
Vīrāsana is that state of sitting while seated, as opposed to lying down against a wall or similar support.
One should stand when they stand, follow when they walk,
and likewise sit when they sit— self-controlled, free from envy, and disciplined.

The rule beginning with "those who stay" and so forth means that where some stay, some go, and some reside, one should follow the practice of the majority. "One from whom envy and greed have departed" refers to one who is free from these two.
And this is for the sake of illustration;
it means one whose mental defects such as passion and so forth have been abandoned, because of the statement regarding the "restrained senses."
Whether she is afflicted by illness or accursed, or threatened by dangers such as thieves and tigers,
or fallen, or mired in the mud— one should rescue her with all one's strength.
"Afflicted" means suffering from disease; "accused" means being apprehended by authorities; "by fears" refers to causes such as tigers and the like.
By its full capacity, the word *prāṇa* refers specifically to the vital breath (*ucchvāsa-pavana*), as seen in usage such as "the great breath" (*mahāprāṇa*) for those with abundant life-force;
therefore, one who is personally incapable must effect the extraction by employing assistance.
Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently,
one should not seek protection for oneself without first having provided protection for the cow to the best of one's ability.
Whether the sun burns intensely with heat, or the rain-god pours down rain, or when cold winds blow, or when the wind blows violently—so it is said.
One should not speak of a cow eating in one's own house, field, or threshing floor, nor of a calf drinking there, whether it be one's own or that of others.
One should not prevent a cow from eating rice and other grains, nor should one call out to others for the purpose of stopping it. However,
if one binds it because there is a fear of harm, then there is no fault in performing the previously mentioned act once the cow is satisfied.
Thus, favor is bestowed even upon the calf as it drinks.
But he who, as a cow-slayer, follows a cow according to this rule,
removes the sin committed by killing a cow within three months.
One who has successfully observed the vow should give ten cows and a bull;
if these are unavailable, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas.
Ten cows and one bull are to be given;
if one is capable, four vows [are required];
if the aforementioned wealth is not available, then everything less than that, even one's entire property, should be given.
[The penance is] for those who know the Vedas, and not when two or even one [of them] are involved.

The mention of "those who know the Vedas" (*vedavid*) is not intended to imply plurality; rather, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) because only those who know the Vedas have been declared to be worthy recipients.

As for the rule in another *Smṛti* stating that if [the victim] dies through burning, being carried away, being bound, being joined with a rope or noose, or through the application of oil or medicinal herbs, one should perform a tonsure including the top-knot (*saśikha-vapana*), perform a *Prājāpatya* penance, and then give a piece of cloth—this is the expiation for an offense arising from negligence on the part of one who engages in these activities without excessive care.
For it is said:
"If misfortune should occur despite efforts made in restraining a cow, in treating it medically, or in dislodging a dead fetus, no expiation is required."
He who provides medicine, oil, or food to cows and Brahmins shall not be tainted by sin, even if misfortune should occur while it is being given.
Thus concludes the section on the Sāṃvarta [penance].

Likewise, his purification is said to be achieved in one month if he drinks the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) at every sixth mealtime; when it is completed, he should gratify the Brāhmaṇas and give a gift of a sesame-cow.
Likewise, another [method] lasts for half a month, consisting of barley meal (*saktu*), barley gruel (*yāvaka*), vegetables, milk, curd, and ghee, each taken once [per day].
I shall explain these various options:

whatever substance one has begun with at the start of the practice must be completed with that very same substance; one should not take barley meal on one day and barley gruel or other items on another.

Even when two substances are offered as alternatives, as in the injunction "one should sacrifice with rice or with barley," one does not take up barley at will once the rice is available; rather, barley is taken up only upon the destruction of these [rice grains].
Thus, the completion of the ritual performance is achieved through a substitute (pratinidhi). In that case as well, the gift of a cow is prescribed.
Likewise, there are exactly these many penances; therefore, one should give a cow along with its calf.
Regarding this, it is stated in the Gautama-smṛti: "For a Vaiśya, as for a cow.

In that context, having killed the milch-cow of a learned Śrotriya who knows the sacrifice, maintains the sacred fires (agnyāhita), possesses much milk, has a young calf, and is destitute of wealth, one follows the rule of Gautama. If, however, she dies somehow while he was running after her with the intention, "I will not kill her," for the purpose of warding her off from entering his fields, gardens, or the rice and other crops, then this monthly penance applies.
Likewise, for the intentional killing of an old, milkless cow belonging to one who is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*), the penance is three months;

for the unintentional killing of such a cow that is entirely devoid of qualities and has a master likewise devoid of qualities, the penance is the *Prājāpatya*; and for the intentional killing of that same cow when it has died, the penance is three months.
Twice-born men who have committed minor offenses (upapātaka),
with the exception of one who has broken his vow of chastity (avakīrṇin), should perform this very same penance for the sake of purification, or else the Cāndrāyaṇa.
The phrase "this very same" extends the penance for killing a cow to all minor offenses (*upapātaka*).
Although the *cāndrāyaṇa* is also an optional alternative,
because specific instructions are given regarding the status of being a minor offender, some authorities do not accept the *cāndrāyaṇa* for the killer of a cow.
Since they are stated to be "upapātakin" (secondary sinners), the purpose for including the killer of a cow must be sought elsewhere.
But one who has broken his vow of chastity shall, at night, sacrifice to Nirṛti at a crossroads with a one-eyed donkey, according to the procedure for a *pākayajña*.

*Avakāra* means that which is scattered; it refers to the transgression of the vows of a religious student (*brahmacārin*), characterized by sexual union with a woman. One who possesses such a transgression is an *avakīrṇin*. As he will state later: "the intentional emission of semen.

The phrase "with a one-eyed donkey" is a specification of the substance along with its quality; "at a crossroads" specifies the location; "at night" specifies the time; and "dedicated to Nirṛti" specifies the deity.
"By means of the procedure for the *pākayajña*" refers to the prescription of the ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
But surely, animal sacrifices are accomplished by means of the *agniṣṭomīya* animal and have the *agniṣomīya* animal as their archetype?
True.
That very [offering] is the archetype of the *pākayajña*, for it possesses the requisite qualification.
And it has been said: "The animal flows, and the milk also flows."
The *pākayajñas* are the *pūrṇamāsa* and other such sacrifices.
Having performed the oblations in the fire according to the rule, and finally having come together with the *ṛc*,
one should offer oblations of clarified butter to Vāta, Indra, Guru, and Agni.
When one performs the oblation in the fire, the *agnihomas* are performed with the verse beginning "In front of the heart.
Finally, when the oblations are completed, one should offer oblations to the Maruts, Indra, Bṛhaspati,
and Agni with this [verse] beginning with "sam."
May the Maruts sprinkle me; may Indra sprinkle me; may Bṛhaspati sprinkle me;
and may this Agni sprinkle me with progeny and with wealth.
One should offer with this [verse].
Since the deities are indicated by the wording of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*), in the verse the words *vāta* and *guru* signify the words *marut* and *Bṛhaspati*.
Therefore, in the offerings to Vāta and the others, when beginning with the utterance of *svāhā*, the words *marut* and *Bṛhaspati* should be employed, not the words *vāta* and *guru*.
Those who know the Dharma and expound the Veda declare that for a twice-born man observing a vow, the intentional emission of semen constitutes a transgression of his vow.
The definition of the term *avakīrṇin*:
Therefore, it should be understood that this refers exclusively to cases other than those involving the violation of undertaken vows;
that "of this vow" means "of one residing in the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya-āśrama*)," as is known from the observation of another Smṛti text.
The emission of semen is especially forbidden for him even without sexual intercourse with a woman;
this rule applies specifically to intentional emission.
The four— Māruta, Puruhūta, Guru, and Pāvaka—
approach the Vedic splendor of the student who has broken his vow.
"He should offer oblations"—this is an explanatory supplement (arthavāda) to the injunction.

For one who has broken his vow (*avakīrṇin*) while remaining under a religious observance (*vratī*), that Brahmanic luster (*brāhmatejas*)—the merit acquired through various forms of knowledge—which belongs to him, goes to, that is, approaches, each respective deity;
the meaning is that it reaches dissolution therein.
What is intended to be expressed is that [the deity] approaches the one who observes the vow.
When this sin has been incurred, having worn the skin of a donkey,
he shall go for alms to seven houses, proclaiming his own deed.
Having worn and covered [them], [one should think]:
"I am one whose own karma has been scattered."
Subsisting on alms obtained from them and eating only once a day,
he becomes purified in one year by performing the ritual ablutions at the three sessions of the day.
By performing ablutions at dawn, midday, and afternoon, while practicing ritual bathing, one becomes purified within a year.
Having intentionally committed any one of those acts that cause loss of caste, one should perform the *sāntapana* penance; if done unintentionally, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance.
The minor offenses (upapātaka) are concluded.
The phrase "any one of them" is a restatement; for it is impossible to collect all the specific causes [of these offenses] together.
When the intention is to refer to the collection [of acts] as a whole, he does not prescribe an expiation for anyone;
for what man would commit all those forbidden acts that cause loss of caste?
If there were only a single word prescribing the expiation, it would result in the undesirable consequence of the scripture being non-authoritative.
Nor has the intention to express a collective [conjunction] been stated, because these causes are heard as defining characteristics with respect to the person.

Therefore, the syntactical completion occurs for each individual [cause]; thus, in the case of "he whose father or grandfather did not drink Soma," the animal sacrifice applies even if only one of them—the father or the grandfather—did not drink Soma.

Just as, despite the hearing of both [conditions], in the rule "if both oblations should meet with ruin," the five-platter offering (*pañcaśarāva*) still takes place upon the destruction of either oblation, so too should it be understood in all cases of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*).
The intention is that [the penance is performed] either intentionally or unintentionally;
the specific nature of the Prājāpatya and Sāntapana penances will be explained later.
For acts causing mixture of castes or the use of improper vessels, purification is achieved by the lunar penance (Cāndrāyaṇa) for one month;
for acts causing defilement, one should perform the hot barley-meal penance (Taptayāvaka) for three days.
"Defiling acts (saṃkarīkaraṇa) and acts rendering one unworthy of receiving gifts (apātrīkaraṇa)" were mentioned previously.
Thus, in the phrase "regarding defiling and unworthy acts," the plural number is used due to the distinction between the names of the categories.
The word *kṛtyā* is connected with each [of the two].
*Kṛtya* means a cause. *Aindava* refers to the lunar month (*cāndrāyaṇa*). *Yāvaka* is a preparation of barley, such as a drink, a confection, or similar food.
Although no distinction is heard here [in the text], the relative weight or lightness of desire and lack of desire should be understood.
The fourth part of the penance for killing a Brahmin is prescribed for the murder of a Kṣatriya;
an eighth part is for a Vaiśya who abides by his duty, while a sixteenth part should be known for a Śūdra.
For the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya engaged in the Soma-sacrifice, it has been stated that they are equal to the Brāhmaṇa;
however, here the case is otherwise.
Regarding those who perform their own specific duties (*svadharma*), there is a rule for a division of one-fourth and one-eighth respectively.
And thus, the mention of "conduct" (vṛtta) is intended to include all ritual actions:
three years for a Kṣatriya, one and a half years for a Vaiśya, and nine months for a Śūdra.
As for the statement regarding "the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya," that refers to those who have abandoned their own duties and are established in unrighteousness.
The conduct (*vṛtta*) of a Śūdra consists of service to the twice-born and so forth, and not the performance of the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*).
Conduct (*vṛtta*), meaning character (*śīla*), remains fixed within the conduct of a Vaiśya—that is, within the duties of a Vaiśya.
Just as in a dense forest, at the proper time, there is an expiation according to the rules for those devoted to their own duty (*svadharma*).
But having unintentionally caused the death of a Kṣatriya, the best of the twice-born,
having performed his vow well, should give a thousand cows and one bull.
This is another expiation for giving.
The author will state that "for one who possesses wealth, there is no penance," and so forth, such as "the purification of killing is through giving.
The phrase "unintentionally" is not intended [to apply here], because of the great magnitude of this expiation.
Alternatively, it should be understood that this refers specifically to two [cows] present at the *savana* sacrifice.
Those thousand cows among which there is one bull are called "one-thousand-with-one-bull" (*vṛṣabhaikasahasrāḥ*).
Or, with his hair matted and remaining self-restrained, he may perform for three years the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa,
dwelling far away from the village and making his abode at the foot of a tree.
The first half-verse is the fourth [quarter]; the other is a restatement [of it].
Some say that the word "jaṭī" (one with matted hair) is for the purpose of excluding the wearing of bark garments, the khaṭvāṅga staff, and so forth;
but that is incorrect.

In that very place, those specific duties are prescribed for him as his fourth share, and not others, even though they might be possible—just as in the case of Sarasvatīparisarpaṇa and other rites, where their purpose is established.
"From afar" means turning away from villages.
"Having built a hut at the foot of a tree."
The best of the twice-born should perform this very same penance for one year after killing a Vaiśya who is established in his proper conduct; alternatively, he should give one hundred and one cows.
In the previous case, an eighth part was prescribed; by this [verse], a twelfth part is ordained.
Because of the inferiority [of the qualities], it is understood that this rule applies to one whose year is deficient.
But is it not heard [in the scripture] that he must be "established in his conduct"?
True;
however, this refers to one who is currently established in good conduct at the time of death but was previously devoid of virtue.
But for one who has always been established in good conduct, it should be understood that the result is as stated before.
A killer of a Śūdra shall perform this entire vow for six months,
or else he should give ten white cows and a bull as the eleventh to a Brāhmaṇa.
Here too, the periods of six months and nine months are to be applied according to the distinction between those who abide in the [prescribed] conduct and others;
and the gift of a cow, in the number as heard in the text, is optional in all cases.
Furthermore, the mention of the "best of the twice-born" is for the sake of illustration.
They are not white by color;
rather, they are so because of their common purity—those cows that yield much milk, have three offspring, and whose progeny has not perished.
Having killed a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay,
a frog, a dog, an iguana, an owl, or a crow, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra.
Because the expiation is so very great, this expiation applies to the killing of a group;
for indeed, it has been stated that in cases such as those causing loss of caste, the collective nature [of the act] is not intended to be significant.
And how could all these [factors] lead to the state of being slain for the sake of a single [person]? If there were an excess [of factors], it would not be caused by that [single person].
This is simply another way of saying that it can only be stated on account of that [specific factor].
By that [act], he becomes a slayer;
however, in the case of excessive killing, there will be another [penalty].
This is not heard [in the texts] regarding minor killing, nor would it apply there.
The injunction "one should drink milk," and so forth, is connected with each [ingredient] individually;
there is neither the completion of the sentence in the collection as a whole nor in each individual part, yet they are able to stand for distinct meanings.
As for what was said—that the conjunction is not intended to be expressed—it is not intended where the meaning of each related term is significant in its own right.
For example: "He whose father and grandfather do not drink Soma.

However, where the literal meaning would otherwise be purposeless if it were not intended to be expressed, then an intention to express that meaning is appropriate for the sake of avoiding such purposelessness;
as he will say: "In the case of killing a thousand, or when the wagon is full."
In this case, if there were no intention to express it, the mention of "of a thousand" would be redundant.
For in this way, because of the contradiction with other treatises, the intention to express it is indeed appropriate given its extreme magnitude.
But surely, even when a word is explicitly mentioned, there is still no intention to express a qualifying attribute that has entered [the meaning] through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā)?

Just as in the case of the rule "for whom both oblations (*havir*) [are spoiled]," the meaning of the word "both" (*ubhaya*) is the same; however, if the two words "here the oblation" and "both" were to be stated, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), as in: "the oblation here is both."

Where there is a difference in state, there must necessarily be a distinction in order to avoid a split in the sentence; otherwise, either the syntactical connection or the subordinate quality must be abandoned. Such is the case with the word "ubhaya" (both), wherein everything is present.

The word "should cut" (*ārcchet*) becomes separated by the word "oblation" (*havis*), because it must correspond to the [preceding] number. Alternatively, this [word] can function as a restatement of a quality (*guṇānuvādaka*). And if that [quality] is not intended to be expressed, the remainder of the sentence is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
Furthermore, here, when there is an intention to express a collective whole or an intention to express the word "thousand," the entire sentence constitutes a single meaningful unit.
For indeed, this much would have to be said:
"In this case, regarding the status of the place and the status of the authority, the penance for killing a Śūdra applies"—this alone would need to be stated.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of killing a Śūdra," it is because injury is possible only to these [specified categories]. Likewise, other qualifiers of this kind would not be intended [to be included], because the same principle applies [to them] as to the clause "of trees that bear fruit."
Consequently, everything would be inconsistent;
this statement would be merely human and not Vedic at all.
Furthermore, in the Veda, which person would have employed it, and for what purpose—why was it employed so pointlessly?

But here, in the case of an intentional application, even regarding a single syllable (*mātrā*), it is improper for there to be pointlessness; likewise, the desire to express their conjunction or the desire to express them as qualifiers is certainly not improper.
And as for what was said—"How could all these [be so]?"—in that regard too, it is established precisely through the context of hunting for the sake of sport or by means of a forest fire.
As for what was said—that in the case of an excess, that [cause] does not exist—that too is incorrect;
for there is no destruction of the preceding [moments] upon an increase, and one should likewise conceive [the cause] in the case of a decrease.
One should drink milk for three nights, or travel a distance of one yojana,
or bathe in a flowing river, or mutter the hymn dedicated to the waters (Ab-daivata Sūkta).
A distinct expiation is prescribed for each individual killing.
The term *payaḥ* refers to milk because its usage is more well-known, and not water, even though it possesses both meanings, as in the expression "one offers with milk" (*payasā juhoti*).
Just as the word *varāha* applies to a cloud, a mountain, and a boar.
In the case of the boar, [the term] is more well-known;
when it occurs in reference to mountains and the like, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is required, as in "The Himavat is a boar" or "The Pāriyātra is a boar.
Furthermore, when ordinary food such as rice-meal has been obtained for the sake of maintaining the body, milk being prescribed in its place excludes other food.
Moreover, because this [act] is of the nature of austerity (*tapas*), it is proper to understand it in this way:
austerity (*tapas*) is so called because it "scorches" or causes suffering.
Therefore, just as in the case of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) the consumption of clarified butter does not exclude the ordinary meal, so here too rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*) is not excluded.
As for the one who consumes clarified butter (*ghṛta*) as the occasion for a subsequent meal,
water is not made optional by the drinking of milk;
rather, [the rule is] "he should sip water from a flowing stream."

Regarding the drinking of milk, the term "journeying on a road" refers to traveling; bathing in a river is prescribed because of the mention of a "flowing stream," which excludes tanks and lakes. The "Pavamāna hymn" refers to the collection of *ṛc* verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," which has the Waters as its deity.
In other Smṛti texts, the meal of *kṛsara* and an iron staff as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) are prescribed for a single purpose.
"He should go" does not mean merely reaching another country; rather, it means traveling on foot.
Having killed a snake, the best of the twice-born should give an iron spade;
having killed a eunuch, a load of straw and one māṣa of lead.
The mention of "the best of the twice-born" (dvijottama) is not restrictive.
"A sharp iron adze" (tīkṣṇām āyasīm abhrīm): the mention of "iron" (kāṣṇāyasī) is for the purpose of excluding wood and other materials.
"In a eunuch" (ṣaṇḍhe) means in a neuter person.

That [offense] is of four kinds: one who has no semen, one whose semen is wind-like (impotent), one whose organs are not active, or one with both sexual characteristics. This penance applies to the contact of any living being whatsoever—whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Śūdra, a ram, or a goat.
For killing a boar, one should give a jar of ghee; for a partridge, a drona of sesame;
for a parrot, a two-year-old calf; and for killing a curlew, a three-year-old calf.
A *varāha* is a boar; when that has been killed, one should give a jar of ghee. Four *āḍhakas* make a *droṇa*.
A *hāyana* is a year.
A calf is a young one of the bovine species.
Having killed a swan, a crane, a heron, or even a peacock, as well as a monkey,
a hawk, or a vulture, one should give a cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
"Haṃsa and so forth" refers to birds;
"vānara" refers to a monkey;
"sparśayet" means one should give.
And this penance applies to the killing of each individual, as it has been stated that there is no mention of them in pairs.
Having killed a horse, one should give a garment; for killing an elephant, five dark-colored bulls; for killing a goat or a sheep, an ox; and for killing a donkey, a one-year-old calf.
A horse (*hayo 'śvaḥ*),
an elephant (*gajo hastī*),
and an ox (*anaḍvān*) [are forbidden] for killing a goat or a sheep (*ajameṣavadhe*).
In the context of slaughter, by association with the ox (*anaḍut*), the term refers to a one-year-old calf (*ekahāyana*).
Having killed carnivorous wild animals, one should give a milch cow;
for non-carnivorous animals, a heifer; and having killed a camel, a *kṛṣṇala* weight of gold.
Carnivorous animals include hyenas, lions, tigers, and the like;
non-carnivorous animals include the ruru deer, the pṛṣata deer, and so forth; and "dhenū" refers specifically to a cow.

A *kṛṣṇala* is gold of a specific measure; this is a technical definition according to the treatises on legal punishment (*daṇḍādhikāra*). Elsewhere, however, it is simply the common [weight], as in the Vedic injunction: "One desiring long life [should offer] a hundred *kṛṣṇalas* of clarified butter."

Having killed women of the four castes who were not protected by their husbands, those who are unstable must give, for the sake of purification, a bow of Jina, a bull, a horse, and a goat respectively.
They are unstable.
Associating with many men and practicing the conduct of a courtesan, they become unstable.
It is not merely a transgression of the scriptures; for if that were the case, [the fault] would not be found solely in sexual union with another man.
According to the sequence of colors, because of the giving of the *jīna* and so forth: *jīna* refers to a leather pouch used for purposes such as holding *muṭaka* (betel nut) and other items;
*kārmuka* means a bow; and *basta* means a goat.
"The ram is for Agni.
The separate mention [of the animal] indicates that the expiation is prescribed according to the specific gender, not for the collective group;
some read the text as "having gone."
That is incorrect, because the context concerns violence.
If a twice-born man is unable to expiate the killing of snakes and other such creatures through the giving of gifts,
he should perform a *kṛcchra* penance for each individual creature in order to remove the sin.
"Purification" means cleansing.
This shows that giving is primary in cases of injury.
Furthermore, because of the grammatical indicator (liṅga) in the phrase "not for each one individually," some maintain that it applies even when the acts are performed collectively.
The words "dvija" and so forth are for the purpose of completing the meter;
when used without qualification, they remember the word *kṛcchra* to mean the *prājāpatya* penance.
But for the killing of a thousand beings possessing bones,
or for the killing of a full thousand boneless beings, one should perform the penance prescribed for the murder of a Śūdra.

"Having a very small body" here means "having bones," due to its association with "boneless" (an-asthi). "Anaḥ" means a cart; this is a calculation based on that. This is true provided the aforementioned meaning holds.
But for killing a vertebrate creature, one should give something to a Brahmin;
indeed, for the injury of boneless creatures, one is purified by a breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
"Something" refers to very small wealth, in terms of quantity, utility, and value.
This constitutes the individual killing of each of the aforementioned animals.
Furthermore, those animals that lack bones should be understood as being subject to expiations not explicitly mentioned here.
The cessation of the self is breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Regarding the mention of "worms, insects, and birds" among the impure [beings], that is for the purpose of defining the measure of those that have accumulated [into larger bodies].
But these [refer to] those that are minute, such as mosquitoes and the like.
For cutting fruit-bearing trees, one hundred ṛc verses should be recited;
likewise for shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering herbs.
The fruit-bearing trees such as the mango and the thorny *kaṇṭakī* and so forth [are for all].
For the twice-born, there is the recitation of a hundred *ṛc*s;
what then is it for the *śūdra*?

Some say that "for the purpose of fuel from [trees] that are not dry" refers to the penance for a minor offense (*upapātaka*); but that is not correct, because it is too severe. If that were not the case, for what purpose would there be an instruction regarding it among the minor offenses?
If it were to recur again and again, [the penance] would have to be increased;
therefore, one should prescribe for a Śūdra a period of two nights, three nights, and so forth.
The *gulma* and other such [penances] have already been explained.
Climbers are the branches of trees.
For all beings born from food, born from fluids,
and those produced from fruits and flowers, the consumption of clarified butter is the complete purification.
The beings or living creatures that arise from food, flour, and the like that have been stored for a long time;
"of those born from liquids" refers to [beings arising] from molasses, whey, and so forth;
and those such as the *udumbara* gnat and others that originate from fruits and flowers.
Regarding *ghṛtaprāśa*: at the beginning of eating, clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is to be consumed.
The prefix *pra-* denotes the commencement of an action;
therefore, it does not exclude ordinary food, as is the case with the *payovrata* (milk-vow) and similar observances.
And just as these living beings are small creatures, for whose killing breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is prescribed,
in comparison to that, fasting is a very great penance;
therefore, the consumption of ghee is like sipping water (ācamana).
For the unauthorized cutting of cultivated plants or those grown spontaneously in the forest,
one should follow a cow for one day while subsisting on milk alone.

The "useless cutting" (*vṛthālambha*) refers to the cutting down of those plants that grow in ploughed land by means of ploughs, spades, and so forth, as well as those that grow spontaneously in the forest, when done without a purpose such as providing for cows and other needs.
[The penance consists of] following a cow and serving her with supreme joy for one day.
The milk-vow (payovrata) is the cessation of all other food.
By these vows, indeed, the sin arising from violence—whether committed intentionally or unintentionally—is entirely removed; now hear [the rules] regarding the consumption of forbidden food.
The sin or evil arising from violence— that is, produced from violence— is to be removed or dispelled by these aforementioned expiations,
whether it was committed intentionally or unintentionally.
Listen now to how the sin incurred in eating what should not be eaten— that is, in consuming forbidden food— is likewise to be removed.
Having drunk liquor through ignorance, one is purified by the sacramental rite alone;
but for intentional drinking, it is beyond prescription—the established rule is that it ends only with life.
From the prohibition of the girdle and other such items, it is understood that this refers to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*);
and according to another *smṛti*, that initiation is accompanied by the *taptakṛcchra* penance.

For Gautama states: "In the case of unintentional drinking of liquor, one should consume hot milk, curd, water, or air for three days each; having performed these *kṛcchra* penances, his consecration (*saṃskāra*) follows."
And the *surā* mentioned here is not that made from flour (*paiṣṭī*), but rather that made from molasses (*gauḍī*) or honey (*mādhvī*). Why is this so?
Because of the observation of other *smṛti* texts.
If the best of the twice-born drinks liquor or *asura* wine even once through negligence,
he becomes pure after ten nights by subsisting on cow's urine and barley gruel.
And regarding the drinking of liquor made from flour through negligence, there is the expiation for the transgression:
having learned the vow according to the rule, one should subsist on grains for a year or practice the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
However, if these two types of liquor are drunk intentionally, this [expiation] is not prescribed.
What then? That by which the end of the vital breaths occurs.
What is that?
It is what has been stated regarding *mukhyā* liquor.
And this should be understood to apply to habitual practice:
"In the case of drinking once, or drinking *asurā* or *madya*, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
This is the settled rule in this matter.
If one intentionally drinks liquor made from flour (paiṣṭī), the penance ends only with death.
If one unintentionally drinks that same liquor even once, there is the practice of eating grains and performing the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Even if the drinking is unintentional but occurs more than once, the penance is the same as for intentional drinking.

Regarding other types of intoxicants, however, if consumed intentionally, one should practice the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. If drunk unintentionally once, the purificatory rites consist of the Taptakṛcchra penance along with cow-urine and barley-gruel (yāvaka). If drunk unintentionally more than once, it is the same as for the *paiṣṭī* liquor.
Having drunk water contained in a vessel for *surā* or likewise situated in a vessel for intoxicants,
one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for five nights.
Where the essence of *surā* is experienced, this penance applies to the drinking of water contained in a vessel that held it.

Now, since the word "intoxicant" (*madya*) is a general term, the phrase "situated in a vessel for intoxicants" would suffice; thus, it need not have been stated that "water [in a vessel] of *surā*" and so forth.
True, provided there were no absolute difference in the penances for drinking *surā* and other intoxicants.

Since that [impurity] exists and imagination (kalpanā) is permitted, there would be a greater degree [of impurity] for those [liquids] situated in a vessel of *surā*; therefore, the statement regarding equal penance (*samaprāyaścitta*) is intended to prevent such imagination.
"For five nights, milk boiled with *saṅkhapuṣpī*";
by the inclusion of the term "boiled" (*śṛta*), it is understood that "milk" (*payas*) refers specifically to cow's milk (*kṣīra*).
The term *śṛta* (boiled) is grammatically correct only when applied to milk and clarified butter.
*Saṅkhapuṣpī* is the name of a medicinal herb;
one should drink milk that has been ground with it and boiled for five days.
Having touched or given liquor, or having accepted it according to the rules,
or having drunk water that is the leavings of a Śūdra, one should drink water infused with Kuśa grass for three days.
Having accepted it according to rule with the recitation of the *svastivācana*,
there is likewise no fault in giving [it] in the case of rice and other such grains.
Kuśa is darbha grass.
But a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk Soma, having smelled the breath of one who has drunk liquor,
becomes pure by suppressing his breath three times in water and consuming clarified butter.

Regarding the phrase "the smell of one who has drunk *surā*": it is easier for the smell of the *surā* itself to be perceived through its contact with the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) and the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).
As for [the smell] residing within a vessel, it is acquired simply by smelling [the air].
Others, however, explain it differently.
For a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk *surā*, even if he merely smells [the breath of such a person], this same [penance] applies.
Because of the statement "one who has drunk *soma*," it does not apply in the ritual manual (*kalpa*) for one who performs the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices;
[therein it says] "he should consume clarified butter."
In this case as well, there is no cessation of other types of food;
because of the specific mention of *surā*, it does not refer to intoxicants in general.
Having unintentionally consumed feces, urine, or anything touched by *surā* liquor,
the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) once again.
The mention of feces and urine is intended as an illustration for semen;
for another Smṛti states: "In the same way [one must fast] upon consuming feces, a corpse, or semen.
To what class does this [penance] apply regarding the consumption of feces and urine?
This applies specifically to human beings;
however, we shall speak of others later.
In this case as well, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is to be performed in conjunction [with the others].
And the reason has been shown;
"twice-born" is what was intended [to be excluded],
for we shall state something else regarding the Śūdra.
"Out of ignorance" is a restatement (anuvāda).
For who, knowing [the consequences], would eat feces and urine?

Just as it is said regarding the drinking of intoxicants: "Having consumed an intoxicant, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance"; if, however, it becomes a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), then by virtue of that scriptural statement, it is exactly the same.
Shaving the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—
all these are dispensed with for the twice-born when the rite of re-consecration is performed.
The "vows" refer to the Vedic vows; that [interpretation] is incorrect, because since those [vows] are for the purpose of learning [the Vedas], how could they be obtained [at this stage]?

Therefore, those vows which were [prescribed] at the time of initiation— such as "Do not sleep during the day," "Offer fuel sticks in the evening and in the morning," and "Be dependent upon the teacher"—
these are now discontinued.
Having eaten the food of those whose food should not be eaten, or the leavings of women or Śūdras,
or having consumed forbidden meat, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights.

Those whose food is not to be eaten are persons unfit for consumption, such as those who have not studied the Vedas (*aśrotriya*), those who live off women, those who subsist by war, those who officiate at sacrifices for those unworthy to offer them (*ayājya-yājaka*), and so forth.

Since the mention of the Śūdra caste already implies the designation of gender through the category of birth, the explicit inclusion of the word "woman" (*strī*) should be understood as intended to include women of the same caste (*savarṇa*).
"Leftover" (*ucchiṣṭa*) refers to that which has been touched by the mouth.
Regarding the statement that "the mouth of women is eternally pure," its specific scope has been shown:
in the previous case, water with *kuśa* grass was prescribed for drinking water left over by a Śūdra;
here, however, it is seven nights of barley.
Since this matter pertains to the future, it should be understood to apply in both cases:
regarding the eating of leftovers such as food offerings, and regarding meat that is unfit for consumption, such as that of frogs, swans, and ruddy geese.
However, this [specific rule] should be understood to apply to intentional and habitual consumption.
"In other remaining cases, one should fast for a day.
This very [penance] applies after drinking milk, provided it is from animals other than pigs, camels, and so forth; for in those specific cases, other expiations are prescribed for each instance.
Drinking of barley-meal (saktu) and drinking of barley-gruel (yāvaka) indeed remain applicable.
Even after drinking fermented acids or astringent decoctions, though they are pure, a twice-born man remains impure as long as that substance has not passed downward.
Impure sour substances, curd, and what is fit for consumption among sour things—these and others are permitted [by the rule].
However, in the case of curd, even though it is sour, this rule does not apply because its fitness for consumption has been specifically ordained;
for they remember in the tradition that "it is indeed pure."
Kāṣāya refers to those decoctions well-known to physicians which are boiled through the combination of many medicinal herbs.
One who is *aprayata* is impure;
as long as he remains so, he goes downward.
Downward movement is the exit of digested [substances] in the form of urine and feces, or alternatively, their arrival at the receptacle of undigested matter (pakvāśaya).
Having consumed the urine or feces of a village pig, a donkey, a camel, a jackal, a monkey, or a crow, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Since no specific distinction is taught, or because it might be due to negligence, it is equally reasonable to assume that negligence involves a lighter penalty.
Having eaten dried meats, mushrooms from the earth,
or meat from a slaughterhouse that was unknown [to be such], one should observe this very same vow.
"Dry" refers to dried meat such as *vallūra* and the like.
"Terrestrial" is stated to exclude those born in hollows (*koṭara*).
"Unknown" means unknown by nature, such as whether it is from a ram or a buffalo.
A *sūnā* is a place of slaughter where animals are killed for the purpose of sale;
for one situated elsewhere than that, the penance is light.
[Objection: Is it not the case that, because of the statement "one who stands at a slaughterhouse," it is logical that there is an absence of penance for one situated elsewhere?
[Response: This is not so;
for there is a prohibition against meat from a slaughterhouse (*sauna*) without qualification.
However, because the word "standing" (*sthā*) is used in the context of penance, it is more appropriate that the gravity or lightness of the offense depends on whether one has risen from it;
and that very penance is the *cāndrāyaṇa*.
But when the specific caste is known and the act is repeated, there is the drinking of barley-gruel for seven nights.
In the case of the remaining [impurities], one should fast for a day.
For eating the flesh of carnivorous animals, pigs, camels, chickens, humans, crows, and donkeys,
the *taptakṛcchra* penance is the means of purification.
And the word "ca" (and) draws in the preceding verse here;
therefore, this very same [penance] applies to the eating of village pigs and the like.
And by the second "ca," it is indicated that for the consumption of the feces and urine of carnivorous animals and the like, the penance is exactly the same as that for village pigs and the like.

Furthermore, in another Smṛti, the mention of "twice-born" (dvija) here—within a context that applies to human beings in general—is not intended to be restrictive; thus it says, "A twice-born man [should perform] the Cāndrāyaṇa.
