In this way, these two verses are required here in connection with the verse beginning "The cat and the crow... and so forth.
Consequently, for these [animals] as well, in the case of consuming what has been left over by them, the penance is like that for cats and the rest.
Therefore, in these three verses,
the consumption of urine and feces by any [creature] is prohibited;
and consequently, that which applies to the consumption of the urine and feces of carnivorous animals also applies to cats and the like.
If a twice-born man who has not yet performed the return ceremony (saṃāvartana) should eat food belonging to a monthly Śrāddha,
he shall fast for three days and dwell in water for one day.
The monthly *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha is performed every month for a year as long as the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has not been performed.

As for the *āmāvāsya* (new moon) śrāddha, however, since it is permitted even under the designation of "monthly" by the rule, "If requested, he may eat at will," how could there be any need for penance?
Others, however, say that because permission is granted only when one is requested, the [penance] previously mentioned applies only to one who is not being requested.
One who remains in the teacher’s family without returning home is, by implication, called a *brahmacārī*.
He should stay in the water on either of the two days [of the three-day period];
since the intention refers specifically to the three-day period, the fourth day is that very day.
If one observing a vow should eat honey or meat in any way whatsoever,
he shall perform the ordinary *kṛcchra* penance and then complete the remainder of his vow.
"One observing a vow" means one who is engaged in the stage of studenthood (*brahmacarya-āśrama*) alone;
"in any way whatsoever" means even in times of distress (*āpad*).

Since this is prescribed for times of distress by the rule "even at the risk of life," there is no fault when such a situation does not exist; therefore, this expiation is not intended for the removal of that [actual] fault.
What then? It is performed by virtue of a statement that concludes with the mere indicative mark (*nimitta*).
"Prākṛta" means "belonging to the archetype" (*prakṛti*); it is called *prājāpatya* because it serves as the archetype for all *kṛcchra* penances. Thus it is said.
One should complete the remainder of the vow.
This states that for one who has not performed the penance, there is no entitlement to the completion of the remaining vow.
Having eaten the leavings of a cat, a crow, or a mouse, or those of a dog or a mongoose, or food contaminated by hair or insects, one should drink *brahmasuvarcalā*.
"Ākhu" means a mouse. "Avapanna" refers to that which has been defiled by contact with it.

One should grind *brahmasuvarcalā* with water and drink it for one day; since there is no specific qualification [regarding the duration], the purpose of the scriptural injunction is fulfilled by that alone.
One who desires purity for oneself must not eat food that is unfit to be consumed;
however, if it was eaten unknowingly, it should be vomited out or quickly purified by means of purificatory rites.
The first half-verse is a restatement;
the phrase "for the sake of purifying what was eaten unknowingly" is what is being prescribed.
The meaning is that immediately thereafter, one must expel [the food] by vomiting.
Or rather, it should be purified quickly by means of purificatory expiations (*prāyaścitta*).

Others, however, say that "purifications" refers to purgatives such as *harītakī* and the like; they cite this passage from Gautama: "In the case of eating what should not be eaten, one must become free of feces.
But this [interpretation] is not conclusive.
Since even fasting can result in the state of being free from feces,
therefore, in the case of vomiting, the expiation should be understood exactly as it is stated in the scriptural texts.
This has been declared as the various rules for the vows regarding the eating of forbidden food;
now hear the rule for those vows which remove the sin of theft.
Regarding the vows for the non-eating of what should not be eaten and the non-consumption of what is unfit to be consumed—
those vows which remove theft along with all its attendant faults— their procedure is now being stated.
Having committed thefts of grain, cooked food, or wealth out of desire from the house of one of his own caste, the best of the twice-born is purified by performing the Kṛcchra penance for one year.
The mention of "the best of the twice-born" is for the purpose of illustration, as it includes Kṣatriyas and others as well;
and because of the application of the term "best of the twice-born," it is understood to mean "from the house of his own kind," that is, from the house of a Brāhmaṇa.
By this, the following is stated.
All social classes (varṇas), having taken wealth from the house of a Brāhmaṇa, shall be purified by a year-long Kṛcchra penance.
Since the taking of "wealth" (dhana) already establishes the rule for all types of property, the specific mention of grain and food is intended to include high-quality grain.
For items of little value, he will state another rule.
Therefore, this [penance] is understood to apply to the theft of essential and principal substances.
For, when there is a mutual theft of goods among them, or when a Brāhmaṇa's wealth is stolen, which penance is prescribed?
It is said:
Just as in the case of penance for violence, a division into fourths, eighths, and so forth, must be applied:
three [fortnights] for a Kṣatriya’s wealth, one and a half for a Vaiśya’s, or twenty-two nights for a Śūdra’s.
This applies when grain of what quantity has been stolen?
It should be slightly less than ten jars, because of the great magnitude of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
It should be understood that even when wealth has been obtained, time is not to be calculated [as a factor].
The phrase "out of desire" (*kāmāt*) is for the purpose of completing the verse.
For it is impossible for one who is unwilling to seize the wealth of another;
"grain" refers specifically to rice and the like when stolen,
while "food" refers to that which has been prepared.

For the theft of each individual item such as grain and the like, the penance is a *kṛcchra* for three years; some, however, maintain that the penance applies to the theft of the entire collection, for that [theft] is indeed more serious.
For the abduction of human beings, women, fields, or houses, as well as for the theft of water from wells or tanks, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed as the means of purification.
Of male servants among humans;
of female servants among women;
and "field" refers to a portion of land that is a site for the production of grains such as rice.
The word "water" (jala) is connected to each of the two terms, "well" (kūpa) and "tank" (vāpī).
This [penance] applies to the theft of water that has been drawn out and is situated in a channel or similar place.
Because of the mention of "water," there is a different rule for wells and tanks when they are dry.
In the case of a step-well, a dug pond, and a tank.
Having stolen articles of small value from another's house,
one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance and restore that property for the sake of self-purification.

Objects of little substance do not endure for long; these include earthenware items such as bowls and jars which are of small value, wooden items such as buckets and measures, and iron tools such as scrapers and spades. Regarding "in the house," there is a greater fault in the theft of items situated within a dwelling than in those located in threshing floors, fields, and the like.
"Having restored" means having given back;
and this applies to all cases without exception because there is no distinction [in the rule].
However, in a case where what was stolen cannot be returned, the penance is double.
For the theft of edible foods, whether chewed or swallowed, as well as vehicles, beds, seats,
flowers, roots, and fruits, the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is the means of purification.
Vehicles include carts and the like;
beds include couches and the like;
seats include grass mats, benches, and cloth cushions and the like.
The distinction between *bhakṣya* (food to be chewed) and *bhojya* (food to be swallowed) should be understood by way of their being rough and coarse versus the opposite.
*Bhakṣya* refers to things such as sweetmeats (*modaka*) and cakes (*śaṣkulī*);
*bhojya* refers to things such as barley-gruel (*yāvaka*).
The five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are well known;
here too, it lasts for only one day.
For grass, wood, trees, dried food, molasses,
cloth, leather, and meat, there shall be a fast of three nights.
This expiation applies when one takes more than the previous amount [of grass and so forth] from a vehicle or similar object;
"wood" refers to unworked bamboo poles and the like, due to its association with trees;
and "tree" refers to one belonging to a dwelling.
Dry food refers to rice and the like, or parched barley.
The mention of "molasses" (guḍa) is intended to include its own derivatives;
by this, pieces of sugar (khaṇḍa), granulated sugar (matsyaṇḍikā), and so forth are included.
*Caila* means cloth; *vastra* refers to many kinds of excellent garments, [to be understood] through the previously mentioned mention of "wealth" in the context of the *kṛcchra* and other penances.
*Carman* means armor.
Flesh is meat.
For stealing gems, pearls, corals, copper, silver, iron,
bronze, and stones, one must subsist on grain-particles for twelve days.
And the reduction of time occurs in relation to the smallness or greatness [of the number of repetitions], as well as in the case of a single repetition.
For cotton, silk, wool, cloven-hoofed animals, single-hoofed animals, birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, and rope, one must subsist on milk alone for three days.
Silk fabrics are produced from insects;
cloven-hoofed animals include cows and the like;
single-hoofed animals include horses and the like.
"Birds" refers to parrots, hawks, and the like;
"rope" refers to that which draws up water from wells and other sources.
By these vows, a twice-born man may remove the sin committed through theft;
however, he should expel the sin of approaching those who should not be approached by means of these following vows.
The meaning of this verse has already been explained.

Having discharged semen into women of one's own lineage, or into the wives of a friend or a son, or into virgins, or into women of the lowest castes, one must perform the vow for violating the Guru’s bed.

Although the expression "the vow for violating the Guru's bed" is stated without qualification, it does not extend [to include] such rules as "one should not sleep with him"; rather, because this is a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance for a year.
For there is no penance ending in death for anything other than mortal sins; however, in the case of repeated practice, such [a severe penance] might apply.
"Those born of one's own womb" refers to uterine sisters;
"among the wives of a friend" refers to the wives of a close companion.
In this case, the sole reason for the relationship is friendship itself; neither the specific nature of a blood relation nor qualities such as being a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya) is a factor.
Likewise, this same [penance] applies to the forcible approach of a son’s wives or daughters-in-law;
and even to the case of approaching unmarried girls of a different caste who have not been given away by their fathers or others,
but have come to him of their own accord through mutual affection.
In this case as well, there is no dependence on [the specific status of] truth.
Even if there is no distinction in the extension of the rule (*atideśa*), nevertheless, two penances (*prāyaścitta*) would apply, because it is so observed.

Thus, due to the relative gravity or lightness of the offense, when [the act is committed] against women of lower castes, the three-month *cāndrāyaṇa*—which is lighter than the year-long *kṛcchra*—should be prescribed.
The term *antyajāḥ* refers to women of the Caṇḍāla, Mleccha, and other such castes.

Regarding sexual intercourse with women of the Caṇḍāla and other such castes, a distinction based on whether the act was intentional or unintentional is stated in another Smṛti: "For approaching a woman of the Antyāvasāyin caste, one shall perform half a Kṛcchra penance; for other [such women], a twelve-night penance."

Having approached a daughter of one's father's sister, a daughter of one's own sister, a daughter of one's mother's sister, or the daughter of one's mother's brother who is a close kinsman, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
The daughter of a paternal aunt is a paternal aunt's sister;
the daughter of a maternal aunt is a maternal aunt's sister;
and the daughter of a mother’s brother is a maternal uncle’s daughter.
The meaning is "of a trustworthy uterine brother."
A wise man, however, should not take these three as wives;
they are not to be approached because of their kinship, for by marrying them he falls low.
But surely, since their non-marriageability is already established by the rule "and not a sapinda," for what purpose is this [additional rule] stating "one should not marry her"?
Some say:
it is for the purpose of permitting other [types of women] who were prohibited in the verse concerning sapindas.
That is incorrect, because there is no distinction in the penance [prescribed] for one who falls downward;
and since this purpose is possible, it is improper to resort to an optional exclusion of the verse concerning *sapiṇḍas*, for an option (*vikalpa*) is resorted to only when there is no other way.
The meaning is: "by virtue of being a kinsman" (*jñāti*) and "by virtue of being a relative" (*bandhu*).
They are not to be approached, not to be married, and not to be had sexual intercourse with. By approaching them or marrying them, one falls downward; that is to say, one reaches hell.
Alternatively, one falls away from birth and becomes one of low caste;
even though there is no loss of the physical body from that birth while it still lives, it is nevertheless said so because of the incapacity for that [higher] karma.
Having emitted semen into non-human females, a woman in her courses, those who are not the proper womb, or into water, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance.
Non-human females include mares and the like.

Even though a cow is non-human, [the penance] for having intercourse with a female friend, a woman born of the same womb (sister), a woman of the same lineage (gotra), a female disciple, a wife, a daughter-in-law, or a cow is equal to that for the bed (talpa).
This is specifically prescribed as "refuse" (avakara).

The distinction between these two penances for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*) and for being an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy) is based on whether the act was unintentional or intentional.
In this treatise, by virtue of its well-known association, the word *talpa* refers specifically to the Guru’s bed;
*avakara* is the cause for being an *avakīrṇin*.
When the indicative mark (*nimitta*) is extended by analogy, its effect is also extended.
Here, "female friend" (*sakhī*) refers to one who has attained friendship with a man like a man himself, and not the wife of a friend;
for in this case, the application [of the term] does not arise from a connection with a male.

Nor does a relationship exist by way of connection with one's wife, because of the intervention of the term "sayoni" (uterine kin). Thus Vasiṣṭha states: "A female friend is a Guru’s [relative], but not so one who is a part of the vessel; a maiden is not a vessel for the year-long Kṛcchra penance, nor are these two [the friend and the maiden] [related] except through the *upastha* (the generative organ).
And regarding the *udakyā*: "An *udakyā* is one who is overwhelmed by menstrual flow for a month."
There is an alternative reading: "having drunk from the lower lip of a man," which refers to [drinking] from a menstruating woman or from non-vaginal openings;
the meaning is the same. A "non-vaginal opening" (ayoni) is any place other than the female organ.
Likewise, others read: "in water and in the sky."
But surely, since it is already established by the very mention of "non-womb" (ayoni), the word "in the sky" (khe) need not be recited; for the word *kha* denotes space (*ākāśa*),
and that is distinct from a womb.
This is not a fault;
for they consider that by the word "womb" (*yoni*), another limb is expressed through association (*sāhacarya*).
[The term *jale* means] directly in the water.
If a twice-born man has engaged in sexual intercourse with a male or a female,
he shall perform a bath with his clothes on in a bullock-cart, in water, or during the daytime.
Immediately after sexual intercourse, one must bathe with one's clothes on;
likewise after riding in a bullock-cart or similar vehicle, and even after being in water.

Having approached women of the Caṇḍāla or other lowest castes, having eaten with them, or having accepted gifts from them, a Brahmin falls [from his caste] through ignorance; but through knowledge, he becomes their equal.

Caṇḍālas and Mlecchas dwell at the ends of the quarters. Regarding sexual intercourse with their women, as well as eating their food or accepting gifts from them, there is a penance greater than a year-long Kṛcchra because of the scriptural statement that "one falls" (patati); however, this does not mean that one actually incurs the state of being an outcaste (pātitya) merely by eating [their food].

Regarding the statement "having eaten the food of those whose food should not be eaten," this declaration is intended for the purpose of a year-long *kṛcchra* penance when such an act has occurred; likewise, regarding the acceptance of gifts, it is for that same purpose as the rule "milk in a cow-pen for a month" would otherwise apply.
Thus, there is equality [of penance] when the act is done intentionally.
This is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) intended to prescribe an expiation even for an act committed intentionally;
it has already been shown that what is stated in another Smṛti using the word "year" refers to the expiation for both intentional and unintentional acts.
Therefore, how could this have the purpose of prescribing a heavier expiation?
With what is "and having eaten" connected? It is connected with the phrase "a *caṇḍāla* or an outcaste. But is it not the case that this [phrase] has become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*)?
Even though [the term *caṇḍāla*] is subordinate, its connection is shown when there is an expectation;

for when the expectation arises, "Of whom [did he eat]?", since no other [subject] is heard and because of the statement of equality, the connection belongs only to the *caṇḍālas* and the lowest castes (*antyajas*).
Therefore, this is the meaning that results: [he who eats the food of these people].

Having eaten the food of a Cāṇḍāla woman, a Mleccha, or having accepted a gift from them, and having had sexual intercourse with one of them—even from a single act—there is an expiation. However, in the case of repetition, it is proper that there be equality [with the sin] itself, by means of an expiation for a loss of eligibility (*anadhikāra-prāyaścitta*).
For there must be a contingent rite for every contingent cause, and those [repetitions] cannot be performed within a single lifetime.
A husband shall confine a corrupt wife in a single room;
he shall compel her to perform that same penance which is prescribed for a man who commits adultery with another's wife.
One should especially restrain a woman who is corrupted and turn her away from her duties as a wife, based on such [scriptural] passages as "and her in the accumulation of wealth," and so forth.
The phrase "in one house" means she should be kept in confinement with fetters;
she must not be allowed to roam about at will in her husband's home.
In that case, one should cause the expiation for what has been committed to be performed.
What then?

Whatever expiation constitutes a minor offense (*upapātaka*) for a Brahmin who has sexual intercourse with the wives of others, that same expiation applies to adultery with women of equal or lower caste.

For those of other castes, it is the same. However, in the case of approaching a woman of superior status, the penalty for a Vaiśya is double, and for a Kṣatriya it is triple when the woman is a Brāhmaṇī.
Likewise, this is the distinction: two years' penance for adultery with another's wife, and three years for the wife of a Śrotriya.

For a Śūdra who has sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman, there is the expiation for a mortal sin (mahāpātaka). For a Vaiśya who has intercourse with a Kṣatriya woman, it is a secondary sin (upapātaka) doubled or tripled.
Some, however, maintain that for a Śūdra’s intercourse with a woman of a higher caste, the penance is the same as for a Brāhmaṇī.
Because of the observation of the indicative mark stating that "for men there is death in the case of the reverse order," this has been stated.
A distinction has also been shown regarding punishments:
just as the rule for men in the case of approaching a woman of higher caste is established, so too is it for women in contact with a man of lower caste.
Even when a fault has been committed, women receive half the expiation. Women, the sick, and boys under sixteen years of age, as well as men over eighty, deserve only half the prescribed penance.

Likewise, in the case of approaching a woman who has been seen to be unfaithful, the penance is lighter. One who has discharged semen in an unchaste *vṛṣalī* woman shall bathe with his clothes on and give a water-pot to a Brāhmaṇa.
In the case of a Vaiśya woman, he should eat only at every fourth meal-time and feed a Brāhmaṇa.
In the case of a Kṣatriya woman, one should fast for three nights and give an *āḍhaka* of barley;
it is also recorded in the Smṛti that this is the same as for a Vaiśya.
Likewise, the same should be understood to apply to a Śūdra man with respect to an Ārya woman.
If the wives of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas have sexual intercourse with a Śūdra during their fertile period or conceive a child from him,
they may be purified by penance if they have not yet given birth; but not otherwise.
Alternatively, there arises a doubt as to whether or not there is an expiation for approaching those women who are not carried away by anyone and who live as Vaiśyas.
Why is there this doubt?
Because the word *dāra* (wife) is a term denoting a sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*).
In the absence of a marriage, they do not deserve to be designated as his "wives," and there would be an expiation for adultery;
therefore, we understand that [the wife] does not exist [in such a case].
Since the rule "one who is devoted to his own wife" has been prescribed, we consider that it follows from this.
But what is correct here?
That it exists.
Why?
Because the rule has been prescribed;
for it is stated that "one who fails to perform what is enjoined," and so forth, and because traditional law (smṛti) prescribes penance upon its transgression.

Granted that it may not be a minor offense (*upapātaka*), there is nonetheless no absence of penance (*prāyaścitta*) on that account alone; for the category of minor offenses, such as those causing loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakara*), is enumerated specifically for the purpose of [prescribing] penance.
However, the general cause applies everywhere, as in the rule: "one who does not perform what is prescribed," and so forth.

And it was stated previously [in verse 163] that "the wanton woman" (*svairiṇī*) and so forth. Now, one might object: is it not the case that only a woman connected with the side of her deceased husband or with the side of her father can be designated as another's wife (*paradāravyapadeśyā*), since those who do not maintain a higher [conjugal] relationship are merely wanton women?
True;
even in the case of courtesans, the term *svairinī* (one who acts according to her own will) is not contradictory, as it relies upon their independence.
And for this reason, there is the requirement for them to bathe with their clothes on and to provide water-jars and other such offerings.
Regarding this, some say:
"This is a vow.

Those rules which are prescribed after beginning with "His vow" and stating "He should observe these vows" are the *snātaka-vratas* (vows of one who has completed his studies), not duties common to all men.
If, however, she should become defiled while being approached by a man of equal status,
the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances are prescribed for her purification.
When solicited by one of the same caste, a subsequent sexual union is established as an *upapātaka* (minor offense), for which the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance is prescribed;
the repeated injunction of the *cāndrāyaṇa* for the sake of one who has killed a cow is intended to prescribe the full extent of the penance.
And this is exactly what has been stated.
Mother, mother’s sister, mother-in-law, maternal uncle’s wife,
father’s sister, paternal uncle’s wife, friend’s wife, female disciple, sister, her friend, and daughter-in-law;
A daughter, a teacher’s wife, one of the same lineage, one who has sought refuge,
a queen, a female renunciant, a virtuous woman, a nurse, and one of the highest caste.
In this case, even though there is an extension of the rule (*atideśa*), the penance is not the same, because a specific punishment is observed.
Regarding that, what was stated for the mother applies:
for those beginning with the mother’s sister and ending with the daughter, the penance is a year-long *kṛcchra*.
For those remaining [cases], there is the repeated performance of the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.

Regarding that, as for those who have been mentioned, it is said whether they are of the same *gotra*—meaning they are designated by the caste (*jāti*) of the one [who gave them]—or whether they are of the *gotra* of the one to whom they were given.
He says it is by both ways, because indicative marks (*liṅga*) are seen in both manners.

*Gotra*, *vaṃśa*, and *abhijana* refer to the paternal lineage and so forth; therefore, because she is related to that [lineage], the mention of the father’s sister (*pitṛṣvasṛ*) would be redundant, for she is not of the same *gotra*. Alternatively, if it is held that those who have attained oneness with someone partake of that person's status, then they ought to be designated by their husband’s *gotra*; in that case, the mention of the paternal uncle’s wife (*pitṛvyastrī*) would be redundant, for she is indeed of the same *gotra*.
[Objection: But surely this [term] applies to both [the father’s sister and the paternal uncle’s wife] because there is no gender marker [to distinguish them].
However, for all [rites], the view is that they belong to the lineage of the husband (bhartṛgotra) and share the same lineage (sagotra).
As for what is said by some—that in the performance of the *śrāddha* rite one should adopt the paternal lineage (*paitrika-gotra*)—that applies only to that specific occasion;
or else, it is done in that manner because of a specific scriptural injunction.
Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by consorting with a *vṛṣalī* for a single night,
he removes that by subsisting on alms and constantly reciting [sacred texts] for three years.
Here, "Vṛṣalī" refers to a Caṇḍālī because of her low status; if the repetition occurs intentionally, it should be understood as such.
Otherwise, the term *kṛcchra* itself [indicates the penance].
Because of the mention of "one night," this should be understood to apply to one who spends the entire night sleeping with her.
"Service" means enjoyment.
The word "vṛṣalī" is used here as a term of reproach, not as a designation for a caste.
Whatever sin one commits or produces, that one removes—that is, destroys—in three years.
Regarding the injunction "subsisting on alms, reciting [mantras]," since no specific [mantra] is prescribed, some say that there is nothing other than these [Vedic texts] in this world or the next.
Others, however, maintain that one may recite other passages from the *Mantra* and *Brāhmaṇa* according to one's faith, but not worldly speech;
for the recitation of mantras is enjoined without distinction for the sake of purification, as in the case of the *Ṛgveda-saṃhitā* and so forth.

As for the claim that having consorted with a *vṛṣalī*— which they define as a *śūdrā*— for three months [constitutes this offense], that too is incorrect; for the marriage of a *śūdrā* is not prescribed [for the twice-born],

and because a lighter penance is taught for a wanton woman (*svairiṇī*), whereas another [type of *vṛṣalī*] is a minor offense (*upapātaka*), this [penalty] would be disproportionately heavy and thus inappropriate.
The expiation for these four types of evildoers has been declared;
now hear these expiations for those who associate with outcasts.
The meaning of this verse is straightforward.
One falls from one's status by associating with an outcast for a year through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or marriage; but not by sharing a vehicle, a seat, or food.

The meaning is that one falls away from the duties of the twice-born; "falls" means one slips away or is deprived of one's qualification. Those who have fallen are the four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.

By associating with them for one year, one becomes fallen; the meaning is that one becomes equal to them. Associating with them means traveling together with them through conversation, physical contact, and so forth, as well as by sharing vehicles, seats, and food.
The vehicle and the seat are likewise the same.
[They may eat] on one bed, on one seat; on one seat, they may eat from a single vessel.
They may engage in officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and matrimonial alliances, provided there is no excessive intimacy.
It must be stated whether loss of caste (pātitya) occurs through officiating at sacrifices and so forth, or not at all, or whether it occurs before or after one year;
[the answer is] that it occurs immediately (sadyaḥ), as seen in other Smṛtis.

The reading "officiating at sacrifices and teaching" (yājanādhyāpanam) with the accusative ending is appropriate, because the sense of the cause is conveyed by the present participle suffix -śatṛ in the word "ācaran" (practicing).
Whichever among these a man associates with through his own downfall,
he must perform that very person's penance for the sake of purification from that association.
Whichever penance has been prescribed for whichever outcaste, that same penance he shall perform for the sake of purifying his association with them.
The genitive case in the word *eṣām* is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*).

Among these outcastes, whichever outcaste one enters into association with—that is, undergoes the aforementioned form of contact—he shall perform that very penance which has been prescribed for that specific outcaste.
"For the purification and destruction of that fault which has arisen from such association"—

this is a restatement (anuvāda) intended to complete the verse. Now, regarding this statement that one falls through the repeated performance of censurable acts, such as "one who does not abandon those who have fallen, etc.," is that which is called "falling" taught here as a primary injunction (upadiśyate), or is it extended by analogy (atidiśyate)?
If it is first taught that "there are five mortal sins," then the basis for that established usage must be stated.

Alternatively, if the teaching of the five [sins] is based on direct extension (*anugama*), then there is no purpose in using a different terminology through indirect extension (*atideśa*) for others.
Since those very same expiations and those very same duties are taught to him, what is the point of using indirect extension in practice?
To this it is replied:
conventional practices do not differ solely because of their purpose;
rather, they may differ for other reasons as well, and in this case, there is a difference based on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Where, having stated the condition of being an outcast (*patitatva*), it is declared that there is a loss of the duties of the twice-born (*dvijāti*) and that water-libations (*udaka*) must be offered for the outcast, and so forth—because the specific duty is mentioned once—this is an *upadeśa* (direct injunction). However, where the acquisition of those duties occurs through a statement of connection with that [original rite], either by name or by association of gender-markers (*liṅga*), that is an *atideśa* (extended application).

Indeed, in the case of the words "Sūrya" and "Agni," no specific duty is heard in the *Saurya* sacrifice such that, upon the existence of an extended application, this particular distinction could be determined as obtainable.
That is incorrect,
because sovereignty belongs only to words such as "Sūrya" and the like, since the Veda is uncreated;
this is a human composition.
And why would a person initiate a new linguistic convention when there is no difference [between things]?
As for the establishment [of a convention] through perception and inference due to the absence of sublation, that is not ever observed in this case.
Furthermore, as for "repetition," that is merely a recurrence; in that regard, activity proceeds from it, yet even among hundreds of recurrences, it remains a single entity in the form of repetition.
In common worldly usage, repetition is simply what constitutes practice (*abhyāsa*).
In that regard, whether an offense is committed twice or a hundred times, both would be equal in terms of penance (*prāyaścitta*),
for a censurable act is by definition prohibited.
In this regard, whether one sleeps twice during the day or repeatedly slaughters cows, there is an equal attainment of downfall due to the habitual practice of censurable acts;
therefore, this must be reflected upon.
What is it that is to be reflected upon here?
First, the status of being an outcast (pātakin) is declared by all authors of Smṛtis for five [offenses], while for some others, there is equality with them.
To refute both of these [views], it will be intended that "there is no distinction therein," based on the consideration of the person's capacity and the gravity of the sin.
For it is not logical to treat that [sin] as identical to its counterpart, as in the case of Gārgava.
Now, there is a distinction among certain factors and a similarity among others in their unity;
therefore, one becomes an equal to those [who have fallen].
Consequently, for one who is slightly less than such an equal, the penance is nearly equal to that of the fallen.
Some say that when the qualification ceases, there is a distinction:
the qualification for the Vedic rites ceases directly, but not for those based on Smṛti.

As for what was said—that if there were two repetitions, there would be no difference between [the first] hundredfold repetition and [the second]—even in that case, there is a difference between the repetitions.

How can there be equality of transgression? As for the claim that because sleeping during the day and killing a cow are equally censured, one becomes an outcast (patita) equally by practicing them—how can the censure be equal when, in the explanatory passages (arthavādas), a difference in the gravity of the transgression is heard, and even though the prohibition is equally extensive, there is a multiplicity of expiatory rites (prāyaścitta)?
In such a case, this is the rule:
"Falling" (pātana) occurs through the habitual practice of censurable acts, not merely by their performance once; thus it is said, "when the cart is full.
Therefore, even when there is habitual practice of censurable acts, there is no falling [from caste] at all.
The sapinda relatives and kinsmen must perform the water-libation for one who has fallen from his caste outside the village on an inauspicious day,
in the evening, in the presence of agnates, officiating priests, and teachers.

It is stated that for one who has fallen from his status while still alive, even if he is unwilling, the offering of the water-pot (*ghaṭodaka*)—as if he were already dead—must be performed as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
"Sapiṇḍas" refers to those within seven generations of a single lineage; others than these are "bandhus" (relatives) and "sagotras" (those of the same clan).
On a censured day, such as the fourteenth [lunar day] and so forth;
in the evening, when the sun has set;
[and in the presence of] a kinsman or a priest.
Relatives and others [should provide maintenance] for those who perform the rites, as well as for one who has fallen from caste.
A female slave should overturn a jar full of water with her foot as if for a deceased person;
the kinsmen, together with her, shall observe impurity for a day and a night.
"Like a *preta*" means this is an instruction on what ought to be done:
a female slave, being sent, should overturn— that is, throw down— the water-jar with her foot, thinking, "This is for such-and-such a person."
When that [corpse] has been cast out, impurity (āśauca) lasting for a day and night is prescribed.
Along with their kinsmen, they should sit together and dwell in one place on that day.
By the mention of the female slave, [the author] prohibits performing the act oneself.

If this is so, then regarding the alternative that one does not perform the rite oneself—namely, "in the presence of kinsmen, officiating priests, and gurus"—what is the distinction between kinsmen (*jñāti*) and *sapiṇḍas*, such that it is stated that the rite must be performed by him in their presence?
For insofar as all of them assist merely by being present, they provide assistance that is not something to be physically brought together (*asaṃnipātyopakāra*).
This is not the case.
The sapindas and others are the agents by virtue of being the instigators;
however, kinsmen and others are merely brought together for the sake of the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa).
From that point on, however, there shall be a cessation of conversation and shared seating,
as well as the giving of inheritance and even ordinary social intercourse.
Now it is explained how one should behave after the water libations have been performed: "Conversation" refers to the mutual exchange of speech;
"inheritance," meaning wealth, that too must not be given to him.

Worldly conduct consists of inquiries after one's welfare and so forth when two people meet, as well as bringing [the guest] to the house and providing food on occasions such as marriages and the like.
But is it not the case that their cessation is already established simply by the prohibition of conversation?
For there is also the possibility of ceasing from rising to greet and leaving one's seat, which likewise take the form of [verbal] interaction.
But conversation consists essentially of sound alone.
The status of being the eldest shall cease, as well as the wealth acquired by the eldest;
moreover, a younger brother who is superior in virtue shall receive the share of the eldest.
And regarding the wealth that is to be obtained by the eldest,
an objection is raised here as well:
since the giving of an inheritance is prohibited, the prohibition of wealth consisting of property obtainable by the eldest is already established.
Some say that this is restated for the purpose of granting a share to a younger brother who is superior by virtue of his qualities;
others, however, believe that by the word "inheritance" (dāyādya) mere wealth is meant, not only that which has come down through lineage.
Accordingly, it is recorded in the lexicons that "inheritance (dāyādya) is considered to be wealth";
therefore, even that which has been taken by someone from him as a debt must not be paid.
What, then, should be done?
It should be delivered to those who inherit the estate, such as sons, brothers, and so forth.

Others, however, hold the view that for those whose wealth has not been partitioned, there is a prohibition against inheriting property; but once partition has taken place, there is only the abolition of the *uddhāra* (preferential share) and the senior share (*jyeṣṭhāṃśa*) itself.
Even when sons exist, they alone shall have authority over everything except the portion set aside for the inheritance.
But when the penance has been performed, they should bathe in a sacred body of water and together with him alone cast a new pitcher full of water into it.
Now, the water-rite for one who has performed expiation is described.

Having bathed together with that very person in a sacred body of water—whether in a river, a great lake, or at a specific holy site such as Prabhāsa or Mānasa—they, having themselves performed the ablution, should personally cast a new jar of water [into it].
Because of the mention of a "new jar" and the mention of a "female slave," it follows that in the previous case, the jar used in the rites was not new.
Having filled it with water, its removal has been described.
He said, "Furthermore, that jar must be thrown back in.
Having cast that jar into the water and entered his own home,
he performed all the duties for his kinsmen just as before.
The jar should be cast into those very waters in which they have bathed;
then, placing it at their head, they should enter his dwelling. Thereafter, they should proceed with the ancestral rites, such as the communal feast and other ceremonies, just as before.
Others, however, connect the phrase "when the penance has been performed" with this.
The throwing of the water-pot (ghaṭaprāsana) must be performed by that very person;

and this rite of offering water for one who has fallen (patitodakakriyā) applies to him alone, not to any other who is to be abandoned, such as one who abandons his father, a regicide, a priest for a Śūdra, and so forth.
One should apply this very same rule even to women who have fallen from their status;
however, they should be provided with clothing, food, and drink, and they should live near the house.

This same rule applies even to women who have become outcasts (*patita*). That is, it applies to those who have become outcasts and have not performed penance. However, even for them, once the water-libation has been performed, clothing and food should be given.
Because of the mention of "giving," clothing and food—which merely suffice for the maintenance of the body—are what should be given, not luxuries and the like.
As for drink, it is water by virtue of propriety;
and because of its abundance, it is obtained even if not specifically offered.
However, even that speech [of instruction] should not be given to them independently, but rather out of affection and in consideration for others;
and just as it is with their drink, so it is with their clothing and food—therefore, inferior clothing and food should be given.
Thus it has been said:
One should cause an unfaithful wife to live deprived of her authority, wearing soiled clothes, subsisting on mere alms, humiliated, and sleeping on the ground.
The causes for loss of caste (*pātitya*) for women are exactly the same as those for men.

As for the statement regarding the killing of an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*) and service to a man of lower caste—that there is no greater [sin] for women in the case of killing an embryo—that is intended to establish equality, not to serve as an exclusive restriction (*parisaṃkhyā*).
And so says Yājñavalkya:
Approaching a low-caste man, causing an abortion, and harming one's husband—
these also certainly constitute acts that cause women to fall specifically.
The mention of "nearby" (antikagrahaṇa) means that they should be made to dwell in small huts after being removed from their principal residences; they should reside close to their own homes.
Some say that this [provision] is to be given to those performing penance (prāyaścitta), but not otherwise.
That is incorrect, because the practice of providing clothing and food is appropriate in that context.
Expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) include subsisting on alms, the milk-vow (*payovrata*), the *cāndrāyaṇa* procedure, and so forth.
Furthermore, subsisting on alms cannot be precluded by this [text], because its purpose is fulfilled by the prescription of one's livelihood (*vṛtti*).

Therefore, the meaning of the verse is that even for her who lacks the qualification for expiatory rites—whether due to incapacity or excessive corpulence—the giving of clothing and other such things must be performed.
One should not engage in any business with those who have committed sins until they have been purified; but once they have undergone purification, one should never despise them.
Since those who have committed offenses (*enasvin*) are the subject under discussion, they are sinners.

With them being "unpurified" (*anirṇikta*), meaning impure and having not performed expiation (*akṛtaprāyaścitta*), no transaction whatsoever—such as lending money, buying, selling, officiating at sacrifices, and so forth—is permitted. Purification (*nirṇejana*) means cleansing, the removal of sin.
When that has been performed, one should not despise her; one should not revile those who have completed their penance.

One should not live together with those who kill children, those who are ungrateful, those who kill those who have sought refuge, or those who kill women— even if they have been purified according to the Dharma.
One who has come for refuge (*śaraṇāgata*) is one who, being struck by enemies or oppressed by another powerful person, runs toward someone else for the sake of protection, saying, "Save me!
In the same way, a wise person who has committed an offense should run to [the teacher], saying, "Lift me up; grant me an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Such a person is one who has come for refuge.

An ungrateful person (*kṛtaghna*) is one who, having forgotten a benefit received, strives to cause harm, or who, having once rendered assistance, seeks to destroy that very benefactor by endeavoring to do them wrong.
Although this is the etymological derivation of the word, according to common worldly usage, he who acts toward the benefactor as if he were an enemy is ungrateful.
In this matter, caste is not a requirement; the very nature of being a fool or the like is the cause.
Women, even though they are unchaste;
although their penance is slight, nevertheless there is a scriptural prohibition against cohabitation.
"Cohabitation" (saṃvāsa) means association as well as residing in the same house.
Those twice-born men for whom the Sāvitrī has not been recited according to the rule,
one should cause them to perform three Kṛcchra penances and then initiate them according to the rule.
The rule regarding the time for initiation has been established by the passage beginning with "For a Brāhmaṇa, up to the sixteenth year. This is the expiation for its transgression:
from the eighth year after conception until the sixteenth year, if the Sāvitrī has not been recited for a Brāhmaṇa.
The sacrament known as initiation (*upanayana*) is indicated by the recitation of the *Sāvitrī*.
If the initiation is not performed at this time,
[the period for it extends] until the twenty-second year for a Kṣatriya and until the twenty-fourth year for a Vaiśya.
Beyond this, he should be made to perform three *kṛcchra* penances;
for when the term *kṛcchra* is heard without a qualifying prefix, it is established in the *smṛti* systems that it refers to the *prājāpatya*.
Others, however, say it refers to the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*.
She should be brought back when difficult circumstances have arisen;
"according to the rule" is a restatement.
This same penance should also be prescribed for those twice-born who, being engaged in improper acts and abandoned by the Veda, desire to perform expiation.
Those who abide in improper action (*vikarmastha*) are, for example, Brahmins devoted to the service of Śūdras and the like.
Whatever action serves as one's means of livelihood is that person's prescribed duty (*vihita-karma*);
whatever is not prescribed for a person is, for that person, improper action (*vikarma*).
This [penance] is prescribed for one of the twice-born classes; for one of a different class, it constitutes a forbidden act (*vikarman*).

This threefold *kṛcchra* penance applies even to those who have been abandoned by the Veda—whether they have been initiated (*upanīta*) but have not accepted the Vedas, or having studied the Veda, have forgotten it.
The phrase "desiring to perform an expiation" (*prāyaścittaṃ cikīrṣantaḥ*) is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).
For it is precisely because one desires that one engages in action.
Whatever wealth Brāhmaṇas acquire through a censurable occupation,
they are purified by relinquishing it, as well as by silent recitation and austerity.

Although the term "by what is censurable" (*garhitena*) is used without qualification, it should be understood as referring specifically to "accepting gifts from the wicked" (*asatpratigraha*), because the specific injunction that follows is taught with reference to that very act, stating: "one is liberated from accepting gifts from the wicked.

"Renunciation" (*utsargaḥ*) means abandonment, the cessation of the sense of ownership, or giving away by means of a gift. Disregarding both visible and invisible rewards, one should cast [the wealth] away through renunciation on royal roads and the like, having declared: "Whoever wishes to take what is mine, let him take it," and so forth; or one may throw it into a pit, a hole, a river, or similar places.
The [author] will explain recitation and austerity in the verse that has been taught.
Others, however, reading the word *varṇa* (caste) in place of the word *brāhmaṇa*, explain it as follows:
whatever is prohibited for a particular caste—whether a twice-born person or a Śūdra—as a means of acquiring wealth, that is contemptible for him.
As it is said: "Neither a Brāhmaṇa nor even a Kṣatriya should ever engage in usury," and so forth.
Therefore, for those who acquire wealth through such [forbidden] action, the three—renunciation, recitation, and austerity—are prescribed as combined penances.
For a Brāhmaṇa, the acceptance of improper gifts constitutes a further specific rule.
Having recited the Sāvitrī mantra three thousand times with a concentrated mind,
and having drunk only milk for a month in a cow-pen, one is released from the sin of accepting improper gifts.
Some say "three thousand recitations of the Sāvitrī" refers to every day;
others, however, connect the three with a month.
And therefore, one hundred [cows] each day;
"goṣṭha" refers to the place of residence.
When he had returned from the cow-pen, emaciated by his fasts and bowing before them, they should ask him: "O gentle one, do you desire equanimity?"
By the mention of "emaciation," he indicates that the drinking of milk should be very little.
[The student] stands on the ground with his knees bent.
Those learned Brahmins should ask him: "O gentle one, do you desire equanimity?"
Furthermore, one must not again disregard the treatise and proceed [to act] out of greed for accepting what is improper.
Having spoken the truth before the Brahmins, he should scatter fodder for the cows;
once the sacred ford has been established by the cows, they should perform his formal reception.
When questioned by him, he should say "truth.

At that bathing place (*tīrtha*) or crossing point on the path where the cows roam to drink water from rivers, springs, and the like, those Brahmins should perform its formal acceptance (*parigraha*); for they would bring a portion of it under their own control by means of the ritual placing of the hand (*hastāropaṇa*).
Having performed sacrifices for Vrātyas, the funeral rites for others,
malevolent magic, or the Ahīna sacrifice, one removes the taint by means of three Kṛcchra penances.
The *vrātyas* are those who have fallen away from the *Sāvitrī*. For these *vrātyas*, the *vrātyastoma* sacrifice is prescribed.
Those who officiate for them through the role of a priest (*ṛtvij*) or as an instructor (*upadeṣṭṛ*) [are likewise affected].

For others—excluding [actions for] one's mother, father, or guru—the *antyakarma* refers to funeral rites at the cremation ground and so forth; *abhicāra* refers to sorcery such as the *śyena* sacrifice and the *cit* fire-altar;
and *ahīna* refers to sacrifices lasting two nights or more.
He is purified by means of arduous penances (*kṛcchra*).
However, others say:
"This rule does not apply to a sacrificer who has performed malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) or a degraded sacrifice (*ahīna*)."
To whom, then, does [the sin] belong? To the officiating priests (ṛtvij).

And thus, their officiating for those who have lost their caste (vrātyas) constitutes precisely such an entitlement. But as for the sacrificer, his engagement is characterized by scriptural injunction; since there is no prohibition against that [engagement], how could there be an expiation?
Let it be that engagement with the *ahīna* sacrifice proceeds on the basis of scripture;
but how can this be the case regarding the *śyena* and other such rites?
For there is no injunction stating, "One should kill one's enemies."
What then? One who desires the killing of an enemy must perform rites such as the Śyena for the sake of achieving that end.
And in the killing of an enemy, there is an engagement characterized by violence;
and that [violence] is prohibited by the rule: "One should not harm any living beings."
Even in the case of the *ahīna* sacrifices, engagement occurs solely out of a desire for gain;
for it is one who desires a fruit who has the qualification (*adhikāra*) for them.
However, the desire for a fruit is not prohibited therein, nor is the activity that accomplishes the desired object prohibited.

In this case, however, both are prohibited: by the injunction "one shall not kill," one must not engage in an action that results in death; and the result of such an action belongs specifically to the Śyena sacrifice and the like. But here, there is no prohibition stating that an action which has heaven and other such things as its fruit should not be performed.
Some say:
"The weapon of a Brāhmaṇa is indeed speech"; thus, even malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) performed by one who practices such magic is traditionally taught as permitted.
Malevolent magic and the *ahīna* sacrifice are equal.

In that case, it is appropriate that the expiation belongs to the officiating priests alone. Now, as for the objection that even optional rites are prohibited because "being driven by desire is not praised," the scope of that [prohibition] has already been explained in that very context.
And the Śruti states that officiating at a sacrifice must be performed without deficiency;
yet it is improper for one who performs an *abhicāra* (malevolent rite) to act as the sacrificer.
How so?

Whatever is prescribed regarding the practice of sorcery (*abhicāra*) against the luminaries, the expiations for that have already been stated; for this [treatise] has jurisdiction over both the officiating priest who performs the sorcery and the person against whom it is directed. Sorcery (*abhicāra*) is the killing of an enemy by means of Vedic recitation, oblations, and so forth.
Having abandoned one who has come for refuge or having caused the Veda to be lost, a twice-born man expiates that sin by subsisting on barley for one year.

The two kinds of those who have sought refuge were mentioned previously. Their abandonment or rejection [is forbidden], provided one has the capacity; this was already examined above. "Having corrupted the Veda" means having performed the study of the *nadhyāya* [prohibited days].

The granting of instruction to one who is studying under authority consists of asking, "What are you reading? or "Has this been lost by you? Alternatively, it may be studied for the sake of wealth at places of examination by one who is not appointed; and having granted such an appointment for the sake of wealth, the Sage declared those fallen from their status.
One bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a donkey, or by domestic carnivorous animals,
as well as by humans, horses, camels, or pigs, becomes pure through breath control (prāṇāyāma).
"Bitten" means bitten by the teeth and fangs;
that is, by domestic carnivorous animals such as cats, mongooses, and the like.
Eating only at the sixth meal-time for a month, or the recitation of the *Saṃhitā*,
as well as daily *homas* with *sāla* wood, are the means of purification for those excluded from the company at meals (*apāṅktya*).
Those who are declared unfit for the company at the third [meal] have a penance prescribed for each specific case elsewhere;
for them, there is a combination of reciting the *Saṃhitā* for a month,
the *Śākalahoma*, and eating only at the sixth meal-time.
Wooden sticks and other materials are offered with the mantras beginning with "devakṛtasya" (of what is done by the gods); that is the *śākalahoma*.
The inclusion of the word "nitya" (constant/regular) is for the purpose of repeating [the rite] again and again even after the recitation of the *saṃhitā* is completed, until the month is fulfilled.
Having mounted a camel-vehicle or a donkey-vehicle out of desire,
a Brahmin who has bathed while naked becomes pure through breath control (prāṇāyāma).

A vehicle yoked with camels refers to a cart or similar conveyance; mounting a camel or such directly, without any intervening barrier, constitutes a more serious offense. The repetition of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) is required.
"Naked" means unclothed.
To remove the fault of being naked, one should again bathe while wearing clothes and perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
If one is distressed and has deposited a corpse in water without water, or even within water, one becomes pure by bathing outside with one's clothes on and touching a cow.
In the absence of water— meaning when water is not present or is beyond the range of sight—
one who is distressed and paralyzed by the urge to defecate,
having discharged his bodily waste of urine and feces, shall remain together with his *cela*, that is, the garment he was wearing.
Having bathed by immersing oneself in a river or similar body of water outside the village, and then having touched a cow, one becomes pure.
In the case of the omission of obligatory rites prescribed by the Vedas,
and in the case of the violation of the vows of a *snātaka*, the penance is fasting.
These include the Vedic rites such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and others, as well as the Smārta rites such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and others;
for these too are declared in the Vedas, since the Smṛtis are rooted in them.
Also included are the vows of a *snātaka*, such as "one should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes," and so forth.
For their omission, there is a fast for one day;
those sacrifices (iṣṭis) that have been prescribed for the transgression of Śrauta rites are to be combined with this [penance].
Having uttered "huṃ" to a Brāhmaṇa, or having addressed an elder with "thou," one should bathe, fast for the remainder of the day, and propitiate him by bowing down.

In the context of angry rebukes, the utterance of the syllable *huṃ*—such as "Be silent! Huṃ! Do not speak thus! and so forth—is employed for the purpose of prohibiting such actions. Whether toward a Brāhmaṇa who is senior, equal, or junior, or toward a disciple or a son; likewise, toward one who is more venerable, one says "you" (*tvam*) and addresses them: "You have spoken thus," or "This was done by you."
This expiation applies to the utterance of the word *yuṣmad* in the singular number;
the specific case endings, such as the nominative and so forth, are not intended to be restrictive.
Accordingly, established practice dictates that when addressing a teacher, the plural form should be employed, as in "among you" (*yuṣmāsu*) and similar expressions.

Having bathed and not eating in the morning, he should abandon food for the day; having offered salutations and performed the ritual clasping of the feet, he should appease [the teacher] by abandoning anger and eat in the evening.
Having struck him even with a blade of grass, or having bound him by the neck with a cloth,
or having defeated him in a dispute, one should propitiate him by bowing down.
Having struck and beaten them even with a blade of grass that causes pain,
or having bound them by the neck even with a garment of soft touch,
and having completely defeated them in a worldly dispute or quarrel;
Having prostrated and become humble, one should seek to propitiate [the opponent];
however, this rule does not apply to formal debate (vāda) and contentious disputation (jalpa).
But by threatening a Brahmin, one falls into hell for a hundred years, and by striking him with intent to kill, for a thousand years.
This is a prohibition against threatening;
the remainder is an explanatory statement (arthavāda).
"Having raised a staff or the like with the intent to kill," that is, with the desire to strike.
He dwells in the hells for a hundred years;
having struck and dealt a blow with the intent to kill, he remains there for a thousand years, but not for mere jesting.
For as many particles of dust as the blood collects upon the surface of the earth,
for that many thousands of years shall the one who caused it go to hell.

If the blood of a Brahmin falls to the ground due to a blow from a staff or similar weapon, his progenitor shall go to and dwell in hell for as many thousands of years as there are particles of dust and soil that the blood absorbs;
this too is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).
Having threatened [a Brahmin], one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; for striking him down, the Atikṛcchra;
and for causing blood to flow from a Brahmin, one should perform both the Kṛcchra and the Atikṛcchra.
This is the expiation for the former [offense].
Regarding the phrase "having caused injury to a Brāhmaṇa," this applies to cases other than the drawing of blood;
or else, it may be considered as an alternative to that.
But for the removal of those sins for which no expiation has been stated,
one should prescribe an expiation after considering both the capacity [of the offender] and the nature of the sin.
Regarding those wrongful acts for which no expiations or penances have been stated—such as the killing of a *caṇḍāla* or others born of inverse unions—one should determine them in that case.
But has it not already been stated here: "In the case of killing animals with bones, one should give something small to a Brahmin"?
Because of their association with boneless creatures, those possessing bones there are understood to be mostly small animals;
however, this rule does not apply to large-bodied beings.
Now, since it is said that "there are four castes and no fifth," those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*) are merely subdivisions of the *śūdra*.
Even if it is true that a fifth caste has not been born, it does not follow from this alone that they must be Śūdras;
for their characteristics are also fixed by the rule: "one born of a woman of the same caste who has been married is a Śūdra. Thus, these are those born from a mixture of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*).
Therefore, the penance for killing a Śūdra does not apply.
Nor, however, is there any room for the alternative conception that "something [small] indeed should be given to the Brahmin";
for the capacity lies in the penance of the one performing the expiation— namely,
whether he is capable of this penance or rather of giving.
And as for sin:
for violence, there is indeed the prescribed expiation;
for eating what is unfit to be eaten, that very same [expiation applies].
Now, the relative gravity or lightness of a sin must be considered.
But how is the gravity or lightness of a sin known?
If it is argued that it is known from the magnitude of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), this reasoning applies only to cases where no specific expiation has been mentioned.
True;
because of the gravity resulting from the hearing of an excessive fault in the case of a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda),
as well as in the case of an act performed intentionally after repeated practice.
Furthermore, one should not assume that this [penance] applies only to cases where no expiation has been mentioned; even when one has been mentioned, it must be applied. Why is this?
Because penance and punishment are equivalent.
By means of the staff (daṇḍa), the scope of both what has been stated and what has not been stated is authorized.
Furthermore, because there is instruction regarding the gravity or lightness of these transgressions, a necessary conceptualization must be applied therein;
therefore, this is the remainder of everything, both that which has been specifically mentioned and that which has not.
I shall describe to you those means practiced by gods, sages, and ancestors, by which a human being removes his sins.
But has it not already been stated that these very means are prescribed here—here the Cāndrāyaṇa, here the Prājāpatya, and here the twelve-year penance?
True;
they were merely indicated by way of their names.
But here, the essential nature [of the means] together with its procedure is stated.
A "subsidiary means" (abhyupāya) is simply a means (upāya). It draws away; it wipes away.
The passage beginning with "devarṣi" (divine sage) is a hymn of praise; the mention of "mānava" (descendant of Manu) is for the sake of including all social classes.
A twice-born man performing the Prājāpatya penance should eat food obtained by begging for three days in the morning, for three days in the evening, and for three days he should not eat at all.
Although "the beginning of the day" (aharmukha) refers to morning (prātar), it nevertheless indicates the forenoon (pūrvāhṇa),
because this excludes the time of the second part of the day. For, in the injunction regarding the morning time, eating at will would otherwise have been the case.
For when a meal that is already established for men— either in the forenoon or at midday— is obtained because it was not specifically requested, yet arises from a state of need,

if that very same meal is prescribed for the morning time, then the midday meal would be excluded, but not the evening meal. However, in the present case, since the meal that was already established as an option between the forenoon and midday times is mentioned again, it results in the exclusion of other times.
And this alone is appropriate because it is a vow (*vrata*);
for eating a single meal is counted as a number among the enumeration of vows. Furthermore, this is austerity (*tapas*) because it heats and causes suffering.
If the second meal is prohibited, then the evening meal would be excluded there.
Others, however, say that by the phrase "morning meals consisting of sacrificial food" (*haviṣyān prātarāśān*), a small quantity of food is indicated;
for indeed, they eat only a little during the morning meal.
Ordinary people are characterized by such behavior;
likewise, when cooking has been accomplished, they designate him an "ordinary eater" before he has actually eaten.
Or, [the word] "sāyam" [may refer to] the third day thereafter.
Immediately thereafter, for three days, the Vedic *haviṣya* food is permitted as long as it is being consumed.
And it has been stated by the authors of the Smṛtis: "One should go to sleep after eating only a little.
Even when food is not requested (*ayācita*), the consumption of *haviṣya* food is to be done only once a day.
Even when servants and others are commanded, "Let food be given to me even in my own house," that too is indeed a request (*yācita*).
A request is merely a petition, common to both commanding and entreating.
Therefore, even in one's own home, one should eat only what is offered by one's wife and others without their explicit permission, and not otherwise.
Cow's urine, cow dung, milk, curd, ghee, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass,
followed by a fast for one night— this is known as the *Sāntapana* penance.
They say that on a single day there is a collection of cow-urine and so forth along with kusha-water;
then there is fasting for one night;
after that, the Sāntapana penance lasts for two days.
Others, however, maintain that one [grain] should be eaten each day, because eating them collectively is not prescribed;
therefore, the *sāntapana* penance lasts for seven days.
Both of these views are accepted in another Smṛti text.
A twice-born man performing the Atikṛcchra penance should eat only a single morsel for three periods of three days as before,
and he should fast for the final three days.
The phrase "as before" extends the rule for the *prājāpatya* penance;
during these very times, one should eat only a single morsel of food.
A Brahmin performing the *taptakṛcchra* penance should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air,
each for three days, bathing once daily and remaining composed in mind.
At those very times, one should consume water and so forth until no excessive satiation occurs;
in some places, a specific measure is recited:
"One should drink three *palas* of water, but only one *pala* of clarified butter."
One should drink two palas of milk, or three palas of warm wind-curing [decoction].
"One who bathes once" is an exception to the rule that one should bathe three times during the day and three times during the night.
For one who is self-restrained and vigilant, fasting for twelve days is this penance called Parāka, which removes all sins.
One who is self-controlled, with senses restrained, having no desire for hearing sounds such as singing,
being vigilant and devoted to that [practice]—
this is a commendatory statement (arthavāda), because this dharma is prescribed for all types of penance (kṛcchra).
One should decrease the morsel by one each day during the dark fortnight and increase it during the bright fortnight;
touching water at the three sessions of the day, this is remembered as the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
Having fasted on the fourteenth day, on the following day, which is the full moon (paurṇamāsī), one should eat fifteen morsels.

Regarding the size of the morsel and the consecration of the morsels, the procedure stated in another Smṛti—namely, "Grow great" (*āpyāyasva*) and "May your milks unite" (*saṃ te payāṃsi*)—is to be expected.
Since all Smṛtis constitute a single scripture, when there is no contradiction, they should be applied in their entirety.

In case of conflict, however, there is an option (*vikalpa*). Beginning from the first lunar day (*pratipad*), one should decrease the morsels (*grāsa*) one by one each day: fourteen on the first, thirteen on the second, and so on, until there is only one morsel on the fourteenth day.
Then, having fasted on the new moon day, he should eat one mouthful on the first day of the lunar fortnight;
on the second day, two; thus he should increase by one each day until there are fifteen mouthfuls on the full moon day, while performing ritual ablutions and bathing.
"Three times a day" means in the morning, at midday, and in the afternoon;
"three times at night" is excluded because it has been specifically prescribed [as a separate rule].
One who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, beginning with the bright fortnight and remaining self-restrained, should carry out this entire procedure for the Yavamadhyama variety.
In the *yavamadhyama* [lunar penance], having fasted on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), one takes one morsel (*grāsa*) on the first day of the fortnight (*pratipad*);

two on the second, and so on until fifteen on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*). Then, beginning again from the first day of the dark fortnight, there is a reduction of one morsel per day until the fast on the new moon day.
Restraining his self and subsisting on sacrificial food, one performing the *yaticāndrāyaṇa* should eat eight morsels when the sun has reached the meridian.
The *yaticāndrāyaṇa* consists of eight morsels of food each day, beginning either from the dark fortnight or from the bright fortnight;
it is performed when midday has arrived,
meaning that the forenoon and afternoon have been avoided.
The remainder is well known.
A Brahmin, with a concentrated mind, should eat four morsels in the morning and four when the sun has set;
this is known as the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa.
Here, by association with "sunset," the word *prātaḥ* (morning) indicates the time proximate to sunrise;
the meaning is that it is "dusk" (*pradoṣa*) when the sun has set.
By eating, with a concentrated mind, eighty-three morsels of sacrificial food (haviṣya) in any manner whatsoever for one month, one attains the same world as the Moon.

On some days he takes four morsels, on some twelve, and on others he does not eat at all; in this manner, the practice continues for thirty nights. If on some days he takes sixteen, this is the rule: three hundred and eighty [morsels] per month, which amounts to two hundred and forty-four.
One attains the world of the moon.
The Rudras, the Ādityas, the Vasus,
and the Maruts, together with the great seers, observed this vow for the sake of liberation from all that is unwholesome.
All the gods practiced this Cāndrāyaṇa vow for the sake of liberation from all unwholesome deeds.
It should be understood that it applies not only where it is explicitly mentioned, but also in cases where it is not;
for it has been said: "The Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and the Cāndrāyaṇa constitute the universal expiation—the universal expiation."
In this regard, the following doubt arises:

regarding this statement on universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*), does it purify all [sins] through a single performance (*tantra*), or does it recur for each individual cause according to the principle of the accomplishment of yoga (*yogasiddhi*)?
It is said:

Although it is logically correct that when the occasion (*nimitta*) recurs, the occasional rite (*naimittika*) should also recur, nevertheless, this [rule] is prescribed for cases where the occasions for which specific penances have been taught are not consciously remembered, yet there is a suspicion that they occurred.

Among those cases, first, regarding those for which purification is effected by mere suspicion—such as "even one [day] of the year"—since the occurrence of the occasion is uncertain, how could a recurrence be possible?

Just as for one who is asleep there occurs the killing of minute living beings on the bed through his turnings over, so too for one wandering in the streets of a city, the sight of another's wife's face occurs repeatedly from the time he leaves home until he reaches his house; in such a case, a state of *tantra* (simultaneous application) alone is appropriate. And this has been demonstrated in the passage beginning with "asthanvatām," where a single expiation is prescribed for the killing of a multitude.
Furthermore, for those most serious sins, expiations have been prescribed in all such cases;
and this [penance] ought to apply precisely to the subject matter as demonstrated.
Moreover, because of its gravity, it is logical that it should apply in the case of non-repetition.
Therefore, even when penances are determined in some way, it is indeed proper that there be a single performance (*tantra*) upon the arising of another occasion;
and thus he shows that the rule of *tantra* alone is logical: "Whatever sin we have committed by day and by night, you are the expiation for that, Svāhā!
Whatever sin we have committed while sleeping and while waking, you are the expiation for that, Svāhā!"
Regarding the passage beginning with "yad vidvāṃsaḥ" (that which the wise...):
the word "yat" (that) is used in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*), indicating the simultaneous abandonment of all sins without exception.
Regarding this, they say:
"One should personally perform the fire-oblation every day with the Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛti);
one should practice non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and straightforwardness."
Regarding all these [rites], this procedure is stated:
in all *homa* offerings, clarified butter (*ājya*) is shown to be the substance when no specific substance has been prescribed.
By the mention of "himself" (*svayam*), the agency of another is excluded.
Furthermore, it is deliberated whether this *homa* belongs to one who does not maintain the domestic fire (*anāvasathya*) in a worldly fire or not.
First, this must be considered: why is there an offering (*homa*) into the fire?
The meaning of the root *hu* (to sacrifice) is an act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) characterized by the limit of casting [the oblation] into [the fire].
In that regard, the *homa* is indeed accomplished by pouring [the offering] into any substrate whatsoever.

Consequently, the *homa* may be performed on land, in water, or in fire; however, for one who maintains the *gṛhya-agni*, the *homa* is not to be performed in a common (*laukika*) fire, because his *homa* is prohibited from being performed in a village fire (*grāmya-agni*).
If it is argued that the fire is established through traditional practice (*samācāra*), then let that very practice be investigated.
The authors of the Gṛhyasūtras, who possess authority regarding the fires established by them, have prescribed a fire-oblation (homa) within the rules for the Kṛcchra penances.
By this observation, it follows that for one who does not maintain a domestic fire (anāvasatha), the Kṛcchras do not involve fire-oblations when performed as expiations (prāyaścitta).

However, for those seeking prosperity (abhyudaya), there are no such [fireless] rites for one who maintains no sacred fire, because the attainment of the fruit requires the performance of all constituent parts (sarvāṅga) of the rite.
Non-violence:
even one's disciples, servants, and others should not be struck; they must not be beaten.
Truthfulness: even in jest, one should not speak untruth.
Or else, it is an injunction for the purpose of establishing as subsidiary elements those [qualities] already obtained as ends in themselves for a person;
namely, straightforwardness and lack of cruelty.
Three times during the day and three times at night, he should enter the water while still wearing his clothes;
and he should never speak with women, Śūdras, or outcasts.

Gautama says that one should touch water at each of the three *savanas* (pressings), that is, three times during the day; likewise, one should do so during the three watches of the night as well, excluding the *mahāniśā* (the dead of night). Beyond that time, there is no prescribed time for bathing. One should enter the water together with the pair of garments appropriate for covering oneself, which have been obtained according to custom.
"He should enter" means he should not do so with water that has been drawn up.
He should not speak to women, even Brāhmaṇa women, except for his mother, elder sisters, and others [of that class].
Conversation with his wife that pertains to the performance of ritual acts is not forbidden.
But another [type of person] should certainly not be made [to do so].
He should spend his time standing or sitting; if unable, he may lie on the ground.
He should be a celibate observer of vows, worshipping his guru, the gods, and the twice-born.
Whether standing, sitting, or even reclining,
he should not sit down anywhere at all;
if unable [to remain upright], he may lie on the ground, but not on a couch.
A *brahmacārī* is one who has desisted from sexual intercourse.
