Being observant of vows (*vratin*), he should undertake restraint regarding what is prescribed by the learned and what is prohibited, thinking: "This must not be done by me.
He should offer worship to his teacher and others with prostration, and present garlands, ointments, and other such offerings.
And he should daily recite the Sāvitrī and purificatory mantras according to his ability;
for in all vows, one who is intent on expiation should act in this manner.
The *sāvitrī* is the *gāyatrī* verse beginning with "tat savituḥ.
Because its deity is Savitṛ, it is entitled everywhere by the term *sāvitrī* in injunctions regarding recitation (*japa*).

The purifiers (*pavitrāṇi*) include the *aghamarṣaṇa*, the *pāvamānī* verses, the *puruṣasūkta*, and so forth; as well as the Sāman chants such as the *śukriya-adhyāya*, the *ajanara*, and the *rauhiṇeya*.
"In all [types of] severe hardships," meaning attentive and diligent;
the phrase "in all" and so forth serves to complete the verse, since only such a person possesses the requisite qualification.
The twice-born whose sins have been made public should be purified by these vows;
however, those whose sins have not been disclosed, one should purify with mantras and burnt offerings.
Those whose sin or evil has been manifested, revealed, and become known to the world must be purified by these arduous penances; however,
for those whose sins are secret, there are no penances consisting of ascetic toil.
What then? One should purify [the person] by means of mantras and fire-offerings (homa).
If it refers to the assembly (pariṣad), then surely in the secret [penances], there would be no disclosure [of the offense] before an assembly.
For the wise have authority in that matter.
It is said:
"One should not purify a future transgression through penance."
Rather, at the time of explaining the treatise, this purification regarding the secrets is to be understood as an instruction for the disciples.
By confession, by remorse, by austerity, and by Vedic study,
as well as by giving in times of distress, the doer of evil is released from evil.
Having been made known by the Brahmins, one should likewise proclaim it to others as well, saying, "I am a doer of such deeds.
This is *khyāpana* (confession) and *anutāpa* (remorse).
Therefore, remorse consists of mental distress such as: "Alas! Through my own heat [of passion], I have committed a great misdeed; for me, a doer of evil, birth is nothing but calamity.
Regarding non-violence, there is the study of the Sāvitrī, the chanting of mantras, or the recitation of the Vedas.
In other cases, for one incapable of asceticism (tapas), there is the giving of gifts.

This is what he says with the phrase "by giving in times of distress": for one who has undertaken ascetic practices, when there is distress—that is, suffering—and when there is no restraint [of the senses], there should be giving.
To the extent that a man, having himself committed an unrighteous act, confesses it,
to that same extent he is freed from that unrighteousness, just as a snake is freed from its slough.
The explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) pertains to the rule of self-proclamation.

In the phrase "a man [should not] proclaim unrighteousness" (*adharmam*), there is an elision (*praśleṣa*) of the negative particle (*nañ*). What is prohibited is the self-proclamation of one's own dharma; it does not mean that one's virtues should not be spoken of at all.
And it is indeed heard that unrighteousness itself was the primary cause, and by means of that unrighteousness [the world was destroyed].
To the extent that his mind reproaches the evil deed he has committed,
to that same extent his body is released from that unrighteousness.
The body is indeed the inner self (antarātman), not the elemental self (bhūtātman), because merit and demerit have that [inner self] as their locus.
For this term "body" should be understood as a metaphorical designation for the self;
this is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) intended to induce remorse.
It is known as censure.
Having committed a sin, one is indeed liberated from that sin by feeling remorse;
however, one is purified through the resolve of abstention, thinking, "I shall not do this again."
They say that this continues until cessation;
however, that is incorrect.
"Distress" (saṃtāpa) is mental exhaustion, consisting of the thought, "I have done this through negligence."
But cessation is the resolve that "it must not be done again";
and it shows a distinction in the action by means of the suffix *ktvā* in the expression "having heated oneself and having desisted."
Therefore, like a formal expiation, confession, remorse, and desistance must be performed by the one who has committed the offense;
thus he is purified and attains success.
Having thus reflected in his mind upon the arising of the fruits of action after death,
he should constantly perform virtuous deeds through his thoughts, words, and physical acts.
The word "thus" (*evam*) refers to the collective reflection upon the entire range of injunctions and prohibitions.

Regarding the emergence of the fruits of action after death: for a virtuous deed, it is the attainment of results such as heaven; for a non-virtuous one, it is rebirth in hell. Furthermore, if expiation (*prāyaścitta*) has not been performed, [the consequences remain]; and expiation itself is of the nature of extreme suffering.
Having reflected upon this in the mind, one should perform virtuous action.
It has been established that "the auspicious is ordained," and likewise, "desire indeed has its root in intention (saṃkalpa)," and "meanings are fixed by words.

Therefore, although the prohibitions such as "one should not kill" do not refer to the raising or striking of a staff or similar instruments when they produce suffering in another, nevertheless, upon considering such scriptural passages, there is a prohibition of the resolve (adhyavasāya) and so forth.

The same should be understood regarding the eating of forbidden food and so forth. Although "eating" extends as far as the actual swallowing of food and the like, nevertheless, the mental resolve [to do so] is indeed prohibited.
The same applies to approaching a woman who should not be approached.

Although physical movement through the senses and the attainment of meditative absorption constitutes "going," nevertheless, the mental determination for that purpose is precisely what is prohibited by other scriptural authorities.
If this were so, then whatever expiation is prescribed for killing, eating [forbidden food], or approaching those who should not be approached would apply even to the mere mental determination.
This is not a fault.
In the case of killing a Brāhmaṇa, it is indeed intended [to include even one who does not kill], because of the statement "even without having killed.
In other cases, however, it is proper to accept the primary meaning of the word.
But regarding a prohibition, through a consideration of the stated scriptures, it is established as having for its scope everything from the mental activity up to the physical action.

If this is so, then since it is taught that "one who practices what is censured" incurs a cause for penance (*prāyaścitta*), such a person would be subject to the penance corresponding to the prohibition. Who says there is no penance? Furthermore, a lighter [penance] cannot be prescribed for someone other than those specifically enjoined by the word "that" (*tat*).
And thus, it is logical that even such cases as these fall within the scope of all expiatory rites (*sarvaprāyaścitta*).
But from what source is this specific distinction obtained?
From the determination [of the act] as being prohibited (*pratiṣedhādhyavasāyāt*).

Regarding expiations (*prāyaścitta*), however, by the statement "vows (*vrata*) and all duties of restraint (*yama-dharma*) have their basis solely in the meanings of words and are born of intention (*saṃkalpa*)," it is precisely injunctions (*vidhi*) and prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*) that are being expressed.

Vows are of the nature of injunctions, while restraints (*niyama*) are characterized by prohibition; since they fulfill their purpose within those [injunctions and prohibitions], they do not need to operate further with respect to occasional rites (*naimittika*).
Furthermore, there exists a general cause for prohibition, and therefore an expiation occurs.
Nor is that [mind] itself;
for we shall demonstrate at the very end of this very section that covetousness consists in longing for the property of others.
Whether through ignorance or knowledge, having committed a censurable deed,
one who seeks liberation from it should not perform it a second time.

"Even for one who has performed penance, if he engages again in what ought not to be done, the penance must be more extensive; it is for this purpose that it is said, 'he should not perform it a second time.
Alternatively, the statement 'he should not perform it a second time' is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) of the cessation [from sin] just taught.
The vow (*vrata*) must not be abandoned."
Therefore, one who desires liberation—that is, one who desires release—from that initial transgression should not commit it again.
Consequently, this is what is being stated:
even if an expiation has been performed, one is not liberated if one commits it once more.
Furthermore, liberation is not logically possible whether an expiation has been performed or not; therefore, the statement "seeking the liberation of one who is already liberated" is untenable.
Consequently, the repetition [of the verse] is for the sake of emphasis.
If, after performing a particular action, one's mind should feel a sense of unease,
one should perform penance for that until it becomes a source of satisfaction.

This [instruction] is for the purpose of performing more than what is prescribed when there is no purity of mind. If there is some hesitation regarding a misdeed, then even after the penance has been performed, it must be repeated until mental clarity arises.
The mention of austerity (tapas) is intended to indicate that giving (dāna) and the other [virtues] are also to be practiced according to the prescribed rules.
All this happiness of gods and men has austerity as its root;
it has been declared by the wise, who perceive the Vedas, that austerity is its middle and austerity its end.

In the world of humans, whatever happiness there is—whether it be the pride-based sovereignty over one's country and so forth, the worldly [happiness] such as health and the like, the social [happiness] consisting of the prosperity of wealth, sons, and so on, the sensory [happiness] characterized by the enjoyment of desired objects such as beloved women, or that which is described in the Vedas as "the hundredfold joys of humans constitute a single joy among the Ājāna-devas," and so on—the root of all that is austerity (*tapas*), being its cause of origination;
austerity is the middle, being the maintenance or intermediate state of what has arisen; and austerity is the end, being its conclusion.
"With reference to that" is the view of those who know the Vedas;
for just as ritual action is the means for achieving desired fruits such as heaven or a village, so too should austerity be understood.
For a Brahmin, austerity is knowledge; for a Kshatriya, austerity is protection;
for a Vaishya, austerity is trade and agriculture; and for a Shudra, austerity is service.

One should not think thus: "By the power of austerity, I shall attain the accomplishment of all fruits through austerity; and by virtue of the excellence of my knowledge, even if I fail to perform what is prescribed, how can I practice dharma without material wealth? For the austerity of a Brahmin is knowledge;
knowledge is the comprehension of the meaning of the Vedas.
In its absence, there is no attainment of that fruit;
therefore, knowledge alone is called austerity.
This verse has the purpose of showing that even in the face of great transgressions, one's own duty must not be abandoned by means of that [knowledge].
The mention of "knowledge" (jñāna) is for the purpose of illustrating all one's own duties, beginning from the formal acquisition and study of the Veda;
likewise, "austerity" (tapas) refers to the Kṣatriya.
For the Śūdra, the remainder is "service to the twice-born," because such service is prescribed for him.
And because this is a restatement (anuvāda).
Sages who have restrained their selves and subsist on fruits, roots, and air perceive the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, through asceticism alone.
The meaning is that even the attainment of the excellence of super-sensory knowledge by the sages occurs solely through the power of austerity (*tapas*).
They are self-restrained through the discipline of speech, mind, and body.
"With fruits and roots" refers to the discipline of diet.
By such asceticism, they perceive the three worlds as if they were before their eyes.
Medicines, antidotes, sciences, and the various states of divine power—
all these are accomplished through austerity alone, for austerity is indeed their means of attainment.
Medicines are elixirs;
antidotes are remedies for the alleviation of diseases;
and sciences concern specific subjects such as spirits.
The divine state consists of the yoga of powers such as *aṇimā* and others, which is of many kinds.
Whatever is difficult to cross, whatever is difficult to attain, whatever is difficult to traverse, and whatever is difficult to accomplish—
all this can be achieved through austerity, for austerity is indeed insurmountable.
That which is crossed with suffering is difficult to cross;
a great calamity caused by disease;
and that which is the siege by enemies of superior strength.
This too is easily accomplished by ascetics.

That which is obtained with great difficulty, such as traveling through the sky and so forth, is "hard to attain" (durāpa). That which is difficult to access, such as ascending to the back of a cloud and so forth, is "difficult to traverse" (durga).
Difficult to perform are such acts as the bestowing of curses or boons; otherwise, they would not be done.
For example, Saṃvarta’s creation of other deities.
Everything indeed is accomplished through ascetic heat (*tapas*).

By means of these three verses, it is stated that the *kṛcchra* penances serve the purpose of attaining prosperity (*abhyudaya*) because of the principle of "separateness despite connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*).

Now, one might object: since the context concerns expiations (*prāyaścitta*), it is more logical that the praise of the *kṛcchras* be understood as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) to that very context, rather than as something to be enjoined for the sake of one desiring prosperity.
Furthermore, it cannot be argued that terms such as "difficult to cross" (*dustara*) are impossible to interpret as mere explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
Such great hardships as these enable one to cross even the ocean and other impassable obstacles;
how much more so will they eliminate evil?
It is said in reply:

In the Gṛhyasmṛtis and in the Sāmavidhāna, the rule for the Kṛcchra penance is handed down without even enumerating the specific expiations. Since it is taught as a general injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*), its purpose is rightly for the sake of spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*).
And it says: "Now, having performed these Kṛcchras, one becomes bathed in all the Vedas; one becomes known by all the gods."
By the phrase "one who has bathed in the Vedas," he states that the fruit which results from the performance of Vedic study according to the prescribed rules is thereby accomplished.
As for the injunction for study intended merely for acquisition, which is otherwise fruitless, that is fulfilled here by the study of even a single Veda.
Thus, it has been stated that the study of multiple Vedas is solely for the sake of dharma.
By the phrase "known by the gods," he states the attainment of the fruits of all sacrifices without exception;
for it is the sacrificer who is known through the Vedas,
and not one who exists merely as a subject of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), nor one who undergoes expiations (*prāyaścitta*) while assuming the state of a donor.
Here too, for one who suspects the cessation of their own duty, the statement that "for a Brahmin, austerity is knowledge" is possible only if it aims at worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*).

Expiations (*prāyaścitta*) are not optional rites for the attainment of specific fruits intended for the purpose of liberation from sin; since their spheres of application are distinct, how could there be any suspicion of cessation on account of expiations?
However, if they aim at worldly prosperity, then because the *kṛcchra* penances and other such rituals are equal [in status], the suspicion of cessation is indeed appropriate.

Likewise, the statement "and those who have committed the great sins" is enjoined for the purpose of liberation from sin by means of the passage beginning with "that which is difficult to cross," while [the other] is for the purpose of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*); thus, these two sentences are indeed distinct.
Consequently, it is entirely appropriate that the context (*prakaraṇa*) be set aside.
And so, the sages such as Dvaipāyana will describe those various types of intellects arising from the power of austerity (*tapas*).
Therefore, all ascetic practices (tapas) yield all fruits.

However, unlike Vedic rituals which, despite being "for all purposes" (sarvārtha), have restricted results—such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices [yielding results] for all [eligible persons], or the Jyotiṣṭoma [yielding results] for all—their status as "for all purposes" there is based solely on the specific fruits like heaven and so forth that are heard of in the Veda; it does not mean that they result in the attainment of every possible excellence or enjoyment.
What then? It is as has been illustrated by the passage beginning with "that which is difficult to cross," and so forth.
Even those who have committed great sins, as well as others who have performed forbidden acts,
are liberated from that evil through well-performed austerity alone.
This has already been explained.
Insects, snakes, moths, beasts, birds,
and even stationary beings go to heaven by the power of austerity.
This is a praise of austerity (*tapas*).
By means of that austerity, because they go everywhere, all [beings] dwell in heaven.
Just as even those not authorized for Vedic rites, such as insects and the like, go to the celestial realm through the power of austerity, how much more so the learned Brahmins?
The object [of their practice] is the suffering innate to their species, such as that of insects; that very suffering constitutes their austerity.
By means of that, through the merit performed in previous lives which has exhausted their defilements, they go to heaven.
Whatever sin people commit through their mind, speech, or body,
those whose wealth is austerity quickly consume it all by means of austerity alone.
It is recorded in the Smṛti that purification from what is committed by speech, mind, and body occurs through recitation (japa) and burnt offerings (homa).
In that regard, cessation [of sin] may be achieved through austerity (tapas).
Therefore, this [section] is commenced; that [purification] is also restated here by means of austerity.
The gods accept the sacrifices of a Brahmin purified by austerity alone, and they fulfill his desires.
At the commencement of rites performed for specific desires, austerity must first be practiced;
that too is now being restated:
as it has been said, "Having first practiced [austerity], one becomes pure, cleansed, and fit for ritual action."

In cases where initiation (*dīkṣā*), the sacred thread ceremony (*upanayana*), and so forth are constituent parts, austerity (*tapas*) is indeed that very [initiation or ceremony] itself; for it is said, "One enters upon austerity as a vow," and it is prescribed for those who are not yet married. Furthermore, even in the case of rites for pacification (*śāntika*) or nourishment (*pauṣṭika*) pertaining to the *Gṛhya* texts and similar subjects, austerity must first be performed—this is the meaning of the verse.
The mention of the "brāhmaṇa" is intended to indicate anyone who is entitled to perform sacrifices and possesses desire;
and it has been said:
"The deities do not accept the oblation from a man who has not performed austerities."
For one who has not taken consecrated food fit for sacrifice, no desire is ever fulfilled.

Even though the deity does not bestow that fruit, nevertheless, because a sacrifice cannot be accomplished without a deity, it is said that the deities "contribute" to it. Furthermore, the deities' status as recipients of the oblation does not imply their personal appropriation;
rather, it consists in the non-rejection of the offering when it is designated for them as a *saṃpradāna* (recipient).
The Lord Prajāpati created this scripture through austerity alone;
likewise, the sages attained the Vedas through austerity.
This foundation of Manor’s work arises solely from the power of his asceticism (*tapas*).

Any other person who desires the establishment of a treatise should likewise compose that work only after first performing ascetic penance. Even as for the sages (*ṛṣi*), the fact that the Vedas manifest to them is due to asceticism alone.
The gods proclaim that this which is called the great fortune of austerity is because they behold the supreme merit of all this austerity.
The conclusion of the praise of austerity:
that which has been described as the great majesty and the great fruitfulness of austerity is proclaimed by the gods, not merely by humans alone;
by the phrase "of all this," he indicates the entire world.
Beholding the merit of the entire world as arising from, and having its auspicious birth in, the presence of austerity.
The daily study of the Vedas according to one's ability and the performance of the great sacrifices (mahāyajña) quickly destroy all sins, even those born of the most heinous crimes (mahāpātaka).

It is stated that the performance of obligatory duties (*nityakarman*), such as the study of the Vedas, serves the purpose of removing sin by way of constituting a distinct qualification (*adhikārāntara*).
This is understood to apply to those for whom no specific expiation has been prescribed, to those acts committed unintentionally, and to those that have already occurred.

Others, however, say: "Just as it was stated that 'for a Brahmin, austerity is knowledge'—a statement made by one who, fearing the cessation of other ritual actions due to the injunction of austerity, [asserted this]—this [present rule] should likewise be understood in the same way."
The mention of "forbearance" (kṣamā) is for the purpose of connection and to demonstrate all the qualities of the Self.

Regarding the phrase "even great sins" (mahāpātakāny api), praise is understood from the word "even" (api); it does not mean the cessation of great sins, nor was it promulgated without cause; thus it is understood through the subjects as they have been demonstrated.
Just as fire, by its own heat, consumes whatever it encounters in an instant,
so does the knower of the Vedas burn away all evil with the fire of knowledge.
This is a praise of knowledge;

it is understood in this context that for the learned man, purification occurs through a very small expiation. And "knowledge" should be understood as pertaining to the meaning of the Vedas along with their secret doctrines (rahasya).

Knowledge of the rules for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is not solely for the sake of purification, because it serves the purpose of ritual performance; for otherwise, the performance of the rite would not be possible. However, as for the knowledge of the existence of gods and so forth, and the knowledge pertaining to the secret sections (*rahasya*), since that is not intended for [worldly] desires, it is appropriate [to consider it a means of purification], for those [knowledges] are indeed the removal of sin.
And it is said: "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil karma does not cling to one who knows thus. *Edhas* means wood for fuel.
Just as dry wood thrown into a fire is quickly consumed by burning, so too is knowledge—on account of its burning away of evil and its commonality with destruction—spoken of as being like fire.
The knowledge "one who knows the Vedas" is distinguished;
by that, the knowledge of logic, arts, poetry, and so forth is set aside.
Thus has the expiation for these sins been declared according to the rule;
hereafter, learn the expiation for secret offenses.
The purpose is to establish the connection between the preceding and subsequent sections.
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the Vyahṛtis and the Praṇava,
performed daily for a month, purify even the slayer of an embryo.
The breath that moves through the mouth and nose is *prāṇa*; its extension (*āyāma*) is its restraint (*nirodha*).
This [restraint] is well known as *recaka*, which occurs either by the gradual outward movement of the flow of *prāṇa* through both pathways or by the inward movement of the flow of *apāna*.
There are seven *vyāhṛtis*.
The *praṇava* is the syllable *oṃ*.
The breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) should be performed together with the *vyāhṛtis* and the *praṇava*.
"Sixteen" refers to the number of repetitions.
What is the nature of this "concomitance" (sahabhāva)?
Some say that after performing breath control (prāṇāyāma), the recitation of the Vyāhṛtis and the Japa of the Praṇava must be performed in reverse order.
Others, however, say:
they should be meditated upon at the time of arresting the breath.
What is the duration of these breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma)?

To the extent that excessive pain from the suppression of breath does not arise, the breath-control practices (prāṇāyāma) of retention (kumbhaka), exhalation (recaka), and inhalation (pūraka) are prescribed; it is not merely the suppression of breath. This is because there is no failure [of the practice] according to the proper measure, since the measures themselves are not something to be accomplished [but rather limits].
"Even for a killer of an embryo";
by the word "even," [it is implied] those equal to him.
Having recited the *kautsa* hymn beginning with "apaḥ," the verse from the *Vasiṣṭha* collection beginning with "pratīcīḥ," the *māhitra*,
and the *śuddhavatī* verses, even a drinker of spirituous liquor is purified.
That which was seen and proclaimed by the seer Kutsa is the *Kautsa*; the eight-verse hymn beginning with "May our sin be burned away" (*apa naḥ śośucad agham*) is recited in the *Bahvṛca* [Ṛgveda],
as is the verse beginning with "O Vasiṣṭha" (*vāsiṣṭhaṃ ca partīti*).

Three verses are collected to form a *ṛc*; and for the purpose of indicating the beginning of hymns and so forth, there is the verse: "The Vasisthas [praise] Ushas with their hymns" (*pratistomebhir uṣasaṃ vasiṣṭhāḥ*). And the *māhitra* [hymn] consists of the very three-verse group beginning with "Great is the [glory] of the three" (*mahi trīṇām*), because the word *mahitṛ* occurs in this hymn due to its insertion among the *vimukta* and other [hymns].

However, for those who read "māhendra," they say that the *payaḥ-sūkta* consists of forty-eight verses beginning with "mahāṃ indro ya ojasā," as well as the *śuddhavatī* verses beginning with "eto nv indraṃ stavāma śuddhaṃ śuddhena.
Here, the word "api" has the same meaning as "ca" (and).
By reciting the Vāmīya hymn and the Śivasaṃkalpa even once,
one becomes stainless in an instant after having stolen gold.
Here, because of the mention of "once," a repetition of the recitation in the preceding [rule] is understood;
and that [repetition] occurs due to established custom and because it is seen elsewhere.
In the case of the requirement [of repetition] in the rule "having muttered the Aghamarṣaṇa three times," there is a connection with the subject under discussion.

The etymology of the word *asyavāma* is derived from the rule "the suffix *cha* is added after the name of a *sūkta* when it occurs in the sense of 'containing this,'" because the word *asyavāma* occurs in this *sūkta*.
The *sūkta* consisting of fifty-two verses begins with "Of this lovely, gray-haired Hotṛ.
The *Śivasamkalpa*, moreover, consists of six verses from the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā beginning with "That which, for one who is awake, rises far away."
Having repeatedly recited the *Haviṣpāntīya* and the verse beginning with "na tamaṃ ha," and having muttered the *Puruṣasūkta*, one who has violated the teacher's bed is liberated from that sin.
The second *iti* has the sense of "quotation" (*pratīka*), which effects a reversal of the word-meaning;
thus, [the phrase] "or rather, the grasping of the essential form of the mantra" is obtained here.
"Pauruṣa" refers to the hymn (*sūkta*) consisting of sixteen verses beginning with "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads."
Desiring to remove gross and subtle sins,
one should mutter for a year either the verse beginning with "Having known" (*avet*) or the verse beginning with "Whatever this" (*yat kiṃcedam*).
Sins smaller than the great sins (mahāpātaka) are called minor offenses (upapātaka) and so forth.
Desiring to remove them, one should mutter the verse beginning with "ava" for a year.
By the word "ava" as a pratīka, the verse "ava te heḷo varuṇa namobhiḥ" is indicated, because it contains the characteristic mark of liberation from sin.
But it does not extend beyond that which is not included therein; thus [the verse] "Whatever here, O Varuṇa, among the divine folk... belongs to these [verses].
Having accepted what should not be accepted, or having eaten food that is censured,
a man is purified in three days by reciting the *taratsamandīya* hymn.

That which is not to be accepted includes liquor and the like; furthermore, even gold and other such things from an evil-doer are likewise not to be accepted. Forbidden food is of four kinds, being defiled by its nature, the time [of its acquisition], the person who possesses it, or through contact.
This fourfold [classification] is found in the *Pāvamānī* verses: "The slow one runs across."
But one who has committed many sins is purified by reciting the *Somāraudra* hymn for a year,
or by performing ritual ablutions in a flowing river while reciting the three-verse hymn beginning with "aryamṇām."
"O Soma and Rudra, hold fast the weapon"—these are four [verses]; and the *ṛc* "The sacrifice, the nourishments, and the sense-organ";
"the year" (*saṃvatsara*) is the same as "the year" (*samā*);
and the invocation (*cāhvāna*).
This is the indicative mark (liṅga) that has been stated: that in some tantras there is also an expiation (prāyaścitta).
By the phrase "in a flowing river," the terms "tank" and "lake" are excluded.
One who has committed an offense should mutter the seven verses beginning with "Indra" for half a year;
however, having performed a blameworthy act, he should subsist on alms for a month while remaining in water.
One who has committed an offense should recite this sevenfold hymn beginning with "Indram mitram varuṇam agnim" for half a year—
that is, for six months;
since the text specifies "one who is sinful" without qualification, this applies to all offenses.
If one performs an improper sexual act or voids excrement there,
having performed that penance in water, one should subsist on alms for a month.
Having offered clarified butter for a year with the Śākala-homa mantras, a twice-born man destroys even a very heavy sin; or he does so by reciting the verse beginning with "namaḥ."
"Thou art the expiation for sin committed against the gods"—these and others are the eight mantras belonging to the Śākala-homa.
By offering clarified butter with them for one year, one destroys even grave sin;
the meaning is that one destroys all the great mortal sins (mahāpātakas) as well.

Having recited the mantra "Namo rudrāya tavase kapardine" for one year, one shall attain this very accomplishment even without the Śākala-homa. This rite of recitation is an optional alternative to the preceding expiation consisting of the Śākala-mantra-homa; or alternatively, having recited another verse, namely the Ṛgvedic hymn beginning with "Vāmana."
But she must be made easily accessible to the learned.
One who is joined with a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) shall follow cows with a concentrated mind;
by practicing the Pāvamānī verses for a year while subsisting on alms, he becomes purified.
By the phrase "one joined with a great sin" (*mahāpātaka-saṃyukta*), it is understood that this [penance] applies even when there is a specific number of such preceding offenses.
It is appropriate to prescribe a single expiation for each minor offense even when they are combined.

The *Pāvamānī* verses consist of the entire *Maṇḍala* of the ten books, beginning with "With the sweetest, most intoxicating [Soma]" (*svādiṣṭhayā madiṣṭhayā*) and ending with "O King, the oblation which has been prepared for you" (*yat te rājañ chṛtaṃ haviḥ*).
Following the cows does not mean merely walking behind them; rather, it means attending to them. And that [attending] is to be understood as the expiation for killing a cow.
Or, having purified himself by three *parāka* penances, one who is self-restrained recites the Vedic *saṃhitā* three times in the forest; he is liberated from all sins.
This is another expiation specifically for one who has committed a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*):
having fasted for thirty-six nights, he is liberated by reciting the *Saṃhitā*— the collection of Mantras and Brāhmaṇas— in the forest.
Restrained, one should fast for three days while approaching water three times a day;
by reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, one is liberated from all sins.
The connection is that one should recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* while entering the water;
therefore, the successful performance of the recitation occurs within the water.
In this way, it is supported by other Smṛti texts.
The specific Aghamarṣaṇa mantra is said to consist of three verses (ṛcas).
Just as the horse sacrifice, the king of rituals, removes all sins,
so too does the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn remove all sins.
This verse is for the purpose of praise.
Even if he has slain these three worlds and eats from here and there,
a Brahmin who maintains the Ṛgveda incurs no sin whatsoever.
This too is a hymn of praise;

it is intended for the secret expiation of one who upholds the Ṛgveda. Others, however, maintain that it applies even to one who has committed a mortal sin (mahāpātaka), beginning from the words "one joined with a mortal sin" and so forth.
Having recited the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā three times, or the Yajurvedic formulas, or the Sāmavedic chants together with their secret doctrines, with a concentrated mind, one is liberated from all sins.
By the specific qualification "Ṛg" and so forth, the Brāhmaṇas are excluded;
the "Rahasyas" are the Sāmans studied in the Āraṇyakas.
Just as a clod of earth thrown into a great lake perishes,
so does all misconduct sink away when immersed in the threefold Veda.
The threefold [Veda] consists of three parts;
because they share a single purpose and are treated as constituent parts, one Veda is a part of another Veda.
The Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, and the various Sāman-chants—this is to be known as the threefold Veda; he who knows this is a knower of the Veda.
He shows that it has three members; the meaning is that the first ones are the primary ones, while the others are those to be studied by Brāhmaṇas and have been recited.
Alternatively, there are the *padakramitāni* (the sequences of words and phrases),
and various *sāmans* distinguished as belonging to either the village or the forest.
That which is the primordial three-syllabled Brahman, in which the triple Veda is established—that is another secret threefold Veda; he who knows it is a knower of the Vedas.
The three-syllabled [syllable] is the *oṃkāra*, which is a collection of three phonemes. It is the primordial Brahman, the secret;
because it has been taught exactly as it is in the section on secrets, it is prescribed as an object of meditation in the form of the Śabdabrahman (the Brahman of Sound).

Or, he is "secret" (guhya) because he denotes the Supreme Self, and not because he is a known syllable; for that [syllable] "Om" is accepted as well-known in the world. In him, this threefold Veda is contracted.
"All colors," and so forth.
Its worship has been described previously, namely: "One should thus meditate upon this syllable Om.
In the preceding verse, the nature of the Veda was stated through the knowledge of the meaning of the mantra; by this [verse], the knowledge of Vedānta is expressed.
However, it is well known that the experience of the results of action is indeed implied by the injunction to study the Veda.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
The *Manusmṛti* is indeed venerable, yet Medhātithi’s appropriate commentary upon it has vanished by the power of fate, such that no manuscript can be found anywhere.
King Madana, together with his son Araṇasuta, brought [the work] from another land.
He then carried out the restoration of the worn-out [text] by means of manuscripts copied here and there.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Commentary on Manu composed by Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi, son of Bhaṭṭa Vīrasvāmin.
Now begins the twelfth chapter:
"O sinless one, you have indeed declared this entire dharma of the four social orders;
now tell us truly the supreme result that arises from actions."
The first half-verse is intended to show the completion of the treatise's subject matter, thereby removing any further expectation for more;
the inclusion of the word "entire" (kṛtsna) is for the sake of honor,
signifying that all these Smṛti-based duties have been taught in this treatise, down to the secret (rahasya) portions.
The fact that the teacher has performed the entire work is presented through the mouth of the disciple, but it is not intended [as literal fact].
Here, one should not understand the disciple and the teacher as distinct entities in reality;
rather, the author of the treatise himself divides this work in this manner.
And the word *dharma*, denoting what ought to be done, reiterates the collection of injunctions and prohibitions.
Therefore, since the connection between action and its fruit has not yet been stated, it is explained hereafter.
"The entirety of *dharma* has been taught by you."
The statement is appropriate with respect to injunctions and prohibitions.
But for which action is the connection with its fruit intended to be investigated, such that it is said, "one should declare the production of the fruits of actions"?
For as many obligatory rites as there are, they are performed simply because they are enjoined by the scriptures; their fruit is not something to be aimed at.

For those [actions] that are impermanent do not have those [results] as their purpose; yet, regarding even those, the results for each respective action have generally already been stated, such as "the giver of water obtains satisfaction, heaven, long life," and so forth.
Even in cases where one might think a result has not been mentioned, heaven and the like are nonetheless established there as well.

Those purificatory rites (*saṃskārakarma*) such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*) and others are fruitful solely through the result of the action as specified for the particular object to be purified; they do not require an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Furthermore, those occasional rites (*naimittika*), such as the purification of substances and bathing upon touching a *caṇḍāla*, also have only visible purposes.
Indeed, these are performed for the sake of purification, because engagement in worldly transactions is prohibited for those who are impure.
The expiations (*prāyaścittāni*) have already been mentioned immediately before with their respective purposes;
therefore, we do not know for which of these prohibited actions the fruit is intended to be understood. [This refers to] the prohibitions.

Because those very [faults] will be explained later in the passage beginning with "by the defects of actions born of the body" (Gītā 13.7), even the performance of prohibitions is indeed enjoined by the scripture. Now, one might object: "In that case, if there were a desire for results, there would be no qualification for all [prohibitions]."
Or perhaps the state of being a seeker (arthitā) would be disqualified?
It is said:
in this case, no such fruit is mentioned that is desired.
In this context, the undesirable result is being demonstrated;
that [result] is not desired at all,
nor does anyone wish for the attainment of what is undesirable.
Therefore, the status of [the scripture] as having all things as its object is established.
As for what is said—that the performance of prohibitions is carried out because the scripture has enjoined them—this is stating far too little;
such is the performance in that case.
Everything indeed is performed as enjoined by the scripture;
however, that scripture establishes its duty for someone who desires a result,
while for another it does so as an occasional rite (naimittika) even without a result.
But here, since there is no scriptural injunction regarding a lifelong commitment as there is in other cases, for what purpose should that which is prohibited not be performed?
Furthermore, a transgression is observed in the case of indifference, as it is said: "By the desire to kill a Brāhmaṇa, one falls into hell.
Now, it might be argued that that which is prohibited, such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, is not enjoined by the scriptures.
For it is logical that what is impelled by scripture should be connected with a scriptural result, as in the case of "one who desires heaven should sacrifice.
Indeed, the understanding of the necessity of performing a sacrifice comes from scripture alone and not from any other source.
In this context, however, activity prompted by hatred and the like is worldly and non-scriptural.
Furthermore, it is not logical for that which is non-scriptural to be connected with a scriptural result.
As for what was said—that transgression (*pratyavāya*) is shown to occur in the case of indifference—what expectation could there be here?
For as soon as the understanding arises from scripture that "one should not act toward one who hates," the meaning of the sentence is complete.
What word is there here that one might desire?
This being analyzed would entail a vast expansion of the text;
this, however, is a summary.
In the prohibitive injunction "one should not harm living beings," the meaning of the verbal root is the object of the prohibition;
furthermore, it is heard [in grammar] that there is a relationship between the agent and the instrument.
In that context, the injunction first has a requirement for the person to be enjoined (niyojya) and its objective domain (viṣaya).
In that case, the understanding of the person to be enjoined (niyojya) is this: "This must not be done by me.
The person is not enjoined toward that [prohibited act], because an injunction consists in the enjoining of a person.
And here, that person to be enjoined is presented through worldly activity characterized by aversion, being prompted by the teaching whose nature is the avoidance of injury.

"One who proceeds to kill by his own will shall kill"—this [interpretation] is not tenable, for that person is the subject of the injunction here. And because the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is already established elsewhere in the case of empty [injunctions], it serves merely as a qualification of the person; thus, the connection with the injunction occurs through its own status as the object.
Furthermore, that person who is to be enjoined does not realize his own status as one to be enjoined by virtue of being a "sacred site" (tīrtha),
so long as he does not determine that the object of that [injunction], which is being prohibited, has an undesirable result;
for such is the linguistic convention in the world.
When it is said, "A finger should be given to the courtier," the performance of that act after the prohibition has been issued is understood to be a cause of misfortune.
Furthermore, one cannot set aside common worldly understanding and demand the presentation of some other reason.

In such a case, even if the result of an undesirable consequence is not explicitly heard, it is proper to infer it from the force of the prohibition itself; how much more so when it is actually stated?
For it is not logical to discard what has been heard [in scripture].

Nor is it appropriate here to regard [the mention of hell] as merely indicative of verbal dispute, since the result consisting of hell and so forth is established by scripture; for, according to the reasoning already stated, there is a connection with a result through its proximity.
Furthermore, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) serve as qualifications of injunctions (*vidhi*).

Furthermore, no injunction (*vidhi*) is heard here, nor is one established by context (*prakṛta*), because it is precisely the connection between action and its fruit that is intended to be demonstrated as the primary subject.
Indeed, actions are not enjoined here;
rather, their connection with the fruit is stated.
And it is not because of this that hundreds of statements become meaningless;
let this view at least serve as a cause for recollection,
for these statements cannot be explained in any other way.
There is no lack of a specific rule here.
If it is argued that this explanation is merely a figurative statement (*guṇavāda*) and that even the authors of the treatises were mistaken, we say:
no.
Those who speak thus do not hold themselves in high esteem, nor do they despise the great seers.
"Agham" means evil or sin.
"Anagha" is a form of address intended as praise on account of being free from stain.
He should recite while remaining restrained in speech.
That righteous-souled Bhṛgu, the son of Manu, said to those great seers:
"Hear the definitive conclusion regarding this entire yoga of action."
This is the reply to what was asked:
listen to that which I have been asked;
the connection is "the application of action" (*karmaṇo yoga*).
And that [subject], being the topic at hand, is to be understood precisely by means of its fruit.
Action, arising from mind, speech, and body, bears auspicious and inauspicious fruits;
the destinies of humans—superior, inferior, and middling—are born of action.
The description of "the auspicious" is by way of illustration; or rather, it is for the purpose of prescribing the activities of mind and speech, since action arises from the mind, speech, and body.
Furthermore, the word *karman* does not refer solely to bodily movement in the sense of ritual sacrifice (*ijyā*);
what then? It refers to action in general, even that consisting of yoga and meditative concentration.
The word "fruit" (phala) is connected with each [term]:
the fruit of the auspicious and the fruit of the inauspicious.
It should not be understood that the attainment of the auspicious and inauspicious fruits occurs solely from the performance of actions accomplished through bodily activity.
Moreover, it is exactly the same with respect to the arising of mind, speech, and body;
therefore, the attainment of results is ordained from these three kinds of action as well.
One should know that for this embodied being— who possesses these three types [of action], who has three bases, and who is endowed with ten characteristics— it is the mind that is the instigator.
Now, one might object: "One should sacrifice those who deserve punishment" and "One should not harm [living beings]"—these refer to both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
All of these are accomplished through bodily activity.

Furthermore, giving consists of the relinquishing of one's own ownership and the effecting of ownership in another; and this has been previously prescribed by such rules as "with the right hand," and so forth.
Even a sacrifice, consisting of its performance and ending with the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), is accomplished through bodily activity.
Likewise, ignorance regarding the community, punishment, and so forth, is well known to be of a physical nature.
In that case, what kind of action is possible for the mind?
Therefore, he says: "One should know that the mind is the activator of this object;
for all the functions of the mind, such as seeing and so forth, do not exist when the three [faculties] are absent."

For instance, first of all, one perceives this object with the mind, thinking, "This is exactly such-and-such," or "Its cause is pleasure or pain"; then, depending on that, the mind resolves: "How shall I accomplish this? or "Therefore, I shall not do this.
In that regard, when the action is primary, there is physical movement and verbal expression.
Therefore, for one who acts with prior intention (*preṣāpūrvakārin*), the mind is the instigator of everything;

however, in cases not preceded by conscious intent (*abuddhipūrvam*), the perception of a preceding form as being of that very nature is not necessarily required—such as, for example, acting with the notion that it is a drink because its color resembles wine, or due to the possibility of darkness, acting toward another's wife; other instances, however, are accidental (*daivopanipatitam*), such as the killing of insects like mosquitoes by the hand-movements or turning over of the side of a sleeping person. Even in those cases, agency has been established as the cause for engaging in penances (*prāyaścitta*).
It is threefold, by way of the distinctions of speech, mind, and body;
it has three bases, by way of the distinctions of superior, inferior, and middling destinies;
and it is endowed with ten characteristics, consisting of the three types of mental and bodily actions and the four types of vocal action.
These are the ten characteristics;
he will explain them further below.
Coveting the property of others, thinking of what is undesirable with the mind,
and adherence to falsehood— this is the threefold mental action.

Covetousness (*abhidhyāna*) is the contemplation of surpassing the wealth of others with a mind of envy regarding their possessions, thinking: "How much wealth of horses and cattle he has! How many goats and sheep! What prosperity his horses possess! Fie on fate! Why does he have such abundance? Now, how might I take this away from him? Or rather, it would be better if he did not have this.
Others, however, say that it is the thought of overwhelming that wealth; they connect it with the contemplation of what is undesirable for another.
If one thinks of a means to kill another, or thinks, "May he die, and let that [wealth] be mine"—
but has not coveting another's property already been mentioned? Since this [covetousness] is established by that very [precept], it is redundant.
For this is a general term:
that which is undesirable or unintended by another should not be contemplated. Even the loss of wealth is certainly not desired by another.
And out of fear of this, they do not say "something belongs to another";
rather, they explain that which is undesirable as being what is prohibited.
Even on this view, coveting the property of another is mentioned specifically for the sake of emphasis.
In this way, there is also adherence to what is false:

grasping the meaning of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) as the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), such as the doctrine of consciousness-only (*vijñānavāda*), the invalidity of the Vedas, the apprehension of non-selfhood (*anātmatā*), and so forth.
Others, however, speak of eternal, worldly-aversionless hatred (*nityanirāmiṣadveṣa*).
And this threefold unwholesome mental activity is distinct from its opposite, which is wholesome:
lack of longing for the property of others, compassion toward all sentient beings, and faith in the existence of phenomena and so forth.

And so the Blessed Vyāsa said: "One should contemplate in three ways with the mind: non-covetousness regarding the property of others, benevolence toward all sentient beings, and that there is fruit for those who possess dharma."
Harsh speech, falsehood, slander in every form,
and incoherent prattle— these constitute the fourfold nature of verbal misconduct.
Taking what is not given, violence contrary to the prescribed rules, and consorting with the wives of others— this is remembered as the threefold bodily [action].
Because of the predominance of scriptural authority, it is both improper and wicked to take what has not been given from the wicked;
the same applies to the wives of others, such as virgins and so forth.
Furthermore, there is the taking up of contrary dharmas, protection, and the restraint of the senses.
This is tenfold through the distinction of mind, speech, and body;
it is twentyfold through the division of wholesome and unwholesome activity.
One experiences the mental [karma], whether auspicious or inauspicious, by means of the mind itself;
verbal action performed by speech, and bodily action likewise by the body.
Some say that one experiences mental suffering through that action by which distress is produced in another.
We, however, maintain that the attainment of mental suffering results from the threefold mental [action] that has been described;
the same applies to the two subsequent types as well.
Through the defects of actions born of the body, a person goes to the state of an immobile being;
through those of speech, to the state of birds or beasts; and through those of the mind, to the status of a low-born caste.
This is intended to indicate a predominance;
for the most part, these are the respective signs of these classes of beings according to their division,
but this is not an absolute rule.
Likewise, it will be stated that those who have committed great sins wander among the animals;
the mention of birds and wild animals is for the purpose of illustrating the animal realm in its entirety.
This is intended primarily to demonstrate that each subsequent type of action—of mind, speech, and body—is more grave than the preceding one.
The restraint of speech, the restraint of mind, and likewise the restraint of body— he in whose intellect these are established is called a *tridaṇḍin*.
Self-restraint is the rod;
the rod of speech is the refraining from harshness;
the same applies to the two that follow.
He in whose mind these three staffs are established—thinking "this must not be done by me"—and who does not falter, is called a *tridaṇḍin*;
it is not the ignoble man who carries a heavy wooden staff.
Having laid down this triple staff toward all beings and having thoroughly restrained desire and anger, a person then attains perfection.

The collection of the three staffs is *tridaṇḍa*; because it is listed alongside items such as the alms-bowl (*pātra*) and because it is stated [in the grammatical tradition] that it is not feminine. "Having placed in the intellect" means having performed [the action] within the intellect.
Non-violence toward all beings is established as his triple staff, or it is laid down;
the restraint of desire and anger is excellent.
From that, he attains and reaches the perfection known as liberation.
This introduction concerning internality is an opening [inquiry]:
To whom, then, does this accomplishment belong? Or to whom belongs the state of being the experiencer of the fruits of transformative actions in the hereafter?
The body ends in ashes.

And yet, we do not perceive this [person] apart from that; therefore, desiring to demonstrate the authoritative person (adhikāripuruṣa) with respect to all dharmas and adharma-s, he begins [the treatise].
That which causes this self to act is called the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field);
but that which performs the actions is called the *bhūtātman* (the elemental self) by the wise.
He is the self-initiator of the activity of this body, which consists of functional movement;
his agency is due to the power of effort.
He is the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field).
In the phrase "of this self" (*asyātmanaḥ*), the genitive case is used in apposition.
The word "self" (*ātman*) refers here to the body, because that too exists for the sake of the [true] self.

That which performs actions characterized by drinking and so forth—the agent known as the body, which is a collection of the elements such as earth—is called the "elemental self" (*bhūtātman*), because it is the lowest [in status].
The self that is a modification of the elements is the "elemental self" (bhūtātmā).
Thus it has been said: "There are two selves: the inner self and the bodily self."
There is another internal self, distinct from the body, known as the *jīva*, which is innate to all embodied beings;
by means of it, one experiences all pleasure and pain throughout successive births.
Furthermore, what indeed is this so-called *jīva*, given that they consider the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) alone to be the *jīva*?
Moreover, two things are perceived here: the body and the inner self (*antarātman*) who is to be known through the notion of "I. Apart from these, what else could there be called a *jīva*?

Some, first of all, say: that which is recited as "the *liṅga*—enveloped by the subtle elements beginning with the *mahat*, devoid of experience, and permeated by dispositions (*bhāva*)—migrates," it is this [which] functions as the instrument (*itikaraṇatva*) with respect to cognition. For that is the substratum of the gross elements, since it alone serves as the substratum for the external elements known as the body.
And while the body exists, the self possesses the state of being an experiencer of pleasure and pain;
therefore, it is expressed by the instrumental case as "by which.
Others, however, believe that the individual soul (jīva) is the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), consisting of mind, intellect, and ego.
And because it is designated as the "internal organ" (antaḥkaraṇa), its indication by means of the instrumental case-ending is indeed appropriate.
Furthermore, the term "inner self" (antarātman) is likewise appropriate because it exists for that purpose.
And the term "innate" (sahaja) is used because it is not separated from that [organ] until the attainment of liberation or until the dissolution of the world.
Both of these— the Great One (Mahat) and the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña)— being conjoined with the elements,
abide pervading that which exists within high and low beings.
He who remains pervading all beings— high and low, manifold, and of various forms—
stands [therein], that is, takes refuge in them; and for this reason, he is the agent of all actions, since the root *sthā* has multiple meanings.

Who is this who remains pervading all beings, both high and low? It is the Supreme Self (paramātman), which is devoid of the world of sentient and insentient things, whose nature is supreme bliss, and which will be explained further on.
Regarding "in contact with the elements," the elements are five.
"It is great" means that by which one experiences;
it refers to the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) of this self.
Just as it is pervasive, so too is it "situated in the second" even within the subject (*pakṣa*).
And its being the "resort" (*saṃśrayaṇa*) is because it is the cause of this entire world;
for an effect resorts to its cause, and thus resorting is simply dependence.
And so you, Vyāsa, have said:
"There are these two persons in the world, the perishable and the imperishable;
the perishable consists of all beings, while the one who stands at the peak is called the imperishable."
All this, consisting of the manifold world of moving and non-moving beings, is denoted by the word "the perishable" (kṣara).
"The imperishable" (akṣara) refers to the causal primordial nature (prakṛti), so called because it does not perish even during dissolution due to its nature as the cause.
Alternatively, the "perishable" is the body and the "imperishable" is the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
But its immutability [is such] until the attainment of liberation, because agency and enjoyership have not ceased.
"The Supreme Person, however, is another, declared as the Supreme Self (paramātman),
the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them."
Innumerable forms issue forth from his body,
which constantly set in motion all beings, both high and low.
By the word "form" (mūrti), whatever is material, whether effect or cause, as well as power (śakti), is denoted.
All this emerges from the body of that Supreme Self;
indeed, His very nature is His body.
The designation by way of distinction is like [the expression] "the body of a stone statue.
They are innumerable and infinite,
like waves from the ocean.
It has been stated that they "issue forth," meaning they manifest. By their manifestation, this world moves; the meaning is that it becomes active.
Since there is no movement without the body, the sense faculties, and consciousness, it is said that they "cause [the world] to move."
Others, however, maintain that the primary principle (pradhāna) is the body of the Supreme Self because its activity is dependent upon Him; in this context, the elements are not meant.
After death, for those men who have committed evil deeds, another body certainly arises from the five elements alone, intended for the purpose of undergoing torment.
"A body composed of the five elements arises after death as something distinct from those five elements.
This is what is meant:
a body consisting of the five elements arises even without semen and blood.

The body of evildoers consists of the five elements, whereas for those who have performed meritorious deeds, it consists merely of light and space, as it has been said: "Becoming wind, he takes on the form of space.
*Yātanā* refers to an excess of torment.
That which aims for this [goal] is that which is extremely firm and capable of enduring supramundane suffering.
Having experienced those torments of Yama with this very body,
they dissolve part by part back into those same elemental constituents.
Yama is a specific deity who performs the punishment and so forth of evildoers;
the torments seen therein are his,
which one experiences with that body composed of the five elements.
Those bodies, in turn, dissolve back into those subtle elemental constituents.
Having experienced those defects born of attachment to sense objects, which result in future suffering,
he— freed from all taints— approaches those same two of great splendor.
From attachment to sense objects, from indulging in prohibited objects, and from those very attachments—whatever faults have arisen, produced by evil;
having experienced the sufferings of hell, and through that experience of suffering, one whose impurities are removed and whose sins are destroyed.
Those two [sons] were both possessed of great splendor.
Which two?
The Great One (mahat) and the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña); these two are the primary causes.
Furthermore, by the following verse, it is the Knower of the Field alone who is experienced as the enjoyer of pleasure and pain.
The word "he" (saḥ) refers back to that very same [Self]; therefore, it follows that [the Self] approaches the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
But that is contradictory:
the same entity would be both the goal to be attained and the attainer.
True; a figurative distinction is intended here.
The meaning of "he approaches" (*abhyeti*) is that he remains with only this much remaining;

that is to say, by way of being the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), he remains as only that much among the fruits, designated as the "Great One" (*mahān*) consisting of the aggregate of the vital breaths and so forth.
The individual soul (liṅgajīva) is the knower of the field (kṣetrajña);

others, however, explain it as the Great Principle (mahat) and the Supreme Self (paramātman). "Having happiness as its sequel" means that when evil has been exhausted, happiness is experienced at a later time.
When evil stands as an obstacle, even if it be slight, no happiness arises;
just as when there is even a slight indigestion, eating does not lead to comfort.
Vigilantly observing both his merit and his evil together,
he attains their combined results— happiness and suffering— both in this world and after death.
Now, if that [Mahat] and the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) were connected, then in the phrase "of him who sees," to whom does "of him" refer? Some say it refers to the individual soul (jīva);
and it has been stated that "He alone is the Knower of the Field; He alone is the individual soul."
Now, regarding the *liṅga*:
but has that not already been expressed by the word "Great" (*mahat*)? Or is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) [meant], such as the Great Intellect (*mahat-buddhi*) and so forth?
Even in that case, what is the connection between the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)?
For that [mark] is indeed a subtle form of the primary elements (*bhūta*),
as was stated in the passage beginning with "Now, this [is the nature] of those seven."

Therefore, we consider that what has been explained by others— that in the preceding verse "those two" refers to both the Great One (mahat) and the Supreme Self (paramātman), and that these two are understood as such— is indeed what we see to be correct; for in their case, the illustration is appropriate, since the agency of the Great One, which is actually an instrument, is figuratively attributed to it, just as one says, "the pieces of wood cook."
The phrase "of him" (tasya) is appropriate as a reference to the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field).

Furthermore, the statement of the analogy regarding merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which reside in the *kṣetrajña* and pertain to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), is for the purpose of making known that the entire experience of pleasure and pain is dependent upon Him.
As it has been said:

Impelled by the Lord, one may go either to heaven or to the state of a donkey; and this impulsion is simply the will itself, as regulated by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). But surely, if merit and demerit act as regulators of the will, then His lordship (*aiśvarya*) is diminished?

This is likewise demonstrated in the Śārīraka [Brahma-sūtra]: just as in this world a king bestows rewards according to service, yet his sovereignty does not thereby diminish, so too it is designated that "one sees both the Great One and the Supreme Self. The word "of him" (tasya) refers to the knowledge of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
That too is incorrect, because it contradicts the subsequent text:
"He reaches [the world] of Yama when conjoined.
For no conjunction or connection with the Supreme Self (paramātman) is ever predicated of anyone.
Nor is there any connection whatsoever with the Supreme Self.
If that is so, then the words "by which two" do not connect with the Great Principle (mahat) and the Supreme Self;
what then? They refer to merit and demerit, as these two are also the subject under discussion.
"He sees both that [which is] dharma and that which is evil.
If the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is denoted by the word "great" (*mahat*), this is all the more untenable;
for when the Supreme Self is the seer, there is no dependence upon an instrument.
For it is the locus itself that attains the nature of the supreme self of awakening, and those two are indeed that very [locus].
Of what kind is this "approaching"?
If it were the attainment of that state, it could certainly not be accomplished merely by the removal of defilements.
Furthermore, regarding the inclination toward attaining that [state], even that does not occur for one who is bodiless once the elements have dissolved.
Therefore, it should be understood as before: those two see the dharma of that very self.
If one practices dharma for the most part and unrighteousness only to a small degree,
being enveloped by those very elements, he enjoys happiness in heaven.

For the most part, that is, in great measure, one attains happiness in heaven by means of those very elements, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and ending with the gross elements (mahābhūta).
But if one mostly practices unrighteousness and righteousness only slightly,
abandoned by those elements, he undergoes the torments of Yama.
But has it not been stated that the body of evildoers is composed of the five elements alone? Why, then, is it now said that they are "abandoned by those elements"? It is replied:
the body is not composed of the elements, nor do the torments belong to one who is bodiless.
Rather, those human bodies are extremely distinct; these [other bodies] are entirely different, being the initiators of soft, supple, and delicate bodies.
He is said to have "renounced" them as a means of expiation for the blow of suffering;
he has renounced those bodies which are to be enjoyed in heaven.
Having undergone those torments in the Yāmis, that living being, freed from defilement,
returns once again to those very five elements, each according to its own portion.
This has been explained previously;
this is the intended meaning of these four verses:

if the demerit (*adharma*) is great, then there are the torments of Yama, but not when the demerit is slight; for even with a small amount of demerit, one attains heaven through the experience of unhappiness in this very world.

Having observed these destinies of the living being by means of his own mind— both those resulting from righteousness and those from unrighteousness— one should always fix the mind upon righteousness.
This has a very limited meaning:
"from dharma and adharma" involves the elision of the negative particle (nañ), meaning "due to the cause of dharma and adharma";
[it refers to] the living being, the knower of the field, the self.
By means of one's own mind, one should experience that [result] through the authority of the treatise;
this is the synthesis of the fruit of the entire meaning of the treatise.
One should know that sattva, rajas, and tamas are the three qualities (guṇas) of the Self;
pervaded by these, the Great One (mahat) stands encompassing all these states without exception.
That which pertains to dharma and adharma, being useful for the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), has already been stated. Now, he intends to begin the section on knowledge (vidyākāṇḍa).
In that regard, first the meaning of the auxiliary limbs (aṅga) is set forth as if it were based upon duality.
The three qualities, sattva and the others, belong to the Self;
here, the "Self" is not the individual soul (jīva),
but rather the Great One (mahat) itself.
The word "ātman" denotes intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and not the state of being the internal subject (*pratyaktva*).
For the *puruṣa* is indeed devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*).
Alternatively, it is designated as belonging to the self, the enjoyer, by virtue of its being the object of enjoyment (*bhogyatā*).
And "the Great" (mahat) refers specifically to the Pradhāna due to proximity;

for the first manifestation of transformation belonging to the Pradhāna is called "the Great. Just as one who is alive remains present throughout all modifications until death, so it is said of this [Pradhāna] because it is the primordial source (prakṛti) of all modifications.
Whichever of these qualities is predominant in the body in its entirety at any given time, it then makes that embodied being consist primarily of that quality.

Although everything consists of the three qualities (guṇas), nevertheless, whenever a particular quality—by virtue of the predominance of past karma—surpasses all others in its entirety and reaches a state of excess, it then overpowers the other qualities of the person (puruṣa).
Consequently, the embodied being becomes characterized by that predominant quality;
he manifests only its specific nature and, as it were, abandons the other qualities.
Sattva is knowledge, tamas is ignorance, and rajas is known as passion and hatred;
this is their pervasive nature, which rests within all beings.
This common characteristic of theirs is pervasive among all living beings:
knowledge is the capacity for cognition, while ignorance is delusion; it is not merely a state of unconsciousness, as in conditions such as intoxication or fainting.
Passion (*rajas*) consists of both forms;
by the terms "attachment" and "aversion," the conjunction with both qualities is expressed.
Furthermore, for those who possess right knowledge, there is neither excessive anger nor excessive negligence.
That is *rajas*;
it is the nature of the body (*vapuḥ-svabhāva*),
because the latent impression of the seed (*bīja-vāsanā*) persists without interruption until the attainment of Brahman.
In that regard, whatever one perceives within oneself as associated with joy,
tranquil and appearing pure— that should be understood as the *sattva* element.

A sensation conjoined with joy appears as pure radiance, as if it were pure, being untainted by *rajas* and *tamas*, and free from the defects of intoxication, pride, passion, hatred, greed, delusion, fear, sorrow, and envy.
This is the case for everything.
And this state occurs at a certain time as something to be personally realized within oneself.
That which is conjoined with suffering and is disagreeable to oneself, one should know that to be the quality of passion (rajas), which constantly carries away embodied beings.

Being conjoined with suffering and intermingled, it is not pure and does not have the nature of joy; therefore, it is said to be "unpleasant" because it is permeated by suffering and is not joined with joy. It is "indirect" (apratyakṣa), meaning it is not immediate but ultimate (pāramārthika).
This is the nature of *rajas*: it impels one toward sense objects and generates longing; such is the meaning.
That which is associated with delusion, unmanifest, consisting of sense objects, inconceivable, and unknowable— one should understand that to be *tamas*.
Delusion (*moha*) is a state of bewilderment, the absence of discrimination between what is appropriate and what is inappropriate.
Its object (*viṣaya*) is the self (*ātman*), which is its own nature (*svabhāva*). But is it not the case that this [self] is not an object at all, precisely because it is the inner self?
How, then, can it have the nature of an object?
It is spoken of in this way because the intellect (buddhi) is colored by its attachment to the objects of delusion;

or rather, through the object, the intellect becomes so thoroughly identified with it that the three qualities (triguṇya) are [attributed] to it, though there is no such designation for the internal or external beings.
It is beyond ratiocination and outside the scope of inference;
it is unknowable, meaning it is not within the range of the internal or external senses.
Furthermore, I shall explain in its entirety the arising of the fruits of these three qualities— the highest, the middling, and the lowest.

It is promised that the fruit which arises from the practice of these three—whether superior, inferior, or middling—will be explained; and it is promised that the specific nature of a person which occurs when a particular quality is predominant will be described. This is the formal proposition (*pratijñā*).
The study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, purity, restraint of the senses,
performance of righteous deeds, and contemplation of the Self— these are the characteristics of the quality of sattva.

It is proposed that this must be stated as "having the quality (guṇa) characterized by connection with that. The term "sāttvika" is to be construed in some way [with the following]. That by which a quality is characterized is "guṇalakṣaṇam."
"To whom does that belong?"— the connection is with the word "sāttvika" (pertaining to sattva).
The purpose is that even parts are seen to be connected with the whole.
Therefore, this is what is meant:
this is the characteristic of the quality (guṇa) of a substance (sattva),
just as "Devadatta’s teacher's house" [indicates the house as the locus of Devadatta].
Just as the teacher, even though he has become subordinate, is connected with the word "Devadatta," so too should this be understood.
The meanings of the words have been explained.
Delight in undertaking enterprises, lack of fortitude, engagement in improper actions, and constant indulgence in sense objects— these are the characteristics of the quality of passion (rājasa).
Delight in the undertaking of actions—whether they be for the sake of desired fruits, for visible purposes, or for invisible purposes—and futile exertion;
this is the characteristic of the passionate (rājasa).
Lack of fortitude is the mind’s lack of composure even when faced with a minor cause of affliction.
The adoption of dejection is the abandonment of enthusiasm.
Improper action is that which is contrary to worldly custom and sacred scripture; its acceptance is its performance.
Attachment to sense objects is constant engagement with them again and again.
Greed, sleepiness, lack of fortitude, cruelty, atheism, deviation from right conduct,
mendicancy, and negligence are the characteristics of the quality of darkness (tamas).
Greed is attachment to wealth and other such things;
cruelty is the persistence of enmity even toward a minor offense;
and atheism is heedlessness.

Deviation from conduct is the falling away from ethical discipline (*śīla*). By the inclusion of "and" (*ca*), the censure of the learned is implied. Begging is the state of being a petitioner; it is one's habitual disposition toward that.
Heedlessness is a lack of attention; it is a disregard for the teachings and so forth, as well as for the avoidance of the miserable states of existence.
"Sleep" and "lack of steadfastness" involve the elision of the negative particle (nañ).
Furthermore, for these three qualities residing in the three [states],
this should be known as the summary definition of their qualities in successive order.
"In the three times," meaning in the states of equilibrium, increase, and decrease, or in the arising of results that are superior, inferior, and middling;
"this" is a reference to what is about to be explained.
Whatever action one feels ashamed of having done, doing, or about to do—
all that should be known by the wise as characterized by the quality of darkness (tamas).
He demonstrates that which was stated as "in the three" by means of the temporal indications: "having done," "doing," and "about to do.
Sometimes [the remorse] occurs in all three times, and sometimes in one or another.
"Why did I act thus? How shall I stand before the disciplined?"—this is shame in the mind, a state of exhaustion.
That action by which one desires abundant fame in this world,
yet does not grieve over its failure to be accomplished, should be known as rajasic.
The practice of sacrifices, austerities, and religious duties with the thought, "May there be praise for me in the world," is for the sake of fame.
For example: giving gifts to crows at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), boasting out of rivalry with a king, or explaining the scriptures to *śūdras*.
By the word "abundant" (*puṣkalām*), he indicates that fame acts as an auxiliary because it is an incidental consequence (*anuṣaṅgin*).
If people proclaim such a dharma for one who is acting for the sake of the Dharma, that dharma does not constitute a fault.
