As it has been said, "just as for the sake of sugarcane," and as was stated by Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana in the narrative of the Mahābhārata.
Just as a farmer intent on sugarcane in his field also gathers grass and creepers,
so too a man walking upon the path of dharma attains fame, desires, and wealth.
And when the fruits of actions are not attained,
one does not grieve and there is no suffering;
or rather, [this refers to] the non-attainment of actions.
That which one desires to know in its entirety, that which one does not feel shame in practicing,
and by means of which one’s own self is satisfied— that is the characteristic mark of the qualities of a sentient being.
This is quite clear.
Desire is said to be the characteristic of *tamas*, while purpose is said to be that of *rajas*;
the characteristic of *sattva* is righteousness (*dharma*). Among these, each succeeding one is superior to the preceding.
But surely there is also pleasure within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
In that case, it follows that whatever is associated with joy (*prīti*) would possess the characteristic of *sattva*;
how then could it be the characteristic of *tamas*?
It is said:
here, darkness consists of the nature of delusion, yet there is cognition;
that too is a characteristic of Being (sattva) alone, because it has been stated that "Being is knowledge."
It is said:
here, the state of being an enjoyer and an object of enjoyment is not intended;
rather, it refers to an excessive longing directed toward sense objects.
Furthermore, in that state, there is no arising of pleasure,
and the object remains unmanifest;
because one who is dominated by desire is devoid of discrimination between what is appropriate and inappropriate, it is indeed of the nature of delusion.
And the desire intended here is of this kind:
it is not the eagerness for approaching one's own wife during her season as being the purpose of the scriptural injunction.
I shall now describe, in brief and in their proper order, those qualities by which one enters into these various states of cyclic existence.
Among these qualities, by whichever quality a person enters into which transmigrations—
where the word *saṃsāra* signifies a state of existence (*gati*),
meaning those births which one attains.
"This will be explained later" is the verse of formal promise.

Those characterized by sattva attain the state of gods; those characterized by rajas, the state of humans; and those characterized by tamas, the state of animals eternally—such is this threefold destiny.
This general indication of the destinies is based on their qualities.
This secondary course of rebirth should be understood as being threefold and of three types:
inferior, middling, and superior, according to the specific nature of one's actions and knowledge.

This threefold secondary [nature] is impelled by the qualities (guṇas) such as sattva and so forth; furthermore, each of these is again threefold through the distinction of superior, inferior, and middling. Thus, it becomes ninefold.

And because of the distinctions in action and knowledge, they are infinite, due to the power of wholesome and unwholesome actions and because of the many varieties of actions resulting from intentional and unintentional application.
This is what is meant by the phrase "due to the distinction between karma and knowledge."
Immovable beings, worms, insects, fish, snakes along with tortoises,
cattle, and wild animals— this is the lowest state, characterized by darkness (tāmasī gati).
Elephants, horses, Śūdras, and despised Mlecchas,
as well as lions, tigers, and boars, constitute the middling state of darkness (tāmasī gati).
Cāraṇas, Suparṇas, deceitful men,
Rākṣasas, and Piśācas constitute the highest state among those in the quality of darkness (tamas).
"Cāraṇas" refers to storytellers, singers, female entertainers, and the like;
"suparṇas" refers to specific types of birds; and "Śūdras" means those who are contemptible—such is the connection [of the terms].
Those who hold Brahmins in contempt, those who live off their service, those possessed by intoxication, pride, and the like,
as well as the violent, thieves, and others of such a kind, are censured.
Jhallas, Mallas, and actors, men who live by the sword, those addicted to gambling and drinking, and the low-born— this is the rajasic state.
*Jhallas* and *mallas* are performers who enter the arena. Among them, *mallas* are those who fight with their arms; *jhallas* are those who strike with clubs or live by means of jesting.
Kings, kṣatriyas, the domestic priests of kings,
and those whose primary concern is the science of weaponry and warfare— this is the intermediate rājasī state.
Kings are lords of the realm;
the kṣatriyas are those who live under them, as are the neighboring vassals.
Those for whom debate is primary engage in mutual discourse regarding the depths of the meaning of the treatises.
Warriors are those whose primary activity is battle.
The Gandharvas, Guhyakas, Yakṣas, and those who are followers of the gods,
as well as all the Apsarases, attain the highest state among the qualities of Rajas.
The Gandharvas and other such beings are gods; their distinction from [the aforementioned] should be understood from the explanatory passages (arthavāda) and historical narratives (itihāsa).
The Vibudhas are gods, and their attendants are the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and so forth.
Ascetics, yogis, brahmins, and the hosts of celestial beings who dwell in vimānas,
as well as the constellations and the daityas— this is the first, sattvic destination.
Ascetics (*tāpasa*) are those such as forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) for whom austerity is paramount;
mendicants (*yati*) are those such as wandering renunciants (*parivrājaka*).
By this, he makes it known that rebirth does not occur solely through the attainment of birth, but also from the performance of actions (*karmācaraṇa*) by one born into a particular destiny (*gati*).
For ascetics and the like are not merely certain specific castes; rather, these designations are based on their actions.
Others, however, believe that there are certain regions inhabited by Mount Meru known as the *yatayaḥ*.
It is heard [in scripture] that Indra gave the Yatis to the hyenas.

"Vimānas" are specific types of celestial vehicles, such as the Puṣpaka and others; those who travel by means of them are the "vaimānikas," certain classes of beings born of the divine race who move through the atmosphere.
The first [category] is the lowest.
Sacrificers, seers, gods, the Vedas, the luminaries, the years, the ancestors, and the Sādhyas— this is the second, the sāttvika goal.
The Veda is sound distinguished by its sequential order.
But surely, in the context of motion, what relevance is there for insentient things?
And sounds and the like are indeed insentient.
To say that sound and the other [objects] are insentient is to state too little.

All these things, from the gods down to the immobile [plants], have bodies as their essence. Among them, while all bodies are insentient, it is only their power that is attained in the form of consciousness, such as that of the Puruṣa.
The Puruṣa is devoid of qualities, yet the bodies presided over by it, though insentient, are called sentient.
Therefore, this is what is meant:
the Veda is dominated by *sattva*, and through its practice, a *sāttvika* state is attained.
Furthermore, the attainment of the status of a Veda by one whose essence is predominantly *sattva* is called the *sāttvikī gati*.
As for the mention of others, it is taught that there are all-pervading knowers (*kṣetrajña*) or Veda-persons (*vedapuruṣa*) who act as presiding deities in the world of Varuṇa.
Brahmā, the creators of the universe, Dharma, Mahat, and the Unmanifest—
these the wise declare to be the supreme state characterized by sattva.
The creators of the universe are the Prajāpatis, such as Marīci and others.
Dharma is the meaning of the Veda.
Previously, the nature of the Veda was described; now, its meaning is being explained.
It is thus stated that the meaning of the essential nature (svarūpa) is more primary.
Alternatively, "dharmas" refers to the Truths and so forth;
their possession of a physical form (vigrahavattva) is to be understood as before.
"Mahat" is another name [for it]. "Avyakta," "pradhāna," and "prakṛti" have one and the same meaning.

But surely, if the *pradhāna* consists of a predominance of *sattva*, then because the world is its modification (*vikāra*), it follows that all modifications would possess a predominance of *sattva*.
And consequently, how could there be an excess of *rajas* or *tamas*?
Therefore, what was stated—that whichever of these qualities (*guṇa*) is entirely predominant in the body—is untenable. To this, it is replied:
This is not intended to mean that the state of being the Pradhāna is what is to be attained.
Rather, three possibilities exist:

either the state of unmanifestness is to be attained, or it refers to an unseen procedure (adṛṣṭavidhi), or else this word "unmanifest" (avyakta) does not apply to the Pradhāna at all as a numerical category.
For this [term] is caused by its function (*kriyā*);
since no manifestation (*vyakti*) of it is found, it is "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) because its appearance is indistinct.
Thus, it applies to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
And its greatness is indeed established by virtue of its omnipresence.
But is it not the case that its course is not purely sattvic?
Indeed, it is so because of the abandonment of the guṇas as well.
For it is understood that when one becomes free from the notions of "I" and "mine"—thinking "I am not, nor is anything mine"—then the state of Brahman arises;
indeed, the attainment of Brahman occurs through *nididhyāsana* alone.
However, only those in whom the quality of *sattva* predominates become intent upon knowledge and the like.
It is neither *tāmasī* nor *rājasī*.
Having established this, it is said that the supreme goal is the *sāttvikī* state;
the other two positions are untenable.
For no accomplishment of the purpose of the person occurs by attaining the state of being the primary cause;
for they designate it as insentient.
Insentience is even more base than stationary things (plants), since some people seek out states such as intoxication and fainting which depend upon it.

However, the view that [the Great Principle and the Unmanifest] are to be seen is not possible, because it is not so heard; for from the scripture, "The Self, my dear, is to be seen," it follows that it is the Self that is to be seen, not the Pradhāna.
Therefore, these two terms, "the Great" and "the Unmanifest," refer exclusively to the Supreme Self.
Thus has been fully described the entire cycle of existence consisting of all living beings, which is threefold and of three kinds, arising from the three types of action.
It is threefold by way of the means of speech, mind, and body;
it is of three kinds according to the distinction of the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth;
and it is again threefold according to the distinctions of superior and so on.

Those destinies which have not been specifically mentioned here should also be included by virtue of their similarity to those already described. This concludes the section on qualities. The following verse also serves as an indicator of what is to be said next.
Through attachment to the sense faculties and by not practicing the Dharma,
the ignorant and lowest of men go to miserable states of existence.

The mention of the senses is for the purpose of demonstrating the practice of what is forbidden. Non-practice of dharma is the failure to perform what is prescribed by the learned; and since this occurs among the ignorant, he says "the ignorant."
They alone are the lowest of men;
and because of these sins, they go to— that is, they attain— evil transmigrations, which are despicable places of birth.
In this regard, the well-known ripening of karma (karmavipāka) shall first be explained.
Learn now all those various wombs into which this living soul enters in this world, one after another, according to its respective actions.
Having experienced terrible hells for many series of years, those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakins) enter these transmigrations upon the exhaustion of that [karmic residue].
Terrible hells;
terrible because of the agony of enduring suffering;
places of torment belonging to the denizens of hell.
At that moment, there is the exhaustion of manifested form through the experience of the fruit of karma;
thereafter, when only a slight remnant of karma remains, one undergoes rebirth in saṃsāra.
But why is all karma not experienced right then and there?
It has been said:
hell is the fruit of the activity of the sense-faculties, not of one who is at peace.
Furthermore, because activities are contrary to their effects, there is a cessation [of suffering] through the fruit of those activities.
In this regard, just as for a blazing fire there is burning, application, and heat—remaining entirely without deceit—so too should it be understood regarding the hells.
For fire has two states: tranquility and flame;
but hell is always of only one form.
Like fires with upward-flaming tongues, karmas possess both increase and decrease.
Therefore, hell is the experience for accumulated karma, while for that which is being diminished, there is experience elsewhere.
In this regard, it is logical [to say] "by the remainder from that."
The killer of a Brahmin enters the womb of a dog, a pig, a donkey, or a camel; or that of a cow, a goat, a sheep, a deer, or a bird; or even that of a Caṇḍāla or a Pukkasa.
A Brahmin who drinks liquor shall go among worms, insects, moths, birds that feed on excrement, and indeed among predatory creatures.
"Those that eat excrement" refers to crows and the like;
"of the predatory" refers to tigers and the like.
A Brahmin who is a thief becomes, by the thousands, spiders, snakes, lizards, aquatic animals, predatory beasts, and Piśācas.
The violator of the Guru's bed becomes [a creature] among grasses, shrubs, and creepers, or among carnivorous beasts with fangs,
or even among those who perform cruel deeds by the hundreds.
Those who perform cruel deeds and are habituated to the slaughter of others.

Those who eat the flesh of others become carnivorous beasts; those who consume impure things become worms; thieves become creatures that devour one another; and those who consort with low-caste women become hungry ghosts.
Carnivorous creatures such as vultures and the like,
and worms that consume impure matter,
devour one another; just as a large cat devours a cat, or a large fish a small fish, as if it were a mere trifle.
Those who consort with women of the lowest castes are themselves considered "low-born," such as the Barbaras and others.
By entering into association with outcasts, by approaching the wife of another,
and by stealing the property of a Brahmin, one becomes a Brahma-rākṣasa.
A person who, out of greed, steals gems, pearls, corals,
and various other jewels, is born among those who work in gold.
The Hemakartas are birds.
By stealing grain one becomes a rat; by stealing bell-metal, a swan; by stealing water, a water-fowl;
by stealing honey, a gadfly; by stealing milk, a crow; by stealing savory food, a dog; and by stealing ghee, a mongoose.
Ākhu means a mouse.
A vulture [eats] meat, a cormorant fat, a *tailapaka* bird oil,
a cricket salt, and a crane curd.
Having stolen silk, a partridge [is reborn as such]; having stolen linen, a frog; having stolen cotton cloth, a curlew; having stolen a cow, a monitor lizard; and having stolen molasses, a guḍa-worm.
*Dardura* means a young frog.
The muskrat [enjoys] auspicious fragrances, the peacock leaf-vegetables,
the porcupine various kinds of prepared food, and the hedgehog unprepared food.
Barhiṇas are peacocks.
By stealing fire, one becomes a cricket; by stealing household utensils, a house-builder;
and by stealing dyed garments, one is born as a jīvajīvaka bird.
A wolf [dreams of] a deer, a tiger an elephant, a monkey fruit and roots,
a bear a woman, a cuckoo water, a camel vehicles, and a goat livestock.
In the phrase "jalaṃ plavaḥ," water is to be understood as that for the purpose of drinking;

in "stokako vārī," it refers to water for the purpose of sprinkling grain and so forth; and regarding "rasa," they say it is the primary juice, or alternatively, it should be seen as medicinal herbs and the like.
Having forcibly seized any kind of another's property whatsoever, or having consumed an oblation that was not consecrated by fire, a man inevitably goes to the state of an animal.
There is nothing here that is hidden, as it were.
Women also, by stealing in this same manner, incur guilt;
they become wives to these very same creatures.
Indeed, when the social classes fall away from their respective duties due to no distress,
they pass through sinful transmigrations and enter into servitude among bandits.

If a Brāhmaṇa, by abandoning his livelihood through such duties as teaching, should subsist on the occupation of a Kṣatriya or others, then likewise Kṣatriyas and the rest, having fallen from their own duties, experience sinful transmigrations and births among animals; and when born again in human form, they attain the status of servants among bandits, thieves, and other violent persons.
The phrase "in times of non-distress" is a restatement; since these occupations are prescribed for times of distress, there is no fault [in their adoption].
A Brahmin who has fallen from his own dharma becomes a preta named Ulkāmukha who eats what has been vomited;
and a Kṣatriya becomes a kūṭapūtana who eats impure matter and corpses.
The evil destinies of those who have fallen from their own dharma are shown:
he eats what has been vomited,
and his mouth is burned by a flaming torch.
*Kuṇapa* means a corpse.
*Kūṭapūtana* is so called because his nose has a foul odor;
or rather, *kaṭapūtana* is an alternative reading.
A *kaṭapūtana* is a type of *piśāca* or similar being; it is a certain invisible class of spirit that frequents cremation grounds.
The Vaiśya who was Maitrākṣijyotika becomes a preta that feeds on pus;
and the Śūdra, fallen from his own dharma, becomes a Cailāśaka.
*Maitrākṣijyotika* is another term for the speech of a *piśāca*, as explained previously.
Alternatively, it means that light (*jyotis*) is seen even in what is called *maitra*;
*maitra* refers to the organ, the anus, and its "eye" is the cavity of the opening.
Others, however,
say that *tūlūka* is the light of the sun,
while *akṣa* is the luminosity pertaining to the senses, which is vision.
For he does not see in the light of the sun.
To the very extent that those whose nature is the objects of sense indulge in those objects,
to that same extent skillfulness in them arises for them.

In order to turn away from the attachment to wife and children and the greed for wealth and so forth— those seized by the perception of duality— the scent of sensual pleasure, which is the adversary of the knowledge that leads to the realization of the oneness of the Self, the nature of worldly existence as it truly is in human birth is restated as something well-known to all.
Just as they proceed toward sense objects through repeated practice,
becoming identified with those objects and craving them.
They say that for one who has engaged [in practice] by means of the word "self," there arises the very nature of that [object].
However, for one who somehow consumes it in combination with other things, no longing arises through such enjoyment for the arising of the memory of that [object].
But he who is utterly inferior [to the object] becomes identical with it through the cultivation of that [object], attaining its very selfhood.
This is what it means by saying "skillful in such and such a way.
The term "skillfulness" refers to the state of being of a single flavor (*ekarasībhāva*).
And for this reason, he is unable to avoid sense objects.
Such indeed is the course of conduct;

even regarding acts such as approaching one's own wife—which are neither enjoined nor prohibited by the cultured—this [prohibition] applies when performed with wealth acquired through improper means or with specific types of food that are forbidden.
Due to the repeated practice of those evil deeds, those of small intelligence encounter sufferings in various wombs here in this world.
And so, due to the repeated practice of those sinful, forbidden actions—
let it be that "falling" occurs through the habituation to censurable deeds—
they experience sufferings in various births as worms, insects, and the like.
There is wandering through the fierce hells such as Tāmisra,
as well as the forests of sword-leaves and other punishments involving binding and cutting.
The hells previously mentioned, such as Tāmisra and Andhatāmisra, are located there.

In those places, "turning" (*vivartana*) refers to rolling over from one side to another after lying on one side; or, for those who are unbound or lying supine, being bound to trees with leaves sharpened like sword-edges;
or, by means of similar leaves fixed to the ground—like fragments of plantain leaves—the limbs of the evildoers are cut off. This is their "friendship" (*maitrī*) with such [trees].
There are various torments, being devoured by crows and owls,
the heat of burning sand mixed with grit, and the dreadful Kumbhīpāka hells.
Karambha is a thick porridge;
for when it is thrown into the jars, it is cooked by the heat of fire like food and other such things.
And there are constant births in non-womb-born states that consist mostly of suffering,
as well as the afflictions of cold and heat and various kinds of fears.
"Non-wombs" refers to animals, hungry ghosts, piśācas, and so forth;
birth therein means being born into states abounding in suffering.
Again and again, there is dwelling in the abodes of the womb, birth that is agonizing,
bonds as rigid as wood, and even the state of being sent on errands by others.
The meaning is clear.
The separation from kinsmen and loved ones, as well as dwelling with wicked people; the acquisition of wealth and its loss, and the gaining of friends and enemies.
And [he saw] old age, which is indeed incurable; the affliction by various diseases; those manifold sufferings; and death itself, which is difficult to overcome.
These two also have their meaning already explained.
With whatever disposition one performs any particular action,
with a body of that same nature one experiences the corresponding fruit.

Whatever action one performs—whether it be sattvic, rājasic, or tāmasic—with a disposition that is sattvic, rājasic, or tāmasic, one reaps a corresponding fruit through a body characterized by an abundance of sattva, rajas, or tamas; that is, a sattvic, rājasic, or tāmasic fruit. Since this is so, from an action abounding in rajas and tamas, which is caused by unwholesome intentions, there follows the attainment of undesirable results.
Therefore, by avoiding those [unwholesome thoughts], one should act with wholesome intentions.
This entire arising of the fruits of your actions has been fully declared;
now learn this action which brings about the supreme good for a Brahmin.
Those actions, both prescribed and prohibited, have been taught as they endure until the production of their results;
therefore, one must desist from them.
Since the enjoyment of sensual pleasure is followed by suffering, one should turn away from it.
One must abide by the injunctions for action leading to the supreme good, which are the means to liberation taught in the section on knowledge (vidyākāṇḍa) to be described hereafter;
that we shall now explain.
The study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, restraint of the senses,
non-violence, and service to the guru are the supreme means for attaining the highest good.

The term *niḥśreyasa* (the supreme good) does not, however, refer here to the attainment of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), but rather to a specific state of joy characterized by the definitive cessation of the connection with pleasure and pain.
The repetition of the study of the Vedas and so forth, which have been mentioned in various places, is for the purpose of praising the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*).
This "knowledge" has as its object the meaning of the Vedas.
The other words have their meanings already explained.
And among all these auspicious actions here,
a certain action has been declared to be more conducive to welfare for a person.
And for all of these, knowledge of the Self is remembered as supreme;
for that is the foremost of all sciences, since immortality is attained from it.

Self-knowledge is twofold: first, the knowledge of the self as distinct from the body, senses, intellect, and so forth, established in its nature as agent and enjoyer, which is the object of the notion of "I," is included within the cognition of objects, and is designated by such synonyms as *jīva*, *kṣetrajña*, and *vijñānātman*; and second, the knowledge of the self as the enjoyer of the fruits of actions—whether pertaining to future lives or otherwise—which remain undestroyed even upon the destruction of the body.

Furthermore, there is the knowledge of the one eternal Being—the sole cause of the birth and so forth of the entire world—who, though appearing in various forms due to the impressions of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*), is perceived as one among animals, humans, and others; this is the knowledge of the essential nature revealed by such scriptural passages as, "Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon.
In that context, the thorough knowledge of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) is employed in the injunctions regarding ritual action (*karma-vidhi*).

For if this [Self] were not distinct from the body and so forth, the injunctions such as "one who desires heaven" regarding rewards for rites pertaining to the afterlife would be purposeless; consequently, no one would engage in them.
Therefore, that [knowledge of the Self] is useful for the performance of ritual action.

However, as for the knowledge of the oneness of the Supreme Self—which arises through the power of practicing the service of concealment and which reveals the Self whose nature is pure, awakened, liberated, blissful, eternal, and indestructible—in that case, the following is appropriate: "This is the foremost of all sciences, for by it immortality is attained."
"Amṛtam" refers to the failure of that [other] path.
"Tataḥ" (from that) is a designation for knowledge; it refers to the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*).
Knowledge of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), however, because it is merely an auxiliary to ritual action, does not suffice for immortality.
Therefore, what is intended by "knowledge of the Self" is the vision of that True Self, which is the subject of both duality and non-duality as taught in its entirety by the Vedānta.
Among these six aforementioned types of action, it should be known that the Vedic rite is always more conducive to welfare, both in this world and after death.
The six duties beginning with the study of the Vedas are conducive to prosperity (*abhyudaya*).
Among them, the Vedic rites such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* lead to the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*).
It is in these that liberation (*mokṣa*) is established.
But surely, if the genitive in *pūrveṣām* is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), that is untenable;
for selection occurs when a specific member of a collective group is distinguished by some attribute that is possible within that same domain, yet not possible among its sub-divisions—
as in "the Kṣatriya is the bravest of men," where the Kṣatriya, being included within the genus "human beings," is selected as the most brave.
How can there be a selection of that which is neither taught nor separated [from others]?
Furthermore, no Vedic ritual action has been previously taught here. Now, it might be argued:
The study of the Vedas and so forth are exclusively Vedic; how then can it be said that a Vedic rite has not been specified?
If this were so, there would be even greater uncertainty regarding the general through the general;
for it does not happen that "among cows, the cow that has just given milk is the best."
For if non-Vedic acts were intended to convey the same purpose [as Vedic ones], then it would follow that one should look to the Vedic as being more conducive to the highest good (*śreyaskaratara*).
Furthermore, what exactly are the "Vedic acts" intended here?
If they refer to the Jyotiṣṭoma and so forth, then an authority must be stated for such a specific selection, since practices such as the study of the Vedas (*vedābhyāsa*) are also Vedic.
Now, it might be argued that because they are based on *smṛti*, those [acts] are not Vedic; only those prescribed by direct *śruti* are Vedic.

For indeed, among all Vedic rites, the study of the Vedas and so forth are not included as constituent parts (*aṅga*). And this is because he will say later: "They are included sequentially in that injunction of action. If that were not the case, then in the *agnihotra* and other such rites, great austerity would have to be performed.
No purpose whatsoever is served by what he has said;
for even the study of the Vedas and so forth must be practiced, as must the Agnihotra and other rites.
In that regard, we do not know in what manner these [latter] constitute a means to the highest good (*śreyaskaratva*).
Nor are the fruits equal, such that it could be said [of one] on account of the excellence of its fruit alone;
for example, from the gift of a cow [comes] heaven, and from the Jyotiṣṭoma [comes] its persistence for a long period of time.
As it has been stated: "In accordance with the world, there would be a distinction of fruits according to their magnitude."
To this it is replied:

regarding what was said— that no purpose is served by this statement— some say that the declaration of the superior efficacy of Vedic [rites] is intended to make known the sublation of Smṛti when there is a conflict with Śruti.
As it has been said: "When there is a conflict between two [authorities] of equal strength, there is an option;
when a Smṛti is of unequal strength, it is sublated by Śruti. But where there may be a duality of Śruti, both those [rules] are recorded as Dharma.
In a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, it is effectively stated that the Smṛti is the restatement (anuvāda);
since this is already understood from that very [preceding statement], it need not have been said. However, there is no fault in stating it again for the sake of clarification.

Alternatively, another such meaning is also possible; and the mention of "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*) pertains to the pure [consciousness]. When there is a conflict between two memories, it is not for the purpose of conceptualizing that [object].
Therefore, this is the meaning:
Vedic [injunctions] are stronger than those based on Smṛti.
The mention of "the study of the Vedas and so forth" is for the purpose of illustrating all that is based on Smṛti.
This was recited thus merely for the sake of metrical conformity.
We, however, say that this matter is established by logic; and it is appropriate to state even what is established by logic out of friendly intent, without having already begun [the discussion].
Here, the knowledge of the Self is recited at every step.
In that case, what relevance does sublation have to it?
Furthermore, the authors of the Smṛtis ought not to seek to validate their own statements by means of their own statements.
If it is argued that the injunction being stated belongs to the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* and not to one's own [work], and thus there is no parity, [we reply: so be it.
Since what has been said regarding one's own [self] also applies here,
the term "study of the Vedas" and so forth is mentioned separately in accordance with the context;
it is not recited here after having first proposed a self as the subject.
And how is it that they have explained self-knowledge as being subordinate to the Vedas?
[They argue: "From the study of the Vedas and so forth, Vedic ritual action such as sacrifice is superior; from that arises knowledge of the supreme self (adhyātmajñāna).
Otherwise, what is being taught in one place would be established elsewhere and fall into another."
Alternatively, the knowledge of the Self alone is what is intended here by the Veda, because the Veda is devoted to its exposition.
The instruction on the Agnihotra and other rites is for the purpose of engaging children and others in practice, like the instruction for an elder to take medicine.

Alternatively, the proponents of Brahman (brahmavādinaḥ) maintain that the learned, having discarded this innate beginningless ignorance—which is the cause of attachment to the objects of latent impressions—by means of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), and through the power of the impressions from the study of the scriptures, gradually attain dispassion; thus, as their firm grasping of thirst and passion becomes loosened, they become fit to be directed toward the instruction for the highest qualification. It is understood that the entire ritual section, as enjoined in the Śrutis and other texts, serves as an aid to that qualification.

Therefore, this statement—"Vedic action is in every way more conducive to the highest good"—should be understood as intending the action called *nivṛtti* (cessation) which will be described hereafter.

Alternatively, the meaning is that even if there is a distinction between all [paths], since both types of unreal perception are like a dream, the knowledge of the oneness of the Self is the highest good; thus, the practice of Vedic study and so forth, which is prompted by the teaching of duality, must be performed.
But the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is not to be raised by them [the opponents], because a distinctness established by the intellect (*buddhi*) is possible through an internal superimposition;
for example, "The people of Mathurā are wealthier than those of Pāṭaliputra.

If it is argued that, such being the case, this should be the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*), here too a counter-argument has been provided, because there is no difference in the underlying property (*dharma*).
But in the Vedic yoga of action, all these [elements] without exception are included in their respective order within each specific ritual injunction.
They describe Vedic ritual as consisting of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such sacrifices; the application of the verse to these very rites is as follows:
"The injunction of action" (kriyāvidhi) refers to the Vedic injunction of ritual (karmavidhi).
In the application of action (*karmayoga*), that is, in the performance of ritual acts, these states are to be accomplished externally;
these include the study of the Upaniṣads and other such practices, which are included therein.
By the word "in that" (*tasmin*), he indicates that some of these are equally included within others by virtue of being pervaded.
When "karmayoga" is mentioned, the inclusion of the term "ritual procedure" (kriyāvidhi) is for the purpose of completing the verse.
Alternatively, the distinction [between these types of sacrifice] should be explained according to the divisions of Soma sacrifices, such as the *kratu* and *yajña*.
Among those, the study of the Vedas (*vedābhyāsa*) is included within the *sattra* sacrifice, because it is useful in all the mantras recited by the sacrificer.
In the initiations for austerity (*tapodīkṣā*), the preparatory rites (*upasada*), and the Soma sacrifices, there are such rules as "milk is the nectar for the Brāhmaṇa," and so forth.

Knowledge, however, applies everywhere, because those who already possess it have no further requirement [to undergo initiation]. Likewise, the restraint of the senses pertains to each specific sacrifice, as in the injunctions: "one should not approach a woman" and "one should not eat meat."

"Even in this night of non-violence, one should not deprive any living being of its life, even a lizard"— thus there is no engagement in such acts as service to the teacher. However, for those who maintain that [the *niyama*] consists solely of abstention (*nivṛtti*), this verse serves the purpose of ensuring the continuation of practices such as the study of the Vedas.
They are included even for one intent upon meditation (*upāsana*), because they are included through the performance of those [meditations].

Thus, the instruction regarding expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for a meditator found in the Upaniṣads is for the purpose of destroying sin; it does not, however, mean that a modification of the remedial measure itself has been stated.
Therefore, when there is the non-performance of what is enjoined or the practice of what is prohibited, demerit (*pratyavāya*) arises.
If that is so, then from what does liberation arise?

It arises from the exhaustion of the demerits produced in other births through the experience of their fruits; from the non-commission of other [acts] by one's own conscious intent; from the performance of expiation for what was done through negligence by means of the excellence of practice in specific breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and knowledge (*vidyā*); and from the direct realization of the nature of the self as free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*). First, one should experience that [self]; liberation is the attainment of its state.
Therefore, even by one intent upon being established in Brahman, the study of the Vedas and other such duties must be performed.
For whomsoever the renunciation of action is prescribed, that has been explained in the sixth [chapter].
The injunction regarding action should be understood as the very injunction for meditation (*upāsanā*), as set forth in such passages as "it is to be seen, it is to be heard," and so forth.
Moreover, because there are many modes of meditation (*upāsanā*), the repetition "in this and in that" (*tasmin tasmin*) is indeed appropriate.

Therefore, in passages such as "one should meditate on him as Brahman," "this golden person who is in the sun," and "he is this Self, free from evil," sometimes that which is superimposed upon the intellect (the individual self) is enjoined; sometimes, in cases like "golden," the meditation is on that very same [Brahman] through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); and sometimes, by virtue of its sovereignty over all meditations—as in "He alone is below, He is above"—that very [Brahman] is enjoined as if stainless. Thus, due to the multiplicity of these injunctions, the repetition is justified.
Vedic action is of two kinds: that which leads to worldly prosperity and that which leads to the supreme good; it is also twofold, being either active (pravṛtta) or withdrawn (nivṛtta).
But has it not already been explained that Vedic action is indeed of one kind?
Why then is it said here that it is "twofold"?
This is not a fault.
In that context, the primary Vedic [tradition] has been explained;
however, the Vedic is uniform everywhere.
One attains, that is, reaches, happiness.

Furthermore, the term *sukhābhyudayika* should be understood etymologically either as "that which brings about happiness and prosperity" (*sukhābhyudayaḥ prayojanam asya*) or as "that whose purpose is happiness and prosperity.
Some also interpret it as "that whose purpose is the supreme good" (*niḥśreyasaṃ prayojanam asya*).
These [terms] should be connected respectively with the words *pravṛtta* (active engagement) and *nivṛtta* (withdrawal), as previously explained.
Action performed with desire for results here or hereafter is called "pravṛtta" (active); however, action free from desire and preceded by knowledge is taught as "nivṛtta" (withdrawn).
In this world, rites such as the Kārīrī and Vaiśvānarī, and in the next world, rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, are actions that accomplish what is desired (*kāmya*).
That which is desired is "kāmya";
because the fruit is what is desired, the action that is its means is also indeed *kāmya*.
It is desireless and constant;
it is preceded by knowledge in both cases, because one who lacks knowledge has no entitlement [to these rites].
Nevertheless, knowledge is taught for one who is entitled to the secret [Upaniṣads].
In that case, there is no remainder for either [term].
Furthermore, the word "pūrva" (prior) indicates the sense of "first" (ādya); the analysis of the compound is: "that of which knowledge is the first, that is, the primary."
That which is present is the world that first acquires its activity;
therefore, this is what is meant:
knowledge is primary, and it is to be practiced primarily.
But the study of the Vedas and so forth [is accomplished] by means of the mere scripture.
By practicing active (pravṛtta) karma, one attains equality with the gods;
but by practicing renounced (nivṛtta) karma, one indeed transcends the five elements.
But has it not been stated that desire-driven action is characterized by engagement?
And among desire-driven actions, some have heaven as their fruit, while others have perceptible fruits;
yet no perceptible action is observed to have the attainment of equality with the gods as its fruit.
Therefore, why is it said that "one attains equality with the gods"?
Even those rites such as the Viśvajit, whose specific fruits are not mentioned in scripture, have heaven as their fruit when performed without desire.
Consequently, we do not understand how the attainment of equality with the gods could be the fruit of ritual action.

Nor can it be said that those rites heard in scripture to have specific fruits should be performed by one free from desire, such that when performed in that way they result in the fruit of divinity; for in that case, there would be the abandonment of what is explicitly stated in scripture and the postulation of what is not so stated. Furthermore, the fruit mentioned in the Veda is something desired, as in "one desiring a village" or "one desiring heaven," and not something produced by the inherent nature of the thing itself, like the effect of consuming poison.
Furthermore, it might be argued that there is a contradiction in saying that the attainment of divinity and so forth occurs, yet it is not something desired (*kāmya*).
If it is asked how it can be undesired within the context of prohibitions, the answer is that such a state itself is connected as the fruit in those cases;
for what is undesirable cannot be something desired.
Now, the fruit of the obligatory rites (*nitya*) is stated here, which is the avoidance of non-eternality (*anityatā*);
for by such terms as "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*), the status of having an obligatory fruit is understood therein.
If something must necessarily be postulated, let it be the avoidance of transgression (*pratyavāya-parihāra*).
For that [state], when being conceptualized, is not contradictory with permanence.
As for the subsequent verse, "He indeed transcends the five elements," we do not understand there what is meant by "transcending" (*atyeti*) other than "being liberated" (*vimucyate*).
Elsewhere, *atyaya* is said to mean dissolution (*laya*).
And here, the dissolution of the individual soul (*jīva*) into the elements is not intended; rather, it is the attainment of the nature of Brahman.
Others also explain: "He transcends the five elements;
his body does not consist of the five elements, but he follows along as a form of light alone."
That too is of no consequence;
for liberation is indeed the non-grasping of a body.
Whether that body consists of a single element or of the five elements, what difference does it make regarding the state of transmigrating?
Therefore, this verse must be explained.

It is said in reply: as for what was stated—that it is not possible to say of which action the fruit is equality with the gods, because obligatory (*nitya*) rites have no fruit, and because optional (*kāmya*) rites are connected with other fruits—we respond to that: by this, the fruit of all Vedic actions is not being stated.

What then? It is a praise [of the teaching] that there exists an action which, having ceased, has a fruit wherein there is engagement; and furthermore, there exists an action by which that fruit is attained. And indeed, there are certain actions that have the attainment of divinity as their fruit.
Therefore, this is what is meant:
that which is known as something to be performed in the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) constitutes its highest goal, namely the attainment of divinity, but not liberation;
whereas that action which is taught in the section concerning the secret doctrine (rahasyādhikāra) is the cause for non-return [to saṃsāra].
In this regard, for one who desires [fruits], action becomes a cause of bondage because it is impaired by the mental resolve for results.
For it is the very nature of actions that they initiate the activity of an agent in order to yield their own fruits.
Likewise, even obligatory rites (*nitya-karmāṇi*), if not performed, become causes of transgression.
Those [karmas] also indeed initiate a body.

If this were so, he would perform obligatory duties (*nitya*) and would not perform optional (*kāmya*) or prohibited (*pratiṣiddha*) ones; because of the absence of karma that initiates a body, he would attain liberation due to the absence of its cause. What, then, would be the use of self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*)? As it has been said:
One should perform the obligatory and occasional rites with the desire to avoid transgression;
one devoid of the desire for liberation should engage in the optional and prohibited rites.
Thus it has been said by the Blessed Ones:
"For one who does not practice knowledge, there is no destruction of ignorance;
and as long as ignorance is not severed by knowledge, there is no attainment of the nature of Brahman."
It is with this very intention that it was said: "free from desire and preceded by knowledge," and likewise, "selfishness born of desire is not praised.
*Sāmārṣṭi* means the performance of equal actions; its state is *sāmyatā*.
The meaning is that one attains a state equal to that of the gods.
Furthermore, the delusion regarding the statement "and that which transcends the elements" is also not tenable;
for even "transcending" (atyaya) is said to mean "deception," in the sense that the entire phenomenal world (prapañca) becomes like frost.
Even with the reading "abhyeti," the state of being bodiless is expressed.
Furthermore, as to how this elaboration (prapañca) is to be performed, he says:
"Seeing the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self, equally, the one who sacrifices to the Self attains self-sovereignty (svārājya)."
By the word "bhūta" (being), everything that exists, whether stationary or moving, sentient or insentient, is denoted.
In that regard, one should perceive the Self [in all], thinking, "This world is just like me.
And so says the Śruti: "I am the swaying branch of the tree."
One should abandon the conventional discourse of self and other.
The notions "this is I," "this is mine," and "this is not mine" constitute bondage.
For one who has relinquished the attachment to self and what belongs to the self, and has cast off the distinction between self and other, there shines forth the absolute unity of the Self alone.
This indeed is the meaning of the state of self-sovereignty (*svārājya*):
"all beings in the Self.
That very world, which consists of the manifold expansion of modifications, exists within Me; thus it is realized that I alone am the creator, the agent, the meditator, and the object of meditation.

The "sacrificer to the Self" (ātmayājī) is one who sacrifices to, or regards, the Self alone as consisting of all the deities; he does not consider fire or the sun to be the deity, but rather perceives, "I myself am the deity"—it is in this way that he becomes a sacrificer to the Self.
It is not, however, enjoined that a sacrifice must be performed with the Self as its objective.
Some say:
in the rites dedicated to Agni and others, the deities such as Agni should not be spoken of even as one's own self;
[the goal is] sovereignty over oneself (*svārājya*).
"Svārājya" means existing in one's own kingdom;
he becomes independent like the Supreme Self (paramātman) and becomes self-luminous.
He does not depend on the light of the moon, the sun, and so forth, nor on the senses such as the eyes, nor on the internal organ such as the mind.
Therefore, the phrase "seeing" is said to mean "one should cultivate [that vision].
It is not mere seeing; rather, when all external and internal activities have been set aside, those intent on that cultivation are traditionally known as such.
Even having abandoned the aforementioned ritual acts, the best of the twice-born should be diligent in self-knowledge, tranquility, and the study of the Vedas.
Regarding the phrase "even the aforementioned actions":

this does not prescribe the abandonment of rituals such as the *agnihotra*; rather, it prescribes the practice of self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*), meaning that one should be diligent in the knowledge of the Self.

As for the expression "having abandoned actions," its basis is that even while performing such acts as circumambulating sacred shrines of exalted deities, reciting mantras, and approaching one's teacher, one should nevertheless practice self-knowledge.
For there is no renunciation at will of obligatory rites; they must be performed according to human duty and so forth, and not without their performance.
For this indeed is the fulfillment of the purpose of birth, especially for a Brahmin;
having attained this, the twice-born becomes one who has accomplished his duty, and not otherwise.
The term "twice-born" (dvija) indicates that even for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, there is eligibility for the knowledge of the Self;
as the Āraṇyaka Śruti states:
"Especially for the Brāhmaṇa."
The phrase "in the study of the Vedas" is to be connected [to the previous context].
These two are possible only for one who knows the Self and has practiced equanimity.
Having attained that knowledge of the Self, the twice-born becomes one who has accomplished his purpose; by this much, the goal of human existence is fulfilled.
For there is indeed no human goal (puruṣārtha) other than liberation (mokṣa).

Now, as for what was said—that one should perceive this [reality] through the oneness of the self of all—this seems to contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), for by direct perception distinct entities appear.
Therefore, how can they be grasped as one?
It would be as if a teaching were given that does not concern its own subject matter.
How can that which is divided be seen as undivided?
For a donkey cannot be grasped by the intellect as if it were a cow;
rather, due to a defect in the sense organ, a mother-of-pearl shell or similar object is perceived in the form of silver through a manifestation elsewhere, and not by means of instruction.
For one who would act upon what another teaches that elephant would not directly obtain the fruit of those words;
therefore, he says:
The Veda is the eternal eye for the ancestors, the gods, and human beings;
it is established that the Vedic scripture is both impossible to master in its entirety and immeasurable.
This is the meaning:
here, the Veda is the authority for the speaker;
it is like an eye, because of the commonality of being a cause of vision.
Just as the cognition of form arises without effort regarding objects delimited by the eye, so too [it arises] from the Veda; thus "the eye" is mentioned.
It is "sanātana," meaning eternal and constant.
By this, he states that it is not created by a person.

For if [the Veda] were the work of a person, there would be no proof for the claim that "even error might occur due to its authority," because one could not ascertain the presence or absence of qualities or defects in a person.
Therefore, due to the absence of such [human agency], the Veda is authoritative by virtue of being authorless (*apauruṣeya*).
Consequently, because of the authority of the Veda, there is no contradiction whatsoever with an object that is perceptible.
But if one were to instruct thus: "one should sprinkle with fire and kindle with water," would there not be a contradiction?
This is an unequal comparison;
for in that case, an actually perceived purpose is indeed taught as something to be performed by means of the perceived power of things.
In that case, it would be logical for that object to fall within the scope of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),

and it is precisely because of the opposite of that [which you claim] that this has been stated. However, here, since the words are intent upon injunction (*vidhi*) and other means of valid cognition do not have injunction as their object— having instead as their scope established entities whose nature is already accomplished— how can there be a contradiction when there is no single common object?
For here, indeed, the vision of things that are not the self as being the self is enjoined for the sake of the fruit of self-sovereignty (*svārājya*).
In this regard, where there is an excessive perception of difference, it is possible to effect a change through practice.
For instance, mental states such as passion and the like can be restrained by the practice of the limbs of yoga through the excellence of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Even regarding an object of hatred, the perception of it as hateful ceases through the cultivation of loving-kindness and the like; this is self-evident to everyone and is observed in experience.
Through the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), the nature of even non-existent things appears [as real];
for example, in the case of a deceptive lover, those filled with passion see everything as if it were their beloved—how much more so when there is actual, ontological unity!
How then can it appear as differentiated, given that its nature is non-dual?
For all phenomena have that [non-dual] nature; yet they are perceived as differentiated.
And herein, such a vision is prescribed as equality, wherein the notions "this is mine" and "this is not mine" are no longer possible.
As it has been said:
"The two syllables 'mine' are death, and 'not mine' is the eternal."
Therefore, there is no contradiction.

Phrases such as "of the ancestors, gods, and humans" are scriptural statements (*śruti*). Even though the gods and others possess supernatural powers when joined [with them], they do not perceive such supersensible objects (*atīndriya-artha*), because it is impossible to know them without the aid of scripture.
It is immeasurable and unlimited because the branches of the Vedas are infinite;
furthermore, it is impossible to measure in terms of its meaning.
"Vedaśāstra" refers to the Vedas.
Whatever scriptures are outside the Veda, and whatever false doctrines there may be—
all of them are fruitless after death, for they are traditionally held to result in darkness.

Having previously stated that the Veda possesses authority because it is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), [the author] now addresses the lack of authority of those Vedas that are of human origin (*pauruṣeya*).

Furthermore, there are well-known scriptural traditions outside the Veda (*vedabāhya*)—contrary to the Veda and lacking a Vedic foundation—which consist of compositions of texts and injunctions such as "Heaven results from bowing to a *caitya*," and so forth; these are the established doctrines of the Nirgranthas, the Śobhas, and others.
These are "bad views" (*kudṛṣṭi*), which are systems of reasoning based on fallacious logic (*asattarka*).
The proofs for the author of the Vedas, the refutation of the *apūrva*, the deities, and so forth—these are false views (*kudṛṣṭayaḥ*).
All of them are fruitless after death, having reached their culmination.
They are stated to be ultimately fruitless because they are established with fallacious reasons and examples, since the arguments therein are merely semblances of reasoning.
Furthermore, those arguments on another's path become as long as the night when expanded into great treatises, whereas here they are presented in a concise form.

Likewise, there is no authority in the instruction of human beings, because humans lack the power to perceive supersensuous objects; and even if such power existed, there would be no means of verifying the instructor.
As for the claim that "this person is omniscient, and therefore this scripture was composed by him," not the slightest proof applies to this point.

Even if there were a prior agent, there would be the undesirable consequence of postulating unseen results for what has a seen purpose; and if that [agent] were the means of valid cognition, the status of being a deity would be established.
Therefore, the meaning is that those arguments are rooted in delusion.
Others, however, explain as follows:
After death, those [actions] are fruitless for one who has died,
because they result in birth from a *tāmasa* womb and culminate in darkness (*tamas*).
In this interpretation, the use of the word "pretya" (having departed) is problematic, as it implies a lack of common agency between the subject of the action and the subject of the gerund.
Alternatively, the locative case ending should be read after the word "preta" as being derived from a form ending in a past passive participle (niṣṭhā).
Whatever other things there may be besides these, which arise and perish,
they are fruitless and false because they belong only to the past.
Therefore, those other teachings that arise from the Veda are subject to origination and destruction;
because they possess the nature of arising and perishing, they are impermanent.
The Veda, however, is eternal, as it is the opposite of that.
Because they are of recent origin, having been composed by some person of the present day, they are therefore fruitless due to the absence of any unseen (adṛṣṭa) result;
such works as those characterized by being rooted in deception and the like.
The four castes, the three worlds, and the four stages of life in their distinctness—
the past, the present, and the future— all these are established through the Veda.
This too is indeed a mere praise.
The fourfold caste system is established through the Veda and exists as a matter of qualification, as in such passages as "In spring, a Brāhmaṇa; in summer, a Rājanya," and so forth.
However, its actual nature is to be understood through worldly usage, since it is common to all castes; this has been shown elsewhere.
The three worlds subsist upon the giving from this [world];

thus, the fact that the Veda is the cause of the maintenance of the triple world is indeed established, as are the Smṛtis, since they have their root in the Veda; even the stages of life (āśrama) originate solely from the Veda.
Whatever has passed— the happiness, suffering, and so forth of past births—
and whatever is currently existing, as well as whatever is yet to come, for all of that the Veda alone is the refuge.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—these are established through the Veda alone; their production arises from qualities and actions.
The establishment of sound and other objects as means of pleasure through their being objects of enjoyment is known from the Veda alone.
From the performance of Vedic rites, there arises the occurrence of sounds such as songs and the like;
from the abandonment of those rites, there follows the hearing of sounds that are harsh to the ear.

Therefore, the intended meaning is that sound and the other [objects] which initiate the body are established by those two [the senses] as their respective objects through the Veda; however, the Veda is not the material cause (upādāna-karaṇa).
Thus, sound and the others which initiate the body [are known] by those two.
This very point he states: "The production [of the body] is from the qualities and the action."
*Prasūtiḥ* is the production of sound and the other sense objects;
for that purpose, there is the *guṇakarma* (subordinate action).

Furthermore, because it is for the sake of a result, the *pradhānakarma* (principal action), such as the *Citrā* sacrifice and others, is said to be a property of the *guṇa* (quality/subordinate element).

An alternative reading is *prasūtir guṇadharmataḥ*. The *guṇas* are *sattva* and the others; their *dharma* is transformation (*vipariṇāma*). The production (*prasūti*) of that [transformation] consists in its departure from the state of equilibrium, its intensification, and its diversification (*viṣvagbhāva*). In this regard, the Veda alone is the cause, because it has the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) as its motive. Other variant readings concerning diversity (*vaicitrya*) are not recorded here, as they serve no purpose.
The eternal Vedic scripture sustains all living beings;
therefore, I consider this to be the supreme means for the accomplishment of the goals of this creature.

The support of all beings is shown in the Vedic scripture in the Brāhmaṇa: "The oblation is offered into the fire; that fire carries it upward to the sun; the sun bears it with his rays; from that comes rain; from that arises their birth and sustenance—thus the oblation is known. Here too it is said: "An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun," and so forth.

Therefore, I consider this to be the supreme cause for the goals of human life: namely, that such instruction in dharma for this living being occurs through such a cause, and from this cause, there arises the justification for those [teachings] as it has been shown. Now, if the purpose is based on grasping (*aupādānika*), why was it called a "worldly purpose" (*laukika-artha*)? It was stated as such because of its distinction.
It is said:
its performance is Vedic, but its purpose, being perceptible, is purely worldly.
One who is learned in the Vedic scriptures is worthy of the command of armies, of sovereignty, of the office of a judge, and of lordship over all the world.
This is an excessive praise.

"Punishers" (daṇḍanetāraḥ) refers to the leaders of punishment (daṇḍanāyakāḥ), those appointed to oversee what has been done and what remains to be done in villages and cities. An "army" (senā) consists of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; its "lord" (patiḥ) is the commander thereof.
Sovereignty is the status of a regional lord;
overlordship of all the world is the status of a universal monarch.
Just as a fire that has gained strength consumes even moist trees,
so too does one who knows the Vedas burn away the defects of his own karma.
This also is as before;
the word-connections are clear and the meanings of the words are well known.
One who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras, dwelling in whatever stage of life he may be,
is fit for becoming Brahman even while remaining in this very world.
"For the sake of becoming Brahman" means for the state of being Brahman, that is to say, for the attainment of the nature of Brahman.
"Wherever that may be" means even by departing from there, or even by deviating from the sequence;
as it has been said: "And having departed even from hostility, the Brāhmaṇas, having announced their intention, go forth on the mendicant's way."

Those who possess the texts are superior to the ignorant; those who retain them are better than those who merely possess them; those who have realized knowledge are superior to those who merely retain them; and those who act with resolve are superior to those who merely possess knowledge.
The ignorant are fools who have not studied; the "bookish" are the learned who merely recite the texts. From these, the "retainers" are those who study with diligence.
But in the previous case, it was not with such great effort; the phrase "of the text" is connected there as well, meaning "of one who upholds the text.
Their superiority [is established] because they possess the qualification for recitation (*japa*), receiving gifts (*pratigraha*), and so forth.
But those possessed of knowledge are superior, as they are authorized in all matters.
When practices such as the recitation of mantras (*japa*) are performed preceded by knowledge, they yield an excellence of fruit.
As it has been said: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*), that alone becomes more powerful."
Those who are resolute are practitioners free from doubt,
for whom it is impossible to think that this [teaching] could be otherwise;
this too is for the purpose of praise.
The Vedas lead to the goals of human life through mere study alone; how much more so, then, does the knowledge of their meaning!
Austerity and knowledge are the supreme means for attaining the highest good for a Brahmin;
through austerity he destroys evil, and through knowledge he partakes of immortality.
By this he shows the following:

even when knowledge exists, there is no liberation for one whose evil has not been exhausted; and even when the exhaustion of karma exists, there is no liberation if the knowledge of the Self does not exist.
Therefore, that which was stated—that they are liberated by their very nature—is incorrect.
Immortality is non-return, which is this state consisting of absolute bliss.
Perception, inference, and scripture consisting of various traditions—
these three must be thoroughly understood by one who desires purity in dharma.
Having become a friend, he instructs him in worldly matters.
Dharma is the meaning of the Veda; its purification is its exposition, which consists in establishing the settled conclusion by means of refuting opposing views.
This occurs when there is certainty regarding the means of valid cognition, such as direct perception and the rest.
For when perception is well-understood, the proof of the permanence of sound and so forth is recognized through the distinction [of sound] from [the case of] a flame and the like;
however, for one who lacks correct discrimination, there would be a determination of perception as being indistinguishable in both cases.

Furthermore, having observed the destruction of flames and the like through direct perception, one might likewise infer it for sound; thus, the Veda would consist of a collection of impermanent sounds. However, for one who considers that the established valid means of knowledge regarding wholesome things do not involve the apprehension of what is not [the object], and who—being ignorant—does not conceive of a distinction such as "white" and "not-white" based on the apprehension of difference (as in the case of a flame), he does not imagine a sublation of sound based on the sublation of the flame. Likewise, inference is well-discriminated, because it serves as an illustration of the authority of texts such as the *Mahābhārata*.
Therefore, at the conclusion of the treatises on valor and other such subjects, there is the attainment of proficiency.

For one who has not discriminated [between valid and fallacious inference], thinking that the operation of inference occurs merely through the observation of presence in the similar class (*pakṣa*) and non-observation in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), would postulate an author even for the Veda.

But when he becomes a person of subtle intellect, he determines its lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) because the specific causes for such an author—namely, the characteristics of one who must have studied it and his own instruments of action—are absent.
And "treatise" (*śāstra*) refers to various scriptures (*āgama*).
Because there are various injunctions and prohibitions within a treatise, its scripture is "various," meaning of many kinds. That wherein one arrives [at knowledge] is a scripture.
Because the Veda has many branches, its diversity is stated through the distinction between Śruti and Smṛti;
and this matter, implied by the injunction for Vedic study (svādhyāya-vidhi), is taught out of friendship, yet neither of these two [the diversity nor the teaching] is merely for the sake of praise.
He who examines the instruction on Dharma given by the seers with reasoning that does not contradict the Vedas and the Shastras knows Dharma, and no other.
The *ṛṣi* is the Veda; that which originates therein is *ārṣa*. This refers to the instruction on Dharma that is Vedic.

The syntactical construction of the words is as follows: he who investigates by means of reasoning (*tarka*), that is, by means of other forms of inference (*anumāna*) and logic (*yukti*), knows Dharma.
Reasoning (*tarka*) is the internal accomplishment of inclusion and exclusion (*ūhāpoha*): "this is fit to be included here," and "this is to be excluded."

When, in the ritual for the Sun (saurya), the mantra obtained from the archetype is "By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour out [the grain] acceptable to Agni," the word *agni* is excluded because its referent is not applicable, and the word *sūrya* is inserted.
This reasoning (*tarka*) is not contradicted by the Veda.

Furthermore, for one who thinks thus: "In the *saurya* rite, because the deity Agni is absent, and because mantras are to be employed according to their meaning, and because a mantra ceases to be a mantra when even a single part is omitted, there must be the complete elision of the mantra"—this reasoning contradicts the meaning of the Veda.

And as for the view that the employment of mantras consists merely in their recitation, and therefore the mantra must be employed in its unmodified form—this too is a reasoning that contradicts the scripture.
Moreover, this is not an injunction (*vidhi*).
This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).

Its purport here is this: such indifference [toward other sciences] is understood from this very inquiry (*mīmāṃsā*); therefore, by this, the necessity of studying *mīmāṃsā* for the sake of the purification of Dharma is enjoined.
Others, however, explain it differently.

Regarding the phrase "by means of reasoning" (*tarkeṇa*), treatises in which reasoning is predominant—namely the Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, and Lokāyata systems, which are devoted to defining worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—are being referred to.
Among these, those that contradict the Veda, such as the Buddhist, Lokāyata, and Nirgrantha (Jaina) schools, are excluded;
for they are indeed opposed to the Veda.
The Veda is not the authority in that regard;
for in the systems of Kapila, Kaṇāda, Kriyā, Aviratha, Tāntrika, Nigraha, Anta, and so forth, it is *śabda* (verbal testimony) that is the authority.
Accordingly, the sūtra of Akṣapāda states: "Perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
The Vaiśeṣikas also state that the authority of the Veda arises from His word,
and that for this reason those scriptures should be heard.
Thus it has been shown by the Blessed Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana in the Mahābhārata:
O King, these dull-witted men of yours are merely Vedic scholars;
their intellects are paralyzed by rote recitation and do not perceive subtle meanings.

By the phrase "struck down by the recitation" (anuvākahatā), he states the logical justification even for those who employ reasoning; this is because [the world] is non-existent due to its being merely [a mental construction].
Likewise, there is this other point:
"A follower of the Smṛti does not serve certain Lokāyata Brahmins."
"For these fools who consider themselves wise are indeed unskilled in what is meaningful.
By this [verse], the hearing of false reasoning is established; by the preceding [verse], the permission of true reasoning is granted—this is precisely that.
Some assert that the authority of the Veda arises from its being composed by God;
however, such a [composer] is not possible.
Furthermore, on that view, the Veda would not be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for in that case, God would merely be the one who establishes the linguistic convention (*samaya*).
When these [arguments] are heard, an unauthoritative and contrary dogmatic adherence arises;
therefore, they are merely fallacious reasonings (asattarka).
Furthermore, they are of no use whatsoever for the comprehension of Vedic statements.
And thus the Sāṃkhyas say: "For that [Vedic knowledge] is joined with impurity, decay, and excess.
Akṣapāda also considers its lack of authority;
likewise, this was determined in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the ritualists (*yājñika*), as it was recited by someone:

The *Karmamīmāṃsā-vedāntabhāṣya* is understood according to the scripture as stating: "The gods went from this world to that world; the seers followed them; men said to them, 'How then shall we exist? To them the seers imparted all ritual action (*sarvakarman*). This is because of the scriptural statement: "Therefore, whatever the best of Brahmins reflect upon becomes truly seer-like (*ārṣa*).
This [work] is a restatement of the categories of reasoning (*tarka*) as they have been described.
This action leading to the supreme good has been declared in its entirety; now the secret doctrine of this treatise of Manu is being taught.
This verse is intended to address the learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) for the purpose of generating an extraordinary degree of reverence for the subject matter about to be explained.
"Secret" (*rahasya*) means hidden;
therefore, it must not be disclosed to everyone.
It should not be revealed to one who is not intent on service, nor to one who has attained supreme devotion, nor to one whose nature is not steadfast.
If it should be asked how one should act regarding those dharmas that have not been explicitly prescribed,
whatever learned Brahmins may declare, that shall be the dharma, free from doubt.
But surely, what doubt can there be regarding those things not mentioned in the traditional texts?
If you say, "I do not know how it would be in this case," [the answer is] because that [result] does not belong to them at all.
This is what is being stated.
What is intended here is not something that has not been mentioned;
rather, it is that which has been mentioned in general but whose specific details are not known.
But surely, even in that case, what doubt could there be?

The purpose of the scripture is established by any [water] whatsoever, because the general rule depends only on a particular instance; for example, regarding the injunction "one should sip water," although waters are divided into various types such as those from wells, stagnant pools, or rivers, any of these being employed fulfill the purpose of the scripture.
True;
this is taught in cases where there is a scriptural prohibition, but no specific expiation has been prescribed.
When a vessel containing the remnants of a Śūdra is impure due to that contact, and someone should eat from it before it has been purified, there arises the doubt: what is the expiation for that?
For that inquiry, which culminates in certainty, is properly established through perception and other means; [it is concluded that] it must indeed be the uneaten remnant of a woman or a Śūdra.
Indeed, it cannot be said that "this is the remnant of a Śūdra."
"What is that? Is it leavings?"—in such cases of doubt, the word of the learned (śiṣṭa) must be accepted as authoritative.
For example, this is the doubt regarding dharma concerning those Śūdras and others who are under the authority of Brāhmaṇas.
It is proper to perform exactly what has been taught by the learned (*śiṣṭa*).
Therefore, whatever conceptualization is made through a state of deficiency or excess, that itself constitutes the *dharma* in that case;
there is no fault even for those who teach in such a manner.
For it has been said: "That [practice] should be considered Dharma without hesitation. There is fault in one who speaks of what is non-Dharma; but as for Dharma, what room is there for doubt?

Likewise, when there is uncertainty regarding lineage (*gotra*) and ancestral sages (*pravara*), and when the traditional memory has somehow been interrupted, the determination of the lineage and the ancestral sages is established through the word of a Brāhmaṇa.

And in that regard, regarding the doubt concerning the *pravara*, it has been stated: "In case there is a doubt among all [regarding the lineage], [the rule] 'of Manu' applies. Well then, this will apply in the case of a doubt concerning the *gotra*.
But in that case, in the absence of a doubt concerning the *gotra*, how could there be a doubt concerning the *pravara*, since the *pravaras* are recited with distinct differences for each *gotra*?
It is indeed appropriate that this be called by the name of a lineage;
for lineages are distinguished and diverse, consisting of various clans.
In that case, even when there is certainty regarding the ancestral lineages, doubt concerning the specific clan arises.
Those by whom the Veda, along with its supplements, has been mastered according to the Dharma,
are to be known as cultured Brahmins (śiṣṭas), who are the direct authorities for the Śruti.
The definition of a cultured person (*śiṣṭa*) is stated by this [verse].
But is it not the case that the definition of a cultured person was already stated in the passage "those who are unattached to wealth and pleasure"?

Another meaning for that term was also suspected there; therefore, that passage does not have the purpose of providing a definition. Furthermore, regarding what Vasiṣṭha stated—"the cultured person, moreover, is one whose nature is free from desire"—in that instance, erudition (*vidvattā*) is not mentioned.
Where [the meaning] is fully complete, it is realized in its essential sense and known; that is "accompanied by expansion.
And so you, Vyāsa, should expand the meaning of the Vedas through the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
Thus,
the Smṛtis also have their objects understood in this same way. The mention of the Brāhmaṇas is a restatement (anuvāda), because they alone have the authority for the proclamation of Dharma.
The causes of scripture and perception;
that is, perception and the causes [of knowledge] are "perception-causes.
By the word "cause," the means of valid cognition other than perception are expressed.
Those for whom scripture (*śruti*) and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) are the means of knowledge are called "those whose means of knowledge are scripture and direct perception.
This is what is meant:

they regard scripture as having authority exactly like direct perception, which is beyond dispute; they place their trust in those means of knowledge that arise from reasoning (*hetu*); they consider scripture itself to be logic (*tarka*), and they do not validate this [scripture] by relying on the treatises of formal reasoning (*hetuśāstra*).
Alternatively, *śruti* means direct revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*); the word "direct" (*pratyakṣa*) is applied to scriptural cognition because it is equivalent to direct perception.
Those for whom that [scriptural cognition] is the cause—the instrument—for the full knowledge of dharma and adharma are described in this way.
Whatever Dharma an assembly of at least ten members may determine,
or even one of at least three who are established in virtuous conduct, that Dharma shall not be overturned.
"Ten at the minimum" means ten as the lowest limit. If many [monks] are not present, ten must certainly be present;
in their absence, there must be at least three.
Regarding the phrase "vṛttatha":
this is a restatement of what was previously said concerning those who are unattached to wealth and desire;
furthermore, this is not a count of persons, but rather a count of qualities.
And so he will say later: "even one who knows the Veda.
