Since a plurality of such a collection of qualities is generally impossible for a single person, the number is specified by making the individual the primary referent.
Now he shows those qualities which serve as causes for [forming] an assembly: "One who possesses the threefold knowledge, a logician, a dialectician, an etymologist, a reciter of the Dharma,
and the first three stages of life— such an assembly shall consist of at least ten members."
Even though the description emphasizes the person, it should be understood as being subordinate to the qualities:
one who is "versed in the three Vedas" (traividya) is a student of the three Vedas and a knower of their meaning,
and one who is skilled in inference and other means of knowledge.
"This man is a logician (*tarkī*), endowed with the intellect for reasoning and refutation (*ūhāpoha*).
[Objection: But has it not been stated that for one who knows such things, the status of being a knower of the meaning of the Veda is simply impossible?
[Response: True.
Even from the instruction of another, there may arise for someone a mere portion of the Vedic meaning accompanied by a request;
therefore, it is said that [the meaning] appears without a [verbal] cognition (pratyaya) which has the purpose of grasping the Vedic meaning.
By this, the etymologist (nairukta) is also explained.
A *dharmapāṭhaka* is one who studies the legal treatises (*smṛti-śāstra*) of Manu and others.

Indeed, these three types of persons belonging to the [first] stages of life (*āśrama*), being devoted to the performance of duties, become more proficient in matters of dharma than those mentioned previously.
"Some say he is a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), a householder (*gṛhastha*), or a mendicant (*bhikṣu*);
for his entry into the village is not forbidden, and Gautama has recited this sequence: 'the celibate student, the householder, the mendicant, and the forest-dweller' (*vaikhānasa*).
Others, however, say: "Since there is no permission for him to commit violence, how could he resort to [worldly] dharma?"
Therefore, one should go into the presence of the ascetic together with others.
One who knows the Ṛgveda, one who knows the Yajurveda, and likewise one who knows the Sāmaveda—
this assembly of at least three persons is to be known as the authority for resolving doubts concerning dharma.
The meaning of the Vedas is understood through etymology (nirukta), grammar (vyākaraṇa), and hermeneutics (mīmāṃsā).
And all of these are common [to all Vedas];
for it is not the case that the meaning of one Veda is understood there and not that of another, as this method is eternally present.
Now, how is the establishment of the distinction between the *Ṛgveda* and the others possible?
Likewise, it has been stated there according to the various *Gṛhyasūtras*:

Even if he is alone, whatever dharma a supreme twice-born man who knows the Vedas determines should be recognized as the highest dharma; it is not [dharma] proclaimed by tens of thousands of the ignorant.
"Should determine" means that one should speak after having reached a certainty;
even if uttered by tens of thousands of ignorant fools,
[this] subsequent [point] is explained first.
Among thousands gathered together who lack vows, lack mantras, and subsist on mere birth, the status of an assembly does not exist.
The meaning already stated previously regarding "those who do not observe vows" is now expressed by way of contrast:
one should not entertain doubt concerning the conclusion that those who observe vows—those who study the Vedas—declare; this applies whether they are learned or unlearned.
For this very reason, it is not to be treated as a minor alternative to be considered as if it were equivalent in merit.
Whatever those who are shrouded in darkness, the fools who do not know the Dharma, declare to be dharma—
that sin becomes tenfold and follows after those who spoke it.
The statement of faults regarding ignorant speakers.
All this has been declared to you, which brings about the supreme good;
a Brahmin who does not fall away from this attains the highest goal.
This verse is a summary of the doctrine already promised.

Regarding what was asked—"You ought to tell us the dharmas"—and what was promised as the subject to be spoken—"O Great Sages, listen"—all of that has now been told; thus he declares the completion of the treatise (*śāstra*).
But surely there is more of the treatise to follow, such as the section on "those to be killed" (*hantavya*) and so forth, and that is heard [in the text] as a formal injunction (*vidhi*).
In that regard, how can it be said that "the scripture is concluded" concerning the subject matter of injunctions? Generally, the conclusion [of the scripture] does not pertain to the speaker.
Furthermore, since after the remainder of ritual action, pure knowledge, which has its own primary status, is taught, there is no contradiction.
The purpose of stating the conclusion—that knowledge, characterized by the dharma which is the meaning of the treatise, is superior in all respects—is as follows.
Thus that Blessed Lord, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
has told me all this, the supreme secret of the Dharma.
Bhṛgu said to his disciples: "That Blessed One, Manu, proclaimed this entire treatise for the welfare of the world.
By this, the desire for further qualification is set at rest.
Whatever was secret regarding the inner self (adhyātma), that too Manu, having instructed me, has made manifest.
I too have revealed this to you according to the tradition; therefore, no further desire for more should be entertained.
One who is composed should perceive everything—both the existent and the non-existent—within the self;
for by perceiving everything within the self, one does not direct the mind toward unrighteousness.
The entire world, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, is subject to the nature of arising and perishing.
Now, one should perceive everything—whether non-existent like the horn of a hare or existent and eternal like space—as established within the Self; one should worship it as abiding in the Self.
Through this worship, which extends until the direct realization of the object to be clearly perceived, it is fully known.
Indeed, direct realization (sākṣātkāra) is not possible through a single vision alone;

thus the secret scripture (rahasyaśāstra) teaches. In that regard, for the purpose of meditating upon the Self, it is said: "It is to be heard, to be reflected upon, and to be meditated upon. Thus, right vision culminates in meditation.
Self-meditation is said to be the practice of knowledge as it has been taught, uninterrupted by heterogeneous cognitions;
or rather, by implication, it entails such practice,
because formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and actions fulfill their own purpose by imparting a specific quality to that which is to be formed.

Just as the statement "one threshes rice" is an introduction of what was not previously heard— since its purpose would otherwise be unseen (adṛṣṭārthatā) through the observation of results such as the removal of husks and chaff—
so too, because it is an injunction regarding an action, there is an abandonment of its status as a purificatory rite (*saṃskārakarma*) involving sixty [preparations].
Therefore, by the words "one should perceive," one should declare the culmination in that single object of knowledge by means of the exclusion of knowledge whose objects are other things to be known.
Regarding this term "in the Self," there is dispute.
What indeed is this so-called Self? If it were the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) whose locus is the body, then that would contradict the subsequent [description]: "the Ruler, golden-hued."
For the origin of death, whose nature is action, is not heard [in scripture]; rather, it is said: "Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, heaven and earth stand held apart.
Therefore, the process of transmigratory existence does not apply even to the Self, which is the object of the notion of "I.
Consequently, some other means for establishing its true nature must be stated.

Furthermore, this being the case, by the words "one should see" and so forth, there is an internal subsumption (*upasaṃhāra*) even of external selves—those established in the form of the elemental (*ādhibhautika*) and the divine (*ādhidaivika*)—into the internal self (*ādhyātmika*). And thus, the Vedic [knowledge] remains as the means; for that which has been acquired through its causal nature attains a state of connection.

Now, as for the statement that one should always perceive within oneself the entire world as delimited by the causal Person (*kāraṇapuruṣa*), it must be explained what kind of perception of the self is meant here, "within the self."
Others, however, think that this arrangement belongs to the embodied self alone;
for it is logical that its possession of those [qualities] occurs through the arrangement of the hearer.
To this it is replied:
First of all, the word "Self" (ātman) has its authority established by the harmony with other scriptural passages which show it to have the Supreme Self as its object.
As for the claim that its own nature must be explained, what else could possibly be said regarding it, other than the injunction for hearing and knowing it?
And those statements are to be understood from all the Upaniṣads across every Vedic branch (*śākhā*).

Since even other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are devoted solely to establishing unity, the effort expended by the Mīmāṃsakas against perception (*pratyakṣa*), which grasps [diversity], has been entirely in vain.
And it has been stated in the *Vākyapadīya*: "There is no such thing as that which is called 'name'," and so forth.
And its status as being understood through injunction is to be inferred from the covering of the body.
As for what was said—"How can that which is non-existent be seen?"—the meaning would be "existent and non-existent";
"existent" is a designation for the aggregate of transformations.
The statement "it is non-existent" is merely a lack of direct perception, because [the Self] is too subtle to be determined [by the senses].

As for what was said—that there is no connection between the Supreme Self and the sense of hearing—what is the point here? For [the Self] has been established as the cause of the maintenance, origination, and destruction of the entire world. Thus, it is indeed connected to everything.
And as for this method of arrangement, its meaning is as follows:
whatever appears as differentiated, all that one should dissolve into non-duality;
"everything is situated in the Self"—this is the reason found for the commonality of cessation from the Supreme Self.
"Concentrated":

the meaning is that "concentration" (samādhi) is the means for the cessation of mental fluctuations, which is to be learned from the Yogaśāstra. He does not direct his mind toward unrighteousness; this refers to the state of immobility of both the intellect (buddhi) and the mind (cetas).
One should practice as long as one's mind is not captivated by disputants;
and for this reason, as long as anyone might cause [the distinction] to dissolve into its opposite.
The Self alone is all the deities; everything is established within the Self.
For the Self indeed produces the connection with action for these embodied beings.
In all cases, sacrificial acts such as the *yāga* and so forth, as well as heaven and the deities, should be viewed as being the Self.
This deity Agni is none other than the Self; there is no deity Agni apart from the Self.
This has also been stated: "The one Self is heard of in many ways."

In this regard, one who is disciplined [should realize]: "I alone am the Self, the deity. Likewise, it is said: "They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni; the wise speak of the One Being as many. By the statement, "He abandons those who see the deity as other than the multiform Supreme Self," it is enjoined that one should view the deities who are parts of ritual action as the Self.
What then? For such a person, there is no longer any function performed by deities and the like.
All accomplishment is achieved through the self alone.
How so?
Because it does not produce these [cognitions] from an external object as their essence.
In the application of action, there is a connection between the action and its fruit;
that Self alone brings those about for them,
not any other deity, nor anything possessing its qualities.
One should place space within the cavities, wind within movement and touch,
the supreme fire within digestion and sight, water within moisture, and earth within solid forms.
One should restrain the external space within these nine apertures;
that external space is indeed that [internal space], for there is nothing external whatsoever.
"Anila" means wind.
One should establish that [consciousness] there. A certain state of the body moves and vibrates therein, characterized by the movement of the hands, feet, and so forth;
and this contact is characterized by external objects and the like.
Therein one should establish the wind;
the digestive process is produced by the gastric fire,
as is vision.

One should cause the supreme fire, which is black and abides as the self of the sun, to enter into those two; that is, one should cause it to be established within the oily substances consisting of fat, marrow, and so forth. This is how the context continues.
The earth (gām) [is placed] upon the forms (mūrtiṣu), that is, upon the parts of the body.
Thus is the withdrawal of the great elements.
Now, the installation of the deities will be described:
one should place the Moon in the mind, the Quarters in the ears, Viṣṇu in the stride, and Hara in the strength.
One should invoke Agni in the case of emission, and Prajāpati in the case of procreation.
One should fix this very moon, Indu, within the mind:
"This is not the moon that moves through the sky;
rather, it is established within my mind."
And those directions are within the power of the sense of hearing;
as for Viṣṇu, whoever strides even a little where Viṣṇu has stridden, he is established there by that very act of striding.
Likewise, [one should assign] Hara to strength.
The sudden rising of the semen is that which provides the occasion for the senses; it is the form of Time and the very activity of the senses.
One should perceive this emission as belonging to the fire of speech through the mantras beginning with "vāyu.
Having thus withdrawn everything into the self, one should perceive all within the Supreme Self.
A cause of such a nature is established in the Supreme Self [with the thought]: "I am not anyone distinct from That.
In this way, this entire practice of worship should be performed.
One should know that Supreme Person as the ruler of all, subtler even than the subtle, radiant like gold, and attainable through the intellect in the state of dream.
Thus he says:
"the ruler," meaning the controller of all beings, from the Brāhmaṇas down to the Śūdras.

This restriction of fire and other elements to their inherent natures such as heat, this incessant internal power of the sun and others in their functions of causing the world’s rotation and illumination, and this fixed regularity of actions regarding their fruits—all of this exists because that Controller exists.
As it has been stated in passages such as, "O Gārgī, by the command of this very Imperishable," and likewise: "The sun shines, and the moon rains."

"Out of fear, fire and wind, and death runs as the fifth"—thus [it is said that Brahman is] "smaller even than the small. If anyone were to suggest that the statement "a hundredth part of the tip of a hair" and so forth establishes for you that its dimension is one-third [of a hair], that is incorrect, because of the negation of all attributes in passages such as "neither gross nor subtle. What then? It is because it is to be understood by an intellect as sharp as the tip of a blade of kusha grass.
This is what is meant:
one who is neither extremely skilled nor fully absorbed in the practice thereof.
Some call this Agni, others Manu, others Prajāpati; some Indra, others Prāṇa, and still others the eternal Brahman.
Pervading all beings with its five forms,
this [Self] perpetually causes them to revolve like a wheel through birth, growth, and decay.
Thus, he who perceives the Self within all beings by means of his own self,
having attained equanimity toward all, reaches Brahman, the supreme state.
"Brahmābhyeti" means he attains the state of Brahman;
by the manifestation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth, he describes the destruction of passion and hatred.
By this, he states that the knowledge of the oneness of the Self, uninterrupted by heterogeneous cognitions, is to be practiced.
For it is not the case that the arising of a cognition of a different class is universally accepted.
Therefore, this is what is meant:
for one who has abandoned the notions of "I" and "mine," Brahman—which consists of unsurpassed, supreme bliss—is attained because [the mind] is restricted to that single cognition.
The meaning is that the accomplishment of the fruit consists in the cessation of the undesired and the attainment of the intended restriction demonstrated by the treatise.
A twice-born man who recites this Mānava Śāstra proclaimed by Bhṛgu becomes constantly possessed of right conduct and shall attain his desired goal.
The word "iti" indicates the completion of the treatise. One who recites it becomes possessed of right conduct (*ācāravān*); other forms of conduct are to be supplied by implication.
Just as the practice of a scripture follows from its study,
so too, if one is of such a kind, one attains the desired state characterized by the deity and so forth.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
The *Manusmṛti* is indeed venerable, and Medhātithi’s commentary upon it is truly appropriate;
yet, by the power of fate, that work has been lost, such that no manuscript can be found anywhere.
However, King Madana, along with his son Araṇasuta, brought it from another land.
He then undertook the restoration of this [work] by having manuscripts of it copied here and there.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter of the Commentary on Manu, composed by Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi, son of Bhaṭṭa Vīrasvāmin.
